a2a-protocol.desc: Agent2Agent (A2A) is an open protocol, hosted by the Linux Foundation, that lets AI agents from different platforms communicate, delegate tasks and collaborate.

faq.a: A2A is an open protocol, hosted by the Linux Foundation, for communication and interoperability between AI agents built on different platforms. It lets agents delegate sub-tasks, exchange information and coordinate actions without exposing their internal memory, tools or proprietary logic.
faq.q: What is the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol?

faq.a: According to the A2A project site, MCP connects an agent to tools, APIs and data, while A2A connects an agent to other agents. The two are described as complementary, and the site recommends using both.
faq.q: How does A2A differ from MCP?

faq.a: The project lists six official SDKs for Python, Go, Java, JavaScript, C# and .NET, and Rust. All of them implement the A2A v1.0 specification.
faq.q: Which SDKs are available for A2A?

a2a-protocol.long:
The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol is an open protocol for communication and interoperability between agentic applications that are opaque to one another. It allows AI agents built on different platforms to find each other, delegate sub-tasks, exchange information and coordinate actions. Frameworks named on the project site include LangGraph, CrewAI and Semantic Kernel. The aim is that such agents can connect without a custom integration being built for every pair of systems.

A central design idea is opacity. An agent that takes part in A2A collaboration does not have to expose its internal memory, its tools or its proprietary logic to the agents it works with. Each agent stays a black box that is reached through the protocol, which supports collaboration across vendor and platform boundaries while the implementation details remain private. The project lists secure and opaque collaboration as one of its highlighted features, alongside interoperability, complex multi-agent workflows, working with MCP, and extensibility.

A2A is hosted by the Linux Foundation under neutral governance and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. The project cites more than 170 community partners and says it has joined the Agentic AI Foundation. Changes to the protocol are handled through a formal process. Extensions and custom bindings are added through a tiered promotion process, so the core of the specification can stay stable while new capabilities are developed and tested around it.

For developers, official SDKs are listed for Python, Go, Java, JavaScript, C# and .NET, and Rust. All of them implement the A2A v1.0 specification, which gives teams a shared baseline regardless of the language in which an agent is written. The short description of the protocol also notes that it builds on standard web technologies such as HTTP and JSON-RPC. The A2A landing page itself does not go into discovery or transport details, so those aspects should be checked in the specification and SDK documentation.

A2A is positioned as complementary to the Model Context Protocol (MCP), not as a replacement for it. According to the project site, MCP connects an agent to tools, APIs and data, whereas A2A connects an agent to other agents. The site recommends using both: MCP for giving an individual agent access to the resources it needs, and A2A for letting several agents work together on a larger task. In practice this separates two questions that come up when designing multi-agent systems, namely what an agent can use and who an agent can delegate work to.

Typical situations where A2A is relevant include multi-agent workflows in which agents come from different vendors or open-source frameworks, and organizations that want to avoid writing point-to-point integrations between each pair of agents. Decisions around adoption usually involve which SDK matches the existing stack, how the agent pairs with MCP-based tool access, and whether any needed capability belongs in the stable core or in an extension.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic, so this page relies on the public description of the protocol only.

ab-100.desc: Microsoft Certified: Agentic AI Business Solutions Architect Expert (AB-100) is a 2026 expert certification for architects designing agentic AI business solutions.

faq.a: AB-100 is the exam for Microsoft Certified: Agentic AI Business Solutions Architect Expert, a 2026 expert-level certification from Microsoft for designing agentic AI business solutions across Copilot, Dynamics 365 and Power Platform.
faq.q: What is the AB-100 certification?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, candidates pass AB-100 and also hold at least one of a listed set of associate certifications. The exam is booked through Pearson VUE.
faq.q: What is required to earn the Agentic AI Business Solutions Architect Expert credential?

faq.a: The listed skills include generative AI and Azure AI services, Azure OpenAI, multi-agent orchestration, Copilot Studio, Azure AI Foundry, Dynamics 365 and Power Platform, open standards such as Agent2Agent and the Model Context Protocol, responsible AI, security, and monitoring and telemetry.
faq.q: Which topics does AB-100 cover?

ab-100.long:
Microsoft Certified: Agentic AI Business Solutions Architect Expert (AB-100) is an expert-level certification from Microsoft, introduced in 2026, for architects who design agentic AI business solutions across Copilot, Dynamics 365 and Power Platform. The exam code is AB-100. The certification is part of the AB series of 2026 certifications that revolve around AI in business applications, and it sits at the expert level, above the associate-oriented certifications in this area.

According to Microsoft Learn, the credential describes a solution architect who drives the transformation of business processes through AI-powered architectures. It validates the ability to design and implement AI and agent-based business solutions that span several Microsoft services. The certification addresses architects who decide how AI agents fit into business processes and which Microsoft services should work together. It is developed by Microsoft and covers Microsoft 365 Copilot.

The skills listed in the official documentation cover a broad range of topics. They include generative AI and Azure AI services, Azure OpenAI, agent-oriented design, multi-agent orchestration, Copilot Studio, Azure AI Foundry, Dynamics 365 and Power Platform, as well as open standards such as Agent2Agent and the Model Context Protocol. Further themes are responsible AI, securing models and data flows, and monitoring and telemetry. The exam areas are planning, designing and deploying AI-powered business solutions, each with a stated weighting range.

The responsibilities attached to the role are architectural rather than operational. They include defining an architecture strategy, a roadmap for agent-oriented processes, guidance during implementation, and an application lifecycle and environment strategy. Architects in this field usually combine an understanding of business requirements with knowledge of the available platforms, and they are responsible for the design rather than the day-to-day configuration.

To earn the credential, candidates pass AB-100 and also hold at least one of a listed set of associate certifications. The exam is booked through Pearson VUE. Exam format and validity period are not stated in the available documentation, so candidates should check the official Microsoft Learn page for current details before planning preparation.

Typical scenarios for the topic include planning where an AI agent can take over steps of a business process, deciding how such agents access company data and applications, and defining the roles of Copilot, Dynamics 365 and Power Platform in one overall solution. Decisions around multi-agent orchestration, security of data flows and responsible AI are part of the same design work.

The M365.FM episodes in the current data do not cover this certification directly. The topic is related to Microsoft 365 Copilot, which the certification covers, and listeners interested in the background of agent-based solutions in the Microsoft ecosystem can find related material through that topic.

faq.a: It covers designing and implementing AI-assisted sales solutions in Dynamics 365 Sales, including Copilot, agent capabilities, lead qualification, opportunity research and extending Sales.
faq.q: What does the AB-210 certification cover?

faq.q: How long is the AB-210 exam and what is the passing score?

faq.a: Candidates should know how to interpret sales processes, build and extend model-driven apps and create Power Automate cloud flows. Intermediate Power Platform configuration training is highly recommended.
faq.q: Which prior knowledge is recommended for AB-210?

ab-210.long:
Microsoft Certified: Dynamics 365 Sales AI Consultant Associate (AB-210) is an associate-level certification from Microsoft, introduced in 2026, that covers the design and implementation of AI-assisted sales solutions on Dynamics 365 Sales. The exam code is AB-210. According to the available data, the certification replaces the MB-280 path. It belongs to the wider group of AB certifications from 2026 that deal with AI in business applications and Copilot.

The certification is aimed at consultants who set up and adapt sales applications so that AI features support sellers in their daily work. Microsoft Learn describes typical roles as business analyst and functional consultant. Candidates are expected to configure Dynamics 365 Sales, Copilot in Dynamics 365 Sales and agent capabilities, and to turn business needs into workflows that use conversational intelligence, predictive insights, guided automation and secure data access. The scope follows seller workflows from lead to cash.

The exam topics listed by Microsoft include configuring core Sales features for AI, optimizing AI-driven sales, qualifying and prioritizing leads, developing deals through intelligent opportunity research, and extending Sales. Dynamics 365 Sales is the application used to manage leads, opportunities and customer relationships, so the content combines knowledge of sales processes with the configuration of AI functions within that application.

Beyond the AI features themselves, candidates must be able to interpret sales processes, build and extend model-driven apps and create Power Automate cloud flows. Microsoft Learn states that intermediate Power Platform configuration training is highly recommended. In practice, this means the role calls for both an understanding of how a sales team works and the ability to translate business requirements into a working configuration.

Typical situations for this topic include configuring a sales application for a specific team, deciding which AI-supported functions help sellers prepare for customer conversations or follow up on opportunities, and adapting the solution to the sales process of a particular company. Choosing between built-in capabilities and extensions through apps and flows is part of the same decision area.

On the exam format, the Microsoft Learn page describes AB-210 as a beta exam that runs 120 minutes, is proctored and has a passing score of 700. It is delivered through Pearson VUE in several languages. Beta results are not scored immediately. The page names no license requirements and no certificate validity period, so candidates should check the official exam page for current details before planning.

The M365.FM episodes in the current data do not cover this certification directly, so no episode-based guidance or recommendations are available for AB-210 at this time. Related topics on the platform include Dynamics 365 Sales as the covered product and Microsoft as the developer of the certification.

ab-410.desc: Microsoft Certified: Intelligent Applications Builder Associate (AB-410) is an associate certification for building AI-enabled solutions on Power Platform.

faq.a: It is an associate-level Microsoft certification from 2026 for building AI-enabled solutions on Power Platform using Copilot, low-code tools and built-in data features. It is earned through the AB-410 exam.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft Certified: Intelligent Applications Builder Associate (AB-410)?

faq.a: According to the available data, AB-410 replaces the PL-200 path. The emphasis moves toward applications that include intelligent features such as agents and Copilot capabilities.
faq.q: How does AB-410 relate to PL-200?

faq.a: The 120-minute proctored exam covers three areas: laying the foundation for intelligent applications, creating intelligent applications, and building business logic and automation. It is booked through Pearson VUE.
faq.q: What does the AB-410 exam cover?

ab-410.long:
Microsoft Certified: Intelligent Applications Builder Associate (AB-410) is an associate-level Microsoft certification introduced in 2026 for people who design, build and deliver AI-enabled solutions on Power Platform. The exam code is AB-410. According to the available data, the certification replaces the PL-200 path, which shifts the emphasis from configured apps and flows toward applications that contain intelligent features.

The certification is developed by Microsoft and covers Power Platform, the low-code platform that brings together apps, automation, data and AI building blocks. Microsoft Learn describes it as an intermediate certification for developers that confirms the ability to build solutions using Copilot, low-code tools and built-in data features. It relates to Power Apps, Power Automate, Power BI and Power Pages.

The target profile described by Microsoft Learn is a builder who creates Dataverse data models, model-driven and canvas apps, and cloud flows with business logic. In addition, this person adds agents and Copilot features to apps and Power Pages sites. Candidates are expected to work alongside administrators, governance teams, agent developers, solution architects and business stakeholders. The expected experience includes creating solution components with natural language, Dataverse modeling, Power Fx and low-code automation. Knowledge of environment governance, roles, policies and the solution lifecycle is also listed as part of the profile.

The AB-410 exam takes 120 minutes, is proctored and is booked through Pearson VUE. It covers three areas: laying the foundation for intelligent applications, creating intelligent applications, and building business logic and automation. The documentation page does not state a passing score, a validity period or license requirements, so candidates who need those details should check the current exam page directly.

Typical scenarios for this certification include building an internal app that supports a team with AI-assisted suggestions, automating a recurring business process that includes steps where content has to be interpreted, and connecting such solutions to company data. Builders in this role often come from a low-code or consulting background and combine platform knowledge with a clear understanding of the business problem the application is meant to solve. For people who previously followed the PL-200 path, AB-410 is the relevant successor to consider when planning a certification route.

The M365.FM episodes in the current data do not cover this certification directly, so this page relies on the certification and exam documentation. Related topics on the site include Power Platform and Microsoft as the developer of the certification.

ab-620.desc: Microsoft Certified: AI Agent Builder Associate (AB-620) is a 2026 beta associate certification from Microsoft for building AI agents in Copilot Studio.

faq.a: AB-620 covers planning and configuring agent solutions, integrating and extending agents in Copilot Studio, and testing and managing agents. Named topics include identity, channels, responsible AI, agent flows, connectors, MCP tools, REST APIs, multi-agent solutions and application lifecycle management.
faq.q: What does the AB-620 exam cover?

faq.a: According to the Microsoft Learn study guide, it targets professional developers or advanced builders such as application developers, consultants and ISV partners. Candidates should know Power Fx, Dataverse and Power Platform and have intermediate generative AI knowledge, including RAG.
faq.q: Who is the AI Agent Builder Associate certification intended for?

faq.a: The study guide states a pass mark of 700. The certification expires yearly and is renewed through a free online assessment.
faq.q: What is the pass mark and how does renewal work?

ab-620.long:
Microsoft Certified: AI Agent Builder Associate (AB-620) is an associate-level certification from Microsoft, introduced in 2026 and currently in beta. It addresses people who build AI agents with Copilot Studio, the environment in which agents are created, configured and published. The exam behind the certification carries the code AB-620, and its official study guide is titled "Designing and Building Integrated AI Agent Solutions in Copilot Studio".

The certification focuses on building custom agents for enterprise solutions. According to the Microsoft Learn study guide, the intended audience is professional developers or advanced builders, such as application developers, consultants and ISV partners. Candidates are expected to know Power Fx, Dataverse and Power Platform, and to have intermediate generative AI knowledge, including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Typical agents in this context answer questions, follow instructions and carry out tasks for users, for example an agent that answers employee questions from company information or an assistant that supports a department with a defined set of tasks.

The skills measured fall into three areas. The first is planning and configuring agent solutions, which includes topics such as identity, channels and responsible AI. The second is integrating and extending agents in Copilot Studio; the study guide names agent flows, topics, adaptive cards, connectors, MCP tools, REST APIs, multi-agent solutions, Foundry agents and the A2A protocol in this area. The third is testing and managing agents, covering test sets, evaluation and application lifecycle management with solutions and pipelines. Together these areas span the path from designing an agent to extending it with external capabilities and operating it over time.

Within the 2026 AB series, AB-620 complements the fundamentals-level AB-900, which deals with the administration of Copilot and agents. AB-620 concentrates instead on the construction of agents themselves, which makes it relevant for makers and developers rather than administrators. The relation to Copilot Studio is direct: the exam content is organized around what can be designed, connected and tested in that product.

On exam logistics, the study guide states a pass mark of 700. The certification expires yearly and is renewed through a free online assessment. The page does not give an exam duration, a question count, a cost or Copilot Studio license requirements, so candidates who need those details should check the official Microsoft Learn page. Because the exam is described as being in beta, its content and availability may still change.

The M365.FM episodes in the current data do not cover this certification directly. For preparation, the study guide's structure is the most concrete orientation: it lists the three skill areas and the technologies named in them, which can serve as a checklist when deciding which topics to practice, such as building agent flows and topics, connecting agents through connectors or MCP tools, or setting up test sets and solution-based deployment with pipelines.

faq.a: It targets people who use generative AI productivity tools and core Microsoft 365 apps to improve business results and decisions. It is not aimed at administrators or developers, and no coding or app development is required.
faq.q: Who is the AB-730 certification intended for?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, it measures understanding of generative AI basics, managing prompts and conversations, and creating and analyzing business content with AI. Microsoft 365 Copilot, Researcher and Analyst are named as tools in scope.
faq.q: What does the AB-730 exam measure?

faq.a: The exam lasts 45 minutes, is proctored with interactive parts, and is offered in English only through Pearson VUE. The price depends on the country, and a failed attempt can be repeated after 24 hours.
faq.q: How is the AB-730 exam delivered?

ab-730.long:
Microsoft Certified: AI Business Professional (AB-730) is a certification from Microsoft, introduced in 2026, that covers the use of generative AI and Copilot in everyday business work. The exam code is AB-730. Unlike many other Microsoft certifications, it is not aimed at administrators or developers. It targets people who use generative AI productivity tools and core Microsoft 365 apps to improve business results and decisions, and no coding or app development is required.

According to the Microsoft Learn exam page, the exam measures understanding of generative AI basics, managing prompts and conversations, and creating and analyzing business content with AI. Microsoft 365 Copilot is the central tool in scope, and the page also names Researcher and Analyst. Candidates are expected to know Microsoft 365 and to be comfortable with Outlook, Word, Teams, PowerPoint and Excel, including tasks such as writing emails, building presentations, generating images and managing documents.

The certification is relevant for office and business roles across departments because Copilot is integrated into applications that many employees already use for writing, analysis, communication and meetings. Typical scenarios include drafting and summarizing documents with an AI assistant, preparing for meetings, analyzing information from different sources and judging the quality of AI-generated answers before using them. A credential of this kind documents that someone can work with generative AI in a business setting, including an awareness of its limitations, without needing technical administration or development skills.

Several practical details are given on the exam page. The exam lasts 45 minutes, is proctored and includes interactive parts. It is offered in English only through Pearson VUE, and the price depends on the country. A failed attempt can be repeated after 24 hours. Microsoft recommends registering with a personal Microsoft account rather than a work account. The page does not state licensing requirements, a passing score or how long the credential stays valid, so candidates who need these details should check the official exam page before planning.

In relation to other topics, the certification is developed by Microsoft and covers Microsoft 365 Copilot. It therefore fits readers who want a structured way to show proficiency with Copilot in the Microsoft 365 apps they already use, rather than a path into administration, security or development. Preparation naturally centers on hands-on practice with prompts, conversations and content creation inside those applications.

The M365.FM episodes in the current data do not cover this certification directly, so no episode-based recommendations or warnings can be attributed to it here. For authoritative and up-to-date information on skills measured, scheduling and pricing, the Microsoft Learn exam page for AB-730 is the reference source.

ab-731.desc: Microsoft Certified: AI Transformation Leader (AB-731) is a 2026 Microsoft certification for business leaders who guide AI adoption and transformation in their organization.

faq.a: It is aimed at business decision makers who guide transformation and innovation in teams or organizations. According to the Microsoft Learn study guide, no coding is expected.
faq.q: Who is the AB-731 certification intended for?

faq.a: The study guide lists three areas: the business value of generative AI, Microsoft AI apps and services such as Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio, and implementation and adoption, including responsible AI principles and adoption structures like an AI council.
faq.q: What topics does the AB-731 exam cover?

faq.a: The certification expires yearly and is renewed through a free online assessment. The pass mark for the exam is 700.
faq.q: How long does the certification stay valid?

ab-731.long:
Microsoft Certified: AI Transformation Leader (AB-731) is a certification from Microsoft, introduced in 2026, for leaders who drive AI adoption and transformation in their organization. The exam code is AB-731. It addresses managers and business decision makers rather than technical specialists. According to the Microsoft Learn study guide, no coding is expected, and the focus lies on guiding teams and organizations through change rather than on configuring tools.

The study guide divides the exam into three areas. The first covers the business value of generative AI. It includes prompt engineering, grounding, retrieval-augmented generation, data quality and security, so candidates need a working understanding of how generative AI behaves and what it depends on. The second area covers Microsoft AI apps and services. The services named in the guide are Microsoft 365 Copilot, Researcher and Analyst, Copilot Studio, Microsoft Graph, Azure AI Search and Microsoft Foundry. The third area covers implementation and adoption. It addresses responsible AI principles, an AI council, an adoption team, an AI champions program and licensing models such as pay-as-you-go and subscription-included.

The certification is linked to Microsoft 365 Copilot. Copilot is a common starting point for organizations that introduce AI at scale, because it reaches many employees through the applications they already use. That makes questions of change management, governance and value measurement especially visible. The exam covers Copilot together with the wider set of Microsoft AI services, so it does not limit itself to a single product.

In practice, the topic matters in situations where leaders must set priorities for AI use cases, align business units and IT around a common approach, and decide how employees are trained and supported. It also matters where responsibilities for oversight and risk have to be defined. Structures such as an AI council, an adoption team and an AI champions program, which the study guide names, are organizational answers to these questions. Candidates should have experience with adoption or change management and should know Microsoft 365 services.

Some exam details are stated in the study guide. The pass mark is 700, and the page lists no formal prerequisites and no exam fee. The certification expires yearly and is renewed through a free online assessment. Most questions address generally available features, although common preview features can appear, so candidates should expect that part of the content may change over time.

The M365.FM episodes in the current data do not cover this certification directly, so there are no episode statements to report here. For related background, the linked topic Microsoft 365 Copilot is the product around which many AI adoption discussions begin. The official documentation on Microsoft Learn remains the primary reference for the current exam skills outline and for any changes to the exam.

faq.a: It covers the administration of Microsoft 365 Copilot and agents, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio and Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat. ab-900.long:
Microsoft Certified: Copilot and Agent Administration Fundamentals (AB-900) is a fundamentals-level certification from Microsoft, introduced in 2026, that focuses on the administrative side of Microsoft 365 Copilot and agents. The exam code is AB-900. It is aimed at IT staff and administrators who are taking their first steps in managing AI assistants in the workplace, and it concentrates on concepts and responsibilities rather than deep specialization.

The certification covers three products: Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio and Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat. Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat is the conversational entry point, Microsoft 365 Copilot brings AI assistance into Microsoft 365 applications, and Copilot Studio is the environment in which agents are created and managed. Administration of these tools means deciding who may use them, understanding which data they can reach, and controlling agents that employees or the organization build.

According to the Microsoft Learn study guide for Exam AB-900, the intended audience is expected to know Microsoft 365 core services, security, identity and access, data protection and governance. Familiarity with the admin centers for Exchange Online, SharePoint, Teams, Entra and Purview is also assumed. The page lists no formal prerequisites and no required licenses for taking the exam.

The skills measured are split into three areas: core features and objects of Microsoft 365 services, data protection and governance for Microsoft 365 and Copilot, and basic administration of Copilot and agents. Topics named in the guide include licensing, Conditional Access, Purview capabilities such as DLP and Information Protection, and oversharing in SharePoint. They also include Researcher and Analyst, custom agents, and agent approval and monitoring in the admin centers. The combination reflects a typical administrative situation: before Copilot and agents are rolled out, the surrounding identity, access and data protection setup determines what the tools can see and do.

The pass mark is 700. The study guide gives no question count, duration or fee. The certification expires after a year and is renewed through a free online assessment on Microsoft Learn. Because it sits at fundamentals level, it can serve as a first step before more specialized certifications on agents and AI solutions.

The M365.FM episodes in the current data do not cover this certification directly, so there are no episode statements to cite. The topics it touches, such as Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio and Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, are linked entities on this site that can be explored for related context.

access.desc: Microsoft Access is a desktop database application in Microsoft 365 Apps for building small relational databases with tables, queries, forms and reports.

faq.a: Microsoft Access is used to build small relational databases with tables, queries, forms and reports. It is typically used for departmental tools, small inventories and data collections that outgrow a spreadsheet but do not need a server database.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Access used for?

faq.a: Yes. Access belongs to Microsoft 365 Apps and is included in the Microsoft 365 licence.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Access part of Microsoft 365?

faq.a: Dataverse is a managed data platform of the Power Platform and is related to Access for larger or shared scenarios. Power Apps is often considered when a small database should become a web or mobile app.
faq.q: How does Access relate to Dataverse and Power Apps?

access.long:
Microsoft Access is a desktop database application developed by Microsoft for building small relational databases. It is part of Microsoft 365 Apps and is included in the Microsoft 365 licence. The product is classified as a Microsoft tool and as a business application, and it was first released in 1992.

An Access database is built from a few core object types. Tables store the data in a structured, relational form. Queries retrieve, filter and combine that data. Forms provide a screen for entering and editing records, and reports present or print the results. Together these objects let a single person or a small team create a working data-entry and reporting tool without a separate server database.

Access is typically used for departmental tools, small inventories and data collections that have outgrown a spreadsheet but do not need a server database. A common decision point is exactly this boundary: when the data has related tables, several people need to enter records through forms, or recurring reports are needed, a relational desktop database can be a better fit than a workbook. When data volumes, sharing needs or access requirements grow beyond a desktop tool, other platforms come into consideration.

Two related products are connected to Access in the Microsoft ecosystem. Dataverse is a managed data platform of the Power Platform and is relevant when data should move from a local database to a centrally managed store. Power Apps is often considered when a small database application should become a web or mobile app. Both relations point to the usual path from a desktop database toward a shared, cloud-based solution, although the details of any migration depend on the individual case and are not covered by the sources used for this page.

The M365.FM episodes linked to Access mostly cover neighbouring Microsoft topics rather than Access itself, and mostly the identity and network security side of the Microsoft 365 environment in which desktop tools like Access are used. "Global Secure Access - Simply Explained" describes how employees now reach business applications from home offices, airports, customer sites, coffee shops and mobile devices instead of sitting inside a corporate network, and why traditional VPNs, designed for applications inside company data centers, fit this situation poorly. "Microsoft Entra Quick Access - Simply Explained" looks at Quick Access, a feature inside Microsoft Entra Private Access, which the episode presents as a replacement for the company VPN.

"Microsoft Entra Private Access - Simply Explained" explains what that service does and where it fits in the Microsoft ecosystem, with considerations for administrators, architects and business stakeholders. "ENTRA PIM EXPLAINED: Securing Privileged Access with Mark Orr [MVP]" is a conversation with the MVP about his career and about securing privileged access with Entra PIM, including the point that passwords remain one of the weakest links. "Conditional Access - Simply Explained" covers Conditional Access in Microsoft Entra as a policy engine that evaluates several signals to decide who can reach applications, from which devices and under what conditions.

These episodes do not describe Access features such as table design, queries, forms or reports. For product details, Microsoft publishes documentation and support pages for Access, and the official Microsoft 365 product page describes the application and its place in the licence.

access-packages.desc: Access packages bundle groups, Teams, enterprise applications and SharePoint sites in Microsoft Entra entitlement management, governed by request, approval and expiry policies.

faq.a: An access package is a bundle of resources, such as groups, Teams, enterprise applications and SharePoint sites, managed in Microsoft Entra entitlement management. Its policies define who can request it, who approves and when access ends.
faq.q: What is an access package in Microsoft Entra?

faq.a: The episodes describe using access packages to grant external users temporary access through an approval process, with expiration dates so guests lose access when it is no longer needed.
faq.q: How are access packages used for guest users?

faq.a: Access packages define how access is requested and for how long, while access reviews check whether users still need the access they hold. The episodes present both as parts of identity governance in Microsoft Entra.
faq.q: How do access packages relate to access reviews?

access-packages.long:
Access packages are bundles of resources in Microsoft Entra entitlement management. A package can contain groups, Teams, enterprise applications and SharePoint sites, so that everything a person needs for a particular job or project is requested and granted together instead of one resource at a time. Each package carries policies that define who can request it, who approves the request and when the access ends. Access packages sit within Microsoft Entra, the broader identity and access management platform in the Microsoft ecosystem, and they are part of its identity governance capabilities.

The main purpose of an access package is to standardize and automate how access is granted and removed. Because the resources are grouped by role or need, administrators can assign a package to users or groups and keep the set of permissions consistent. When someone changes roles, access can be updated by changing which package is assigned rather than editing many individual permissions. The episode "Microsoft Entra as a Complete IAM Platform" describes this in terms of automating onboarding and offboarding: new employees receive what they need quickly, and access is removed when someone leaves, which reduces the risk of forgotten accounts and unused permissions.

The policy side is what distinguishes an access package from a plain group membership. A policy states which users may request the package, whether an approval step is required and how long the access remains valid. Expiration is a central idea: access is granted for a defined period and ends automatically unless it is renewed. This supports least-privilege access and keeps the directory from accumulating stale permissions over time.

Access packages are especially relevant for external users. The episode "Govern Microsoft 365 Guest Access and Offboarding" recommends using access packages for guests so that temporary access can be granted through an approval process, with expiration dates that remove access when it is no longer needed. It presents automated processes such as expiration and regular permission checks as a way to reduce manual work and keep the environment secure. The episode "Fix Microsoft 365 Guest Access Risks Across Services" lists access packages for guests, set up through Entitlement Management, as one step among several protective measures. The others it names are controlling who can send guest invites, scheduling regular access reviews, applying Conditional Access policies such as multi-factor authentication, and managing sharing settings in SharePoint and OneDrive.

Access packages are also one component of a wider identity governance setup. The episode "Lock Down Microsoft Entra ID Before Phishing Hits" lists automated access reviews, entitlement management with access packages linked to roles, and automated lifecycle events such as onboarding or role changes as building blocks that support compliance and regulatory requirements. Access reviews complement packages: where a package defines how access is requested and how long it lasts, a review checks whether people who hold access still need it, and reviews can be scheduled to run automatically for sensitive data.

The episode "Entra ID Governance: Access Reviews, Entitlement Management and Lifecycle Workflows" addresses how these parts work together and how to introduce governance step by step, starting from joiner-mover-leaver basics and moving toward access packages. It is aimed at identity architects and IAM and compliance teams. In practice, this suggests a typical decision path: first establish how people join, move and leave, then group the resulting access needs into packages with clear policies, and finally add reviews and lifecycle workflows to keep the arrangement accurate over time.

access-reviews.desc: Access reviews are recurring Microsoft Entra reviews that ask designated reviewers whether a person still needs access to a group, app or role.

faq.a: Access reviews are recurring reviews in Microsoft Entra in which designated reviewers confirm whether a person still needs access to a group, application, access package or privileged role. Removals can optionally be applied automatically.
faq.q: What are access reviews in Microsoft Entra?

faq.a: According to the concept description, access reviews apply to groups, applications, access packages and privileged roles.
faq.q: Which resources can access reviews cover?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode on Entra ID Governance presents the three as working together: entitlement management and lifecycle workflows shape how access is granted and changed, while access reviews recurrently check that existing access is still needed.
faq.q: How do access reviews relate to entitlement management and lifecycle workflows?

access-reviews.long:
Access reviews are a Microsoft Entra capability for checking, on a recurring basis, whether people still need the access they hold. Designated reviewers are asked to confirm or deny access to a group, an application, an access package or a privileged role. Depending on how a review is configured, removals can be applied automatically once the decision is made. The concept sits under Microsoft Entra and is part of the identity governance area described in Microsoft's documentation.

The purpose of access reviews is to keep permissions from accumulating unnoticed. The M365.FM episode "Entra ID Governance: Access Reviews, Entitlement Management and Lifecycle Workflows" opens with the observation that access which is never reviewed tends to grow, and that identity governance puts lifecycle and accountability around it. Access reviews are the recurring checkpoint in that model: instead of assuming that a permission granted once remains appropriate, the organization asks a named reviewer to re-confirm it at defined intervals.

In practice, a review is scoped to a resource type: membership of a group, assignment to an application, holders of an access package, or assignment to a privileged role. Reviewers are designated to make the decision, and the outcome can be enforced automatically so that denied access is removed without a separate manual cleanup step. This makes the review both a decision process and an enforcement mechanism, which is relevant when a team needs to demonstrate that least-privilege access is actively maintained rather than merely documented.

Access reviews are usually discussed together with other identity governance features. The episode on Entra ID Governance covers access reviews alongside entitlement management and lifecycle workflows and looks at how the three work together, including how to introduce governance step by step, starting from joiner-mover-leaver processes. In this combination, entitlement management and lifecycle workflows cover how access is requested, granted and adjusted over a person's time in the organization, while access reviews check afterwards whether what was granted is still justified.

Several other M365.FM episodes mention access reviews as one control among many. "Secure Microsoft Copilot with Entra ID and Zero Trust" recommends periodic access reviews to maintain least-privilege access and prevent data exposure, as part of an identity-first approach built on Microsoft Entra and Zero Trust principles. "Microsoft 365 Governance as Code Beyond Written Policies" lists inconsistent access governance as a common governance failure, including broad permissions, missing least privilege and a lack of periodic access reviews and entitlement management. "Automate Microsoft 365 Governance Beyond Static Checklists" describes how role-based access reviews, entitlement management and automated access reviews can be orchestrated so that permissions are continuously validated and adjusted across Microsoft 365. "Microsoft 365 Audit Readiness and Governance Debt" recommends regular audits and access reviews to maintain visibility and accountability, alongside tools such as Entra and Purview.

Taken together, the episodes position access reviews as a recurring, accountable control rather than a one-time cleanup. Typical decisions around them include which resources to review first, who should act as reviewer, how often the review should recur, and whether denied access should be removed automatically. The official documentation page for access reviews in Microsoft Entra ID Governance is the reference for the exact scenarios, settings and licensing requirements, none of which are specified in the episode excerpts summarized here.

access-token.desc: An access token is a short-lived, signed token from an identity provider such as Microsoft Entra ID that lets a client call a protected API within defined scopes or roles.

faq.a: It is a short-lived, signed token issued by Microsoft Entra ID that lets a client call a protected API within defined scopes or roles. The client sends it with each request to prove it is authorized.
faq.q: What is an access token in Microsoft Entra ID?

faq.a: According to the episode "Graph API - Simply Explained", the request includes an Authorization header with the word Bearer followed by the access token.
faq.q: How is an access token sent to Microsoft Graph?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Graph Webhooks - Simply Explained" says renewing the subscription may fail, and the app then needs to obtain a new access token.
faq.q: What happens if an app's authorization is lost during a Graph webhook subscription?

access-token.long:
An access token is a short-lived, signed token issued by an identity provider such as Microsoft Entra ID. It lets a client application call a protected API within defined scopes or roles. The token acts as proof that the caller has been authenticated and authorized, so the API does not need to receive the user's password or the application's credentials with every request. Microsoft documents the format and behavior of these tokens in its Microsoft Entra identity platform documentation.

The typical flow starts with registration. According to the episode "Use Managed Identity with PowerShell for Microsoft Graph", an application is first registered in Azure Active Directory (Azure AD), which provides client credentials such as an application ID and a secret or certificate. When a script requests an access token, it presents these credentials to Azure AD. Azure AD verifies the identity and issues a short-lived token. The script then includes this token in its API requests to show that it has the right to access the requested resources. The episode describes this as a way to support fine-grained permissions, so that scripts only receive the access they need.

How the token is sent to an API is also covered in the episodes. The episode "Graph API - Simply Explained" shows that a request to Microsoft Graph, with a path appended to the v1.0 endpoint, must carry an Authorization header in the form "Bearer" followed by the access token. This is how the API receives the token and checks it. The same episode notes that Microsoft Entra ID supports several authentication methods for users, including passwords, phone (SMS and voice calls), FIDO2 security keys and Microsoft Authenticator.

What a token contains depends on the access model. The episode "Microsoft Graph Permissions and Consent Models Explained" describes delegated access, where the app works as the user and both the app and the user need permission. Scopes decide what the app can do for the user, and the app can only do what the user can do. After sign-in, the app receives an access token that carries details about the app and the user, and Microsoft Graph checks this token to see whether the app has the right permissions. OAuth is described as the usual way to sign in and obtain that permission. The short description of this entity also mentions roles, which apply alongside scopes when a token is issued for an application rather than for a signed-in user.

Access tokens also matter for long-running scenarios. The episode "Microsoft Graph Webhooks - Simply Explained" explains that when a subscription's authorization is challenged, the app receives a notification at its lifecycleNotificationUrl. The app must validate the authenticity of that notification and make sure it holds a valid access token. If the app is no longer authorized, renewing the subscription may fail, and a new access token must be obtained. The episode presents managing these stages well as a way to avoid missed notifications, and it also advises handling subscriptionRemoved notifications by acknowledging receipt, validating authenticity and creating a new subscription if needed.

The term is also used outside Microsoft identity flows. In the episode "Figma to Power Apps Development with Lukas Pavelka [MVP]", a Figma access token and the PowerApps for Figma plugin are listed as requirements for connecting Figma designs to Power Apps and Power BI. In that context the token is issued by Figma rather than by Microsoft Entra ID, but it serves the same general purpose of granting a tool authorized access to a service.

In practice, the decisions around an access token concern which scopes or roles to request, which credentials the client uses to obtain the token, and how the app reacts when a token expires or authorization is withdrawn. Because the token is short-lived and scoped, an app is expected to request a new one when needed rather than store one indefinitely, and to request only the permissions it requires.

account-reconciliation-agent.desc: The Account Reconciliation Agent is an AI agent in Dynamics 365 Finance that helps reconcile the general ledger against subledgers such as payables, receivables, tax and bank.

faq.a: It is an AI agent in Dynamics 365 Finance that helps reconcile the general ledger against subledgers such as accounts payable, accounts receivable, tax and bank.
faq.q: What is the Account Reconciliation Agent in Dynamics 365 Finance?

faq.a: It is part of Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations.
faq.q: Which product is the Account Reconciliation Agent part of?

faq.a: Microsoft provides a configuration article for the agent in the general ledger section of the Dynamics 365 Finance documentation on Microsoft Learn.
faq.q: Where can configuration information be found?

account-reconciliation-agent.long:
The Account Reconciliation Agent (Dynamics 365 Finance) is an AI agent in Dynamics 365 Finance that supports the reconciliation of the general ledger against subledgers. The subledgers named in its description include accounts payable, accounts receivable, tax and bank.

In finance operations, reconciliation compares balances and transactions recorded in the general ledger with the detail held in subledgers, so that differences can be identified and resolved. The Account Reconciliation Agent is intended to assist with this task within Dynamics 365 Finance rather than leaving the comparison entirely to manual work.

The agent is part of Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations. Microsoft documents how to set it up in a configuration article in the general ledger section of the Dynamics 365 Finance documentation on Microsoft Learn. That article is the reference point for configuration details, which are not described further here.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity. Readers looking for specifics on setup, prerequisites or supported scenarios should consult the official Microsoft documentation.

accounts-payable.desc: Accounts payable is the finance function and set of records that track what a company owes its vendors and prepare and process vendor payments.

faq.a: Accounts payable is the finance function and the records that track what a company owes its vendors and that prepare and process vendor payments. It also appears as an account in the general ledger.
faq.q: What is accounts payable?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode, vendor records, invoices, purchase orders, receiving, invoice matching and approvals come together in one controlled process before a payment run and settlement take place.
faq.q: What happens before an invoice is paid in Dynamics 365 Accounts Payable?

faq.a: No. The episode on Dynamics 365 Finance states that an invoice does not necessarily require immediate payment; Finance decides the timing based on the supplier's payment terms, such as thirty-day terms, and the organization's payment processes.
faq.q: Does an approved supplier invoice have to be paid immediately?

accounts-payable.long:
Accounts payable is the finance function and the associated records that track what a company owes its vendors and that prepare and process payments to them. It covers the period from the moment a supplier invoice arrives to the point where the payment is made and the liability is closed. In accounting terms it appears as one of the accounts in the ledger, alongside accounts such as cash, sales revenue, inventory and rent expense.

The purpose of accounts payable is to make sure that money leaves the company only after the right checks have taken place. A supplier invoice may arrive when the goods are already in the warehouse or the service is already complete, but that alone does not mean it should be paid immediately. The episode "Dynamics 365 Accounts Payable - Simply Explained" describes this as the question of what has to happen before money leaves the company, and presents Dynamics 365 Finance as a system that connects vendor records, invoices, purchase orders, receiving, invoice matching, approvals, payment runs, bank accounts and settlement into one controlled financial process.

Payment timing is a central part of the function. According to the episode "Dynamics 365 Finance - Simply Explained", an invoice does not necessarily require immediate payment. Once an invoice has passed the appropriate checks, Finance determines when it should be paid according to the supplier's payment terms and the organization's own payment processes. A supplier might, for example, grant thirty-day terms, so the payment is scheduled accordingly rather than made on receipt. The same episode points out a practical benefit of keeping invoices inside a controlled process: if something does not match, for instance because the products have not arrived or the receipt has not yet been recorded, the organization can investigate while the invoice is still pending instead of discovering the problem after payment through a long email conversation.

Accounts payable is closely tied to the general ledger. The episode "Dynamics 365 General Ledger - Simply Explained" explains that the ledger holds debit and credit entries organized into accounts, that every financial event has two sides, and that total debits and credits must remain balanced. Accounts payable is named there as one of those ledger accounts. The same episode notes that Dynamics 365 Finance maintains a ledger for each legal entity, so individual companies within a larger organization keep their own financial records, reporting responsibilities, currencies and accounting periods. Payables transactions therefore sit within that per-entity accounting structure.

Several M365.FM episodes also look at how automation and AI relate to payables work. In "AI and Copilot in D365FO Finance with Billur Samdancioglu [MVP-MCT]", the invoice processing scenario with a Copilot payables agent is described. When an invoice is opened in the Dynamics 365 invoice capture workbench, the agent can be asked for suggestions. According to the episode, it retrieves historical postings and supplier patterns from the ERP and returns a summary with recommended general ledger accounts and dimension values for each line item, which the user can accept, adjust or apply. The episode "Use Copilot in Dynamics 365 Business Central" similarly says that Copilot automates invoice and accounts payable processes by extracting and matching invoice data and flagging discrepancies for review, and that it can help correct errors by scanning statement lines and auto-matching transactions.

Typical decisions around accounts payable include how strictly to match invoices against purchase orders and receipts, who approves which invoices, how payment runs are organized, and which bank accounts are used. These choices determine how tightly the process controls outgoing money. The episodes treat the topic from two angles: the foundational process in Dynamics 365 Finance, and the emerging use of Copilot and agent features to reduce manual entry and speed up review while leaving discrepancies visible for people to check.

acid-transactions.desc: ACID transactions are database transactions that guarantee atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, a contrast to Excel files with concurrent edits.

faq.a: ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. Together these four properties describe reliable database transactions.
faq.q: What does ACID stand for?

faq.a: The episodes contrast them because Excel offers none of these guarantees for concurrent edits. "Fix Power Apps After a Schema Change" lists no transactions and no version checks for Excel versus ACID transactions and referential constraints in Dataverse.
faq.q: Why are ACID transactions compared with Excel files?

faq.a: According to "Optimize Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Performance", Lakehouse ACID guarantees through versions and commits add metadata and compaction costs. This can make short-lived micro-batches faster than large monolithic Warehouse loads.
faq.q: How do ACID transactions affect Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse performance?

acid-transactions.long:
ACID transactions are a core concept in reliable data management. The acronym stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, the four properties that describe how a database transaction should behave. A transaction groups several read and write operations into one unit of work, and the ACID properties define what a system promises about that unit: it is applied as a whole, it leaves the data in a valid state, it does not interfere with other concurrent work, and its result is kept once it has been committed.

The concept is most useful when it is compared with tools that offer none of these guarantees. The M365.FM material contrasts ACID-backed data stores with Excel files, which provide no such guarantees for concurrent edits. When several people change the same workbook, there is no transaction boundary, no version check and no mechanism that keeps two changes from overwriting each other. This is why the topic appears in discussions about moving business data out of spreadsheets and into governed platforms.

The episode "Fix Power Apps After a Schema Change" makes this comparison concrete for Power Apps. It lists Excel limitations, such as no required fields, no audit log, no transactions and no version checks, next to the improvements Dataverse offers: enforced required fields, audit logs, ACID transactions and referential constraints. The episode also notes that Excel offers limited multi-user support and unoptimized queries, whereas Dataverse offers optimized queries and scalable storage. In that framing, ACID transactions are one of several reasons to migrate from Excel to Dataverse, and the episode adds that a clear migration strategy can make the move less daunting.

In Microsoft Fabric, ACID transactions come up in three different contexts. The episode "Fix Bad Data Upstream with T-SQL Contracts" describes T-SQL as a query language that supports data integrity and governance, and says that data mirrored in Microsoft Fabric stays consistent across analytics workloads. According to the episode, this approach supports robust ACID transactions, so that grouped read and write operations can be performed with confidence. The episode presents this as part of keeping data trustworthy and accessible for reporting and analysis.

The episode "Fix Wrong Copilot Numbers in Microsoft Fabric" connects ACID transactions to the layered Bronze, Silver and Gold approach, where data is cleaned, processed and refined step by step. It lists ACID transactions as a benefit that guarantees consistency and reliability across all layers, alongside improved data quality and time travel. Time travel is described as a way to audit and troubleshoot by reverting to previous data states. The episode argues that focusing on the integrity of these layers improves the accuracy and reliability of Microsoft Fabric Copilot.

The performance side is covered in "Optimize Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Performance". The episode says that the ACID guarantees of a Lakehouse, provided through versions and commits, change optimization tradeoffs. They add metadata and compaction costs, which can make short-lived micro-batches faster than large monolithic Warehouse loads, contrary to what might be expected. The same episode states that many small columnar files with good partitioning can outperform fewer huge files in some high-concurrency scenarios, because of parallel read efficiency and predicate pushdown. It also notes that IO patterns matter more than raw compute, since adding compute helps only in certain cases.

Taken together, the episodes treat ACID transactions as both a reliability feature and a design factor. They give protection against inconsistent or partially applied changes, which matters for governance, auditing and trustworthy reporting. They also carry a cost in metadata and compaction work that influences how data should be loaded and organized. Decisions around the concept typically involve choosing between a spreadsheet and a governed store such as Dataverse, and choosing load patterns in a Fabric Lakehouse or Warehouse.

active-directory.desc: Active Directory is Microsoft's on-premises directory service for Windows domains, managing users, computers and permissions and authenticating them, including via Kerberos.

faq.a: Active Directory is the on-premises directory service for Windows domains. It manages users, computers and permissions centrally and authenticates them within a domain, with Kerberos being part of how authentication works.
faq.q: What is Active Directory used for?

faq.a: Many organizations run Active Directory alongside Microsoft Entra ID, the cloud identity service. Identities from on-premises Active Directory can be synchronized into Microsoft Entra ID with tools such as Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync or Microsoft Entra Connect.
faq.q: How does Active Directory relate to Microsoft Entra ID?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Stop Active Directory Security Drift Before a Breach", it is the gradual move of an environment away from its original secure configuration through daily changes, admin actions or incomplete processes. The episode says it often goes unnoticed and calls for proactive governance and visibility.
faq.q: What is Active Directory security drift?

active-directory.long:
Active Directory (AD), also called Active Directory Domain Services, is the on-premises directory service for Windows domains. It manages users, computers and permissions centrally and authenticates them within a domain. The Kerberos protocol is part of how it does this, which is why Kerberos appears among the aliases of the product. Active Directory was developed by Microsoft and is classed as an identity and security tool. For many years it has been the backbone of identity in company networks, and in hybrid environments it often remains the source of user accounts.

In practice, Active Directory is the place where an organization defines who its users are, which computers belong to the domain and which permissions apply to them. Because these records sit in one directory, administrators can apply access rules consistently across the Windows environment. That central role is also why decisions around Active Directory affect many other systems: sign-in, group-based access and the identities that later appear in the cloud all depend on how the directory is organized and maintained.

Active Directory is closely related to Microsoft Entra ID, the cloud identity service that many organizations run alongside it. When both directories are in use, identities have to be kept consistent between them. Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync is one of the ways to synchronize identities from on-premises Active Directory into Microsoft Entra ID, and Microsoft Entra Connect is another. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Entra Connect - Simply Explained" describes hybrid identity from the starting point that companies managed employee identities primarily on premises for many years, and breaks Microsoft Entra Connect down into synchronization, authentication and health monitoring. The episode "Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync - Simply Explained" covers the cloud-managed alternative and looks at architecture, high availability, scoping, security, hybrid environments and the decision between Cloud Sync and Entra Connect.

Security is a recurring theme in the episodes. "Stop Active Directory Security Drift Before a Breach" explores security drift, meaning how an environment gradually moves away from its original secure configuration over time. According to the episode, even well-designed setups become vulnerable as changes accumulate through daily operations, admin actions or incomplete processes, and this drift is often subtle and goes unnoticed. The episode emphasizes that drift is inevitable but unmanaged drift is dangerous, and it points to proactive governance and visibility as the response. A related episode, "How Ransomware Moves Through Active Directory", describes security drift in Active Directory and Azure AD as the slow, invisible decay of identity, permissions and governance posture when environments are not routinely managed and remediated. The episode says this decay weakens access controls and creates blind spots that attackers can exploit.

Migration and operating model are the other focus. "Move Active Directory Groups to Microsoft Entra ID" describes the real cost of relying on both on-premises Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID at once. The episode names mismatched policies, sync drift, failed Conditional Access checks and recurring sign-in problems as typical symptoms of a dual-directory setup. It frames the way forward as clarifying identity practices and giving Microsoft Entra ID full control in a safe and predictable way without breaking the environment.

Typical decisions around Active Directory therefore include how to keep its configuration from drifting, how to synchronize identities into Microsoft Entra ID, which synchronization tool to choose, and how far to move group management and the source of authority into the cloud. Identity lifecycle management is a related topic, because users, groups and permissions in the directory change over time and need to be governed as they do.

active-directory-certificate-services.desc: Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) is a Windows Server role for issuing and managing PKI certificates, reportedly adding ML-DSA support for post-quantum certificates in 2026.

faq.a: AD CS is a Windows Server role for issuing and managing PKI certificates. It lets an organization operate its own certificate infrastructure.
faq.q: What is Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS)?

faq.a: According to the episode, AD CS added ML-DSA support for post-quantum certificates in 2026. No further technical details are given in the available information.
faq.q: Does AD CS support post-quantum certificates?

faq.a: Microsoft publishes an overview of Active Directory Certificate Services in its Windows Server documentation on Microsoft Learn, under the identity section for AD CS.
faq.q: Where can I find official documentation for AD CS?

active-directory-certificate-services.long:
Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) is a Windows Server role used to issue and manage certificates as part of a public key infrastructure (PKI). Organizations use such a role to run their own certification authority and to provide certificates for identity, authentication and related security scenarios inside a Windows environment.

According to the episode that references it, AD CS added support for ML-DSA, a post-quantum signature algorithm, in 2026. This would allow certificates based on post-quantum cryptography to be issued from the role. The available information on this change is limited to that statement, so details such as supported versions, configuration steps or rollout timing are not covered here.

Microsoft provides an overview of the role in its Windows Server documentation under the identity section for AD CS. That documentation is the reference point for the role's general purpose and capabilities.

On M365.FM, AD CS appears in the context of a discussion of post-quantum certificate support. No specific episode titles or related topic links are listed for this entity at this time.

active-directory-forest.desc: An Active Directory forest is the top-level, self-contained Active Directory environment, grouping domains that share one schema, configuration and global catalog.

faq.a: It is a separate, self-contained Active Directory environment at the top of the logical hierarchy. It consists of one or more domains that share a schema, a common configuration and a global catalog.
faq.q: What is an Active Directory forest?

faq.a: A common reason is a merger or acquisition, where an acquired company keeps using its own Active Directory environment. The episode on AD tiering also notes that some organizations use a separate forest for tier 0 accounts to enhance security.
faq.q: Why do organizations have more than one forest?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync - Simply Explained", an agent can run near each forest while all of them synchronize toward the same Microsoft Entra tenant. The forests do not need a direct connection to each other for this.
faq.q: How can several forests work with Microsoft Entra?

active-directory-forest.long:
An Active Directory forest is a separate, self-contained Active Directory environment. According to Microsoft Learn's description of the Active Directory logical model, the forest sits at the top of the logical hierarchy, above domains and organizational units. It is a collection of one or more Active Directory domains that share a common logical structure. Because of this, the forest is the broadest unit of organization in Active Directory, the broader concept it belongs to.

The domains in one forest share three things. The first is a single directory schema, which holds the class and attribute definitions for directory objects. The second is a common directory configuration, which covers site and replication information. The third is a global catalog, which allows searching across the whole forest. Domains inside one forest are linked automatically by two-way transitive trusts. The documentation also stresses that this logical model is independent of the physical deployment, such as the number of domain controllers or the network topology. The page does not describe the forest as a security boundary and gives no numeric limits, so those points are not covered here.

Organizations can have several forests. A typical reason is a merger or acquisition: one organization may operate one Active Directory environment while an acquired company continues using another. Establishing full network connectivity between such environments, or restructuring the directories into one, may take months. Running more than one forest is therefore a common situation in practice, and decisions about identity often have to account for it.

The episode "Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync - Simply Explained" discusses this multi-forest situation. It says Cloud Sync allows an agent to operate near each Active Directory forest while the separate environments synchronize toward the same Microsoft Entra tenant. The cloud becomes the common destination, and the forests do not need a direct connection between them just for synchronization. According to the episode, this can give organizations additional time to complete larger identity and infrastructure integration projects without preventing employees from accessing the resources they need.

A second use of separate forests appears in the episode "AD Tiering and Privileged Access with Viktor Hedberg [MVP-MCT]". In the context of administrative tiering, the episode says some organizations use a separate Active Directory forest for tier 0 accounts to enhance security. It describes enforcing a one-way trust boundary so that credentials from lower tiers cannot access tier 0 systems, and it notes that isolating tier 0 assets prevents attackers from moving laterally and limits the impact of a breach. The episode also mentions monitoring tier 0 accounts closely and working from Privileged Access Workstations to reduce exposure.

Taken together, the sources show two different reasons for having more than one forest: organizational history, such as an acquisition, and deliberate isolation of the most privileged administrative accounts. In both cases the forest defines the shared schema, configuration and global catalog, and design questions concern whether and how separate forests are connected or synchronized, for example toward a common Microsoft Entra tenant.

active-directory-tiering.desc: Active Directory administrative tiering is a security model that separates admin accounts and systems into tiers to limit credential exposure and lateral movement.

faq.a: It is a security model for Active Directory that separates administrative accounts and systems into tiers, with tier zero holding domain controllers and other identity-critical systems. Its aim is to limit credential exposure, privilege escalation and lateral movement.
faq.q: What is Active Directory administrative tiering?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn describes the enterprise access model as the successor of the on-premises Active Directory tier model. Tier 0 maps to the control plane, Tier 1 splits into the management plane and the data and workload plane, and Tier 2 splits into user access and app access.
faq.q: How does administrative tiering relate to the enterprise access model?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, the required principles are Zero Trust, pervasive security and policy for all access types, and mitigating privilege escalation. The last is done by enforcing hierarchy, auditing configuration weaknesses and monitoring anomalies.
faq.q: Which principles does the enterprise access model require?

active-directory-tiering.long:
Active Directory administrative tiering is a security model for Active Directory that separates administrative accounts and systems into tiers. Tier zero holds the domain controllers and other identity-critical systems. The purpose of the model is to limit credential exposure, privilege escalation and lateral movement, so that the compromise of a less sensitive system does not hand an attacker control over the systems that govern identity for the whole environment.

Microsoft Learn describes the original tier model as a way of containing unauthorized privilege escalation in a Windows Server Active Directory environment. In practice this means that the accounts, workstations and servers used to administer one tier are kept apart from those of the other tiers, and that higher-privileged credentials are not used on systems in lower tiers. The Microsoft Learn page presents the legacy tier model only as a diagram, and the sources available here do not spell out further operational details such as the exact contents of each tier or the technical controls used to enforce separation.

The model is the starting point for what Microsoft calls the enterprise access model. According to the Microsoft Learn page, the enterprise access model is the successor of the on-premises Active Directory tier model. It organizes the environment into three planes: a control plane of enterprise identity systems, a management plane for IT management infrastructure, and a data and workload plane that holds applications and data. Each plane controls those beneath it. Three access pathways cross these planes: user access, application access through APIs, and privileged access for administrators and developers, which must be stringently protected.

The page also maps the older tiers onto the newer structure. Tier 0 becomes the control plane, widened to cover all access control, including networking for legacy operational technology. Tier 1 splits into the management plane and the data and workload plane. Tier 2 splits into user access and app access, so that the model also covers B2B, B2C and API surfaces. This mapping shows how the original three-tier idea was extended beyond on-premises Active Directory to cover cloud and application scenarios.

The required principles named for the enterprise access model are Zero Trust, pervasive security and policy for all access types, and mitigating privilege escalation. The last of these is achieved by enforcing hierarchy, auditing configuration weaknesses and monitoring anomalies. These principles indicate how administrative tiering is meant to be applied today: as part of a broader access strategy rather than as an isolated Active Directory setting.

Active Directory administrative tiering is a narrower topic within Active Directory, the broader concept it belongs to. Typical decisions around it include which systems count as identity-critical and therefore belong in tier zero, how administrator accounts are separated by tier, and whether an environment should continue to use the classic tier model or move toward the plane-based enterprise access model. No M365.FM episodes are linked to this topic at present, so there are no episode-specific recommendations or warnings to report.

activity-explorer.desc: Activity explorer is a Microsoft Purview tool that gives a historical view of activities on labeled content, such as label changes and DLP events, drawn from the unified audit log.

faq.a: Activity explorer shows a historical view of activities on labeled content, such as labels applied, changed or removed and DLP events. The data is based on the unified audit log.
faq.q: What does Activity explorer show?

faq.a: According to the episodes, it is used to filter and view DLP events and to provide forensic detail such as who accessed, modified or shared sensitive items. This supports investigations and compliance reviews beyond simple blocking rules.
faq.q: How is Activity explorer used with DLP?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Purview Information Protection - Simply Explained" lists it, together with content explorer, as a way to view sensitive items for deeper analysis during the assessment of the data landscape, before policies are configured.
faq.q: Where does Activity explorer fit in an information protection rollout?

activity-explorer.long:
Activity explorer is a tool in Microsoft Purview that provides a historical view of activities on labeled content. It shows events such as sensitivity labels being applied, changed or removed, as well as data loss prevention (DLP) events. The underlying data comes from the unified audit log, so the tool presents audit information in a form that is easier to filter and review than raw log entries. It belongs to the data classification area of Microsoft Purview, where it sits alongside tools such as content explorer.

The main purpose of Activity explorer is to make the use of labels and the behavior of protection policies visible. A label alone does not show how content is handled in daily work. By surfacing who accessed, modified or shared sensitive items, the tool lets security and compliance teams see how labeled data moves through an organization. The episode "Microsoft Purview vs Azure Information Protection" describes this as activity and telemetry that make labels actionable, showing where labeled data is accessed, shared or exfiltrated, which helps security teams prioritize controls and demonstrate compliance.

In practice, Activity explorer is used most often together with DLP and sensitivity labels.
