The episode "Configure Microsoft 365 DLP Policies in Purview" explains that DLP can use sensitivity labels from Microsoft Information Protection as conditions and actions, so labeling and DLP policies work together in one setup strategy. In that context, Activity explorer is described as providing forensic detail: DLP logs include detailed alerts and activity explorer entries that support investigations and compliance reviews beyond what simple blocking rules show. This gives administrators a way to check what a policy actually did, not only what it was configured to do.

The tool also appears in the assessment phase of an information protection rollout. The episode "Microsoft Purview Information Protection - Simply Explained" lists viewing sensitive items with content explorer and activity explorer as a step for deeper analysis, after valuable information types have been identified and data has been discovered and classified. According to the episode, this assessment helps organizations understand their data landscape and tailor protection strategies before configuring policies.

For monitoring DLP, the episode "Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) - Simply Explained" describes using Activity explorer to filter and view DLP events over the last 30 days, with a focus on sensitive information and policy detections. The episode contrasts this with other reporting routes, such as accessing DLP reports through PowerShell cmdlets, which requires connections to both Security & Compliance and Exchange PowerShell. Activity explorer therefore serves as the interactive, filter-based option for reviewing recent DLP activity.

Activity explorer also plays a role in incident handling. The episode "Protect Microsoft Copilot with Purview, DLP, and Insider Risk with Alan Cox [MVP]" names the DLP alert management dashboard, activity explorer and content explorer as tools for collecting evidence and tracking file activities during an incident. According to the episode, these tools help teams understand what happened and guide the response, alongside practices such as keeping accurate logs, notifying affected parties and running regular incident response exercises.

Taken together, the episodes position Activity explorer as an analysis and evidence tool rather than an enforcement tool. It does not apply labels or block actions itself; it reports on label activity and DLP events after they occur, based on the unified audit log. Decisions around it typically concern how to review label adoption, how to validate DLP policy behavior, and how to support investigations and compliance reviews with a historical record of activity on labeled content.

activity-protocol.desc: Activity Protocol is the communication standard used by Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, Teams and the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK to exchange activities between a channel and agent code.

faq.a: Activity Protocol is the communication standard used by Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, Teams and the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK. It defines the activities that a channel and agent code exchange.
faq.q: What is Activity Protocol?

faq.a: It defines activities such as messages, events and typing. These are the units of communication passed between a channel and an agent.
faq.q: What kinds of activities does Activity Protocol define?

faq.a: It is documented in Microsoft Learn, within the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK documentation.
faq.q: Where is Activity Protocol documented?

activity-protocol.long:
Activity Protocol is a communication standard that defines how a channel and agent code exchange information. It is used across several parts of the Microsoft ecosystem, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, Teams and the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK.

The protocol is built around activities. An activity is a unit of communication between a channel and an agent, and the protocol names examples such as messages, events and typing. By giving these exchanges a shared structure, Activity Protocol lets the same agent logic work with the different channels that send and receive them.

For developers working with the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK, Activity Protocol describes the format of the data moving between the channel the user interacts with and the code that implements the agent. For people working with Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio or Teams, it is the underlying standard that these products share when conversations are handled by an agent.

The official reference for Activity Protocol is published in Microsoft Learn as part of the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK documentation. No episodes on M365.FM are currently linked to this topic.

adaptive-card-designer.desc: The Adaptive Cards Designer is a browser-based visual tool for authoring Adaptive Cards, and it can also be embedded in custom web applications via an SDK.

faq.a: It is a web-based visual tool from Microsoft for authoring Adaptive Cards. Elements can be dragged and dropped, cards previewed with sample data, and the resulting JSON template copied.
faq.q: What is the Adaptive Cards Designer?

faq.a: Yes. Microsoft Learn describes an SDK that lets the designer be embedded in a custom web application. It is distributed as the npm package adaptivecards-designer, or it can be loaded as a script from a content delivery network.
faq.q: Can the Adaptive Cards Designer be embedded in another application?

faq.a: The episode "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions" lists designing cards with the Adaptive Cards Designer tool as one step, alongside adding the Adaptive Cards SDK and Fluent UI, building the interface with Fluent UI React components, and testing in Teams.
faq.q: How does the episode on Teams apps use the designer?

adaptive-card-designer.long:
The Adaptive Cards Designer is a web-based visual tool from Microsoft for authoring Adaptive Cards. It is part of the Adaptive Cards ecosystem and gives card authors an interactive, design-time surface in which cards are built and checked without setting up a local development environment. Because it runs in the browser, it can be opened and used directly, which lowers the barrier for people who want to prototype a card quickly.

In practice, the designer is used to compose the layout of a card by dragging and dropping elements onto a canvas, to preview the card with sample data, and to copy the resulting JSON template. That JSON template is the artifact that developers then take into their own solutions, such as bots, tabs or message extensions in Microsoft Teams. Working visually first and exporting JSON afterwards can save time compared with writing the card payload by hand, especially when a card has several nested containers or many fields.

Beyond the standalone page, Microsoft Learn documents a software development kit for the designer. This SDK allows the designer to be embedded in a custom web application, so that users can build cards without leaving that application for the external designer page. The component is distributed as the npm package adaptivecards-designer, and it can alternatively be loaded as a script from a content delivery network. According to the documentation, the package itself holds the complete documentation for the SDK. Embedding requires a web application and the npm package. The documentation pages do not describe individual designer functions beyond authoring cards, and they do not state prerequisites for browser use, license terms, costs or known limits.

The designer sits alongside other tooling for Adaptive Cards. A related tools page in the documentation mentions a JSON schema for Adaptive Cards that supports validation and IntelliSense in Visual Studio and VS Code. The documentation does not say whether the designer itself uses that schema, so the two should be treated as separate aids: the designer for visual authoring and previewing, and the schema for editor support when working with the JSON directly.

Typical decisions around the tool concern where the design work should happen. Teams that only need to create or tweak a few cards can use the browser-based designer as is. Teams that want card authoring to be part of their own product, for example an internal portal where business users define notifications, can consider the SDK and embed the designer in that application. In both cases the output remains an Adaptive Card JSON template that is rendered by a host application.

The M365.FM episode "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions" mentions the tool in the context of building Teams apps. It recommends adding the Adaptive Cards SDK and the Fluent UI library to a project, designing cards with the Adaptive Cards Designer tool, building the interface with Fluent UI React components, and testing the app in Teams to confirm that everything looks and works as expected. The episode also notes that Teams message extensions use Adaptive Cards to display live data and actions in chat, and that using Adaptive Cards improves accessibility and responsiveness. In that workflow, the designer covers the card-design step, while Fluent UI is used for the main interface in tabs and task modules.

adaptive-card-extensions.desc: Adaptive Card Extensions (ACEs) are SharePoint Framework components that render Adaptive Cards on Viva Connections dashboards in desktop and mobile.

faq.a: ACEs are SharePoint Framework (SPFx) components that use Adaptive Cards to render cards on Viva Connections dashboards, in both the desktop and mobile experience, optionally with a quick view.
faq.q: What are Adaptive Card Extensions (ACEs)?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, ACEs appear in the desktop experience through the Microsoft Teams client, on tablets and in the Teams mobile app. The mobile view shows the same ACEs as the desktop by default, adapted for mobile.
faq.q: Where do ACEs appear?

faq.a: The episode "Customize Microsoft Viva Connections Dashboards" describes ACEs, together with SPFx web parts, as a way to surface live business data and actions in Teams, such as approving, submitting and tracking, and links this to role-based personalization and a change plan.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode say about ACEs?

adaptive-card-extensions.long:
Adaptive Card Extensions (ACEs) are SharePoint Framework (SPFx) components that use Adaptive Cards to render cards on Viva Connections dashboards. They appear in both the desktop and the mobile experience and can optionally include a quick view. According to Microsoft Learn, ACEs are the foundation of the personalization and extensibility model in Viva Connections, and all customization and extension work for Viva Connections relies on the SharePoint Framework.

The purpose of ACEs is to shape the Viva Connections dashboard around the needs of an organization. They add new cards and experiences that surface the information and apps relevant to a person's role. Because dashboards can be personalized or set up separately for different audiences, ACEs can be used to give different groups of employees different sets of cards. They are built as client-side extensions, which means developers create them with the same framework used for other SharePoint Framework solutions.

ACEs appear in several places. In the desktop experience they are shown through the Microsoft Teams client. They are also available on tablets and in the Teams mobile app. By default, the mobile view shows the same ACEs as the desktop, adapted for mobile use. The Microsoft Learn overview names Card View and Quick View as topics covered in further articles: the card is the tile shown on the dashboard, and the quick view is the optional extended view that can open from it. The overview page itself does not explain these two parts in detail, and it does not state licensing requirements or technical limits.

In practice, decisions around ACEs concern which business data and actions belong on a dashboard, which audience should see which cards, and how the cards behave on mobile. The M365.FM episode "Customize Microsoft Viva Connections Dashboards" (13 August 2025) treats ACEs as a way to move Viva Connections beyond a SharePoint homepage. The episode says that a solid foundation of navigation, targeting, permissions and mobile should be paired with SPFx web parts and ACEs to surface live business data and actions inside Teams.

The same episode describes ACE-based tiles as elements that do work, with approving, submitting and tracking given as examples. It also connects the technical side to adoption: role-based personalization, performance discipline and a measured change plan are named as the means of driving use of the customized dashboard. The episode frames customization as a way for teams to shape a Viva Connections dashboard to their own needs and create a meaningful experience for everyone.

In summary, ACEs are the SPFx-based mechanism for placing Adaptive Card content on Viva Connections dashboards. They tie the dashboard to a person's role through targeted cards, work across desktop, tablet and the Teams mobile app, and rely on the SharePoint Framework for all extension work, as described in the Microsoft Learn overview and discussed in the M365.FM episode.

adaptive-cards.desc: Adaptive Cards are platform-agnostic JSON UI snippets that host apps such as Teams, Outlook and Copilot Studio render as native UI, including Power Automate approvals.

faq.a: Adaptive Cards are platform-agnostic UI snippets written in JSON. Host apps such as Microsoft Teams, Outlook and Copilot Studio render them as native UI.
faq.q: What are Adaptive Cards?

faq.a: Power Automate uses Adaptive Cards for interactive approval and notification messages. The M365.FM episode on interactive Teams cards also describes wiring Action.Submit and Action.Execute to Power Automate or a bot.
faq.q: How does Power Automate use Adaptive Cards?

faq.a: The episode "Build Interactive Microsoft Teams Adaptive Cards" names the JSON essentials as body, actions and data binding, with personalization and conditional logic as additional techniques.
faq.q: What are the core parts of an Adaptive Card in Teams?

adaptive-cards.long:
Adaptive Cards are platform-agnostic UI snippets written in JSON. A host application, such as Microsoft Teams, Outlook or Copilot Studio, takes the JSON description and renders it as native user interface in its own look and feel. Because the card is described as data rather than as platform-specific code, the same card definition can be shown in different hosts. Microsoft documents the format in the Adaptive Cards section of Microsoft Learn.

In practice, Adaptive Cards are used to put small, focused pieces of interface into the places where people already work. Power Automate uses them for interactive approval and notification messages, so a flow can post a card into Teams or Outlook that asks someone to approve a request or acknowledge an alert. Cards can also be returned by bots and Teams extensions, which lets structured, interactive results appear directly in a chat or channel instead of a plain text reply.

The M365.FM episode "Build Interactive Microsoft Teams Adaptive Cards" describes the JSON essentials as body, actions and data binding. The episode says that cards can capture input, fire approvals, update themselves and even drive bots without users leaving Teams. It covers wiring Action.Submit and Action.Execute to Power Automate or to a bot, and it mentions personalization and conditional logic as ways to make cards more useful. Its framing is that cards should do something, rather than being pretty but pointless.

The episode "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions" places Adaptive Cards inside the wider Teams extensibility model. It distinguishes search extensions, which surface existing records on demand, action extensions, which collect input, trigger back-end workflows and return results via adaptive cards, and link unfurling, which turns pasted URLs into rich previews. The walkthrough builds an action-based extension with the Teams SDK and Bot Framework that queries external systems such as CRM or ticketing tools and posts structured, interactive results into the chat. The same episode lists rollout considerations such as OAuth and SSO, permissions, privacy scope and the app manifest.

Meeting scenarios are covered in "Build Microsoft Teams Meeting Apps and Bots". There, Adaptive Cards are named alongside tab apps and bots as one of the app types for in-meeting experiences, providing rich and adaptive UI, while the meeting APIs and meeting SDK support things like polls, Q&A, whiteboards and live reactions.

A service-management example appears in "Integrate Jira Service Management with Microsoft Teams". The episode notes that interactive Adaptive Cards in that integration let users transition issue status, assign owners or add comments from the chat card without opening Jira, and that card actions can trigger Jira automations as part of a larger workflow. The episode "Build Actionable Teams Notifications with Adaptive Cards" approaches the topic from the notification side, discussing how Teams notifications work and how to configure alerts so that they inform without constant interruption.

Typical decisions around Adaptive Cards include where the card is produced, which action type handles the response, and which host will render it. A card sent from a Power Automate flow suits approvals and notifications, while a bot or extension suits conversational or lookup scenarios. Since rendering is left to the host, the card author describes content and intent in JSON and relies on the host to present it as native UI.

adaptive-protection.desc: Adaptive Protection is a Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management capability that assigns user risk levels and applies data loss prevention and Conditional Access controls accordingly.

faq.a: Adaptive Protection is a capability of Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management. It assigns users risk levels and dynamically applies data loss prevention and Conditional Access controls based on those levels.
faq.q: What is Adaptive Protection in Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: It applies data loss prevention and Conditional Access controls. The controls applied depend on the risk level assigned to each user.
faq.q: Which controls does Adaptive Protection apply?

faq.a: It is part of Microsoft Purview, specifically the Insider Risk Management capability.
faq.q: Which product is Adaptive Protection part of?

adaptive-protection.long:
Adaptive Protection is a capability of Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management. It assigns risk levels to users and dynamically applies data loss prevention and Conditional Access controls based on those levels. It is part of Microsoft Purview.

The feature is used to link the assessment of insider risk to enforcement. Rather than applying the same policies to every user, controls can vary with the risk level a user has been assigned. Two kinds of controls are involved: data loss prevention, which governs how sensitive data may be handled, and Conditional Access, which governs access to resources.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, Adaptive Protection connects the insider risk signals gathered in Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management with protective measures that respond to them. The entity is listed under Microsoft Purview as its parent product.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to Adaptive Protection (Microsoft Purview).

adaptive-scopes.desc: Adaptive scopes in Microsoft Purview use attributes such as department or job title to decide dynamically which users, groups or sites a policy covers.

faq.a: Static scopes target specific users, mailboxes or SharePoint sites from a fixed list and suit stable environments. Adaptive scopes use a query on attributes such as department or job title, so membership is determined dynamically.
faq.q: What is the difference between adaptive and static scopes in Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, the query is evaluated once a day. Changes are not validated immediately and can take several days to take effect.
faq.q: How quickly do changes take effect in an adaptive scope?

faq.a: Administrators need the Scope Manager role. Queries can be built with a simple or advanced query builder, using OPATH syntax for users and groups and KeyQL for sites, and licensing is covered in the Purview service description.
faq.q: What is needed to create adaptive scopes?

adaptive-scopes.long:
Adaptive scopes are a feature of Microsoft Purview. An adaptive scope is a query-based scope whose membership is determined dynamically from attributes or properties, such as Microsoft Entra attributes, instead of a manually maintained list. They are used to decide which locations a retention policy covers, and they stand in contrast to static scopes, which rely on fixed lists of targets.

The purpose of adaptive scopes is to reduce administrative effort while keeping policy coverage accurate. With a static scope, an administrator names specific users, mailboxes or SharePoint sites, which suits stable environments where the list rarely changes. With an adaptive scope, users or locations are included automatically when they match the defined attributes, for example a department or a job title. According to the M365.FM episode "Data Lifecycle Management - Simply Explained", this significantly reduces administration in large organizations, because the policy follows changes in the directory rather than requiring manual updates.

According to Microsoft Learn documentation, adaptive scopes can be used to target policies for communication compliance, retention and auto-labeling at users, SharePoint sites or Microsoft 365 groups. Membership is defined by a query. The query can be built with a simple query builder or with an advanced builder. The advanced builder uses OPATH syntax for users and groups and KeyQL for sites. A typical example is limiting a policy to people in a particular country or department. The documentation also lists limits for query length, attribute counts and group counts, which matter when designing more complex queries.

Several behaviors are worth knowing when planning a deployment. The query is evaluated once a day, so changes are not validated immediately and can take several days to take effect. This means that a user who changes department, or a site whose properties change, is not picked up by the policy instantly. One scope can be assigned to several policies, and one policy can contain several scopes, so scopes can be defined once and reused across different retention or labeling policies. Administrators who create and manage adaptive scopes need the Scope Manager role, and licensing is described in the Purview service description.

The choice between static and adaptive scopes is typically a question of how stable the target population is. A small, unchanging set of mailboxes or sites can be covered by a static scope. A large or frequently changing population, where the relevant attribute already exists in Microsoft Entra ID, is a typical case for an adaptive scope. The quality of the underlying attributes then becomes important, since the scope is only as accurate as the data it queries.

Adaptive scopes also interact with the wider retention logic in Microsoft Purview. The episode "Data Lifecycle Management - Simply Explained" describes that where multiple retention rules overlap, Purview follows predictable conflict resolution principles. Scopes determine where a rule applies, while the conflict resolution logic determines which rule prevails when several apply to the same item. Adaptive scopes are therefore one building block within data lifecycle management, which the episode presents as a way to apply retention to business-critical information with more granular control based on predefined conditions.

adkar-model.desc: The ADKAR model is a change management framework by Jeff Hiatt (Prosci) that guides individual change through awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement.

faq.a: The five stages are awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement. They describe why a change is needed, the willingness to support it, what to do, the capacity to do it and how the results are kept in place.
faq.q: What are the five stages of the ADKAR model?

faq.a: Jeff Hiatt developed it and first published it in 1999 in a white paper called The Perfect Change. Later work from 2006 is associated with his organization Prosci.
faq.q: Who developed the ADKAR model?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes mention ADKAR as a guide for change management in a Dynamics 365 Project Operations migration. They also say that the Microsoft Engagement Framework for Copilot adoption follows the ADKAR model.
faq.q: How does ADKAR relate to Microsoft Copilot and Dynamics 365 adoption?

adkar-model.long:
The ADKAR model is a change management model developed by Jeff Hiatt, associated with the organization Prosci. It structures change at the level of the individual and breaks it into five sequential building blocks, which give the model its name: awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement. Hiatt first published the model in 1999 in a white paper called The Perfect Change, and later work from 2006 is associated with Prosci.

Each of the five building blocks answers a specific question about a person affected by a change. Awareness covers why the change is needed. Desire describes the willingness to take part in the change and support it. Knowledge refers to what a person has to do during and after the change. Ability is the capacity to carry out the change as required. Reinforcement keeps the results in place once the change has been made. Because the focus is on the individual, ADKAR is typically used to understand why a particular person or group is not yet adopting a new way of working, rather than to describe an organization as a whole.

ADKAR is described as prescriptive and goal-oriented. Each milestone has to be achieved for the change to count as successful, and individuals can be scored from 1 to 5 on each of them. A score of 3 or below is called a barrier point and has to be addressed before moving on to the next step. According to Hiatt, the steps run in order, begin from each person's current level and cannot be skipped or reordered. The strict sequencing is presented as a design feature of the model.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, ADKAR comes up in discussions of technology adoption and change management. The M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Project Operations with Joe Griffin [MVP]" mentions it in the context of a migration to Dynamics 365 Project Operations. The episode says that teams need awareness and buy-in, and that the benefits of the new system, such as improved AI-driven automation and better project visibility, should be communicated. Experts are quoted as recommending the ADKAR model to guide change management efforts. The episode also advises customizing training programs for different roles, monitoring resistance, listening to feedback and addressing concerns quickly. For the final stage, it suggests recognizing team members who adapt well and tracking adoption metrics to reinforce and sustain the change.

The second episode, "Microsoft Copilot Adoption with Edyta Gorzoń [MVP]", links ADKAR to the Microsoft Engagement Framework, which the episode says follows the ADKAR model. It describes the framework as working well for change management, guiding users through awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement so that they move from learning about Copilot to using it confidently. In the same discussion, the episode lists concerns such as privacy and trusting AI-generated content, and recommends open communication, simple language and real examples while avoiding technical jargon. It also notes that building new habits takes time and support, that instant results should not be expected, and that teams should be encouraged to use Copilot daily with ongoing training.

Taken together, the sources show how ADKAR is applied in practice: as a checklist of individual stages that helps decide where a rollout is stuck. A lack of awareness calls for communication about the reasons for a change. Low desire points to resistance that needs to be heard. Gaps in knowledge and ability call for role-specific training and support. Weak reinforcement calls for recognition and adoption tracking. The article on ADKAR does not describe criticism aimed specifically at the model; the criticism it mentions concerns Kurt Lewin's three-step model, which some scholars called simplistic.

administrative-units.desc: Administrative units are containers in Microsoft Entra ID that hold users, groups or devices and limit an administrator role to that subset of an organization.

faq.a: They are containers in Microsoft Entra ID that hold users, groups or devices and restrict the scope of an administrator role to that subset of the organization.
faq.q: What are administrative units in Microsoft Entra ID?

faq.a: They support delegation and least privilege by letting an administrator role apply only to a defined set of objects instead of the whole tenant. The episodes describe this as limiting scope and reducing exposure.
faq.q: Why are administrative units used?

faq.a: In the episode on auditing Microsoft 365 user activity, admin units are listed as a filter that scopes an audit log search to specific administrative units.
faq.q: How do administrative units relate to Purview audit searches?

administrative-units.long:
Administrative units are containers in Microsoft Entra ID that hold users, groups or devices. Their purpose is to restrict the scope of an administrator role to that subset of the organization. Instead of granting an administrator a role across the whole tenant, an organization can place a defined set of objects into an administrative unit and let the role apply only there. The concept sits under Microsoft Entra ID, the identity platform in the Microsoft ecosystem, and is closely tied to role-based access control and the principle of least privilege.

The typical use is delegation. Large or complex organizations often need local or departmental administrators who manage a limited group of accounts without being able to touch the rest of the directory. Administrative units provide a way to express that boundary inside the identity platform. Common situations include separating responsibilities by region, business unit or customer, and giving each administrator rights only over the objects assigned to their unit. Because the container can hold users, groups or devices, the scope of a delegated role can be tailored to the kinds of objects an administrator is expected to handle.

In practice, an administrative unit works as a scoping layer on top of an administrator role. The role defines what actions an administrator can perform, while the administrative unit defines which objects those actions apply to. This keeps broad permissions from reaching the entire tenant and reduces exposure if an administrator account is misused or compromised. The approach complements custom roles, which let an organization define the set of permissions, whereas administrative units define the set of objects.

The episode "Building a Secure Microsoft-First MSP: Intune, Defender & Entra ID at Scale with Albin Klinaku [MVP]" mentions administrative units in the context of managed service providers. According to the episode, Entra ID provides custom roles and administrative units for secure delegation of responsibilities, which can help navigate complex organizational structures. The episode presents this as part of building an identity protection framework that aligns with modern security practices and supports the growth of an MSP.

The episode "Microsoft 365 Structural Debt from Default Governance" lists administrative units among the capabilities that support role-based access control and least privilege. Together with role-based access control, administrative units are described as a way to limit scope and reduce exposure. In that discussion they appear as one of several governance building blocks, alongside automation such as templates, lifecycle policies and provisioning, and monitoring and reporting, which together address tenant hygiene and operational efficiency.

Administrative units also appear in auditing. The episode "Audit Microsoft 365 User Activity with Purview" lists admin units among the filters available when searching the audit log. The search can be scoped to specific administrative units, next to filters such as the date and time range in UTC (with a maximum of 180 days), keywords, friendly activity names, operation names and record types. The episode notes that these filters help focus on relevant data, making it easier to identify trends or suspicious activities.

Taken together, the episodes show administrative units as a scoping tool used in three connected areas: delegating administration safely, enforcing least privilege as part of governance, and narrowing audit searches to a defined part of the organization. Decisions around them usually involve which objects belong in each unit, which roles are assigned at that scope, and how the structure maps to the organization's departments, regions or customers.

advanced-connector-policies.desc: Advanced connector policies (ACP) are a Power Platform governance capability for controlling which connectors, including MCP servers, may be used in an environment.

faq.a: Advanced connector policies are a Power Platform governance capability for controlling which connectors, including MCP servers, may be used in an environment.
faq.q: What are Advanced connector policies (ACP)?

faq.a: They complement classic data loss prevention (DLP) policies. They are described as an addition to DLP rather than a replacement for it.
faq.q: How do Advanced connector policies relate to DLP policies?

faq.a: Yes. MCP servers are included among the connectors whose use in an environment can be controlled with advanced connector policies.
faq.q: Do Advanced connector policies cover MCP servers?

advanced-connector-policies.long:
Advanced connector policies (ACP) are a Power Platform governance capability used to control which connectors may be used in an environment. The scope includes MCP servers, which are treated as connectors that can be allowed or restricted under these policies.

ACP complement classic data loss prevention (DLP) policies rather than replacing them. Classic DLP policies are the established mechanism for governing connector usage in Power Platform, and advanced connector policies add a further layer of control on top of that approach. Administrators responsible for Power Platform governance would use this capability when they need finer or additional control over connector availability in a given environment.

The available information about Advanced connector policies (ACP) is limited. No specific configuration steps, licensing details, supported connector types beyond MCP servers, or release information are stated here, so those points are not covered. For authoritative details, the official Microsoft documentation for Power Platform governance is the appropriate reference.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

advanced-hunting.desc: Advanced hunting is a query-based threat hunting capability in Microsoft Defender that lets analysts search raw security data using Kusto Query Language (KQL).

faq.a: Advanced hunting is a query-based threat hunting capability in Microsoft Defender. Analysts use Kusto Query Language (KQL) to search raw security data rather than depending only on automatically generated alerts.
faq.q: What is advanced hunting in Microsoft Defender?

faq.a: It uses Kusto Query Language (KQL). The episode "Correlate Microsoft 365 Telemetry for Better Insights" provides KQL examples usable in Microsoft Sentinel or Microsoft 365 Defender Advanced Hunting, noting that table names differ slightly.
faq.q: Which query language does advanced hunting use?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Defender XDR: Building Detection Beyond the Defaults" covers custom detections, advanced hunting, tuning and response automation as parts of a repeatable detection practice that adds organizational context to default detections.
faq.q: How does advanced hunting relate to custom detections?

advanced-hunting.long:
Advanced hunting is a query-based threat hunting capability in Microsoft Defender. It lets security analysts search raw security data with Kusto Query Language (KQL) instead of relying only on the alerts and incidents that the platform generates automatically. The capability sits under the broader Microsoft Defender family and is used wherever analysts need to look beyond prebuilt detections and ask their own questions of the data.

In practice, advanced hunting is used for proactive investigation. An analyst writes a KQL query to look for patterns that default detections may not surface, such as unusual sign-in behavior, suspicious file activity or signs of lateral movement. Because the queries run against raw data, the same approach can also support follow-up on an alert, validation of a suspected compromise or checks across many devices and identities at once. The episode "Microsoft Defender vs Sentinel: When You Need Both" lists advanced hunting among the tools in endpoint detection and response, where it supports detecting, investigating and responding to advanced threats.

Advanced hunting also appears in the context of Microsoft Defender XDR. The episode "Microsoft Defender XDR - Simply Explained" names it as one of the key concepts alongside incidents, alerts, automated investigation and remediation, threat intelligence and AI-powered attack disruption. In that framing, Defender XDR correlates events across identities, devices, email, cloud apps and Microsoft Teams, and advanced hunting gives analysts a way to explore that correlated data directly. The episode discusses scenarios such as phishing, ransomware, credential theft, insider threats and lateral movement, where hunting queries complement the automated correlation.

KQL is the working language of advanced hunting, and the episode "Correlate Microsoft 365 Telemetry for Better Insights" shows what this looks like. It provides copy-paste KQL that can be used in Microsoft Sentinel (Log Analytics) or in Microsoft 365 Defender Advanced Hunting, and it notes that table names differ slightly between the two. One example query looks at high-risk sign-ins combined with a download spike over the past 24 hours, joining sign-in risk information with Office activity. The episode also describes correlation ideas such as new external Teams chats and meetings appearing together with external SharePoint shares, which shows how hunting queries can connect signals from different Microsoft 365 workloads.

Advanced hunting is closely tied to detection engineering. The episode "Microsoft Defender XDR: Building Detection Beyond the Defaults" argues that default detections are a starting point and that good detection engineering adds an organization's own context on top. It covers custom detections, advanced hunting, tuning and response automation, and aims to help teams move from handling alerts to a repeatable detection practice. It is aimed at SOC analysts and related security roles. Seen this way, a hunting query that proves useful can become the basis for a custom detection rather than remaining a one-off search.

Advanced hunting is also listed as part of monitoring and oversight for AI workloads. In "Azure Copilot Agents: Building a Synthetic Platform Team", "Advanced Hunting & Threat Detection in Defender" appears in a list of tools used to monitor and audit AI operations, next to Purview audit logs, Microsoft Sentinel, Application Insights and other platforms. The episode connects such monitoring to detecting suspicious query patterns and flagging high-risk usage.

A recurring decision around advanced hunting is where to run queries and how to combine it with other tools. The episodes show that similar KQL can be used in Microsoft Sentinel or in Defender's advanced hunting, with adjustments for table names. They also frame Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel as products that can be needed together, with advanced hunting representing the query-driven side of Defender's endpoint detection and response capabilities.

advanced-planning-and-scheduling.desc: Advanced planning and scheduling (APS) is planning software that calculates a feasible production schedule from capacity, calendars, material, routing rules and priorities.

faq.a: APS is planning software that calculates a feasible production schedule. It builds the schedule from inputs such as capacity, calendars, material, routing rules and priorities.
faq.q: What does advanced planning and scheduling (APS) do?

faq.a: The described inputs are capacity, calendars, material, routing rules and priorities. Together they determine what can realistically be produced and in which order.
faq.q: Which inputs does an APS schedule rely on?

advanced-planning-and-scheduling.long:
Advanced planning and scheduling (APS) is a category of planning software that produces a feasible production schedule. Rather than listing what should be made, it calculates what can actually be made, taking into account the constraints that apply in a given operation.

According to the available description, an APS calculation draws on capacity, calendars, material availability, routing rules and priorities. Capacity and calendars describe when resources are available. Material availability limits what can start. Routing rules define the sequence of steps a product follows, and priorities determine which orders take precedence when resources are contested. The result is a schedule that respects these inputs instead of assuming unlimited resources.

The concept is relevant to people who search for how production planning differs from simple order lists or unconstrained planning, and who want to understand what inputs a scheduling engine needs. No specific product, vendor, version or implementation is tied to the concept on this page, and no related topics or episodes are currently linked to it on M365.FM.

advanced-specialization.desc: Advanced specialization is a Microsoft partner credential built on a Solutions Partner designation that validates deep workload expertise via audit or customer references.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft partner credential that builds on a Solutions Partner designation and validates deep expertise in a specific workload. The expertise is verified through an audit or customer references.
faq.q: What is an Advanced specialization?

faq.a: A partner generally needs an active Solutions Partner designation in a matching solution area plus the specialization's own requirements. These can include performance criteria, skilling criteria based on individual certifications, and sometimes a marketplace offer.
faq.q: What is required to earn an Advanced specialization?

faq.a: Depending on the specialization, verification is either an audit by a third-party auditor or customer references from separate recent customer projects. A failed audit can be repeated after a waiting period.
faq.q: How is expertise verified for a specialization?

advanced-specialization.long:
Advanced specialization is a credential within the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program that shows a partner's deeper expertise in a specific workload. It builds on a Solutions Partner designation: a partner generally needs an active designation in a matching solution area before applying. The credential is verified, not self-declared, through either an audit by a third-party auditor or customer references, depending on the specialization.

Specializations are grouped under four areas: Azure, Modern Work, Security and Business Applications. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Partner Journey: From Enrollment to Growth" lists examples of advanced specialization areas and their prerequisites. It names AI Business Solutions, which requires a Solutions Partner designation for Business Applications or Modern Work. It also names Business Applications specializations such as Business Intelligence, Finance, Intelligent Automation, Low Code Application Development and Microsoft Copilot, and a Security Solutions area that depends on a Solutions Partner designation for Security. The episode also notes that specializations often come with additional resources, training and support from Microsoft, which can help a partner grow its business, and that they can increase exposure to potential customers.

The requirements for a specialization combine several criteria. According to Partner Center documentation, these include performance criteria, such as consumed Azure revenue or the number of unique customers, and skilling criteria based on individual certifications held by staff. Some specializations also require a marketplace offer. Trial, benefit, support and internal consumption does not count toward revenue requirements, which matters when a partner plans how to reach a threshold.

Proof of capability is the distinguishing step. Depending on the specialization, a partner either undergoes an audit conducted by a third-party auditor or submits customer references drawn from separate recent customer projects. A partner choosing a specialization therefore needs to check which verification method applies and prepare the matching evidence, such as documented projects or audit-ready processes. A failed audit can be repeated after a waiting period.

In practice, applications and tracking happen in Partner Center. Only users with the partner admin role see the Specializations area, where progress against the requirements is shown and audits are scheduled. This makes role assignment an early practical decision for organizations that want to pursue a specialization. Some specializations have been retired and no longer accept new applications, so it is worth confirming that a target specialization is still open before investing in its requirements.

A typical decision path starts with the existing Solutions Partner designation, since it determines which specializations are available. A partner then compares the performance, skilling and verification requirements of candidate specializations against its current customer base, certified staff and project history. Advanced specialization sits above the designation level in this structure: the designation establishes broad capability in a solution area, while the specialization signals focused depth in one workload within it.

adx-studio.desc: ADX Studio was a Canadian software company whose portal product for Dynamics CRM was acquired by Microsoft in 2015 and became the basis of Power Pages.
adx-studio.long:
ADX Studio was a Canadian software company that developed a portal product for Dynamics CRM. The product allowed organizations to build web portals connected to their Dynamics CRM data.

In 2015, Microsoft acquired ADX Studio. The acquired portal technology later served as the basis of Power Pages, the Microsoft low-code platform for building external-facing websites. Readers researching the history of Power Pages, or the origins of Dynamics 365 portals, will encounter ADX Studio as the starting point of that product line.

No episodes on M365.FM are currently linked to this entity, and no further relations to other topics are recorded here. The company's name appears mainly in the context of the Microsoft acquisition and the lineage from a Dynamics CRM portal product to Power Pages.

aerospace.desc: Aerospace (Luftfahrt, Luft- und Raumfahrt, Aviation) designs, builds and maintains aircraft, spacecraft and components under strict quality and certification rules.

faq.a: Aerospace is the industry that designs, builds and maintains aircraft, spacecraft and their components, with strict quality, traceability and certification requirements. On M365.FM it appears as an industry context for simulation, digital twins, auditing and automation.
faq.q: What does Aerospace mean in the context of M365.FM?

faq.a: "Microsoft Fabric Digital Twin Builder Explained" says digital twins help predict issues in airframes and engines before they happen. "Codify Business Logic into a Digital Twin for AI Agents" adds product development, prototyping, training and mixed-reality work instructions for maintenance.
faq.q: How are digital twins used in aerospace according to the episodes?

faq.a: The episode "Private LoRA for Secure AI on Proprietary Enterprise Data" says time-stamped logs, location evidence and usage trails support audits and compliance checks, which is especially important in industries like aviation.
faq.q: Why do auditing and monitoring matter for aviation?

aerospace.long:
Aerospace, also referred to as Luftfahrt, Luft- und Raumfahrt or Aviation, is the industry that designs, builds and maintains aircraft, spacecraft and their components. It is characterised by strict quality, traceability and certification requirements. On M365.FM the term appears as an industry context for Microsoft and partner technologies rather than as a product of its own: the episodes mention aerospace when they describe where simulation, digital twins, automation and governed AI are applied.

Because quality, traceability and certification define the sector, the data and engineering work around it tends to be demanding. Product development depends on simulation, prototyping and the ability to follow parts and decisions over their lifetime. This is the background against which the episodes place their examples: tools that help engineers analyse complex systems, represent physical assets digitally, and keep records that can be audited.

One recurring theme is simulation and machine learning. The episode "Mainframe Architecture Lessons for Azure Cloud Design" describes a platform that integrates with Altair simulation tools so that engineers can use machine learning to analyse and optimise complex systems. According to the episode, this is particularly valuable in industries such as automotive, aerospace and energy, where simulation plays a crucial role in product development. Combining simulation with machine learning is presented as a way to predict performance, identify potential issues and optimise designs more effectively than traditional methods.

A second theme is the digital twin. In "Microsoft Fabric Digital Twin Builder Explained", aerospace is listed alongside automotive, retail and architecture as a field where Microsoft Fabric digital twin technology has had an impact. The episode says that in aerospace, issues in airframes and engines can be predicted before they happen, and it ties predictive maintenance and diagnostics to anticipating equipment problems. The episode "Codify Business Logic into a Digital Twin for AI Agents" returns to the idea in a different form. It says aerospace teams use digital twins for product development and prototyping, that designers and engineers can work together more easily, and that simulation and training become more engaging with AR and VR. It also describes maintenance and operations teams using digital twins to create work instructions in mixed reality, which makes inspections and repairs more efficient, and it names Boeing as an example company.

A third theme is auditability and governance, where the wording is aviation. The episode "Private LoRA for Secure AI on Proprietary Enterprise Data" notes that auditing and monitoring features, such as time-stamped movement logs, location evidence and usage trails, support internal audits, compliance checks and operational reviews. The episode says this level of monitoring is especially important for industries like government, healthcare, aviation and critical infrastructure, and that it helps organisations operate across multiple countries and regions while staying compliant. This connects directly to the traceability expectations that define the sector.

Aviation also appears in a Power Platform context. The episode "From SharePoint Developer to Power Platform Architect with Michel Mendes [MVP]" lists customer examples for Power Platform applications, including Choice Aviation, which the episode says created a logistics system with Power Apps, Power Automate and Power BI for higher efficiency. This shows the low-code side of the topic: operational and logistics processes around the industry can be addressed with Power Apps, Power Automate and Power BI.

In practice, the decisions around aerospace in the Microsoft ecosystem concern how to bring simulation output, asset data and operational records together, how to keep an auditable trail, and how to apply automation or AI without losing traceability. The episodes treat aerospace as one example among several industries, so the guidance is general: connect simulation and machine learning for design work, use digital twins for prediction, maintenance and training, and apply monitoring and governance where compliance matters.

agent-card.desc: An agent card is a machine-readable A2A document at a well-known path that describes an agent's name, capabilities, endpoint and formats so others can discover it.

faq.a: It is a machine-readable document, published at a well-known URL, that describes an agent's name, capabilities, skills, endpoint, authentication requirements and input/output formats so other agents can discover it.
faq.q: What is an agent card in the A2A protocol?

faq.a: In the ASP.NET Core hosting example it is served at a well-known path ending in agent-card.json, using a mapping method from the A2A SDK package rather than from the Agent Framework hosting packages.
faq.q: Where is the agent card served in the Microsoft Agent Framework example?

faq.a: According to the Microsoft Learn page, a single host can publish only one agent card at the well-known path, so only one agent is discoverable there; other agents stay reachable by their own URLs, which clients must already know.
faq.q: Can one host publish several agent cards?

agent-card.long:
An agent card is a machine-readable document used in the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol to describe an agent. It is published at a well-known URL and carries metadata such as the agent's name, description, version, capabilities, skills, endpoint, authentication requirements and the input and output formats it supports. Its core purpose is discovery: a client or another agent can read the card to learn what an agent offers before sending any request to it.

The A2A protocol addresses interoperability between agents by emphasizing a standardized language, which removes the need for custom code in each agent-to-agent interaction. The agent card is the part of that approach that lets an agent advertise its identity and capabilities. Instead of hard-coding assumptions about a remote agent, a calling agent reads the published card and works out how to reach the agent and what kinds of data it can exchange.

The Microsoft Learn page on A2A hosting in the Microsoft Agent Framework shows how this looks in practice. In the ASP.NET Core hosting example, the card is served at a well-known path ending in agent-card.json. The mapping method that exposes the card comes from the A2A SDK package rather than from the Agent Framework hosting packages. The sample card sets a name, a description and a version, default input and output modes, and a supported interface that includes a URL, a protocol binding and a protocol version. The page recommends that the card be fully populated for production use, so that clients receive complete information about the agent they are about to call.

A practical limitation described in the documentation concerns hosting. A single host can publish only one agent card at the well-known path, which means only one agent is discoverable there. Other agents hosted alongside it remain reachable through their own URLs, but clients must already know those endpoints, since the shared well-known location does not list them. When planning a deployment with several agents, this affects how discovery is designed and how endpoint information is shared with consumers. The documentation page does not cover skills, authentication details or card signatures, so those aspects of the card are described here only at the level of the general definition.

The episode "Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Communication - Simply Explained" touches on the concept as part of a wider discussion of interoperability. It presents the agent card as the mechanism through which agents advertise their identity and capabilities, making discovery and interaction easier. The same episode connects this to structured communication, where agents exchange various types of data, which supports collaboration and the tracking of task state. It also stresses that privacy and security concerns are central in agent-to-agent communication, and that anyone working with these systems should be aware of the risks associated with data handling. Because an agent card publishes information about an agent and how to reach it, deciding what to include and how access is controlled is part of that broader security consideration.

In summary, the agent card functions as the public description of an A2A agent. It is read by clients before any task is sent, it is served from a predictable location, and it should be complete and accurate in production. Its single-card-per-well-known-path constraint in the ASP.NET Core hosting example is a design point to account for whenever more than one agent is exposed from the same host.

agent-feed.desc: Agent feed (Copilot Studio) is a supervision view for autonomous Copilot Studio agents, showing which actions were completed, needed user input, or failed.

faq.a: It is a supervision view for autonomous Copilot Studio agents. It lets people review what an agent has done and step in where needed.
faq.q: What is the Agent feed in Copilot Studio?

faq.a: It shows which actions an agent completed autonomously, which required user input, and which failed.
faq.q: What information does the Agent feed show?

faq.a: It supports human oversight of autonomous agents, so reviewers can check outcomes and intervene when an action needs input or has failed.
faq.q: Why is the Agent feed useful?

agent-feed.long:
Agent feed (Copilot Studio) is a supervision view for autonomous agents built in Copilot Studio. It gives people a place to follow what an agent has done on its own, so that its work can be reviewed rather than taken on trust.

The view sorts an agent's activity by outcome. It shows which actions the agent completed autonomously, which actions required input from a user, and which actions failed. This separation helps reviewers see where an agent worked without help, where it stopped to ask a human, and where something went wrong.

The main purpose of the Agent feed is human oversight. By surfacing completed, blocked and failed actions in one view, it allows people to check the agent's results and to intervene when an action needs attention, for example when a user response is outstanding or an action did not succeed.

The available facts describe the Agent feed only at this level. No further details about configuration, licensing, availability or related products are stated here, so this page does not go beyond that description. No M365.FM episodes are linked to this topic yet.
