agent-harness.desc: An agent harness is the software layer around a language model that provides tools, permissions, memory, evaluation and limits for safe, reproducible agents.

faq.a: An agent harness is the software layer around a language model that provides tools, permissions, memory, evaluation and limits. It allows an AI agent to act safely and reproducibly rather than only generating text.
faq.q: What is an agent harness?

faq.a: The agent loop is the repeated cycle in which an agent acts and observes results, and the agent harness is the surrounding runtime in which that loop runs. The harness is also where limits and approvals are enforced.
faq.q: How does an agent harness relate to the agent loop?

faq.a: The episode "From AI Hype to AI Harness Engineering – Building AI That People Can Actually Trust with Alan Buscaglia [MVP] from Gentleman Programming" says that enterprise AI success depends on more than choosing a model. It points to harness engineering as a way to build systems that are secure, governed, observable and trustworthy.
faq.q: Why does the agent harness matter for enterprise AI?

agent-harness.long:
An agent harness is the software layer built around a language model that supplies tools, permissions, memory, evaluation and limits so that an agent can act safely and reproducibly. The model provides the reasoning; the harness decides which tools are available, what the agent is allowed to touch, what it remembers across steps, and when it has to stop. The terms "Harness" and "Agent-Harness" are used as aliases for the same idea.

The concept exists because a language model on its own can generate text but cannot complete real work. According to the episode "Microsoft AI Agent Harness - Simply Explained", the agent harness is the runtime layer that transforms a large language model into a capable AI agent. It provides what is needed to complete real work: planning tasks, calling tools, managing memory, handling approvals, and maintaining context across long-running workflows. Without such a layer, the same model has no controlled way to act on systems, remember earlier results or ask a person for approval.

The agent harness is closely tied to the Agent loop. The loop is the repeated cycle in which an agent reasons, selects an action, observes the result and continues, and the harness is the surrounding runtime in which that cycle runs. This is also where limits are enforced in practice, for example by restricting which tools can be called, requiring approvals for sensitive steps, or ending a run that exceeds its boundaries. Because these rules sit outside the model, they can be applied consistently and reviewed, which supports reproducibility.

The harness relates to several other topics. It is the runtime that makes an AI agent usable in practice, since the agent concept describes goal-directed behavior while the harness supplies the controlled environment for it. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is related as a way to attach tools and context to an agent. GitHub Copilot and Copilot Studio are linked as products in which a surrounding layer shapes what the underlying model can do and how an agent can be configured and constrained.

Governance is a recurring theme in the M365.FM material. The episode "From AI Hype to AI Harness Engineering – Building AI That People Can Actually Trust with Alan Buscaglia [MVP] from Gentleman Programming" discusses why enterprise AI success depends on far more than choosing the latest language model. It describes a shift from AI hype to AI Harness Engineering, a practical approach to building AI systems that are secure, governed, observable and trustworthy, and it explains why prompt engineering alone is no longer enough. The episode "Prevent Shadow IT in Microsoft Foundry AI Agent Programs" looks at the risk side: when agents are easy to create, unsupervised use can expose sensitive data and cause compliance problems through lack of oversight and excessive permissions, which is why controls need to exist around the agent rather than only inside the model.

Typical decisions around an agent harness include which tools an agent may call, what permissions it receives, what it is allowed to remember, which actions need human approval, and how its behavior is evaluated and observed over time. Related M365.FM episodes on agent topics, such as those on Agent-to-Agent (A2A) communication, Microsoft Entra Agent ID and Microsoft AI Agent Runtimes, cover neighboring areas of the same ecosystem.

agent-id.desc: Microsoft Entra Agent ID is an identity type in Microsoft Entra that gives AI agents their own identity, permissions and lifecycle instead of borrowed credentials.

faq.a: Microsoft Entra Agent ID is an identity type in Microsoft Entra for AI agents. It gives each agent its own identity, permissions and lifecycle instead of reusing a user's or an application's credentials.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Entra Agent ID?

faq.a: Without one, agents often run under shared service accounts or accounts nobody can name, which makes it unclear who acted and what was permitted. An own identity allows an organization to see which agent did what, limit its access and retire it when it is no longer needed.
faq.q: Why do AI agents need their own identity?

faq.a: It is part of Microsoft Entra and a close relative of Microsoft Entra ID. Conditional Access is related because access rules are one way to control what an agent identity may do.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Entra Agent ID relate to Microsoft Entra ID and Conditional Access?

agent-id.long:
Microsoft Entra Agent ID is an identity type in Microsoft Entra designed for AI agents. Instead of letting an agent borrow the credentials of a user or an application, it gives the agent its own identity with its own permissions and lifecycle. It is also referred to as Agent ID, Entra Agent ID or agent identity. The product is developed by Microsoft, belongs to the family of Microsoft tools for identity and security, and is part of Microsoft Entra. Licensing is listed as paid.

The purpose of the identity type follows from a common problem. AI agents increasingly act as autonomous digital workers inside a tenant: they read mail, open files and answer questions in Teams. Many organizations still manage such agents like traditional applications or shared service accounts, or let them sign in with an account that no one can name. When something goes wrong in that situation, it is hard to say which agent acted, what it was allowed to do, and who is responsible. A dedicated agent identity addresses this by making each agent a separately identifiable and governable object.

In practical terms, giving an agent its own identity makes it possible to see which agent did what, to limit what that agent may access, and to retire it cleanly when it is no longer needed. This reflects the idea of a lifecycle: an agent identity is created, receives permissions, is reviewed over time and is eventually removed, in the same way that other identities in a tenant are handled. Microsoft publishes official documentation for the product in its Microsoft Learn library under the Entra Agent ID section.

Microsoft Entra Agent ID sits close to several related topics. It is a relative of Microsoft Entra ID, the identity service that the wider Microsoft Entra family builds on. It is related to Conditional Access, because access rules are one way to control what an agent identity may do. It is often discussed together with Microsoft Agent 365, which deals with managing agents, and with the broader concept of an AI agent as an autonomous actor in a tenant. Typical decisions around it include whether agents should keep running under shared service accounts or personal accounts, how permissions are scoped per agent, and who owns each agent's lifecycle.

The M365.FM episodes return to this theme several times. "Microsoft Entra Agent ID: Secure Identity for AI Agents" explores why treating agents like ordinary applications or shared service accounts no longer works and why governing every agent with its own identity matters for enterprise AI. The episode describes Agent ID as more than a new feature, presenting it as an architectural foundation for scaling enterprise AI safely. "AI Agent Identity Security: Beyond Service Accounts" covers why agents should be treated as digital identities with lifecycle, permissions and accountability, and points to a related episode on service principal security about not using personal accounts. "Microsoft Entra Agent ID - Simply Explained" starts from the scenario of an agent signing in with an account nobody can name, and walks through why agents need their own identity.

Two further episodes place agent identity in a broader architecture. "Security Agent Fabric: Autonomous AI for Cyber Defense" describes an identity control plane at the center of an agent fabric, used to manage agent identity, access and accountability and to support zero trust by verifying every agent and action instead of relying on network perimeters. "Enterprise AI Agent Fabric: Architecture Beyond Chatbots" touches on persistent sessions and agent identity as part of building agents that behave as participants in a digital workforce. Taken together, the episodes frame Microsoft Entra Agent ID as the identity layer that makes agent governance possible.

agent-identity-blueprint.desc: An agent identity blueprint is an object in Microsoft Entra Agent ID that acts as a template for agent identities and holds the credentials used to obtain tokens.

faq.a: It is an object in Microsoft Entra Agent ID that acts as a template for agent identities. It holds shared properties and the credentials used to request access tokens, and it defines how agents are created, authenticated and managed.
faq.q: What is an agent identity blueprint?

faq.a: Disabling a blueprint stops authentication for all agent identities created from it, so none of them can sign in.
faq.q: What happens when an agent identity blueprint is disabled?

faq.a: It is created through Microsoft Graph. As an identity itself, it has one allowed operation, provisioning or deprovisioning agent identities, and for this it needs an OAuth client ID, credentials and the Graph permission AgentIdentity.CreateAsManager.
faq.q: How is an agent identity blueprint created and what can it do itself?

agent-identity-blueprint.long:
An agent identity blueprint is an object in Microsoft Entra ID, within Microsoft Entra Agent ID, that acts as a template for agent identities and defines how agents are created, authenticated and managed. It works as a container: many agent identities of one kind can be administered centrally, while each agent identity keeps its own identity, credentials and permissions. The concept addresses a common problem with non-human identities, which is the lack of a repeatable and consistent way to create, manage and retire them.

The blueprint holds the properties that agent identities of one kind share. According to Microsoft Learn, these include a description, app roles, the verified publisher and authentication protocol settings such as optional claims. Credentials used to request access tokens are configured on the blueprint, so agent identities created from it can obtain tokens on that basis. OAuth permissions granted to the blueprint apply to every identity created from it. Required resource access and inheritable permissions on a blueprint are only declarations, so administrators must still give consent before they take effect. Blueprints can be single-tenant or multitenant, and the documentation reviewed here names no licensing requirements.

A blueprint is also an identity in its own right, with exactly one allowed operation: provisioning or deprovisioning agent identities. For that purpose it needs an OAuth client ID, credentials and the Microsoft Graph permission AgentIdentity.CreateAsManager. Blueprints are created through Microsoft Graph.

The blueprint is also a central control point. Conditional Access policies applied to a blueprint reach all of its agent identities. Disabling a blueprint stops authentication for every agent identity created from it, which gives administrators a single action to stop a whole group of agents from signing in. This is relevant for incident response, retirement of a class of agents, or policy enforcement across many similar agents without editing each identity separately.

The M365.FM episode "AI Agent Identity Security: Beyond Service Accounts" (2026-06-26) discusses the blueprint as a repeatable, secure way to create, manage and retire agent identities. The episode says it ensures every agent follows the same rules and security controls, and presents it as a way to avoid unmanaged non-human identity sprawl. It breaks a strong blueprint into components: a template that records shared characteristics for consistent configuration across agent identities; an identity that acts as a special identity type able to provision or deprovision agent identities; a credential container that holds the credentials used for authentication so that agent identities can request access tokens; and a management container.

In practice, the decision around a blueprint is about granularity. Because credentials, OAuth permissions and Conditional Access policies set on the blueprint apply to all agent identities created from it, the choice of what belongs in one blueprint determines the shared blast radius, and the extent of central control, for those agents. Its broader context is Microsoft Entra Agent ID, the area of Microsoft Entra that deals with identities for AI agents.

agent-kill-switch.desc: An agent kill switch is a tested procedure that lets an authorized person disable an AI agent or revoke its identity, permissions and tool access within seconds.

faq.a: It is a tested procedure that lets an authorized person disable an AI agent or revoke its identity, permissions and tool access within seconds when the agent misbehaves.
faq.q: What is an agent kill switch?

faq.a: According to the definition, it can disable the agent itself or revoke its identity, its permissions and its tool access.
faq.q: What can an agent kill switch revoke?

faq.a: The definition describes it as a tested procedure, which indicates it should be verified in advance so it can act within seconds when needed.
faq.q: Why does the procedure need to be tested?

agent-kill-switch.long:
An agent kill switch is a tested procedure that allows an authorized person to disable an AI agent, or to revoke its identity, permissions and tool access, within seconds when the agent misbehaves. The term describes an operational control rather than a single product feature.

The concept covers several elements named in its definition: switching the agent off, removing the identity it acts under, withdrawing the permissions it holds, and cutting its access to the tools it can call. Because the procedure is described as tested, it is meant to be rehearsed and verified in advance instead of improvised during an incident. The reference to an authorized person indicates that the ability to trigger it is restricted to people with a defined responsibility.

A kill switch is typically discussed as part of governing AI agents, alongside questions of agent identity, permission scoping and tool access, since these are the points at which an agent can be stopped. The stated goal is speed: the response is measured in seconds, not in the time needed to investigate or redesign the agent.

No specific products, configurations or episode references are linked to this concept in the available information, so this page covers only the general definition of the term.

agent-loop.desc: The agent loop is the control cycle in which an AI agent plans, calls tools, observes the result and repeats until the goal is met or a human takes over.

faq.a: It is the control cycle in which an AI agent plans a step, calls a tool, observes the result and repeats until the goal is reached or it hands over to a human. The episode "Microsoft AI Agent Harness - Simply Explained" describes it as following a ReAct pattern of reasoning, acting through a tool and observing the outcome.
faq.q: What is an agent loop?

faq.a: The loop can pause for a person when judgment or approval is needed. "Dynamics 365 Agents - Simply Explained" describes the cycle as notice, understand, act, check, and hand over, and "Azure Logic Apps for Multi-Agent AI Orchestration" advises designing human checkpoints into the orchestration.
faq.q: How does the agent loop relate to human oversight?

faq.a: Azure Logic Apps offers an agent loop feature that lets a workflow check progress and make decisions until it reaches a goal, as described in "Build Enterprise Automation with Azure Logic Apps". It can also connect agents to enterprise systems through connectors.
faq.q: Where does Azure Logic Apps fit into the agent loop?

agent-loop.long:
The agent loop, also called the agentic loop or Agent-Schleife, is the control cycle in which an AI agent plans a step, calls a tool, observes the result and repeats until the goal is reached or the work must be handed to a human. It is the core working pattern of an AI agent, and it is what separates an agent from a single model call: the model does not only produce one answer but keeps deciding what to do next based on what happened in the previous step.

The loop is typically described as a sequence of recurring stages. The episode "Microsoft AI Agent Harness - Simply Explained" says the Microsoft AI Agent operates through a process known as the agent loop and that it follows a ReAct pattern, where the model continuously reasons, takes action by invoking a tool, observes the outcome, and repeats this cycle. According to that episode, this iterative approach lets the agent adapt and respond to varying situations, which strengthens its problem-solving capabilities. The Agent harness is the software layer that runs this loop and supplies tools, permissions and limits, so the two concepts are closely related.

A second description comes from the Dynamics 365 context. The episode "Dynamics 365 Agents - Simply Explained" frames the basic agent process as: notice, understand, act, check, and hand over. The agent notices a defined event such as a new message or lead, understands the situation using information and rules it is permitted to access, performs allowed actions, checks whether the result remains within its boundaries, and hands the work to a person when judgment or approval is needed. The same episode contrasts Copilot, described as an assistant sitting beside a user, with an agent, described as a specialized team member with a narrow job description, specific permissions and clear rules.

The loop also appears in runtime and workflow topics. In "Microsoft AI Agent Runtimes: Beyond Enterprise Chatbots", a runtime agent uses an orchestration and workflow engine to coordinate the agent loop, which includes getting the user's input, calling models, using tools, updating state, and making decisions. The episode says the agent can handle multi-step tasks and branching workflows, and can ask for human approval when needed. This connects the loop to Human in the loop, the point at which the cycle pauses and a person decides.

Azure Logic Apps is the other recurring link. In "Azure Logic Apps for Multi-Agent AI Orchestration", the agent loop is listed among effective orchestration strategies: workflows think and act in cycles until they reach a goal. The same episode lists integration with enterprise systems through connectors and support for both human and autonomous execution, and it advises identifying where human input is needed and building those checkpoints into the orchestration. "Build Enterprise Automation with Azure Logic Apps" describes the agent loop feature as allowing a workflow to check progress and make decisions until it reaches a goal, alongside loops, parallel branches and conditional logic.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is related as one way to expose tools that the loop can call. In practice, decisions around an agent loop concern which tools the agent may invoke, what state is kept between iterations, what boundaries the agent checks its results against, and where the loop must stop and hand over to a person. The episodes treat these as design choices of the surrounding harness or orchestration layer rather than of the model itself.

agent-mesh.desc: Agent mesh is an enterprise architecture in which many AI agents share common layers for identity, reasoning, governance and observability rather than running as isolated chatbots.

faq.a: An agent mesh is an enterprise architecture in which many AI agents run on shared layers for identity, reasoning, governance and observability instead of existing as isolated chatbots.
faq.q: What is an agent mesh?

faq.a: Isolated chatbots are built and managed individually, while an agent mesh provides common layers, such as identity, ontology-based reasoning, governance and observability, that multiple agents use together.
faq.q: How does an agent mesh differ from isolated chatbots?

faq.a: The concept is covered in the episode "The Death of the Chatbot: Why Your Dataverse Strategy Is Broken", published on 2026-07-29.
faq.q: Where is the agent mesh discussed on M365.FM?

agent-mesh.long:
Agent mesh is an enterprise architecture concept for deploying AI agents at scale. Instead of building each agent as a standalone chatbot with its own logic and data access, an agent mesh runs many agents on shared foundational layers. These layers cover identity, reasoning (for example through ontologies), governance and observability.

The idea contrasts with isolated chatbot deployments, where each assistant is built and managed separately. In an agent mesh, common capabilities are provided once and reused across agents. Shared identity, a shared reasoning layer, central governance and unified observability are meant to keep a growing number of agents consistent and controllable within one organization.

On M365.FM, the term appears in the episode "The Death of the Chatbot: Why Your Dataverse Strategy Is Broken" (2026-07-29). The episode frames the agent mesh as an alternative to the chatbot-centered approach and connects it to how data strategy, including Dataverse, is planned. No further details about specific products, versions or implementation steps are given in the available material.

agent-observability.desc: Agent observability is the practice of collecting traces, metrics, evaluations and audit data of AI agents to show what they did, why, and at what cost.

faq.a: Agent observability is the collection of traces, metrics, evaluations and audit data of AI agents to see what they did, why, and at what cost. It supports trust in agents running in production.
faq.q: What is agent observability?

faq.a: Usage data and logs show which applications and models consume tokens. The AI Gateway episodes describe quotas, token budgets, semantic caching and detailed monitoring as ways to manage these variable costs, which connects the topic to FinOps.
faq.q: How does agent observability relate to cost control?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft AI Agent Runtimes: Beyond Enterprise Chatbots" names response time, task completion rate and resource usage, and recommends testing observability tools in staging before deployment.
faq.q: Which metrics are mentioned for monitoring agents?

agent-observability.long:
Agent observability, also called AI observability or Agenten-Observability, is the practice of collecting traces, metrics, evaluations and audit data of AI agents so that it is possible to see what an agent did, why it did it and what it cost. It is a narrower and more operational view of the broader topic of the AI agent: once an agent is running in production, an organization needs evidence about its behavior rather than assumptions based on a successful demo.

The purpose is practical. Without observability, an agent that works in a demo becomes hard to trust in production, because failures, drifting quality and rising spend stay invisible until someone complains. Traces show the steps an agent took, metrics describe how it performs, evaluations assess the quality of its output, and audit data records its actions. Together these sources let teams reconstruct decisions, compare behavior over time and attribute usage to specific agents or applications.

The episode material points to several concrete signals. The episode "Microsoft AI Agent Runtimes: Beyond Enterprise Chatbots" describes performance metrics such as response time, task completion rate and resource usage, which help measure reliability and efficiency. It mentions platforms like Fiddler AI Observability and Rubrik Agent Cloud as ways to get unified analytics and to monitor agent-to-agent interactions. It also advises testing observability tools in staging before deployment so that telemetry and alerts work as expected, and says that continuous monitoring, logging and performance metrics support oversight and control. According to the episode, centralized platforms connect agent behavior with data risk signals.

Cost is a second major driver. The episodes "Microsoft AI Gateway - Simply Explained" and "Azure Local - Simply Explained" note that generative AI introduces variable consumption costs based on token usage, unlike traditional software licensing. They describe Microsoft AI Gateway as a way to control these expenses through request throttling, quotas, token budgets, semantic caching, traffic prioritization and detailed monitoring, with AI requests logged along with information such as the calling application. The same episodes tie this to governance: when an agent receives only the minimum permissions required for its task, visibility into every AI-driven action becomes complete. This links agent observability directly to FinOps, since traces and usage data are the basis for understanding and controlling the cost of agents.

Agent observability also appears in the development and platform context. The episode "Microsoft Agent Framework - Simply Explained" lists observability among the capabilities discussed around the framework, including how OpenAPI tooling standardizes agent observability and API interactions alongside protocols such as Agent2Agent (A2A) and Model Context Protocol (MCP). The episode "Beyond Copilot: Building Enterprise AI Agents That Actually Work with Copilot Studio with Manpreet Singh [MVP-MCT]" places AI observability and tracing in a list with agent testing and evaluation, hallucination reduction, AI consumption and cost management, agent lifecycle management, agent inventories and Agent 365, and Microsoft Purview and DLP. Its key takeaway is that the next phase of enterprise AI is about moving from answers to outcomes, which makes visible, verifiable agent behavior more important.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, agent observability is related to Microsoft Agent 365, which deals with managing agents in an organization, and to Microsoft Foundry, where evaluation and observability are part of the platform. It connects to AI governance and Audit logs, which need evidence of agent behavior, and to FinOps. Typical decisions around the topic include which signals to collect, where to centralize them, how to test telemetry before go-live, and how to link agent activity to cost and risk reporting.

agent-orchestrator.desc: Agent orchestrator is the component of an AI agent that interprets a user's request and decides which skills and tools to load into context for each turn.

faq.a: It reads a user's request, compares its intent with the names and descriptions of available skills and tools, and decides what to load into context for each turn.
faq.q: What does an agent orchestrator do?

faq.a: It matches the intent of the request against the names and descriptions of the skills and tools available to the agent.
faq.q: How does an agent orchestrator choose skills and tools?

faq.a: It decides what to load into context for each turn, so the selection is made per turn rather than once in advance.
faq.q: When does the agent orchestrator make its decisions?

agent-orchestrator.long:
Agent orchestrator is a concept describing the component of an AI agent that reads a user's request and determines how the agent should respond to it. It works by matching the intent of the request against the names and descriptions of the skills and tools that are available to the agent.

Based on that match, the agent orchestrator decides what to load into context for each turn. This means the selection of skills and tools is not fixed in advance but is made per turn, depending on what the user asks. Because the matching relies on names and descriptions, the way a skill or tool is named and described directly affects whether the orchestrator can recognize it as relevant to a request.

The term is used to separate the decision-making step of an agent, which chooses what is relevant, from the skills and tools themselves, which carry out specific work once selected. The agent orchestrator therefore sits between the user's input and the capabilities the agent can draw on.

No related topics, official documentation links or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, so this page covers only the general definition of the concept.

agent-quarantine.desc: Agent quarantine in Copilot Studio is an admin control that temporarily blocks a deployed agent from user interaction while it stays visible, pending investigation.

faq.a: It temporarily blocks a deployed agent so that users can still see it but cannot interact with it until an investigation is complete.
faq.q: What does agent quarantine do in Copilot Studio?

faq.a: It can be set via the Power Platform API, according to the Microsoft documentation for the Copilot Studio quarantine API.
faq.q: How can agent quarantine be set?

faq.a: No. The agent remains visible to users; only interaction with it is blocked while the investigation is ongoing.
faq.q: Is a quarantined agent deleted?

agent-quarantine.long:
Agent quarantine (Copilot Studio) is an administrative control for agents built in Copilot Studio. When an agent is quarantined, it is temporarily blocked: users can still see the deployed agent, but they cannot interact with it until an investigation is complete.

The control is intended for situations where an administrator needs to stop an agent from being used without removing it. Because the agent remains visible, the quarantine acts as a pause rather than a deletion, and the agent can be examined while interaction is disabled.

Quarantine can be set via the Power Platform API, which allows administrators to apply the block programmatically rather than only through a manual interface. The topic sits under Copilot Studio, the broader product in which these agents are created and deployed. Microsoft documents the quarantine API in its Copilot Studio administration documentation.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this concept, and the available information does not describe further details such as the exact steps, required permissions or how quarantine is lifted.

agent-registry.desc: Agent Registry is the unified inventory in Microsoft Agent 365 that lists every agent in an organization, so admins can find, quarantine or block them.

faq.a: Agent Registry is the unified inventory in Microsoft Agent 365 that lists every agent operating in an organization, including Microsoft and non-Microsoft agents. Admins use it to find agents and to quarantine or block them.
faq.q: What is Agent Registry in Microsoft Agent 365?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Agent Builder — Simply Explained" describes selecting an agent from the Agent Registry and using the Users tab to set who has it pre-installed and who can install it. Options include just me, the entire organization, or specific users and groups.
faq.q: How is Agent Registry used to manage who can use an agent?

faq.a: The episodes link it to visibility, compliance and governance. They describe it as a way to track every agent, its builder and its data, and to support least privilege, recertification and zero trust controls.
faq.q: Why do the M365.FM episodes recommend a central agent registry?

agent-registry.long:
Agent Registry is the unified inventory in Microsoft Agent 365 that lists every agent operating in an organization. It covers both Microsoft agents and non-Microsoft agents, which gives administrators a single place to see what is running in the environment. According to the short description of the product, admins use it to find agents and, where needed, to quarantine or block them. The registry is documented in connection with Microsoft Entra Agent ID under the topic of registry convergence.

The main purpose of an agent registry is visibility. As organizations build and adopt more AI agents, it becomes difficult to know which agents exist, who built them and which data they use. A central registry answers those questions in one location. The M365.FM episode "Codify Business Logic into a Digital Twin for AI Agents" describes a centralized agent registry that tracks every agent and shows who built it and what data it uses, and it pairs this with security policies, access controls, data classification and lifecycle governance that includes review, deployment and monitoring.

The registry also serves as an administrative control point. In the episode "Microsoft Agent Builder — Simply Explained", the steps for managing an agent begin with selecting that agent from the Agent Registry. From the agent details pane, an admin opens the Users tab and decides who gets the agent. The Installed option assigns users who will have the agent pre-installed, with choices such as just me, the entire organization, or specific users and groups. The Available option controls who can install and use the agent, ranging from no users in the organization to all users or specific users and groups. This shows the registry acting as the place where availability and assignment of an agent are managed.

Several M365.FM episodes treat a central registry as a governance best practice rather than an optional extra. The episode "Graph-Powered AI Agents: An Enterprise Architecture Guide" lists maintaining an agent registry alongside defining clear decision rights and implementing centralized policy configuration. It recommends narrow permission bundles and short-lived credentials for agents, continuous authorization that evaluates risk and policy at each action, and guardrails that limit delegation and tool use to prevent impersonation and excessive privilege accumulation. The episode also mentions emergency controls such as kill switches, which fit with the ability to quarantine or block an agent that the registry supports.

In security operations, the episode "Security Agent Fabric: Autonomous AI for Cyber Defense" advises establishing a central agent registry to manage all agents effectively and to maintain visibility and compliance across the security environment. It combines this with a strong identity control plane that enforces zero trust principles, so that every agent's actions are verified and controlled, and with agent orchestration over secure communication protocols. The registry here is one component of a wider approach in which agents are identified, governed and monitored.

The episode "Secure Microsoft Copilot with Entra ID and Zero Trust" connects the registry to identity governance. It states that Microsoft Entra allows least privilege to be applied so that agents operate with only the permissions they need, and that ongoing governance through periodic recertification campaigns and a centralized agent registry strengthens the security posture. Its summary of best practices names a permissions audit, least privilege for users and AI agents, and ongoing governance with recertification and a centralized registry.

Taken together, the sources describe Agent Registry as the inventory layer of agent governance: it establishes what agents exist, supports decisions about who can install or use them, and provides the means to quarantine or block an agent. Identity, permissions, policy and lifecycle controls then build on that inventory.

agent-run-steps.desc: Run steps in Azure AI Foundry Agent Service are step-by-step records of a run, such as tool calls and generated messages, used for debugging and auditing agent behaviour.

faq.a: Run steps are the step-by-step records of what happened during a run, such as tool calls and generated messages. They show the individual actions an agent took while the run was executing.
faq.q: What are run steps in Azure AI Foundry Agent Service?

faq.a: They are used for debugging and auditing agent behaviour. Reviewing the recorded steps helps explain how an agent produced its output and which tools it called.
faq.q: What are run steps used for?

faq.a: No. Run steps describe the progression of a run, including intermediate actions like tool calls and generated messages, rather than only the end result.
faq.q: Do run steps record only the final answer of an agent?

agent-run-steps.long:
Run steps (Azure AI Foundry Agent Service) are the step-by-step records of what happened during a run of an agent. Each record captures an individual action taken while the run was in progress, such as a tool call or a generated message.

The main purposes of run steps are debugging and auditing agent behaviour. By reviewing the sequence of steps, a developer or administrator can see how an agent arrived at its output, which tools it invoked, and which messages it produced along the way. This makes run steps a useful reference when an agent does not behave as expected or when its activity needs to be reviewed after the fact.

Run steps belong to Azure AI Foundry Agent Service, the Azure service in which agents are executed as runs. They describe the internal progression of a single run rather than the final result alone.

No related topics, episodes or official links are listed for this term on M365.FM at this time. Further details, such as the specific fields available in each step or how steps are retrieved, are not covered here and should be checked in the official Azure AI Foundry documentation.

agent-skill.desc: An agent skill is a reusable package of instructions, scripts and resources that an AI agent loads on demand to perform a specific task consistently.

faq.a: An agent skill is a reusable package of instructions, scripts and resources that an AI agent loads on demand to perform a specific task consistently. It lets the agent follow the same procedure each time without long, repeated prompts.
faq.q: What is an agent skill?

faq.a: MCP supplies tools that an agent can use, while a skill supplies the know-how about when and how to use them. In the layered view discussed in an M365.FM episode, tools and skills are separate layers.
faq.q: How do agent skills relate to the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

faq.a: Skills shape what an agent does, so organizations need to decide which skills are approved and who maintains them. The episode with Rishi Sapra lists governance as its own layer covering permissions, policies, security and controls.
faq.q: Why does governance matter for agent skills?

agent-skill.long:
An agent skill is a reusable package of instructions, scripts and resources that an AI agent loads on demand to perform a specific task consistently. The term also appears as Skills, Agent Skills, Copilot skills and, in German, Skills für Agenten. Instead of repeating the same long instructions in every prompt, an agent picks up the relevant skill when it is needed and follows the same procedure each time. A skill is therefore a narrower, more specialized concept than the AI agent that uses it.

The main purpose of a skill is to give an agent repeatable expertise for a defined business task. A skill acts like a predefined capability that teaches the agent how to carry out that task in a consistent way. This keeps prompts short and makes the agent's behavior more predictable. Because the package can contain instructions, scripts and other resources, it can describe both the reasoning steps and the concrete material needed to complete the work. The agent does not need to hold all of this in its context at all times; it loads the skill on demand.

Skills are closely connected to several other topics in the Microsoft ecosystem. They relate to Copilot Cowork and Copilot Studio, where skills extend what a Microsoft assistant or agent is able to do. They also relate to the Model Context Protocol (MCP): MCP servers are one of the tools an agent can call, while a skill supplies the know-how about when and how to use such tools and how to interpret what they return. Because skills shape what an agent does and how it behaves, they also touch Governance. Organizations need to decide which skills are approved, who maintains them and which permissions and policies apply to the agents that use them.

The M365.FM episode "The End of AI Bloat: Why Modern Agents Need Skills" describes a common pattern. Agents start out fast, responsive and capable, but after a few months of real-world use response times increase, costs rise, prompts become enormous and accuracy declines. The episode says organizations often respond by moving to larger models, expanding prompts or adding more orchestration, while the underlying issue is the architecture rather than the model. It presents skills as an answer to monolithic prompts.

"Copilot Skills - Simply Explained" introduces Copilot Skills as a way to make Microsoft Copilot more capable by giving it reusable expertise rather than long, repetitive prompts. The episode explains the idea in simple terms and shows how skills differ from prompts, plugins and AI agents. A skill teaches Copilot how to perform a specific business task consistently, so the same instructions do not have to be restated for each request.

The episode "From Financial Data to AI-Ready Decisions: Power BI, Microsoft Fabric, Semantic Models & AI Agents with Rishi Sapra [MVP]" places skills inside a layered view of AI-ready environments. In that discussion, skills form one of five interconnected layers alongside data, logic, tools and governance. Skills are described as the instructions and business processes that describe how agents should use tools and interpret information, while governance covers permissions, policies, security and controls on what agents may do. The stated goal is a governed environment in which AI understands which data, logic, tools and processes to use, rather than simply having access to more data.

Other M365.FM episodes use the word in related ways. "Dataverse Business Skills for Scalable Power Platform Solutions" covers business skills on Dataverse for scalable Power Platform solutions, and "Microsoft Fabric AI Skills: Natural Language Data Insights" discusses AI Skills in Microsoft Fabric for natural language access to data insights. These episodes concern specific product areas and should be read in their own context.

agent-sponsor.desc: Agent sponsor is the named human in Microsoft Entra Agent ID who is accountable for an agent identity, including its purpose, access and retirement.

faq.a: An agent sponsor is the named human accountable for an agent identity. The sponsor is responsible for why the agent exists, what it may access and whether it should be retired.
faq.q: What is an agent sponsor in Microsoft Entra Agent ID?

faq.a: A named sponsor gives each agent identity an accountable person who can answer for its purpose and access and decide on its retirement.
faq.q: Why does an agent identity need a human sponsor?

faq.a: Microsoft documents sponsors together with owners and managers on Microsoft Learn, on the page about agent owners, sponsors and managers for Microsoft Entra Agent ID.
faq.q: Where can the official details about sponsors be found?

agent-sponsor.long:
An agent sponsor is a concept in Microsoft Entra Agent ID. It refers to the named human who is accountable for an agent identity. The sponsor answers for why the agent exists, what resources it may access and whether it should be retired.

The concept ties an automated agent identity to a responsible person. Because an agent can hold access in the same way a user or application can, a named accountable human gives organizations a point of contact for review and lifecycle decisions. The sponsor role is described alongside the related roles of owners and managers in Microsoft's documentation on agent owners, sponsors and managers.

In practice, the sponsor is the person asked to justify an agent's continued existence and access, and to decide when the agent identity is no longer needed. This frames agent identity governance around human accountability rather than leaving agent identities unattended.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity, and no further relations are recorded. Details on how sponsors differ from owners and managers, and how the roles are assigned, are covered in the official Microsoft Learn documentation referenced for this topic.

agent-sprawl.desc: Agent sprawl is the uncontrolled growth of AI agents in an organization without a clear owner or a central list of which agents exist.

faq.a: Agent sprawl is the uncontrolled growth of AI agents in an organization without a clear owner or a central list of what exists. It leaves administrators unsure which agents are running, what data they use and who controls them.
faq.q: What is agent sprawl?

faq.a: According to the episode "Computer-Using Agents: How CUA Could Transform SaaS", each agent increases the attack surface and can expose sensitive data when access controls are missing. Inconsistent permissions and identity misconfigurations also create access chains that are hard to audit.
faq.q: Why is agent sprawl a security risk?

faq.a: The episodes point to a central inventory or registry of agents, named ownership, controlled permissions and identities, and lifecycle management. They also mention an AI Center of Excellence and emerging management capabilities around Agent 365.
faq.q: How can organizations limit agent sprawl?

agent-sprawl.long:
Agent sprawl is the uncontrolled growth of AI agents across an organization without a clear owner and without a central list of what exists. It describes a situation in which agents are created quickly and by many different people or teams, while nobody keeps track of how many agents are running, what data they can reach, or who is responsible for maintaining them. The term appears across several M365.FM episodes on governance, security and agent development.

The core problem is a loss of visibility. As the episode "Microsoft 365 Global Admin Power, Identity, and Governance" puts it, creating many AI agents has become easy, which can lead administrators to lose track of which agents exist, which data they use and who controls them. The episode lists several governance issues that follow from this: visibility, because it is hard to track all agents and their data access; maintenance, because it is often unclear who updates or manages each agent; and accuracy, because agents must provide correct information. Missing oversight, in the episode's description, creates security blind spots.

The security side is addressed in "Computer-Using Agents: How CUA Could Transform SaaS". The episode says decentralized deployment leads to fragmented environments, with agent sprawl and inconsistent permissions. Each additional agent increases the attack surface and can expose sensitive data when access controls are unclear. It also points to OAuth and identity misconfigurations that create complex access chains that are hard to audit, and it stresses tracking agent actions so that blind spots are avoided and misuse can be detected.

Several episodes describe the measures that counter agent sprawl. "Security Agent Fabric: Autonomous AI for Cyber Defense" presents an agent registry that helps discover new agents quickly, supports governance and compliance by showing where agents are deployed, and lets teams visualize the agent network and the way agents interact. The same episode describes an identity control plane that manages agent identity, access and accountability, so that access decisions rest on identity rather than on network perimeters.

The episode "Beyond Copilot: Building Enterprise AI Agents That Actually Work with Copilot Studio with Manpreet Singh [MVP-MCT]" describes how organizations can move quickly from a handful of experimental agents to hundreds or thousands. It covers agent lifecycle management, parent-child agent relationships, centralized inventories, ownership, connected data sources, permissions, consumption and emerging management capabilities around Agent 365. The stated goal is to give administrators visibility into which agents exist. The episode also mentions establishing an AI Center of Excellence before agent development expands across an organization, and it notes that governance should protect enterprise information without becoming so restrictive that agent performance and usability suffer.

In "AI Governance for Microsoft 365 with Christian Buckley [MVP]", agent sprawl is named together with shadow AI, uncontrolled permissions and poor data quality as risks that can undermine security, compliance and trust. The episode argues that most governance frameworks were designed for static content and predictable user behavior, not for AI systems that can generate, access and act on information across the tenant. It adds that governance is no longer only an IT responsibility; it requires a balance between innovation and control, with clear ownership, lifecycle management and automation.

Taken together, the episodes treat agent sprawl as a governance problem rather than a purely technical one. The recurring answers are an inventory of agents, named owners, controlled permissions and identities, and lifecycle management from creation through maintenance.

agentic-ai.desc: Agentic AI describes AI systems that pursue goals over multiple steps with limited human oversight, using tools and context to decide on and carry out actions.

faq.a: Agentic AI refers to AI systems that pursue goals over multiple steps with limited human intervention, using tools and context to decide on and carry out actions rather than only answering single prompts.
faq.q: What is agentic AI?

faq.a: An AI agent is the broader concept of an individual AI component acting on a task. Agentic AI describes the goal-driven, multi-step way such agents operate.
faq.q: How does agentic AI relate to an AI agent?

faq.a: The episode "Use Agentic AI in DevOps Safely" names failures, security blind spots and the need to revert safely when automation goes wrong. Other episodes stress governance and security when deploying autonomous AI solutions.
faq.q: Which risks do the M365.FM episodes mention?

agentic-ai.long:
Agentic AI describes AI systems that pursue goals over multiple steps with limited human intervention. Instead of only answering a single prompt, such a system uses tools and context to decide on actions and then carries them out. The concept is closely tied to the AI agent, which is its broader term: an AI agent is the individual software component, while agentic AI describes the way of working in which agents plan, act and follow through on a goal.

In the Microsoft ecosystem the topic appears in several places. The M365.FM episodes connect it to Copilot Studio, Dataverse and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), to Windows 365 and Microsoft Intune, to Agent 365, to Microsoft Foundry, and to DevOps pipelines. A recurring theme is the move from simple chatbots toward agents that understand intent and can reach data and systems, rather than only producing text answers.

The episode "Agentic AI with Copilot Studio and Dataverse MCP with Nathan Rose [MVP]" looks at how Copilot Studio, Dataverse and MCP shape agentic AI in Microsoft 365. It discusses how organizations can build agents that understand intent and access data, and it covers governance, security, custom MCP servers, multi-agent architectures and the challenges of deploying autonomous AI solutions. According to the episode description, the guidance is practical rather than focused on hype.

In IT operations, the episode "Agentic AI for IT Operations: Windows 365, Intune & Microsoft's AI Vision with Christiaan Brinkhoff [Nerdio]" explains how Windows 365, Microsoft Intune, Agent 365, Microsoft Foundry and an emerging agentic operating system could change endpoint management, security and cloud operations. A related episode, "How Do You Successfully Deploy Microsoft 365 Copilot Across an Enterprise?", describes agentic systems in Windows 365 and Intune as managed, autonomous software agents or agent-like capabilities running within Windows 365 Cloud PCs and controlled through Intune policies. These agents perform tasks on behalf of users or administrators. The episode also states that organizations adopting agentic AI can reduce operational overhead and cut manual administrative workloads by up to 80%; this is a figure from the episode, not an independently verified result.

For software delivery, "Use Agentic AI in DevOps Safely" explores how agentic AI can automate CI/CD, incident response and cloud operations. It reports stories of teams speeding up deployments, and it also addresses the risks: failures, security blind spots and ways to revert safely when automation goes wrong. The episode offers a practical framework for using these systems with control in place.

Another angle is covered in "Beyond Copilot: Building AI That Works in the Real World with Azure AI Foundry and Agentic AI for Frontline Workers with Fergus Kidd [MVP]". The conversation moves enterprise AI beyond the desk and toward people who maintain infrastructure and carry out repairs. One example is an agent that flags missing information so that photos, serial numbers and job data are collected while they are still available.

Taken together, the episodes point to the same decisions: how much autonomy an agent should receive, which tools and data it may use, how its actions are governed and secured, and how changes can be reversed. Because agentic AI acts with limited human intervention, governance and security are treated as part of the design rather than an afterthought.

agentic-rag.desc: Agentic RAG extends retrieval-augmented generation: the model plans, picks sources, checks what it retrieves and queries again in a loop instead of one pass.

faq.a: Classic RAG answers from a single retrieval pass. In agentic RAG the language model plans, chooses data sources, evaluates retrieved results and queries again in a loop.
faq.q: What is the difference between RAG and agentic RAG?

faq.a: The episodes mention Azure AI Agent Service with Planner, Retriever and Verifier agents, and Azure AI Search together with agents that use tools to reach sources such as SharePoint, APIs, databases or custom connectors.
faq.q: Which Azure components do the episodes associate with agentic RAG?

faq.a: According to the episode with Fergus Kidd, keeping answers focused on the organisation's own knowledge reduces irrelevant responses and hallucinations, but it makes information architecture and content quality essential.
faq.q: Why does content quality matter in agentic RAG?

agentic-rag.long:
Agentic RAG is an evolution of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in which the language model does more than answer from a single retrieval pass. Instead of retrieving a set of passages once and generating a reply, the model plans its approach, chooses which data sources to use, evaluates the results it gets back and queries again when the evidence is not sufficient. The result is a loop of planning, retrieval and checking rather than a straight line from question to answer. It is a more specific form of the broader concept Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

The distinction matters most when relevant knowledge is spread across several systems. Classic RAG retrieves from one index and hands the passages to the model for generation. The episode "Build Traceable Copilots with Agentic RAG on Azure" argues that this approach quietly fails once the truth lives in more than one system, and describes how agentic RAG on Azure turns a Copilot into a reasoning engine. In that episode, Planner, Retriever and Verifier agents running on Azure AI Agent Service divide the work: one decides what to look for, one fetches the information, and one checks the outcome. The title's focus on traceability points to a further goal, which is being able to follow how an answer was assembled.

The same shift is described from the Microsoft Copilot side in "The Copilot Assumption That's Holding You Back — Agentic RAG". The episode challenges the common mental model of Copilot as a question-and-answer system that searches and then lets an LLM generate text. According to the episode, Copilot is moving toward an orchestration system that can determine where to search, evaluate what it finds, decide whether additional information is required, and increasingly take action. For teams planning Copilot rollouts, the takeaway is that the retrieval step is no longer a fixed pipeline but a set of decisions made at run time.

Practical examples appear in "Beyond Copilot: Building AI That Works in the Real World with Azure AI Foundry and Agentic AI for Frontline Workers with Fergus Kidd [MVP]". Fergus Kidd describes an agentic RAG approach in which Azure AI Search retrieves relevant information and agents use tools to reach the right sources. Depending on the scenario, those sources can be SharePoint repositories, APIs, databases or custom connectors, and different agents can switch between knowledge retrieval, notes and reporting within the same session. The episode also names a trade-off: because retrieval stays anchored to the organisation's own knowledge, irrelevant answers and hallucinations are reduced, but information architecture and content quality become essential.

Enterprise delivery is the angle in "From Pilot to Production: Building Enterprise AI That Actually Delivers with Leon Gordon [MVP]". Among the features of Microsoft Fabric listed in that episode is reliable knowledge access with enterprise and agentic RAG, alongside built-in AI governance, auditability and compliance. This places agentic RAG in the context of moving from pilots to production, where governance and data quality determine whether results can be trusted.

The episode "RAG on Azure — Simply Explained" lists related M365.FM material for readers who want the foundations first, including conversations on Copilot Studio agents and RAG, authorization-aware data retrieval in private RAG, building private RAG with SharePoint and n8n, and when to use RAG versus Microsoft 365 Copilot. Together, these episodes frame agentic RAG as an architectural pattern: decisions about source selection, evaluation and repeated retrieval are made by the model and its agents, while content quality, access control and traceability remain design responsibilities for the organisation.

agentic-sdlc.desc: Agentic SDLC is a software development lifecycle in which AI agents take part in requirements, coding, testing, review and operations under human oversight.

faq.a: Agentic SDLC is a software development lifecycle in which AI agents take part in requirements, coding, testing, review and operations, with humans keeping oversight. The familiar phases remain, but agents handle part of the work inside them.
faq.q: What is Agentic SDLC?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode "Agentic Coding with Nick Doelman [MVP-MCT]" says developers no longer just write code but orchestrate agents that plan, generate, test, review and execute changes. The agents are described as autonomous collaborators that work from high-level goals.
faq.q: How does the developer's role change in an agentic SDLC?

faq.a: Related topics include GitHub Copilot, GitHub Actions, AI agent, Agent harness and Requirements management. Governance also plays a role, since it determines how much autonomy agents are given.
faq.q: Which topics are related to Agentic SDLC?

agentic-sdlc.long:
Agentic SDLC, also described as the AI-driven software development lifecycle or agentic software development, is a model of the software development lifecycle in which AI agents take part in requirements, coding, testing, review and operations, while humans keep oversight. The classic phases of development stay recognizable. What changes is that some of the work inside each phase is done by agents that plan, write, check and report, and people decide where to intervene.

The term describes a shift in the developer's role. According to the M365.FM episode "Agentic Coding with Nick Doelman [MVP-MCT]", a developer in this paradigm no longer just writes code. Instead, the developer orchestrates intelligent agents that plan, generate, test, review and execute changes. The episode describes these agents as autonomous collaborators that understand high-level goals and manage complex processes such as requirements. In that framing, agentic AI is seen as a partner rather than only a tool, which is presented as a way to move faster and build better software.

The episode lists a set of capabilities that characterize this way of working: models for code, inline generation, conversation, codebase awareness, tool use, background execution, persistent memory, and review and validation. Taken together, these describe how an agent can understand the surrounding project, act through tools, keep working without constant prompting, retain context between tasks, and check its own output before a person looks at it.

Several related topics help place the concept. GitHub Copilot is a common entry point for AI help in development, and GitHub Actions automates build and test steps that agents can trigger or respond to. Agentic SDLC builds on the idea of an AI agent and on the agent harness, the layer that gives an agent tools and limits. Requirements management also belongs here, since clear requirements are the input an agent works from. Governance determines how much autonomy is acceptable in a given team or organization.

In practice, teams adopting this model face decisions about where agents act on their own and where a human must approve. Typical questions include which phases are suitable for delegation, how requirements are written so an agent can act on them, which tools and permissions an agent receives, and how generated changes are reviewed and validated before they reach production. The emphasis on oversight in the definition means that responsibility for the outcome stays with people, even when much of the intermediate work is performed by agents.

The M365.FM episode "Agentic Coding with Nick Doelman [MVP-MCT]" is the main reference on this site. Host Mirko Peters speaks with Nick Doelman about the rapid evolution of agentic coding and how AI is transforming software development. Nick describes his path from traditional development into low-code, Power Platform and AI-assisted application building, and the conversation explores how modern AI agents change the way developers create solutions. The discussion connects the concept to hands-on experience rather than treating it only as theory, and it frames agentic SDLC as a new phase of software development rather than a single product or feature.

faq.a: No. The catalog data states that the exam was retired on 30 June 2026, and it names AI-103 as the successor.
faq.q: Is the AI-102 exam still available?

faq.a: It is aimed at engineers who build AI-enabled applications on Azure, for example by integrating language, vision or generative AI services into software, and it covers Microsoft Foundry.
faq.q: What does the Azure AI Engineer Associate certification cover?

faq.a: It is listed in a learning-path section of the episode "AI, Power Platform & Developer Experience: The Next Frontier with Reza Niroomand [MVP]", next to the DP-100 and DP-600 certifications. The episode itself focuses on AI-powered development on Power Platform rather than on the exam.
faq.q: Where does AI-102 appear in the M365.FM episodes?

ai-102.long:
Microsoft Certified: Azure AI Engineer Associate (AI-102) is a Microsoft certification at the associate level, based on the exam AI-102. It is aimed at engineers who build AI-enabled applications on Azure, for example by integrating language, vision or generative AI services into software. The catalog data states that the exam was retired on 30 June 2026 and names AI-103 as its successor. Anyone looking at this certification today therefore deals with a credential that is no longer available to newly register for.

The certification is developed by Microsoft and covers Microsoft Foundry, the Azure environment for building and managing AI applications and models. In practice, an engineer working in this area connects AI capabilities to application code, so that an app can analyze text, interpret images or generate content through managed services rather than through models built from scratch. That role definition explains why the exam sat at the associate level: it focuses on applying and integrating AI services in solutions, not on research-oriented model development.

For people planning a learning path, the most important decision is how to handle the retirement. Because AI-102 is retired, preparation material written for it may no longer match what Microsoft currently tests. The successor exam, AI-103, is the item to check first, and the current Microsoft Learn exam page is the reliable place to verify the skills measured. The platform that the exam is tied to changes quickly, which is a general reason to confirm the scope of any Azure AI exam against official documentation before investing study time.

AI-102 also appears as one entry among several in a learning-path list shared in the M365.FM episode "AI, Power Platform & Developer Experience: The Next Frontier with Reza Niroomand [MVP]". In the excerpt, the certification is listed next to Microsoft Certified: Azure Data Scientist Associate (Exam DP-100) and Microsoft Certified: Fabric Analytics Engineer Associate (Exam DP-600), alongside AI productivity pathways for Copilot, ChatGPT, Gemini and AI for project managers. The same excerpt then turns to soft skills, stating that communication and teamwork are essential when collaborating on AI projects, in addition to technical skills.

The episode does not cover the exam content itself. Instead, Mirko Peters and Reza Niroomand discuss how AI-powered development changes the way builders work on Microsoft Power Platform and what that means for the developer experience. This makes it useful background for readers who want to see where AI skills of the kind AI-102 once tested fit into everyday Microsoft development work, and how technical certification sits next to collaboration and communication skills.

In summary, Microsoft Certified: Azure AI Engineer Associate (AI-102) is best understood as a retired Microsoft credential for engineers who integrate AI services into Azure-based applications, tied to Microsoft Foundry and replaced by AI-103. Readers who meet the name in older articles, course lists or learning-path recommendations should treat it as a historical reference point and verify the current exam landscape on the official Microsoft Learn pages.

ai-103.desc: Microsoft Certified: Azure AI App and Agent Developer Associate (AI-103) is a 2026 associate certification for building AI apps and agents on Azure, replacing AI-102.

faq.a: Microsoft Certified: Azure AI App and Agent Developer Associate (AI-103) is a 2026 associate certification for building, managing and deploying AI apps and agents on Azure. It is based on the AI-103 exam and covers Microsoft Foundry.
faq.q: What is the AI-103 certification?

faq.a: According to the available data, AI-103 replaces AI-102. Candidates who planned to take AI-102 should check the official Microsoft documentation for the current exam status and the recommended path.
faq.q: Does AI-103 replace AI-102?

faq.a: The study guide lists five areas: planning and managing an Azure AI solution, generative AI and agentic solutions, computer vision, text analysis, and information extraction. The pass mark is 700, and the certification is renewed yearly through a free online assessment.
faq.q: What topics does the AI-103 exam cover?

ai-103.long:
Microsoft Certified: Azure AI App and Agent Developer Associate (AI-103) is an associate-level certification from Microsoft for developers who build AI applications and agents on Azure. It was introduced in 2026 and, according to the available data, replaces the earlier AI-102 exam. The exam code is AI-103, and Microsoft's study guide titles the exam "Developing AI Apps and Agents on Azure".

The certification is developed by Microsoft and covers Microsoft Foundry, the platform on which candidates build, manage and deploy agents and AI solutions. It targets people who integrate AI models and agent capabilities into cloud applications. According to the Microsoft Learn study guide, candidates are expected to have experience developing applications in Python, along with basic knowledge of AI, generative AI and Azure services. The page lists no formal prerequisites.

The study guide divides the exam into five areas: planning and managing an Azure AI solution, implementing generative AI and agentic solutions, computer vision, text analysis, and information extraction. The examples named in the guide show the breadth of the content. They include model selection, deployment and monitoring, managed identity, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), tool calling, multi-agent solutions and tracing. The vision and language areas mention image generation, speech input and output, semantic and vector search, and document extraction. Together these areas reflect a mix of platform management, agent development and classic AI services.

Several practical details come from the same documentation. The pass mark is 700. The certification expires after one year and is renewed through a free online assessment. A practice assessment and an exam sandbox are available for preparation. The study guide page does not list a price, an exam duration or Azure subscription requirements, so candidates should check the official credential page for those details before booking.

Typical scenarios behind the content include adding a language model to an existing business application, building an agent that uses company data and external tools, and checking the quality and safety of AI responses before a release. Because AI-103 replaces an earlier developer exam, professionals who had planned to take AI-102 should consult the official Microsoft documentation for the current exam status and the recommended path.

The M365.FM episodes in the current data do not cover this certification directly, so there are no episode statements to summarize. The relation to Microsoft Foundry is the main link to other topics in the knowledge base: the exam content centers on the platform on which AI apps and agents are planned, built, deployed and monitored. Readers who want to prepare can start with the study guide on Microsoft Learn, which describes the skills measured in each area.

ai-200.desc: Microsoft Certified: Azure AI Cloud Developer Associate (AI-200) is a 2026 associate certification for building AI-enabled cloud applications on Azure.

faq.a: Microsoft Certified: Azure AI Cloud Developer Associate (AI-200) is an associate-level Microsoft certification from 2026 for developing cloud applications with AI on Azure. According to the available data, it replaces AZ-204.
faq.q: What is the AI-200 certification?

faq.a: The study guide lists four areas: containerized solutions, AI solutions on data services such as Cosmos DB, PostgreSQL with pgvector and Azure Managed Redis, service connectivity through Service Bus, Event Grid and Functions, and security, monitoring and troubleshooting.
faq.q: Which areas does the AI-200 exam cover?

faq.a: The pass mark is 700. The certification expires after a year and is renewed through a free online assessment, according to the Microsoft Learn study guide.
faq.q: What is the pass mark and how does renewal work?

ai-200.long:
Microsoft Certified: Azure AI Cloud Developer Associate (AI-200) is an associate-level certification from Microsoft for developing cloud applications with AI on Azure. It was introduced in 2026, and according to the available data it replaces AZ-204. The exam code is AI-200. The certification covers Microsoft Azure and is aimed at developers who treat AI services as a regular part of the applications they build.

According to the Microsoft Learn study guide for Exam AI-200, titled "Developing AI Cloud Solutions on Azure", the exam targets people who implement AI solutions on Azure with an emphasis on back-end services and components. The role supports design, development, deployment, security and monitoring. Expected skills include working with SDKs, data management services, messaging and eventing, vector databases, Python and containerized applications. As the successor of AZ-204, the certification continues the line of Azure developer credentials, but places AI capabilities at the center of cloud application development instead of treating them as an optional addition.

The exam is organized into four areas. The first covers developing containerized solutions and names Azure Container Registry, App Service, Container Apps and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS). The second covers building AI solutions on data services, naming Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL with pgvector, and Azure Managed Redis. The third covers connecting services through Service Bus, Event Grid and Azure Functions. The fourth covers securing, monitoring and troubleshooting solutions with Key Vault, App Configuration, OpenTelemetry and KQL.

Some practical details are stated in the study guide. The pass mark is 700, and most questions address generally available features. The certification expires after a year and is renewed through a free online assessment. The guide names no formal prerequisites, cost, duration or question format, and it notes that related topics beyond the listed bullet points may be tested. Candidates should therefore check the current official documentation for the latest skills outline and exam conditions.

Typical situations in which the certification is relevant include building web or service-based applications on Azure, packaging them as containers, storing and searching data with vector-capable databases, connecting components through messaging and events, and operating the result with secrets management, configuration and telemetry. Developers who previously considered AZ-204 as an entry point for Azure development can use the AI-200 skills outline to compare the new focus areas with their current experience and decide on a learning path.

The M365.FM episodes in the current data do not cover this certification directly, so no episode-specific statements about AI-200 can be made here. The topic connects to the linked entities Microsoft, as the developer of the certification, and Microsoft Azure, as the platform whose services the exam addresses.

faq.q: What does the AI-300 certification validate?
