It also refers to learning materials for Microsoft Azure as a compilation of resources for beginners, and to the DevOps resource center for Azure DevOps as a central hub for learning about DevOps practices. These pointers suggest a preparation path that starts with the platform fundamentals and then moves to the exam-specific study guide.

The same episode gives the working context on which the certification builds. It describes Azure DevOps as Microsoft's all-in-one platform for planning, developing, testing and delivering software, and explains that it replaces separate tools for project management, source control, build automation, testing and deployments. The episode also stresses that the platform helps development and operations teams collaborate and automate repetitive tasks. Among the benefits it lists are quick release cycles for deploying new systems and applications, and built-in security and compliance, so that security and control are applied directly in the pipelines.

In relation to other topics on M365.FM, the certification is closely tied to Microsoft Azure as the covered platform and to Microsoft as the vendor that defines the exam. Anyone reading about Azure DevOps features, pipelines or release practices will find that the AZ-400 exam objectives follow the same themes: planning and tracking work, managing source code, building and releasing automatically, and keeping security and compliance part of the delivery process rather than an afterthought.

az-500.desc: Microsoft Certified: Azure Security Engineer Associate (AZ-500) was an associate-level Microsoft certification for Azure security, retired on 31 August 2026 and succeeded by SC-500.

faq.a: No. According to the catalog data, AZ-500 was retired on 31 August 2026. The successor exam is SC-500.
faq.q: Is the AZ-500 exam still available?

faq.a: It addresses security engineers who protect workloads, identities, networks and data on Azure. It is developed by Microsoft and covers Microsoft Azure.
faq.q: What does Microsoft Certified: Azure Security Engineer Associate cover?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Defender XDR - Simply Explained" names AZ-500 among certifications that listeners may be preparing for. It introduces Microsoft Defender XDR in general terms and does not cover the AZ-500 exam topics.
faq.q: How does the M365.FM episode relate to AZ-500?

az-500.long:
Microsoft Certified: Azure Security Engineer Associate (AZ-500) is a Microsoft certification built on the exam AZ-500. It is positioned at the associate level and is aimed at security engineers who protect workloads, identities, networks and data on Azure. The certification is developed by Microsoft and covers Microsoft Azure. According to the catalog data, the exam was retired on 31 August 2026, and the successor exam is SC-500.

In practice, a certification like this serves two purposes. For individuals, it provides a structured way to show and verify skills in securing Azure environments. For employers and project teams, it offers a common reference point when staffing roles that deal with cloud security. Because AZ-500 is retired, its main relevance today is historical: it appears in older study material, job descriptions and training paths that have not yet been updated. Anyone who encounters AZ-500 in such material should check SC-500 on Microsoft Learn to find the current exam and its skills outline, since the retired exam no longer reflects the current offering.

The scope named for the certification is the protection of four areas on Azure: workloads, identities, networks and data. These areas are not isolated from the wider Microsoft security portfolio. Security work on Azure normally interacts with tools that detect threats and coordinate responses across many sources, and the surrounding Microsoft security products are often studied together with Azure security skills. The exam page on Microsoft Learn is the official place to look up details about the certification and its lifecycle status.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Defender XDR - Simply Explained" mentions AZ-500 in its introduction. It addresses an audience that includes security analysts, Microsoft 365 administrators, Azure professionals and cloud architects, and it names AZ-500 alongside SC-200, SC-300 and SC-100 as certifications that listeners may be preparing for. The episode describes Microsoft Defender XDR as a unified Extended Detection and Response platform that brings security signals from endpoints, identities, email, cloud applications and collaboration tools into one experience, so that security teams do not have to investigate isolated alerts from several separate products. It also refers to the connection with Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Intune and Microsoft Entra in support of a modern Zero Trust security strategy.

The episode gives a practical introduction to Defender XDR and says it aims to explain how the platform helps organizations unify security operations, detect advanced threats, automate investigations and protect modern hybrid environments from a single platform. It is an overview of that platform in general terms and does not review the AZ-500 exam topics themselves. Its link to the certification is therefore contextual: it shows the operational security landscape in which Azure security engineers, and candidates for related Microsoft security exams, work.

For anyone deciding how to approach this topic today, the facts point to a simple path. AZ-500 is retired, SC-500 is its documented successor, and Microsoft Learn is the source for current exam details. Existing knowledge gained while studying for AZ-500 remains conceptually tied to Azure security, but the current exam content and skills outline should be taken from the SC-500 documentation rather than from older AZ-500 material.

az-700.desc: Microsoft Certified: Azure Network Engineer Associate (AZ-700) is an associate-level Microsoft certification for designing, implementing and maintaining Azure networking solutions.

faq.a: AZ-700 is the exam code for Microsoft Certified: Azure Network Engineer Associate, an associate-level certification developed by Microsoft. It covers designing, implementing and maintaining Azure networking solutions.
faq.q: What is the AZ-700 certification?

faq.a: The certification covers Microsoft Azure, with a focus on networking. Network security services such as Azure Firewall belong to this topic area.
faq.q: Which technology area does AZ-700 cover?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" describes Azure Firewall as a cloud-native, fully managed network security service. It also lists study resources, including the Microsoft Press AZ-700 cert prep course, a demo repository, documentation and a deployment tutorial.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode on Azure Firewall offer for AZ-700 preparation?

az-700.long:
Microsoft Certified: Azure Network Engineer Associate (AZ-700) is an associate-level certification from Microsoft that focuses on designing, implementing and maintaining networking solutions in Azure. The related exam code is AZ-700, and the credential is often referred to simply by that code. It addresses professionals who plan how Azure workloads are connected, secured and made reachable.

The certification covers Microsoft Azure and is developed by Microsoft. Networking is a foundation for almost every other Azure workload, which is why the subject matters well beyond dedicated network teams. Architects, administrators and engineers who need to understand how traffic flows between cloud resources, on-premises environments and users are the typical audience. Decisions about how services are connected and protected tend to shape the reliability and security of an entire Azure environment, and AZ-700 is positioned as the credential that addresses this area.

In practice, the role described by the certification covers three broad activities that are reflected in its short description: designing networking solutions, implementing them, and maintaining them over time. Design involves deciding how Azure resources should be connected and exposed. Implementation turns those decisions into working configurations. Maintenance covers keeping the network operating as workloads and requirements change. The certification is aimed at people who carry responsibility across all three activities rather than only one of them.

Network security is a central part of this topic area. The M365.FM episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" (July 2026) touches on it directly. The episode presents Azure Firewall as Microsoft's cloud-native, fully managed network security service that protects Azure workloads from internal and external threats. Instead of deploying and maintaining traditional firewall appliances, teams get centralized traffic filtering, threat intelligence and application-aware security that scales with the environment. The episode also points to a modular economic model that allows scaling based on network traffic. For anyone preparing for AZ-700, this gives a practical view of how network protection is delivered as a managed service rather than as hardware or self-maintained software.

The same episode lists learning resources for people who want to go deeper. Among them is a course titled "Designing and Implementing Microsoft Azure Networking Solutions (AZ-700) Cert Prep" by Microsoft Press, which is named as a way to study the exam content. The episode also mentions a demo repository for quick deployment of Azure Firewall, the Azure Firewall documentation, and a step-by-step tutorial for deploying and configuring it. These resources are presented as tools for strengthening both understanding and hands-on implementation, which fits the implement-and-maintain emphasis of the certification.

Typical situations in which this certification becomes relevant include building a structured learning path in Azure networking, validating existing hands-on experience with a recognized credential, or preparing for roles in which responsibility for connectivity and network protection in Azure is part of the job. The official Microsoft Learn page for the AZ-700 exam is the place to check the current exam details, such as the skills measured, since those are maintained by Microsoft and may change over time.

az-800.desc: Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate – exam AZ-800 is a Microsoft certification exam on hybrid Windows Server administration, retired on 30 September 2026; successor: AZ-802.

faq.a: No. The catalog data and a warning on the Microsoft Learn page state that AZ-800 was retired on 30 September 2026 and can no longer be taken for the certification. The successor named in the catalog is AZ-802.
faq.q: Is exam AZ-800 still available?

faq.a: The exam covers AD DS in on-premises and cloud settings, hybrid server and workload management, virtual machines and containers, on-premises and hybrid networking, and storage and file services. Tools named include Windows Admin Center, PowerShell, Azure Arc, Azure Policy, Azure Monitor and Azure Update Manager.
faq.q: What topics does AZ-800 cover?

faq.a: Both are exams of the Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate certification. AZ-800 deals with core infrastructure, while AZ-801 covers advanced services, and the catalog data lists both as retired on the same date.
faq.q: How does AZ-800 relate to AZ-801?

az-800.long:
Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate – exam AZ-800 is a Microsoft certification exam for administrators who run Windows Server in on-premises and hybrid environments. It is one of the two exams of the Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate certification, the other being AZ-801. According to the catalog data, AZ-800 was retired on 30 September 2026, and AZ-802 is named as its successor. The exam is developed by Microsoft and covers Microsoft Azure, because the hybrid scenarios connect local Windows Server infrastructure with cloud services.

The Microsoft Learn exam page, titled "Administering Windows Server Hybrid Core Infrastructure", describes the role behind the exam. It concerns deploying, managing and troubleshooting Windows Server, including servers running in Azure, migrating workloads, and handling identity, security, compute, networking, storage and monitoring. The exam is aimed at candidates with several years of Windows Server experience, and the pass mark is 700. The related exam AZ-801 covers advanced services, while AZ-800 addresses the core infrastructure side.

The skill areas measured by AZ-800 are grouped around a few themes. These include Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) in on-premises and cloud settings, hybrid server and workload management, virtual machines and containers, on-premises and hybrid networking, and storage and file services. The tools named in the documentation include Windows Admin Center, PowerShell, Azure Arc, Azure Policy, Azure Monitor, Azure Update Manager and the Defender products. Together they show the typical shape of the work: managing servers and identity services consistently across a data center and the cloud rather than treating the two as separate worlds.

In practice, candidates preparing for hybrid administration tend to combine the official Microsoft Learn material with hands-on practice in a test environment, since many of the subjects, such as joining servers to Azure management through Azure Arc or applying policy and update management to hybrid machines, are operational skills. The exact skills measured should always be taken from the current Microsoft Learn exam page rather than from older study guides, because exam outlines change over time.

Retirement is the most important point for anyone planning a certification path. A warning on the Microsoft Learn page states that the exam was retired on 30 September 2026, after which it can no longer be taken for the certification. The scheduling section of the same page still shows no retirement date, so the two statements on the page do not fully line up, and the warning text and the catalog data should be treated as the reference. Anyone starting now should orient themselves on AZ-802 and check how it relates to AZ-801, which is retired on the same date according to the catalog data.

No M365.FM episode in the catalog is currently linked to this exam, so there is no episode commentary to summarize here. The topic connects most directly to Microsoft Azure, the platform that the hybrid scenarios of this certification build on. The documentation page names no license requirements and no price for the exam, so those details should be checked through Microsoft directly.

az-801.desc: AZ-801 is the Microsoft exam on advanced Windows Server hybrid services, part of the Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate; retired 30 September 2026, successor AZ-802.

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, it covers advanced Windows Server administration in on-premises and hybrid setups: securing Windows Server, high availability, disaster recovery, migration to Azure, and monitoring and troubleshooting.
faq.q: What does the AZ-801 exam cover?

faq.a: No. The catalog data records that AZ-801 was retired on 30 September 2026, and AZ-802 is listed as its successor.
faq.q: Is AZ-801 still available?

faq.a: The Microsoft Learn page names Windows Admin Center, PowerShell, Azure Arc, Azure Policy, Azure Monitor, Azure Update Manager and the Defender products.
faq.q: Which tools are associated with AZ-801?

az-801.long:
Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate – exam AZ-801 is a Microsoft certification exam, titled "Configuring Windows Server Hybrid Advanced Services" on Microsoft Learn. It belongs to the Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate certification, alongside AZ-800, and is aimed at administrators who run Windows Server in on-premises and hybrid infrastructures. The catalog data records that AZ-801 was retired on 30 September 2026, with AZ-802 listed as the successor.

The exam is developed by Microsoft and covers Microsoft Azure, because hybrid administration means extending on-premises Windows Server environments with Azure services. According to the Microsoft Learn page, AZ-801 deals with advanced services for administering Windows Server, including migration of servers and workloads to Azure. The role it describes is about keeping servers secure, available and recoverable across on-premises and cloud locations.

The skills measured fall into several areas: securing Windows Server, implementing and managing high availability, implementing disaster recovery, migrating servers and workloads, and monitoring and troubleshooting Windows Server environments. The Microsoft Learn page names a range of tools in this context, among them Windows Admin Center, PowerShell, Azure Arc, Azure Policy, Azure Monitor, Azure Update Manager and the Defender products. In practice, these cover tasks such as hardening servers, planning failover and backup strategies, moving workloads to Azure, and tracking the health of a mixed server estate.

On the preparation side, Microsoft Learn recommends several years of Windows Server experience and gives the pass mark as 700. The page lists no formal prerequisites; AZ-800 appears only as a related exam. A free practice assessment, a study guide and an exam sandbox are offered for candidates. Details such as exam duration, number of questions, format and certificate validity are not stated on the page.

The retirement matters for anyone planning a certification path. A warning on the Microsoft Learn page states that the exam was retired on 30 September 2026, after which the certification can no longer be earned or renewed through it, although the scheduling section of the page still shows no retirement date. Candidates who encounter older AZ-801 study material should therefore compare it with the current AZ-802 outline on Microsoft Learn, since earlier skills outlines may no longer apply.

Within the wider Microsoft certification landscape, AZ-801 sits in the infrastructure branch, in contrast to the Microsoft 365 administrator exams, which focus on the productivity cloud. No M365.FM episode is linked to AZ-801 in the catalog, so there are no episode statements to report for this topic.

az-802.desc: Microsoft Certified: Windows Server Administrator Associate (AZ-802) is a 2026 consolidated exam for Windows Server hybrid administration, replacing AZ-800 and AZ-801.

faq.a: AZ-802 is the exam for the Microsoft Certified: Windows Server Administrator Associate certification. It validates skills in deploying, implementing, managing and troubleshooting Windows Server workloads in on-premises, cloud and hybrid environments.
faq.q: What is the AZ-802 exam?

faq.a: According to the facts provided, AZ-802 is a new consolidated exam from 2026 that replaces AZ-800 and AZ-801. The official Microsoft documentation should be consulted for the current status of those older exams.
faq.q: Does AZ-802 replace AZ-800 and AZ-801?

faq.a: The Microsoft Learn page recommends experience with Windows Admin Center, Hyper-V, PowerShell, Azure Arc, Azure Monitor, Azure Update Manager, Microsoft Defender for Cloud and AD DS basics. No formal prerequisites are listed.
faq.q: What experience is recommended for AZ-802?

az-802.long:
Microsoft Certified: Windows Server Administrator Associate (AZ-802) is an associate-level certification from Microsoft for Windows Server hybrid administration. It is built around the exam code AZ-802 and, according to the facts available, was introduced in 2026 as a consolidated exam that replaces the earlier AZ-800 and AZ-801 exams. The certification covers Microsoft Azure alongside Windows Server, reflecting the way many administrators run servers in their own data centers while also using cloud services.

The exam is described on Microsoft Learn as validating skills in deploying, implementing, managing and troubleshooting Windows Server workloads in on-premises, cloud and hybrid environments. Its content areas include deploying and managing AD DS, managing Windows Server instances and workloads in hybrid settings, managing virtual machines, implementing on-premises and hybrid networking, managing storage and file services, securing the Windows Server infrastructure, and monitoring and troubleshooting. Merging two earlier exams into one puts these areas under a single credential, which matches the idea that they belong together in the daily work of a server administrator.

The documentation lists recommended experience rather than formal prerequisites. The recommended background covers Windows Admin Center, Hyper-V, PowerShell, Azure Arc, Azure Monitor, Azure Update Manager, Microsoft Defender for Cloud and AD DS basics. This mix shows how hybrid administration is framed: classic server roles and virtualization on one side, and Azure-based management, update, monitoring and security services on the other. Typical scenarios for the topic include running core server roles in an existing infrastructure, connecting on-premises servers to cloud management services, and planning the availability and recovery of important systems.

On the practical side, the exam is available in English and is booked through Pearson VUE. The price depends on the country. Microsoft offers a course called Administer Windows Server that supports preparation. The official exam page does not list formal prerequisites, license requirements, a validity period or renewal rules, and it states no retirement date for the exam, so candidates who need those details should check the current Microsoft documentation directly.

For administrators who had already started preparing for AZ-800 or AZ-801, the main decision is how that earlier preparation maps to the new exam. Because AZ-802 is stated to replace both, the official Microsoft documentation is the place to confirm the current status of the older exams and the transition. The topic areas listed for AZ-802 give a way to compare earlier study material against what the new exam covers.

The M365.FM episodes in the current data do not cover this certification directly, so there are no episode statements to report on AZ-802. The certification is relevant to listeners of M365.FM mainly through its connection to Microsoft Azure and to the hybrid server administration topics that surround the Microsoft ecosystem.

az-900.desc: Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals (AZ-900) is Microsoft's entry-level certification covering basic cloud concepts and core Azure services.

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, it covers describing cloud concepts, describing Azure architecture and services such as compute, networking and storage, and describing Azure management and governance, including security, governance and administration tools.
faq.q: What does the AZ-900 exam cover?

faq.a: No formal prerequisite is listed. Microsoft Learn recommends experience in an IT area such as infrastructure, database administration or software development, but this is not required.
faq.q: Are there prerequisites for Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals?

faq.a: The exam is proctored, offered in many languages, and booked through Pearson VUE, or through Certiport for students and educators. Microsoft lists a practice assessment, an exam sandbox and a study guide as preparation options.
faq.q: How is the AZ-900 exam taken?

az-900.long:
Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals is an entry-level certification developed by Microsoft. It is earned by passing the exam with the code AZ-900, and the exam code is often used as the short name for the certification itself. It covers basic cloud concepts and core services of Microsoft Azure and is aimed at people who are new to cloud computing or to Azure, for example in business, sales or early IT roles.

According to Microsoft Learn, the certification demonstrates foundational knowledge of cloud concepts in general and of Microsoft Azure in particular. It is described as a common starting point for a career in the Azure space. Microsoft Azure is the cloud platform on which many Microsoft 365 integrations, data services and AI services run, which is one reason a fundamentals-level overview of the platform is useful for people working anywhere in the Microsoft ecosystem.

The exam covers three areas. The first is describing cloud concepts. The second is describing Azure architecture and services, including compute, networking and storage. The third is describing Azure management and governance, which includes security, governance and administration tools. The scope is conceptual and descriptive rather than deeply hands-on, which fits the fundamentals level.

No formal prerequisite is listed for AZ-900. Microsoft Learn notes that experience in an IT area such as infrastructure, database administration or software development is recommended but not required. The exam is proctored and offered in many languages. It is booked through Pearson VUE, or through Certiport for students and educators. Preparation options listed by Microsoft include a practice assessment, an exam sandbox and a study guide. The documentation reviewed here does not state a passing score, a question count or renewal rules, so those details should be checked on the official exam page before booking.

In practice, AZ-900 is typically chosen as a first step before more specialized, role-based Azure exams, or as a way for non-engineering staff to learn the vocabulary used by cloud teams. Typical decisions around it include whether the learner needs only a conceptual overview or a path toward administration and architecture roles, and which preparation materials to use.

The M365.FM catalog has no episode dedicated solely to AZ-900, but the episode "7 Levels of Azure Administration: Beginner to Cloud Architect" places the certification at the start of a career progression. The episode excerpt lists, as a key takeaway, to start the Azure journey with the AZ-900 certification, since it provides essential knowledge of cloud concepts and Azure services. It also stresses understanding key Azure terms such as subscriptions, resource groups and workloads in order to manage resources effectively, and mentions managing Azure subscriptions to control costs and ensure compliance, with strategies such as rightsizing and autoscaling. The episode further says that professionals who excel in Azure administration can move into roles like Solutions Architect or DevOps Engineer, and it describes a seven-level model from beginner to cloud architect, in which a fundamentals exam such as AZ-900 marks the beginning.

azure.desc: Microsoft Azure is Microsoft's cloud platform offering compute, storage, networking, databases, analytics and AI services for running applications and data workloads.

faq.a: Microsoft Azure is Microsoft's cloud platform with services for computing, storage, networking, databases, analytics and AI. It lets organizations run applications and store data without operating their own data centers.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Azure?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Azure OpenAI Service - Simply Explained", it runs the same models but Microsoft hosts them inside the customer's own Azure space, with their own keys, limits and privacy rules.
faq.q: How does Azure OpenAI Service differ from ChatGPT?

faq.a: Related topics include Azure Logic Apps, Azure Functions, Azure landing zone, Azure Virtual Desktop and Bicep, the language used to describe Azure resources as code.
faq.q: Which services are related to Azure on M365.FM?

azure.long:
Microsoft Azure, often shortened to Azure, is Microsoft's cloud platform. It provides services for computing, storage, networking, databases, analytics and AI. Organizations use it to run applications, store data and build solutions without operating their own data centers. Microsoft develops the platform, and on M365.FM it is classified both as a Microsoft tool and as a cloud platform.

Azure is not a single product but a broad collection of services that can be combined. Several of them are linked to the platform on M365.FM: Azure Logic Apps and Azure Functions for automation and event-driven logic, Azure Virtual Desktop for delivering desktops from the cloud, and the Azure landing zone as a foundation for structuring an Azure environment. Bicep, the language used to describe Azure resources as code, is part of the same ecosystem. Many Microsoft 365 solutions depend on Azure services, for example for identity, automation and AI, which is why Azure appears so often in discussions of the wider Microsoft ecosystem.

The M365.FM episodes in the "Simply Explained" series describe individual Azure services in plain language. "Azure OpenAI Service - Simply Explained" says the service is not ChatGPT with a Microsoft logo on it. It runs the same models, but Microsoft hosts them inside the customer's own Azure space, with the customer's own keys, limits and privacy rules. The episode covers topics such as deployments as your own copy of a model, endpoints and keys, built-in content filtering, data privacy, and how the service differs from the OpenAI API.

"Azure SQL Database - Simply Explained" describes a relational database that Microsoft runs for you in its cloud. The episode walks through the two ways to pay for it, how to pick a service tier, elastic pools described as a timeshare trick, and which tasks Azure handles so the customer does not have to. It also touches on security.

"Azure Data Factory - Simply Explained" compares the service to a courier for company data: it picks up raw information from wherever it lives, cleans it on the way, and delivers it somewhere reports can use it. The episode explains the building blocks, including pipelines and activities, linked services and datasets, integration runtimes, triggers and scheduling, and mapping data flows for transformation.

"Azure Event Grid - Simply Explained" covers the part of Azure that tells apps what has already happened. A file lands in storage, a device connects or an order comes in, and instead of code asking repeatedly, Event Grid delivers the news. The episode discusses why event-driven designs keep coming up, the different kinds of topics, push versus pull delivery, retries and dead-lettering when delivery fails, and how Event Grid compares with Service Bus and Event Hubs.

Azure also appears in an industry context. The episode "Predictive Maintenance on Azure for Manufacturers: What You Actually Need Before the Model" is aimed at maintenance managers, reliability engineers, plant and production leaders, OT and IT architects, and data teams planning predictive maintenance, condition monitoring and industrial AI on Microsoft Azure in manufacturing. It stresses the preparation needed before a model is built and the maintenance process technicians already follow.

Typical decisions around Azure include which service fits a workload, how to structure the environment through a landing zone, how to define resources as code with Bicep, and how to handle data privacy and access for AI services. The linked topics and episodes above give entry points for each of these areas.

azure-ad-b2c.desc: Azure AD B2C is Microsoft's earlier customer identity service for consumer-facing apps, configured with user flows or XML custom policies and succeeded by Microsoft Entra External ID.

faq.a: Azure AD B2C is Microsoft's earlier customer identity service for consumer-facing apps. According to the M365.FM episodes, it is used for sign-in to customer portals and multi-tenant SaaS platforms, including social accounts, tenant-specific credentials and single sign-on.
faq.q: What is Azure AD B2C used for?

faq.a: It is configured with user flows or with XML-based custom policies. User flows cover common scenarios, while custom policies allow more tailored identity journeys.
faq.q: How is Azure AD B2C configured?

faq.a: Microsoft Entra External ID succeeds Azure AD B2C. The episode "Microsoft Entra External ID for Digital Trust and Growth" covers migration realities and how organizations can modernize without abandoning existing CIAM investments.
faq.q: What replaced Azure AD B2C?

azure-ad-b2c.long:
Azure AD B2C (Azure Active Directory B2C) is Microsoft's earlier customer identity service for consumer-facing applications. It is part of Microsoft Azure and handles sign-up and sign-in for external users such as customers, rather than for an organization's own workforce. The service has been succeeded by Microsoft Entra External ID, which is why most current discussion of it concerns existing deployments, comparison with its successor, and migration.

The service is configured in one of two ways: with user flows or with XML-based custom policies. User flows are the predefined route for common scenarios, while custom policies are written in XML and allow more tailored identity journeys. Choosing between the two is a typical design decision, since it affects how much of the sign-in experience can be adapted and how much configuration effort is involved. Official documentation describes the service in its overview pages on Microsoft Learn.

The M365.FM episode "Building Multi-Tenant SaaS with Power Pages and Dataverse" discusses Azure AD B2C in the context of multi-tenant software-as-a-service platforms. According to the episode, Azure AD B2C works well for such platforms because tenants can use their own credentials or connect with social accounts, which it describes as giving flexibility and strong security. The episode adds that user flows, policies and branding can be managed for each tenant, and that the service supports single sign-on (SSO), which makes the login process smoother for users. It also mentions custom identity providers as a further option and stresses tenant-specific authentication and authorization, with separation between tenants to support privacy and legal requirements.

The episode "Build Customer Portals with Power Pages and Dataverse" places Azure AD B2C in a customer portal setting. Its field guide lists external identities, either Azure AD B2C or local authentication, combined with multi-factor authentication as the authentication layer of a portal. Access is then controlled through web roles such as Customer, Partner and Manager, mapped to Dataverse table permissions scoped by Contact or Account, so that users read and write only their own records. The episode also lists a go-live checklist covering authentication, data scope, branding and audit, including sign-in logs, data access logs and change history.

The relationship to its successor is covered in "Microsoft Entra External ID for Digital Trust and Growth". The episode describes Microsoft Entra External ID as the layer for external identities and Verified ID as the means of portable trust through verifiable credentials. It says that together they help organizations modernize customer and partner identity without abandoning existing CIAM (customer identity and access management) investments. The same episode addresses Azure AD B2C migration realities, governance challenges, digital sovereignty, lifecycle management and the balance between user control and enterprise policy enforcement.

The broader positioning appears in "Microsoft Entra as a Complete IAM Platform". The episode notes that what used to be several consoles, including Azure AD, Azure AD B2C and B2B, is now a coordinated platform under the Microsoft Entra umbrella for managing users, devices and apps from a single control plane. For readers searching for Azure AD B2C, the practical takeaways from the episodes are that the service remains relevant for understanding existing customer-facing sign-in setups, that its policy-based configuration model shapes migration planning, and that Microsoft Entra External ID is the direction Microsoft has taken for external identities.

azure-ad-graph.desc: Azure AD Graph is the legacy Microsoft directory API, part of Microsoft Azure, that was deprecated and retired in favor of Microsoft Graph.

faq.a: Azure AD Graph is the legacy Microsoft directory API that Microsoft deprecated and retired in favor of Microsoft Graph. It is part of Microsoft Azure and did not provide API-level activity logging.
faq.q: What is Azure AD Graph?

faq.a: The episode "Migrate Exchange Web Services to Microsoft Graph with Glen Scales [MVP]" says the Azure AD Graph API enters its retirement phase on June 30, 2023, and that all apps must enable extended access by February 1, 2025.
faq.q: When was Azure AD Graph retired according to the episodes?

faq.a: The episodes point to Microsoft Graph as the replacement, with a unified endpoint, OAuth 2.0 authentication and a permissions model that controls what each app can do. They recommend testing the migration as a modernisation project rather than only changing endpoints.
faq.q: What should replace Azure AD Graph in applications?

azure-ad-graph.long:
Azure AD Graph is the legacy Microsoft directory API that Microsoft deprecated and retired in favor of Microsoft Graph. It belongs to the Microsoft Azure ecosystem and was used by applications to work with directory data. According to the facts available, it did not provide API-level activity logging, which is one of the gaps that matters when teams review how older integrations behaved and what can be audited afterwards.

Azure AD Graph sits in a sequence of API generations. The episode "Microsoft Graph Automation Architecture: Beyond Scripts" describes the path: in 2015 Microsoft launched the Office 365 Unified API, which allowed interaction with users across Office 365. The API was then expanded to cover more services, moving from Office Graph to Microsoft Graph. The episode says that Microsoft will retire the Azure AD Graph API and that anyone relying on it must migrate to Microsoft Graph to keep access. Microsoft Graph is presented there as a single, unified interface for service APIs and endpoints, which suits automation projects that need to keep working as the platform changes.

The retirement timeline appears in the episode "Migrate Exchange Web Services to Microsoft Graph with Glen Scales [MVP]". The episode states that the Azure AD Graph API enters its retirement phase on June 30, 2023, and that all apps must enable extended access by February 1, 2025. The same episode covers Exchange Web Services (EWS), for which Microsoft will start retirement in October 2026 and fully disable it by April 2027. The episode frames this as an application-modernisation project rather than a simple URL or endpoint change. Its suggested approach includes reviewing authentication methods, permissions and mailbox operations, and then testing Microsoft Graph replacements with representative users.

The episode "How Microsoft Graph Connects Microsoft 365 Data and Context" compares Microsoft Graph with older APIs. According to that comparison, Microsoft Graph offers a unified endpoint, support for multiple platforms, advanced features such as delta sync and batching, OAuth 2.0 authentication, and extensive integration with Microsoft services. For Azure AD Graph, the comparison lists no unified endpoint, limited advanced features and limited integration with Microsoft services. The episode also notes that the Microsoft Graph permissions model lets administrators decide exactly what each app can do, which reduces risks that older APIs could not address.

Identity design is the other theme linked to Azure AD Graph. The episode "Service Principal Security: Stop Using Personal Accounts" says that, as Microsoft moves toward the 2026 identity model, legacy authentication patterns are being deprecated and old Azure AD Graph integrations are disappearing. Workloads are being pushed toward identity-first architecture. The episode argues that Service Principals, Managed Identities, Federated Credentials and zero-secret authentication are foundational requirements rather than optional modernization projects, and warns that automation tied to an individual employee's account breaks when that person leaves.

In practice, teams that still have applications calling Azure AD Graph typically need to inventory those apps, identify which directory operations they perform, and map them to Microsoft Graph equivalents. The episodes recommend treating the work as a modernisation effort that includes authentication and permissions, not only a change of endpoint, and testing replacements before the legacy API stops working.

azure-advisor.desc: Azure Advisor is a free, built-in Azure service that analyzes resource configuration and usage and gives recommendations on cost, security, reliability, performance and operations.

faq.a: Azure Advisor analyzes the configuration and usage of Azure resources and gives personalized recommendations in five areas: cost, security, reliability, performance and operational excellence. It is a free, built-in part of Microsoft Azure.
faq.q: What does Azure Advisor do?

faq.a: According to the episodes, it provides cost recommendations such as rightsizing virtual machines, reserving capacity and optimizing storage tiers. It is named alongside Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, Azure Hybrid Benefit and tagging as a cost optimization strategy.
faq.q: How does Azure Advisor help reduce Azure costs?

faq.a: No. The episodes describe it as a complement: Azure Monitor supplies metrics and logs for diagnosing performance, and Azure Cost Management handles budgets, alerts and forecasting, while Azure Advisor contributes recommendations.
faq.q: Is Azure Advisor a replacement for Azure Monitor or Azure Cost Management?

azure-advisor.long:
Azure Advisor is a free, built-in service within Microsoft Azure that analyzes the configuration and usage of Azure resources and returns personalized recommendations. The recommendations are grouped into five areas: cost, security, reliability, performance and operational excellence. Because the service is part of Microsoft Azure itself, it needs no separate deployment and works on the resources that already exist in a subscription.

The purpose of Azure Advisor is to point out best-practice improvements that administrators and architects might otherwise miss. The episode "Azure Advisor - Simply Explained" describes it as Microsoft's personalized cloud optimization service that continuously analyzes an Azure environment and provides actionable recommendations. According to that episode, the goal is to help organizations optimize workloads, reduce unnecessary spending and strengthen their cloud infrastructure with minimal effort. The five categories reflect typical concerns in cloud operations: keeping costs under control, protecting resources, keeping workloads available, maintaining acceptable speed, and running the environment in a well-managed way.

In practice, Azure Advisor is most often mentioned in connection with cost optimization. The episode "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud" recommends reviewing an Azure environment for unattached disks, unused storage accounts and idle virtual machines, and using Azure Advisor to obtain cost recommendations such as rightsizing virtual machines, reserving capacity or optimizing storage tiers. The same episode advises scheduling non-production resources to shut down outside business hours, moving infrequently accessed data to cool or archive tiers, and removing over-provisioned resources such as oversized virtual machines or excessive backup retention. Azure Advisor serves there as one source of findings alongside these housekeeping steps.

The service also appears in the wider discussion of cost governance. The episode "Azure Cost Management - Simply Explained" lists Azure Advisor recommendations among practical cost optimization strategies, next to Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, Azure Hybrid Benefit, rightsizing, tagging for cost allocation and identifying underutilized services. In that context, Azure Advisor complements Azure Cost Management, which covers budgets, alerts, forecasting and cost analysis by group, service or tag. Similarly, "Stop Azure Cost Entropy with Ownership and Budget Controls" presents a case in which a company used Azure Advisor to receive personalized recommendations on cost, performance and security, alongside Azure Monitor and resource tagging. The episode draws the lesson that governance and resource management are central to controlling costs.

Azure Advisor is also relevant for performance work. The episode "Design Reliable and Resilient Azure Architectures" suggests starting with Azure Monitor and performance diagnostics to collect metrics and logs for App Service, Azure virtual machines and Azure SQL Database, and then using Azure Advisor recommendations together with Application Insights traces and performance monitor counters to locate CPU, memory or I/O hotspots. Here the service acts as a pointer toward likely problem areas, while the detailed diagnosis relies on monitoring data.

A typical decision around Azure Advisor is how to treat its output: as input to review rather than as an automatic action. The recommendations indicate where configuration or usage deviates from best practice, and teams decide which ones fit their workloads, such as whether a virtual machine can be resized or a reservation makes sense. Used alongside Azure Monitor, Azure Cost Management and tagging, the service supports a regular optimization routine across all five of its categories.

azure-ai-content-safety.long:
Azure AI Content Safety is a product within Microsoft Azure. The name places it in the Azure AI portfolio, and the knowledge base records it as part of Microsoft Azure.

Beyond that relationship, no further details are currently recorded for this entry. No feature list, pricing, supported scenarios, version information or official documentation links are included in the facts available for this page, so none are described here to avoid stating anything that cannot be verified.

On M365.FM, the entity is tracked as part of the broader Microsoft Azure topic area. No episodes are currently linked to Azure AI Content Safety. As episodes covering the product are added, this page can be expanded with more specific context drawn from them. azure-ai-content-understanding.desc: Azure AI Content Understanding is a Microsoft Azure service that turns documents, images, video and audio into structured results defined by a field schema.

faq.a: It takes unstructured content such as documents, images, video and audio and returns structured output based on a schema, either as JSON that follows the schema or as Markdown for search and retrieval scenarios.
faq.q: What does Azure AI Content Understanding do?

faq.a: An analyzer drives the processing and defines the extraction settings, the field schema and the model deployments. Prebuilt analyzers cover common scenarios and custom analyzers cover specific ones.
faq.q: What is an analyzer in Azure AI Content Understanding?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode "Copilot Studio AI Agents and RAG with Nilüfer Doğan [MVP]" says that connecting Copilot Studio with the service lets an agent use structured data pulled from emails or documents, for example to extract invoice details and trigger approval workflows.
faq.q: How does it relate to Copilot Studio?

azure-ai-content-understanding.long:
Azure AI Content Understanding is a Microsoft AI service within Microsoft Azure that takes unstructured content, such as documents, images, video and audio, and returns structured results based on fields defined in a schema. Microsoft Learn describes it as a Foundry tool that uses generative AI to turn unstructured content into structured output for automation and analytics workflows. The aim is that business processes can work directly with the extracted information instead of relying on manual reading and data entry.

Processing is driven by an analyzer. According to the documentation, an analyzer defines the extraction settings, the field schema and the model deployments. Prebuilt analyzers cover common scenarios, while custom analyzers can be created for specific ones. Inside the pipeline, content extraction comes first and covers steps such as OCR, layout analysis and transcription. Optional segmentation can then split the content into parts. Field extraction follows, and it can extract values directly, classify content, or generate values based on the schema that was defined.

Results are returned in one of two forms. Markdown output is intended for search and retrieval scenarios, while JSON output follows the schema and suits automation and data integration. For document analyzers, confidence scores and grounding to source regions are available, which helps in judging how reliable an extracted value is and where in the source it came from. The service requires a Foundry resource and deployments of supported models. Content safety guardrails can restrict extraction, so the documentation advises checking warnings. Some features exist only in the preview API version, which is relevant when planning production use.

Typical uses named in the documentation include document processing, inputs for agents, search indexing, process automation and routing documents by class. In practice this means a solution can read an incoming document, determine what kind of document it is, pull out the fields that matter and pass them on to the next step in a workflow. Choosing between a prebuilt and a custom analyzer, deciding how fields are defined in the schema, and deciding when low-confidence values should be reviewed by a person are the main design decisions around the service.

The M365.FM episode "Copilot Studio AI Agents and RAG with Nilüfer Doğan [MVP]" places the service in the context of Copilot Studio. The episode says that connecting Copilot Studio with Azure AI Content Understanding allows an AI agent to deliver context-aware responses by pulling structured data from unstructured sources, such as emails or documents, and using it to answer questions or make decisions. One example from the episode is invoice processing, where key details such as vendor name, amount and due date are extracted and approval workflows can be triggered automatically. The episode states that this reduces manual effort and errors and speeds up business processes, with faster invoice processing given as a measurable result.

As part of Microsoft Azure, Azure AI Content Understanding sits alongside other Azure AI capabilities and is consumed through a Foundry resource. For teams building agents or retrieval solutions, it serves as the layer that converts raw files into data an agent or workflow can act on, while the schema keeps the output predictable and the confidence and grounding information supports review and control.

azure-ai-document-intelligence.desc: Azure AI Document Intelligence, formerly Azure Form Recognizer, is a cloud AI service that extracts text, key-value pairs, tables and structure from documents.

faq.a: Azure AI Document Intelligence is a cloud AI service that extracts text, key-value pairs, tables and structure from documents. It provides prebuilt and custom models and is accessed through REST APIs and SDKs.
faq.q: What is Azure AI Document Intelligence?

faq.a: It was formerly named Azure Form Recognizer.
faq.q: What was Azure AI Document Intelligence called before?

faq.a: Developers call the service through REST APIs and SDKs, using either prebuilt models or custom models to extract structured data from documents.
faq.q: How do developers use Azure AI Document Intelligence?

azure-ai-document-intelligence.long:
Azure AI Document Intelligence is a cloud AI service from Microsoft for extracting information from documents. It was previously known as Azure Form Recognizer. The service reads documents and returns text, key-value pairs, tables and document structure as structured output.

The service offers prebuilt models as well as custom models. Prebuilt models cover common document extraction scenarios without additional training, while custom models allow the extraction to be adapted to specific document types. Developers access the service through REST APIs and SDKs, which makes it possible to integrate document processing into applications and workflows.

Typical uses include turning scanned or digital documents into structured data that other systems can process, for example by pulling field values and table contents out of forms. Official technical documentation is published on Microsoft Learn.

This page is a reference entry on M365.FM. No episodes or related topics are currently linked to Azure AI Document Intelligence in the knowledge base.

azure-ai-search.desc: Azure AI Search, formerly Azure Cognitive Search, is a Microsoft Azure service that indexes content and supports keyword, vector and hybrid search, often for RAG.

faq.a: Azure AI Search is a Microsoft Azure service that indexes content and supports keyword, vector and hybrid search. It was previously called Azure Cognitive Search and is often used for retrieval-augmented generation.
faq.q: What is Azure AI Search?

faq.a: In a RAG setup, the search index supplies relevant passages from company data, and a language model uses them to formulate an answer. This grounds responses in an organization's own knowledge rather than only the model's training data.
faq.q: How does Azure AI Search relate to RAG?

faq.a: They are two vector search algorithms available in Azure AI Search. The episode "HNSW vs DiskANN for Vector Search in Azure AI Search" compares them and says the choice depends on the size and growth of the vector data.
faq.q: What do HNSW and DiskANN have to do with Azure AI Search?

azure-ai-search.long:
Azure AI Search is a search and information retrieval service from Microsoft that indexes content and supports vector and hybrid search. It was previously known as Azure Cognitive Search. It is part of Microsoft Azure and is classed as a Microsoft tool. Organizations use it to build search experiences over their own documents and data, and it is frequently used as the retrieval layer in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) setups.

The service combines several approaches to finding information. Traditional keyword search matches the exact words a user types, which works well for things like policy codes. Vector search compares embeddings so that a query about time off can still find a document that says vacation. The episode "Azure AI Search Hybrid Retrieval - Simply Explained" frames this as the reason a search box that relies on only one method keeps falling short: keyword search alone misses meaning, while semantic matching alone can miss exact terms. Azure AI Search also offers semantic ranking and AI enrichment, so results can be reordered by relevance and content can be enriched during indexing.

In a RAG architecture, the search index supplies relevant passages from company data, and a language model uses them to formulate an answer instead of relying only on its training knowledge. The episode "RAG on Azure — Simply Explained" walks through the steps involved: ingesting documents, creating vector embeddings, storing them in a vector database, and retrieving the most relevant information for each user query. It names concepts such as embeddings, chunking, semantic search and grounding, and describes Azure AI Search and Azure OpenAI as building blocks. According to the episode, grounding answers in an organization's private knowledge reduces hallucinations and produces more accurate, up-to-date and source-aware responses. Use cases mentioned include AI chatbots, internal knowledge assistants, customer support, document search and enterprise copilots.

A central design decision concerns vector search at scale. The episode "HNSW vs DiskANN for Vector Search in Azure AI Search" describes the "billion-vector problem": how to search through very large numbers of vector embeddings without excessive infrastructure cost. It compares two vector search algorithms available in the service, HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) and DiskANN. The episode notes that HNSW has become widely used, and that the right choice depends on the size and growth trajectory of the vector data. It offers practical guidance for both proof-of-concept projects and planning for billion-scale workloads.

The overview episode "Azure AI Search – Simply Explained" presents the service as a core component for RAG, AI agents and enterprise search solutions, combining keyword search with vector search, semantic ranking and AI enrichment. It is part of the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets series.

The service also appears in applied scenarios. In "Beyond Copilot: Building AI That Works in the Real World with Azure AI Foundry and Agentic AI for Frontline Workers with Fergus Kidd [MVP]", Azure AI Search is named as one of the components behind FieldPal AI, alongside models, speech capabilities, retrieval-augmented generation, APIs, Kubernetes and other Azure services. The episode describes this combination as forming a full product rather than a single assistant experience, with the option to connect the same backend capabilities to Copilot Studio and Microsoft 365.

Azure AI Search relates most closely to Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), Microsoft Azure and the wider set of Azure AI services. Official documentation is available on Microsoft Learn under the Azure Search section.

azure-ai-services.desc: Azure AI services is Microsoft's family of prebuilt AI APIs on Azure, formerly Azure Cognitive Services, covering vision, speech, language and decision capabilities.

faq.a: Azure AI services is Microsoft's family of prebuilt AI APIs on Azure, formerly called Azure Cognitive Services. It covers vision, speech, language and decision capabilities that apps and flows can call.
faq.q: What is Azure AI services?

faq.a: According to the episode "Fix Common Azure AI Foundry Project Failures", Azure AI Foundry is a hub-based solution that brings together Azure AI services, Azure Machine Learning, Azure OpenAI Service and other Azure services into a single managed Azure resource.
faq.q: How does Azure AI services relate to Azure AI Foundry?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Private Link - Simply Explained" lists Azure AI services among the services that Azure Private Link integrates with, alongside Azure Storage, Azure SQL Database, Key Vault and App Service.
faq.q: Can Azure AI services be accessed over a private network connection?

azure-ai-services.long:
Azure AI services is a family of prebuilt AI APIs offered on Microsoft Azure. It was formerly known as Azure Cognitive Services and groups vision, speech, language and decision capabilities that applications and automation flows can call without building and training models from scratch. As a part of Microsoft Azure, it sits alongside other Azure offerings such as Azure Machine Learning and Azure OpenAI Service, and it is often used together with them.

The central idea is to add AI capabilities to an application through a service call instead of through custom model development. The episode "Azure AI Infrastructure Architecture for C-Level Leaders" places this kind of service on the consumption side of the decision between infrastructure-level, platform-level and ready-made options. According to the episode, a ready-made service may not offer the same degree of customization as IaaS or PaaS approaches, but it allows quick deployment and ease of use. The episode adds that choosing the right model depends on the specific needs and capabilities of the organization. In its service overview table, it lists Azure Machine Learning for model training and development, with use cases such as predictive maintenance, customer churn prediction, fraud detection and demand forecasting, and Azure Cognitive Services for adding pre-built AI capabilities.

Azure AI services also appears as one component of a wider platform. The episode "Fix Common Azure AI Foundry Project Failures" describes Azure AI Foundry as Microsoft's hub-based solution that brings together Azure AI services, Azure Machine Learning, Azure OpenAI Service and other Azure services into a single managed Azure resource for enterprise AI. In that description, the Foundry portal and control plane support AI development teams with collaboration, governance, deployment and monitoring across hubs and projects. Here Azure AI services is one of the building blocks inside a managed environment rather than a standalone product.

A recurring decision is whether to use Azure AI services or the AI options built into Microsoft Power Platform. The episode "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform" says to choose AI Builder when prebuilt, no-code or low-code AI such as prediction, document processing or object detection is needed within Microsoft Power Platform. It names developer skills, compliance, latency and cost as factors when comparing Azure AI services with Power Platform AI options. The same episode lists common integration patterns: Power Automate triggering Azure OpenAI calls, generative responses embedded in Dynamics 365 forms through Power Apps, and copilot experiences that surface knowledge and automate case resolution.

In practice, Azure AI services is combined with other Azure components to form complete solutions. In the episode "Beyond Copilot: Building AI That Works in the Real World with Azure AI Foundry and Agentic AI for Frontline Workers with Fergus Kidd [MVP]", the guest explains why FieldPal AI is built on Azure AI Foundry and Azure AI services. According to the episode, the platform combines models, speech capabilities, Azure AI Search, retrieval-augmented generation, APIs, Kubernetes and other Azure services to create a full product rather than a single assistant experience. The episode presents this as a way to build an end-to-end application for workers who may not use Teams every day, while keeping the worker's interaction simple.

Network security is another topic connected to the service. The episode "Azure Private Link - Simply Explained" covers Private Link services, private IP addresses, DNS integration, virtual networks and secure access to Azure PaaS services. It states that Azure Private Link integrates with services such as Azure Storage, Azure SQL Database, Key Vault, App Service and Azure AI services, as well as on-premises environments connected through VPN or ExpressRoute. According to the episode, this helps reduce the risk of data exfiltration while simplifying secure connectivity across hybrid and multi-region deployments, and it also explains the differences between Azure Private Link and Service Endpoints.

Taken together, the episodes show Azure AI services in three roles: as a set of ready-to-use AI APIs, as a component inside Azure AI Foundry, and as a resource that can be reached privately over Azure networking. Decisions around it typically involve how much customization is needed, whether Power Platform's AI options are sufficient, and how the service is secured and connected to other Azure resources.

azure-ai-translator.desc: Azure Translator in Foundry Tools is a Microsoft cloud neural machine translation service for text and documents, available through REST API, SDKs, Microsoft Foundry and containers.

azure-api-center.desc: Azure API Center is an Azure service that keeps a central inventory of an organization's APIs and MCP servers for discovery, reuse and governance.

faq.a: It provides a central inventory of an organization's APIs and MCP servers, including versions, definition files and metadata, so that they can be discovered, reused and governed.
faq.q: What is Azure API Center used for?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, Azure API Center focuses on design-time governance and discovery, while Azure API Management covers runtime governance through a gateway. Azure API Center is not a runtime gateway.
faq.q: How does Azure API Center differ from Azure API Management?

faq.a: The episode "Azure MCP Server - Simply Explained" describes opening the Azure API Center resource in the Azure portal, selecting Assets under Inventory, choosing Register an asset and then MCP server, and then providing the required information and configuring environments and deployments.
faq.q: How is an MCP server registered in Azure API Center?

azure-api-center.long:
Azure API Center is a service in Microsoft Azure that lets an organization register its APIs and MCP servers in one central inventory. Each entry can carry versions, definition files and shared metadata, regardless of the API's type, its lifecycle stage or the place where it is deployed. The stated aims are discovery, reuse and governance: teams can find what already exists instead of building the same interface again, and platform owners get a single place to see what is in use.

According to Microsoft Learn, the service is positioned around design-time governance and discovery. This distinguishes it from Azure API Management, which covers runtime governance through a gateway. Azure API Center is not a runtime gateway and does not route traffic. It describes and organizes APIs, while a gateway product handles requests at run time. The two can be combined, since APIs can be added to the inventory from API Management as well as from other platforms, unmanaged sources and APIs that are still in development.

Registration can be done through the Azure portal, the Azure CLI or pipelines. This allows the inventory to be filled manually for a small set of interfaces or automated as part of a delivery process. Because the sources can be varied, the inventory is not limited to APIs hosted in Azure; it is meant to hold the whole portfolio an organization wants to keep track of.

Governance features form a large part of the service. Built-in and custom metadata describe each API consistently, and linting and analysis of definitions such as OpenAPI help enforce quality standards. A Visual Studio Code extension offers linting, breaking-change detection and GitHub Copilot integration, which brings these checks into the developer's editor. A portal supports discovery for people who want to find and consume registered APIs. Integration with Dev Proxy can reveal unregistered shadow APIs, meaning interfaces that are in use but were never added to the inventory.

MCP servers are treated as a type of asset alongside APIs. The M365.FM episode "Azure MCP Server - Simply Explained" describes the steps for registering one: sign in to the Azure portal, open the Azure API Center resource, expand Inventory in the left navigation pane and select Assets, then choose Register an asset and pick MCP server. After providing the required information about the server, environments and deployments are configured following the tutorial on adding environments and deployments for APIs in Azure API Center. The episode also mentions that authentication for the MCP server can optionally be configured afterwards.

For planning, Microsoft Learn describes two plans. A free plan suits evaluation and comes without Microsoft support, while a standard plan targets production use. The service is offered only in the regions listed in the documentation, which is a point to check before choosing it for a given environment.

Typical decisions around Azure API Center concern scope and ownership: which APIs and MCP servers belong in the inventory, which metadata fields are mandatory, which linting rules apply to definitions, and how shadow APIs are brought under governance. Organizations that already run Azure API Management usually keep it for gateway functions and use Azure API Center as the catalog and governance layer above their APIs.

azure-api-management.desc: Azure API Management (APIM) is a Microsoft Azure service for publishing, securing, throttling and monitoring APIs, placed between API consumers and backend services.

faq.a: It is used to publish, secure, throttle and monitor APIs from a central point between API consumers and backend services. It helps manage authentication, versioning, monitoring and developer access as the number of APIs grows.
faq.q: What is Azure API Management used for?

faq.a: Both are related Azure services that can serve as backends. APIM can expose and protect Azure Functions endpoints and Azure Logic Apps workflows as APIs, for example by adding authentication or restricting access by IP.
faq.q: How does Azure API Management relate to Azure Functions and Azure Logic Apps?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft AI Gateway - Simply Explained", it extends Azure API Management with centralized control over AI traffic, model endpoints, agents, MCP tools and Agent-to-Agent communication, aiming at governance, monitoring and cost visibility.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft AI Gateway in connection with Azure API Management?

azure-api-management.long:
Azure API Management, often shortened to APIM, is a service from Microsoft for publishing, securing, throttling and monitoring APIs. It belongs to Microsoft Azure and is classed as a developer tool. The service sits between API consumers and backend services and gives teams a single place to control access, apply policies and observe traffic. It is aimed at organizations that run many APIs, microservices or enterprise integrations.

The core problem it addresses is growth. As the number of APIs increases, managing security, authentication, monitoring, versioning and developer access quickly becomes complex. Instead of solving each of these concerns separately in every backend service, an API management layer lets them be handled centrally. This is the same idea described for API gateways in general: a single entry point that handles concerns such as request routing, caching, logging and monitoring while simplifying access to multiple backend services.

Within the Azure landscape, APIM is related to Azure Functions and Azure Logic Apps. Azure Functions can act as a backend whose endpoints are exposed through APIM, and Azure Logic Apps workflows can likewise be published and protected as APIs. In both cases APIM provides the front door, while the backend service provides the actual logic.

The episode "Azure API Management - Simply Explained" from Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets introduces APIM in plain English and describes it as one of the most important services in Microsoft Azure for organizations building modern cloud applications, microservices and enterprise integrations. It focuses on why security, authentication, monitoring, versioning and developer access become hard to manage as API estates grow. The episode "API Gateway - Simply Explained" covers the broader concept, compares API gateways with reverse proxies and load balancers, explores common deployment patterns and names Azure API Management alongside Amazon API Gateway and other enterprise solutions as platforms that implement these capabilities.

A newer use of the service is the Microsoft AI Gateway. According to the episode "Microsoft AI Gateway - Simply Explained", presented by Mirko Peters, the AI Gateway extends Azure API Management by introducing centralized control over AI traffic, model endpoints, intelligent agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and Agent-to-Agent (A2A) communication. The episode describes the motivation as increasing security risks, inconsistent access controls, rising token costs and limited visibility into AI usage, and presents Azure API Management as a secure front door for enterprise AI traffic that simplifies governance, monitoring and operational management. The episode "Azure Local - Simply Explained" carries the same summary for this gateway scenario in its listing.

Security is another recurring theme. In the episode "Secure Azure Networking with Rex de Koning [MVP-MCT]", Azure API Management is named as an option for protecting Azure Functions: it provides additional security options for incoming requests and can restrict access based on IP. This appears alongside other measures such as enforcing HTTPS and the latest TLS version, managing access keys and deploying the function app within a virtual network, which together form a security framework for function endpoints.

In practice, the decision to use APIM usually arises when several backends, teams or consumers need consistent authentication, throttling, versioning and monitoring. Official documentation for the service is available from Microsoft Learn under the Azure API Management section.

azure-app-configuration.desc: Azure App Configuration is a managed Microsoft Azure service that stores application settings and feature flags centrally as key-value pairs for shared use.

faq.a: It stores application settings and feature flags centrally as key-value pairs. This lets multiple applications share configuration and lets settings change without redeploying or restarting an application.
faq.q: What is Azure App Configuration used for?

faq.a: The service complements Azure Key Vault. Key Vault remains the place for application secrets, while App Configuration holds settings and feature flags.
faq.q: How does Azure App Configuration relate to Azure Key Vault?

faq.a: Client libraries exist for .NET, ASP.NET Core, Java Spring, JavaScript, Python and Go. Typical consumers include microservices on Azure Kubernetes Service or Service Fabric, Azure Functions and continuous deployment pipelines.
faq.q: Which languages and platforms can use Azure App Configuration?

azure-app-configuration.long:
Azure App Configuration is a managed service in Microsoft Azure for storing application settings and feature flags in one central place. Configuration is kept as key-value pairs, so several applications can share the same settings and update them without each application carrying its own copy. The service is part of Microsoft Azure and is documented on Microsoft Learn.

The main purpose is to separate configuration from code, in line with the twelve-factor app recommendation. According to the documentation notes, spreading settings across individual deployments can lead to errors that are hard to trace. Keeping them in a single store reduces that risk and makes it clear where a given value comes from. A common scenario is managing hierarchical configuration for different environments and regions. Another is changing settings without redeploying or restarting an application. A third is controlling the availability of features in real time through feature flags.

The service provides several capabilities that support these scenarios. Keys can be represented and mapped flexibly, and labels can be used to tag values. Settings can be replayed to an earlier point in time, which helps when investigating what a configuration looked like at a given moment. A dedicated interface exists for feature flags, and two configuration sets can be compared along custom dimensions. For security, the service relies on Azure managed identities, and sensitive data is encrypted at rest and in transit.

Azure App Configuration is meant to complement Azure Key Vault, not replace it. Key Vault remains the place for application secrets, while App Configuration holds ordinary settings and feature flags. This division is relevant when deciding where a particular value belongs: credentials and other secrets go to Key Vault, whereas non-secret configuration that changes per environment or per release goes to App Configuration.

Typical consumers include microservices running on Azure Kubernetes Service or Service Fabric, serverless applications such as Azure Functions, and continuous deployment pipelines. Client libraries are available for .NET, ASP.NET Core, Java Spring, JavaScript, Python and Go, so applications written in these languages can read their settings from the service. The page used as a source does not cover prerequisites, licensing, pricing tiers or limits, so those details need to be checked in the current Azure documentation.

The M365.FM episode "Build Fusion Apps with Power Apps and Azure Functions" (2025-08-11) mentions the service in the context of securing an Azure Function that is connected to Power Apps through a custom connector. Among its security recommendations, the episode says that sensitive information and configuration settings should be protected with Azure Key Vault or Azure App Configuration. It adds that managed identities and OAuth make an Azure Function safer and easier to handle, because passwords no longer need to be placed in the code. In that discussion, App Configuration is therefore one of the building blocks for keeping configuration out of application code.

azure-app-service.desc: Azure App Service is a Microsoft platform-as-a-service for hosting web apps, REST APIs and mobile back ends with built-in scaling and deployment slots.

faq.a: Azure App Service is a platform-as-a-service from Microsoft for hosting web apps, REST APIs and mobile back ends. It provides built-in scaling, deployment slots and CI/CD integration.
faq.q: What is Azure App Service used for?

faq.a: The episode "Azure App Service - Simply Explained" says the tier chosen decides what an app is allowed to do, since it unlocks a feature set, controls billing and affects how workloads scale.
faq.q: Why does the App Service plan matter?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Virtual Network - Simply Explained", Azure App Service uses VNet Integration through subnet delegation, so web applications can reach VNet resources as if they were within the network.
faq.q: How can Azure App Service connect to a virtual network?

azure-app-service.long:
Azure App Service is a platform-as-a-service (PaaS) offering from Microsoft, available as part of Microsoft Azure. It is used to host web applications, REST APIs and mobile back ends without managing the underlying servers. The service includes built-in scaling, deployment slots and integration with CI/CD workflows, which lets development teams move code into the cloud while the platform handles the infrastructure. Within the Microsoft ecosystem it is categorized as both a Microsoft tool and a developer tool.

The central concept in the service is the App Service plan. According to the M365.FM episode "Azure App Service - Simply Explained", the tier chosen on Azure App Service determines what an app is allowed to do. The choice is therefore not only about hosting capacity: it unlocks a particular feature set, controls billing and shapes how a cloud workload scales. The episode describes the App Service plan as the element that dictates the resources available to the app, which makes the plan selection one of the first and most consequential decisions when adopting the service.

The same episode points out several common traps. These include forgetting the "Always On" setting, misconfiguring continuous deployment slots, and leaving forgotten paid plans running. Each of these relates to everyday operation rather than initial setup: an app that is not kept warm may behave differently from one that is, deployment slots need to be set up deliberately to support continuous deployment, and a plan that is no longer needed can keep generating cost if it is not removed.

For deployment, the episode "Deploy Web Apps to Azure App Service Without Boilerplate" describes Azure App Service as one of the more efficient ways to move an application into the cloud on a fully managed platform. It states that the service supports all major development frameworks, handles infrastructure responsibilities behind the scenes and simplifies hosting and scaling. A related episode with Gábor Ruzsinszki, "Modern .NET: WPF, ASP.NET Core, and gRPC with Gábor Ruzsinszki [MVP]", lists Azure App Service alongside Azure Functions as an example of deep .NET integration on Azure, and notes that code can be uploaded while Azure handles the rest.
