Azure DevOps is mentioned there as a way to automate deployments.

Security is another recurring topic. The episode "Replace Hard-Coded SQL Logins in Azure App Service" covers securing web applications on Azure with the built-in security capabilities of Azure App Service. It highlights authentication and authorization options, IP restrictions and TLS encryption, as well as integration with Azure DDoS protection, Azure Front Door and Azure SQL Database. The title of the episode reflects a practical decision: moving away from credentials embedded in application code toward the platform's own mechanisms.

Networking is addressed in the episode "Azure Virtual Network - Simply Explained". It explains that Azure App Service can connect to resources in a virtual network through VNet Integration, which uses subnet delegation. With this integration, web applications can reach VNet resources as if they were inside the network, which allows applications to access required resources securely.

Taken together, the episodes position Azure App Service as a managed hosting layer whose behavior depends heavily on configuration choices: the plan tier, the deployment approach, the security settings and the network integration. Official documentation for the service is published on Microsoft Learn.

azure-app-service-plan.desc: An Azure App Service plan is the set of compute resources an Azure App Service app runs on, fixing the operating system, region, instance count and size, and pricing tier.

faq.a: It defines the operating system, the region, the number and size of VM instances and the pricing tier. All apps in the plan share these resources.
faq.q: What does an Azure App Service plan define?

faq.a: Yes, all apps and slots in a plan run on all its instances and scale together. Per-app scaling can limit an app to a subset of instances, and Free and Shared tiers do not scale out.
faq.q: Do all apps in one App Service plan scale together?

faq.a: For Basic and above, billing is per VM instance. Shared is billed by CPU quota per app, and Free has no compute cost.
faq.q: How is an App Service plan billed?

azure-app-service-plan.long:
An Azure App Service plan is the set of compute resources on which an Azure App Service app runs. It belongs to the broader topic Azure App Service, and every App Service app always runs in a plan. Azure Functions can also use such plans in some scenarios. The plan is the unit that holds the hosting capacity, while the apps are the workloads placed on it.

A plan defines several fixed characteristics: the operating system, the region, the number and size of the virtual machine instances, and the pricing tier. These settings determine what the apps inside the plan can do and what they cost. Because the region and operating system are set at the plan level, apps that need a different region or operating system need a different plan.

Pricing tiers fall into three groups according to Microsoft Learn. Shared compute covers the Free and Shared tiers. Dedicated compute runs from Basic up to the Premium tiers. Isolated uses dedicated virtual networks. Which features are available depends on the tier, including custom domains, TLS certificates, autoscaling, deployment slots and backups. Choosing a tier is therefore both a cost decision and a feature decision.

Scaling is one of the central ideas behind the plan. All apps and slots in a plan run on all of its instances and scale together. Free and Shared tiers do not scale out. Per-app scaling can limit an individual app to a subset of the plan's instances, which helps when apps in one plan have different load. A plan can also be scaled up or down by switching to a different tier. The documentation gives recommended maximum app counts per plan size, which is relevant when deciding how many apps to place in one plan.

Billing follows the plan rather than each app in most cases. For Basic and above, billing is per VM instance. The Shared tier is billed by CPU quota per app, and the Free tier has no compute cost. Because apps in a plan share the same instances, placing several apps in one plan shares the cost, but it also means they compete for the same resources. The documentation also notes that Windows apps support 32-bit and 64-bit, while Linux apps run only as 64-bit, and that a managed instance option exists for Windows web apps on selected SKUs.

In practice, the plan often appears as a resource to be declared next to the app itself. The M365.FM episode "Deploy Web Apps to Azure App Service Without Boilerplate" describes starting from a template with azd init, choosing the Starter - Bicep option, and editing the Bicep files in the infra folder to set up an Azure App Service Plan together with an Azure App Service. After editing the azure.yaml file with the app's details, running azd up sets up and launches the resources. The episode presents this as a way to avoid configuring everything by hand and to spend more time writing code.

Typical decisions around an App Service plan include which tier provides the required features, how many instances are needed, whether apps should share a plan or be separated, and whether per-app scaling is appropriate. Reviewing the plan's tier and instance count is also the starting point when an app needs more capacity or when costs need to be reduced.

azure-application-gateway.desc: Azure Application Gateway is a Layer 7 web traffic load balancer in Microsoft Azure that routes HTTP and HTTPS requests by web rules and can terminate TLS.

faq.a: Azure Application Gateway is a Layer 7 web traffic load balancer in Azure that understands HTTP and HTTPS, routes requests by web rules and can handle TLS termination before traffic reaches back-end servers.
faq.q: What is Azure Application Gateway?

faq.a: Azure Load Balancer works at Layer 4, while Azure Application Gateway works at Layer 7 and reads the web request itself. The M365.FM episode "Azure Load Balancer — Simply Explained" discusses when to choose one over the other.
faq.q: How does Azure Application Gateway differ from Azure Load Balancer?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Run Azure Application Gateway Without Public IP Exposure", the newer Network Isolation model removes the earlier need for a public IP and outbound Internet access for control plane communication. The episode describes registering the feature flag and redeploying the gateway.
faq.q: Can Azure Application Gateway run without a public IP?

azure-application-gateway.long:
Azure Application Gateway is a Layer 7 web traffic load balancer in Microsoft Azure. Unlike a load balancer that forwards packets without examining them, it understands HTTP and HTTPS and makes routing decisions based on the content of each web request. It is part of Microsoft Azure and is documented in the official Microsoft Learn overview for the service.

The core idea is that the gateway reads the request it is delivering. Based on web rules, it decides which back-end servers should receive the traffic. It can also handle TLS termination, meaning that encrypted HTTPS traffic is decrypted at the gateway before the request is passed on to the back-end servers. The M365.FM episode "Azure Application Gateway - Simply Explained" builds on this point, noting that most load balancers never read the request they are delivering, while Azure Application Gateway does, and that this habit changes where traffic lands.

The same episode outlines the main building blocks of the service: listeners and routing rules, backend pools and health probes, where HTTPS gets handled, what stops attacks, and how scaling works without manual intervention. In practical terms, a listener accepts incoming requests, routing rules map those requests to a backend pool, and health probes help ensure that traffic is sent only to healthy back-end resources. The episode also compares the three Azure load balancing options, which helps place Application Gateway among the other services in Azure networking.

Choosing between Azure networking services is a recurring design decision. The M365.FM episode "Azure Load Balancer — Simply Explained" describes Azure Load Balancer as a Layer 4 service and discusses when to choose it over Azure Application Gateway or Azure Front Door. The episode "Azure Traffic Manager - Simply Explained" covers DNS-based global load balancing and notes that Azure Traffic Manager can be combined with services such as Azure Firewall and Azure Application Gateway to build a multi-region application architecture with high availability and security. The episode "Azure API Management - Simply Explained" addresses a further boundary, explaining when Azure API Management should be used instead of Azure Application Gateway or Azure Front Door for exposing and managing APIs.

A separate area of attention is network exposure. The episode "Run Azure Application Gateway Without Public IP Exposure" describes a long-standing limitation: for years, a so-called private Azure Application Gateway still needed a public IP and outbound Internet access to communicate with Microsoft's control plane. According to the episode, management traffic (control plane) and user traffic (data plane) shared the same entry point, which led to firewall exceptions, Azure DNS dependencies, and discomfort for auditors. The episode presents the newer Network Isolation model as a fix for this, with isolation achieved by structure rather than by exception, and describes registering the feature flag, redeploying the gateway, and retiring the temporary rules that had kept a supposedly private gateway partly public.

Taken together, the episodes position Azure Application Gateway as the web-aware entry point for HTTP and HTTPS workloads in Azure. It is typically considered when requests need to be routed by web rules, when TLS must be terminated before traffic reaches back-end servers, or when a private deployment without public IP exposure is required. For non-web traffic, global DNS-based distribution, or API lifecycle management, the episodes point to other Azure services and describe how they relate to it.

azure-arc.desc: Azure Arc is a Microsoft Azure service that connects servers and Kubernetes clusters outside Azure to Azure management, governance and security from one control plane.

faq.a: Azure Arc is a Microsoft service, part of Microsoft Azure, that connects servers and Kubernetes clusters running outside Azure, such as on-premises or at the edge, to Azure management. It brings Azure's management, security and governance to those resources from a single control plane.
faq.q: What is Azure Arc?

faq.a: No. According to the episode "Azure Arc - Simply Explained", Azure Arc brings Azure services to wherever the infrastructure already exists instead of moving workloads into Azure.
faq.q: Does Azure Arc require moving workloads into Azure?

faq.a: In the M365.FM episodes, Azure Arc is discussed together with Azure Local, which combines familiar infrastructure with Azure-based management, governance and security. Azure Arc is named as part of the connection between local environments and the broader Azure architecture.
faq.q: How does Azure Arc relate to Azure Local?

azure-arc.long:
Azure Arc is a Microsoft service within Microsoft Azure that connects servers and Kubernetes clusters running outside Azure, for example on-premises or at the edge, to Azure management. Instead of requiring workloads to be moved into the cloud, it brings Azure's management, security and governance capabilities to the place where the infrastructure already exists. Resources are then handled from a single control plane, regardless of where they physically run.

According to the M365.FM episode "Azure Arc - Simply Explained", Azure Arc extends Azure's management, security and governance beyond the Azure cloud. It covers servers, Kubernetes clusters, databases and other resources running on-premises, at the edge or at other cloud providers. The central idea is that the infrastructure stays where it is, while Azure services reach out to it. This makes Azure Arc relevant for organizations with a mixed estate in which not every workload can or should be hosted in Azure.

A typical use is applying consistent controls to machines that are not part of Azure itself. The episode "Cut Cloud Costs with Azure Arc and Azure Local on Mini PCs" describes how Azure Arc lets a company's own mini PCs and edge boxes carry an Azure badge, so they follow the same policies, Defender rules, role-based access control (RBAC) and monitoring as cloud resources. The episode frames this as a way to keep governance, security and automation while reducing spending on cloud virtual machines, and it cites the figure that 70% of enterprises plan to adopt hybrid cloud strategies by 2026. This figure is attributed to the episode, not independently verified here.

Azure Arc also appears in architecture discussions around hybrid cloud. In "Azure Local and Landing Zones: How to Build Hybrid Cloud the Right Way with Christoffer Klarskov Jakobsen [MVP]", Mirko Peters talks with Microsoft MVP Christoffer Klarskov Jakobsen about making Azure Local part of a broader Azure architecture instead of an isolated on-premises platform. Azure Arc is one of the topics alongside Azure Local, Azure Landing Zones, governance, Infrastructure as Code, Bicep, Azure DevOps and modernization. Azure Local is described there as combining familiar infrastructure technologies with Azure-based management, governance and security, with workloads such as virtual machines running locally while the environment stays connected to Azure.

For operational technology and industrial scenarios, the episode "Azure IoT Operations at Scale: Managing Hundreds of Sites With Azure Arc" looks at how Azure Arc supports managing many locations. The discussion covers architecture, rollout, configuration management and monitoring across sites, with the aim of standardizing deployments and keeping control as the footprint grows. It is aimed at industrial IoT architects, platform engineers and OT/IT teams.

Azure Arc is also mentioned in the context of automation. The episode "Secure Azure Automation with Ahmed Uzejnovic [MVP]" lists integrating Azure Arc among its recommendations for consistent management across hybrid cloud environments, alongside regularly reviewing permissions, automating identity management tasks and monitoring automation logs.

Taken together, the episodes position Azure Arc as the connecting layer between Azure and infrastructure that lives elsewhere. Decisions around it usually concern which resources to onboard, which policies and security rules should apply to them, and how to roll the same configuration out across many sites or machines. Further technical detail is available in the official Microsoft documentation overview for Azure Arc.

azure-artifacts.desc: Azure Artifacts is the Azure DevOps package management service for hosting private NuGet, npm, Maven, Python and Universal package feeds, with support for upstream sources.

faq.a: Azure Artifacts is the package management service in Azure DevOps. It hosts private feeds for NuGet, npm, Maven, Python and Universal packages.
faq.q: What is Azure Artifacts?

faq.a: It supports NuGet, npm, Maven, Python and Universal packages.
faq.q: Which package types does Azure Artifacts support?

faq.a: Yes. Feeds in Azure Artifacts can proxy public upstream sources, so public packages can be accessed through the same feed as private ones.
faq.q: Can Azure Artifacts use public package sources?

azure-artifacts.long:
Azure Artifacts is the package management service within Azure DevOps. It hosts private feeds for several package types: NuGet, npm, Maven, Python and Universal packages. Teams use it to publish and consume the packages their own code produces, and to keep those packages in a controlled location instead of distributing them informally.

A feed in Azure Artifacts can also proxy public upstream sources. This means that packages from public registries can be reached through the same feed that holds a team's private packages, giving developers a single source to configure in their build and development tools.

Azure Artifacts is one of the services that make up Azure DevOps, alongside the other components used to plan, build and release software. It is typically referenced when discussing how dependencies and build outputs are stored and shared in a delivery pipeline.

On M365.FM, Azure Artifacts appears in the context of Azure DevOps topics. The episode "Azure DevOps - Simply Explained" covers Azure DevOps as a whole, and "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD" looks at how Azure DevOps compares with GitHub for continuous integration and delivery with Microsoft Fabric. Official documentation for getting started with the service is available on Microsoft Learn.

azure-automation.desc: Azure Automation is Microsoft's cloud-based service for automating repetitive operational tasks across Azure, on-premises and other cloud environments.

faq.a: It is used to automate repetitive operational tasks across Azure, on-premises environments and other clouds, using runbooks, configuration management and update management. The episodes cite examples such as device cleanup, patching and removing orphaned Azure resources.
faq.q: What is Azure Automation used for?

faq.a: The episodes recommend avoiding hard-coded credentials, using managed identities instead of outdated service accounts, and applying version control, testing, logging, approval workflows and governance to automation.
faq.q: What security practices do the episodes recommend for Azure Automation?

faq.a: The episodes mention Azure Functions, Microsoft Graph, Logic Apps, Azure Resource Graph, Azure Policy, Log Analytics, Microsoft Intune and managed identities, depending on the scenario.
faq.q: Which services are commonly combined with Azure Automation?

azure-automation.long:
Azure Automation is a cloud-based automation service developed by Microsoft and part of Microsoft Azure. It supports process automation with runbooks, configuration management and update management across Azure and on-premises environments. The M365.FM episode "Azure Automation - Simply Explained" describes it as a service that helps organizations automate repetitive, time-consuming and error-prone operational tasks, including in environments that span other cloud platforms.

The main purpose of the service is to replace manual administration with automated workflows. According to the episode, IT teams that build such workflows can improve consistency, reduce operational costs and free up time for more valuable work. Typical use cases covered in the episodes include device cleanup, patch management, reporting and the removal of unused cloud resources. The official documentation for the service is published on Microsoft Learn.

In practice, work with Azure Automation starts with an Automation account. The episode "PowerShell Automation for Azure and Microsoft 365 with Matthew Dowst [MVP]" walks through creating and configuring Azure Automation accounts as the foundation for automating tasks. It says the account needs the right structure and permissions so that workflows run reliably, and it stresses avoiding hard-coded credentials. The episode also frames PowerShell as the scripting layer used to automate both Azure and Microsoft 365 tasks.

Security is a recurring theme. The episode "Secure Azure Automation with Ahmed Uzejnovic [MVP]" argues that automation is no longer optional in large Microsoft cloud environments, but that poorly designed automation can become a major attack surface. It points out that many companies still rely on outdated service accounts, and it describes automation as an engineering discipline that calls for version control, testing, logging, approval workflows and governance. According to the episode, reusable automation frameworks are safer and more scalable than one-off administrative scripts.

Azure Automation is often combined with other services. In "Automate Intune Device Cleanup with Azure Automation", the service is paired with Microsoft Intune, Azure Functions, Microsoft Graph, managed identities and Log Analytics. The episode presents this combination as a way to address configuration drift, stale devices and manual reporting, and to avoid granting global administrator rights for everything. It also mentions keeping synchronization and cleanup in Microsoft Entra ID as part of a secure environment.

Cost control is another application. The episode "Build an Automated Azure Cleanup Engine to Reduce Cloud Waste" describes orphaned Azure resources that silently increase monthly bills. It outlines how Azure Automation, Azure Functions, Azure Resource Graph, Logic Apps, tagging strategies and Azure Policy can be used to detect and clean up such resources continuously. The episode adds that approval workflows, lifecycle management, reporting and governance practices help ensure that automated cleanup does not affect production workloads.

Taken together, the episodes position Azure Automation as a building block for operations that must be repeatable and controlled. Decisions around it typically concern which identity the automation runs under, how credentials are handled, how changes are reviewed and logged, and which companion Azure services handle detection, orchestration or reporting.

azure-automation-state-configuration.desc: Azure Automation State Configuration is a PowerShell Desired State Configuration (DSC) based service that keeps machines in a defined state and reports compliance.

faq.a: It is a configuration management service based on PowerShell Desired State Configuration (DSC). It keeps machines in a defined desired state and reports their compliance.
faq.q: What is Azure Automation State Configuration?

faq.a: Microsoft is moving this capability to Azure Machine Configuration. The Microsoft Learn documentation should be checked for current details on the transition.
faq.q: Is Azure Automation State Configuration being replaced?

faq.a: It is based on PowerShell Desired State Configuration (DSC), which describes the intended configuration of a machine and enforces it.
faq.q: What technology is Azure Automation State Configuration based on?

azure-automation-state-configuration.long:
Azure Automation State Configuration is a configuration management service built on PowerShell Desired State Configuration (DSC). It is used to define how machines should be configured and to keep them in that defined desired state over time.

Beyond applying configurations, the service reports on compliance, showing whether managed machines match the state that was declared for them. This makes it relevant for administrators who want a consistent, auditable configuration baseline across their systems.

Microsoft is moving this capability to Azure Machine Configuration. Anyone evaluating or maintaining solutions built on Azure Automation State Configuration should therefore review the current Microsoft documentation for the latest guidance on the transition.

No episodes on M365.FM currently reference Azure Automation State Configuration, and no related topics are linked to this entry at present. Official details are available in the Microsoft Learn documentation for the Azure Automation DSC overview.

azure-autoscale.desc: Azure Autoscale is a Microsoft Azure capability that automatically adds or removes instances based on metric rules, schedules or predictive patterns within set limits.

faq.a: Azure Autoscale automatically adds or removes instances, for example in a virtual machine scale set. It does this based on metric rules, schedules or predictive patterns.
faq.q: What does Azure Autoscale do?

faq.a: No. Scaling takes place within a defined minimum and maximum, which sets the lower and upper bounds for the number of instances.
faq.q: Can Azure Autoscale add an unlimited number of instances?

faq.a: Azure Autoscale is a capability of Microsoft Azure, which is its broader parent topic.
faq.q: How does Azure Autoscale relate to Microsoft Azure?

azure-autoscale.long:
Azure Autoscale is a capability of Microsoft Azure that adjusts the number of running instances automatically. A common example is a virtual machine scale set, where instances are added or removed depending on demand rather than being managed by hand.

Scaling decisions can be driven by metric rules, by schedules or by predictive patterns. Every configuration operates within a defined minimum and maximum, which bounds how few or how many instances can run at any time. This keeps capacity aligned with workload while staying inside the limits that were set.

Azure Autoscale sits under the broader topic of Microsoft Azure. It is relevant for anyone sizing and operating Azure-hosted workloads where load varies over time and where fixed capacity would either leave resources idle or fall short at peak demand.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity, and no further product details are available in the source facts beyond this description.

azure-backup.desc: Azure Backup is Microsoft's managed cloud backup service within Microsoft Azure, protecting Azure and hybrid workloads with policy-based retention in a vault.

faq.a: According to the facts, Azure Backup protects Azure VMs, databases, file shares, blobs, disks and on-premises servers, storing recovery points in a vault with policy-based retention.
faq.q: What does Azure Backup protect?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Site Recovery - Simply Explained" says Azure Backup focuses on protecting data and restoring files or workloads after data loss, while Azure Site Recovery keeps applications running by orchestrating disaster recovery during infrastructure failures.
faq.q: What is the difference between Azure Backup and Azure Site Recovery?

faq.a: The episode "Harden Azure Backup with Soft Delete, MUA, and Vault Lock" says they are not, because an over-privileged identity can delete items or purge soft-deleted points. It recommends least privilege and hardening controls such as soft delete, MUA and vault lock.
faq.q: Are Azure backups safe by default?

azure-backup.long:
Azure Backup is Microsoft's native, managed cloud backup service and part of Microsoft Azure. It protects Azure virtual machines, databases, file shares, blobs, disks and on-premises servers by storing recovery points in a vault, with retention controlled through policies. Instead of operating their own backup infrastructure, organizations manage protection directly from Azure, where backup is automated, secured and scaled by the platform.

The service is used to guard against accidental deletion, hardware failures, ransomware and disasters. The episode "Azure Backup - Simply Explained" describes it as the native service for protecting Azure and hybrid workloads, covering virtual machines, databases, Azure Files and many other workloads. The central building blocks are the vault, which holds the recovery points, and the policy, which defines how long those recovery points are kept. A typical workflow is to assign a workload to a vault, apply a retention policy, and then monitor the resulting backup jobs and restore points.

A recurring theme in the M365.FM episodes is that having a backup does not by itself mean the data is safe. The episode "Harden Azure Backup with Soft Delete, MUA, and Vault Lock" argues that Azure backups are not safe by default. It describes attack paths in which a single over-privileged identity, such as compromised automation, a shadow admin, or a broad Contributor or Owner role, can delete backup items, purge soft-deleted recovery points and reduce retention settings, even when the backups are meant to be immutable. The episode recommends following the principle of least privilege, limiting user permissions, reviewing permissions regularly and removing unnecessary Owner permissions. Its title also points to three hardening controls: soft delete, multi-user authorization (MUA) and vault lock.

Operational discipline is the second theme. The episode "Hidden Microsoft 365 and Azure Cloud Security Risks" lists common backup problems: vaults that are in the wrong location or lack the needed permissions, and database applications that do not restore properly when the wrong backup strategy is used. Its advice is to check backup logs, set up alerts for failed jobs and use Azure-native tools such as Azure Backup to automate monitoring and reporting. It also recommends assigning clear responsibility for backup monitoring, so that someone is accountable for noticing failures, and holding regular reviews to find problems before they become disasters. The same episode stresses that disaster recovery plans should be tested often, since plans that look sound on paper can fail in real emergencies.

Azure Backup is closely related to, but distinct from, Azure Site Recovery. The episode "Azure Site Recovery - Simply Explained" explains that Azure Backup focuses on protecting data and restoring files or workloads after data loss, whereas Azure Site Recovery is designed to keep applications running by orchestrating disaster recovery and business continuity during infrastructure failures. According to the episode, understanding when to use each service, or both together, is essential for building resilient cloud architectures.

Azure Backup also appears in the context of file storage. The episode "Azure Files - Simply Explained" notes that Azure Files integrates with Azure Backup, alongside Azure Virtual Desktop, FSLogix and hybrid Windows Server environments, and covers snapshots and backups among its key concepts. For teams moving file servers to Azure or storing user profiles in Azure Files, Azure Backup is the service that provides the recovery layer for those shares.

In practice, decisions around Azure Backup come down to which workloads to place in which vault, how retention policies should be set, who is allowed to modify or delete protected items, and how failures are detected and acted on. The episodes together suggest treating backup as both a data protection feature and a security-sensitive resource that needs access control, monitoring and regular restore testing.

azure-backup-soft-delete.desc: Soft delete for Azure Backup keeps deleted backup items and recovery points in a soft-deleted state for a retention period, so they can be restored instead of lost.
azure-backup-soft-delete.long:
Soft delete for Azure Backup is a protection feature of Azure Backup. When a backup item or its recovery points are deleted, they are not removed immediately. Instead, they remain in a soft-deleted state for a defined retention period, which allows them to be restored rather than being lost right away.

The feature is used as a safeguard against accidental or unwanted deletion of backup data. Because deleted items stay recoverable during the retention period, an administrator can bring back backup items and recovery points that were removed by mistake. This supports data-protection and recovery planning for workloads that rely on Azure Backup.

The official Microsoft documentation describes an enhanced soft delete capability for Azure Backup. Details such as supported workloads, configurable retention periods, and how to enable or disable the setting are covered there and are not specified here.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic, and no related entities have been recorded for it yet.

azure-bastion.desc: Azure Bastion is a managed Microsoft Azure service for secure RDP and SSH access to virtual machines through the Azure portal, without exposing public IP addresses.

faq.a: Azure Bastion provides secure RDP and SSH access to Azure virtual machines through the Azure portal. It avoids exposing public IP addresses and open management ports on the machines.
faq.q: What is Azure Bastion used for?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Azure Bastion - Simply Explained", it replaces opened RDP or SSH ports with browser-based access through the Azure portal. This keeps virtual machines off the public internet.
faq.q: How does Azure Bastion reduce the attack surface?

faq.a: Azure Bastion integrates with Azure Virtual Network and is named alongside Azure Firewall in a layered security strategy. Azure Firewall provides centralized network protection, while Azure Bastion handles secure administrative access.
faq.q: How does Azure Bastion relate to Azure Firewall and Azure Virtual Network?

azure-bastion.long:
Azure Bastion is a managed remote access service in Microsoft Azure that lets administrators connect to Azure virtual machines over RDP and SSH without exposing those machines to the public internet. It is developed by Microsoft, is part of Microsoft Azure, and is classified as both a Microsoft tool and an identity and security tool. Official documentation is available in the Microsoft Learn section for Azure Bastion.

The core idea is to remove the need to open RDP or SSH ports on virtual machines. Instead of assigning public IP addresses and publishing management ports, access runs through the Azure portal, where the connection is provided in the browser. According to the M365.FM episode "Azure Bastion - Simply Explained", this significantly reduces the attack surface while improving security and simplifying remote administration. Because the service is managed, there is no separate jump host that has to be built, patched and hardened by the customer, which is the situation Azure Bastion is meant to address.

In practice, Azure Bastion is used wherever virtual machines need administrative access but should remain unreachable from the internet. Typical situations include managing Windows machines over RDP and Linux machines over SSH in a private network, supporting operations teams that would otherwise rely on public management endpoints, and reducing exposure in hybrid or multi-region environments. The main design decision is whether administrators connect through the portal-based service or keep traditional direct connectivity; the episodes frame the portal-based path as the way to avoid public IP exposure on the virtual machines themselves.

Azure Bastion sits within a wider networking and security architecture. The episode "Azure Virtual Network - Simply Explained" lists Azure Bastion among the services that integrate with Azure Virtual Network, alongside Azure VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, Azure Firewall, Load Balancer, Private Link and Azure Kubernetes Service. Virtual networks, subnets, route tables, network security groups, VNet peering, DNS and hybrid connectivity form the environment in which the service operates, so understanding how a VNet is designed and structured is a prerequisite for placing remote access correctly.

The episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" describes how Azure Firewall integrates with Azure Bastion, Azure Virtual WAN, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor and Azure Policy to create a layered security strategy for enterprise workloads. In that picture, Azure Firewall provides centralized network protection, for example controlling outbound internet access and filtering application traffic, while Azure Bastion covers the specific problem of secure administrative access to virtual machines. The two address different layers rather than replacing each other.

In the episode "Secure Azure Networking with Rex de Koning [MVP-MCT]", Azure Bastion appears as part of a set of recommendations for securing Azure networking. The episode advises using it for secure remote access without exposing public IPs, noting that it allows connections to virtual machines directly through the Azure portal. It places this next to related measures: enabling just-in-time VM access to limit the time that virtual machines are accessible, enabling DDoS protection to preserve availability for internet-facing workloads, and deploying virtual network appliances for protection at higher OSI layers. Taken together, the episodes treat Azure Bastion as one building block of a defense-in-depth approach rather than a standalone security solution.

azure-blob-storage.desc: Azure Blob Storage is Microsoft's object storage service for unstructured data, with hot, cool, cold and archive access tiers that balance storage cost against access cost.

faq.a: It stores unstructured data such as images, videos, documents, backups, logs and application files as blobs inside containers, accessible via REST APIs or Azure SDKs.
faq.q: What is Azure Blob Storage used for?

faq.a: The documentation describes hot, cool, cold and archive tiers. Cooler tiers lower storage charges but raise access costs, and the archive tier adds rehydration delays before data can be read.
faq.q: What are the access tiers in Azure Blob Storage?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode on Azure Disk Storage, Blob Storage stores files and objects, while Azure Disks provide persistent block storage that works like the hard drives of Azure Virtual Machines.
faq.q: How does Azure Blob Storage differ from Azure Disk Storage?

azure-blob-storage.long:
Azure Blob Storage is Microsoft's scalable object storage service for unstructured data such as images, videos, documents, backups, logs and application files. It is part of Microsoft Azure. Instead of a traditional file system, data is stored as objects called blobs inside containers. Blobs are accessible from anywhere through REST APIs or the Azure SDKs, which is how applications, scripts and other services typically read and write the data.

The service is organised under an Azure storage account. The M365.FM episode "Azure Storage Accounts - Simply Explained" describes Blob Storage as designed for unstructured data and lists scalability among its key features, noting that large amounts of data can be stored without worrying about capacity limits. The same episode mentions a choice of data replication options and describes encryption of data in transit together with role-based access control (RBAC) to enforce least privilege and support compliance requirements.

A central design decision with Azure Blob Storage is the access tier. The official documentation describes hot, cool, cold and archive tiers that trade lower storage charges for higher access costs or, in the case of the archive tier, rehydration delays. In practice this means that data accessed often is suited to a warmer tier, while data that is rarely read can be placed in a cooler tier to reduce storage charges. Data in the archive tier cannot be read immediately and must first be rehydrated, so the tier choice depends on how quickly and how often the data needs to be retrieved. Choosing a tier is therefore a decision about expected access patterns as much as about price.

The episode "Azure Blob Storage - Simply Explained", part of the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets series, introduces the service as highly durable, cost-effective and reachable via REST APIs or Azure SDKs, and frames the blob-and-container model as the alternative to a conventional file system. It is a good starting point for the basic vocabulary of objects, containers and API-based access.

Blob Storage also appears in a Microsoft 365 context. In "Archive Inactive SharePoint Sites with Azure Blob Storage", the episode argues that SharePoint accumulates duplicates, forgotten drafts and many "final final V2" files, which it describes as a relevance problem rather than only a storage problem, affecting search results and Copilot answers. In that discussion, Azure Blob Storage serves as a destination for archiving inactive content, and the episode points to its security features, including encryption at rest and access controls, as protection for sensitive information.

Blob Storage is distinct from other Azure storage offerings. The episode "Azure Disk Storage - Simply Explained" contrasts it with Azure Disk Storage: blobs store files and objects, whereas Azure Disks provide persistent block storage that acts like the physical hard drives of Azure Virtual Machines, holding the operating system, applications and data. Knowing this difference helps when deciding whether a workload needs object storage or VM disks.

Blob Storage can also act as a source of events. In "Event Grid - Simply Explained", Azure Blob Storage is named as an example of an event publisher that sends events to Event Grid. Those events can then be routed through topics and subscriptions to event handlers such as Azure Functions or Logic Apps, which allows processing to be triggered when something happens to stored data.

azure-boards.desc: Azure Boards is the Azure DevOps service for planning and tracking work with work items, backlogs, sprints, queries, dashboards and Kanban boards.

faq.a: Azure Boards is the Azure DevOps service for planning and tracking work. It provides work items, backlogs, sprints, queries, dashboards and Kanban boards so teams can organize and follow their tasks.
faq.q: What is Azure Boards used for?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure DevOps - Simply Explained", Azure Boards works together with Repos, Pipelines, Test Plans and Artifacts. Azure Boards handles planning and tracking, while the other services cover source control, automation, testing and packages.
faq.q: How does Azure Boards relate to other Azure DevOps services?

faq.a: The episode "Monitor Compliance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud" mentions using Azure Boards to track vulnerabilities and manage them as backlog items, supporting regular reviews between development and security teams.
faq.q: Can Azure Boards be used for security findings?

azure-boards.long:
Azure Boards is the service within Azure DevOps that teams use to plan, organize and track work. It is built around work items, which represent the units of work a team manages, and offers backlogs, sprints, queries, dashboards and Kanban boards as the main ways to view and organize that work. The product is listed as part of Microsoft Azure and is documented in Microsoft's Azure DevOps documentation under the heading "What is Azure Boards?".

The purpose of Azure Boards is to give software teams a single place to see what needs to be done, who is working on it and how far along it is. Work items can be arranged in a backlog, pulled into sprints for time-boxed iterations, and moved across a Kanban board to show status. Queries allow teams to filter and list work items according to chosen criteria, while dashboards bring selected information together in one view. Together these elements support both planning at the start of a cycle and day-to-day tracking while work is in progress.

Azure Boards is one of several services that make up Azure DevOps. The episode "Azure DevOps - Simply Explained" describes how Azure Boards, Repos, Pipelines, Test Plans and Artifacts work together to support modern software development. In that picture, Azure Boards covers the planning and tracking side, while the other services address source control, build and release automation, testing and package management. The episode presents these pieces in plain language for both technical and business audiences, using concepts such as continuous integration, continuous deployment, Git repositories, YAML pipelines and automated testing.

The comparison between Azure DevOps and GitHub is another place where Azure Boards appears. The episode "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD" describes Azure DevOps as a suite of developer tools that includes Azure Boards, Pipelines, Repos, Test Plans and artifact management, with a focus on enterprise project management and CI/CD. GitHub, in contrast, is characterized in that episode as a Git-first platform centered on repositories, pull requests and the developer community. The episode notes that Azure DevOps is often preferred where integrated work item tracking is wanted, which is the area Azure Boards covers.

Azure Boards also shows up in security and compliance workflows. The episode "Monitor Compliance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud" lists a strategy of regularly reviewing cloud security posture management findings and using tools like Azure Boards to track vulnerabilities and manage them as backlog items. In this use, findings become tracked work, and regular reviews with development and security teams help prioritize and fix issues. The episode ties this to shared ownership between development, security and operations, and to feedback loops that keep remediation visible.

In practice, decisions around Azure Boards usually concern how a team wants to structure its work: whether to organize around a backlog and sprints, a continuous Kanban flow, or both, and how to use queries and dashboards to keep stakeholders informed. Because Azure Boards belongs to the wider Azure DevOps suite, teams also weigh whether to keep planning, code and pipelines in one platform or to combine Azure DevOps services with other tools, as the GitHub comparison episode discusses. The facts available here do not specify licensing, pricing or detailed feature configuration, so those details should be checked in the official documentation.

azure-bot-service.desc: Azure Bot Service is a Microsoft Azure service for building and deploying intelligent bots, used for scenarios such as customer support and appointment scheduling.

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure AI Infrastructure Architecture for C-Level Leaders", it is used to build and deploy intelligent bots, with examples such as a customer support bot, appointment scheduling and employee onboarding.
faq.q: What is Azure Bot Service used for?

faq.a: The episode "Production AI Agents with Microsoft Foundry and Edgar McOchieng [MVP]" names it as the way to deploy an agent after testing, followed by ongoing monitoring with dashboards and alerts.
faq.q: How does Azure Bot Service relate to production AI agents?

faq.a: The episode "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform" lists a range of free to $0.50 per 1,000 messages and says the free tier covers moderate usage.
faq.q: What does Azure Bot Service cost?

azure-bot-service.long:
Azure Bot Service is a service within Microsoft Azure for building and deploying intelligent bots. In the M365.FM episodes it appears as one building block in a wider set of Azure AI and application services, rather than as a stand-alone topic. The sources describe it as a way to put conversational agents into production and to connect them with other Microsoft services.

The episode "Azure AI Infrastructure Architecture for C-Level Leaders" lists Azure Bot Service in a table of Azure AI services next to Azure Cognitive Services, Azure Cognitive Search, Azure Document Intelligence and Azure Video Indexer. There it is described as the service to build and deploy intelligent bots, with typical use cases named as a customer support bot, appointment scheduling and employee onboarding. This framing positions the service as a business-facing capability that executives and architects can map to concrete scenarios, in the same way that the neighboring services are mapped to tasks such as search, document extraction or video analysis.

The episode "Power Platform - Simply Explained" mentions Azure Bot Service in the context of Copilot Studio. It names the service among the Microsoft services that connect with Copilot Studio, alongside Azure OpenAI Studio and Azure Cognitive Services, while Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Outlook, Microsoft Loop, Microsoft Word and Microsoft PowerPoint are listed as the Microsoft 365 applications it works with. The episode presents these connections as part of a cohesive user experience and as a way to create a more dynamic and responsive environment for users.

In "Production AI Agents with Microsoft Foundry and Edgar McOchieng [MVP]", Azure Bot Service is named as the deployment step. After an agent has been tested, the episode says to deploy it using Azure Bot Service and then keep monitoring its performance, using dashboards and alerts to track how well it works. The testing advice in the same episode is to compare the agent's answers with what is expected and to measure results with both numbers and feedback, so that quality standards and task coverage can be checked before and after release. The episode also lists scaling and productionization, enterprise governance and compliance, and a unified control plane as aspects of running agents in production.

Cost is addressed in the episode "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform". Its cost table gives Azure Bot Service a range of free to $0.50 per 1,000 messages and notes that the free tier covers moderate usage. By comparison, the same table shows Azure OpenAI Service with GPT-4o at $50 to $800 per month, scaling with token volume, and Azure Cognitive Search at $73 to $300 or more, depending on index size and queries. The episode frames these figures as typical ranges and recommends controlling costs by monitoring idle resources and scheduling workloads during low-usage periods.

Taken together, the episodes treat Azure Bot Service as the layer that makes a bot or agent available to users, while other services supply language models, search, document processing or low-code tooling. Decisions around it typically involve which scenario the bot serves, how it is tested, how it is monitored after deployment and how message volume affects cost. The sources do not describe the service's internal architecture, supported channels or versions, so those details are outside what these episodes cover.

azure-chaos-studio.desc: Azure Chaos Studio is Microsoft's managed chaos engineering service for injecting controlled faults into Azure workloads to test how applications withstand failures.

faq.a: Azure Chaos Studio is Microsoft's managed chaos engineering service within Microsoft Azure. It supports controlled fault injection so teams can test how their applications withstand outages and failures.
faq.q: What is Azure Chaos Studio?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Chaos Studio - Simply Explained", the goal is to build more resilient cloud applications by simulating failures before they happen for real. It works like a fire drill, checking that applications, monitoring and recovery processes are ready.
faq.q: Why would an organization use chaos engineering on Azure?

faq.a: The official documentation on Microsoft Learn is the reference for technical details. The M365.FM episodes cover the concept and its role in resilience and architecture testing at an overview level.
faq.q: Where can technical details about Azure Chaos Studio be found?

azure-chaos-studio.long:
Azure Chaos Studio is a managed service from Microsoft for chaos engineering, part of Microsoft Azure. It allows teams to run controlled fault injection against their cloud workloads in order to test how applications and supporting systems behave when something goes wrong. The idea is to find weaknesses on purpose and under supervision, rather than waiting for a real outage to expose them. The service is classed as a Microsoft tool and sits within the broader Azure platform.

Chaos engineering is the practice behind the product. Instead of assuming that a design is resilient because it looks redundant on paper, teams deliberately create disruptions and observe the outcome. The episode "Azure Chaos Studio - Simply Explained" describes this with the image of a fire drill for an Azure environment: failures are practiced in a safe, controlled way so that applications, monitoring and recovery processes are ready when a real incident occurs. The episode presents the service as a way to build more resilient cloud applications by safely simulating failures before they happen in the real world.

In practice, the service is used when an organization wants evidence about resilience instead of assumptions. Typical questions include whether an application keeps working when part of its environment is disrupted, whether monitoring and alerting notice the problem, and whether recovery steps work as intended. The sources provided describe the purpose of the service at this level and do not go into individual fault types, experiment design or configuration details. For those, the official documentation published by Microsoft on Microsoft Learn is the reference.

The topic also appears in the context of cost and architecture decisions. The episode "Stop Azure Cost Entropy with Ownership and Budget Controls" mentions Azure Chaos Studio as one of the tools to use when testing and adapting an architecture to business needs. In that episode it appears alongside advice such as governance guardrails, right-sizing, efficient networking, reservations and forecasting, and a culture of accountability. Testing resilience is presented there as part of keeping an Azure architecture deliberate and predictable rather than accidental.

Azure Chaos Studio is also listed among related episodes about automation and infrastructure. The episode "Frictionless Automation Can Digitize Business Chaos" recommends it together with other Azure automation topics, including Azure Automation, a comparison of PowerShell and Bicep for Azure infrastructure automation, and Microsoft Graph security automation for Microsoft 365. This grouping reflects that resilience testing is often considered alongside how environments are built and operated.

For readers deciding whether the service fits their situation, the main considerations drawn from the sources are the following. The service targets organizations running workloads on Azure that want to validate resilience before real failures occur. It works through intentional, controlled disruption, which implies that experiments should be planned and observed rather than run casually. The outcome of such tests is information about how systems, monitoring and recovery processes respond, which can then feed back into architecture and operational decisions. Further technical specifics, such as supported targets or pricing, are not covered in the material available here and should be checked in the official Azure Chaos Studio documentation.

azure-cli.desc: Azure CLI is the Azure command-line tool for signing in and for creating and managing Azure resources from a terminal, including inside WSL.

faq.a: Azure CLI is used to sign in to Azure and to create and manage Azure resources from a terminal, including inside WSL. It supports both quick one-off commands and scripted automation.
faq.q: What is Azure CLI used for?

faq.a: The episodes describe Azure CLI as the tool used to validate and deploy ARM templates and Bicep files. One episode gives the az deployment group create command with a template file and a resource group as the way to deploy a Bicep file.
faq.q: How does Azure CLI relate to Bicep and ARM templates?

faq.a: The episode "Azure CLI vs PowerShell: Which Should You Use?" compares the two in scripting, automation and one-off commands and provides a decision checklist. Another episode lists Azure CLI and the Azure PowerShell module as alternatives for managing resources and deploying Bicep files.
faq.q: Should Azure CLI or PowerShell be used for Azure work?

azure-cli.long:
Azure CLI is a command-line tool for working with Microsoft Azure. It is used to sign in to Azure and to create and manage Azure resources from a terminal, and it can also be used inside WSL. As a component of Microsoft Azure, it gives administrators and developers a text-based way to carry out tasks that would otherwise be done in a graphical portal, which makes those tasks easy to repeat and to script.

In practice, Azure CLI covers two broad kinds of work. The first is quick, one-off commands, such as signing in or checking and changing a single resource. The second is scripting and automation, where the same commands are combined into repeatable procedures. The M365.FM episode "Azure CLI vs PowerShell: Which Should You Use?" compares the tool with PowerShell along exactly these lines. According to its description, the episode looks at how each option performs in scripting, automation and quick one-off commands, and it includes live demos, a look at performance under load, error handling and reliability, and experiences from cloud engineers. It also touches on migrations, cross-platform usage and common mistakes, and ends with a practical decision checklist for choosing between the two tools.

Azure CLI also appears regularly in infrastructure-as-code workflows. The episode "Bicep - Simply Explained" describes a sequence in which the Bicep CLI is installed locally, .bicep files are authored to define Azure resources, and those files are compiled into ARM templates. Deployment then uses Azure CLI. The episode gives the command az deployment group create with a template file and a resource group name as the way to deploy a Bicep file directly, noting that the simplified syntax and Azure integration help manage resources more effectively.

The same pattern shows up for ARM templates. In "ARM Templates - Simply Explained", Azure CLI is listed among the recommended tools for setting up an environment, described as a command-line interface for validating and deploying ARM templates. It is named alongside Visual Studio Code, which offers extensions for Azure, and the ARM template test toolkit, which checks templates against best practices and provides feedback on compliance. In this setup, Azure CLI is the part that sends the finished template to Azure.

The episode "Azure Bicep Fundamentals for Production Projects" treats Azure CLI as one of two interchangeable options for the deployment side of the setup. Its setup steps include installing Azure Bicep to compile Bicep files into ARM templates, installing either Azure CLI or the Azure PowerShell module to manage Azure resources and deploy Bicep files, and installing Visual Studio Code with the Bicep extension. This reflects a common decision: whether to standardize on Azure CLI or on PowerShell for management and deployment tasks, which is the question the dedicated comparison episode addresses.

Finally, "Bicep vs ARM Templates vs Terraform for Azure" mentions Azure CLI in the context of tooling support. The episode says that integration with Visual Studio Code and Azure CLI provides features such as linting and IntelliSense for Bicep, alongside a simplified syntax, modular and reusable code, and improved maintainability compared with ARM templates.

Taken together, the episodes position Azure CLI as the command-line layer used for sign-in, deployment and day-to-day resource management in Azure, usable on its own for scripts and ad hoc commands and as the deployment tool for Bicep and ARM template projects.

azure-compute-fleet.desc: Azure Compute Fleet is an Azure service that provisions large pools of virtual machines in one request, mixing several VM sizes with Spot and standard pricing.

faq.a: Azure Compute Fleet is an Azure service that provisions large pools of virtual machines in one request by mixing several acceptable VM sizes and Spot and standard pricing models. A single API call can deploy up to 10,000 VMs.
faq.q: What is Azure Compute Fleet?

faq.a: In managed mode the fleet stays in place and maintains capacity. In launch mode, which is in preview, the VMs are provisioned in one request and the fleet object is deleted afterward. The mode is chosen at creation and cannot be changed.
faq.q: What is the difference between managed mode and launch mode?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn there is no extra fee for the service; only the VMs are billed, and normal VM and vCPU quotas still apply.
faq.q: Does Azure Compute Fleet cost extra?

azure-compute-fleet.long:
Azure Compute Fleet is a service within Microsoft Azure that provisions large pools of virtual machine capacity through a single request. Instead of choosing one exact VM size, a fleet can combine several acceptable VM sizes and mix Spot and standard (on-demand) pricing models. Microsoft Learn describes it as a building block that gives accelerated access to Azure capacity in a region by launching a mix of virtual machines chosen for lowest price and highest capacity.

The service addresses a scale problem. Creating one virtual machine is straightforward, but when a workload suddenly needs hundreds or thousands of workers, tying the request to one VM size becomes a limitation. The selected size may not have enough capacity in the preferred region, another size may work at a different price, and Spot VMs can reduce costs but can be reclaimed by Azure. Managing all of those options by hand quickly becomes difficult. Azure Compute Fleet moves that decision-making into the request itself.

According to the documentation, a single API call can deploy up to 10,000 VMs. A fleet can combine Spot and standard VMs and different pricing models such as reserved instances, savings plans, Spot and pay-as-you-go. Allocation strategies for standard and Spot VMs can optimize for cost, capacity or both, and evicted Spot VMs are replaced automatically. Attribute-based VM selection and multi-region distribution are listed as preview features, and a fleet can span up to three regions.

Two modes exist, and the mode is chosen at creation and cannot be changed later. In managed mode, the fleet stays in place and maintains the desired capacity. In launch mode, which is in preview, the VMs are provisioned in one request and the fleet object is then deleted, leaving the VMs to the customer or to an orchestrator. The choice depends on whether the fleet itself should keep managing capacity or whether another system takes over after provisioning.

Named workloads in the documentation include stateless web services, big data clusters, CI pipelines, risk analysis and rendering. These are typically jobs that can run on interchangeable workers and tolerate some VMs being replaced. Normal VM and vCPU quotas still apply, so quota planning remains part of using the service. There is no extra fee for Azure Compute Fleet itself; only the VMs are billed.

The documentation also draws a boundary with virtual machine scale sets. A scale set remains the better fit for long-running services that need autoscaling and rolling updates, while Azure Compute Fleet is aimed at obtaining large amounts of capacity quickly across sizes and pricing models.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Compute Fleet – Simply Explained" (2026-08-10) introduces the service as designed for a very different scale of compute problem. It describes the situation in which a workload suddenly needs hundreds or thousands of workers and choosing one exact VM size becomes a major limitation, noting that capacity, pricing and Spot reclaim risk all complicate a manual approach.

azure-compute-gallery.desc: Azure Compute Gallery is a library in Microsoft Azure that organizes approved virtual machine images into definitions and versions and replicates them to regions.

faq.a: It is used to store, organize and share approved virtual machine images and VM applications, with versioning, grouping and replication of image versions to the Azure regions where they are needed.
faq.q: What is Azure Compute Gallery used for?

faq.a: According to the documentation, the gallery itself is free. Storage for each replica and network egress are billed, so the number of replicas and replicated versions affects cost.
faq.q: Does Azure Compute Gallery cost money?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Image Builder - Simply Explained" notes that Azure Image Builder can use images stored in Azure Compute Gallery as a starting point, so images need not be rebuilt from scratch when something changes.
faq.q: How does Azure Compute Gallery relate to Azure Image Builder?

azure-compute-gallery.long:
Azure Compute Gallery is a service in Microsoft Azure that gives structure and organization to resources such as virtual machine images and VM applications. It works as a library for approved images: instead of leaving images scattered across subscriptions and regions, a team keeps them in one gallery, groups them logically, and tracks changes through versions. Official documentation describes global replication, versioning and grouping as its core capabilities.

The service is built from three main parts. The gallery is the top-level container. Inside it, image definitions group related images, and each definition contains image versions. The image versions are the items that are replicated to target regions, so that virtual machines can be created from an image close to where the workload runs. In regions that offer availability zones, zone-redundant storage is available for the stored images. VM applications are handled as separate resources, which means that changing an application does not require building a new image.

Sharing is another central function. A gallery can be shared with subscriptions, with tenants, or with a community. The documentation recommends sharing at the gallery level rather than for single image versions, which keeps access management simpler. This makes the gallery useful for organizations that maintain a standard set of images for many teams or environments.

Several operational points matter when planning a gallery. Azure Compute Gallery is not a global resource, so the documentation advises keeping galleries in separate regions for disaster recovery. Replica counts per image version can be scaled up for large parallel deployments, since more replicas can support more virtual machines being created at the same time. Replicating only the newest version widely, and older versions to fewer regions, can save cost. Per-subscription limits apply to the number of galleries, image definitions, image versions and replicas, and moving gallery resources is not supported. On cost, the gallery itself is free, while storage for each replica and network egress are billed.

The gallery also appears in image build workflows. The M365.FM episode "Azure Image Builder - Simply Explained" explains that Azure Image Builder can start from Linux or Windows images from Azure Marketplace, such as Windows Server, Windows 11 or Ubuntu, but also from images an organization already has, including images stored in Azure Compute Gallery. According to the episode, this means images do not have to be rebuilt from scratch every time something changes. The episode also clarifies that Azure Image Builder does not primarily create the production virtual machines that users or applications consume; it prepares the image first, and virtual machines are created from that image afterward. In that picture, Azure Compute Gallery is the place where prepared images can be kept, versioned and distributed.

Typical decisions around the service include how to structure image definitions, which regions should receive replicas, how many replicas a large rollout needs, and how to protect against a regional outage by placing galleries in more than one region. Because storage per replica is billed, the choice of replication targets and the number of retained versions directly affects cost.

azure-connected-machine-agent.desc: The Azure Connected Machine agent connects Windows and Linux servers outside Azure to Azure Arc over outbound HTTPS, so they appear as Azure resources.

faq.a: It connects Windows and Linux machines running outside Azure to Azure Arc, handles the machine's identity, enforces policy compliance, manages VM extensions and reports inventory so the server appears as an Azure resource.
faq.q: What does the Azure Connected Machine agent do?

faq.a: It connects outbound over HTTPS on TCP port 443, with options for proxy configuration. The episode "Azure Arc - Simply Explained" lists this as a requirement for connecting servers.
faq.q: What network access does the agent need?

faq.a: No. According to the Microsoft documentation, the Azure Monitor Agent is a separate agent and does not replace the Connected Machine agent.
faq.q: Does the Azure Monitor Agent replace the Azure Connected Machine agent?

azure-connected-machine-agent.long:
The Azure Connected Machine agent is the software installed on Windows and Linux machines that run outside Azure so they can be managed from Azure through Azure Arc. These machines may sit in a corporate network or at another cloud provider. Once the agent is installed and connected, the server becomes an Azure Arc-enabled server and is projected into Azure's control plane as an Azure resource. The agent is part of Microsoft Azure and is described in Microsoft documentation as a lightweight component.

The agent is built from several parts. The Hybrid Instance Metadata Service handles the connection to Azure and the machine's identity. A machine configuration agent checks and enforces policy compliance on the server. An extension agent installs, removes and updates VM extensions. An Azure Arc proxy bundles the network traffic of these services. According to the documentation, the agent also reports inventory: collected metadata covers the operating system, computer name, hardware details, network interfaces and detected database software, and the documentation states that no personal data is collected.

On the network side, the agent connects outbound over HTTPS, using TCP port 443, with options for proxy configuration. The episode "Azure Arc - Simply Explained" lists this outbound communication on port 443 as a requirement before servers can be connected, and names supported Linux distributions such as Red Hat Enterprise Linux versions 7 to 9, along with others like CentOS, Debian and Oracle Linux. Because the connection is initiated from the server toward Azure, the approach does not depend on opening inbound access to the machine.

Installation differs by platform. On Windows the agent is delivered as an MSI package. On Linux it is installed from an rpm or deb package or through a script. After installation the agent sends a heartbeat to Azure every five minutes. The documentation notes that a gap longer than fifteen minutes can indicate that the server is offline or that the connection is blocked, which makes the heartbeat a practical starting point when troubleshooting a machine that no longer reports in.

Typical decisions around the agent involve version currency and resource use. Only agent versions not older than one year are supported, so environments with many connected servers need a process for keeping the agent updated. CPU limits apply to the machine configuration and extension services, and from version 1.39 these limits can be adjusted. The documentation also points out that the Azure Monitor Agent is a separate agent and does not replace the Connected Machine agent; the two serve different purposes, and the Connected Machine agent is the one that establishes the Azure Arc connection.

The agent is what makes the unified management model of Azure Arc possible. The episode "Azure Arc - Simply Explained" says that installing the Azure Connected Machine Agent transforms a server into an Azure Arc-enabled server, integrating it into Azure's control plane. From there, servers can be managed through a single interface, with consistent policies and governance applied across on-premises and multi-cloud environments. In that framing, the agent is the entry point: without it, a server outside Azure remains outside Azure Arc management.

azure-container-apps.desc: Azure Container Apps is a fully managed, serverless container platform in Microsoft Azure built on Kubernetes, KEDA, Dapr and Envoy, with scale-to-zero support.

faq.a: Azure Container Apps is a fully managed, serverless container platform in Microsoft Azure. It is built on Kubernetes, KEDA, Dapr and Envoy, and Microsoft runs the underlying cluster so that apps can scale to zero.
faq.q: What is Azure Container Apps?

faq.a: No. According to the M365.FM episode "Azure Container Apps - Simply Explained", the platform lets teams run containerized applications without managing Kubernetes clusters or virtual machines, while Azure handles deployment, networking, scaling and operations.
faq.q: Does Azure Container Apps require managing Kubernetes clusters?

faq.a: The episode "MCP Architecture for Microsoft Copilot and AI Agents" says MCP servers can run on Azure Container Apps for persistent services, while "RAG on Azure — Simply Explained" names Azure Container Apps and AKS as options for scaling AI workloads.
faq.q: How does Azure Container Apps relate to AI and MCP workloads?

azure-container-apps.long:
Azure Container Apps is a fully managed, serverless container platform that is part of Microsoft Azure. It is built on Kubernetes, KEDA, Dapr and Envoy, but Microsoft operates the underlying cluster, so teams that run containerized applications do not have to manage Kubernetes clusters or virtual machines themselves. Apps running on the platform can scale to zero when there is no demand.

The core idea behind the service is to separate the application from the infrastructure it runs on. Instead of dealing with orchestration, node pools or cluster upgrades, developers package their code as a container and let Azure handle deployment, networking, scaling and operations. The building blocks named in the product description each cover a different concern: Kubernetes provides the orchestration foundation, KEDA drives event-based scaling, Dapr supplies building blocks for distributed applications, and Envoy handles traffic routing. Because these components are managed by the platform, they are not something the application team has to install or patch separately.

Typical situations for Azure Container Apps are services and APIs that run as containers and benefit from automatic scaling, workloads that are idle for long periods and therefore profit from scaling to zero, and persistent services that need to stay available. The choice of a platform usually comes down to how much control over the cluster a team wants. Azure Container Apps suits teams that want the container model without the operational overhead of running Kubernetes directly. Teams that need direct access to the cluster layer typically look at other options within Azure, such as Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), which is mentioned alongside Azure Container Apps in the M365.FM material.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Container Apps - Simply Explained" (July 2026) describes the service as Microsoft's serverless platform for running containerized applications without managing Kubernetes clusters or virtual machines. The episode says that developers can focus on building applications while Azure automatically handles deployment, networking, scaling and operations. It is aimed at listeners who want a practical understanding of what the service does before planning or supporting it.

Azure Container Apps also appears in two other episodes in connection with AI workloads. The episode "RAG on Azure — Simply Explained" says that Azure Container Apps and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) enable scaling of AI workloads, and that this flexibility supports large-scale AI deployments, including organizations with strict data residency requirements. The episode "MCP Architecture for Microsoft Copilot and AI Agents" says that MCP servers can run on Azure Functions for event-driven workloads or on Azure Container Apps for persistent services, and that this setup supports both small and large-scale deployment. In the same episode, VNet support is described as a way to use private networking, with outbound traffic routed through the VNet to Azure PaaS services over private endpoints.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, Azure Container Apps sits within the broader Azure platform and is referenced as a related topic in episodes about Power Apps and Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, where it is listed among suggested follow-up listening. Those episodes do not describe the service in detail, but they show how the topic is positioned in the wider catalog of Microsoft subjects covered by M365.FM.

azure-container-storage.desc: Azure Container Storage is a volume management and orchestration service for Kubernetes and AKS; version 2 uses local NVMe disks of cluster nodes as backing storage.

faq.a: Version 2 supports two storage types: local NVMe disks on AKS nodes of certain storage-optimized and GPU VM sizes, and Elastic SAN as a managed resource. Azure Disks are not supported in version 2 and remain with version 1.
faq.q: What does Azure Container Storage version 2 use as backing storage?

faq.a: No. Local NVMe volumes are ephemeral by default, offer no snapshots or replication, and keep no data after the pod is deleted unless the application replicates the data itself.
faq.q: Is data on local NVMe volumes kept after a pod is deleted?

faq.a: Only Linux-based Kubernetes clusters are supported, and availability is limited to a subset of regions. It can be installed as an AKS extension or through Helm.
faq.q: Which clusters and regions does Azure Container Storage support?

azure-container-storage.long:
Azure Container Storage is a cloud-based service in Microsoft Azure for managing, provisioning and orchestrating volumes for containers. It integrates with Kubernetes, including Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), and creates persistent volumes dynamically for stateful applications. Volumes are handled with standard Kubernetes tooling, so CSI drivers do not have to be installed manually. The product is part of Microsoft Azure and is documented on Microsoft Learn.

The current documentation covers version 2, which supports two storage types. The first is local NVMe, which uses local NVMe disks on AKS nodes of certain storage-optimized and GPU VM sizes. The documentation names latency-critical workloads such as PostgreSQL, and AI or machine learning frameworks such as Ray and Kubeflow, as typical fits. The second is Elastic SAN, a managed resource provisioned per volume or snapshot. Elastic SAN supports snapshots, replication with LRS and ZRS, and encryption. Volumes attach to the workload through NVMe over Fabrics or iSCSI.

The choice between the two types mainly follows from durability needs. Local NVMe volumes are ephemeral by default. They offer no snapshots or replication, and no data is kept after the pod is deleted unless the application replicates it itself. That makes local NVMe a fit for hot or temporary data, while Elastic SAN is the option when snapshots, replication and encryption are needed. Anyone planning a deployment should also know the stated limits: only Linux-based Kubernetes clusters are supported, version 2 does not support Azure Disks (which remain with version 1), and availability is limited to a subset of regions. Installation works as an AKS extension or through Helm, and the source is open. Licensing terms are not stated in the documentation, and prices are covered on a separate page.

The M365.FM episode "Speed Fabric and AKS Workloads with Local NVMe Storage" (2025-11-03) looks at the local NVMe side of version 2, which it abbreviates as ACStor v2. The episode argues that data-platform workloads are often slow because data sits far from compute, and that managed storage adds network hops, IOPS caps and latency on every read and write. Its proposed remedy is proximity: placing hot data on local NVMe inside the AKS nodes. According to the episode, this is done through a lean, CSI-based, ephemeral driver that stripes across all NVMe disks of a node, with throughput described as multi-GB/s and roughly one million IOPS. The episode also says that no SAN, LVM or etcd is involved and that the capacity comes from VM families such as L-series, Dv6 and NC, which are already paid for. It suggests uses such as Spark shuffles, Dataflows Gen2 staging and Direct Lake caches. These figures and recommendations are the episode's own statements rather than values from the product documentation.
