Taken together, Azure Container Storage v2 is a storage layer for Kubernetes workloads that moves the choice of backing storage into a Kubernetes-native workflow. The local NVMe option trades durability for speed and proximity, so applications that use it need their own replication or a way to rebuild the data. The Elastic SAN option gives managed durability features instead. Teams evaluating the service typically weigh latency requirements, data-loss tolerance, VM size availability, region coverage and the Linux-only restriction against each other.

azure-copilot-agents.desc: Azure Copilot agents are specialized agents in Azure Copilot for migration, deployment, optimization, observability, resiliency and troubleshooting, acting only with approval.

faq.a: They are specialized agents in Azure Copilot for migration, deployment, optimization, observability, resiliency and troubleshooting. They reason over Azure resources and act only with approval.
faq.q: What are Azure Copilot agents?

faq.a: No. According to the product description, they act only with approval, so a person must consent before an action is carried out.
faq.q: Do Azure Copilot agents make changes on their own?

faq.a: "Azure Copilot Agents: Building a Synthetic Platform Team" discusses operationalizing Azure Copilot Agents at enterprise scale through the concept of a synthetic platform team, with attention to governance, compliance and operations.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode on Azure Copilot agents cover?

azure-copilot-agents.long:
Azure Copilot agents are specialized agents within Azure Copilot, part of Microsoft Azure. Each agent is focused on a particular area of cloud work: migration, deployment, optimization, observability, resiliency and troubleshooting. They reason over Azure resources and act only with approval, which means a person stays in the loop before any change is made to an environment. The product is documented by Microsoft in its Azure Copilot documentation.

The purpose of this agent model is to take recurring cloud operations tasks and give them a dedicated, task-oriented assistant instead of a single general-purpose chat experience. A migration agent, for example, is aimed at moving workloads to Azure, while an observability or troubleshooting agent is aimed at understanding what is happening in an existing environment. Because the agents reason over Azure resources, their output is tied to the resources actually present in a subscription rather than to generic advice. The approval requirement is the central control: an agent can analyze and propose, but an action is carried out only after explicit consent.

Typical situations where these agents come into play include planning and executing a migration, deploying new infrastructure, tuning cost and performance, improving monitoring coverage, strengthening resilience, and diagnosing incidents. In each case the decision for an organization is less about whether an agent can suggest something and more about how much it is allowed to do, who approves its actions, and how its activity is governed. This is why the approval model matters: it keeps accountability with the people who own the environment while still letting the agents reduce manual investigation and repetitive work.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Copilot Agents: Building a Synthetic Platform Team" treats these agents as an operational topic rather than only a development one. According to the episode, building AI agents is no longer just a development challenge but an operational one, and it introduces the idea of a synthetic platform team as a way to operationalize Azure Copilot Agents at enterprise scale. Instead of handling agents as isolated applications, the discussion frames them as part of a shared platform, with attention to governance, compliance and operational excellence. The episode is aimed at cloud engineers, DevOps professionals and IT leaders who want an AI platform that supports long-term innovation.

The topic also appears as a related listening suggestion in other M365.FM episodes, including "Microsoft 365 Copilot Agents: Real Business Value with Steve Corey [MVP]", "MCP Architecture for Microsoft Copilot and AI Agents", "Building a Synthetic Market for Microsoft 365 Strategy" and "Why Microsoft Copilot Agents Fail—and How to Fix Them". These cross-references place Azure Copilot agents next to broader discussions of Copilot agents, architecture patterns and strategy, which helps readers see how the Azure-focused agents relate to agent work elsewhere in the Microsoft ecosystem.

In short, Azure Copilot agents combine task specialization with an approval-based action model. Their value in practice depends on how an organization defines scope, review and governance around them, which is the angle the M365.FM material emphasizes when it discusses operating agents as a platform capability rather than as one-off tools.

azure-data-explorer.desc: Azure Data Explorer (ADX) is a fully managed Azure service for fast analysis of large volumes of log and telemetry data using Kusto Query Language.

faq.a: Azure Data Explorer (ADX) is a fully managed Azure service for fast analysis of large volumes of log and telemetry data. Data is queried with Kusto Query Language (KQL).
faq.q: What is Azure Data Explorer used for?

faq.a: KQL databases in Microsoft Fabric share the Kusto engine heritage of Azure Data Explorer. The episode "Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence - Simply Explained" describes Fabric as suited to end-to-end analytics with Power BI integration, while ADX excels at ultra-fast ingestion and analytics of high-volume, time-series or log data.
faq.q: How does Azure Data Explorer relate to Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: According to the episodes, Azure Event Hubs integrates with Azure Data Explorer for event streams. In the "Microsoft Defender EASM - Simply Explained" episode, ADX supports larger-scale analysis and custom reporting of exported data alongside Log Analytics, Microsoft Sentinel and Security Copilot.
faq.q: Which other services does Azure Data Explorer work with?

azure-data-explorer.long:
Azure Data Explorer, often abbreviated ADX, is a fully managed service within Microsoft Azure for the fast analysis of large volumes of log and telemetry data. Data in the service is queried with Kusto Query Language (KQL). The service is aimed at workloads where large amounts of data arrive continuously and need to be searched and analyzed quickly, such as application logs, device telemetry and other time-based records. KQL databases in Microsoft Fabric share the Kusto engine heritage of Azure Data Explorer, which makes the two closely related in how data is stored and queried.

As a managed Azure service, Azure Data Explorer removes the need to operate the underlying analytics infrastructure directly. Its role in an architecture is typically that of an analytics store and query engine placed behind an ingestion path. Streaming platforms such as Azure Event Hubs are a common source of events, and the episode "Azure Event Hubs - Simply Explained" lists Azure Data Explorer among the services that Event Hubs integrates with, alongside Azure Functions, Azure Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Apache Kafka and other analytics platforms. In that picture, Event Hubs collects and buffers the event stream, while Azure Data Explorer supports the analysis of what arrives.

The positioning of Azure Data Explorer relative to Microsoft Fabric is discussed in the episode "Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence - Simply Explained". According to the episode, Microsoft Fabric is designed for end-to-end analytics and integrates tightly with Power BI and other Microsoft tools, which makes it suitable for structured data and moderate real-time needs. Azure Data Explorer, by contrast, is described as excelling in scenarios that require ultra-fast ingestion and analytics, particularly for high-volume, time-series or log data. The episode frames this as a comparison of fit rather than a ranking, helping listeners decide which approach matches the volume and speed requirements of a project. The same episode walks through building a real-time intelligence dashboard for project monitoring, beginning with defining the objectives and the metrics or KPIs that matter.

Azure Data Explorer also appears in security operations. The episode "Microsoft Defender EASM - Simply Explained" describes how Defender EASM asset data and attack-surface insights can be exported for analysis. In that discussion, Log Analytics provides a place to search information from multiple Microsoft services, while Azure Data Explorer can support larger-scale analysis and custom reporting. Microsoft Sentinel can use the exported information alongside security alerts and logs, helping analysts determine whether incidents involve public-facing assets and which other resources may be connected, and Security Copilot can offer a natural-language interface for investigating the same information.

Typical decisions around Azure Data Explorer therefore concern where it sits relative to neighboring services. For log and telemetry analysis at scale with custom reporting, the episodes point to Azure Data Explorer as a candidate. For broader end-to-end analytics tightly connected to Power BI, they point to Microsoft Fabric, whose KQL databases build on the same Kusto engine lineage. For collecting events before analysis, Azure Event Hubs is the ingestion-side service, and the Event Hubs episode also compares it with Event Grid and Service Bus to clarify when each messaging service is appropriate.

Official documentation for the service is published under the Azure Kusto section of Microsoft Learn. The material in the episodes is introductory in nature, aimed at developers, cloud architects and data engineers, and it presents Azure Data Explorer mainly through its relationships with Fabric, Event Hubs and the Defender and Sentinel security stack rather than as a standalone deep dive.

azure-data-factory.desc: Azure Data Factory is Microsoft's cloud-based data integration service for orchestrating data movement and transforming data at scale using pipelines.

faq.a: It is used to orchestrate data movement and transform data at scale in the cloud. The episode "Azure Data Factory - Simply Explained" compares it to a courier that picks up raw data, cleans it on the way and delivers it where reports can use it.
faq.q: What is Azure Data Factory used for?

faq.a: The service is built from pipelines, activities, linked services, datasets, integration runtimes and triggers. Mapping data flows are used for transforming data within it.
faq.q: What are the main components of Azure Data Factory?

faq.a: Microsoft describes Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric as its next generation. According to "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines", Fabric Data Factory builds on familiar Azure Data Factory concepts with pipelines optimized for Fabric's data platform.
faq.q: How does Azure Data Factory relate to Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric?

azure-data-factory.long:
Azure Data Factory is Microsoft's cloud-based data integration service for orchestrating data movement and transforming data at scale. It is part of Microsoft Azure and is built around a small set of concepts: pipelines, activities, linked services, datasets, integration runtimes and triggers. Microsoft describes Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric as the next generation of the service, which matters for anyone deciding where new integration work should live.

The episode "Azure Data Factory - Simply Explained" describes the service with an everyday image: a courier service for a company's data. It picks up raw information from wherever it lives, cleans it on the way, and drops it off somewhere reports can actually use it. That framing captures the main use of the product, which is moving data from source systems to destinations used for analytics and reporting, with transformation along the route.

The building blocks follow the structure laid out in that episode. Pipelines and activities define the work: a pipeline groups a set of activities, and each activity performs a step such as copying or transforming data. Linked services and datasets describe what the pipeline connects to. The episode compares linked services to the keys and datasets to the address, meaning that one holds the connection information for a data store or compute resource while the other points to the specific data being read or written. Integration runtimes are called the engine room, the compute infrastructure that actually executes the movement and transformation. Triggers and scheduling make pipelines run on their own, so that data movement does not depend on someone starting it manually. The episode also covers mapping data flows as the way to transform data within the service.

In practice, teams use Azure Data Factory to build ETL-style processes, to bring data from many locations into a central store, and to schedule recurring loads. Typical decisions include how to organize work into pipelines, which integration runtime fits a given source, and which trigger type matches the required refresh pattern. Because the service orchestrates rather than stores data, it is usually combined with storage and analytics platforms.

Several other M365.FM episodes place Azure Data Factory next to related services. "Microsoft Graph Data Connect - Simply Explained" lists Azure Data Factory, together with Microsoft Fabric and Azure Synapse Analytics, as an analytics platform that can receive large volumes of Microsoft 365 data extracted in batches, in contrast to the request-by-request approach of the Microsoft Graph API. "Microsoft Fabric OneLake - Simply Explained" notes that OneLake integrates with Azure Data Factory, Azure Databricks and Synapse Analytics as part of a platform for data engineering, warehousing and analytics. "Build Reusable Dataflows Gen2 in Microsoft Fabric" mentions that Power BI dataflows stored in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 can be consumed directly by Azure Data Factory and other tools.

The relationship to Fabric is addressed in "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines". The episode explains that Fabric Data Factory builds on familiar concepts from Azure Data Factory by providing pipelines in Fabric and a unified experience for data integration. Pipeline copy and ETL pipelines operate similarly but are optimized for Fabric's data platform, supporting data movement and transformation into Fabric lakehouse and warehouse destinations. For readers working with existing Azure Data Factory pipelines, this means the core vocabulary carries over, while Fabric is positioned as the direction for the service going forward.

azure-data-lake-storage.desc: Azure Data Lake Storage is a set of capabilities built on Azure Blob Storage for holding large volumes of data for analytics workloads in Microsoft Azure.

faq.a: Azure Data Lake Storage is a set of capabilities on Azure Blob Storage for storing large volumes of data for analytics workloads. It is part of Microsoft Azure.
faq.q: What is Azure Data Lake Storage?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Azure Data Lake Storage - Simply Explained", it is the one setting that gives Azure storage real folders. The episode "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" also recommends enabling it for better organization.
faq.q: What does the hierarchical namespace do in Azure Data Lake Storage?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Fabric OneLake - Simply Explained" states that OneLake is built on Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) Gen2 and can accommodate various file types.
faq.q: How does Azure Data Lake Storage relate to Microsoft Fabric OneLake?

azure-data-lake-storage.long:
Azure Data Lake Storage is a set of capabilities on Azure Blob Storage designed for storing large volumes of data for analytics workloads. It is part of Microsoft Azure. The M365.FM episode "Azure Data Lake Storage - Simply Explained" describes it as not a whole new product to learn, but as the same inexpensive Azure storage with one setting switched on that gives it real folders. That setting is the hierarchical namespace, which turns a flat pool of stored objects into an organized structure of directories and files.

The main purpose is to give analytics platforms a single place to land and keep data of many kinds. The same episode raises the point that a data lake is not just a folder full of files, which indicates that organization, access control and structure matter as much as raw capacity. Because Azure Data Lake Storage builds on Blob Storage rather than replacing it, teams that already know Azure storage accounts work with familiar concepts such as containers, and add directory-style organization on top.

Security and configuration are covered in the episode "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines". For Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 accounts, the episode recommends aligning the storage region with the Fabric capacity region and enabling the hierarchical namespace for better organization. It advises granting the Storage Blob Data Reader role only at the container level to limit access and follow the least privilege principle, and granting the Fabric Workspace Identity the right Azure RBAC roles. It also mentions using a private endpoint as part of securing the connection.

Azure Data Lake Storage also appears in several integration scenarios in the Microsoft ecosystem. In "Microsoft Fabric OneLake - Simply Explained", OneLake is described as the single place for all analytics data and as built on Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) Gen2, able to accommodate various file types. The episode says this reduces the need to maintain multiple separate systems for data processing and links OneLake's integration with Data Factory and Power BI to simpler infrastructure management.

The episode "Microsoft Graph Data Connect - Simply Explained" lists Azure Data Lake Storage among the systems that Microsoft Graph Data Connect can integrate with, alongside Microsoft Fabric Lakehouses, Azure Blob Storage, Azure Synapse Analytics and Azure Data Factory pipelines. The episode says this allows Microsoft 365 productivity data to be combined with project data for predictive insights into initiative execution and outcomes.

In the episode "Build Reusable Dataflows Gen2 in Microsoft Fabric", preparing data for a data warehouse or Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 is named as one common use case for dataflows. Other use cases listed there include centralizing shared data preparation logic across reports, creating a single source of truth for the enterprise, handling large data volumes with scheduled refresh, and reusing the prepared data across multiple Power BI datasets and Power Platform apps.

Taken together, the episodes position Azure Data Lake Storage as a storage foundation. Typical decisions around it include whether to enable the hierarchical namespace, how to scope access roles to containers rather than whole accounts, where to place the storage relative to the compute capacity that reads from it, and whether to use it directly or through a service such as Microsoft Fabric OneLake that sits on top of it.

azure-database-for-postgresql-flexible-s.desc: Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server is a fully managed Azure database service built on the community PostgreSQL engine, with three compute tiers.

faq.a: It is a fully managed Azure database service built on the community PostgreSQL engine. It is part of Microsoft Azure.
faq.q: What is Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server?

faq.a: It offers Burstable, General Purpose and Memory Optimized compute tiers.
faq.q: Which compute tiers does Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server offer?

faq.a: Microsoft provides documentation for the service on Microsoft Learn, in the Azure PostgreSQL section.
faq.q: Where can the official documentation be found?

azure-database-for-postgresql-flexible-s.long:
Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server is a fully managed database service in Microsoft Azure. It is built on the community PostgreSQL engine, which means it runs the open-source PostgreSQL database as a managed platform service rather than as software that an organization installs and operates on its own virtual machines.

The service is offered in three compute tiers: Burstable, General Purpose and Memory Optimized. These tiers allow a deployment to be matched to different workload profiles, from smaller or intermittent workloads to those that need more memory relative to processing capacity. Specific sizes, limits and pricing for each tier are documented by Microsoft and are not covered here.

Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server is part of Microsoft Azure and sits within the broader set of Azure data and database services. Teams that use PostgreSQL for application back ends, data-driven services or other relational workloads may consider it as a way to run PostgreSQL on Azure with the operational management handled by the platform.

Official technical documentation is available on Microsoft Learn under the Azure PostgreSQL section. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity.

azure-databricks.desc: Azure Databricks is a first-party managed Apache Spark analytics service on Azure for data engineering, analytics and machine learning on data in your own storage.

faq.a: Azure Databricks is a first-party managed Apache Spark analytics service on Azure, built by Microsoft and Databricks. It is used for data engineering, analytics and machine learning on data kept in the customer's own storage.
faq.q: What is Azure Databricks?

faq.a: The episode "Azure AI Foundry - Simply Explained" describes Azure AI Foundry as focused on generative AI application and agent development. Azure Databricks is described as focused on large-scale data engineering, analytics, traditional machine learning and AI workflows.
faq.q: How does Azure Databricks differ from Azure AI Foundry?

faq.a: The episodes mention Microsoft Fabric OneLake, Azure Data Factory, Synapse Analytics, Azure NetApp Files, Azure Open Datasets, Azure Machine Learning and Power BI in connection with Azure Databricks.
faq.q: Which other Azure services are mentioned together with Azure Databricks?

azure-databricks.long:
Azure Databricks is a first-party managed Apache Spark analytics service on Azure, built by Microsoft and Databricks. It is used for data engineering, analytics and machine learning on data that stays in the customer's own storage. As a part of Microsoft Azure, it gives teams a way to run the Spark engine as a service inside their Azure environment instead of assembling and operating that engine themselves.

The background of the service is tied to Apache Spark itself. According to the episode "Azure Databricks - Simply Explained", Apache Spark started as a research project at a university in 2009 and grew into the engine that most big data platforms still run on today. Azure Databricks is described there as the way Microsoft and the people who built Spark turned that engine into a service that can be spun up inside Azure. The same episode also covers what Azure Databricks actually is and why the lakehouse idea is discussed in connection with it.

In practice, the service is relevant wherever large volumes of data have to be prepared, transformed and analysed, or where machine learning models are developed on that data. Because the data is kept in the customer's own storage, a typical design decision is how the compute service and the storage layer are separated and connected. Teams that already run workloads in Azure often consider Azure Databricks when the focus is on data engineering and analytics at scale rather than on a single reporting tool.

The M365.FM episodes place Azure Databricks next to several neighbouring services. The episode "Azure AI Foundry - Simply Explained" compares Azure AI Foundry with Azure Databricks in a feature table. In that comparison, Azure AI Foundry is described as focused on generative AI application and agent development, with foundation models, prompt engineering, RAG, agent orchestration, model evaluation, content safety and responsible AI tooling. Azure Databricks is described as focused on large-scale data engineering, analytics, traditional machine learning and AI workflows, including supervised and unsupervised learning, deep learning, feature engineering and MLflow for lifecycle management. The comparison shows that the two services address different primary needs and are not direct substitutes.

The episode "Microsoft Fabric OneLake - Simply Explained" mentions that OneLake integrates with Azure Data Factory, Azure Databricks and Synapse Analytics, forming a platform for data engineering, warehousing and analytics. In that framing, OneLake acts as a centralized repository for analytics data, and Azure Databricks is one of the services that can work with it. This is relevant for organisations that want a single data foundation while still using Spark-based processing.

Storage is another recurring theme. The episode "Azure NetApp Files - Simply Explained" lists direct operation with Azure Databricks on file-based datasets among the use cases of Azure NetApp Files, alongside advanced data analytics, AI workflows and integration with Microsoft OneLake for governed analytics. The episode "Azure Open Datasets - Simply Explained" notes that curated public datasets are ready to use with Azure Machine Learning, Azure Databricks, Power BI, Azure Data Factory and other Azure services, which makes them a possible starting point for experiments and training data.

Taken together, the available material describes Azure Databricks as a managed Spark platform that sits in the data and AI layer of Azure. It connects to storage, to OneLake, to open datasets and to other Azure data services, and it covers the engineering and machine learning side of analytics. The episode "Azure Databricks - Simply Explained" is the dedicated introduction, while the other episodes mention the service in the context of storage, data platforms and AI tooling.

azure-ddos-protection.desc: Azure DDoS Protection is a Microsoft Azure service that detects and mitigates network-layer distributed denial-of-service attacks against Azure resources.

faq.a: It is an Azure service that defends Azure resources against distributed denial-of-service attacks at the network layer. According to the M365.FM episode "Azure DDoS Protection - Simply Explained", it automatically detects and mitigates malicious traffic meant to overwhelm infrastructure, helping keep applications available during large-scale attacks.
faq.q: What does Azure DDoS Protection do?

faq.a: They protect different layers. Azure DDoS Protection works at the network layer, while Azure Web Application Firewall provides application-layer protection, so the two complement each other.
faq.q: How does Azure DDoS Protection relate to Azure Web Application Firewall?

faq.a: No. The episode "Azure Virtual Network - Simply Explained" lists it alongside Azure Firewall, VNet Encryption, Azure Bastion, Network Security Groups and Traffic Mirroring, and describes it as essential for internet-facing workloads rather than as a complete solution on its own.
faq.q: Is Azure DDoS Protection the only network security control needed for Azure workloads?

azure-ddos-protection.long:
Azure DDoS Protection is a managed service within Microsoft Azure that defends Azure resources against distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks. It works at the network layer and is designed to complement application-layer protection such as Azure Web Application Firewall. A DDoS attack tries to overwhelm an application or its infrastructure with malicious traffic so that legitimate users can no longer reach it. The service is intended to keep applications and services available even while such an attack is under way.

According to the M365.FM episode "Azure DDoS Protection - Simply Explained", Azure DDoS Protection is Microsoft's managed service for defending applications and services against DDoS attacks. It automatically detects and mitigates malicious traffic that is designed to overwhelm infrastructure. The episode describes the protection as built directly into Azure's global network and as providing enterprise-grade protection without requiring complex security appliances. In practice, this means the defence sits in the platform itself rather than in separate devices that an organisation would have to deploy, size and maintain.

The service is typically considered for internet-facing workloads, where exposure to volumetric or protocol-based attack traffic is highest. The episode "Azure Virtual Network - Simply Explained" places Azure DDoS Protection in a list of virtual network security capabilities. There it is described as providing always-on monitoring and automatic attack mitigation, and as essential for internet-facing workloads. The same list names Azure Firewall, VNet Encryption, Azure Bastion, Network Security Groups (NSGs) and Traffic Mirroring, which shows that Azure DDoS Protection is one layer in a broader set of network controls rather than a standalone answer to every threat.

This layering is the main design consideration around the service. Network-layer DDoS protection addresses traffic floods aimed at the network and transport level, while application-layer threats, such as malicious requests to a web application, are handled by other tools like Azure Web Application Firewall. Network Security Groups filter traffic at the subnet and network interface level, and Azure Firewall adds managed filtering with threat intelligence. Choosing between or combining these controls depends on what an organisation exposes to the internet and which kinds of attacks it needs to withstand.

Azure DDoS Protection also appears in the context of platform services. The episode "Replace Hard-Coded SQL Logins in Azure App Service" lists Azure DDoS protection among the core features discussed for Azure Web Apps, alongside authentication and authorization options, IP restrictions, TLS encryption, and integration with Azure Front Door, Azure SQL Database and Microsoft Entra ID. In that discussion it is one of several security features that support running web workloads on Azure, together with network security fundamentals and practices such as managed identities and secret storage in Azure Key Vault.

As part of Microsoft Azure, the service is documented in Microsoft's official Azure DDoS Protection overview on Microsoft Learn. Readers who need details on tiers, supported resources, configuration or pricing should consult that documentation, since the episodes summarised here describe the service at an introductory level and focus on what it does and where it fits among other Azure network security options.

azure-dedicated-host.desc: Azure Dedicated Host reserves a whole physical server in an Azure datacenter for one subscription, with host-level isolation and control over maintenance timing.

faq.a: Azure Dedicated Host is an Azure service that provides physical servers whose virtual machines belong to a single Azure subscription. It gives hardware isolation at the server level and control over platform maintenance timing.
faq.q: What is Azure Dedicated Host?

faq.a: Billing is per host rather than per virtual machine. Licenses, storage and networking are charged separately.
faq.q: How is Azure Dedicated Host billed?

faq.a: No. A host's size and type cannot be changed after deployment, and live migration is not supported. A hardware failure leads to service healing with brief unavailability.
faq.q: Can a dedicated host be resized or live-migrated?

azure-dedicated-host.long:
Azure Dedicated Host is an Azure service that provides physical servers for running virtual machines that belong to a single Azure subscription. It is part of Microsoft Azure. The servers are the same type of hardware used across Azure datacenters, but they are exposed to the customer as a hardware resource rather than as shared capacity. A customer places compatible virtual machines on the host and, in return, gets isolation at the server level and more say over how the underlying hardware is managed.

The documentation names several benefits. The first is hardware isolation at the server level: only virtual machines from the owning subscription run on the host. The second is control over the timing of platform maintenance, which matters for workloads that cannot tolerate maintenance at arbitrary moments. The third is the ability to choose which workloads share the same physical resources. The fourth is the option to bring Windows and SQL licenses through Azure Hybrid Benefit. These points are the usual reasons teams consider a dedicated host instead of ordinary virtual machines.

The service is built from a few components. A host is a single physical server, and its SKU determines which virtual machine sizes it can run. A host group is a collection of hosts tied to one availability zone. Placement is organized by region, availability zone and fault domain. Only virtual machines from the same family as the host can be placed on it, so the choice of host SKU follows directly from the virtual machine sizes that will be deployed.

There are also limits to plan around. The size and type of a host cannot be changed after deployment, so the SKU decision needs care up front. Live migration is not supported. If the underlying hardware fails, the result is service healing, which means brief unavailability for the virtual machines on that host. Deployment requires dedicated host quota as well as matching virtual machine family quota, so quota has to be arranged before a host can be created.

Billing works differently from standard virtual machines. Charges apply per host rather than per virtual machine, so cost is tied to the reserved server and not to the number of machines placed on it. Licenses, storage and networking are charged separately. This changes how teams reason about cost: the question becomes how well a host is filled and whether the isolation and maintenance control justify paying for the whole server.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Dedicated Host - Simply Explained" approaches the topic from the question of why anyone would rent an entire physical server in Azure when a virtual machine could simply be created and paid for. According to its outline, the episode covers the problem Dedicated Host solves, what the service actually is, how the building blocks fit together, isolation, security and maintenance control, and pricing. It serves as an introduction to the decision between standard virtual machines and a dedicated physical server.

In practice, Azure Dedicated Host fits situations where server-level isolation, control over maintenance timing, or the reuse of existing Windows and SQL licenses through Azure Hybrid Benefit are requirements. Where those needs do not exist, the per-host billing model and the fixed host SKU are trade-offs worth weighing against standard virtual machine deployments.

azure-deployment-stacks.desc: Azure deployment stacks manage the resources of a Bicep or ARM template as one unit, track ownership, and can block out-of-band changes with deny settings.

faq.a: It depends on the unmanaged resources setting. By default they are detached and remain in Azure, but the stack can also be configured to delete them, either as resources or as a whole including resource groups.
faq.q: What happens to resources that are removed from the template of a deployment stack?

faq.a: They block changes to managed resources outside the stack. The options are none, deny delete, and deny write and delete, with excluded actions and up to five excluded Entra principals possible. They only affect control plane operations and explicitly defined resources.
faq.q: What do deny settings in a deployment stack do?

faq.a: Deployment stacks can be created at resource group, subscription or management group scope.
faq.q: At which scopes can a deployment stack be created?

azure-deployment-stacks.long:
A deployment stack is an Azure resource that manages a group of resources as one unit. The group is defined by a Bicep file or an ARM JSON template, and the stack keeps track of which resources it owns. The feature is part of Microsoft Azure and is documented under Azure Resource Manager. Its purpose is lifecycle management: instead of treating a template deployment as a one-off action, the stack remembers what was deployed and can act on the difference when the template changes.

A stack can be created at resource group, subscription or management group scope, which allows resources spread across several scopes to be handled together. When a resource is removed from the template and the stack is updated, the setting for unmanaged resources decides what happens to it. By default the resource is detached, meaning it stays in Azure but is no longer managed by the stack. Alternatively, unmanaged resources can be deleted, either as resources only or as a whole including resource groups. Because these delete flags are applied in a single update, stacks can also be used to clean up an environment in one operation.

Protection against unwanted changes is handled through deny settings. These can be set to none, deny delete, or deny write and delete. They can apply to child scopes and can allow excluded actions as well as up to five excluded Microsoft Entra principals. Deny settings only affect control plane operations, not data plane ones, and they only cover resources that are explicitly defined in the template, not implicitly created ones such as the virtual machines of an Azure Kubernetes Service cluster. Teams that rely on deny settings should keep this scope in mind.

Access to stacks is governed by Azure RBAC. The built-in roles are Azure Deployment Stack Contributor and Azure Deployment Stack Owner. The resources managed by a stack can be exported as JSON. In the Azure portal there is no graphical view of the managed resources, so PowerShell or the Azure CLI is needed to work with them, with Azure PowerShell 12.0.0 or Azure CLI 2.61.0 as the minimum versions according to the documentation.

Typical decisions around deployment stacks include which scope the stack should live at, whether removed resources should be detached or deleted, and which deny setting fits the environment. A detach default is the more conservative choice, while delete options suit short-lived or test environments that should be removed completely. Deny settings fit shared or production environments where changes made outside the template should be prevented, with excluded principals reserved for cases that need an exception.

The M365.FM episode "Design Reliable and Resilient Azure Architectures" mentions deployment stacks in the context of infrastructure as code. It lists using Azure Deployment Stacks among practices such as CI/CD pipelines, Azure Policy to enforce standards, and regular audits and drift detection. The episode says that stacks let teams create repeatable resource definitions for their infrastructure, and that these practices keep infrastructure predictable and reduce hidden risks to Azure solutions. Deployment stacks therefore sit alongside Bicep and ARM templates as a way to keep deployed resources consistent with their definitions over time.

azure-developer-cli.desc: The Azure Developer CLI (azd) is an open-source command-line tool for creating environments, provisioning Azure resources and deploying application code in Microsoft Azure.
azure-developer-cli.long:
The Azure Developer CLI (azd) is an open-source command-line tool that provides a consistent workflow for working with Azure. It is used to create environments, provision Azure resources and deploy application code from the command line.

azd belongs to Microsoft Azure and acts as a developer-focused layer for the steps between writing an application and running it in the cloud. Rather than handling each step separately, developers can use a single set of commands for setting up an environment, provisioning the required Azure resources and deploying the application code to them.

The tool's commands are documented in the official Microsoft Learn reference for the Azure Developer CLI, which lists the available azd commands. This reference is the primary source for details about how individual commands behave.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity.

azure-device-registry.desc: Azure Device Registry is a Microsoft Azure service that represents connected devices and industrial assets as Azure resources for registration, discovery and governance.

faq.a: Azure Device Registry is an Azure service that represents connected devices and industrial assets as Azure resources. This allows them to be registered, discovered and governed across edge and cloud.
faq.q: What is Azure Device Registry?

faq.a: Azure IoT Operations is given as an example of where Azure Device Registry is used. The registry provides the Azure resource representation of the devices and assets involved.
faq.q: How does Azure Device Registry relate to Azure IoT Operations?

faq.a: Azure Device Registry is part of Microsoft Azure.
faq.q: Which Microsoft product family does Azure Device Registry belong to?

azure-device-registry.long:
Azure Device Registry is a service within Microsoft Azure that represents connected devices and industrial assets as Azure resources. Because these items exist as resources in Azure, they can be registered, discovered and governed across both edge and cloud environments.

The service is used where physical equipment and devices need a consistent presence in the cloud alongside other Azure resources. One example named in its description is Azure IoT Operations, where Azure Device Registry provides the resource representation of the devices and assets involved.

Azure Device Registry is part of Microsoft Azure. Official documentation is available on Microsoft Learn under the Azure IoT section, in the device registry overview.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity, so this page is limited to the product definition and its relationship to Microsoft Azure and Azure IoT Operations.

azure-devops.desc: Azure DevOps is Microsoft's suite of developer services for planning, versioning, building, testing and delivering software across Boards, Repos, Pipelines, Test Plans and Artifacts.

faq.a: Azure DevOps includes Azure Boards, Azure Repos, Azure Pipelines, Azure Test Plans and Azure Artifacts. Together they cover planning, source control, build and release automation, testing and package storage.
faq.q: What services are part of Azure DevOps?

faq.a: Both are Microsoft platforms for source control and CI/CD, and the M365.FM episode "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD" compares them for Fabric delivery. Azure DevOps offers an integrated suite of work tracking, repositories, pipelines, testing and artifacts.
faq.q: How does Azure DevOps relate to GitHub?

faq.a: Yes, according to the episodes. "Implement Power Platform CI/CD with Azure DevOps" covers pipelines for Power Platform solutions, and "Power BI Version Control with GitHub and Azure DevOps" covers Git-based version control for Power BI.
faq.q: Can Azure DevOps be used for Power Platform and Power BI?

azure-devops.long:
Azure DevOps is a suite of developer services from Microsoft that supports the full software delivery lifecycle. It combines Azure Boards, Azure Repos, Azure Pipelines, Azure Test Plans and Azure Artifacts in one platform. The product is also referred to as Azure DevOps Services, and Azure Pipelines is the part most often associated with build and release automation. It is classed as a Microsoft tool and a developer tool, and it is related to both GitHub and Microsoft Azure.

The services each cover a separate stage of the work. Azure Boards handles planning and tracking and supports agile methods such as Scrum and Kanban. Azure Repos provides source control, Azure Pipelines builds and deploys code, Azure Test Plans supports testing, and Azure Artifacts stores packages and build output. Because these pieces sit together, a team can trace a pipeline run back to specific commits, pull requests or work items, which gives visibility into how a change moved from idea to release. Official product documentation is published on Microsoft Learn.

Typical decisions around Azure DevOps involve how to organize repositories, how to structure pipelines, and how to secure access and secrets. The M365.FM episode "Azure DevOps - Simply Explained" walks through the individual services, including the features of Azure Boards, and mentions that integration with Azure Cost Management gives better visibility and control over cloud spending in CI/CD pipelines. The episode presents these capabilities as a way to respond to market changes while maintaining quality.

A recurring theme in the episodes is governance. In "Azure DevOps in 2026: The Quiet Backbone of Enterprise AI", the framing is that Azure DevOps gives enterprise teams a governed way to plan, build, test and release both software and infrastructure. The episode argues that disciplined source control, pipelines, security and traceability remain essential even as GitHub, Copilot and AI-powered development speed up the pace of change. In that view, faster development increases the need for controlled release processes rather than reducing it.

Azure DevOps is also used as the delivery backbone for other Microsoft platforms. The episode "Implement Power Platform CI/CD with Azure DevOps" describes building a pipeline for Power Platform solutions and addresses trouble spots such as environment variables, connection references, service connections and secure secrets. It notes that a solution package does not carry everything: environment variables are placeholders and connection references must be bound after import, so per-environment settings need to be parameterized in the pipeline.

Version control for analytics content is another use. The episode "Power BI Version Control with GitHub and Azure DevOps" covers Git-based workflows for Power BI, which keep a clear list of changes and help teams work faster, and recommends integrating Git as a first step toward version control and CI/CD. The related episode "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD" compares the two platforms for Microsoft Fabric. It describes Azure DevOps as a unified platform that brings together code repositories, work tracking, testing tools and artifact storage, and lists regular audits of repository access, secrets and security settings among its recommendations.

The relationship to GitHub is therefore a practical choice rather than a replacement story in these episodes. Both platforms can host source code and drive CI/CD, and the comparison episode treats them as alternatives for the same delivery problems, with Azure DevOps offering its integrated set of planning, repository, pipeline, testing and artifact services under one ownership model. Its link to Microsoft Azure appears in the cost-visibility point above and in its use for deploying infrastructure.

azure-digital-twins.desc: Azure Digital Twins is an Azure platform service that builds a live twin graph from DTDL models of real environments and supports queries and event routing.

faq.a: Azure Digital Twins is an Azure platform-as-a-service offering for building a live graph of digital twins from DTDL models. The graph represents the entities and relationships of a real environment such as a building, factory or city.
faq.q: What is Azure Digital Twins?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, data can arrive from IoT Hub, through REST APIs or via connectors such as Logic Apps. Events update the graph, and custom processing is often done in Azure Functions.
faq.q: How does data get into an Azure Digital Twins graph?

faq.a: No. The documentation distinguishes Azure Digital Twins from Digital Twin Builder in Fabric and from IoT Hub device twins. The episode "Microsoft Fabric Digital Twin Builder Explained" describes Fabric as able to integrate with Azure Digital Twins.
faq.q: Is Azure Digital Twins the same as Digital Twin Builder in Fabric?

azure-digital-twins.long:
Azure Digital Twins is a platform-as-a-service offering in Microsoft Azure for building a live graph of digital twins. The graph represents the entities of a real environment and the relationships between them. Microsoft Learn names buildings, factories, farms, energy networks, railways, stadiums and cities as examples of whole environments that can be modeled this way. The service is part of Microsoft Azure and is documented there as its own product.

The starting point is a set of digital models. Types are described in the Digital Twins Definition Language (DTDL), a JSON-like language in which a model is defined through properties, components and relationships. Ready-made industry ontologies exist, so a model does not have to be written from scratch in every case. Concrete twins are then created from these models and linked by relationships into a twin graph. The graph can be explored visually in the Azure Digital Twins Explorer.

Data reaches the graph from several directions. According to the documentation, it can arrive from IoT Hub, through REST APIs, or via connectors such as Logic Apps. Incoming events update the twins in the graph, and custom processing is often done in Azure Functions. In this way the graph reflects the current state of the environment it describes rather than a static snapshot.

Once the graph exists, it can be used in two main ways. A query API allows searching by property values, by relationships and by model information, which makes it possible to ask questions across connected twins instead of looking at single devices in isolation. Event routes forward data to downstream services through Event Hubs, Event Grid or Service Bus, so that changes in the graph can trigger further processing elsewhere in an Azure solution.

Two further capabilities are described in the documentation. A data history feature records graph updates into an Azure Data Explorer cluster, which keeps a record of how the twin graph has changed. 3D Scenes Studio, which the documentation still lists as a preview, maps 3D elements to twins. The overview page does not list prerequisites or licensing details and points to a separate article for service limits, so those aspects need to be checked there before planning a solution.

The documentation also separates the service from similarly named offerings. It distinguishes Azure Digital Twins from Digital Twin Builder in Fabric and from IoT Hub device twins. This distinction matters in practice because the names are close but the products are not the same thing.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Fabric Digital Twin Builder Explained" touches on the Fabric side of this relationship. The episode says that Fabric can integrate with Azure Digital Twins, Azure IoT Hub and other Azure services. It describes combining Microsoft Fabric as an all-in-one platform with Azure resources for storage, compute and device connectivity. The episode presents this as enabling hybrid scenarios in which both Fabric and Azure Digital Twins are used for large-scale digital twin creation and for real-time intelligence workloads.

azure-disk-storage.desc: Azure Disk Storage, also called Azure Managed Disks, is Microsoft's block storage for Azure virtual machines, offered in HDD, SSD and Ultra tiers.

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Disk Storage - Simply Explained", Azure Blob Storage stores files and objects, while Azure disks act like the physical hard drives in a traditional server and provide persistent block storage for virtual machines.
faq.q: What is the difference between Azure Disk Storage and Azure Blob Storage?

faq.a: The episode names Standard HDD, Standard SSD, Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disks. They let administrators balance cost and performance based on the workload.
faq.q: Which disk types does Azure Disk Storage include?

faq.a: Azure Managed Disks is listed as an alias of Azure Disk Storage. The episode on Azure Managed Disks describes them as fully managed block storage for Azure Virtual Machines, with provisioning, availability, redundancy and lifecycle management handled by Azure.
faq.q: Is Azure Disk Storage the same as Azure Managed Disks?

azure-disk-storage.long:
Azure Disk Storage is the persistent block storage service used by Azure Virtual Machines. It is also referred to as Azure Managed Disks. Microsoft develops it as part of Microsoft Azure, and it is described as a fully managed block storage solution. The product page for it summarizes the range as block storage volumes for Azure virtual machines, from Standard HDD to Premium and Ultra SSD.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Disk Storage - Simply Explained" explains the role of a disk by comparison. Unlike Azure Blob Storage, which stores files and objects, Azure disks act like the physical hard drives in a traditional server. Every Azure VM relies on managed disks for its operating system, applications and data. Microsoft handles availability, durability, redundancy and infrastructure, so the person running the virtual machine works with a disk as a volume rather than with the hardware underneath it.

The companion episode "Azure Managed Disks - Simply Explained" focuses on the managed aspect. It says that, instead of manually creating and maintaining storage accounts, Azure automatically handles provisioning, availability, redundancy and lifecycle management. The stated benefit is that administrators can concentrate on their workloads rather than on storage operations, while still getting reliable, scalable and high-performance storage.

Azure offers several disk types so that cost and performance can be balanced according to the workload. The episode names Standard HDD, Standard SSD, Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disks. Choosing between them is the central design decision: a disk type is picked per workload, depending on how much performance the application needs and how much the organization wants to spend on storage.

The overview of Azure storage in the episode "Azure Storage Accounts - Simply Explained" lists key features of Azure Disk Storage. It describes high-performance, durable block storage for Azure VMs. Data remains intact when a VM is stopped or deallocated, which means information is not lost during maintenance or updates. The same episode also notes that Azure Disk Storage supports encryption.

Disks also appear in discussions of shared storage. The episode "Azure Elastic SAN — Simply Explained" notes that Azure Managed Disks work very well for many individual virtual machines. The difficulty it describes arises in environments with many workloads that have different performance patterns. Examples given are a SQL database with its highest load at month-end, a reporting server that is busy every morning, and backup workloads that use significant storage bandwidth overnight. Because each disk has its own capacity and performance, one workload can leave performance unused while another needs more that it cannot borrow. Azure Elastic SAN approaches this by providing high-performance block storage through a shared pool.

In practice, Azure Disk Storage sits next to other Azure storage services rather than replacing them. Disks serve the operating system and data volumes of virtual machines, Azure Blob Storage covers files and objects, and Azure Elastic SAN offers a pooled alternative for block storage. The related episodes on Azure Storage Accounts, Azure Blob Storage and local NVMe storage for Fabric and AKS workloads place disks within that wider set of storage choices.

azure-dns.desc: Azure DNS is Microsoft's managed service in Azure for hosting public DNS domains and private DNS zones and resolving names without self-run DNS servers.

faq.a: Azure DNS hosts DNS domains in Azure and provides name resolution for applications. It supports public internet domains through Azure Public DNS and name resolution inside virtual networks through Azure Private DNS.
faq.q: What is Azure DNS used for?

faq.a: Azure DNS Private Resolver allows queries from on-premises environments to private zones and the reverse, without VM-based DNS servers. This enables name resolution between Azure and on-premises networks.
faq.q: How does Azure DNS support hybrid environments?

faq.a: No. Azure Traffic Manager is a DNS-based traffic load balancer, but it is a separate service with its own documentation, while Azure DNS focuses on DNS hosting and name resolution.
faq.q: Is Azure Traffic Manager the same as Azure DNS?

azure-dns.long:
Azure DNS is a hosting and name resolution service for DNS domains that runs on Azure infrastructure. It is developed by Microsoft and is part of Microsoft Azure, where it belongs to the network foundations category alongside services such as virtual networks and Private Link. In short, it lets organizations host their DNS zones in Azure and resolve names for cloud and hybrid environments without operating their own DNS servers.

The service covers two main areas. Azure Public DNS hosts domains for the public internet. Records are managed with the same credentials, APIs, tools and billing as other Azure services, so DNS administration can sit in the same environment as the rest of an Azure deployment. Azure Private DNS manages and resolves names inside virtual networks, so a custom DNS solution is not needed for name resolution between resources in those networks.

Further components extend the service to hybrid and security scenarios. Azure DNS Private Resolver allows queries from on-premises environments to reach private zones and the other way round, without VM-based DNS servers. DNS Resolver Policy filters and logs DNS queries at virtual network level and includes a threat intelligence feed, which means known malicious domains can be blocked from resolution. These parts address typical situations in which an organization runs workloads both in Azure and in its own data center and needs consistent name resolution across both.

The Microsoft Learn overview names several typical scenarios: hosting public domains, automatic registration of virtual machines, name resolution between Azure and on-premises networks, monitoring through metrics and alerts, protection of zones and records, and failover. Azure Traffic Manager is described there as a DNS-based traffic load balancer, but it is a separate service with its own documentation. This is a useful distinction when deciding between hosting DNS records and distributing traffic across endpoints. Prerequisites, prices and limits are not covered in the overview and are left to the FAQ pages of the documentation.

The M365.FM episode "Azure DNS - Simply Explained" presents Azure DNS as Microsoft's managed Domain Name System service that hosts and resolves domain names using Azure's global infrastructure. According to the episode, it allows organizations to manage public and private DNS zones, automate DNS management, and provide fast, reliable name resolution for cloud and hybrid environments, all without maintaining their own DNS servers. The episode is part of the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets format.

For planning, the main decisions revolve around which zones are public and which are private, how on-premises name resolution connects to Azure through the Private Resolver, and whether query filtering at virtual network level is required. Because Azure DNS uses the same management model as other Azure resources, it fits teams that already administer their infrastructure through Azure tools and want DNS handled in the same way.

azure-dns-alias-record.desc: An Azure DNS alias record points a DNS name directly at an Azure resource, such as a load balancer or CDN endpoint, and updates automatically when the resource's IP address changes.
azure-dns-alias-record.long:
An Azure DNS alias record is an Azure-specific DNS record type that points a name directly at an Azure resource instead of at a fixed IP address or another hostname. Examples of target resources include a load balancer or a CDN endpoint. It is a feature of Azure DNS, the service within which the record is created and managed.

The main purpose of an alias record is to keep a DNS name aligned with the resource it references. When the IP address of the referenced Azure resource changes, the alias record updates automatically, so the DNS entry does not need to be edited by hand. This reduces the risk of stale records that continue to point at an address the resource no longer uses.

Within the Azure DNS topic, alias records sit alongside the standard DNS record types as a way to link a zone's names to Azure resources. Administrators use them when a name should follow a resource rather than a manually maintained address. The official Microsoft Learn documentation on Azure DNS alias records describes the supported scenarios and configuration in detail.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity.

azure-elastic-san.desc: Azure Elastic SAN is a managed Azure storage area network that pools block storage into volume groups and volumes, which workloads attach to over iSCSI.

faq.a: Azure Elastic SAN is a managed storage area network service in Microsoft Azure that provides pooled block storage. It is organized into volume groups and volumes, and workloads connect to volumes over iSCSI.
faq.q: What is Azure Elastic SAN?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, Azure Elastic SAN can serve as shared backend storage for Azure Virtual Machines, Azure VMware Solution and Azure Kubernetes Service.
faq.q: Which Azure services can use Azure Elastic SAN as storage?

faq.a: It supports encryption at rest, LRS or ZRS redundancy, private endpoints, VNet-restricted access and snapshots. Encryption in transit and soft delete are not supported, and a single volume can reach up to 80,000 IOPS as an upper bound.
faq.q: What features and limits does Azure Elastic SAN have?

azure-elastic-san.long:
Azure Elastic SAN is a managed storage area network service in Microsoft Azure that provides pooled, high-performance block storage. Microsoft Learn describes it as a fully integrated SAN offering that simplifies provisioning, scaling and managing a storage area network, with cloud capabilities such as high availability built in. Workloads connect to its volumes over iSCSI. It belongs to Microsoft Azure and is aimed at performance-heavy workloads and large databases.

The service addresses a problem that often appears only after an Azure environment grows. One virtual machine with one Managed Disk is simple, but as more virtual machines, databases and applications appear, each workload can end up with its own disks, its own performance limits and its own capacity decisions. The episode "Azure Elastic SAN — Simply Explained" describes the resulting inefficiency: one workload may pay for storage performance it rarely uses while another needs additional capacity or performance. Consolidating many IO-intensive workloads onto one SAN, instead of managing storage separately for each compute resource, can be more cost-efficient, according to the documentation.

Azure Elastic SAN is organized into three levels. The Elastic SAN itself is the top-level resource, where redundancy and provisioned capacity are set. Volume groups sit beneath it and pass settings, such as virtual network rules, down to the volumes they contain. Volumes are the partitions of capacity that clients attach to over iSCSI. Because performance is shared across all volumes in the SAN, volumes typically do not need to be overprovisioned individually. According to the documentation, a single volume can reach up to 80,000 IOPS depending on the SAN's limits and the volume's size, and these figures are upper bounds rather than guarantees.

Azure Elastic SAN can act as shared backend storage for several Azure compute services: Azure Virtual Machines, Azure VMware Solution and Azure Kubernetes Service. This makes it relevant for scenarios where many workloads draw on one storage pool and where sizing each disk separately would lead to stranded capacity or unused performance.

The documented feature set includes encryption at rest, locally redundant storage (LRS) or zone-redundant storage (ZRS) redundancy, private endpoints, access restricted to virtual networks, and snapshots. Two limits are worth noting when planning: encryption in transit and soft delete are not supported. Teams evaluating Azure Elastic SAN against per-VM Managed Disks should weigh the pooled-performance model against these constraints, as well as the redundancy option chosen at the SAN level.

The second episode, "Shared Data Reservoirs for Multi-Tenant Microsoft 365", places Azure Elastic SAN within a wider architectural discussion. It covers centralized, scalable resource pools as an alternative to isolated storage silos and fixed allocations, alongside concepts such as Azure SQL Hyperscale, elastic storage pools, shared performance layers and tenant-wide scaling models for multi-tenant Microsoft 365 environments. The episode also discusses automation, orchestration, governance and dynamic scaling as ways to improve operational efficiency and reduce infrastructure waste.

In short, Azure Elastic SAN is a pooled block-storage option in Azure where capacity and performance are provisioned at the SAN level and distributed across volumes, rather than assigned workload by workload.

azure-event-grid.desc: Azure Event Grid is a managed publish-subscribe service in Microsoft Azure that routes events from publishers to subscribed handlers over HTTP or MQTT.

faq.a: Azure Event Grid is a fully managed publish-subscribe service in Microsoft Azure that routes events from publishers such as Azure services or custom apps to subscribed handlers. It supports HTTP and MQTT, with push and pull delivery.
faq.q: What is Azure Event Grid?

faq.a: According to the episode "IoT Hub Message Routing vs Event Grid — Why Telemetry and Events Are Not the Same Problem", IoT Hub Message Routing is designed around preserving and distributing operational data, while Event Grid is designed around notifying systems that something changed and may require a response.
faq.q: How does Azure Event Grid differ from IoT Hub Message Routing?

faq.a: The episode "Event Grid - Simply Explained" compares Event Grid with Azure Service Bus and Event Hubs to help listeners decide which messaging service fits a given situation.
faq.q: Which Azure services are compared with Event Grid in the episodes?

azure-event-grid.long:
Azure Event Grid is a fully managed publish-subscribe service in Microsoft Azure. It routes events from publishers, such as Azure services or custom applications, to subscribed handlers. Delivery works over HTTP or MQTT, and both push and pull delivery are supported. The service is part of Microsoft Azure and is documented on Microsoft Learn.

The core idea is event-driven design. The M365.FM episode "Azure Event Grid - Simply Explained" describes Event Grid as the part of Azure that tells applications what has already happened. A file lands in storage, a device connects, or an order comes in, and instead of application code asking over and over whether something changed, Event Grid delivers the news. The episode "Event Grid - Simply Explained" makes the same point: instead of constantly polling for changes, Event Grid delivers notifications in real time, which lets services react instantly when something happens.

In practical terms, a publisher emits an event, and subscribers register interest in the events they care about. Event Grid sits between the two and moves the event from source to handler, so publishers and handlers do not need to know about each other directly. The episode "Azure Event Grid - Simply Explained" structures its explanation around a small set of terms, including why event-driven architecture keeps coming up, what the service actually is, and the kinds of delivery it supports. The episodes frame Event Grid as a building block for cloud-native, serverless and microservices architectures, where components respond to changes rather than checking for them on a schedule.

A frequent design decision is choosing between Event Grid and other Azure messaging services. The episode "Event Grid - Simply Explained" compares Event Grid with Azure Service Bus and Event Hubs so listeners can judge when each service is the right choice. A second episode theme concerns separating telemetry from events. In "IoT Hub Message Routing vs Event Grid — Why Telemetry and Events Are Not the Same Problem", the hosts follow a manufacturing scenario in which a press line continuously sends temperature, vibration, cycle count, energy consumption and machine-state data through an industrial gateway. That stream forms an operational history that engineers, data teams and maintenance teams may need to analyze later. A device disconnect is different, because it is a discrete change that may require a response.

According to that episode, Azure IoT Hub Message Routing and Azure Event Grid solve different problems. One path is designed around preserving and distributing operational data. The other is designed around notifying systems that something changed and may require a response. The episode warns that treating the two as interchangeable can lead to expensive workflows processing routine sensor data, or to important signals buried inside a telemetry pipeline that nobody is actively watching. It also notes that treating routine measurements as discrete events can create noisy workflows, incomplete production histories, unnecessary processing, and systems that react without enough context.

Event Grid also appears in the modernization discussion in "Replace Legacy Middleware with Policy-Driven Architecture". That episode names Microsoft Azure Event Grid and Service Bus as enabling real-time, event-driven architectures that reduce what it calls the coordination tax of legacy middleware, and links modernization to faster response to market changes and improved customer experience.

In summary, Azure Event Grid is the routing layer for "something happened" notifications in Azure. It is most relevant where applications should react to state changes from Azure services or custom sources, and less suited to being used as a store or pipeline for continuous measurement data, a distinction the M365.FM episodes return to repeatedly.

azure-event-hubs.desc: Azure Event Hubs is Microsoft's big-data streaming and event ingestion service in Azure, handling millions of events per second and compatible with Apache Kafka.

faq.a: Azure Event Hubs is Microsoft's big-data streaming platform and event ingestion service in Microsoft Azure. It receives and processes millions of events per second and is compatible with Apache Kafka.
faq.q: What is Azure Event Hubs?

faq.a: According to the episode "IoT Hub vs Event Hubs — Why Most Manufacturers Pick the Wrong Service", Event Hubs focuses on stream processing and high-volume data movement via partitions and consumer groups. It does not manage device lifecycles, firmware or desired configurations.
faq.q: How does Azure Event Hubs differ from IoT Hub?

faq.a: The episodes mention Azure Functions, Azure Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Data Explorer, Apache Kafka, Event Grid, Microsoft Graph change notifications and Fabric Data Activator as integrations or related services.
faq.q: Which services work with Azure Event Hubs?

azure-event-hubs.long:
Azure Event Hubs is a big-data streaming platform and event ingestion service developed by Microsoft and offered as part of Microsoft Azure. It receives and processes millions of events per second and is compatible with Apache Kafka. In everyday usage it is often shortened to Event Hubs. Microsoft documents the service in its Azure documentation, and it is classified as a Microsoft tool within the wider Azure portfolio.

The core purpose of Event Hubs is high-throughput, low-latency movement of event data from many producers to many independent readers. The episode "IoT Hub vs Event Hubs — Why Most Manufacturers Pick the Wrong Service" describes it as a data highway that focuses entirely on stream processing and high-volume movement. According to that episode, its primary job is keeping traffic moving efficiently through partitions and consumer groups. Partitions and consumer groups are therefore central concepts: they allow data to be spread across parallel streams and read by several consumers independently.

An important distinction made in the same episode is what Event Hubs does not do. It does not manage device lifecycles, firmware or desired configurations. Those responsibilities belong to a device-management service, and the episode contrasts Event Hubs with Azure IoT Hub, where individual gateways can be identified, authenticated, enabled or disabled. For example, a single suspect gateway on a production line can be isolated without shutting down the whole plant's telemetry path. The episode's argument is that manufacturers often choose the wrong service by overlooking this difference between a device-aware service and a pure streaming pipeline.

The episode "Azure Event Hubs - Simply Explained" presents the service as a high-throughput event streaming platform for cloud-native applications, IoT solutions, real-time analytics and large-scale data pipelines. It also covers how Event Hubs integrates with Azure Functions, Azure Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Data Explorer, Apache Kafka and other analytics platforms to support real-time processing and insights. Kafka compatibility is relevant for teams that already use Kafka-based tooling and want to work with an Azure-hosted streaming endpoint.

Event Hubs also appears as a building block in other Microsoft services covered by M365.FM. In "Microsoft Graph Change Notifications - Simply Explained", Event Hubs is named as an alternative to webhooks for receiving change notifications: webhooks suit instant push notifications, while Event Hubs is the choice for handling large volumes of notifications securely and reliably. In "Event Grid - Simply Explained", Azure Event Hubs is listed as an example of an event publisher that sends events to Event Grid, alongside Azure Blob Storage. In "Power BI Alerts vs Fabric Data Activator", it is mentioned as one of the sources, along with Power BI, that Fabric Data Activator can connect to in order to watch live data and trigger alerts or actions, such as messages in Teams, emails or workflows.

Taken together, the episodes position Event Hubs as an ingestion and streaming layer rather than a complete solution on its own. Typical decisions around it concern whether device management is needed (pointing to IoT Hub), whether volume justifies Event Hubs over webhooks for notification delivery, and which downstream consumers, such as Stream Analytics, Functions, Fabric or Data Explorer, will process the incoming events.

azure-expressroute.desc: Azure ExpressRoute is Microsoft's private, dedicated connection between on-premises networks and Azure that avoids the public internet.

faq.a: Azure ExpressRoute is a Microsoft product that provides a private, dedicated connection between on-premises networks and Microsoft cloud services. The traffic does not traverse the public internet.
faq.q: What is Azure ExpressRoute?

faq.a: ExpressRoute is a private dedicated connection, while VPN Gateway is the VPN option for connecting networks to Azure. The M365.FM episode "Azure VPN Gateway - Simply Explained" includes a section comparing VPN Gateway versus ExpressRoute.
faq.q: How does ExpressRoute differ from Azure VPN Gateway?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Virtual Network - Simply Explained", Azure Virtual Network integrates with services such as VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, Azure Firewall, Load Balancer, Private Link, Azure Bastion and Azure Kubernetes Service. Azure Virtual WAN can also centralize ExpressRoute connections.
faq.q: Which Azure services does ExpressRoute work alongside?

azure-expressroute.long:
Azure ExpressRoute is a Microsoft networking product that provides a private, dedicated connection between on-premises networks and Microsoft cloud services. Unlike a standard internet connection, the traffic does not traverse the public internet. ExpressRoute is developed by Microsoft and is part of Microsoft Azure. The product is documented on Microsoft Learn under the Azure ExpressRoute documentation.

The main purpose of ExpressRoute is to connect enterprise infrastructure to Azure in a way that supports demanding networking requirements. The M365.FM episode "Azure ExpressRoute - Simply Explained" describes it as Microsoft's dedicated private network connection for securely connecting on-premises infrastructure to Azure without sending traffic over the public internet. According to that episode, it is designed for enterprise and mission-critical workloads and delivers predictable performance, low latency, higher reliability and enhanced security. This is why it is described as a preferred connectivity option for organizations with demanding networking needs.

Typical situations in which ExpressRoute comes into consideration are hybrid cloud scenarios, where an organization runs workloads both in its own datacenters and in Azure and needs a stable, controlled path between the two. In these cases the choice is usually between a private dedicated circuit and an internet-based alternative. The episode "Azure VPN Gateway - Simply Explained" covers this decision directly under the heading "VPN Gateway Versus ExpressRoute", alongside topics such as site-to-site versus point-to-site connections, gateway SKUs and tunnels, route-based versus policy-based VPNs, and BGP and active-active configurations. VPN Gateway is the encrypted-tunnel option over the internet, while ExpressRoute is the private-connection option, so the two are often compared when planning hybrid connectivity.

ExpressRoute does not exist in isolation but fits into the wider Azure networking stack. The episode "Azure Virtual Network - Simply Explained" explains that Azure Virtual Network integrates with services such as Azure VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, Azure Firewall, Load Balancer, Private Link, Azure Bastion and Azure Kubernetes Service to build secure and scalable cloud architectures. In that context, ExpressRoute provides the hybrid connectivity path into a virtual network, while concepts such as subnets, IP address spaces, route tables, network security groups and VNet peering shape what happens inside Azure.

ExpressRoute also appears in discussions of centralized network management. The episode "Azure Virtual WAN - Simply Explained" presents Azure Virtual WAN as Microsoft's global networking service that connects branch offices, remote users, virtual networks and on-premises datacenters through the Microsoft global backbone. The episode notes that instead of managing multiple VPN gateways, ExpressRoute connections and complex routing configurations individually, Virtual WAN offers a centralized platform for building secure, scalable and high-performance enterprise networks. ExpressRoute is therefore one of the connection types that Virtual WAN can consolidate.

Cost is another topic raised in the episodes. The episode "Azure Private Link - Simply Explained" compares Azure Private Link with traditional solutions such as ExpressRoute.
