faq.a: No. According to Microsoft Learn there is no additional cost, and any Azure customer or partner can use it. EA, CSP and pay-as-you-go licensing are supported.
faq.q: Does Azure Lighthouse cost extra?

faq.a: No. Microsoft 365 Lighthouse is a separate offering. Azure Lighthouse concerns delegated management of Azure resources across tenants.
faq.q: Is Azure Lighthouse the same as Microsoft 365 Lighthouse?

azure-lighthouse.long:
Azure Lighthouse is a service that is part of Microsoft Azure. It allows a service provider, or an enterprise with several tenants, to manage resources in other Azure tenants through delegated resource management, without needing accounts in those tenants. The aim is multitenant management with greater automation and governance across resources. According to Microsoft Learn, Azure Lighthouse is a non-regional service.

The problem it addresses is often described as the "two houses" problem: an outside company has to work in a customer's Azure environment, but handing over passwords or creating separate accounts in every customer tenant is cumbersome and hard to control. The M365.FM episode "Azure Lighthouse - Simply Explained" frames it this way: an outside company can manage an Azure setup without ever holding the customer's password. The episode outline covers what Azure Lighthouse is, how the connection between the two sides is created ("The Handshake: How the Door Gets Built"), who uses it and who approves it, and the security question of who really holds access.

The mechanism is Azure Delegated Resource Management. A customer delegates a subscription or a resource group to users and roles in the managing tenant, and the managing users then work on those resources from their own tenant. The customer stays in control of who has access, which resources can be reached and what actions are permitted. The delegation can be revoked at any time. Onboarding can be done with Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates, or through managed service offers published in the Microsoft Marketplace.

Visibility is handled in the Azure portal. A "My customers" view gives the service provider cross-tenant information, while a "Service providers" view lets customers review the delegations they have granted. The activity log in the customer tenant shows who made changes, which supports auditing of delegated work. Other services work together with Azure Lighthouse, including Azure Policy, Microsoft Sentinel and Azure Arc, so that governance, security monitoring and hybrid resources can be handled across tenants.

Several practical points are stated in the documentation. There is no additional cost for Azure Lighthouse, and any Azure customer or partner can use it. Enterprise Agreement (EA), Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) and pay-as-you-go licensing are supported. There are limits as well: delegation across a national cloud and the public cloud, or between two national clouds, is not possible. Azure Lighthouse should also not be confused with Microsoft 365 Lighthouse, which is a separate offering.

Azure Lighthouse also appears in the context of the Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider program. In the episode "Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) - Simply Explained", a tip for partners is to use Azure Lighthouse for administering on behalf of (AOBO) access in support scenarios, which the episode says helps manage customer accounts more efficiently. Typical decisions around the service therefore concern which subscriptions or resource groups to delegate, which roles the managing tenant receives, how onboarding is performed (templates or Marketplace offers), and how customers review and, if needed, revoke the delegations.

azure-load-balancer.desc: Azure Load Balancer is a Layer 4 service in Microsoft Azure that spreads TCP and UDP traffic across virtual machines or scale set instances using health probes.

faq.a: It distributes TCP and UDP traffic across virtual machines or scale set instances and uses health probes so that traffic goes only to healthy instances.
faq.q: What does Azure Load Balancer do?

faq.a: According to the episodes, Load Balancer distributes traffic within a region at Layer 4, Front Door acts as a global application delivery network, and Traffic Manager works at the DNS layer.
faq.q: How does Azure Load Balancer differ from Azure Front Door and Traffic Manager?

faq.a: Health probes let the service send traffic only to healthy instances. The episode "Design Reliable and Resilient Azure Architectures" recommends reviewing Load Balancer and Application Gateway health probes and session persistence as part of a network checklist.
faq.q: Why are health probes important for Azure Load Balancer?

azure-load-balancer.long:
Azure Load Balancer is a Layer 4 load-balancing service in Microsoft Azure. It distributes TCP and UDP traffic across virtual machines or virtual machine scale set instances and uses health probes to send traffic only to instances that are healthy. It is one of the core networking services in Azure and is documented as part of the platform's load-balancing options.

The main purpose of the service is to keep applications available, scalable and resilient as traffic grows. Relying on a single virtual machine creates a single point of failure: if that machine fails or becomes overloaded, the application is affected. Placing several similar instances behind a load balancer spreads the incoming connections, and the health probes allow unhealthy instances to be left out of rotation. The episode "Azure Load Balancer — Simply Explained" presents these ideas in plain English as part of the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets series, focusing on how the service supports availability, scalability and resilience.

Because Azure Load Balancer operates at Layer 4, it works with TCP and UDP traffic rather than inspecting application-level content such as URLs or HTTP headers. This distinction matters when choosing between Azure's traffic-distribution services. The episode "Azure Traffic Manager - Simply Explained" describes Load Balancer as distributing traffic within a region, while Azure Front Door acts as a global application delivery network and Traffic Manager operates at the DNS layer. The episode "Azure Front Door - Simply Explained" likewise covers how Front Door differs from Azure Load Balancer, Azure Traffic Manager and Azure Application Gateway, and lists global load balancing, URL routing, caching, Web Application Firewall and SSL/TLS termination as Front Door concepts. In practice, the choice depends on whether the requirement is regional TCP/UDP distribution, DNS-based routing, or global HTTP-focused delivery.

Typical scenarios involve long-running application tiers where several machines perform similar roles. The episode "Azure Compute Fleet – Simply Explained" names customer-facing websites, APIs, line-of-business applications and application servers behind Azure Load Balancer or Application Gateway as suitable workloads for virtual machine scale sets. In those cases, application health, traffic handling and scaling the number of similar instances are the central requirements, which is exactly where a load balancer and its health probes fit. The same episode contrasts this with Compute Fleet, which targets obtaining large amounts of compute for work spread across many independent workers.

The service also appears in reliability and troubleshooting guidance. The episode "Design Reliable and Resilient Azure Architectures" includes a network checklist that recommends reviewing Azure Load Balancer and Application Gateway health probes and session persistence, alongside checking network security group and user-defined route rules for unintended packet drops, measuring latency between tiers and across regions, and enabling Accelerated Networking where supported. This reflects the practical point that a load balancer's behavior depends on correctly configured probes and on the surrounding network configuration.

Azure Load Balancer is part of Microsoft Azure and is commonly combined with other Azure services. It sits in front of virtual machines and scale sets, can be used together with Application Gateway for application-tier designs, and is discussed alongside Traffic Manager and Front Door when planning regional and global traffic flow. Official documentation is available from Microsoft Learn in its load balancer overview.

azure-local.desc: Azure Local, formerly Azure Stack HCI, is a Microsoft distributed infrastructure solution that runs Azure services, VMs and containers on customer-owned hardware via Azure Arc.

faq.a: Azure Local is a Microsoft distributed infrastructure solution, formerly called Azure Stack HCI, that runs Azure services, virtual machines and containers on customer-owned hardware managed through Azure Arc.
faq.q: What is Azure Local?

faq.a: It is managed through Azure Arc, which gives local hardware an Azure identity so that policies, Defender rules, RBAC and monitoring can apply in the same way as for Azure resources.
faq.q: How is Azure Local managed?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, some workloads must remain close to factories, offices or regulated environments, or are latency-sensitive, and Azure Local also supports in-country data processing for data residency needs.
faq.q: Why would an organization use Azure Local instead of only the public cloud?

azure-local.long:
Azure Local is a distributed infrastructure solution from Microsoft that brings Azure services, virtual machines and containers to hardware owned by the customer. It was formerly known as Azure Stack HCI, and that older name still appears in documentation and discussions, including in M365.FM episodes. Azure Local is part of Microsoft Azure and is managed through Azure Arc, which means that on-premises or edge systems can be handled with the same control plane concepts used for resources in the public cloud.

The core idea is hybrid infrastructure. Some workloads cannot live entirely in the public cloud, for example because they must stay close to factories, offices or regulated environments, depend on existing infrastructure, or are sensitive to latency. Azure Local addresses these situations by placing compute on local hardware while keeping the management model aligned with Azure. In practice, this connects to topics such as Azure Landing Zones, Infrastructure as Code and automated deployment pipelines, which organizations use to standardize their Azure environments and which can be extended to hybrid scenarios.

Azure Arc is the link between the local hardware and Azure. According to the M365.FM episode "Cut Cloud Costs with Azure Arc and Azure Local on Mini PCs", Azure Arc lets self-owned mini PCs and edge boxes receive an Azure identity, so that they can follow the same policies, Defender rules, RBAC and monitoring as resources running in Azure. The episode frames this as a way to reduce cloud spending while keeping governance, security and automation in place. The statements about cost reduction are the episode's perspective and depend on the individual workload and setup.

Pricing is another recurring decision point. The episode "Azure Arc - Simply Explained" notes that Azure Arc uses a flexible, usage-based pricing model and states that Azure Stack HCI, the earlier name of the product, is charged according to the number of physical cores, while Arc-enabled services typically incur costs per resource or per feature. The episode advises tracking usage carefully to manage expenses. Anyone planning a deployment should check current official documentation for the actual licensing terms.

Data residency and sovereignty are a further area where Azure Local appears. The episode "Microsoft 365 Data Sovereignty Beyond Technical Custody" says that Azure Local and sovereign Azure offerings provide local infrastructure, isolated control planes and contractual assurances intended to keep data stored and processed within a region. According to the episode, they support in-country data processing and can help organizations meet strict data residency requirements, including for AI workloads. This places Azure Local in discussions about digital sovereignty rather than only in infrastructure design.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Local and Landing Zones: How to Build Hybrid Cloud the Right Way with Christoffer Klarskov Jakobsen [MVP]" covers how Azure Local fits into a broader cloud strategy that includes platform services, Infrastructure as Code and Azure Landing Zones. A separate episode, "Azure Local - Simply Explained", offers an introductory overview of the product.

In summary, Azure Local is relevant when an organization wants Azure-style management, governance and services but needs the workloads themselves to run on its own hardware. Typical decisions concern which workloads stay local, how Azure Arc governance is applied, how licensing is calculated, and how landing zone practices are extended to the hybrid environment.

azure-management-group.desc: An Azure management group is a container above Azure subscriptions that organizes them into a hierarchy, with access and policies inherited by every subscription beneath it.

faq.a: An Azure management group is a container above Azure subscriptions that lets an organization arrange many subscriptions into one hierarchy.
faq.q: What is an Azure management group?

faq.a: Access and policies assigned at a management group are inherited by every subscription underneath it.
faq.q: What do subscriptions inherit from a management group?

faq.a: It is a concept within Microsoft Azure, used to organize subscriptions into a hierarchy for consistent access and policy assignment.
faq.q: How does an Azure management group relate to Microsoft Azure?

azure-management-group.long:
An Azure management group is a container that sits above Azure subscriptions within Microsoft Azure. It allows an organization to arrange many subscriptions into a single hierarchy instead of managing each one separately.

The main purpose of a management group is inheritance. Access assignments and policies applied at a management group are inherited by every subscription underneath it. This lets administrators define a setting once at a higher level and have it apply consistently across all the subscriptions in that branch of the hierarchy.

Management groups are part of the broader Microsoft Azure platform and relate to how larger environments with many subscriptions are structured and governed. No episodes on M365.FM are currently linked to this topic, and no further details are recorded here beyond this core definition.

azure-maps.desc: Azure Maps is a set of geospatial services and SDKs in Microsoft Azure, and in Power BI its visual replaces the deprecated Bing Maps-based map visuals.

faq.a: Azure Maps is a collection of geospatial services and SDKs in Microsoft Azure that give web and mobile applications geographic context. Its services include Render, Search, Route, Traffic, Weather, Geolocation, Timezone and Geofencing.
faq.q: What is Azure Maps?

faq.a: In Power BI the Azure Maps visual replaces the deprecated Bing Maps-based map and filled map visuals. It must be enabled in the tenant settings before it can be used.
faq.q: How does Azure Maps relate to Power BI?

faq.a: The episode "Migrate Bing Maps to Azure Maps in Power BI" says the Bing Maps visuals are deprecated as of October 2025 and that, without migration, map visuals become blank boxes.
faq.q: What happens to Bing Maps visuals in Power BI?

azure-maps.long:
Azure Maps is a collection of geospatial services and SDKs in Microsoft Azure. It uses current map data to give web and mobile applications geographic context, such as showing locations, finding addresses or calculating routes. It is part of Microsoft Azure and is created and managed through an Azure Maps account in the Azure portal.

The service suite covers several functional areas. According to the Microsoft Learn overview, Render provides vector and raster map tiles and satellite imagery. Search handles addresses, places and points of interest. Route supports point-to-point, multipoint and vehicle-specific routing. Traffic offers flow and incident data, and further services include Weather, Geolocation, Timezone and Geofencing. The services are language-agnostic REST APIs that return JSON, so they can be called from many programming environments. The Web SDK adds interactive maps for JavaScript and TypeScript. Authentication relies on keys that are provided with the Azure Maps account.

For people working with reports rather than code, Azure Maps also appears as a Power BI visual that makes it possible to plot geospatial data without writing code. In Power BI this visual replaces the deprecated Bing Maps-based map and filled map visuals, and it must be enabled in the tenant settings before report authors can use it. A Maps preview in Microsoft Fabric additionally supports geovisualization within Real-Time Intelligence.

The episode "Migrate Bing Maps to Azure Maps in Power BI" (published 2025-11-04) addresses this transition directly. It describes the move from Bing Maps to Azure Maps as not optional, not cosmetic and not just a visual upgrade. The episode states that as of October 2025 the Bing Maps visuals are deprecated and that, without migration, map visuals turn into blank boxes. It frames Azure Maps as a compliance-era replacement rather than a simple change of appearance, and it treats the migration as a countdown for teams that depend on map visuals in production reports.

Several practical points follow from the documentation. The documented limits include that the service is not available in China and Korea. When Azure Maps tiles are used in third-party map controls, a copyright attribution is required. The Geolocation service returns only a country code for an IP address. The documentation also notes that address and location requests are passed to the subprocessor TomTom, which is relevant when organisations review data handling and compliance for map-based reporting.

Typical decisions around Azure Maps therefore concern whether the Azure Maps visual is enabled in the tenant settings, which existing reports still use Bing Maps-based visuals and need migration, and whether the regional availability and data-handling characteristics fit the organisation's requirements. For application scenarios beyond Power BI, the choice of individual services, such as Search or Route, and of the Web SDK or direct REST calls depends on what the application needs to display or calculate.

In summary, Azure Maps is both a developer-oriented geospatial platform and the supported mapping option behind Power BI's map visual. Reports built on the deprecated Bing Maps-based visuals are the main reason the topic comes up for Power BI teams, and the M365.FM episode on the migration is the relevant reference for that situation.

azure-marketplace.desc: Azure Marketplace is Microsoft's online store for certified applications, services and solutions from Microsoft and partners that run on or integrate with Azure.

faq.a: Azure Marketplace is Microsoft's online store for certified applications, services and solutions from Microsoft and partners that run on or integrate with Azure. It is part of Microsoft Azure.
faq.q: What is Azure Marketplace?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, Azure Marketplace mainly serves technical buyers such as architects, developers and Azure administrators looking for items like virtual machines, managed applications and containers. AppSource targets organizations seeking business solutions that work with Microsoft 365. Microsoft now presents them as one unified Marketplace experience.
faq.q: How does Azure Marketplace differ from Microsoft AppSource?

faq.a: The episode "The Hard Way to Get Listed on Microsoft Marketplace" points to meeting requirements, passing certification and creating offers customers can find and buy. It also covers eligibility, co-sell opportunities, private offers and transactable listings, noting that approval is only the beginning.
faq.q: What do partners need to consider when listing on Azure Marketplace?

azure-marketplace.long:
Azure Marketplace is an online store for certified applications, services and solutions from Microsoft and its partners that run on or integrate with Azure. It was developed by Microsoft, is classed as a Microsoft tool, and forms part of Microsoft Azure. Official documentation describes it in the Microsoft Learn marketplace overview.

The marketplace connects two groups. Customers use it to find and deploy technology for their Azure environment. Partners such as independent software vendors, managed service providers and other software vendors use it to list and sell their offerings. According to the episode "Microsoft Marketplace - Simply Explained", buying through a marketplace tied to Azure subscriptions and Microsoft 365 tenants means customers spend less time managing vendors and more time deploying technology that solves business problems.

A point that often causes confusion is the relationship between Azure Marketplace and Microsoft AppSource. The episodes explain that Microsoft now presents one unified Marketplace experience, yet the platform still serves two audiences. Azure Marketplace is primarily aimed at technical buyers: cloud architects, developers, infrastructure engineers and Azure administrators who search for items such as virtual machines, managed applications and containers. Microsoft AppSource, covered in the episode "Microsoft AppSource - Simply Explained", is designed for organizations looking for business solutions, including applications, consulting services, templates and industry-specific offerings that work with Microsoft 365 applications. The same episode describes the two as combined into a single platform that simplifies the search for applications and services.

For partners, the episode "The Hard Way to Get Listed on Microsoft Marketplace" frames listing as more demanding than uploading a product. It covers meeting requirements and passing certification, creating offers that customers can actually find and buy, and understanding how Microsoft evaluates submissions. The discussion also touches on marketplace eligibility, co-sell opportunities, private offers and transactable listings, and notes that many partners underestimate the complexity and learn that approval is only the beginning. The episode also helps partners decide when Azure Marketplace or Microsoft AppSource is the appropriate platform for an offer.

Azure Marketplace also appears in infrastructure workflows. The episode "Azure Image Builder - Simply Explained" notes that Azure Image Builder can start from Windows or Linux images in Azure Marketplace, for example Windows Server, Windows 11 or Ubuntu. Organizations can alternatively start from images they have already created, including images stored in Azure Compute Gallery. In this role the marketplace acts as a known source image, and the result becomes a standardized starting point for future virtual machines.

On the go-to-market side, the episode "How to Build a Winning Microsoft Partner Strategy" lists examples of partners that aligned with Microsoft's approach. It says Databricks coordinated its sales strategy on Azure Marketplace, citing faster customer acquisition, and that a financial services company optimized its marketplace presence and achieved $75,000 in annual savings from a $45,000 investment, described as a 67% ROI. These figures are attributed to the episode.

In summary, Azure Marketplace is the technically oriented storefront within the broader Microsoft Marketplace. Buyers use it to source certified Azure-related software and services, and partners use it as a distribution and sales channel that involves certification, listing quality and co-sell considerations.

azure-mcp-server.desc: Azure MCP Server is Microsoft's open-source Model Context Protocol implementation that lets AI agents work with Azure resources through natural language.

faq.a: Azure MCP Server is Microsoft's open-source implementation of the Model Context Protocol for Azure. It lets MCP-compatible AI agents and clients work with Azure resources through natural language.
faq.q: What is Azure MCP Server?

faq.a: The facts name Storage, Cosmos DB, Azure Monitor and App Configuration as examples of Azure resources that MCP-compatible clients can work with through the server.
faq.q: Which Azure services can it work with?

faq.a: The episode "Azure MCP Server - Simply Explained" covers what it is and how it works, and "MCP (Model Context Protocol) - Simply Explained" explains the underlying protocol.
faq.q: Where can more be learned about it on M365.FM?

azure-mcp-server.long:
Azure MCP Server is Microsoft's open-source implementation of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for Azure. It allows MCP-compatible AI agents and clients to work with Azure resources such as Storage, Cosmos DB, Azure Monitor and App Configuration using natural language. It is part of Microsoft Azure, and getting-started guidance is published in Microsoft's Azure developer documentation on Microsoft Learn.

The product builds on the Model Context Protocol, an open protocol that standardizes how AI assistants and agents connect to external tools and data sources. Instead of writing a separate custom integration for every combination of AI client and cloud service, an MCP server exposes a defined set of capabilities that any compatible client can discover and call. In the case of Azure MCP Server, those capabilities map to Azure services. A user or agent can describe a task in plain language, and the MCP-compatible client uses the server to carry out the corresponding operation against Azure resources.

The typical purpose is to extend AI assistance beyond chat. A conversation with an assistant normally produces text; with an MCP server attached, the assistant can interact with real cloud resources. Examples drawn from the supported services include working with data held in Storage or Cosmos DB, inspecting information in Azure Monitor, and reading or managing settings in App Configuration. This makes the server relevant for developers, cloud administrators and architects who want to use AI agents for cloud management and automation while keeping the interaction tied to their existing Azure environment.

Because an agent acting on cloud resources raises questions of access and governance, decisions around Azure MCP Server usually involve security and operations as much as convenience. The episode "Azure MCP Server - Simply Explained" describes the server as a way for AI assistants and agents to securely interact with Azure resources through the open Model Context Protocol. Planning typically includes deciding which clients are allowed to connect, which Azure resources they may reach, and how those permissions are controlled, in the same way as for any other automation that touches cloud resources.

In the M365.FM series, the episode "Azure MCP Server - Simply Explained", presented by Mirko Peters in the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets format, explains what the Azure MCP Server is, how it works, and why it represents a major step toward AI-driven cloud management and automation. A companion episode, "MCP (Model Context Protocol) - Simply Explained", covers the underlying protocol and is aimed at Microsoft 365 administrators, architects, IT leaders and practitioners who need a practical understanding of MCP before planning or implementing it. Further related episodes include "Dynamics 365 ERP MCP Server - Simply Explained" and "Dataverse MCP Integration with Nathan Rose [MVP]", which show how MCP is applied to other Microsoft platforms alongside Azure.

Placed in context, Azure MCP Server is one of several MCP servers in the Microsoft ecosystem. Where the Dynamics 365 ERP MCP Server and Dataverse MCP integrations connect agents to business applications and data, Azure MCP Server addresses the cloud infrastructure and platform services layer. Together they illustrate the pattern the episodes describe: a common protocol on the client side, with product-specific servers exposing the capabilities of each Microsoft service.

azure-migrate.desc: Azure Migrate is a free Microsoft service and hub within Microsoft Azure that discovers on-premises servers, databases and web apps and assesses them for migration.

faq.a: Azure Migrate is a free Microsoft service and hub within Microsoft Azure. It discovers on-premises servers, databases and web apps, assesses readiness, sizing and cost for Azure, maps dependencies and helps carry out the migration.
faq.q: What is Azure Migrate?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Migrate - Simply Explained" states that Azure Migrate is free and that it will show what your own servers are really costing you.
faq.q: Does Azure Migrate cost anything?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Governance Is Enforced Architecture, Not Documentation", it is the key tool in the Assessment phase, which comes before planning the architecture, readying the environment and migrating workloads.
faq.q: Where does Azure Migrate fit in a migration project?

azure-migrate.long:
Azure Migrate is a free Microsoft service and hub that belongs to Microsoft Azure. It discovers on-premises servers, databases and web apps, assesses their readiness, sizing and cost for Azure, maps dependencies and helps carry out the migration itself. It is used at the start of a cloud migration, when an organization needs a factual picture of what it runs today and what moving it to Azure would involve.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Migrate - Simply Explained" frames the service around one idea: Azure Migrate is free, and it will tell you what your own servers are really costing you. The episode points out that the hard part of a migration usually happens before anyone opens the cloud portal, because nobody mapped what was connected to what. Its outline covers what Azure Migrate actually is, how discovery works, and the assessment stage with its readiness and sizing results. In other words, the service is presented as a way to replace assumptions about the existing environment with discovered data.

The functions described in the sources follow a recognizable sequence. Discovery inventories the on-premises estate, including servers, databases and web apps. The assessment then evaluates readiness for Azure, proposes sizing and estimates cost, which supports the decision of what to move and in what form. Dependency mapping shows which systems communicate with each other, which matters when workloads are moved in groups rather than one by one. Finally, the service helps with the migration step, moving workloads into Azure once the plan is set.

In the episode "Move Legacy Systems to Azure Without Disrupting Work", Azure Migrate is listed among recommended tools for assessing legacy systems. The episode describes it as providing a comprehensive assessment of the on-premises environment, helping to understand dependencies and readiness for migration. It names other tools alongside it for different tasks, such as CloudHealth for analyzing cloud costs and performance and ServiceNow for cataloging IT assets, which shows that Azure Migrate is treated as one part of a wider assessment toolkit rather than the only tool involved.

The episode "Azure Governance Is Enforced Architecture, Not Documentation" places Azure Migrate in the first phase of an Azure cloud migration framework. In that breakdown, the Assessment phase defines business objectives and evaluates the current IT landscape, with Azure Migrate as the key tool. Later phases are planning and designing the architecture with Azure Landing Zones, readying the environment with Azure Policy, migrating workloads in phases with Azure Database Migration Service, and optimizing and modernizing. This positions Azure Migrate as the entry point whose findings feed the landing zone design and the phased migration order.

The episode "Plan a Secure and Cost-Controlled Azure Migration" mentions Azure Migrate as helping to move to the cloud and to find risks. It lists it together with Azure Monitor for continuous monitoring and alerting, Azure Site Recovery for recovery when something goes wrong, and Azure Security Center and Azure Sentinel for threat detection and compliance. The episode also advises checking the system often and testing backup plans.

Finally, "Deploy Web Apps to Azure App Service Without Boilerplate" covers migration strategies for web applications, including assessing existing apps, moving workloads with Azure Migrate, validating performance after the move and resolving common challenges during the transition. Taken together, the episodes treat Azure Migrate as the service for assessment and movement at the beginning of an Azure adoption, closely tied to governance, cost control and monitoring decisions that follow.

azure-monitor.desc: Azure Monitor is Microsoft's monitoring and observability platform in Microsoft Azure, collecting metrics and logs from cloud and on-premises resources.

faq.a: Azure Monitor is Azure's monitoring and observability service. It collects metrics and logs from cloud and on-premises resources, and its log half is Log Analytics.
faq.q: What is Azure Monitor?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Azure Monitor — Simply Explained", it continuously collects metrics, logs, traces, and events to give real-time visibility into infrastructure.
faq.q: What kinds of data does Azure Monitor collect?

faq.a: Episodes on Azure DDoS Protection, Azure Firewall, Azure Functions, and Event Grid mention it for telemetry, alerting, monitoring, and tracking event deliveries. It acts as a shared monitoring layer across these services.
faq.q: How does Azure Monitor relate to other Azure services?

azure-monitor.long:
Azure Monitor is Azure's monitoring service. It collects metrics and logs from cloud and on-premises resources and is part of Microsoft Azure. Its log half is Log Analytics. In the M365.FM episode "Azure Monitor — Simply Explained", it is described as Microsoft's comprehensive monitoring and observability platform that helps organizations understand the health, performance, and availability of their cloud and on-premises environments.

The purpose of Azure Monitor is to replace manual checking of servers, applications, and services with continuous data collection. According to the episode, Azure Monitor continuously collects metrics, logs, traces, and events and gives IT teams real-time visibility into what is running across their infrastructure. Metrics and logs are the two broad kinds of telemetry named in the short description, with Log Analytics serving as the log-focused part of the service. Because the scope covers both cloud and on-premises environments, it applies to hybrid setups as well as to workloads that run entirely in Azure.

In practice, Azure Monitor tends to appear as the common monitoring layer behind other Azure services rather than as a stand-alone topic. Several M365.FM episodes on neighboring services mention it in that role. The episode "Azure DDoS Protection - Simply Explained" lists telemetry, alerting, and integration with Azure Monitor among the key concepts of that service, alongside automatic detection and traffic mitigation. The episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" names Azure Monitor as one of the services Azure Firewall integrates with, together with Azure Bastion, Azure Virtual WAN, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, and Azure Policy, as part of a layered security strategy for enterprise workloads.

The same pattern appears in the application and event-driven side of Azure. In "Azure Functions - Simply Explained", the recommendation is to use Azure Monitor and Application Insights for effective monitoring and troubleshooting of functions. In "Event Grid - Simply Explained", Azure Monitor is listed in the monitor-and-manage step of an Event Grid setup, where it is used to track event deliveries and configure alerts. These examples show a typical decision: instead of building separate monitoring for each service, teams route health and delivery information into Azure Monitor and use alerts to react to problems.

Taken together, the episodes position Azure Monitor as the place where visibility and alerting for Azure workloads come together. For security services such as Azure DDoS Protection and Azure Firewall, it supplies telemetry and alerting. For compute and messaging services such as Azure Functions and Event Grid, it supports troubleshooting and delivery tracking. The sources provided here do not go into pricing, configuration steps, or specific features beyond these roles, so anyone planning a deployment would need to consult the official Microsoft documentation for those details.

azure-monitor-agent.desc: Azure Monitor Agent is a lightweight agent that collects guest OS metrics and logs from Azure, on-premises and other-cloud machines for Azure Monitor using data collection rules.
azure-monitor-agent.long:
Azure Monitor Agent is a lightweight agent that is installed inside a machine to collect guest operating system metrics and logs. It can be deployed on machines running in Azure, on-premises or in other clouds, and it sends the collected data to Azure Monitor.

What the agent gathers is controlled through data collection rules. These rules define which data is collected from a machine and how it is handled, so the agent's behavior is configured through rules rather than being fixed. Azure Monitor Agent replaces the retired Log Analytics agent, which means it is the agent used for guest-level monitoring in place of that earlier component.

Azure Monitor Agent is part of Azure Monitor, the Microsoft monitoring service it feeds. It is relevant wherever telemetry from inside virtual machines or servers needs to reach Azure Monitor, including hybrid and multicloud environments.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity.

azure-monitor-workbooks.desc: Azure Monitor Workbooks are interactive reports in Azure Monitor that combine text, metrics, logs and parameters into custom dashboards for data analysis and visual reporting.

faq.a: They are interactive reports in Azure Monitor that combine text, log queries, metrics and parameters on a flexible canvas in the Azure portal. They can draw on several Azure data sources in one view.
faq.q: What are Azure Monitor Workbooks?

faq.a: Workbooks are opened through Azure Monitor and then Workbooks, or from a Log Analytics workspace page. Access follows a person's permissions on the resources used, and the roles Monitoring Reader, Monitoring Contributor and Workbooks Contributor cover reading and saving shared workbooks.
faq.q: How do users get access to Azure Monitor Workbooks?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn lists investigating VM usage, explaining performance of a new deployment, sharing results of a resizing experiment, and documenting the impact of an outage. They are suited to open-ended exploration when the relevant metrics are not yet known.
faq.q: What are typical uses for Azure Monitor Workbooks?

azure-monitor-workbooks.long:
Azure Monitor Workbooks, also called Azure Workbooks, are interactive reports within Azure Monitor that combine text, log queries, metrics and parameters into custom dashboards. They provide a flexible canvas in the Azure portal for data analysis and visual reporting, and they can pull data from several Azure data sources into one unified view.

The main purpose of Azure Monitor Workbooks is open-ended exploration and custom reporting. According to Microsoft Learn, they suit situations where the relevant metrics are not yet known, for example when investigating how a virtual machine is being used. Because a single workbook can aggregate data from multiple sources, it can include composite resource views or cross-resource joins. Typical uses named in the documentation include investigating VM usage, explaining the performance of a new deployment, sharing the results of a resizing experiment, and documenting the impact of an outage.

Workbooks are reached through Azure Monitor and then the Workbooks section, or from the page of a Log Analytics workspace. A gallery lists saved workbooks, public templates published by Microsoft, and templates that a user has deployed. This template-based approach gives a starting point, while the content can still be adjusted. The M365.FM episode "Azure Monitor — Simply Explained" describes the feature in the same way, noting that it is template-based with full KQL control, which lets the author shape exactly which data a report shows.

Access to a workbook follows the permissions a person has on the resources used in it. The built-in roles Monitoring Reader, Monitoring Contributor and Workbooks Contributor cover reading and saving shared workbooks, and custom roles need the workbooks write permission. The episode summarizes sharing as basic role-based access control, so sharing decisions largely depend on how roles are assigned on the underlying resources and on the workbook itself.

Azure Monitor Workbooks are part of Azure Monitor and sit alongside other visualization options. The episode "Azure Monitor — Simply Explained" places them next to Azure Dashboards, which provide a single view of Azure infrastructure and services, and Power BI, which it describes as useful for business-centric dashboards and for analyzing long-term KPI trends. In that comparison, Workbooks serve as the tool for custom reporting and data visualization that aggregates data from multiple sources, which allows a comprehensive analysis of the data.

When deciding how to present monitoring data, the choice usually depends on the purpose of the view. A fixed overview of infrastructure fits a dashboard, long-term business KPI analysis fits Power BI, and interactive, parameter-driven investigation across metrics and logs fits a workbook. Since workbooks rely on KQL for the log-based parts, familiarity with that query language helps when building or changing reports.

azure-nd-gb200-v6.desc: Azure ND GB200 v6 series is a family of GPU virtual machines on Microsoft Azure that pairs NVIDIA Grace CPUs with Blackwell GPUs for AI and HPC workloads.

faq.a: It is a series of GPU virtual machines in Microsoft Azure built on NVIDIA Grace CPUs and Blackwell GPUs. It is intended for deep learning training, generative AI and HPC workloads.
faq.q: What is the Azure ND GB200 v6 series?

faq.a: The series is based on NVIDIA Grace CPUs and NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, as stated in its product description.
faq.q: Which hardware does the Azure ND GB200 v6 series use?

faq.a: Detailed sizes and specifications are published in Microsoft's official Azure documentation for the ND GB200 v6 series within the GPU-accelerated virtual machine sizes.
faq.q: Where can detailed specifications for the Azure ND GB200 v6 series be found?

azure-nd-gb200-v6.long:
Azure ND GB200 v6 series is a GPU-accelerated virtual machine series offered as part of Microsoft Azure. It is built on NVIDIA Grace CPUs and NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, a combination aimed at compute-intensive tasks.

According to the product description, the series is designed for deep learning training, generative AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. These are scenarios in which large models or simulations require substantial GPU capacity, and the series belongs to Azure's family of GPU-accelerated virtual machine sizes.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, the ND GB200 v6 series sits under Microsoft Azure as one of the virtual machine options available for AI infrastructure. Detailed specifications, sizes and availability are documented by Microsoft in the official Azure virtual machine sizes documentation for the ND GB200 v6 series.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity, so this page serves as a reference definition of the series and its place within Azure.

azure-netapp-files.desc: Azure NetApp Files is a Microsoft Azure file storage service built on NetApp technology, offering NFS and SMB shares for demanding workloads such as SAP and HPC.

faq.a: Azure NetApp Files is an enterprise-grade, high-performance file storage service in Microsoft Azure that provides NFS and SMB file shares. It is powered by NetApp technology and developed by Microsoft.
faq.q: What is Azure NetApp Files?

faq.a: It is aimed at demanding workloads such as SAP and HPC that need very low latency, massive throughput, and advanced data management. The episode "Azure NetApp Files - Simply Explained" describes it as suited to migrating business-critical applications without redesigning storage architecture.
faq.q: Which workloads is Azure NetApp Files designed for?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Files - Simply Explained" notes that Azure Files suits scenarios like file server migration, application data sharing, user profiles, and hybrid architectures, while Azure NetApp Files may be more appropriate in other cases. Choosing between them can help optimize cost and performance.
faq.q: How does Azure NetApp Files differ from Azure Files?

azure-netapp-files.long:
Azure NetApp Files is an enterprise-grade file storage service in Microsoft Azure. It provides NFS and SMB file shares and runs on NetApp technology, while being developed by Microsoft and integrated into Microsoft Azure as one of its services. It is aimed at demanding workloads such as SAP and high-performance computing (HPC), where file access needs to be fast and predictable.

The service is positioned for applications that require extremely low latency, massive throughput, and advanced data management capabilities. Because it is fully integrated into Azure, organizations can move business-critical applications to the cloud without redesigning their storage architecture. This is the central idea behind the service: workloads that previously depended on a particular kind of enterprise file storage can keep that storage model while running in Azure, instead of being rebuilt around a different storage paradigm.

Azure NetApp Files sits alongside other Azure storage options, and choosing between them is a common architectural decision. The M365.FM episode "Azure Files - Simply Explained" describes Azure Files as a service for use cases such as migrating file servers to Azure, sharing application data, storing user profiles, supporting container workloads, and enabling hybrid cloud architectures. That episode also notes that understanding when Azure Files is the right choice, and when Blob Storage or Azure NetApp Files may be more appropriate, can help optimize both cost and performance. In practice, this means Azure NetApp Files is typically considered when performance, latency, or data management requirements go beyond what general-purpose file shares are meant to cover.

The product also appears in virtual desktop scenarios. The episode "Azure Virtual Desktop - Simply Explained" explains that Azure Virtual Desktop integrates with Microsoft 365, Azure Files, Azure NetApp Files, Intune, and Azure Monitor to provide a secure, scalable, and high-performance virtual desktop experience. In the same context, FSLogix user profiles are mentioned as part of the Azure Virtual Desktop feature set, and storage for those profile containers is one of the places where the storage choice matters.

The episode "AVD vs Windows 365: Which Virtual Desktop Strategy Wins: with Shabaz Darr [MVP]" places Azure NetApp Files within a broader discussion of virtual desktop architecture. The conversation covers Azure Landing Zones, Cloud Adoption Framework principles, identity, networking, storage, Azure Files, Azure NetApp Files, FSLogix profile containers, host pools, workspaces, autoscaling, monitoring, and performance optimization. According to the episode, proper planning, governance, and infrastructure design have a far greater impact on long-term success than simply deploying virtual machines, and organizations that invest in architecture from the beginning gain better security and lower operational costs.

The dedicated episode "Azure NetApp Files - Simply Explained", part of the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets format, introduces the service as Microsoft's enterprise-grade, high-performance file storage offering. It describes it as built for demanding workloads, powered by NetApp technology, and fully integrated into Azure. The service is also listed as a related episode in the M365.FM piece "How to Run Local Llama on SharePoint Files Securely", alongside "Azure Files - Simply Explained".

For administrators and architects, the practical takeaways from these sources are about fit. Azure NetApp Files is relevant when an organization needs NFS or SMB storage with strong performance characteristics, such as for SAP or HPC workloads, or when a high-performance storage layer is wanted for virtual desktop profiles. For simpler file sharing, server migration, or hybrid scenarios, the episodes point to Azure Files, and for object data to Blob Storage. Official documentation for the service is available on Microsoft Learn.

azure-open-datasets.desc: Azure Open Datasets is a Microsoft Azure product offering curated public datasets on weather, census, holidays and more for machine learning and analytics.

faq.a: Azure Open Datasets is a Microsoft Azure product with curated public datasets, including weather, census, holiday, public safety and location data, that can be added to machine learning solutions as scenario-specific features.
faq.q: What is Azure Open Datasets?

faq.a: According to the documentation, it integrates with Azure Machine Learning (UI and SDK), Azure Databricks and notebooks, and data can be reached through APIs, Power BI and Azure Data Factory.
faq.q: Which tools can be used with Azure Open Datasets?

faq.a: Access works with an Azure account, but the documentation says the Python package azureml-opendatasets can also be used in any Python environment, with or without Spark, without an account.
faq.q: Is an Azure account required to use Azure Open Datasets?

azure-open-datasets.long:
Azure Open Datasets is a Microsoft product within Microsoft Azure that provides curated public datasets for use in machine learning and analytics solutions. The datasets contain public-domain data on topics such as weather, census, holidays, public safety and location. According to Microsoft Learn, they can be added to machine learning solutions as scenario-specific features, with the aim of obtaining more accurate models.

The service is used to reduce the effort of finding, collecting and preparing outside data. Instead of downloading files from many different websites, a team can draw on datasets that are already hosted in Azure. The M365.FM episode "Azure Open Datasets - Simply Explained" describes it as instant access to curated public datasets hosted by Microsoft, so that less time goes into searching for and cleaning data and more into building AI, analytics and machine learning solutions. The episode also describes the data as trusted and regularly updated.

The documentation explains how the data is prepared. Data is copied into the Azure cloud and reloaded from its original sources at regular intervals; one example given is data from NOAA retrieved over FTP. It is then parsed into a structured format and, where needed, enriched. Examples of enrichment named in the documentation are adding ZIP codes or the locations of the nearest weather stations. The datasets are placed alongside cloud compute, which is intended to ease access and processing. The documentation does not specify the refresh intervals.

Azure Open Datasets connects to several other Azure and Microsoft tools. It integrates with Azure Machine Learning through the user interface and the SDK, and works with Azure Databricks and notebooks. Data can also be reached through APIs, Power BI and Azure Data Factory. The episode lists Azure Machine Learning, Azure Databricks, Power BI and Azure Data Factory among the services it can be used with. Users also have the option to share their own public datasets.

Example datasets mentioned in the documentation include New York taxi trip records, US labor force statistics and US employment, hours and earnings data. A typical situation is enriching a forecasting or prediction model with weather or holiday information that the organization does not collect itself, or exploring public census or labor statistics in a notebook or a Power BI report.

Regarding access, the documentation states that an Azure account works, but that the Python package azureml-opendatasets can also be used in any Python environment, with or without Spark, without an account. This makes the datasets usable outside a full Azure setup. The reviewed sources give no information on prices, service levels or usage limits, so these points need to be checked in the official Microsoft documentation before planning a solution around the service.

In short, Azure Open Datasets sits between public data sources and Azure-based data and AI workloads: Microsoft copies, structures and in some cases enriches public-domain data, and users connect to it through the tools they already use for machine learning, analytics and data integration.

azure-openai.desc: Azure OpenAI Service provides OpenAI models such as GPT through Microsoft Azure, with the security, keys, limits and privacy rules of the customer's own Azure space.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft service that provides OpenAI models such as GPT through Azure with enterprise security and compliance. The models run inside the customer's own Azure space with their own keys, limits and privacy rules.
faq.q: What is Azure OpenAI Service?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure OpenAI Service - Simply Explained", it is not ChatGPT with a Microsoft logo on it. It runs the same models, but Microsoft hosts them in the customer's own Azure environment.
faq.q: Is Azure OpenAI Service the same as ChatGPT?

faq.a: The episode "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform" says it can be connected through built-in connectors in Power Apps and Power Automate, and describes pairing it with Azure API Management for security, throttling and observability.
faq.q: How can Azure OpenAI Service be used with Power Platform?

azure-openai.long:
Azure OpenAI Service is a Microsoft service that provides OpenAI models such as GPT through Azure, with enterprise security and compliance. It is developed by Microsoft, is part of Microsoft Azure and is classed as a Microsoft tool. The M365.FM episode "Azure OpenAI Service - Simply Explained" puts the core idea plainly: it is not ChatGPT with a Microsoft logo on it. It runs the same models, but Microsoft hosts them inside the customer's own Azure space, with the customer's own keys, own limits and own privacy rules.

The service is used when an organization wants to add generative AI features to its own applications and processes rather than rely on a consumer chat product. Because the models are hosted in the customer's Azure environment, the surrounding controls follow the Azure model of ownership: access is governed through keys, usage is bounded by limits, and privacy settings are defined at the customer level. The same episode walks through the building blocks in order: what the service is, the models behind it, deployments as "your own copy of a model", and endpoints and keys as the way applications connect to those deployments.

The model family accessible through the service includes GPT models, and the service is related to GPT-5 in the Microsoft ecosystem. The episodes also mention GPT-4o in a cost context. In "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud", the discussion is that smaller models handle simple tasks well and cost less, while larger models such as GPT-4o offer advanced reasoning but increase expenses. Choosing a model is therefore a cost and capability decision, not only a technical one.

In practice, Azure OpenAI Service is rarely used alone. The episode "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform" describes a pattern in which Power Apps or Dynamics 365 and Power Automate are paired with Azure OpenAI and Azure API Management for security, throttling and observability. According to the episode, Azure OpenAI Service can be connected directly in Power Platform through built-in connectors, so makers can use GPT models in Power Apps and Power Automate without building custom APIs. The same episode also points to low-code prompt engineering in Power Platform and recommends community resources and documentation for troubleshooting and continuous learning.

Other episodes show the service as one component in larger solutions. "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud" combines Azure OpenAI with Copilot Studio, Power Platform and practical cost controls to build agents. "How to Build Private RAG with SharePoint and n8n" lists an Azure OpenAI account as a prerequisite for generating embeddings and using language models, alongside SharePoint for documents, n8n for workflows, Microsoft Graph access, a PostgreSQL or Supabase vector store, Mistral OCR and Open WebUI. That episode also advises having admin rights or the correct permissions on each platform before starting.

For developers, "Build AI Applications with .NET 10" describes connecting a .NET 10 project to Azure OpenAI Service to add generative AI features, using Semantic Kernel for tasks such as text generation and calling GPT models with async and await, with JSON used to handle responses.

Typical decisions around the service therefore include which model to deploy, how to manage keys and limits, how to place a gateway such as Azure API Management in front of it, and how to keep costs under control. The episodes treat these as design choices made together with the surrounding Azure and Power Platform services.

azure-policy.desc: Azure Policy is the Microsoft Azure service for defining rules, bundled as initiatives, that are assigned to a scope to audit, deny, modify or deploy resources.

faq.a: Azure Policy is the Azure service for defining rules, called policy definitions and bundled as initiatives, that are assigned to a scope and inherited downward. It is used to audit, deny, modify or deploy resources so that environments follow organizational standards.
faq.q: What is Azure Policy?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Policy - Simply Explained", it can deny, audit, modify or automatically remediate deployments that do not meet organizational requirements. The effect used depends on how strictly the rule needs to be enforced.
faq.q: What can Azure Policy do when a resource does not meet a rule?

faq.a: The episodes list Azure Policy as a building block of Azure Landing Zones and as a capability used with Azure Arc, which projects non-Azure resources into Azure Resource Manager. This allows consistent governance across Azure, other clouds and on-premises environments.
faq.q: How does Azure Policy relate to Azure Arc and Azure Landing Zones?

azure-policy.long:
Azure Policy is the governance and compliance service of Microsoft Azure. It lets organizations define rules, called policy definitions, and bundle them into initiatives. These rules are assigned to a scope and inherited downward, so a rule set at a higher level applies to everything beneath it. Instead of relying on administrators to follow best practices manually, Azure Policy evaluates resources against the defined rules automatically.

The core idea is to enforce standards and prevent misconfigurations at scale. According to the episode "Azure Policy - Simply Explained", the service can deny, audit, modify or automatically remediate deployments that do not meet organizational requirements. Those effects map to the different ways a rule can be used: auditing reports on resources that fall outside a standard, deny stops a non-compliant resource from being created, modify changes properties on a resource, and deploy-style behavior adds required configuration or related resources. Which effect fits depends on how strictly a standard has to be enforced.

Because assignments are made to a scope and inherited downward, Azure Policy fits naturally into how Azure environments are structured. The episode "Azure Landing Zones - Simply Explained" lists Azure Policy among the core building blocks of a Landing Zone, alongside management groups, subscriptions, resource organization, identity, networking, Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), monitoring and security baselines. In that model, policy assignments at the management group level apply a consistent set of rules as new subscriptions and business units are onboarded, which supports a repeatable architecture and helps avoid redesigns as an Azure environment grows.

Cost control is another use covered in the show. In "Real-Time Azure Cost Control with Azure Policy", Mirko Peters argues that traditional FinOps and Azure cost management approaches often fail because they depend on dashboards, alerts and monthly reviews. By the time overspending appears in a report, the expensive resources already exist and the cleanup has become costly and political. The episode frames Azure Policy as a way to act earlier, at the point where resources are created, rather than reviewing spend after the fact.

Azure Policy also extends beyond resources that run natively in Azure. The episode "Azure Arc - Simply Explained" describes how Azure Arc projects non-Azure resources into Azure Resource Manager, enabling centralized management without migrating workloads. Azure Policy is named there as one of the capabilities used together with Azure Arc, next to Azure Monitor, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, GitOps and Infrastructure as Code. This supports a consistent operational model across Azure, AWS, Google Cloud and on-premises datacenters, including the governance of hybrid servers and Kubernetes clusters.

In the broader compliance context, the episode "Compliance as Code: The Architect’s Blueprint for Automated Trust" discusses how governance rules can become executable code that validates systems in real time. It lists Azure Policy together with Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Purview, Infrastructure as Code and Power Platform governance as technologies that help make compliance part of the platform itself rather than an afterthought. The stated benefit is that organizations can continuously prove compliance through automated controls and evidence instead of asking only at audit time whether a system is compliant, while reducing human error and improving consistency.

Typical decisions around Azure Policy therefore concern which rules to express as policy definitions, how to group them into initiatives, at which scope to assign them, and which effect to use for each rule. Together these choices determine how much of an organization's standards are enforced automatically versus reported for review.

azure-policy-initiative.desc: An Azure Policy initiative is a collection of Azure Policy definitions grouped into one assignable object, also called a policy set, for example to apply regulatory frameworks.
azure-policy-initiative.long:
An Azure Policy initiative is a collection of Azure Policy definitions that are grouped together into a single object that can be assigned as a unit. It is also referred to as a policy set. The concept is part of Azure Policy, the governance capability in the Microsoft ecosystem that it is classified under.

Initiatives are used to manage related policy definitions together instead of assigning each definition on its own. A common use is applying a regulatory framework, such as ISO 27001 or NIST, at a management group scope. By bundling the definitions that correspond to a framework into one initiative, the whole set can be assigned in a single step and handled as one object.

The structure of an initiative definition is described in the Azure Policy documentation on Microsoft Learn, in the article on initiative definition structure.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

azure-portal.desc: The Azure portal is Microsoft's web-based console for creating and managing Azure resources and subscriptions through a graphical interface, part of Microsoft Azure.

faq.a: It is Microsoft's web-based console for creating and managing Azure resources and subscriptions through a graphical interface. The M365.FM episodes show it used for tasks such as creating virtual networks and DNS zones, configuring backups and connecting to virtual machines.
faq.q: What is the Azure portal used for?

faq.a: No. The episode "Secure Azure Networking with Rex de Koning [MVP-MCT]" describes creating a virtual network using both the Azure portal and Azure CLI, showing that the portal is one option among several.
faq.q: Is the Azure portal the only way to manage Azure resources?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Bastion - Simply Explained", Azure Bastion provides browser-based RDP and SSH access to Azure virtual machines through the Azure portal, so RDP or SSH ports do not need to be exposed to the public internet.
faq.q: How does Azure Bastion relate to the Azure portal?

azure-portal.long:
The Azure portal is Microsoft's web-based console for creating and managing Azure resources and subscriptions through a graphical interface. It is part of Microsoft Azure and is the entry point many administrators use when they want to deploy, configure and monitor cloud services without writing scripts. An overview of the portal is maintained in the official Microsoft Learn documentation.

In practice, the Azure portal is the place where subscriptions, resource groups and individual resources are created and organised. The M365.FM episodes that touch on it describe a recurring pattern: sign in, choose a subscription and resource group, enter a name and region, and then fill in the service-specific settings. The episode "Secure Azure Networking with Rex de Koning [MVP-MCT]" walks through creating a virtual network this way, starting from the Create resource option, searching for the resource type, and then selecting the subscription, resource group, name and region. The same episode notes that the identical task can also be done with Azure CLI, which shows that the portal is one of several ways to manage Azure rather than the only one.

Several service-focused episodes use the Azure portal as the working surface for setup. The episode "Azure DNS - Simply Explained" describes the DNS resolution process as starting with logging into the Azure portal and creating a DNS zone with a unique domain name, selecting the subscription and resource group, and then opening the zone resource to add records such as A and CNAME records. After that, the Azure DNS name servers are obtained and entered at the domain registrar. In this flow the portal covers the creation and record management steps, while the registrar change happens outside it.

The episode "Azure Backup - Simply Explained" calls the Azure portal the primary interface for managing Azure Backup. It describes the portal as a user-friendly environment for configuring and monitoring backup operations, and lists features such as long-term retention, where on-demand backups of file shares can be kept for up to 10 years and are configurable via the Azure portal, as well as cross-region capabilities. This illustrates the dual role of the portal: configuration at set-up time and ongoing monitoring afterwards.

Security-related episodes also tie the portal to specific services. In "Azure DDoS Protection - Simply Explained", native integration is listed as a benefit, meaning deployment and administration can be set up directly in the Azure portal. The episode describes turnkey protection that applies as soon as it is activated, along with a Network Protection tier for larger organisations that covers resources in virtual networks enabled for DDoS Protection. The episode "Azure Bastion - Simply Explained" describes Azure Bastion as a managed remote access service that provides browser-based RDP and SSH access to Azure virtual machines through the Azure portal, so that RDP or SSH ports do not have to be opened to the public internet. Here the portal acts not only as an administration console but also as the access path to the virtual machines.

Taken together, the episodes position the Azure portal as the graphical front end for everyday Azure tasks: creating networking resources, DNS zones, backup configurations and protection features, and connecting to virtual machines. Decisions around its use typically concern whether a task is done interactively in the portal or through another tool such as Azure CLI, and which subscription and resource group a new resource should belong to. The portal sits within the wider Microsoft Azure platform, and the services mentioned above are examples of what can be reached from it rather than a complete list.

azure-private-5g-core.desc: Azure Private 5G Core is an Azure service for running 5G core network functions on Azure Stack Edge in an on-premises private mobile network; retirement is listed for September 30, 2025.

faq.a: Azure Private 5G Core is an Azure service for deploying and managing 5G core network functions on Azure Stack Edge. It is used as part of an on-premises private mobile network.
faq.q: What is Azure Private 5G Core?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn lists the retirement of Azure Private 5G Core for September 30, 2025. The official documentation should be consulted for current details.
faq.q: Is Azure Private 5G Core being retired?

faq.a: It is part of Microsoft Azure and runs its 5G core network functions on Azure Stack Edge.
faq.q: Which Microsoft product family does Azure Private 5G Core belong to?

azure-private-5g-core.long:
Azure Private 5G Core is a service within Microsoft Azure for deploying and managing 5G core network functions on Azure Stack Edge. It forms the core network component of an on-premises private mobile network, so that the packet core runs at the customer's own site rather than only in a public cloud region.

The service is part of Microsoft Azure and relies on Azure Stack Edge as the hardware platform on which the core network functions run. Management of the deployment is handled through Azure, which links the on-premises mobile network to the rest of the Azure environment.

Microsoft Learn lists the retirement of Azure Private 5G Core for September 30, 2025. Anyone evaluating or maintaining a private mobile network based on this service should check the official Microsoft Learn documentation for current status, timelines and any guidance related to the retirement.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity. The official product documentation is available on Microsoft Learn under the Azure Private 5G Core section.

azure-private-dns-zone.desc: Azure Private DNS zone is an Azure DNS zone that resolves records only within linked Azure virtual networks, with optional automatic registration of virtual machine records.
azure-private-dns-zone.long:
An Azure Private DNS zone is a DNS zone in Microsoft Azure whose records resolve only inside the Azure virtual networks that are linked to it. Records in the zone are not exposed to the public internet, which makes it suited to name resolution for internal workloads.

The zone can be set up with automatic registration of virtual machine records. When this option is enabled for a linked virtual network, DNS records for the virtual machines in that network are maintained in the zone without manual entries. Name resolution is therefore tied to the virtual network links configured for the zone.

Azure Private DNS zone is part of Microsoft Azure and belongs to the Azure DNS area. Microsoft documents the service in its Azure DNS private zone overview on Microsoft Learn.

No episodes on M365.FM are currently linked to this entity.

azure-private-link.desc: Azure Private Link is a Microsoft Azure networking service that connects virtual networks to Azure PaaS and partner services over private endpoints, not the public internet.

faq.a: Azure Private Link is a Microsoft Azure service that provides private connectivity from virtual networks to Azure PaaS services and partner services through private endpoints, instead of using the public internet.
faq.q: What is Azure Private Link?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Private Link - Simply Explained" names Azure Storage, SQL Database and Key Vault as examples, and says many other services can be connected as well.
faq.q: Which Azure services can be reached through private endpoints?

faq.a: Yes, according to the episode "Azure Files - Simply Explained", when a private endpoint is used with Azure Files, the CNAME entry in Active Directory DNS Manager should be mapped to the private endpoint name.
faq.q: Does Azure Private Link affect DNS configuration?

azure-private-link.long:
Azure Private Link is a networking service within Microsoft Azure, developed by Microsoft, that provides private connectivity from virtual networks to Azure platform-as-a-service (PaaS) offerings and partner services. Instead of reaching a service through its public endpoint over the internet, traffic is routed through a private endpoint inside the customer's own virtual network. The feature is also referred to as Private Endpoint, which is the name of the network resource that represents the connection. In the Microsoft ecosystem it is categorized as a Microsoft tool and as an identity and security tool, since its main purpose is to reduce the exposure of services to the public internet.

The core idea is that a service such as Azure Storage, SQL Database or Key Vault becomes reachable through a private IP address in a virtual network. The episode "Azure Private Link - Simply Explained" describes it as Microsoft's networking service for securely accessing Azure services over a private connection instead of the public internet. According to that episode, using private endpoints lets organizations connect services such as Azure Storage, SQL Database, Key Vault and many others directly to their virtual network, with all traffic staying on Microsoft's private backbone network, which is described as significantly improving security.

Typical situations where Azure Private Link comes into play are those in which a workload in a virtual network needs to talk to a PaaS service without any public path. Examples that appear in related M365.FM episodes illustrate this. In "Azure Files - Simply Explained", the setup of Azure Files with Active Directory authentication includes a step where a CNAME entry is added in Active Directory DNS Manager, and the episode notes that when a private endpoint is used, the CNAME entry should be mapped to the private endpoint name. This shows that DNS configuration is a practical part of working with private endpoints. In "Secure Azure Automation with Ahmed Uzejnovic [MVP]", network isolation with Azure Private Link is listed among the measures that keep connections of an Azure Automation account secure, alongside encryption, secure credential management, resource logs, managed identities and service principals.

The episode "Run Azure Application Gateway Without Public IP Exposure" also touches on the topic. It explains network isolation as keeping an application's control traffic separate from user data, and states that a private endpoint connects an application directly to a virtual network. This avoids public IP addresses and keeps traffic inside Azure's network, which the episode says lowers the risk of external attacks. The same episode notes that network isolation requires deploying new gateways with the feature enabled, while existing gateways keep their prior behavior.

Azure Private Link sits next to other Azure networking building blocks. The episode "Azure Bastion - Simply Explained" recommends it as a practical next step, together with Azure Network Security Groups and Azure Virtual Network, for listeners who want to extend their understanding of Azure network design. Because private endpoints live inside a virtual network, decisions around Private Link usually involve virtual network layout, name resolution and the access controls of the target service. The service is documented by Microsoft in its Azure Private Link documentation on Microsoft Learn.

For administrators and architects, the main decision is whether a given PaaS service should remain reachable over its public endpoint or be exposed only through a private endpoint. The M365.FM episodes frame Azure Private Link as a way to keep traffic on Microsoft's backbone network and to reduce public exposure, and they present it as one component of a broader secure design rather than a standalone control.

azure-quantum.desc: Azure Quantum is Microsoft's cloud quantum computing service in Azure, including the Quantum Development Kit and the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator.

faq.a: Azure Quantum is Microsoft's cloud quantum computing service in Azure. It includes the Quantum Development Kit and the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator.
faq.q: What is Azure Quantum?

faq.a: According to the episode "Debug Quantum Programs with VS Code and Azure Quantum", the QDK combines the Q# language, quantum simulators, Python integrations and Visual Studio Code tooling for building and debugging quantum programs.
faq.q: What does the Quantum Development Kit include?

faq.a: It is used to understand what it takes to run quantum code on real quantum machines, as described in the episode on debugging quantum programs with VS Code and Azure Quantum.
faq.q: What is the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator used for?

azure-quantum.long:
Azure Quantum is Microsoft's cloud quantum computing service within Microsoft Azure. It gives developers and teams a place to write, test and run quantum programs, and it bundles the tooling that surrounds that work. Two components named in the available material are the Quantum Development Kit (QDK) and the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator. Official documentation for the service is published on Microsoft Learn under the Azure Quantum overview.

The Quantum Development Kit brings together the pieces needed to build quantum programs. According to the episode "Debug Quantum Programs with VS Code and Azure Quantum", the QDK combines the Q# language, quantum simulators, Python integrations and Visual Studio Code tooling into one developer-oriented platform. The episode presents this as a way to start building and testing real quantum programs today, and it walks through writing and debugging a first quantum algorithm. Debugging in a familiar editor is treated as part of the normal development loop rather than as a specialist activity.

The Azure Quantum Resource Estimator addresses a different question: what it would take to run a given piece of quantum code on real quantum machines. The same episode describes using the resource estimator to understand those requirements before a program is run on hardware. This separates the work of designing an algorithm from the work of judging whether current or future machines could execute it.

Azure Quantum also supports hybrid workflows in which classical and quantum computation work together. The episode "Run Hybrid Quantum Jobs in Azure with Python and QAOA" describes how Azure Quantum workspaces, simulators and quantum processing units (QPUs) fit into ordinary Python- and DevOps-driven processes. It uses the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), where a classical optimizer steers parameters while the quantum part explores many possibilities at once, drawing on concepts such as qubits, superposition, entanglement and interference.
