Business email compromise (BEC) is a fraud attack in which an attacker impersonates or takes over a trusted mailbox in order to trick people into moving money. Typical examples are changing the bank details of a supplier or getting a payment approved. Because the message appears to come from someone the recipient already trusts, such as an executive or a vendor, BEC relies on social engineering rather than on malicious attachments or obviously suspicious links.

The M365.FM episode "Detect Microsoft 365 Attack Chains with Entra and Sentinel" describes BEC as a sophisticated attack that targets organizations through their email systems. Attackers impersonate trusted individuals, such as executives or vendors, to manipulate employees into transferring funds or sharing sensitive information. The episode presents it as one stage in a wider set of Microsoft 365 attack chains, alongside topics such as OAuth app abuse, and stresses that understanding BEC tactics is essential for protecting an organization.

BEC is difficult to stop with basic email filtering. The episode "Exchange Online Protection (EOP) - Simply Explained" says that EOP primarily filters spam, malware and basic phishing attempts. It states that advanced phishing, Business Email Compromise and impersonation of executives often slip through EOP's defenses, and its coverage table lists BEC as not covered by EOP. The episode concludes that such threats call for more advanced threat protection measures on top of the baseline filtering.

One such measure is covered in "Microsoft Defender for Office 365 - Simply Explained". The episode explains that the system analyzes incoming messages in real time to identify potential phishing attempts, and it cites a Microsoft-reported 99.995% accuracy rate in detecting malicious intent and around 140,000 BEC emails blocked daily. The detection methods it names include anti-phishing policies that can be configured against impersonation and phishing, with adjustable thresholds for detecting phishing emails, and real-time scanning of links and attachments so that malicious content does not reach the inbox.

Sender authentication is another layer. In "SPF, DKIM and DMARC - Simply Explained", the hosts explain why anyone can send email as someone else: legacy SMTP protocols were built for an era of trust, and the hidden envelope address can differ from the visible "From" line. The episode walks through SPF, DKIM and DMARC as a blueprint for protecting an email infrastructure, framed explicitly for administrators of a Microsoft 365 tenant and for organizations that want to protect themselves from BEC, so that a stranger cannot use the company's name.

The newest development discussed is the use of AI. The episode "Stop Deepfake Business Email Compromise with Verified ID" explores how deepfake-enabled BEC attacks are becoming more convincing and dangerous. It says that traditional trust signals, such as email addresses, writing style or even voice messages, are no longer reliable because attackers can imitate executives and employees with AI-generated content. The episode argues that organizations should move away from trust based on appearance and adopt identity verification as a core principle, with Verified ID in the title as the approach it examines.

Taken together, the episodes treat BEC as a problem that spans several layers: baseline filtering, advanced anti-phishing protection, authentication of sending domains, detection of attack chains, and verification of identity for sensitive requests such as payments and bank detail changes. Typical decisions for administrators include whether EOP alone is sufficient, which anti-phishing policies and thresholds to configure, and how to authenticate email so the company's domain cannot be easily spoofed.

business-performance-analytics.desc: Business Performance Analytics (BPA) is a Microsoft add-on that turns Dynamics 365 ERP data into prebuilt Fabric and Power BI reports and exposes it to agents via MCP.

faq.a: Business Performance Analytics (BPA) is a Microsoft analytics offering for Dynamics 365 ERP data. It provides prebuilt reports on Fabric and Power BI and exposes ERP analytics to AI agents through an MCP server.
faq.q: What is Business Performance Analytics?

faq.a: It is a preview MCP server that supports natural-language queries, DAX generation by AI agents and role-based row-level security. According to the documentation, it integrates with Visual Studio Code and Copilot Studio.
faq.q: What is the ERP Analytics MCP server?

faq.a: The documentation lists reporting over a maximum of eight quarters, data volume bound by the Power BI Embedded A6 capacity, and refreshes twice a day. Near real-time analysis and predictive insights are announced for later releases.
faq.q: What limits apply to Business Performance Analytics?

business-performance-analytics.long:
Business Performance Analytics (BPA) is an analytics offering for Dynamics 365 ERP data. It builds prebuilt reports on Microsoft Fabric and Power BI and exposes ERP analytics to agents through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, which is why it is also known as the ERP Analytics MCP. Microsoft developed it as part of Dynamics 365, and it is classified as a Microsoft tool and an analytics and BI tool. It is listed as an add-on.

The purpose of Business Performance Analytics is to turn an organization's operational and financial data into actionable insights without building every report and data model from scratch. According to Microsoft's documentation, it works with Dynamics 365, Dataverse and Power BI. The documented goals are consolidating key performance indicators, automating reporting and allowing custom analysis. Typical business areas named in the documentation are finance, supply chain, project operations and commerce reporting. The offering is related to Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations, whose data it analyses.

The offering provides preconfigured reports and interactive dashboards for several business areas. It also provides dimensional data models that can be used in a SaaS or data-as-a-service approach. Teams that need more than the standard content can build custom models on top of these models, for example in Microsoft Fabric. Access to the data lake relies on shared Dataverse permissions, so existing security concepts carry over to the analytical layer.

The link to agents is a distinguishing part of Business Performance Analytics. A preview ERP Analytics MCP server supports natural-language queries, lets AI agents generate DAX, and applies row-level security based on roles. The documentation names integration with Visual Studio Code and Copilot Studio. This means an AI agent can ask questions about business performance in plain language while the results respect the same role-based access rules as the reports. Because this server is described as a preview, its behaviour and scope may change, and current documentation should be consulted before relying on it.

Several limits are documented. Reporting covers a maximum of eight quarters, data volume is bound by the Power BI Embedded A6 capacity, and data refreshes twice a day. Near real-time analysis and predictive insights are announced for later releases rather than being part of the current scope. These points matter in practice: organizations that need long history, very large data volumes or frequent refreshes should check whether the limits fit their requirements, and may consider custom models in Fabric for needs beyond the prebuilt content.

On licensing, the documentation states that the capability is included in the Dynamics 365 Finance license scope, while the product is also described as an add-on. Anyone evaluating it should verify current licensing and availability in Microsoft's own documentation. Typical situations in which it is considered include finance and operations teams that want standard ERP reports in Power BI without a custom data project, analysts who want to work with ERP data in Fabric, and scenarios in which AI agents answer questions about business performance through the MCP server.

No M365.FM episode is currently recorded for Business Performance Analytics, so this description relies on the product's own documentation and metadata. Related topics on the site include Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations, Microsoft Fabric, Power BI, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and AI agents, which together describe the data sources, the analytical platform and the agent access that the offering combines.

business-process-flow.desc: A business process flow is a guided process bar across a Dynamics 365 record that leads users through defined stages, such as Qualify, Develop, Propose and Close.

faq.a: It is a guided process shown as a bar at the top of a record form. It leads users through defined stages and steps, for example Qualify, Develop, Propose and Close for sales opportunities.
faq.q: What is a business process flow in Dynamics 365?

faq.a: Yes. Steps can be marked as required, so the stage cannot be left and the form cannot be saved until the data is entered.
faq.q: Can a business process flow enforce that data is filled in?

faq.a: No, not by itself. According to the Microsoft Learn overview, workflows, business rules or form scripts are needed when conditional business logic is required.
faq.q: Does a business process flow include conditional logic?

business-process-flow.long:
A business process flow is a guided process that leads users through the steps an organization has defined until a result is reached. In Dynamics 365 it appears as a process bar at the top of a form, and it shows the user which stage a record is in and what remains to be done. A familiar example is the sales pipeline in Dynamics 365 Sales, where an opportunity moves through the stages Qualify, Develop, Propose and Close.

The main purpose is consistent data entry. According to the Microsoft Learn overview on which this page draws, a business process flow reduces training effort and mistakes, because users see the same defined path for every record instead of deciding on their own what to capture next. Typical scenarios named there are sales and customer service, where a team wants records to be handled in the same order and with the same information.

A business process flow is built from stages and steps. Each step corresponds to a column on the record, and a Next Stage button moves the record forward to the following stage. Steps can be marked as required. A required step means that the stage cannot be left, and the form cannot be saved, until the data has been filled in. This is the mechanism that enforces data quality along the flow.

In the sales pipeline, the stages carry specific meaning. The episode "Dynamics 365 Opportunity Management - Simply Explained" says that Dynamics 365 Sales uses a business process flow to guide opportunities through four standard stages: Qualify, Develop, Propose and Close. During Qualify, sellers establish facts such as the customer, timeframe, potential budget, purchasing process and decision maker. Develop focuses on understanding customer needs, identifying stakeholders and competitors, and defining the proposed solution. The episode also describes how opportunities can arise from several sources, for example customers requesting additional products or services, partners introducing potential buyers, or account managers discovering expansion and renewal opportunities during customer conversations.

A flow does not have to stay within one table. The documentation gives Opportunity to Quote to Order to Invoice as an example of a flow that spans several tables. Several flows can also be attached to one record, and users can switch between them. Flows can be tied to security roles, so that different groups see the processes that apply to them, and the tables used by a flow can also be used for views, charts and dashboards. The documentation states limits, such as a maximum number of active flows per table, stages per process and tables per multi-table process, so larger designs should be checked against those limits.

There are decisions and constraints to keep in mind when planning a business process flow. Business process flows do not provide conditional business logic by themselves. Where behavior must depend on conditions, the documentation points to workflows, business rules or form scripts. Another point concerns custom tables: enabling the business process flow feature on a custom table cannot be undone, so that choice should be made deliberately.

In short, a business process flow gives a record a visible, staged path, uses required steps to secure the data that each stage needs, and works alongside other automation options when conditional logic is required. The M365.FM episode on opportunity management shows this in the concrete setting of the Dynamics 365 Sales pipeline.

bystander-effect.desc: The bystander effect is a social psychology phenomenon in which individuals are less likely to act when other people are present, because responsibility is spread across the group.

faq.a: The bystander effect is a social psychology phenomenon in which individuals are less likely to act when other people are present. It is attributed to the diffusion of responsibility across the group.
faq.q: What is the bystander effect?

faq.a: Responsibility is spread across everyone who is aware of the situation, so each individual may feel less personally obligated to act and may assume someone else will.
faq.q: Why does the presence of others reduce the likelihood of action?

bystander-effect.long:
The bystander effect is a social psychology phenomenon in which individuals are less likely to take action when other people are present. The central explanation is diffusion of responsibility: when several people are aware of a situation, each person may assume that someone else will respond, so the sense of individual obligation is reduced.

The concept is used to describe and analyze group behavior in situations where action is needed but no one is clearly assigned to take it. Because it describes how shared awareness can lower the likelihood that any single person acts, the term is applied to discussions of responsibility, accountability and group dynamics.

This entity page is based on a general definition of the term. No related topics, products or official documentation are linked to it at this time, and no M365.FM episodes are currently associated with the concept.

caching.desc: Caching keeps frequently accessed data in fast memory so repeated requests avoid slower storage; it is a core performance lever in APIs, cloud apps and Microsoft Fabric.

faq.a: Caching keeps frequently accessed data in fast memory so repeated queries or requests do not have to read from slower storage. It improves response times and reduces load on the underlying system.
faq.q: What is caching?

faq.a: The episodes name Redis and Memcached for in-memory caching, content delivery networks (CDNs) for caching static assets closer to users, API gateway caching such as in Azure API Management, and semantic caching for AI agents.
faq.q: Which technologies do the M365.FM episodes mention for caching?

faq.a: The episode "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud" says that semantic caching reduces API calls, which can lower costs and improve response times for AI agents.
faq.q: How does caching help with AI agent costs?

caching.long:
Caching is the practice of keeping frequently accessed data in fast memory so that repeated queries or requests do not have to read from slower storage every time. It is used wherever the same information is requested again and again: in analytics platforms such as Microsoft Fabric, where it is described as a key lever for query performance, but also in API gateways, application back ends and cloud-hosted services.

The basic idea is simple. When data is requested for the first time, it is fetched from its original source, such as a database or a backend service. A copy is then held in a faster layer. Later requests for the same data can be answered from that copy, which shortens response times and takes load off the underlying storage or service. The main decisions around caching therefore concern what to keep, where to keep it, and how long the stored copy should be considered valid.

The M365.FM episodes place caching in several contexts. In "API Gateway - Simply Explained", caching is listed alongside authentication, authorization, rate limiting, request routing, logging and monitoring as one of the capabilities an API Gateway provides while simplifying access to multiple backend services. The episode "Azure API Management - Simply Explained" covers caching in the same way, as one of the concepts of Azure API Management, which acts as a secure gateway between applications and backend services. There it appears together with products, subscriptions, policies, rate limiting, authentication, transformations, versioning and revisions.

The episode "Why Microservice Architecture Slows Software Delivery" treats caching as a way to address scaling problems and improve performance. It says that database calls and API responses can be cached to reduce load on the backend, and that the data store used for caching should be selected based on need. Redis and Memcached are named as popular choices. The episode also says that fragments can be cached based on their volatility and update frequency, which means that data that changes rarely can be held longer than data that changes often.

The episode "High-Performance Azure Cloud Governance to Reduce Waste" lists caching strategies for cloud applications. It states that storing frequently accessed data in a cache reduces the time needed to retrieve information. Suggested approaches include in-memory caching solutions such as Redis or Memcached to speed up data retrieval, and content delivery networks (CDNs) that cache static assets closer to users. In that episode, caching is one part of keeping a cloud environment responsive and efficient, including during peak usage.

Caching also appears in the context of AI workloads. The episode "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud" recommends semantic caching to reduce API calls, and says this strategy can lower costs and improve response times for AI agents. It is mentioned together with other cost measures such as prompt compression to minimize token usage, choosing the right billing model in Azure, and monitoring resource usage with alerts for spending spikes.

Across these sources, caching serves two goals: faster responses and reduced load on or cost of the backing system. The choice of layer depends on the situation, whether that is a gateway policy in front of backend services, an in-memory store such as Redis or Memcached, a CDN for static assets, or a semantic cache in front of AI calls. In each case the trade-off is the same: cached data is quicker to read, but its freshness has to be managed according to how often the underlying data changes.

calculated-column.desc: A calculated column is a Power BI table column defined by a DAX formula, computed row by row and stored in the model, which adds to model size and refresh work.

faq.a: According to the episode "Power BI DAX and Semantic Models with Bernat Agulló Roselló [MVP]", a calculated column adds data to each row, is static and is used for data preparation, while a measure calculates values based on filters, is dynamic and is used for analysis.
faq.q: What is the difference between a calculated column and a measure?

faq.a: Yes. Its values are computed row by row and stored in the model, which increases model size and adds work to each refresh. The episode "Power BI Calculated Columns vs Measures - Simply Explained" discusses this as a memory cost.
faq.q: Does a calculated column affect model size?

faq.a: The episode "Implement Power BI Row-Level Security in Microsoft Fabric" lists a calculated column used for identity as a pitfall because it has no per-user effect, and suggests moving that logic into role filter DAX over model tables.
faq.q: Can a calculated column be used for row-level security by user identity?

calculated-column.long:
A calculated column is a column added to a table in a Power BI model using a DAX formula. The formula is evaluated for every row of the table, and the resulting values are stored in the model alongside the imported data. Because the values are materialized rather than computed at query time, a calculated column increases the size of the model and adds work to each data refresh. Microsoft's documentation covers the creation of calculated columns in a Power BI Desktop tutorial.

The central idea behind a calculated column is that it adds data to each row. The episode "Power BI DAX and Semantic Models with Bernat Agulló Roselló [MVP]" contrasts it with a measure in a simple comparison: a calculated column adds data to each row, is static, and is used for data preparation, whereas a measure calculates values based on filters, is dynamic, and is used for analysis. In practice this means a calculated column behaves like any other column in the table. It can be placed on an axis, used in a slicer, or used as a field in a visual, because its value already exists on every row.

The episode "Power BI Calculated Columns vs Measures - Simply Explained" frames the difference as a question of where the calculation stands. It describes the two options as ways of doing something similar that behave very differently, noting that a calculated column is stored inside the data model and follows every single row. The episode also addresses the memory cost of that storage, which it describes as a bill that can lead to a slow report, and it lists common beginner mistakes around choosing between the two. It places the topic in the wider context of Microsoft 365, Fabric and Azure.

Choosing between a calculated column and a measure is a recurring modeling decision. When a value must exist per row, for example to categorize or prepare data, a calculated column fits. When a value should respond to the filters applied in a report, a measure is the appropriate tool. The episode "Bulk Rename Power BI Measures with PBIP" touches on this decision when it discusses replacing a measure: the process includes analyzing the existing DAX and deciding between a new calculated column or a revised measure, then updating visuals so results remain accurate. The same episode mentions common troubleshooting issues such as broken visuals, context-related errors and performance bottlenecks, and covers DAX fundamentals including functions like CALCULATE, VAR, SUM and SWITCH.

Calculated columns also appear in the context of security. The episode "Implement Power BI Row-Level Security in Microsoft Fabric" lists a calculated column used for identity as a pitfall, noting that it has no per-user effect. Its suggested fix is to move that logic into the role filter DAX over model tables instead of relying on calculated columns. This illustrates a limit of the concept: because a calculated column is stored and static, it does not adapt to the identity of the person viewing the report.

In day-to-day work, the main trade-offs are model size, refresh duration and flexibility. Since every calculated column is stored, adding many of them to large tables grows the model and lengthens refresh. Testing DAX before using it in reports is recommended in the first episode, which mentions DAX Studio as a way to check formulas, find errors and improve performance. Taken together, the episodes position the calculated column as a data-preparation tool whose convenience should be weighed against its storage and refresh cost.

calculation-groups.desc: Calculation groups are a tabular model feature that applies reusable DAX calculation items, such as time intelligence, to many measures at once.

faq.a: A calculation group is a tabular model feature that applies reusable DAX calculation items, such as time intelligence, to many measures. This reduces the number of redundant measures in a model.
faq.q: What is a calculation group?

faq.a: According to the episode "Power BI Calculation Groups - Simply Explained", models often accumulate dozens or hundreds of measures that are copies of one another for different periods. Calculation groups define the variation once and apply it to the base measures.
faq.q: Which problem do calculation groups solve?

faq.a: The episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" describes calculation groups as a way to keep time intelligence, KPIs, and business rules centralized and auditable within a semantic model reused across reports and teams.
faq.q: How do calculation groups relate to semantic models in Microsoft Fabric?

calculation-groups.long:
Calculation groups are a feature of tabular models, available in Power BI semantic models, that lets a modeler define reusable DAX calculation items and apply them to many measures. Instead of building a separate measure for every combination of a base figure and a variation, such as the current period, year to date, or prior year, the logic is written once as a calculation item and then applied to whichever measures a report uses. The main purpose is to reduce redundant measures and keep repeated logic in one place.

The problem they address is a familiar one in growing models. The episode "Power BI Calculation Groups - Simply Explained" describes a model with dozens of measures, most of them copies: one sales number is built, then rebuilt for this month, this year, and last year, until nobody can tell which version is right. A simple report turns into a hundred measures. A calculation group replaces that pattern by separating the base measure from the variation applied to it, so the base measure is defined once and the variations are defined once.

In practice, a calculation group is a table-like object in the model that contains calculation items. Each item holds a DAX expression that modifies how a selected measure is evaluated. A typical use is time intelligence, where items such as YTD, QTD, and TTM sit in a single group and can be combined with any measure in the model. The episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" names this use directly: calculation groups remove the need for endless YTD/QTD/TTM variants and keep time intelligence, KPIs, and business rules centralized and auditable.

Calculation groups also fit into a wider modeling approach. The episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" presents the semantic model as an enterprise asset, a single definitional layer reused across reports, workspaces, and teams, with row-level security enforced in the model. In "Extend Microsoft Fabric with Custom APIs and Power BI Models", the semantic model is described as a contract: business logic goes into measures rather than reports, calculation groups handle time intelligence, and KPI definitions are centralized. Keeping logic in the model rather than in individual reports is what allows several reports to show consistent numbers.

The topic also appears in discussions of DAX practice. The episode "Power BI DAX and Semantic Models with Bernat Agulló Roselló [MVP]" lists calculation groups among recommended practices for scalable analytics models, alongside variables for readability, efficient data types, pattern-based measure design for modularity and reusability, and a star schema. In "Bulk Rename Power BI Measures with PBIP", the connection is to maintenance: tools such as Tabular Editor can support bulk edits and advanced features like calculation groups, which centralize logic and reduce repeated formulas, and the episode stresses validating changes and refreshing datasets afterwards.

Typical decisions around calculation groups concern where repeated patterns exist. If a model contains many measures that differ only by a time period or a similar transformation, a calculation group is a candidate for consolidation. If a model has few measures, the added concept may not be needed. Because calculation groups are defined at the model level, they are usually created and maintained with modeling tools rather than inside individual reports, and changes should be tested against existing measures and visuals. Official documentation on calculation groups is available from Microsoft Learn under the Analysis Services tabular models section.

canary-release.desc: A canary release is a deployment technique that sends a small share of production traffic to a new version, compares it with the stable one and scales up or rolls back.

faq.a: A canary release is a deployment technique that routes a small percentage of production traffic to a new version and compares it against the stable version. The share of traffic is then increased step by step or the change is rolled back.
faq.q: What is a canary release?

faq.a: If the new version performs worse than the stable version, the rollout can be rolled back automatically. Because only a small portion of traffic is affected at first, the impact of a faulty release is limited.
faq.q: How does a canary release handle problems?

canary-release.long:
A canary release is a deployment technique in which a new version of an application is exposed to only a small percentage of production traffic while the stable version continues to serve the rest. The new version is compared against the stable version, and the share of traffic it receives is increased gradually or the change is rolled back automatically.

The approach is used to limit the impact of a faulty release. Because only a fraction of users or requests reach the new version at first, problems can be detected early and contained before a full rollout. Comparing the new version against the stable one provides a basis for deciding whether to continue the rollout, pause it or revert.

The technique is commonly discussed alongside other progressive delivery and deployment practices, where traffic routing and automated rollback play a central role. No specific products, tools or Microsoft services are tied to the term in the information available for this entry, and no M365.FM episodes are currently linked to it.

canvas-app.desc: Canvas app: a Power Apps app type where the maker designs the screen layout freely, like a slide, and connects it to data with Power Fx formulas.

faq.a: A canvas app is a Power Apps app type where the maker designs the screen layout freely, like a slide, and connects controls to data using Power Fx formulas. Data can come from many sources through connectors.
faq.q: What is a canvas app in Power Apps?

faq.a: A model-driven app is generated from the Dataverse data model, while a canvas app starts from the screen design chosen by the maker. The episode "Canvas Apps vs Model-Driven Apps - Simply Explained" says the right choice depends on the business requirements.
faq.q: How does a canvas app differ from a model-driven app?

faq.a: Power Fx is the formula language used to define behavior and connect data in a canvas app. It is closely related to Power Apps and the Power Platform.
faq.q: Which language is used to build logic in a canvas app?

canvas-app.long:
A canvas app is one of the two primary app types in Power Apps. The maker designs the screen layout freely, in a way comparable to arranging objects on a slide, and then connects the controls on those screens to data by writing Power Fx formulas. The name is also written "Canvas apps" or, in German, "Canvas-App". Because the starting point is the visual design rather than a data model, canvas apps are the Power Apps option where the maker decides exactly how each screen looks and behaves.

In practice, canvas apps are used for task-focused business applications that need a specific design. Typical examples mentioned in the M365.FM material on Power Apps include employee onboarding, asset management, inspections, help desk solutions, inventory tracking, approval processes and field service applications. Data can be brought in through connectors from many different sources, and the apps can integrate with Microsoft 365 services such as SharePoint, Teams, Excel, Outlook, Dynamics 365 and Azure. The freedom of the layout comes with a trade-off: the maker is responsible for how the screens are arranged and how they respond.

The two building blocks that define a canvas app are the screen design and Power Fx. Controls are placed on screens, and Power Fx, the formula language of the Power Platform, defines behavior, data connections and logic. A canvas app therefore sits inside Power Apps as its broader platform and relies on Power Fx for everything that goes beyond the visual layout.

The main decision around canvas apps is the choice against the other app type, the model-driven app. A model-driven app is generated from the Dataverse data model, while a canvas app starts from the screen design. The episode "Canvas Apps vs Model-Driven Apps - Simply Explained" presents these as the two primary ways to build business applications with Microsoft Power Apps and says the right choice depends entirely on the business requirements. It is aimed at IT professionals, citizen developers and Microsoft partners who need to know when each approach delivers the most value. The episode "Power Apps - Simply Explained" places both app types within the wider Power Platform, alongside Power Automate, Power BI, Dataverse and Power Pages.

Several episodes look at how canvas apps relate to newer approaches and to data governance. "Canvas App UI vs Generative Pages: Which Should You Use?" compares manual canvas work with Generative Pages, which turn plain-English prompts into responsive, Dataverse-aware React pages. The episode describes the upside as speed, consistency, accessibility and governance through Dataverse metadata and roles, and the downside as possible fragility, such as read-only generated output, prompt ambiguity and hidden licensing. It also says the technical debt shifts from messy one-offs to platform dependency and regeneration discipline.

"Power Apps Code Apps - Simply Explained" describes Code Apps as a way to build modern React-based web applications with familiar tools such as Visual Studio Code while keeping Power Platform features like Dataverse, Microsoft Entra authentication, connectors, security policies and managed deployments. The episode contrasts them with traditional canvas apps and model-driven apps, and says they extend the platform rather than replace low-code development.

"Move Canvas Apps from SharePoint to Dataverse" addresses where a canvas app's data lives. The episode describes a fork between a fast personal Copilot lane and a governed enterprise Power Platform lane, and discusses stopping accidental data exposure, the point that Copilot amplifies whatever governance already exists, and the role of sensitivity labels in protecting a tenant. For makers, this frames moving a canvas app's data from SharePoint to Dataverse as a governance decision as much as a technical one.

capa.desc: Corrective and preventive action (CAPA) is a formal quality process that addresses the causes of nonconformances and prevents potential problems before they occur.
capa.long:
Corrective and preventive action (CAPA) is a formal quality process. It addresses the cause of a nonconformance so that the issue does not recur, and it addresses potential problems before they occur.

The term combines two related activities. Corrective action focuses on an issue that has already happened: the aim is to identify and address its cause rather than only the visible symptom, so the same nonconformance does not appear again. Preventive action looks ahead: it deals with potential problems before they take place, reducing the likelihood that a nonconformance occurs at all.

CAPA is used as a structured way to manage quality issues. Treating both activities as one defined process gives organizations a consistent way to respond to existing problems and to anticipate future ones.

No related topics, episodes or official documentation links are currently listed for this entry on M365.FM, so this page limits itself to the definition of the concept.

capable-to-promise.desc: Capable to promise (CTP) is an order promising approach that derives a delivery date from current factory capability rather than from a static lead time.

faq.a: Capable to promise is an order promising approach that sets a delivery date based on what the factory can currently do, given material, routing, resource, labor and shipping limits, instead of a static lead time.
faq.q: What is capable to promise (CTP)?

faq.a: According to the Infor LN documentation, CTP is a group of techniques that includes basic ATP checks on standard items as well as approaches such as capacity CTP, component CTP, channel ATP and family CTP, each drawing on a different source of availability.
faq.q: How does CTP differ from available to promise (ATP)?

faq.a: The Infor LN documentation states that with multisite functionality active, CTP and ATP calculations run per planning cluster. If a cluster is linked to several sites, the checks use the combined supply across those sites.
faq.q: How does CTP work in multisite setups?

capable-to-promise.long:
Capable to promise (CTP) is an order promising approach in which the delivery date offered to a customer is derived from what the factory can currently do, given constraints such as material, routing, resources, labor and shipping, rather than from a fixed, static lead time. The idea is to answer a sales question with a date that reflects real production conditions instead of a standard estimate that may no longer hold.

In practice, CTP is used when a salesperson or customer service team needs to know whether a quantity of an item can be delivered by a requested date, how soon a quantity could arrive, or how much could ship before a month ends. Because the answer rests on the state of supply and capacity at the time of the request, it can change from one request to the next as orders, stock and resource loads change.

The Infor LN documentation describes CTP as a group of order-promising techniques rather than a single method. They range from basic available-to-promise (ATP) checks on standard items to more advanced approaches, and each one draws on a different source of availability. Standard ATP uses supply that is already planned for the product. Capacity CTP looks at capacity that could be converted into deliverable supply. Component CTP uses the ATP of components linked to the product. Channel ATP considers the maximum volume that can be sold through a particular channel, and family CTP supports long-term promising at product-family level. The same documentation notes that CTP is also supported for customised items.

These variants matter for the decision of which technique to apply. A check against planned supply answers a different question than a check that converts spare capacity into new supply, and a check that depends on component availability answers yet another. The choice depends on what limits delivery for a given product: finished stock already planned, free production capacity, or the availability of the parts that go into it. Family-level promising, by contrast, serves longer-term commitments where item-level detail is not yet available.

Multisite environments add a further consideration. According to the Infor LN documentation, when multisite functionality is active, CTP and ATP calculations run per planning cluster. If a cluster is linked to several sites, the checks use the combined supply across those sites, so a promise can reflect more than a single location.

The documentation identifies the kinds of information consulted when a promise request is answered, but it does not describe step by step how a delivery date is calculated. This page therefore stays at the level of the concept: CTP ties a promise date to present capability and supply, in contrast to relying on a static lead time, and it sits alongside ATP as part of the wider set of order-promising techniques. No M365.FM episodes are linked to this topic at present.

capture-the-flag.desc: Capture the flag is a team game in which each side defends its own flag while trying to capture the opposing team's flag, used here to expose communication gaps under time pressure.
capture-the-flag.long:
Capture the flag is a team game in which two sides each protect their own flag while attempting to capture the flag of the opposing team. The structure combines defense and attack at the same time, so every team has to divide attention between guarding its own position and pursuing the other side's.

On M365.FM, the concept is referenced as an exercise that exposes communication gaps under time pressure. Because players must coordinate roles, share information and react quickly, weaknesses in how a team talks to each other tend to become visible during play.

The available information about this entry is limited. No related products, technologies or episodes are linked to it at this time, and no official documentation or site is associated with the term. The description here is therefore restricted to the game's basic rules as stated and its use as a way to surface team communication issues.

carbon-removal.desc: Carbon removal (carbon dioxide removal) is the deliberate extraction of CO2 from the atmosphere and its durable storage in land, ocean, geological reservoirs or products.

faq.a: Carbon removal, or carbon dioxide removal (CDR), is the deliberate removal of CO2 from the atmosphere and its durable storage in geological, land or ocean reservoirs, or in products. It is also called greenhouse gas removal or negative emissions.
faq.q: What is carbon removal?

faq.a: Carbon capture and storage at point sources such as power plants cuts new emissions but does not lower CO2 already in the air. Carbon removal takes CO2 out of the atmosphere itself.
faq.q: How is carbon removal different from carbon capture and storage?

faq.a: Land-based methods include planting forests, improving soil carbon, bioenergy with carbon capture, and direct air capture with storage. Ocean and water-based methods include ocean fertilisation, ocean alkalinity enhancement, wetland restoration and blue carbon management.
faq.q: Which methods count as carbon removal?

carbon-removal.long:
Carbon removal, also called carbon dioxide removal (CDR), greenhouse gas removal or negative emissions, is the deliberate removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and its durable storage in geological, land or ocean reservoirs, or in products. It is a human-led activity: the aim is to lower the amount of CO2 already present in the air, not only to avoid adding more. Organisations buy removal credits to counterbalance residual emissions in net claims, which is why the term appears in corporate climate and sustainability reporting.

The methods fall into two broad groups. Land-based approaches include planting forests, improving soil carbon through farming, bioenergy combined with carbon capture, and direct air capture with storage. Ocean and water-based approaches include ocean fertilisation, ocean alkalinity enhancement, wetland restoration and blue carbon management. The approaches differ in where the carbon ends up and in how reliably it stays there.

Permanence is a central point when comparing methods. Biological stores such as forests are considered volatile, because fire, disease or policy shifts can release the stored carbon again. Geological and mineral storage can last far longer. For anyone evaluating removal credits, the type of storage therefore matters as much as the quantity claimed.

According to the source material, CDR currently removes about 2 gigatons of CO2 per year, roughly 4 percent of annual human greenhouse gas emissions, mostly through reforestation. Studies suggest that methods deployable today could reach around 10 gigatons per year. The same material notes that measuring removals precisely is difficult, which affects how credible and comparable removal claims are.

Carbon removal should be distinguished from carbon capture and storage at point sources such as power plants. Point-source capture cuts new emissions but does not lower CO2 that is already in the atmosphere. Removal, by contrast, works on the existing stock of atmospheric CO2. In practice the two address different parts of the problem, and net claims typically refer to removal when counterbalancing emissions that remain after reductions.

In a business and sustainability context, the typical decisions around carbon removal concern which method to fund, how durable the storage is, how the removal is measured and verified, and how purchased credits are described in net claims. Choosing between volatile biological stores and longer-lasting geological or mineral storage is one of the main trade-offs.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no related topics are listed for it. The description above rests on the general definition and the figures from the cited reference article.

cardinality.desc: Cardinality in Power BI data modeling describes how often values repeat on each side of a relationship: one-to-many, many-to-one, one-to-one or many-to-many.

faq.a: It describes how often values can repeat on each side of a relationship between two tables. The options are one-to-many, many-to-one, one-to-one and many-to-many.
faq.q: What does cardinality mean in a Power BI relationship?

faq.a: The episode "Reduce Power BI Premium Costs with Better Data Models" says high cardinality in a column can inflate model size and slow performance. "Build a Power BI Star Schema for Faster Reports" adds that high-cardinality text keys in relationships can degrade performance compared with surrogate integer keys.
faq.q: Why does high cardinality matter for Power BI performance?

faq.a: The episode "Reduce Power BI Premium Costs with Better Data Models" suggests keeping only the necessary columns, testing splitting columns or replacing decimal columns with whole numbers, and limiting rows to what the report needs.
faq.q: How can cardinality be reduced in a data model?

cardinality.long:
Cardinality is a concept in Power BI data modeling that describes how often values can repeat on each side of a relationship between two tables. The common settings are one-to-many, many-to-one, one-to-one and many-to-many. The term also has a second, related meaning: it can refer to the uniqueness of the values in a single column. Both meanings appear in the M365.FM episodes, and they matter for how a semantic model behaves and performs.

When a relationship is defined, the cardinality tells the model whether one row on one side matches a single row or many rows on the other side. A one-to-many relationship, for example, lets multiple records from one table be related to a single record in another. The episode "Power BI Paginated Reports: Service vs Report Builder vs SSRS" notes that managing cardinality is essential when working with lookup functions: the relationships between tables must be defined correctly to avoid errors, and a one-to-many relationship allows multiple records to be pulled from one table into another, for instance when customer details from a separate table are added to a sales report.

In Power BI Desktop, relationships are created and reviewed in a visual interface. The episode "Power BI DAX and Semantic Models with Bernat Agulló Roselló [MVP]" describes dragging fields between tables to define relationships, using the relationship view to check for errors or missing links, and adjusting cardinality and cross-filter direction for more advanced modeling. Choosing between one-to-many and many-to-many relationships is part of this modeling work, alongside formatting tasks such as naming tables and fields and setting data types, which the episode says make a model easier to maintain.

Cardinality also affects performance and model size. The episode "Reduce Power BI Premium Costs with Better Data Models" defines cardinality as the uniqueness of data values in a column and states that high cardinality can inflate the data model size and slow down performance. Its suggested strategies include keeping only the columns a report needs, testing ways to lower column cardinality such as splitting columns or replacing decimal columns with whole numbers, and limiting rows to what is required. The episode attributes to Shahid Umar the remark that performance bottlenecks are often caused not just by large datasets but by how those datasets are structured.

The same point appears in the context of relationship keys. The episode "Build a Power BI Star Schema for Faster Reports" says that using high-cardinality text keys in relationships can degrade performance, and that replacing them with surrogate integer keys in a star schema usually yields much faster joins and a smaller model. In a star schema, relationships between a fact table and its dimension tables are typically many-to-one, so the choice of key column and its cardinality directly influences how efficiently those joins run.

In the episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric", cardinality is listed among the design factors behind performance tuning. The episode says that suboptimal model design, cardinality, or a lack of appropriate aggregations can cause slow queries and an inconsistent user experience in semantic models. Reviewing relationship cardinality and column uniqueness is therefore part of making a semantic model reusable across reports.

In practice, decisions around cardinality come down to a few checks: whether each relationship uses the intended setting, whether the key columns are as lean as possible, and whether unnecessary high-cardinality columns can be removed or simplified. The episodes treat these as routine modeling tasks rather than one-off fixes, since relationship definitions and column uniqueness shape both the correctness of results and the resource use of a model.

cash-flow-forecasting.desc: Cash flow forecasting estimates a business's future cash inflows and outflows over a period so finance teams can anticipate liquidity problems and plan decisions.
cash-flow-forecasting.long:
Cash flow forecasting is the practice of estimating a business's future cash inflows and outflows over a defined period. The resulting projection shows how much cash an organization expects to have available at different points in time.

Finance teams use cash flow forecasting to anticipate liquidity problems before they occur and to plan decisions around the expected cash position. By comparing projected inflows with projected outflows, a forecast helps indicate whether a business is likely to have enough cash to meet its obligations over the forecast period.

On M365.FM, Cash flow forecasting is listed as a concept in the knowledge base. No related topics, episodes or official documentation links are currently associated with this entry, so the page limits itself to the general definition of the term.

certificate-authority.desc: A certificate authority (CA) is a trusted entity in a public key infrastructure that issues and signs digital certificates, binding identities to public keys.

faq.a: A certificate authority issues and signs digital certificates that bind an identity to a public key. It hashes the certificate content, signs the hash with its private key and embeds the signature in the certificate.
faq.q: What does a certificate authority do?

faq.a: A root CA typically anchors trust in the hierarchy, while an issuing CA signs certificates for devices and users. The root CA publishes its public key in a self-signed CA certificate.
faq.q: What is the difference between a root CA and an issuing CA?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Key Vault - Simply Explained" describes Key Vault sending a TLS/SSL certificate request to the CA, which responds with an X509 certificate that is then merged to complete the certificate creation.
faq.q: How does a CA relate to Azure Key Vault?

certificate-authority.long:
A certificate authority (CA) is a trusted entity in a public key infrastructure (PKI) that issues and signs digital certificates. In a typical hierarchy, a root CA anchors trust, while an issuing CA signs certificates for devices and users. According to Microsoft Learn, the certification authority is the trusted third party that acts as the root of trust, offering services that authenticate the identity of people, computers and other entities on a network.

The problem a CA addresses is one of ownership. Someone who receives a public key cannot be sure that it truly belongs to the claimed sender, because a third party on the communication channel might have swapped it for another. The CA resolves this by binding an identity to a public key through a certificate. A public key infrastructure as a whole is described as a set of software and hardware elements that lets a trusted third party establish the integrity and ownership of a public key, and the CA is the central element of that arrangement.

The mechanism rests on digital signatures. To issue a certificate, the CA hashes the certificate content, signs that hash with its private key and embeds the signature in the certificate. The CA publishes its own public key in a self-signed CA certificate. A recipient who wants to verify a certificate decrypts the signature with the CA's public key and compares the resulting hash with a hash of the certificate content. If the two match, the content has not been altered and the certificate was signed by that CA. Trust in the whole chain therefore depends on the CA verifying identities correctly before it issues a certificate.

A CA usually operates together with other PKI components. The Microsoft Learn material lists a registration authority, which in Microsoft PKIs is usually called a subordinate CA, a certificate database, a certificate store on the local computer and a key archival server. The split between a root CA and subordinate or issuing CAs reflects the hierarchy described above: the root anchors trust, and the issuing CAs sign the certificates that devices and users actually present.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the CA appears wherever certificates are requested and consumed. The M365.FM episode "Azure Key Vault - Simply Explained" walks through how certificates are handled in Azure Key Vault and shows where the CA fits into that process. According to the episode, the steps are: create a certificate by starting with a key in the Key Vault; have Key Vault send a TLS/SSL certificate request to the certificate authority; let the application poll Key Vault to see whether the certificate is ready; receive an X509 TLS/SSL certificate from the CA; and complete the creation by merging the CA's X509 certificate. The episode presents this as a simple way to manage secrets, keys and certificates in one place.

Seen from a decision-making perspective, the key points are which CA is trusted and how its identity checks are performed. Because every certificate inherits its credibility from the CA that signed it, the choice of root and issuing CAs, the protection of their private keys and the way identities are validated determine how much confidence relying parties can place in the certificates. The sources treat the underlying signing and verification process in simplified form, and the details of a real deployment can be more involved.

In summary, a certificate authority provides the trust anchor for certificate-based security. It signs certificates with its private key, publishes its public key in a self-signed certificate, and lets others verify that a public key belongs to the identity named in the certificate. Services such as Azure Key Vault rely on this relationship when they request and receive TLS/SSL certificates from a CA on behalf of an application.

champions-network.desc: A champions network is a group of trained employees who carry adoption of platforms such as Microsoft 365 or Copilot into their own teams through peer support.

faq.a: A champions network is a group of trained employees who carry adoption of a new platform such as Microsoft 365 or Copilot into their own teams through peer support and real workflows.
faq.q: What is a champions network?

faq.a: The episode "Power Platform Governance Best Practices with Craig White [MVP]" suggests aligning the community with business goals, gaining stakeholder support, setting clear participation expectations, holding regular meetings, and offering advanced training and recognition.
faq.q: How can a champions network be built according to the episodes?

faq.a: The episodes describe champions as employees who are passionate about technology, ready to learn and willing to help others, such as early adopters or members of a pilot group who can share their experience.
faq.q: Who are suitable champions?

champions-network.long:
A champions network is a group of trained employees who carry the adoption of a new platform, such as Microsoft 365 or Microsoft Copilot, into their own teams. The members help colleagues through peer support and by showing real workflows, rather than relying only on central training or announcements from IT. The concept appears repeatedly in M365.FM episodes on Copilot adoption, Power BI Copilot, Power Platform governance and scaling Copilot agents.

The purpose of a champions network is to make change management local and repeatable. Instead of every question going to a central team, people who work next to the users act as the first point of contact. The episode "Why Microsoft Copilot Agents Fail—and How to Fix Them" lists coaching and peer learning as an effective training practice and says that a champions network enhances local support and consistency. In this view, champions complement formal training by giving employees someone nearby who understands their daily tasks.

The episodes also describe who champions tend to be and how a network can be built. The episode "Power Platform Governance Best Practices with Craig White [MVP]" says champions are employees who show passion for technology and a willingness to help others, for example by creating an app. According to the episode, champions inspire their peers and drive user adoption. To build a strong network, it suggests aligning the champions community with business goals, getting support from key stakeholders, setting clear expectations for participation, holding regular meetings to share updates and celebrate success, and offering advanced training and recognition programs. The episode adds that champions often become leaders in a center of excellence, where they help others follow best practices and encourage a culture of sharing.

Champions networks are usually combined with other adoption measures. In "Microsoft 365 Copilot Adoption with Chris Hinch [Microsoft]", building a champions network is named alongside pilot programs and continuous training as ways to help teams adapt and maintain momentum. The episode ties successful Copilot adoption to strong leadership, clear governance and ongoing support, and suggests that leaders assess readiness and set clear goals. Similarly, "Connect Microsoft Copilot to Predictive Power BI" recommends starting with a pilot group and choosing users who are ready to learn and can share their experience with others. It also advises building an internal champions network to support new users, using contextual training tools that provide real-time help, and embedding AI governance in the training to support compliance and security.

A champions network also addresses adoption barriers when organizations scale AI. The episode "Scale Copilot Agents Safely in Microsoft 365" describes resistance and uneven skill levels among employees. It recommends visible leadership support, listening to feedback, answering questions and explaining how data stays safe and private. Its tip is to create a champions network in which early adopters share their success stories and help others learn. This links the network to trust-building: peers who have already used the tools can demonstrate them in context.

In practice, organizations deciding on a champions network typically consider whom to select, how to prepare them, and how to keep them engaged. The episodes point to early adopters or pilot participants as a natural source of champions, to regular community meetings, advanced training and recognition as ways to sustain involvement, and to governance topics such as compliance and security as content that champions should be able to pass on. The network is not a technical feature of Microsoft 365 but an organizational approach that supports platforms such as Microsoft 365, Copilot, Power BI and the Power Platform.

change-notifications.desc: Change notifications and webhooks are a Microsoft Graph pattern that pushes a message to an endpoint when data changes, replacing repeated polling.

faq.a: With polling, an application repeatedly asks Microsoft Graph whether data has changed, which often returns nothing new. With change notifications, the application registers a subscription and Microsoft Graph sends a message to its endpoint when the data changes.
faq.q: What is the difference between change notifications and polling?

faq.a: The episode "Fix Microsoft Graph Change Notifications and Webhooks" names a mishandled validation echo as the most common reason: the endpoint must return the raw token within the first five seconds, without JSON or wrappers. It also points to subscription renewals and monitoring as safeguards.
faq.q: Why do Microsoft Graph webhooks sometimes stop delivering notifications?

faq.a: The episodes recommend combining them. Delta query retrieves the changes since a previous point in time, and a saved deltaLink allows continued tracking, while webhooks supply the real-time trigger.
faq.q: How are change notifications related to delta query?

change-notifications.long:
Change notifications and webhooks are a Microsoft Graph pattern in which an application is told when data changes instead of asking for it repeatedly. The application registers a subscription, and Microsoft Graph then sends a message to the application's notification endpoint when the relevant data changes. This replaces constant polling, which, as the episode "Microsoft Graph Webhooks - Simply Explained" notes, often returns nothing new. The pattern is part of Microsoft Graph, the API that connects data across Microsoft 365.

The main purpose is to let applications respond almost immediately to events, such as calendar updates or document modifications. According to the episode "Microsoft Graph Change Notifications - Simply Explained", notifications can cover create, update and delete changes on various resources such as users, groups and security entities. Creating a subscription requires three settings: the resource to watch, the notification endpoint, and the change types. The request is then sent to the Microsoft Graph API. The same episode describes a choice of delivery channel: webhooks for instant push notifications, or Azure Event Hubs for handling large volumes of notifications securely and reliably.

Operating a subscription involves several recurring tasks. The episode says subscriptions should be renewed automatically so that notifications are not interrupted and no manual effort is needed. Incoming notifications should be processed quickly and securely, which includes validating the data, responding within 30 seconds and monitoring the status of the subscription. The episode also covers troubleshooting of common issues.

The episode "Fix Microsoft Graph Change Notifications and Webhooks" focuses on the situation where webhooks go silent, for example when SharePoint updates stop arriving. It names the most frequent cause as a validation echo that the endpoint handles incorrectly within the first five seconds: the endpoint is expected to return the raw token, with no JSON and no wrappers. The episode then lists measures that make the pipeline more reliable, compliant and auditable: thorough token checks, smart retries, automated subscription renewals and real monitoring.

Change notifications are frequently combined with delta query. The episode "Microsoft Graph Delta Queries - Simply Explained" describes delta queries as a way to query for changes in resources without retrieving the whole dataset, tracking additions, deletions and updates. It advises saving the deltaLink after the first request in order to keep tracking changes, and recommends combining delta queries with webhooks for real-time updates and better performance. In this combination, the notification signals that something changed, and the delta query retrieves what exactly changed.

The pattern also appears in architecture guidance. The episode "Microsoft Graph Automation Architecture: Beyond Scripts" lists webhooks for real-time notifications as one element of a governance-first automation design, alongside batching of requests and regular audits of permissions and access. Webhooks there let systems respond instantly to changes in Microsoft 365.

Typical decisions around the topic include whether push notifications are needed at all or polling is sufficient, whether webhooks or Azure Event Hubs suit the expected notification volume, how subscription renewal is automated, and how the endpoint is monitored. The episodes address administrators, architects and business stakeholders and stress safe implementation and operational value alongside the technical mechanics.

chaos-engineering.desc: Chaos engineering is the practice of injecting controlled failures into a system to test resilience hypotheses and find weaknesses before real outages occur.

faq.a: Chaos engineering is the practice of deliberately injecting controlled failures into a system to test hypotheses about its resilience and to find weaknesses before real outages occur.
faq.q: What is chaos engineering?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Chaos Studio - Simply Explained" describes Azure Chaos Studio as Microsoft's chaos engineering service for safely simulating failures in Azure environments, such as virtual machine failures, network latency, CPU stress and service outages.
faq.q: Which Microsoft service is associated with chaos engineering?

faq.a: According to the episode "Build Resilient Azure Architecture for Regional Outages", simulating failures lets teams validate that recovery mechanisms work during disruptions, and regular chaos testing builds confidence in the system's resilience.
faq.q: How does chaos engineering relate to disaster recovery?

chaos-engineering.long:
Chaos engineering is the practice of deliberately injecting controlled failures into a system in order to test hypotheses about its resilience and to find weaknesses before real outages occur. Rather than waiting for an incident to expose a gap in an architecture, teams create disruptions on purpose, observe how the system responds and recovers, and use the results to improve the design. The approach treats resilience as something that has to be verified by experiment, not assumed from the architecture diagram.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, this practice is most closely tied to Azure. The M365.FM episode "Azure Chaos Studio - Simply Explained" describes Azure Chaos Studio as Microsoft's chaos engineering service, which helps organizations build more resilient cloud applications by safely simulating failures before they happen in the real world. The episode compares it to a fire drill for an Azure environment: failures are rehearsed in a safe, controlled way so that teams know how systems behave when something actually goes wrong. According to the episode, such experiments can simulate virtual machine failures, network latency, CPU stress, service outages and many other real-world scenarios.

The core idea is the same regardless of tooling. A team states an expectation about how a system should behave under a given fault, introduces that fault in a controlled way, and compares the observed behavior with the expectation. If the system does not respond as hoped, the experiment has revealed a weakness that can be fixed while the stakes are still low. The word controlled matters: the goal is not to cause damage but to learn, so experiments are scoped and deliberate rather than random.

Chaos engineering also appears as one element of wider resilience and disaster recovery work. The episode "Build Resilient Azure Architecture for Regional Outages" places chaos engineering and testing alongside topics such as warm standby, automated failover and infrastructure as code. It says that chaos engineering helps find weaknesses in a cloud architecture, that simulating failures shows how a system responds, and that the practice lets teams validate recovery mechanisms and confirm they work during disruptions. The episode also states that regular chaos testing builds confidence in a system's resilience and that it identifies gaps in architectural resilience. In the same context, it notes that disaster recovery improves when failover is monitored and tested regularly.

The practice is also named in the context of migration and long-term operation. In "Move Legacy Systems to Azure Without Disrupting Work", chaos engineering is listed among ongoing optimization strategies after a move to Azure, next to continuous testing frameworks, load and stress testing, performance tuning with Azure Application Insights, recommendations from Azure Advisor, autoscaling based on real-time metrics and storage and network optimization. Here it serves to test system resilience by simulating failures once workloads are running in the cloud.

A further mention comes from the episode "Build an Auditable Multi-Agent Copilot in Microsoft 365", where chaos engineering scenarios appear in a list of compliance and governance mechanisms for multi-agent systems, alongside circuit-breaker mechanisms that isolate non-compliant agents and behavior baselining that detects compliance drift. In that list, chaos engineering scenarios are described as testing compliance resilience during disruptions or failures. This shows the concept being applied beyond infrastructure, to the behavior of agent-based systems as well.

Typical decisions around chaos engineering include which failures to simulate, how to keep experiments safe and controlled, and how to connect the findings to concrete changes such as failover design, standby capacity or monitoring. Because the episodes frame it as a recurring activity rather than a one-time test, it fits naturally into regular resilience reviews and continuous testing routines.

character-drift.desc: Character drift is the loss of a character's visual identity, such as face, proportions or outfit, across frames or shots in AI-generated video.

faq.a: Character drift is the loss of a character's visual identity, including face, proportions and outfit, across frames or shots in AI-generated video.
faq.q: What is character drift?

faq.a: It is typically caused by inconsistent references, inconsistent prompts or excessive motion in the generated footage.
faq.q: What causes character drift?

faq.a: It appears in the episode "AI Movie Production with Copilot, Seedance, and Higgsfield", published on 2026-06-02.
faq.q: Where is character drift discussed on M365.FM?

character-drift.long:
Character drift is the loss of a character's visual identity across frames or shots in AI-generated video. The affected attributes include the face, body proportions and outfit, so that a character appears to change subtly or noticeably from one moment to the next.

According to the available description, character drift is typically caused by inconsistent references, inconsistent prompts or excessive motion. When a generation model receives differing reference material or varying prompt wording between shots, or when a scene contains a lot of movement, the character's appearance can deviate from the intended look. The term is used in AI video production to describe this consistency problem and to guide how references, prompts and shot design are prepared.

In practice, the concept matters for any multi-shot AI video workflow in which the same character must remain recognizable, such as short films or narrative sequences. Keeping references and prompts consistent and limiting excessive motion are the factors named as relevant to the problem.

On M365.FM, character drift appears in the episode "AI Movie Production with Copilot, Seedance, and Higgsfield" (2026-06-02), which covers AI-assisted movie production.

chargeback.desc: Chargeback is a FinOps practice in which each team or cost center is billed for allocated technology costs through an internal budget transfer.

faq.a: Showback reports costs back to the consuming teams, while chargeback actually bills them through an internal budget transfer. The episode "Showback vs Chargeback for Cloud and Microsoft 365 Costs" notes that reporting without consequence often fails to change behavior.
faq.q: What is the difference between showback and chargeback?

faq.a: The episodes point to consistent tagging, such as cost center, project and environment tags, to attribute costs accurately. They also mention Azure Policy to enforce tagging and Azure Cost Management to analyze usage.
faq.q: What is needed to run a chargeback model for cloud resources?

faq.a: The episode "Reduce Microsoft Fabric Costs by Optimizing Compute Workloads" mentions the Fabric Chargeback App, which attributes compute usage to organizational units to make cost allocation easier.
faq.q: Is there a chargeback tool for Microsoft Fabric?

chargeback.long:
Chargeback is a FinOps practice in which each team or cost center is actually billed for the technology costs allocated to it. The billing happens as an internal budget transfer: money moves from the budget of the consuming unit to the budget of the central IT or platform owner. This separates chargeback from showback, which only reports costs back to the consumer without moving any money.

The practice is used in enterprise IT cost management for cloud and Microsoft 365 workloads. Its purpose is to make the people who drive consumption responsible for what that consumption costs. Several M365.FM episodes treat chargeback as part of a larger cost-accountability setup rather than a stand-alone control, and they connect it to tagging, cost allocation, monitoring and governance.

The episode "Showback vs Chargeback for Cloud and Microsoft 365 Costs" challenges the common belief that showback and chargeback alone create accountability. According to the episode, many organizations introduce showback dashboards or reports and expect behavior to change, only to find that business units ignore, dispute or game the numbers. The core message of the episode is that transparency without consequence is not enough. It argues that cost reporting needs clear ownership, meaningful incentives and integration into enterprise processes in order to influence decisions and deliver sustainable cost optimization. The discussion begins by defining showback as reporting costs back to the consuming units and then contrasts it with chargeback, where those costs are actually billed.

A recurring prerequisite for chargeback is the ability to attribute costs accurately. The episode "Azure Service Bus - Simply Explained" recommends consistent tagging strategies for Service Bus namespaces, including cost center, project and environment tags. The episode states that such tags enable accurate cost allocation and support chargeback models, and that tagging allows cost attribution across shared infrastructure, including structured chargeback for multi-tenant Service Bus deployments. It also suggests using Azure Cost Management to analyze message volume patterns and operation counts, so that tier selection rests on data.

The episode "Azure Policy - Simply Explained" links chargeback to governance. It lists cost management as one use of Azure Policy and says that enforcing tagging supports cost control and ownership, which aids chargeback and lifecycle management. In this view, policies that require tags on resources create the data foundation on which allocation and billing between teams can be built.

For Microsoft Fabric, the episode "Reduce Microsoft Fabric Costs by Optimizing Compute Workloads" mentions the Fabric Chargeback App. According to the episode, the app enables financial accountability by attributing compute usage to organizational units, which makes cost allocation easier. It is listed alongside the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics App, which is used for operational monitoring, so that usage can be observed technically and also assigned to the units responsible for it.

The episode "Build an Automated Azure Cleanup Engine to Reduce Cloud Waste" places chargeback in the context of waste reduction. It notes that many organizations use chargeback or showback practices to encourage teams to manage their own costs, and it pairs them with dashboards, budgets, automated alerts, native recommendations and regular reviews of budget and usage metrics. The aim named in the episode is to motivate teams to optimize their own usage.

Taken together, the episodes describe chargeback as one element of a FinOps approach. It depends on reliable allocation data such as tags, on tooling that attributes usage to organizational units, and on ownership and incentives that give the resulting numbers consequences. A typical decision is whether to start with showback reporting or to bill teams directly, and the episodes caution that either choice depends on those supporting elements to change behavior.

chart-of-accounts.desc: A chart of accounts is the list of general ledger accounts, usually with a name and number, that categorizes money movements such as sales income, rent or supplier debt.

faq.a: It is the list of accounts used in a company's general ledger, each typically with a name and number. The accounts categorize money movements such as sales income, rent or supplier debt.
faq.q: What is a chart of accounts?

faq.a: The episode "Why Your Business Central Won't Scale to Finance & Operations" advises designing the chart of accounts and dimensions with future consolidation in mind for organizations that may grow through acquisitions.
faq.q: Why does the chart of accounts matter for consolidation?

faq.a: According to "Financial Forecasting with Dynamics 365 Finance and Fabric", the chart of accounts is standardized in the transform step using translation tables, and an account dimension (DimAccount) is part of the semantic model alongside a general ledger fact table.
faq.q: How is the chart of accounts used in forecasting with Fabric?

chart-of-accounts.long:
A chart of accounts is the list of accounts used in a company's general ledger. Each account typically carries a name and a number, and together the accounts categorize money movements such as sales income, rent or amounts owed to suppliers. The chart of accounts defines the categories used to organize financial activity, so every posting can be placed in an appropriate account and later summarized for reporting.

The purpose of the chart of accounts is to answer one basic question for every transaction: what kind of financial activity was this? The episode "Dynamics 365 Finance - Simply Explained" gives examples of accounts an organization might have: sales revenue, rent, software costs, travel, salaries, taxes, cash, money owed by customers, and money owed to suppliers. If the organization pays office rent, that amount belongs in the account designed for rent.
