Instead of prompting for stronger verification on every sign-in to an app, an organization can target only the operations that carry higher risk. One example is each Privileged Identity Management (PIM) role activation, where a step-up requirement can be applied at the point of activation.

Because the requirement is attached to a specific action or resource, it allows different levels of assurance within the same application. Everyday access can stay low-friction, while sensitive operations trigger an additional check. This fits the broader Microsoft Entra approach of using Conditional Access policies to decide when and how access is granted.

Microsoft publishes developer-oriented documentation for authentication context in its Entra identity platform guidance, which describes how applications can work with the feature. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

conditional-access-report-only-mode.desc: Report-only mode is a Conditional Access policy state in Microsoft Entra ID that logs how a policy would apply at sign-in without enforcing it, helping assess impact first.
conditional-access-report-only-mode.long:
Report-only mode (Conditional Access) is a policy state in Microsoft Entra ID. In this state, a Conditional Access policy is evaluated whenever a sign-in occurs and the result is recorded in the logs, but the policy's controls are not enforced. Users are not blocked or prompted for additional requirements because of a policy that is set to report-only.

The mode is used to assess the potential impact of a Conditional Access policy before turning it on. By reviewing the logged evaluation results, administrators can see how a policy would have applied to real sign-ins and decide whether its conditions and controls behave as intended. This allows a policy to be tested and adjusted before enforcement begins, rather than discovering unintended effects after users are affected.

Report-only mode is one of the states a Conditional Access policy can be placed in, alongside enforced and disabled states. It is part of the broader Conditional Access capability in Microsoft Entra ID, which evaluates signals at sign-in to make access decisions.

Microsoft documents the feature in its Learn article on Conditional Access report-only mode. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity, and no related topics are recorded for it yet.

conditional-formatting.desc: Conditional formatting automatically changes cell appearance based on value rules in Excel, and similar rule-based formatting appears in Power BI and Microsoft Lists.

faq.a: It automatically changes the appearance of cells based on rules about their values, for example to highlight outliers. Typical tools mentioned in the episodes are color scales and icon sets.
faq.q: What does conditional formatting do in Excel?

faq.a: Yes. According to the entity description, Copilot in Excel can create such rules from natural-language prompts.
faq.q: Can Copilot in Excel create conditional formatting rules?

faq.a: The episode "Fix Excel Shadow Systems and Broken Business Processes" states that overuse of conditional formatting can significantly slow down calculations and refresh times, especially as data grows.
faq.q: Can conditional formatting slow down a workbook?

conditional-formatting.long:
Conditional formatting is an Excel feature that automatically changes the appearance of cells based on rules about their values. Instead of coloring cells by hand, a user defines a rule, and the formatting follows the data whenever it changes. A typical use is to highlight outliers so that unusual values stand out in a large table. Copilot in Excel can also create such rules from natural-language prompts, which lowers the effort of setting them up.

The idea is not limited to Excel. The M365.FM episodes mention rule-based visual formatting in several parts of the Microsoft ecosystem, including Power BI reports and Microsoft Lists. In each case the purpose is similar: make important patterns, trends or exceptions visible without requiring the reader to scan every value.

In the episode "From Excel Expert to Microsoft MVP: Empowering Millions with Data, Dashboards & AI with Karen Abecia [Microsoft MVP]", conditional formatting is described as a way to highlight important data trends and patterns visually, which improves data comprehension and supports decision-making. The tips listed there include using color scales to represent data ranges visually, applying icon sets to indicate performance levels or trends, and creating rules that highlight cells based on specific conditions. The episode places this next to dynamic charts built on named ranges, as part of presenting data so that stakeholders can grasp it more easily.

In Power BI, the episode "Power BI DAX and Semantic Models with Bernat Agulló Roselló [MVP]" describes conditional formatting as using DAX formulas to change the appearance of visuals based on values. Colors or icons can mark important trends or outliers, which improves the visual appeal of dashboards and helps users spot key insights quickly. The same episode mentions DAX functions such as CALCULATE, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR and PARALLELPERIOD for creating measures that adapt to the context of a report. The episode "From Raw Data to Real Business Impact: Mastering Power BI and Microsoft Fabric with Thummalacherla Krishnakanth" lists conditional formatting among the topics of report design, alongside KPI design, drill-down analysis, drill-through navigation, decomposition trees and report layouts. The framing there is that reports should help business users make faster and better decisions rather than overwhelm them with charts.

Microsoft Lists is a third setting. The episode "Use the Eisenhower Matrix with Microsoft 365 Copilot" says that Lists supports conditional formatting and rules that visually highlight overdue Asks, priority changes or status updates, so that to-do lists appear dynamically based on the data. It combines this with Power Automate for notifications and reminders and with Power Apps for custom forms.

Conditional formatting also has a cost. The episode "Fix Excel Shadow Systems and Broken Business Processes" lists excessive formatting as a performance issue in growing workbooks, stating that overuse of conditional formatting can significantly slow down calculations and refresh times. It appears there next to slow calculations on large datasets, memory limits in the 32-bit version of Excel, improper PivotTable use and the complexity added by defined names. The practical decision is therefore balance: rules should serve a clear reading purpose, and large or heavily used workbooks should limit how many rules are applied.

In summary, conditional formatting turns data values into visual signals. It is used for spotting outliers and trends in Excel, for emphasizing key figures in Power BI visuals, and for flagging status in Microsoft Lists, while the episodes advise keeping an eye on its effect on workbook performance.

confidence-score.desc: A confidence score is an estimate attached to an individual AI extraction result that shows how sure the system is about a value, not a guarantee it is correct.

faq.a: A confidence score is an estimate attached to an individual AI extraction result that indicates how sure the system is about that value. It is not a guarantee that the value is correct.
faq.q: What is a confidence score?

faq.a: No. The episode "Content Understanding & Document AI - Simply Explained" says a high score does not automatically mean a value should be trusted, and critical values like invoice totals or bank details may still need validation against business rules and existing systems.
faq.q: Does a high confidence score mean a value can be trusted?

faq.a: According to the episode "Agentic Operating Model for Enterprise AI and Copilot", confidence thresholds mean agents only act when their reasoning meets a set confidence score, which blocks risky actions. This is one mechanism alongside behavioral baselines and guardrail agents.
faq.q: How are confidence scores used with AI agents?

confidence-score.long:
A confidence score is an estimate attached to an individual AI extraction result. It indicates how sure the system is about that specific value, such as a field read from a document or a link found between two items. It is an indication of certainty, not a guarantee that the value is correct. This distinction runs through the M365.FM episodes that mention the term, and it shapes how scores should be used in practice.

In document processing, a confidence score is typically produced for each extracted value. The episode "Content Understanding & Document AI - Simply Explained" places confidence scores at the center of one of the most important parts of Document AI, together with human-in-the-loop review. In that setup, Power Apps can provide a human review interface where people correct uncertain or missing information, and records and process history keep track of what happened to each document. The score helps decide which values can pass through automatically and which should be routed to a person.

The episode is explicit about the limits of the score: a high confidence score does not automatically mean a value should be trusted. Critical information such as invoice totals, payment instructions, bank details, or contract dates may still require additional validation against business rules and existing systems. The episode describes validation that can check whether suppliers exist, purchase orders match, totals make sense, dates are valid, and duplicate invoices are caught. In this approach, the confidence score is one input alongside deterministic checks, and it does not replace them.

Confidence scores also appear in the context of controlling AI agents. The episode "Agentic Operating Model for Enterprise AI and Copilot" lists confidence thresholds as a control-layer mechanism: agents only act when their reasoning meets a set confidence score, which blocks risky actions. The episode presents this alongside behavioral baselines, which set limits on what agents can do, and guardrail agents, which monitor outputs and step in if actions go beyond safe limits. Here the score works as a gate: below the threshold, the agent does not act. Choosing the threshold is a design decision, and the episode frames it as one layer among several rather than a standalone safeguard.

A third use appears in large-scale document analysis. The episode "Scaling Microsoft Copilot to 35 Million Pages: The Epstein Files" describes AI linking names, places, themes, and timelines across very large sets of files, with a confidence score for each connection so that users know which findings are most reliable. The same episode stresses using and citing sources to counteract fears of hallucinations, which again shows that a score helps prioritize findings but does not replace checking them against sources.

Taken together, the episodes describe the same practical pattern. A confidence score ranks and filters results, decides what is routed to human review, and can gate automated actions. It should be combined with business-rule validation, lookups against existing systems, and review for high-impact values. Typical decisions include where to set the threshold for automatic processing, which fields always require validation regardless of score, and how reviewers see and correct uncertain values.

confidential-computing.desc: Confidential computing protects data in use by processing it inside attested, hardware-based trusted execution environments that host administrators and cloud operators cannot read or alter.

faq.a: It protects data in use, meaning data that is actively being processed in memory. It does this by running the processing inside hardware-based, attested trusted execution environments that code outside the TEE, including host administrators and the cloud operator, cannot read or alter.
faq.q: What does confidential computing protect?

faq.a: Encryption at rest protects stored data, for example with BitLocker, and encryption in transit protects data on the network, for example with TLS. Confidential computing covers the remaining case, data in use, and complements the other two.
faq.q: How is confidential computing different from encryption at rest and in transit?

faq.a: Attestation is the step in which the environment is checked before it is trusted. The M365.FM episode "Azure Confidential Computing - Simply Explained" describes it as checking the room before you trust it.
faq.q: What is attestation in confidential computing?

confidential-computing.long:
Confidential computing is an approach to data protection that secures data while it is being processed, not only while it is stored or transmitted. It works by running code inside hardware-based, attested trusted execution environments (TEEs). Code outside the TEE, including host administrators and the cloud operator, cannot read or alter what happens inside. In Microsoft's ecosystem the topic is documented under Azure Confidential Computing, and Microsoft Learn hosts the official documentation for it.

The concept addresses what the M365.FM episode "Azure Confidential Computing - Simply Explained" calls the encryption gap: data in use. Encryption at rest and in transit are well established, but data has traditionally had to be decrypted in memory in order to be processed. Another episode, "Build Auditable AI Agents with Azure AI Foundry", lays out the same three-part split. Data at rest is protected with encryption such as BitLocker for disk storage, data in transit is protected with TLS, and data in use is protected with confidential computing during processing. Confidential computing is therefore usually described as the layer that completes an existing encryption strategy rather than replacing it.

The mechanism rests on two ideas. The first is the trusted execution environment, a protected area of a system where code and data are isolated from the rest of the machine, including privileged software. The second is attestation, which allows a party to check the environment before trusting it. The outline of "Azure Confidential Computing - Simply Explained" describes this as checking the room before you trust it: instead of assuming a workload runs in a protected environment, the environment can be verified against the expected hardware and software state before sensitive data is released to it.

The same episode outline lists Azure building blocks, including virtual machines and containers, as the ways the technology is offered. Another episode, "Azure Infrastructure as Code and DevOps with Maik van der Gaag [MVP]", mentions that Azure supports confidential virtual machines with NVIDIA H100 GPUs. According to that episode, this allows sensitive AI applications to run while keeping data private, which it describes as relevant for fields such as healthcare and finance that require strict data protection.

Confidential computing also appears in governance discussions. The episode "7-Step Microsoft 365 Sovereign Tenant Governance Framework" lists it as one principle alongside data residency and encryption. In that framing, data residency keeps data within specific national or regional boundaries, such as the EU Data Boundary for Azure. Encryption protects information in transit and at rest, using customer-managed keys and HSMs. Confidential computing extends protection to data in use through secure enclaves and trusted execution environments, preventing unauthorized access. The episode presents these principles as a combined framework that supports regulatory requirements in industries such as healthcare and finance.

Typical decisions around confidential computing include which workloads justify the extra isolation, for example processing of regulated or sensitive data and AI workloads that handle private inputs. They also include which Azure offering fits, such as confidential virtual machines or containers, and how attestation is verified before keys or data are released. The sources in this entity do not give pricing, performance figures or version details, so those aspects should be checked in the official Azure Confidential Computing documentation.

configuration-drift.desc: Configuration drift is the gradual gap between the documented, intended state of infrastructure and its actual running state, often caused by manual changes.

faq.a: Configuration drift is the gradual gap between the intended, documented state of infrastructure and its actual running state. It is typically caused by manual changes made outside infrastructure as code.
faq.q: What is configuration drift?

faq.a: According to the episodes, IaC with tools such as Terraform and Bicep automates deployments and produces consistent results across environments, which reduces the risk of errors and configuration drift. Version control of the infrastructure code also adds transparency.
faq.q: How does Infrastructure as Code help reduce configuration drift?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft 365 Security Through Clear Accountability" says undocumented setting or policy changes accumulate and make the environment deviate from its security baseline. This can weaken defenses and open new vulnerabilities.
faq.q: Why is configuration drift a security concern in Microsoft 365?

configuration-drift.long:
Configuration drift is the gradual gap between the intended, documented state of infrastructure and its actual running state. It typically arises when manual changes are made outside infrastructure as code (IaC), so the environment slowly moves away from the baseline that teams believe is in place. The term appears across several areas of the Microsoft ecosystem, including Azure resources, Microsoft 365 tenant settings, Active Directory and Intune-managed endpoints.

The core mechanism is simple: a setting or policy is changed, often with good intent, and the change is not recorded or fed back into the documented configuration. One episode, "Microsoft 365 Security Through Clear Accountability", describes this for Microsoft 365: someone updates a policy or changes a security setting but forgets to document it. Individually these changes may look small, but the episode says they add up and cause the environment to deviate from its security baseline, which can weaken defenses and open new vulnerabilities. The same episode links drift to permission changes made without proper tracking, arguing that organizations need visibility into who holds which permissions and why.

The practical concern is mainly security and predictability. When the running state no longer matches the documented state, it becomes harder to know what protections are actually active, who can access what, and why a system behaves as it does. The episode "Stop Active Directory Security Drift Before a Breach" frames Active Directory configuration management as the way to prevent drift: organizations maintain consistent and secure configurations to minimize vulnerabilities, so that systems operate as intended with fewer interruptions and errors. It also describes monitoring tools as playing a vital role in tracking changes, and presents continuous monitoring and proactive management of configurations as essential for a secure environment and for compliance.

Infrastructure as Code is presented as a primary countermeasure. In "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained", IaC is described as making deployments faster and less error-prone, enabling version control of infrastructure code, and producing consistent deployments across environments, which reduces the risk of errors and configuration drift. Tools named there are Terraform and Bicep, which simplify the management of cloud resources. The episode "Azure Infrastructure as Code and DevOps with Maik van der Gaag [MVP]" covers the same ground for Azure: Terraform and Bicep let teams automate deployments, improve consistency and reduce configuration drift. That conversation also stresses that tooling is only part of the picture; collaboration between development, operations, security and business teams, along with topics such as GitOps, governance and security, belongs to a successful cloud transformation.

Drift also shows up in endpoint management. The episode "Automate Intune Device Cleanup with Azure Automation" lists configuration drift together with stale devices, manual reports and broad administrator rights as factors that silently open the door to attackers. It describes combining Intune with Azure Automation, Functions, Microsoft Graph, managed identities and Log Analytics so that event-driven automation cleans up stale devices, enforces zero trust and fixes non-compliant devices before users notice. According to the episode, example enterprise scenarios include more than 40 percent fewer ghost devices and onboarding times dropping from days to minutes.

Taken together, the episodes suggest a common set of decisions around configuration drift: define the intended state explicitly, keep that definition in version control, deploy through automation rather than manual edits, record every change that must be made by hand, and monitor continuously so that deviations are detected and corrected. Drift is therefore less a single product feature than a condition to be managed through process, tooling and accountability.

configuration-manager.desc: Microsoft Configuration Manager is Microsoft's on-premises device management product, often compared with Intune and used in co-management scenarios.

faq.a: It is Microsoft's on-premises device management product, also called SCCM in the M365.FM episodes. It is typically compared with Microsoft Intune, the cloud-based endpoint management service.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Configuration Manager?

faq.a: In co-management, workload sliders decide which system owns particular functions, including Windows Update policies. This lets management responsibilities move between Configuration Manager and Intune workload by workload.
faq.q: How does co-management with Intune work?

faq.a: According to the episode "Manage Microsoft 365 Update Overload", it can synchronize software updates, control Office 365 update channel assignments, schedule update options and monitor deployment status. It requires the current branch version and WSUS 4.0, among other things.
faq.q: What does Configuration Manager do for Microsoft 365 Apps updates?

configuration-manager.long:
Microsoft Configuration Manager is Microsoft's on-premises device management product. It is also referred to as SCCM in the M365.FM episodes, and one episode uses the name Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager (MECM). Organizations use it to manage devices and software from infrastructure they run themselves, and it is frequently discussed alongside Microsoft Intune, the cloud-based endpoint management service.

One of the main decisions around Microsoft Configuration Manager is how it relates to Intune. In co-management, both systems manage the same Windows devices. Workload sliders decide which system owns particular management functions, including Windows Update policies. This lets an organization move individual workloads from Configuration Manager to Intune at its own pace instead of switching everything at once. The episode "SCCM vs Intune: Key Differences | Simply Explained" frames the comparison as an input to an organization's IT management strategy.

The infrastructure side is where the two products differ most. According to that episode, Configuration Manager requires a robust on-premises setup. For deploying it in a large organization, the episode lists several guidelines: choose one primary site for central management with normal WAN connectivity; opt for multiple sites when scale, geography or network costs make a single site inefficient; and add secondary sites only when local distribution and management benefit from them. Intune takes a different approach, since it is a cloud-based service and does not depend on that kind of site hierarchy.

Configuration Manager is also used for software update management. The episode "Manage Microsoft 365 Update Overload" describes how it can handle updates for Microsoft 365 Apps. In the console, an administrator selects Microsoft 365 Apps/Office 2019/Office LTSC under Products, picks Updates on the Classifications tab, and then synchronizes software updates so they appear in the console. The episode lists these requirements: the current branch version of Microsoft Configuration Manager, an enterprise or business subscription for Microsoft 365 Apps, Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) 4.0, and device access to specific Microsoft URLs. It says Configuration Manager lets administrators control Office 365 update channel assignments, schedule update options and monitor deployment status.

Configuration Manager also appears as a delivery mechanism for Microsoft 365 Copilot. In "How Do You Successfully Deploy Microsoft 365 Copilot Across an Enterprise?", the episode names Microsoft Configuration Manager, the Microsoft 365 apps admin center and Microsoft Store strategies as options for installing the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on devices. That deployment sits alongside other steps the episode lists, such as assigning licenses, preparing enterprise data and security controls, configuring network requirements and testing with pilot groups.

In virtual desktop scenarios, Configuration Manager is positioned as the bridge to existing infrastructure. The episodes "Windows 365 – Simply Explained" and "Azure Virtual Desktop vs Windows 365 with Dieter Kempeneers [MVP] & Dominiek Verham [MVP]" list Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager among the components of a Windows 365 environment. They describe it as integrating with existing on-premises infrastructure for unified management alongside cloud tools such as Microsoft Intune and Windows Autopatch. One episode adds that this gives a unified toolchain for policy enforcement, inventory and reporting across Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows 365.

Taken together, the episodes treat Microsoft Configuration Manager as an established on-premises tool that continues to matter in hybrid environments, where it works next to Intune rather than being replaced outright. The decision usually concerns which workloads each system should own and how much on-premises infrastructure an organization wants to keep operating.

confluence.desc: Confluence is Atlassian's web-based corporate wiki, covered on M365.FM as a knowledge source for Microsoft 365 Copilot, connectors and Copilot Studio agents.

faq.a: According to the episodes, a Microsoft Copilot connector (formerly Graph Connector) can index Confluence content and sync it into Microsoft Search and Copilot. Security trimming is applied so results respect access rights.
faq.q: How can Confluence content be used with Microsoft 365 Copilot?

faq.a: The facts describe indexing an on-premises Confluence with Azure AI Search and using that index as a knowledge source for a Copilot Studio agent.
faq.q: How can Confluence serve as a knowledge source for a Copilot Studio agent?

faq.a: In the episode on integrating Jira Service Management with Microsoft Teams, Teams can suggest helpful articles from the Confluence database while a user raises a request, which can help resolve issues without a ticket.
faq.q: How does Confluence relate to Jira Service Management in Microsoft Teams?

confluence.long:
Confluence is Atlassian's web-based corporate wiki. Organizations use it to store and share documentation, policies and project pages in one place. On M365.FM it appears mainly from the Microsoft side: as an external content source that can be made available to Microsoft 365 Copilot and to agents built in Copilot Studio, alongside the Microsoft 365 data that these tools already reach.

The episode "Connect External Business Data with Microsoft 365 Copilot Connectors" describes Microsoft Copilot connectors as integrations that bring external content into Microsoft 365 and Copilot experiences. Confluence is named there together with MediaWiki, Google services and custom data stores. According to the episode, connectors index the external content and sync it into Microsoft Search and Copilot, which improves discoverability in search and Copilot search scenarios. The practical effect is that wiki knowledge kept in Confluence does not have to be copied into Microsoft 365 by hand to be found.

The episode "Microsoft Graph Connectors - Simply Explained" from the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets format, presented by Mirko Peters, covers the same mechanism under its earlier name. It lists Confluence among third-party platforms, such as Salesforce, ServiceNow and Jira, whose information organizations can securely index. The episode explains that Graph Connectors crawl external data sources, create searchable indexes and apply security trimming, so that relevant results can surface in Microsoft Search, Microsoft Copilot and other Microsoft 365 experiences. Security trimming matters for a wiki in particular, because pages often carry different audiences, and results should respect those boundaries.

Another route is described in the facts about the Copilot Studio scenario: an on-premises Confluence is indexed with Azure AI Search and then used as a knowledge source for a Copilot Studio agent. This is a decision point for teams. A connector-based approach feeds Microsoft Search and Copilot, while an Azure AI Search index serves as a knowledge source for a custom agent. Which path fits depends on where Confluence is hosted and which Microsoft experience should consume the content.

The episode "Beyond Copilot: Building Enterprise AI Agents That Actually Work with Copilot Studio with Manpreet Singh [MVP-MCT]" places Confluence among enterprise systems that agents can connect to, next to Workday, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, Jira and PeopleSoft. The episode's argument is that the shift happens when an agent does more than retrieve information. Instead of navigating several applications manually, employees interact with an agent in Microsoft Teams or another conversational interface. In the leave-request example from the episode, an agent checks available leave, consults HR policies, starts the request in the HR system, asks the manager for approval and returns the result. Policy documents of this kind are a typical use of a wiki as a knowledge source.

Confluence also appears in the Atlassian-to-Microsoft integration discussed in "Integrate Jira Service Management with Microsoft Teams". The episode says that when a user starts a new request from a chat or channel conversation and fills out the summary field, Teams may suggest helpful articles from the Confluence database, which can help people solve issues on their own. Requests are then tracked under a "My Requests" tab, similar to the Jira Service Management portal.

Finally, "Make Your Cloud Migration Ready for Enterprise AI" lists cloud-side Confluence capabilities in the context of AI project workflows: independently configurable workflows, fields and permissions per team, a project template library, mobile apps, and external collaboration that allows sharing Confluence pages with clients and partners without requiring full licenses. The episode connects moving to the cloud with operational efficiency and with integrating data from multiple sources for AI work.

connected-organizations.desc: Connected organizations in Microsoft Entra entitlement management are external partners, defined by domain or identity provider, whose users may request access packages.

faq.a: It is an external organization with which a business relationship exists, declared by domain or identity provider. Its users can be allowed to request specific access packages under a policy.
faq.q: What is a connected organization in Microsoft Entra entitlement management?

faq.a: Users can come from another Microsoft Entra directory, a non-Microsoft directory using SAML or WS-Fed federation, a shared email domain with one-time passcodes, or Microsoft accounts. One connected organization can cover several directories and domains.
faq.q: How can users of a connected organization be defined?

faq.a: A configured one is the default when created manually. A proposed one is created automatically when a requester has no matching organization and applies only to policies that target it directly.
faq.q: What is the difference between configured and proposed connected organizations?

connected-organizations.long:
Connected organizations are a concept in Microsoft Entra entitlement management. A connected organization is another organization with which a business relationship exists. For its users to reach resources in a directory, a representation of those users has to exist in that directory, and entitlement management can bring it in on demand. The purpose is to simplify access for groups of people from specific external organizations and to control which of them are allowed to request access packages under a given policy.

A connected organization defines its users in one of four ways. The first is another Microsoft Entra directory. The second is a non-Microsoft directory that uses SAML or WS-Fed federation. The third is a shared domain used by email addresses, where users sign in with one-time passcodes. The fourth is Microsoft accounts. A single connected organization can cover several directories and domains, so one partner with multiple tenants or domains can be represented as one entry. For domains that have no directory, email one-time passcodes must be enabled. Domain search requires the full domain name, and domains can be blocked by B2B allow or deny lists, which can affect whether a partner's users are accepted.

Each connected organization can have sponsors. Sponsors can be internal members or external guests, and they can act as contacts and approvers for requests that come from that organization. This allows approval to be handled by someone who knows the business relationship rather than by a central team alone.

Connected organizations have one of two states. A configured organization is the default when an administrator creates one manually. A proposed organization is created automatically when a requester has no matching connected organization, and it applies only to policies that target it directly. Managing connected organizations requires at least the Identity Governance Administrator role.

In practice, connected organizations are used together with access packages. A policy on an access package can be scoped so that only users from selected connected organizations may request it. When a request from such a user is approved, Microsoft invites the user into the directory so that access can be granted. Because access packages support multi-stage approval and time-limited assignments, guest access granted this way can expire and be removed automatically, which supports offboarding and lifecycle governance of external users.

The M365.FM episode "Govern Microsoft 365 Guest Access and Offboarding" (2025-11-03) places connected organizations within this broader picture of access governance. The episode describes capabilities such as controlling who can access applications and resources through multi-stage approval and time-limited assignments, granting access based on identity properties and removing it when those properties change, and letting identities from connected organizations request access, with Microsoft inviting them into the directory upon approval. It also states that guest access is removed automatically when packages expire.

Typical decisions around the concept include which partners to declare as connected organizations, whether to define them by Microsoft Entra directory, federated identity provider, domain or Microsoft account, who should act as sponsors, and which access package policies should be limited to specific organizations. Another consideration is whether B2B allow or deny lists, or the lack of email one-time passcodes, could prevent users from a partner domain from signing in.

connection-references.desc: Connection references are a Power Platform concept; this page defines the term and notes its place under Power Platform, with limited detail available.

faq.a: Connection references is a concept listed under the broader topic Power Platform. The facts recorded for this entry do not include a detailed definition, so specifics should be confirmed in official Microsoft documentation.
faq.q: What are connection references in Power Platform?

faq.a: They are categorized under Power Platform, which is the broader topic in this knowledge base's relation structure.
faq.q: Which topic do connection references belong to?

faq.a: No episodes are currently linked to this entry in the available information.
faq.q: Is there an M365.FM episode about connection references?

connection-references.long:
Connection references (Power Platform) is a concept within the Microsoft Power Platform ecosystem. In the M365.FM knowledge base it is classified as a concept and sits under the broader topic Power Platform.

The available information for this entry is limited. No short description, documentation link or episode references are recorded for it, so this page does not describe specific features, behaviors or configuration steps. Readers looking for technical details should consult the official Microsoft documentation for Power Platform.

Within the knowledge base, the term is linked to Power Platform as its parent subject. Any coverage of Power Platform on M365.FM may be relevant context for understanding where connection references fit, though no individual episodes are currently associated with this entry.

connector.desc: A connector is a prebuilt API wrapper that lets Power Apps, Power Automate and Copilot Studio read and write data in hundreds of services without direct API calls.

faq.a: A connector is a prebuilt wrapper around an API that lets Power Apps, Power Automate and Copilot Studio read and write data in hundreds of services. It exposes actions, triggers and data sources so makers do not handle API calls directly.
faq.q: What is a connector in the Power Platform?

faq.a: DLP policies classify connectors and control which of them may be used together in the same app or flow. This makes connectors a central point for governance decisions in the Power Platform.
faq.q: How do connectors relate to data loss prevention (DLP)?

faq.a: No. According to the episode "Microsoft Graph Connectors - Simply Explained", Graph connectors bring external data into Microsoft 365 so it becomes searchable, for example in Microsoft 365 Copilot. A Power Platform connector wraps an API for use in apps and flows.
faq.q: Is a Microsoft Graph connector the same as a Power Platform connector?

connector.long:
A connector, also referred to as a Power Platform connector or Konnektor, is a prebuilt wrapper around an API. It allows Power Apps, Power Automate and Copilot Studio to read and write data in hundreds of services. Instead of building and handling raw API calls, a maker selects a connector and works with the actions, triggers and data sources it exposes. Connectors sit under the broader Power Platform concept and are one of the main ways the platform reaches data and services outside of itself.

In practice, connectors supply the building blocks of automation and app logic. In Power Automate, triggers and actions in a flow come from connectors. In Power Apps, connectors provide the data sources that an app reads from and writes to. In Copilot Studio, connectors give a copilot access to external systems. A reference list of available connectors is maintained in Microsoft's official connector reference documentation. When a service has no ready-made connector, a custom connector can be created so that the same low-code tooling can still reach it.

Connectors are also a central point for governance. Data loss prevention (DLP) policies classify connectors and control which of them may be used together in the same app or flow. Because every connection to a service passes through a connector, DLP gives administrators a way to separate business data from non-business data and to limit where information can move. Decisions about which connectors are allowed, and how they are grouped, therefore shape what makers can build and what risks they can introduce.

The M365.FM episode "MCP Custom Connector in Copilot Studio: The Complete Integration Guide" covers a concrete use of custom connectors. It describes connecting an MCP server to Copilot Studio through a custom connector, and walks through authentication, schemas, testing, streaming and troubleshooting. This shows that a custom connector can serve as the bridge between Copilot Studio and an external tool server.

A more critical view appears in the episode "Custom Connectors vs Model Context Protocol for Enterprise AI". The episode argues that organizations have treated managed connectors as an easy button for automation, and it presents them as a fragile transport model. It names hidden latency, throttling limits, middleware bottlenecks, retry storms and black-box infrastructure that the organization does not control as concerns. The related episode "Dataverse MCP Integration with Nathan Rose [MVP]" discusses the end of custom integration, noting that building a custom connector for each tool and platform takes considerable time and money, and that standardized solutions can reduce the need to build every connection from scratch. These are positions taken in the episodes rather than universal statements.

The term connector is also used for different technologies, which can cause confusion. The episode "Microsoft Graph Connectors - Simply Explained" describes Microsoft Graph connectors, which integrate external data with Microsoft 365 services so that content from other business applications becomes searchable, for example in Microsoft 365 Copilot. This is distinct from a Power Platform connector, which wraps an API for use in apps and flows. Likewise, the episode "Microsoft Entra Private Access - Simply Explained" mentions verifying connector configurations when troubleshooting connection issues, which refers to a connector in the Microsoft Entra context rather than to a Power Platform connector. When searching for the term, it helps to confirm which product area is meant.

Typical decisions around connectors include whether a prebuilt connector is sufficient or a custom connector is needed, how connectors are classified in DLP policies, and how authentication and testing are handled for custom ones. Understanding the connector concept therefore supports both building solutions in Power Apps, Power Automate and Copilot Studio and governing them across the Power Platform.

consent-management.desc: Consent management is the process of obtaining, recording and respecting a person's permission to collect and use their data, such as for marketing by channel or purpose.

faq.a: Consent management is the process of obtaining, recording and respecting a person's permission for the collection and use of their data, for example for marketing communications by channel, brand or purpose.
faq.q: What is consent management?

faq.a: The episode "Find Missing Microsoft Teams and Channels" names the need for user consent under GDPR and suggests using a consent management platform, together with documentation to support user rights such as access and deletion. The episode "Stop Prompt Injection in LangChain4j and Copilot Studio" lists clear user consent alongside GDPR and CCPA compliance.
faq.q: How does consent management relate to GDPR in the M365.FM episodes?

faq.a: The episode "Graph API - Simply Explained" names consent management alongside permissions, least-privilege access and API security as essential for enterprise data. The Copilot episode lists it among the security assessments to run before rollout.
faq.q: Why does consent management appear in Microsoft Graph and Copilot discussions?

consent-management.long:
Consent management is the process of obtaining, recording and respecting a person's permission for the collection and use of their data. Consent can be tied to specific scopes, for example marketing communications by channel, brand or purpose. In practice it covers the full cycle: asking for permission in a clear way, storing evidence of what was agreed, and making sure later data handling follows that choice.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the term appears in several different contexts, and the M365.FM episodes treat it as a recurring building block of compliance and security work rather than as a standalone product. It shows up in discussions of analytics tooling, API access, AI governance and Copilot rollout planning. The common thread is that data is only collected or accessed when the relevant permission exists and can be shown to exist.

The episode "Find Missing Microsoft Teams and Channels" touches on consent in the context of session recording and analytics. It lists the need for user consent under GDPR as a limitation, and the suggested approach is to use a consent management platform to manage user consent and support compliance. The same excerpt connects this to handling user data rights, advising that documentation and processes be kept in place to support rights such as access and deletion. It also notes that session tracking can fail when data protection requirements are not followed or when user consent is missing.

The episode "Graph API - Simply Explained" places consent management in a more technical setting. It describes Microsoft Graph as providing secure, contextual access to business data across Microsoft 365, and states that understanding permissions, least-privilege access, consent management and API security is essential when working with enterprise data. Here consent is closely tied to which permissions an application or user has been granted, and to the principle of limiting access to what is needed.

The episode "Stop Prompt Injection in LangChain4j and Copilot Studio" lists consent management within a compliance checklist for AI solutions. The entry reads as securing clear consent from users regarding data handling practices. In the same list it appears alongside risk management, user rights management under data privacy laws such as GDPR and CCPA, data minimization, security measures and regular staff training. The pairing with data minimization reflects a practical point: limiting data collection to what is strictly necessary reduces both the scope of consent that must be obtained and the exposure if something goes wrong.

The episode "Microsoft 365 Security Through Clear Accountability" frames consent within broader governance trends. It expects tighter governance and regulatory frameworks around consumer data, including expanded consent requirements and stricter breach notification timelines. It also says organizations are increasingly focusing on AI governance and data consent management, which it links to the need for comprehensive accountability frameworks.

The episode "Measure Microsoft 365 Copilot Productivity and Efficiency" includes consent management in a readiness checklist for Copilot. Security assessments covering identity, authentication, encryption and consent management appear next to reviews of compliance, privacy and data residency requirements, and the setup of governance policies for prompt use, data sharing and access control. In this view, consent management is one of several checks performed before and during adoption, not a one-time task.

Taken together, the episodes describe consent management as a cross-cutting practice: it supports user rights, depends on documentation and repeatable processes, and interacts with permissions, governance and data minimization. Decisions around it typically involve whether a dedicated consent management platform is needed, how consent records are kept, and how consent choices are respected across analytics, integrations and AI features.

constraint-based-scheduling.desc: Constraint-based scheduling places each production operation on a real resource and time slot only when hard constraints are met, then compares feasible options against business goals.

faq.a: It is a production scheduling approach that places each operation on a real resource and time slot only when hard constraints such as machine capability, tooling, labor skills, material release and precedence are met. Feasible options are then compared against business objectives.
faq.q: What is constraint-based scheduling?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes describe ERP plans that look correct but ignore real shop-floor conditions, such as a machine failure or missing material. Constraint-based scheduling checks whether the work fits the capacity actually available instead of discovering overload later.
faq.q: How does constraint-based scheduling differ from simple ERP planning?

faq.a: The episode "Production Schedule Optimization - How to Build Better Production Schedules" lists machine availability and capability, setup and changeover time, material and batch availability, and operator availability. The other episode adds tooling, fixtures and operator qualifications.
faq.q: Which constraints are typically considered?

constraint-based-scheduling.long:
Constraint-based scheduling is a production scheduling approach that assigns each operation to an actual resource and time slot only when the hard constraints of the shop floor are satisfied. Typical constraints include machine capability, tooling, labor skills, material release and precedence between operations. Once a set of feasible placements exists, the approach compares those options against business objectives. The result is a plan that the factory can actually execute rather than one that merely looks acceptable in a planning report.

The idea addresses a familiar gap between planning and execution. An ERP system may show a work order as released, the routing as correct and capacity as available, and still produce a date that cannot be met. The M365.FM episode "Constraint-Based Scheduling: The Architecture That Makes Production Plans Real" describes this situation: the ERP says an order ships on Friday, and then a critical five-axis machining center goes down on Monday morning. One order is already in production, another waits for material, and a third might theoretically be moved. The episode frames the core questions as whether a machine has the correct tooling, whether the fixture is available, whether the material has been released and whether an operator with the required qualification is available during the planned setup.

The second M365.FM episode, "Production Schedule Optimization - How to Build Better Production Schedules", places constraint-based scheduling alongside finite-capacity scheduling. Instead of loading orders against preferred dates and discovering overload later, the scheduler checks whether the work fits the capacity that is really available. The episode lists typical constraints such as machine availability and capability, setup and changeover time, material and batch availability, and operator availability. It also argues that a credible schedule combines several information sources: business priorities from ERP, current execution information from MES and relevant shop-floor events from OT systems. According to the episode, none of these systems provides the complete scheduling picture alone.

Constraint-based scheduling belongs to the wider field of advanced planning and scheduling (APS). APS is a manufacturing management process that allocates raw materials and production capacity as well as possible to meet demand. It is used where simpler planning methods cannot handle complex trade-offs between competing priorities. Reference material on APS notes that scheduling is inherently hard because the solution space grows roughly factorially with the number of products. It also criticizes traditional approaches such as manufacturing resource planning, which allocate materials and capacity stepwise and separately, often ignore constraints and can therefore produce infeasible plans that adapt poorly to changes in demand, capacity or material availability. APS instead plans and schedules simultaneously based on available materials, labor and plant capacity.

The approach is relevant in environments such as make-to-order manufacturing, capital-intensive processes with constrained plant capacity, plants where many products compete for the same capacity, products with many components or tasks, and production that needs frequent and unpredictable schedule changes. In these settings, a plan that ignores a hard constraint tends to fail at the point of execution, which then forces manual rework by planners and supervisors.

A practical decision around constraint-based scheduling is which constraints count as hard and which are treated as preferences. Hard constraints, such as tooling availability or precedence, must be met for a placement to be feasible at all. Business objectives, such as delivery dates, then guide the choice among the feasible options. Another decision concerns data: the quality of a constraint-based schedule depends on how current and accurate the information about machines, materials and labor is, which is why the episodes stress combining ERP, MES and OT information rather than relying on one source.

In summary, constraint-based scheduling treats feasibility as the starting point of planning. It checks what the factory can support before optimizing for business goals, and it is positioned in the sources as a way to make production plans realistic enough to hold when conditions on the shop floor change.

consulting.desc: Consulting is the industry of advisory firms and independent consultants helping organisations with strategy, processes, technology and change, including Microsoft 365 work.

faq.a: Consulting consists of advisory firms and independent consultants who help organisations with strategy, processes, technology and change. In the Microsoft context this includes work on Microsoft 365, governance, identity and automation.
faq.q: What does the Consulting industry do?

faq.a: The episode "Build a High-Value Productized Microsoft 365 Service" says services sold as tasks such as deployments or migrations become commoditized, because technical expertise is no longer a differentiator. It argues that services designed around outcomes and risk reduction avoid this trap.
faq.q: Why do the M365.FM episodes say Microsoft 365 consulting is becoming commoditized?

faq.a: The episodes recommend focusing on architecture, strategic impact and business transformation rather than basic implementation, and choosing a high-value niche. The episode "How to Become a High-Value Microsoft 365 Consultant" describes this as engineering architectural necessity instead of selling hours.
faq.q: How can consultants differentiate themselves according to the episodes?

consulting.long:
Consulting, also called management consulting or Unternehmensberatung, is the industry of advisory firms and independent consultants who help organisations with strategy, processes, technology and change. Clients typically bring in outside advisors when they need specialist knowledge, additional capacity or an independent view on a problem they cannot easily solve alone. In the Microsoft ecosystem, consulting covers a wide range of work, from deploying and configuring Microsoft 365 to advising on governance, identity, automation and wider business transformation.

Within M365.FM, the term appears mainly in discussions about how consulting practices around Microsoft 365 are built, priced and positioned. The episode "5 High-Margin Microsoft 365 Business Models" argues that traditional Microsoft 365 consulting is rapidly losing value. It describes Microsoft 365 as a distributed decision engine rather than a set of tools, and says the real opportunity lies in controlling how that system behaves. According to the episode, five modern business models can generate high-margin, recurring revenue by focusing on governance, identity, automation and system-level outcomes instead of implementation work.

A related theme is commoditisation. The episode "Build a High-Value Productized Microsoft 365 Service" says that most Microsoft 365 consulting services become commoditized because they are sold as tasks and activities such as deployments, governance setups or migrations. The episode argues that technical expertise is no longer a differentiator and that service architecture is. In its view, clients do not actually buy those activities; they buy certainty, risk reduction and measurable business results. It recommends designing services around outcomes rather than tasks and choosing high-value niches, with specialisation as part of that approach.

The episode "How to Become a High-Value Microsoft 365 Consultant" looks at the same question from the perspective of the individual advisor. It says many Microsoft consultants never break out of commodity consulting, competing on hourly rates, implementation speed and certifications while struggling to be seen as strategic advisors. The episode presents a blueprint centred on architecture, strategic impact and business transformation rather than basic implementation work. Instead of selling hours, it describes consultants who engineer architectural necessity, meaning solutions that clients' organisations come to depend on.

Consulting also intersects with the tools clients and consultants use. The episode "Microsoft AppSource - Simply Explained" describes Microsoft AppSource as an online marketplace for business applications that combines business applications and consulting services in one place. It notes that users can find industry-specific solutions for their business challenges, that many applications offer free trials, and that solutions integrate with Microsoft 365. This shows one route by which organisations find both software and advisory support.

The episode "Dynamics 365 Project Operations - Simply Explained" touches on consulting from the operational side. It describes Microsoft Dynamics 365 Project Operations as designed for organisations that sell project-based services, including consulting hours, engineering work and implementation projects. In such businesses, people, time, costs, contracts and billing need to stay connected, and the episode says that without a connected system different departments often create their own version of a project, with sales, delivery and time recording each holding separate information.

Taken together, the episodes present consulting as an industry under pressure to move from selling hours and implementation effort toward selling outcomes, governance and long-term system behaviour. Typical decisions for advisors include which niche to specialise in, whether to package services as defined products, and how to demonstrate measurable results such as risk reduction, automation and efficiency gains. For client organisations, the decisions centre on what they are actually buying: activities, or a dependable outcome.

container.desc: A container packages an application with everything it needs to run and shares the host operating system, so it behaves the same on a laptop, server or cloud.

faq.a: A container packages an application with everything it needs to run and shares the host operating system. This lets it run the same way on a laptop, a server or in the cloud.
faq.q: What is a container?

faq.a: Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform that automates deployment, scaling, management and recovery of containerized applications. The episode "Kubernetes - Simply Explained" describes it as keeping applications running, healthy and available across many servers.
faq.q: How do containers relate to Kubernetes?

faq.a: The episodes cover Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) and Azure Container Apps. Azure Container Apps is described as a serverless option that avoids managing Kubernetes clusters or virtual machines, while AKS offers more flexibility with more operational complexity.
faq.q: Which Azure services run containers according to the episodes?

container.long:
A container is a software unit that packages an application together with everything it needs to run, while sharing the operating system of the host. Because the application and its dependencies travel together, a container runs the same way on a developer laptop, on a server or in the cloud. This consistency is the main reason containers are used as a building block in modern development and operations.

Containers are used to solve the familiar "works on my machine" problem. When the runtime environment is defined once and shipped with the application, differences between development, test and production environments shrink. The M365.FM episode "Stop Environment Drift with VS Code Dev Containers" explains this idea from the development side. It describes how development containers give teams a consistent coding environment and how container images, Docker, GitHub Actions and command-line tooling can be combined to automate build and deployment steps in a CI pipeline. According to the episode, containerization has become foundational to DevOps workflows.

Running a handful of containers on a single machine is manageable, but running many of them across multiple servers requires coordination. This is where orchestration comes in. The episode "Kubernetes - Simply Explained" describes Kubernetes as a widely used container orchestration platform that automates the deployment, scaling, management and recovery of containerized applications. Instead of managing hundreds or thousands of containers by hand, Kubernetes continuously checks that applications are running, healthy and available, and it can place workloads and replace failed ones automatically. The episode also covers the architecture, benefits, common use cases and challenges of the platform.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, containers can be run on several Azure services that differ in how much infrastructure the user manages. The episode "Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) - Simply Explained" walks through the building blocks of AKS, including clusters, node pools, pods, deployments, services, ingress and autoscaling. It also explains how AKS works together with Azure Container Registry, Azure Monitor, Azure Key Vault, Managed Identities, networking and security features to form production-ready environments. The episode stresses that the choice involves trade-offs between flexibility, operational complexity and cost, and that simpler services such as Azure Container Apps or App Service may be a better fit in some cases.

"Azure Container Apps - Simply Explained" covers that simpler option. The episode presents Azure Container Apps as Microsoft's serverless platform for running containerized applications without managing Kubernetes clusters or virtual machines. In that model, Azure handles deployment, networking, scaling and operations, so developers can concentrate on the application itself rather than on infrastructure and orchestration.

The word "container" also appears in a different sense in low-code design. In the episode "Build Responsive Power Apps with Containers and Components", containers are layout elements in Power Apps rather than runtime packages. The episode describes building screens like modern web layouts, with a top-level vertical container holding a header, a main area with sidebar and content in a horizontal container, and an optional footer. Properties such as gap, padding, align, justify and flexible width and height control the arrangement, so no positioning formulas are needed. This layout approach is combined with a central component library to keep look and feel consistent across apps.

Taken together, the episodes show containers as a common unit across development, deployment and app design. For software containers, typical decisions concern how to build consistent environments, how much orchestration is needed, and whether a managed or serverless platform is sufficient or a full Kubernetes service is justified.

container-image.desc: A container image is a read-only, layered template holding an application, its files and start instructions; containers are the running instances started from it.

faq.a: A container image is a read-only, layered template containing an application, its files and its start instructions. A container is a running instance started from that image.
faq.q: What is the difference between a container image and a container?

faq.a: A Dockerfile defines the build instructions for an application, and building it produces the image. The episode "Stop Environment Drift with VS Code Dev Containers" notes that the base image influences performance and security and that multi-stage builds can shrink image size.
faq.q: How does a Dockerfile relate to a container image?

faq.a: The episodes mention them in Azure Container Apps, where an image is built to run a job, and in Azure Functions, where the setup asks whether to deploy code or a container image.
faq.q: Where do container images appear in Azure services?

container-image.long:
A container image is a read-only, layered template that holds an application, its files and the instructions needed to start it. Containers are the running instances created from an image. Because the image itself does not change at runtime, the same image can be started repeatedly and in different places, which is the basis for reproducible and portable application packaging.

Images are typically described by a Dockerfile, which defines the build instructions. The episode "Stop Environment Drift with VS Code Dev Containers" explains how Dockerfiles define an application's build steps and how the choice of base image affects both performance and security. It also covers multi-stage builds, which the episode says can drastically shrink image size. A smaller image generally means less to store, transfer and maintain, so the build structure is a practical design decision rather than an afterthought.

Container images also play a central role in continuous integration. According to the same episode, the core components of a CI pipeline include source control triggers, automatic builds, container image creation and deployment stages that rely on Docker and container registries. In this flow, a change in source control triggers a build, the build produces an image, the image is stored in a registry, and a deployment stage then runs it. Configuration is kept separate from the image: the episode describes environment variables, YAML files and container runtimes as the means by which an application behaves consistently across environments without being rebuilt for each one.

The same idea supports development environments. The episode describes dev containers, powered by devcontainer.json and VS Code, as a way to give developers reproducible, portable workspaces and to address environment drift and the "works on my machine" problem. The workspace is defined by an image and configuration rather than by whatever happens to be installed on a given computer.

Container images also appear in Azure hosting scenarios. In "Azure Container Apps - Simply Explained", building a container image that runs a job is one step in an event-driven setup: create a Container Apps environment, set up an Azure Storage queue to send messages to the container app, build the image, deploy the job to the environment, and verify that queue messages are processed. The episode also mentions Azure Key Vault and environment variables in connection with configuration. In "Azure Functions - Simply Explained", the function app creation page asks whether to deploy code or a container image, showing that an image is one of two deployment forms for a function app alongside plain code.

Images are also relevant to AI workloads. The episode "How to Run Local Llama on SharePoint Files Securely" lists a Google Vertex AI container image among the points in a comparison table of ways to connect SharePoint and OneDrive content to a local model, which shows that prebuilt images can be part of such integration choices.

Typical decisions around container images include which base image to start from, whether to use multi-stage builds to reduce size, where to store images in a container registry, and how to inject configuration at runtime instead of baking it into the image. Together these choices determine how portable, small and consistent the resulting containers are across development, build and deployment.

container-labels.desc: Sensitivity labels for containers apply workspace rules such as privacy, guest access and sharing to Teams, Microsoft 365 groups and SharePoint sites, not to the files inside.

faq.a: No. Items inside a container do not inherit its label, and content markings or encryption are not applied automatically. File protection needs separate sensitivity labels.
faq.q: Do container labels label the files inside a team or site?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn lists Teams sites, Microsoft 365 groups, SharePoint sites, Viva Engage communities and Loop workspaces. Some apps, such as Dynamics 365, Project and Power BI, are not supported.
faq.q: Which containers support sensitivity labels?

faq.a: The feature is enabled once in Microsoft Entra ID, labels are synced, a label with the Groups and sites scope is created, and it is published through a label policy.
faq.q: What is needed to set up container labels?

container-labels.long:
Sensitivity labels for containers are sensitivity labels that are applied to a workspace instead of to an individual document or email. According to Microsoft Learn, sensitivity labels can protect containers as well as documents and emails. The supported containers are Teams sites, Microsoft 365 groups, SharePoint sites, Viva Engage communities and Loop workspaces. When a label is applied to one of these containers, the container takes on the label's classification and the protection settings that were configured for it.

The settings a container label can control cover privacy, external user access, external sharing from SharePoint sites, access from unmanaged devices, authentication contexts and the discovery of private teams. In practice this means that one label can define whether a team is private or public, whether guests may be added, whether content can be shared externally and how users on unmanaged devices are treated. Some of these options depend on Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies, so the label alone does not enforce them. Default sharing link settings are available through PowerShell only.

An important point is the boundary of what a container label does. It governs the workspace rules, not the content stored in it. Items inside a container do not inherit its label, and content markings or encryption are not applied automatically to files. Protecting the documents themselves requires separate sensitivity labels for files and emails. Container labels and file labels are therefore complementary and answer different questions: who can reach the workspace, and how a particular item is protected.

Setup follows a defined sequence in the Microsoft documentation. The feature is enabled once in Microsoft Entra ID, labels are synced, a label is created with the Groups and sites scope, and the label is published through a label policy. After that, users can pick a label from the sensitivity dropdown when they create a new team, group or site. For existing workspaces, labels can be applied in bulk with PowerShell, which is relevant when many containers need to be classified after the policy has been rolled out.

Several operational details matter when planning. Site owners may be able to change some label-controlled settings, so the effective configuration should be checked rather than assumed. Replication after a change can take at least a day, which affects how quickly a new setting is visible. Shared channels inherit the label of their parent team. The documentation also notes that several apps are not supported, such as Dynamics 365, Project and Power BI, so coverage of the label should be verified for the workloads in use.

Typical decisions around container labels include how many labels to offer, which privacy and guest settings each level should enforce, and whether Conditional Access policies are available to back the unmanaged-device and authentication-context options. The topic sits within the wider area of Microsoft Purview information protection and Microsoft 365 governance. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic, so the description here rests on the Microsoft Learn documentation.

container-registry.desc: A container registry is a service that stores container images so they can be pushed, shared and pulled by others, and it can be public or run privately.

faq.a: A container registry is a service that stores container images so they can be pushed, shared and pulled by others. Registries can be public or run privately.
faq.q: What is a container registry?

faq.a: According to the episode "Stop Environment Drift with VS Code Dev Containers", a CI pipeline builds the code, runs tests and packages the application into a container image, with container registry integration as a key component. In the GitOps episode, CI pushes the updated image version to the registry.
faq.q: How does a container registry fit into a CI pipeline?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes mention Azure Container Registry in connection with Azure Container Apps and Azure Kubernetes Service. Azure Container Apps also supports Docker images from any container registry, and Azure Functions can use continuous deployment from a container registry.
faq.q: Which Azure services work with a container registry?

container-registry.long:
A container registry is a service that stores container images so that they can be pushed, shared and pulled by other people and systems. Registries can be public, which makes images broadly available, or run privately, which keeps images inside an organisation. In practice the registry sits between the place where an image is built and the place where it runs, acting as the shared storage point for the packaged application.

The typical purpose of a container registry is to hold the output of a build so that it can be reused in later stages. In the M365.FM episode "Stop Environment Drift with VS Code Dev Containers", the registry appears as a key component of a continuous integration (CI) pipeline. The episode describes a pipeline that starts when a developer commits code to a repository, which triggers an automated build. That build compiles the code, runs tests and packages the application into a container image using tools such as Docker and npm, and container registry integration is listed alongside automated testing, source code management, container build processes and deployment stages.

The registry also plays a central role in GitOps workflows. The episode "GitOps - Simply Explained" describes a flow in which a change to application code is pushed to a Git repository, CI builds the change, and the updated image version is pushed to the container registry. A CI job then commits a change to the GitOps repository, updating YAML files to reflect the new application version. A GitOps operator such as Argo CD or Flux monitors the live state of the cluster and applies changes so that it matches the desired state. In this flow Git acts as the single source of truth, while the registry holds the image artifacts that the Kubernetes infrastructure pulls.

Container registries are also referenced throughout the Azure container and compute services covered by M365.FM. The episode "Azure Container Apps - Simply Explained" notes that Azure Container Apps supports Docker images from any container registry, which simplifies deployment and operations, and it lists integration with Azure Container Registry alongside Azure AI Foundry, Azure Monitor, GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps. The episode "Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) - Simply Explained" similarly names Azure Container Registry among the Azure services that AKS integrates with, together with Azure Monitor, Azure Key Vault, Managed Identities, networking and security features, to create production-ready environments.

Container registries matter for serverless and app-hosting scenarios as well. The episode "Azure Functions - Simply Explained" lists container deployments among the deployment options, describing continuous deployment (CI/CD) from source control or from a container registry as one of the App Service-managed methods. Other options in the same overview include external pipelines such as Azure Pipelines and GitHub Actions for production pipelines that include validation and testing, and tools like Core Tools publish for deployments during development.

Typical decisions around a container registry concern visibility and integration. Teams choose between a public registry and a privately run one depending on who needs to pull the images, and they decide which build pipeline pushes images and which runtime pulls them. Because the registry is a neutral storage layer, the same image can serve several runtimes, such as Azure Kubernetes Service, Azure Container Apps or container-based Azure Functions deployments, which is why the episodes mention it in the context of each of these services.

Taken together, the M365.FM episodes present the container registry as connective infrastructure rather than a standalone product feature. It receives images from CI pipelines, supplies them to deployment targets, and supports workflows such as GitOps in which an updated image version triggers a tracked, auditable change to the desired state of a cluster. The facts available do not go deeper into specific registry products beyond the mentions of Azure Container Registry and the general description of registries as public or private image stores.

content-assessment.desc: Content assessment is an evaluation of stored content that examines structure, usage behavior and business context to decide what to keep, improve or archive.

faq.a: A content assessment is an evaluation of stored content that looks at its structure, actual usage behavior and business context. It is used to decide what to keep, improve or archive.
faq.q: What is a content assessment?

faq.a: Mapping records where content is and how it is organized. A content assessment goes further by also examining how the content is used and what role it plays in the business.
faq.q: How does a content assessment differ from content mapping?

faq.a: It supports deciding whether content should be kept, improved or archived.
faq.q: What decisions does a content assessment support?

content-assessment.long:
Content assessment is an evaluation of stored content that goes beyond mapping. Where mapping records where content lives and how it is organized, a content assessment also looks at the structure of that content, how it is actually used, and the business context around it.

The purpose is to support a decision about each body of content: keep it as it is, improve it, or archive it. By combining structural information with real usage behavior and business relevance, an assessment gives a basis for those decisions rather than relying on location or age alone.
