copilot-connectors.desc: Copilot connectors, formerly Microsoft Graph connectors, index content from external systems so Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Search can use it.

faq.a: Copilot connectors, formerly called Microsoft Graph connectors, index content from external systems so that Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Search can use it. They extend Microsoft Graph with data from third-party platforms and custom applications.
faq.q: What are Copilot connectors?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Graph Connectors - Simply Explained" mentions Salesforce, ServiceNow, Confluence, Jira, file shares, websites, databases and custom business applications as examples.
faq.q: Which external systems can Copilot connectors bring into Microsoft 365?

faq.a: Yes. According to the episode "Connect External Business Data with Microsoft 365 Copilot Connectors", developers can build custom connectors through the Graph Connectors API and the Microsoft 365 agents toolkit, in addition to using prebuilt connectors from Microsoft.
faq.q: Can Copilot connectors be customized?

copilot-connectors.long:
Copilot connectors are connectors that bring content from external systems into Microsoft 365 so that it can be searched and used by Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Search. They were formerly called Microsoft Graph connectors, and the older names "Microsoft Graph connectors" and "Graph connectors" still appear in documentation and in discussions of the product. Microsoft develops the feature as part of Microsoft 365, and it is closely related to Microsoft Graph and to Microsoft 365 Copilot.

The basic purpose is to close a data gap. Much enterprise knowledge sits outside Microsoft 365, in line-of-business platforms, file shares, websites, databases and custom applications. Without a way to reach that information, an AI assistant or a search experience can only work with content that already lives in Microsoft 365. Copilot connectors extend Microsoft Graph by indexing data from third-party sources, so that this content becomes searchable and accessible in Microsoft Search, Microsoft 365 Copilot and other Microsoft 365 experiences. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Graph Connectors - Simply Explained" names examples of such sources: Salesforce, ServiceNow, Confluence, Jira, file shares, websites, databases and custom business applications.

In terms of how they are built, the episode "Connect External Business Data with Microsoft 365 Copilot Connectors" distinguishes between prebuilt connectors from Microsoft and fully customizable options that developers can create through the Graph Connectors API and the Microsoft 365 agents toolkit. Custom connectors are described there as a way to bring niche or legacy systems into the Copilot experience. The same episode says that Microsoft Entra secures the data pipeline, that a Copilot Connectors Gallery serves as a discovery hub for organizations connecting more of their stack, and that Copilot Studio lets teams configure, test and validate connections.

Typical decisions around Copilot connectors concern which external systems hold knowledge that users or agents actually need, whether a prebuilt connector covers that system, and whether a custom connector is required for a specialized or older application. The episode "Microsoft Graph Connectors for Enterprise AI and Copilot" frames the topic from an AI-value perspective. It argues that many enterprise AI initiatives fall short not because of weak models but because the AI lacks access to the right data, which is fragmented across systems, apps and repositories. According to the episode, Graph Connectors are the missing link, and without such integration AI outputs remain shallow, incomplete and disconnected from real business workflows. Its key takeaway is that successful enterprise AI depends on connecting and structuring data, not only on deploying models.

Copilot connectors also appear in discussions of extensibility. The episodes "Agentic AI with Copilot Studio and Dataverse MCP with Nathan Rose [MVP]" and "Microsoft 365 Copilot Extensibility with Gautam Sheth [MVP]" place connectors alongside APIs as tools for bringing outside data into Microsoft 365 Copilot and for extending what agents can reach. The Copilot Studio episode lists Copilot connectors as available in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Microsoft Search and the Microsoft 365 Copilot app, and describes related connector types for linking agents to services such as Power Automate, Power Apps and Azure Logic Apps. The extensibility episode describes Microsoft Graph connectors as a bridge between Microsoft 365 and external data, useful for systems such as ERP and CRM, so that information from many places can be accessed without leaving the main workspace. It also points to APIs as a means of automating data flow.

For readers searching for the term, the practical distinction is between two ideas that are easy to confuse. Copilot connectors, in the sense described here, index external content into the Microsoft Graph so it can be found and used in Microsoft 365 experiences. Other connector types, such as those used with Power Automate or Logic Apps, mainly let agents perform actions or retrieve data on demand. Official documentation for Copilot connectors is available on Microsoft Learn under the connectors overview for Microsoft Search.

copilot-control-system.desc: Copilot Control System is Microsoft's set of admin controls for governing Microsoft 365 Copilot, covering security, deployment, agent policies and usage monitoring.

faq.a: It gives administrators a central place to manage settings, monitor usage and enforce compliance for Microsoft 365 Copilot, including agent policies for access, sharing and publishing.
faq.q: What is Copilot Control System used for?

faq.a: The episodes describe them as complementary: the Copilot Control System handles Copilot and agent controls, while Microsoft Purview provides audit logs, retention, data loss prevention and policy enforcement.
faq.q: Does Copilot Control System work together with Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: According to the episode on Copilot settings, the admin should review license assignments and permissions in the Microsoft 365 admin center and use the Copilot Control System to review settings.
faq.q: What should an admin check if a Copilot feature cannot be activated?

copilot-control-system.long:
Copilot Control System is a product area within the Microsoft ecosystem that gives administrators a central place to govern Microsoft 365 Copilot and the agents built around it. According to the M365.FM episodes that mention it, it brings together settings for user access, data access, Copilot actions, compliance enforcement and monitoring, so that an organization can roll out Copilot in line with its own security and governance policies.

The episode "How to Govern Microsoft Copilot in the Enterprise" describes what a Copilot control system should provide at enterprise scale: visibility, control and actionable insights. The listed capabilities are integrated security and governance to protect sensitive data and reduce AI risks, centralized deployment management for configuration and license control, and usage and adoption analytics. The same episode places the control system alongside related data-protection measures such as Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) for Dataverse, which helps discover and classify sensitive data, and protection status information used to assess risks and obtain remediation guidance.

Agent governance is a recurring theme. In "Microsoft Copilot Security Readiness with Åsne Holtklimpen [MVP-MCT]", the discussion states that Microsoft 365 Copilot agents follow strict tenant policies and admin configurations, which prevent unrestricted access to organizational data. Agent policies that manage access, sharing and publishing settings are handled through the Copilot Control System. The episode also mentions lifecycle management features such as versioning, staged deployments and rollback processes, which support a controlled rollout and a quick response when changes are needed. Admins can restrict user access and set sharing controls for Copilot, while Microsoft Purview contributes audit logs, retention and data loss prevention on the compliance side.

For compliance and monitoring, "Fix Copilot Notebooks GDPR and Governance Risks" recommends using the Copilot Control System as a monitoring tool that provides comprehensive controls for Microsoft 365 Copilot, enabling compliance enforcement and data protection. The episode pairs this with regular audits of user interactions and admin activities, and with feedback loops, as practices for maintaining governance over Copilot outputs.

In day-to-day administration, the system also appears as the place where settings are managed when features do not work as expected. "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Settings and Configuration" explains that admins can use the Copilot Control System to manage settings, monitor usage and ensure compliance with security protocols. If a user cannot activate a feature, the episode advises asking the admin to check license assignments and permissions in the Microsoft 365 admin center.

The topic also connects to multi-platform strategies. "Scale Copilot Agents Safely in Microsoft 365" suggests treating services such as Azure AI Foundry, Microsoft Copilot and custom LLMs as components of one enterprise AI platform. In that picture, an orchestration layer and a copilot control system handle routing, fallback and agentic coordination, while policies are enforced through Microsoft Purview and governance frameworks to support end-to-end compliance. SharePoint is mentioned in the same episode as a central knowledge repository that Copilot uses through documents, metadata and search.

Taken together, the episodes treat Copilot Control System as the governance layer that connects licensing, deployment, agent policies, security and usage analytics for Microsoft 365 Copilot, working together with Microsoft Purview and related data-classification tools rather than replacing them.

copilot-cowork.desc: Copilot Cowork is a Microsoft 365 Copilot capability that carries out multi-step work on a user's behalf across Outlook, Teams, Word and Excel.

faq.a: Copilot Cowork is a capability of Microsoft 365 Copilot in which the assistant carries out multi-step work on the user's behalf across Outlook, Teams, Word and Excel, rather than only answering single prompts.
faq.q: What is Copilot Cowork?

faq.a: The episode "Copilot Cowork - Simply Explained" says the user describes the outcome they want, and Cowork creates a plan, performs the work and keeps the user informed, instead of just generating an answer or content.
faq.q: How does Copilot Cowork differ from a normal Copilot prompt?

faq.a: Because it acts on a user's behalf, it is related to Human in the loop, meaning a person reviews or approves results at suitable points. Cowork is also described as keeping the user informed while it works.
faq.q: How does Copilot Cowork relate to human oversight?

copilot-cowork.long:
Copilot Cowork, also referred to as Cowork or Microsoft 365 Copilot Cowork, is a capability of Microsoft 365 Copilot developed by Microsoft. It is an AI assistant that carries out multi-step work on the user's behalf across Outlook, Teams, Word and Excel, instead of only answering a single prompt and stopping. The idea is that a person describes the outcome they want, and the assistant takes ownership of the steps needed to reach it.

The main purpose is to move work forward rather than to produce one-off answers or content. According to the episode "Copilot Cowork - Simply Explained", Cowork represents the next evolution of Microsoft 365 Copilot. The user states the desired result, and Cowork creates a plan, performs the work, and keeps the user informed along the way. This differs from a prompt-and-response pattern, where each request is handled in isolation and the user must connect the pieces manually.

Copilot Cowork is part of Microsoft 365 Copilot and is closely related to the concept of an AI agent, since it acts toward a goal across several applications. It also relates to Agent skill. Reusable skills can give an assistant consistent methods and expertise, so that similar tasks are handled in the same way across projects. The episode "Microsoft Cowork IQ Knowledge Graph Architecture" mentions that built-in and custom skills streamline processes, that tasks can be delegated to agents so work progresses in the background, and that deeper connections link Microsoft products and third-party solutions.

Because Cowork acts on a user's behalf, Human in the loop is a relevant companion topic. When an assistant performs actions rather than only suggesting text, there need to be points at which a person reviews, approves or corrects the result. The description of Cowork as keeping the user informed while it works fits this pattern: the user sets the outcome, the assistant executes, and the person stays aware of progress and decisions. Questions about how much to delegate, and where to require approval, are typical decisions for organizations adopting this kind of capability.

Several M365.FM episodes place Copilot Cowork in a wider context. "Copilot Cowork with Vesa "Vesku" Nopanen [MVP]" discusses how Microsoft 365 Copilot is evolving from a simple AI assistant into a collaborative coworker inside organizations. It covers the future of AI-driven work, the rise of agentic collaboration, and how businesses can prepare for AI that takes part in daily workflows. The conversation highlights a move away from isolated AI prompts toward integrated AI ecosystems that can automate processes and assist decision-making.

The episode "Microsoft Copilot Cowork Engine for Context-Driven Work" connects Cowork to the problem of finding information. It describes constant file searching as a sign of a poorly designed system, with scattered documents, duplicate versions and unclear structures producing what the host calls a "search tax". Rather than relying only on better search, the episode suggests rethinking how information is organized and accessed, which is relevant to any assistant that needs reliable context to do multi-step work.

The episode "AI and Copilot in D365FO Finance with Billur Samdancioglu [MVP-MCT]" refers to Microsoft's "Cowork" vision in a finance setting. There, autonomous AI systems proactively monitor workflows, detect anomalies, trigger processes and assist finance teams with operational tasks. The episode says that AI is expected to reduce repetitive administrative work so that finance professionals can focus on strategy, analysis and business value, and it emphasizes data quality and governance as important foundations.

Taken together, the sources describe Copilot Cowork as a delegation-oriented layer of Microsoft 365 Copilot. Its value depends on clear task descriptions, well-organized information, suitable skills and sensible review points. Official documentation for Microsoft 365 Copilot is available through Microsoft Learn.

copilot-credit-pre-purchase-plan.desc: Copilot Credit Pre-Purchase Plan (P3) is a Microsoft one-year option to pay up front for Copilot Credits, with tiered volume discounts and credits that expire at term end.
copilot-credit-pre-purchase-plan.long:
Copilot Credit Pre-Purchase Plan (P3) is a Microsoft purchase option for Copilot Credits. It is structured as a one-year commitment in which the full amount is paid in advance, rather than being billed as credits are consumed.

The plan includes tiered volume discounts, meaning the pricing advantage depends on the size of the up-front purchase. A defining condition of the plan is that any Copilot Credits left unused at the end of the one-year term expire, so the purchased volume needs to be consumed within that period to be fully used.

The plan is relevant to organizations that expect predictable, sustained use of Copilot Credits and want to plan spending ahead of time. The trade-off described in the available information is between a discounted rate for committing in advance and the risk that unused credits are lost at the end of the term.

No further details, such as specific tier thresholds, discount percentages, pricing or eligibility rules, are covered here. For current terms, Microsoft's official licensing and pricing documentation is the authoritative source. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

copilot-credits.desc: Copilot Credits are the consumption unit that bills agent and Copilot Studio usage, so spending follows what agents do instead of how many licenses exist.

faq.a: Copilot Credits are a consumption unit used to bill agent and Copilot Studio usage. They measure what agents do, so costs follow activity instead of per-user licenses.
faq.q: What are Copilot Credits?

faq.a: The episodes "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud" and "AI and Copilot in D365FO Finance with Billur Samdancioglu [MVP-MCT]" both cite $0.01 per credit for pay-as-you-go use. The first episode also mentions prepaid packs for lower costs when usage is predictable.
faq.q: How much does a Copilot Credit cost?

faq.a: According to "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud", billing for agent work is enabled in the Microsoft Admin Center, where billing policies, usage caps and alert configurations can be set. "The Copilot Credit Trap- Why Your AI Economy is Already Broken" adds that governance and FinOps practices become central.
faq.q: How can spending on Copilot Credits be controlled?

copilot-credits.long:
Copilot Credits are a consumption unit used to bill agent and Copilot Studio usage. Where traditional software is licensed per person, Copilot Credits measure what agents actually do, so costs follow activity rather than headcount. The concept is also referred to as Copilot Studio credits or, in older wording, messages and credits. Copilot Credits sit under the broader topic of Copilot Studio, where the billed usage takes place.

The core idea is a shift from fixed licensing to consumption. The episode "The Copilot Credit Trap- Why Your AI Economy is Already Broken" describes autonomous agents performing work on an organization's behalf, where every action, reasoning cycle and orchestration task consumes credits instead of simply using a fixed license. According to the episode, this changes enterprise budgeting and makes governance more important than licensing, and it argues that organizations need to rethink identity, permissions, auditing, FinOps and AI compliance before autonomous agents become part of everyday operations. This is why Copilot Credits are closely related to FinOps, the practice of making cloud and AI spending visible and accountable, and to Copilot governance, since decisions about who may build and publish agents influence how much consumption an organization generates.

The episodes give concrete price points. "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud" says that pay-as-you-go pricing is $0.01 per Copilot Credit, with prepaid packs offered for lower costs when usage is predictable. The same episode says that Microsoft 365 Copilot billing stays per user for tasks such as typing in Word or summarizing emails, while agent work shifts to a consumption-based model measured in Copilot Credits. To activate billing for agent work, the episode says it must be enabled in the Microsoft Admin Center, where billing policies, usage caps and alert configurations can be set to control spending. The episode also advises preparing for major changes in Azure billing and architecture by November 2026.

The episode "AI and Copilot in D365FO Finance with Billur Samdancioglu [MVP-MCT]" places Copilot Credits in a finance operations context. Its cost table lists Copilot Credits at $0.01 per credit and states that D365 Supply Chain Management includes 1,000 Copilot Credits per month pooled at the tenant. It adds that most credit consumption is covered under interactive use with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license, which is listed at $30 per user per month and described as required for Copilot Studio agent authoring. The same table shows an autonomous trigger cost of $0.25 per event, with every autonomous event incurring a charge.

Hidden cost drivers are a recurring theme. "The Copilot Tax: Hidden Costs of Enterprise AI Strategy" lists several reasons why spending grows beyond the license fee: billing rates that change with the features used, credits that are consumed as agents are designed and run, licensing structures that pool capacity across an organization and make it hard to see where money goes, token consumption that rises as more users interact with Copilot, compute usage that grows with large documents or complex tasks, and unused seats that still cost money.

Copilot Credits also appear in practical build scenarios. In "Cut Contract Review Time with SharePoint AI Agents", configuring an AI stage in an approval workflow requires that Copilot Studio Copilot Credits are assigned. This shows that credits are not only a finance topic but a prerequisite for certain agent-based features.

In practice, the decisions around Copilot Credits come down to choosing between pay-as-you-go and prepaid capacity, setting usage caps and alerts, deciding who may create and run agents, and monitoring consumption so that a popular agent does not use more than planned.

copilot-extensibility.desc: Microsoft 365 Copilot extensibility covers how Microsoft 365 Copilot is extended with agents, connectors, plugins and APIs to reach business data and processes.

faq.a: It is the set of options for extending Microsoft 365 Copilot beyond its built-in experience, for example with agents, connectors, APIs and custom orchestration, so that Copilot can work with business data and processes.
faq.q: What is Microsoft 365 Copilot extensibility?

faq.a: The episode with Gautam Sheth names declarative agents, custom engine agents, Copilot connectors and plugins. Other episodes also cover Copilot Studio, Microsoft Foundry, Model Context Protocol (MCP), RAG and multi-agent architectures.
faq.q: Which extensibility options are discussed in the M365.FM episodes?

faq.a: The episode "Extend Microsoft 365 Copilot with Agents, Plugins, and Connectors" mentions Copilot Studio and Visual Studio Code as Microsoft 365 tools for development, and recommends monitoring and updating solutions to keep them effective and secure.
faq.q: Which tools are mentioned for building Copilot extensions?

copilot-extensibility.long:
Microsoft 365 Copilot extensibility is the set of options for extending Microsoft 365 Copilot beyond its built-in experience. Instead of using Copilot only as it ships, organizations can connect it to their own business data, systems and processes by adding agents, connectors, APIs and custom orchestration. It is a subtopic of Microsoft 365 Copilot, and Microsoft documents it on its Learn site under the extensibility section.

The central idea is that the out-of-the-box Copilot experience works with Microsoft 365 content such as Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive, while many organizations also hold knowledge and workflows in other places. Extensibility is how those sources and actions are brought into Copilot. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft 365 Copilot Extensibility with Gautam Sheth [MVP]" describes the different extensibility options as declarative agents, custom engine agents, Copilot connectors and plugins, and frames the discussion around helping listeners understand when each option fits and how organizations can go beyond the standard experience.

In practice, the choice between these options is a design decision. A declarative agent builds on Copilot's existing capabilities and is shaped for a particular task or audience, whereas a custom engine agent implies more control over how the solution is orchestrated. Copilot connectors bring external data into the reach of Copilot, and plugins let Copilot call into other systems. The episode with Gautam Sheth also covers the surrounding ecosystem, common implementation patterns, and recommendations for developers and architects who want to build intelligent, enterprise-ready Copilot experiences.

The episode "Extend Microsoft 365 Copilot with Agents, Plugins, and Connectors" looks at the tooling side. It points to Microsoft 365 tools such as Copilot Studio and Visual Studio Code for development, and advises regularly monitoring and updating solutions to keep them effective and secure. It also lists features of custom solutions in Copilot Studio: custom copilots can access and act on Microsoft 365 data through sanctioned connectors without moving data out of the tenant, and reusable building blocks such as skills, actions and prompts can be composed so that one solution can lead to multiple specialized copilots.

A further perspective comes from "Extending Microsoft 365 Copilot: Agents, MCP & Production-Grade AI with Yves Habersaat [MVP]". This episode ties extensibility to Copilot Studio, Microsoft Foundry, Model Context Protocol (MCP), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), multi-agent architectures and enterprise search. It stresses that connecting Copilot to Microsoft Graph, organizational knowledge, APIs, workflows and enterprise data has to be done while maintaining security, permissions and governance. The episode also contrasts prompt engineering, which can help employees get more from generative AI, with the broader requirements of enterprise AI, framing the move from prompts toward AI architecture and production-grade solutions.

Taken together, the episodes treat Microsoft 365 Copilot extensibility less as a single feature and more as an architectural area. Typical decisions include which extension type matches a scenario, where the data should come from, how access is governed, and how the solution is maintained over time. Developers and architects usually weigh these points together, since the same connectors, agents and APIs that increase Copilot's usefulness also widen the surface that security and governance have to cover.

copilot-flex-routing.desc: Copilot flex routing is a Microsoft 365 Copilot setting that lets LLM inferencing for EU and EFTA tenants run outside the EU Data Boundary during peak demand.

faq.a: Copilot flex routing is a Microsoft 365 Copilot setting that allows LLM inferencing for EU and EFTA tenants to run outside the EU Data Boundary during peak demand.
faq.q: What is Copilot flex routing?

faq.a: The setting applies to tenants in the EU and EFTA, whose LLM inferencing can be routed outside the EU Data Boundary when demand is high.
faq.q: Who is affected by Copilot flex routing?

faq.a: Yes. Administrators can disable flex routing in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
faq.q: Can administrators turn off Copilot flex routing?

copilot-flex-routing.long:
Copilot flex routing is a setting in Microsoft 365 Copilot that concerns where large language model (LLM) inferencing takes place. For tenants in the European Union and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), it allows LLM inferencing to run outside the EU Data Boundary when demand is at its peak.

The setting is relevant for administrators who need to understand where Copilot processing can occur and how that relates to data residency requirements. Administrators can disable flex routing in the Microsoft 365 admin center, which gives organizations a way to decide whether their tenant may use capacity outside the EU Data Boundary during high-demand periods.

Microsoft documents the feature on its Microsoft Learn site under the Microsoft 365 Copilot section. No related topics or M365.FM episodes are linked to this entry at the moment, and the facts available here are limited to the scope and administrative control described above.

copilot-governance.desc: Copilot governance covers the permissions, data access controls and oversight that apply when Copilot is used in a Microsoft 365 tenant.

faq.a: It covers controls for permissions, data access and oversight when Copilot is used in a Microsoft 365 tenant. This includes permission hygiene, data classification, monitoring and compliance, often supported by Microsoft Purview capabilities.
faq.q: What does Copilot governance cover?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Copilot Governance Without Waiting for Perfect Data", treating governance as a gate is an architectural mistake. It describes governance as a continuous track that evolves alongside deployment, using automation, prioritization and real-time controls.
faq.q: Does governance have to be finished before a Copilot rollout?

faq.a: The episode "Multi-Tenant Microsoft Copilot Governance Strategy" says that multi-tenant deployment is not just a scaling exercise. It introduces governance, security and data boundary risks, including inconsistent rules between tenants that create compliance blind spots.
faq.q: Why is multi-tenant Copilot governance treated as a separate topic?

copilot-governance.long:
Copilot governance is the set of controls for permissions, data access and oversight that apply when Copilot is used in a Microsoft 365 tenant. It sits under the broader heading of AI governance and is closely tied to Microsoft 365 Copilot, general Governance practice and Microsoft Purview. The central idea is that Copilot works with the content a user is already allowed to see, so the condition of permissions, site ownership and data classification directly shapes what the assistant can surface in prompts and responses.

In practice, the topic covers several areas. One is access: who holds which permissions, and whether those permissions have drifted over time. Another is data quality and hygiene, including orphaned sites, outdated content, inconsistent classification and shadow sites. A third is protection and monitoring, where Microsoft Purview capabilities come into play. A rollout checklist discussed in one episode mentions sensitivity labels combined with data loss prevention to restrict highly confidential content, unified auditing with retention, and Communication Compliance to review risky prompts. Training on AI risks and compliance is also named as part of building a responsible culture around the tool.

A recurring decision is how to sequence governance and deployment. The episode "Microsoft Copilot Governance Without Waiting for Perfect Data" argues that treating governance as a gate that must be perfect before rollout is an architectural mistake. Real environments are messy, with orphaned sites and inconsistent data classification, and waiting for perfection delays value. The episode instead describes governance as a continuous track that evolves alongside deployment, using automation, prioritization and real-time controls to manage risk. "How to Govern Microsoft Copilot in the Enterprise" takes a similar line, recommending continuous governance in which Copilot is deployed carefully while data quality, permissions, monitoring and compliance are improved in parallel. It also states that successful Copilot governance combines technology, process and culture, with security teams working alongside business leaders, architects and end users to set scalable policies and shared accountability. User training, prompt awareness and change management are described as essential.

Scale introduces further complexity. "Multi-Tenant Microsoft Copilot Governance Strategy" says that deploying Microsoft 365 Copilot across several tenants is not simply a scaling exercise but brings governance, security and data boundary risks. The episode warns about fragmented oversight, where different tenants develop inconsistent rules, creating blind spots for compliance and raising the chance of sensitive data exposure.

Other episodes approach the subject from the contractual and operational side. "Microsoft Copilot Rollout: DPA and Product Terms Checklist" frames governance as a question of structured frameworks for responsible AI use and observes that stated policies often have unclear effectiveness. It describes Copilot as a mirror of the underlying directory and data: when those are cleaned up, the AI appears more disciplined. "Secure and Govern Microsoft 365 Copilot" recommends gathering user feedback to refine governance policies so they match real-world needs, alongside regular training on AI risks and compliance. It also lists tenant-wide policy options and notes that Copilot uses Microsoft Graph signals and data stored in the tenant rather than creating a separate store of documents.

Taken together, the sources present Copilot governance less as a one-time project than as an ongoing discipline. It links permission hygiene, data classification, compliance tooling and user behavior, and it applies to single-tenant and multi-tenant environments alike.

copilot-grounding.desc: Grounding in Microsoft 365 Copilot is the step where relevant work context such as files, emails and meetings is gathered via Microsoft Graph before Copilot answers.
copilot-grounding.long:
Grounding (Copilot) is the step in which Microsoft 365 Copilot gathers relevant work context before it produces an answer. The context can include files, emails and meetings, and it is retrieved through Microsoft Graph.

The purpose of grounding is to change what kind of answer the user receives. Without it, a response would be generic. With grounding, the response is based on the user's actual work, because the material Copilot draws on comes from the user's own Microsoft 365 content rather than only from general knowledge.

In practice, grounding sits between the user's prompt and the generated response. The prompt describes what the user wants, and the grounding step supplies the surrounding information that makes the answer specific and relevant to the situation at hand.

On M365.FM, Grounding (Copilot) is treated as a concept within the Microsoft 365 Copilot ecosystem. No dedicated episodes or official documentation links are currently associated with this entry, so the description here is limited to the definition above.

copilot-in-fabric.desc: Copilot in Microsoft Fabric is the generative AI assistant built into Fabric that supports data work such as queries, notebook code and Power BI report pages.

faq.a: It is used for data work such as writing queries, fixing notebook code and drafting Power BI report pages. Episodes on M365.FM also describe it suggesting fixes at ingestion and producing DAX and documentation.
faq.q: What is Copilot in Microsoft Fabric used for?

faq.a: Yes. It runs on paid Fabric capacities and consumes capacity compute. The episode "Can Copilot Replace Power BI Developers?" also mentions that capacity and workspace setup may need to be configured for Copilot to be enabled.
faq.q: Does Copilot in Microsoft Fabric require a paid capacity?

faq.a: According to the episode "Build Data Models with Copilot in Microsoft Fabric", Copilot speeds up parts of the work, but a human is still needed in the loop for tasks where its output has to be checked.
faq.q: Does Copilot remove the need for human review in Fabric?

copilot-in-fabric.long:
Copilot in Microsoft Fabric is the generative AI assistant integrated into Microsoft Fabric. It helps with everyday data work such as writing queries, fixing notebook code and drafting Power BI report pages. It runs on paid Fabric capacities and consumes capacity compute, so its use is tied to the capacity that a workspace is assigned to.

The assistant is used across the workloads of the platform. According to the M365.FM episode "Copilot for Microsoft Fabric - Simply Explained", it can support many Fabric tasks and offers suggestions that follow Microsoft's best practices, whether the work happens in Data Factory, Data Engineering or Power BI. The same episode describes data analysis and reporting as a main area of use, where Copilot helps to create reports and build data models in Power BI more quickly so that the focus can stay on insights rather than on technical detail.

The episode "Build Data Models with Copilot in Microsoft Fabric" looks at where Copilot speeds up data work and where a human still needs to stay in the loop. It describes Copilot catching schema issues at ingestion and suggesting fixes for naming, data types, dates and partitions before pipelines break. After ingestion, it is described as accelerating transformation with optimized steps, ready-to-use DAX and automatic documentation. The episode also touches on performance tuning. Its framing is that Copilot shortens routine steps but does not remove the need for review by someone who understands the data.

Setup and prerequisites are a recurring practical topic. The episode "Can Copilot Replace Power BI Developers?" notes that general requirements for Copilot in Microsoft Fabric and Power BI include appropriate licensing, a suitable workspace setup and enabling the Copilot features. It also mentions that Fabric capacity or Power BI capacity may need to be configured so that Copilot is enabled and can reach the necessary data sources and models. In the Power BI service, the same episode describes Copilot helping to generate reports, explain metrics and create dashboard tiles. Because it consumes capacity compute, administrators typically weigh which workspaces and capacities should have it enabled.

The title of the episode "Can Copilot Replace Power BI Developers?" points to a common decision: how far to rely on generated output. The episodes covered here present Copilot as an accelerator for tasks like drafting, code suggestions and documentation, with human review remaining part of the process. Teams that adopt it usually combine it with existing practices around data modeling, governance and testing rather than treating it as a replacement for them.

Copilot in Microsoft Fabric also appears in the context of broader Fabric topics on M365.FM. Episodes such as "Build a Bronze-Silver-Gold Data Pipeline in Microsoft Fabric" and "How to Build a Microsoft Copilot Agent Fabric" list "Build Data Models with Copilot in Microsoft Fabric" among related listening, which connects the assistant to pipeline design, data modeling and agent-oriented scenarios. Official documentation for the feature is available in the Microsoft Learn overview of Copilot in Fabric.

copilot-in-power-apps.desc: Copilot in Power Apps is an AI assistant that builds app structures from natural-language descriptions and answers questions about data inside running apps.

faq.a: It generates app structures from natural-language descriptions and lets users ask questions about, summarise and visualise data inside running apps. It also supports building apps and writing expressions conversationally.
faq.q: What does Copilot in Power Apps do?

faq.a: The episodes describe it as making app creation accessible to people without coding skills, since the app is described in natural language and Copilot generates the components.
faq.q: Do users need coding skills to use Copilot in Power Apps?

faq.a: The episode "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform" names custom connectors, Azure Functions and Microsoft Copilot Studio as ways to integrate the OpenAI API or Azure OpenAI Service into Power Apps.
faq.q: How can OpenAI capabilities be added to Power Apps beyond Copilot?

copilot-in-power-apps.long:
Copilot in Power Apps is an AI assistant built into Power Apps, Microsoft's low-code platform for building business applications. It generates app structures from natural-language descriptions and lets users ask questions about, summarise and visualise data inside running apps. In practice this means a maker can describe the application they need in plain language and receive the components needed to start building, rather than assembling every screen and control by hand.

The main purpose is to make app creation faster and more accessible. According to the episode "Power Apps - Simply Explained", Microsoft Copilot is an AI-driven feature that assists with app creation: the maker describes the app in natural language, and Copilot generates the necessary components. The episode "AI, Power Platform & Developer Experience: The Next Frontier with Reza Niroomand [MVP]" makes a similar point, describing how Copilot in Power Apps allows the system to be instructed in natural language, which opens app creation to people without coding skills. It also mentions a vehicle inspection app as an example of an application that can be created by instructing Copilot.

Copilot also supports the developer side of the work. The episode "AI-First UX for Microsoft Power Platform with Tchesco Ayih [MVP-MCT]" says that AI tools such as Copilot in Power Apps allow apps to be built and expressions to be written conversationally. The episode presents this as a way to generate applications from a description of the data or workflow, which reduces manual coding effort and raises developer productivity. It contrasts this with earlier versions of the platform that had no AI assistance.

A typical working sequence is outlined in the episode "Enterprise AI Experiences in Power Apps with Sara Lagerquist [MVP]". The suggested steps are to define the business requirements and the specific problem to solve, use Copilot in Power Apps to create the application by entering a prompt for the desired features, and connect to relevant data sources such as Microsoft Dataverse or SharePoint. After that, AI features such as document processing and text generation can be added, business processes can be automated with Power Automate, and the app can be integrated with Microsoft 365 services. The same episode stresses governance, citizen development and redesigning workflows so that AI is used effectively.

Copilot in Power Apps sits within a wider set of AI options on the Power Platform. The episode "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform" distinguishes between Azure OpenAI for complex generative scenarios and OpenAI API workloads, and AI Builder for faster low-code solutions that are tightly integrated with Power Apps and Power Automate. It states that OpenAI API or Azure OpenAI Service can be integrated into Power Apps through custom connectors, Azure Functions or Microsoft Copilot Studio, which can embed conversational agents. According to the episode, this enables Copilot in Power Apps scenarios in which the assistant offers contextual suggestions, generates content and acts as an AI assistant for power users and business users.

The choice between these approaches depends on the scenario. Copilot in Power Apps covers describing an app and working with data in a running app, while custom connectors, Azure Functions and Copilot Studio are the routes the episodes name for adding more specialised generative or conversational capabilities. The episodes do not give detailed limits, licensing terms or availability by region, so those points should be checked in the official Power Apps documentation on AI features.

copilot-in-power-bi.desc: Copilot in Power BI is the generative AI assistant in Power BI Desktop and the service that drafts DAX, builds report pages, answers data questions and writes summaries.

faq.a: It drafts DAX measures, creates report pages, answers data questions and writes narrative summaries, all based on the semantic model, in both Power BI Desktop and the Power BI service.
faq.q: What can Copilot in Power BI do?

faq.a: The episode "Connect Microsoft Copilot to Predictive Power BI" says to check tenant settings, ensure the organization has the right capacity, and use Power BI Premium or eligible Pro licenses. It also recommends role-based access to protect sensitive data.
faq.q: What is needed to enable Copilot in Power BI?

faq.a: According to the episode "Can Copilot Replace Power BI Developers?", it adapts to corrections within a session but does not automatically inherit enterprise modeling conventions unless they are encoded in templates, developer-defined measures or governance rules.
faq.q: Does Copilot in Power BI follow an organization's modeling conventions automatically?

copilot-in-power-bi.long:
Copilot in Power BI is the generative AI assistant built into Power BI Desktop and the Power BI service. It works on top of the semantic model and is used to draft DAX measures, create report pages, answer questions about data and write narrative summaries. The product is documented by Microsoft in the Power BI report-creation documentation under the Copilot integration topic.

The central idea is natural-language interaction. According to the M365.FM episode "Can Copilot Replace Power BI Developers?", a user describes what should be shown, and the assistant interprets the request in plain language. Questions and requests for visuals do not require knowledge of technical terms or a manually built query. This lowers the entry barrier for business users who need answers quickly, while report authors can use the same capability to speed up the creation of pages and measures.

The same episode also describes limits that matter for planning. It says Copilot adapts to corrections made during a session, which improves immediate suggestions, but it does not automatically inherit enterprise modeling conventions. Such conventions have to be encoded in templates, developer-defined measures or governance rules. In practice this means the quality and consistency of the output depend heavily on how well the underlying semantic model and its governing rules are prepared. The title of the episode frames the broader question of how far Copilot can take over work traditionally done by Power BI developers, and the excerpt points to modeling standards as the area where human-defined structure remains important.

Before Copilot in Power BI can be used, the environment has to be prepared. The episode "Connect Microsoft Copilot to Predictive Power BI" lists several steps: checking tenant settings, making sure the organization has the right capacity, and using Power BI Premium or eligible Pro licenses to access the AI features. It also recommends connecting to dependable data sources such as Excel and SQL Server so that AI-driven insights and dashboards rest on accurate data, and assigning role-based access to protect sensitive data. The episode presents Copilot as a way to connect a team to predictive models and to bridge the gap between traditional reporting and more intelligent decision-making.

Copilot in Power BI also appears in integration scenarios. In the episode "Microsoft 365 Copilot Extensibility with Gautam Sheth [MVP]", it is mentioned alongside connectors and workflow tools. The excerpt describes using Copilot in Power BI to fetch and analyze SAP ERP data after enabling the Power Platform SAP connector, and to generate Jira project reports and sprint insights after installing the Jira Cloud Connector in Power Automate. In these scenarios, Power Automate, Azure Logic Apps and API connections move data between systems, and Copilot in Power BI serves as the analysis and reporting layer on top.

Typical decisions around the product therefore include which tenant and capacity settings to enable, which licenses users need, which data sources feed the semantic model, and how access is restricted by role. A further decision is how to document modeling conventions, for example through templates and developer-defined measures, so that AI-generated measures and pages follow organizational standards. Taken together, the sources present Copilot in Power BI as an assistant that accelerates authoring and exploration within a governed model, not as a replacement for that model.

copilot-memory.desc: Copilot Memory is a Microsoft Copilot feature that stores user-requested details such as tone, format and project tags to personalize later responses.

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Copilot Memory vs Windows Recall vs Vision", it saves only what the user explicitly asks it to remember, for example tone, format or project tags. Each save is announced with "Memory updated."
faq.q: What does Copilot Memory store?

faq.a: Yes. The episode says entries can be reviewed, edited or wiped at any time, and that users and administrators have controls such as toggles, deletions and tenant policies.
faq.q: Can stored Copilot Memory entries be removed?

faq.a: The episode describes Windows Recall as automatic, device-local screenshots on Copilot+ PCs and Vision as opt-in, realtime screen assistance. Copilot Memory, by contrast, only saves what the user explicitly asks it to remember.
faq.q: How does Copilot Memory differ from Windows Recall and Vision?

copilot-memory.long:
Copilot Memory is a personalization feature of Microsoft Copilot. It lets Copilot retain details from earlier interactions, such as preferred tone, output format or project tags, so that later responses fit the user's working context more closely without the same instructions being repeated.

According to the M365.FM episode "Copilot Memory vs Windows Recall vs Vision", Copilot Memory is not stealth surveillance. It only saves what the user explicitly asks it to remember, and every save is announced with the message "Memory updated." Entries can be reviewed, edited or wiped at any time. This explicit, user-driven behavior is the central design point the episode emphasizes: the feature personalizes output based on what has been deliberately stored, not on passive observation.

The same episode stresses that the real privacy risk lies in confusing Copilot Memory with two other capabilities. Windows Recall is described as automatic, device-local screenshots on Copilot+ PCs. Vision is described as opt-in, realtime screen-based assistance. These are different mechanisms with different data flows, and treating them as one feature leads to wrong assumptions about what is collected and where. The episode therefore frames the three as separate topics that should be evaluated individually when deciding what to enable.

Governance is a recurring theme. The episode states that users and administrators both have hard controls: toggles, deletions, tenant policies and eDiscovery visibility. On this reading, personalization through Copilot Memory is governed rather than guessed. Users can manage their own stored entries, while administrators can apply tenant-level policy, and stored memory content remains visible to eDiscovery processes. Organizations considering the feature can use these controls to decide whether and how it is made available.

Copilot Memory also appears in prompt-writing guidance. The episode "Microsoft 365 Copilot Prompts That Deliver Better Results" lists Memory alongside elements such as source, detailed persona and custom instructions. There, Copilot Memory is described as a way to pull details from past conversations for more relevant responses, while custom instructions add background on the user's role and preferred communication style. The episode's tip is that the more detail is included in the instructions, the more Copilot can personalize its output. Memory and custom instructions are thus complementary: one carries context forward from earlier conversations, the other states standing preferences.

Typical situations for using Copilot Memory include asking Copilot to keep a consistent writing style, apply a preferred document or answer format, or associate work with a named project. A practical decision for users is what is worth storing explicitly, and for administrators whether to allow the feature, how to communicate its behavior, and how to explain the difference between Memory, Recall and Vision to staff.

The topic is also cross-referenced from the M365.FM episodes "Windows 365 – Simply Explained" and "Azure Virtual Desktop vs Windows 365 with Dieter Kempeneers [MVP] & Dominiek Verham [MVP]", which list "Copilot Memory vs Windows Recall vs Vision" as a related listen. In those cases the link is a recommendation for further reading within the Microsoft ecosystem rather than a detailed discussion of Copilot Memory itself.

copilot-notebooks.desc: Copilot Notebooks are Loop-based Microsoft 365 Copilot workspaces that gather pages, files and links on one topic so Copilot can reason over that content.

faq.a: Copilot Notebooks are Loop-based Microsoft 365 Copilot workspaces that collect pages, files and links on a topic so Copilot can reason over that content, for example to create summaries or audio overviews.
faq.q: What are Copilot Notebooks?

faq.a: According to the episode "Copilot in Office Apps: The Governance Checklist", Copilot Notebooks suggest relevant files from the notebook's title or theme, support custom instructions per notebook and can generate audio overviews, while OneNote notebooks offer none of these.
faq.q: How do Copilot Notebooks differ from OneNote notebooks?

faq.a: The episode "Fix Copilot Notebooks GDPR and Governance Risks" says Copilot outputs are derived content that can contain fragments of sensitive sources and lose their parent context. It recommends limiting sharing, review-gating AI summaries and forcing inheritance on outputs.
faq.q: What governance risks do the episodes raise about Copilot Notebooks?

copilot-notebooks.long:
Copilot Notebooks are workspaces in Microsoft 365 Copilot that are based on Loop. A notebook collects pages, files and links around a single topic so that Copilot can reason over that specific set of content instead of answering from a blank chat window. Typical outputs include summaries and audio overviews of the collected material.

The core idea, as described in the M365.FM episode "Microsoft Copilot Notebooks - Simply Explained", is to give Copilot a home. The episode argues that many people use Copilot like a search box and then find the answers random, for example when ten files belong to one project and the chat has no way of knowing which of them matter. A notebook addresses this by defining the context up front. The episode walks through what a Copilot Notebook actually is, how one is set up in a few minutes, and what it does well.

A related conversation appears in "OneNote vs Loop vs Copilot with Karinne Diamond Bessette [MVP]". There, Copilot Pages and Copilot Notebooks are described as the next step in contextual AI collaboration. They let organizations gather several information sources into a centralized workspace and then ground AI responses in the context of one project. The guest's practical example comes from a large event project, where emails, Teams messages, planning calls and Loop pages were combined into one place. The same episode places this next to persistent collaborative workspaces that connect to tasks, updates and shared action items, as an alternative to information scattered across Teams chats.

The episode "Copilot in Office Apps: The Governance Checklist" compares Copilot Notebooks with OneNote notebooks. According to its comparison, Copilot Notebooks automatically recommend relevant files based on the notebook's title or theme, while OneNote notebooks offer no content suggestions and leave the structure to the user. Copilot Notebooks also allow custom instructions, such as tone, format or other AI behavior guidelines, set per notebook, which OneNote does not offer. A further listed difference is the audio overview, which generates a summary of the notebook content for quick consumption.

Governance is the main risk theme in the episodes. "Fix Copilot Notebooks GDPR and Governance Risks" describes the notebook experience as a conversational workspace that pulls context from SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, decks, sheets and emails and synthesizes answers instantly. Its warning is that users who trust this experience generate data with no parents: every Copilot output, whether a summary, paragraph or bullet list, is derived content that can contain fragments of sensitive source material. The episode's recommendations include limiting sharing, making AI summaries review-gated, and forcing inheritance of source protections onto the outputs, since AI productivity accelerates compliance debt otherwise.

The same episode is listed among related reading in "Fix Microsoft Copilot Agent Governance with a Control Plane", which places Copilot Notebooks within a wider discussion of governing Copilot and agents. In practice, decisions around Copilot Notebooks therefore combine two questions: which sources belong in a notebook so Copilot has useful, focused context, and how sharing, review and sensitivity of the generated content are controlled once summaries and overviews exist.

copilot-pages.desc: Copilot Pages is a Microsoft 365 Copilot capability that turns Copilot chat results into a shared, editable page built on the Loop framework for team collaboration.

faq.a: Copilot Pages is a Microsoft 365 Copilot capability that turns Copilot chat results into a shared, editable page built on the Loop framework, so colleagues can collaborate on the content with Copilot.
faq.q: What is Copilot Pages?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Copilot Pages - Simply Explained", a useful answer from an AI chat can vanish once the chat is closed. Copilot Pages gives that result a lasting, shareable place so it can be edited and developed with others.
faq.q: What problem does Copilot Pages address?

faq.a: Copilot Pages is built on the Loop framework. The episode "Microsoft Loop and Copilot Pages: Where Collaboration Content Should Live" discusses how Loop, Copilot Pages, SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams fit together and how storage, sharing and lifecycle behave.
faq.q: How does Copilot Pages relate to Loop, SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams?

copilot-pages.long:
Copilot Pages is a Microsoft 365 Copilot capability that turns the results of a Copilot chat into a shared, editable page. It is built on the Loop framework, which means the content is not a one-off answer that disappears when a chat is closed, but a page that colleagues can open, edit and develop together with Copilot. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Copilot Pages - Simply Explained" describes the underlying problem: a useful answer from an AI chat is easily lost once the user scrolls away or closes the conversation.

The main purpose of Copilot Pages is to give good chat output a durable place to live. According to the episode "Replace Traditional M365 Training with In-Flow Learning", Copilot Pages lets users modify, share and collaborate on any Copilot Chat result, so that ideas that start in Copilot Chat are solidified and developed more quickly. In that sense the page acts as a bridge between an individual conversation with Copilot and shared team work. Instead of copying a response into a separate document, the result can be turned into a page and worked on by several people.

Because Copilot Pages is based on Loop, it sits alongside other Loop-powered content. The episode "Microsoft Loop and Copilot Pages: Where Collaboration Content Should Live" looks at how Loop components and Copilot Pages add new places where content can live, and which questions follow from that. It covers how Loop, Copilot Pages, SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams fit together and how storage, sharing and lifecycle behave. The practical decision for organizations is where each kind of collaboration content belongs, and the episode frames this as setting guidance rather than leaving the choice to chance.

Copilot Pages also appears in the wider discussion of how Microsoft 365 collaboration tools relate to one another. In the episode "OneNote vs Loop vs Copilot with Karinne Diamond Bessette [MVP]", the conversation touches on Copilot Pages and Copilot Notebooks as the next evolution of contextual AI collaboration. Copilot Notebooks, as described there, gather multiple information sources into a centralized workspace that can then ground AI responses against a specific project context. Copilot Pages is mentioned in that same line of development, with Loop-powered collaborative pages offering persistent shared workspaces instead of content that is lost inside long chat threads.

The episode "Copilot Cowork with Vesa "Vesku" Nopanen [MVP]" places Copilot Pages in a broader picture as well. It describes Microsoft 365 Copilot, Loop and Copilot Pages working together so that information flows between them, moving away from static documents toward dynamic, AI-enhanced collaboration with real-time updates. This framing treats Copilot Pages as one part of a connected knowledge ecosystem rather than a standalone feature.

In day-to-day use, the typical situation is straightforward: a user asks Copilot a question in chat, receives a result worth keeping, and turns it into a page that others can edit. The episode "Microsoft Copilot Pages - Simply Explained" walks through what the capability is, where it came from, how it works and how it is used. Because the content lives in the Loop framework, questions about sharing, storage location and lifecycle become relevant, which is why the Loop-focused episode recommends clear practical guidance on where collaboration content should reside.

For administrators and champions, the related topics are Microsoft 365 Copilot, Loop, Copilot Notebooks, SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams. Copilot Pages connects the first two directly, while the others come into play when deciding where pages and related content are stored and shared. Listeners who want the concept explained from first principles can start with "Microsoft Copilot Pages - Simply Explained", and those weighing governance and placement can follow with "Microsoft Loop and Copilot Pages: Where Collaboration Content Should Live".

copilot-plus-pc.desc: Copilot+ PC is a category of Windows 11 PCs with an NPU above 40 TOPS, required for on-device AI features such as Recall and Click to Do.

faq.a: A Copilot+ PC is a Windows 11 device with a neural processing unit capable of more than 40 trillion operations per second (TOPS). This NPU requirement is what separates it from a general AI PC.
faq.q: What makes a PC a Copilot+ PC?

faq.a: Many of the new Windows AI features require an NPU above 40 TOPS, including on-device functions such as Recall and Click to Do, as well as real-time translation and image generation.
faq.q: Which features require a Copilot+ PC?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn recommends Windows ML, which builds on ONNX Runtime, detects the hardware and loads a fitting execution provider, falling back to GPU or CPU when needed. Models often need quantization because most NPUs work with low-precision integer formats.
faq.q: How do developers target the NPU in a Copilot+ PC?

copilot-plus-pc.long:
Copilot+ PC is a category of Windows 11 devices built around a neural processing unit (NPU), a specialized chip designed for AI-heavy work. The defining criterion is the performance of that chip: an NPU delivering more than 40 trillion operations per second (TOPS). Microsoft's documentation describes this class of devices as the hardware basis for many of the newer Windows AI features, including on-device functions such as Recall and Click to Do, as well as tasks like real-time translation and image generation.

The NPU is the component that separates a Copilot+ PC from an ordinary laptop that is merely marketed as an AI PC. According to the Microsoft Learn developer guide, running AI tasks on the NPU is more efficient than running them on the CPU or GPU, which helps battery life. Windows 11 distributes work across the CPU, GPU and NPU depending on what suits each task, so the NPU does not replace the other processors but takes over the workloads it handles well. The Task Manager shows NPU utilization, which makes it possible to see when AI work is actually running on the chip. The documentation names the Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite as an example chip and lists devices from several manufacturers, with support for other chip families described as arriving later.

The M365.FM episode "Copilot+ PCs - Simply Explained" frames the topic around a single number: forty. The episode says that every new Windows laptop claims to be an AI PC, but only a smaller group earns the Copilot+ badge. Its outline covers what makes a PC a Copilot+ PC, the chip that many people have never heard of, what runs directly on the laptop, where data actually goes, how a Copilot+ PC differs from an ordinary AI PC, and who benefits now versus who can wait. The episode is aimed at people deciding whether their next laptop purchase needs to meet this threshold.

For developers, the Microsoft Learn guide recommends Windows ML, which builds on ONNX Runtime. It detects the available hardware, loads a fitting execution provider and falls back to the GPU or CPU when needed. Models can be sourced from Qualcomm AI Hub or the ONNX Model Zoo, or optimized with the Olive tool. Because most NPUs handle low-precision integer formats, models often need quantization before they run well on this hardware. The guide also notes that some Windows AI APIs are not yet shipped and are tied to an upcoming Windows App SDK release, so developers should check availability before building on them.

In practice, the central decision around Copilot+ PC is whether the on-device AI features justify choosing hardware that meets the NPU requirement. Organizations and individuals planning device purchases can use the 40 TOPS threshold as the dividing line between devices that qualify for these features and those that do not. The documentation reviewed here gives no pricing or licensing information, so cost comparisons require other sources. The topic connects to Windows 11 as the operating system, to local versus cloud processing of AI workloads, and to the broader question of how AI features are delivered on managed Microsoft devices.

copilot-prompt-gallery.desc: The Copilot Prompt Gallery is a catalog of suggested and saved prompts in Microsoft 365 Copilot that also lets organizations add their own custom prompts.

faq.a: It is a catalog of suggested and saved prompts inside Microsoft 365 Copilot, containing Microsoft-created prompts, videos and articles. Organizations can also add their own custom prompts, for example sorted by department.
faq.q: What is the Copilot Prompt Gallery?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, it has three areas: Suggested prompts curated by Microsoft, Your Prompts that a user creates and saves, and Teams prompts shared by a team.
faq.q: Which areas does the Copilot Prompt Gallery contain?

faq.a: User and group prompts are stored in collections within the Microsoft 365 Substrate data store inside the tenant boundary, encrypted and reachable only through Substrate APIs. Microsoft-created prompts come from a public catalog.
faq.q: Where are saved and shared prompts stored?

copilot-prompt-gallery.long:
The Copilot Prompt Gallery is a catalog of suggested and saved prompts inside Microsoft 365 Copilot. Microsoft describes it as a resource of Microsoft-created prompts, videos and articles meant to help people understand and use Microsoft Copilot effectively. Organizations can now add their own custom prompts to the gallery, for example sorted by department, which makes it a place for company-specific starting points as well as general guidance.

The gallery is reachable from within Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Chat. According to the Microsoft Learn documentation, it is divided into three areas: Suggested prompts curated by Microsoft, Your Prompts that a user creates and saves, and Teams prompts shared by a team. Each prompt includes hints on how to personalize and extend it, so a suggested prompt can serve as a template rather than a fixed instruction. Users can save prompts and share them across teams, which the documentation presents as a way to encourage consistency and collaboration.

Access works differently depending on sign-in status. Opening the gallery from Copilot requires authentication. People who are not signed in can only browse the Microsoft-created prompts on the web and need to sign in to try them. The Microsoft prompts come from a public catalog, while user and group prompts are stored in collections within the Microsoft 365 Substrate data store inside the tenant boundary. The documentation states that this data is encrypted and reachable only through Substrate APIs.

For administrators, the documentation mentions analytics and reporting on saved, liked and shared prompts, as well as on prompts shared with a team. A separate article covers exporting this information. The documentation page does not state license requirements, concrete limits, regional availability or supported languages, so those details need to be checked in the current product documentation before planning a rollout.

Typical situations for the gallery include onboarding people who are new to Copilot, standardizing how a team phrases recurring requests, and giving departments a curated set of prompts that fit their daily work. Because saved and team prompts can be reused, the gallery reduces the need for each person to write prompts from scratch. The option to add organization-defined prompts by department points toward using it as an internal library, where the contents reflect local processes and terminology rather than only the Microsoft-curated catalog.

The M365.FM episode "Use SharePoint Lists as a Copilot Knowledge Base" (2025-11-03) mentions the gallery in a short list of quick tips for getting started with Copilot. The episode suggests adding Copilot to the daily routine, asking it for help with planning and sorting tasks, checking the Copilot Prompt Gallery for prompts that match individual needs, and using Copilot in Microsoft 365 apps such as Outlook and Teams to stay organized. In that context the gallery is presented as a practical entry point for people who want ready-made prompts instead of formulating each request themselves.

copilot-search.desc: Microsoft 365 Copilot Search is an AI-powered enterprise search module in the Microsoft Copilot app, part of Microsoft 365 Copilot, using semantic and keyword matching.

faq.a: It is an AI-powered enterprise search built into the Microsoft Copilot app as its own Search module. It finds results from across the organization, including sources outside Microsoft 365, and shows short AI-generated Copilot Answers.
faq.q: What is Microsoft 365 Copilot Search?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, it is available to users with a suitable Copilot license at no additional cost and needs no setup. It supports Entra work or school accounts.
faq.q: Does Microsoft 365 Copilot Search cost extra?

faq.a: The episode "MCP Custom Connector in Copilot Studio: The Complete Integration Guide" names it as a service that is only available as an MCP server. The episode recommends MCP servers for connecting to Copilot Studio.
faq.q: How does Microsoft 365 Copilot Search relate to MCP and Copilot Studio?

copilot-search.long:
Microsoft 365 Copilot Search is an AI-powered universal search designed for enterprises. According to Microsoft Learn, it is built into the Microsoft Copilot app as its own Search module and is part of Microsoft 365 Copilot. Its aim is to find relevant results from across the organization quickly, including sources that sit outside Microsoft 365.

In the Copilot app, Search acts as an organizing layer. Users start with a query to locate information, and they move to Chat when they want to carry out tasks or interact with the content in more depth. This marks the main difference between the two modules: search is query-based, while chat is conversation-based. Choosing between them usually depends on whether the goal is to find something or to work with it.

Several capabilities are described in the documentation. Unified search spans a large catalog of connectors, plus custom connectors and partner connectors. Queries are interpreted with semantic understanding of natural language and combined with classic keyword matching. At the top of the results, Copilot Answers provide short AI-generated answers. Administrators can curate answers for acronyms, bookmarks and people, which gives organizations some control over what appears for common lookups. Copilot Answers can draw on web content according to the Copilot Chat settings.

On availability, the documentation says the feature is offered to users with a suitable Copilot license at no additional cost. It needs no setup and supports Entra work or school accounts. Compared with the free Microsoft Search, Microsoft 365 Copilot Search requires a Copilot license and adds semantic search and integration with Copilot Chat answers. The documentation also notes that several features are still missing in US government clouds, which is a relevant point for organizations in those environments.

The product also appears in the M365.FM episode "MCP Custom Connector in Copilot Studio: The Complete Integration Guide" (2025-11-12). In that episode, Microsoft 365 Copilot Search is cited as an example of a service that is only available as an MCP server. The episode argues that MCP servers offer portability across multiple agent platforms, support complex logic unlike connectors limited to the Power Platform ecosystem, and provide automatic tool updates and additional protocol features. It describes this as a recommended way to connect to Copilot Studio and warns against the misconception that custom connectors are always required for integration.

For people evaluating the product, the practical questions are the license that users hold, which connectors feed the search results, whether curated answers are needed for internal terms, and whether the tenant runs in a cloud where some features are not yet available. For those building agents, the episode points to the MCP route when connecting Microsoft 365 Copilot Search to Copilot Studio.

copilot-service-workspace.desc: Copilot Service workspace, formerly Dynamics 365 Customer Service workspace, is the multisession agent app in Dynamics 365 Customer Service with Copilot assistance.

faq.a: It is the multisession agent app for Dynamics 365 Customer Service, formerly named Dynamics 365 Customer Service workspace. It keeps each customer issue in its own session with tabs, an inbox, a productivity pane and Copilot assistance.
faq.q: What is Copilot Service workspace?

faq.a: Yes. Copilot Service workspace is the newer name for Dynamics 365 Customer Service workspace, as described in the M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Customer Service Workspace - Simply Explained".
faq.q: Is Copilot Service workspace the same as Dynamics 365 Customer Service workspace?

faq.a: Unified Routing distributes incoming work to the most suitable agent based on factors such as availability and workload, and the episode on Unified Routing mentions Copilot Service workspace as the app where agents handle that work.
faq.q: How does Copilot Service workspace relate to Unified Routing?

copilot-service-workspace.long:
Copilot Service workspace is the agent-facing application for Dynamics 365 Customer Service. It was previously called Dynamics 365 Customer Service workspace, and the name change reflects the Copilot assistance built into the app. It is described as a multisession app: each customer issue is kept in its own session, so an agent can handle several conversations or cases without losing the context of any one of them. Instead of jumping between browser tabs, inboxes, CRM records, notes, knowledge bases and communication tools, the agent works in a single place.

The app is organized around a few building blocks named in the sources. Sessions hold the work for one customer issue, and tabs within a session hold the related records, such as the case and its timeline. An inbox gives the agent a view of incoming work. A productivity pane sits alongside the main work area and provides supporting tools, and Copilot assists the agent during the interaction. Together these elements are intended to reduce the manual switching between systems that customer service work otherwise involves.

The episode "Dynamics 365 Customer Service Workspace - Simply Explained" on M365.FM, presented by Mirko Peters, covers the workspace in plain English under its newer name. It walks through sessions and tabs, cases and timelines, omnichannel customer service and the agent inbox. It also covers Smart Assist, knowledge management, agent scripts, macros and quick replies, along with Copilot and collaboration through Microsoft Teams. On the operations side, the episode touches on Unified Routing, queues, presence, capacity, SLA management and escalation, as well as self-service, dashboards and customer service analytics.

Routing is closely tied to how the workspace is used day to day. The episode "Dynamics 365 Unified Routing - Simply Explained" describes Unified Routing as an intelligent capability that distributes incoming customer service work, considers agent availability and workload, and sends each item to the most appropriate person. It likens this to a smart front desk in a large office building. The same episode explains workstreams, queues, skills, capacity profiles, presence, push assignment, pick assignment, machine learning and fallback queues, and mentions Copilot Service workspace as the place where agents receive that routed work.

The workspace also appears in the context of supervising AI agents. The episode "Agent Feed - Simply Explained" describes steps for setting up monitoring of AI agents through Agent Feed. An administrator signs in to Power Apps, selects the contact center environment, opens Apps in the site map, and edits the Copilot Service workspace app. Agent Feed is enabled by selecting the Agents icon in the site map, choosing the agent that corresponds to Case Management Agent (for example, Case Processing Agent), using the ellipses menu to add it to the app, and then saving and publishing the changes. The episode also describes adding an Agent Supervisor view by selecting the Case view and choosing views in the Cases pane. This shows that the app is configurable through the Power Apps app designer rather than being a fixed, closed interface.

Typical decisions around the workspace concern how work reaches agents and which assistance features are exposed to them. Organizations choose how routing is configured, how queues and capacity are set up, and whether supporting tools such as scripts, macros, quick replies, knowledge articles and Copilot are surfaced in the agent experience. Because the product was renamed from Dynamics 365 Customer Service workspace, older documentation, training material and conversations may use the earlier name for the same app.

copilot-studio.desc: Copilot Studio is Microsoft's low-code platform for building, customising and publishing AI agents and copilots to Teams, websites or Microsoft 365 Copilot.

faq.a: Copilot Studio is Microsoft's low-code platform for building, customising and publishing AI agents and copilots. Makers define topics, knowledge sources, actions and flows, and can publish the result to Teams, websites or Microsoft 365 Copilot.
faq.q: What is Copilot Studio?

faq.a: Power Virtual Agents is the former name of Copilot Studio, and the two are listed as related on m365.fm. Copilot Studio is part of the Power Platform.
faq.q: How does Copilot Studio relate to Power Virtual Agents?

faq.a: The episodes describe a move from demos to production, stressing secure and governed solutions, RAG, multi-agent systems and MCP for connecting agents to tools and data. They present reliability across large organisations with sensitive data as the harder challenge compared with building a demo.
faq.q: What do the M365.FM episodes say about using Copilot Studio in enterprises?

copilot-studio.long:
