Copilot Studio, also called Microsoft Copilot Studio and formerly known as Power Virtual Agents, is a low-code platform from Microsoft for building, customising and publishing AI agents and copilots. It is classified as a Microsoft tool and a low-code tool, it is part of the Power Platform, and it is a paid product. Makers use it to define the behaviour of an agent without writing a full application from scratch.

The building blocks named in the product description are topics, knowledge sources, actions and flows. Topics describe the conversations an agent can handle, knowledge sources give it content to draw on, and actions and flows let it do work in other systems. Once an agent is configured, it can be published to Teams, to websites or to Microsoft 365 Copilot. Related concepts on m365.fm include Power Fx, connectors, agent skills, Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, Microsoft Agent 365 and Copilot Credits, which together describe how agents are expressed, connected, extended, surfaced to users, managed and metered.

Typical decisions around the product concern scope and reliability. A simple agent that answers questions from a knowledge source differs from one that connects to enterprise systems, orchestrates workflows and acts on behalf of users. The episodes on this topic stress that agents are moving beyond chatbots that only answer questions, and that the harder task is making them work in real organisations with sensitive data and many users.

The M365.FM episode "Beyond Copilot: Building Enterprise AI Agents That Actually Work with Copilot Studio with Manpreet Singh [MVP-MCT]" discusses this shift. Its description says that building an impressive AI agent demo is easy, while building an agent that works reliably across a global enterprise, with sensitive data and measurable outcomes, is a very different challenge. The next generation of agents, according to the episode, can understand business context, connect to enterprise systems, orchestrate workflows and take action.

The episode "From Demo to Production- Building Enterprise AI Agents That Actually Work with Microsoft Copilot Studio with Elliot Margot [MVP]" takes the same theme from the production side. Elliot Margot is described as a Microsoft MVP for Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio Team Lead at Witivio. The conversation covers moving from an impressive demo to a secure, governed and genuinely useful enterprise solution, and it touches on multi-agent systems and on MCP. The description says that MCP can help package connections in a more consistent, secure and reusable way than treating every API as an isolated endpoint.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation is the focus of "Copilot Studio AI Agents and RAG with Nilüfer Doğan [MVP]". The episode explores how Copilot Studio is changing enterprise automation through AI agents, RAG and low-code development, and it describes agents that understand business context, access enterprise knowledge and automate complex workflows rather than acting as simple chatbots. This links directly to the knowledge source concept in the product.

Two further episodes look at architecture and data. "Multi-Agent AI with Copilot Studio and David Lorenzo Lopez [MVP]" covers multi-agent systems alongside Microsoft Agent Framework, AI orchestration and Microsoft Foundry. "Agentic AI with Copilot Studio and Dataverse MCP with Nathan Rose [MVP]" looks at how Copilot Studio, Dataverse and the Model Context Protocol shape agentic AI in Microsoft 365. According to that description, MCP is an emerging open standard that lets AI agents connect to external tools, data sources and business systems in a more consistent and scalable way. Together, the episodes present Copilot Studio as a platform whose value depends on governance, data access and integration choices as much as on the agent itself.

copilot-studio-kit.desc: Copilot Studio Kit is a toolkit within Copilot Studio for testing and evaluating agents, tracking conversation KPIs and supporting governance.

faq.a: It is a toolkit for Copilot Studio used to test and evaluate agents and to track conversation KPIs. The episodes also describe it as a way to measure the business value of agents and to support governance.
faq.q: What is Copilot Studio Kit used for?

faq.a: According to the episode "Replace Legacy RPA with Copilot Studio Computer Use", it is imported as a solution in the chosen Power Apps environment using the CopilotStudioKit_managed.zip file. The administrator reviews the solution information and creates any required connections.
faq.q: How is Copilot Studio Kit installed?

faq.a: The Power Platform governance episode names it alongside the Power Platform Admin Center, the Center of Excellence Starter Kit and a custom inventory built with Power Platform APIs as a source of visibility into what exists.
faq.q: How does Copilot Studio Kit relate to governance and inventory?

copilot-studio-kit.long:
Copilot Studio Kit is a product that belongs to Copilot Studio, Microsoft's environment for building agents. It is described as a toolkit for testing and evaluating agents and for tracking conversation KPIs. In the M365.FM episodes it appears in two main roles: as a means of measuring the business value of agents, and as a building block for governance.

The kit is delivered as a solution that is installed into a Power Apps environment. The episode "Replace Legacy RPA with Copilot Studio Computer Use" walks through the connection steps. The administrator signs in to Power Apps with an organizational account and selects the environment in which the kit should be installed, so that work happens in the correct workspace. In the left-hand menu the administrator opens Solutions and chooses Import Solution. After clicking Browse, the downloaded managed solution file named CopilotStudioKit_managed.zip is selected. The administrator then continues with Next, reviews the solution information and, if prompted, creates the required connections, which allow the Power Apps side to work with Copilot Studio. Because the kit is installed per environment, the choice of environment is a real decision rather than a formality.

A typical use case is evaluating agents before and after they go into production. Testing and evaluation help show whether an agent behaves as intended, while conversation KPIs give a view of how agents are actually used. In the Replace Legacy RPA episode, this measurement is tied to the question of business value: when an organization moves from legacy robotic process automation to agents that use Copilot Studio computer use, it needs evidence of what those agents deliver, and the kit is the tool the episode uses for that purpose.

Governance is the second theme. In the episode "Power Platform Governance Without Killing Innovation: Security, DLP, Environments & Citizen Development with Michael Roth [MVP]", the Copilot Studio Kit is mentioned in the discussion of inventory. The episode makes the point that administrators can only make sensible decisions after they can see what exists. It examines several sources of inventory information: the native inventory capabilities in the Power Platform Admin Center, the changing role of the Center of Excellence Starter Kit, the Copilot Studio Kit, and the option of building a customized inventory with Power Platform APIs. The episode notes that, for many organizations, a purpose-built inventory can align better with their licenses, services, risks and governance requirements. The Copilot Studio Kit is therefore one option among several for gaining visibility into agents, not a replacement for the other approaches.

The kit also comes up in the context of integration work. The episode "MCP Custom Connector in Copilot Studio: The Complete Integration Guide" refers to resources such as the Copilot Studio Kit and the Architecture Bootcamp as providing reusable assets and templates. According to the episode, these can help avoid common pitfalls when integrating MCP with Copilot Studio. The same episode lists challenges to watch for, including the lack of account ID reuse across tools and performance differences between various connectors, and it recommends learning from real-world examples when preparing an integration.

Taken together, the episodes position Copilot Studio Kit as a supporting layer around Copilot Studio rather than a standalone product. It helps teams verify agent quality, observe conversation KPIs, contribute to an inventory for governance, and reuse assets when building integrations. Related topics include Copilot Studio itself, Power Apps environments and solutions, the Power Platform Admin Center, and the Center of Excellence Starter Kit.

copilot-studio-topics.desc: Copilot Studio topics are designed conversation portions of a Copilot Studio agent, built with steps, questions and conditions for answers that must be exact.

faq.a: They are designed portions of a Copilot Studio agent conversation, made up of steps, questions and conditions. They are used for answers that must be exact.
faq.q: What are Copilot Studio topics?

faq.a: Requests outside the defined topics can fall back to generated answers.
faq.q: What happens when a request does not match any topic?

faq.a: Copilot Studio is the broader product, and topics are one of the elements used to design an agent's conversation within it.
faq.q: How do topics relate to Copilot Studio?

copilot-studio-topics.long:
Copilot Studio topics are designed portions of a Copilot Studio agent conversation. Each topic is built from steps, questions and conditions that define how the agent responds in a particular part of a dialogue.

Topics are used where answers must be exact. Because the conversation path is authored in advance, the agent follows the defined steps rather than composing a reply on its own. Requests that fall outside the defined topics can fall back to generated answers, so topics and generated responses can work together within the same agent.

Topics are a core authoring element of Copilot Studio, the broader product in which agents are created and edited. Microsoft documents how to create and edit topics in its Copilot Studio documentation.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

copilot-ux-components.desc: Copilot UX components are reusable interface building blocks from Microsoft for extending Microsoft 365 Copilot with interactive experiences in custom apps and agents.

faq.a: They are reusable user-interface building blocks from Microsoft for extending Microsoft 365 Copilot in custom apps and agents. They let a conversation show branded, interactive interfaces instead of plain text.
faq.q: What are Copilot UX components?

faq.a: They are built with the SharePoint Framework (SPFx), derive from BaseCopilotComponent and declare tools and display modes in a manifest. They are packaged with a declarative agent as an .sppkg file and deployed through the SharePoint App Catalog.
faq.q: How are Copilot UX components built and deployed?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, a user-specific Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on license is needed on top of E3, E5 or E7, even for development. Limits include a 10 KB text context for Copilot and no mobile support.
faq.q: What requirements and limits apply to Copilot UX components?

copilot-ux-components.long:
Copilot UX components are reusable user-interface building blocks for extending Microsoft 365 Copilot experiences in custom apps and agents. They are developed by Microsoft and classed as a developer tool. Instead of designing every chat element, response display or interaction from scratch, developers use ready-made pieces so that their extensions look and behave consistently with the Copilot experience around them.

According to the Microsoft Learn overview, the components extend Microsoft 365 Copilot with custom interactive interfaces built with the SharePoint Framework (SPFx). A conversation can then show branded, interactive experiences rather than plain text. A solution packages one or more components together with a declarative agent, which makes them discoverable and callable from Copilot. The components derive from BaseCopilotComponent, declare their tools and display modes in a manifest, and render either inline or fullscreen, with the host controlling the layout. Tools receive their input through a properties schema.

The same shared UI can be reused elsewhere. Through separate adapters, the interface logic can also run in an SPFx web part or in a Teams tab, so a team does not have to build the same view several times. Packages are delivered as .sppkg files and deployed through the SharePoint App Catalog. Assets are hosted automatically when includeClientSideAssets is set. Distribution can be private within an organization or go through the SharePoint Store. For local testing, a Copilot Workbench is available.

Copilot UX components are part of Microsoft 365 Copilot and are related to Copilot Studio, where custom agents are built, and to Microsoft 365 as the environment in which these experiences appear. The underlying idea is the same as for any component library: shared building blocks reduce effort and keep the result consistent across apps built by different teams. A typical scenario is a team that builds a custom app or agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot and wants the interface to match the surrounding Copilot experience without maintaining its own design system.

Several conditions and limits are listed in the documentation. The page states that the components are generally available from SPFx 1.24, released on 28 October 2026. It also states that a user-specific Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on license is required on top of E3, E5 or E7, even for development. Copilot receives a text context of at most 10 KB. Mobile is not supported, a sync mismatch can occur when the components are combined with Teams functionality, and additional surfaces are not yet covered. These points matter when deciding whether the components fit a planned scenario and how licensing and testing should be organized.

No M365.FM episode in the knowledge base is linked directly to Copilot UX components. For the exact list of components, the manifest structure and the deployment steps, the official Microsoft documentation is the reliable source.

copilot-vision.desc: Copilot Vision lets Microsoft Copilot see a shared Windows or web screen or a phone camera feed and answer questions about it during a voice conversation.

faq.a: Copilot Vision is a capability of Microsoft Copilot that lets it analyze a shared Windows or web screen, or a mobile camera view, in real time and answer questions about the visible content.
faq.q: What is Copilot Vision?

faq.a: No. According to Microsoft's support documentation, Copilot may highlight parts of the screen in this mode but does not click, type or scroll on the user's behalf.
faq.q: Can Copilot Vision click or type for the user?

faq.a: Work or school accounts need a Microsoft Copilot license, and personal accounts need a Microsoft 365 Personal, Family or Premium subscription. Microphone access is required, and mobile use also needs camera permission, since the feature runs only during a voice conversation.
faq.q: What is needed to use Copilot Vision?

copilot-vision.long:
Copilot Vision is a capability of Microsoft Copilot that allows the assistant to look at what a user shares and answer questions about it. The shared content can be a Windows or web desktop screen or the view from a mobile device camera. Copilot analyzes the shared material in real time and grounds its answers in that content and, for work accounts, in work data. In Microsoft's support documentation the feature is described as vision capabilities in Microsoft Copilot.

Vision works only during a voice conversation. A user starts a voice chat from the Copilot Chat input, with the Copilot key, with Win+C, or in the mobile app. On desktop the user then selects the screen-share arrow, and on mobile the camera icon. Sharing ends when the user selects Stop sharing. Microphone access is needed, and on mobile the camera permission must be granted as well. A privacy notice may appear the first time the feature is used.

The requirements depend on the account type. Work or school accounts need a Microsoft Copilot license, while personal accounts need a Microsoft 365 Personal, Family or Premium subscription. Availability, regions and supported languages vary while features roll out, so the experience can differ between users and devices.

Two design points shape how Copilot Vision is used in practice. First, each vision conversation is independent, so screens or camera input shared earlier are not reused in a later session. Second, Copilot does not act on the user's behalf in this mode. It may highlight parts of the screen, but it does not click, type or scroll. The feature therefore works as a guide that explains or points out what is visible, not as an automation tool that completes tasks for the user.

Typical situations include asking Copilot about an application window the user is working in, getting an explanation of something displayed on screen, or pointing a phone camera at an object and asking about it. For work accounts, the grounding in work data means answers can draw on organizational context in addition to the shared content, as described in the documentation.

The episode "Beyond the Prompt: Mastering Microsoft Copilot for Real Productivity with Jess Stratton [MVP]" mentions Copilot Vision in its overview of recent Copilot developments. According to the episode notes, an enhanced Copilot Vision offers real-time visual "show me how" guidance and simultaneous dual-app analysis, integrated into a multi-app workspace in Windows. The notes state that it was available to U.S. Windows Insiders before the full public release. The same notes describe a staged feature deployment strategy driven by user feedback, with an incremental release schedule intended to test system stability, and mention an Android assistant for messaging, timers, alarms and rideshare booking.

For anyone evaluating the feature, the main decisions concern licensing, device access and rollout status. Because voice conversation is required, microphone availability matters, and because regions and languages vary, availability in a given tenant or country is worth checking against current Microsoft documentation before planning around it.

copilot-web-search.desc: Copilot web search is a setting that lets Microsoft 365 Copilot reference public web content alongside internal data, with admin options to allow, block or selectively enable it.
copilot-web-search.long:
Copilot web search is a setting in Microsoft 365 Copilot that allows the assistant to reference public web content in addition to the internal data it can already access. It governs whether answers may draw on information from outside the organization's own environment.

Administrators control how the setting is applied. The available choices are to allow it, block it, or enable it selectively. Because the setting changes what sources Copilot can consider when responding, admins are advised to test its effect in their own tenant before deciding on a configuration.

The concept is relevant to governance and data-handling decisions around Microsoft 365 Copilot, since it determines whether responses may combine internal organizational content with material from the public web. The facts available for this entry do not specify further technical details, licensing requirements or related products, so those are not described here.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

corporate-social-responsibility.desc: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) describes how a company accounts for the social and environmental impact of its business decisions.

faq.a: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) describes how a company accounts for the social and environmental impact of its business decisions. It is often framed as people, planet and profit.
faq.q: What does corporate social responsibility (CSR) mean?

faq.a: CSR is commonly grouped into four categories: environmental, ethical, philanthropic and economic responsibility.
faq.q: What are the main categories of CSR?

corporate-social-responsibility.long:
Corporate social responsibility (CSR) describes how a company accounts for the social and environmental impact of its business decisions. It is commonly framed as people, planet and profit, a shorthand that places social and environmental outcomes alongside financial results.

CSR is typically grouped into four areas: environmental, ethical, philanthropic and economic responsibility. Environmental responsibility concerns a company's effect on the natural environment. Ethical responsibility concerns how a company conducts itself toward people and stakeholders. Philanthropic responsibility concerns voluntary contributions to society, and economic responsibility concerns the financial viability of the business itself.

On M365.FM, CSR is catalogued as a concept within the knowledge base covering the Microsoft ecosystem. No related topics, episodes or official documentation links are currently associated with this entry, so it serves as a general definition of the term rather than a description of any specific product, program or Microsoft offering.

cosmos-db.desc: Azure Cosmos DB is a globally distributed NoSQL database service on Azure, developed by Microsoft, used behind web, SaaS and AI applications.

faq.a: Azure Cosmos DB is a globally distributed NoSQL database service on Azure, developed by Microsoft. It stores data in flexible, non-relational formats and is part of Microsoft Azure.
faq.q: What is Azure Cosmos DB?

faq.a: According to the episode "Building Multi-Tenant SaaS with Power Pages and Dataverse", Power Pages Elastic Tables are powered by Azure Cosmos DB, which supports performance and tenant isolation in multi-tenant SaaS applications.
faq.q: How does Azure Cosmos DB relate to Power Pages?

faq.a: The episode "Deploy Web Apps to Azure App Service Without Boilerplate" mentions the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator as a way to run integration tests in a local testing environment.
faq.q: Can Azure Cosmos DB be tested locally?

cosmos-db.long:
Azure Cosmos DB is a globally distributed NoSQL database service on Azure. It is developed by Microsoft, is part of Microsoft Azure and is listed as a Microsoft tool. It is also referred to simply as Cosmos DB. The service was released in 2017. As a NoSQL service it stores data in flexible, non-relational formats rather than in fixed table schemas.

The purpose of Azure Cosmos DB is to give applications a managed data store, so that teams do not have to run database servers themselves, and to serve data to users in several regions where that is needed. Within Azure it commonly sits behind web applications, APIs and AI applications as the place where their data lives. The knowledge base lists no further relations for it, so it is best understood as one data service among the many that make up the Azure platform.

In the M365.FM episodes, Azure Cosmos DB appears as a building block inside larger architectures rather than as the main subject. The episode "Building Multi-Tenant SaaS with Power Pages and Dataverse" describes Power Pages Elastic Tables as being powered by Azure Cosmos DB. According to the episode, this gives multi-tenant SaaS applications fast, reliable performance and robust security for each tenant, while keeping tenant data isolated as the user base grows. The same episode names multi-tenant architecture as a way to reduce costs and simplify scaling for SaaS applications.

The episode "Fix Common Azure AI Foundry Project Failures" touches on Azure Cosmos DB from a troubleshooting angle. It describes checking whether the managed identity of an Azure AI Foundry project has access to Cosmos DB, Storage or Search when API calls fail, permissions errors appear or models do not fully deploy. It also points to the network layer and recent security updates as possible causes if communication between these resources is cut off, and mentions that a role assignment that was never applied can be behind such failures.

For development and testing, the episode "Deploy Web Apps to Azure App Service Without Boilerplate" mentions the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator as a way to set up a local testing environment for integration tests. It places this within a testing pyramid of many unit tests, some integration tests and a few end-to-end tests, and recommends using dependency injection to control what the code uses during tests.

The episode "Build AI Applications with .NET 10" lists Cosmos DB, together with Entity Framework Core, under data management in the infrastructure layer of an AI application, next to semantic search and vector databases such as Qdrant and Weaviate. The episode "Azure AI Search – Simply Explained" lists Azure Cosmos DB as one of the supported data sources for Azure AI Search and advises setting clear field mappings and creating custom metadata flags when connecting it.

Taken together, the episodes show Azure Cosmos DB in several roles: as the storage behind Power Pages Elastic Tables, as a resource that Azure AI Foundry projects and their managed identities must be able to reach, as a data source for search indexing, and as a database that can be emulated locally during testing.

cost-to-serve.desc: Cost to serve is a business metric for the total operational effort and expense required to run a process or deliver a service, including manual handling and rework.
cost-to-serve.long:
Cost to serve is a business metric that describes the total operational effort and expense needed to run a process or deliver a service. It covers not only the direct work involved but also manual handling, rework and exception management.

The metric is used to understand what it actually takes to operate a process or service over time. Because it includes manual handling, rework and exceptions, it reflects effort that is often less visible than the headline cost of a process step. Looking at these components together gives a fuller picture of operational expense than a narrow view of the main workflow alone.

On M365.FM, Cost to serve is listed as a concept in the knowledge base. No related entities, official documentation links or specific episodes are currently associated with it, so this page limits itself to the definition above.

credential-guard.desc: Windows Defender Credential Guard uses virtualization-based security to isolate NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets from the LSASS process memory on Windows 11 and related platforms.

faq.a: It isolates NTLM password hashes, Kerberos ticket-granting tickets and credentials stored by applications as domain credentials using virtualization-based security, which makes pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket attacks harder.
faq.q: What does Windows Defender Credential Guard protect?

faq.a: It is supported on Windows Enterprise and Education editions with matching E3, E5, A3 or A5 licenses, but not on Pro. VBS and Secure Boot are required, and a TPM and UEFI lock are recommended.
faq.q: Which Windows editions support Credential Guard?

faq.a: The episode "Move Active Directory Groups to Microsoft Entra ID" states that ADMT will not run on devices with Credential Guard enabled, so the feature should be temporarily disabled on the ADMT server.
faq.q: Why might Credential Guard need to be disabled during an ADMT migration?

credential-guard.long:
Windows Defender Credential Guard is a Windows security feature that protects credentials against theft. It uses virtualization-based security (VBS) to isolate secrets such as NTLM password hashes, Kerberos ticket-granting tickets and credentials that applications store as domain credentials. In this model, the secrets are kept out of reach of the LSASS process memory, so that only privileged system software can access them. In the product structure it is part of Windows 11 and is also related to Windows 10 and Windows Server.

The purpose of Credential Guard is to make common credential-theft techniques harder, in particular pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket attacks. Because the protected secrets are isolated through virtualization-based security, even malware running with administrator rights cannot extract them from the operating system in the usual way. Microsoft's documentation notes that attackers are expected to adopt new techniques, so the feature is one layer of protection and not a complete defense on its own.

There are several hardware and platform requirements. VBS and Secure Boot are required, while a TPM and UEFI lock are recommended. Hyper-V guests must be generation 2, and the host needs an IOMMU. Credential Guard is supported on Windows Enterprise and Education editions with matching E3, E5, A3 or A5 licenses, but not on Pro. On recent Windows 11 and Windows Server releases it is enabled by default for domain-joined devices that meet the requirements, without UEFI lock. Microsoft advises against enabling it on domain controllers.

The feature has defined limits. It does not protect the Active Directory database or the SAM. Applications that depend on Kerberos DES, unconstrained delegation, TGT extraction or NTLMv1 stop working when Credential Guard is active. Other mechanisms, such as CredSSP, MS-CHAPv2 and digest authentication, can still expose credentials because the protection does not cover them. Administrators therefore usually check application and authentication dependencies before turning the feature on broadly.

Credential Guard also appears in identity migration work. The M365.FM episode "Move Active Directory Groups to Microsoft Entra ID" lists it among the issues that can arise from differences between a local Active Directory environment and the cloud-based Microsoft Entra ID. According to the episode, the Active Directory Migration Tool (ADMT) will not run on devices that have Windows Defender Credential Guard enabled, and the suggested solution is to temporarily disable Credential Guard on the ADMT server. The same episode mentions a related restriction, that domain controllers cannot use unconstrained delegation, which fits the compatibility limits described in the official documentation.

In practice, decisions around Credential Guard involve weighing the protection it adds against the compatibility of legacy authentication methods and the licensing and hardware prerequisites. Environments that still rely on NTLMv1, Kerberos DES or unconstrained delegation need to review those dependencies, while tools such as ADMT may require the feature to be disabled for the duration of a migration. Further details are published in the Credential Guard overview on Microsoft Learn.

critical-data-element.desc: A critical data element is a logical grouping of the same important field, such as a customer ID, across different tables so it can be governed with the same rules everywhere.

faq.a: It is a logical grouping of the same important field, such as a customer ID, across different tables. Grouping them allows the field to be governed with the same rules everywhere.
faq.q: What is a critical data element?

faq.a: Grouping lets the same governance rules apply wherever the field appears. This avoids managing each occurrence of the field separately.
faq.q: Why group a field across different tables?

critical-data-element.long:
A critical data element is a logical grouping of the same important field across different tables. A typical example is a customer ID that appears in several tables. Treating these separate occurrences as one element makes it possible to apply the same governance rules to all of them.

The concept is used in data governance. Instead of managing each column in each table on its own, an organization defines the field once as a critical data element and governs it consistently wherever it appears. This supports a shared understanding of which fields matter most and keeps the rules for those fields uniform.

No related products, documentation or M365.FM episodes are linked to this entry at present, so this page is limited to the definition and its general purpose.

critical-path-method.desc: The critical path method (CPM) is a scheduling technique that finds the chain of dependent tasks with no float that sets the earliest possible completion date.

faq.a: It identifies the longest chain of dependent tasks with zero total float, which determines the shortest possible project duration. Any delay on those tasks delays the whole plan.
faq.q: What does the critical path method identify?

faq.a: Managers can use fast-tracking, which adds more parallel work, or crashing, which adds resources at extra cost. Both focus on the activities that control the finish date.
faq.q: How can a schedule be shortened using CPM results?

faq.a: Non-critical tasks can exceed their float and create a new critical path. The M365.FM episode "Why Your Critical Path Changes When Production Changes" argues that in manufacturing the path should be treated as a live chain of dependencies rather than a fixed sequence.
faq.q: Why can the critical path change during a project or production run?

critical-path-method.long:
The critical path method (CPM) is a scheduling method that identifies the chain of dependent tasks with no float, which determines the earliest possible completion date of a plan. Tasks on that chain delay the whole plan when they slip. In the form described in reference material, CPM is a scheduling algorithm for a set of project activities: from a list of activities, their durations, dependencies and milestones, it finds the longest chain of dependent activities. That longest chain sets the shortest possible project duration.

The method works by computing earliest and latest start and finish times for each activity. Activities on the critical path have zero total float, meaning any slip pushes out the end date of the entire project. Activities off the critical path have slack, so they can run late by a limited amount without affecting completion. Related concepts include critical path drag, near-critical paths and the effect of constraints. Extensions of the basic approach add resource leveling and the resource critical path.

CPM is used to decide where management attention and effort should go. Because the critical path shows which tasks actually control the finish date, managers can prioritize that work and look for ways to shorten the schedule. Two common techniques are fast-tracking, which means doing more work in parallel, and crashing, which means adding resources at extra cost. CPM was developed in the late 1950s by Morgan Walker of DuPont and James Kelley Jr. of Remington Rand, is related to PERT, and was used in 1966 on the World Trade Center towers. It is applied in construction, aerospace, software, research and manufacturing.

The method has known limits. Results are sensitive to errors in duration estimates. A plan also has to be monitored continuously, because non-critical tasks can exceed their float and thereby create a new critical path. As-built critical path analysis has additionally drawn criticism when used in court.

The M365.FM episode "Why Your Critical Path Changes When Production Changes" applies CPM to manufacturing and production planning. It describes situations such as a qualified operator becoming unavailable, a quality inspection taking longer than expected, or a batch missing its furnace window, where a delay of only a few hours can put an entire customer delivery at risk. The central idea in the episode is that the critical path in manufacturing should not be treated as a fixed sequence created when the production order was released. Instead, manufacturers need to understand the live chain of dependencies that currently determines the earliest possible completion. This matches the general caution that a critical path can shift as conditions change, so the plan has to be re-examined rather than computed once.

In practice, the decisions around CPM concern how detailed the dependency model should be, how reliable the duration estimates are, and how often the critical path is recalculated. A static path may be adequate for a stable project, while an environment where resources, inspections and equipment windows change frequently calls for a path that is updated as events occur. The episode frames this adaptation of a traditional project management technique to modern production as the main theme.

cross-cutting-concerns.desc: Cross-cutting concerns are program aspects such as logging, authentication, validation and telemetry that affect many modules and are centralized outside business logic.

faq.a: They are aspects of a program, such as logging, authentication, validation and telemetry, that affect many modules and cannot be contained in any one of them. They are usually handled separately from business logic.
faq.q: What are cross-cutting concerns in software?

faq.a: They often cannot be separated cleanly from the rest of the system, which leads to scattering, where the same code is duplicated in many places, and tangling, where components become heavily interdependent.
faq.q: Why can cross-cutting concerns cause problems?

faq.a: The episode "Azure API Management - Simply Explained" says that, as an API gateway in a microservices architecture, it addresses cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, authorization, throttling, caching, transformation and monitoring.
faq.q: How does Azure API Management relate to cross-cutting concerns?

cross-cutting-concerns.long:
Cross-cutting concerns are aspects of a program that affect several modules and cannot be contained in any one of them. Typical examples are logging, authentication, validation, monitoring and telemetry. Because these concerns span many parts of a system, they do not belong inside the business logic of any single component. In practice they are usually centralized with mechanisms such as middleware, decorators or filters, so that the core code can stay focused on its primary purpose.

The term comes from aspect-oriented software development. According to the description of the concept in the sources, a cross-cutting concern often cannot be separated cleanly from the rest of the system in design or implementation. This leads to two recurring problems. The first is scattering, where the same code is duplicated in many places. The second is tangling, where components become heavily interdependent. Either problem can appear on its own, or both can occur together. Procedural, functional and object-oriented styles offer no direct way to handle a primary goal together with a cross-cutting concern, which is why modularity tends to suffer when these concerns are handled ad hoc.

A commonly cited illustration is a medical records application. In that example, indexing records is the core function, while logging changes and authentication cut across many parts of the application. The wider list of cross-cutting concerns named in the sources includes logging, monitoring, caching, validation, persistence, transaction processing, synchronization, security and privacy, error handling, internationalization and memory management. The concept is therefore not limited to one technology or layer; it describes a recurring structural problem in software design.

Aspect-oriented programming addresses these concerns by encapsulating each one in an aspect, which keeps the related code isolated, reusable and easier to maintain. The 1997 paper on aspect-oriented programming by Kiczales and AspectJ are cited as foundations of this approach. In everyday engineering, teams often reach the same goal without a dedicated aspect-oriented language, by placing shared behavior in a single layer that wraps or intercepts requests, which is where middleware, decorators and filters come in.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the idea appears in the discussion of API gateways. The M365.FM episode "Azure API Management - Simply Explained" describes Azure API Management as an API gateway in a microservices architecture. According to the episode, it manages communication between microservices and clients and addresses cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, authorization, throttling, caching, transformation and monitoring. The episode lists several benefits of this approach: APIM decouples clients from microservices, adds a layer of security, simplifies client integration, and routes incoming requests based on path, method, headers or query parameters. Handling these concerns at the gateway means individual microservices do not each need to implement them separately.

When deciding how to deal with cross-cutting concerns, the central question is where the shared behavior should live. Keeping it inside each module risks duplication and tight coupling between components. Moving it into a shared layer, whether a gateway, middleware, a decorator or a filter, keeps business logic focused and makes the shared behavior easier to change in one place. The sources do not prescribe specific implementation mechanisms, so the choice depends on the architecture and tooling in use.

cross-filter-direction.desc: Cross filter direction is the Power BI relationship setting that controls whether filters flow from the one side to the many side only, or in both directions.

faq.a: It is a relationship setting that determines whether filters travel only from the one side to the many side (single) or in both directions (bidirectional).
faq.q: What is cross filter direction in Power BI?

faq.a: The two options are single, where filtering flows from the one side to the many side, and bidirectional, where filtering flows in both directions.
faq.q: What are the available cross filter direction options?

cross-filter-direction.long:
Cross filter direction is a setting on relationships in Power BI data models. It determines how a filter applied to one table propagates to the table on the other end of the relationship. The setting has two options: single, where filters travel only from the one side to the many side, and bidirectional, where filters travel in both directions.

The setting is used when designing a data model to decide how slicers, visuals and other filter selections affect related tables. With a single direction, a selection on the one-side table narrows the many-side table, but a selection on the many-side table does not narrow the one-side table. With a bidirectional direction, the filter also passes back from the many side to the one side.

Choosing between the two options is a modeling decision that affects which values appear in reports and how the relationships between tables behave. Because the setting is defined per relationship, it can differ from one relationship to another within the same model.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this concept, and no further relations are recorded for it in the knowledge base.

cross-tenant-access-settings.desc: Cross-tenant access settings in Microsoft Entra control inbound and outbound collaboration with other Entra organizations and whether their MFA and device claims are trusted.

faq.a: They control inbound and outbound B2B collaboration and B2B direct connect with other Microsoft Entra organizations, and whether Conditional Access trusts MFA, compliant-device and hybrid-joined claims from a partner's home tenant.
faq.q: What do cross-tenant access settings control?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, B2B collaboration is on by default, B2B direct connect is blocked, and claims from other organizations are not trusted. Organization-specific settings can override these defaults for individual partners.
faq.q: What are the default cross-tenant access settings?

faq.a: Trust settings and targeted rules for users, groups or applications need Microsoft Entra ID P1, and B2B direct connect needs it in both tenants.
faq.q: Do cross-tenant access settings require a specific license?

cross-tenant-access-settings.long:
Cross-tenant access settings are a set of Microsoft Entra controls that let an organization manage how it collaborates with other Microsoft Entra organizations and Azure clouds. They apply to two collaboration models, B2B collaboration and B2B direct connect, and they determine which users, groups and applications can reach resources in another tenant, and which of the organization's own resources partners can reach.

The settings are organized into inbound and outbound controls. Each direction can be applied to all users or limited to chosen users, groups and applications. Alongside these controls sit inbound trust settings. These decide whether Conditional Access in the resource tenant accepts claims issued in a partner's home tenant, specifically multifactor authentication (MFA), compliant-device and hybrid-joined claims. Without that trust, a partner user who has already completed MFA or signed in from a managed device may be asked to satisfy those requirements again in the tenant being accessed.

The configuration works in two layers. Default settings apply to every external organization. Organization-specific settings can then be added for individual partners, and these override the defaults for that partner. Per the Microsoft Learn overview, the out-of-the-box defaults are that B2B collaboration is on, B2B direct connect is blocked, and claims from other organizations are not trusted. Further options include automatic redemption of invitations, a configurable redemption order for identity providers, and controls for cross-tenant synchronization.

Several licensing and scope points affect planning. Trust settings and targeted rules for specific users, groups or applications require Microsoft Entra ID P1, and direct connect requires it in both tenants. Direct connect is not supported between clouds. The documentation also warns that blocking default access can interrupt business-critical access, and it advises planning changes together with business owners before applying them.

In practice, these settings sit close to Conditional Access. The M365.FM episode "Fix Conditional Access Loopholes in Microsoft 365" describes overlapping policies, for example one policy requiring controls while another blocks access from specific geographic locations. Such overlaps can block legitimate users or expose resources through unintended interactions. The episode recommends regularly reviewing cross-tenant access settings so that policies work together and the environment stays secure while user trust is preserved. The same episode lists frequent MFA prompts among the common causes of user frustration with Conditional Access, which is the situation that trust for partner MFA claims is designed to address.

The episode "Fix Microsoft Entra B2B Direct Connect Issues" treats the settings as part of troubleshooting and ongoing hygiene for cross-tenant chat and meetings. Its guardrails include using named locations or cross-tenant access settings to target Conditional Access precisely, keeping a partner registry that records domain, identity provider mode, Conditional Access posture and contact, and keeping a change log of identity provider changes, Conditional Access updates and Teams policy edits. It also suggests a quarterly health check covering federation tests, sync error review and a Conditional Access audit, and it names the success rate of external chat and meeting joins as a metric to watch.

Typical decisions around the settings include whether to leave B2B collaboration open by default or restrict it to named partners, whether to enable B2B direct connect for specific organizations, and whether to trust a partner's MFA and device claims or require them again locally. Because organization-specific entries override defaults, many tenants keep restrictive defaults and add partner-specific exceptions.

cryptographic-agility.desc: Cryptographic agility is the capability to discover, replace and evolve cryptographic algorithms across systems without destabilizing critical services.

faq.a: It is an organization's ability to change which cryptographic algorithms it relies on quickly and safely, and to adapt repeatedly as standards, threats and implementations evolve. The M365.FM episode describes it as a permanent operational discipline rather than a one-time migration.
faq.q: What is cryptographic agility?

faq.a: Post-quantum cryptography creates the immediate need to migrate away from algorithms such as RSA and ECC, while cryptographic agility provides the lasting capacity to adapt when cryptography changes again. Microsoft Learn presents agility as the foundation for becoming quantum-safe.
faq.q: How does cryptographic agility relate to post-quantum cryptography?

faq.a: With discovery: keeping an inventory of cryptographic dependencies and trust chains and building dependency maps to find vulnerable algorithms. The Microsoft Learn guidance then proceeds through strategy and governance, architecture, risk-ordered implementation, and operations with validation.
faq.q: Where does an organization start with cryptographic agility?

cryptographic-agility.long:
Cryptographic agility is the capability of an organization to discover, replace and evolve the cryptographic algorithms it depends on without destabilizing critical services. The Microsoft Learn planning article describes it as the ability to change which algorithms are relied on quickly and safely, and to do so repeatedly as standards, threats, implementations and the understanding of cryptanalysis change. The M365.FM episode "Cryptographic Agility for Post-Quantum Security" frames it as a permanent operational discipline rather than a one-time migration.

The topic has gained attention because of post-quantum cryptography. As quantum computing moves from theory toward reality, many organizations focus on replacing RSA and ECC with post-quantum algorithms. The episode, presented by Mirko Peters, argues that choosing a new algorithm is not enough. The real challenge is being able to adapt, replace and evolve cryptographic systems as threats and standards change. The Microsoft Learn page makes a similar point: post-quantum cryptography creates the immediate need to migrate, while cryptographic agility provides the lasting capacity to adapt when cryptography changes again. It is presented as the foundation for becoming quantum-safe.

In practice, cryptographic agility starts with discovery. The Microsoft Learn guidance describes keeping an inventory of enterprise cryptography and trust chains and building dependency maps, so that it is clear which systems use which algorithms and where vulnerable algorithms are in use. The episode likewise argues that organizations should begin inventorying cryptographic dependencies today, identify vulnerable systems and prepare migration strategies before regulatory requirements or technological breakthroughs force emergency action.

The Microsoft Learn article organizes the work into four steps. The first is strategy and governance. The second is architecture. The third is disciplined implementation, ordered by risk, business criticality and attack-path impact. The fourth is operations with validation. Typical activities include assessing vendor support for quantum-resistant options and planning phased migration waves with change windows that allow rollback. The page notes that the changes involved can range from configuration updates to new libraries, certificates, firmware or hardware, which is one reason a visibility-first approach matters: the effort differs widely between systems.

The central decision the concept raises is whether cryptography is treated as a fixed component or as something that is expected to change. A one-time migration to a new algorithm would leave an organization in the same position the next time standards or threats shift. Treating agility as an ongoing capability means maintaining the inventory, governance and operational processes so that later replacements can be carried out in a controlled way and without disrupting critical services.

The Microsoft Learn source is a conceptual planning article. It does not prescribe specific algorithms or technical implementation patterns, and this overview does not either. For readers following the M365.FM coverage, the episode "Cryptographic Agility for Post-Quantum Security" is the main reference on how cryptographic agility relates to post-quantum readiness and why the episode positions inventory and migration preparation as work to start before external pressure arrives.

csharp.desc: C# is a general-purpose, multi-paradigm programming language from Microsoft and the primary language of the .NET platform.

faq.a: C# is a general-purpose, multi-paradigm programming language from Microsoft. It is the primary language of the .NET platform.
faq.q: What is C#?

faq.a: C# is a programming language from Microsoft.
faq.q: Who develops C#?

faq.a: C# is the primary language of the .NET platform, so .NET applications are most commonly written in it.
faq.q: How does C# relate to .NET?

csharp.long:
C# is a general-purpose, multi-paradigm programming language from Microsoft. It is the primary language of the .NET platform, which means that applications built on .NET are most commonly written in C#.

As a general-purpose language, C# is not tied to a single kind of workload. Its multi-paradigm design allows developers to combine different programming styles within the same codebase. Within the Microsoft ecosystem, C# is typically encountered wherever .NET is used as the development foundation.

The knowledge base currently holds no linked topics, related entities or episode references for C#, so no further connections are documented here. This page will be extended as related content on M365.FM is added.

custom-connectors.desc: Custom connectors wrap a REST or SOAP API, usually described with OpenAPI, so Logic Apps, Power Automate, Power Apps and Copilot Studio can call it with typed actions.

faq.a: A custom connector wraps a REST or SOAP API, typically described with OpenAPI, so that Azure Logic Apps, Power Automate, Power Apps and Copilot Studio can call it like a built-in connector. It offers typed actions and configured authentication.
faq.q: What is a custom connector?

faq.a: They are used when no built-in connector exists for a system, for example a line-of-business or legacy application, or when Dynamics 365 APIs need to be exposed to Power Platform. The M365.FM episodes also mention them for linking AI agents to systems without ready-made connectors.
faq.q: When are custom connectors used?

faq.a: The episode "Scale Azure Logic Apps Beyond Custom Connectors" describes a "custom connector trap" in which easy-to-build connectors lead to fragmentation, poor governance and hidden operational risk at scale. The Dynamics 365 episode adds that improper configuration can create security, performance and governance gaps.
faq.q: What risks do the M365.FM episodes associate with custom connectors?

custom-connectors.long:
A custom connector is a wrapper around a REST or SOAP API that makes the API usable inside the Microsoft low-code and integration stack. The API is typically described with OpenAPI. Once wrapped, Azure Logic Apps, Power Automate, Power Apps and Copilot Studio can call it in the same way as a built-in connector, with typed actions and configured authentication. Official documentation for the feature is published on Microsoft Learn under the connectors section.

The main purpose of a custom connector is to close gaps where no ready-made connector exists. A maker who needs live data from a line-of-business or legacy system, or from a third-party service, can describe that API once and then reuse it across apps, flows and agents instead of repeating raw HTTP calls. The description of the API defines the available operations and their inputs and outputs, and the authentication settings define how calls are secured. The episode "Build Secure Custom Connectors for Power Apps" walks through this idea step by step, covering authentication (including OAuth quirks), OpenAPI, error handling, throttling, testing and production hardening. It is aimed at app makers who need live data beyond Microsoft 365, and at Power Platform admins and architects connecting line-of-business and legacy systems.

Custom connectors also appear in scenarios around business applications. The episode "Expose Dynamics 365 APIs with Power Platform Custom Connectors" describes exposing Dynamics 365 APIs through custom connectors to enable integration between business applications, automation workflows and external systems. It points out that improper configuration can introduce security risks, performance issues and governance gaps, and it names permission management, environment isolation and monitoring as areas that need attention.

In agent scenarios, custom connectors are one way to link AI agents to systems without ready-made connectors. The episode "Azure Logic Apps for Multi-Agent AI Orchestration" lists custom connectors among best practices for agent integration. It describes them as a way to build tailored links for unique integration challenges so that agents can work with the systems a business uses.

The episodes also raise cautions about relying on custom connectors at scale. "Scale Azure Logic Apps Beyond Custom Connectors" argues that custom connectors are useful for quick wins but can create long-term architectural problems. The episode calls this the "custom connector trap": connectors are easy to build but hard to manage, and what feels like agility can turn into fragmentation, weak governance and hidden operational risk. It describes the hidden costs of custom integrations as an "API tax" and says that moving to a centralized automation platform such as Logic Apps Standard can reduce those costs. "Custom Connectors vs Model Context Protocol for Enterprise AI" takes a related line of criticism, questioning the managed connector as a foundation for enterprise integration and comparing it with the Model Context Protocol.

Taken together, the episodes treat custom connectors as a practical tool with clear strengths and clear limits. They are a fast way to expose an API to Power Platform, Logic Apps and Copilot Studio, provided that authentication, permissions, environment boundaries, monitoring and ownership are planned. Decisions around them usually concern whether a one-off connector is enough, whether a reusable and governed integration layer is needed, and whether newer approaches such as the Model Context Protocol fit AI-driven scenarios better.

custom-engine-agent.desc: A custom engine agent is a Microsoft 365 Copilot agent type in which the developer chooses the model and orchestrator instead of using Copilot's own orchestrator.

faq.a: It is a Copilot agent type in which the developer chooses the model and the orchestrator, in contrast to declarative agents that use Copilot's own orchestrator.
faq.q: What is a custom engine agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot?

faq.a: The episodes list Copilot Studio as the low-code option and Visual Studio Code with the Teams SDK or Visual Studio 2022 as pro-code options. The Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit is also mentioned as a way to build such agents.
faq.q: Which tools can be used to build a custom engine agent?

faq.a: The episodes give a legal research AI that integrates legal databases for case law analysis as an example for a custom engine agent, while a healthcare compliance assistant is paired with a declarative agent plus an API plugin.
faq.q: When is a custom engine agent used instead of a declarative agent?

custom-engine-agent.long:
A custom engine agent is a type of Microsoft 365 Copilot agent in which the developer selects the AI model and the orchestrator. This sets it apart from declarative agents, which run on Copilot's own orchestrator. In practice, a custom engine agent is used when a team wants full control over how requests are interpreted, which model produces answers, and how external data or actions are handled, while still making the result available inside the Microsoft 365 Copilot experience.

According to the episode "Extend Microsoft 365 Copilot with Agents, Plugins, and Connectors", a custom engine or custom engine agent plugs into the Copilot extensibility landscape as an external or hosted processing component. It can provide grounding, domain-specific reasoning, or actions. Developers can register a custom engine to surface specialized knowledge or run workflows, so that Copilot can call the engine and return its responses to the user. The episode places this within enterprise AI scenarios in which developers extend Microsoft 365 Copilot's capabilities, ground responses with organizational data, and let users take actions directly from Copilot chat or other Copilot experiences.

The tooling differs by skill level and agent type. The episode "Connect External Business Data with Microsoft 365 Copilot Connectors" lays out a comparison: for declarative agents, low-code options are Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio, while the pro-code option is Visual Studio Code with the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit. For custom engine agents, the low-code option listed is Copilot Studio, and the pro-code options are Visual Studio Code with the Teams SDK, or Visual Studio 2022. The same episode notes that plugins can be added to give Copilot new abilities or to connect to unique data, for instance through Microsoft Graph Connectors, so that Copilot can be tailored to tasks such as analyzing sales data, managing customer support, or accessing custom databases. The short description for this concept also mentions that a custom engine agent can be built with the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit.

The episode "Build Custom Microsoft 365 Copilot Plugins" gives example scenarios that show where each approach fits. A Copilot connector suits customer information integration, for example a Salesforce connector for quick access to customer data. A declarative agent with an API plugin suits a case such as a healthcare compliance assistant. A custom engine agent is listed for a legal research AI that integrates legal databases for case law analysis. The same episode describes project templates as a way to start quickly and avoid setup mistakes, naming the Yeoman generator, Visual Studio, and the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit as tools that create the basic files and folders needed.

The term also appears in the context of Microsoft Teams. In the episode "Build Microsoft Teams Meeting Apps and Bots", a custom engine agent is listed among the main bot types for Teams meetings. It is described as using AI to perform automated tasks, understanding natural language, and being able to engage in conversations. The episode contrasts it with a conversational bot that simulates interactions through text and interactive cards, a notification bot that sends alerts in channels or chats, and a workflow bot that automates business processes by managing tasks.

When deciding between agent types, the sources point to a few considerations. A declarative agent relies on Copilot's own orchestrator and is configured rather than coded around a chosen model. A custom engine agent is the option when the developer needs to bring their own model and orchestration logic, for example for domain-specific reasoning over specialized data. The choice of low-code or pro-code tooling then follows the team's skills: Copilot Studio on the low-code side, and Visual Studio Code with the Teams SDK or Visual Studio 2022 on the pro-code side, with the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit also named as a build option.

custom-pages.desc: Custom pages are a page type in Power Apps model-driven apps that bring canvas-app design and Power Fx into a model-driven app as full pages, dialogs or side panes.

faq.a: Custom pages are a page type in Power Apps model-driven apps. They bring canvas-app design and Power Fx into a model-driven app.
faq.q: What are custom pages in Power Apps?

faq.a: A custom page can be used as a full page, as a dialog, or as a side pane within a model-driven app.
faq.q: How can a custom page be displayed in a model-driven app?

faq.a: Custom pages are part of Power Apps, specifically its model-driven apps.
faq.q: Which product do custom pages belong to?

custom-pages.long:
Custom pages (Power Apps) are a page type available in Power Apps model-driven apps. They bring canvas-app design capabilities and Power Fx into a model-driven app, which allows makers to build page content with the canvas approach while keeping it inside a model-driven app.

A custom page can be used in different ways within a model-driven app: as a full page, as a dialog, or as a side pane. This gives makers a choice of how the page is presented to users, depending on the scenario the app needs to support.

Custom pages are part of Power Apps. They connect two app-building approaches within the platform: the structured, data-driven layout of model-driven apps and the flexible, design-focused authoring of canvas apps, with Power Fx used as the formula language for logic.

The Microsoft Learn documentation for model-driven apps includes an overview of this page type. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

customer-managed-keys.desc: Customer-managed keys (CMK) are encryption keys a customer creates and controls, usually in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM, to protect data keys in a cloud service.

faq.a: CMK are encryption keys that a customer creates and controls, typically in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM, to protect the keys that encrypt their data in a cloud service, instead of relying on provider-managed keys.
faq.q: What are customer-managed keys (CMK)?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, the key must be in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM with soft delete and purge protection, and it must be an RSA or RSA-HSM key of an allowed size. A managed identity needs permission on the key.
faq.q: What must be in place to use CMK with Azure Storage?

faq.a: For Azure Storage, covered operations fail with a forbidden error for all users when the key is disabled.
faq.q: What happens if a customer-managed key is disabled?

customer-managed-keys.long:
Customer-managed keys (CMK) are encryption keys that a customer creates and controls, typically in Azure Key Vault or Azure Key Vault Managed HSM, to protect the keys that encrypt their data in a cloud service. They are used instead of relying on provider-managed (platform-managed) keys, and they give the customer more control over how data is protected at rest.

Microsoft Learn documentation for Azure Storage shows how this works in practice. The customer's own key does not encrypt the data directly. It protects the account encryption key, which in turn encrypts the data in a storage account. The customer key must be held in Azure Key Vault or Azure Key Vault Managed HSM, which can be in a different tenant, region or subscription than the storage account. A managed identity is granted permission on the key. Azure Storage authenticates with Microsoft Entra ID, wraps the account encryption key with the customer key, and unwraps it when data is read or written.

The documentation also names several requirements and operational duties. The key vault needs soft delete and purge protection enabled. The key must be an RSA or RSA-HSM key of an allowed size. For Azure Storage, Blob Storage and Azure Files are always protected, whereas protection for queues and tables is optional and is chosen when the account is created. Rotation is the customer's responsibility, handled through a Key Vault policy; when no key version is pinned, Storage checks daily for new versions. Disabling the key causes covered operations to fail with a forbidden error for all users, which makes access to the key a control point over access to the data. Key Vault and Managed HSM also carry their own costs, which belong in any decision about adopting CMK.

Typical decisions around CMK involve weighing the extra control against the extra responsibility. Using CMK means the organization must manage key lifecycle, rotation, permissions and availability of the vault, since a disabled or unavailable key affects the data it protects. Organizations usually consider it when compliance, regulatory or sovereignty requirements call for more direct control over encryption than platform-managed keys provide.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Bicep Fundamentals for Production Projects" lists CMK among security practices for production deployments. Its recommendations include using Private Endpoints for services such as Storage Accounts and SQL Databases instead of public IPs, enabling diagnostic logging through Azure Monitor, enforcing compliance with Azure Policy, and enabling encryption at rest with Customer-Managed Keys for greater control rather than relying on platform-managed keys.

The episode "Microsoft 365 Data Sovereignty Beyond Technical Custody" places CMK in a data sovereignty checklist. Under data protection and controls, it recommends ensuring encryption at rest and in transit and evaluating customer-managed keys and HSM options within the required region. The same list covers DLP policies tailored to classification and residency, retention and records management rules, and sensitivity labels with Microsoft Purview and Azure Information Protection. In this context CMK is one control among several that support sovereignty requirements, alongside legal and contractual mapping of applicable laws and regulations.

customer-segment.desc: A customer segment is a group of customers chosen by rules on profile details, activities and measures, updating automatically as customer data changes.

faq.a: A customer segment is a group of customers selected by rules based on profile details, activities and measures. It updates automatically as customer data changes.
faq.q: What is a customer segment?

faq.a: The documentation lists a quick segment with a single operator, the segment builder for complex rules, an AI-based search for similar customers, suggested segments, and segments built from behavioral data in Customer Insights - Journeys.
faq.q: How are segments created in Dynamics 365 Customer Insights?

faq.a: A rule contains one or more conditions, and each condition consists of an attribute, an operator and a value. Rules can be nested as subrules, and their position and nesting controls the AND/OR logic.
faq.q: How do rules work in the segment builder?

customer-segment.long:
A customer segment is a group of customers selected by rules based on profile details, activities and measures. Because the selection is rule-driven, the group updates automatically as the underlying customer data changes. In Dynamics 365 Customer Insights, a segment groups customers according to demographic, transactional or behavioral attributes. Customer or contact profiles that satisfy the filters of the segment definition become its members.

Segments are used to find target audiences. According to the Microsoft Learn documentation on segments in Dynamics 365 Customer Insights, typical uses are marketing campaigns, sales activities and customer support actions. Instead of maintaining a list of customers by hand, a team defines the criteria once and the membership follows the data. This is the core idea behind the concept: the definition stays stable while the members change.

Several ways of creating a segment are described in the documentation. A quick segment uses a single operator and suits simple selections. The segment builder handles more complex rules. An AI-based search can be used to find customers similar to a given group, and suggested segments are offered as a starting point. Segments can also be built from behavioral data in Customer Insights - Journeys. Which method fits depends on how complex the selection logic needs to be and whether the criteria are already known.

In the segment builder, a rule contains one or more conditions, and rules can be nested as subrules. Each condition consists of an attribute, an operator and a value. For example, a condition compares a profile attribute against a given value using a chosen operator. The position and nesting of rules controls the AND/OR logic, so the way rules are grouped determines whether a customer must meet all conditions or any of them. A relationship path links related tables to the unified customer table and decides which attributes can be used in a condition. Designers therefore need to consider how data tables are connected to the unified customer profile when planning a segment.

The documentation also notes that service limits apply to segments, and that usage tracking is available only for certain segment types. These points matter when planning how many segments to create and how to monitor where they are used.

The topic also appears in the M365.FM episode "Extend Copilot in Dynamics 365 for CRM and ERP". In that episode, customer segment data is mentioned in the context of Dynamics 365 Customer Service. The episode says that Copilot and AI agent capabilities give support agents suggested replies, knowledge article recommendations and case summarization, and that by analyzing historical tickets and customer segment data, Copilot assists agents in delivering faster, more consistent customer experiences. The episode also says that Copilot can pull in Dynamics 365 Customer Insights and customer data platform information to personalize responses and recommend tailored offers.

Taken together, a customer segment links data and action. The rules define who belongs to the group, the automatic updates keep the group current, and the resulting audience can feed marketing, sales and customer support work. Choosing the right creation method, designing the rule logic carefully and respecting the service limits are the main practical decisions around the concept.

d365-data-entities.desc: Data entities in Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations wrap business data from several tables into one view for OData, data management and Excel.

faq.a: A data entity is an abstraction that wraps a business concept in a de-normalized view, combining data from a main table and its related tables. It is exposed through OData, data management and Excel.
faq.q: What is a data entity in Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations?

faq.a: They can be exposed as OData services, for example for Office integration, or used asynchronously through the data management pipeline for file-based or recurring integrations. Azure Logic Apps and Microsoft Excel can work with entities as well.
faq.q: How can data entities be accessed?

faq.a: The documentation notes name five categories: parameter, reference, master, document and transaction.
faq.q: Which categories of data entities exist?

d365-data-entities.long:
Data entities in Dynamics 365 are abstractions in Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations that expose business data through OData, data management and Excel. According to the documentation notes provided, a data entity abstracts the physical database tables and wraps a business concept in a de-normalized view. Each row of such a view combines data from a main table and its related tables. A customer entity, for example, merges several directory, customer and address tables into a single, easier to handle record. The concept is also known as D365 data entities, OData entities or, in German, Datenentitäten.

The purpose of data entities is to read, import and integrate records such as customers, vendors or orders without requiring direct work against the underlying table structure. They replace older concepts such as AXD, DIXF entities and aggregate queries with one concept that bundles business logic for import and export, integration and programmability. Because application code and integrations work against the entity rather than the physical tables, entities also insulate consumers from changes to those tables between versions.

Entities fall into five categories: parameter, reference, master, document and transaction. This classification helps to decide what kind of data an entity represents, for instance configuration values, shared reference data, master records or business documents. In application lifecycle scenarios, data entities carry configuration data and support data migration. The documentation notes that posted transactions are usually excluded or migrated only in summary form, which is a relevant point when a migration is planned.

There are two main ways to use entities. They can be exposed as OData services, for example for Office integration, so that other applications or Microsoft Excel can read and write records directly. Alternatively, they can be used asynchronously through the data management pipeline for file-based or recurring integrations. Azure Logic Apps can call entities via OData to read or write data as part of a workflow, and Microsoft Excel can use entities to view and edit data from a spreadsheet. The choice between the paths usually depends on whether the scenario needs interactive, record-level access or scheduled bulk loading.

A few practical details are mentioned in the documentation notes. Each entity needs a unique label, and the entity list must be refreshed manually after code deployments or configuration key changes. The page lists no license requirements.

Data entities are the usual starting point when an integration or a data migration with Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations has to be planned. They belong to the broader Dynamics 365 family and are one of the integration building blocks of Finance and Operations. No M365.FM episode is recorded for this topic, so this overview rests on the product documentation and the short description of the concept.

dapr.desc: Dapr (Distributed Application Runtime) is an open-source microservices runtime that runs as a sidecar and offers building blocks like state management and pub/sub messaging.

faq.a: Dapr, short for Distributed Application Runtime, is an open-source runtime for microservices. It runs as a sidecar next to an application and provides building blocks for common distributed-system needs.
faq.q: What is Dapr?

faq.a: Dapr provides building blocks such as state management, pub/sub messaging and service discovery.
faq.q: What building blocks does Dapr provide?

faq.a: Dapr runs as a sidecar, meaning it operates next to the application and supplies its capabilities to the service rather than being built into the application code.
faq.q: How does Dapr run alongside an application?

dapr.long:
Dapr (Distributed Application Runtime) is an open-source runtime for building microservices. It runs as a sidecar alongside an application and exposes common distributed-system capabilities as reusable building blocks, so that application code does not have to implement them directly.

Among the building blocks described for Dapr are state management, pub/sub messaging and service discovery. Because these capabilities are provided by the sidecar rather than embedded in the application, services can use them through a consistent interface while the runtime handles the underlying mechanics.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, Dapr is relevant to teams designing microservice-based and cloud-native applications. This page is a short reference entry; no related topics, episodes or official documentation links have been linked to it yet on M365.FM.

dark-data.desc: Dark data is information an organization stores but does not use for insight or decisions, often because it cannot be found, classified or governed.
