faq.a: Dark data is information an organization collects and stores but does not use for insight or decision-making, often because it cannot be found, classified or governed.
faq.q: What is dark data?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes point to poor or manual tagging, fragmented storage silos created by static quotas, and general document chaos such as duplicate or inconsistent data.
faq.q: What causes dark data in Microsoft 365?

faq.a: According to the episode "Real-Time AI Sensitivity Labeling in Microsoft Purview", Microsoft Purview uses semantic inference to discover dark data and categorize it based on real context rather than metadata alone.
faq.q: How can dark data be discovered?

dark-data.long:
Dark data is information that an organization collects and stores but does not use for insight or decision-making. In most cases the reason is not that the data is worthless, but that it cannot be found, classified or governed. Files sit in storage, hidden from the people and tools that could draw value from them, while still carrying cost and potential risk. In the Microsoft 365 context, the term comes up in discussions of governance, compliance, storage management and AI readiness.

The M365.FM episodes describe several ways dark data comes about. In "AI-Powered Metadata Classification for Microsoft 365 Governance", the argument is that manual tagging does not keep pace with growing data volumes. Errors, inconsistency and limited scalability are named as problems of manual processes, and the episode says poor tagging leads to dark data that hides important files from the organization. It adds that compliance suffers and AI tools become less effective when content is not properly described. The episode frames this as a shift away from dropdown-based tagging toward automation and AI, and states that such approaches can reduce human effort in data classification by up to 80%.

A second cause appears in "Shared Data Reservoirs for Multi-Tenant Microsoft 365". That episode explains how static quota models across SharePoint Online, OneDrive, Teams, Power Platform, Azure storage and multi-tenant workloads create fragmented infrastructure and dark data silos. It also criticizes what it calls a "buffer mentality", in which organizations keep adding extra capacity to avoid outages, leaving idle resources and inflated cloud spending. As an alternative, the episode discusses elastic shared data reservoirs, where centralized capacity replaces isolated storage silos and fixed allocations.

A third angle is discovery through classification. "Real-Time AI Sensitivity Labeling in Microsoft Purview" says that semantic inference lets AI understand the meaning and context of data rather than relying only on pattern matching. According to the episode, Microsoft Purview uses inference to discover dark data and categorize it based on real context, not just metadata. The episode states that this keeps classifications current as data changes and supports continuous compliance and protection for sensitive information. It also describes AI using natural language processing and computer vision to scan, classify and tag data automatically, which matters for large amounts of structured and unstructured content. It cites an accuracy improvement of 25-40% over manual tagging.

Dark data also overlaps with general document chaos. "Build Audit-Ready Document Management with SharePoint and Purview" lists shadowed and dark data alongside inaccurate or incomplete data, duplicate data and inconsistent data formats as common causes of document chaos. The episode links these issues to operational inefficiencies such as reduced trust in communications, missed marketing opportunities and flawed business strategies, and says organizations often spend up to 30% of their revenue managing these challenges. It also mentions the use of personal or unsecured corporate storage as part of the problem.

Taken together, the episodes treat dark data as a governance problem rather than only a storage problem. Typical decisions around it include whether to keep relying on manual metadata and dropdown tagging, whether to automate classification and sensitivity labeling, and whether to replace fixed storage quotas with shared, elastic capacity. The common thread is visibility: content that is findable, classified and governed can support compliance, search and AI features, while content that is not remains hidden and unused.

dashboards.desc: Dashboards are visual displays that bring key metrics onto one screen, often built in Excel or Power BI; M365.FM episodes discuss their limits and alternatives.

faq.a: A dashboard is a visual display that brings key information and metrics together on one screen. It is often built in tools such as Excel or Power BI.
faq.q: What is a dashboard?

faq.a: The episode "Replace Reactive Dashboards with Proactive Notifications" says dashboards depend on people checking them, which rarely happens consistently, so signals get missed and decisions are delayed. "Make Power BI Dashboards Drive Better Decisions" adds that missing planning and unclear objectives are a major cause.
faq.q: Why do dashboards often fail according to M365.FM?

faq.a: The episode "Replace Reactive Dashboards with Proactive Notifications" proposes a proactive notification model, where information reaches people instead of requiring them to check a dashboard.
faq.q: What alternative to dashboards do the episodes describe?

dashboards.long:
Dashboards are visual displays that bring key information and metrics together on one screen. They are commonly built in tools such as Excel or Power BI, and the idea behind them is simple: instead of searching through separate reports, a reader sees the most relevant figures in a single place and can judge the state of a process, project or business area at a glance.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, dashboards appear in several forms. Power BI is the most frequently mentioned tool for building them, and Excel remains another common option. The M365.FM episode "Customize Microsoft Viva Connections Dashboards" covers a different kind of dashboard, one that lives inside Teams. It describes how Viva Connections can serve as more than a SharePoint homepage when a solid foundation of navigation, targeting, permissions and mobile support is combined with SPFx web parts and Adaptive Card Extensions. According to the episode, these cards can surface live business data and actions, such as approving, submitting or tracking, and they are designed to be lightweight and to load progressively, which improves perceived performance across desktop, web and mobile clients. The episode also points to role-based personalization, performance discipline and a measured change plan as ways to drive adoption.

Much of the discussion on M365.FM concerns why dashboards often fail to deliver value despite being technically sound. The episode "Make Power BI Dashboards Drive Better Decisions" argues that Power BI projects frequently fall short because of missing planning rather than weak visuals. It cites a share of 60 to 70 percent of BI projects becoming expensive wallpaper, and describes three disciplined steps that separate strategic intelligence from dashboard vanity. A central recommendation is to align Power BI efforts with clear objectives from the start, so that the dashboard supports informed decisions and helps reach business goals instead of simply reporting activity.

A second line of argument concerns behavior. The episode "Replace Reactive Dashboards with Proactive Notifications" says the issue is not the data but the habit dashboards depend on: people have to check them actively, and in practice that rarely happens consistently. The episode describes dashboards as inherently reactive, since they show what has already happened and do not prompt action at the moment it matters. As a result, important signals are missed, decisions are delayed and problems continue unnoticed. The episode proposes a proactive notification model as the alternative, in which information reaches people instead of waiting for them to look.

The episode "Why Executives Ignore Power BI Dashboards" frames the problem as one of changing expectations. It states that dashboards did not fail but expired, because the business decision model changed while dashboards did not. The episode says executives are no longer asking for numbers; they are asking for answers, such as what changed and why it changed. In this view, visualization quality and adoption are not the core issue.

A further caution comes from "Fix Microsoft 365 Compliance Drift Beyond Green Dashboards". The episode follows an investigation into a Microsoft 365 tenant where compliance, retention, versioning and discovery all appeared healthy on dashboards, with policies applied and audit logs reconciled. It reframes green status as a color rather than proof of control and encourages measuring behavior, not just outcomes. For anyone designing or relying on dashboards, the episodes together suggest asking what decision a dashboard supports, whether people will actually look at it, and whether a status indicator reflects real control.

data-access-governance-reports.desc: Data access governance reports are SharePoint admin center reports that show overshared sites, permission gaps and sensitive content that may be exposed.

faq.a: They are opened in the SharePoint admin center under Reports and require SharePoint administrator rights. The requirements of SharePoint Advanced Management apply.
faq.q: Where are Data access governance reports found?

faq.a: Snapshot reports show the current state, such as site permissions, sensitivity labels on files and content shared through broad groups. Activity reports cover recent sharing link creation and sharing with Everyone except external users.
faq.q: What is the difference between snapshot reports and activity reports?

faq.a: No. Organizations with Microsoft 365 E5 alone get the reports but not snapshot reports or remediation actions. Those depend on SharePoint Advanced Management.
faq.q: Does Microsoft 365 E5 alone include everything?

data-access-governance-reports.long:
Data access governance reports (DAG) are a set of reports in the SharePoint admin center. They help administrators control access to SharePoint data by surfacing sites that may be overshared or hold sensitive content, so that suitable security and compliance policies can be applied. In short, the reports show where permissions do not match policy and where content may be more widely accessible than intended.

The reports are opened in the SharePoint admin center under Reports and need SharePoint administrator rights. They fall under the requirements of SharePoint Advanced Management and are unavailable for Microsoft 365 operated by 21Vianet. Organizations that hold Microsoft 365 E5 alone get the reports, but not snapshot reports or remediation actions. Without SharePoint Advanced Management, data collection must be switched on before the activity reports can be used.

There are two groups of reports. Snapshot reports show the current state of the environment: site permissions across the organization, site permissions for a given user, sensitivity labels applied to files, and content shared through broad groups such as Everyone except external users. Activity reports cover recent events, namely the creation of sharing links and sharing with Everyone except external users. Microsoft suggests running the snapshot reports first as a baseline and the activity reports afterwards for ongoing monitoring.

Typical situations for these reports include a review of oversharing before a wider rollout of content-based tools, a check of which sites expose content to large internal groups, and an assessment of where labeled or sensitive files sit in relation to site permissions. A per-user permission report answers the question of which sites a particular person can reach. Because the activity reports track recent sharing behavior, they support continuous monitoring after the initial baseline has been established and any clean-up has been done.

One limitation is noted in the documentation: reports may fail when concealed user, group and site names are enabled in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Administrators who see failures should check that setting. Licensing also shapes what is possible, since remediation actions and snapshot reports depend on SharePoint Advanced Management rather than on Microsoft 365 E5 alone.

In the M365.FM episode "What Is SharePoint Premium - Simply Explained", Data Access Governance reports appear within the Content Governance pillar of SharePoint Premium. The episode describes them as providing sitewide reports on overshared content and exposure levels. It lists them alongside restricted access control, which limits site access to specific security groups, the block download policy for view-only access, the inactive site policy that detects inactive sites for review and potential deletion, and site lifecycle governance. Together these features are presented as ways to keep documents in line with industry standards and organizational policies.

data-analyst.desc: A data analyst collects, cleans and analyses data and presents findings in reports and dashboards, for example with Power BI, to support business decisions.

faq.a: A data analyst collects, cleans and analyses data and presents the findings in reports and dashboards, for example with Power BI, to support decisions.
faq.q: What does a data analyst do?

faq.a: Power BI is named as an example for building the reports and dashboards in which a data analyst presents findings.
faq.q: Which Microsoft tool is named for presenting a data analyst's results?

faq.a: The episode "Automate Compliance Workflows with Microsoft Power Automate" says certification helps a person stand out in the growing field of data analytics and that employers value turning raw data into clear reports and dashboards.
faq.q: What do the M365.FM episodes say about careers in data analytics?

data-analyst.long:
A data analyst is a professional role that collects, cleans and analyses data and presents the findings in reports and dashboards so that decisions can rest on evidence rather than assumption. The role is also described with the terms Datenanalyst, Datenanalystin and data analytics. A common tool for presenting results is Power BI, which is named as an example in the role description. The core idea is a path from raw data to clear, usable information: gather the data, correct and prepare it, examine it for patterns, and communicate what it shows.

In practice, the work covers several connected steps. Data has to be collected from the sources where it lives, then cleaned so that errors, gaps and inconsistencies do not distort the results. The prepared data is then analysed to find trends and answer business questions. Finally, the findings are turned into reports and dashboards that colleagues and decision makers can read without needing to handle the underlying data themselves. This presentation step is what separates analysis that stays on a single desk from analysis that actually informs an organisation.

The role appears in several M365.FM episodes, mostly as part of the wider data analytics field rather than as the main subject. The episode "Automate Compliance Workflows with Microsoft Power Automate" discusses certifications and lists roles that work with data, among them Data Scientist and Business Intelligence Analyst, the latter described as analysing data to help businesses make informed decisions. The episode says that a certification helps a person stand out in the growing field of data analytics, and that employers value the ability to turn raw data into clear reports and dashboards. It also notes that such skills open doors to roles that influence strategy and business growth, and advises planning a certification path around current skills and career goals. According to the episode, fundamentals certifications take about 1 to 2 weeks to prepare, associate certifications 4 to 6 weeks, and expert-level certifications longer.

Data analytics as a discipline is also referenced in the episode "Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse - Simply Explained", where it appears alongside real-time intelligence as capabilities that become available once an account for Microsoft Fabric has been created. The episode stresses checking the supported regions before creating an account, since availability depends on the region. In "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD", Microsoft Fabric is characterised in a comparison table as a platform for data analytics and unified control, linked to either GitHub or Azure DevOps. This is relevant to analysts because the reports and data items they build can be managed in a repository, which matters when several people work on the same analytical content.

The broader theme of using data to guide decisions comes up in other episodes as well. "Build Safe Guardrails for Microsoft 365 Copilot" recommends leveraging data analytics to make informed decisions, using real-time insights to optimise workflows and identify trends that drive growth, together with regular audits and strict access controls to protect sensitive data. "Public vs Hybrid vs Multi-Cloud Azure Architecture" lists big data analytics as a cloud use case, in which cloud computing power is used to analyse large datasets for insights and improved decision-making. Taken together, these references show that the work of a data analyst sits within a wider environment of platforms, security practices and cloud capacity.

Typical decisions around the role include which tool to use for reporting, how to keep data trustworthy through cleaning and access control, and how to build skills through certification. The sources describe the role at a general level and do not set out a detailed tool stack, a salary range or a formal career ladder, so these points are left open here. What the material does establish is the purpose of the role: to make data understandable, to present it in reports and dashboards such as those built with Power BI, and to support decisions with the results.

data-classification.desc: Data classification is the practice of categorizing data by sensitivity or business value so that protection policies such as DLP can target the right content.

faq.a: Data classification is the practice of identifying and categorizing data by sensitivity or business value, for example with sensitive information types and labels. The results let protection policies such as DLP target the data that matters.
faq.q: What is data classification?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes describe data classification and labeling as fundamental components of Microsoft Purview Information Protection, alongside automatic protection measures. They also list sensitive data classification among the key Purview features for data governance.
faq.q: How does data classification relate to Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: According to the episode with Åsne Holtklimpen, Copilot uses data classification to identify sensitive data and apply protection. Labeled files and emails let Copilot respect access rules, which supports compliance.
faq.q: Why does data classification matter for Microsoft Copilot?

data-classification.long:
Data classification is the practice of identifying and categorizing data according to its sensitivity or business value. Typical tools for this are sensitive information types and labels. The purpose is practical: once data is classified, protection policies such as data loss prevention (DLP) can focus on the content that matters instead of treating every file and message the same way. In the Microsoft ecosystem the concept is closely tied to Microsoft Purview, where classification and labeling are described as fundamental components of the information protection capabilities.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Purview Information Protection - Simply Explained" presents data classification and labeling as core features that help organizations identify and manage sensitive information. The episode groups these capabilities with automatic protection measures and says they help keep sensitive information secure across various platforms, including data stored outside Microsoft 365. In this view, classification is the starting point: a label or a detected information type tells downstream controls what level of protection a piece of data needs.

The episode "Microsoft Purview - Simply Explained" places classification within the wider field of data governance. It lists sensitive data classification next to automated data discovery and role-based access controls as key features that improve data visibility and security. The episode also recommends establishing clear governance objectives, engaging stakeholders early and regularly reviewing governance policies as part of a successful implementation. Classification is therefore treated as one element of a governance program rather than a one-time task.

A recurring theme in the episodes is the limit of manual work. "Real-Time AI Sensitivity Labeling in Microsoft Purview" says that manual tagging is outdated and covers only a small portion of data, which leaves security gaps. The episode describes real-time AI classification that applies security labels to data instantly, saving time, reducing manual analysis and helping organizations handle large amounts of unstructured data. According to the episode, this makes governance scale and lets security oversight become faster and more responsive.

Classification also matters for AI assistants. In "Microsoft Copilot Security Readiness with Åsne Holtklimpen [MVP-MCT]", the show notes say Microsoft Copilot uses data classification to identify sensitive data and apply protection. Files and emails are labeled so that Copilot respects access rules, which keeps sensitive content secure and supports compliance. The same episode ties readiness to strong governance, clear permissions, user education, cleaning up data and setting up policies. The episode "Secure Microsoft Copilot with Entra ID and Zero Trust" adds that users should be educated on data classification and secure sharing practices to reduce the risk of data leaks, alongside periodic access reviews for least privilege access.

Taken together, the sources describe a consistent pattern. Data is first discovered and categorized, labels or information types are applied, and policies such as DLP then act on those categories. Automation helps cover the volume of data that manual tagging cannot reach, while user awareness and governance reviews keep the approach current. The decisions around data classification usually involve which categories an organization needs, how much to automate, and how classification results feed into access control, sharing rules and AI tooling.

data-contract.desc: A data contract is a written, versioned agreement defining what a data signal means, how its records are formed, and how receiving systems respond to non-conforming records.

faq.a: A data contract is a written, versioned agreement that defines what a data signal means, how its records are formed and what receiving systems should do when records do not meet the agreement.
faq.q: What is a data contract?

faq.a: According to the episode "Connect ERP, MES, and IoT — Without Replacing Anything", technical integration answers whether data can move, while a business data contract defines what the message means, who owns the field, allowed values and how late arrivals are handled.
faq.q: How does a data contract differ from technical integration?

faq.a: They are discussed for managing OT, ERP, MES and Fabric interfaces, for classifying connectors under DLP policies with limits such as labels, volume caps and retention, and for documenting per-solution requirements like connectors, permissions and feature flags in Power Platform deployments.
faq.q: Where do data contracts appear in the M365.FM episodes?

data-contract.long:
A data contract is a written, versioned agreement that defines what a data signal means, how its records are formed and what receiving systems should do when records do not meet the agreement. It turns implicit assumptions between a data producer and its consumers into an explicit, reviewable artifact that can change over time through versions.

The concept addresses a gap between technical integration and shared meaning. One M365.FM episode, "Connect ERP, MES, and IoT — Without Replacing Anything", frames the distinction this way: technical integration answers whether data can move, while a business data contract dictates what the message means, who owns the field, which values are allowed, and how late arrivals are handled. According to the episode, a misconfigured mapping that silently alters an asset ID or a unit of measurement can run for weeks and generate confident nonsense. A contract gives the parties a reference point against which such drift can be detected and discussed instead of going unnoticed.

The same episode ties the idea to protecting system boundaries. Data platforms and low-code applications, it says, should not become shadow systems in which users freely alter live production orders or inventory balances outside approved workflows. A contract that names ownership and allowed values supports that boundary by stating who may define or change a field and which workflows are approved.

A second episode, "Your Machine Data Never Becomes a Decision. Here's the Missing Pipeline.", places data contracts in the context of a connected factory. It argues that such a project should begin close to the machine, at the edge, where the first trustworthy fact appears, rather than with a dashboard requirement. The interfaces between OT, ERP, MES and Fabric, according to the episode, should be managed as data contracts. In this reading, each hand-off between the shop floor, business systems and the analytics platform has an agreement that describes the signal and the expected behavior of the receiver.

The term also appears in the Power Platform and governance episodes as a way of documenting expectations around a solution or a data flow. In "DLP Policies for Microsoft Fabric and Power Platform", attaching a data contract is listed as part of classifying connectors, alongside ownership and business justification. In that episode the contract covers allowed labels, volume caps, retention and a revocation path, and is paired with re-certifying connectors quarterly or when scope changes. Here the agreement describes what a connector or flow is permitted to do with data, not only how the data is structured.

In "Azure DevOps Pipelines for Power Platform Deployments", the episode recommends keeping a data contract for each solution. It lists required connectors, permissions and feature flags as the contents, and pairs the contract with environment configuration stored as code, such as environment variables, connection reference mappings and role assignments kept as JSON or YAML. The contract in this setting records what a solution needs in order to run in each environment, which helps pipelines fail early when a requirement such as a connection reference is unresolved.

Across these sources, the common elements of a data contract are a clear description of meaning, named ownership, allowed values or limits, and a defined response when records or requests fall outside the agreement. Versioning allows the agreement to evolve while producers and consumers stay aligned. Typical decisions around a data contract include who owns each field, what counts as a valid record, how late or malformed data is treated, and how often the agreement is reviewed.

data-entropy.desc: Data entropy describes the gradual degradation of data quality over time, appearing as duplicates, outdated records and conflicting versions of the truth across systems.
data-entropy.long:
Data entropy is the gradual degradation of data quality over time. It typically shows up as duplicate entries, records that are no longer current, and conflicting versions of the same information held in different systems.

The term is used to describe how data tends to become less reliable the longer it is stored, copied and modified without consistent upkeep. Because the same information can exist in several places, changes made in one system may not be reflected in another, which leads to competing versions of the truth. People searching for the term are usually trying to understand why data that was once accurate becomes harder to trust, and what the visible symptoms look like in practice.

In a Microsoft-focused context, the concept is relevant wherever organizations keep information across multiple applications and repositories. The same underlying idea applies to any environment where data is created, duplicated and left to age: quality declines unless it is actively managed.

The available information on this topic does not include linked products, related topics or specific episodes, so this page limits itself to the definition and the common symptoms: duplicates, outdated records and conflicting versions of data across systems.

data-governance.desc: Data governance is the set of rules, roles and tools that keep data classified, protected and used correctly, especially before and during Copilot and agent rollouts.

faq.a: It is the set of rules, roles and tools that keep data classified, protected and used correctly. In Microsoft 365 it relies on tooling such as Microsoft Purview, sensitivity labels and data loss prevention (DLP), combined with decisions about ownership and allowed use.
faq.q: What is data governance in the Microsoft context?

faq.a: Copilot and agents surface data that users can already reach, so gaps in classification, ownership or permissions become visible once they are enabled. Governance is therefore treated as essential both before and during deployment.
faq.q: Why does data governance matter for Copilot and agents?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Purview is a Trap: The Hard Truth About Data Governance", treating it as one is a mistake. Without a clear strategy, relying on the tool alone can lead to chaotic data environments and confusion over permissions.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Purview a complete data governance solution?

data-governance.long:
Data governance is the set of rules, roles and tools that keep an organization's data classified, protected and used correctly. It defines who owns data, how it is labeled, who may access it and which uses are allowed. In the Microsoft ecosystem the term is closely tied to Microsoft Purview, but it is broader than any single product. It is also known as Datengovernance, and the phrase "Data governance for Copilot" is used when the focus is on preparing data for AI assistants. Data governance sits under the wider concept of Governance.

The topic gained weight with the arrival of Copilot and agents. These tools work with whatever data a user can already reach, so weak classification, unclear ownership or loose permissions become visible quickly once AI features are switched on. For that reason data governance is treated as essential both before a Copilot or agent deployment and while it is running. The same thinking is carried into Copilot governance and AI governance, which apply governance principles to how AI tools are configured, monitored and used.

In practice, data governance combines organizational decisions with technical controls. On the organizational side it covers data ownership, quality rules, retention expectations and access models. On the technical side Microsoft Purview provides tooling for classification, retention and compliance. Sensitivity labels categorize data into classifications and can trigger protections such as encryption and access restrictions. Data loss prevention (DLP) adds rules that limit how sensitive content is shared or moved. Many of these rules exist to support Compliance with legal and regulatory requirements, which is why the two topics overlap.

M365.FM discusses the subject from several angles. The episode "Microsoft Purview is a Trap: The Hard Truth About Data Governance" warns that organizations often see Microsoft Purview as a complete data governance solution. According to the episode, relying on the tool without a clear strategy can result in chaotic data environments and confusion over permissions, and recognizing the limits of the tool is essential. The takeaway is that tooling supports governance but does not replace the decisions about ownership, rules and responsibilities.

"Microsoft Purview Data Governance for Information Architects" takes a more practical view and covers information architecture, Data Map, classification, retention, DLP and practical enterprise controls. This episode is aimed at people who design how information is structured and protected across an organization. "Microsoft Purview Information Protection - Simply Explained" describes a unified framework for data governance in which sensitivity labels categorize data, built-in classifiers detect sensitive content automatically, and real-time monitoring and compliance dashboards give insight into data protection.

The topic also appears outside the Microsoft 365 core. "Industrial Data Governance: Who Owns the Machine Data?" asks who owns machine data: the plant, IT or the supplier. It covers ownership, data contracts, quality rules, access models between OT, IT and suppliers, retention, and how Microsoft Purview fits in, with the aim of building a governance practice that plants accept instead of ignore. "The Death of the Chatbot: Why Your Dataverse Strategy Is Broken" lists strong data governance among its key takeaways, describing clear ownership rules that keep company information accurate and secure, alongside centralized control to protect against unmanaged AI tools and security risks.

Typical decisions around data governance include who owns which data, which classification scheme to use, which labels and DLP rules to apply, how long data is retained, and how these choices are checked once Copilot and agents are in use. The episodes consistently point to the same pattern: tools such as Microsoft Purview are enablers, and the results depend on a defined strategy, clear roles and rules that people actually follow.

data-gravity.desc: Data gravity describes how large accumulated data sets attract applications, services, copies and teams, which makes the data increasingly costly and slow to move.

faq.a: Data gravity is the tendency of large data sets to attract applications, services and other data, which makes the data harder and costlier to move as it grows. The term was coined by Dave McCrory in 2010.
faq.q: What is data gravity?

faq.a: Moving large data sets is slow and costly, cloud egress fees can make a migration uneconomical, and every dependent application needs extra work. Planning for the eventual data size and co-locating applications with their data are suggested responses.
faq.q: Why does data gravity matter for cloud migration?

faq.a: One episode uses it to judge what data should move upstream from manufacturing sites, while another cites it as a reason to host data and AI together in Azure to reduce latency and complexity.
faq.q: How do the M365.FM episodes relate data gravity to architecture choices?

data-gravity.long:
Data gravity is a concept from IT architecture describing how a large body of data attracts applications, services and other data, much as mass attracts objects in physics. The more data accumulates in one place, the more compute, tools, copies and teams gather around it, and the harder it becomes to relocate. Data lakes and data warehouses are commonly given as prime examples of systems that exhibit this effect.

The term was coined in 2010 by IT expert Dave McCrory. He later distinguished two forms: natural data gravity, which arises as data moves to the cloud, and artificial gravity, which is caused by outside forces such as legislation, throttling or manipulative pricing. In 2020 he released the Data Gravity Index, which measures the effect for large enterprises by metro area and industry.

The core mechanism is scale. Gravity grows with data volume, and moving large data sets is expensive and slow. As a result, applications and services tend to be placed near the data they use rather than the other way around. This has several practical consequences. Applications that sit far from their data face higher latency. Cloud egress fees can make a migration uneconomical. A migration also creates extra work for every application that depends on the data being moved. New gravity keeps appearing as AI, machine learning and edge sources generate additional data.

Typical decisions around data gravity concern where to place workloads and how much data to keep. Suggested responses include co-locating applications and data, applying strong governance and standards, integrating sources into a unified store, planning migrations for the eventual data size rather than the current one, and filtering or analyzing data at the edge before it travels upstream.

The M365.FM episode "Edge vs. Cloud in Manufacturing- Why the Wrong Architecture Costs You More" uses data gravity as one of several placement criteria. It asks how much data is created and what format it actually needs when moving upstream. The episode says that a design that collects everything forever ends up paying for every unnecessary byte more than once. In that discussion, data gravity is weighed alongside outage behavior, where a function should degrade gracefully and keep production running within defined local limits, and alongside scope, where a single sensor or asset favors local placement and broader fleet operations push work upstream.

The episode "Fix Common Azure AI Foundry Project Failures" treats data gravity as an argument for centralizing on one platform. It says that hosting data and AI in Azure reduces latency and complexity, and presents this as a reason teams choose Azure for larger AI projects. The same episode notes that Azure also supports on-premises, hybrid and edge inference, so AI can run where data is generated rather than moving the data.

Taken together, the two episodes show the concept from both directions: moving compute to where data already sits, and reducing or processing data near its source so that less of it needs to move at all.

data-historian.desc: A data historian is an industrial system that records process measurements over time and provides an interface for retrieving that recorded history.

faq.a: A data historian is an industrial system that records process measurements over time. It also provides an interface that makes the recorded history available for retrieval.
faq.q: What is a data historian?

faq.a: It captures process measurements as they occur and keeps them as a time-based record. Users or systems can then retrieve that history through the interface it offers.
faq.q: What does a data historian do?

data-historian.long:
A data historian is an industrial system that records process measurements over time and offers an interface to retrieve that history. It stores time-based values from a process so they can be looked up again later, rather than being limited to the current reading.

The core idea is the combination of two functions: capturing measurements as they occur and making the accumulated record accessible. This allows past process behavior to be reviewed alongside present values.

On M365.FM, the topic is catalogued as a concept within the Microsoft ecosystem knowledge base. No related products, linked topics or specific episodes are currently associated with this entry, so there is no further detail to add beyond the definition above.

data-lineage.desc: Data lineage is the trail of where data came from and how it moved and changed between systems, as covered in M365.FM episodes on Microsoft Fabric and Purview.

faq.a: Data lineage is the trail of where data came from and how it moved and changed between systems. It lets teams trace a result such as a report figure back through transformations to its source.
faq.q: What is data lineage?

faq.a: No. The episode "Microsoft Fabric Governance Beyond Data Lineage" says lineage only shows what already happened and does not prevent anything, so visibility should not be mistaken for control. Governance also needs preventive controls such as classification, ownership and access decisions.
faq.q: Is data lineage the same as data governance?

faq.a: The episodes describe Fabric as capturing lineage automatically across Data Factory, the Lakehouse, notebooks, SQL, Dataflows, semantic models and Power BI. Microsoft Purview is described as offering end-to-end lineage tracking as part of a broader governance and catalog capability.
faq.q: Where does lineage appear in Microsoft Fabric and Purview?

data-lineage.long:
Data lineage is the trail of where data came from and how it moved and changed between systems. It answers questions such as which source produced a figure in a report, which transformations were applied along the way, and which downstream assets depend on a given table. Teams use it to trace the origin of a number, to judge the impact of a change before making it, and to support the traceability that compliance work requires.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, lineage appears most prominently in Microsoft Fabric and Microsoft Purview. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Governance and Data Lineage" describes Fabric as capturing each hop of a data flow automatically, from ingestion through transformation to the report. It names Data Factory, the Lakehouse, notebooks, SQL and Dataflows, semantic models and Power BI as parts of that journey. The episode presents this automatic lineage, together with workspace-based permissions and the Purview enterprise catalog, as a way to turn opaque pipelines into auditable, end-to-end flows. It also cites the figure that over 65% of data leaders put governance at the top of their strategy, and attributes this to the episode itself rather than to an independent source.

Microsoft Purview is the second place where lineage shows up. In the episode "Microsoft Purview - Simply Explained", Purview is compared with Azure Data Catalog, which is described as having reached end of life and as limited to a metadata repository. In that comparison, Purview offers end-to-end data lineage tracking, automated data discovery, sensitive data classification and a federated governance model, while Azure Data Catalog does not provide lineage tracking. The same episode mentions concepts such as governance domains, data products and glossary terms, which place lineage inside a broader governance approach instead of treating it as a standalone feature.

Lineage also appears in smaller supporting roles. The episode "Build a Bronze-Silver-Gold Data Pipeline in Microsoft Fabric" lists data lineage among the governance tools in Fabric, next to information protection labels, as a means of managing data security in a layered pipeline. The episode "Stop Stale Power BI Reports with Strong Governance" links clear ownership and defined responsibilities to better lineage and to a culture of trust in analytics, which shows that lineage depends on people and process as well as on tooling.

A central point in the M365.FM material is the limit of what lineage can do. The episode "Microsoft Fabric Governance Beyond Data Lineage" argues that many organizations believe they have governance in Microsoft Fabric because they can see lineage. According to the episode, lineage only shows what already happened and does not prevent anything from happening, so visibility is often mistaken for control. The episode states that real governance requires a decision engine that can say no before data is accessed. It recommends using Microsoft Purview to ensure correct data usage, traceability, classification, ownership and accountability, and to serve as a centralized metadata catalog that standardizes definitions and improves understanding of data.

Taken together, the episodes treat data lineage as a necessary building block rather than a complete governance answer. It provides the audit trail and the impact view, while preventive controls such as access enforcement, classification and ownership decide who may use data in the first place. Typical decisions around it include whether to rely on the automatic lineage that Fabric records, whether to extend visibility across the wider estate through a Purview catalog, and how to pair lineage with ownership and policy so that the trail is backed by real control.

data-literacy.desc: Data literacy is the ability of people across an organization to ask precise questions of data and to read, interpret and question the answers they receive.

faq.a: Data literacy is the ability of people across an organization to ask precise questions of data and to read, interpret and question the answers they get.
faq.q: What is data literacy?

faq.a: The episode "Shadow Data Discovery and Governance with Microsoft Purview" lists data literacy and training as a governance program role that builds literacy programs, delivers role-based training and supports adoption. The Fabric governance episode also names enhancing data literacy as a trend.
faq.q: How does data literacy relate to governance according to the episodes?

faq.a: The episode on executive reporting says that questioning data reduces the risk of misinterpretation and over-reliance on dashboards. The in-flow learning episode says Copilot training often helps users ask better questions and interpret AI-generated insights.
faq.q: Why does data literacy matter for dashboards and Copilot?

data-literacy.long:
Data literacy is the ability of people across an organization to ask precise questions of data and to read, interpret and question the answers they get. It is a skill set for everyday work with information, not a product or a single tool. In the M365.FM episodes, the term appears in several contexts: governance programs, executive reporting, Copilot training and Power BI licensing and capacity decisions. In each of them, data literacy is described as a human capability that supports the technical setup rather than replacing it.

In the episode "Shadow Data Discovery and Governance with Microsoft Purview", data literacy appears as a named part of a governance program. The episode lists a group responsible for "Data Literacy and Training", covering training, employee development and communications. Its tasks are to build data literacy programs, deliver role-based training and support adoption. The episode advises involving these groups early, noting that clear communication and training help everyone understand their role in protecting data. Here data literacy is treated as one of several roles alongside the governance program owner and the executive sponsors, and as part of sustaining data security and compliance over time.

The episode "Sentiment Analysis for Executive Leadership Reporting" connects data literacy to organizational culture and to the risk of misleading dashboards. It says a healthy culture values transparency and encourages questions, and that leaders who model data literacy and invite questions build trust. According to the episode, a culture that prioritizes data literacy and encourages questioning of data can reduce the risk of misinterpretation, while the absence of these cultural elements can lead to over-reliance on dashboards and flawed decision-making. The point made is that decisions should rest on reliable information, and that people need the habit of questioning what a dashboard shows.

In "Microsoft Fabric Governance to Prevent Cost and Metric Chaos", data literacy is listed among the trends in data governance. The episode names a focus on enhancing data literacy and democratizing data access within organizations, next to topics such as data ethics, privacy regulations like GDPR and CCPA, the integration of ESG factors and the use of AI technologies to automate governance tasks. In this framing, wider access to data and the skills to use it responsibly are seen as developments that go together.

The episode "Replace Traditional M365 Training with In-Flow Learning" links data literacy to Microsoft 365 Copilot training. It states that effective Copilot training often improves employees' data literacy because users learn to ask better questions and to interpret AI-generated insights, which increases trust in and usefulness of analytics. The same episode says that off-the-shelf training yields limited gains, while tailored role-based scenarios and organization-specific prompts increase real-world results. This matches the definition: asking precise questions and judging the answers are the core of the skill, and AI assistants make that practice part of daily work for non-technical teams such as marketing, HR and legal.

In "Choose the Right Power BI License and Capacity", data literacy appears in the discussion of a data mesh approach. The episode says a data mesh can reduce the divide between IT and business expectations and encourages a culture of data literacy and shared accountability, which it describes as vital for long-term success. Its tip is to combine a strong governance framework with a data mesh approach, balancing control and flexibility so that users can explore and analyze data with confidence.

Taken together, the episodes treat data literacy as a recurring condition for governance, reporting and analytics to work in practice. It shows up in role-based training and communication plans, in leadership behavior that invites questions, and in the way people phrase prompts and read results from AI tools and dashboards. The sources do not define a formal maturity model or measurement method for it, so the episodes describe it mainly through the activities and cultural conditions that support it.

data-management-framework.desc: Data management framework (DIXF) is the data import/export framework in Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations for bulk loading and extracting data through data entities.
data-management-framework.long:
The Data management framework (DIXF), short for the data import/export framework, is a feature of Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations. It is used for the bulk import and export of data and works through data entities, which define the data that is moved in or out of the system.

DIXF is well suited for master data and for batch loads, where larger volumes of records are transferred in a single run. It is not intended for real-time integration, so scenarios that depend on immediate, record-by-record data exchange call for a different approach.

The topic is relevant for anyone planning data migration, initial data loads or recurring bulk transfers into or out of Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations. Understanding the framework's batch-oriented character helps in choosing between bulk data management and other integration patterns.

No specific episodes of M365.FM are linked to this term at the moment, and no further related topics are recorded here.

data-mesh.desc: Data mesh is a data architecture approach that gives business domains ownership of their data while a platform team provides shared infrastructure and governance.

faq.a: Data mesh is a data architecture approach in which ownership of data is distributed to business domains, while a platform team provides shared infrastructure and governance.
faq.q: What is data mesh?

faq.a: According to the episode "Use Microsoft Fabric Domains for Data Mesh Governance", Fabric domains group workspaces and data assets logically and support a data mesh architecture with clear boundaries for access management and responsibility.
faq.q: How does data mesh relate to Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: No. The episode with Amit Chandak says Fabric does not automatically mean one large centralized environment. A centralized setup can suit smaller organizations, while larger ones may benefit from domain-oriented architectures.
faq.q: Does Fabric require a data mesh?

data-mesh.long:
Data mesh is a data architecture approach in which ownership of data is distributed to business domains, while a platform team provides shared infrastructure and governance. Instead of collecting all data in one central environment managed by a single team, the people closest to a subject area, such as sales, finance or purchasing, take responsibility for the data they produce and use. The central platform function does not own the data itself. Its role is to supply the common tooling and the rules that keep the whole landscape consistent and secure.

The concept is used to scale analytics and AI without losing control. When many teams need data and a single central group becomes a bottleneck, distributing ownership lets each domain manage its own data quality and collaboration, while shared governance keeps access, compliance and data integrity under common standards. Decisions around data mesh typically concern where ownership should sit, how much should remain centralized, and which governance mechanisms apply across domains.

The M365.FM episode "Use Microsoft Fabric Domains for Data Mesh Governance" connects the idea to Microsoft Fabric. According to the episode, Fabric domains create logical groupings of workspaces and data assets, support a data mesh architecture, and let organizations manage, govern and secure data in a way that matches how the company works. Domains also create clear boundaries for data access management and responsibility, which reflects the core mesh principle of assigning accountability to the owning area.

The episode "Microsoft Fabric End-to-End: From Raw Data to Business Decisions with Amit Chandak [MVP]" discusses the choice between centralized data and a data mesh. It says that Fabric does not automatically mean putting everything into one large centralized analytics environment. For smaller organizations a centralized architecture may still work well. As organizations grow, the episode describes increasing value in domain-oriented architectures where areas such as sales, finance and purchasing have their own workspaces and responsibilities, while the resources still sit within a common Fabric storage architecture. This is presented as particularly relevant when organizations want to reduce unnecessary duplication while maintaining security and organizational boundaries.

Governance is a recurring theme. In "Copilot Cowork with Vesa "Vesku" Nopanen [MVP]", a data mesh strategy is listed as a practice that enables scaling analytics and AI while maintaining ownership and governance. The same episode points to Microsoft Purview for monitoring data attributes for accuracy and completeness, and to compliance with regulations such as GDPR and CDPA. The episode also notes that security risks increase as AI systems gain access to more information, which makes consistent governance across domains important.

Two further episodes link data mesh to self-service. "Build a Bronze-Silver-Gold Data Pipeline in Microsoft Fabric" describes how simplifying data interactions lets business users perform self-service data activities with less reliance on technical teams, promoting a culture of data mesh where collaboration and accessibility thrive, with Microsoft Purview supporting consistent governance and compliance. "Choose the Right Power BI License and Capacity" states that adopting a data mesh approach allows teams to manage their own data, improving quality and collaboration, and pairs this with strong governance frameworks and monitoring of adoption and business outcomes in self-service BI initiatives.

Taken together, the episodes treat data mesh as a combination of decentralized ownership and centralized guardrails. Domains hold responsibility for their data, a platform team supplies shared infrastructure, and governance tooling keeps access, quality and compliance consistent across the organization.

data-partitioning.desc: Data partitioning divides a table or data set into separate segments, for example by date or region, so queries scan only relevant slices and data stays manageable.

faq.a: Data partitioning splits a table or data set into separate segments, for example by date or region, so queries only scan the relevant slices. The Azure Architecture Center describes it as physically dividing data into separate data stores.
faq.q: What is data partitioning?

faq.a: The Azure Architecture Center guidance names horizontal partitioning (sharding), where each shard holds a subset of rows with the same schema, vertical partitioning, where fields are split by usage pattern, and functional partitioning, where data is grouped by bounded context or business area.
faq.q: What are the main partitioning strategies?

faq.a: The guidance lists slower cross-partition queries, limited cross-partition transactions handled in application logic, referential integrity left to the application, eventual consistency, and complex rebalancing, backup and restore.
faq.q: What are the drawbacks of data partitioning?

data-partitioning.long:
Data partitioning is the practice of dividing a table or data set into separate segments, for example by date, region or another attribute, so that queries only need to scan the relevant slices. The Azure Architecture Center guidance defines it as physically dividing data into separate data stores and distinguishes it from SQL Server table partitioning. The goals named there are scalability, performance, security, operational flexibility, matching data stores to usage patterns, and availability.

The guidance describes three main strategies. In horizontal partitioning, also called sharding, every shard has the same schema but holds a subset of the rows. In vertical partitioning, fields are split according to how they are used, so that frequently accessed fields are kept apart from rarely accessed ones. In functional partitioning, data is grouped by bounded context or business area, for example separating data that belongs to different parts of an application. Which strategy fits depends on the access patterns, the volume of data and the way the workload is expected to grow.

The shard key is described as the most important design factor in a partitioning scheme. It determines which partition a record belongs to, and it is hard to change once the system is in operation. The guidance also points out that balanced access matters more than equal shard sizes: a partition that receives a disproportionate share of requests becomes a bottleneck even if its data volume is similar to the others. For this reason, partitioning should be considered early in the design rather than added late.

Partitioning also brings trade-offs. According to the Azure Architecture Center, queries that span several partitions are slower, and transactions across partitions are limited, so they must be handled in application logic. Referential integrity is left to the application, consistency is often eventual, and rebalancing, backup and restore become more complex. These costs are the main factors to weigh when deciding whether and how to partition.

Data partitioning appears in two M365.FM episodes in different contexts. In "Microsoft Fabric Digital Twin Builder Explained", fine-grained data partitioning is listed as one of the security features of the digital twin builder, alongside role-based access control and immutable data lineage. The episode describes it as a way to selectively expose insights that are relevant to each participant's operational role while keeping other information private, which ties partitioning to access control and not only to performance.

In "Vector Databases - Simply Explained", data partitioning is mentioned as a technique for dealing with scalability when large language models are integrated with vector databases. The episode says that the increased complexity of processing and comparing vectors can lead to performance degradation, and that techniques such as data partitioning and load balancing are needed to manage it. Together, the two episodes show the same idea used for access separation and for spreading load.

In practice, the decision around data partitioning usually involves choosing the partitioning dimension, such as time or geography, checking whether typical queries can be limited to a single partition, and planning for how the design will cope with changing data volumes. The guidance's warnings about cross-partition queries and rebalancing are a reminder that partitioning is a design decision with ongoing operational consequences, not only a tuning step.

data-plane.desc: The data plane is the system layer that carries out operational requests at scale, such as user interactions, flow runs and data transactions, unlike the control plane.

faq.a: The data plane executes operational requests at scale, such as user interactions, flow runs and data transactions. The control plane defines policy and configuration for the system.
faq.q: What is the difference between the data plane and the control plane?

faq.a: Not entirely. According to the episode "Azure Event Hubs - Simply Explained", data-in-transit encryption for the data plane is enabled by default, while Azure AD authentication for data plane access is supported but not enabled by default and is configured by the customer.
faq.q: Is data plane protection always enabled by default in Azure Event Hubs?

faq.a: The episode "How to Design Sovereign Cloud Architecture for Microsoft Azure" lists data plane placement as one of five layers of the sovereignty stack, alongside jurisdiction, identity authority, control plane authority and cryptographic custody.
faq.q: Why does the data plane matter for sovereign cloud design?

data-plane.long:
The data plane is the layer of a system that executes operational requests at scale. Typical examples are user interactions, flow runs and data transactions. It is usually contrasted with the control plane, which defines policy and configuration. In short, the control plane decides how a system is set up and governed, while the data plane does the work that the configuration describes.

The distinction matters in cloud architecture because the two planes can be secured, governed and placed differently. The M365.FM episode "How to Design Sovereign Cloud Architecture for Microsoft Azure" treats this separation as part of a sovereignty stack with five layers: jurisdiction, identity authority, control plane authority, data plane placement, and cryptographic custody. In that framing, data plane placement is one of the layers that organizations consider when they want to keep control over where their data is processed and stored. The episode describes knowing these layers as important for managing digital assets well.

Security is another area where the term appears. The episode "Azure Event Hubs - Simply Explained" summarizes the security capabilities of Azure Event Hubs in a table that refers to the data plane in several places. According to that summary, the service supports data-in-transit encryption for the data plane, and this is enabled by default with Microsoft as the responsible party. The same summary lists Azure AD authentication for data plane access as supported but not enabled by default, with the configuration responsibility on the customer side. This shows a common pattern: some data plane protections are provided by the platform, while others must be switched on and configured by the customer.

The term also shows up in streaming and IoT designs. The episode "IoT Hub Message Routing vs Event Grid — Why Telemetry and Events Are Not the Same Problem" describes Azure IoT Hub Message Routing as part of a telemetry data plane. The episode contrasts this with Azure Event Grid, which fits event-driven and reactive architectures. It argues that machine telemetry and discrete business or lifecycle events call for different patterns, that message ordering matters for manufacturing telemetry, and that Event Grid should not become the primary high-volume telemetry bus. It also says IoT Hub routing should not be forced into every notification workflow, and that the two services can work together in the same architecture.

In manufacturing and edge scenarios, the episode "MQTT and OPC UA in Microsoft Manufacturing: Azure IoT Operations + Fabric Architecture" refers to Microsoft's edge data plane pattern. In this pattern, modular services run on Arc-enabled Kubernetes together with Azure IoT Operations and Microsoft Fabric. The episode also discusses the boundary between the control plane and the data plane, stating that local control loops must remain independent of the cloud and that a broker is never a safety controller. It notes that a production-ready deployment of this pattern requires hybrid IT/OT skills.

A further use of the term appears in analytics. The episode "Your Machine Data Never Becomes a Decision. Here's the Missing Pipeline." describes Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric as a common data plane for ingestion, event shaping and time-series query with the KQL database, built for investigation while data is moving. Eventstream handles basic shaping, transformation and routing of streaming sources to multiple destinations, and Activator watches defined conditions across streams, dashboards or KQL results and triggers defined actions.

Taken together, the episodes use data plane to mean the path where operational traffic and data actually flow, whether that is encrypted Event Hubs traffic, routed IoT telemetry, edge messaging or real-time analytics. Decisions around it usually concern placement, authentication, encryption, and keeping the data plane separate from the control plane that governs it.

data-processing-agreement.desc: A data processing agreement (DPA) is the contract between a data controller and a data processor governing how personal data is processed, as required by GDPR Article 28.

faq.a: A DPA is the contract between a data controller and a data processor that governs how personal data is processed on the controller's behalf. It is required by GDPR Article 28.
faq.q: What is a data processing agreement (DPA)?

faq.a: A DPA covers how personal data is processed on the controller's behalf, including sub-processors, security measures and breach notification.
faq.q: What does a DPA cover?

faq.a: The two parties are the data controller and the data processor. The processor handles personal data on behalf of the controller under the terms of the agreement.
faq.q: Which parties are involved in a DPA?

data-processing-agreement.long:
A data processing agreement (DPA) is the contract between a data controller and a data processor that governs how personal data is processed on the controller's behalf. It is required by GDPR Article 28 and sets out the terms under which a processor may handle personal data for the controller.

A DPA typically addresses the use of sub-processors, the security measures applied to the data, and the obligations around breach notification. By putting these points in writing, the agreement documents the division of responsibility between the party that decides why and how personal data is processed (the controller) and the party that carries out the processing (the processor).

In practice, a DPA is relevant whenever an organization relies on an external provider, such as a cloud or software service, to process personal data. Reviewing the DPA is a common step in assessing whether a service can be used in line with data protection requirements.

This page is a concept entry on M365.FM. No linked topics or episodes are currently listed for it.

data-product.desc: A data product is a bundle of related data assets, such as tables, files and Power BI reports, packaged for a defined use case with owners and a business description.

faq.a: It is a bundle of related data assets, such as tables, files and Power BI reports, packaged for a defined use case. It also has owners and a business description so others can discover it and request access.
faq.q: What does a data product contain?

faq.a: They are created and managed in the Unified Catalog, within governance domains. The episode on Purview Data Governance says data product owners are assigned and users receive Unified Catalog reader permissions to view and explore them.
faq.q: Where are data products managed in Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: Episodes on Fabric recommend one workspace per data product unless specific constraints justify otherwise. They describe this as moderate isolation, with multiple workspaces and strict separation of duties for high isolation.
faq.q: How do data products relate to Microsoft Fabric workspaces?

data-product.long:
A data product is a bundle of related data assets, such as tables, files and Power BI reports, packaged for a defined use case. It carries named owners and a business description, so that other people in an organization can discover it and request access to it. The idea shifts attention from individual technical objects to a collection that is organized around a business purpose and presented in terms that business users can understand.

The concept is closely tied to the Unified Catalog in Microsoft Purview, and the official documentation describes how data products are created and managed there. According to the episode "Microsoft Purview Data Map - Simply Explained", the Unified Catalog offers a more business-oriented discovery experience in which users can search for understandable data products rather than relying exclusively on technical names. In that setting, a data product acts as the unit that people look for, evaluate and ask to use.

The same episode gives an illustrative example. Finance could publish a pricing analytics data product that contains relevant source information, cleaned data in Microsoft Fabric, and the approved reporting assets used for monthly analysis. Instead of employees hunting through folders and asking colleagues which spreadsheet is correct, the data product gathers the relevant assets in one place and presents them with a description and responsible owners. This is what makes the packaging useful: the owners and the business description tell consumers what the data is for and who stands behind it.

The episode "Microsoft Purview Data Governance for Information Architects" describes the roles and steps needed to set data products up. Users are assigned the governance domain creator role, which allows them to build governance domains. At least one governance domain is created and a governance domain owner is assigned. Data product owners are then assigned, and at least one data product is created within the governance domains. To let others explore the results, users are given Unified Catalog reader permissions, which allows them to view and explore data products within the governance domain. The episode also notes that a unified catalog helps consolidate five catalogs into one, and it lists better scale, higher adoption and faster time-to-insight among the benefits.

Data products also appear as an organizing principle in Microsoft Fabric guidance. The episode "Fix Wrong Copilot Numbers in Microsoft Fabric" recommends using one workspace per data product unless specific constraints justify otherwise. It pairs this with documenting the default pattern and approved exceptions, and with educating teams on the intent of governance, not just the rules. Similarly, "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" says that one workspace per data product gives moderate isolation, while multiple workspaces with strict separation of duties give high isolation, and that data products should be consolidated only when necessary.

In practice, decisions around a data product concern its scope, its ownership and its boundaries. Teams decide which related assets belong together for a use case, who is accountable as owner, and how the product is described so that it can be found. They also decide how it maps to Fabric workspaces and how much isolation sensitive workloads require. Taken together, the sources treat a data product as both a discovery unit in the Unified Catalog and a structuring unit for governance and workspace design.

data-protection-addendum.desc: The Microsoft Products and Services Data Protection Addendum (DPA) is a contractual document covering data protection terms for Microsoft products and services.

faq.a: It is a data protection addendum associated with Microsoft products and services, tracked on M365.FM as a concept. Detailed terms are not covered in the facts available here.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft Products and Services Data Protection Addendum (DPA)?

faq.a: The authoritative wording is published by Microsoft in its official licensing and compliance documentation. M365.FM does not currently list a source link or episode for this entity.
faq.q: Where can the exact terms of the DPA be found?

data-protection-addendum.long:
The Microsoft Products and Services Data Protection Addendum (DPA) is a concept in the Microsoft ecosystem that refers to a data protection addendum associated with Microsoft products and services. As its name indicates, it concerns the handling of data within the scope of those offerings.

This page is an entity placeholder on M365.FM. The knowledge base currently holds no further verified details about the document's contents, scope, version history or how it is applied, so none are stated here. Readers who need the exact terms, applicable products or current wording should consult Microsoft's official licensing and compliance documentation directly.

No related topics or podcast episodes are linked to this entity at present. As more material on M365.FM references the Microsoft Products and Services Data Protection Addendum (DPA), this page can be expanded with connections to the relevant discussions.

data-protection-baseline.desc: Data Protection Baseline is the default assessment in Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager, built from controls of standards and regulations such as NIST, ISO, FedRAMP and GDPR.
data-protection-baseline.long:
Data Protection Baseline is the default assessment in Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager. It is available at every subscription level, which makes it the starting point for organizations that begin to track their compliance posture in Compliance Manager.

The baseline is assembled from controls drawn from common standards and regulations, including NIST, ISO, FedRAMP and GDPR. Rather than mapping to a single framework, it brings together controls that recur across several of them. This gives administrators a general view of data protection and compliance requirements without first selecting a specific regulatory template.

Within Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager, an assessment groups controls and tracks progress against them. The Data Protection Baseline serves as the default assessment of this kind, so it is typically the first assessment present in a tenant.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no further related topics are recorded for it.

data-protection-impact-assessment.desc: A data protection impact assessment (DPIA) is a GDPR-required assessment for processing likely to create a high risk to people's rights, documenting risks and mitigating measures.
data-protection-impact-assessment.long:
A data protection impact assessment (DPIA) is an assessment required under the GDPR when a type of processing is likely to result in a high risk to people's rights. It is a structured way of examining a processing activity before and during its operation, rather than a one-off formality.

A DPIA documents the processing itself, including what it involves and why it is carried out. It also assesses the necessity and proportionality of that processing, identifies the risks it creates for individuals, and records the measures intended to mitigate those risks. The result is a written record that shows how the risks were considered and addressed.

In the context of the Microsoft ecosystem, a DPIA is a concept that organizations may need to consider when evaluating processing that is likely to be high risk. The facts available for this entry do not link it to specific Microsoft products or services, and no M365.FM episodes are currently associated with the term.

data-provenance.desc: Data provenance is the documented history of a data asset's origin, custody and transformations, used to validate and audit where data came from and how it changed.

faq.a: Data provenance is the documented history of a data asset's origin, custody and transformations. It is used to validate and audit where data came from and how it changed.
faq.q: What is data provenance?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, lineage supports governance by making it easier to track data provenance. Weak metadata and missing lineage obscure provenance and make audits and impact analysis slower.
faq.q: How does data provenance relate to data lineage?

faq.a: The episode on auditable ESG compliance recommends documenting every data input, transformation and output so that clear audit evidence exists for verification.
faq.q: Why is data provenance important for audits?

data-provenance.long:
Data provenance is the documented history of a data asset's origin, custody and transformations. It records where data came from, who held it, and what was done to it along the way. The main purpose is to make data verifiable: when a figure, a report or a training dataset is questioned, provenance makes it possible to trace it back to its source and to check how it reached its current form. This is why the concept appears so often in discussions of audits, compliance and governance.

In practice, data provenance is rarely handled as a standalone feature. It is usually described together with related governance capabilities such as metadata management and data lineage. The episode "Microsoft Fabric OneLake - Simply Explained" lists data lineage tracking among OneLake's governance capabilities and states that it helps teams understand data provenance for audits. The same list includes data discovery and classification, which automatically identify and label sensitive data, and access control management with fine-grained permissions. In that framing, provenance is one element of a broader approach in which governance is managed centrally across tenants, domains and workspaces.

The episode "Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Governance and Data Lineage" connects the two ideas directly. It says that lineage supports data governance by making it easier to enforce policies and track data provenance. Combined with access controls in the data platform and Azure, lineage helps ensure that sensitive data is handled correctly and that audit trails can be tied back to specific Fabric items and processes. The same episode also points to common limitations of lineage across Fabric, such as incomplete metadata for certain sources, and discusses how these gaps can be mitigated. Provenance information is only as complete as the metadata and lineage that feed it.

Provenance also matters for compliance programs. The episode "Turn Microsoft 365 Compliance into Competitive Advantage" lists ineffective metadata and data lineage as a common pitfall. According to the episode, weak metadata management and missing lineage obscure data provenance, which makes risk assessments, audits and impact analysis slow and error-prone. The practical lesson is that provenance has to be captured as data is created and changed, because reconstructing it afterwards is difficult.
