faq.q: Which related topics do the M365.FM episodes connect to dependency injection?

dependency-injection.long:
Dependency injection is a software engineering technique in which an object does not create the things it depends on itself. Instead, those dependencies are supplied from outside, typically through interfaces. The result is a design made of loosely coupled and replaceable components: one implementation of a dependency can be swapped for another without rewriting the code that uses it.

In practice, dependency injection is used to keep application code flexible and testable. Because a class receives its collaborators rather than constructing them, the surrounding application decides which concrete implementation is used. This makes it possible to change behavior, replace services, or substitute test doubles without touching the consuming code. The M365.FM episodes treat it as one of several established design patterns that improve code maintainability and testability.

The episode "Modern .NET: WPF, ASP.NET Core, and gRPC with Gábor Ruzsinszki [MVP]" lists dependency injection alongside MVVM as a design pattern to adopt in order to improve code maintainability and testability in modern .NET applications. In that context it sits in a set of recommendations that also includes securing applications with HTTPS and token-based authentication and adopting CI/CD pipelines for automated testing and deployment.

The episode ".NET Extensibility and Clean Architecture with Miguel Castro [MVP]" places dependency injection among the principles behind clean architecture and modular design. The discussion connects it with abstractions, strategy patterns, plugin architectures, and event-driven development, and describes how designing for change helps applications survive new business requirements, emerging technologies, and growing complexity. The episode also stresses avoiding overengineering and presents extensibility as creating flexible foundations rather than unnecessary complexity, which frames dependency injection as a means to flexibility rather than an end in itself.

Testing is a recurring theme. In "Deploy Web Apps to Azure App Service Without Boilerplate", the advice for unit and integration testing is to use dependency injection to control what the code uses during tests, alongside a local testing environment such as the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator and a testing pyramid with many unit tests, some integration tests, and a few end-to-end tests. Similarly, "Azure Functions - Simply Explained" recommends using dependency injection to enhance testability and maintainability, together with mocking external dependencies so test runs are consistent and faster.

Dependency injection also appears as a built-in convention in the .NET platform. In "Build AI Applications with .NET 10", a table of features lists dependency injection as the way to register AI services using familiar .NET patterns. The same table names provider flexibility, a middleware pipeline, OpenTelemetry-based telemetry, and unified abstractions for vector data. Together these describe how AI providers can be switched without code changes, with caching, logging, or custom behavior added around AI calls.

Taken together, the episodes describe dependency injection as a low-level technique that supports higher-level goals: replaceable components, easier testing, and architectures that can adapt as requirements change. It is usually discussed together with interfaces and abstractions, since those are what allow one implementation to stand in for another.

deployment-slots.desc: Deployment slots in Azure App Service are live copies of an app with their own address, used to deploy and test a new version before swapping it into production.
deployment-slots.long:
Deployment slots (Azure App Service) are live copies of an Azure App Service app. Each slot has its own address, which makes it possible to deploy a new version of an app and test it separately from the version that serves production traffic.

The typical use is a staged release: a new version is deployed to a non-production slot, checked there, and then swapped into production. Because the slot is a running copy of the app rather than a static package, the new version can be exercised in its own environment before it replaces the current one. Deployment slots are available from the Standard tier of Azure App Service.

Deployment slots are a feature of Azure App Service, which is the broader topic they belong to. Microsoft documents the feature in its Azure App Service documentation on setting up staging environments.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

desire-paths.desc: Desire paths are unplanned trails worn by people taking shorter or easier routes, and a metaphor for workarounds that reveal where a designed workflow fails real work.

faq.a: Desire paths are unplanned trails worn by people who take a shorter or easier route than the official one. The term is also used as a metaphor for repeated workarounds.
faq.q: What are desire paths?

faq.a: Repeated workarounds show where a designed workflow does not match real work. They act as a signal of where the intended process creates friction for the people using it.
faq.q: Why are desire paths used as a metaphor for workflows?

desire-paths.long:
Desire paths are unplanned trails worn into the ground by people who take a shorter or easier route than the official one. The term is also used as a metaphor: repeated workarounds in a system or process that show where a designed workflow does not fit the way people actually work.

In a workplace or software context, a desire path appears when users consistently bypass the intended steps, tools or approvals to reach a goal. Examples of the pattern include copying data by hand instead of using a prescribed form, or choosing a different tool than the one provided. Because these behaviors repeat across many people, they are treated as a signal about unmet needs rather than as simple misuse.

The concept is used as an observation aid: noticing where people deviate can point to friction in a design, which can then be reviewed and adjusted. The idea does not prescribe a specific method or product.

No related topics or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no official documentation is associated with the concept.

desktop-flow.desc: A desktop flow is a Power Automate automation that runs on a Windows machine and drives apps through mouse and keyboard actions where no API or connector exists.

faq.a: A desktop flow is a Power Automate automation that runs on a Windows machine. It performs tasks by driving the user interface through mouse and keyboard actions.
faq.q: What is a desktop flow?

faq.a: A desktop flow is used to automate applications that have no API or connector. Since it works through the user interface, it can handle software that other integration methods cannot access.
faq.q: When is a desktop flow used?

faq.a: A desktop flow runs on a Windows machine, as part of Power Automate for desktop.
faq.q: Where does a desktop flow run?

desktop-flow.long:
A desktop flow is a type of automation in Power Automate for desktop. It runs on a Windows machine and operates the user interface by simulating mouse and keyboard actions, in the way a person would work with an application on screen.

Desktop flows are used to automate applications that offer no API or connector. Because the automation interacts with the visible interface rather than a programmatic endpoint, it can cover legacy or desktop-only software that other integration methods cannot reach.

The facts available here describe the concept in general terms and do not list related topics or specific M365.FM episodes. Detailed guidance on how desktop flows are built and run is provided in the official Microsoft Learn documentation for desktop flows.

dev-containers.desc: Dev Containers are container-based development environments defined in a devcontainer.json file, giving every developer, VS Code instance and CI pipeline the same runtimes, tools and extensions.

faq.a: It is the configuration file that describes a dev container. It lives in the project repository, usually in a .devcontainer folder, and defines the environment that is built when a folder is reopened in the container.
faq.q: What is a devcontainer.json file?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn lists WSL 2, Docker Desktop with the WSL 2 based engine enabled, Visual Studio Code and the Dev Containers extension. Docker Desktop must be running before VS Code is opened.
faq.q: What is needed to use Dev Containers on Windows?

faq.a: Projects stored in the Windows file system are noticeably slower than those in the WSL 2 file system, and file changes may not be detected there, according to the Microsoft Learn documentation.
faq.q: Why does the storage location of a project matter?

dev-containers.long:
Dev Containers are container-based development environments in which a Docker container serves as the complete workspace for a project. The environment is described in a devcontainer.json file that lives in the project repository, usually inside a .devcontainer folder. Because the definition travels with the code, everyone who opens the project gets the same runtimes, tools, extensions and settings, regardless of what is installed on their own machine. This addresses what the M365.FM episode "Stop Environment Drift with VS Code Dev Containers" calls environment drift: the gradual divergence between the setups of different developers, editors and build servers.

In practice, a developer opens a folder in Visual Studio Code and reopens it in the container. At that point the image is built from the configuration, and the editor works inside that environment. A configuration can be added to an existing project through a Visual Studio Code command, which asks for a base image such as Node.js, Python or Debian/Ubuntu. A separate command returns to the local environment when the container is not needed. The full list of options is documented in the Dev Container Specification, which is the reference for what devcontainer.json can contain.

On Windows, Microsoft Learn describes a setup that expects WSL 2, Docker Desktop with the WSL 2 based engine enabled, Visual Studio Code and the Dev Containers extension. Docker Desktop must be running before VS Code is opened, and WSL integration must be enabled for the Linux distribution in use. These prerequisites are a typical stumbling block when a team first adopts the approach, so they are worth checking before troubleshooting anything inside the container itself.

Where the project files are stored matters for performance. According to the Microsoft Learn documentation, projects kept in the Windows file system are noticeably slower than those kept in the WSL 2 file system, and file changes may not be detected when the project sits on the Windows side. Teams deciding how to organize repositories on Windows machines therefore have a concrete reason to place dev container projects inside the WSL 2 file system.

The central idea is that one definition can be reused beyond the individual workstation. The episode "Stop Environment Drift with VS Code Dev Containers" discusses how development teams can automate continuous integration pipelines using dev containers, container images and command-line tooling. It frames containerization as foundational to DevOps workflows and explains how development containers keep coding environments consistent, with tools such as Docker, GitHub Actions and CLI utilities supporting the path from build to deployment. In that picture, the same environment definition used in VS Code can also run in a CI pipeline, which reduces the situation where code works locally but fails in the build.

Typical decisions around Dev Containers include which base image to start from, which extensions and settings to include in the shared configuration, and how the container definition is versioned together with the code. Since the configuration lives in the repository, changes to the environment can be reviewed and tracked like any other change. The episode also appears in a later M365.FM episode, "Stop Active Directory Security Drift Before a Breach", which lists it among related practical conversations on the topic of drift. The sources available here do not go into further detail on that connection.

developer-experience.desc: Developer experience (DX) describes the quality of the tooling, workflows and conventions developers work with in a code base or organization, with a focus on removing friction.

faq.a: Developer experience (DX) is the quality of the tooling, workflows and conventions that developers work with in a code base or organization. It focuses on removing friction from development work.
faq.q: What is developer experience (DX)?

faq.a: DX covers the tools, workflows and conventions developers encounter, whether within a single code base or across an organization. The emphasis is on reducing friction in these areas.
faq.q: What does DX cover?

developer-experience.long:
Developer experience (DX) is the overall quality of the tooling, workflows and conventions that developers work with in a code base or across an organization. The central aim is to remove friction from everyday development work, so that building, testing and maintaining software is as smooth as possible.

In practice, DX is a way of looking at the environment around the code rather than the code alone. It covers how easy it is to set up a project, how consistent the conventions are, how clear the workflows feel, and how much unnecessary effort developers spend on obstacles that do not relate to the task at hand. Because it concerns both the tools and the habits around them, DX can apply to a single repository as well as to a whole organization.

The term is used as a lens for evaluating and improving how development work is organized. Attention to DX typically means identifying points of friction and addressing them through better tooling, clearer processes or more consistent conventions.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this concept, and no related entities or official documentation are listed for it at this time.

developer-tool.desc: Developer tool is an M365.FM category for tools that help developers write, test and ship software, from editors and build pipelines to APIs and platforms.

faq.a: A developer tool is a tool that helps developers write, test and ship software. Examples include editors, source control, build and deployment pipelines, APIs, and platforms for building and running applications.
faq.q: What is a developer tool?

faq.a: Microsoft Graph and Azure AI Foundry are classified as instances of this category. Graph provides one API for Microsoft 365 data, and Azure AI Foundry is a platform for building and deploying AI applications.
faq.q: Which M365.FM topics are classified as developer tools?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Files - Simply Explained" lists developer tool shares as a scenario, where IDE plugins, build tools and scripts are shared across a development team using Azure Files.
faq.q: How does Azure Files relate to developer tools?

developer-tool.long:
A developer tool is a tool that helps developers write, test and ship software. The term covers editors, source control, build and deployment pipelines, APIs, and platforms on which applications are built and run. In general software engineering usage, a programming tool is a program used to develop another program, usually by helping the developer manage files. The boundary is not always sharp: a compiler collection exists only for development, while a plain text editor was not designed for programming but is often used for it, so whether something counts as a development tool can be subjective.

Tools are typically combined into a workflow. A common example is a source code editor for writing source files, a compiler that turns source code into machine code, and build automation that packages programs for distribution. A set of tools run one after another, each passing its output to the next, is called a toolchain. An integrated development environment combines several of these tools, usually an editor plus compiling, debugging and testing, in one place.

The category is broad. Common groups include assemblers, compilers, decompilers and disassemblers; linkers, loaders and build automation; static analyzers, lint tools, code review, pretty-printers and minifiers; debuggers, memory debuggers and performance profilers; version control and bug tracking, with Git and GitHub as familiar names; documentation generators and GUI builders; parser generators and software development kits; unit testing frameworks; and AI-assisted tools. Valgrind is a named example of profiling and memory debugging.

On M365.FM, Developer tool is a parent category. Microsoft Graph and Azure AI Foundry are classified as instances of it: Graph gives developers one API for Microsoft 365 data, while Azure AI Foundry is a platform for building and deploying AI applications. Developer tools are normally used together with source control, cloud platforms and identity services that protect access to the code and its environments, so choices about tooling usually involve decisions about where code lives, how it is built and who may reach it.

The linked episode, "Azure Files - Simply Explained", touches the category from the storage side. It presents Azure Files as Microsoft's fully managed cloud file sharing service, which lets organizations create secure, scalable and highly available file shares without maintaining traditional file servers, using the familiar SMB and NFS protocols. Among the scenarios the episode lists is developer tool shares: sharing IDE plugins, build tools and scripts across a development team. It also mentions hybrid access, where on-premises servers and Azure VMs can mount the same share using Azure File Sync, and configuration and settings shares that store config files in a share accessible from multiple App Service instances or containers.

The episode describes Azure Files as a flexible and scalable option for organizations that want to modernize their file storage without disrupting existing workflows, with various deployment models and redundancy options that let businesses tailor a setup to performance requirements and budget. For development teams, this means shared storage that applications and Windows or Linux systems can reach in the usual way, which can keep shared tooling and scripts consistent across machines. The M365.FM material otherwise provides only a general definition for this category, so details about individual tools are found on the pages for the specific products.

devops.desc: DevOps is a software delivery approach in which development and operations work together; M365.FM episodes cover its platforms, costs, Azure DevOps and AI automation.

faq.a: DevOps is an approach in which development and operations collaborate across planning, building, testing, releasing and running software. The M365.FM episode "The DevOps Tax: Why Your Platform is Failing" describes its original vision as "You build it, you run it."
faq.q: What is DevOps?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "The DevOps Tax: Why Your Platform is Failing", it is the hidden cost of teams handling infrastructure, cost optimization and CI/CD on top of feature work. The episode says it reduces productivity and increases cognitive overload.
faq.q: What is the DevOps Tax?

faq.a: Azure DevOps is Microsoft's platform that combines project management, source control, build automation, testing and deployments. The episode "Azure DevOps - Simply Explained" presents it as a way to help development and operations teams collaborate and automate repetitive tasks.
faq.q: How does Azure DevOps relate to DevOps?

devops.long:
DevOps is an approach to building and running software in which development and operations work closely together instead of operating as separate groups. Microsoft documents the concept in its "What is DevOps" overview. The idea is to bring planning, building, testing, releasing and operating software into one connected flow, so that teams can deliver changes more consistently and with less manual hand-off between roles.

The M365.FM episode "The DevOps Tax: Why Your Platform is Failing" describes the original vision of DevOps as "You build it, you run it." In that model, small, autonomous teams own their software from development through production. The episode points out a side effect of this model: teams ended up carrying work well beyond business features, including infrastructure management, cost optimization and CI/CD. It calls this hidden cost the DevOps Tax and says it reduces engineering productivity and increases cognitive overload, so that teams spend more time managing infrastructure than delivering customer value. This framing is useful for organizations that are deciding how much responsibility to place on individual product teams and how much to centralize in a shared platform.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, DevOps practice is often tied to Azure DevOps. The episode "Azure DevOps - Simply Explained" describes Azure DevOps as Microsoft's all-in-one platform for planning, developing, testing and delivering software. Instead of separate tools for project management, source control, build automation, testing and deployments, it combines them in a single platform. According to the episode, this helps development and operations teams collaborate and automates repetitive tasks across the software development lifecycle.

The episode "Azure DevOps in 2026: The Quiet Backbone of Enterprise AI" looks at the role of Azure DevOps when AI speeds up development. Its quick answer is that Azure DevOps gives enterprise teams a governed way to plan, build, test and release software and infrastructure. The episode argues that disciplined source control, pipelines, security and traceability remain essential when AI accelerates development and increases the speed of change. It also notes that much of the public conversation centers on GitHub, Copilot and AI-powered development, while governance and traceability stay important for enterprise delivery.

Infrastructure is another recurring theme. In "Azure Infrastructure as Code and DevOps with Maik van der Gaag [MVP]", host Mirko Peters talks with Microsoft Azure MVP Maik van der Gaag about modern cloud engineering and automation. The episode explains how tools such as Terraform and Bicep let teams automate deployments, improve consistency, reduce configuration drift and speed up delivery across Azure environments. In this context, DevOps and Infrastructure as Code go together: environments are defined and deployed through repeatable automation rather than manual configuration.

Automation is also moving toward autonomous systems. The episode "Use Agentic AI in DevOps Safely" explores how agentic AI is changing DevOps by automating CI/CD, incident response and cloud operations. It shares stories of teams speeding up deployments dramatically, but also covers the risks: failures, security blind spots and new attack surfaces created by AI-driven systems. The episode discusses how to revert safely when automation goes wrong and gives guidance on when to rely on automation versus keeping human oversight, along with tool comparisons and tactics to reduce risk.

Taken together, the episodes treat DevOps as both a working model and a set of practices. Typical decisions include how far teams should own their own infrastructure, which platform holds source control, pipelines and work tracking, how environments are defined as code, and how much autonomy to give AI-driven automation. The recurring caution across the episodes is that speed gains need governance, traceability and a deliberate way to manage the extra load placed on teams.

differential-privacy.desc: Differential privacy is a mathematical framework that limits how much any single record can influence a model's output, using clipping and calibrated noise.

faq.a: Differential privacy is a mathematical framework that bounds how much any single record can influence a model's output. It relies on techniques such as gradient clipping and calibrated noise, with the strength of the guarantee quantified by epsilon and delta parameters.
faq.q: What is differential privacy?

faq.a: The episode "AI Security and Microsoft Purview with Danilo Nogueira [Microsoft]" lists it as a mitigation for membership inference attacks, which involve privacy risks from training data exposure. Other episodes mention it for inferring sensitive user attributes and for protecting customer data in chatbot platforms.
faq.q: Which risk does differential privacy help address according to the episodes?

faq.a: The episodes present it as one layer among several controls. It is mentioned alongside data access audits, federated learning, encryption, data minimization and governance measures rather than as a single complete solution.
faq.q: Is differential privacy used on its own?

differential-privacy.long:
Differential privacy is a mathematical framework that bounds how much any single record can influence the output of a model or analysis. It is used to reduce the privacy risk that arises when models are trained on or answer questions about sensitive data. The idea is that the result should look nearly the same whether or not one individual's data was included, so that little can be learned about any specific person from the output.

In practice, the framework is implemented with techniques such as gradient clipping and calibrated noise. Gradient clipping limits how strongly any one training example can affect the model's parameters, and noise is added in a controlled amount so that individual contributions are masked. The strength of the guarantee is quantified by two parameters, epsilon and delta. These values express how much privacy loss is permitted, which makes the protection something that can be measured and reasoned about rather than only described qualitatively.

Differential privacy appears in the M365.FM episodes mainly as one item in a wider set of privacy and security controls for AI systems. The episode "AI Security and Microsoft Purview with Danilo Nogueira [Microsoft]" lists it as a mitigation for membership inference attacks, which are described as privacy risks arising from the exposure of training data. In that episode it is paired with data access audits, and it sits alongside other measures such as regular security audits, adversarial testing and comprehensive data validation. The same discussion treats data privacy as a concern whenever employees interact with AI-driven tools, since sensitive data can be exposed in the process.

The episode "How AI-Generated Identity Configuration Breaks Entra Security" mentions differential privacy together with federated learning as privacy-preserving techniques to apply against the risk of inferring sensitive user attributes without consent. It frames this as part of a broader risk view that also includes process risks such as weak governance and missing continuous monitoring, and it points to data retention governance and routine audits as complementary controls.

In retrieval-focused scenarios, the episode "Improve Microsoft Copilot Accuracy Beyond Vector Search" describes hybrid graph-vector RAG as supporting privacy-preserving techniques. It gives the example of a bank that can use differential privacy to answer customer questions about financial products without exposing personal details, and it relates this to regulated industries that need to keep client data safe. The episode also notes trade-offs: on-device solutions may run slightly slower than cloud-based ones but offer better privacy, and some privacy methods, such as homomorphic encryption, carry their own costs.

The episode "Govern Microsoft Fabric Data Agents in Copilot Studio" lists differential privacy among the measures AI chatbot platforms can use to protect customer data while offering generative AI features. These are named together with model governance, data minimization, private model hosting, on-premises inference and training data controls. The episode "Private LoRA for Secure AI on Proprietary Enterprise Data" places differential privacy under the heading of encryption and extra protection, next to layered encryption with a Network Session Key and an Application Session Key, in a setup where each customer's data stays separate and is not mixed with anyone else's.

Across these episodes, differential privacy is presented as one layer in a defence-in-depth approach rather than a standalone solution. Typical decisions around it involve how much privacy protection a use case requires, how that interacts with accuracy and performance, and how it combines with access controls, auditing and governance in regulated settings.

digital-debt.desc: Digital debt is the build-up of unverified, unmanaged digital artifacts, such as AI-generated drafts, summaries and automations, that outpaces people's ability to validate it.

faq.a: Digital debt is the accumulation of unverified and unmanaged digital artifacts, such as AI-generated drafts, summaries and automations, that grows faster than people can validate it and slows down decisions. Microsoft's Work Trend Index uses the term for the point at which incoming data, email, meetings and notifications outpace people's ability to process them.
faq.q: What is digital debt?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "How Microsoft Copilot Creates Digital Debt", the cause is not the AI itself but messy, ungoverned Microsoft 365 environments. Copilot exposes all accessible data, so problems like oversharing and poor structure are scaled rather than fixed.
faq.q: How can Microsoft Copilot contribute to digital debt?

faq.a: The episode points to proper data governance, security controls and clear operating models. Without them, it says, organizations risk building long-term complexity instead of productivity.
faq.q: What does the episode recommend to avoid digital debt?

digital-debt.long:
Digital debt is the accumulation of unverified and unmanaged digital artifacts, such as AI-generated drafts, summaries and automations, that grows faster than people can validate it and slows down decisions. The term borrows its wording from finance: just as financial debt accumulates when obligations outrun what can be paid, digital debt accumulates when the inflow of content outruns the capacity to review, organize and trust it.

The concept appears in two related framings. Microsoft's Work Trend Index, published through Microsoft WorkLab, uses the term for a situation in which the inflow of data, email, meetings and notifications has outpaced people's ability to process it. The report describes the cause as a steadily growing flood of information and always-on communication in which everything seems important, so employees spend much of their time sorting and searching rather than creating. It links this overload to too little uninterrupted focus time, time lost looking for information, and difficulty finding the energy and time for the work itself. Leaders report that it shows up as missing innovation and breakthrough ideas in their teams. The report frames digital debt as a tax on individual productivity that also weighs on organizations and the wider economy, and it positions AI copilots as a way to help people work free of that debt. The page gives a business framing rather than a formal glossary definition.

A second framing focuses on what AI itself can add to the pile. When AI tools produce drafts, summaries and automations quickly, each output is another artifact that someone has to check, own and maintain. If verification does not keep pace with generation, unvalidated material accumulates, and decisions slow down because people must first work out what can be trusted. In this reading, digital debt is not only incoming information but also the unverified material an organization creates for itself.

The M365.FM episode "How Microsoft Copilot Creates Digital Debt" (2026-04-24) develops this second view. The episode explains that treating AI as a simple add-on tool, especially Microsoft Copilot, can quietly create digital debt inside organizations. According to the episode, the problem is not the AI itself but the messy, ungoverned Microsoft 365 environments it relies on. Copilot is described as a powerful coworker that instantly exposes all accessible data, so existing issues such as oversharing and poor structure become visible and are amplified. The episode says that AI does not fix such weaknesses but scales them: if an environment is chaotic, AI will accelerate that chaos.

From this follows the practical emphasis the episode places on preparation. Without proper data governance, security controls and clear operating models, the episode argues, companies risk building long-term complexity rather than productivity. The decision that matters is therefore less which AI feature to switch on and more whether the underlying content, permissions and ownership are in a state where generated output can be trusted and managed.

Typical situations where the term applies include teams that receive more email, meeting recordings and notifications than they can read, and organizations where AI-generated summaries, drafts and automations multiply without anyone responsible for checking or retiring them. In both cases the signal is the same: validation capacity, not production capacity, becomes the bottleneck, and the time spent sorting, searching and verifying displaces the work itself.

digital-fluency.desc: Digital fluency extends digital literacy by treating technology use as a life skill: using tools correctly, efficiently, effectively and responsibly, including AI.

faq.a: Digital fluency is an extension of digital literacy that treats technology use as a life skill. It means using tools correctly, efficiently, effectively and responsibly, including AI.
faq.q: What is digital fluency?

faq.a: Digital fluency builds on digital literacy by framing technology use as a broader life skill. It adds an emphasis on efficiency, effectiveness and responsible use, and it includes AI.
faq.q: How does digital fluency differ from digital literacy?

faq.a: It appears in the episodes "How Microsoft 365 & Copilot Are Redesigning the Way We Work with Tracy van der Schyff [MVP]" and "The Future of Work with Fabio Bonolo [MVP]".
faq.q: Where is digital fluency discussed on M365.FM?

digital-fluency.long:
Digital fluency is an extension of digital literacy. Where digital literacy is often understood as knowing how to operate digital tools, digital fluency treats technology use as a life skill. It covers using tools correctly, efficiently, effectively and responsibly, and it explicitly includes working with AI.

The concept is used to describe what people need in order to work well with modern technology, not only to perform individual tasks. The emphasis on responsible use means that fluency is not limited to speed or technical skill. It also concerns how and why tools are applied, which becomes more relevant as AI features become part of everyday work.

On M365.FM, digital fluency appears in conversations about how people work with Microsoft technology. It is discussed in the episode "How Microsoft 365 & Copilot Are Redesigning the Way We Work with Tracy van der Schyff [MVP]" and in "The Future of Work with Fabio Bonolo [MVP]". Both episodes place the topic in the context of changing ways of working.

digital-literacy.desc: Digital literacy is the ability to find, evaluate, use, create and communicate information with digital tools in a purposeful and responsible way.

faq.a: Digital literacy is the ability to find, evaluate, use, create and communicate information with digital tools in a purposeful and responsible way. It covers both practical skills and the judgment about how to use technology.
faq.q: What is digital literacy?

faq.a: The episode "Scale Microsoft Copilot Adoption in 90 Days with Carina de Vries [MVP]" lists improving digital literacy among the goals of AI adoption programs, together with reducing AI anxiety and building long-term engagement with Copilot.
faq.q: How does digital literacy relate to Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption?

faq.a: No. The episode with Tracy van der Schyff describes the focus as helping people understand technology and use it with purpose, not just teaching which buttons to click. The leadership episode also includes knowing what generative AI cannot do and discussing ethics.
faq.q: Is digital literacy only about technical skills?

digital-literacy.long:
Digital literacy is the ability to find, evaluate, use, create and communicate information with digital tools in a purposeful and responsible way. It describes a set of capabilities rather than a single product or technology. The term covers both the practical skills needed to work with software and the judgment needed to decide when and how a digital tool should be used. In the Microsoft ecosystem, it comes up most often in discussions about adoption, training and the introduction of AI assistants such as Microsoft 365 Copilot.

The definition contains several distinct activities. Finding and evaluating information means locating relevant material and judging whether it can be trusted. Using and creating information means applying digital tools to produce documents, analyses and other work results. Communicating means sharing and collaborating through digital channels. The words "purposeful" and "responsible" matter in this definition: digital literacy is not only about knowing which buttons to click, but about using technology with a clear goal and with awareness of its limits and consequences.

The M365.FM episode "How Microsoft 365 & Copilot Are Redesigning the Way We Work with Tracy van der Schyff [MVP]" places digital literacy next to digital fluency, training, adoption and organizational change. According to the episode description, the focus is not simply on teaching people which buttons to click, but on helping people understand technology, use it with purpose, and become more capable because of it. The conversation also touches on information management, AI readiness and change management, which shows how closely digital literacy is tied to the human side of Microsoft 365 rollouts.

The topic also appears in the context of AI adoption programs. The episode "Scale Microsoft Copilot Adoption in 90 Days with Carina de Vries [MVP]" describes designing scalable AI adoption programs, reducing AI anxiety among employees, improving digital literacy and creating long-term engagement with Copilot. In that framing, digital literacy is one of several levers, alongside change management, AI habits and a use-case-first approach that connects AI to practical tasks such as writing, summarizing meetings, improving quality and saving time.

Career development is another recurring angle. The episode "How to Futureproof Your Career in the AI Era with Sarah Jones" lists developing AI and digital literacy first in a checklist that also includes critical thinking and problem-solving, communication and storytelling, leadership and collaboration, and continuous learning. The episode suggests that certifications or professional education programs can show employers a commitment to growth. Similarly, "Dataverse MCP Integration with Nathan Rose [MVP]" says that digital literacy helps integration professionals understand and manage complex integration platforms, alongside skills such as data analytics, automation, adaptability and collaboration with other teams.

For leaders, the episode "Leadership in the AI Era Beyond Approvals and Control" names digital literacy as one of several challenges. It describes the need to know how generative AI works and what it cannot do, to balance human judgment with AI-generated input, to discuss bias and fairness, to help teams see AI as a tool for growth, and to support creativity and innovation. Here digital literacy is less about operating a tool and more about understanding its behavior well enough to lead a team that uses it.

Taken together, the episodes treat digital literacy as a foundation for working with Microsoft 365 and AI rather than a one-time training topic. Typical decisions around it include how to structure training and adoption programs, how to address employee concerns about AI, and which skills individuals should build as tools and platforms change. No fixed curriculum or framework is specified in the sources; the concept is described by its purpose, which is helping people use digital tools with understanding, intent and responsibility.

digital-signal-processor.desc: A digital signal processor (DSP) processes audio signals, handling tasks such as mixing, echo and reverb reduction and noise removal, including in conference rooms.
digital-signal-processor.long:
A digital signal processor (DSP) is a component or software function that processes audio signals digitally. Typical tasks include mixing multiple audio sources, reducing echo and reverb, and removing noise from a signal.

In conference rooms, DSP functionality is used to make speech clearer for remote participants and to manage the audio coming from microphones and speakers in the room. Instead of relying on a separate, dedicated hardware device, a DSP can run as onboard software inside microphones and room systems. This allows the audio processing to be built into the equipment already present in the space.

The concept is relevant for anyone planning or evaluating audio setups for meeting rooms, since it affects whether audio processing is handled by an additional device or integrated into the room's existing hardware.

No related products, documentation links or episodes are currently linked to this entry on M365.FM.

digital-thread.desc: Digital thread is the connected context linking product information from engineering to service, while each system keeps ownership of its own records.

faq.a: A digital thread is the connected context that links product information across the lifecycle, from engineering through planning, production, quality, maintenance and service. Each system keeps ownership of its own records.
faq.q: What is a digital thread?

faq.a: According to a Microsoft industry blog post, it integrates data from PLM, ERP and MES systems and draws on operational technology, information technology and engineering data.
faq.q: Which systems does a digital thread connect?

faq.a: The Microsoft post says fragmented systems and heterogeneous environments, along with the difficulty of connecting modern solutions to legacy infrastructure, have kept them more aspiration than reality. Data quality, standardization and integration are also often unreliable when data stays trapped in separate systems.
faq.q: Why have digital threads been hard to achieve?

digital-thread.long:
Digital thread is a concept for linking product information across the whole lifecycle, from engineering through planning, production, quality, maintenance and service. Its defining feature is that the connection happens at the level of context, not ownership: each system continues to own and manage its own records, while the thread ties those records together so that people and software can follow a product or process from one stage to the next.

A Microsoft industry blog post, "Industrial AI in action: How AI agents and digital threads will transform the manufacturing industries", describes digital threads as the nervous system of industrial operations. According to the post, they connect information, processes and people across manufacturing and are built on unified operational technology, information technology and engineering data. The intent is for data to flow from the first concept through to customer support, moving away from static, separate records toward dynamic networks of related information.

In practice, the approach draws on data from systems such as PLM, ERP and MES. Each of these holds a different part of the picture: product definition, business planning and shop-floor execution. A digital thread does not replace them. It connects what they contain so that questions spanning several systems can be answered without manually reconciling separate sources. The same Microsoft post says employees could use AI agents to retrieve measures such as OEE, total cost of ownership and return on investment once this connected context is in place. It names two examples: a shared, AI-assisted digital thread built with Autodesk Fusion and Microsoft Fabric, and an enterprise data framework with a multi-agent model from PTC.

The post is also direct about why digital threads have often remained more aspiration than reality. Fragmented systems and heterogeneous environments make integration difficult, and connecting modern solutions to legacy infrastructure is described as hard. Without AI, data quality, standardization and integration are often unreliable because data stays trapped in separate systems. Typical decisions around a digital thread therefore concern which systems stay authoritative for which records, how data is standardized across them, and how legacy environments are connected to newer platforms.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Graph Architecture Beyond Folders and Hierarchies" (2026-05-27) touches on the idea from a different angle. The episode says knowledge graphs connect data, workflows and applications, creating a digital thread that enhances every business process. It also says that combining AI with graph databases enables real-time, automated decision-making and dynamic IT governance, and that graph-based mapping supports compliance and governance through automated mapping, risk flagging and consistent auditability. In that framing, the digital thread is the result of relationships between data, workflows and applications being made explicit, rather than information being filed in folders and hierarchies.

Taken together, the sources present digital thread as a way to keep information connected across the stages of a product's life while leaving record ownership with the systems that already hold it. The manufacturing view emphasizes engineering, production and service data from PLM, ERP and MES, whereas the Microsoft 365 view emphasizes graph-based connections across data, workflows and applications. Both stress that the value comes from connected context that AI can use, and both imply that integration, data quality and standardization are the practical hurdles.

digital-twin.desc: A digital twin is a maintained digital representation of a physical resource, its relationships and operating conditions, kept current from observations.

faq.a: A digital twin is a maintained digital representation of a physical resource, its relationships, and its operating conditions, kept up to date from observations such as sensor data or transactions.
faq.q: What is a digital twin?

faq.a: According to the episode "Why AI Can't Optimize a Factory It Doesn't Understand", a live dashboard is not automatically a digital twin. A useful twin connects structure, state, rules, and source data around a specific purpose.
faq.q: Is a live dashboard the same as a digital twin?

faq.a: The episode "Digital Twins on Azure: What Should You Actually Model?" recommends starting with the decision the twin should support, rather than with the asset hierarchy or an architecture diagram.
faq.q: What should be modeled first in a digital twin project?

digital-twin.long:
A digital twin is a maintained digital representation of a physical resource, its relationships to other things, and the conditions under which it operates. The representation is kept up to date from observations, such as sensor readings, equipment activity, or transactions, so that it reflects the current state of the physical operation rather than a one-time snapshot. In the Microsoft ecosystem the term appears in several contexts, including Microsoft Fabric, Azure, and discussions about how AI agents can work with business logic.

The core idea is that a twin is more than a dashboard. The episode "Why AI Can't Optimize a Factory It Doesn't Understand" makes this point directly: a live dashboard is not automatically a digital twin. A useful twin represents a defined part of the physical operation and connects structure, state, rules, and source data around a specific purpose. The episode gives examples of scope. An asset twin might support maintenance decisions, a line twin might help understand flow and bottlenecks, and a production-system twin might connect equipment state to orders and related constraints. According to the episode, a twin without a job is hard to justify, and an AI system working on top of it can only give useful answers if the underlying model captures why something is or is not feasible, for instance because a required fixture is unavailable, a product revision lacks approval, or a downstream quality condition blocks a route.

This leads to the question of what should be modeled in the first place. The episode "Digital Twins on Azure: What Should You Actually Model?" argues that projects often start from the wish for a twin rather than from a real problem. It notes that data typically already lives across ERP, MES, historians, and IoT layers, yet operators still rely on phone calls, spreadsheets, and scattered alarms to work out what a fault actually affects. The episode's advice is to begin with the decision to be supported, not with the asset hierarchy or an elaborate architecture diagram, and to model only what that decision needs.

On the Microsoft Fabric side, the episode "Microsoft Fabric Digital Twin Builder Explained" describes the Digital Twin Builder, which was in preview at the time of recording. The episode presents it as a way to take things already known in an environment, such as machines, rooms, sensors, movements, and transactions, and give them a modeled counterpart inside Fabric. Event streams feed the model, so that changes such as temperature shifts, equipment activity, stock movement, or environmental readings update the twin continuously. This reflects the general mechanism of a digital twin: a structured model of entities and relationships combined with a stream of observations that keeps it current.

Governance is a further concern. The episode "Govern 3D Models and Digital Twins in Microsoft Fabric" addresses the challenge of managing large 3D assets and twins. It warns against relying on folders, shared drives, and good intentions to protect multi-gigabyte 3D files, and it raises the problem of "latest" becoming unreliable when versions are not controlled. The episode frames governance of a 1:1 digital twin as a demanding test case; if the estate can govern that, other assets become easier to manage. Compliance and consistent version control are presented as central to keeping twins trustworthy.

A different angle comes from the episode "Codify Business Logic into a Digital Twin for AI Agents," which challenges the habit of treating AI chatbots as the main interface for automation. The episode argues that chatbots are easy to deploy and demonstrate but often miss the business value held in organizational processes and decision-making logic. Its central message is to codify that logic into a digital twin, so that AI agents work against an explicit model of how the business operates instead of relying on conversation alone.

Taken together, the episodes describe a consistent pattern. A digital twin needs a defined purpose, a deliberately scoped model of structure and rules, a reliable flow of observations from source systems, and governance over the model and its assets. Decisions around it usually concern what to model, which data sources to connect, how to keep versions controlled, and whether the twin serves human operators, AI agents, or both.

digital-twin-builder.desc: Digital twin builder is a preview item in Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence for modeling real-world assets and relationships as an ontology, with data stored in OneLake.

faq.a: It is a preview item in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence for modeling real-world assets and their relationships as an ontology on a low-code semantic canvas.
faq.q: What is digital twin builder in Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: Twin data is stored in OneLake, the data lake used by Microsoft Fabric.
faq.q: Where is the data from a digital twin stored?

faq.a: No. It is described as a preview item, so its features may change before general availability.
faq.q: Is digital twin builder generally available?

digital-twin-builder.long:
Digital twin builder (Microsoft Fabric) is a preview item in Real-Time Intelligence within Microsoft Fabric. It is used to model real-world assets and the relationships between them as an ontology, working on a low-code semantic canvas.

The data behind the twin is stored in OneLake, the unified data lake that underpins Microsoft Fabric. The item belongs to the Microsoft Fabric platform and sits within its Real-Time Intelligence workload, which places it alongside other Fabric capabilities for working with data on that platform.

Because the feature is in preview, its scope and behavior may change before general availability. Microsoft's documentation for Real-Time Intelligence provides an overview of digital twin builder and is the reference for current capabilities and limitations.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

digital-twins-definition-language.desc: Digital Twins Definition Language (DTDL) is a JSON-LD based language for modeling digital twins, used by Azure Digital Twins and IoT Plug and Play.

faq.a: DTDL is a JSON-LD based language for describing digital twin models. It defines elements such as properties, telemetry, components, commands and relationships.
faq.q: What is Digital Twins Definition Language (DTDL)?

faq.a: DTDL is used by Azure Digital Twins and by IoT Plug and Play to describe models of twins and devices.
faq.q: Where is DTDL used?

faq.a: A DTDL model can describe properties, telemetry, components, commands and relationships.
faq.q: Which elements can a DTDL model contain?

digital-twins-definition-language.long:
Digital Twins Definition Language (DTDL) is a language for describing digital twin models. It is based on JSON-LD, so models are written as JSON documents that follow a defined structure. DTDL is used by Azure Digital Twins and by IoT Plug and Play.

A DTDL model describes the shape of a twin or device through a set of building blocks. These include properties, telemetry, components, commands and relationships. Properties describe the state of an entity, telemetry covers data emitted by it, and commands represent operations that can be invoked. Components allow one model to be composed of others, while relationships describe how twins connect to each other. Together these elements let a model capture both the characteristics of a single entity and the links within a larger environment.

In practice, DTDL provides the vocabulary for defining the models that Azure Digital Twins uses to represent real-world environments, and the same language is applied to describe the capabilities of devices in IoT Plug and Play. Further details on how models are defined in Azure Digital Twins are available in the Microsoft Learn documentation on models.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

direct-lake.desc: Direct Lake is a Power BI semantic model storage mode in Microsoft Fabric that reads Delta tables straight from OneLake, without importing a copy or querying the source per click.

faq.a: Direct Lake is a storage mode for Power BI semantic models in Microsoft Fabric. It reads Delta tables directly from OneLake instead of importing a copy of the data or querying the source on every click.
faq.q: What is Direct Lake in Power BI?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Fabric Direct Lake - Simply Explained" frames Import as fast but stale and DirectQuery as fresh but slow. Direct Lake aims to combine both by querying lakehouse Delta tables in place with performance similar to Import mode.
faq.q: How does Direct Lake differ from Import and DirectQuery?

faq.a: It relies on OneLake as the unified storage layer and on Delta tables, which provide ACID transactions, versioning and schema evolution. A semantic model in Fabric then sits on top and serves reports.
faq.q: Which Fabric components does Direct Lake rely on?

direct-lake.long:
Direct Lake is a storage mode for Power BI semantic models in Microsoft Fabric. Instead of importing a copy of the data into the model, or sending a query to the source system on every interaction, the semantic model reads Delta tables directly from OneLake. This addresses a long-standing trade-off in Power BI. Import mode is fast but can be stale, while DirectQuery is fresh but can be slow. Direct Lake is positioned to deliver both, so that reports can query lakehouse tables with performance similar to Import mode and without maintaining duplicate copies or complex refresh cycles.

The concept depends on several Fabric building blocks. OneLake provides the unified storage layer and supports the Delta Lake format. Delta tables add transactional features such as ACID transactions, data versioning and schema evolution, which keep the underlying data reliable and easy to update. Direct Lake mode then allows queries to run immediately, without a prior load into a warehouse. Semantic models in Fabric combine classic tabular modeling capabilities, including measures, hierarchies and calculated columns, with lake-based governance, so that business semantics and data governance travel together. Row- and column-level controls are part of that governance picture.

The episode "Speed Power BI with OneLake and Direct Lake" describes a pattern built around this mode: Dataflows Gen2 hydrate a lakehouse, pipelines keep it current and raise alerts, a semantic model sits on top, and a Direct Lake report consumes it. In that framing, OneLake becomes the governed source of truth. The episode also notes that Fabric admin controls allow the feature to be enabled safely, starting in a trial capacity rather than directly in production.

A second recurring theme is reuse. "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" explains that semantic models act as a shared metrics and business-logic layer that many reports and teams can use from one central place, which reduces duplication and inconsistency. According to that episode, Direct Lake support lets such models query parquet and Delta files in place with near-real-time freshness, avoiding full imports while keeping query performance highly optimized. The related episode "Optimize Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Performance" lists Direct Lake mode alongside OneLake and Delta tables as one of the components of a lakehouse setup, with the point that queries can run without waiting for data to load into a warehouse.

For analysts and admins, the practical decisions are which flavour of Direct Lake to choose, what licensing it needs, and which modeling mistakes make it slow. The episode "Microsoft Fabric Direct Lake - Simply Explained" is aimed at exactly these questions. It covers how framing works, which of the two flavours to pick, the licensing requirements and the common causes of poor performance, starting from the framing that import reports are fast but stale while DirectQuery reports are fresh but slow.

Direct Lake also appears in broader architecture discussions. In "From Financial Data to AI-Ready Decisions: Power BI, Microsoft Fabric, Semantic Models & AI Agents with Rishi Sapra [MVP]", it is named together with semantic models, DAX, lakehouses, OneLake, Copilot Studio, data agents, ontologies and MCP-based tools as part of a stack that has become harder for individual business users to understand. The episode raises the possibility that AI agents could build and operate parts of that technical stack, so that business users do not each need to become data engineers or BI developers.

In short, Direct Lake connects the lakehouse side of Microsoft Fabric with the semantic model layer of Power BI. Its value in the sources comes from reading Delta tables in place from OneLake, which keeps data fresh, avoids duplicate copies and lets governance and business logic stay close to the data.

direct-routing.desc: Direct Routing is a Teams Phone connectivity option where an organization connects its own certified session border controller and carrier trunks to Microsoft's SIP proxies.

faq.a: Direct Routing is a Teams Phone connectivity option in which an organization connects its own certified session border controller and chosen carrier trunks to Microsoft's SIP proxies. The organization owns routing, certificates and operations.
faq.q: What is Direct Routing in Microsoft Teams Phone?

faq.a: Microsoft's documentation lists a Microsoft-certified SBC, a Microsoft 365 tenant with users homed online, a verified custom domain that is not onmicrosoft.com, a public IP and DNS record for the SBC, a publicly trusted certificate, and firewall openings for Teams traffic. Licensing involves Teams and Teams Phone.
faq.q: What is needed to set up Direct Routing?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Teams Phone and Telephony | Simply Explained" presents all three as connectivity options. With Direct Routing the organization brings its own SBC and carrier trunks and manages routing itself.
faq.q: How does Direct Routing differ from Calling Plans and Operator Connect?

direct-routing.long:
Direct Routing is a connectivity option for Microsoft Teams Phone. It links an organization's own telephony infrastructure to Microsoft Teams through a supported, customer-provided session border controller (SBC) and the carrier trunks the organization chooses. In this model the organization owns routing, certificates and day-to-day operations, rather than handing these over to Microsoft or an operator.

The main purpose of Direct Routing is to let an organization keep its existing PSTN carriers while still using Teams Phone for calling. It also allows integration of third-party phone systems and gives more control over the voice infrastructure. According to Microsoft's planning documentation, typical uses include existing carrier relationships, third-party PBX systems or analog devices, and contact centers.

Technically, the SBC sits between the PSTN and Microsoft. Only Microsoft-certified SBCs are supported, and support for uncertified SBCs may be declined. One or more PSTN trunks attach to the SBC. Signaling uses TLS toward Microsoft SIP proxy hosts, which come with primary and failover FQDNs. Media flows over UDP and SRTP through defined port ranges, and media bypass is optional. The supported codecs are SILK, G.711, G.722, G.729 and AMR-WB, the last only when media bypass is not used.

The documentation lists several requirements. The organization needs a Microsoft 365 tenant with users homed online, and a verified custom domain that is not an onmicrosoft.com domain. The SBC needs a public IP address and a DNS record, plus a publicly trusted certificate. Firewalls must allow the Teams traffic. Licensing involves Teams and Teams Phone. Direct Routing is not supported in Islands mode.

Because the organization operates the SBC, certificates and routing itself, the choice of Direct Routing is mainly a decision about control versus effort. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Teams Phone and Telephony | Simply Explained" describes it as one of three connectivity options alongside Microsoft Calling Plans and Operator Connect. The episode explains these options so listeners can judge which approach fits their business requirements, and also covers Teams Telephony features such as voicemail, call forwarding, Auto Attendants, Call Queues, presence integration, call transfers and hybrid work support.

The episode "Teams Phone Migration: Moving From a PBX to Cloud Calling Without Surprises" places Direct Routing within migration planning. It treats the move from a PBX to cloud calling as rarely a pure technology project, since numbers, devices, sites and people each have their own timelines. The episode covers inventory and number planning, the choice between calling plans and Direct Routing, devices, emergency calling and user adoption, as well as how to sequence the migration and which surprises tend to appear.

In practice, organizations weigh Direct Routing when they already have carrier contracts, need to connect equipment that does not speak Teams natively, or want to keep control over how calls are routed. The trade-off is the responsibility for operating a certified SBC and keeping certificates, DNS and firewall rules in order.

directquery.desc: DirectQuery is a Power BI storage mode that copies no data into the model and sends each report interaction to the source database, keeping data live.

faq.a: DirectQuery is a storage mode in which no data is copied into the model. Each report interaction queries the source database directly, so the data shown is live.
faq.q: What is DirectQuery in Power BI?

faq.a: Report performance depends on the source and the network. The episode "Optimize Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Performance" warns that using DirectQuery without caching or aggregations increases dependence on source performance and latency.
faq.q: What is the main drawback of DirectQuery?

faq.a: Semantic models can use import, DirectQuery or Direct Lake storage modes. The episodes also describe composite models and aggregation tables, and one episode pairs DirectQuery for fast-changing facts with import for reference dimensions.
faq.q: How can DirectQuery be combined with other storage modes?

directquery.long:
DirectQuery is a storage mode in Power BI in which no data is copied into the semantic model. Instead, every interaction with a report, such as applying a filter or opening a visual, sends a query directly to the underlying source database. Because the data stays in the source, what a report shows is always live and does not depend on a scheduled refresh.

The main reason to choose DirectQuery is freshness. When reports need to reflect the current state of an operational system, a model that holds a periodic copy of the data can fall behind. With DirectQuery the report reads the source each time, so the result matches the source at the moment of the query. It is also relevant where the source data should not be duplicated, for example in sensitive systems or under strict compliance requirements, since the model does not store a second copy.

DirectQuery is one of several storage modes for Power BI semantic models. The episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" describes semantic models as holding tables, measures, relationships and calculations, and notes that they can be created with import, DirectQuery or Direct Lake storage modes to serve datasets and semantic layers to consumers. The choice of mode therefore sits at the level of the semantic model and shapes how reports behave once published.

The trade-off is that report performance depends on the source. The episode "Optimize Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Performance" lists relying on DirectQuery without assessing trade-offs as a common mistake. According to that episode, using DirectQuery against a lakehouse or external sources without caching or aggregations increases runtime dependence on source performance and network latency. The same episode points to aggregation tables and composite models as ways to serve common queries from small in-memory aggregates instead of sending every request to the source.

The Fabric-focused episodes show DirectQuery inside larger designs. In "Extend Microsoft Fabric with Custom APIs and Power BI Models", one pattern routes webhook events through an API receiver and a stream processor into a Delta table and KQL cache, and then serves them to a Power BI DirectQuery or hybrid table for alerts and live operational dashboards. Another pattern uses a rate-limited API gateway with Fabric Dataflows Gen2 or Power BI DirectQuery into a governed semantic model, which the episode recommends for sensitive systems, small result sets and strict compliance. In "Real-Time Dynamics 365 Campaign Analytics in Fabric", gold-layer tables are served to Power BI with DirectQuery or a short refresh for frequently changing facts, while import is kept for reference dimensions, with row-level security by region or business unit and caching for critical visuals.

The episode "Teams vs SharePoint for Power BI Dashboards" mentions DirectQuery in the context of how current a dashboard feels. It says a dashboard in Teams can feel live through DirectQuery or short refresh intervals, but that every viewer needs the right license, and missing licenses can result in blank tabs. SharePoint, by comparison, is described as relying on a stable nightly refresh by default, which suits scheduled reporting better than hour-by-hour operations.

In practice, the decision around DirectQuery weighs live data against query speed and source load. The episodes consistently pair it with mitigation measures: gold or curated tables as the source, aggregations, composite models that mix import and DirectQuery, caching of critical visuals and short refresh where near-real-time is sufficient. Official documentation for DirectQuery in Power BI Desktop is available from Microsoft Learn.

disaster-recovery.desc: Disaster recovery is the set of policies, tools and procedures for restoring IT systems and data after a major outage, usually derived from a business continuity plan.

faq.a: Disaster recovery is the set of policies, tools and procedures for restoring IT systems and data after a major outage or disaster. It is typically derived from a business continuity plan.
faq.q: What is disaster recovery?

faq.a: The episodes cover Azure Site Recovery, which replicates virtual machines and physical servers to a secondary region or site, Azure Traffic Manager for routing traffic during outages, and storage services such as Azure Storage Accounts (Blob Storage) and Azure NetApp Files.
faq.q: Which Azure services are discussed in connection with disaster recovery on M365.FM?

faq.a: The episode "Disaster Recovery for Plant Systems: Designing Resilience With Azure" says the recovery plan has to work on the shop floor, not only in a document, so it covers recovery objectives, backup, failover and testing to align IT recovery with production reality.
faq.q: Why does the plant systems episode stress testing?

disaster-recovery.long:
Disaster recovery is the set of policies, tools and procedures used to restore IT systems and data after a major outage or disaster. It is typically derived from a business continuity plan: the continuity plan describes what the organization must keep running, and the disaster recovery plan describes how the supporting systems and data are brought back. The term covers both the technical side, such as replication, backup and failover, and the organizational side, such as documented procedures and responsibilities.

In practice, disaster recovery work starts with deciding what must be recovered and how quickly. The M365.FM episode "Disaster Recovery for Plant Systems: Designing Resilience With Azure", part of the iFAKT series, frames this around recovery objectives, backup, failover and testing. Its central point is that a recovery plan has to work on the shop floor and not only in a document, so IT recovery needs to be aligned with production reality. The episode is aimed at plant IT and infrastructure teams who run systems where downtime has direct operational consequences.

Several Azure services appear in the M365.FM catalog as building blocks for disaster recovery. The episode "Azure Site Recovery - Simply Explained" describes Azure Site Recovery (ASR) as Microsoft's disaster recovery service for keeping business applications and workloads running during planned and unplanned outages. According to the episode, ASR continuously replicates virtual machines and physical servers to a secondary Azure region or recovery site, which allows organizations to recover quickly from failures while minimizing downtime and data loss. The episode is presented by Mirko Peters in the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets format.

Networking and routing are another part of the picture. In "Azure Traffic Manager - Simply Explained", disaster recovery is described as crucial for maintaining business continuity, and the episode lists several methods Azure Traffic Manager offers to keep applications available during outages. Among them are performance-based routing, which directs traffic to the region with the lowest network latency, and weighted routing, which splits traffic between endpoints according to assigned weights. The episode also mentions DNS-based global load balancing and multi-region application architectures as ways to support high availability for global applications.

Storage is the third area covered. The episode "Azure Storage Accounts - Simply Explained" lists backup and disaster recovery as a common use case for Blob Storage, where data is stored for backup, restore and disaster recovery to support business continuity. The episode "Azure NetApp Files - Simply Explained" notes that the file storage service integrates with Azure networking, identity, monitoring and disaster recovery features, and that it is used for enterprise workloads such as SAP HANA, Oracle databases, Azure VMware Solution and Azure Virtual Desktop.

Taken together, the episodes show that disaster recovery is not a single product but a combination of decisions: which workloads matter most, how data is replicated or backed up, how traffic is redirected when a region or site fails, and how the whole procedure is tested. Typical decisions include the choice of a secondary region or site, the balance between downtime and data loss that the business can accept, and how recovery steps are verified against real operating conditions. The M365.FM material treats testing and alignment with operational reality as part of the design, not as an afterthought.

diskann.desc: DiskANN is a Microsoft Research graph-based nearest neighbor search algorithm that keeps a compressed layer in RAM and the full graph on SSD for large vector workloads.

faq.a: DiskANN is a graph-based approximate nearest neighbor search algorithm from Microsoft Research. It keeps a compressed navigation layer in RAM and the full-precision graph on SSD.
faq.q: What is DiskANN?

faq.a: It is used in services such as Azure Cosmos DB and SQL Server vector search. It is also one of two vector search algorithms, alongside HNSW, discussed for Azure AI Search in the M365.FM episode "HNSW vs DiskANN for Vector Search in Azure AI Search".
faq.q: Where is DiskANN used?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode, HNSW is known for fast in-memory performance and high recall but requires significant RAM. DiskANN instead keeps only a compressed layer in RAM and places the full-precision graph on SSD.
faq.q: How does DiskANN differ from HNSW?

diskann.long:
DiskANN is a graph-based approximate nearest neighbor search algorithm developed at Microsoft Research. It is designed for vector search, the task of finding the stored embeddings that lie closest to a query embedding. Its defining characteristic is a split between memory and disk: a compressed navigation layer is kept in RAM, while the full-precision graph is kept on SSD. This design allows very large vector collections to be searched without holding every full-precision vector in memory. DiskANN is used in services such as Azure Cosmos DB and SQL Server vector search.

Vector search sits behind many AI-powered applications, including retrieval for copilots and semantic search over documents. Each item is converted into an embedding, and a query is answered by locating the nearest embeddings rather than matching keywords. When the number of vectors grows very large, the cost of the infrastructure needed to serve them becomes a central concern. The M365.FM episode "HNSW vs DiskANN for Vector Search in Azure AI Search" frames this as the "billion-vector problem": how to search through billions of vector embeddings without exploding infrastructure costs.

In practice, the main decision DiskANN is associated with is the choice of index algorithm. The episode compares two vector search algorithms available in Azure AI Search: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) and DiskANN. According to the episode, HNSW has become the industry standard thanks to its fast in-memory performance and high recall, but it requires significant RAM. DiskANN addresses the same search problem with a different resource profile, since only the compressed navigation layer needs to reside in memory and the full-precision graph stays on SSD. The trade-off between memory footprint, speed and recall is therefore the core of the comparison.

How it works can be summarized from the short description. The algorithm builds a graph over the vectors and navigates that graph to reach close neighbors, which is why it is described as graph-based and approximate: it aims to find very close matches quickly rather than guaranteeing an exhaustive comparison against every vector. The compressed representation held in RAM guides the navigation, and the full-precision data on SSD is consulted where needed. This arrangement is what lets storage capacity, rather than memory alone, determine how large an index can grow.

DiskANN also appears in the wider Microsoft ecosystem beyond Azure AI Search. The facts available name Azure Cosmos DB and SQL Server vector search as services that use it, which shows that the same approach is applied across both cloud database and relational database offerings. For teams evaluating where to run vector workloads, this means the algorithm is not tied to a single product but is a building block that surfaces in several places.

The topic connects to several other M365.FM episodes. "Azure AI Search – Simply Explained" presents the key concepts behind Azure AI Search and how it fits into the wider Microsoft technology ecosystem, and lists the HNSW versus DiskANN episode as related listening. "Vector Databases - Simply Explained" covers the key concepts behind vector databases and likewise points to the HNSW versus DiskANN comparison. "Improve Microsoft Copilot Accuracy Beyond Vector Search" discusses accuracy in Microsoft Copilot beyond vector search alone, again referencing the same comparison episode. Together these episodes place DiskANN as one of the algorithm choices underneath vector search, which in turn supports retrieval for AI scenarios.

dispatch-list.desc: A dispatch list is the immediate shop-floor instruction that tells a person or machine which operation to run next, distinct from a broader plan or detailed schedule.

faq.a: A dispatch list is the immediate shop-floor instruction that tells a person or machine which operation to run next in the current situation. It is narrower than a production plan or a detailed schedule.
faq.q: What is a dispatch list?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode, a production plan works at a broader level, covering demand, product families and capacity across a longer horizon, while a detailed schedule arranges specific operations. The dispatch list is the short-term instruction for what to run next.
faq.q: How does a dispatch list differ from a production plan and a detailed schedule?
