faq.a: The episode explains that the factory produces newer information than the ERP holds, for example a person on the workforce calendar who lacks the qualification needed for the next operation. The ERP is not necessarily wrong; the situation has simply changed.
faq.q: Why can a dispatch decision differ from what the ERP system shows?

dispatch-list.long:
A dispatch list is the immediate shop-floor instruction that tells a person or machine which operation to run next, given the situation as it currently stands. It is the most short-term layer of production decision-making. Where a production plan and a detailed schedule describe what should happen over a longer horizon, a dispatch list answers a narrower question at the moment of execution: what should be started now, at this work centre, by this operator or on this machine.

The term is easiest to understand by contrasting it with two other things that are often both called a schedule. According to the M365.FM episode "Why Your Production Schedule Is Wrong Before It Even Starts", one reason production planning becomes confusing is that several different decisions are described with the same word. A production plan works at a broader level. It determines what demand needs to be covered, which product families should be produced, and whether enough capacity and material appear to exist across a longer planning horizon. A detailed production schedule then arranges specific operations in time. The dispatch list sits below both and reflects what is actually possible right now rather than what was assumed when the plan was made.

This distinction matters because the factory continually generates newer information than the planning system holds. The episode gives an example: a person may appear on the workforce calendar while lacking the specific qualification required for the next operation. In that case, the episode says, the ERP system is not necessarily wrong; the factory has simply produced newer information. A dispatch decision is where that newer information is taken into account, for instance by choosing an operation that can really be run with the people, machines and materials available.

The broader context is described in general manufacturing-systems documentation. A manufacturing execution system (MES) tracks and documents how raw materials become finished goods and monitors plant-floor conditions in real time. One of its core functions is dispatching production orders, meaning the distribution of batches, runs and work orders to work centres and the adjustment to unexpected conditions. This sits alongside scheduling, which turns production requirements from ERP or planning systems into work orders that make good use of local resources, and alongside resource management, which tracks capability and availability. The control systems carry out the actual execution, while the MES checks resources and reports progress. In the ISA-95 model, MES sits at Level 3, between ERP at Level 4 and process control at Levels 0 to 2. Note that this documentation describes the dispatching function and does not itself use the term dispatch list.

In practice, a dispatch list is therefore the point where planning meets execution. Typical decisions around it include which of the waiting operations to run next, whether the required qualification, tooling and material are actually present, and how to react when conditions differ from the plan. Treating the plan, the detailed schedule and the dispatch list as separate levels helps clarify which decision is being discussed and which system or role is responsible for it, instead of relying on the single word schedule for all three.

disposition-review.desc: Disposition review is a Microsoft Purview process in which designated reviewers decide whether content at the end of its retention period may be permanently deleted.

faq.a: It is a process in which designated reviewers decide whether content that has reached the end of its retention period can be permanently deleted. It adds a human approval step before deletion.
faq.q: What is a disposition review in Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Purview Records Management - Simply Explained", it provides structured approval workflows so records are evaluated by designated reviewers before permanent deletion, once retention requirements have been satisfied.
faq.q: Why use disposition review instead of automatic deletion?

faq.a: The episode "Automate Document Processing with Microsoft Syntex" suggests tracking the disposition review completion rate, meaning reviews completed on time, with a target of 95% or above as part of its compliance metrics.
faq.q: How can disposition review be monitored?

disposition-review.long:
Disposition review is a Microsoft Purview process in which designated reviewers decide whether content that has reached the end of its retention period can be permanently deleted. Instead of letting items disappear automatically once a retention requirement has been met, the organization places a human approval step between the end of retention and the actual deletion. The official Microsoft documentation describes it as part of the records and retention capabilities in Microsoft Purview.

The purpose is controlled disposal. Keeping records is only one side of governance; organizations also need a defined way to dispose of them once retention requirements have been satisfied. The episode "Microsoft Purview Records Management - Simply Explained" describes Disposition Review as introducing structured approval workflows that require designated reviewers to evaluate records before permanent deletion. This helps ensure that records still needed for other reasons are not removed simply because a timer has expired.

In practice, disposition review is configured as part of the retention rules that apply to a content class. The episode "Microsoft 365 Retention Policies vs Records Management" lists it among the items to define for each class of content: the retention period, the event or creation date that starts the period, whether the item needs to be declared a record, whether a disposition review is required, and whether holds apply. That makes it one of several design decisions made together rather than a stand-alone setting. The same episode frames the choice of control by risk level: records for high-risk or high-regulatory items such as contracts and patient or financial records, retention labels for item-level control where immutability is not required, and location policies for broad, low-risk baselines.

Disposition review also appears in governance planning for the wider platform. The episode "Microsoft 365 Structural Debt from Default Governance" includes implementing retention labels and disposition review processes in its list of governance tasks, alongside defining the lifecycle of sites, groups, Teams and mailboxes (creation, review, archive and deletion), enabling audit logging, and configuring eDiscovery and legal hold. In that framing, disposition review belongs to the compliance and records management layer, where regulatory and legal requirements are mapped to Microsoft 365 controls.

Because the process depends on people acting on review requests, it can be measured. The episode "Automate Document Processing with Microsoft Syntex" lists disposition review completion rate, described as reviews completed on time, with a target of 95% or above, among its compliance metrics. Other metrics in the same list include retention label coverage and sensitivity label coverage. The episode attributes these figures to its own suggested scorecard; they are not a Microsoft requirement.

Disposition review works alongside other Microsoft Purview technologies. The episode on records management mentions Sensitivity Labels, which protect document access through encryption, and Data Loss Prevention, which monitors the movement of sensitive information, as technologies that together secure business information throughout its lifecycle. Disposition review covers the end of that lifecycle: it adds an accountable decision before content is permanently removed, and the episode also connects it to an audit history of those decisions.

Typical decisions around the feature include who should act as reviewers, which content classes warrant a review step rather than automatic deletion, how reviews are tracked to completion, and how the review step interacts with holds and record declarations. The sources provided do not go into further technical detail, so licensing, exact configuration steps and reviewer permissions should be checked against the current Microsoft Purview documentation.

distributed-order-management.desc: Distributed order management (DOM) in Dynamics 365 Commerce applies business rules to select a store or warehouse for fulfilling an order, based on stock and delivery promise.
distributed-order-management.long:
Distributed order management (DOM) is a concept in Dynamics 365 Commerce that uses business rules to decide which store or warehouse should fulfill a given order. It is relevant where an organization has several possible fulfillment locations and needs a consistent way to choose among them.

The selection of a fulfillment location is based on factors such as available stock, the delivery promise made to the customer, and the set of locations that can fulfill orders. By expressing these considerations as business rules, DOM replaces ad hoc, manual decisions about where an order should be processed with a rule-driven approach.

Typical use of DOM concerns order fulfillment scenarios in retail and commerce, where an order may be placed through one channel and fulfilled from a different store or warehouse. The concept sits within the broader Dynamics 365 Commerce area of the Microsoft ecosystem.

No specific episodes on M365.FM are currently linked to this term, and no further details such as configuration steps, versions or related products are recorded here.

distributed-transactions.desc: Distributed transactions are operations that must commit or roll back atomically across multiple services or databases, classically coordinated through a two-phase commit.
distributed-transactions.long:
Distributed transactions are transactions that span more than one service or database and must either commit everywhere or roll back everywhere. The goal is atomicity: all participating resources end up in a consistent state, even though the work is spread across separate systems.

The classic way to coordinate such a transaction is a two-phase commit. In this approach, a coordinator first asks every participant whether it can commit, and only then instructs all of them to commit or to roll back. This is used when a single logical operation touches several data stores or services that cannot share one local transaction.

In .NET, support for distributed transactions has platform restrictions. In .NET 7 and later, this support is Windows-only and must be explicitly enabled rather than being available by default. Developers working with cross-database or cross-service operations in .NET therefore need to account for the operating system and configuration requirements.

The topic is relevant to anyone designing data access and service integration in the Microsoft ecosystem, since it affects how consistency is maintained when one business operation involves multiple resources. No M365.FM episodes are linked to this entry at this time.

distribution-list.desc: A distribution list is a static mail-enabled group in Exchange Online whose membership changes only when an administrator or owner adjusts it.

faq.a: A distribution list is a static mail-enabled group in Exchange Online. Messages sent to its email address are delivered to its members.
faq.q: What is a distribution list in Exchange Online?

faq.a: Membership is static and only changes when an administrator or the group owner adjusts it.
faq.q: How does membership of a distribution list change?

faq.a: Microsoft publishes documentation on managing distribution groups in Exchange Online, linked as the official documentation for this concept.
faq.q: Where can administration details be found?

distribution-list.long:
A distribution list is a static mail-enabled group in Exchange Online. Its membership does not update automatically; it only changes when an administrator or the group's owner adds or removes members.

The defining trait of a distribution list is this manual, fixed membership. Unlike groups whose membership is driven by rules or queries, the list of recipients stays the same until someone with the right permissions edits it. Because the group is mail-enabled, it has an email address, so a message sent to that address is delivered to every member.

Distribution lists are typically used to reach a defined set of people with a single address, such as a team, a project group or a mailing audience. Administration of distribution groups in Exchange Online is described in the official Microsoft documentation on managing distribution groups.

No related topics or episodes are currently linked to this entry on M365.FM, so this page limits itself to the core definition of the concept.

dkim.desc: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) is an email authentication method where the sending server signs messages with a private key and publishes the public key in DNS.
dkim.long:
DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) is an email authentication method. The sending mail server signs outgoing messages with a private key, and the matching public key is published in DNS. A receiving server can look up that public key and use it to check the signature.

The signature is used to show two things: that the message content has not been altered in transit (integrity) and that the message originated from a system authorized to sign for the signing domain (origin). Because verification relies on a published DNS record, the domain owner controls which keys are valid for their mail.

DKIM is one of several email authentication mechanisms that organizations configure for the domains they send mail from. It is typically managed by administrators who handle DNS records and mail flow settings.

No further details about DKIM, such as specific product implementations, configuration steps, or related topics, are available in the material provided for this page. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

dlp.desc: Data loss prevention (DLP) uses policies to detect sensitive information and stop it from being shared, copied or uploaded in ways that break company rules.

faq.a: DLP uses policies to detect sensitive information such as credit card numbers or personal data and prevent it from being shared, copied or uploaded in ways that violate company rules. Controls can warn users, block risky sharing and give security and compliance teams visibility.
faq.q: What does data loss prevention (DLP) do?

faq.a: DLP is part of Microsoft Purview and applies to content across Microsoft 365. The episodes also mention DLP as a capability in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps and as a mechanism used with Adaptive Protection in Insider Risk Management.
faq.q: Which Microsoft product includes DLP?

faq.a: The episode "Data Loss Prevention in Microsoft 365: Policies That Actually Work" says policies fail when they either block everything or catch nothing. It recommends scoping, sensitive information types, policy tips, simulation mode and tuning, and rolling out DLP in stages.
faq.q: Why do DLP policies sometimes fail?

dlp.long:
Data loss prevention (DLP) is a set of policies that detect sensitive information, such as credit card numbers or personal data, and prevent it from being shared, copied or uploaded in ways that violate company rules. In the Microsoft ecosystem, DLP is part of Microsoft Purview and works on content across Microsoft 365. The aim is to protect data while still allowing approved business work to continue.

A DLP policy follows a simple logic: it identifies content that matches defined criteria and then applies a control. According to the episode "Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) - Simply Explained", Microsoft Purview DLP detects sensitive information and applies policy-based controls across Microsoft 365. Those controls can warn users, block risky sharing, and give security and compliance teams visibility into what is happening. This range of responses matters in practice, because not every situation calls for a hard block. A warning may be enough for a low-risk case, while a block fits content that must never leave the organization.

DLP is often combined with sensitivity labels. Labels classify content, and DLP rules can then act on that classification. The episode "Microsoft Purview Information Protection - Simply Explained" describes labels that can restrict access, encrypt content or add visual markings such as watermarks, and notes that policies can block sharing or trigger alerts when sensitive data is at risk of exposure. It also says this works together with data loss prevention and insider risk management to prevent data leaks and support compliance. In that sense, labeling and DLP are complementary: one identifies and marks the data, the other enforces how it may be handled.

Design choices decide whether a DLP deployment succeeds. The episode "Data Loss Prevention in Microsoft 365: Policies That Actually Work" states that DLP policies fail when they either block everything or catch nothing, and that the sweet spot takes iteration. It covers how to design Microsoft Purview DLP policies through scoping, sensitive information types, policy tips, simulation mode and tuning. It also recommends rolling out DLP in stages and measuring whether the policies actually work, rather than switching on strict enforcement at once. Simulation mode and tuning are the practical tools for that approach, since they allow a policy to be observed and adjusted before it affects users.

DLP also appears in other parts of the Microsoft security portfolio. The episode "Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps - Simply Explained" lists data loss prevention among the capabilities it covers, alongside Cloud Discovery, app governance, SaaS Security Posture Management, threat detection, OAuth app protection and adaptive access controls. It also describes how that platform integrates with Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Sentinel and Microsoft 365, and mentions scenarios such as preventing sensitive data exposure.

There is a link to insider risk as well. The episode "Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management - Simply Explained" says the system uses Adaptive Protection to identify high-risk actors and to enforce strict data loss prevention policies, so that organizations can act quickly when needed. It also describes analysis of user behavior patterns and contextual signals across services including Exchange, SharePoint and Teams. Here DLP acts as an enforcement mechanism that can be tightened when risk signals rise.

Typical decisions around DLP include which locations and users a policy covers, which sensitive information types it looks for, whether it should only warn or also block, and how long to observe results in simulation before enforcing. The episodes suggest treating DLP as an iterative process of scoping, testing and tuning, with visibility for security and compliance teams, instead of a one-time configuration.

dlp-simulation-mode.desc: DLP simulation mode in Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention runs a policy without blocking anything, letting admins review matches and tune rules before enforcement.

faq.a: DLP simulation mode is a Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention mode in which a policy runs as if it were enforced but does not block anything. It is used to see what a policy would match before enforcement.
faq.q: What is DLP simulation mode?

faq.a: It lets admins review the matches a policy produces and tune its rules before enforcement. This helps ensure the policy targets the intended content without blocking activity during testing.
faq.q: Why use simulation mode before enforcing a DLP policy?

faq.a: No. In simulation mode the policy behaves as if it were enforced, but it does not block anything.
faq.q: Does DLP simulation mode block users or content?

dlp-simulation-mode.long:
DLP simulation mode is a mode in Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) in which a policy runs as if it were enforced, but without blocking any activity. Because nothing is actually stopped, the policy can be evaluated against real content and user behavior without disrupting work.

The main use of simulation mode is to test a policy before it goes live. Administrators can review the matches the policy generates, see which items and activities would have been affected, and adjust the rules accordingly. This tuning step helps refine conditions and scope before the policy moves to enforcement.

In practice, simulation mode sits between drafting a Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention policy and turning it on. It gives admins a way to check whether a rule is matching the intended content and whether the volume of matches is reasonable, so that enforcement settings can be applied with more information.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry. Further details on how the mode works are available in the official Microsoft Learn documentation on DLP simulation mode.

dmarc.desc: DMARC is an email authentication standard published in DNS that checks SPF and DKIM alignment with the From domain and tells receivers how to handle failures.

faq.a: DMARC checks whether SPF or DKIM results align with the visible From domain and instructs receivers to do nothing, quarantine, or reject mail that fails. The policy is published as a record in DNS.
faq.q: What does DMARC do?

faq.a: According to the episode "Stop Deepfake Business Email Compromise with Verified ID", SPF, DKIM, and DMARC verify that the sender is authentic but do not examine content or intent. They therefore do not cover deepfake-based attacks on their own.
faq.q: Is DMARC enough to stop business email compromise?

faq.a: DMARC works alongside SPF and DKIM, which are the other two DNS records described in "SPF, DKIM and DMARC - Simply Explained". It ties their results to the domain in the visible From address.
faq.q: How does DMARC relate to SPF and DKIM?

dmarc.long:
DMARC is an email authentication standard published as a record in DNS. It checks whether the results of SPF and DKIM align with the domain shown in the visible From address, and it tells receiving mail systems what to do with messages that fail: do nothing, quarantine the message, or reject it. In this way DMARC connects two other authentication mechanisms to the address that a human recipient actually sees, which is the part of a message most easily faked.

The need for DMARC follows from how email was designed. The episode "SPF, DKIM and DMARC - Simply Explained" points out that the email system was built to move messages rather than to verify who is sending them, so anyone with a laptop can send a message that pretends to come from a company. A fake invoice or a fraudulent note that appears to come from a manager can reach a real inbox with the organization's name on it. The episode describes three DNS records that close this gap and notes that a surprising number of organizations set up only one of them. DMARC is the third of those records, working alongside SPF and DKIM rather than replacing them.

In practice, a DMARC record is published for a domain and sets a policy that receivers apply. The three outcomes named in the standard's description are to take no action, to quarantine failing mail, or to reject it. Because the policy is expressed in DNS, the domain owner controls it without changing how individual messages are sent. The key idea is alignment: it is not enough for a message to pass SPF or DKIM in isolation; the passing result has to line up with the domain in the From header.

DMARC also appears in the context of mail flow in Microsoft environments. In the episode "When Microsoft Messaging Looks Secure but Isn’t — Exchange Server, Hybrid and Microsoft 365 Security with Thomas Stensitzki [MVP]", the guest explains the roles of SPF, DKIM, and DMARC in authenticating messages sent from an organization's domain. The discussion stresses understanding the full route an email takes, especially in complex setups that combine gateways, Exchange Server, Exchange Online Protection, and Microsoft Defender. He also recommends dedicated subdomains for third-party services such as marketing platforms, which keeps the authentication setup for those senders separate from the main domain.

DMARC is part of a wider hardening checklist as well. The episode "Harden Microsoft 365 Security Without User Friction" lists publishing SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records as a step to reduce spoofing and phishing, next to items such as tracking Microsoft Secure Score, tightening SharePoint and OneDrive sharing, and restricting legacy authentication. In hybrid scenarios, "Maintain Hybrid Exchange Beyond the Configuration Wizard" notes that inbound and outbound connectors, TLS, and SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment together govern delivery and reputation.

The limits of DMARC matter when judging what it protects against. The episode "Stop Deepfake Business Email Compromise with Verified ID" cautions that SPF, DKIM, and DMARC only check whether the sender is authentic; they do not examine the content or intent of a message. According to that episode, deepfake-based business email compromise attacks rose from less than 5% in 2023 to 40% by 2026, and it argues that enterprise security increasingly depends on provable digital identity rather than on how legitimate a message looks. DMARC therefore addresses sender spoofing of a domain, while content-based and identity-based threats call for additional controls.

docker.desc: Docker is a set of tools that package and run applications in portable containers; on Windows, Docker Desktop runs on top of WSL 2.

faq.a: Docker is a set of tools that package and run applications in portable containers. A container bundles an application with its dependencies so it can run consistently across environments.
faq.q: What is Docker?

faq.a: Docker Desktop on Windows runs on top of WSL 2.
faq.q: How does Docker Desktop run on Windows?

faq.a: The episode "Kubernetes - Simply Explained" says Docker is primarily a platform for creating and running containers, while Kubernetes serves a different purpose in managing containerized applications. Both are central to containerization but are not the same tool.
faq.q: What is the difference between Docker and Kubernetes?

docker.long:
Docker is a set of tools that package and run applications in portable containers. A container bundles an application together with its dependencies into a single unit, so the same software can be moved between machines and environments. On Windows, Docker Desktop runs on top of WSL 2. In the M365.FM catalog, Docker appears in episodes about cloud development, DevOps workflows, Azure hosting and self-hosted automation tooling.

The core problem Docker addresses is the familiar "works on my machine" situation, where software behaves differently across developer laptops, build servers and production. The episode "Docker and Containers - Simply Explained" describes Docker as the most-used tool in cloud development and walks through the problem it solves, what a container actually is, images, Dockerfiles and the role of layers, registries where images are stored and shared, and how containers compare with virtual machines. Those topics make up the basic vocabulary needed to work with Docker: a Dockerfile describes how an image is built, an image is the packaged result, a registry stores and distributes images, and a container is a running instance of an image.

A common point of confusion is the relationship between Docker and Kubernetes. The episode "Kubernetes - Simply Explained" contrasts the two and says they serve different purposes. According to that episode, Docker is primarily a platform for creating and running containers, packaging applications and their dependencies into a single unit, while Kubernetes deals with deploying and managing containerized applications. The two are therefore often mentioned together in discussions of containerization, but they are not interchangeable.

Docker also plays a role in development environments. The episode "Stop Environment Drift with VS Code Dev Containers" covers how containerization has become foundational to DevOps workflows and how development containers keep coding environments consistent. It describes dev containers, configured with a devcontainer.json file and used from VS Code, as reproducible and portable workspaces, and it names Docker, GitHub Actions and command-line utilities as tools that streamline work from build to deployment. In that context, Docker supplies the container runtime that makes a shared, repeatable developer setup possible and helps address environment drift.

On the hosting side, the episode "Azure Container Apps - Simply Explained" notes that Azure Container Apps supports Docker images from any container registry while simplifying deployment and operations. The episode covers concepts such as containers, revisions, ingress, environments, autoscaling, scale-to-zero, KEDA and Dapr, and scenarios including web APIs, microservices, background jobs, AI agents and event-driven applications. For teams that already build Docker images, this shows how an image can be run on a managed Azure service rather than on infrastructure they operate themselves.

Docker is also a common way to install and run self-hosted tools. The episode "How to Build Private RAG with SharePoint and n8n" lists Docker as one hosting option for n8n, alongside installing on a virtual machine or using a managed cloud service, and notes that many organizations choose self-hosting for privacy and compliance. The episode shows a docker run command that publishes port 5678, mounts a local folder for n8n data and starts the n8nio/n8n image, after which the n8n dashboard is opened in a browser.

Taken together, the episodes place Docker at the base of several workflows: building and packaging applications as images, sharing them through registries, running them locally or on Windows through Docker Desktop with WSL 2, using them for consistent development environments, and deploying them to services such as Azure Container Apps. Decisions around Docker typically involve whether a container or a virtual machine fits the workload, where images are stored, and whether an orchestrator or a managed container service is needed once more than a single container is involved.

docker-hub.desc: Docker Hub is Docker's default public registry for finding, storing and sharing container images, with public and private repositories and curated base images.

faq.a: Docker Hub is Docker's default public registry for finding, storing and sharing container images. Teams use it to pull pre-built images as a starting point and to publish their own images in public or private repositories.
faq.q: What is Docker Hub used for?

faq.a: According to Docker's documentation, it can be used through the web interface, the Docker Hub API, an experimental CLI tool, and a Docker Hub MCP server for integrating AI agents.
faq.q: How can Docker Hub be accessed?

faq.a: The episode "Stop Environment Drift with VS Code Dev Containers" notes that Docker offers many official images on Docker Hub that can serve as base images, and recommends keeping them updated with security patches and using multi-stage builds.
faq.q: How does Docker Hub relate to base images in Dockerfiles?

docker-hub.long:
Docker Hub is a container image registry and Docker's default public registry for finding, storing and sharing container images. Docker's documentation describes it as the world's largest registry for storing, managing and sharing Docker images. It integrates with developer tools to support deployment and distribution of containerized applications and offers pre-built images and assets that are meant to speed up development.

In practice, Docker Hub serves two roles. First, it is a source of ready-made images that teams use as a starting point for their own applications. Second, it is a place to publish and distribute images that a team builds itself. The documentation lists unlimited public repositories and private repositories as core features, so the same service can hold openly shared images as well as images meant only for an organization. Further listed features include webhooks for automating workflows, integrations with GitHub and Bitbucket, concurrent and automated builds, and trusted content, which the documentation defines as curated, high-quality, secure images. In the documentation's navigation, automated builds are marked as deprecated.

Users can work with Docker Hub in several ways: through the web interface, through the Docker Hub API, through an experimental CLI tool, and through a Docker Hub MCP server intended for integrating AI agents. The documentation hub also points to sections on a quickstart, the library with search, trusted content and mirrors, repositories, settings, organizations, usage and limits, and release notes. The page itself acts as an overview and entry point rather than a detailed reference for each feature, so questions about limits or organization settings are answered in the linked sections.

Two M365.FM episodes mention Docker Hub in the context of .NET and developer environments. In "Stop Environment Drift with VS Code Dev Containers", the discussion centers on building container images and choosing a base image. The episode notes that Docker provides a large selection of official images on Docker Hub, which makes it easier to find an appropriate base image for an application. It also recommends keeping the base image updated with the latest security patches to reduce potential vulnerabilities, and it describes multi-stage builds in a Dockerfile, where larger images are used for building and smaller images for runtime, to optimize the container build process and reduce image size.

In "Fix OWASP Architectural Risks in .NET Applications", Docker Hub appears in a list of tools for tracking images and artifacts. The episode describes it as a container registry that also serves as an artifact repository for Docker images, with public and private options. In the same list it places Harness Artifact Registry, described as an AI-native solution for centralized artifact management integrated with CI/CD pipelines and security features, and NuGet, the package manager for .NET that provides a centralized repository for .NET libraries and tools. The context given is the need for a clear migration plan, since without one parts of an application may have to be re-engineered, and tracking images and artifacts helps with that problem.

Typical decisions around Docker Hub therefore involve which base images to trust, whether images should be public or private, and how to keep images current. Using official or curated images, updating base images for security patches, and keeping runtime images small are the practices the episodes connect with it. Teams that automate workflows can look at webhooks and the GitHub and Bitbucket integrations, while keeping in mind that the documentation marks automated builds as deprecated.

dockerfile.desc: A Dockerfile is a plain-text file listing the instructions for building a Docker image, one instruction per line, with each step producing a layer.

faq.a: A Dockerfile is a plain-text file that lists the instructions for building a Docker image. Each instruction is on its own line, and each step produces a layer of the image.
faq.q: What is a Dockerfile?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode on modern .NET shows an example that sets an ASP.NET 8.0 base image, copies the application into an app folder, sets the working directory and defines an entry point that runs the application's DLL.
faq.q: What does a simple Dockerfile contain?

faq.a: According to the episode "Kubernetes - Simply Explained", writing a Dockerfile to package the application and its dependencies is the first step. The image is then built, pushed to a container registry and referenced by Kubernetes manifests.
faq.q: How does a Dockerfile fit into a Kubernetes deployment?

dockerfile.long:
A Dockerfile is a plain-text file that lists the instructions for building a Docker image. Each instruction sits on its own line, and each step in the file produces a layer of the resulting image. Because the build is described in a file rather than performed by hand, the same steps can be repeated by anyone with access to the file, which is why the Dockerfile shows up in so many containerization and automation workflows.

The main purpose of a Dockerfile is to define the environment in which an application runs. The M365.FM episode "Modern .NET: WPF, ASP.NET Core, and gRPC with Gábor Ruzsinszki [MVP]" describes it in this way: a simple Dockerfile defines the app's environment, so the application can be packaged in a container that is portable and easy to deploy anywhere. The episode gives a short example for an ASP.NET application. It starts from a Microsoft-published ASP.NET 8.0 base image, copies the application files into an app folder, sets that folder as the working directory, and defines an entry point that launches the application's DLL with the dotnet command. That example shows the typical shape of a Dockerfile: a base image, the files to include, a working directory and a command to run.

The Dockerfile is also the first step in the path from source code to a running container service. The episode "Kubernetes - Simply Explained" lists, as the first step of a first Kubernetes deployment, containerizing the application by writing a Dockerfile that packages the application and its dependencies. After that, the image is built and pushed to a container registry, Kubernetes manifests are defined as YAML files for objects such as deployments and services, and a CI/CD pipeline is set up to build, test and deploy. The episode mentions tools like Helm or Kustomize for managing the manifest files. In this sequence the Dockerfile produces the artifact, the image, that the later Kubernetes objects refer to.

In continuous integration, the Dockerfile serves as one of the configuration files that define the pipeline's steps and dependencies. The episode "Stop Environment Drift with VS Code Dev Containers" describes a pipeline in which a developer commits code to a repository, which triggers an automated build. That build compiles the code, runs tests and packages the application into a container image using tools like Docker and npm. According to the episode, configuration files such as the Dockerfile and the YAML files for GitHub Actions define these steps and dependencies, which helps keep the process consistent and reliable. Docker is presented there as a standardized way to package applications and their dependencies into container images, and the Dockerfile is the place where that packaging is spelled out.

A few practical points follow from the sources. Since the file is plain text and describes the build step by step, it can be stored in the same repository as the application code and reviewed like other code. Since each step produces a layer, the order and content of the instructions determine how the image is assembled. And since the image built from a Dockerfile can be pushed to a container registry, the same definition can be used to deploy to environments such as Kubernetes or cloud services like Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), as mentioned in the .NET episode. Teams deciding how to package an application typically weigh the portability of a container image against the extra step of maintaining the Dockerfile and the registry workflow around it.

The Dockerfile is therefore best understood as the build recipe at the center of container-based development: it records what an image contains, supports repeatable builds in CI pipelines, and provides the starting point for deployments to container platforms.

domain-controller.desc: A domain controller is a server running Active Directory Domain Services that authenticates users and computers and supplies group policy to domain members.

faq.a: A domain controller is a server that runs Active Directory Domain Services for a Windows domain. It authenticates users and computers and holds the group policy that domain members download.
faq.q: What does a domain controller do?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Entra Domain Services - Simply Explained", organizations can keep an existing Active Directory environment connected to Azure or deploy their own domain controller VMs in Azure. Both approaches bring infrastructure and operational responsibilities. Microsoft Entra Domain Services is the managed alternative, where Microsoft operates the domain controllers.
faq.q: How can domain controllers be provided in Azure?

faq.a: The episode "AD Tiering and Privileged Access with Viktor Hedberg [MVP-MCT]" recommends Privileged Access Workstations for administrators, multi-factor authentication, Just Enough Admin for domain controller maintenance, and Advanced Threat Analytics for attack detection.
faq.q: How are domain controllers protected from attacks?

domain-controller.long:
A domain controller is a server that runs Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) for a Windows domain. It authenticates users and computers and holds the group policy that domain members download. In a traditional Windows environment, the domain controller is the central point of trust: a sign-in to a domain-joined device is validated against it, and the policy settings that shape how that device behaves are distributed from it.

The role matters because many applications and workloads still expect to talk directly to a Windows domain. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Entra Domain Services - Simply Explained" notes that, instead of consuming modern cloud authentication, such workloads expect to communicate with a domain using technologies such as LDAP and Kerberos. Those protocols are served by domain controllers, so any environment that depends on them needs access to one, whether on-premises or in the cloud.

The same episode describes the options organizations have when they move or extend workloads into Azure. They can keep an existing Active Directory environment connected to Azure, or they can deploy their own domain controller VMs in Azure. According to the episode, both approaches introduce infrastructure and operational responsibilities, because someone has to run, patch and maintain the servers. As an alternative, Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides a managed Windows domain inside an Azure virtual network, where Microsoft operates the underlying domain controllers while Azure workloads consume traditional Active Directory capabilities.

Domain controllers also appear in setup guidance for other services. The episode "Azure Virtual Desktop - Simply Explained" lists, among its setup steps, connecting a virtual network to the domain controller as part of linking an Azure subscription to Azure Active Directory or an on-premises identity platform. In that scenario the domain controller is part of the identity plumbing that lets session hosts and users authenticate.

Because a domain controller holds authentication data, it is also a prime target. The episode "Harden Azure AD Connect Against Hybrid Identity Breaches" describes several attacks against Active Directory. A Golden Ticket attack lets attackers create forged Kerberos tickets and reach resources across the network. A DCSync attack involves cybercriminals mimicking a domain controller to request password data from other domain controllers. The episode also states that attackers often target Active Directory to maximize the impact of ransomware.

Securing these servers is the focus of "AD Tiering and Privileged Access with Viktor Hedberg [MVP-MCT]". Its excerpt recommends deploying Privileged Access Workstations for all administrators, requiring multi-factor authentication, using Just Enough Admin for domain controller maintenance, and deploying Advanced Threat Analytics for attack detection. The reasoning given is that dedicated administration workstations protect the environment from common threats and keep privileged accounts secure.

Domain controllers also come up in migration work. The episode "Move Active Directory Groups to Microsoft Entra ID" includes a troubleshooting table in which one entry states that domain controllers cannot use unconstrained delegation, with the suggested fix of installing and running the ADMT apps on the target domain controller to remove the need for delegation. This shows that the choice of where a tool runs can depend on how the domain controller is configured.

Taken together, the episodes treat the domain controller as a foundational identity component: required by LDAP- and Kerberos-based workloads, replaceable in Azure by either self-managed VMs or a managed service, and deserving of tight administrative controls.

domain-name-system.desc: The Domain Name System (DNS) is the internet's public directory for domain names, holding records such as SPF, DKIM and DMARC that any receiving server can read.

faq.a: DNS is the internet's public directory for domain names. It translates names into the data needed to reach services, and it also stores records such as SPF, DKIM and DMARC that receiving servers can read.
faq.q: What is the Domain Name System (DNS)?

faq.a: SPF information must be stored as a TXT record, because the dedicated SPF record type is not supported in Azure DNS.
faq.q: How is SPF stored in Azure DNS?

faq.a: No. Azure DNS hosts zones on name servers but does not sell domains. The Azure name servers must be entered at the registrar that owns the domain.
faq.q: Does Azure DNS register domain names?

domain-name-system.long:
The Domain Name System (DNS) is the internet's public directory for domain names. It translates names into the data needed to reach services, and it also serves as the place where certain configuration data is published so that other systems can look it up. Email authentication is a typical example: SPF, DKIM and DMARC records are published as DNS records that any receiving mail server can read and evaluate.

DNS data is organised in zones. A DNS zone hosts all the records of one domain. To host a domain in a service such as Azure DNS, a zone with the domain's name is created and every record for that domain is added to it. Each record has a name and a type, and the type depends on the data it holds. Microsoft Learn lists common record types: A for an IPv4 address, AAAA, CNAME, MX for a mail server, NS, PTR, SOA, SRV, CAA and TXT. A record set is the collection of records in a zone that share the same name and type, and the time to live (TTL) is configured per record set rather than per individual record.

Several rules shape how records are managed. SPF information must be stored as a TXT record in Azure DNS, because the dedicated SPF record type is not supported. A CNAME cannot coexist with other record sets of the same name, and it cannot sit at the zone apex. These constraints matter in practice when a domain needs to point at a service and also carry mail-related records at the same name.

Hosting and registration are separate concerns. Azure DNS hosts zones on name servers, but it does not sell domains. The domain itself is held at a registrar, and the Azure name servers must be entered there so that the registrar delegates the domain to the hosted zone. Until that delegation is in place, queries for the domain do not reach the zone hosted in Azure DNS.

The M365.FM episode "Azure DNS - Simply Explained" (Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets) describes Azure DNS as Microsoft's managed DNS service that hosts and resolves domain names on Azure's global infrastructure. According to the episode, it allows organizations to manage public and private DNS zones, automate DNS management, and provide name resolution for cloud and hybrid environments without maintaining their own DNS servers. The episode frames this in terms of reducing errors and improving operational efficiency for IT teams, and of supporting the performance and availability of websites.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, DNS comes up wherever a custom domain is connected to a service. Typical tasks include adding MX records so mail is routed correctly, adding TXT records for SPF and other verification data, and publishing DKIM and DMARC records so receiving servers can validate messages from the domain. Because these records are public and read by external servers, accuracy in the zone directly affects whether services resolve and whether mail authentication works as intended.

dora-metrics.desc: DORA metrics are the software delivery measures from the DevOps Research and Assessment program, covering throughput and stability of change delivery.

faq.a: They are software delivery metrics from the DevOps Research and Assessment program. They cover throughput (change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time) and instability (change fail rate, deployment rework rate).
faq.q: What are the DORA metrics?

faq.a: No. DORA's research says speed and stability are not trade-offs, because the metrics generally correlate.
faq.q: Do DORA metrics assume speed and stability are a trade-off?

faq.a: DORA guidance advises applying them to one application or service at a time, using several metrics together, sharing ownership across teams and avoiding their use as targets, since that invites gaming.
faq.q: How should DORA metrics be used in practice?

dora-metrics.long:
DORA metrics are the software delivery performance metrics from the DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) program, which is run by Google Cloud. They are used to describe how quickly and how reliably a team delivers software changes to production. The measures were originally known as the four keys: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. DORA's current guidance describes a model that has moved from four keys to five metrics.

The metrics fall into two groups. The throughput metrics are change lead time, which is the time from commit to production, deployment frequency, and failed deployment recovery time, which replaced the older mean time to restore. The instability metrics are change fail rate, the share of deployments that need immediate intervention such as a rollback or hotfix, and deployment rework rate, the share of unplanned deployments caused by production incidents. Together they give a view of delivery speed on one side and delivery stability on the other.

DORA's research links these metrics to better organisational performance and to team well-being. A central point in the guidance is that speed and stability are not trade-offs: the metrics generally correlate, so teams that deliver quickly tend not to do so at the expense of stability. This is why the metrics are presented as a set rather than as separate numbers to optimise one by one.

The guidance also sets out how the metrics should be applied. They are meant to be used for one application or service at a time, and comparing very different applications with one another is discouraged. They should not be turned into targets, because that invites gaming of the numbers. Several metrics should be used together instead of relying on a single one, and ownership should be shared across development, operations and release teams. Reducing batch size is named as a common way to improve all five metrics. The guidance gives no numeric tier thresholds.

The M365.FM episode "The Productivity Illusion: Why AI is Breaking Your Engineering KPIs" discusses DORA metrics in the context of AI-assisted development. The episode says AI has shifted engineering constraints from development toward review and verification, which makes flow measurement more valuable than raw throughput metrics. One of its practical recommendations is to expand the traditional DORA metrics with a fifth dimension, Rework Rate, which tracks how much recently written code has to be rewritten shortly afterward.

According to the episode, high rework can indicate weak verification, poor code durability, fragile architectures, inadequate reviews or incorrect AI usage. It presents rework as a stronger indicator of long-term engineering quality than deployment speed alone. This fits the stability side of the DORA model, where a measure of unplanned work sits next to the throughput measures. Teams that adopt DORA metrics typically decide which service to measure, how to collect the underlying deployment and incident data, and how to discuss results without turning them into performance targets for individuals.

dotnet.desc: .NET is Microsoft's free, open-source, cross-platform developer platform for building web, cloud, desktop, mobile, CLI and AI applications in C#, F# and Visual Basic.

faq.a: .NET is used to build web, cloud, desktop, mobile, command-line and AI applications with C#, F# and Visual Basic. It is commonly used for applications that run on Microsoft Azure, including Azure Functions.
faq.q: What is .NET used for?

faq.a: The name .NET Core refers to an earlier stage of the same platform line, and the platform is also listed under the aliases dotnet and DotNet. It is open source, cross-platform and free to use.
faq.q: Is .NET Core the same as .NET?

faq.a: According to the episode "Fix OWASP Architectural Risks in .NET Applications", no. It notes that default templates leave settings like CSP, secure cookies and strict transport to developers, and that BinaryFormatter deserialization remains a concern.
faq.q: Does using the latest .NET version make an application secure?

dotnet.long:
.NET, also written dotnet or DotNet, is Microsoft's open-source, cross-platform developer platform. It is used to build web, cloud, desktop, mobile, command-line and AI applications with languages such as C#, F# and Visual Basic. The platform is free to use and was first released in 2002. The name .NET Core refers to an earlier stage of the same platform line, which is why the terms .NET and .NET Core often appear side by side in documentation, job descriptions and community discussions.

In practice, .NET serves as the foundation for many kinds of software in the Microsoft ecosystem. Teams use it for ASP.NET Core web applications and services, for Windows desktop applications built with WPF, and for backend components that run on Microsoft Azure, including Azure Functions. Because the platform is cross-platform, the same codebase can be deployed to Windows, Linux and macOS, a point raised in the episode on modern .NET. The platform also includes data access technologies such as LINQ to SQL and EF Core, which connect object-oriented code to relational databases.

.NET is also closely tied to the current wave of AI tooling. The episode "Build AI Applications with .NET 10" describes AI as becoming a first-class citizen in the .NET ecosystem and presents .NET 10 as a unified platform for training models, running inference, orchestrating AI agents and integrating services such as Azure OpenAI and Semantic Kernel. Related topics in the knowledge base include GitHub Copilot for AI-assisted coding, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the concept of an AI agent, since .NET is one of the platforms used to build such tools and agents.

Architecture and maintainability are a recurring theme. The episode ".NET Extensibility and Clean Architecture with Miguel Castro [MVP]" argues that software does not become difficult to maintain because developers write bad code, but because it was not designed to evolve. It places extensibility at the center of modern .NET design and states that AI may accelerate implementation but cannot replace the experience needed to build resilient enterprise systems. Design patterns such as Dependency Injection and MVVM are also named in the modernization episode as ways to improve maintainability and testability.

Modernization of existing applications is another typical decision area. "Modern .NET: WPF, ASP.NET Core, and gRPC with Gábor Ruzsinszki [MVP]" follows the path from legacy WPF desktop applications to ASP.NET Core, cloud-native designs and gRPC services. Its listed takeaways include maintaining consistent business logic across WPF and ASP.NET applications to reduce code duplication, migrating legacy applications to ASP.NET Core with gRPC for fast communication, using HTTPS and token-based authentication, and adopting CI/CD pipelines to automate testing and deployment.

Security is covered in "Fix OWASP Architectural Risks in .NET Applications". The episode maps many OWASP Top 10 risks, such as Injection, Broken Authentication and XSS, to mitigations available in .NET Core and ASP.NET Core, including parameterized EF Core queries, Identity and automatic Razor encoding. It also says that default project templates are not automatically secure: settings such as Content Security Policy, secure cookies and strict transport may be left to developers, and BinaryFormatter deserialization is described as a persistent concern. The episode challenges the idea that upgrading to the latest framework makes an application safe.

For data access, the episode "LINQ to SQL vs EF Core for .NET Data Access" explains how LINQ to SQL bridges object-oriented programming with relational data, how data contexts map to database structures, and how it compares with traditional SQL and ADO.NET patterns, with EF Core as the comparison point. Together, the four episodes cover .NET from architecture and modernization through security, AI and data access.

dotnet-aspire.desc: .NET Aspire is Microsoft's opinionated, cloud-ready stack for building observable distributed .NET applications, with local orchestration, components and a dashboard.

faq.a: .NET Aspire is Microsoft's opinionated, cloud-ready stack for building observable, production-ready distributed applications. It is delivered as NuGet packages and covers orchestration, components and tooling.
faq.q: What is .NET Aspire?

faq.a: The dashboard shows logs, health and traces across the services of an application. The telemetry and health checks come from the components and the ServiceDefaults project.
faq.q: What does the .NET Aspire dashboard show?

faq.a: No. The Microsoft Learn overview states that the orchestration is intended mainly for local development and does not replace production platforms such as Kubernetes.
faq.q: Does .NET Aspire replace Kubernetes in production?

dotnet-aspire.long:
.NET Aspire is an opinionated, cloud-ready stack from Microsoft for building observable, production-ready distributed applications. It is part of .NET and is delivered as a set of NuGet packages, each of which addresses a specific cloud-native concern. Its main purpose is to remove much of the manual work involved in wiring together the frontend, backend services, databases and other dependencies of a multi-service application, especially during local development.

The stack has three main parts. The first is orchestration, which runs and connects multiple projects and their dependencies in local development. An application can be composed from .NET projects, containers, executables and cloud resources, and the orchestration handles service discovery and connection strings so that the individual pieces can find one another. The second part is components: NuGet packages for common services such as Redis or PostgreSQL that expose standardized interfaces and bring health checks and telemetry along with them. The third part is tooling, which consists of project templates and support in Visual Studio and the dotnet command line.

A typical .NET Aspire solution contains the application projects themselves, an AppHost project that handles orchestration, and a ServiceDefaults project. The ServiceDefaults call wires up OpenTelemetry logging, metrics and tracing, default health check endpoints, and service discovery for HttpClient. Two starter templates exist: a minimal one and one that includes sample UI and API projects. Because observability is configured through these defaults, a developer gets a consistent view of how services behave without building the instrumentation separately for each project.

A notable part of the experience is the built-in dashboard, which shows logs, health and traces across the services that make up the application. This turns the question of why a distributed app is misbehaving into something that can be inspected in one place instead of across several terminals and tools. The dashboard works together with the telemetry and health checks that the components and ServiceDefaults provide.

One point of scope is worth stating clearly. According to the Microsoft Learn overview, the orchestration capability is intended mainly for local development and does not replace production platforms such as Kubernetes. The stack is therefore a way to compose, run and observe a distributed application while building it, rather than a hosting platform for production workloads. The overview does not cover prerequisites or licensing, so those details need to be checked separately.

The M365.FM episode "Run Your Full Stack Locally with .NET Aspire" approaches the topic from the perspective of local setup that should not consume half of a developer's working time. The episode describes the promise of a single command that starts the frontend, backend, databases and queues together, along with a dashboard that shows health, logs and traces across services. It walks through running the command, touring the dashboard and plugging the stack into tooling a team already uses, framing the benefit as less time hunting for setup steps and more time shipping.

Typical decisions around .NET Aspire include whether a solution has enough moving parts to justify an AppHost project, which components to use for services such as Redis or PostgreSQL, and which starter template fits the project. Teams also need to keep in mind the boundary between local orchestration and the production platform they deploy to, since the two serve different roles.

dotnet-maui.desc: .NET MAUI is a cross-platform framework in .NET for building native mobile and desktop apps with C# and XAML from a single shared code base.

faq.a: .NET MAUI is used to build native mobile and desktop apps for Android, iOS, macOS and Windows with C# and XAML from a single shared code base, while still allowing access to native platform APIs.
faq.q: What is .NET MAUI used for?

faq.a: Microsoft documentation describes .NET MAUI as the evolution of Xamarin.Forms, extended to desktop scenarios and with UI controls rebuilt for performance and extensibility.
faq.q: How does .NET MAUI relate to Xamarin.Forms?

faq.a: A Mac is required when building for iOS and macOS. Platform-specific code can also still be needed, even though most code can be shared.
faq.q: Is a Mac required to build apps with .NET MAUI?

dotnet-maui.long:
.NET MAUI, short for .NET Multi-platform App UI, is an open-source, cross-platform framework for building native mobile and desktop apps with C# and XAML. It is part of .NET and is described in Microsoft documentation as the evolution of Xamarin.Forms, extended to cover desktop scenarios, with UI controls rebuilt for performance and extensibility. The central idea is a single code base that can target Android, iOS, macOS and Windows.

The framework is used when a team wants to share as much as possible across platforms while still producing native apps. Layout, design, code, tests and business logic can be shared, and native platform APIs remain reachable when a scenario requires them. .NET MAUI provides a set of controls, a layout engine, several page types, data binding and customizable handlers. It also includes cross-platform APIs for common device features such as sensors, network status, device information, the clipboard, file picking, secure storage and browser-based authentication.

Structurally, .NET MAUI simplifies project layout through a single project that uses multi-targeting and a shared app manifest, rather than separate projects per platform. For iteration speed, it supports .NET Hot Reload and XAML Hot Reload, so changes can be applied while an app is running. Under the surface, it builds on .NET 6 or later together with .NET for Android, .NET for iOS, Mac Catalyst and WinUI 3. The execution model differs by platform: Android code is compiled to IL and just-in-time compiled at startup, while iOS uses full ahead-of-time compilation.

Several practical constraints shape decisions around the framework. Building for iOS and macOS requires a Mac, and platform-specific code can still be needed even with a shared code base. Teams therefore weigh how much of an app's logic and interface can be shared against how much must be adapted for each platform.

In the broader .NET ecosystem, .NET MAUI sits alongside other UI technologies. The M365.FM episode "Modern .NET: WPF, ASP.NET Core, and gRPC with Gábor Ruzsinszki [MVP]" discusses WPF and its XAML-based architecture, and explains how that architecture influenced newer technologies such as .NET MAUI and WinUI. The same episode compares alternatives such as Avalonia and Uno Platform and touches on migration challenges for large legacy systems, which is relevant for organizations that rely on WPF and are considering newer UI frameworks.

The episode "Build AI Applications with .NET 10" addresses the cross-platform UI question directly. It says that .NET 10 continues to support .NET MAUI for cross-platform UI and updates Windows Forms on Windows with performance and high-DPI improvements. According to the episode, the release focuses on enabling modern app experiences while delivering core runtime enhancements that benefit both UI frameworks. It also mentions that development tools are being updated to support .NET 10 features, including templates, debugging support and profiling.

Taken together, the sources position .NET MAUI as the .NET option for native, cross-platform mobile and desktop apps built with C# and XAML, with XAML knowledge carrying over from earlier technologies such as WPF.

dp-100.desc: Microsoft Certified: Azure Data Scientist Associate (DP-100) was a Microsoft certification for machine learning on Azure; it was retired on 1 June 2026 and succeeded by AI-300.

faq.a: No. According to the catalog data, the DP-100 exam was retired on 1 June 2026. Its successor is AI-300.
faq.q: Is the DP-100 exam still available?

faq.a: It is built around the exam DP-100 and targets people who train, evaluate and operate machine learning models on Azure. It is developed by Microsoft and covers Microsoft Azure.
faq.q: What does Microsoft Certified: Azure Data Scientist Associate (DP-100) cover?

faq.a: It appears in a resource list in the episode "AI, Power Platform & Developer Experience: The Next Frontier with Reza Niroomand [MVP]", next to the AI-102 and DP-600 certifications. The episode does not cover the exam content itself.
faq.q: Where is DP-100 mentioned in M365.FM?

dp-100.long:
Microsoft Certified: Azure Data Scientist Associate (DP-100) is a Microsoft certification built around the exam DP-100. It targets people who train, evaluate and operate machine learning models on Azure, and it was used as proof of practical data science skills in the Microsoft ecosystem. According to the catalog data, the exam was retired on 1 June 2026, and its successor is AI-300. The credential sits at the associate level.

The certification is developed by Microsoft and covers Microsoft Azure, the cloud platform on which the machine learning workloads of this role run. In practice, a certification of this kind serves several purposes. It gives individuals a structured way to show data science skills on a specific platform. It gives employers and project teams a common reference when staffing machine learning work. It also gives learners a defined scope to study against, instead of an open-ended list of topics. The authoritative description of the exam, including its skills outline, is kept on the Microsoft Learn certification pages, and any exact skill list or exam detail should be checked there rather than in secondary summaries.

Because the exam has been retired, the main decision for anyone meeting the DP-100 name today is how to treat it. Existing study material, course outlines and older job descriptions may still refer to Microsoft Certified: Azure Data Scientist Associate (DP-100). Such references should be read as pointing to a credential that can no longer be newly earned. People planning a certification path in this area should look at AI-300, which the catalog data names as the successor. Anyone who already holds the credential can still describe it accurately as a retired certification rather than as a current one.

DP-100 is often mentioned together with other Microsoft role-based certifications. In the M365.FM episode "AI, Power Platform & Developer Experience: The Next Frontier with Reza Niroomand [MVP]", the DP-100 certification appears in a list of resources alongside Microsoft Certified: Azure AI Engineer Associate (Exam AI-102) and Microsoft Certified: Fabric Analytics Engineer Associate (Exam DP-600). The same list includes productivity pathways for ChatGPT, Gemini and AI for Project Managers. This grouping shows that the exam was treated as one option among several for building AI and data skills in the Microsoft ecosystem.

The episode itself is only indirectly related to the exam. In it, Mirko Peters and Reza Niroomand discuss how artificial intelligence changes the way developers build solutions on Microsoft Power Platform and how the developer experience is shifting. The excerpt also stresses that technical skills are not enough on their own: the episode says that soft skills such as clear communication, active listening and teamwork matter when collaborating on AI projects. It gives context on why AI skills have become part of many Microsoft roles, but it does not walk through DP-100 exam content.

For readers comparing certifications, the practical takeaway is to separate the credential's history from its present availability. DP-100 describes a role focused on machine learning on Azure and is tied to Microsoft as its developer and to Microsoft Azure as the platform it covers. Its retirement on 1 June 2026 and the named successor AI-300 mean that current planning should start from the Microsoft Learn pages for the replacement exam, while the DP-100 page remains useful as a record of what the earlier credential covered.

dp-600.desc: Microsoft Certified: Fabric Analytics Engineer Associate (DP-600) is an associate certification for designing and deploying analytics solutions with Microsoft Fabric.

faq.a: Microsoft Certified: Fabric Analytics Engineer Associate (DP-600) is an associate certification from Microsoft for designing and deploying analytics solutions with Microsoft Fabric. It covers Microsoft Fabric, Power BI, DAX and Power Query.
faq.q: What is the DP-600 certification?

faq.a: The four-part series covers planning Fabric solutions, data flows, pipelines and notebooks, performance optimization with the Monitoring Hub, DMVs and Query Insights, and Power BI security through incremental refresh, Row-Level Security and Object-Level Security.
faq.q: Which topics does the M365.FM DP-600 training series cover?

faq.a: An M365.FM episode with Thummalacherla Krishnakanth discusses certification paths that include both PL-300 and DP-600 as part of career advice for aspiring analytics professionals.
faq.q: How does DP-600 relate to PL-300?

dp-600.long:
Microsoft Certified: Fabric Analytics Engineer Associate (DP-600) is an associate-level certification from Microsoft for designing and deploying analytics solutions with Microsoft Fabric. The exam code is DP-600, and the credential is aimed at professionals who build the data and semantic layers on which reports and analyses depend. It is commonly referred to simply as DP-600.

The certification covers Microsoft Fabric, Power BI, DAX and Power Query. Fabric provides the unified analytics platform, Power BI supplies the reporting layer, Power Query is used to shape and prepare data, and DAX is used to define calculations. Taken together, these topics connect data engineering tasks with analysis and reporting, which is why the credential spans both the platform side and the semantic-model side of an analytics project. Microsoft maintains the official exam page in its Microsoft Learn credentials documentation, which is the reference for the current skills measured and exam details.

In practice, candidates preparing for DP-600 typically need to understand how data moves through Fabric and how it is made usable for reporting. That includes choosing between the available orchestration and transformation tools, tuning performance, and securing data in the semantic model. These themes also shape how the exam content is organized in the M365.FM training material.

M365.FM offers a four-part DP-600 training series. The first episode, "DP-600 Training 1/4: Planning Microsoft Fabric Solutions", opens the series with the planning stage of a Fabric solution. The second, "DP-600 Training 2/4: Fabric Dataflows, Pipelines & Notebooks", features a discussion of Microsoft Fabric's data management tools, namely data flows, pipelines, notebooks, shortcuts and stored procedures. It emphasizes the strengths and limitations of each tool and how they complement one another in data orchestration and transformation.

The third episode, "DP-600 Training 3/4: Data Flow, SQL, and Delta Optimization", focuses on performance optimization for data flows and SQL queries. The speakers discuss tools such as the Monitoring Hub, DMVs and Query Insights, and stress monitoring key metrics, such as refresh errors and resource consumption, to diagnose performance issues effectively. The fourth episode, "DP-600 Training 4/4: Incremental Refresh, RLS, and OLS", turns to data security and analytics in Power BI. It describes Row-Level Security (RLS) as a way for companies to restrict data visibility at a granular level, alongside Object-Level Security (OLS), and says these features support data trust and better decision-making in organizations.

DP-600 also appears in career discussions on the show. In the episode "From Raw Data to Real Business Impact: Mastering Power BI and Microsoft Fabric with Thummalacherla Krishnakanth", the conversation covers certification paths including PL-300 and DP-600, along with career advice for aspiring analytics professionals. The episode also stresses that developers must still understand data modeling, DAX, governance and business requirements, even as AI-assisted development and Microsoft Copilot become more common.

For anyone weighing whether to pursue the certification, the decision usually depends on role and focus. DP-600 sits between data platform work and Power BI-based reporting, so it fits people who design the Fabric data layer and the semantic models that analysts consume. Related Microsoft Learn material and the four M365.FM episodes together give a structured route through the main topics: planning, orchestration and transformation, performance tuning, and security.

Microsoft Certified: Fabric Data Engineer Associate (DP-700) is an associate-level certification from Microsoft that covers ingesting, transforming and securing data with Microsoft Fabric. It is earned by passing exam DP-700 and is aimed at data engineers who work with Microsoft Fabric at an intermediate level. The certification is meant to demonstrate expertise in data loading patterns, data architectures and orchestration processes.

The role behind the certification is that of a data engineer who brings data from different sources into the platform, prepares it for analysis and makes sure access to it is controlled. According to Microsoft Learn, this includes ingesting and transforming data, securing and managing an analytics solution, and monitoring and optimizing an analytics solution. Data engineers in this role work closely with analytics engineers, architects, analysts and administrators to design and deploy data engineering solutions for analytics. Skills in SQL, PySpark and Kusto Query Language are named as part of the profile.

The exam covers three areas: implementing and managing an analytics solution, ingesting and transforming data, and monitoring and optimizing an analytics solution. Candidates usually bring experience with data pipelines and a basic understanding of how analytics platforms are organized.

DP-700 puts more weight on data movement, transformation and protection, while DP-600 leans toward modeling and reporting. The choice between the two usually follows the role: people who build and operate the data flows tend to look at DP-700, while those who shape semantic models and reports tend to look at DP-600.

Typical scenarios for the topic include consolidating data from several operational systems into one analytical platform, building repeatable processes that clean and reshape incoming data, and applying security rules so that only authorized people can reach sensitive datasets. The prepared data is then used by analytics engineers and report authors for models and dashboards, which is why collaboration across roles is part of the role description.

Like other Microsoft certifications, this one expires unless it is renewed. Microsoft Learn states that renewal is free and done through an online assessment. This keeps the credential tied to current platform knowledge, which matters for a product such as Microsoft Fabric that continues to develop.

The M365.FM episodes in the current data are not tagged to this certification directly, so no episode-specific guidance on DP-700 can be summarized here.
