explainability.desc: Explainability in automation governance is an organization's ability to trace and prove, with evidence, how an automated outcome was produced.

faq.a: It is the ability of an organization to trace and prove, with evidence, how an automated outcome was produced. This covers what triggered it, which rules and data applied, and who changed the logic.
faq.q: What does explainability mean in automation governance?

faq.a: It relies on evidence showing the trigger of an outcome, the rules and data that applied, and the record of who changed the logic. The focus is on proof that can be traced, not on a general description of the process.
faq.q: What kind of evidence does explainability rely on?

faq.a: No product is linked to this entry. On M365.FM it is treated as a governance concept used in an episode on automation, not as a feature of a particular service.
faq.q: Is explainability tied to a specific Microsoft product?

explainability.long:
Explainability (automation governance) is the ability of an organization to trace and prove, with evidence, how an automated outcome was produced. In the sense used on M365.FM, it means being able to show what triggered the outcome, which rules and data applied, and who changed the underlying logic.

The concept centers on evidence rather than on general descriptions of how a process is supposed to work. An organization that can explain an automated result can reconstruct the chain of events behind it: the initiating trigger, the rules and data that were in effect at the time, and the history of changes made to the logic. This links an individual outcome back to the people and decisions that shaped the automation.

In governance terms, explainability supports accountability for automated processes. It allows questions about a specific result to be answered with a verifiable record instead of assumptions, including questions about who altered the rules and when.

The term appears on M365.FM as a concept discussed in an episode on automation governance. No specific products, tools or episode titles are linked to this entry at this time, so it is described here as a general governance idea rather than a feature of a particular Microsoft service.

exposure-window.desc: Exposure window is the time a risky condition, such as an oversharing event or unprotected sensitive file, stays unresolved before a governance control contains it.

faq.a: An exposure window is the time a risky condition, such as an oversharing event or an unprotected sensitive file, stays unresolved before a control contains it.
faq.q: What is an exposure window?

faq.a: It indicates how close governance controls sit to the point of action. A shorter window suggests controls respond nearer to the moment the risky condition arises.
faq.q: Why is the exposure window used as a metric?

faq.a: It appears in the episode "Real-Time AI Sensitivity Labeling in Microsoft Purview", published on 2026-05-12.
faq.q: Where is the exposure window discussed on M365.FM?

exposure-window.long:
Exposure window is a concept describing how long a risky condition remains unresolved before a control contains it. Typical examples are an oversharing event or a sensitive file that has no protection applied. The longer the condition persists, the longer the window during which the data or the sharing arrangement stays exposed.

The concept is used as a metric for how close governance controls sit to the point of action. Controls that act at or near the moment a file is created, shared or changed tend to leave a shorter window than controls that act later or in batches. Measuring the exposure window gives a way to compare governance approaches by how quickly they respond, rather than only by whether a control exists.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the idea is relevant to sensitivity labeling and data protection work, where the interval between a sensitive item appearing and a label or restriction being applied determines how long that item is unprotected.

On M365.FM, the term appears in the episode "Real-Time AI Sensitivity Labeling in Microsoft Purview" (2026-05-12), which discusses labeling in the context of Microsoft Purview.

express-js.desc: Express.js is an open-source back-end web application framework for Node.js, used to build web applications and APIs.

faq.a: Express.js is an open-source back-end web application framework for Node.js. It is used to build web applications and APIs.
faq.q: What is Express.js?

faq.a: Express.js is built for Node.js, so applications written with it run on the Node.js runtime.
faq.q: What runtime does Express.js run on?

faq.a: Yes. Express.js is described as an open-source framework.
faq.q: Is Express.js open source?

express-js.long:
Express.js is an open-source back-end web application framework for Node.js. It is used to build web applications and APIs on the Node.js runtime.

As a framework for the server side, Express.js sits between the Node.js runtime and the application code that handles requests and returns responses. Developers use it to structure back-end services, including the API layers that front ends and other systems call.

This page is a short reference entry. No related Microsoft products, linked topics, or M365.FM episodes are currently associated with Express.js in the knowledge base, so no further details on its role in the Microsoft ecosystem are stated here.

expression-trees.desc: Expression trees represent code as a data structure that can be examined at run time; Entity Framework Core uses them to analyze LINQ queries before translating them to SQL.

faq.a: Expression trees represent code as a data structure that can be examined at run time. This makes it possible to inspect the logic of an expression instead of only running it.
faq.q: What are expression trees?

faq.a: Entity Framework Core uses expression trees to analyze LINQ queries before translating them to SQL.
faq.q: How does Entity Framework Core use expression trees?

expression-trees.long:
Expression trees are a concept in .NET and C# in which code is represented as a data structure instead of being compiled only into executable instructions. Because the structure can be examined at run time, a program can inspect the logic of an expression and work with its individual parts.

A common use is query translation. Entity Framework Core uses expression trees to analyze LINQ queries before translating them to SQL. This allows a query written in C# to be interpreted as a structure and then converted into the query language of a database, rather than being executed directly in memory.

Expression trees are documented by Microsoft as part of the C# documentation on Microsoft Learn. The facts available for this entry do not list related topics or M365.FM episodes, so no specific episode coverage is described here.

expressroute-peering.desc: ExpressRoute peering refers to the routing domains on an Azure ExpressRoute circuit, including private peering for virtual networks and Microsoft peering for Microsoft services.
expressroute-peering.long:
ExpressRoute peering describes the routing domains that are configured on an Azure ExpressRoute circuit. Each peering defines which kind of Microsoft-hosted resources a connected network can reach over that circuit.

Private peering connects to Azure virtual networks. It is used to extend an on-premises network into Azure resources that sit inside virtual networks. Microsoft peering connects to Microsoft public services, such as Microsoft 365, rather than to resources inside a customer's virtual network.

Because the two peering types serve different destinations, the choice of peering determines how traffic to Azure workloads and to Microsoft public services is routed over an ExpressRoute circuit. Planning ExpressRoute connectivity therefore involves deciding which routing domains the circuit needs.

The term appears in discussions of hybrid networking and connectivity in the Microsoft ecosystem. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

extended-security-updates.desc: Extended Security Updates (ESU) is a Microsoft program that supplies security patches for out-of-support products such as Windows Server 2012 and SQL Server 2012.

faq.a: Extended Security Updates (ESU) is a Microsoft program that provides security patches for products that are out of support, such as Windows Server 2012 and SQL Server 2012.
faq.q: What is Extended Security Updates (ESU)?

faq.a: No. With Azure Arc, the extended security updates can be received on-premises, so a migration to Azure is not required.
faq.q: Do systems need to move to Azure to receive ESU patches?

extended-security-updates.long:
Extended Security Updates (ESU) is a Microsoft program that delivers security patches for products that have reached the end of their regular support lifecycle. Examples named for the program include Windows Server 2012 and SQL Server 2012. The updates address security issues in these older products after standard support has ended.

ESU is relevant for organizations that still run legacy server and database workloads and need more time before upgrading or replacing them. The program gives those environments a way to continue receiving security patches while a longer-term plan is carried out.

With Azure Arc, ESU patches can be received on-premises. This means the covered products do not have to be migrated to Azure in order to obtain the extended updates, and servers can stay in their existing location while still being connected to the program.

No specific M365.FM episodes are linked to this entry yet, and no further details such as pricing, coverage periods or enrollment steps are included here. Official Microsoft documentation is the place to confirm current terms for a given product.

external-tenant.desc: An external tenant is a separate Microsoft Entra tenant, isolated from the workforce tenant, that stores customer identities for consumer-facing apps in Microsoft Entra External ID.

faq.a: An external tenant is a separate Microsoft Entra tenant, isolated from the workforce tenant, that holds customer identities for consumer-facing apps in Microsoft Entra External ID.
faq.q: What is an external tenant?

faq.a: The external tenant is isolated from the workforce tenant. It is used for customer identities, while the workforce tenant is separate from it.
faq.q: How does an external tenant differ from a workforce tenant?

faq.a: It belongs to Microsoft Entra External ID, where it holds customer identities for consumer-facing applications.
faq.q: Which product area does an external tenant belong to?

external-tenant.long:
An external tenant is a separate Microsoft Entra tenant that is isolated from the workforce tenant. It is used to hold customer identities for consumer-facing applications and is part of Microsoft Entra External ID.

The separation from the workforce tenant means that customer accounts are kept apart from the identities of employees and other internal users. This keeps the organization's own directory distinct from the directory that serves the people who sign in to its public or customer-facing apps.

In practice, an external tenant is the place where an organization manages the identities of its customers within Microsoft Entra External ID, rather than adding those customers to the directory used for its workforce.

The External tenant concept has no linked episodes or related topics listed on M365.FM at this time. Further detail on configuration and capabilities is not covered here.

fabric.desc: Microsoft Fabric is an all-in-one analytics platform from Microsoft that combines data engineering, warehousing, real-time analytics and Power BI on OneLake.

faq.a: Microsoft Fabric is an all-in-one analytics platform from Microsoft that combines data engineering, data warehousing, real-time analytics and Power BI on a shared storage layer called OneLake.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: Fabric is billed through shared capacity rather than per person. The episode "Fabric Capacity Pricing - Simply Explained" describes capacity as a pool of computing power sold in sizes such as F2, F8 and F64.
faq.q: How is Microsoft Fabric billed?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Fabric for Microsoft 365 Admins: What You Need to Know", admins meet Fabric through capacities, tenant settings, workspaces, OneLake, security, licensing and governance.
faq.q: Why does Microsoft Fabric matter to Microsoft 365 admins?

fabric.long:
Microsoft Fabric, often shortened to Fabric, is an all-in-one analytics platform developed by Microsoft. It brings data engineering, data warehousing, real-time analytics and Power BI together on a shared storage layer called OneLake. Instead of running separate products for each analytics discipline, teams work in a single environment where data from many sources can be prepared, stored, analyzed and reported on. Fabric is classed as a Microsoft tool and as an analytics and BI tool.

Costs in Fabric are billed through shared capacity rather than per person. The episode "Fabric Capacity Pricing - Simply Explained" describes this as buying a pool of computing power called a capacity, sold in sizes such as F2, F8 and F64. The episode explains why this model can feel confusing at first and makes the point that a capacity can keep running, and keep being billed, even when nobody is using it. For anyone planning a Fabric rollout, choosing and monitoring capacity is therefore one of the first decisions.

Several related concepts shape how Fabric is used day to day. A Fabric workspace is where items are organized. A semantic model defines business meaning for reports, and the star schema is a related topic because model design affects how well the analytics side works. Fabric notebooks support code-based data work, and Semantic Link Labs is another related topic connected to working with models. Together these cover the path from raw data to reports that business users can read.

Fabric also reaches roles beyond data engineers. The episode "Microsoft Fabric for Microsoft 365 Admins: What You Need to Know" states that Fabric is not just a data engineer topic. Administrators meet it through capacities, workspaces, licensing and governance. The episode introduces the parts that matter to them, namely capacities, tenant settings, workspaces, OneLake and security, and covers what to expect, what to ask and where admins should get involved.

For data that arrives continuously, the episode "Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Hub - Simply Explained" presents Real-Time Hub as the one place where live, flowing data shows up. According to the episode, every Fabric tenant already has it switched on, so it does not need to be installed. The episode walks through what Real-Time Hub is, the three jobs it does and the four kinds of items it surfaces.

Fabric also covers transactional workloads. In "Fabric SQL Database - Simply Explained", a SQL database in Fabric is described as running the same engine that powers Azure SQL Database. The episode discusses where it feels like Azure SQL and where it differs, how a copy of the data makes itself, and how one database can serve two jobs.

Industrial scenarios are covered in "How Machine Data Reaches Microsoft Fabric - From OPC UA to Real-Time Analytics". The episode follows a machine signal from the factory floor: OPC UA exposes the signal, an edge layer collects it, MQTT can distribute it locally, and Fabric can ingest and analyze the resulting stream. The episode stresses that the difficult part starts after the data arrives, because raw telemetry needs production context before it can support an actual decision.

Taken together, the episodes show Fabric as a platform where decisions about capacity, governance, data modeling and ingestion are connected. Which of these matters most depends on the role: administrators focus on capacities, tenant settings and security, while analytics teams focus on workspaces, models, notebooks and the data paths feeding them.

fabric-capacity.desc: Fabric capacity is a shared pool of Microsoft Fabric compute, measured in capacity units (CUs), that workspaces and items draw from and pay for as a pool.

faq.a: Fabric capacity is a shared pool of Microsoft Fabric compute measured in capacity units (CUs). Workspaces and items draw from it, and consumption is smoothed over time.
faq.q: What is Fabric capacity?

faq.a: According to the episode "Fabric Capacity Pricing - Simply Explained", Fabric does not charge per person; a capacity is bought as a pool of computing power in sizes like F2, F8, and F64.
faq.q: How is Fabric capacity sold?

faq.a: The episode "Reduce Microsoft Fabric Costs by Optimizing Compute Workloads" describes the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics App, with Health, Compute and Timepoint pages that show consumption, a 14-day compute history and throttling events.
faq.q: How can capacity usage be monitored?

fabric-capacity.long:
Fabric capacity is the shared pool of compute that Microsoft Fabric workloads run on. It is measured in capacity units (CUs), and the workspaces and items inside Fabric draw from this pool rather than being billed per person. Consumption is smoothed over time, and sustained overuse of the pool can lead to throttling. Microsoft's licensing documentation for Fabric covers how capacities and licences relate.

The episode "Fabric Capacity Pricing - Simply Explained" describes the basic idea: Fabric does not charge per user, because what is bought is a pool of computing power called a capacity, sold in sizes such as F2, F8, and F64. The episode points out that a capacity can sit idle while the meter keeps running, which is one reason Fabric pricing can feel confusing at first. Choosing a size is therefore a decision about how much shared compute an organization wants to provision, not about how many people will use it.

In practice, a capacity is assigned to workspaces, and the items in those workspaces, such as notebooks, lakehouses, semantic models and reports, consume CUs from the pool when they run. The episode "What Microsoft Fabric Means for Power BI Professionals" notes that teams moving to Fabric need to map workspaces and capacities carefully, assigning each workspace to the right capacity to avoid performance slowdowns. It also recommends reviewing refresh strategies for large datasets, since refresh patterns affect how the pool is used. Notebook work follows the same model: "Train AI Models with Microsoft Fabric Notebooks" mentions attaching a notebook to a Fabric capacity or Spark runtime when creating it in a workspace.

Monitoring is a central part of managing a capacity. The episode "Reduce Microsoft Fabric Costs by Optimizing Compute Workloads" says that tracking how workloads use capacity units helps identify patterns that lead to overspending. It describes the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics App, whose Health Page summarizes capacities and highlights high consumption and critical issues. Its Compute Page shows a 14-day history of compute performance, including usage patterns and throttling events, and Timepoint Pages allow analysis of the specific operations that consumed compute. The episode also mentions the Fabric Chargeback App in the context of attributing consumption.

Capacity planning also appears in discussions of Power BI and Copilot. The episode "Can Copilot Replace Power BI Developers?" says that complex data engineering, advanced DAX and architecture decisions still require developer knowledge, including experience with BI tools and Fabric capacity planning. Sizing, workspace assignment and workload design are therefore treated as skills that remain with people.

Typical decisions around Fabric capacity include which size to provision, which workspaces share a pool, how to spread heavy workloads such as refreshes and Spark jobs so they do not compete for the same CUs, and how to watch for throttling before users notice slowdowns. Because consumption is smoothed over time, short spikes are treated differently from sustained overuse, which is the situation that can lead to throttling. The episodes frame cost control as largely a matter of understanding what consumes CUs and optimizing those workloads.

fabric-copy-job.desc: Copy job is a Data Factory item in Microsoft Fabric that copies data from a source to a destination without a pipeline, supporting batch and incremental patterns.

faq.a: A Copy job is a Data Factory item in Microsoft Fabric that copies data from a source to a destination. It does not require building a pipeline.
faq.q: What is a Copy job in Fabric Data Factory?

faq.a: Copy job has built-in batch and incremental patterns. The incremental pattern uses change tracking.
faq.q: Which copy patterns does Copy job support?

faq.a: No. Copy job is designed to move data without building a pipeline.
faq.q: Is a pipeline needed to use Copy job?

fabric-copy-job.long:
Copy job (Fabric Data Factory) is an item in Data Factory within Microsoft Fabric. It copies data from a source to a destination without requiring a pipeline to be built, which makes it a lighter-weight option for straightforward data movement tasks.

Copy job includes built-in patterns for common data movement scenarios. These cover batch copying as well as incremental copying that relies on change tracking, so that data transfers can be set up without custom pipeline logic. The aim of the item is to reduce the setup effort for copy scenarios that do not need the orchestration capabilities of a full pipeline.

The feature is part of the Data Factory experience in Microsoft Fabric and is documented in Microsoft Learn under the Data Factory section. No episodes on M365.FM currently reference Copy job, and no related entities are linked to this page yet.

fabric-data-activator.desc: Fabric Data Activator, also called Activator, is a Microsoft Fabric feature that detects data patterns and thresholds and triggers alerts or actions automatically.

faq.a: Fabric Data Activator, also called Activator, is a real-time intelligence feature in Microsoft Fabric that triggers actions and alerts automatically when it detects data patterns or thresholds.
faq.q: What is Fabric Data Activator?

faq.a: The episode "Automate Real-Time Actions with Fabric Data Activator" names pausing bad pipelines, placing purchase orders, opening Dynamics 365 work orders and triggering API calls as examples.
faq.q: What kinds of actions can Fabric Data Activator trigger?

faq.a: The episode "Power BI Alerts vs Fabric Data Activator" presents Fabric Data Activator as acting on changing data itself, rather than waiting for someone to notice a problem on a dashboard or report.
faq.q: How does Fabric Data Activator differ from Power BI alerts?

fabric-data-activator.long:
Fabric Data Activator, also referred to as Activator or Data Activator, is a real-time intelligence feature in Microsoft Fabric. It is developed by Microsoft and belongs to the group of Microsoft analytics and BI tools. Its purpose is to watch data and, when a defined pattern or threshold is detected, trigger an action or alert automatically instead of waiting for a person to notice a change in a report.

The core idea is a shift from passive reporting to active response. A dashboard or report shows what has happened and relies on someone to look at it. Fabric Data Activator takes the opposite approach: it monitors the data on its own and responds when a condition is met. The M365.FM episode "Power BI Alerts vs Fabric Data Activator" describes this as data that "wakes up", with the activator noticing a problem rather than a report quietly updating in the background. The episode contrasts planning for tomorrow with responding to something now, and points to businesses where timing matters, such as retail, manufacturing, logistics and finance, as typical candidates for acting the moment something changes.

Because Fabric Data Activator is part of Microsoft Fabric, it works with data that already lives in the platform. According to the episode "Automate Real-Time Actions with Fabric Data Activator", it listens to streams and models from Power BI, Synapse and the Lakehouse. When a threshold is reached, it can execute pre-approved playbooks with minimal latency. The examples named in that episode include pausing a faulty pipeline, placing a purchase order, opening a Dynamics 365 work order and triggering an API call. The value lies in connecting a live signal directly to a downstream step, so that the response does not depend on manual follow-up.

The same episode offers practical guidance for adoption. It recommends starting small with high-value triggers, designing with capacity and downstream service levels in mind, and building in guardrails so that the result is meaningful signal rather than alert spam. These points reflect the typical decisions around the feature: which conditions justify an automatic action, how many triggers the environment can support, and how to keep notifications useful.

The comparison with Power BI alerts is a recurring theme. Power BI alerts are tied to report content, while Fabric Data Activator is positioned as a broader mechanism that reacts to changing data and can start actions beyond a notification. The episode "Power BI Alerts vs Fabric Data Activator" frames the choice as one between noticing a change after the fact and acting at the time it occurs.

Fabric Data Activator also appears in the context of data quality and governance. The episode "Govern Semantic and AI Model Drift in Power BI and Fabric" lists it among the Fabric capabilities for monitoring, alongside notebooks and dataflows, in a discussion of tools that help track architectural drift and maintain data correctness. Other tools mentioned there, such as Microsoft Purview, pipeline-native validation tools and observability tools, complement it rather than replace it.

Fabric Data Activator is also listed as a related topic in several other M365.FM episodes on real-time scenarios, including those covering Real-Time Dynamics 365 Campaign Analytics in Fabric, Real-Time Azure Cost Control with Azure Policy and Real-Time AI Sensitivity Labeling in Microsoft Purview. Official documentation is available through Microsoft Learn under the Real-Time Intelligence section of Fabric, in an introduction to Activator.

fabric-data-agents.desc: Fabric data agents are AI agents in Microsoft Fabric that answer natural-language questions over lakehouses, warehouses and semantic models with controlled data access.

faq.a: Fabric data agents are AI agents in Microsoft Fabric that answer natural-language questions over lakehouses, warehouses and semantic models. They are also called data agents and are developed by Microsoft as part of Microsoft Fabric.
faq.q: What are Fabric data agents?

faq.a: According to the episode "Query Microsoft Fabric in Plain English with Copilot Studio", the data agent must be operational and published with a detailed description. It also states that the data agent and Copilot Studio must be in the same tenant and that both are accessed with the same signed-in account.
faq.q: What is needed to connect a Fabric data agent to Copilot Studio?

faq.a: The episode "Govern Microsoft Fabric Data Agents in Copilot Studio" says that controls such as sensitivity labels and data access policies apply to every query. Another episode adds that administrators can turn Copilot access on or off and set limits for data processing.
faq.q: How do Fabric data agents handle data security?

fabric-data-agents.long:
Fabric data agents, also referred to as a data agent, are AI agents in Microsoft Fabric that answer natural-language questions over data stored in lakehouses, warehouses and semantic models. Microsoft develops the product, and it is part of Microsoft Fabric. It belongs to the groups of Microsoft tools, analytics and BI tools, and AI assistants. The official documentation describes the concept on the Microsoft Learn page for data agents in the Fabric data science area.

The core purpose of a Fabric data agent is to let people ask questions in plain language instead of writing queries or navigating semantic models by hand. The episode "Govern Microsoft Fabric Data Agents in Copilot Studio" describes a Fabric data agent as an AI-driven intermediary that gives users controlled access to selected data stored in Microsoft Fabric. The agent sits between the person asking and the underlying data, so what a user can retrieve depends on what the agent has been configured to expose and on the governance rules that apply to that data.

Governance is a recurring theme in the episodes. According to "Govern Microsoft Fabric Data Agents in Copilot Studio", controls such as sensitivity labels and data access policies apply to every query, which is meant to keep data safe while making it easy to get information. The episode "Copilot for Microsoft Fabric - Simply Explained" makes a related point: it says Copilot uses Fabric data agents so that queries follow the rules for data security and governance, and that administrators can control Copilot settings, such as turning access on or off, and set limits for data processing to stay compliant.

Fabric data agents can also be consumed from Copilot Studio. The episode "Query Microsoft Fabric in Plain English with Copilot Studio" lists the setup steps for connecting Copilot Studio to Fabric data agents. The Fabric data agent must be operational and responsive, and it must be published with a detailed description before use. Both the Fabric data agent and Copilot Studio must reside in the same tenant, and authentication means signing into Microsoft Fabric and Copilot Studio with the same account. The episode also refers to model layouts as a factor in getting accurate insights.

The agents are also discussed as one building block of a wider data foundation. In "From Financial Data to AI-Ready Decisions: Power BI, Microsoft Fabric, Semantic Models & AI Agents with Rishi Sapra [MVP]", the episode names OneLake, lakehouses, Delta tables, semantic models, Direct Lake, Fabric data agents and the integration with Copilot Studio as components that can form a unified foundation for structured and unstructured organizational data. It argues that these layers give AI agents stronger grounding. Direct Lake is explained as allowing Power BI to work directly with data stored in Delta format, rather than repeatedly importing and refreshing data into traditional Power BI semantic models, while maintaining analytical performance.

In a broader architectural context, "Enterprise AI Agent Fabric: Architecture Beyond Chatbots" discusses agent fabric as a backbone that connects multiple data agents and other agents so they can work together. The episode contrasts this with traditional chatbots, noting that such an architecture supports persistent context, memory and identity. This is a separate concept from the product, but it shows where data agents can fit in enterprise designs.

Typical decisions around Fabric data agents include which lakehouses, warehouses or semantic models to expose, how to describe the agent so it is usable once published, how sensitivity labels and access policies should constrain results, and whether to surface the agent through Copilot Studio. The episodes position the agents as a way to combine natural-language access with the governance already applied to the data in Microsoft Fabric.

fabric-data-factory.desc: Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric is the data integration experience in Microsoft Fabric, covering pipelines, Dataflow Gen2, copy jobs and mirroring for moving and transforming data.

faq.a: It is the data integration service in Microsoft Fabric for moving and transforming data using pipelines, Dataflow Gen2, copy jobs and mirroring. Microsoft describes it as the next generation of Azure Data Factory.
faq.q: What is Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: A copy job is the preferred option and handles bulk, incremental and change data capture copies. Copy activity offers manual control over parallelism, and mirroring keeps a near-real-time replica of an operational database in OneLake.
faq.q: Which options exist for moving data in Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: The episode "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" recommends managed identity authentication, which connects to resources without storing passwords or secrets in pipelines. It also advises reviewing data movement policies regularly.
faq.q: How can pipelines be secured according to M365.FM?

fabric-data-factory.long:
Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric is the data integration service built into Microsoft Fabric. Microsoft describes it as the next generation of Azure Data Factory. Its purpose is to bring together data that is scattered across databases, files, cloud services and legacy systems, clean it, and prepare it for analytics in a lakehouse or data warehouse. Movement and transformation are orchestrated from a single interface. Using it requires a Fabric tenant account with an active subscription and a workspace with Fabric enabled.

The service connects to well over a hundred data sources. These include multicloud and hybrid sources, which can be reached through on-premises gateways. Both ETL and ELT patterns are supported, so teams can choose whether data is transformed before or after it lands in the target.

For moving data, the documentation names several options. A copy job is the preferred option and handles bulk copies, incremental copies and change data capture copies. Copy activity inside a pipeline gives manual control over parallelism. Mirroring keeps a near-real-time replica of an operational database in OneLake. Choosing between them typically depends on whether a one-time load, a recurring incremental load or a continuously updated replica is needed, and how much control over the copy process is required.

Transformations can run in several ways. Pipeline activities can call notebooks, Spark job definitions, stored procedures and SQL scripts. Dataflow Gen2 offers a low-code interface for shaping data. dbt jobs can be run against a Fabric data warehouse. This allows both code-first and low-code teams to work in the same environment.

Orchestration covers schedules, event-based triggers, control flow in the pipeline designer and Apache Airflow DAGs. Copilot can create pipelines and dataflows from natural-language prompts and can explain errors, which can help when building or troubleshooting integration logic.

Security is a recurring theme in the M365.FM coverage. The episode "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" advises reviewing data movement policies regularly and updating them as the organization grows or as new threats appear. It states that strong data movement security protects sensitive information and supports compliance with regulations. The episode also discusses managed identity authentication for securing Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric. According to the episode, this method lets pipelines connect to resources without storing passwords or secrets, which avoids the risks that come with hardcoded credentials.

In practice, teams working with Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric decide which movement method fits each source, which transformation approach suits their skills, and how to authenticate and govern pipelines. Because the service sits inside Fabric, its output feeds directly into the lakehouse and warehouse experiences that the rest of the platform uses for analytics.

fabric-data-pipelines.desc: Fabric Data Pipelines is the Microsoft Fabric orchestration feature that chains copy, dataflow and notebook activities into scheduled or triggered workflows.

faq.a: It is the orchestration feature of Microsoft Fabric that chains activities such as copy data, dataflows and notebooks into a scheduled or triggered workflow, with handling for success, failure, retry and timeout.
faq.q: What is Fabric Data Pipelines?

faq.a: The episode "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" recommends managed identities instead of passwords, Azure Key Vault for centralized and audited secrets, and least-privilege role-based access control at the workspace, pipeline and dataset layers.
faq.q: How can Fabric Data Pipelines be secured?

faq.a: The episode "Monitor Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" describes four pillars: performance metrics, error logging, data lineage and automated recovery, combined with alert patterns and runbooks so issues surface early and reach the right owners.
faq.q: How should Fabric Data Pipelines be monitored?

fabric-data-pipelines.long:
Fabric Data Pipelines is the orchestration feature of Microsoft Fabric. It chains activities such as copy data, dataflows and notebooks into a single workflow that runs on a schedule or is started by a trigger. The workflow includes handling for success, failure, retry and timeout conditions, so that a sequence of data tasks can run in a defined order without manual intervention.

The typical problem it addresses is a data landscape in which files and records arrive at different times and from different sources. The episode "Fabric Data Pipelines - Simply Explained" describes the situation: a sales file arrives at seven in the morning, customer records update at eight, and application data shows up whenever it is ready, while someone on the team opens spreadsheets, presses refresh, fixes columns and hopes the report matches the previous day's story. A pipeline replaces that manual coordination with a defined sequence. The episode frames the underlying question as one of control: the data is moving, but who is in control of how and when it moves. It also touches on ETL as the background concept for this kind of work.

In practice, a pipeline is built from activities. A copy data activity moves data from a source to a destination, a dataflow activity applies transformations, and a notebook activity runs code. Linking these activities and defining what should happen when one of them succeeds, fails, needs a retry or exceeds a time limit turns individual steps into a managed process. Scheduling and triggering determine when the process starts, which matters for decisions about whether data should be refreshed at fixed times or in response to an event.

Security is one of the recurring themes in the M365.FM coverage. The episode "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" says that pipelines often feel secure by default, but that silent data exposure usually comes from misconfigured permissions, hardcoded secrets and overbroad workspace roles. As described in the episode, hardening an end-to-end pipeline involves using managed identities in place of passwords, centralizing and auditing secrets in Azure Key Vault, and applying precise role-based access control with least privilege at the workspace, pipeline and dataset layers. The episode also advises planning for disaster recovery and regularly testing backup procedures so that sensitive data can be restored quickly if needed.

Operations are the second recurring theme. The episode "Monitor Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" argues for a proactive, system-level monitoring strategy instead of working without visibility. It breaks monitoring into four pillars: performance metrics, error logging, data lineage and automated recovery. According to the episode, these are wired together so that issues surface early, are routed to the right owners and, where possible, are resolved automatically. It offers concrete runbooks and alert patterns for this purpose. The episode "Azure Monitor — Simply Explained" lists the monitoring episode among related listening, which reflects how pipeline operations connect to broader monitoring practices in the Microsoft ecosystem.

Fabric Data Pipelines also appears as a related reference in other episodes. The episode "Private LoRA for Secure AI on Proprietary Enterprise Data" lists "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" among its related conversations and points listeners to Microsoft Fabric as a next step, which places pipelines within the wider Fabric platform and the data preparation that precedes enterprise AI work.

For teams evaluating the feature, the questions that follow from these sources are practical ones: which activities need to run in what order, what should happen on failure or timeout, who owns alerts, which identity each connection uses, and how secrets and workspace roles are governed. The M365.FM episodes treat security and monitoring as parts of pipeline design from the start rather than additions made afterward.

fabric-deployment-pipelines.desc: Deployment pipelines in Microsoft Fabric and Power BI promote workspace content through development, test and production stages, with REST APIs for automation.

faq.a: They are a feature that promotes workspace content through stages such as development, test and production. They are available for both Fabric and Power BI content.
faq.q: What are deployment pipelines in Microsoft Fabric and Power BI?

faq.a: Yes. Deployment pipelines offer REST APIs, which allow promotion steps to be automated rather than run manually.
faq.q: Can deployment be automated?

faq.a: Not necessarily. The feature supports both full deployment and selective deployment, so either an entire stage or chosen items can be promoted.
faq.q: Does it move all content at once?

fabric-deployment-pipelines.long:
Deployment pipelines (Microsoft Fabric and Power BI) is a feature that moves workspace content through a series of stages, such as development, test and production. It gives teams a structured way to manage how content progresses from authoring to the environment where it is used.

Content can be promoted in two ways: a full deployment, which moves everything in a stage forward, or a selective deployment, which moves only chosen items. This allows changes to be reviewed in an earlier stage before they reach later ones.

Deployment pipelines also provide REST APIs, which make it possible to automate promotion steps instead of performing them manually in the interface. This supports repeatable release processes and fits into continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) practices for Fabric and Power BI content.

The feature is documented by Microsoft within the Fabric CI/CD section of Microsoft Learn. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic, and no related entities have been defined for it yet.

fabric-domains.desc: Fabric domains group Microsoft Fabric workspaces by business area, such as sales or finance, to set ownership and governance boundaries in a data mesh style setup.

faq.a: Fabric domains are logical groupings of workspaces in Microsoft Fabric organized by business area, such as sales or finance. They define ownership and governance boundaries in a data mesh style setup.
faq.q: What are Fabric domains?

faq.a: They give organizations a scalable way to manage ownership, access, and compliance across workspaces and data assets by tying them to the business area that is responsible for them.
faq.q: What problem do Fabric domains address?

faq.a: No. Fabric domains concern governance and organization of data workspaces in Microsoft Fabric, while Microsoft Mesh is a separate technology covered in its own M365.FM episode.
faq.q: Are Fabric domains the same as Microsoft Mesh?

fabric-domains.long:
Fabric domains are a governance and organization concept in Microsoft Fabric. A domain groups workspaces and the data assets they contain by business area, for example sales or finance. The purpose is to give each area a clear boundary for ownership and governance, so that data is managed close to the people who understand it rather than in one central pile of workspaces. This approach is commonly described as data mesh style: responsibility is distributed across business domains while shared rules still apply.

In practice, a domain acts as a logical container above individual workspaces. Instead of treating each workspace in isolation, an organization can place related workspaces under the same domain and reason about them together. This makes it easier to answer questions that matter for governance: which business area owns a given dataset, who is accountable for its quality, and how access and compliance expectations apply to everything within that area. The episode "Use Microsoft Fabric Domains for Data Mesh Governance" describes domains as logical groupings of workspaces and data assets that support a data mesh architecture and give organizations a scalable way to manage ownership, access, and compliance.

Typical decisions around Fabric domains concern how to divide the organization. Teams have to decide which business areas deserve their own domain, which workspaces belong under which domain, and who is responsible for each one. Aligning domains with real business structure, such as sales or finance, keeps ownership understandable. The grouping also supports consistency: when workspaces sit under a shared domain, governance practices can be applied across them in a more uniform way than with ad hoc, workspace-by-workspace handling.

Fabric domains are one piece of the broader governance picture in Microsoft Fabric. Several M365.FM episodes place them alongside related topics. "Microsoft Fabric Governance Beyond Data Lineage" and "Microsoft Fabric Exposes Data Engineering and Governance Gaps" both list the domains episode as related listening, as does "Microsoft Fabric Governance to Prevent Cost and Metric Chaos". These pairings suggest that domains are meant to be understood together with other governance concerns such as lineage, roles, labels, and cost control rather than as a standalone feature.

The data mesh framing is central to why domains matter. In a data mesh style setup, ownership is organized by business area, with each area responsible for its own data. Fabric domains provide a way to express that structure inside the platform, linking workspaces to the part of the business that owns them. This helps keep governance boundaries visible as the number of workspaces and data assets grows.

For people searching for the term, it helps to distinguish Fabric domains from similarly named products. Microsoft Mesh is a separate Microsoft technology covered in its own M365.FM episode, "Microsoft Mesh - Simply Explained", and it is unrelated to the data mesh concept that Fabric domains support. Fabric domains concern the organization and governance of data workspaces in Microsoft Fabric, not immersive collaboration.

In summary, Fabric domains offer a way to structure Microsoft Fabric around business areas, define who owns what, and set governance boundaries that scale with the organization. The M365.FM episode "Use Microsoft Fabric Domains for Data Mesh Governance" is the main source for how they work and why they matter, and the related governance episodes provide the surrounding context.

fabric-eventhouse.desc: Microsoft Fabric Eventhouse is the Microsoft Fabric container for real-time event analysis, holding KQL databases of time-stamped events for fast queries.

faq.a: Microsoft Fabric Eventhouse is the Microsoft Fabric container for real-time event analysis. It holds KQL databases that store time-stamped events.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Fabric Eventhouse?

faq.a: It holds time-stamped events, such as recent machine states, alarms and condition data. These are stored in KQL databases for fast queries.
faq.q: What kind of data does an Eventhouse hold?

faq.a: Microsoft Fabric Eventhouse is part of Microsoft Fabric. It provides the real-time event analysis container within that platform.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Fabric Eventhouse relate to Microsoft Fabric?

fabric-eventhouse.long:
Microsoft Fabric Eventhouse is a component of Microsoft Fabric designed for real-time event analysis. It acts as a container that holds KQL databases, which store time-stamped events.

The data held in an Eventhouse is typically recent and time-oriented, such as machine states, alarms and condition data. Because the KQL databases are built for this kind of event data, queries over recent states can be run quickly. This makes the Eventhouse relevant to scenarios where current conditions need to be observed and analyzed as they change, rather than after the fact.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, Microsoft Fabric Eventhouse is part of Microsoft Fabric, the broader analytics platform. It sits alongside other Fabric items and provides the real-time, event-focused storage and query layer. The reference to KQL databases indicates that data in an Eventhouse is queried with Kusto Query Language.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity, and no official documentation link is recorded here. The description above is limited to the established role of Microsoft Fabric Eventhouse as a container for KQL databases that store time-stamped events within Microsoft Fabric.

fabric-iq.desc: Fabric IQ is a Microsoft Fabric workload in preview that combines an ontology and Power BI semantic models to give AI agents context about business data.

faq.a: Fabric IQ is a Microsoft Fabric workload, currently in preview, that brings unified data and semantics together. It includes an ontology and Power BI semantic models to give AI agents context about business entities and data.
faq.q: What is Fabric IQ?

faq.a: Semantic drift is when the meaning of data metrics changes over time and causes inconsistent reporting. The episode "Build a Trusted Semantic Layer in Microsoft Fabric" describes Fabric IQ as aiming to unify data semantics so analytics and AI agents share consistent context.
faq.q: How does Fabric IQ relate to semantic drift?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Cowork IQ Knowledge Graph Architecture", Work IQ interprets intent and organizational language to find the right documents, while Fabric IQ organizes business data into a unified semantic layer with consistent definitions and metrics.
faq.q: How is Fabric IQ different from Work IQ?

fabric-iq.long:
Fabric IQ is a workload in Microsoft Fabric, currently in preview, that brings unified data and semantics together. According to the description of the product, it includes an ontology and Power BI semantic models, and its purpose is to give AI agents context about business entities and the data that describes them. Rather than adding another storage or compute engine, it focuses on meaning: what a customer, an order or a metric actually stands for across the data estate.

The problem it addresses is described in the M365.FM episode "Fabric IQ - Simply Explained". The episode opens with a common situation: somewhere in a Fabric workspace, two teams call the same customer two different things. The data itself may be sound, but the meaning behind it has quietly drifted apart. The episode uses this scenario to explain why data alone is not enough and why a shared layer of definitions matters, especially once AI agents start reading and acting on that data.

The ontology is the central building block. In plain terms, an ontology describes the business entities in an organization and how they relate to one another, so that people, reports and agents refer to the same things in the same way. The episode walks through the ontology, how it connects to semantic models, how it grounds AI agents, and where Fabric IQ stops. Power BI semantic models are the second component named in the product description, which means existing semantic modeling work is part of the picture rather than something to be replaced.

Fabric IQ is closely tied to the idea of a trusted semantic layer. The episode "Build a Trusted Semantic Layer in Microsoft Fabric" discusses semantic drift, meaning the situation in which the meaning of data metrics changes over time and leads to confusion and discrepancies in reporting. That episode names Microsoft Purview as the component that supports data quality, lineage and accessibility for effective governance, and it describes Fabric IQ's contribution as an effort to unify data semantics so that analytics and AI agents work with consistent context. Governance and semantics are presented as complementary: one keeps data trustworthy and traceable, the other keeps its meaning consistent.

The episode "Microsoft Cowork IQ Knowledge Graph Architecture" places Fabric IQ alongside Work IQ. It says that Work IQ interprets intent and organizational language so the right documents are found even when phrasing differs, while Fabric IQ organizes business data into a unified semantic layer that guarantees consistent definitions and metrics across all sources. The same episode points to integration with Microsoft 365 Copilot as part of that architecture. Read together, the two are presented as covering different kinds of organizational knowledge: work content on one side and business data on the other.

For practitioners, the practical questions are where to start and how much to rely on a preview workload. The episode "Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse - Simply Explained" lists a training module titled "Understand Microsoft Fabric IQ fundamentals" among its learning resources, alongside modules on designing semantic models for scale. Those pointers suggest that solid semantic modeling and an understanding of Fabric IQ fundamentals go together. Because Fabric IQ is in preview, its scope and behavior can change, and the official overview in Microsoft Learn is the reference for the current state of the workload.

fabric-lakehouse.desc: Fabric lakehouse is a Microsoft Fabric item for storing and analyzing structured and unstructured data, organized into a Tables folder and a Files folder.

faq.a: A Fabric lakehouse is a Microsoft Fabric item for storing and analyzing large amounts of structured and unstructured data. It is organized into a Tables folder and a Files folder.
faq.q: What is a Fabric lakehouse?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Governance and Data Lineage" describes automatic lineage across Fabric items, workspace-based permissions, Purview cataloging and classifications, and unified audit logs for compliance.
faq.q: How is governance handled for a Fabric lakehouse?

faq.a: The episode "Optimize Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Performance" covers data modeling, partitioning, query tuning, workload management and storage optimization as ways to support scalability, cost control and reliable reporting.
faq.q: What do the M365.FM episodes say about lakehouse performance?

fabric-lakehouse.long:
A Fabric lakehouse is an item in Microsoft Fabric used to store and analyze large amounts of structured and unstructured data in one place. According to the product description, a lakehouse is organized into two main areas: a Tables folder and a Files folder. This layout reflects the idea behind the lakehouse approach, in which data of different shapes sits side by side instead of being split across separate systems.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse - Simply Explained" frames the lakehouse against an older division in data architecture: the data lake on one side and the data warehouse on the other. The episode describes a common problem in which one team keeps spreadsheets, another keeps a database, and the data lives in disconnected places. Its outline covers what a Fabric lakehouse actually is, how OneLake and Delta tables form the shared foundation, how raw files become trusted tables through the medallion flow, and the role of a SQL analytics layer on top.

In practice, the lakehouse acts as a landing and working area for data coming from many sources. The episode "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" describes data workflows that move source data, whether from cloud or on-premises systems, into a Fabric Lakehouse or a Fabric Data Warehouse. It treats ingestion, pipeline copy, data movement, transformation and storage as stages that should protect sensitive data and remain auditable. Fabric Data Factory is discussed there as the pipeline tooling that builds on concepts familiar from Azure Data Factory.

Lakehouse data also feeds other Fabric workloads. The episode "Microsoft Fabric Digital Twin Builder Explained" describes data from sensors, logs and operational systems flowing into the Fabric lakehouse, where the digital twin builder reshapes it into a digital model of the physical world and connects it to real-time event streams. This illustrates the lakehouse as a shared storage layer that other Fabric experiences read from and build on.

Governance is a recurring theme. The episode "Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Governance and Data Lineage" says Fabric captures lineage automatically across steps such as Data Factory, the Lakehouse, notebooks, SQL, Dataflows, semantic models and Power BI. It also describes workspace-based permissions and Purview's enterprise catalog, with classifications that make sensitive fields searchable across workspaces and unified audit logs that support compliance evidence. The stated aim is to replace guesswork about where data went with auditable, end-to-end flows from ingestion through transformation to the report, and to make broken KPIs faster to trace.

Performance and cost are the focus of "Optimize Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Performance". The episode presents optimization as necessary for scalability, cost control and reliable reporting, and covers data modeling strategies, partitioning practices, query tuning, workload management and storage optimization. It positions these recommendations for large datasets, real-time analytics and enterprise reporting, with the goal of preventing bottlenecks.

Taken together, the episodes treat the Fabric lakehouse as a central building block: a place to land raw files, shape them into curated tables, secure the movement of data into it, trace its lineage, and tune it for the workloads that depend on it. Decisions around it typically concern how to structure the Tables and Files areas, how to protect and govern the data, and how to keep queries and storage efficient as volumes grow.

fabric-mirroring.desc: Fabric Mirroring is a managed Microsoft Fabric capability that continuously replicates external databases, or their metadata, into OneLake as Delta tables.

faq.a: Fabric Mirroring is a managed Microsoft Fabric capability that continuously replicates external databases, or their metadata, into OneLake as Parquet-based Delta tables without requiring pipelines to be built.
faq.q: What is Fabric Mirroring?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn describes database mirroring, which copies whole databases or selected tables; metadata mirroring, which syncs catalog names, schemas and tables and exposes data via shortcuts; and open mirroring, which lets applications write change data through public APIs.
faq.q: What types of mirroring exist in Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: It is described as near real time, not guaranteed real time. The M365.FM episode mentions that changes can arrive as fast as fifteen seconds later, and replication requires a running Fabric capacity.
faq.q: Is Fabric Mirroring real time?

fabric-mirroring.long:
Fabric Mirroring is a managed capability in Microsoft Fabric that continuously replicates data from external databases, or only their metadata, into OneLake. The replicated data is stored as Parquet-based Delta tables in near real time, and no data pipelines have to be built to move it. Microsoft Learn describes Mirroring as a low-cost, low-latency way to bring data from different systems together in one analytics platform, covering existing data estates that include Azure databases and other external sources.

The documentation distinguishes three types of mirroring. Database mirroring copies whole databases or selected tables and keeps changes in sync. Metadata mirroring syncs only catalog names, schemas and tables, and exposes the underlying data through OneLake shortcuts instead of copying it. Open mirroring lets applications write change data into a mirrored database through public APIs, which makes it possible to feed the same mechanism from sources that are not natively supported. Choosing between these types depends on whether the data should physically land in OneLake, be referenced in place, or be delivered by a custom application.

When a mirrored item is created, Fabric sets up a replication process and a SQL analytics endpoint in the workspace. Once the data is in OneLake as Delta tables, it can be used by other Fabric workloads. The Learn page names Spark, notebooks and Power BI, including Direct Lake, as ways to consume it, and notes that the data can be shared with row-level and object-level security. This keeps analytical work separate from the operational source system, since queries run against the replicated copy in OneLake.

There are practical constraints to consider. A running Fabric capacity is required, and replication stops if the capacity is paused or deleted. Replication is described as near real time, not guaranteed real time, so designs that depend on strict timing should account for latency. Several sources are still in preview, which is relevant when planning production use. The available source list therefore deserves a check against current documentation before a project commits to a particular database.

The M365.FM episode "Fabric Mirroring - Simply Explained" covers the topic in an accessible format. It states that changes to a database can land in Microsoft Fabric as fast as fifteen seconds later, and stresses that this is not the same as copying data once. The episode outline walks through why data is often stuck in source systems, how the copy actually gets to Fabric, what is available once the data has arrived, and which sources can be mirrored. It also compares Mirroring with Shortcuts and pipelines, which helps frame when each approach fits: Mirroring for continuous replication, Shortcuts for referencing data in place, and pipelines for custom movement and transformation logic.

In short, Fabric Mirroring addresses the common problem of operational data sitting in separate databases that analytics teams cannot easily reach. By landing that data in OneLake as Delta tables and keeping it synchronized, it lets reporting, notebooks and Spark workloads work from one consistent storage layer, while the capacity requirement and preview status of some sources remain points to verify during planning.

fabric-notebooks.desc: Fabric notebooks are the notebook experience in Microsoft Fabric for data engineering and data science, using PySpark, Python and SQL on lakehouse data.

faq.a: They are used for data engineering and data science in Microsoft Fabric, running PySpark, Python and SQL on lakehouse data. Typical tasks include cleaning and joining data, feature engineering, training models and publishing results.
faq.q: What are Fabric notebooks used for?

faq.a: According to the episode "Manage Git Integration for Microsoft Fabric Notebooks", code and metadata sync to Git, while Lakehouse data does not. The episode recommends a dev, test and prod branching model with pull requests.
faq.q: What does Git integration sync for Fabric notebooks?

faq.a: The episode "Train AI Models with Microsoft Fabric Notebooks" says that running on Spark next to the Lakehouse avoids CSV exports and memory crashes. It also allows transforms to be pushed to the data and long runs to be monitored in real time.
faq.q: Why train models in Fabric notebooks instead of on a laptop?

fabric-notebooks.long:
Fabric notebooks are the notebook experience in Microsoft Fabric for data engineering and data science. They let users work with PySpark, Python and SQL directly on lakehouse data, so that code runs on Spark next to the data instead of on a local laptop. The tool is also referred to as Python in Fabric, Microsoft Fabric notebooks or PySpark notebooks. It was developed by Microsoft, is classified as a Microsoft tool and as an analytics and BI tool, and is part of Microsoft Fabric. The license is included with Fabric.

The main purpose is to prepare, model and analyze data in the place where it already lives. Typical tasks named in the M365.FM episodes are cleaning and joining data, engineering features at scale, training models, evaluating them across large test sets and publishing results to Power BI or to machine learning scenarios. Because the notebooks run on Spark beside the Lakehouse, there is no need to export data to CSV files or to hold everything in the memory of a single machine. The episode "Train AI Models with Microsoft Fabric Notebooks" says this approach avoids memory crashes, allows transforms to be pushed to the data, and makes it possible to monitor long-running jobs in real time and to checkpoint models. Work can be done in Python or R.

A common organizing pattern described in "Use Fabric Notebooks for Data Transformation and ML" is a layered workflow: ingest raw data into a Bronze layer, clean and join it into Silver, feature-engineer it into Gold, and then publish the result to Power BI or to ML. According to the episode, this can be done end to end from one notebook inside the Lakehouse, combined with Git governance. This makes the notebook a single place for transformation logic rather than a series of manual steps in a reporting tool.

Collaboration and change control are a further topic. The episode "Manage Git Integration for Microsoft Fabric Notebooks" describes Fabric's Git integration not as a backup but as the basis for safe, scalable teamwork on notebooks, pipelines and models. It explains that code and metadata sync to Git, while Lakehouse data does not. The recommended approach in that episode is a simple branching model that moves from dev to test to prod using pull requests, supported by automated testing in CI/CD pipelines and alerts for important deployment events. These practices are meant to reduce merge conflicts and surprises when several people edit the same notebooks.

Fabric notebooks relate to other parts of the Microsoft ecosystem in several ways. The product is listed as related to Semantic Link Labs and to the semantic model, which reflects its use alongside Power BI-oriented data modeling. A newer episode, "Fabric Notebooks - Simply Explained", addresses the first-time experience of opening a Fabric Spark notebook and meeting code, data, unfamiliar errors and new terminology, framing the goal as getting data that can be trusted rather than becoming a developer. Another episode, "When to Use Python in Power Platform Automation", draws a boundary: it says Python suits analytics, machine learning and Fabric notebooks, but is a poor fit as everyday glue code inside Power Automate, Dataflows Gen2, Dataverse or Microsoft 365, where it points to Office Scripts, Copilot and agent-style orchestration instead.

In practice, decisions around Fabric notebooks usually concern where logic should live and how it is governed. Heavy transformation and model training fit a Spark notebook next to the Lakehouse, whereas lightweight orchestration across Microsoft 365 services is described in the episodes as better handled by other tools. Teams that adopt notebooks are advised in the episodes to connect them to Git early, separate environments, and treat notebooks as versioned code. Official documentation on using notebooks is available through Microsoft Learn.

fabric-ontology.desc: Ontology in Microsoft Fabric is a capability for modeling business entities and their relationships on top of existing data and semantic models, usable by data agents.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft Fabric capability for modeling business entities and their relationships on top of existing data and semantic models.
faq.q: What is Ontology in Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: Data agents can use the modeled entities and relationships to answer questions about the underlying data.
faq.q: How do data agents use an ontology?

faq.a: No. It is described as being built on top of existing data and semantic models rather than replacing them.
faq.q: Does an ontology replace existing semantic models?

fabric-ontology.long:
Ontology in Microsoft Fabric is a Microsoft Fabric capability for modeling business entities and the relationships between them. It is built on top of data and semantic models that already exist in a Fabric environment, rather than replacing them.

The purpose of an ontology is to give business concepts an explicit structure: which entities exist, and how they relate to one another. This shared description of the business domain can then be used by data agents, which rely on it to answer questions about the underlying data.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, Ontology in Microsoft Fabric sits alongside Fabric data and semantic models and the data agents that consume them. No further technical details, such as configuration steps, licensing or supported data sources, are stated in the information available for this entry.

This page does not yet list related M365.FM episodes or official documentation links.

fabric-real-time-intelligence.desc: Fabric Real-Time Intelligence is the Microsoft Fabric workload for streaming and event data, combining eventstreams, eventhouses, KQL databases, dashboards and Activator.

faq.a: It is the Microsoft Fabric workload for streaming and event data. It combines eventstreams, eventhouses with KQL databases, real-time dashboards and Activator alerts.
faq.q: What is Fabric Real-Time Intelligence?

faq.a: The components are eventstreams, eventhouses with KQL databases, real-time dashboards and Activator alerts. Together they cover ingesting event data, storing and querying it, visualizing it and reacting to it.
faq.q: Which components make up Fabric Real-Time Intelligence?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence - Simply Explained" covers what the workload does, where it fits in the Microsoft ecosystem and key considerations for administrators, architects and business stakeholders.
faq.q: Which M365.FM episode explains Fabric Real-Time Intelligence?

fabric-real-time-intelligence.long:
Fabric Real-Time Intelligence is the Microsoft Fabric workload for streaming and event data. It combines several components: eventstreams, eventhouses with KQL databases, real-time dashboards and Activator alerts. Together they cover the path from data that arrives continuously to a visible result or an automated reaction, so that teams can see what is happening in their operations while it is still happening rather than after a delay.

The workload is used where data is generated as a constant flow of events and where the value of that data depends on how quickly it is available. In the M365.FM episode "Microsoft Fabric Digital Twin Builder Explained", real-time intelligence is described as bringing together data from many sources and using AI to turn it into actionable insights. The episode says this lets teams spot problems early, respond quickly and keep the business running smoothly. That framing places the workload as a basis for faster and better-informed decisions in operational settings.

The components named in the description each play a distinct role. Eventstreams handle the incoming flow of events. Eventhouses, together with their KQL databases, are the place where event data is stored and queried using the Kusto Query Language. Real-time dashboards present the results of those queries in a visual form that follows the data as it changes. Activator alerts allow a defined condition in the data to trigger a notification or action, which moves the workload from observation to response. Read in sequence, these parts describe a pipeline from ingestion to storage and analysis, then to visualization and automated reaction.

Typical decisions around the workload concern where it fits in a wider Microsoft Fabric design and who is responsible for it. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence - Simply Explained" presents the topic for teams that need clearer technical decisions, safer implementation and practical operational value. According to the episode, it explains what the workload does, where it fits in the Microsoft ecosystem and the key considerations for administrators, architects and business stakeholders. This indicates that the subject is relevant to several roles: administrators who run the environment, architects who design the data flow, and business stakeholders who rely on the resulting insight.

The workload also appears as a connected topic in other episodes. "Microsoft Fabric Digital Twin Builder Explained" discusses it as part of the Fabric picture for operational scenarios, and the same episode points to security and compliance as important when scaling such projects. Several further episodes, including "Agent Governance Explained- How IT Can Enable the AI Agent Revolution with Thomas Zou [Microsoft]", "Agent Feed - Simply Explained" and "Microsoft Agent Framework - Simply Explained", recommend "Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence - Simply Explained" as a next practical learning step. This suggests the topic is treated as useful background for listeners who are also interested in AI agents and the Microsoft Agent Framework.

For readers who search for the term, the practical takeaway is that Fabric Real-Time Intelligence is not a single tool but a set of cooperating parts inside Microsoft Fabric. Understanding the role of eventstreams, eventhouses with KQL databases, real-time dashboards and Activator alerts is the starting point for judging whether a streaming or event-driven scenario fits the workload. The episodes referenced here are the places on M365.FM where the topic is explained in more depth.

fabric-task-flow.desc: Fabric task flow is a visual design in a Microsoft Fabric workspace that maps the tasks of a data solution to items, making architecture and ownership visible.

faq.a: It is a visual design in a Microsoft Fabric workspace that maps the tasks of a data solution to the items that implement them. This makes the architecture and the ownership of the solution visible.
faq.q: What is a Fabric task flow?

faq.a: The task flow is displayed and maintained in the Fabric workspace, and the items it points to live in that same workspace. It acts as an organizing layer over the workspace contents.
faq.q: How does a task flow relate to a Fabric workspace?

faq.a: Not in detail. The only linked episode, "Build Your First Power App: Beginner Step-by-Step Guide", mentions planning task flows in a Power Apps context and is only loosely related to the Fabric feature.
faq.q: Do the M365.FM episodes cover Fabric task flows?

fabric-task-flow.long:
A Fabric task flow is a visual design inside a Microsoft Fabric workspace. It maps the tasks of a data solution to the items that carry them out, so that the structure of a solution and the responsibility for its parts can be seen on one canvas. The concept is also referred to as Task flows or Fabric Task Flow Studio. Official documentation describes it in the Fabric getting-started material under the title task flow overview.

The core idea is to separate the question of what a data solution needs to do from the question of which items implement it. A data solution usually consists of several kinds of work: bringing data in, storing it, transforming it, and presenting it in a form that people can use. A task flow represents these kinds of work as tasks in a diagram, and each task can then be connected to the concrete items in the workspace that fulfil it. In this way the diagram acts as a map between the intended design and the actual contents of the workspace.

Task flows are closely tied to the Fabric workspace. The flow is displayed and maintained there, and the items it refers to live in the same workspace. They are also part of the broader Microsoft Fabric platform, where they serve as an organizing layer rather than as a separate service. Because the diagram sits next to the items, it helps people who open a workspace to understand what it contains and how the pieces relate, without having to inspect each item individually.

Typical situations in which a task flow is useful follow from this purpose. A team starting a new analytics project can begin from a recognizable pattern of tasks instead of an empty workspace. A team that inherits or reviews an existing workspace can use the flow as documentation to see which items belong to which stage. Stakeholders who are not working in the items directly can read the diagram to follow how a solution is put together. Because ownership becomes visible, it is also easier to discuss who is responsible for which part of a solution.

The M365.FM episodes linked to this topic do not discuss task flows in depth. The only episode in the data is "Build Your First Power App: Beginner Step-by-Step Guide", which deals with building a Power App and mentions planning task flows in the context of reviewing interaction design and testing. That usage concerns app design for users rather than the Fabric feature, so the episode is only a loose neighbor of this topic and does not describe how Fabric task flows work.

For practical decisions, the main questions around a Fabric task flow are about scope and upkeep. A flow is only as useful as the match between its tasks and the items in the workspace, so teams that adopt it generally need to decide who keeps the diagram aligned with the workspace as items are added or changed. For details on the available task types and how items are attached to them, the official task flow overview documentation is the reference to consult.

fabric-tenant-settings.desc: Fabric tenant settings are admin portal controls in Microsoft Fabric that determine which features, such as lakehouses, warehouses and notebooks, are available to which users.

faq.a: They are tenant-level settings in the Microsoft Fabric admin portal. They control which features, such as creating warehouses, lakehouses or notebooks, sharing and exporting, are available to which users in an organization.
faq.q: What are Fabric tenant settings?

faq.a: They are managed in the Microsoft Fabric admin portal. Microsoft describes them in its Fabric administration documentation on tenant settings.
faq.q: Where are Fabric tenant settings managed?

faq.a: Examples include creating warehouses, lakehouses and notebooks, as well as sharing and exporting. Each setting determines whether the feature is available and to which users.
faq.q: What kinds of capabilities do tenant settings affect?

fabric-tenant-settings.long:
Fabric tenant settings are tenant-level settings in the Microsoft Fabric admin portal. They control which features are available to which users in an organization, covering capabilities such as creating warehouses, lakehouses or notebooks, as well as sharing and exporting.

Administrators use these settings to govern how Microsoft Fabric is used across a tenant. Instead of managing each workload separately, a tenant admin can decide at the organizational level whether a given capability is switched on and for whom. This makes the settings a central part of governance and access planning in a Fabric deployment.

The settings are documented by Microsoft in the Fabric administration documentation under the topic about tenant settings. That documentation is the reference for the individual settings and how they are applied.

No related topics or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry. It is included as a reference term for anyone looking up how feature availability is controlled in Microsoft Fabric at the tenant level.

fabric-warehouse.desc: Fabric Data Warehouse is the relational data warehouse in Microsoft Fabric, used to prepare and query well-defined tables with SQL.

faq.a: Fabric Data Warehouse is the relational data warehouse in Microsoft Fabric. It is used to prepare and query well-defined tables with SQL.
faq.q: What is Fabric Data Warehouse?
