faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, data is ingested and transformed through Fabric items such as pipelines, dataflows and notebooks. One episode walks through extracting data from Amazon S3, transforming it with Python and loading it into a Fabric data warehouse.
faq.q: How does data get into a Fabric Data Warehouse?

faq.a: The episode "What Microsoft Fabric Means for Power BI Professionals" lists the data warehouse among the Fabric components BI developers should know. Data is transformed and stored in Fabric, and semantic models are then published for business users to consume in Power BI.
faq.q: How does Fabric Data Warehouse relate to Power BI?

fabric-warehouse.long:
Fabric Data Warehouse is the relational data warehouse within Microsoft Fabric. It is used to prepare and query well-defined tables with SQL, and it sits alongside other Fabric items such as the Fabric Lakehouse, OneLake, data pipelines and semantic models. Microsoft documents the product in its data warehousing section of Microsoft Learn, which serves as the reference for how the warehouse is built and used.

In practice, the warehouse is the part of a Fabric solution where structured, analytics-ready data is stored and served. Data typically arrives from source systems, whether cloud data or on-premises data, through ingestion and transformation steps, and is then modeled into tables that analysts, report authors and applications can query with SQL. This makes it a natural fit for teams that already think in terms of relational schemas, fact and dimension tables, and T-SQL-style querying, as opposed to file-based or notebook-driven exploration.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse - Simply Explained" frames the topic as relevant for teams that need clearer technical decisions, safer implementation and practical operational value. According to the episode, it explains what the warehouse does, where it fits in the Microsoft ecosystem, and which considerations matter for administrators, architects and business stakeholders. The episode also points to a 46% adoption rate for data warehousing solutions as a sign of how many organizations see value in streamlined data warehousing for informed decision-making.

A recurring question around the product is how data gets into it. The episode "DP-600 Training 2/4: Fabric Dataflows, Pipelines & Notebooks" works through a scenario in which data is extracted from Amazon S3, transformed with Python and loaded into a Fabric data warehouse. The episode uses this to walk through how to choose between ingestion methods in Microsoft Fabric, which is also relevant for exam preparation. The companion episode "Microsoft Fabric Data Factory - Simply Explained" recommends connecting data ingestion and transformation with analytics-ready warehouse data, pointing listeners to the Fabric Data Warehouse topic after the Data Factory overview.

Security and governance come up as well. The episode "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" describes end-to-end data workflows covering ingestion, pipeline copy, data movement, transformation and storage, designed to protect sensitive data as it moves from source data into a Fabric Lakehouse or a Fabric Data Warehouse. The stated aims are to reduce leakage risk, ensure secure access, maintain compliance, and keep ETL pipelines and dataflow processes auditable and resilient. It also notes that Fabric Data Factory builds on familiar concepts from Azure Data Factory by providing pipeline capabilities within Fabric.

For people coming from reporting, "What Microsoft Fabric Means for Power BI Professionals" lists the warehouse among the key components BI developers should know about, next to OneLake, data factory-like orchestration, the semantic model layer and the lakehouse. The episode describes a workflow in which fabric items such as notebooks, dataflows and pipelines are used to transform data, after which semantic models are published for business users to consume in Power BI. In that picture, the Fabric Data Warehouse is one of the storage and modeling layers that sits between ingestion and the semantic model.

Typical decisions around the product therefore concern where it belongs in the overall design: whether a given workload is better suited to the relational warehouse or to a lakehouse, how data is ingested and transformed before it lands in warehouse tables, how access to sensitive data is controlled, and how the resulting tables are exposed to Power BI. The episodes treat these as platform-level choices that involve administrators, architects and business stakeholders together rather than as purely technical details.

fabric-warehouse-snapshots.desc: Fabric warehouse snapshots are read-only, point-in-time views of a Microsoft Fabric warehouse that give consumers consistent data and can be rolled forward on demand.

faq.a: It is a read-only representation of a warehouse at a specific point in time, created as a child item of the parent warehouse. It gives consumers a consistent view of the data while updates continue in the source warehouse.
faq.q: What is a warehouse snapshot in Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: No. The episode "Use Microsoft Fabric Warehouse Snapshots Correctly" states that snapshots are not traditional backups. A snapshot has no storage of its own and relies on the source warehouse, and its retention is bounded by the parent warehouse.
faq.q: Is a Fabric warehouse snapshot the same as a backup?

faq.a: No. According to the documentation, Power BI can use only DirectQuery or Import mode with a warehouse snapshot, not Direct Lake.
faq.q: Can Power BI use Direct Lake with a warehouse snapshot?

fabric-warehouse-snapshots.long:
Fabric warehouse snapshots are a feature of the Microsoft Fabric data warehouse. A warehouse snapshot is a read-only representation of a warehouse item at a specific point in time. It is created as a child item of its parent warehouse and offers a transactionally consistent view of the data while the underlying warehouse continues to receive updates.

The main purpose is stability for consumers. According to Microsoft Learn, a snapshot gives analysts a consistent view of the data while real-time updates continue, and it protects reports from partial changes made by ETL processes. The documented uses include providing a stable warehouse version, keeping ETL runs consistent, supporting historical analysis, improving reporting accuracy and refreshing snapshots on a regular basis. A common pattern is to let loading processes write to the warehouse and let reports read from a snapshot, so that report users never see a half-loaded state.

The snapshot timestamp can be rolled forward on demand. This operation is described as instant and atomic. Queries that are already running finish against the data version they started with, and consumers can keep using the same connection string, so no reconfiguration is needed when a snapshot is advanced to a newer point in time. Updating the timestamp is the only change allowed through T-SQL beyond querying.

A snapshot does not hold its own copy of the data. It has no storage of its own and relies on the source warehouse. T-SQL access is limited to queries: data modifications and DDL statements are not permitted, apart from updating the timestamp. Permissions follow the workspace roles. Admins, members and contributors can create and manage snapshots, while viewers can query them. Security settings are applied in the source warehouse and take effect immediately in the snapshot.

The documentation lists several limitations that matter for design decisions. Schema changes in the parent warehouse carry over and can break reports that depend on the previous structure. Retention is bounded by the parent warehouse, which means a snapshot cannot reach further back than the parent allows. Power BI can use a snapshot only through DirectQuery or Import mode, not Direct Lake. Snapshots are also not supported on a lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint.

The M365.FM episode "Use Microsoft Fabric Warehouse Snapshots Correctly" (2025-11-25) addresses how the feature is commonly misunderstood. The episode says that snapshots are not traditional backups and that relying on them as such can lead to architectural and governance issues. Its guide covers what warehouse snapshots are and how they function within Microsoft Fabric. This matches the documentation: because a snapshot depends on the source warehouse and has no storage of its own, it offers consistency and a stable view for reading rather than independent protection of the data.

In practice, the decision around warehouse snapshots comes down to whether the goal is a stable, consistent read layer or data protection. For the first goal, snapshots with a scheduled or on-demand timestamp roll-forward fit well, provided that the reporting tools use DirectQuery or Import and that schema changes in the parent warehouse are coordinated with report owners. For recovery needs, the limits on retention and the dependency on the parent warehouse need to be taken into account separately.

fabric-workspace.desc: A Fabric workspace is a Microsoft Fabric container that groups lakehouses, notebooks and reports and sets access, capacity and deployment boundaries.

faq.a: A Fabric workspace is a container in Microsoft Fabric that groups items such as lakehouses, notebooks and reports. It defines access, capacity and deployment boundaries for those items.
faq.q: What is a Fabric workspace?

faq.a: Workspaces already existed in the Power BI Service as the place to publish and share reports. Fabric builds on this idea and uses workspaces for a wider set of item types.
faq.q: How does a Fabric workspace relate to the Power BI Service?

faq.a: Typical scenarios are separating development, test and production content and giving a department its own area with its own members. A workspace can also be assigned to a capacity.
faq.q: When are separate Fabric workspaces used?

fabric-workspace.long:
A Fabric workspace is a container in Microsoft Fabric that groups items such as lakehouses, notebooks and reports. It also defines access, capacity and deployment boundaries. In practice it is the unit that teams use to organize analytics work and to decide who may see or change which content. The term is sometimes shortened to "Workspace", and the German-language product term is "Fabric-Arbeitsbereich".

The concept sits inside Microsoft Fabric and is closely related to the Power BI Service. In the Power BI Service, workspaces were already the place where reports and other content were published and shared. Fabric extends that idea to a wider range of item types, so a single workspace can hold the lakehouses, notebooks and reports that belong to one piece of analytics work. Because of this, the workspace is a broader concept than a simple report folder: it is the organizing boundary for everything a team builds on the platform.

Three functions are tied to a Fabric workspace according to the available description. The first is grouping: related items live together, which makes it easier to see which assets belong to the same project or team. The second is access: membership in the workspace and the roles assigned there determine who can view, change or manage the items inside. The third is capacity and deployment: the workspace is the boundary to which capacity is assigned and along which content can be separated into stages. Exact settings, available roles and licensing details should be checked in the official Microsoft documentation, since they are not spelled out here.

Typical decisions around workspaces include how many to create and how to split them. Common scenarios are separating development, test and production content, and giving a department its own area with its own members. Each of these choices affects who has access and how content moves from one environment to another. A Fabric task flow can help here, because it visualizes how the items inside a workspace belong together and gives a team a clearer picture of what the workspace contains.

Workspaces are also a Governance topic. The way workspaces are named, owned and secured shapes how well an organization can control its data and its analytics assets. The M365.FM episode "Copilot Inherits Your Mess: Modernizing Microsoft 365 for AI with Richard Harbridge [MVP]" discusses this from a wider Microsoft 365 view. The episode says that AI does not necessarily create entirely new governance problems but makes existing ones more visible, and it describes accumulated decisions around permissions, sharing, workspace creation and ownership as "sprawl". It also says that sprawl itself is not automatically bad, because growth can be a sign of successful adoption; the problem begins when growth outpaces the organization's ability to manage it. That discussion is not specific to Fabric, but the same reasoning applies to how workspaces are created and owned.

Other M365.FM episodes use the word "workspace" for different products. "Power BI Workspace Roles - Simply Explained" covers the roles that control what people can do in a Power BI workspace, and the episode notes that the real control sits in the role chosen for a person rather than in the share button. "Dynamics 365 Customer Service Workspace - Simply Explained", "Dynamics 365 Omnichannel - Simply Explained" and "Microsoft Places - Simply Explained" deal with an agent workspace, a unified agent workspace and workspace management in hybrid offices, so they are not about Fabric workspaces.

face-check.desc: Face Check is a Microsoft Entra Verified ID feature that compares a live selfie with the photo in a Verified ID credential to support higher-assurance identity checks.

faq.a: Face Check compares a live selfie with the photo stored in a Microsoft Entra Verified ID credential. It uses the Azure AI Vision Face API and includes a liveness check to confirm that the person presenting the credential is its holder.
faq.q: What does Face Check do?

faq.a: The verifier receives only a confidence score. The selfie and liveness data are processed in the cloud and are not stored or passed on to the verifier. The match threshold can be set between 50 and 100, with a default of 70.
faq.q: What does the verifier receive from a Face Check?

faq.a: Verified ID must be set up in the tenant, along with an Azure subscription and the Contributor role. Either the Face Check add-on or the Microsoft Entra Suite is required, and users need Microsoft Authenticator on a device that meets integrity requirements.
faq.q: What is needed to use Face Check?

face-check.long:
Face Check is a premium feature of Microsoft Entra Verified ID. It compares a live selfie with the photo stored in a Verified ID credential. The aim is to confirm that the person presenting a credential is the person the credential was issued to. Because it adds a biometric comparison to a credential check, it is used in situations where a credential alone is not considered strong enough proof of who is on the other end.

According to Microsoft Learn, Face Check relies on the Azure AI Vision Face API. The user takes a selfie with the camera of a mobile device, and the selfie is compared with the photo contained in the credential. The process includes a liveness check that is meant to rule out static photos or 2D videos. The verifier does not receive the selfie or the liveness data. Processing happens in the cloud, and the selfie and liveness data are not stored or passed on. The verifier only receives the outcome as a confidence score.

The match threshold is configurable. It is an integer between 50 and 100, with a default of 70. Choosing a value is a design decision for each verifier: it determines how strict the comparison is. Photo quality matters for the result, and large changes in appearance between the stored photo and the live selfie can lower the score. Supported credentials include VerifiedEmployee, government-issued IDs and custom credentials that contain a trusted photo.

There are practical prerequisites. Verification works only with Microsoft Authenticator on devices that meet integrity requirements. Setup requires Verified ID in the tenant, an Azure subscription and the Contributor role. Face Check must also be licensed, either through the Face Check add-on or through the Microsoft Entra Suite. Typical uses named in the documentation are help desk verification and access to sensitive information, where an organization wants more confidence than a simple credential presentation provides.

Face Check sits within the broader Microsoft Entra Verified ID model, in which a person holds a credential and presents it to a verifier instead of handing over documents. The episode "Microsoft Entra Verified ID - Simply Explained" describes this model as reducing document handling and unnecessary sharing of personal information. It presents Face Check as the part intended for higher-risk scenarios, where it helps organizations confirm that the individual presenting the credential is the legitimate holder. The episode goes on to explore practical uses of the feature.

The episode "Microsoft Entra as a Complete IAM Platform" covers Face Check in the context of Verified ID as one component of a wider identity and access management platform. It describes Face Check as real-time verification, in which users prove who they are with the camera on their mobile device before they can take action. It also states that Microsoft Entra Verified ID uses Azure AI services for facial identity verification and mentions scenarios such as onboarding users and recovering credentials securely.

In short, Face Check does not replace the credential. It adds a live check on top of it, binding the credential to the person present at the time of verification. Decisions around it include which credentials to accept, which confidence threshold to set, which licensing route to use, and which processes, such as help desk calls or access to sensitive data, justify the added step.

facilitator-agent.desc: Facilitator agent (Microsoft Teams) is a Microsoft 365 Copilot agent for Teams meetings that takes notes and answers questions visibly to all participants.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft 365 Copilot agent that works in Teams meetings. It takes notes and answers questions, and its output is visible to all meeting participants.
faq.q: What is the Facilitator agent in Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: It takes notes and answers questions during the meeting. Both the notes and the answers are shown to everyone taking part, not only to one person.
faq.q: What does the Facilitator agent do in a meeting?

faq.a: It is part of Microsoft Teams and is described as a Microsoft 365 Copilot agent used in Teams meetings.
faq.q: Which product is the Facilitator agent part of?

facilitator-agent.long:
Facilitator agent (Microsoft Teams) is a Microsoft 365 Copilot agent that operates inside Teams meetings. It takes notes during a meeting and answers questions, and its output is visible to all meeting participants rather than to a single user.

The agent is part of Microsoft Teams. Because notes and answers appear for everyone in the meeting, it serves as a shared aid for keeping track of discussion points and responding to questions that come up during a session. This differs from an assistant that returns results only to the person who asked.

On M365.FM, the Facilitator agent (Microsoft Teams) is recorded as a product entity connected to Microsoft Teams. No episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no official documentation or site links are listed for it. This page therefore limits itself to the confirmed description: a Microsoft 365 Copilot agent for Teams meetings that handles note-taking and question answering in a way that all participants can see.

factory-simulation.desc: Factory simulation is a controlled model of how work flows through part of a factory, used to test changes such as an extra shift or a new machine before making them.

faq.a: Factory simulation is a controlled model of how work moves through part of a factory, built from current operating rules, resources, orders and normal variation. It lets a proposed change, such as an extra shift, a new machine or a smaller buffer, be tested before it is made.
faq.q: What is factory simulation?

faq.a: Factories are interconnected systems, so improving capacity at one resource can simply move the bottleneck elsewhere. The M365.FM episode notes that more machine hours do not automatically mean more customer orders shipped.
faq.q: Why is it hard to predict the effect of a change in a factory?

faq.a: The usual technique is discrete-event simulation, which models a system as a sequence of events in time and jumps the clock from one event to the next. Randomness comes from pseudorandom number generators, and results are averaged over replications.
faq.q: Which modeling technique is behind factory simulation?

factory-simulation.long:
Factory simulation is a controlled model of how work moves through part of a factory. It uses the current operating rules, resources, orders and normal variation, so that a proposed change can be tested before it is made on the real shop floor. Typical candidates for such a test include an extra shift, a new machine or a smaller buffer.

The reason for building such a model is that factories are interconnected systems. A change that looks obvious in one place can have little effect on overall output. The M365.FM episode "Can You Simulate Your Factory Before Changing It?" makes this point directly: improving capacity at one resource can simply move the bottleneck somewhere else, and more machine hours do not automatically mean more customer orders shipped. Adding buffers, changing staffing or accepting a different product mix can all look like straightforward fixes, yet their combined effect on the whole line is hard to predict by inspection alone. The episode places factory simulation alongside production planning, Digital Twins, finite capacity, bottleneck management and manufacturing optimization.

The underlying technique is usually discrete-event simulation. According to the Wikipedia article on discrete-event simulation, this approach models a system as a sequence of events in time. Each event marks a change of state at a specific instant, and the state is assumed to stay constant between events. Instead of advancing time in small steps, the simulation clock jumps to the next event, which is faster. A pending event set, normally a time-ordered priority queue, holds the scheduled events. The article's own example is a teller queue, with arrival, service-start and service-end events and queue length as the state. The article does not use the term factory simulation itself, so this describes the modeling method rather than a specific product or standard.

Randomness in such models comes from pseudorandom number generators, which means runs can be repeated exactly. Because early output may be misleading until the model reaches steady state, results are typically averaged over several replications and reported with confidence intervals, and a stopping rule has to be defined. These practices matter when interpreting the output: a single run is not a reliable basis for a decision about a real production line.

In manufacturing, simulation is described as a way to find bottlenecks caused by excess inventory, overproduction, process variability and varying routing. It gives a whole-system view with indicators such as worker utilization, on-time delivery and scrap rate. Managers can also test Lean or Six Sigma changes within the full system before committing resources. The same source gives a healthcare example with a similar lesson: extra hours help only if the true bottleneck is solved.

Typical decisions around factory simulation therefore start with a specific question about a change, for example whether adding capacity at one resource will raise the number of orders shipped or only shift the constraint to another step. The model is built from the current operating rules, resources and orders, so that the baseline reflects how the factory actually runs, and the proposed change is then applied to the model rather than to the shop floor. Comparing the two runs, with normal variation included, shows whether the change is worth making. The relationship to Digital Twins, production planning and finite capacity is raised in the episode as part of the same discussion of how manufacturers can test operational changes before introducing them.

For listeners of M365.FM, the episode "Can You Simulate Your Factory Before Changing It?" (dated 2026-09-16) is the reference on this topic. It frames factory simulation as a way to avoid acting on intuition about isolated resources and to look at the factory as a connected system.

fault-domains.desc: Fault domains are groups of hardware in an Azure datacenter that share power and network equipment, used to limit rack-level failures across hosts or VMs.
fault-domains.long:
Fault domains are groups of hardware in an Azure datacenter that share common power and network equipment. Because machines in the same fault domain depend on the same underlying infrastructure, a failure affecting that shared equipment can impact every host or virtual machine placed within it.

The concept is used when planning the placement of workloads. Spreading hosts or VMs across multiple fault domains reduces the risk that a single rack-level failure takes down all of them at once. In this way, fault domains serve as a basic building block for designing resilient deployments in Azure, where the goal is to avoid having every instance of a workload depend on the same physical hardware group.

The notion of isolating failures by shared power and networking applies at the level of individual racks and the equipment serving them, which makes it narrower in scope than larger availability boundaries. It describes how hardware is grouped rather than any specific service or product feature.

No related topics or episodes are currently linked to Fault domains on M365.FM, so this entry is limited to the definition and purpose of the concept itself.

feature-engineering.desc: Feature engineering turns raw data into model-ready features through cleaning, aggregation and encoding, as covered in M365.FM episodes on Fabric, Azure and AI.

faq.a: Feature engineering is the process of transforming raw data into input variables, called features, for machine learning models, for example through cleaning, aggregation and encoding.
faq.q: What is feature engineering?

faq.a: According to the episode "Train AI Models with Microsoft Fabric Notebooks", Python-based tools in Fabric notebooks can be used to build new variables from an existing dataset, and Spark applies the transformations across the whole dataset, even with millions of rows.
faq.q: How is feature engineering done in Microsoft Fabric notebooks?

faq.a: The episode "Architect a High-Performance Autonomous Enterprise with Microsoft 365" says that variations in data collection methods or feature engineering can introduce inconsistencies that degrade model accuracy.
faq.q: Why can feature engineering cause problems in production models?

feature-engineering.long:
Feature engineering is the process of transforming raw data into input variables, called features, for machine learning models. Typical steps include cleaning data, aggregating records and encoding values so that a model can use them. The quality and relevance of the features strongly influence how well a model performs, which is why the step is treated as a core part of any machine learning workflow rather than a minor preparation task.

In practice, feature engineering means creating new variables from an existing dataset. The M365.FM episode "Train AI Models with Microsoft Fabric Notebooks" describes this in the context of Fabric notebooks. It says that Python-based tools in notebooks can be used to transform data and build features that improve model accuracy, and that Spark makes it possible to apply these transformations across an entire dataset, even with millions of rows. The same episode mentions a data-cleaning tool that can generate code automatically for common tasks such as filling in missing values or removing incomplete rows, and that these cleaning steps can be exported as reusable functions in pandas or PySpark. Its stated best practice is to use Spark and Python tools to clean and transform data.

Feature engineering also depends on where the data lives and how it can be accessed. The episode "Optimize Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Performance" lists native support for analytics and machine learning as an advantage of a lakehouse, because it enables direct access to large datasets for feature engineering and model training without ETL bottlenecks. The same episode notes that a performant lakehouse requires expertise in data formats, partitioning, compaction and metadata management, so the quality of the underlying data platform affects how smoothly features can be prepared.

Public and curated data can support the same work. The episode "Azure Open Datasets - Simply Explained" says that Azure Open Datasets can be used for training and testing models as well as for feature engineering. It stresses that high-quality data is crucial when training models and that clean, curated datasets help in building robust machine learning models. The MNIST database of handwritten digits is given as an example for training an image recognition model.

Feature engineering is also named as one of the traditional machine learning capabilities in the comparison presented in "Azure AI Foundry - Simply Explained". There it appears alongside supervised and unsupervised learning, deep learning, MLflow for lifecycle management and Databricks AI/BI Genie, as part of a platform oriented toward training and serving custom machine learning models. By contrast, the same comparison lists foundation models, prompt engineering, RAG and agent orchestration as capabilities of the Azure AI Foundry side, which shows that feature engineering belongs mainly to the classical, data-centric approach to building models.

The topic matters for operations as well as for model building. The episode "Architect a High-Performance Autonomous Enterprise with Microsoft 365" lists data pipeline issues among the causes of model drift. It says that variations in data collection methods or feature engineering introduce inconsistencies that degrade model accuracy. Features therefore need to be defined and produced consistently over time, not only when a model is first trained. Other drivers of drift named in that episode include external disruptions, seasonality and trends, and product or service changes, all of which alter the data a model sees.

In summary, the episodes describe feature engineering as a step that connects data preparation to model training: cleaning and transforming data, scaling the transformations with Spark, relying on accessible and well-managed storage, and keeping the feature logic consistent so that deployed models remain accurate.

federated-connectors.desc: Federated connectors let Microsoft 365 Copilot query external systems in real time via the Model Context Protocol, without indexing content into Microsoft 365.

faq.a: Synced connectors index external data into Microsoft Graph and work at organization level. Federated connectors query the external system in real time via the Model Context Protocol, do not index the content, and work per user.
faq.q: What is the difference between federated and synced connectors?

faq.a: Each user authenticates with the source system using their own credentials via OAuth 2.0, so Copilot accesses data under that user's identity and permissions.
faq.q: How do users sign in to a federated connector?

faq.a: Where the connector offers matching tools, Copilot can create, change or delete data in the connected system. These write actions require the user's approval, and the Researcher agent only reads.
faq.q: Can Copilot change data through a federated connector?

federated-connectors.long:
Federated connectors are a type of Microsoft 365 Copilot connector in which Copilot queries an external system live, through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), instead of copying that system's content into Microsoft 365. The data is retrieved at the moment it is needed and is not indexed in Microsoft 365. It stays where it originated, and the source system remains the system of record.

The model contrasts with synced connectors. According to the M365.FM episodes, synced connectors index external data into Microsoft Graph, which allows quick searches across Microsoft 365 applications. Federated connectors, by comparison, provide real-time access to live data without indexing, so the information reflects the current state of the source. The episode "Connect External Business Data with Microsoft 365 Copilot Connectors" describes these as the two main connector types, one for indexed data and one for real-time access. The episode "Microsoft Graph Connectors - Simply Explained" covers the same split and notes that connecting external sources helps reduce data silos.

A defining property is how identity and access work. Each user authenticates with the source system using their own credentials via OAuth 2.0, and access runs under the identity and permissions of that signed-in user. Federation therefore works per user. Synced connectors, by contrast, work at organization level. Users also need a Microsoft 365 Copilot license to use federated connectors.

Federated connectors are not limited to reading data. Where a connector offers the matching tools, Copilot can create, change or delete data in the connected system on the user's behalf. Such write actions require the user's approval, while read tools do not. The available actions depend on the tools the connector publisher exposes. Typical examples named in the documentation are summarizing open project issues, turning an email into an issue, or updating a CRM record.

There are some limits and management points to consider. The Researcher agent only reads from federated connectors and does not perform write actions. Activity can be audited in Microsoft Purview, which matters for organizations that need traceability. Administrators manage connectors in the Microsoft 365 admin center, and connectors are either published by Microsoft or submitted by partners and approved before use.

In practice, the choice between the two models comes down to the data and the requirements. Where live, current data and keeping content in the source system are priorities, the federated approach fits, because nothing is copied into the Microsoft 365 index and each user sees only what their own permissions allow. Where fast cross-application search over a prepared index is the aim, synced connectors are the alternative described in the episodes. The episodes also point to unified search from a single search box, productivity gains from streamlined routine tasks, and customization with low-code and pro-code tools as wider benefits of Copilot connectors in general.

For teams evaluating federated connectors, the main questions are which external systems expose MCP-based tools, whether those tools cover the needed actions, how users will authenticate, and how auditing in Microsoft Purview will be used. Because behavior depends on the tools a publisher provides, the scope of what Copilot can do varies from one connector to another.

federated-learning.desc: Federated learning trains models across organizations or locations without sharing raw data; only model updates, such as LoRA adapter matrices, travel across the network.

faq.a: Federated learning is a way of training models collaboratively across multiple organizations, business units or locations without sharing raw data. Only model updates, such as LoRA adapter matrices, are exchanged across the network.
faq.q: What is federated learning?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes name it as a privacy-preserving technique, for example to address data privacy concerns in "Real-Time AI Sensitivity Labeling in Microsoft Purview" and to reduce inference of sensitive attributes in "How AI-Generated Identity Configuration Breaks Entra Security".
faq.q: Why is federated learning mentioned in privacy and governance discussions?

faq.a: Not necessarily. The episode "Autonomous Microsoft Enterprise with Altera and Copilot" lists federated learning and privacy compliance among data management challenges that can complicate data handling.
faq.q: Does federated learning make data management simpler?

federated-learning.long:
Federated learning is an approach to training machine learning models collaboratively across multiple organizations, business units or locations without sharing the underlying raw data. Instead of pooling records in one central place, each participant keeps its data where it is, and only model updates move across the network. One example of such an update named in the available description is the set of LoRA adapter matrices. The idea is that the shared learning benefits from many data sources while the sensitive source material stays with its owner.

In practice, federated learning is used where data cannot or should not be centralized, for instance because of privacy concerns, compliance requirements or organizational boundaries. This makes it relevant for enterprise AI scenarios in which several departments, subsidiaries or partner companies hold valuable but sensitive data. The core principle is a separation between the data, which stays local, and the learned parameters, which are exchanged. How the updates are aggregated and secured depends on the specific implementation, and the sources provided here do not go into those technical details.

Several M365.FM episodes mention federated learning in the context of privacy and governance rather than as a standalone technical topic. In "Real-Time AI Sensitivity Labeling in Microsoft Purview", the episode lists data privacy concerns as a challenge when adopting such a solution and names privacy techniques like federated learning as a response. The implementation tip given alongside it is to start with non-sensitive data to build trust. This frames federated learning as one option for addressing privacy worries during rollout, together with other measures such as phased migration and bias audits.

The episode "Improve Microsoft Copilot Accuracy Beyond Vector Search" looks ahead at enterprise AI and states that neural federated learning will let organizations train models without sharing raw data. It appears there in a forward-looking list alongside ideas such as neural privacy controls, neural auditing and neural edge computing, and the episode treats it as part of a future direction for enterprise AI instead of a configuration step.

In "Autonomous Microsoft Enterprise with Altera and Copilot", federated learning is named among data management challenges. The episode says that federated learning and privacy compliance can complicate data handling as organizations scale autonomous systems. This is a useful counterpoint: while federated learning keeps raw data local, the episode presents it as something that also adds complexity to data management and must be weighed against infrastructure readiness, cybersecurity risks and workforce readiness.

Security-oriented treatments appear in two further episodes. "AI Governance from Microsoft Copilot to Quantum Computing" lists, as a medium-term challenge, integrating federated learning with quantum-safe cryptographic protocols to protect sensitive data. "How AI-Generated Identity Configuration Breaks Entra Security" recommends applying privacy-preserving techniques like differential privacy and federated learning in response to a documented case of inferring sensitive user attributes without consent. In both cases, federated learning is positioned as one building block within a broader privacy and security posture.

Taken together, the episodes treat federated learning as a privacy-preserving training approach that supports governance goals: keeping raw data local, reducing exposure of sensitive information and enabling collaboration across boundaries. Decisions around it typically involve balancing these benefits against added data management complexity, the need for suitable infrastructure and the importance of combining it with other controls such as auditing, monitoring and cryptographic protection.

fido-alliance.desc: The FIDO Alliance is an open industry association that develops the FIDO authentication standards, including FIDO2 and WebAuthn, which underlie passkeys.

faq.a: It is an open industry association, based in Beaverton, Oregon, that was launched in February 2013 to reduce reliance on passwords. It develops and promotes authentication standards such as UAF, U2F and FIDO2.
faq.q: What is the FIDO Alliance?

faq.a: Passkeys build on the FIDO authentication standards, including FIDO2, which combines WebAuthn and CTAP2. The M365.FM episode "Passkeys and FIDO2 - Simply Explained" cites the FIDO Alliance as the source of the figure of five billion passkeys in use worldwide.
faq.q: How does the FIDO Alliance relate to passkeys?

faq.a: FIDO2 is a joint project of the FIDO Alliance and the W3C. It consists of WebAuthn, which became a W3C Recommendation in March 2019, and CTAP2.
faq.q: What is FIDO2?

fido-alliance.long:
The FIDO Alliance, short for Fast IDentity Online Alliance, is an open industry association based in Beaverton, Oregon. It was launched in February 2013 with the aim of reducing reliance on passwords. Its work centers on authentication standards that are now the technical foundation of passkeys, the sign-in method Microsoft has made the default way to sign in to Microsoft 365.

The Alliance targets two problems. The first is that strong authentication devices have not interoperated with one another. The second is the burden placed on people who must manage many usernames and passwords. To address both, the FIDO model is device-centric. A device registers a public key with a server. When the user later signs in, the device signs a challenge sent by the server with a private key, and that private key is unlocked by a local gesture such as a fingerprint scan or a button press. Because the approach relies on public-key cryptography, authentication can take place over an insecure channel, and no shared secret has to travel to the server.

Over time the Alliance has published several specifications. UAF covers password-free authentication, and U2F defines a second factor that is used alongside a password. FIDO2 is a joint project with the W3C and consists of two parts: WebAuthn, the web API that lets sites and apps request this type of sign-in, and CTAP2, the protocol that lets an external authenticator communicate with a browser or device. WebAuthn became a W3C Recommendation in March 2019. Authenticators that work within this framework can take several forms, including hardware security keys, smartphones, TPMs, smart cards and NFC devices.

Membership in the Alliance spans large technology, payment and government organizations. Named members include Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Samsung, Intel, Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Yubico and NIST. This mix of platform vendors, hardware makers and payment companies is relevant because the standards only help if browsers, operating systems, services and authenticators all support them.

In practice, the FIDO Alliance matters to administrators and users because its specifications define how modern phishing-resistant sign-in works. When a service accepts a FIDO2 credential, the secret never leaves the device, so there is nothing for an attacker to capture and replay on a fake site. Organizations weighing a move away from passwords typically look at which authenticator types they can support, such as security keys or built-in device authenticators, and how these map onto the standards the Alliance maintains.

The M365.FM episode "Passkeys and FIDO2 - Simply Explained" refers to the FIDO Alliance directly. The episode says that, according to the FIDO Alliance, five billion passkeys are already in use worldwide, and it notes that this is a large shift for something many people still cannot explain. It also points out that Microsoft has made passkeys the default way to sign in to Microsoft 365. The episode walks through what a passkey actually is, how the keys do their work without ever sharing a secret, and why phishing stops working once the secret is gone.

It is worth keeping the roles clear. The FIDO Alliance is a standards and promotion body, not a product or a service that people sign in to. It develops and promotes the specifications, while vendors such as Microsoft implement them in their own sign-in experiences. Passkeys are a user-facing result of this standards work rather than a separate offering from the Alliance itself.

fido2.desc: FIDO2 is an open authentication standard, including WebAuthn and CTAP, that defines how passkeys and security keys work for phishing-resistant, passwordless sign-in.

faq.a: FIDO2 is an open authentication standard, including WebAuthn and CTAP, that defines how passkeys and security keys work. It supports passwordless sign-in.
faq.q: What is FIDO2?

faq.a: Passkeys are built on the FIDO2 standard. The episode "Passkeys and FIDO2 - Simply Explained" covers what a passkey is and notes that Microsoft has made passkeys the default way to sign in to Microsoft 365.
faq.q: How does FIDO2 relate to passkeys?

faq.a: The episode "Passkeys vs Passwords in Microsoft Entra ID" describes FIDO2 security keys as one of the passwordless methods, alongside Windows Hello and the Microsoft Authenticator app.
faq.q: Where does FIDO2 appear in Microsoft Entra ID?

fido2.long:
FIDO2 is an open authentication standard that defines how passkeys and security keys work. It includes two parts, WebAuthn and CTAP, which together describe how a sign-in is carried out between a service, a browser or operating system, and an authenticator such as a hardware security key. The standard is maintained within the FIDO Alliance, and it is the technical basis for what most people now know as passkeys.

The main purpose of FIDO2 is to replace passwords with a stronger way to prove identity. Passwords can be guessed, reused, phished or stolen, and credential theft is a recurring theme in the M365.FM episodes that touch on the topic. FIDO2 changes the model: instead of typing a shared secret, the user proves possession of a cryptographic credential held on a device or security key. Because the sign-in does not depend on a password being entered and transmitted, the approach is described in the episodes as designed to resist modern attacks such as phishing, which still affects methods like a password plus a one-time code.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, FIDO2 shows up most often in connection with Microsoft Entra ID. The episode "Passkeys vs Passwords in Microsoft Entra ID" describes how organizations move away from passwords by using passwordless authentication, and it explains how FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello and the Microsoft Authenticator app work. It also covers case studies on lower breach risk, faster onboarding and cost savings, along with a practical playbook for piloting passwordless authentication, including common pitfalls, quick wins and the new security trade-offs that come with dropping passwords.

The episode "Passkeys and FIDO2 - Simply Explained" looks at the same standard from a broader angle. It cites the FIDO Alliance figure of five billion passkeys already in use worldwide, and it notes that Microsoft has made passkeys the default way to sign in to Microsoft 365. The episode aims to explain what a passkey actually is and how it relates to FIDO2, since the term is widely used but often not well understood.

FIDO2 also appears in security-hardening discussions. In "Lock Down Microsoft Entra ID Before Phishing Hits", FIDO2 keys are named as a passwordless option that removes the need for passwords, alongside multi-factor authentication, identity protection alerts and automated risk remediation. In "Hidden Microsoft 365 Tenant Security Risks", a comparison of authentication methods lists SMS one-time codes as vulnerable to SIM swap attacks, push notifications as exposed to MFA fatigue, and password plus one-time code as still open to phishing, while FIDO2 and passkeys are described as designed to resist modern attacks. The episode recommends moving toward passwordless authentication and using conditional access policies, and it suggests regularly reviewing authentication methods.

FIDO2 is also mentioned as one of several passwordless solutions in an episode on Azure, where it is listed together with managed identities. That episode presents passwordless authentication as a way to reduce the risk of breaches caused by weak passwords and to bring cost and operational benefits.

Typical decisions around FIDO2 include whether to use hardware security keys, platform authenticators such as Windows Hello, or the Microsoft Authenticator app, how to run a pilot before a wider rollout, and how to combine passwordless sign-in with conditional access. FIDO2 is the common standard underneath these choices, which is why it is often discussed together with passkeys, Windows Hello and Microsoft Entra ID.

figma.desc: Figma is a collaborative interface design tool; in Power Platform, a plugin turns Figma designs into Power Apps screens to support designer-maker hand-off.

faq.a: Figma is a collaborative interface design tool, and a plugin turns Figma designs into Power Apps screens. This supports hand-off between designers and the makers who build the app.
faq.q: What is Figma used for in the Power Platform?

faq.a: A canvas app is the flexible, screen-based kind of Power Apps app where layout is designed freely. Screens converted from Figma designs are used in Power Apps, so the screen-by-screen design maps onto that app type.
faq.q: How is Figma related to canvas apps?

faq.a: The episode "Figma to Power Apps Development with Lukas Pavelka [MVP]" covers it. Mirko Peters talks with Lukas Pavelka about tools such as PowerApps for Figma and Power BI for Figma, which bridge UI design and low-code development.
faq.q: Which M365.FM episode covers Figma and Power Apps?

figma.long:
Figma, also referred to as Figma Design, is a collaborative interface design tool. It is classified as a developer tool and is used to create and share the visual design of applications and user interfaces. Within the Microsoft ecosystem it appears mainly in two places: as a source of designs for Power Apps, and as a design reference in other Microsoft products such as Microsoft Teams.

In the Power Platform context, a plugin turns Figma designs into Power Apps screens. This supports hand-off between designers and makers. Designers can work in a tool built for visual design, and the makers who build the app start from that work instead of redrawing every screen by hand. The approach is most relevant for apps whose appearance matters, because it narrows the gap between the design file and the finished app.

Figma is related to Power Apps, where the converted screens are used, and to the Canvas app type. A canvas app is the flexible, screen-based kind of Power Apps app in which layout is designed freely, which is why a screen-by-screen design from Figma maps onto it naturally. The typical decision for a team is whether the interface design should be created in a dedicated design tool first and then brought into Power Apps, or built directly inside Power Apps by the maker.

The M365.FM episode "Figma to Power Apps Development with Lukas Pavelka [MVP]" is the main reference on this topic. In it, Mirko Peters talks with Lukas Pavelka about the future of enterprise app development, AI-assisted coding and the growing connection between Figma and Microsoft Power Platform. The episode says that Lukas Pavelka moved from Java development into building tools such as PowerApps for Figma and Power BI for Figma, which are designed to bridge the gap between modern UI design and low-code development.

Figma also shows up in other episodes as part of wider Microsoft workflows. The episode "Organize Projects Properly in Microsoft Teams" mentions embedding design files from tools like Figma in Teams to streamline feedback, alongside integrations with project management apps such as Jira or Azure DevOps. The episode "Build Actionable Teams Notifications with Adaptive Cards" lists a Microsoft Teams UI Kit for Figma, which provides design guidelines, theming, accessibility and responsive sizing guidance for adaptive cards. In "Canvas App UI vs Generative Pages: Which Should You Use?", Figma is named among the tools commonly used in interface design work, together with Sketch, Adobe XD, Miro and Maze, and the episode notes that mastering such tools can improve design capabilities and streamline a workflow.

The episode "Model Context Protocol vs Custom AI Integration Glue" mentions Figma in a different setting. It says that companies such as Atlassian, Figma and Asana favor remote MCP servers for their ease of deployment and scalability, as part of the rapid adoption of the Model Context Protocol since its launch in November 2024.

In short, Figma is the design side of a designer-maker workflow. Power Apps and the canvas app type are where designs become working screens, and the related episodes describe how the tool connects to AI-assisted development, Teams collaboration and design guidance.

figma-make.desc: Figma Make is Figma's AI prompt-to-app feature that generates working prototypes and code from a written description.

faq.a: Figma Make is Figma's AI prompt-to-app feature. It generates working prototypes and code from a description provided by the user.
faq.q: What is Figma Make?

faq.a: According to its short description, it generates working prototypes and code based on a written description of the desired app or interface.
faq.q: What does Figma Make produce?

faq.a: Figma Make is a feature offered by Figma.
faq.q: Who makes Figma Make?

figma-make.long:
Figma Make is an AI feature from Figma that turns a written description into a working prototype and code. It follows a prompt-to-app approach: a user describes what they want, and the tool produces an interactive result instead of a static design.

The feature is aimed at the early stages of building an app or interface, where an idea needs to become something that can be tested and discussed. Because it produces both a working prototype and underlying code, it connects design work with development work.

No further details, such as supported inputs, integrations, pricing or availability, are included in the information available for this entry, so none are stated here. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to Figma Make, and no related topics have been associated with it yet.

filter-context.desc: Filter context in DAX is the set of active filters from slicers, visuals, pages and rows that determines which data a measure sees when it is evaluated.

faq.a: Filter context is the set of filters active when a measure is evaluated, coming from slicers, visuals, the page and rows. It determines which data the measure sees and therefore which result it returns.
faq.q: What is filter context in DAX?

faq.a: The episode "Data Analysis Expressions (DAX) - Simply Explained" says filter context determines which data is included in each calculation, so the same measure automatically adapts to regions, products, dates and visuals.
faq.q: Why does one measure show different values in different visuals?

faq.a: Relationships carry filters between tables, and bi-directional filtering can make filter context ambiguous, according to "Build a Power BI Star Schema for Faster Reports". CALCULATE is introduced in the episodes as a key function for working with filter context.
faq.q: How do relationships and CALCULATE relate to filter context?

filter-context.long:
Filter context is a core concept in DAX (Data Analysis Expressions). It describes the set of filters that are active at the moment a measure is evaluated. These filters come from several places in a report: slicers, the visual that displays the measure, the page, and the rows or columns of the visual itself. Together they decide which part of the data a calculation is allowed to see, and therefore which number a measure returns.

The main practical consequence is that a single measure can return different results in different places without being rewritten. The episode "Data Analysis Expressions (DAX) - Simply Explained" describes filter context as the mechanism that determines which data is included in every calculation, and explains how one DAX measure can automatically show the correct result across different regions, products, dates and report visuals. The measure does not change; the filters around it do. This is also why measures differ from calculated columns. As the same episode puts it, calculated columns are created during data refresh and remain static, while measures recalculate dynamically whenever users apply filters, select slicers or interact with a report.

Understanding filter context is often presented as the dividing line between writing DAX like Excel formulas and writing it as DAX is meant to be written. In "Power BI DAX and Semantic Models with Bernat Agulló Roselló [MVP]", the discussion of common misconceptions centers on the mistake of treating DAX like Excel formulas. The episode lists filter context together with semantic models, relationships, and the difference between measures and calculated columns as foundational topics. Filter context depends on the model it runs against: relationships between tables determine how a filter applied to one table propagates to another, so the shape of the semantic model directly affects what a measure returns.

Filter context is closely tied to the CALCULATE function, which the episode "Data Analysis Expressions (DAX) - Simply Explained" introduces alongside SUMX, row context, variables, date tables, running totals, year-over-year comparisons and time intelligence. Filter context is distinct from row context, which is the concept used when a calculation iterates row by row, as with SUMX. The episode "From Raw Data to Real Business Impact: Mastering Power BI and Microsoft Fabric with Thummalacherla Krishnakanth" lists understanding filter context among practical techniques for debugging DAX calculations, improving measures with variables, using Performance Analyzer and working with advanced functions such as CALCULATE, so that reports stay fast as datasets grow.

Model design influences filter context as well. The episode "Build a Power BI Star Schema for Faster Reports" warns that enabling many-to-many or bi-directional cross-filtering can turn a clean star model into a complex network, harming performance and producing ambiguous filter context. It also notes that inactive relationships can be useful for time intelligence: keeping multiple date relationships inactive and activating them inside measures with USERELATIONSHIP preserves a star design while supporting cases such as invoice date versus ship date.

Filter context also appears in the episode "DAX UDF VAL vs EXPR: Prevent Timeouts and Wrong Totals", which covers user-defined functions. There, EXPR parameters let a function receive a measure or calculation that depends on the current row or filter context, so that a result such as a margin is calculated dynamically based on the current filters. The episode advises wrapping EXPR parameters inside CALCULATE when the filter expression should be evaluated in the context supplied by the caller.

In practice, filter context matters whenever a measure returns an unexpected total, a value that does not respond to a slicer, or a result that differs between visuals. Diagnosing such cases usually involves asking which filters reach the measure, which relationships carry them, and whether a function such as CALCULATE changes them.

financial-close.desc: Financial close is the recurring period-end process in which a finance team reconciles accounts, posts adjustments, validates results and reports the financial statements.

faq.a: It is the recurring period-end process in which a finance team reconciles accounts, posts adjustments, validates results and reports the financial statements for the month or year.
faq.q: What does the financial close involve?

faq.a: The Financial period close workspace tracks closing work across companies, task areas and people. Tasks are defined in a template with due dates relative to the period end, and a closing schedule generates them for a specific period and set of companies.
faq.q: How does Dynamics 365 Finance support the financial close?

faq.a: The episode "ERP Modernization with Alicia King [MVP]" says that ignoring financial close windows, payment cycles or audit periods during implementation can delay approvals and create reconciliation backlogs.
faq.q: Why does financial close matter during ERP modernization?

financial-close.long:
Financial close is the recurring period-end process in which a finance team reconciles accounts, posts adjustments, validates results and reports the financial statements for the month or year. It marks the point at which the books for a period are finalized so that the resulting figures can be relied on for management reporting, external reporting and audit. Because it repeats on a fixed rhythm, it is usually treated as a managed process with defined tasks, owners and deadlines rather than as a one-off activity.

In practice the close consists of several kinds of work: reconciling accounts, posting adjustments, validating results and producing the financial statements. These activities are typically spread across responsibility areas inside a finance organization, and they depend on one another. A task such as a ledger adjustment cannot sensibly be completed before the reconciliations that feed it, which is why sequencing and dependency tracking matter as much as the individual tasks themselves.

In Dynamics 365 Finance, the Financial period close workspace supports this work. According to Microsoft Learn, it is the place to track period-end closing work across companies, task areas and people. Closing tasks are defined once in a template, each with a due date expressed relative to the period end. A closing schedule then ties that template to a concrete period and a set of companies, and the system generates the tasks from the schedule. Where a task spans several companies, a separate task is created for each one. Each schedule allows only one template, and setup is done under General ledger, Period close.

Task areas group the work by responsibility, for example accounts payable, accounts receivable or general ledger. An optional calendar can limit planning to open working days. Responsible users complete their tasks and can attach notes, files or links. A task that still depends on unfinished tasks cannot be finished, which enforces the order of work. Summary tiles and markers show overdue, blocked and remaining tasks, giving the team a running view of how far the close has progressed. When a schedule is set to closed, it leaves the workspace, but its history remains in the list of all period close tasks, which can be exported to Excel.

Financial close also matters when an organization changes its finance systems. The M365.FM episode "ERP Modernization with Alicia King [MVP]" notes that many organizations run into problems not because of the ERP platform itself, but because of decisions made during implementation. The episode says that rushing deployment or skipping planning around finance operations can disrupt critical processes, and it gives the example of ignoring financial close windows, payment cycles or audit periods. According to the episode, this can delay approvals and create reconciliation backlogs, which in turn can erode executive support and lead to operational inefficiency.

The same episode names poorly sequenced deployment as something that can delay financial close processes, and it states that disruptions can affect approval workflows and create backlogs. It also identifies weak process design and poor data migration as major contributors to these problems. For teams planning an ERP rollout or change, the practical consequence is that the close calendar is a constraint to plan around: go-live timing, data migration and process design are weighed against the periods in which the close must run without interruption.

Taken together, financial close is both a finance process and a planning consideration for system projects. Defining the tasks once in a template, generating them per period and company, tracking dependencies and status, and keeping a history of completed schedules are the elements the Dynamics 365 Finance documentation describes. Protecting close windows during implementation work is the point the episode emphasizes.

financial-consolidation.desc: Financial consolidation is the accounting process of combining the results of multiple legal entities into one consolidated view, including the elimination of intercompany transactions.

faq.a: Financial consolidation is the accounting process of combining the financial results of multiple legal entities into one consolidated view. It includes eliminating intercompany transactions.
faq.q: What is financial consolidation?

faq.a: Transactions between entities in the same group would otherwise be counted twice in the combined results. Eliminating them leaves a consolidated view that reflects only external activity.
faq.q: Why are intercompany transactions eliminated?

financial-consolidation.long:
Financial consolidation is the accounting process of combining the financial results of multiple legal entities into a single consolidated view. It is used when a group of companies needs to report its overall financial position and performance as if it were one organization, rather than as a set of separate entities.

A central part of the process is the elimination of intercompany transactions. When one legal entity within a group transacts with another, those amounts would otherwise be counted twice in the combined figures. Removing them ensures the consolidated result reflects only activity with parties outside the group.

The term describes an accounting concept rather than a specific product, so it applies regardless of which systems or tools an organization uses to carry it out. No related topics, official documentation or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, so this page limits itself to the definition and the two core ideas above: combining entity results and eliminating intercompany activity.

financial-dimensions.desc: Financial dimensions in Dynamics 365 Finance are labels such as department, cost center, location or project that add detail to ledger entries beyond the main account.

faq.a: They are additional labels, such as department, cost center, location or project, attached to ledger entries to categorize transactions beyond the main account. Their values become segments within a main account, enabling reporting by dimension.
faq.q: What are financial dimensions in Dynamics 365 Finance?

faq.a: Custom dimensions have manually maintained values that always apply across legal entities. Entity-backed dimensions take their values from a system entity such as projects, customers or stores, can be shared or company-specific, and are edited in the source entity.
faq.q: What is the difference between custom and entity-backed dimensions?

faq.a: Not necessarily. Microsoft Learn notes that some reports do not include dimensions, and that sales tax works with legal entities rather than dimensions, so the planned reporting needs should be checked when designing them.
faq.q: Do financial dimensions appear in every report?

financial-dimensions.long:
Financial dimensions are additional labels in Dynamics 365 Finance that are attached to ledger entries to describe a transaction in more detail than the main account alone can. Typical examples are department, cost center, location or project. According to Microsoft Learn, financial dimensions categorize financial transactions further, and their values become segments within a main account. This is what makes it possible to report by dimension, for example in a profit and loss statement or a trial balance.

The documentation distinguishes between two kinds of dimensions. Custom dimensions have values that are maintained manually and always apply across legal entities. Entity-backed dimensions take their values from a system entity such as projects, customers or stores. These can be shared or specific to a company, and they must be edited in the source entity rather than on the dimension values page. Choosing between the two types is a common design decision: values that exist anyway in another area of the system are typically better drawn from that source, while values that only exist for reporting purposes can be maintained as custom values.

Financial dimensions are not applied in isolation. Microsoft Learn describes several controls around them. Legal entity overrides make it possible to suspend a dimension value or a main account for particular legal entities, to assign responsible people and to set validity periods. Dimension data validation checks whether an account combination or a default dimension combination is structurally valid. Financial tags are named as an alternative to dimensions for cases where a lighter labeling approach is wanted.

The same documentation lists limits that matter when planning a dimension structure. Custom dimension values have a maximum length. Dimensions are not meant to represent the operational needs of legal entities. Intercompany functions cover postings only, sales tax works with legal entities rather than dimensions, and some reports do not include dimensions. The page lists no licensing requirements. These points are relevant when deciding how many dimensions to define and what each should represent.

In the M365.FM episodes, financial dimensions appear as one building block of the finance data model. The episode "Dynamics 365 General Ledger - Simply Explained" presents them alongside the chart of accounts, subledgers, posting profiles, vouchers, journals, allocations, tax, period close and consolidation, as part of how financial transactions come together in one structured and traceable accounting record. The episode "Dynamics 365 Financial Reporting - Simply Explained" describes how the general ledger, main accounts, financial dimensions, reporting categories and predefined report structures are used to create consistent income statements, balance sheets, cash flow reports, trial balances and budget-versus-actual reports, instead of rebuilding financial statements in multiple spreadsheets every month.

In practice, this means that the dimension design influences what finance teams, managers, auditors and executives can later see in their reports. Detail that is not captured as a dimension on the ledger entry cannot easily be reported by that dimension afterwards, which is why the choice of dimensions, their value sources and their scope across legal entities is usually settled before reporting structures are built on top of them.

financial-services.desc: Financial services covers banks, insurers and asset managers; on M365.FM it appears in Microsoft contexts of compliance, data security, governance and AI agents.

faq.a: It refers to the industry of banks, insurers, asset managers and other providers of financial products, which is subject to strict regulation. The episodes use it as a context for security, compliance, governance and AI use with Microsoft technologies.
faq.q: What does financial services mean on M365.FM?

faq.a: The episodes mention Microsoft Purview with Communication Compliance, Microsoft Copilot Studio agents for risk and compliance automation, row-level security in Microsoft Fabric, Power Platform control planes and Microsoft Copilot grounding.
faq.q: Which Microsoft topics are linked to financial services in the episodes?

faq.a: The episode "Power Platform Control Planes for Scalable Governance" describes a financial services company whose control plane handled loan restructuring decisions. It kept loan terms consistent, monitored exposure levels, escalated conflicting signals and logged every decision.
faq.q: What example of governance in financial services is given?

financial-services.long:
Financial services is the industry of banks, insurers, asset managers and other providers of financial products and services. It is subject to strict regulation, which shapes how these organizations handle data, document decisions and manage risk. The term is also known as Finanzbranche or Finanzwesen in German, and as banking and insurance in English. On M365.FM it is treated as an industry entity: a vertical in which Microsoft technologies are applied under demanding security and compliance requirements.

The episodes on M365.FM return to the same theme: regulated data and the need to prove control over it. In "Automate Compliance Workflows with Microsoft Power Automate", financial services is described as an area where Microsoft technologies enhance security and compliance. The episode explains that organizations rely on various Microsoft solutions to protect sensitive data and manage risks effectively, and it lists Microsoft solutions together with their roles in security and compliance. One of those named is Microsoft Purview, including its Communication Compliance capability.

A second recurring topic is automation of risk and compliance work through AI agents. The episode "Scaling Copilot Studio with Isha Kapoor [MVP]" describes industry use cases for Microsoft Copilot Studio in financial services, healthcare and the public sector. For financial services, it states that organizations face strict rules and fast-changing risks, and that Copilot Studio agents can help automate key tasks and support compliance. According to the episode, these agents can analyze large amounts of data, flag unusual activity and support a compliance team, so that threats can be answered faster and manual effort reduced.

Data access control is a further area. The episode "DP-600 Training 4/4: Incremental Refresh, RLS, and OLS" recalls a conversation with a financial services client who was concerned about who could access sensitive sales data. The episode uses this to illustrate that many organizations overlook robust measures such as row-level security (RLS) and tend to act only after a breach. It then explores how RLS in Microsoft Fabric can be used to safeguard sensitive data, alongside incremental refresh and object-level security.

Governance of automated decisions is covered in "Power Platform Control Planes for Scalable Governance". That episode presents a case study of a financial services company that engineered a control plane to handle loan restructuring decisions. According to the episode, the organization used the control plane to keep loan terms consistent, monitor exposure levels, escalate conflicting signals and log every decision. The episode states that these functions helped improve service speed while avoiding systemic risks.

The episode "Grounding Microsoft Copilot for Trusted Enterprise AI" places financial services among several industries with measurable effects from Copilot. It mentions that financial services automate month-end reporting and thereby reduce manual errors, next to examples from government, healthcare and software engineering. The same episode recommends preparing for change with a tailored change management strategy, including early adopter programs and guided sessions.

Taken together, the episodes show typical decisions in this industry: which Microsoft solutions to use for data protection and communication compliance, how to restrict data access at row or object level, how to log and escalate automated decisions, and how to introduce AI assistants and agents without weakening regulatory obligations. The material on M365.FM treats strict regulation not as a side note but as the starting point for design choices in Microsoft 365, Power Platform, Fabric and Copilot environments.

findability.desc: Findability describes how easily users can locate the content they need, shaped by structure, metadata, search behavior and navigation in Microsoft 365.

faq.a: Findability is the ease with which users can locate the content they need. It is influenced by structure, metadata, search behavior and navigation.
faq.q: What is findability?

faq.a: The episode "SharePoint Network Drive vs OneDrive Sync" says managed metadata and metadata columns often outperform deep folder hierarchies for findability and reuse. It adds that consistent metadata and content types improve search results more than tweaking search settings.
faq.q: How can metadata improve findability in SharePoint?

faq.a: No. The episode "Govern SPFx Adaptive Card Extensions in Teams and Viva" lists poor team naming as a findability challenge, since it makes it hard for users to locate the right team.
faq.q: Does findability only apply to documents?

findability.long:
Findability is the ease with which users can locate the content they need. It is influenced by how content is structured, which metadata is attached to it, how people search, and how navigation is set up. In the Microsoft 365 context it comes up mainly around SharePoint sites, knowledge bases, document libraries and Teams, where large volumes of documents and workspaces make it hard to reach the right item quickly.

The concept is used as a design goal rather than a single feature. When teams plan a site, a library or a knowledge base, findability is a way to judge whether the planned structure will actually help people get to answers. It also acts as a reason to invest in information architecture, taxonomy and naming rules. Because it depends on several factors at once, it is usually discussed together with metadata strategy, content types, navigation and governance.

The M365.FM episode "Fix SharePoint Knowledge Management" links findability to the design of a knowledge base. It describes using templates to present collections of knowledge in flexible ways, make it easy for content owners to share resources, and improve findability with scoped search and browse features. The episode adds that a template should match the goals of the knowledge base, and that consistent layouts help users scan and understand articles faster. It also recommends categorizing knowledge pages, for example by topic, department or project, so that users can find what they need more easily. Features such as an A-to-Z listing and a search facility are named as part of clear, easy navigation.

The episode "SharePoint Network Drive vs OneDrive Sync" connects findability to information architecture. It states that managed metadata can replace complex folder structures, and that taxonomy-driven navigation and metadata columns often outperform deep folder hierarchies for findability and reuse. It also says that search relevance depends more on information architecture than on search settings: consistent metadata and content types improve search results more effectively than tweaking the search engine. A well-designed architecture is described as reducing duplicate documents and unused libraries by guiding users to the right location.
