Content types are presented as a way to standardize retention, policies and templates across sites, and hub sites are noted as changing navigation strategy.

Metadata planning is the focus of "Fixing the SharePoint Metadata Gap for AI and Governance". The episode lists search needs as one input to a metadata strategy, alongside the business reality of which document types are managed and which fields help locate them, and controlled terms such as departments and policy types. It suggests using a planning worksheet to capture business areas and document categories, aligning the strategy with IT and business goals, and implementing lifecycle management with regular review. In this framing, defining what users need to search for comes before deciding which columns and terms to create.

"Microsoft 365 Maturity Model Based on 500 Tenant Audits" places findability among the outcomes of content management practices. The model it outlines covers taxonomy, content types, metadata policies, versioning, retention and the document management lifecycle, and the episode says these measures help organizations manage content consistently, improve findability and ensure compliance with policies.

Findability also applies to collaboration spaces, not only documents. In "Govern SPFx Adaptive Card Extensions in Teams and Viva", findability challenges are listed as one consequence of ineffective team naming, together with duplication, inconsistent naming, unmanageable sprawl, access issues and uncontrolled content growth. The episode notes that undefined naming conventions create uncertainty about a team's purpose and make it hard for users to locate the right team, which is why policies and regular reviews are recommended.

Taken together, the episodes treat findability as the result of deliberate choices: a consistent structure, meaningful metadata and content types, clear categorization and navigation, and governance that keeps naming and content growth under control.

fine-tuning.desc: Fine-tuning further trains a pre-trained model on additional data, often compared with retrieval-augmented generation for keeping enterprise AI answers current.

faq.a: Fine-tuning further trains a pre-trained model on additional data so that its behavior and accuracy better fit a specific task or organization. The M365.FM episodes describe it as starting with a pre-trained model and making small adjustments to improve performance.
faq.q: What is fine-tuning in AI?

faq.a: The two are often compared as ways to keep AI answers aligned with company data. The episodes also describe combining them, for example connecting a fine-tuned model to live databases or pairing private deployments with retrieval architectures.
faq.q: How does fine-tuning relate to retrieval-augmented generation?

faq.a: According to the episode on Private LoRA, LoRA modifies only a small subset of model parameters, so specialized capabilities can be created without retraining an entire large language model. The episode contrasts this with traditional fine-tuning, which it describes as often expensive and harder to govern.
faq.q: What is the difference between fine-tuning and LoRA?

fine-tuning.long:
Fine-tuning is the practice of taking a pre-trained model and training it further on additional data so that its behavior fits a particular task or organization. Instead of building a model from scratch, the starting point is an existing foundation model, and the adjustments are made on top of it. In enterprise AI discussions, fine-tuning is frequently compared with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as a way to keep AI answers aligned with company data.

The M365.FM episode "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform" describes fine-tuning as part of model adaptation. The sequence it outlines is to learn what a model can and cannot do, pick a model that fits the task, fine-tune it with your own data, adjust settings for better results, and update the model as needs change. It summarizes fine-tuning as starting with a pre-trained model and making small adjustments to improve performance. The episode also advises careful testing and a review of outputs before a model moves into production, so that results meet the required standards.

The episode "Small Language Models for Faster, Cheaper Enterprise AI" treats fine-tuning and customization as a way to fit Small Language Models to business needs. According to the episode, fine-tuning adjusts a model's behavior and can improve accuracy for specific tasks. The described workflow begins with preparing and cleaning data and selecting a suitable base model. It then connects the model to live databases so answers stay up to date, and applies security protocols such as masking. This shows how fine-tuning and live data access can be combined in one deployment plan rather than treated as mutually exclusive.

Cost, governance, and security are recurring concerns. The episode "Private LoRA for Secure AI on Proprietary Enterprise Data" states that traditional fine-tuning approaches are often expensive, difficult to govern, and associated with significant security and compliance concerns, especially when intellectual property, customer records, or internal knowledge would otherwise be sent to public AI services. The episode presents Private LoRA as an alternative that lets organizations adapt and customize foundation models while keeping data within controlled environments. LoRA works by modifying only a small subset of model parameters, which allows specialized AI capabilities without retraining an entire large language model. The episode also discusses combining private deployments with retrieval architectures.

Platform choice is another decision point. The episode "Copilot Studio vs Azure AI Foundry: Which Should You Use?" says that Azure AI Foundry commonly supports bringing your own models and fine-tuning or customization at scale. Copilot Studio, by contrast, encourages managed models optimized for conversational tasks. The episode describes Foundry as the more flexible option for bespoke models, while noting that Copilot Studio can reduce development cost and time for single-purpose copilots and that Foundry can be more cost-effective when scaling many models and high-throughput workloads.

The term also appears in a different sense in the episode "Configure Microsoft 365 DLP Policies in Purview", where fine-tuning refers to adjusting data loss prevention policy thresholds, for example by starting in Test or Monitoring mode and using policy tips. That usage concerns tuning policy settings, not training an AI model, so the two meanings should be kept apart when searching for the term.

In practice, the decision around fine-tuning usually weighs several factors covered in the episodes: the cost of training, the ability to govern and secure the data used, how current the model's answers need to be, and whether a lighter technique such as LoRA or a retrieval-based approach meets the requirement. The episodes present these as trade-offs to evaluate for each workload, not as a single recommended path.

finite-capacity-scheduling.desc: Finite capacity scheduling plans production operations onto real resource calendars, treating each machine, person or station as limited so order conflicts become visible.

faq.a: It is a planning approach that schedules production operations onto real resource calendars and treats each machine, person or station as limited, so conflicts between orders become visible instead of being left to the shop floor.
faq.q: What is finite capacity scheduling?

faq.a: No. The episode "Constraint-Based Scheduling: The Architecture That Makes Production Plans Real" states that it does not add another machine; it shows where demand exceeds what resources can deliver so that trade-offs can be decided.
faq.q: Does finite capacity scheduling create more capacity?

faq.a: The episode "APS Software vs. ERP: What's the Difference?" names finite capacity scheduling as a major difference between APS and traditional production planning, with optimization for goals such as on-time delivery or throughput built on top of a feasible schedule.
faq.q: How does it relate to APS and ERP?

finite-capacity-scheduling.long:
Finite capacity scheduling is a production planning approach that places operations onto real resource calendars and treats every machine, person or station as limited. Instead of assuming that a work center can absorb whatever demand is assigned to it, the method forces conflicts between orders into the open before production has to discover them on the shop floor. It is used to close the gap between planning demand and scheduling reality.

The starting point, as described in the M365.FM episode "How Finite Capacity Scheduling Actually Works in Manufacturing", is a familiar situation: an ERP system says a production order should finish next Thursday, the routing looks correct and material is planned. On the shop floor, however, the machine may already be overloaded, the required operator may be booked elsewhere, a fixture may be in use, or material that exists in ERP may not yet have been inspected and released. Finite capacity scheduling addresses exactly this kind of mismatch between what the plan promises and what the factory can execute.

How it works is tied to the physical limits of the factory. According to the episode "Constraint-Based Scheduling: The Architecture That Makes Production Plans Real", two urgent orders can both appear to require the same machine at the same time, and on paper both remain urgent. On the factory floor, one spindle can still run only one operation at a time. Finite capacity scheduling accounts for resource calendars, maintenance, setup time, fixtures, tooling and other limitations, so the conflict becomes visible rather than hidden inside an overloaded time period.

The same episode makes an important distinction: finite capacity scheduling does not create capacity. It does not add another machine or extra hours. What it does is show where demand exceeds what the resources can deliver, so that people can decide how to respond. In the episode "APS Software vs. ERP: What's the Difference?", the consequences are described as trade-offs: one resource may be contended, another order may be delayed, overtime may be required, the production sequence may change, or the customer promise may simply be impossible under the current constraints. Advanced planning and scheduling (APS) makes those trade-offs visible before production runs into them.

That episode also separates feasibility from desirability. Creating a feasible schedule is only the first step, because a schedule can respect every physical constraint and still be commercially undesirable. Manufacturers may therefore want to optimize for different objectives, such as on-time delivery, higher throughput or reduced setup effort, on top of the finite capacity logic. Finite capacity scheduling provides the realistic baseline; optimization then chooses among the feasible options according to business priorities.

Typical decisions around the concept include whether a delivery date can really be promised, which order should be sequenced first when two compete for the same resource, and whether overtime or a delay is the better response to an overload. These questions are hard to answer in a planning model that treats capacity as unlimited, which is why the episodes position finite capacity scheduling as a core feature that separates scheduling-oriented tools from traditional production planning in ERP.

In summary, finite capacity scheduling turns a demand-based plan into one that respects resource calendars, maintenance, setups, fixtures and tooling. It does not remove constraints, but it exposes them early, so that conflicts are resolved in planning instead of on the shop floor.

finops-foundation.desc: The FinOps Foundation is a nonprofit project of the Linux Foundation that maintains the FinOps Framework and publishes the annual State of FinOps survey.

faq.a: The FinOps Foundation is a nonprofit project of the Linux Foundation. It maintains the FinOps Framework, including its principles and phases.
faq.q: What is the FinOps Foundation?

faq.a: It publishes the annual State of FinOps survey in addition to maintaining the FinOps Framework.
faq.q: What does the FinOps Foundation publish?

finops-foundation.long:
The FinOps Foundation is a nonprofit project of the Linux Foundation. It maintains the FinOps Framework, which sets out the principles and phases associated with the FinOps practice.

Beyond the framework, the organization publishes the annual State of FinOps survey. Teams working on cloud financial management may consult the framework and the survey as reference material when describing how FinOps is structured and how the practice is understood across the industry.

No relations to specific Microsoft products or services, and no M365.FM episodes, are recorded for this entity at present. The page will be extended if connections to topics in the Microsoft ecosystem are added.

flex-consumption-plan.desc: The Azure Functions Flex Consumption plan is a serverless hosting plan for Azure Functions with pay-for-what-you-use billing and scale-out to up to one thousand instances.
flex-consumption-plan.long:
The Azure Functions Flex Consumption plan is a serverless hosting plan within Azure Functions. Microsoft recommends it for new serverless apps. It is one of the hosting options available for running Azure Functions code without managing the underlying servers.

The plan builds on the pay-for-what-you-use billing model associated with serverless hosting, so charges follow actual usage rather than a fixed provisioned capacity. It can scale out to as many as one thousand instances, which makes it relevant for workloads where demand varies and the number of running instances needs to grow or shrink with load.

As part of Azure Functions, the Flex Consumption plan applies to apps built with that service, such as event-driven or HTTP-triggered functions. People evaluating where to host a new serverless app on Azure typically compare it with other Azure Functions hosting plans, and the official Microsoft Learn documentation covers its details and configuration.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

fluent-ui.desc: Fluent UI is Microsoft's UI framework and component library for building interfaces that look and behave like Microsoft 365 and SharePoint.

faq.a: Fluent UI is Microsoft's UI framework and component library for building user interfaces that look and behave like Microsoft 365 and SharePoint. The episodes describe its use in Teams apps, SPFx solutions, Power Apps generative pages and Microsoft Graph Toolkit components.
faq.q: What is Fluent UI used for?

faq.a: According to the episode with Siddharth Vaghasia, it is one part of a stack that also includes TypeScript, React, PnPjs and PnP React Controls. In that stack, Fluent UI helps custom solutions retain the familiar Microsoft user experience.
faq.q: How does Fluent UI fit into an SPFx project?

faq.a: The Graph Toolkit episode says its components have a Fluent UI look and accessibility, including keyboard use, screen readers and right-to-left support.
faq.q: Does Fluent UI support accessibility?

fluent-ui.long:
Fluent UI is Microsoft's user interface framework and component library. It is used to build interfaces that look and behave like Microsoft 365 and SharePoint, so that custom solutions feel familiar to people who already work in those products. Rather than designing buttons, pickers, layouts and other controls from scratch, developers draw on a shared set of components that follow the Microsoft look and interaction patterns.

The M365.FM episodes mention Fluent UI in several development contexts. In the episode "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions", Fluent UI appears alongside Adaptive Cards as a tool for creating engaging and interactive experiences in a Microsoft Teams app. The episode says these technologies help build interfaces that look modern and work well across devices, and that using them makes an app feel like a natural part of Teams. The same episode stresses responsive design more broadly: using flexible grids and layouts, testing on multiple devices and screen sizes, and making touch targets large enough for mobile users.

In SharePoint Framework (SPFx) development, Fluent UI is one part of a larger technology stack. The episode "Stop Reinventing SPFx- Building Better SharePoint Solutions with PnP React Controls with Siddharth Vaghasia [MVP]" describes a modern SPFx project as bringing together several technologies rather than relying on one framework. Siddharth breaks down the roles of TypeScript, React, Fluent UI, PnPjs and PnP React Controls. According to the episode, TypeScript provides stronger typing and compile-time checks, while Fluent UI helps custom solutions retain the familiar Microsoft user experience. PnPjs simplifies interaction with SharePoint, Microsoft Graph and other Microsoft 365 services by replacing repetitive REST request code with reusable abstractions. The episode also argues for not rebuilding controls that already exist.

Fluent UI also shows up in low-code and generated experiences. The episode "Create Power Apps Faster with Generative Pages" lists Fluent UI controls with default alignment to an app's theme among the features of generative pages, together with solution-aware components that move across environments and GPT-5 as the engine for code generation. The episode presents these features as a way to go from concept to a working experience in a day, where earlier work required weeks of coordination between design and development teams.

In the episode "Build Consistent M365 Apps with Microsoft Graph Toolkit", Fluent UI is named as the basis for the look and accessibility of the Graph Toolkit components. The episode says the toolkit gives developers Microsoft-branded React components that work with Microsoft Graph, with built-in authentication and consent, handling of caching, throttling and error states, and a Fluent UI look with accessibility support for keyboard use, screen readers and right-to-left languages. Components such as Login and PeoplePicker are given as examples of what can be used from day one.

Taken together, the episodes treat Fluent UI as a consistency layer. It supports a uniform visual and interaction experience across Teams apps, SPFx web parts, Power Apps generative pages and Graph Toolkit components. Typical decisions around it include whether to use ready-made Fluent UI-based components instead of custom controls, how to combine it with React and TypeScript in SPFx projects, and how to check that an interface stays usable on different devices and for people who rely on assistive technology.

flux-cd.desc: Flux is an open-source GitOps operator and CNCF graduated project that keeps Kubernetes clusters in sync with Git, built into AKS and Azure Arc.

faq.a: Flux is an open-source GitOps operator and CNCF graduated project that runs as Kubernetes controllers and continuously reconciles a cluster with the state defined in Git. It is the built-in GitOps option on AKS and Azure Arc.
faq.q: What is Flux?

faq.a: Flux works pull-based: it runs on the cluster and pulls the declared state from sources such as Git repositories, Helm repositories, buckets or Azure Blob Storage. Neither the source repository nor other clusters need access to the cluster.
faq.q: How does Flux fetch configuration from Git?

faq.a: According to the Microsoft Learn documentation, there is no extra Flux charge on AKS. Other Arc-connected distributions are billed per vCPU after a free allowance.
faq.q: Does Flux cost extra on AKS?

flux-cd.long:
Flux is an open-source GitOps operator and a CNCF graduated project. It runs as a set of Kubernetes controllers inside a cluster and continuously reconciles the cluster with the state that is declared in Git. It is the built-in GitOps option on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) and on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes, where Microsoft documents it as Flux v2.

The core idea behind Flux is that the desired state of a cluster is written down in files rather than applied by hand. According to the Microsoft Learn documentation, these files can be YAML manifests, Helm charts and Kustomize files stored in Git repositories. Controllers in the cluster compare this declared state with what is actually running and bring the cluster back into line when the two differ. Supported sources include Git repositories, Helm repositories, buckets and Azure Blob Storage.

Flux is built from several controllers. The default set consists of the Source, Kustomize, Helm and Notification controllers, and optional image automation and image reflector controllers can be added. Flux works purely pull-based: it runs on the cluster and fetches its configuration, so neither the source repository nor other clusters need access to the cluster. On AKS and Azure Arc, Azure adds a configuration agent and a configuration controller that transfer configurations from Azure into the cluster and report status back to Azure.

Typical situations for Flux involve deploying applications to Kubernetes, managing AKS clusters, automating infrastructure changes and rolling back failed deployments by reverting a change in Git. Because every change goes through a Git repository, change management becomes auditable, and pull requests serve as the review step. The documentation also describes rolling Flux out at scale through Azure Policy, and it supports multi-tenancy and dependency control between deployments.

There are limits to be aware of when using Flux through Azure. Azure supports only part of the Flux parameters. Changes apply only when the agent can reach Azure. Cross-namespace references are blocked while multi-tenancy is enforced. On billing, the documentation states that there is no extra Flux charge on AKS, while other Arc-connected distributions are billed per vCPU after a free allowance.

The M365.FM episode "GitOps - Simply Explained" covers GitOps concepts such as Git repositories, pull requests, continuous reconciliation, Infrastructure as Code, Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts, and names Flux and Argo CD as popular GitOps tools. It also looks at scenarios such as deploying to Kubernetes, managing AKS, rolling back failed deployments and how GitOps fits with Azure DevOps, GitHub, Bicep, Terraform and CI/CD pipelines. The episode "Azure Arc - Simply Explained" explains that Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes uses GitOps for configuration management and employs Flux to deploy application configurations from Git repositories. The desired state is defined in a Git repository, so clusters automatically converge to that state, including clusters running outside Azure.

In practice, the decision around Flux is often about where the source of truth lives and how clusters are managed. Teams that already keep Kubernetes configuration in Git can use Flux to apply it consistently across AKS and Azure Arc-enabled clusters, while Azure Policy can be used to apply Flux configurations broadly. Teams should also check that the Flux parameters they rely on are among those Azure supports.

focus-time.desc: Focus time is protected calendar time for uninterrupted work; Microsoft Viva Insights lets users book focus blocks during which Teams notifications can be silenced.

faq.a: Focus time is protected calendar time for uninterrupted work. Microsoft Viva Insights lets users book focus blocks during which Teams notifications can be silenced.
faq.q: What is focus time in Microsoft 365?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, Microsoft Viva Insights supports booking focus blocks, Copilot can manage a calendar and protect focus time, and Microsoft Scout can block focus time when deliverables are due.
faq.q: Which tools can protect focus time on the calendar?

faq.a: The episode on task management apps presents a table linking 4.4 hours of focus time to higher output and lower burnout, and 2.7 hours to lower output and higher burnout. The notification overload episode describes meeting overload as a cause of more context switching and less focus time.
faq.q: Why does focus time matter according to the episodes?

focus-time.long:
Focus time is protected calendar time set aside for uninterrupted work. Instead of leaving the whole day open to meeting invitations, messages and alerts, a person reserves blocks in the calendar for tasks that need sustained attention. In the Microsoft 365 ecosystem, Microsoft Viva Insights is the tool most closely tied to the idea: it lets users book focus blocks, and during those blocks Teams notifications can be silenced.

The concept addresses a common problem in the workday: constant interruption. The M365.FM episode "Reduce Microsoft 365 Notification Overload and Protect Focus" describes how email pop-ups can distract from the current task, especially when there is a pull to answer right away. It also names meeting overload from email invites as a driver of more context switching and less focus time. Calendar reminders keep a person on schedule but add to the noise as well, and a packed calendar means alerts all day. The episode cites analytics showing that some departments spend 80% of their time in meetings or calls, and describes one company that audited its calendars, found redundant weekly check-ins and reclaimed dozens of hours.

Microsoft Viva Insights is where focus time is most visible to individual users. The episode "Microsoft Viva Insights - Simply Explained" points out that the tool may look like something a manager uses to watch employees, but the first view it opens is the one meant just for the user. Under the heading "Your Own Insights" the episode lists focus time, quiet time and switching off as the personal topics. The same data appears in four views, for the individual, for the manager and for leaders across the company, with an analyst role where deeper questions get answered; the episode also covers what Viva Insights can and cannot see.

Focus time also connects to task management. The episode "Microsoft To Do vs Planner vs Lists vs Loop" argues that sticking to one task at a time helps avoid distractions and that calendar bookings can be automated so the day is managed proactively. It presents a table in which 4.4 hours of focus time goes with a higher output level and a lower burnout rate, while 2.7 hours goes with a lower output level and a higher burnout rate. The episode draws the conclusion that choosing the right Microsoft 365 task tool should support focus and productivity.

AI assistants are described in the same context. The episode "Copilot Cowork - Simply Explained" says Copilot can manage a calendar and protect focus time, so that a person stays productive through the day instead of spending hours on repetitive tasks. The episode "Microsoft Scout - Simply Explained" states that Scout can proactively schedule meetings, generate prep materials and block focus time on the calendar when deliverables are due, working through connections to other Microsoft 365 applications.

In practice, decisions around focus time come down to a few questions: how many blocks to book, which notifications to silence during them, and how to keep meeting invitations from consuming the calendar. A calendar audit, as in the example from the notification overload episode, is one way to find time to reclaim. Booking blocks manually, through Viva Insights, or through an assistant that places them automatically are the approaches the episodes mention.

forecast-category.desc: Forecast category is a Dynamics 365 Sales opportunity label (pipeline, best case, committed, omitted, won, lost) that sets the forecast column and signals seller confidence.

faq.a: The values are pipeline, best case, committed, omitted, won and lost. Pipeline is the default, and won and lost are set automatically when an opportunity is closed.
faq.q: What are the forecast category values in Dynamics 365 Sales?

faq.a: Omitted removes an opportunity from all forecast totals. It is used to keep a deal out of the forecast without closing it.
faq.q: What does the omitted forecast category do?

faq.a: No. The documentation says won and lost are set automatically on closing and should not be picked by hand, since doing so can make the opportunity vanish from the forecast or distort rolled-up values.
faq.q: Should won or lost be selected manually as a forecast category?

forecast-category.long:
A forecast category is a label on an opportunity in Dynamics 365 Sales that expresses how confident the seller is that the deal will close. It also decides which column of the forecast grid includes the opportunity's amount, so the forecast can reflect the real state of the pipeline. The available values are pipeline, best case, committed, omitted, won and lost.

Each value has a defined meaning. Pipeline is the default and marks early or stalled deals. Best case marks deals that are progressing, for example when proposals have been sent, but where no commitment exists yet. Committed marks deals where the customer has given a verbal or contractual commitment. Omitted removes an opportunity from all forecast totals. Won and lost are set automatically when an opportunity is closed. According to the documentation, these two values should not be picked by hand, because doing so can make the opportunity vanish from the forecast or distort rolled-up values.

In daily use, the field is changed on the opportunity form. Sellers adjust the category as the customer situation develops, for instance moving a deal from pipeline to best case once a proposal is out, and to committed once a commitment is given. Because managers in the hierarchy see totals that include these choices, the category affects how the forecast is rolled up across a team. The documentation notes that the feature must be enabled by an administrator, and the described steps apply to the standard Sales Hub and Sales Professional apps.

The label matters because forecasting depends on the quality of the underlying sales data. The episode "Dynamics 365 Forecasting - Simply Explained" says that even sophisticated forecasting technology cannot compensate for inaccurate sales data. It names an outdated close date, incorrect expected revenue and an unrealistic forecast category as examples of errors that can flow directly into the forecast. The episode recommends that sellers keep opportunity amounts, expected close dates, ownership and forecast categories current whenever the customer situation changes, and summarizes the point as: accurate forecasting starts with accurate opportunity management.

The same episode also stresses that human judgment still matters. Sales data cannot capture every detail of a customer relationship, so the category a seller chooses is a judgment about confidence rather than an automatic calculation. In practice, this means the forecast category is only as reliable as the discipline applied to updating it, and a forecast built from stale or optimistic categories will mislead the managers who rely on the rolled-up totals.

Typical decisions around the forecast category include when to promote a deal from pipeline to best case or committed, and when to use omitted to keep an opportunity out of the totals entirely. Choosing omitted is different from closing the deal: it removes the opportunity from forecast totals while it remains an open record. Closing the opportunity as won or lost is the route that sets those categories correctly, which avoids the distortions described for manual selection.

forecast-grid.desc: The forecast grid is the table view of a forecast in Dynamics 365 Sales, showing quota, forecast amounts and pipeline status that can be drilled into opportunities.

faq.a: It shows quota attainment, pipeline status and revenue at risk, aggregated by user or territory at each level of the hierarchy and for each period. In an organization-chart forecast, the default columns are users, quota, committed, best case, pipeline, omitted, won and lost.
faq.q: What does the forecast grid show in Dynamics 365 Sales?

faq.a: Users open it in Sales Hub under Performance and Forecasts, then choose a forecast and a period. From there they can drill into the underlying opportunities, adjust values, or run a manual recalculate to refresh the data.
faq.q: How do users open and work with the forecast grid?

faq.a: No. According to the documentation, the grid is not supported on mobile devices.
faq.q: Is the forecast grid available on mobile devices?

forecast-grid.long:
The forecast grid is the main forecasting view in Dynamics 365 Sales. It is the table view of a forecast and shows quota attainment, pipeline status and revenue at risk, aggregated by user or territory at each level of the hierarchy and for each period. Rows can represent sellers, teams, territories or products, depending on how forecasting is configured, and the figures can be drilled into the opportunities behind them.

The grid draws on opportunity data that the sales organization already maintains. In a forecast based on the organization chart, the default columns are users, quota, committed, best case, pipeline, omitted, won and lost. The middle columns are filled from the forecast category of each opportunity, so the quality of the grid depends on how consistently sellers categorize and update their opportunities. The episode "Dynamics 365 Forecasting - Simply Explained" describes the forecast grid as a shared sales scorecard: because everyone works from the same underlying opportunity information, forecasting becomes part of everyday sales management instead of a separate reporting process.

Sellers and managers open the grid in Sales Hub under Performance and Forecasts. After choosing a forecast and a period, they can view the aggregated numbers, drill into the underlying opportunities, or adjust values. A manual recalculate action refreshes the data. An administrator or forecast manager can enable a currency selector, which matters in organizations that work with more than one currency. What a user sees depends on the permissions set during configuration, so a seller, a team manager and a higher-level manager may see different parts of the same forecast.

The episode explains that the columns can show quota, forecast amounts and different levels of forecast confidence. This lets managers look beyond headline revenue numbers and inspect the opportunities behind a total, for example to understand how much of a figure is committed, how much is best case, and how much is still only pipeline. The documentation adds that the grid also shows won and lost amounts and omitted opportunities, which gives a view of both progress and revenue at risk.

There are a few practical points to consider when planning a rollout. The out-of-the-box forecast covers only the current month and is not stored. A configured forecast keeps several periods and refreshes on a schedule or on demand, which is the option to choose when period-over-period comparison or a stored history is needed. The grid is not supported on mobile devices, so reviews that depend on it are best done in the browser-based Sales Hub.

In day-to-day use, the forecast grid typically supports regular pipeline reviews. A manager selects a period, checks quota against committed and best-case amounts, and drills into individual opportunities where a number looks too high or too low. Sellers use the same view to see how their own opportunities contribute to their forecast. Because both groups work from the same opportunity records, discussions can focus on specific deals rather than on reconciling separate spreadsheets.

In summary, the forecast grid is the place where Dynamics 365 Sales turns opportunity data into a forecast that can be reviewed by seller, team, territory or product. Its usefulness rests on accurate forecast categories on opportunities, a configuration that fits the sales hierarchy, and permissions that give each role the right level of visibility.

forgetting-curve.desc: The forgetting curve is a psychological model from Hermann Ebbinghaus describing how newly learned information fades over time without reinforcement or practice.

faq.a: The forgetting curve is a psychological model, originating with Hermann Ebbinghaus, that describes how newly learned information is lost over time without reinforcement or practice.
faq.q: What is the forgetting curve?

faq.a: The model originated with Hermann Ebbinghaus.
faq.q: Who originated the forgetting curve?

faq.a: According to the model, information is lost over time when it is not reinforced or practiced, so reinforcement and practice are what counter the loss.
faq.q: How can the forgetting curve be counteracted?

forgetting-curve.long:
The forgetting curve is a psychological model that originated with Hermann Ebbinghaus. It describes how newly learned information is lost over time when it is not reinforced or practiced. The concept is commonly used to explain why knowledge acquired in a single session tends to decline unless it is revisited.

In practice, the idea is relevant wherever people need to learn and retain information, such as training programs, onboarding, and ongoing skills development. The model points to the role of reinforcement and repeated practice in slowing the loss of what has been learned.

On M365.FM, the forgetting curve is listed as a concept entity within the knowledge base about the Microsoft ecosystem. No related topics, product links, or specific episodes are currently associated with this entry, so the page serves as a short reference definition of the term.

forrester-research.desc: Forrester Research is a market research and advisory firm whose Total Economic Impact (TEI) studies model the costs, benefits and ROI of technology investments such as Microsoft Power Platform.

faq.a: Forrester Research is a market research and advisory firm. Its Total Economic Impact (TEI) studies model the costs, benefits and ROI of technology investments.
faq.q: What is Forrester Research?

faq.a: A TEI study models the costs, benefits and ROI of a technology investment. Forrester Research has produced such studies for technologies like Microsoft Power Platform.
faq.q: What is a Total Economic Impact (TEI) study?

faq.a: It is referenced in the episodes "How to Build a Microsoft Copilot Agent Fabric" (2026-05-31) and "Power BI Version Control with GitHub and Azure DevOps" (2025-11-03).
faq.q: Where does Forrester Research appear on M365.FM?

forrester-research.long:
Forrester Research is a market research and advisory firm. It is known in the Microsoft ecosystem for its Total Economic Impact (TEI) studies, which model the costs, benefits and return on investment (ROI) of technology investments, including Microsoft Power Platform.

TEI studies are used by organizations that want a structured, financially framed view of what a technology investment may cost and what benefits it may deliver. In discussions about Microsoft products, references to Forrester Research typically point to this kind of cost-benefit and ROI modeling rather than to hands-on implementation guidance.

On M365.FM, Forrester Research appears as a referenced organization in two episodes: "How to Build a Microsoft Copilot Agent Fabric" (2026-05-31) and "Power BI Version Control with GitHub and Azure DevOps" (2025-11-03). No further details about the firm are recorded in the available facts, so this page is limited to its role as a market research and advisory firm and its TEI studies.

foundry-agent-service.desc: Foundry Agent Service is a managed Microsoft Foundry service for hosting AI agents with threads, tool calling, knowledge, MCP servers and enterprise security.

faq.a: It is a managed service in Microsoft Foundry for hosting AI agents, with threads, tool calling, knowledge, MCP server support and enterprise security. It is developed by Microsoft.
faq.q: What is Foundry Agent Service?

faq.a: Azure AI Agent Service and Microsoft Foundry Agent Service are listed as alternative names for the same product. The episodes use these names interchangeably.
faq.q: Is Foundry Agent Service the same as Azure AI Agent Service?

faq.a: MCP servers are one way to give an agent access to tools and data, and Azure Logic Apps can provide workflow steps and connections to other systems. Both are related topics for building agents on the service.
faq.q: How does Foundry Agent Service relate to MCP and Azure Logic Apps?

foundry-agent-service.long:
Foundry Agent Service is a managed service in Microsoft Foundry for hosting AI agents. It is developed by Microsoft, is listed as a paid product, and is described as a Microsoft tool and a developer tool. It has also been referred to as Azure AI Agent Service and Microsoft Foundry Agent Service. The service provides threads for conversations, tool calling, knowledge, support for MCP servers and enterprise security, so that teams can run an AI agent without building the surrounding runtime themselves.

The service sits between the models in the Foundry catalog and the applications that need agents to take action. An AI agent combines a model, which acts as the swappable brain, with tools and knowledge that let it do work rather than only produce text. Conversations are organised through threads and runs, which keep the state of an interaction together. Tool calling lets an agent invoke external capabilities, and knowledge connections give it access to business context. Documentation for the service is published by Microsoft under the Foundry agents section of Microsoft Learn.

Two related technologies appear in connection with the service. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is one way to give an agent access to tools and data, and Foundry Agent Service supports MCP servers for this purpose. Azure Logic Apps is another related topic, since it can supply workflow steps and connections to other systems that an agent can use. Because Foundry Agent Service is part of Microsoft Foundry, it works alongside the model experimentation, orchestration and governance features of the wider platform.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Foundry Agent Service - Simply Explained" starts from the point that the Foundry catalog holds more than ten thousand AI models, and that this number only matters if a model can be turned into something that does work. The episode covers what an AI agent is, what Foundry Agent Service is, models as the brain that can be swapped, tools and knowledge as the way agents take action, and threads and runs for conversations.

The episode "Microsoft AI Agent Runtimes: Beyond Enterprise Chatbots" looks at lifecycle and operations. It describes a layered approach in which agent code, configurations and infrastructure as code live in a repository layer, a CI pipeline handles building, testing and evaluation, and a CD pipeline promotes agent versions through development, testing and production environments. In that picture, Microsoft Foundry Agent Service manages runtime and lifecycle operations, while monitoring and governance provide ongoing quality and compliance. The episode advises monitoring agents after deployment and points to the observability tools in Foundry for tracking performance and compliance.

The episode "Production AI Agents with Microsoft Foundry and Edgar McOchieng [MVP]" discusses the platform's core capabilities, including model experimentation, hosted agents and orchestration pipelines, which help move from prototypes to enterprise-ready solutions. It mentions real-time monitoring, security and business context awareness, along with managing data, tracking usage and ensuring compliance. The episode "Microsoft Foundry AI Apps with Jannik Reinhard [MVP]" lists Azure AI Agent Service among commonly integrated services, for building conversational agents connected to knowledge sources, next to prebuilt AI services, the model catalog, an agent runtime and a governance layer.

The earlier episode "Fix Common Azure AI Foundry Project Failures" describes the Azure AI Agent Service as a managed capability for running conversational agents and orchestrations, with agent instances provisioned through the Foundry portal and integrated via agent service APIs for scalable, secure, enterprise-grade agents.

foundry-iq.desc: Foundry IQ is a Microsoft Foundry capability offering shared knowledge bases that ground AI agents with permission-aware, cited retrieval via an MCP connector.

faq.a: Foundry IQ is a Microsoft Foundry capability that provides shared knowledge bases for grounding AI agents. Retrieval is permission-aware and returns cited results.
faq.q: What is Foundry IQ?

faq.a: Agents, including Copilot Studio agents, can connect to Foundry IQ through an MCP connector. This lets different agents use the same shared knowledge bases.
faq.q: How do agents connect to Foundry IQ?

faq.a: The episode "Foundry IQ - Simply Explained" is dedicated to the topic. It is also mentioned in "Building a Synthetic Market for Microsoft 365 Strategy" and "Fix Common Azure AI Foundry Project Failures".
faq.q: Which M365.FM episodes cover Foundry IQ?

foundry-iq.long:
Foundry IQ is a capability of Microsoft Foundry that provides shared knowledge bases for grounding AI agents. Its purpose is to give agents access to organizational content so that answers are based on actual documents rather than on guesses. According to the product description, retrieval through Foundry IQ is permission-aware and returns cited results, which means an answer can point back to the material it draws on and respects who is allowed to see that material.

The problem it addresses is described plainly in the M365.FM episode "Foundry IQ - Simply Explained". The episode opens with the observation that a company's AI assistant has never read a single one of the company's documents, yet still answers with total confidence, and it describes this as the way trust in AI erodes. The episode is structured around a set of questions: why an AI assistant keeps guessing, what Foundry IQ actually is, where the knowledge comes from, what happens when a question is asked, and a dial that decides how the retrieval behaves. These headings indicate that the topic is approached from the angle of grounding: connecting an agent to a curated knowledge source so that its output can be traced.

A central design idea is that the knowledge bases are shared. Rather than each agent maintaining its own separate retrieval setup, a knowledge base in Foundry IQ can be used by several agents. Agents, including Copilot Studio agents, can connect to it through an MCP connector. This makes Foundry IQ relevant for teams that build agents in Microsoft Foundry as well as for those who build agents in Copilot Studio and want both to draw on the same governed content.

In practice, the decisions around Foundry IQ concern what content goes into a knowledge base, how access rights are honored at query time, and how much effort the retrieval step should spend on a question. The episode "Building a Synthetic Market for Microsoft 365 Strategy" mentions Foundry IQ knowledge bases in the context of end-to-end RAG systems. It states that these knowledge bases help steer queries, plan, rerank, and synthesize answers, and it connects this to use cases such as enterprise search and SLA validation, alongside dashboards for monitoring availability and service health. In that framing, Foundry IQ sits in the retrieval layer of a retrieval-augmented generation setup, where retrieval is combined with a generative model to produce context-aware answers.

The name also appears in a broader context in the episode "Fix Common Azure AI Foundry Project Failures", which describes Foundry IQ as a capability within the Foundry ecosystem that provides insights, recommendations and best practices to accelerate the AI journey, helping developers and decision-makers measure readiness, prioritize investments and adopt architectures that integrate with Azure AI services. That description differs in emphasis from the knowledge-base description given in the product facts, so the two should be read as separate framings found in the episodes rather than as one definition. The product description and the Microsoft Learn module on exploring Foundry IQ are the more direct reference for the knowledge-base and grounding role.

For readers evaluating the capability, the main points to take from the available material are the grounding purpose, the permission-aware and cited nature of retrieval, the shared knowledge base model, and the MCP connector that lets agents, including those built in Copilot Studio, reach it. Details such as supported data sources, configuration options, pricing or limits are not covered in the material summarized here and should be checked in the official documentation.

foundry-local.desc: Foundry Local is a Microsoft runtime and CLI that runs AI models on a PC or device with an OpenAI-compatible API, keeping data off the cloud.

faq.a: Foundry Local is a Microsoft runtime and command-line tool for running AI models locally on a PC or device. It provides an OpenAI-compatible API, so data does not have to be sent to the cloud.
faq.q: What is Foundry Local?

faq.a: Foundry Local is part of Microsoft Foundry and serves as the local counterpart to the hosted parts of the platform. It supports hybrid and edge scenarios where models run close to the data.
faq.q: How does Foundry Local relate to Microsoft Foundry?

faq.a: The episodes mention running RAG workflows on-premises or at the edge, manufacturing use such as quality assurance and predictive maintenance, and fully offline AI in sovereign cloud designs.
faq.q: Where is Foundry Local used according to the M365.FM episodes?

foundry-local.long:
Foundry Local, also referred to as Azure AI Foundry Local, is a runtime and command-line tool for running AI models locally on a PC or other device. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, which means applications written against that interface can talk to a model running on the same machine. No data has to be sent to the cloud. The product is developed by Microsoft, is listed as free, and is classified as both a Microsoft tool and a developer tool.

Foundry Local is part of Microsoft Foundry and acts as the local counterpart to the hosted parts of that platform. Microsoft Foundry, in the wording of the M365.FM episode "Azure AI Foundry - Simply Explained", is a central platform for building, deploying and managing AI applications and agents at scale. Foundry Local extends this idea to situations where the model should run close to where data is generated or stored, instead of in a remote service. Because the API follows the OpenAI-compatible convention, developers can use familiar client code and point it at a local endpoint rather than a cloud one.

The product is closely tied to the concept of Local-first AI, in which models and agents run on the user's device so that data stays there. It is also related to the AI agent topic: an agent can use a local model as its reasoning engine when cloud access is undesirable or impossible. Typical decisions around Foundry Local therefore concern data residency, privacy requirements, offline operation and the choice between running a model on the device or in a hosted service.

Several M365.FM episodes mention Foundry Local in the context of the wider platform. "Azure AI Foundry - Simply Explained" lists support for hybrid and edge computing among the platform's themes, bringing AI closer to data generation through Foundry Local and Azure Arc. "RAG on Azure — Simply Explained" says that Azure AI Foundry Local allows developers to run RAG workflows on-premises or at the edge. The same episode describes deploying RAG at the edge on AKS clusters running on Azure Local as a way to use generative AI capabilities while maintaining data sovereignty, and notes that this flexibility matters for organizations with strict data residency requirements.

The episode "Microsoft Foundry AI Apps with Jannik Reinhard [MVP]" gives an industry example. It says manufacturing teams use Foundry Local to support AI-powered quality assurance and predictive maintenance, even at the edge. In "How to Design Sovereign Cloud Architecture for Microsoft Azure", the product appears in a sovereignty setting. The episode says Foundry Local supports large AI models in fully offline settings, letting organizations run AI tasks locally while staying within strict boundaries. It presents this alongside disconnected operations and Microsoft 365 Local as ways to keep key systems working under governance and policy control without cloud access.

Foundry Local is not the main subject of any M365.FM episode, so the available detail on its installation steps, supported models and hardware requirements is limited here. Official documentation is available through Microsoft Learn under the Foundry Local section of the Azure AI Foundry documentation. Readers who need specifics on supported model catalogs, commands or system prerequisites should consult that documentation.

foundry-model-catalog.desc: The Foundry model catalog is the hub in Microsoft Foundry for discovering, comparing, testing and deploying AI models from Microsoft and partners.

faq.a: It is the hub in Microsoft Foundry for discovering, evaluating and deploying models for generative AI applications. It lists foundation, reasoning, small language, multimodal, domain-specific and industry models from Microsoft and partners.
faq.q: What is the Foundry model catalog?

faq.a: Models sold by Azure are hosted and sold by Microsoft under Microsoft Product Terms, with Microsoft support, enterprise SLAs and a responsible AI review. Partner and community models are billed through the Azure Marketplace and supported by their providers rather than Microsoft.
faq.q: What is the difference between models sold by Azure and models from partners and community?

faq.a: Either as managed compute on dedicated virtual machines, billed by VM core hours, or as serverless deployment through a Microsoft-hosted API, billed mostly by tokens. Managed compute needs VM quota and a hub-based project.
faq.q: How can models from the catalog be deployed?

foundry-model-catalog.long:
The Foundry model catalog is the part of Microsoft Foundry where models for generative AI applications are discovered, evaluated and deployed. It brings together foundation, reasoning, small language, multimodal, domain-specific and industry models in one place. The catalog lists models from Microsoft and from partners such as OpenAI, Meta, Mistral and Cohere, so that teams can work with a range of providers through the same portal instead of handling each model source separately.

According to Microsoft Learn, the catalog is organized into two categories. Models sold by Azure are hosted and sold by Microsoft under Microsoft Product Terms. They come with Microsoft support, enterprise SLAs and a responsible AI review. Models from partners and community come from third parties, research labs and other contributors. These are billed through the Azure Marketplace and are supported by their providers rather than by Microsoft. This split matters in practice, because it determines who handles support, how the model is billed and which terms apply.

Finding a suitable model is the first step. Users can search and filter the catalog by collection, region, deployment option, lifecycle stage, supported features and inference task. For comparison, the catalog offers a leaderboard and benchmarks, and each model has a model card. The model card is organized into tabs for quick facts, details, deployments, benchmarks and license, which gives a compact view of what a model offers and under which conditions it can be used.

Deployment follows one of two main options. Managed compute runs the model on dedicated virtual machines and is billed by VM core hours; it requires VM quota and a hub-based project. Serverless deployment exposes the model through a Microsoft-hosted API and is billed mostly by tokens. Choosing between them is a typical decision: dedicated capacity versus pay-per-use consumption, with different prerequisites. The documentation also notes that content filtering is not available for embedding and time-series models, which is relevant when planning responsible AI controls around a deployment.

Typical uses of models from the catalog include copilots, agents, retrieval-augmented generation and fine-tuning. The M365.FM episode "Build Auditable AI Agents with Azure AI Foundry" touches on this role. It lists the Foundry model catalog among the customization options for agents: developers can select from the ecosystem of models available there to fit different industry needs. The same overview names further options, including grounding agents with knowledge from Bing, SharePoint, Microsoft Fabric and Azure AI Search, over 1,400 action connectors through Azure Logic Apps, data upload options, and API and function calls. In that picture, the model catalog supplies the model choice, while the other options shape what the agent knows and can do.

In summary, the Foundry model catalog serves as the entry point for model selection in Microsoft Foundry. It combines discovery, comparison, testing and deployment, and it distinguishes clearly between Microsoft-supported models and partner or community models with their own support and billing arrangements.

foundry-project.desc: A Foundry project is an isolated workspace inside a Microsoft Foundry resource for one AI solution, holding its own deployments, agents, knowledge stores and monitoring.

faq.a: A Foundry project is an isolated workspace inside a Microsoft Foundry resource for one AI solution. It contains its own model deployments, agents, knowledge stores, evaluations and monitoring.
faq.q: What is a Foundry project?

faq.a: A Foundry project shares the security boundary of the Microsoft Foundry resource it sits in. The resource defines the security posture, while the project scopes the individual AI solution.
faq.q: How does a Foundry project relate to the Foundry resource's security?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Agent Framework - Simply Explained" lists creating a Foundry resource and project as a setup step. "Fix Common Azure AI Foundry Project Failures" covers what happens when the Agent Service or deployments in Azure AI Foundry misbehave.
faq.q: Where does a Foundry project appear in the M365.FM episodes?

foundry-project.long:
A Foundry project is an isolated workspace inside a Microsoft Foundry resource, created for a single AI solution. It holds that solution's own model deployments, agents, knowledge stores, evaluations and monitoring, while sharing the security boundary of the resource it belongs to. In practice, the project is the unit in which a team builds, tests and operates one AI application, separate from other applications that live under the same resource.

The main purpose of a project is separation of concerns. Because each project carries its own deployments, agents, knowledge stores, evaluations and monitoring, one solution can be developed and observed without mixing its assets with those of another. The shared security boundary is the other half of the design: projects inside the same Microsoft Foundry resource do not each define a separate perimeter, but inherit the one set at the resource level. This matters when deciding how many projects to create and where to place them, since the resource determines the security posture and the project determines the scope of the individual solution.

Typical decisions around a Foundry project include how to group solutions, which model deployments a given project needs, and which knowledge stores its agents should use. Setting up a project is also an early step in Microsoft's Agent Framework scenarios. The episode "Microsoft Agent Framework - Simply Explained" lists the creation of an Azure AI Foundry resource and project as part of the setup, followed by deploying the required models and services and configuring an Azure Search Service. It also describes connecting the Azure Search resource to the Foundry project in order to configure grounding with Bing Search. In that walkthrough, the project is the place where models, search and grounding are wired together before an agent is built.

Because a project ties together many connected services, problems often show up at the project level. The episode "Fix Common Azure AI Foundry Project Failures" examines what happens when Azure AI Foundry does not behave as expected, especially when the Agent Service or deployments start acting up. It describes Azure AI Foundry as meant to feel smooth and almost invisible, connecting OpenAI models, search, storage and the other moving parts behind an AI application, and notes that things can slip, for example when an agent stops communicating with the components it depends on. The same episode touches on building a strong pipeline and unified data access to avoid data versioning problems and support the performance of AI models, and it points to governance and security gaps, such as undefined roles and accountability, as recurring sources of trouble.

The episode "Fix Silent Failures in Automated Customer Journeys" does not centre on Foundry projects, but it lists "Fix Common Azure AI Foundry Project Failures" among related M365.FM episodes, which places the topic alongside broader discussions of automation reliability in the Microsoft ecosystem.

For readers who need the authoritative procedure for creating and configuring a project, the official Microsoft Learn documentation for creating projects in Foundry is the reference. The M365.FM episodes complement it with practical context: what a project is used for in an agent scenario, which supporting services are configured around it, and where failures and governance gaps tend to appear when several connected components have to work together.

foundry-toolbox.desc: Foundry toolbox is a Microsoft Foundry feature that collects tools in one place, exposes them through a single connection, and lets multiple agents reuse them.
foundry-toolbox.long:
Foundry toolbox is a feature in Microsoft Foundry that gathers tools once and makes them available through a single connection. Rather than configuring the same tools separately for each agent, the toolbox acts as a shared collection that many agents can draw on.

A central aim of the feature is reuse. Several agents can use the same set of tools, and they do so with shared sign-in and shared controls. This keeps tool access consistent across agents instead of repeating setup and authentication for each one.

The available facts describe Foundry toolbox at this level only: tools are collected once, exposed through one connection, and reused by many agents under common sign-in and controls. Further details, such as specific supported tools, configuration steps or limits, are not covered here.

Foundry toolbox is part of the Microsoft Foundry ecosystem and is relevant to anyone working with agents in that environment who wants a single, reusable point of access to tools. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

freelancing.desc: Freelancing is self-employed work for several clients without a long-term tie to one employer, a model common in IT consulting and the Microsoft partner ecosystem.

faq.a: Freelancing is self-employed work for multiple clients without a long-term commitment to a single employer. In legal and financial contexts the person is often called an independent contractor.
faq.q: What is freelancing?

faq.a: Typical drawbacks are the lack of pensions, sick pay, paid holidays and employer health insurance, as well as late payments and gaps between jobs. Payment is never guaranteed.
faq.q: What are the main drawbacks of freelancing?

faq.a: The episode "How to Futureproof Your Career in the AI Era with Sarah Jones" says more people are choosing freelancing or flexible jobs over traditional office roles, and that AI plays a big part in this shift by opening new doors.
faq.q: How does the M365.FM episode with Sarah Jones relate freelancing to AI?

freelancing.long:
Freelancing is self-employed work carried out for multiple clients without a long-term commitment to a single employer. A person who works this way is called a freelancer, and in legal and financial contexts the term independent contractor is usually used instead. The model is common in IT consulting and in the Microsoft partner ecosystem, and it is also widespread in fields such as music, writing, acting, programming, web and graphic design, translation, illustration and film production.

In practice, a freelancer sells skills or finished results to clients and handles the surrounding business tasks personally. Freelancers may work through agencies or find clients themselves, and they manage contracts, accounting and marketing on their own. Pricing varies: rates may be hourly, daily, per piece, per project or value-based, and payment can be due upfront, on completion or by milestones. Payment is never guaranteed, so the terms agreed in a contract matter a great deal.

The commonly cited benefits are flexibility and the ability to choose clients and projects. The drawbacks are equally well documented. Freelancers typically have no pension, sick pay, paid holidays or employer health insurance, and they may face late payments and gaps between jobs. These trade-offs are central to the decision between freelancing and traditional employment, and they explain why people weigh income stability against control over their schedule and workload.

Legal questions form another major part of the topic. One issue is misclassification, where people who are effectively employees are treated as contractors. The United Kingdom has its own IR35 rules in this area. Copyright is also relevant: by default, the author owns the work unless a contract states that it is work for hire. The European Union has no legal definition of a freelancer, so the status depends on national rules and on the contract in each case. Available statistics are mostly Western; for example, about 10.3 million US independent contractors were counted in 2005, and an estimated 162 million independent workers were reported in Europe and the US in 2018.

The M365.FM episode "How to Futureproof Your Career in the AI Era with Sarah Jones" discusses freelancing under the heading of new work models. According to the excerpt, the world of work is changing quickly, and more people are choosing freelancing or flexible jobs instead of traditional office roles. The episode says AI plays a big part in this shift, opening new doors and changing how people approach their careers. It describes freelancing as a popular choice because it lets people pick their projects, set their schedule and decide how they work.

The same episode places freelancing next to networking advice. It suggests finding groups or individuals with similar goals, sharing ideas through posts or comments to raise visibility, and helping others in order to build genuine relationships. For anyone considering independent work, this connects to a practical point: without an employer, visibility and relationships with potential clients are a main route to new projects.

For readers in the Microsoft ecosystem, freelancing is one way to offer consulting or technical services to organizations that need specialist skills for a limited time. The considerations are the same as for other independent professionals: clear contracts, awareness of the legal classification of the working relationship, a plan for ongoing client acquisition, and provisions for the benefits that an employer would otherwise supply.

freight-reconciliation.desc: Freight reconciliation compares a carrier's freight invoice with the expected charge and shipment details from planning before payment, as in Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management.

faq.a: It is the process of comparing a carrier's freight invoice with the expected transport charge, rate and shipment details recorded during planning before the invoice is paid. In Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management it is also called matching.
faq.q: What is freight reconciliation?

faq.a: Differences are treated as variances and resolved with reconciliation reason codes, which determine how amounts are posted in the general ledger. After variances are handled, the invoice is submitted for approval before the journal is posted.
faq.q: How are differences between the invoice and the freight bill handled?

faq.a: An audit master with minimum and maximum tolerances blocks automatic reconciliation when differences are too large. Such invoices then need review rather than automatic matching.
faq.q: What stops automatic matching when an invoice differs too much?

freight-reconciliation.long:
Freight reconciliation is the process of comparing a carrier's freight invoice with the expected transport charge, rate and shipment details recorded during planning before the invoice is paid. In Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management it is part of Transportation Management and is also called matching. The goal is to confirm that what a carrier bills agrees with what was planned and shipped, and to handle any differences in a controlled way before the amount is posted.

According to Microsoft Learn, the comparison is made between system-generated freight bills and the actual invoices received from carriers. Freight bills carry estimated freight costs. The carrier rate engine calculates the rates, and a freight bill is created when a load is confirmed. Once the carrier invoice arrives, either electronically or on paper, it is matched to the freight bill. Matching can be done line by line or automatically.

Differences between the estimated and the invoiced amounts are called variances. They are resolved with reconciliation reason codes, and these codes determine how the amounts are posted in the general ledger. After variances are handled, the invoice is submitted for approval, and only then is the journal posted. This sequence places a review step between the carrier's bill and the accounting entry, so that charges are checked against planning data before payment.

Several setup elements support the process. Freight reconciliation is enabled in the transportation parameters. Reconciliation reasons, billing groups and freight bill types are then defined, with the freight bill types specifying the matching criteria. An audit master holds minimum and maximum tolerances; when a difference falls outside those tolerances, automatic reconciliation is blocked, so large discrepancies are not matched without review.

Automatic matching follows a defined order. Invoices are sorted by amount, largest first, and applied until the freight bill is fully matched. The documentation advises matching invoices with negative amounts manually and first. It also recommends a match interval of at least 120 seconds when automatic matching is turned on. Typical decisions around the topic therefore include how wide the tolerances should be, which reason codes to offer for variances, and which invoices should be matched by hand instead of automatically.

The M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Transportation Management - Simply Explained" places freight reconciliation within the wider transportation flow. The episode, presented by Mirko Peters, describes how Transportation Management works from the moment goods need to move through load planning, carrier selection, warehouse execution, delivery and freight reconciliation. It describes Dynamics 365 Transportation Management as the transportation planning capability inside Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management, connecting warehouses, vendors, customers, carriers, orders, shipments and freight costs. In that picture, freight reconciliation is the final step, where the cost side of a shipment is checked after planning, execution and delivery.

frequency-capping.desc: Frequency capping limits how many times the same person receives a message or ad within a defined time window, helping prevent fatigue and over-contacting.
frequency-capping.long:
Frequency capping is a concept in messaging and advertising that sets an upper limit on how many times the same person receives a given message or ad within a defined time window. The goal is to prevent audience fatigue and avoid over-contacting recipients.

In practice, a frequency cap is defined by two parameters: a maximum number of contacts and a time period over which those contacts are counted. Once a person has reached the limit within that period, further messages or ad impressions to that person are held back until the window resets or the rule no longer applies. This approach is used where the same audience may be reached repeatedly, such as in marketing communications or ad delivery.

The concept is relevant to anyone managing outbound communication, because unrestricted repetition can reduce attention and leave recipients with a negative impression of the sender. Applying a cap helps balance reach with recipient experience.

No specific products, platforms or episodes on M365.FM are linked to this entry at present. The explanation here is limited to the general definition of frequency capping as a method for limiting repeated contact within a set time window.

front-matter.desc: Front matter is a small metadata block at the top of a file, such as a skill file, that summarizes its name, domain and purpose so relevance can be judged without loading the full file.

faq.a: Front matter is a small metadata section at the top of a file, such as a skill file. It summarizes the file with fields like name, domain and purpose.
faq.q: What is front matter?

faq.a: It lets a system judge whether a file is relevant without loading the whole file. Reading only the short summary at the top is enough to decide if the rest is needed.
faq.q: Why is front matter used?

faq.a: Typical examples are a name, a domain and a purpose. These fields describe what the file is about in a few lines.
faq.q: What kind of information does front matter contain?

front-matter.long:
Front matter is a small metadata section placed at the top of a file, such as a skill file. It summarizes the file's content with a few fields, for example a name, a domain and a purpose, so that a system can quickly see what the file is about.

The main use of front matter is to help judge relevance without loading the entire file. Because the summary sits at the start of the file and is short, a system can read only that part and decide whether the rest of the file is worth opening. This keeps the amount of content that has to be processed small, especially when many files are available and only a few apply to a given task.

In the context of skill files, the front matter acts as a compact description of what the skill covers and when it applies. The details that follow in the body of the file are only needed once the summary indicates a match.

No specific episodes, product documentation or related topics are currently linked to this entry on M365.FM, so the description here is limited to the general concept of front matter as a metadata header.

frontier-program.desc: The Microsoft Frontier program is an early access preview program that lets organizations enable new Microsoft 365 Copilot features before general availability.

faq.a: It is Microsoft's early access preview program. Organizations can use it to enable new Microsoft 365 Copilot features before general availability.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft Frontier program?

faq.a: It provides access to new Microsoft 365 Copilot features ahead of their general availability release.
faq.q: What does the Frontier program provide access to?

faq.a: The features are offered before general availability, so they are preview capabilities. Specific details on how they may change are not covered in the available information.
faq.q: Are the features in the Microsoft Frontier program final?

frontier-program.long:
The Microsoft Frontier program is Microsoft's early access preview program for Microsoft 365 Copilot. Through it, organizations can enable new Copilot features before those features reach general availability.

The program is relevant to administrators and decision-makers who want to evaluate upcoming Microsoft 365 Copilot capabilities ahead of broad release. Because the features are made available before general availability, they are previews and may differ from what is eventually released. Organizations considering participation typically weigh the value of early insight against the maturity of preview functionality.

No further details about eligibility, enablement steps, specific features or timelines are provided in the source information for this entry, so those points are not described here. Readers looking for current requirements or the list of available preview features should consult Microsoft's official documentation.

On M365.FM, the Microsoft Frontier program is tracked as a concept within the Microsoft ecosystem. No episodes are linked to this entry at present.

fslogix.desc: FSLogix is a Microsoft profile technology that stores Windows user profiles in containers and attaches them at sign-in across session hosts.

faq.a: FSLogix is a Microsoft profile technology that stores Windows user profiles in containers (virtual disks) and attaches them at sign-in. This gives users a consistent profile across session hosts in virtual desktop environments.
faq.q: What is FSLogix?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes connect FSLogix with Azure Files and Azure NetApp Files as storage options. The episode "Azure Files - Simply Explained" names storing user profiles as a common use case for Azure Files.
faq.q: Where are FSLogix profile containers stored?

faq.a: FSLogix user profiles are one of the key concepts covered in the episode "Azure Virtual Desktop - Simply Explained", next to host pools, session hosts, personal and pooled desktops and autoscaling. FSLogix handles the profile layer within that architecture.
faq.q: How does FSLogix relate to Azure Virtual Desktop?

fslogix.long:
FSLogix is a Microsoft profile technology for virtual desktop environments. It stores a Windows user profile in a container, which is a virtual disk, and attaches that container when the user signs in. The result is a consistent profile for the same user across multiple session hosts, so settings and data follow the person rather than being tied to a single machine.

The core purpose of FSLogix is to solve the profile problem that appears when users do not always land on the same desktop. In pooled virtual desktop deployments, a user may be connected to a different session host from one sign-in to the next. Because the profile lives in a container that is attached at sign-in, the user experience stays the same regardless of which session host handles the session. Microsoft documents the product in its FSLogix overview, which describes the technology as a way to manage user profiles in such environments.

In practice, profile containers are stored on shared storage that the session hosts can reach. The M365.FM episodes place FSLogix next to storage services such as Azure Files and Azure NetApp Files, since the profile container needs a file share to live on. The episode "Azure Files - Simply Explained" lists Azure Virtual Desktop and FSLogix among the services Azure Files integrates with, and names storing user profiles as one of the common use cases for Azure Files. That connection makes the choice of storage platform a direct design decision for any FSLogix deployment.
