FSLogix appears most often as part of an Azure Virtual Desktop architecture. The episode "Azure Virtual Desktop - Simply Explained" covers FSLogix user profiles among the key concepts of the service, alongside host pools, session hosts, personal and pooled desktops, RemoteApp, autoscaling, image management and identity integration with Microsoft Entra ID. In that overview, FSLogix is one building block that works together with the other components to deliver a secure and scalable virtual desktop experience, including integration with Microsoft 365, Intune and Azure Monitor.

The episode "AVD vs Windows 365: Which Virtual Desktop Strategy Wins: with Shabaz Darr [MVP]" treats FSLogix profile containers as part of the architectural foundation of a successful Azure Virtual Desktop implementation. The conversation groups them with Azure Landing Zones, Cloud Adoption Framework principles, identity, networking, storage, host pools, workspaces, autoscaling, monitoring and performance optimization. According to the episode, proper planning, governance and infrastructure design have a far greater impact on long-term success than simply deploying virtual machines, and organizations that invest in architecture from the start gain better security, lower operational costs and an improved user experience.

When planning around FSLogix, the typical decisions follow from these sources. First, where the profile containers are stored, with Azure Files and Azure NetApp Files named as the options in the episodes. Second, how the storage design, networking and identity fit together with the host pools and session hosts that attach the containers. Third, how performance and monitoring are handled, since profile loading at sign-in is part of the overall user experience. FSLogix itself does not provide the desktop or the hosting platform; it addresses the profile layer, and the surrounding virtual desktop service and storage determine how it is deployed.

fully-qualified-domain-name.desc: A fully qualified domain name (FQDN) specifies a host's exact location in the DNS hierarchy and is used in firewall rules to allow traffic to named services.
fully-qualified-domain-name.long:
A fully qualified domain name (FQDN) is a domain name that specifies a host's exact location in the DNS hierarchy. Rather than identifying a machine or service only by a partial or relative name, an FQDN describes the complete path to it within DNS.

One practical use of FQDNs is in firewall configuration. Firewall rules based on FQDNs allow traffic to named services instead of relying on IP address ranges, which can change over time. Because the rule is tied to a stable name rather than a set of addresses, administrators do not need to update the rule each time the underlying IP addresses change.

In the context of the Microsoft ecosystem, FQDN-based rules are one way to control outbound or inbound access to named endpoints and services. The approach is commonly considered when the destination is described by name and its IP ranges are not fixed.

No linked topics or specific M365.FM episodes are associated with this entry at the moment, so this page covers the concept in general terms only.

function-calling.desc: Function calling lets a language model request a named function with structured inputs so frameworks like Semantic Kernel can run application code and return the result.

faq.a: Function calling is a capability of language models to request a specific function by name with structured inputs. A framework such as Semantic Kernel runs the application code and returns the result to the model.
faq.q: What is function calling?

faq.a: The episode "Model Context Protocol vs Custom AI Integration Glue" argues that MCP is not merely standardized function calling. In "MCP Architecture for Microsoft Copilot and AI Agents", function calling takes place through a manifest of functions, parameters, and constraints that a host reads before sending requests to an MCP server.
faq.q: How is function calling related to MCP?

faq.a: The episode "Phi-4 is the Runtime. MAI-1 is the Reason." mentions Phi-4-mini and Phi-4-multimodal, noting that capabilities such as function calling let the model participate in agentic workflows.
faq.q: Which models are mentioned as supporting function calling?

function-calling.long:
Function calling is a capability of language models that allows a model to request a specific function by name, together with structured inputs. Instead of only producing free text, the model signals which piece of application code should run and with which arguments. A framework such as Semantic Kernel then executes that code and returns the result to the model, which can use it in the rest of the interaction. The concept therefore sits at the boundary between a model and the software around it.

The basic idea is a division of labor. The model decides that a function is needed and describes the call in a structured form; the surrounding application performs the actual work. This keeps execution inside code that developers control rather than inside the model itself. The episode "Semantic Kernel - Simply Explained" describes Semantic Kernel as a kit that lets your own code talk to a large language model and lets that model call your code back. Its agenda lists plugins and functions, planning and function calling, memory and RAG, and connectors and prompts, which places function calling alongside the other building blocks of the framework.

Function calling also appears in discussions of smaller models and agentic workflows. The episode "Phi-4 is the Runtime. MAI-1 is the Reason." notes that Phi-4-mini and Phi-4-multimodal are designed around relatively small footprints, and that capabilities such as function calling allow the model to participate in agentic workflows rather than merely generate text. The episode gives examples of the kind of situation this supports: a local coding assistant examining a file, an endpoint agent classifying a request, or an application deciding which internal function should execute. In each case the model chooses an action, and application code carries it out. The episode also points to MIT licensing as a source of flexibility for embedded and specialized deployments.

The relationship between function calling and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is addressed directly in "Model Context Protocol vs Custom AI Integration Glue". The episode argues that MCP is not a plugin system, an API wrapper, or merely standardized function calling, and that such descriptions miss the point and can lead teams back into brittle "AI glue" patterns. According to the episode, custom glue such as ad hoc connectors, bespoke wrappers, temporary service principals, and middleware seems reasonable in small projects but, when combined across teams, produces tool sprawl, permission creep, policy drift, and inconsistent logging. The episode attributes these failures to unbounded action and brittle integrations rather than to model intelligence. Function calling, in this reading, is one mechanism within a larger integration picture and does not by itself solve governance of actions.

The episode "MCP Architecture for Microsoft Copilot and AI Agents" shows function calling in the context of MCP. It describes a manifest file, a JSON document that defines functions, parameters, and constraints so that hosts can understand tool capabilities programmatically. Capability discovery and function calling follow a sequence: the host scans for available MCP servers, fetches the manifest from each server, parses it to understand the available functions, constructs a request payload based on the manifest, and sends it to the server. The server executes the function and returns a response, and the host processes that response for further actions. Here the function definition is declared in a structured manifest, and calls are validated and answered by a server.

Typical decisions around function calling include which functions to expose, how their parameters and constraints are described, and where execution happens. Exposing code to a model means defining named functions with structured inputs, as in the plugins and functions of Semantic Kernel or the manifest entries of an MCP server. The episodes suggest that how those definitions are organized and governed matters as much as the model's ability to request them, particularly when many teams build integrations independently.

functional-governance.desc: Functional governance is the organizational side of Microsoft 365 governance: how sites and teams are created, templated, archived or deleted, and how guests are managed.

faq.a: Functional governance covers the organizational decisions: how sites and teams are created, templates, lifecycle handling such as archiving or deletion, and guest management. Technical governance covers configuration such as device and conditional access settings.
faq.q: How does functional governance differ from technical governance?

faq.a: The framework says first decisions should cover provisioning, naming and external access. It then asks for policies on group and team creation, naming, expiration and archiving.
faq.q: Which decisions does Microsoft's collaboration governance framework recommend making first?

faq.a: The episode "Close the Microsoft Teams Channel Governance Gap" says many security and compliance features require tiers such as E5 or Purview add-ons, and that overly broad admin roles and delegated permissions widen the governance gap.
faq.q: Why do licensing and permissions matter for functional governance?

functional-governance.long:
Functional governance is the organizational side of Microsoft 365 governance. It covers how sites and teams are created, which templates are used, how data is archived or deleted across its lifecycle and how guest users are managed. It is usually contrasted with technical governance, which deals with configuration topics such as device management and conditional access. In practice the two halves depend on each other: functional decisions say what should happen, and technical settings enforce it.

A Microsoft Learn collaboration governance framework describes the goals behind this work: managing access to resources, keeping collaboration compliant with business standards and securing data, partly to limit shadow IT. Within that framework, functional and organizational governance is presented as a checklist rather than a single tool. It suggests talking to heavy collaborators, balancing risk and benefit, adapting to departments and content types, and aligning effort to business priorities. It also advises embedding decisions in settings that switch features on or off, rolling out in phases while watching help desk tickets, training users, and publishing policies on an adoption site. Roles are defined through a governance core team, and decisions are revisited regularly.

The same framework names the first decisions to make: provisioning, naming and external access. Its organization and lifecycle area asks for policies on group and team creation, naming, expiration and archiving. It also calls for end-of-life options for groups, teams, sites and Viva Engage communities. These questions are functional in nature, because they concern who may create a workspace, what it should be called, how long it lives and what happens when it is no longer needed.

Technical governance builds on Microsoft 365 Groups and gives these decisions an enforcement mechanism. The framework lists controls such as external sharing settings, domain allow and block lists, restricted group creation, naming policy, expiration policy and per-group guest access. According to the notes on that page, these controls mostly require E3 or E5 licensing and sometimes Entra ID P1 or P2. The page is marked as archived and was last updated in July 2023, and it does not cover templates, so template decisions fall outside what that source describes.

The episode "Close the Microsoft Teams Channel Governance Gap" (2025-11-03) approaches a related problem. It describes a governance gap as the difference between intended and actual governance in Microsoft 365. The episode says that many security and compliance features depend on licensing tiers such as E5 and Purview add-ons, and that organizations often assume capabilities are included when they are not. It also says that role-based access controls are frequently underused or misconfigured, and that excessive admin roles and delegated permissions are among the largest practical contributors to the gap. It further notes that auto-classification can mislabel content and deepen the gap. These points show why functional policies need to be checked against licensing and permissions.

Typical situations for functional governance include deciding who can create teams, agreeing naming conventions, setting expiration and archiving rules for inactive workspaces, and defining how external guests are invited and reviewed. The framework's advice to roll out in phases, train users and review decisions regularly applies to each of these. A written policy that is not reflected in settings, or settings that rely on features the organization is not licensed for, leaves the gap that the episode describes.

functional-location.desc: A functional location in Dynamics 365 Asset Management is the place where an asset does its job, arranged in a parent-child hierarchy that also carries cost details.

faq.a: It is the place where an asset does its job, such as a site, building, warehouse, workshop or production line. Functional locations are created in a parent-child hierarchy, and assets are installed on them.
faq.q: What is a functional location in Dynamics 365 Asset Management?

faq.a: An asset can be installed on several functional locations during its life. Costs are always assigned to the functional location where the asset was installed at that time.
faq.q: How are costs handled for assets that move between functional locations?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, the structure is not flexible, and locations cannot be moved within a hierarchy once it has been built. The hierarchy should therefore be planned carefully before it is created.
faq.q: Can a functional location be moved after the hierarchy is built?

functional-location.long:
A functional location in Dynamics 365 Asset Management is the place where an asset performs its job. It can describe a site, building, warehouse, workshop, production line or another operational location. Functional locations are elements of a technical structure, such as the functional units of a system, and they are created in a hierarchy of parent and child records. Assets are then installed on these locations, which separates the question of where work happens from the question of which physical item is doing it.

The hierarchy can follow the needs of the organization. According to Microsoft Learn, typical approaches include a functional layout, used to manage assets with similar behavior, a process-oriented layout based on workflows, and a spatial layout based on geographic locations or sites. A simple example from the M365.FM material is a plant that contains a packing area, which contains a conveyor line, which in turn contains individual motors, sensors and rollers. Each level is its own functional location, and the levels together describe how the operation is organized.

From a functional location, users can set up specifications and maintenance sequences for both preventive and reactive maintenance. They can also manage the assets installed there and follow the active requests, work orders and faults registered against those assets. Each functional location is managed independently within Asset Management, so it works as a working record in its own right and not only as a label in a tree.

Costs are a central reason for the concept. An asset can be installed on several functional locations during its life, for example when a pump is moved from one line to another. Costs are always assigned to the functional location where the asset was installed at that time. This keeps maintenance spending tied to the place where it occurred, even when the same asset appears in different locations over the years. The hierarchy therefore also serves as a structure for cost details.

One limitation is stated in the documentation: the structure is not flexible. Once a hierarchy has been built, locations cannot be moved within it. This makes the design of the hierarchy an early decision. Choosing between a functional, process-oriented or spatial layout, and deciding how many levels to model, determines how reporting, maintenance planning and cost tracking will behave later.

The episode "Dynamics 365 Asset Management - Simply Explained" places functional locations next to the asset record. Instead of relying on somebody remembering which machine is which, the asset record provides a consistent reference point, and functional locations describe where that equipment performs its job. The episode uses the plant, packing area, conveyor line and motor example to show how a hierarchy gives technicians context when a motor fails. They do not simply see a serial number, but also where in the operation the failing item sits.

fusion-development.desc: Fusion development is an approach in which business experts, makers, IT professionals and developers build solutions together on a shared platform such as Power Platform.

faq.a: Fusion development is an approach in which fusion teams of makers, business experts, IT professionals, architects and professional developers build solutions together on a shared platform such as Power Platform. Each contributes at the appropriate abstraction level.
faq.q: What is fusion development?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn names the citizen developer or maker, the professional developer, and the IT professional or DevOps engineer. They cover business process knowledge, code-first engineering and application lifecycle management.
faq.q: Which roles take part in fusion development?

faq.a: Low-code capabilities can be mixed with code-first components. The M365.FM episode "Build Fusion Apps with Power Apps and Azure Functions" describes Power Apps for the interface, Dataverse for data and governance, and Azure Functions for scalable compute and custom APIs.
faq.q: How does fusion development combine low-code and code?

fusion-development.long:
Fusion development is an approach to application development in which fusion teams of business experts, low-code makers, IT professionals, architects and professional developers build solutions together on a shared platform such as Power Platform. Each group contributes at the abstraction level that suits its skills. Microsoft Learn describes it as a way of scaling application development with low-code, in which professional developers work together with citizen developers and other makers.

The documentation cites Gartner's description of fusion teams as distributed, multidisciplinary digital business teams that combine technology and business skills. The idea is that people who understand a business process and people who write and operate code do not work in separate silos. Low-code capabilities can also be mixed with code-first components, so that a single solution contains both visually built parts and custom code.

Three personas are named in the Microsoft Learn material. The citizen developer, or maker, knows the business process and uses visual low-code tools. The professional developer works with tools such as Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code and languages such as C# or JavaScript. The IT professional or DevOps engineer is responsible for application lifecycle management. Together these roles cover the business knowledge, the specialized engineering and the operational discipline that a solution needs.

The stated aim is to build better apps faster. In practice this means a division of labor: professional developers take on specialized problems, while simpler, recurring tasks are handed to makers. Pro developers and IT professionals provide a safe, managed environment in which makers can work with little friction. Power Platform is described as one tool in the toolset rather than the whole approach, and the page names no licensing prerequisites or limits.

The M365.FM episode "Build Fusion Apps with Power Apps and Azure Functions" shows what this looks like technically. The episode describes Power Apps for the interface and light workflow, Dataverse for data and governance, and Azure Functions for scalable compute and custom APIs. It frames fusion development as a way to go beyond low-code limits by combining Power Apps with Azure Functions, so that low-code and pro-code work together in one Microsoft system and the app can use more advanced Azure capabilities.

According to the episode, this matters for real problems such as bringing in thousands of suppliers or moving large amounts of data, where a purely low-code solution may reach its limits. The episode also offers patterns, pitfalls and a step-by-step checklist aimed at shipping quickly, staying secure and scaling with confidence.

Typical decisions around fusion development include which parts of a solution makers should build visually, which parts call for custom code, and how the managed environment and lifecycle management are organized by IT. The sources frame the approach as a collaboration model between these groups, not as a replacement of professional development by low-code.

fuzzy-matching.desc: Fuzzy matching links records that are not identical by scoring their similarity, using methods such as edit distance or semantic similarity instead of exact equality.

faq.a: Fuzzy matching is a technique that links non-identical records by calculating a similarity score, for example with character-based edit distance or semantic similarity. Values that are similar enough are treated as a match even if they are not exactly equal.
faq.q: What is fuzzy matching?

faq.a: Fuzzy merge is enabled with a checkbox in the Merge dialog and uses the Jaccard similarity algorithm to compare text values. Options include a similarity threshold between zero and one, ignore case, combining text parts, a maximum number of matches per row and a transformation table. It works only on text columns.
faq.q: How does fuzzy merge work in Power Query?

faq.a: According to the episode "SC-900 Exam Prep Part 2/8: Microsoft Entra ID", Entra ID uses fuzzy matching so that passwords close to entries on the blocked list, such as "P@ssw0rd1" versus "P@ssw0rd", are still recognised as weak.
faq.q: How is fuzzy matching used in Microsoft Entra ID?

fuzzy-matching.long:
Fuzzy matching is a technique that identifies and links non-identical records by calculating a similarity score. Instead of requiring two values to be exactly equal, it measures how alike they are, for example with a character-based edit distance or with semantic similarity. Values that score above a chosen level are treated as the same thing, even when they differ in spelling, case, word form or wording.

The most direct use is data preparation. In Power Query, the fuzzy merge feature applies approximate matching when columns of two tables are compared, so rows can be joined even if the values are not exactly equal. According to Microsoft Learn, a typical case is free-text survey answers that contain typos, singular and plural variants, or differences in letter case. Fuzzy matching is switched on with a checkbox at the bottom of the Merge dialog and uses the Jaccard similarity algorithm to measure how alike two values are. It is supported only for merges on text columns, and rows without a match stay empty.

The fuzzy merge dialog exposes several options that control how loose or strict the matching is. A similarity threshold between zero and one sets the cutoff, where one means an exact match. An ignore-case setting removes capitalisation differences, and an option to combine text parts lets split words, such as two fragments of a name, still match. A maximum number of matches per input row limits how many candidates a single row can pick up. A transformation table with From and To columns maps chosen values explicitly, for cases where the algorithm alone would not connect them. An option to show similarity scores helps decide whether the threshold should be raised or lowered. The example on the documentation page reduces nine different survey answers to four after tuning the settings, which illustrates that the result depends on the configuration and usually needs a few iterations.

The same idea appears outside of data merging. The episode "SC-900 Exam Prep Part 2/8: Microsoft Entra ID" describes it in the context of password protection. Blocked password lists remove predictable passwords, reduce the chance of password spray attacks and enforce a baseline of password security. The episode says that Entra ID employs fuzzy matching techniques to catch variations of blocked passwords: if someone tries "P@ssw0rd1" instead of "P@ssw0rd", the system can still identify it as a weak password, so that minor tweaks do not slip through.

A broader view comes from the episode "How Probabilistic AI Changes Power Platform Design". It argues that workflow designs should embrace uncertainty instead of trying to eliminate it. By combining AI with governance models such as human review and escalation paths, organizations can build workflows that remain resilient even when inputs are imperfect. In that framing, fuzzy matching, semantic understanding and adaptive reasoning become central parts of the design process. The episode describes a move toward what the article calls the "Approximate Enterprise", where automation rests less on exact logic and more on contextual judgment and probability, and where success depends on balancing automation speed with oversight.

In practice, the main decision around fuzzy matching is how permissive it should be. A low threshold links more records but increases the risk of false matches, while a high threshold behaves almost like an exact comparison. Because the similarity score is available, results can be inspected and the settings adjusted. In probabilistic workflows, uncertain matches can additionally be routed to human review rather than being accepted automatically.

gamification.desc: Gamification applies game design elements such as points, challenges, progress indicators and competition to business apps and adoption programs to raise engagement.

faq.a: Gamification applies game design elements such as points, challenges, progress indicators, competition and social features to non-game contexts like business apps and adoption programs. Its purpose is to increase engagement and motivation.
faq.q: What is gamification?

faq.a: Several episodes name rewards, badges and leaderboards for completing training modules, and interactive walkthroughs during onboarding, as ways to motivate users. They position it alongside change management, ongoing support and feedback loops.
faq.q: How do the M365.FM episodes use gamification in adoption work?

faq.a: According to the episode "Game-Inspired Enterprise UX with Sandra Kiel [MVP]", the emphasis should be on designing experiences with clear goals, instant feedback and progression that make users feel confident and capable, rather than on points and badges alone.
faq.q: Is gamification only about points and badges?

gamification.long:
Gamification is the use of game design elements in contexts that are not games, such as business applications, training programs and adoption initiatives. Typical elements include points, challenges, progress indicators, competition and social features. The goal is to increase engagement and motivation among people who use workplace software or take part in change programs. In the Microsoft ecosystem, the concept appears most often in discussions about user adoption, onboarding, training and portal design.

How the elements are applied varies by situation. The M365.FM episode "Architect Scalable SharePoint Automation for Enterprise Workflows" lists gamification as one part of an adoption strategy and describes it as encouraging adoption through rewards, badges or leaderboards for completing training modules. It sits alongside change management communication and ongoing support, so it is treated as one lever among several rather than a standalone solution. The episode "Build an Autonomous Microsoft 365 Tenant with Zero-Touch Workflows" mentions gamification together with interactive walkthroughs and integrated support features as ways to make onboarding more enjoyable, and it connects engagement during onboarding with user satisfaction and retention.

Gamification is also discussed for customer-facing and partner-facing scenarios. The episode "Power Pages - Simply Explained" says that elements like rewards and badges can motivate users to engage more with a portal, and that leaderboards can foster competition and make the experience enjoyable, which the episode links to higher satisfaction. In that context it is mentioned next to customizable forms, secure data access, responsive layouts and self-service capabilities that streamline processes.

For Copilot adoption, the episode "Scale Microsoft Copilot Adoption in 90 Days with Carina de Vries [MVP]" cites a gamification study in which 85% of participants felt more engaged and gamified courses improved retention rates by up to 60%. The episode presents these figures as coming from the cited source and recommends combining AI-powered reminders, gamification and personalized challenges to keep a team engaged and motivated. It pairs this with building a supportive culture: celebrating small wins, sharing success stories and encouraging people to help each other.

A more cautious view comes from the episode "Game-Inspired Enterprise UX with Sandra Kiel [MVP]". It examines the psychology behind successful game design and how those principles can shape workplace software. The discussion covers clear goals, instant feedback, progression systems and user motivation. The episode stresses that the aim is not gamification understood as points and badges, but designing experiences that make users feel confident, capable and motivated to continue. It also looks at why many enterprise tools overwhelm users with complexity and how game-inspired design patterns can improve onboarding, learning and long-term adoption, including in the growing role of AI and Microsoft Copilot.

Taken together, the episodes suggest two decisions around gamification. The first is where to use visible mechanics such as rewards, badges and leaderboards, for example around training modules, onboarding or portal engagement. The second is how far to go beyond surface mechanics toward game-inspired design principles like clear goals, immediate feedback and visible progression. Gamification in the episodes is consistently tied to broader adoption work, including communication, support and feedback loops, rather than offered as a replacement for them.

gcc-high.desc: GCC High is Microsoft's isolated U.S. government cloud for Microsoft 365, used by defense contractors handling controlled unclassified information.

faq.a: GCC High is Microsoft's isolated U.S. government cloud environment for Microsoft 365. It is designed for organizations such as defense agencies and contractors that handle controlled unclassified information and need elevated compliance and sovereignty.
faq.q: What is GCC High?

faq.a: The move requires a re-tenanting migration, meaning the organization is moved into a separate tenant in the isolated environment. Customers should also confirm their eligibility for government cloud offerings before planning the move.
faq.q: How does a company move from commercial Microsoft 365 to GCC High?

faq.a: No. Feature availability may differ from commercial environments, releases usually arrive later, and third-party integrations are more restricted. The episode "Power BI Copilot - Simply Explained" notes, for example, that Power BI Copilot is not supported in GCC, GCC High, or DoD because of GPU requirements.
faq.q: Are all Microsoft 365 features available in GCC High?

gcc-high.long:
GCC High is one of the Microsoft 365 government cloud environments and part of the U.S. sovereign cloud for government. It is described as a more isolated environment built for elevated compliance and sovereignty requirements. On the spectrum of isolation it sits between GCC and DoD, the other two primary government cloud environments for Microsoft 365. Typical customers are U.S. defense agencies and the contractors that work with them.

The environment is aimed at organizations that handle controlled unclassified information. It also applies where contracts require FedRAMP High, DFARS, or ITAR and EAR compliance, or where an organization needs stronger separation from the commercial cloud. In practice, a defense contractor whose contract language references these obligations will usually have to decide whether its current Microsoft 365 setup meets them. If it does not, GCC High is one of the government cloud options to evaluate.

Moving from commercial Microsoft 365 to GCC High is not a simple switch of settings. The migration requires re-tenanting, meaning the organization moves into a separate tenant in the isolated environment rather than converting its existing one. Planning for this move is a significant part of any adoption decision, since it affects identities, data, and the way users and administrators work day to day.

Eligibility and responsibility are two points the official documentation stresses. Customers must check whether they are eligible for government cloud offerings, and they remain responsible for configuring Microsoft 365 so that it meets their own regulatory duties. The environment supplies the isolated platform, but compliance with the specific obligations in a contract stays with the customer.

There are also practical trade-offs. Feature availability in GCC High may differ from commercial environments, and releases usually arrive later than in the commercial cloud. Third-party integrations are more restricted in highly isolated environments. Organizations therefore tend to compare the features they depend on against what is available in the government cloud before committing to a move.

Microsoft Copilot is one area where this applies. According to the documentation, Microsoft Copilot can run entirely inside the customer's government cloud tenant, which keeps prompts, responses, and generated content within that cloud. This is relevant for contractors who want AI assistance without moving controlled data outside the isolated boundary.

The M365.FM episode "Power BI Copilot - Simply Explained" touches on GCC High from the feature-availability side. Its requirements list notes that Power BI Copilot is not supported in sovereign cloud environments, naming GCC, GCC High, and DoD, and describes this as a hard limit due to GPU requirements. For teams in these environments, that is an example of how a capability available in the commercial cloud can be unavailable in a government cloud, which is why checking availability early matters when planning around GCC High.

gdpr.desc: GDPR (DSGVO) is the EU regulation on processing personal data; M365.FM episodes cover it in Copilot governance, Purview classification and shadow data.

faq.a: The GDPR is the EU General Data Protection Regulation, which governs how personal data may be processed. In German-speaking countries it is called the DSGVO.
faq.q: What is the GDPR?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Purview Information Protection - Simply Explained" says Purview scans and classifies data, identifies sensitive PII and tags it according to GDPR requirements, with a compliance dashboard for visibility.
faq.q: How does the GDPR relate to Microsoft Purview in the episodes?

faq.a: The episode "Fix Copilot Notebooks GDPR and Governance Risks" explains that Copilot outputs are derived content that can contain fragments of sensitive sources and have no clear parents, which creates governance and GDPR risks.
faq.q: Why does the GDPR matter for Copilot Notebooks?

gdpr.long:
The GDPR, short for the EU General Data Protection Regulation and known in German-speaking countries as the DSGVO, is the legal framework that governs how personal data may be processed. It is closely connected to the broader topic of Datenschutz. In the Microsoft ecosystem it becomes relevant wherever user content such as mail, chats, documents and files contains personal data, because those workloads are exactly where such information accumulates.

The GDPR is a regulation, not a product feature. It is therefore related to, and falls under, the broader subject of compliance, which describes the task of meeting legal and internal requirements. Organizations typically support their GDPR obligations with technical and organizational measures: classifying data, labelling it, applying retention rules and keeping audit trails. These tools help demonstrate control over personal data, but they do not replace the legal obligations themselves.

The M365.FM episodes mention the GDPR mostly alongside AI and information protection. The episode "Fix Copilot Notebooks GDPR and Governance Risks" focuses on Copilot Notebooks, described as a conversational workspace that pulls context from SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, decks, sheets and emails and synthesizes answers. According to the episode, every Copilot output, such as a summary, paragraph or bullet list, is derived content that can contain fragments of sensitive sources, which creates data that has no clear parents. The episode frames this as a governance and GDPR risk and points to the need to identify types of confidential data, such as personal information and financial records, and to apply strict controls to protect them.

The episode "Microsoft Purview Information Protection - Simply Explained" places the GDPR in the context of compliance support. It says organizations face strict regulations such as GDPR and HIPAA and describes how Microsoft Purview scans and classifies data, identifies sensitive PII and tags it according to GDPR requirements. It also mentions a compliance dashboard that gives visibility into the compliance posture. The stated aim is to meet compliance standards with less manual effort.

Shadow data is another recurring theme. In "Shadow Data Discovery and Governance with Microsoft Purview", the episode says unmanaged shadow data can lead to fines and legal consequences under frameworks such as GDPR and CCPA, and that shadow data often contains sensitive information that puts audits at risk. It stresses that regulators expect organizations to know where their data lives and how it is protected, so discovering hidden data is part of keeping a compliance posture strong.

The GDPR also appears in discussions about where AI processing takes place. "How to Run Local Llama on SharePoint Files Securely" lists GDPR among compliance frameworks, together with NIST AI RMF, CMMC and ISO/IEC 27001, that require strict data handling. The episode argues that a private, local LLM keeps information inside the organization and gives direct control over sensitive documents and PII, and that local AI offers clearer compliance paths than some cloud-based tools.

Finally, "Fix Sensitivity Labels and Data Silos for Microsoft Copilot" addresses common myths about Copilot and privacy. The episode states that Microsoft uses industry-standard encryption and follows privacy laws like GDPR, and that customer data is not used to train models. It also cautions that over-permissioning and misconfigurations can still lead to data exposure, and that Copilot can surface the wrong data, so access controls and sensitivity labels need careful attention.

Taken together, the episodes treat the GDPR as a regulatory reference point for decisions about classification, labelling, access control, shadow data discovery and the placement of AI workloads, all under the umbrella of compliance.

general-ledger.desc: The general ledger is a company's main bookkeeping record of all financial transactions by account; in Dynamics 365 Finance it holds every posted money movement.

faq.a: It is the central financial record behind Dynamics 365 Finance and the official home for every posted money movement. It brings accounting entries from payments, invoices, inventory, payroll, bank transactions and taxes together in a structured and traceable way.
faq.q: What is the general ledger in Dynamics 365 Finance?

faq.a: Configuration such as vendor posting profiles and item group settings determines which general ledger accounts receive the accounting impact of invoices, purchases, sales, adjustments and production activities.
faq.q: How do transactions from other areas reach the general ledger?

faq.a: Financial Reporting uses data already posted in the general ledger, together with main accounts, financial dimensions and report structures, to produce income statements, balance sheets, cash flow reports, trial balances and budget-versus-actual reports.
faq.q: How is the general ledger related to financial reporting?

general-ledger.long:
The general ledger is the main bookkeeping record of a company. It collects all financial transactions and organizes them by account, so that the financial position of the organization can be traced back to individual accounting entries. In Dynamics 365 Finance, the general ledger is the official home for every posted money movement.

According to the M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 General Ledger - Simply Explained", Dynamics 365 General Ledger provides the central financial record behind Dynamics 365 Finance. Customer payments, supplier invoices, inventory movements, payroll, bank transactions, taxes, accruals and other financial events ultimately affect the company's financial position. The general ledger brings the resulting accounting entries together in a structured and traceable way. In practice, this means the ledger is where activity from many different business areas ends up as accounting data in one place.

The general ledger does not work in isolation. Other Dynamics 365 Finance areas post into it. The episode "Dynamics 365 Accounts Payable - Simply Explained" describes vendor posting profiles, which tell Dynamics 365 where vendor transactions belong in the General Ledger. When an invoice is posted, the system records what the organization owes and connects the transaction with the appropriate financial accounts. The posting profile acts as the accounting map behind this process, so finance employees do not have to determine the relevant vendor ledger account manually for every invoice.

Inventory follows a similar pattern. In "Dynamics 365 Inventory Management - Simply Explained", item groups help organize similar products, such as raw materials, spare parts and finished products, and influence how inventory transactions connect with financial accounts. The associated financial configuration determines which general ledger accounts receive the accounting impact of purchases, sales, adjustments and production activities. This keeps the operational inventory record and the company's financial records connected, so quantity and value stay aligned.

The general ledger is also the foundation for reporting. The episode "Dynamics 365 Financial Reporting - Simply Explained" explains that Financial Reporting turns data already posted in Dynamics 365 Finance into structured reports for finance teams, managers, auditors and executives. Instead of rebuilding financial statements in multiple spreadsheets every month, organizations can use the general ledger, main accounts, financial dimensions, reporting categories and predefined report structures to create consistent income statements, balance sheets, cash flow reports, trial balances and budget-versus-actual reports. The quality of those reports therefore depends on the transactions that were posted to the ledger.

The broader overview episode "Dynamics 365 Finance - Simply Explained" places the general ledger within the full flow of the system, from the first purchase request through the general ledger, budgeting, reporting, security and the wider Microsoft platform. Taken together, the episodes describe the general ledger as the point where operational events become official financial records, and as the source that downstream reporting relies on.

Typical decisions around the general ledger include how main accounts and financial dimensions are structured, how posting profiles and item group configurations map transactions to accounts, and which report structures are built on top of the posted data. The episodes present these setup choices as the way to keep accounting entries consistent, traceable and usable for reporting.

generative-ai.desc: Generative AI is artificial intelligence that produces text, images or other content from natural-language prompts, used across Microsoft 365, Azure and development.

faq.a: Generative AI is artificial intelligence that generates text, images or other content in response to natural-language prompts. It produces new output from written instructions rather than only analyzing existing data.
faq.q: What is generative AI?

faq.a: According to the episode "RAG on Azure — Simply Explained", RAG combines information retrieval with generative AI so responses draw on external data sources. The episode says hybrid keyword and vector queries help reduce hallucinations in generated content.
faq.q: How does RAG relate to generative AI?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Purview for Copilot Security with Peter Rising [Microsoft]" explains that adopting Microsoft 365 Copilot and AI agents requires data to be secure, governed and compliant. It describes Microsoft Purview as helping organizations prepare for AI at scale.
faq.q: Why is governance discussed alongside generative AI in Microsoft 365?

generative-ai.long:
Generative AI is a form of artificial intelligence that generates text, images or other content in response to natural-language prompts. Instead of only classifying or predicting, a generative system produces new output from an instruction written in everyday language. In the Microsoft ecosystem, the term appears in discussions of Microsoft 365 Copilot, AI agents, Azure-based retrieval architectures, software development tooling and creative production.

The M365.FM episodes describe several practical uses. In software development, the episode "How AI Changed Software Development Forever — Building the Agentic Future with Andre Baltieri [MVP]" covers the transition from traditional development to AI-assisted development, coding agents, agentic architectures, Microsoft Agent Framework, .NET, RAG, context engineering, security and the economics of generative AI. The guest argues that this transition feels fundamentally different from earlier shifts such as desktop, web, mobile, cloud, containers, microservices and serverless computing.

A recurring concern is the accuracy of generated content. The episode "RAG on Azure — Simply Explained" presents retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as a way to combine information retrieval with generative AI. According to the episode, integrating external data sources lets RAG provide evidence-based answers, and hybrid queries that combine keyword and vector search lead to contextually accurate results and reduce hallucination rates in AI-generated content. The episode names retrievers and generators as key components of a RAG architecture on Azure and cites reductions of 40-50% in customer support response times; these figures come from the episode itself.

Governance and security form a second theme. In "Microsoft Purview for Copilot Security with Peter Rising [Microsoft]", the discussion centers on organizations adopting Microsoft 365 Copilot, AI agents and generative AI technologies, and on the challenge of keeping data secure, governed and compliant. The episode explains that AI readiness is not only about deploying Copilot licenses but also about understanding and governing the data those tools can reach, and it describes how Microsoft Purview supports that work and addresses AI risks.

A third theme is business value. The episode "From AI Hype to Business Value with Kayode Ajayi [MVP-MCT]" refers to MIT research that found a measurement gap: according to the episode, about 88% of AI pilots stall before production and only 5% of generative AI projects show measurable impact. The episode's advice is to set clear objectives for each AI project, align them with business goals and track progress with meaningful metrics such as cost savings and productivity improvements, rather than following the hype.

Generative AI is also used in creative work. "AI Movie Production with Copilot, Seedance, and Higgsfield" describes AI film production as an orchestrated workflow in which different models and platforms handle specific stages, including ideation, scripting, storyboarding, shot planning, character consistency, motion generation, editing and post-production. The episode names Microsoft Copilot, Seedance and Higgsfield as examples and highlights a shift from prompt engineering to architecture design, where the challenge is no longer a single prompt but how the pieces fit together.

Taken together, the episodes show that generative AI is rarely used as an isolated model. It is combined with retrieval over trusted data, protected by governance tooling, measured against business outcomes and embedded in agent-based or multi-tool workflows. Decisions around it typically involve which data the system may access, how answers are grounded, how risk is controlled and how value is demonstrated.

generative-engine-optimization.desc: Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the practice of improving content so AI systems such as ChatGPT, Copilot and Perplexity reference and cite it in their answers.
generative-engine-optimization.long:
Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the practice of improving content so that it is referenced and cited in answers generated by AI systems such as ChatGPT, Copilot or Perplexity. Rather than aiming only for a ranking position in a list of search results, GEO focuses on whether a piece of content is used as a source when an AI system composes a response.

The concept is used by people who publish information online and want that information to be visible in AI-generated answers. It applies to AI assistants and answer engines that summarize or synthesize material from multiple sources and, in some cases, show which sources were used. Copilot is part of the Microsoft ecosystem, which makes the topic relevant to organizations that think about how their content appears in Microsoft-based AI experiences.

This page describes GEO at a definitional level. No related topics, documentation links or specific techniques are listed in the underlying facts, so the page does not describe particular methods or measurements.

On M365.FM, Generative engine optimization (GEO) is recorded as a concept entity. No episodes are currently linked to it.

generative-orchestration.desc: Generative orchestration is a mode in Microsoft Copilot Studio where a large language model selects the tools, topics or knowledge sources for each request.

faq.a: It is an orchestration mode in Microsoft Copilot Studio in which a large language model chooses which tools, topics or knowledge to use for a request. The choice is guided by the names and descriptions of those components.
faq.q: What is generative orchestration in Copilot Studio?

faq.a: The model uses the names and descriptions of tools, topics and knowledge sources to decide what to use. Clear descriptions therefore help the model route a request to the right component.
faq.q: Why do names and descriptions matter in generative orchestration?

faq.a: The episode "MCP Custom Connector in Copilot Studio: The Complete Integration Guide" lists Generative Orchestration being enabled in the Copilot Studio environment as one of the requirements for the integration.
faq.q: Is generative orchestration required for connecting an MCP server?

generative-orchestration.long:
Generative orchestration is an orchestration mode in Microsoft Copilot Studio. In this mode, a large language model decides which tools, topics or knowledge sources to use in order to handle a given request. The model makes this choice based on the names and descriptions of the available components, so those descriptions work as the main signal that guides how an agent routes a request.

The concept matters because it changes how an agent is built and maintained. In a more rule-driven approach, a request is matched to a predefined path. With generative orchestration, the agent's behavior depends on how clearly each tool, topic and knowledge source is named and described. A component with a vague or misleading description is harder for the model to select correctly, while a precise description helps the model pick the right capability for the request. This is why the topic is closely tied to design choices such as naming conventions, scoping of tools and the quality of the knowledge that is connected to an agent.

Generative orchestration appears as a prerequisite or a recommended setting in several integration scenarios discussed on M365.FM. The episode "MCP Custom Connector in Copilot Studio: The Complete Integration Guide" lists Generative Orchestration as one of the requirements for connecting an MCP server to Copilot Studio. According to the episode, the checklist includes access to Microsoft Copilot Studio with the System Customizer or System Administrator role, together with Generative Orchestration being enabled in the Copilot Studio environment. In that context, enabling the mode is a precondition for the integration steps that follow.

The episode "Automate Document Processing with Microsoft Syntex" mentions generative orchestration in the context of improving how an agent handles queries. Among the tips it lists are enabling Generative Orchestration for better query handling, indexing content in SharePoint so that Copilot can find current information, focusing on internal SharePoint data rather than general AI knowledge, and avoiding unsupported file types. The episode also advises testing workflows with real examples, cleaning up old or duplicate content, and monitoring settings so they can be adjusted for performance. Here, generative orchestration is one part of a wider set of practices around retrieval and content quality.

The episode "Will Copilot Studio Replace Low-Code Developers?" places the concept within a broader shift toward multi-agent systems. The episode recommends moving from single-agent setups to coordinated agent ecosystems and using both classic and generative orchestration methods depending on needs. This framing treats generative orchestration not as a replacement for every other approach but as one option alongside classic orchestration, chosen according to the situation. The episode also connects this to change management, saying that each agent should contribute to larger business outcomes and that teams need to adapt to new processes and mindsets.

In practice, decisions around generative orchestration usually come down to a few questions. One is whether the agent should let a model choose among components or follow a more fixed path. Another is how components are named and described, since those texts guide the model's choice. A third is which knowledge sources and tools are connected, and whether the required environment settings and roles are in place. The M365.FM episodes treat the mode as an enabling setting for agent integrations and for query handling, and as one of two orchestration styles that can be combined within a larger design of collaborating agents.

generative-pages.desc: Generative pages are a Power Apps feature from Microsoft that uses AI to build Dataverse-aware app pages from a plain-English description.

faq.a: Generative pages are a Power Apps feature from Microsoft that uses AI to generate app pages from a natural-language description. The generated pages are responsive and work with Dataverse data.
faq.q: What are generative pages in Power Apps?

faq.a: According to the episode "Govern Power Apps Generative Pages After Edit Code", opening the code ends the shielding of the managed experience. The maker then takes on npm drift, security patches, schema changes and authentication gaps.
faq.q: What happens when someone uses Edit Code on a generative page?

faq.a: The episode "Avoid the Generative Pages Power Apps Licensing Trap" says that generating a page puts the app on Dataverse, which it describes as premium territory. It recommends planning the architecture and environments deliberately to avoid unexpected license costs.
faq.q: Do generative pages affect Power Apps licensing?

generative-pages.long:
Generative pages are a Power Apps feature that generates app pages from a natural-language description on top of Dataverse data, using AI. A maker describes the page in plain English, and the result is a responsive page that reads and writes Dataverse data. The feature is developed by Microsoft, is part of Power Apps and is classed as a low-code tool. It is also known as Power Apps generative pages.

The feature is used to shorten the path from an idea to a working page. Instead of arranging containers and writing formulas by hand, as is typical in canvas apps, the maker states an intent, for example an ideas tracker with category filters and a bar chart. The AI then produces a page bound to Dataverse. Because the data layer is Dataverse, the generated page respects the metadata and roles defined there, which is the basis for the governance benefits described in the episodes. Generative pages are the Power Apps form of vibe coding and sit alongside Microsoft 365 Copilot in the broader AI-assisted experience.

The M365.FM episode "Create Power Apps Faster with Generative Pages" describes the change as a shift from craft to command. It contrasts canvas apps, which offer pixel-level freedom but can become fragile through many containers and brittle Power FX, with generated pages that are described as responsive, accessible, Dataverse-aware and themed with tokens. The episode says developers do not disappear but move toward owning schema, governance, performance and policy while AI handles layout.

A central decision is when to use generative pages and when to build the interface manually. The episode "Canvas App UI vs Generative Pages: Which Should You Use?" lists speed, consistency, accessibility and built-in governance through Dataverse metadata and roles as upsides. It also names risks: generated output can be read-only, prompt ambiguity can produce unexpected results, and licensing can be hidden. According to the episode, real efficiency comes from standard prompts, governed environments and treating language like source code, and manual UI remains the better choice where fine-grained interaction control is needed.

The episode "Govern Power Apps Generative Pages After Edit Code" focuses on what happens after generation. It says that the Edit Code option exposes the generated React code, and that once a maker opens it, Power Apps no longer shields them from the consequences. The episode lists npm drift, security patches, schema changes, authentication gaps and AI assistance that can overwrite intent as responsibilities the maker then inherits. Its recommendation is to keep declarative, safe work in the managed experience and to fence pro-code for exceptions, with the point that AI can generate pages but not governance.

Licensing is the third recurring theme. The episode "Avoid the Generative Pages Power Apps Licensing Trap" explains that generating a page puts the app on Dataverse, which it describes as premium territory, so an experience that looks free can change the license requirements for everyone who uses it. The episode suggests reserving Dataverse for genuine relational needs, isolating premium workloads in dedicated environments, keeping virtual tables read-only and locking sharing until finance has signed off.

Generative pages also appear in the episode "Enterprise AI Experiences in Power Apps with Sara Lagerquist [MVP]", in the context of designing user interfaces for AI applications. There they are presented as a way to build complex interfaces quickly with AI assistance, which can accelerate development and allow customization to fit specific needs. Taken together, the episodes treat generative pages as a fast way to create Dataverse-backed pages that still require decisions about governance, code ownership and licensing.

gentle-ai.desc: Gentle AI is open-source AI tooling by Alan Buscaglia under Gentleman Programming, described as a set of harnesses and reasoning approaches for coding agents.
gentle-ai.long:
Gentle AI is an open-source AI tooling project created by Alan Buscaglia under the Gentleman Programming name. It is described as a collection of harnesses and ways of thinking and reasoning for coding agents.

In that description, the project focuses on how coding agents are structured and guided, rather than on a single application. A harness, in this context, refers to the scaffolding around an agent, and the reasoning approaches refer to how the agent is encouraged to think through a task.

The available information about Gentle AI is limited. No official site, documentation link, version details or feature list are provided in the source facts, so this page does not describe specific capabilities, installation steps or supported tools.

Gentle AI is mentioned in an episode of M365.FM, where it is characterized in the terms above. No related Microsoft products or topics are linked to it in the current knowledge base.

gentleman-programming.desc: Gentleman Programming is a Spanish-speaking developer community and content channel by Alan Buscaglia covering programming, software architecture and AI-assisted development.

faq.a: Gentleman Programming is a Spanish-speaking developer community and content channel created by Alan Buscaglia. It covers programming, software architecture and AI-assisted development across YouTube, Twitch, Discord and GitHub.
faq.q: What is Gentleman Programming?

faq.a: Alan Buscaglia created Gentleman Programming. M365.FM describes him as an MVP and as the creator of the Gentleman Programming YouTube channel.
faq.q: Who is behind Gentleman Programming?

faq.a: The episode "From AI Hype to AI Harness Engineering – Building AI That People Can Actually Trust with Alan Buscaglia [MVP] from Gentleman Programming" discusses why enterprise AI success depends on more than choosing the latest language model. It describes AI Harness Engineering as an approach to building AI systems that are secure, governed, observable and trustworthy.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode with Alan Buscaglia discuss?

gentleman-programming.long:
Gentleman Programming is a Spanish-speaking developer community and content channel created by Alan Buscaglia. It covers programming, software architecture and AI-assisted development, and it is present on several platforms: YouTube, Twitch, Discord and GitHub. The name refers both to the channel and to the community that has formed around it, so the term can mean the video content, the live streams, the chat server or the open-source repositories, depending on the context.

The topics of Gentleman Programming sit at the intersection of everyday software development and the growing role of AI tools in that work. Software architecture is one of the recurring subjects, and so is AI-assisted development, meaning the use of AI systems to support how code is planned, written and reviewed. Because the material is produced for a Spanish-speaking audience, it fills a language niche in a field where much of the learning content is published in English. The mix of platforms reflects different formats: video for structured explanations, live streaming for real-time work and discussion, Discord for community conversation, and GitHub for code and shared projects.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, Gentleman Programming appears mainly through its creator. M365.FM published the episode "From AI Hype to AI Harness Engineering – Building AI That People Can Actually Trust with Alan Buscaglia [MVP] from Gentleman Programming". In that episode Alan Buscaglia, who is credited as an MVP and as the creator of the Gentleman Programming YouTube channel, discusses why enterprise AI success depends on far more than choosing the latest language model. The conversation moves from AI hype toward what the episode calls AI Harness Engineering, a practical approach to building AI systems that are secure, governed, observable and trustworthy. The excerpt also indicates that the discussion touches on why prompt engineering alone is not enough, which fits the broader theme of building dependable AI rather than relying on a single model choice.

That episode is referenced by several other M365.FM episodes as a related listen, which shows how the AI harness idea connects to neighbouring topics. "Microsoft AI Agent Harness - Simply Explained" lists it alongside episodes on agent-to-agent communication, Microsoft Agent Builder and Microsoft Entra Agent ID. "Platform Engineering - Simply Explained" and "Platform Engineering: The New Operating Model for Azure" both point to it as well, linking the harness concept to platform engineering and to an operating model for enterprise AI. "Compliance as Code: The Architect's Blueprint for Automated Trust" also cites the episode, next to material on Infrastructure as Code, CI-CD governance and Zero Trust. Taken together, these cross-references place the Gentleman Programming conversation within a cluster about governance, automation and trust in AI systems.

For readers deciding how to approach the topic, the relevant points are practical. Someone looking for Spanish-language programming and architecture content can use the Gentleman Programming channels directly. Someone responsible for enterprise AI in a Microsoft environment can use the M365.FM episode as an introduction to the argument that security, governance and observability matter as much as model selection. The related episodes on agents, platform engineering and compliance as code give further context on the same themes from the Microsoft side.

ghost-agents.desc: Ghost agents are AI agents that keep running, consuming tokens and holding access after their project has ended and their owner has moved on.

faq.a: Ghost agents are AI agents that keep running after their project has ended and their owner has moved on. They continue to consume tokens and hold access without anyone actively responsible for them.
faq.q: What are ghost agents?

faq.a: They create cost, because they keep consuming tokens, and security risk, because they retain access to systems and data after they are no longer needed.
faq.q: Why are ghost agents a problem?

faq.a: The topic appears in the episode "The Death of the Chatbot: Why Your Dataverse Strategy Is Broken", published on 2026-07-29.
faq.q: Where are ghost agents covered on M365.FM?

ghost-agents.long:
Ghost agents are AI agents that continue to operate after the project they were built for has ended and the person who owned them has moved on. Because nobody is responsible for them any longer, they keep consuming tokens and retain the access they were originally granted.

The concept points to two kinds of risk. The first is cost: an agent that is still running continues to use tokens even though it no longer serves a purpose. The second is security: an agent that still holds access to systems and data represents an exposure that no one is actively reviewing or managing.

The term is relevant to anyone who deploys or governs AI agents, since agents can outlive the initiative that created them if ownership and lifecycle are not tracked. Identifying owners, reviewing access and retiring agents that are no longer needed are the practical concerns the idea draws attention to.

Ghost agents are discussed on M365.FM in the episode "The Death of the Chatbot: Why Your Dataverse Strategy Is Broken" (2026-07-29).

git.desc: Git is a distributed version control system that records changes to project files over time, letting teams compare versions, revert changes and collaborate on shared code.

faq.a: Git is a distributed version control system that records changes to project files over time. It allows teams to compare versions, revert changes and collaborate on the same code.
faq.q: What is Git?

faq.a: Git is used to track the history of project files and to support collaboration. Teams rely on it to compare versions, undo changes and work together on shared code.
faq.q: What is Git used for?

git.long:
Git is a distributed version control system. It records changes to project files over time, so that earlier versions can be compared, restored or reverted when needed.

The main use of Git is collaboration on code. Because it tracks the history of a project, several people can work on the same set of files while keeping a record of who changed what and when. Teams use this history to review modifications, undo unwanted changes and keep a clear picture of how a project has developed.

On M365.FM, Git is listed as a product entity within the Microsoft ecosystem knowledge base. No related topics, linked episodes or official documentation links are currently associated with this entry, so this page limits itself to a basic definition of the tool and its purpose.

git-branch.desc: A branch in Git is a separate line of work that starts from an existing version of a project and is later merged back into the main line of development.

faq.a: A branch is a separate line of work in a version control system such as Git. It starts from an existing version and is later merged back.
faq.q: What is a branch in Git?

faq.a: Branches allow work to proceed on a separate line, starting from an existing version, without changing that original version directly. The work can then be merged back when it is ready.
faq.q: Why are branches used in version control?

git-branch.long:
A branch in Git is a separate line of work within a version control system. It starts from an existing version of the project and develops independently of other lines of work, so changes can be made without directly altering the version it was created from.

Branches are used to keep different pieces of work apart, for example when several changes are developed at the same time. Once the work on a branch is complete, it is later merged back, which brings the changes into another line of work. This pattern is a basic part of how version control systems such as Git are used to organize collaboration and track changes.

This page describes the general concept only. No related topics or specific episodes on M365.FM are linked to the Branch (Git) entry at this time.

gitflow.desc: Gitflow is a Git branching model by Vincent Driessen (2010) using master and develop plus feature, release and hotfix branches for versioned software.

faq.a: Gitflow uses two permanent branches, master (or main) and develop, plus feature, release and hotfix branches. Feature branches start from develop, release branches fork from develop for stabilization, and hotfix branches fork from main to patch production.
faq.q: What branches does Gitflow use?

faq.a: It suits software that ships in numbered versions, projects with scheduled release cycles, and teams that want separate release and development phases with pull-request review. Atlassian describes it as a legacy workflow that is harder to combine with continuous integration and delivery.
faq.q: When is Gitflow a suitable choice?

faq.a: The episode "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD" names Gitflow as an example of a strong branching strategy for managing development, releases and hotfixes, alongside advice to use separate branches per feature and to require code reviews before merging.
faq.q: How does the M365.FM episode on Fabric CI/CD refer to Gitflow?

gitflow.long:
Gitflow is a Git branching model published by Vincent Driessen in 2010. It assigns defined roles to branches so that development, release preparation and production fixes are kept apart. The model uses two permanent branches, master and develop, plus three kinds of supporting branches: feature, release and hotfix. It is intended for software that ships in numbered versions.

In the common description of the workflow, the main branch (called master in the original model) holds the official release history and is usually tagged with version numbers. The develop branch is the integration branch where finished features come together. Feature branches start from develop and are merged back into it when the work is complete. When enough features are ready for a release, a release branch is forked from develop. That branch is used for stabilization only, such as bug fixes and documentation. It is then merged into main with a tag and also merged back into develop so that the fixes are not lost. Hotfix branches fork directly from main to patch a problem in production and are merged into both main and develop.

Gitflow adds no new Git commands beyond the feature branch workflow; it only defines roles for branches. A git-flow extension exists that wraps the individual steps into shorter commands. The model fits projects with scheduled release cycles, teams that want separate release and development phases, and teams that use code review through pull requests.

There are trade-offs. Atlassian's tutorial labels Gitflow a legacy workflow that has fallen out of favor compared with trunk-based development. Long-lived branches can lead to hard merges and drift between branches, and the model is harder to combine with continuous integration and continuous delivery. Teams that deploy continuously therefore weigh these costs against the clear separation of releases that Gitflow provides.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, Gitflow comes up in discussions of source control for CI/CD. The M365.FM episode "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD" mentions it as an example of a strong branching strategy that helps manage development, releases and hotfixes. The episode also advises keeping separate branches for each developer or feature to avoid merge conflicts, and requiring code reviews before merging so that other team members check and approve updates. It adds that Microsoft Fabric lets users compare the content of source and target workspaces before deploying changes, which helps catch mistakes early and keeps environments consistent.

When choosing a branching model, the main decision is how releases are delivered. Gitflow suits numbered, scheduled releases with a stabilization phase. For teams that integrate and deploy frequently, the sources point to trunk-based development as the approach that has largely replaced it. In either case, the practices the episode stresses, such as isolated branches and reviewed merges, apply to how changes move through a deployment pipeline.

github.desc: GitHub is a platform for hosting code and collaborating on software projects, and it is part of Microsoft; M365.FM episodes cover Copilot, CI/CD and version control.

faq.a: GitHub is a platform for hosting code and collaborating on software projects. It is part of Microsoft and is used to store repositories, review changes through pull requests and coordinate shared work.
faq.q: What is GitHub?

faq.a: GitHub Copilot brings AI help into the development workflow. M365.FM episodes describe it moving from autocomplete and chat toward agents that inspect repositories, change multiple files, run tests and create pull requests.
faq.q: How does GitHub relate to GitHub Copilot?

faq.a: Yes. M365.FM episodes cover GitHub Actions for Power Platform ALM and GitHub as one of the Git options for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD, alongside Azure DevOps.
faq.q: Can GitHub be used for CI/CD in the Microsoft ecosystem?

github.long:
GitHub is a platform for hosting code and collaborating on software projects. It is part of Microsoft. Teams use it to store repositories, review changes through pull requests and coordinate work on shared code. Within the Microsoft ecosystem it appears in several roles: as the home of source code, as the place where AI-assisted development happens through GitHub Copilot, and as a base for automated build and deployment workflows.

In day-to-day use, GitHub gives a team a shared location for a codebase and a structured way to change it. Contributors propose modifications, colleagues review them, and the history of the project stays traceable. This version-control foundation is also what other tools build on. Several M365.FM episodes treat GitHub less as a standalone product and more as a connection point between development work and the wider Microsoft platform, including Azure, Microsoft Fabric and the Power Platform.

AI-assisted development is one of the topics the episodes return to. "GitHub Copilot, Clean Context, Automated Testing & AI Coding Agents with Lars Gyrup Brink Nielsen [MVP]" describes how AI help is moving beyond autocomplete and chat. According to the episode description, modern AI coding agents can inspect repositories, modify files, run tests, analyze failures, create pull requests and execute increasingly complex development tasks. The conversation is between Mirko Peters and Microsoft MVP Lars Gyrup Brink Nielsen. A related episode, "Use GitHub Copilot Agent Mode for Multi-File Changes", is a hands-on walkthrough inside a real .NET and Azure solution. The episode says agent mode holds cross-file context, so that services, bindings, dependency injection, configuration and infrastructure can be updated in one coordinated flow. It shows a before and after diff and presents the agents as a way to focus on building features rather than fixing scattered errors, not as a replacement for developers.

GitHub also plays a role in continuous integration and delivery. "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD" explains how Microsoft Fabric Git integration connects to both Azure DevOps and GitHub. The episode describes the benefits as version control, automated deployments and an end-to-end CI/CD workflow, with Git integration bringing collaboration, code tracking and environment consistency to the process. The comparison in the title reflects a common decision: which of the two services should host the repositories and pipelines for a given project.

The same pattern appears for low-code and reporting work. "Power BI Version Control with GitHub and Azure DevOps" looks at how teams can bring version control to Power BI, where datasets, dataflows and models are shared between people and benefit from being built once and reused. "Set Up Power Platform ALM with GitHub Actions" addresses application lifecycle management for the Power Platform. The episode names typical reasons deployments fail, such as connector references, environment variables and manual imports. It describes wiring service principals and scoped secrets, and structuring GitHub workflows with triggers, jobs and environment-specific vaults so solutions can be validated, remapped and deployed from dev to test to prod in an auditable way.

Taken together, the episodes position GitHub as a central tool for source control, review, automation and AI-assisted coding across Azure, Fabric, Power BI and the Power Platform.
