Choosing between GitHub and Azure DevOps, and deciding how far to trust AI agents with multi-file changes, are the practical questions the episodes raise.

github-actions.desc: GitHub Actions is a CI/CD and automation service built into GitHub that runs workflows defined with a project whenever events such as pushes or pull requests occur.

faq.a: GitHub Actions is used for CI/CD and automation inside GitHub. Workflows run automatically when events such as a push or pull request happen, and they can also be used to deploy solutions, for example in Power Platform ALM.
faq.q: What is GitHub Actions used for?

faq.a: The instructions live in files stored with the project. A workflow is built from jobs, and each job consists of steps, as explained in the episode "GitHub Actions - Simply Explained".
faq.q: Where are GitHub Actions workflows defined?

faq.a: The episode "Set Up Power Platform ALM with GitHub Actions" shows how workflows, service principals and scoped secrets can be used to validate and deploy Power Platform solutions across dev, test and prod in a repeatable way.
faq.q: How does GitHub Actions relate to Power Platform?

github-actions.long:
GitHub Actions is a CI/CD and automation service built into GitHub. It runs work automatically whenever something happens in a project, such as a push or a pull request. The service was developed by GitHub and is classed as a developer tool. According to the knowledge base it was released on 2019-11-13 and is listed as free. It is also referred to simply as Actions.

The core idea is that the instructions live together with the project. Workflows are defined in files stored in the repository, so the automation is versioned alongside the code it acts on. Each workflow is made of jobs, and each job is made of steps. What starts a workflow is an event in the project. The episode "GitHub Actions - Simply Explained" walks through exactly these parts: what GitHub Actions really is, where the instructions live, what wakes it up through events, and how jobs and steps work, including the role of runners and reusable building blocks.

A central feature is the large supply of ready-made building blocks, which are themselves called actions. The episode "GitHub Actions - Simply Explained" notes that more than ten thousand of them are available inside GitHub and that they plug into GitHub Actions, which then runs the work whenever something happens in the project. Instead of writing every step from scratch, a workflow can combine these existing actions with its own steps. The naming can be confusing, since the service is called GitHub Actions while the individual reusable pieces are called actions.

The episodes show the service used well beyond plain software builds. In "Set Up Power Platform ALM with GitHub Actions", it is applied to application lifecycle management for Power Platform. That episode explains why such deployments tend to fail, pointing to connector references, environment variables and human-led imports, and it describes how to wire up service principals and scoped secrets. It also covers structuring GitHub workflows with triggers, jobs and environment-specific vaults so that solutions are validated, remapped and deployed predictably across dev, test and prod. The stated aim is reliable, auditable releases in which every step is visible and every secret is controlled.

This points to a typical pattern around the product: GitHub Actions is commonly combined with secrets storage and service principals so that pipelines can deploy safely without people importing artifacts by hand. Decisions that come up in practice include which events should trigger a workflow, how to separate jobs per environment, and how to scope secrets so each stage only has the access it needs.

The name also appears in neighboring topics that should not be mixed up with it. The episode "Automate Real-Time Actions with Fabric Data Activator" is about turning live signals in Microsoft Fabric into automated actions, and it is listed alongside GitHub Actions because of the shared theme of automation. Likewise, "Use Copilot Studio Actions for Business Automation" and "Microsoft Copilot Actions - Simply Explained" deal with actions in the Copilot context rather than with the GitHub service. Official documentation for GitHub Actions is available in the GitHub docs under the Actions section.

github-advanced-security.desc: GitHub Advanced Security is GitHub's security offering for repositories, covering code scanning, secret scanning and dependency checks for GitHub Enterprise and Azure DevOps.

faq.a: For GitHub Enterprise it consists of GitHub Code Security and GitHub Secret Protection. These cover code scanning, secret scanning with push protection, dependency updates, security campaigns and a security overview across repositories.
faq.q: What does GitHub Advanced Security include?

faq.a: No. It is described as the native static application security testing offering for both GitHub Enterprise and Azure DevOps, and it is sold as an add-on for GitHub Enterprise Cloud, GitHub Enterprise Server and Azure DevOps.
faq.q: Is GitHub Advanced Security only for GitHub?

faq.a: Autofix is built on GitHub Copilot and suggests targeted fixes for the alerts raised by code scanning, so developers can address vulnerabilities and coding errors while they work.
faq.q: What is Autofix in GitHub Advanced Security?

github-advanced-security.long:
GitHub Advanced Security is a security offering for source code repositories. It combines code scanning, secret scanning and dependency checks so that developers are alerted to leaked secrets and vulnerable packages while they work. According to Microsoft Azure material, it is presented as the native static application security testing offering for GitHub Enterprise and Azure DevOps, and it is sold as an add-on for GitHub Enterprise Cloud, GitHub Enterprise Server and Azure DevOps.

For GitHub Enterprise, the offering consists of two parts: GitHub Code Security and GitHub Secret Protection. Secret scanning with push protection looks for many types of tokens from a wide range of service providers, which targets credentials that are accidentally committed to a repository. Code scanning analyzes the code in GitHub repositories for vulnerabilities and coding errors. Autofix, which is built on GitHub Copilot, suggests targeted fixes for the alerts that code scanning raises, so a finding can come with a proposed change rather than only a warning.

The supply-chain side of the offering covers dependencies. Automated security updates and version updates help keep the packages a project relies on current, and dependency checks flag packages with known vulnerabilities. Security campaigns group many alerts together so that fixes can be generated for them at the same time, which is relevant when a large number of findings accumulate across a codebase. A security overview shows the security posture across repositories, giving a consolidated view rather than a repository-by-repository one.

A connection to Microsoft Defender for Cloud links code to runtime context. This ties findings in source code to what is running in the cloud environment, so that the development side and the operations side of security can be read together. The stated goal of the offering is to let developers fix vulnerabilities while they are working, instead of discovering them late in the delivery process. The available documentation summary does not give pricing, supported languages or scan configuration details, so those points need to be checked against current official material before planning a rollout.

In practice, the product comes up when teams choose between GitHub and Azure DevOps as their source control and CI/CD platform. The M365.FM episode "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD" (published 2025-11-03) discusses this comparison in the context of Microsoft Fabric. The episode says both platforms offer enterprise capabilities. It describes Azure DevOps as providing fine-grained access control, Azure AD integration and advanced compliance features, while GitHub Enterprise Cloud includes enterprise managed users and GitHub Advanced Security for Azure, which brings code scanning, secret scanning and dependency management. The episode frames the choice as dependent on organizational needs: Azure DevOps may integrate better with existing Microsoft tooling, while GitHub provides stronger open-source and community features plus advanced security options.

Because GitHub Advanced Security is available for both GitHub Enterprise and Azure DevOps, the security capabilities do not by themselves decide which platform a team uses. Decisions around it typically involve which repositories and pipelines should be covered, how alerts are triaged, and how findings from code scanning and secret scanning fit into existing review and release processes. Teams evaluating the product usually also weigh licensing as an add-on, since it is sold separately from the underlying GitHub or Azure DevOps plans.

github-copilot.desc: GitHub Copilot is an AI coding assistant from GitHub that suggests code, explains it, writes tests and carries out multi-step changes in agent mode.

faq.a: GitHub Copilot is a paid AI coding assistant from GitHub. It suggests and explains code, writes tests and, in agent mode, performs multi-step changes in a repository under the developer's review.
faq.q: What is GitHub Copilot?

faq.a: In agent mode, Copilot carries out multi-step changes across a repository. The M365.FM episode on multi-file changes shows it updating services, configuration and infrastructure in one coordinated flow in a .NET and Azure solution.
faq.q: What does agent mode do in GitHub Copilot?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Is Microsoft 365 Copilot Worth the Cost?", GitHub Copilot complements Microsoft 365 Copilot by serving developer workflows, while Microsoft 365 Copilot is embedded in Teams and Office apps.
faq.q: How does GitHub Copilot differ from Microsoft 365 Copilot?

github-copilot.long:
GitHub Copilot is an AI coding assistant developed by GitHub. It suggests code, explains existing code and writes tests, and in agent mode it carries out multi-step changes in a repository while the developer stays in control and reviews the result. It is a paid product, released in 2022, and it is classified both as an AI assistant and as a developer tool.

The core idea is that the assistant works inside the developer's normal environment instead of replacing it. Day to day, that means getting suggestions while writing code, asking for an explanation of an unfamiliar piece of code, or generating tests for existing logic. The M365.FM episode "GitHub Copilot - Simply Explained" frames the topic for newcomers and challenges the common assumption that Copilot simply writes code so that nobody else has to. The episode covers what Copilot actually is, three ways to talk to it, how it knows about your code, what it costs, privacy and ownership of the code, and typical beginner mistakes.

Agent mode extends this from single suggestions to coordinated work across a repository. The episode "Use GitHub Copilot Agent Mode for Multi-File Changes" demonstrates this inside a .NET and Azure solution. Instead of fixing one file at a time, the agent holds context across files and updates services, bindings, dependency injection, configuration and infrastructure in one flow. The walkthrough presents a before-and-after diff and argues that multi-file errors can be resolved faster this way. The same episode stresses that such agents do not replace developers; they let developers focus on building features rather than fixing scattered problems.

The topic goes further in "GitHub Copilot, Clean Context, Automated Testing & AI Coding Agents with Lars Gyrup Brink Nielsen [MVP]". According to the episode description, AI-assisted development is moving beyond autocomplete and chat. Modern AI coding agents can inspect repositories, modify files, run tests, analyze failures, create pull requests and execute increasingly complex development tasks. Clean context and automated testing appear in the title as themes of the conversation between Mirko Peters and Microsoft MVP Lars Gyrup Brink Nielsen.

GitHub Copilot is also related to several wider concepts. The agent harness is the software around a model that lets it use tools, which is the layer that makes agent behavior such as running tests or editing files possible. The agentic software development lifecycle describes a way of working in which AI agents take part in the stages of software delivery, with GitHub Copilot as one practical example. Microsoft Foundry is a related topic in the Microsoft ecosystem.

Grounding is another recurring theme. The episode "Grounding Microsoft Copilot for Trusted Enterprise AI" notes that developers rely on grounded copilots to access accurate information and streamline their workflows, and it describes a grounding gap that arises when AI lacks access to an organization's specific data. In that discussion GitHub Copilot is named alongside Microsoft Copilot as a tool whose usefulness depends on connecting to the organization's systems. The episode "Is Microsoft 365 Copilot Worth the Cost?" separates the two products: it describes GitHub Copilot as a solution that complements Microsoft 365 Copilot for developer workflows.

Typical decisions around GitHub Copilot include how far to let the assistant act on its own, how to review agent-made changes, and how to handle privacy and code ownership. The sources consistently place the developer in the reviewing role: suggestions and agent changes are reviewed before they are accepted.

github-copilot-agent-mode.desc: GitHub Copilot agent mode lets developers hand Copilot a goal; it opens files, edits code and runs commands to check its work, with developer review.

faq.a: It is a mode of GitHub Copilot where the developer gives a goal instead of a question. The agent decides which files to open, makes edits and runs commands to check its own work until the task is finished.
faq.q: What is GitHub Copilot agent mode?

faq.a: No. The changes it makes still need to be reviewed by the developer. The M365.FM episodes describe agents as supporting developers rather than replacing them.
faq.q: Does agent mode remove the need for code review?

faq.a: The episode "Use GitHub Copilot Agent Mode for Multi-File Changes" shows agent mode in a real .NET and Azure solution, updating services, bindings, dependency injection, configs and infrastructure in one coordinated flow, with a before and after diff.
faq.q: What kind of changes does the M365.FM episode demonstrate?

github-copilot-agent-mode.long:
GitHub Copilot agent mode is a mode of GitHub Copilot in which a developer hands over a goal instead of asking a single question. Rather than answering one prompt and waiting for the next, it decides which files to open, makes the edits itself and runs commands to check its own work until the task is finished. It is part of GitHub Copilot, and its changes still need to be reviewed by the developer before they are accepted.

The difference from a conversational assistant lies in who drives the steps. In a chat-style exchange, the developer chooses the file, pastes the code and applies the suggestion. In agent mode, the developer states the outcome and the agent works out the sequence: locating the relevant files, changing them, and running commands such as builds or tests to see whether the change holds up. Because it can check its own output, it can iterate until the result matches the goal, instead of leaving verification entirely to the person.

This matters most for work that spans several files. A change that touches a service, its bindings, dependency injection registration, configuration and infrastructure definitions normally means keeping the context of all those pieces in mind at once, and a missed edit in one place surfaces later as a rebuild failure. The M365.FM episode "Use GitHub Copilot Agent Mode for Multi-File Changes" (3 November 2025) walks through this scenario inside a real .NET and Azure solution. The episode describes agent mode holding cross-file context and updating services, bindings, DI, configs and infra in one coordinated flow, and it presents a before and after diff to show how multi-file errors resolve faster. It frames the problem as patchwork debugging that consumes a day through many small rebuilds, and positions agents as tools that help developers focus on building features rather than fixing broken wiring. The episode also stresses that these agents do not replace developers but support them.

Typical situations for using agent mode are refactors, cross-cutting configuration changes and tasks where a single logical change ripples through several layers of an application. A developer describes the goal in plain language, the agent proposes and applies edits across the affected files, and the developer then reads the resulting diff. Review remains the control point: the agent can run commands to validate its work, but acceptance of the changes stays with the person responsible for the code.

Decisions around adopting agent mode therefore concern scope and oversight rather than replacement of skills. Teams weigh which tasks are well-defined enough to hand over as a goal, how closely to inspect the generated diffs, and how the agent's command execution fits into their existing build and test practices. Since the developer remains accountable for what gets merged, reviewing every multi-file change carefully is part of using the mode as intended.

Agent mode also appears in the wider conversation about AI agents in the Microsoft ecosystem. The episode "Multi-Agent AI with Copilot Studio and David Lorenzo Lopez [MVP]" (15 June 2026) and "Multi-Agent AI with Microsoft Copilot and SharePoint – Reshmee Auckloo [MVP]" (6 July 2026) list the multi-file changes episode among related listening. Those episodes address multi-agent patterns in Copilot Studio and SharePoint, which are separate from the developer-focused coding workflow, but they sit in the same theme of agents that act on a goal instead of answering one question at a time.

github-copilot-cli.desc: GitHub Copilot CLI brings GitHub Copilot to the terminal as an agent that takes natural-language tasks, plans the steps and runs commands in the local environment.

faq.a: GitHub Copilot CLI brings GitHub Copilot to the terminal as an agent. It accepts natural-language tasks, plans the steps and runs commands in the local environment.
faq.q: What is GitHub Copilot CLI?

faq.a: GitHub Copilot CLI is part of GitHub Copilot. It extends Copilot's capabilities to the command-line terminal.
faq.q: How does GitHub Copilot CLI relate to GitHub Copilot?

faq.a: It takes a task described in natural language, plans the required steps and executes commands in the local environment to carry them out.
faq.q: What does GitHub Copilot CLI do with a task?

github-copilot-cli.long:
GitHub Copilot CLI is a command-line product that brings GitHub Copilot to the terminal. It works as an agent: a user describes a task in natural language, and the tool plans the steps needed to complete it and runs commands in the local environment.

The product is part of GitHub Copilot, the broader family of AI-assisted tools from GitHub. Placing the agent in the terminal allows task descriptions to be turned into concrete command-line actions without leaving the shell. Instead of looking up syntax or writing each command by hand, a user can state the intended outcome and let the agent work out and carry out the sequence of steps.

The available information about GitHub Copilot CLI is limited to this description. Details such as supported platforms, installation methods, pricing, available models or configuration options are not covered here and should be checked against official GitHub documentation.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity.

github-copilot-coding-agent.desc: GitHub Copilot coding agent is a part of GitHub Copilot that works asynchronously on tasks such as assigned issues and delivers changes as a pull request.
github-copilot-coding-agent.long:
GitHub Copilot coding agent is a capability within GitHub Copilot that works on development tasks asynchronously. Instead of responding line by line inside an editor, it takes on a task, such as a GitHub issue assigned to it, and carries out the work in a cloud environment.

The results are delivered as a pull request. This keeps the outcome in the usual GitHub review flow, so a person can examine the proposed changes before anything is accepted. The human review step is a defining part of how the agent's output is handled.

GitHub Copilot coding agent is part of the broader GitHub Copilot product family, which is the context in which it is offered and described. Readers looking for background on the wider set of Copilot features should consult the GitHub Copilot entity.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity, and no official documentation or site links are listed here. Further details such as supported task types, configuration, availability or pricing are not stated in the available facts and are therefore not covered on this page.

github-copilot-for-azure.desc: GitHub Copilot for Azure is a GitHub Copilot extension that lets developers use natural language to learn about Azure, deploy resources and diagnose problems.

faq.a: GitHub Copilot for Azure is a GitHub Copilot extension that lets developers use natural language to learn about Azure, deploy resources and diagnose problems.
faq.q: What is GitHub Copilot for Azure?

faq.a: Yes. According to its description, it can generate infrastructure-as-code scaffolding as a starting point for defining Azure resources.
faq.q: Can GitHub Copilot for Azure generate infrastructure as code?

faq.a: It is part of GitHub Copilot, working as an extension that adds Azure-focused capabilities to the assistant.
faq.q: How does GitHub Copilot for Azure relate to GitHub Copilot?

github-copilot-for-azure.long:
GitHub Copilot for Azure is an extension for GitHub Copilot that allows developers to work with Azure through natural language. Instead of switching between documentation, portals and command-line tools, a developer can ask questions and give instructions in a chat-style interaction.

According to its description, the extension supports three main kinds of tasks: learning about Azure, deploying resources, and diagnosing problems. It can also generate infrastructure-as-code scaffolding, which gives developers a starting point for defining Azure resources in code. The product is part of GitHub Copilot and extends that assistant with Azure-specific capabilities.

GitHub Copilot for Azure is relevant to developers, platform engineers and cloud practitioners who build and operate workloads on Azure and want help from an AI assistant within their existing GitHub Copilot workflow. Official documentation is available on Microsoft Learn under the Azure developer section for GitHub Copilot for Azure.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity.

github-copilot-sdk.desc: The GitHub Copilot SDK lets developers embed the agent runtime behind GitHub Copilot CLI into their own apps and services, with custom tools and agents.

faq.a: It is a multi-platform SDK for embedding the Copilot agent in apps and services, exposing the same engine as the Copilot CLI as a programmable agent runtime. Developers define agent behaviour while Copilot handles planning, tool calls and file edits.
faq.q: What is the GitHub Copilot SDK?

faq.a: SDKs exist for Node.js and TypeScript, Python, Go, .NET, Rust and Java. The Copilot CLI is bundled for Node.js, Python and .NET, but must be installed separately for Go, Java and Rust.
faq.q: Which programming languages does the GitHub Copilot SDK support?

faq.a: A Copilot subscription is required unless bring-your-own-key is used. That option supports providers such as OpenAI, Microsoft Foundry and Anthropic with key-based authentication only.
faq.q: Is a Copilot subscription required to use the GitHub Copilot SDK?

github-copilot-sdk.long:
The GitHub Copilot SDK is a multi-platform software development kit for embedding the Copilot agent in applications and services. It belongs to GitHub Copilot and exposes the same engine that powers the Copilot CLI as a programmable agent runtime. Developers define how an agent should behave, while Copilot handles planning, tool calls and file edits. The SDK is therefore aimed at teams that want agent behaviour inside their own products or internal tools rather than only in a chat window or terminal.

Technically, the SDK is delivered in several language flavours: Node.js and TypeScript, Python, Go, .NET, Rust and Java. Each client communicates with the Copilot CLI running in server mode over JSON-RPC and manages that process automatically. For Node.js, Python and .NET the CLI is bundled with the SDK, whereas for Go, Java and Rust it has to be installed separately. This is a practical point when choosing a language, since it affects packaging and deployment of an application built on the SDK.

The SDK offers several extension points. Developers can define custom agents, skills and tools that the runtime can call. By default the first-party CLI tools are exposed, and a permission handler governs each call, which gives an application a place to approve, restrict or log what the agent is allowed to do. All models available through the Copilot CLI are supported. Authentication normally relies on a Copilot subscription. Alternatively, a bring-your-own-key setup is available, which supports providers such as OpenAI, Microsoft Foundry and Anthropic, with key-based authentication only.

On licensing and lifecycle, the repository describes the SDK as generally available under semantic versioning and licensed under MIT. It also states that the product is being renamed Microsoft Copilot SDK, with the repository moving to the Microsoft organisation in phases. Anyone referencing the project should expect names and locations to change during that transition. The repository page does not describe MCP integration in detail, so the extent of MCP server support should be checked in the current documentation rather than assumed.

The M365.FM episode "Enterprise AI Agent Fabric: Architecture Beyond Chatbots" mentions the GitHub Copilot SDK in the context of designing and managing agent interfaces. According to the episode, tools such as the GitHub Copilot SDK and Agent Builder can be used to brainstorm ideas and set up projects, giving a structured way to build specialised agents and implement core features. The episode places these tools among UI frameworks that help create visual dashboards for agent monitoring, set up project templates for new agents, and test agent behaviour and make changes quickly. In that framing, the SDK is one building block in a wider agent architecture that goes beyond simple chatbots, where control and monitoring of agent actions matter as much as the agents themselves.

Typical decisions around the SDK include which language binding fits the existing stack, whether to rely on a Copilot subscription or bring-your-own-key, how strictly to configure the permission handler for tool calls, and which custom tools and skills an agent needs. Because the runtime is the same one used by the Copilot CLI, behaviour observed in the CLI can serve as a reference when building and testing an embedded agent.

github-flow.desc: GitHub flow is a lightweight, branch-based workflow in which short-lived feature branches are reviewed through pull requests before merging into the main branch.

faq.a: According to GitHub Docs, the steps are: create a branch, make changes, open a pull request, address review comments, merge the pull request, and delete the branch.
faq.q: What are the steps of GitHub flow?

faq.a: No. GitHub Docs presents it as useful for anyone working with files in a shared repository, and its steps can be done in the web interface, the GitHub CLI or GitHub Desktop.
faq.q: Is GitHub flow only for software developers?

faq.a: Deleting the branch does not remove the pull request or its history, and a deleted branch can be restored.
faq.q: What happens to the pull request when the branch is deleted?

github-flow.long:
GitHub flow is a lightweight, branch-based workflow for collaborating on projects. Its central rule is that anything on the main branch is deployable, so changes stay off the default branch until they have been reviewed and merged. Work happens in short-lived feature branches, and each branch is merged back through a pull request. According to GitHub Docs, GitHub itself uses this workflow for its own policy, documentation and roadmap repositories.

The workflow is not limited to software developers. The documentation presents it as useful for anyone working with files in a shared repository. Every step can be carried out in the GitHub web interface, with the GitHub CLI or in GitHub Desktop, so teams can choose the tooling that suits them.

GitHub flow consists of six steps. First, a branch is created from the default branch, ideally with a short, descriptive name, so that the default branch remains untouched. Second, changes are made on that branch using small, descriptive and isolated commits. Third, a pull request is opened, optionally as a draft, with a summary of the change and a linked issue where relevant. Fourth, review comments are addressed by pushing additional commits to the same branch. Fifth, the pull request is merged once it has been approved. Sixth, the branch is deleted to mark the work as complete.

Some details matter in practice. A merge can be blocked by conflicts or by branch protection rules, such as a requirement for a certain number of approvals. Deleting a branch after merging does not remove the pull request or its history, and a deleted branch can be restored if needed. This means the review discussion and the record of the change remain available after the branch itself is gone.

GitHub flow is usually compared with other branching strategies, and the M365.FM episode "Git Branching Strategies - Simply Explained" does exactly that. The episode covers what a branch is, why branching strategies exist and the three building blocks involved, then walks through Git Flow as the structured approach, GitHub Flow as the simple one and trunk-based development as the fast one. It also explains pull requests, discusses merge versus rebase, and addresses choosing a strategy for small and large teams as well as common mistakes beginners make. The episode frames the underlying problem as one of knowing which version of the code is the real one, which is a branching problem.

The typical decision around GitHub flow is how much process a team needs. Because it uses a single long-lived branch plus short-lived feature branches, it has fewer moving parts than a model with several permanent branches. Teams weigh this simplicity against their own release and review needs, and the choice often depends on team size and how work is shipped. Pull requests are the core mechanism in all of this: they provide the place for discussion, review and approval before a change reaches the main branch.

gitops.desc: GitOps is an operating model that manages environments, deployments and releases declaratively, using a Git repository as the single source of truth.

faq.a: GitOps is an operating model in which environments, deployments and releases are managed declaratively through a Git repository. Every configuration change is stored, reviewed and version-controlled, with Git as the single source of truth.
faq.q: What is GitOps?

faq.a: The episode "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained" lists GitOps as a 2020 milestone that extended IaC practices by synchronizing infrastructure with Git repositories for better auditability.
faq.q: How does GitOps relate to Infrastructure as Code?

faq.a: The episodes mention Bicep, Terraform, Azure DevOps Pipelines, GitHub Actions, Azure Kubernetes Service and Azure Arc in contexts where GitOps stores or applies the desired configuration.
faq.q: Which tools are mentioned together with GitOps in the episodes?

gitops.long:
GitOps is an operating model in which environments, deployments and releases are managed declaratively through a Git repository. Instead of making manual changes directly to a cloud environment, teams record every configuration change in Git, where it is stored, reviewed and version-controlled. Git therefore acts as the single source of truth for how infrastructure and applications should look and behave.

The approach is used to deploy and manage infrastructure and applications in a traceable and repeatable way. Because the desired configuration lives in a repository, each change to an environment becomes a reviewable and traceable change to code or configuration. The M365.FM episode "GitOps - Simply Explained", part of Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets, describes GitOps in plain English as a modern approach and presents it as a best practice for Kubernetes, cloud-native development and DevOps teams.

GitOps is closely tied to Infrastructure as Code. The episode "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained" places GitOps in a timeline of IaC milestones, listing it under 2020 as an extension of IaC practices that synchronizes infrastructure with Git repositories for better auditability. In that view, GitOps builds on earlier automation and configuration-management tools by adding Git as the place where the desired state is defined and where changes are tracked.

In practice, GitOps often appears alongside provisioning and automation tooling. The episode "Internal Developer Platforms (IDPs) - Simply Explained" says GitOps can store the desired configuration in Git, providing reviewable and traceable infrastructure changes. In the same context, technologies such as Bicep or Terraform can provision infrastructure, while Azure DevOps Pipelines or GitHub Actions can automate testing and deployment. Applications might then run on Azure App Service, Azure Kubernetes Service or other approved environments. In an internal developer platform, developers describe the desired result and let automation create the required environment, with GitOps supplying the reviewable record of that desired state.

GitOps also appears in discussions of operating hybrid and multicloud estates. The episode "Azure Arc - Simply Explained" lists GitOps among the key concepts it covers, together with Arc-enabled servers, Kubernetes, Azure Policy, Azure Monitor, Microsoft Defender for Cloud and Infrastructure as Code. It names deploying applications with GitOps as one of the real-world scenarios, next to managing hybrid servers, governing Kubernetes clusters and monitoring distributed environments, all aimed at a consistent operational model across Azure, other clouds and on-premises datacenters.

The episode "Platform Engineering - Simply Explained" connects GitOps to platform teams. It describes Platform Engineering as working alongside Azure, GitHub, Azure DevOps, Bicep, Terraform and GitOps to create scalable, secure and consistent cloud operations, reducing operational overhead and letting developers provision resources without compromising security or compliance.

Typical decisions around GitOps include how to structure the repositories that hold the desired state, how reviews of configuration changes are handled, and which provisioning and pipeline tools sit alongside it. Related topics in the M365.FM episodes are Infrastructure as Code, Azure Arc, Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms, all of which use declarative, version-controlled configuration as a shared foundation.

global-administrator.desc: Global Administrator is the most privileged built-in role in Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365, granting access to all administrative features and data in a tenant.

faq.a: It is the most privileged built-in administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365, with access to all administrative features and data in a tenant.
faq.q: What is a Global Administrator in Microsoft 365?

faq.a: Microsoft recommends assigning it to as few people as possible and limiting its use. The M365.FM episodes also advise the least privilege principle, assigning only the roles needed for specific tasks.
faq.q: How many people should hold the Global Administrator role?

faq.a: The episodes mention configuration changes in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps and the prerequisite that at least one user holds the role for Microsoft Graph Data Connect. It is also listed among roles that permit managing Microsoft 365 with PowerShell.
faq.q: Which tasks mentioned in the episodes require Global Administrator?

global-administrator.long:
Global Administrator is the most privileged built-in administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365. It gives access to all administrative features and data in a tenant. Microsoft recommends limiting its use and assigning it to as few people as possible, because the scope of the role means that one misused or compromised account can affect the entire organization.

The role is used for tasks that no narrower role can cover. M365.FM episodes mention several concrete situations. In "Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps - Simply Explained", the Global Administrator role appears in a table of required roles, where configuration changes need Global Administrator, Security Administrator, or Cloud App Administrator, and the Defender for Cloud Apps role itself is listed as Global Administrator. In "Microsoft Graph Data Connect - Simply Explained", the prerequisites state that at least one user in the Microsoft 365 tenant must have the Global Administrator role enabled. The same episode lists further requirements: a tenant admin enables the Data Connect service, the Microsoft 365 and Azure tenants share the same Microsoft Entra tenancy, the Azure subscription sits in that tenant, and a different user holds an Application Administrator or Developer role.

The role also appears in lists of permissions for managing Microsoft 365 with PowerShell. The episode "Run Your Full Stack Locally with .NET Aspire" names Global Administrator alongside Exchange Administrator, SharePoint Administrator, and Teams Administrator as roles that allow this kind of management. It advises checking assigned roles in the Microsoft 365 admin center and applying the least privilege principle, meaning only the roles needed for the specific management tasks should be assigned. That list shows a practical choice: service-specific administrator roles can cover work within a single workload, while Global Administrator spans all of them.

The main decision around the role is who should hold it. The episode "SC-900 Exam Prep 3/8: Microsoft Entra Roles Explained" describes a common pattern of over-assignment, with justifications such as "it's easier than having to go back and update later" or "they might need these permissions later, so let's add them all." It gives the example of a junior admin who is made Global Administrator because working out the exact permissions seemed harder. The admin is productive on Monday afternoon, but by Tuesday morning has accidentally deleted a critical application, assuming it was a test instance. The episode uses this to illustrate why high-level roles should not be assigned without a real need.

The episode "Microsoft 365 Global Admin Power, Identity, and Governance" looks at the role from the standpoint of responsibility. It says the Global Administrator role requires trust, technical skill, and a strong sense of responsibility, because decisions can affect everyone in the organization. It describes situations in which a Global Administrator must contain threats and balance requests to bypass normal procedures against company policy and security best practices. One example it gives is an executive asking to share confidential data with a partner. The episode argues that the authority of the role often surpasses traditional executive power within the digital environment of a company, since the holder shapes that environment, enforces security, and supports business continuity.

In practice, the guidance across these sources is consistent. Global Administrator is reserved for work that genuinely needs tenant-wide authority, for example enabling certain services or changing sensitive configuration. Everything else is better handled with narrower roles such as Security Administrator, Cloud App Administrator, Exchange Administrator, SharePoint Administrator, or Teams Administrator. Keeping the number of Global Administrators small, and checking regularly which roles each account actually holds, follows from the recommendation to limit use of the role and from the least privilege principle that the episodes repeat.

global-secure-access.desc: Microsoft Entra Global Secure Access is Microsoft's cloud-delivered Security Service Edge that combines Private Access and Internet Access under identity-based policy.

faq.a: It is Microsoft's cloud-delivered Security Service Edge solution and the umbrella for Microsoft Entra Private Access and Microsoft Entra Internet Access. It secures access to private apps and internet resources based on identity and policy.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Entra Global Secure Access?

faq.a: Instead of giving broad network connectivity, Private Access provides zero trust network access to specific private applications, including per-app access for TCP and UDP apps, private DNS and single sign-on. Access is tied to identity and policy rather than network location.
faq.q: How does Global Secure Access differ from a traditional VPN?

faq.a: The documentation states that Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 is generally required per user, and that the services are also available in the Entra Suite. Some capabilities are in preview and not every feature is available in every traffic profile.
faq.q: What licensing does Global Secure Access need?

global-secure-access.long:
Microsoft Entra Global Secure Access is Microsoft's cloud-delivered Security Service Edge (SSE) offering. It is the umbrella name for two services, Microsoft Entra Private Access and Microsoft Entra Internet Access, and it is part of Microsoft Entra. Both services are managed centrally in the Microsoft Entra admin center and are built on zero-trust principles. The stated aim is to give identity-aware access control and visibility for users and devices both inside and outside the office, and to converge network, identity and endpoint access controls in one place.

The product addresses a shift in how organizations think about network boundaries. Traditional VPNs were designed for an era when applications lived inside company data centers and the network perimeter was the primary layer of security. Global Secure Access replaces broad network connectivity with identity-driven access that grants users only the specific applications and services they need, rather than placing a user on the whole corporate network.

Microsoft Entra Internet Access acts as an identity-based secure web gateway. Traffic is forwarded through a user-specific profile, either via a desktop client or via a remote network such as a branch office. Documented capabilities include traffic logs, integration with Conditional Access, and web content filtering by category or domain name. A Microsoft services variant of the profile adds a compliant network check, universal tenant restrictions and source IP restoration for sign-in logs.

Microsoft Entra Private Access provides zero trust network access to private resources without a classic VPN. It supports per-app access for TCP and UDP applications, private DNS and single sign-on for private apps. This lets administrators publish specific internal applications and apply identity and policy controls to them, instead of opening a network segment.

On licensing, the documentation states that Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 is generally required per user, and that the services are also available in the Entra Suite. Several capabilities are marked as preview, and not every feature is available in every traffic profile, so planning typically involves checking which profile and feature set applies to a given scenario before rollout.

Typical decisions around Global Secure Access include whether to retire or reduce reliance on a traditional VPN, how to route internet and Microsoft 365 traffic through a policy-controlled gateway, and how to connect branch offices as remote networks versus individual devices through the client. Because policy is tied to identity, the product is closely related to Conditional Access and to the wider Microsoft Entra identity platform.

The M365.FM episode "Global Secure Access - Simply Explained" (Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets, with Mirko Peters) presents Global Secure Access in plain English. The episode describes it as a cloud-delivered SSE platform and explains how Microsoft moves from broad network connectivity to identity-driven Zero Trust access limited to the applications and services a user needs. It frames traditional VPNs as designed for a time when applications lived inside corporate data centers.

glossary-term.desc: A glossary term is a shared business word with a definition attached to data; in Microsoft Purview Unified Catalog, terms live in governance domains and can carry policies.

faq.a: It is a shared business word with a definition that is attached to data. In Unified Catalog, terms live in governance domains.
faq.q: What is a glossary term in Microsoft Purview Unified Catalog?

faq.a: Yes. In Microsoft Purview Unified Catalog, glossary terms can carry policies in addition to their definitions.
faq.q: Can a glossary term carry policies?

faq.a: They live in governance domains within Microsoft Purview Unified Catalog.
faq.q: Where are glossary terms stored in Unified Catalog?

glossary-term.long:
A glossary term is a shared business word with a definition that is attached to data. It gives teams a common vocabulary so that the same word means the same thing wherever the data is used.

In Microsoft Purview Unified Catalog, glossary terms are organized within governance domains. A term can also carry policies, which links the business meaning of a word to the rules that apply to the data it describes. The Microsoft documentation page on the enterprise glossary in Unified Catalog covers the details of how terms are created and managed.

Glossary terms are typically used to document business concepts, support data discovery, and connect governance practices to the data assets they describe. The facts available for this entry do not specify further relationships to other topics or products, and no M365.FM episodes are currently associated with it.

golden-image.desc: A golden image is a preconfigured virtual machine image that bundles the OS, updates, applications and customizations and serves as a template for virtual desktops or session hosts.

faq.a: A golden image is a custom, preconfigured virtual machine image that includes the operating system, updates, applications and customizations. It is captured as the template for deploying virtual desktops or session hosts.
faq.q: What is a golden image?

faq.a: A golden image has to be maintained and updated over time so that the template used for new deployments stays current with updates and application changes.
faq.q: Why does a golden image need to be maintained?

faq.a: It is covered in the episode "Image Management for Virtual Desktops – Simply Explained", published 2026-11-21.
faq.q: Where is the golden image concept discussed on M365.FM?

golden-image.long:
A golden image is a custom, preconfigured virtual machine image. It combines the operating system, updates, applications and customizations in a single captured state. That captured image acts as the template from which virtual desktops or session hosts are deployed.

The main purpose of a golden image is to make deployments consistent: each desktop or session host created from the template starts with the same baseline configuration. Because the image holds the operating system, installed applications and settings together, it defines what users receive when a new virtual machine is provisioned.

A golden image is not a one-time artifact. It has to be maintained and updated over time, so that updates and application changes are reflected in the template used for later deployments. This ongoing upkeep is a central part of image management for virtual desktop environments.

On M365.FM, the concept appears in the episode "Image Management for Virtual Desktops – Simply Explained" (2026-11-21), which covers image management for virtual desktops.

golden-path.desc: A golden path is an approved, repeatable route in an internal developer platform that turns code into a running service using sensible defaults instead of setup from scratch.

faq.a: A golden path is an approved, repeatable route for a common development task, such as turning code into a running service. It provides sensible defaults for repositories, CI/CD, Azure resources, identities, monitoring, and security so teams do not set everything up from scratch.
faq.q: What is a golden path in an internal developer platform?

faq.a: No. The M365.FM episode on IDPs says good golden paths offer controlled escape routes for applications with special needs. The Spotify Engineering article similarly states that engineers can leave the path but without the same support.
faq.q: Do developers have to follow a golden path?

faq.a: The sources include a Spotify Engineering article that describes Golden Paths as the opinionated and supported way to build something. Spotify created them to address a fragmented tooling landscape and delivers them as tutorials in its Backstage developer portal.
faq.q: Where does the golden path concept come from?

golden-path.long:
A golden path is an approved and repeatable route inside an internal developer platform (IDP) for a common development task, such as turning code into a running service. Instead of requiring each development team to design its infrastructure from scratch, a golden path supplies sensible defaults. The idea is to make the recommended way of working the easiest way to work, so that standards, tools, and policies already established by an organization are applied without every team having to rediscover them.

The M365.FM episode "Internal Developer Platforms (IDPs) - Simply Explained" describes golden paths as covering defaults for repositories, CI/CD, Azure resources, identities, monitoring, security, and other standard requirements. Developers provide only the information that matters, such as the service name, owner, environment, runtime, and approved options, while the platform handles the underlying setup. The episode also notes that good golden paths provide controlled escape routes for applications with needs that the standard route does not cover, so the path guides rather than traps.

The episode "The DevOps Tax: Why Your Platform is Failing" presents the golden path as an opinionated, pre-built workflow that covers the majority of common engineering scenarios. According to the episode, rather than presenting dozens of infrastructure choices, the platform offers a standard approach that already includes CI/CD pipelines, security scanning, monitoring, logging, deployment strategies, compliance validation, and rollback procedures. Developers customize only the business-specific parts. The episode links this to centralized expertise with preserved developer autonomy, and to greater consistency, improved governance, and lower cognitive overhead.

The term has a documented origin in software engineering practice. A Spotify Engineering article defines a Golden Path as the opinionated and supported way to build something, such as a backend service, website, or data pipeline, accompanied by a step-by-step tutorial that walks engineers along it. According to that article, Spotify introduced them because autonomous teams had produced a fragmented tooling landscape in which engineers learned by asking colleagues, a pattern the author calls rumour-driven development. The aim was to make recommended tools easy to find and the route through them clear, not to restrict engineers. Engineers who leave the path can still do so, but without the same level of support.

The Spotify article adds practical detail on how such paths are delivered. The first tutorial, for backend engineering, began as a Hack Week project by eight engineers in the platform organization. Tutorials now exist for several disciplines, including data engineering, machine learning, web, and audio. They are written with TechDocs and shown in the Backstage developer portal, form part of onboarding, and are usually completed by new engineers within their first two weeks. The article describes them as Spotify's most read technical documentation. It also outlines a proposed Golden State of checks that would show whether a system follows the path.

Typical decisions around a golden path include which common jobs deserve a path, which defaults to build in, and how to handle workloads that do not fit. Because a path bundles security, monitoring, and compliance steps, it also shifts part of the governance effort from individual teams to the platform. The sources agree on two design points: the path should be the supported default, and leaving it should remain possible, with the trade-off that off-path work receives less support.

Golden paths are closely tied to the internal developer platform concept, since the platform is where the routes are made available to developers. The two episodes cited here treat the golden path as one of the core building blocks of an IDP, alongside the shared standards, tools, and policies the platform exposes to development teams.

golden-ticket-attack.desc: A golden ticket attack forges Kerberos ticket-granting tickets with a stolen KRBTGT key, giving an attacker persistent, arbitrary identity in an Active Directory domain.

faq.a: It requires the password hash of the KRBTGT account, which is typically obtained through OS credential dumping and needs privileged access to a domain controller.
faq.q: What does a golden ticket attack require?

faq.a: MITRE ATT&CK recommends resetting the KRBTGT password twice with replication between the resets, rotating it roughly every 180 days, and limiting domain admin rights to domain controllers and a small set of servers.
faq.q: How can a golden ticket be contained?

faq.a: Indicators include abnormal ticket lifetimes, unexpected encryption types such as RC4 in modern domains, malformed logon fields, and service ticket requests without a preceding ticket-granting ticket request.
faq.q: How can golden ticket activity be detected?

golden-ticket-attack.long:
A golden ticket attack is a technique in which an adversary forges Kerberos ticket-granting tickets (TGTs) after obtaining the password hash of the KRBTGT account in an Active Directory domain. MITRE ATT&CK catalogs it as sub-technique T1558.001, "Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket", under the credential access tactic on Windows. The KRBTGT account is the service account of the key distribution center (KDC), and its key is used to encrypt and sign all Kerberos tickets in the domain. Whoever holds that key can produce tickets that the domain treats as genuine.

The practical effect is persistent, arbitrary identity. With a forged TGT, an attacker can obtain authentication material for any account in Active Directory, which in turn allows access to resources across the network. One M365.FM episode describes this as a method that lets attackers create forged Kerberos tickets and access resources within the network without detection. The forged ticket still has to be presented to the KDC to request service tickets for specific resources, so the attack does not bypass the KDC entirely; it abuses the trust the KDC places in tickets signed with the KRBTGT key.

Obtaining the KRBTGT hash is the prerequisite. According to the MITRE ATT&CK description, the hash is typically gathered through OS credential dumping, which requires privileged access to a domain controller. This means a golden ticket is usually a post-compromise technique: an attacker who has already gained high privileges uses it to keep access and to impersonate accounts. Tools and groups listed as having forged golden tickets include Empire, Mimikatz, Rubeus, Sliver and the Ke3chang group.

The episode "Harden Azure AD Connect Against Hybrid Identity Breaches" (2025-11-03) places the golden ticket attack among several prevalent methods used against hybrid identity environments. It names it alongside credential theft, where phishing emails or malicious software are used to steal user credentials, and the DCSync attack, in which cybercriminals mimic a domain controller to request password data from other domain controllers. The episode groups these because each leads to unauthorized access, and it notes that such attacks can have severe consequences.

Containment and prevention follow from how the attack works. The MITRE ATT&CK page recommends resetting the KRBTGT password twice, with replication between the two resets, so that older keys can no longer validate forged tickets. It also suggests rotating the KRBTGT password roughly every 180 days. A second mitigation is limiting domain admin rights to domain controllers and a small set of servers, which reduces the chance that an attacker can reach a domain controller and dump the hash in the first place.

Detection relies on spotting tickets or requests that do not match normal Kerberos behavior. The documented indicators include abnormal ticket lifetimes, unexpected encryption types such as RC4 in modern domains, malformed logon fields, and service ticket requests that have no preceding TGT request. Because forged tickets are created offline rather than issued by the KDC, the absence of the usual authentication sequence is one of the more telling signs.

In hybrid identity discussions, the golden ticket attack matters because it targets the foundation of on-premises Active Directory trust. Hardening connected components such as Azure AD Connect, controlling privileged access to domain controllers, and maintaining a routine KRBTGT rotation schedule are the measures the sources associate with reducing exposure.

google-cloud-interconnect.desc: Google Cloud Interconnect is a Google Cloud service for private, high-availability, low-latency connections between external networks, including other clouds, and Google's network.

faq.a: Google Cloud Interconnect is a Google Cloud service that provides high-availability, low-latency private connections between external networks, including other clouds, and Google's network.
faq.q: What is Google Cloud Interconnect?

faq.a: Yes. According to its description, the service provides private connections between Google's network and external networks, including other clouds.
faq.q: Can Google Cloud Interconnect connect to other clouds?

google-cloud-interconnect.long:
Google Cloud Interconnect is a Google Cloud service that provides private connections between external networks and Google's network. The connections are described as high-availability and low-latency, and they can link other clouds to Google's network as well as other external environments.

The service is relevant where organizations want network connectivity that does not rely solely on the public internet. Typical scenarios include linking an existing network to Google Cloud or connecting resources hosted in another cloud with workloads that run on Google's network.

The available information on this entity is limited to this short description. No related topics, episodes or official links are currently associated with Google Cloud Interconnect on M365.FM, so no further detail on configuration options, connection types or pricing is given here.

google-cloud-platform.desc: Google Cloud Platform (GCP) is Google's suite of public cloud services, often managed alongside Azure and AWS in multi-cloud setups covered by M365.FM.

faq.a: Google Cloud Platform (GCP) is Google's suite of public cloud computing services. In Microsoft contexts it often appears as part of multi-cloud environments managed alongside Azure.
faq.q: What is Google Cloud Platform (GCP)?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Entra Permissions Management - Simply Explained" says the platform provides visibility across Azure, AWS, and GCP. This helps security teams find excessive privileges and permission creep across all three clouds.
faq.q: How does GCP relate to Microsoft Entra Permissions Management?

faq.a: The episode "AWS vs Microsoft Entra for Enterprise Cloud Identity" describes GCP as using a declarative policy model with organizational guardrails. Azure, by contrast, is described as emphasizing a separation between access and compliance.
faq.q: How does the GCP identity model differ from Azure's according to the episodes?

google-cloud-platform.long:
Google Cloud Platform (GCP) is Google's suite of public cloud computing services. In Microsoft-focused discussions it most often appears as one part of a multi-cloud environment, where an organization runs workloads on GCP while also using Azure and, in many cases, Amazon Web Services (AWS). Because of that, GCP shows up in M365.FM material mainly as a point of comparison and as something that identity, security, and governance tools have to cover, rather than as a product the Microsoft ecosystem is built around.

One recurring context is cloud identity and permissions. The episode "Microsoft Entra Permissions Management - Simply Explained" describes a platform that continuously discovers identities, analyzes permissions, detects excessive privileges, and identifies permission creep before attackers can exploit it. According to the episode, this visibility extends across Azure, AWS, and GCP, helping security teams reduce unnecessary access while maintaining productivity. The episode also looks at situations where organizations struggle with overprivileged users, service principals, and workload identities, and explains how Permissions Management complements Microsoft Entra ID, Privileged Identity Management (PIM), and Microsoft Defender for Cloud. In this setting, GCP is one of the three major cloud environments whose permissions need to be assessed together.

A second context is the comparison of identity and governance models between cloud providers. The episode "AWS vs Microsoft Entra for Enterprise Cloud Identity" contrasts the approaches of the different platforms. It says that Azure emphasizes a separation between access and compliance, which allows governance to be managed without complicating role assignments. For GCP, the episode describes a declarative policy model with organizational guardrails, which it says provides clarity and predictability in permissions management. The same episode points to Azure Arc as offering a unified view of resources across environments, and to Google Cloud Anthos as providing visibility into Kubernetes clusters and workloads. These points frame GCP as having its own distinct design philosophy for access control and cluster management.

A third context is application hosting. In "Modern .NET: WPF, ASP.NET Core, and gRPC with Gábor Ruzsinszki [MVP]", cloud deployment is presented as one option for running an ASP.NET Core application. The episode lists Microsoft Azure, AWS, and GCP as popular choices and notes that cloud platforms offer easy scaling, high availability, and managed services. In its comparison table, Azure is associated with deep .NET integration, App Service, and Functions, AWS with flexible compute and global reach through AWS Elastic Beanstalk, and GCP with container support and managed VMs through Google App Engine. This shows GCP as a viable hosting target for .NET workloads even though Azure is described as having the deepest .NET integration.

Taken together, the episodes suggest a few typical decisions around GCP in a Microsoft-centered environment. Teams that already use Azure may need to decide how to extend permission reviews and least-privilege practices to GCP resources, and whether a cross-cloud tool such as Microsoft Entra Permissions Management fits that need. Teams choosing a hosting platform for .NET applications weigh the integration depth of Azure against the container-oriented services described for GCP. Teams working with Kubernetes across providers consider which tooling gives consistent visibility, with Azure Arc and Google Cloud Anthos named in the episode as the respective options.

The source material does not go into GCP's individual services, pricing, or architecture in detail, so this page limits itself to the roles GCP plays in the discussed scenarios: a major public cloud in multi-cloud estates, a distinct model for declarative policy and guardrails, and an alternative deployment target for applications that might otherwise run on Azure.

google-gemini.desc: Google Gemini, formerly Bard, is Google's generative AI assistant, also built into Google Workspace apps such as Google Sheets, and a model provider in multi-model setups.

faq.a: Google Gemini, formerly Bard, is Google's generative AI assistant. It is also built into Google Workspace apps such as Google Sheets.
faq.q: What is Google Gemini?

faq.a: The episodes on Microsoft AI Gateway and Azure Local list Google Gemini among the model providers a gateway can route requests to, alongside Azure OpenAI, Microsoft Foundry, Anthropic and Amazon Bedrock. Applications talk to a stable endpoint rather than to each provider directly.
faq.q: How does Google Gemini relate to a Microsoft AI Gateway?

faq.a: The episode "Is Microsoft 365 Copilot Worth the Cost?" describes Copilot as deeply embedded in Office apps with full administrative control, and Gemini as having limited integration with core apps and fewer controls. Another episode cites approximate Excel-related AI tool shares of about 14% for Copilot and about 13% for Gemini.
faq.q: How do the episodes compare Google Gemini with Microsoft Copilot?

google-gemini.long:
Google Gemini is Google's generative AI assistant. It was previously known as Bard and is also built into Google Workspace apps such as Google Sheets. Within the M365.FM knowledge base, Google Gemini appears mainly as a point of comparison for Microsoft's own AI offerings and as one of several model providers that organizations may connect to when building AI-enabled applications.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, Google Gemini comes up in two typical situations. The first is the choice of an AI assistant for everyday productivity work, where Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini are weighed against each other. The second is architecture: enterprises that run AI workloads across several vendors need a way to reach different models without tying every application to one provider.

The second situation is covered in the episodes "Microsoft AI Gateway - Simply Explained" and "Azure Local - Simply Explained". Both describe a gateway approach in which applications communicate with a stable endpoint instead of hardcoding connections to specific providers. The gateway then routes requests to Azure OpenAI, Microsoft Foundry, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Amazon Bedrock, or other approved model providers. According to the episodes, organizations can balance workloads across multiple regions, optimize performance, reduce operational risk, implement failover strategies, and migrate between models without requiring application developers to rewrite existing integrations. In this picture, Google Gemini is one possible back-end model among several, and the gateway layer is what keeps applications independent of any single provider.

The comparison with Microsoft Copilot is the focus of other episodes. In "Is Microsoft 365 Copilot Worth the Cost?", the episode presents a feature comparison between Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini. It describes Microsoft Copilot as deeply embedded in Office apps, with full administrative control over deployment and user access, and built on a secure environment with existing policies. For Google Gemini, the same comparison lists limited integration with core apps, fewer administrative controls that are generally enabled across the domain, and a need for additional configuration for data access. These are the episode's own assessments and reflect its Microsoft-centered perspective.

The episode "From Excel Expert to Microsoft MVP: Empowering Millions with Data, Dashboards & AI with Karen Abecia [Microsoft MVP]" places Google Gemini in the context of AI tools used with spreadsheets. It cites approximate market-share figures for AI tools integrated with Excel: ChatGPT at roughly 61%, Microsoft Copilot at roughly 14%, and Google Gemini at roughly 13%, noting that Gemini is growing fast. The episode attributes these figures to its own table, and they should be read as the episode's statement rather than an independent measurement. The same episode discusses benefits of Microsoft Copilot for data analysis, such as reported time savings, which frames the Gemini figure within a Copilot-focused discussion.

For readers deciding between assistants, the episodes suggest looking at several factors: how deeply the assistant is integrated with the apps already in use, what administrative controls exist for deployment and user access, how data access and security are handled, and whether a multi-provider architecture is needed. Because Gemini is built into Google Workspace apps such as Google Sheets, it fits most naturally where Workspace is the main productivity platform, while a gateway pattern allows it to be used alongside Microsoft services when a mixed environment is required.

In summary, Google Gemini on M365.FM is treated as a generative AI assistant from Google, a comparison point for Microsoft 365 Copilot in the Office and Excel context, and a selectable model provider behind a Microsoft AI Gateway-style routing layer.

google-sheets.desc: Google Sheets is Google's web-based spreadsheet application in the Docs Editors suite, known for real-time collaboration and compatibility with Excel file formats.

faq.a: Google Sheets is a web-based spreadsheet program in Google's Docs Editors suite and part of Google Workspace. It is also available as Android and iOS apps and as a ChromeOS desktop app.
faq.q: What is Google Sheets?

faq.a: Yes. It can view, convert and export formats including xls, xlsx, xlsm, csv, tsv and ods. It handles the 1900 leap year bug differently from Excel, and documents are capped at 10 million cells.
faq.q: Can Google Sheets open and save Excel files?

faq.a: The episode "Excel vs Google Sheets with David Benaim [MVP]" says the answer depends on the task, the team and the business requirements, with Sheets strong in collaboration and sharing and Excel ahead in areas such as Power Query, advanced analysis and enterprise reporting. "Fix Excel Shadow Systems and Broken Business Processes" lists Google Sheets as a cloud-based option for small to medium-sized teams.
faq.q: How do the M365.FM episodes compare Google Sheets with Excel?

google-sheets.long:
Google Sheets is a web-based spreadsheet program in Google's free Docs Editors suite. It is also available as Android and iOS apps and as a ChromeOS desktop app, and it forms part of Google Workspace. Its core purpose is to let people build, share and analyze tabular data directly in a browser, without installing a desktop application. For readers of a Microsoft-focused knowledge base, it is mainly relevant as the most common point of comparison with Microsoft Excel.

The product began as XL2Web from 2Web Technologies, which Google acquired in 2006. It launched in June 2006 as Google Labs Spreadsheets and was renamed Google Sheets in October 2012. Its main strength is real-time collaboration: several users can edit the same file at once, with coloured cursors showing where each person is working and a chat sidebar for discussion. Changes are saved automatically, a revision history allows earlier versions to be restored, and a permissions system together with tagging controls who can see or edit a file. The Explore feature uses machine learning to answer questions about the data in a sheet, and Gemini was integrated in late 2025 to help with formulas, charts and summaries. Add-ons extend the application further.

Compatibility with Excel is an important consideration for mixed environments. Google Sheets can view, convert and export formats including xls, xlsx, xlsm, csv, tsv and ods. One documented difference is that it handles the 1900 leap year bug differently from Excel. Documents are capped at 10 million cells. Offline editing is available in Chromium browsers through an extension and natively in the mobile apps. Sheets is free for individuals and included in paid Workspace plans. Password managers warn that it lacks end-to-end encryption, which can matter when deciding what kind of data to store in it.

In practice, choosing between Google Sheets and Excel tends to depend on the task, the team and the business requirements rather than on a single winner. The M365.FM episode "Excel vs Google Sheets with David Benaim [MVP]" (2026-07-08) frames the question this way. In that conversation, host Mirko Peters talks with Microsoft MVP David Benaim about whether Google Sheets can really compete with Microsoft Excel. According to the episode description, the discussion covers where Google Sheets is strong, including collaboration and rapid sharing, and where Excel continues to dominate. The areas named for Excel include Power Query, advanced data analysis, automation, large datasets, financial modeling and enterprise reporting.

Google Sheets also appears in the M365.FM episode "Fix Excel Shadow Systems and Broken Business Processes" (2026-04-15). There it is listed among cloud-based alternatives to emailing spreadsheet files back and forth. The episode describes such tools as updating instantly, so everyone sees the most current data without sending files around or dealing with conflicting edits. In its comparison table, Google Sheets is described with real-time collaboration, a cloud-native design and integration with Google Workspace, and is positioned as suited to small to medium-sized teams. Other tools in the same table include Airtable, Smartsheet and Numbers, which the episode distinguishes by their database-style, project-management or template-oriented strengths.

Taken together, the available material presents Google Sheets as a collaboration-first spreadsheet that works well for shared, lightweight data work and can exchange files with Excel, while Excel remains the reference point for heavy analysis, automation and enterprise reporting. Decisions around it usually involve how much collaboration speed matters, how large and complex the data is, which file formats must be exchanged with Excel users, and what security expectations apply to the stored data.

governance.desc: Governance in Microsoft 365: the rules, roles and controls that define who may use which data and tools, including permissions, labelling and agent lifecycle.

faq.a: It refers to the rules, roles and controls that define who may use which data and tools and how that is monitored. For Copilot and agents it covers permissions, labelling, agent lifecycle and auditability.
faq.q: What does governance mean in Microsoft 365?

faq.a: According to the episode with Paul Keijzers, Copilot's answers depend on the content and permissions already present in the tenant, so the state of that content and those permissions shapes the results.
faq.q: Why does governance matter for Microsoft 365 Copilot?

faq.a: No. The episode "Microsoft Purview is a Trap: The Hard Truth About Data Governance" argues that Purview should not be treated as a complete solution on its own, and that a clear strategy is needed alongside the tool.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Purview the same as governance?

governance.long:
Governance is the set of rules, roles and controls that define who may use which data and tools in an organization, and how that use is monitored. In the Microsoft ecosystem the term covers Microsoft 365 collaboration workloads such as Teams and SharePoint, the Power Platform, and, more recently, Microsoft 365 Copilot and AI agents. It is less a single product than a discipline: decisions about ownership, access and oversight that are then supported by technical controls.

For Copilot and agents, governance is commonly described through a few recurring areas: permissions, labelling, the lifecycle of agents and auditability. Permissions determine which content a person, and therefore Copilot acting for that person, can reach. Labelling classifies information so that handling rules can follow the data. The lifecycle of an agent addresses how agents are created, owned, changed and eventually retired. Auditability makes it possible to review what happened, which supports both compliance and day-to-day administration.

Governance is closely related to Microsoft Purview, which provides many of the tools for classification, protection and compliance, and to Microsoft 365 Copilot, whose answers depend on the content and permissions that already exist in a tenant. This connection explains why governance is often raised before a Copilot rollout: the quality and safety of results reflect how well information in the tenant has been organized and secured. The episode "Microsoft 365 Copilot Without the Hype: Adoption, Governance & Getting Your Tenant Ready with Paul Keijzers [MVP]" discusses this dependency, noting that Copilot can help people find information and get work done faster, but that its answers rely on existing content and permissions, and it looks at the foundations that shape results beyond demos and licensing.

Growth is another typical trigger for governance work. The episode "From Garage Band to Symphony Orchestra- How Microsoft 365 Governance Creates Harmony at Scale — with Heiko Brenn" uses a musical metaphor: a small environment works informally, with Teams created when needed, SharePoint sites appearing naturally and external guests invited without complicated processes. As the organization grows, Teams multiply, SharePoint sites accumulate, naming conventions become inconsistent, ownership becomes unclear and manual administration can no longer keep pace. Governance in this setting means introducing structure that scales.

The Power Platform raises a different set of questions. The episode "Power Platform Governance Without Killing Innovation: Security, DLP, Environments & Citizen Development with Michael Roth [MVP]" notes that the platform lets people across an organization build applications and automate processes faster than traditional development, and that this accessibility creates enterprise questions: who can build what, where company data goes, how environments should be structured, and how to limit shadow IT without becoming the department that rejects every new idea. Data loss prevention policies, environments and support for citizen development are among the topics it covers.

Governance and tooling are not the same thing, a point made in "Microsoft Purview is a Trap: The Hard Truth About Data Governance". The episode argues that many organizations mistakenly treat Microsoft Purview as a complete data governance solution, and that relying on it without a clear strategy can result in chaotic data environments and confusion over permissions.
