The episode "Azure AI Search – Simply Explained" lists hybrid search next to search indexes, indexers, full-text search, vector search, semantic search, AI enrichment, embeddings and data connectors as core concepts of Azure AI Search, and describes the service as a foundation for RAG applications. The episode "HNSW vs DiskANN for Vector Search in Azure AI Search" mentions hybrid search as a way to get stronger results by combining keyword and vector search, and also names ranking and relevance tuning as a way to adjust how results appear.

The episode "Improve Microsoft Copilot Accuracy Beyond Vector Search" makes the case for hybrid retrieval over pure vector search. It says that combining vector and keyword search improves precision and trust in AI responses, and that context loss in pure vector search can lead to poor business decisions, whereas hybrid methods keep important details. It further says that hybrid RAG improves recall and accuracy, helps systems understand internal jargon, and can answer faster and more reliably than pure vector search, which it associates with high latency. It also states that compliance and security are enhanced and that privacy risks are reduced, and it notes that moving to hybrid RAG takes some effort.

The same principle appears on the Microsoft 365 side. According to the episode "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Accuracy with Information Architecture", Copilot combines semantic and keyword searches to optimize results, so relevant, specific keywords in a prompt can improve the accuracy of the information retrieved. In practice this affects how content is written and labelled: precise terms still matter even when semantic matching is available.

Typical decisions around hybrid search include whether keyword matching alone is too literal, whether vector search alone loses exact terms such as product names or internal abbreviations, and how the two result lists should be weighted or fused. Related topics are semantic search, vector indexes such as HNSW and DiskANN, chunking, and the Azure services that support vector search, including Azure AI Search, Azure Cosmos DB and Azure SQL. Official documentation for the approach is available in the Azure AI Search hybrid search overview.

hybrid-work.desc: Hybrid work is a working model in which employees split their time between the office and remote work, which requires coordinating who is on site and when.

faq.a: Hybrid work is a working model in which employees split their time between working in the office and working remotely. This creates a need to coordinate who is in the office and when.
faq.q: What is hybrid work?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, Microsoft Places helps coordinate hybrid work by connecting calendars, colleagues, and available workspaces. It integrates with Outlook and Teams so it is clearer when and where people work.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Places relate to hybrid work?

faq.a: No. The episode with Onyinye Madubuko [MVP] says successful hybrid workplaces also depend on accessibility, collaboration, meeting room design, and organizational culture. The episode with Fabio Bonolo [MVP] adds leadership, change management, and employee education.
faq.q: Is hybrid work only a technology topic?

hybrid-work.long:
Hybrid work is a working model in which employees divide their time between working in the office and working remotely. Because people are no longer all in the same place on the same days, the model creates a practical need to coordinate who is in the office and when. Organizations that adopt it therefore have to think about more than where individual people sit: they need ways to see availability, plan shared days, and keep teams connected regardless of location.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, hybrid work is mostly approached through tools that sit inside the Microsoft 365 applications employees already use. The M365.FM episode "Coordinate Hybrid Work with Microsoft Places" describes Microsoft Places as a way to turn scattered office coordination into a connected, AI-driven experience. According to the episode, Places weaves itself into Outlook and Teams so that it becomes clearer when and where people work, rather than leaving colleagues to guess who will be on site. A second episode, "Microsoft Places - Simply Explained", presents Places as a solution that simplifies workspace management and supports collaboration among teams. It states that the platform connects a person's calendar, colleagues, and available workspaces, which makes it easier to coordinate in-office days. The episode also cites a figure that 51% of hybrid employees are likely to go fully remote in the next year, and uses it to argue why tools of this kind become important.

The topic also has a data and knowledge dimension. The episode "Microsoft Cowork IQ Knowledge Graph Architecture" discusses how organizations can build intelligent knowledge graph architectures to support modern hybrid work environments. It describes Microsoft Graph, Microsoft 365, AI-powered search, and Copilot-related capabilities as ways to connect people, content, conversations, and business processes into a unified knowledge ecosystem. In a hybrid setting, where colleagues cannot simply ask someone at the next desk, improving information discovery and reducing data silos is presented as a way to deliver more relevant insights.

The human and organizational side of hybrid work features in two conversations with Microsoft MVPs. In "Designing an Inclusive Hybrid Workplace with Onyinye Madubuko [MVP]", the discussion covers the rapid shift to hybrid work, the importance of employee experience, and how technologies such as Microsoft Teams, Viva, and Teams Rooms can improve communication and productivity. The episode emphasizes that successful hybrid strategies go beyond technology and require planning around accessibility, collaboration, meeting room design, and organizational culture. In "The Future of Work with Fabio Bonolo [MVP]", hybrid work appears alongside the evolution of Microsoft Copilot, autonomous AI agents, and the changing role of productivity. That episode stresses that adoption depends on leadership, change management, employee education, and a culture focused on empowerment rather than fear of automation, with practical points on Copilot adoption, data governance, and AI readiness.

Taken together, the episodes treat hybrid work as both a scheduling problem and a design problem. On the scheduling side, decisions center on how to make presence and availability visible and how to connect calendars, colleagues, and workspaces. On the design side, decisions involve meeting rooms, accessibility, communication tools, and the culture that surrounds them. The sources do not prescribe one fixed approach; they describe how Microsoft 365 components can support the model and where non-technical factors such as inclusion, leadership, and change management shape the outcome.

hyper-v.desc: Hyper-V is Microsoft's type-1 hypervisor in Windows Server and Windows for running virtual machines; Azure Migrate and Site Recovery can work with Hyper-V VMs.

faq.a: Hyper-V is Microsoft's type-1 hypervisor, built into Windows Server and Windows, used to create and run virtual machines for consolidation, resilience and disaster recovery.
faq.q: What is Hyper-V?

faq.a: It is a role in all editions of Windows Server 2025 and is included in the Pro, Enterprise and Education editions of Windows 11, where it mainly serves local development and test needs.
faq.q: Which Windows editions include Hyper-V?

faq.a: Azure Site Recovery can protect Hyper-V virtual machines as part of disaster recovery, and Azure Migrate can discover, assess and replicate them for migration to Azure.
faq.q: How does Hyper-V relate to Azure Site Recovery and Azure Migrate?

hyper-v.long:
Hyper-V is Microsoft's hypervisor technology for running virtual machines on Windows hosts. It is built into Windows Server and Windows and runs as a type-1 hypervisor directly on the hardware. Organizations use it to create and run virtual machines for server consolidation, better use of hardware, resilience and disaster recovery. Guest systems can be Windows, Linux or FreeBSD.

Hyper-V is available as a role in all editions of Windows Server 2025. It is also included in the Pro, Enterprise and Education editions of Windows 11, where it mainly serves local development and test needs. This gives the same virtualization technology a place both in the data center and on an individual workstation. The official documentation consulted for this page does not give concrete limits for vCPUs, memory or the number of virtual machines, so those figures are not covered here.

Several capabilities concern the security and configuration of virtual machines. Generation 2 virtual machines add UEFI, Secure Boot and a virtual TPM 2.0. Shielded VMs combine BitLocker, Secure Boot and attestation, and the Host Guardian Service limits which hosts may run them. For storage, the documentation lists Storage Spaces Direct, Storage Spaces, iSCSI, Fibre Channel, SMB and NFS as options, so virtual machines can sit on a range of local, shared and networked storage designs.

Availability and recovery are a central part of the platform. Failover clustering with Cluster Shared Volumes and live migration support keeping workloads running across hosts. For disaster recovery, Hyper-V Replica and Azure Site Recovery are named as the relevant options. This is where Hyper-V connects to the wider Azure ecosystem: Azure Migrate can discover, assess and replicate Hyper-V virtual machines, which makes it a common source environment when workloads move to Azure.

Management is possible through several tools. Hyper-V Manager provides a graphical console, PowerShell and PowerShell Direct allow scripted administration, Windows Admin Center offers a browser-based approach, and System Center Virtual Machine Manager covers larger managed environments. Which tool fits depends on the size of the estate and on whether administrators prefer interactive or automated workflows.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Site Recovery - Simply Explained" places Hyper-V in the context of disaster recovery. The episode says Azure Site Recovery protects Azure Virtual Machines, VMware, Hyper-V, physical servers and hybrid environments, and that it integrates with Azure networking, Azure Monitor and Azure Automation to simplify disaster recovery management. It covers concepts such as Recovery Services Vaults, replication policies, recovery points, planned versus unplanned failovers, test failovers and automated recovery plans. The episode also explains the difference between Azure Site Recovery and Azure Backup: Azure Backup focuses on protecting data and restoring files or workloads after data loss, while Azure Site Recovery is designed to keep applications running during an outage.

Typical decisions around Hyper-V therefore include where to host virtual machines, which management tool to use, how to protect workloads, and whether to keep them on premises or migrate them to Azure. Hyper-V Replica and Azure Site Recovery address disaster recovery, while Azure Migrate addresses discovery, assessment and replication for migration scenarios.

hyperconverged-infrastructure.desc: Hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) is a software-defined design where one cluster of servers provides compute, storage and networking instead of separate systems.

faq.a: Hyperconverged infrastructure is a software-defined design in which the same cluster of servers provides compute, storage and networking. It replaces the model of separate server and storage systems.
faq.q: What is hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI)?

faq.a: Traditional setups use separate server and storage systems, while HCI delivers compute, storage and networking from one cluster of servers using software-defined methods.
faq.q: How does HCI differ from traditional infrastructure?

hyperconverged-infrastructure.long:
Hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) is a software-defined infrastructure design in which the same cluster of servers provides compute, storage and networking. This differs from traditional architectures that use separate server and storage systems.

In an HCI design, these resources are combined within one set of servers and managed through software rather than through dedicated hardware for each function. The approach is typically used to run virtualized workloads on a unified cluster and to simplify how infrastructure is built and operated.

On M365.FM, Hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) is documented as a concept within the Microsoft ecosystem knowledge base. No related entities, official documentation links or specific episodes are currently linked to this entry, so this page limits itself to the core definition of the term.

idempotency.desc: Idempotency is the property of an operation or deployment that yields the same result however many times it runs, a core idea in infrastructure as code and integrations.

faq.a: It means that re-running a deployment produces the same result and only changes what differs from the desired state. If the environment already matches the definition, nothing further is altered.
faq.q: What does idempotency mean in infrastructure as code?

faq.a: The episode on D365FO integration architecture says repeated messages should not cause errors or data corruption. Designing for idempotency keeps data accurate and avoids unnecessary processing.
faq.q: Why does idempotency matter for integrations?

faq.a: The episode on Power Platform custom connectors recommends upserts, using PATCH with If-Match or an alternate key, together with stored source IDs. This avoids creating duplicate records when a run is repeated.
faq.q: How is idempotency achieved when writing data through APIs?

idempotency.long:
Idempotency is a property of an operation or deployment that produces the same result no matter how many times it is run. In infrastructure as code, this means that re-running a deployment only changes what differs from the desired state: if the environment already matches the definition, running it again leaves everything as it is. The term appears across the Microsoft ecosystem, from infrastructure deployment to integration design and automation of Microsoft 365 services.

The idea matters because real systems rarely run an operation exactly once. Jobs get retried after errors, messages are delivered twice, and deployments are repeated across development, testing and production environments. An idempotent design makes these repetitions safe. Without it, a retry can create duplicate records, corrupt data or leave an environment in an unexpected state. With it, repeated runs converge on the same outcome, which keeps automation predictable and reduces operational risk.

The episode "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained" places idempotency among the core concepts of infrastructure as code, alongside declarative versus imperative deployments, version control and automation. The episode describes how infrastructure can be deployed automatically, consistently and repeatedly across environments instead of relying on manual "click operations", and it compares technologies such as Azure Bicep, ARM Templates, Terraform and PowerShell and where each fits in the Microsoft ecosystem. In this context, idempotency is what allows the same definition to be applied again and again, with only the differences from the desired state being changed.

In integration work, idempotency is mainly about duplicate handling. The episode "D365FO Integration Architecture with Anitha Eswaran [MVP-MCT]" says that integrations should be designed so that repeated messages do not cause errors or data corruption. The episode presents this as a practice that keeps data accurate and prevents unnecessary processing. It sits next to other design decisions discussed there, such as batching messages to process many records at once and using service-level agreements to set expectations for data freshness and to guide monitoring and alerting.

The episode "Expose Dynamics 365 APIs with Power Platform Custom Connectors" gives a concrete pattern. Its notes recommend upserts, using PATCH with If-Match or an alternate key, to avoid duplicates, and storing source IDs so that records can be matched on later runs. This appears in a list of design concerns that also includes pagination, delta loads using a persisted watermark based on the last successful run, and schema evolution. Together these practices let a flow be re-run or resumed without creating duplicate data.

Idempotency also shows up in platform management and automation. In "Enterprise Architecture for Power Platform Management", the notes list retry and idempotency in flows, including handling 429 and 5xx responses and using de-duplication keys, as part of building for resilience. In "Automate Viva Connections, Topics, Learning, and News", the notes name logging, backoff and idempotency as the measures that keep automated jobs running reliably when publishing topics, pushing courses into Viva Learning or posting Connections content programmatically with targeting and retries.

Across these episodes the pattern is consistent. Retries and re-runs are expected, so operations are designed to be safe to repeat: declarative definitions for infrastructure, upserts and alternate keys for data writes, de-duplication keys in flows, and tolerance for duplicate messages in integrations. Teams choosing a design typically weigh how a failed or repeated run will behave, and whether the result after a second execution is identical to the first.

identity-debt.desc: Identity debt is the build-up of non-human identities, secrets and Conditional Access exceptions that an organization relies on but can no longer fully explain.

faq.a: Identity debt is the accumulation of non-human identities and entitlements, such as service principals, managed identities, app registrations, secrets and Conditional Access exceptions, that an organization depends on but can no longer explain.
faq.q: What is identity debt?

faq.a: The episodes describe Conditional Access exceptions as one component of identity debt. Temporary exclusions and poorly maintained policies accumulate over time and weaken the decisions that Microsoft Entra ID makes for every authorization.
faq.q: How does identity debt relate to Conditional Access?

faq.a: The episode with Jonathan Hope covers Zero Trust principles, well-designed Conditional Access policies, least-privilege access and protecting privileged accounts, and it introduces the idea of managing identity as code.
faq.q: What do the M365.FM episodes recommend against identity debt?

identity-debt.long:
Identity debt is the accumulation of non-human identities and entitlements that an organization depends on but can no longer explain. The concept covers items such as service principals, managed identities, app registrations, secrets and Conditional Access exceptions. In the same way that technical debt describes shortcuts that pile up in code, identity debt describes identity-related shortcuts, leftovers and exceptions that gather over time and weaken the security posture of an environment such as Microsoft Entra ID.

The term appears in M365.FM episodes that treat identity as the control plane of the Microsoft cloud. The episode "Fix Microsoft Entra ID Conditional Access and Identity Debt" argues that Azure outages and breaches often begin higher up than networks, costs or misconfigured virtual machines, namely in identity itself. It reframes identity not as a simple login service but as a distributed decision engine that compiles signals about users, devices, risk, roles and exceptions into every authorization decision. According to the episode, small "temporary" exceptions in Conditional Access, hybrid identity sync and workload identities add up over time, and the decision engine then works with a growing set of assumptions nobody has reviewed.

The episode "Conditional Access and Identity as Code with Jonathan Hope [MVP]" describes identity debt as the gradual accumulation of exceptions, legacy configurations, guest accounts, workload identities and hybrid synchronization issues. In that conversation, Microsoft Entra ID is presented as the control plane for security, and mismanaged identities, excessive permissions and poorly maintained Conditional Access policies are named as sources of significant risk. The discussion also covers practical countermeasures: implementing Zero Trust principles, designing effective Conditional Access policies, enforcing least-privilege access and protecting privileged accounts.

In practice, identity debt shows up in situations that many administrators will recognize. An app registration created for a project remains after the project ends. A secret is issued with no clear owner. A Conditional Access exclusion is added to unblock one team and is never removed. A service principal holds permissions that nobody can map back to a business need. Each item may look harmless on its own, but together they form a set of identities and entitlements that the organization depends on without being able to justify or confidently remove them. The key characteristic in the definition is the loss of explanation: the dependency exists, the understanding does not.

Dealing with identity debt is mainly a question of visibility and ownership. The sources behind the episodes point toward reviewing exceptions, tightening least-privilege access and treating identity configuration with the discipline applied to other engineering artifacts, which is the idea behind "identity as code" in the Jonathan Hope episode. A related episode, "Solve the Microsoft 365 Permission and Access Problem", links permission sprawl to governance, and the episode list around it frames Microsoft 365 governance as a people and ownership problem rather than a purely technical one. This fits the definition of identity debt, since an identity nobody owns is by nature one nobody can explain.

The topic also extends to newer identity types. The episode "Microsoft Entra Agent ID: Secure Identity for AI Agents" appears in the same cluster of related listening and points to the need for governed identities for AI agents, a category that goes beyond traditional service accounts. As more non-human identities are created, the same questions about ownership, purpose and lifecycle apply. The shorter overview "Conditional Access - Simply Explained" ties back to the topic by listing the identity debt episode among its related recommendations, showing that Conditional Access design and identity debt are usually discussed together.

identity-drift.desc: Identity drift is the gradual loss of clear accountability when automations and AI agents run under maker credentials or shared service accounts instead of dedicated non-human identities.

faq.a: Identity drift is the gradual loss of clear accountability when automations and AI agents run under maker credentials, shared service accounts or ambiguous connection contexts instead of dedicated, isolatable non-human identities.
faq.q: What is identity drift?

faq.a: The episode "High-Performance Automation Control Plane for Power Automate" recommends giving each automation a unique identity for audit trails and safe rollback, defining execution contracts, running a lifecycle from creation to retirement, and continuously monitoring for identity drift and permission creep.
faq.q: How do the episodes suggest reducing identity drift in Power Automate?

faq.a: According to "Protect Enterprise Architecture from Agentic Copilot Risk", agents that can change state act within the existing permission graph, so without governed non-human identities their actions multiply authority without explicit approval or controls.
faq.q: Why does identity drift matter more with agentic Copilot?

identity-drift.long:
Identity drift is the gradual loss of clear accountability that occurs when automations and AI agents run under maker credentials, shared service accounts or ambiguous connection contexts, rather than under dedicated, isolatable non-human identities. In the M365.FM episodes it is treated as a governance failure pattern: it is rarely a single event, and it builds up as flows, agents and connections accumulate without anyone clearly owning the identity they act under.

The core problem is attribution and control. When an automation runs with the credentials of the person who built it, or through an account shared by many processes, it becomes hard to answer basic questions: who or what performed an action, under whose authority, and what permissions were involved. Over time, people change roles, accounts are reused, and permissions are added and rarely reviewed. The episode "Microsoft 365 Governance Is a People and Ownership Problem" describes identity drift as organizations losing track of identities and their associated permissions, and links it to missing executive sponsorship, weak collaboration with business units and inadequate discovery of identities and entitlements.

The concept becomes more pressing with agentic AI. According to "Protect Enterprise Architecture from Agentic Copilot Risk", once Copilot can take actions that change state, it multiplies executive authority across the environment without explicit approval or controls. The episode says this leads to identity drift, tool and connector sprawl and obedient data leakage, because agents execute within the existing permission graph and data sprawl rather than within a governed system. It lists non-human identities as one of four safeguards, alongside standardized tool contracts, authoritative data boundaries and runtime controls. "Scale Autonomous Agents in Microsoft 365 Without Chaos" makes a similar argument: agents are actors that execute actions with authority and side effects, so the real risks at scale are uncontrolled authority, identity drift, data leakage and cost sprawl rather than accuracy. It proposes a four-layer control plane covering identity, tool contracts, data governance and behavioral monitoring.

For Power Automate, "High-Performance Automation Control Plane for Power Automate" turns the idea into practice. Its recommendations include assigning each automation a unique identity so that audit trails and safe rollback are possible, defining execution contracts that state which actions and conditions are permitted, and establishing a lifecycle covering creation, versioning, review and retirement. It also calls for continuous monitoring of identity drift, permission creep and behavioral changes, treating each automation as a product with clear ownership and measurable KPIs, and using drift detection and containment to keep behavior within defined limits.

Identity drift also appears outside automation. "Move Legacy Systems to Azure Without Disrupting Work" argues that cloud migration amplifies organizational behavior rather than fixing it, exposing identity drift, policy gaps, unmanaged exceptions and teams improvising at scale. The episode's point is about sequencing: workloads are moved before a platform exists that can enforce intent through identity, policy, networking, logging and subscription boundaries.

Taken together, the episodes frame identity drift as an ownership problem as much as a technical one. The practical decisions they point to are which identity each automation or agent runs under, who is accountable for it, how its permissions are reviewed over time, and how deviations are detected and contained. Dedicated, isolatable non-human identities are presented as the way to keep actions attributable and to limit how far a misbehaving automation can reach.

identity-lifecycle.desc: Identity lifecycle management automates how identities are created, changed and removed as people join, move within and leave an organization, using Microsoft Entra.

faq.a: Joiner-mover-leaver (JML) describes the three phases of a person's relationship with an organization: joining, changing roles and leaving. Identity lifecycle management automates the access changes that belong to each phase.
faq.q: What does joiner-mover-leaver mean?

faq.a: It is implemented through provisioning and Lifecycle Workflows in Microsoft Entra ID Governance. These work together with access reviews and entitlement management, as discussed in the episode on Entra ID Governance.
faq.q: How is identity lifecycle management implemented in Microsoft Entra?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft AI Agent Runtimes: Beyond Enterprise Chatbots" describes AI identity lifecycle management as controlling agent identities with policy-driven frameworks. Microsoft Entra Agent ID is a related topic.
faq.q: Does identity lifecycle management apply to AI agents?

identity-lifecycle.long:
Identity lifecycle management is the practice of automating how identities are created, changed and removed as people join, move within and leave an organization. It is commonly described as joiner-mover-leaver (JML), and the topic is also known under the aliases Lifecycle Workflows and Identitäts-Lebenszyklus. In the Microsoft ecosystem it is implemented through provisioning and through Lifecycle Workflows in Microsoft Entra ID Governance. The central idea is that access follows a person's role and employment status instead of depending on manual tickets that are easily forgotten.

The concept is used wherever organizations need consistent onboarding and offboarding. When a person joins, the identity and the access that the role requires should be set up automatically. When someone moves to a different role, access should be adjusted so that permissions from the previous position do not simply accumulate. When someone leaves, access should be removed in a controlled and traceable way. Automating these steps reduces manual work, lowers the chance of human error and supports compliance, because policies are applied the same way every time and actions can be audited.

The topic is closely tied to Microsoft Entra ID, where the identities live, and to Active Directory, from which many organizations still start. Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync connects these two worlds by synchronizing on-premises identities to the cloud, so that lifecycle processes can build on a consistent identity source. Lifecycle management also sits inside the wider area of governance, where it works together with access reviews and entitlement management. Access reviews check whether existing access is still needed, entitlement management bundles access into packages, and lifecycle workflows handle the timing of changes around joiners, movers and leavers.

A newer extension of the topic is the lifecycle of non-human identities. Microsoft Entra Agent ID is related to this subject, and the episode "Microsoft AI Agent Runtimes: Beyond Enterprise Chatbots" describes AI identity lifecycle management as controlling agent identities with policy-driven frameworks. According to that episode, each agent has a unique identity tied to enterprise policies, access is restricted by role and necessity, agent credentials are monitored, and the least-privilege principle applies so that each agent receives only the access it needs for its tasks.

Several M365.FM episodes touch the subject. "Entra ID Governance: Access Reviews, Entitlement Management and Lifecycle Workflows" looks at how these three capabilities work together and how to introduce governance step by step, starting from joiner-mover-leaver basics and moving toward access packages. It is aimed at identity architects and IAM and compliance teams. "Microsoft Entra Permissions Management - Simply Explained" says that Microsoft Entra automates the joiner-mover-leaver process, that this ensures users have only the necessary permissions, and that managing all lifecycle workflows from a single location can reduce time consumption and enhance security, with audit trails supporting transparency. "How Microsoft Graph Connects Microsoft 365 Data and Context" describes managing identity governance through Microsoft Graph, including automating onboarding and offboarding to reduce manual work and improve compliance. "Copilot in Microsoft Entra ID - Simply Explained" mentions that Copilot can help streamline lifecycle workflows and group management and evaluate risks associated with users and applications.

In practice, a common decision is where to begin. The episode on Entra ID Governance recommends introducing governance in steps rather than all at once, with the joiner-mover-leaver basics as the starting point. Teams typically need to decide which identity source drives the process, which access should be granted automatically for a role, and which steps should run when employment status changes. Official documentation for Lifecycle Workflows is available on Microsoft Learn.

identity-security-tool.desc: Identity and security tool is a category for tools that protect identities, devices, data and applications, including Microsoft Entra, Purview, Defender and Intune.

faq.a: It is a tool for protecting identities, devices, data and applications. The category covers controls for sign-in, device trust, handling of sensitive information and threat detection and response.
faq.q: What is an identity and security tool?

faq.a: On M365.FM, Microsoft Entra, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Intune are classified as instances of the category. Entra covers identity and access, Intune devices and apps, Purview data protection and compliance, and Defender threat detection and response.
faq.q: Which Microsoft products belong to this category?

faq.a: The Microsoft Learn overview on Zero Trust describes the principles behind them: verify explicitly, use least privilege access, and assume breach. The tools put these principles into practice by checking identity, device and risk signals and by limiting the impact of a compromise.
faq.q: How do these tools relate to Zero Trust?

identity-security-tool.long:
An identity and security tool is a tool for protecting identities, devices, data and applications. The term describes a category rather than a single product. It covers the controls that decide who may sign in, which devices are trusted, how sensitive information is handled and how threats are detected and answered. Taken together, these controls form the protective layer around the other services of an organization.

On M365.FM this is a parent category. Microsoft Entra, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Intune are classified as instances of it. They divide the work roughly by area. Microsoft Entra handles identity and access, Microsoft Intune manages devices and apps, Microsoft Purview covers data protection and compliance, and Microsoft Defender focuses on threat detection and response. Because each tool addresses a different area, an organization usually combines several of them rather than relying on one.

The tools are often used together. A common example is device status from Microsoft Intune feeding sign-in decisions made through Conditional Access. In that case a device-management signal becomes an input to an identity-based access decision, which shows how the categories depend on one another instead of working in isolation.

The design thinking behind this category is described in the Microsoft Learn overview "Zero Trust as a security foundation". Zero Trust follows the idea of never trust, always verify: access is granted only after checking who is asking, which device is used, location, behavior and risk, and verification continues throughout a session. The overview names three principles. The first is to verify explicitly using all available signals. The second is to use least privilege access for the shortest time needed. The third is to assume breach, which focuses controls on limiting impact and speeding detection and response.

Compared with traditional perimeter models, which trusted assets inside the network, Zero Trust treats every request as untrusted. The overview explains this by noting that modern attacks rely on identity compromise, phishing and session hijacking rather than network position. Outcomes it lists include continuously evaluated and temporary access, tightly scoped permissions, consistent controls across on-premises, cloud, SaaS and AI workloads, and built-in detection and response. It also stresses that security concerns human behavior and processes as well as technology, and that responsibility is shared.

Typical scenarios for identity and security tools include requiring multifactor authentication for administrators, allowing access to company mail only from managed devices, labelling and restricting confidential documents, and collecting alerts from endpoints and email in one place for investigation. The aim is always the same: verify requests explicitly, grant least privilege and limit the damage if one account or device is compromised.

This entry has no linked M365.FM episodes yet. Readers looking for more detail can follow the individual tools in the category, which are covered on their own pages.

identity-threat-detection-and-response.desc: Identity threat detection and response (ITDR) is a security discipline that detects compromised or misused identities from identity signals and contains them quickly.

faq.a: ITDR is a security discipline that detects compromised or misused identities from identity signals and contains them quickly, for example by revoking sessions or disabling accounts. It covers prevention, detection and response for attacks aimed at identities.
faq.q: What is identity threat detection and response (ITDR)?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Microsoft Defender for Identity - Simply Explained", traditional IAM relies on static rules and is reactive, while ITDR provides continuous oversight, analyzes behavior patterns and enables an immediate response to potential threats.
faq.q: How does ITDR differ from traditional IAM?

faq.a: Microsoft names Microsoft Entra ID Protection and Microsoft Defender for Identity as the products involved, with the capabilities offered through the Microsoft Defender Suite.
faq.q: Which Microsoft products are associated with ITDR?

identity-threat-detection-and-response.long:
Identity threat detection and response (ITDR) is a security discipline that detects compromised or misused identities from identity signals and contains them quickly, for example by revoking sessions or disabling accounts. It focuses on attacks aimed at identities rather than at devices or networks alone. Microsoft describes it as a security focus area with solutions that prevent, detect and respond to such attacks.

The starting point is the observation, stated in Microsoft's description, that many identity attacks begin with stolen credentials, for example through phishing or social engineering. Attackers also increasingly target the identity infrastructure itself and weaknesses in its configuration. A purely preventive approach built around authentication therefore leaves gaps: once an account has been taken over, the activity that follows can look like normal use unless behavior is observed continuously.

The capabilities listed in Microsoft's description show how the discipline works in practice. Adaptive access control evaluates risk in real time. Signals from endpoints, email, collaboration tools and SaaS apps are correlated, so that an identity-related event can be judged in context. Anomaly detection based on user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA) can trigger step-up authentication or block access. Further functions are automated disruption of attacks and lateral movement, and autonomous investigation of risky identities. Coverage extends to human and non-human identities across cloud, hybrid and on-premises environments.

A central idea in this description is that identity administrators and security operations teams should work together instead of separately. Identity teams typically own access policies and directory configuration, while security operations teams own detection and incident response. ITDR is the area where the two meet, because a risky sign-in or a suspicious change to an identity needs both a detection and an access-control decision.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, Microsoft Entra ID Protection and Microsoft Defender for Identity are the products named in this context, and the capabilities are offered through the Microsoft Defender Suite according to the page's FAQ. The source does not name specific license SKUs or technical limits, so questions about licensing or scope need to be checked against current product documentation.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Defender for Identity - Simply Explained" places ITDR next to traditional identity and access management (IAM). The episode contrasts the two in a comparison: traditional IAM relies on static rules, while ITDR offers continuous oversight. It describes IAM as reactive to issues and limited in visibility after authentication, whereas ITDR is presented as enabling an immediate response to potential threats, analyzing behavior patterns, preventing threats proactively and giving real-time visibility into identity activity. In that framing, Microsoft Defender for Identity provides the continuous oversight that supports immediate responses and strengthens the security posture.

Typical decisions around ITDR therefore concern how identity signals are collected and correlated, which response actions can be automated (such as revoking sessions or disabling accounts), and how responsibilities are divided between identity administration and security operations. Non-human identities, such as service accounts, are part of the scope alongside user accounts.

illicit-consent-grant.desc: An illicit consent grant attack tricks a user into approving an attacker-controlled OAuth application, giving it access to mail or files without a stolen password.

faq.a: It is an attack in which a user is tricked into granting an attacker-controlled OAuth application permissions, such as mail or file access. The app then has account-level access to data.
faq.q: What is an illicit consent grant attack?

faq.a: No. The attack works by getting the user to consent to the application's permission request, so access is gained without stealing the user's password.
faq.q: Does an illicit consent grant attack require a stolen password?

faq.a: Microsoft publishes documentation on detecting and remediating illicit consent grants as part of its Microsoft Defender for Office 365 guidance.
faq.q: Where can guidance on responding to illicit consent grants be found?

illicit-consent-grant.long:
An illicit consent grant attack is a technique in which an attacker persuades a user to grant an OAuth application permissions to the user's data. The application is controlled by the attacker. Once the user consents, the app can act with the granted permissions, such as reading mail or accessing files, giving it account-level access to data.

The attack does not depend on stealing a password. Instead of capturing credentials, the attacker relies on the user's own approval of a permission request. Because access comes through a legitimate consent flow, the resulting access is tied to the app and its granted permissions rather than to a compromised sign-in.

The concept is relevant to anyone administering or securing Microsoft 365 environments, where third-party and custom applications can request delegated permissions. Microsoft documents how to detect and remediate illicit consent grants in Microsoft Defender for Office 365, and that guidance is the reference for investigating and responding to this kind of activity.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic, and no related entities are listed. The official Microsoft documentation on detecting and remediating illicit consent grants is the primary source for further detail.

immersive-spaces-in-teams.desc: Immersive spaces in Microsoft Teams are a 3D meeting view powered by Microsoft Mesh, where participants join as avatars with spatial audio, up to 16 per space.

faq.a: They are a 3D meeting view in Microsoft Teams, powered by Microsoft Mesh, in which participants join as avatars with spatial audio.
faq.q: What are immersive spaces in Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: A space holds up to 16 participants.
faq.q: How many people can join an immersive space?

faq.a: Immersive spaces are powered by Microsoft Mesh.
faq.q: Which technology powers immersive spaces?

immersive-spaces-in-teams.long:
Immersive spaces in Microsoft Teams are a 3D meeting view in which participants appear as avatars inside a shared virtual environment. The feature is powered by Microsoft Mesh and uses spatial audio, so voices are positioned within the space rather than heard as a single flat stream. A single space holds up to 16 participants.

The feature is used for meetings that take place in a three-dimensional setting instead of the standard grid of video tiles. Participants join as avatars, which allows them to take part without relying on a camera feed. The use of Microsoft Mesh as the underlying technology ties the experience to Microsoft's broader work on shared virtual spaces inside the Microsoft 365 ecosystem.

The available facts do not describe licensing, supported devices, setup steps or administration options, so those details are not covered here. Official documentation for immersive spaces in Teams meetings is published on Microsoft Learn.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

immutable-backup.desc: An immutable backup is stored in a write-once-read-many (WORM) state, so recovery points cannot be changed or deleted, even by administrators, until retention expires.

faq.a: It means the backup is held in a write-once-read-many (WORM) state. Its recovery points cannot be changed or deleted, even by administrators, until the retention period expires.
faq.q: What does immutable mean for a backup?

faq.a: No one can. The protection applies even to administrators, and it lasts until the retention period expires.
faq.q: Who can delete an immutable backup before retention ends?

faq.a: WORM stands for write-once-read-many. Data can be written once and read repeatedly, but not altered or removed during the protection period.
faq.q: What does WORM stand for?

immutable-backup.long:
An immutable backup is a backup stored in a write-once-read-many (WORM) state. Once a recovery point has been written, it cannot be modified or deleted, even by administrators, until its configured retention period has expired.

The concept is used to keep recovery points intact when accounts, credentials or administrative access are compromised or misused. Because the stored data cannot be altered or removed during the retention period, it remains available as a restore source. This is relevant to scenarios such as accidental deletion, tampering and attacks that target backup data.

Immutability depends on the retention period. Until that period ends, the recovery point stays in its protected state; after it ends, the backup can be handled according to the applicable retention policy.

No related products, linked topics or M365.FM episodes are listed for this entry at present, so it serves as a general definition of the term.

immutable-storage.desc: Immutable storage (WORM) is a write once, read many storage behavior in Azure Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2 that prevents data from being modified or deleted.

faq.a: WORM stands for write once, read many. Data can be written and read repeatedly, but it cannot be modified or deleted while the protection applies.
faq.q: What does WORM mean in immutable storage?

faq.a: It is offered for Azure Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2.
faq.q: Where is immutable storage (WORM) offered?

faq.a: It is applied through time-based retention policies and legal holds, which prevent the data from being modified or deleted.
faq.q: How is immutability applied to stored data?

immutable-storage.long:
Immutable storage (WORM) is a storage behavior in which data, once written, can be read many times but cannot be modified or deleted. WORM stands for write once, read many. In the Microsoft ecosystem, this behavior is offered for Azure Blob Storage and ADLS Gen2.

The protection is applied through time-based retention policies and legal holds. A time-based retention policy keeps data protected from change or deletion for a defined period, while a legal hold preserves data until the hold is explicitly removed. Both mechanisms are aimed at situations where the integrity and preservation of stored data must be ensured.

The concept is relevant wherever stored data has to remain unaltered, such as for records that must be preserved over time or data that must be kept available for review. Because the restriction applies to modification and deletion, it differs from ordinary storage behavior, where data can normally be overwritten or removed.

No episodes of M365.FM are currently linked to this entry, and no additional related topics have been recorded for it so far.

impossible-travel.desc: Impossible travel is a risk detection that flags sign-ins by one user from locations too far apart to reach in the time between them, hinting at compromised credentials.

faq.a: It is a risk detection that flags sign-ins by the same user from locations too far apart to be reached in the time between them. It is considered a common signal of compromised credentials or replayed tokens.
faq.q: What does impossible travel mean in Microsoft Entra ID?

faq.a: The episode "Detect Impossible Travel and Token Replay in Microsoft Entra ID" describes an attack where a phishing email steals a session token instead of a password. The stolen identity then reappears from impossible locations, which is how the detection can reveal the replay.
faq.q: How is impossible travel connected to token replay?

faq.a: The episode "Modern Authentication and Token Lifecycle in Microsoft 365" describes setting user risk to High, revoking refresh tokens and sign-in sessions, requiring a password reset and device health check, and notifying the SOC and manager.
faq.q: What can be done after an impossible travel alert is confirmed?

impossible-travel.long:
Impossible travel is a risk detection that flags sign-ins by the same user from locations too far apart to be reached in the time between them. It is treated as a common signal of compromised credentials or replayed tokens. If an account signs in from one region and then appears in a distant region shortly afterwards, no ordinary journey could explain the gap, so the activity is marked as suspicious and surfaced for review.

The purpose of the detection is to catch account takeover that bypasses the usual perimeter. In the M365.FM episode "Detect Impossible Travel and Token Replay in Microsoft Entra ID", the scenario opens with a phishing email that does not steal a password but a session token. Within minutes, the identity reappears from impossible locations, and the episode uses this pattern to show why impossible travel and token replay need to be monitored together. The same episode describes monitoring as providing visibility into user activity and cloud events so that suspicious behaviors, such as unusual login attempts from unexpected places, can be spotted.

Impossible travel also appears as one of several behavioral signals in identity threat detection. The episode "Microsoft Defender for Identity - Simply Explained" lists impossible travel together with unusual devices and abnormal access times as patterns that can indicate compromised credentials. It cites the Verizon 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report, according to which 22% of breaches start with compromised credentials, and argues that monitoring user behavior helps reveal deviations that suggest unauthorized access or privilege escalation.

In Microsoft Entra ID, the detection feeds into risk scoring. The episode "Lock Down Microsoft Entra ID Before Phishing Hits" describes using Microsoft Entra ID to identify and score risky sign-ins and users automatically. Risk policies can be configured to block access or to require secure remediation when risk is detected. Insight into suspicious activities such as unfamiliar sign-ins and impossible travel supports the response, and regular review of audit logs keeps administrators informed. The episode also covers automated risk remediation, where Microsoft Entra ID can enforce strong authentication or a secure password reset depending on the detected risk level.

Impossible travel is also part of wider operational monitoring. The episode "Fix a Failing Microsoft 365 Rollout" recommends watching for brute force attempts, credential stuffing and impossible travel events as part of early detection. It suggests setting up alerts for risky sign-ins, using automated remediations, and running regular threat hunts with Microsoft 365 Defender Advanced Hunting. Those hunts look for unusual activity such as new forwarding rules or large file downloads outside work hours. The episode also advises creating and testing incident response playbooks that define roles and steps for quick action.

When an impossible travel alert is confirmed as a real compromise, the response usually involves containment. The episode "Modern Authentication and Token Lifecycle in Microsoft 365" outlines a playbook triggered by a high-severity identity alert, with impossible travel and Defender for Identity lateral movement named as examples. Its actions include confirming the user is compromised by setting user risk to High, revoking refresh tokens and sign-in sessions, requiring a password reset and device health check, and notifying the SOC and the user's manager. The episode suggests automating these steps with a Logic App and notes that sessions can be revoked through Microsoft Graph.

Taken together, the episodes treat impossible travel as an early indicator rather than proof. The signal points to credentials or tokens possibly in the wrong hands, and the surrounding controls, such as risk policies, session revocation and password resets, determine how quickly access is cut off.

imposter-syndrome.desc: Imposter syndrome is a pattern of self-doubt and fear of being exposed as a fraud, common among high achievers in tech, and discussed in several M365.FM episodes.

faq.a: Imposter syndrome is a psychological pattern in which people doubt their accomplishments and fear being exposed as a fraud. It is described as common among high achievers in tech.
faq.q: What is imposter syndrome?

faq.a: The episode "Why High Performers Burn Out from Workplace Isolation" suggests sharing experiences with trusted peers and being honest about one's feelings. The episode with Heather Cook encourages creators to publish their work confidently, since each piece adds to a lasting knowledge archive.
faq.q: How do M365.FM episodes suggest dealing with imposter syndrome?

faq.a: The topic appears in "Leadership, AI, and Imposter Syndrome with Daniel "Dan" Barber [MVP]", "Why High Performers Burn Out from Workplace Isolation" and "Building Communities That Last: Copilot Adoption, Microsoft 365, and the Human Side of Technology with Heather Cook [Microsoft]".
faq.q: Which M365.FM episodes discuss imposter syndrome?

imposter-syndrome.long:
Imposter syndrome is a psychological pattern in which people doubt their accomplishments and fear being exposed as a fraud, despite evidence of their success. It is commonly described among high achievers, and the description used on M365.FM places it particularly in the technology field. It is not a technical subject in the Microsoft ecosystem, but it appears repeatedly in conversations about careers, leadership and community work around Microsoft 365, AI and related technologies.

In practice, the pattern shows up as persistent feelings of inadequacy that do not match a person's actual track record. People who experience it may hesitate to share their work, question whether their expertise is real, or feel that colleagues will eventually notice a supposed lack of ability. In technology, where tools, platforms and skills change quickly, the sense of always being behind can reinforce this feeling, especially during periods of large-scale change such as AI transformation.

The M365.FM episode "Leadership, AI, and Imposter Syndrome with Daniel "Dan" Barber [MVP]" addresses the topic directly. In that conversation, host Mirko Peters speaks with Daniel "Dan" Barber, founder of Strathos and Microsoft MVP, about the human side of leadership, the emotional impact of AI transformation and the often-hidden reality of imposter syndrome. According to the episode description, the discussion offers an honest reflection on career growth, mental resilience, community building, AI disruption and what it means to lead in a constantly changing digital world. The episode frames imposter syndrome as part of a broader look at the personal side of working in technology rather than as an isolated issue.

The episode "Why High Performers Burn Out from Workplace Isolation" connects imposter syndrome with loneliness and burnout. It states that imposter syndrome affects many high achievers and suggests that sharing experiences with trusted peers can help reduce feelings of inadequacy. The same episode points to related themes: the pressure to maintain a polished image can lead to internal struggles, workplace culture plays a significant role in loneliness, and leaders often feel isolated because of their responsibilities. Its recommendations include being honest about one's own feelings, seeking environments that favor support and collaboration over competition, and encouraging open communication to build trust within a team.

A further angle comes from "Building Communities That Last: Copilot Adoption, Microsoft 365, and the Human Side of Technology with Heather Cook [Microsoft]". There, imposter syndrome is discussed in the context of content creation. The episode description says the conversation encourages creators to publish their work confidently, because every podcast, article or presentation becomes part of a lasting knowledge archive. The same episode links this to authenticity, which it describes as the most valuable asset a creator has, and to Women in Technology initiatives, inclusive communities and mentorship across the Microsoft ecosystem.

Taken together, the episodes treat imposter syndrome as a shared experience instead of an individual flaw. The recurring suggestions are practical and social: talk openly with peers, build supportive communities, share work publicly, and lead in ways that make honest conversation possible. The episode "Sentiment Analysis for Executive Leadership Reporting" also lists the Dan Barber conversation among related M365.FM episodes on leadership, alongside titles on leadership in the AI era and on Microsoft 365 governance beyond central control, which places the topic within the wider discussion of how leaders and teams handle change in the Microsoft ecosystem.

improvement-actions.desc: Improvement actions are recommended tasks in Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager that can be assigned to owners, hold evidence and add points to the compliance score.

faq.a: They are recommended tasks that help meet the controls in an assessment. They can be assigned to owners, hold evidence, be tested manually or automatically, and add points to the compliance score.
faq.q: What are improvement actions in Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager?

faq.a: Completing and verifying an improvement action adds points to the compliance score. The score therefore reflects progress on the actions and highlights areas that still need work.
faq.q: How do improvement actions relate to the compliance score?

faq.a: Actions can be assigned to owners, such as the teams that operate the relevant systems. Episodes recommend assigning improvement actions to teams and tracking evidence and status in Compliance Manager.
faq.q: Who works on improvement actions?

improvement-actions.long:
Improvement actions are the recommended tasks inside Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager. Each one describes a concrete step that helps an organization move closer to the requirements of a regulation or standard. An improvement action can be assigned to an owner, can hold evidence that the work was done, and can be tested either manually or automatically. When an action is completed and verified, it adds points to the compliance score, which is how Compliance Manager turns a broad compliance question into a number that can be tracked over time.

In practice, improvement actions sit at the center of the Compliance Manager workflow. Assessments are built from regulatory templates, including pre-built assessments for industry and regional standards as well as custom ones. Each assessment is broken down into controls, and the improvement actions are the recommended steps that address those controls. The episode "Microsoft 365 as an Enterprise Operating System" describes how regulatory templates and improvement actions centralize compliance activities, which makes it easier to track evidence and update status. It also notes the step-by-step guidance that Compliance Manager provides, with detailed recommendations for each improvement action, and the risk-based compliance score that measures progress and highlights areas for improvement.

Because improvement actions can be assigned, they also define who does what. A compliance lead can distribute actions to the teams that actually operate the relevant systems, and those owners can attach evidence and update the status as work proceeds. The episode "Fix Microsoft 365 Compliance Drift Beyond Green Dashboards" lists using Compliance Manager with pre-built templates to align with regulations and assigning improvement actions to teams as one of its recommended practices. The idea is that a green dashboard alone does not prove ongoing compliance, while assigned, evidenced and tested actions give a traceable record.

The ability to test actions manually or automatically matters for how the compliance score stays meaningful. Some actions can be verified by the system based on the configuration it can observe, while others depend on a person confirming that a procedure or control is in place and uploading supporting evidence. The episode "Microsoft 365 Audit Readiness and Governance Debt" explains the division of labor with Microsoft Purview: Purview provides the technical capabilities for audit, data governance and retention, while Compliance Manager offers risk assessments, control templates and improvement actions. According to the episode, Purview captures and stores audit logs and retention policies, while Compliance Manager maps controls, recommends changes and tracks evidence for audits.

The episode "Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager - Simply Explained" covers improvement actions as one of its named topics, alongside what Compliance Manager is, the compliance score, assessments, regulations and templates, who does what, and the workflow from start to finish. It presents improvement actions as the part of the tool where the compliance score actually moves, since the score reflects the actions that have been completed and verified.

The term also appears in a more general sense elsewhere. In the episode "D365FO Integration Architecture with Anitha Eswaran [MVP-MCT]", improvement actions refers to a simple table used to track continuous improvement of an integration, with columns for improvement area, action taken and next review date. That usage is separate from the Compliance Manager feature, but it shares the idea of recording a concrete action, an owner or outcome, and a follow-up point so that improvement becomes a routine rather than a one-time effort.

Typical decisions around improvement actions include which assessments to enable, how to prioritize actions by their effect on the score, whom to assign each action to, and how to keep evidence current so that the status stays accurate. Used this way, improvement actions connect regulatory requirements to day-to-day operational work and to audit preparation.

inactive-site-policy.desc: Inactive site policy in SharePoint is a SharePoint Advanced Management lifecycle policy that detects sites with no activity and asks owners to confirm they are still needed.

faq.a: It detects SharePoint sites that have had no activity for a set period and notifies the owners so they can confirm whether the sites are still needed.
faq.q: What does the inactive site policy in SharePoint do?

faq.a: If the site is not claimed or confirmed by its owners, the policy can make it read-only or archive it.
faq.q: What happens to a site that no one claims?

faq.a: It is a site lifecycle policy in SharePoint Advanced Management, related to the broader SharePoint topic.
faq.q: Which product area does this policy belong to?

inactive-site-policy.long:
Inactive site policy (SharePoint) is a site lifecycle policy within SharePoint Advanced Management. It identifies SharePoint sites that have shown no activity for a defined period and starts a process to decide what should happen to them.

When the policy detects an inactive site, it notifies the site owners and asks them to confirm whether the site is still needed. If the site is not claimed or confirmed, the policy can make it read-only or archive it. This gives administrators a structured way to reduce unused content in a SharePoint environment without having to review each site manually.

The policy is used for site lifecycle management and for keeping SharePoint tenants tidy over time. It relies on owner confirmation as part of the process, so responsibility for deciding the fate of a site stays with the people closest to its content. It belongs to the broader SharePoint topic and sits among the governance capabilities provided by SharePoint Advanced Management.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity. Details on configuring the policy are available in the official Microsoft documentation for the inactive site policy.

incremental-refresh.desc: Incremental refresh loads only new or changed data since the last run instead of reloading everything, and is used in Power BI and Fabric Dataflow Gen2.

faq.a: Incremental refresh is a data loading technique that processes only new or changed data since the last run instead of reloading the full data set. It is used in Power BI and in Fabric Dataflow Gen2.
faq.q: What is incremental refresh?

faq.a: According to the episode "Power BI Incremental Refresh - Simply Explained", refreshes are slow because Power BI keeps pulling back years of data that has not changed, not simply because the report is large.
faq.q: Why is a Power BI refresh slow without incremental refresh?

faq.a: Yes. The episode "Build ETL with Microsoft Fabric Dataflows Gen2" states that Gen2 dataflows support incremental refresh at the dataflow level with built-in change detection.
faq.q: Does incremental refresh work in Microsoft Fabric as well as Power BI?

incremental-refresh.long:
Incremental refresh is a data loading technique that processes only new or changed data since the last run, rather than reloading the full data set each time. It is used in Power BI semantic models and in Microsoft Fabric Dataflow Gen2. The core idea is simple: data that has already been loaded and has not changed does not need to be fetched again, so each refresh handles a much smaller slice of the source.

The main purpose of incremental refresh is to shorten refresh times and reduce the compute and memory resources a refresh consumes. The episode "Power BI Incremental Refresh - Simply Explained" frames the problem this way: a Power BI refresh is often slow not because the report is large, but because Power BI keeps pulling back years of data that has not changed. Incremental refresh addresses that by limiting each run to the data that is actually new or modified. The same episode lists several building blocks of the technique, including what incremental refresh actually does, why simply hitting refresh stops working as data grows, the two date markers behind every refresh, and the rolling window that keeps the model small.

In practice, incremental refresh is applied to large tables that grow over time, typically fact-style data with a date column. A rolling window means that the model keeps a defined period of history and moves that period forward as time passes, so older data can fall out of the window while recent data is refreshed. Because the refresh touches only the recent portion, the full history does not have to be re-read from the source on every run. This is especially relevant when a dataset has grown to the point where a complete reload is slow or puts a heavy load on the source system.

Incremental refresh also appears in the context of performance and cost optimization. The episode "Reduce Power BI Premium Costs with Better Data Models" lists implementing incremental refresh strategies, meaning refreshing only changed data, alongside other model-design measures such as using a star schema and choosing the right data types. The stated benefit there is saving time and resources. Similarly, the episode "Power Query Folding and Execution Order in Power BI" names configuring incremental refresh for large datasets as a way to drastically reduce refresh times, and presents it together with removing unused columns and optimizing data loading and transformations in Power Query. Together these episodes position incremental refresh as one tool among several for keeping Power BI models efficient, rather than a standalone fix.

On the Fabric side, the episode "Build ETL with Microsoft Fabric Dataflows Gen2" states that Gen2 dataflows support incremental refresh at the dataflow level with built-in change detection, and that this cuts compute and time for large datasets. This extends the same principle from a Power BI semantic model to ETL pipelines built with Dataflow Gen2, where only the changed portion of the source data needs to be processed on each run.

Incremental refresh also appears in certification-oriented material. The episode "DP-600 Training 4/4: Incremental Refresh, RLS, and OLS" groups it with Row-Level Security (RLS) and Object-Level Security (OLS) as part of a DP-600 training session on data security and analytics in Power BI. According to that episode, RLS restricts data visibility at a granular level so users only see the data they are allowed to see, while OLS restricts access to entire objects. These security features are a separate concern from refresh behavior, but they are covered together in the same training because both are part of designing and maintaining production-ready Power BI models.

When deciding whether to use incremental refresh, the relevant considerations drawn from the episodes are the size and growth of the data, how long full refreshes take, and whether the source data has a date field that allows new or changed rows to be identified. For small data sets that refresh quickly, a full reload may be sufficient. For large, growing tables, limiting each refresh to a rolling window of recent data is the approach the episodes recommend to keep refresh times and resource use under control.

independent-software-vendor.desc: An independent software vendor (ISV) is a software company that builds and sells apps for many customers of a platform, such as Business Central apps on Microsoft AppSource.

faq.a: An independent software vendor is a software company that builds and sells an app for many customers of a platform. It develops a product for broad use rather than a one-off solution for a single customer.
faq.q: What is an independent software vendor (ISV)?

faq.a: One example is Business Central apps offered through Microsoft AppSource, where an ISV makes its app available to customers of the platform.
faq.q: Where do ISVs offer their apps in the Microsoft ecosystem?

independent-software-vendor.long:
An independent software vendor (ISV) is a software company that develops an application and sells it to many customers of a given platform, rather than building a one-off solution for a single customer. The term is used across the software industry for companies that create products designed to run on or extend someone else's platform.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, one example is the vendor that builds apps for Business Central and offers them through Microsoft AppSource. In this model, the platform provides the core product, and the ISV supplies additional functionality that customers of the platform can adopt.

The concept is useful for understanding how a platform ecosystem is structured. The platform owner maintains the underlying product, while ISVs package specialized capabilities as repeatable products for a broad customer base. This differs from a custom development project, where a partner builds something for a single organization.

No specific M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no further related topics are listed in the available data.

indicators-of-compromise.desc: Indicators of compromise (IoC) are pieces of evidence on a network, device or in email, such as malicious IP addresses, domains or file hashes, suggesting an intrusion has occurred.

faq.a: Indicators of compromise (IoC) are pieces of evidence on a network, device or in email that suggest an intrusion has happened. Examples include malicious IP addresses, domains and file hashes.
faq.q: What are indicators of compromise (IoC)?

faq.a: Common examples are malicious IP addresses, malicious domains and file hashes. These can appear on a network, on a device or in email.
faq.q: What are examples of an IoC?

indicators-of-compromise.long:
Indicators of compromise (IoC) are pieces of evidence found on a network, on a device or in email that suggest an intrusion has happened. Typical examples include malicious IP addresses, malicious domains and file hashes associated with harmful files.

In security work, IoCs are used to help recognize that a system may have been breached or targeted. Because they are concrete, observable artifacts, they can be compared against logs, device data and email content to check whether a known sign of compromise is present in an environment.

The facts available for this entry do not link Indicators of compromise (IoC) to specific Microsoft products, documentation or M365.FM episodes, so no product-specific behavior is described here. The term is listed on M365.FM as a security concept within the broader Microsoft ecosystem knowledge base.

industrial-data-model.desc: An industrial data model is a shared set of rules describing factory objects such as products, orders, operations, resources and states, with stable identities across systems.

faq.a: It is a shared set of rules that describes the objects that matter in a factory, such as products, orders, operations, resources and states, with stable identities and relationships between them across systems like ERP, MES and maintenance.
faq.q: What is an industrial data model?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode "What Is an Industrial Data Model" says the problem is usually not missing data but that ERP, MES, SCADA, maintenance, quality and engineering describe the same factory through different structures, which makes it hard to tell what an event affects.
faq.q: Why do factories need one if they already collect a lot of data?

faq.a: ISA-95 (also IEC 62264) defines terminology, object models and attributes for exchanging information between enterprise and control systems. The source does not use the phrase industrial data model, so it serves as a standards-based example rather than a definition.
faq.q: How does ISA-95 relate to an industrial data model?

industrial-data-model.long:
An industrial data model is a shared set of rules that describes the objects that matter in a factory, such as products, orders, operations, resources and states. It gives these objects stable identities and defines the relationships between them, so that the same object can be recognized across systems such as ERP, MES and maintenance. The concept addresses a common situation: a factory can collect large amounts of data and still struggle to answer a basic operational question about what a given event actually affects.

The starting point is that each system in a plant describes the same factory from its own viewpoint. According to the M365.FM episode "What Is an Industrial Data Model", ERP knows customer orders, materials, planned dates and inventory. MES knows what is executing on the shop floor. PLCs and SCADA know machine states, alarms and process values. Maintenance knows asset condition and service history. Quality knows inspection and release status, and engineering knows the product definition. The episode frames the core problem as one of description rather than collection: the issue is usually not a lack of data, but that these systems describe the same factory through different structures and identifiers. An industrial data model supplies the common layer that ties those descriptions together.

In practice, such a model is used to connect events and records that would otherwise stay isolated. A machine alarm, for example, only becomes meaningful for planning or quality when it can be traced to the resource, the operation, the order and the product involved. Stable identities for objects and explicit relationships between them make that tracing possible. Typical decisions around a model include which objects to represent, how to identify them consistently across source systems, which states to track, and how the relationships between orders, operations, resources and products should be expressed.

Standards offer one established example of this kind of thinking. ISA-95, also standardized as ANSI/ISA-95 and IEC 62264, is an international standard from the International Society of Automation for building an automated interface between enterprise systems and control systems. It applies to batch, continuous and repetitive processes in any industry. Its objectives are consistent terminology, consistent information models and consistent operations models, so that suppliers and manufacturers share a common foundation. The sources note that the ISA-95 page does not use the phrase industrial data model, so it should be read as a standards-based example rather than a definition of the term.

The structure of ISA-95 illustrates how a shared model can be organized. Part 1 sets terminology and object models that determine which information should be exchanged and helps define the boundary between enterprise and control systems. It includes a Purdue-style scheduling and control hierarchy, an equipment hierarchy, a functional data flow model, and object models with relationships and attributes. Part 2 defines attributes for every object in Part 1, which can underpin information exchange and relational databases. Part 3 models manufacturing operations management at level 3, the production or MES layer, and later parts address object models for operations management, business-to-manufacturing transactions, messaging and information exchange profiles.

Taken together, an industrial data model is less a single product than an agreement about how a factory's objects, identities and relationships are described. It sits between the enterprise level, where ERP holds orders and materials, and the control level, where PLCs and SCADA hold machine states and process values, and it helps the systems in between, such as MES, maintenance and quality, refer to the same things in the same way.
