In "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD", the episode advises looking for a DevOps platform that supports service ownership, having developers enter service metadata when they create new services, and using automation to keep that metadata accurate. It suggests that a deployment platform can evolve into an Internal Developer Platform to centralize ownership and streamline DevOps processes, and recommends asking these questions early to avoid confusion later.

Taken together, the sources frame an IDP as the result of platform engineering rather than a single product. Typical decisions around it include which approved environments to offer, how to expose self-service workflows, how to encode security policies and standards, and who owns and maintains the platform over time.

internet-of-things.desc: Internet of Things (IoT) is the network of physical devices such as sensors, appliances and industrial controllers that connect to the internet to collect and exchange data.

faq.a: IoT is the network of physical devices such as sensors, appliances and industrial controllers that connect to the internet to collect and exchange data.
faq.q: What is the Internet of Things (IoT)?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Sphere - Simply Explained", Azure Sphere is Microsoft's end-to-end security platform for IoT devices, combining certified secure hardware, a custom Linux-based operating system and a cloud security service that authenticates devices and delivers automatic security updates.
faq.q: How does Azure Sphere relate to IoT?

faq.a: The episodes describe Azure Event Hubs for real-time ingestion of telemetry from devices and sensors, and Event Grid for routing telemetry data for real-time processing and alerts.
faq.q: Which Azure services handle IoT telemetry according to the episodes?

internet-of-things.long:
Internet of Things (IoT) describes the network of physical devices, such as sensors, appliances and industrial controllers, that connect to the internet to collect and exchange data. Instead of being isolated machines, these devices send information to other systems and can receive instructions or updates in return. The term covers a wide range of equipment, from small sensors that report measurements to controllers that run industrial processes.

In practice, IoT matters because connected devices produce data that organizations can monitor, analyze and act on. The M365.FM episodes touch on this from several angles: how devices are secured, how their data is ingested at scale, how events from them are routed to other services, and how they feed automation. Taken together, they show that IoT is less a single product than a pattern that spans hardware, networking, cloud services and security.

Security is one central concern. The episode "Azure Sphere - Simply Explained" describes Azure Sphere as Microsoft's end-to-end security platform for IoT devices. According to the episode, it protects connected devices from the silicon chip all the way to the cloud rather than focusing only on software security. The platform combines three core components: certified secure hardware, a custom Linux-based operating system, and a cloud security service that continuously authenticates devices and delivers automatic security updates throughout their lifetime. This illustrates one typical decision around IoT: because devices stay deployed for a long time and are exposed to a network, security and update delivery have to be considered across the whole device lifecycle.

Data ingestion is another recurring theme. The episode "Azure Event Hubs - Simply Explained" describes Azure Event Hubs as scalable and reliable in the IoT sector. According to the episode, it supports real-time ingestion of telemetry data from devices and sensors, which allows organizations to monitor, analyze and alert based on the data received. The episode also says it supports processing of large data volumes, which helps data-driven decision-making. Telemetry in this context means the continuous stream of readings and status information that devices send to a central service.

Event routing and automation form a third area. The episode "Event Grid - Simply Explained" lists IoT among the use cases for Event Grid, where telemetry data can be routed for real-time processing and alerts. It places this next to other scenarios such as triggering Azure Functions for tasks like image processing, notifying teams about builds and deployments, and implementing monitoring for security alerts. The episode presents serverless architectures built on Event Grid as offering dynamic scaling and reduced operational overhead compared with automation approaches that rely on fixed infrastructure.

IoT also appears in the discussion of automation governance. In "High-Performance Automation Control Plane for Power Automate", IoT is named alongside artificial intelligence, machine learning and service-as-software as a technology that will shape how automation is managed. The episode describes IoT as connecting various devices and systems and providing data and context for automation processes. In that framing, device data becomes an input that makes automated workflows more informed and responsive.

For people searching for the term, the main takeaways from these episodes are that an IoT solution usually involves several layers: secured devices, a way to ingest large streams of telemetry, a mechanism to route events to the right consumers, and automation or analytics that act on the results. The sources do not prescribe a single architecture, and the episodes discuss each layer through specific Azure services rather than as one unified product.

intranet.desc: An intranet is a private company website or network for internal news, policies and tools; M365.FM covers it through SharePoint, Viva Connections and AI-driven design.

faq.a: An intranet is a private company website or network for internal information such as news, policies and tools. Classic static versions are described as having suffered from low engagement and poor mobile access.
faq.q: What is an intranet?

faq.a: The episodes treat SharePoint as the platform for building intranets, covering navigation, metadata, search and pages. One episode says modern SharePoint sites and pages can act as lightweight knowledge hubs that replace many traditional intranet portal needs.
faq.q: How does SharePoint relate to the intranet in the M365.FM episodes?

faq.a: According to the episode "Viva Connections - Simply Explained", Viva Connections integrates with Microsoft Teams and SharePoint to give access to the company's intranet, with a personalized dashboard and a News Reader that tailors updates to a person's role.
faq.q: What role does Viva Connections play for an intranet?

intranet.long:
An intranet is a private company website or network that gives employees access to internal information such as news, policies and tools. It is separate from the public internet and is meant for the people inside an organization. Classic static intranets are described as having suffered from low engagement and poor mobile access, which is one reason the topic keeps returning in discussions about modern workplace design.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the intranet is most often built on SharePoint. The M365.FM episode "Make SharePoint Search Show the Right Files First" frames intranet quality as an Information Architecture (IA) question. It breaks IA into six core elements: global navigation, hub navigation, local navigation, metadata, search and personalization. According to the episode, each element supports the others, and a user who pastes the exact title of a file into intranet search and gets nothing back has an IA problem rather than a user problem. The episode also mentions Viva Connections as a way to deliver the right content to the right roles without manual tinkering.

Navigation is a recurring theme. The episode "SharePoint Network Drive vs OneDrive Sync" describes site maps as a way to give an overview of a SharePoint environment, showing how sites connect and where important content sits. It says top navigation helps employees move around the intranet quickly and that custom navigation options go beyond the default settings, supporting branding and user experience goals. It also lists common navigation bar types, including an informative navigation bar with a logo, Quick Links, real-time updates and a clean design.

Knowledge management is another angle. In "Fix SharePoint Knowledge Management", the episode argues that metadata-driven content delivery often outperforms folder structures, because properly applied metadata enables dynamic views, rollups and targeted content without moving files. It also says SharePoint pages and modern sites can act as lightweight knowledge hubs, replacing many traditional intranet portal needs with less custom code. On search, the episode states that relevance can be improved considerably by tuning managed properties, synonyms and result sources, so that search becomes more of a configuration task than a development one. It further mentions that Viva Topics can build topic pages and curate experts by analyzing documents and communications, reducing manual taxonomy work.

The intranet is also discussed as something that is changing in form. "AI-Powered SharePoint Intranets: Beyond Static Design" says the traditional SharePoint intranet is reaching the end of its lifecycle, because manually designed sites, static navigation structures and curated content pages quickly become outdated. The episode explores how artificial intelligence can shift intranet design from a static publishing model to a dynamic, adaptive experience, where intranets become intelligent knowledge experiences rather than static websites. Topics named include personalization, knowledge discovery and content recommendation.

On the employee-facing side, "Viva Connections - Simply Explained" describes how Viva Connections integrates with Microsoft Teams and SharePoint to provide access to a company's intranet. The episode says it offers a personalized dashboard for organizing essential resources and a News Reader feature that tailors updates to a person's role. It presents resource centralization as a one-stop platform for emails, documents and meetings, with the stated aim of higher engagement and less time spent searching for information.

Taken together, the episodes treat the intranet less as a single product and more as a combination of structure, content and delivery: navigation and metadata decide how content is organized, search decides how it is found, and personalization and AI decide who sees what. Typical decisions around an intranet include how to structure navigation across hubs and sites, whether to rely on metadata instead of folders, how much to tune search, and whether to surface intranet content inside Teams through Viva Connections.

intrusion-detection-and-prevention-syste.desc: Intrusion detection and prevention system (IDPS): signature-based monitoring of network traffic that alerts on or blocks malicious activity, offered in Azure Firewall Premium.

faq.a: In Azure, the intrusion detection and prevention system is a feature of the Azure Firewall Premium SKU. The episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" also lists it alongside TLS inspection as a Premium tier capability.
faq.q: Where is IDPS available in Azure?

faq.a: Each signature can run in one of three modes: disabled, alert, or alert and deny. The effective mode depends on the policy, a parent policy, an override or the system default.
faq.q: What modes can an IDPS signature use?

faq.a: Encrypted HTTPS traffic is only inspected in content when TLS inspection is enabled. Without it, the payload of encrypted sessions is not matched against signatures.
faq.q: Does IDPS inspect encrypted HTTPS traffic?

intrusion-detection-and-prevention-syste.long:
An intrusion detection and prevention system (IDPS) is a security capability that monitors a network for malicious activity, logs and reports what it finds, and can optionally block that activity. In the Azure ecosystem, this capability is delivered as a feature of the Azure Firewall Premium SKU rather than as a separate product. It is used to add inspection of traffic patterns on top of ordinary firewall rules, so that known attack techniques can be recognized even when the traffic would otherwise be allowed by address, port or protocol.

The approach in Azure Firewall Premium is signature based. A signature describes a specific pattern, such as a byte sequence in network traffic or a command sequence known from malware, and the firewall compares passing traffic against these patterns. According to the Microsoft Learn implementation guide, the signatures cover the application layer and the network layer, are fully managed, and are updated continuously. Because the signature set is maintained and refreshed by the platform, administrators do not need to author or distribute detection patterns themselves for the managed set.

The inspection applies to several traffic paths: inbound traffic, spoke-to-spoke traffic and outbound traffic, including traffic to and from on-premises networks. This makes the capability relevant in hub-and-spoke network designs, where the firewall sits between workloads, and in hybrid scenarios where traffic crosses into or out of a private network.

Behavior is controlled per signature. Each signature can run in one of three modes: disabled, alert, or alert and deny. The effective mode depends on the firewall policy, a parent policy, an override, or the system default. Signatures also carry a severity and a traffic direction. Private IP ranges follow RFC 1918 by default and can be adjusted to match the actual address space of an environment. A bypass list allows certain addresses or subnets to be excluded from filtering, which is a typical decision point when a known, trusted source produces traffic that would otherwise trigger detections. Alerts can be found in the network rule logs, so reviewing those logs is part of operating the feature. The number of custom IDPS rules is capped, which matters when planning policy beyond the managed signatures.

One limitation concerns encryption. Encrypted HTTPS traffic is only inspected in content when TLS inspection is enabled. Without TLS inspection, the firewall cannot match signatures against the payload of encrypted sessions, so the two Premium features are closely linked in practice.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" places the IDPS within the Premium tier. The episode says that with the Premium tier, users gain access to features like TLS inspection and an Intrusion Detection and Prevention System (IDPS), and describes this tier as suited to enterprises that demand the highest level of network security. It also gives a pricing breakdown for Azure Firewall Premium: a deployment hour rate of $1.75, data processing at $0.065 per GB, and extra cost for capacity units if enabled. As an example, the episode states that processing 50 TB of data monthly would cost around £2,880. Because the IDPS is part of Premium, these figures are relevant when deciding whether the added inspection capabilities justify the tier.

intune.desc: Microsoft Intune is Microsoft's cloud service for managing devices and apps, enforcing policies on Windows, macOS, iOS and Android and informing Conditional Access.

faq.a: Microsoft Intune is Microsoft's cloud service for managing devices and apps. It enforces configuration and compliance policies on Windows, macOS, iOS and Android, deploys applications and helps protect company data.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Intune used for?

faq.a: Microsoft Intune feeds device status into Conditional Access, so access to company data can depend on device compliance. Microsoft Entra ID holds the identities of the users who own the managed devices.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Intune relate to Conditional Access and Microsoft Entra ID?

faq.a: The episode "SCCM vs Intune: Key Differences | Simply Explained" presents Intune as Microsoft's cloud-first approach and SCCM as the long-standing enterprise standard. It notes that many organizations use both together during their transition to the cloud.
faq.q: Does Microsoft Intune replace SCCM?

intune.long:
Microsoft Intune is Microsoft's cloud-based endpoint management solution. It is used to manage devices, applications and users across Windows, macOS, iOS, Android and Linux from a single cloud platform. Microsoft develops it, and it is a paid product. On M365.FM it is classified as a Microsoft tool and as an identity and security tool, and it is closely related to Microsoft Entra ID.

In practice, Microsoft Intune lets IT teams deploy applications, enforce security policies, protect company data and manage endpoints centrally. It enforces configuration and compliance policies on managed devices, so that settings and security requirements are applied consistently rather than device by device. The M365.FM overview episode "Microsoft Intune - Simply Explained" describes it as a cornerstone of modern workplace management. Related material in the show notes also mentions remote support, where administrators can resolve problems and offer assistance remotely, and security enforcement that checks devices against organizational standards.

A key part of how Microsoft Intune works is the link to identity. Microsoft Entra ID holds the identities of the users who own the devices, while Intune reports the status of those devices. That device status is fed into Conditional Access, which means access to company data can depend on whether a device is compliant. This is why Intune sits at the boundary between endpoint management and identity protection, and why it is listed as an identity and security tool as well as a management tool.

A common decision around Microsoft Intune is how it relates to System Center Configuration Manager (SCCM). The episode "SCCM vs Intune: Key Differences | Simply Explained" presents SCCM as the long-standing enterprise standard and Intune as Microsoft's cloud-first approach to managing modern devices. The episode notes that the choice is not always one or the other: many organizations use both together while they transition to the cloud.

Licensing and security architecture are another recurring theme. In "Licensing, Security & Management: Making Microsoft 365 Defender and Intune Work Together with Videsh Chavan", the discussion frames Microsoft 365 licensing as an architecture decision rather than purely procurement. The episode says that licensing choices directly influence security architecture, endpoint management, identity protection and operational costs, and it explores how licensing, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Defender, identity and endpoint security can work together instead of operating as separate silos.

Managed service providers also appear in the episodes. "Building a Secure Microsoft-First MSP: Intune, Defender & Entra ID at Scale with Albin Klinaku [MVP]" features a Microsoft Intune MVP and discusses how an MSP can build a scalable, Microsoft-first security practice using Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Entra ID. The episode argues that customers now expect proactive security, cloud expertise and modern identity protection from day one, and that identity has become the new security perimeter.

Looking ahead, "Agentic AI for IT Operations: Windows 365, Intune & Microsoft's AI Vision with Christiaan Brinkhoff [Nerdio]" explores where Windows 365 and Microsoft Intune can support more autonomous IT operations and Cloud PC management. It places Intune alongside Agent 365, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Entra, with governed workflows, observability, identity and human oversight as part of the picture. Taken together, the episodes position Microsoft Intune as the device and app management layer that connects endpoint operations, identity and security in the Microsoft ecosystem.

intune-update-rings.desc: Update rings for Windows in Intune are a policy type that bundles Windows Update for Business settings and is assigned to device groups for staged rollouts.

faq.a: They are an Intune policy type that bundles Windows Update for Business settings, such as quality and feature update deferrals, deadlines, grace periods and restart behavior. The policy is assigned to groups of devices.
faq.q: What are update rings for Windows in Intune?

faq.a: Assigning rings to different groups of devices supports staged rollouts, so updates can reach devices at different times based on the settings in each ring.
faq.q: What is the purpose of assigning update rings to device groups?

faq.a: They are part of Microsoft Intune, which is the broader topic this concept falls under.
faq.q: Which product do update rings for Windows belong to?

intune-update-rings.long:
Update rings for Windows (Intune) are a policy type in Microsoft Intune that bundles Windows Update for Business settings into a single configuration. The settings include quality and feature update deferrals, deadlines, grace periods and restart behavior.

The policy is assigned to groups of devices, which allows updates to be rolled out in stages. Different device groups can receive different ring configurations, so that changes reach some devices earlier and others later according to the deferral and deadline values defined in each ring.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, update rings sit under the broader topic of Microsoft Intune, the management service in which the policy is created and assigned. They are one way to control how Windows devices receive quality and feature updates, with the timing and restart behavior set centrally through policy rather than on each device individually.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity, and no official documentation link is listed in the available facts.

inventory-dimensions.desc: Inventory dimensions in Dynamics 365 are the product, storage and tracking attributes that distinguish stock records, such as site, warehouse, location, batch and serial number.

faq.a: The Microsoft Learn training unit names three: product dimensions (configuration, size, style, color, version), storage dimensions that control how items are stored and removed, and tracking dimensions (batch and serial numbers).
faq.q: What are the main categories of inventory dimensions in Dynamics 365?

faq.a: They let companies trace products and support quality assurance and warranty handling, according to the Microsoft Learn training unit.
faq.q: Why are batch and serial numbers treated as tracking dimensions?

faq.a: The Learn unit advises planning how inventory should work before creating dimensions, so that they reflect how the company actually categorizes and handles each item.
faq.q: How should inventory dimensions be planned?

inventory-dimensions.long:
Inventory dimensions in Dynamics 365 are the labels that distinguish one stock record from another. Instead of holding a single quantity per item, the system records stock against combinations of dimensions, so that the same product can be tracked separately by where it is, what it looks like and how it can be traced. They are a core part of how Dynamics 365 Inventory Management answers questions about quantities, locations, availability, ownership and movements.

According to the Microsoft Learn training unit on Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management, inventory dimensions fall into three categories. Product dimensions describe the physical characteristics of an item: configuration, size, style, color and version. Storage dimensions control how items are stored and removed from inventory, for example site, warehouse and location. Tracking dimensions are batch and serial numbers, which let companies trace products and support quality assurance and warranty handling. The version dimension, which tracks multiple versions of a product, must be enabled through a configuration key.

The Learn unit advises planning how inventory should work before creating dimensions. The dimensions that are set up should reflect how the company actually categorizes and handles each item, rather than being added without a clear purpose. This planning step matters because the choice of dimensions determines at what level stock is recorded, reserved, moved and counted.

A packaging product dimensions feature adds three physical dimension types. Storage is used together with location volumetrics to decide how many items fit in warehouse locations, and it is the default. Packing is used for containerization and manual packing. Nested packing is used for multilevel packing. Volume is calculated from depth, height, width, weight and the units entered on the released product. If a product is placed where it will not fit, the system returns an error. The unit does not explain dimension groups.

In the M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Inventory Management - Simply Explained", Mirko Peters walks through how Dynamics 365 Inventory Management works from supplier receipt to customer shipment. The episode lists inventory dimensions among the topics covered, alongside reservations, transfers, costing, cycle counting, safety stock, consignment inventory and the connection between inventory and finance. It frames inventory management as a shared stock record across the business that connects quantities, locations, availability, ownership, movements and financial value, with dimensions being one of the mechanisms that make that record specific enough to answer where stock is and whether it can be used.

Typical decisions around inventory dimensions include which items need batch or serial tracking for traceability or warranty reasons, how detailed the site, warehouse and location structure should be, and which product attributes such as size or color must be tracked as separate stock. Because these choices shape how stock is stored, reserved and counted, they are usually settled early in an implementation and aligned with real warehouse and product handling practice.

inventory-visibility.desc: Inventory Visibility is a Dynamics 365 service that provides a central, near real-time view of inventory across locations, legal entities and data sources, with support for reservations.
inventory-visibility.long:
Inventory Visibility (Dynamics 365) is a service within Dynamics 365 that offers a central, near real-time view of inventory. It consolidates stock information across multiple locations, legal entities and data sources, so that inventory can be viewed in one place rather than in separate systems.

The service is used to check on-hand inventory availability and to support reservations. By bringing together data from different sources, it gives organizations that hold stock in several places a shared reference for what is available.

Inventory Visibility is part of Dynamics 365 and sits within the supply chain area of the platform. Microsoft documents the service in its Dynamics 365 supply chain inventory documentation on Microsoft Learn, which is the main source for configuration and usage details.

No M365.FM episodes are linked to this entity at present.

iops.desc: IOPS (input/output operations per second) measures how many read or write requests a storage system handles each second; it is a core Azure storage metric.

faq.a: IOPS stands for input/output operations per second. It describes how many individual read or write operations a storage system can perform each second.
faq.q: What does IOPS mean?

faq.a: IOPS counts individual storage operations per second, while throughput describes how much data can move during a period. Per the Elastic SAN episode, databases often issue many small reads and writes, which makes IOPS especially important for them.
faq.q: What is the difference between IOPS and throughput?

faq.a: They appear as specifications of storage options. The Azure Managed Disks episode lists Ultra Disks with a maximum of 400,000 IOPS and a maximum throughput of 10,000 MB/s.
faq.q: Where do IOPS limits appear in Azure storage?

iops.long:
IOPS stands for input/output operations per second. It is a measure of storage performance that describes how many individual read or write requests a storage system can handle in one second. In the M365.FM episode "Azure Elastic SAN — Simply Explained", the term is defined as the number of individual storage operations that can be performed each second, and it is discussed next to throughput as one of the two central concepts when talking about storage performance.

IOPS and throughput describe different things. IOPS counts operations, while throughput describes how much data can move during a given period. The Elastic SAN episode points out that databases frequently generate large numbers of small reads and writes, which makes IOPS particularly important for database-style workloads. A workload that moves large files in a few big transfers is mostly a throughput question, whereas a workload that issues many small requests is mostly an IOPS question. When sizing storage, both values are therefore looked at together.

In the Azure context, IOPS appears as a published specification of storage options. The episode "Azure Managed Disks - Simply Explained" lists Ultra Disks with a maximum of 400,000 IOPS and a maximum throughput of 10,000 MB/s, alongside a maximum disk size of 65,536 GiB. According to the episode, Ultra Disks suit data-intensive applications such as SAP HANA and Oracle Database and transaction-heavy workloads that need consistent performance and low latency, and they cannot be used as an OS disk. The episode "Azure Disk Storage - Simply Explained" explains that disk performance is measured through IOPS and throughput, and it places this alongside OS disks, data disks, temporary disks, snapshots, backups, encryption, redundancy and resizing as part of choosing the right disk type for a scenario such as a production database or an enterprise application.

IOPS also plays a role in cost and capacity planning. The Elastic SAN episode notes that when every workload is sized individually for its own peak, organizations can end up paying for performance that remains unused for much of the time, because some systems consume significant storage bandwidth overnight while others stay almost idle. Understanding IOPS requirements per workload is therefore a prerequisite for deciding whether performance should be provisioned per disk or pooled and shared.

IOPS is equally relevant for diagnosing problems. The episode "Design Reliable and Resilient Azure Architectures" includes a checklist for Azure VM performance issues that starts with confirming baseline metrics per VM, including CPU, memory, disk IOPS, throughput and network, over expected workloads. It recommends enabling Azure Monitor metrics with a Log Analytics workspace, checking collection frequency and retention, and creating alerts for sustained high CPU, memory pressure, disk queue length or network saturation. Baselines of disk IOPS make it possible to tell whether a slowdown stems from storage limits or from another resource.

The episode "Speed Fabric and AKS Workloads with Local NVMe Storage" connects IOPS to the location of data. It argues that managed storage adds network hops, caps IOPS and adds latency to every read and write, and that proximity is the fix rather than adding more nodes. Azure Container Storage v2 is described as placing hot data on local NVMe inside AKS nodes through a CSI-based, ephemeral driver that stripes across all NVMe disks, with multi-GB/s throughput and roughly a million IOPS, as the episode puts it. Taken together, the episodes treat IOPS as a figure that must be matched to the access pattern of the workload, checked against the limits of the chosen storage service, and monitored over time.

iot-hub-device-twin.desc: IoT Hub device twin is an Azure IoT Hub feature that synchronizes device state using desired properties set by the cloud and reported properties set by the device.

faq.a: An IoT Hub device twin is a state synchronization feature of Azure IoT Hub. It uses desired properties written by the cloud and reported properties written by the device to keep both sides informed about device state.
faq.q: What is an IoT Hub device twin?

faq.a: Desired properties are written by the cloud to describe the state or configuration a device should have. Reported properties are written by the device to describe its current state.
faq.q: What is the difference between desired and reported properties?

faq.a: It is described in the Azure IoT Hub developer guide on Microsoft Learn, which is the official documentation linked for this entry.
faq.q: Where is the device twin feature documented?

iot-hub-device-twin.long:
IoT Hub device twin is a state synchronization feature of Azure IoT Hub. It maintains a record for each registered device that holds information about that device's configuration and condition, and it allows the cloud side and the device side to exchange state data through a shared structure.

The feature is built around two kinds of properties. Desired properties are written by the cloud, typically by a back-end application, to express the configuration or state a device should adopt. Reported properties are written by the device to communicate its current state back to the cloud. Comparing the two allows a solution to see whether a device has applied a requested change.

Device twins are used in Azure IoT Hub solutions that need to manage device configuration, track device status, and coordinate changes between a back end and many connected devices. Because the exchange happens through properties rather than direct commands, it supports scenarios in which a device may be offline or intermittently connected when a change is requested.

The concept is documented in the Azure IoT Hub developer guide on Microsoft Learn. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no related topics have been recorded for it yet.

iot-hub-message-routing.desc: IoT Hub message routing is an Azure IoT Hub feature that applies rules to device-to-cloud messages and sends them to the built-in endpoint or custom endpoints.

faq.a: Once any route exists, data stops flowing to the built-in endpoint unless a route or the fallback route targets it. Messages that match no route go to the built-in endpoint only if the fallback route is in place.
faq.q: What happens to the built-in endpoint when a route is created?

faq.a: By default messages go to the built-in endpoint, which is compatible with Event Hubs. Custom endpoints include storage containers, Service Bus queues and topics, Event Hubs, Cosmos DB, and Fabric eventstreams in preview.
faq.q: Which endpoints can IoT Hub message routing send messages to?

faq.a: Yes, a message can reach several endpoints when several routes match it. It is delivered only once to any single endpoint.
faq.q: Can a message be delivered to more than one endpoint?

iot-hub-message-routing.long:
IoT Hub message routing is a feature of Azure IoT Hub that evaluates rules against device-to-cloud messages and sends each matching message to one or more endpoints. It is meant to move device data to other cloud services in an automated, scalable and reliable way, without the receiving application having to sort every message itself. Besides ordinary telemetry, routing can also carry non-telemetry events: device lifecycle events, device twin change events, digital twin change events and device connection state events.

A route consists of four parts: a name, a source, a condition and an endpoint. The source defines which kind of message the route looks at, and the condition is a query that decides whether a message matches. According to Microsoft Learn, such queries can filter on message properties, on the message body, and on twin tags or properties. By default, all messages go to the built-in endpoint, which is compatible with Event Hubs. Custom endpoints can be storage containers, Service Bus queues and topics, Event Hubs, Cosmos DB, and Fabric eventstreams, the last of which is listed as a preview option.

Several behaviors matter when designing routes. A single message can reach several endpoints if several routes match, but it is delivered only once to any single endpoint. A fallback route sends messages that match no route to the built-in endpoint. Once any route exists, data stops flowing to the built-in endpoint unless a route or the fallback route targets it, so adding a first route to an existing solution can unexpectedly cut off a consumer that reads from the built-in endpoint. Routes can be tested with sample messages before they are relied on. Adding the first route typically raises latency by under 500 ms, according to the documentation.

Connection state events have their own constraints. They appear only for devices that use MQTT or AMQP, and they are reported as snapshots roughly every minute rather than as a continuous stream. This is one reason why lifecycle and connection events should not be treated the same way as high-frequency telemetry.

That distinction is the subject of the M365.FM episode "IoT Hub Message Routing vs Event Grid — Why Telemetry and Events Are Not the Same Problem", which appears twice in the feed. The episode argues that a temperature reading, a vibration sample, a machine cycle and a device disconnect may all be called events, yet they do not represent the same architectural problem. In industrial IoT and manufacturing settings, it says, confusing continuous telemetry with discrete events can lead to noisy workflows, incomplete production histories, unnecessary processing and systems that react without enough context. The episode sets IoT Hub message routing against Event Grid and discusses where services such as Event Hubs, Microsoft Fabric, Power BI, MES, ERP, Functions and Logic Apps fit in such a design.

In practice, the decision around message routing is usually which messages go where. Continuous machine data such as temperature, vibration, cycle counts and power consumption sent every few seconds suits routing to streaming or storage endpoints, while discrete business or lifecycle events call for different handling. Routing conditions based on message properties or twin data let a single IoT Hub separate these flows at the point of ingestion. The official documentation for device-to-cloud messages in IoT Hub describes the endpoint types, query options and fallback behavior in detail.

isa-95.desc: ISA-95 is an international standard that defines how enterprise systems and manufacturing control systems exchange information, using a common hierarchy and object models.

faq.a: ISA-95, or ANSI/ISA-95, is an international standard from the International Society of Automation that describes how enterprise systems and control systems exchange information through an automated interface. It covers batch, continuous and repetitive manufacturing.
faq.q: What is ISA-95?

faq.a: Part 1 defines terminology and object models, Part 2 gives object attributes, Part 3 covers manufacturing operations management at level 3, Part 4 covers operations management objects and attributes, and Part 5 covers business-to-manufacturing transactions. Further parts address messaging, alias services and information exchange profiles.
faq.q: What do the parts of ISA-95 cover?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode on MQTT and OPC UA describes the ISA-95 enterprise-to-cell hierarchy as a naming contract for locating assets consistently. It also says a Unified Namespace is a common event space for publishing facts, not a new master database.
faq.q: How does ISA-95 relate to a Unified Namespace?

isa-95.long:
ISA-95, formally ANSI/ISA-95, is an international standard from the International Society of Automation. It describes how enterprise systems and control systems should exchange information through an automated interface. The standard applies to batch, continuous and repetitive manufacturing. Its stated goals are consistent terminology, shared information models and shared operations models between suppliers and manufacturers, so that responsibilities and interfaces can be placed in a predictable way.

The standard is organised in several parts. Part 1 defines terminology and object models, including a hierarchy model based on the Purdue model, an equipment hierarchy, functional data-flow models and operations activity models. Part 2 gives the attributes of each object. Part 3 covers manufacturing operations management activities at level 3, the production and MES layer. Part 4 covers objects and attributes for operations management, and Part 5 covers business-to-manufacturing transactions. Further parts address messaging, alias services and information exchange profiles. The standard also supplies reference models for production, quality, maintenance and inventory activities and for the information passed between them.

In practice, ISA-95 is used as a map. The levels run from the physical process and its control, through manufacturing operations management, up to enterprise planning. This makes it possible to say which system owns which data, where an interface belongs, and how a plant-floor event relates to business-level processes. Teams use it when they need to decide where a piece of logic should live, for example whether a function belongs in a control system, in a manufacturing execution layer or in enterprise planning.

The M365.FM episode "MQTT and OPC UA in Microsoft Manufacturing: Azure IoT Operations + Fabric Architecture" discusses ISA-95 in the context of Microsoft-based manufacturing data architectures. According to the episode, the enterprise-to-cell hierarchy of ISA-95 can serve as a naming contract: a stable map used to locate assets consistently before changing business context such as work orders and products is applied. The idea is that asset identity stays fixed while context around it changes. The same episode argues for normalizing data once near the source, at the edge, rather than mapping it several times in different downstream systems, and notes that a raw state code means little without context from the machine.

The episode also places ISA-95 next to the Unified Namespace (UNS) discussion. It describes UNS as a common event space where IT and OT publish facts, and cautions that it is not a new master database and not a shortcut to a shared operating model without effort. In that framing, an ISA-95-style hierarchy gives the namespace a consistent structure for naming and locating assets, while the work of agreeing on meaning and ownership still has to be done.

A caveat applies to the available sources: the public description of the standard does not detail each individual level, and edition dates are reported inconsistently, so anyone adopting it for a project should consult the standard itself for exact definitions of the levels and object attributes.

iscsi.desc: iSCSI (Internet Small Computer Systems Interface) carries SCSI storage commands over IP networks, giving servers network access to block storage.

faq.a: iSCSI (Internet Small Computer Systems Interface) is a protocol that carries SCSI storage commands over IP networks, giving servers network access to block storage.
faq.q: What is iSCSI?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Elastic SAN — Simply Explained" states that Azure Elastic SAN volumes connect to workloads using iSCSI, which carries storage commands between the server and the Elastic SAN across the network.
faq.q: How does iSCSI relate to Azure Elastic SAN?

faq.a: The episode "Speed Fabric and AKS Workloads with Local NVMe Storage" mentions setting the MTU to 9000 at both the cluster and virtual machine levels to reduce packet fragmentation, and keeping the Layer 2 network on the same fabric interconnects for low latency.
faq.q: Which network setting does an M365.FM episode mention for iSCSI performance?

iscsi.long:
iSCSI stands for Internet Small Computer Systems Interface. It is a protocol that carries SCSI storage commands over IP networks, which gives servers network access to block storage. Instead of attaching a disk directly to a machine, the server sends its storage requests across an ordinary network connection, and the storage system on the other end answers them as if the disk were local.

The main purpose of iSCSI is to provide a disk-like, block-storage model through a network. Workloads that need large numbers of controlled reads and writes, such as database files, transaction logs and indexes, work with block storage rather than with ordinary files. With iSCSI, a virtual machine or server requests a particular block of data or sends a write operation, and the protocol transports that command between the server and the storage system across the network.

The episode "Azure Elastic SAN — Simply Explained" uses iSCSI as the connection method for Azure Elastic SAN. According to the episode, Azure Elastic SAN volumes connect to workloads using iSCSI. The episode describes the terminology as sounding complicated while the basic concept is straightforward: iSCSI carries storage commands between the server and the Elastic SAN. In that model, a VM asks for a block of data or issues a write, and the request travels over the network to the volume that holds the data.

iSCSI also appears in planning discussions around Kubernetes and fast storage. In the episode "Kubernetes - Simply Explained", iSCSI is listed alongside NFS and SAN as an option for shared storage that holds persistent data in a basic Kubernetes setup. In that layout, the nodes themselves can stay stateless, while the data that has to survive is kept on shared storage reached over the network.

Network configuration matters when iSCSI is part of the design. The episode "Speed Fabric and AKS Workloads with Local NVMe Storage" advises evaluating network settings, especially when iSCSI or similar protocols are used. It names setting the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) to 9000 at both the cluster and virtual machine levels as a way to improve performance by reducing packet fragmentation. It also recommends confirming that the Layer 2 network operates on the same fabric interconnects, to maintain low latency and high throughput. The same episode suggests checking whether hardware supports NVMe protocols and whether the network can handle the added data flow from NVMe drives.

Taken together, the episodes treat iSCSI as a way to attach block storage over a network rather than as a product in itself. It appears as the connection layer behind Azure Elastic SAN, as one of several shared-storage choices for Kubernetes persistent data, and as a protocol whose performance depends on how the underlying network is set up. Decisions around it typically involve the type of workload, the available network capacity and latency, and whether block storage, as opposed to file-based storage, is what the application expects.

iso-27001.desc: ISO/IEC 27001 is the international standard from ISO and IEC that sets requirements for an information security management system (ISMS) and allows certification.

faq.a: It is the international standard published by ISO and IEC that specifies requirements for an information security management system (ISMS). Organizations can be certified against it.
faq.q: What is ISO/IEC 27001?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Landing Zones - Simply Explained" says Azure Policy provides built-in initiatives that map to ISO/IEC 27001 compliance domains and is used to enforce compliance across standards such as ISO 27001 and GDPR.
faq.q: How does ISO/IEC 27001 relate to Azure Policy?

faq.a: The episodes mention Azure, Azure Key Vault, Viva Connections and Power Pages in connection with ISO/IEC 27001. The Power Pages episode lists the accreditation body as Alcumus with an accreditation date of 29/03/2022.
faq.q: Which Microsoft services are mentioned with ISO/IEC 27001 in the episodes?

iso-27001.long:
ISO/IEC 27001 is the international standard published by ISO and IEC that specifies requirements for an information security management system, usually abbreviated as ISMS. Organizations can be certified against it, which means an independent party assesses whether the organization's ISMS meets the standard's requirements. In the Microsoft ecosystem the standard appears mainly as a compliance reference point: a framework that cloud services are audited against and that customers map their own governance controls to.

The M365.FM episodes treat ISO/IEC 27001 in the context of governance and compliance rather than as a stand-alone topic. The episode "Azure Landing Zones - Simply Explained" says that Azure Landing Zones use Azure Policy to enforce compliance across various standards, including ISO 27001 and GDPR. According to the episode, Microsoft Azure undergoes regular independent audits for ISO/IEC 27001 compliance, and Azure Policy provides built-in initiatives that map to ISO/IEC 27001 compliance domains. The episode also notes that deployment accelerators help organizations apply governance initiatives aligned with ISO 27001 during initial setup, which it describes as reducing manual effort and improving audit readiness.

A second use of the standard is as an alignment target for security tooling. The episode "Azure Key Vault - Simply Explained" lists compliance with standards as one reason to adopt customer-managed keys. It says this approach gives tighter control over key ownership, rotation and access logging, and it names alignment with frameworks like ISO/IEC 27001 for encryption and governance. The episode describes this as relevant for regulated industries, large enterprises and public sector environments that need strict governance, and for organizations that must meet specific legal and operational compliance standards.

Certification status also serves as a signal when organizations evaluate individual Microsoft services. The episode "Viva Connections - Simply Explained" presents a table of certifications and audits for Viva Connections that includes the ISMS standard ISO/IEC 27001, PCI DSS and SOC 2. The episode "Power Pages - Simply Explained" lists ISO/IEC 27001 among the certifications held by Microsoft Power Pages, with the accreditation body given as Alcumus and an accreditation date of 29/03/2022, and a note that all aspects are covered. The same table shows PCI DSS with a note that certain PCI controls are excluded, and lists Cyber Essentials and Cyber Essentials Plus without further details. Such a table lets readers see which standards a service has been assessed against and where limits apply.

ISO/IEC 27001 is also mentioned alongside other frameworks in discussions of AI and data handling. The episode "How to Run Local Llama on SharePoint Files Securely" says many compliance frameworks, including NIST AI RMF, CMMC, ISO/IEC 27001 and GDPR, require strict data handling. The episode argues that running a private, local LLM keeps information inside the organization and gives direct control over sensitive documents and personally identifiable information, which it presents as safer than cloud-based tools for those cases.

A practical point follows from these episodes. A vendor's or a platform's ISO/IEC 27001 certification covers that provider's own ISMS and services. It does not by itself certify the customer's own environment. Organizations that want to demonstrate alignment typically combine the provider's certification with their own policies, controls and audit evidence, for example by assigning built-in policy initiatives that map to the standard's compliance domains and by documenting key management and access logging. The standard therefore appears in the episodes as a common reference for governance decisions, audit readiness and vendor assessment across Azure, Power Pages, Viva Connections and AI scenarios.

isolated-storage.desc: Isolated storage is a Business Central key/value data store kept separate for each extension, so other extensions cannot read the values saved in it.

faq.a: It is a data store that keeps extensions separated from each other. An extension saves key-value pairs in it, and other extensions cannot retrieve those pairs.
faq.q: What is isolated storage in Business Central?

faq.a: Through the IsolatedStorage data type in the AL language. Its methods set a value for a key, read it, check whether a key exists, and delete it, and they can take a data scope argument.
faq.q: How does an extension use isolated storage?

faq.a: Yes, there is a method that encrypts the value before storing it. That method limits the plain-text input to a fixed number of characters, and special characters take up more space.
faq.q: Can isolated storage hold encrypted values?

isolated-storage.long:
Isolated storage is a data store in Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central that keeps extensions separated from each other. An extension saves its values as key-value pairs, and other extensions cannot retrieve those pairs. This separation is the defining property of the concept: whatever one extension writes into isolated storage stays out of reach of every other extension running in the same environment.

Because of that isolation, isolated storage is often used for secrets, particularly in development and test scenarios. Typical examples are values an extension needs to remember but that should not be exposed to unrelated code, such as credentials or tokens used to reach an external service. The documentation itself describes the purpose in general terms, as protecting an extension's values from other extensions, and does not list further usage scenarios.

Access to isolated storage goes through an API exposed as the IsolatedStorage data type in the AL language. The available methods let an extension set a value for a key, read it back, check whether a key exists, and delete it. A developer therefore works with simple key-based operations rather than with tables or records, which keeps the pattern small and easy to apply for configuration-like or sensitive values.

Each of these methods can take a data scope argument, which classifies the stored data. The DataScope option type is named in the documentation as related reference material, alongside the IsolatedStorage data type. Choosing the scope is a design decision, because it determines how the stored value is classified and therefore who it is associated with. The documentation excerpt available here does not spell out the individual scope values, so the AL reference for the DataScope option type is the place to confirm them.

There is also a method that encrypts the value before storing it. This is relevant when the stored value is a secret rather than ordinary configuration. The encrypting method limits the plain-text input to a fixed number of characters, and special characters take up more space than ordinary ones, so longer secrets or values with many special characters need to be planned for. The documentation page does not describe size limits for isolated storage as a whole or how it behaves across environments, so those points should be checked in the official reference before relying on them.

In practice, the decision around isolated storage is whether a value belongs in a regular table or in a store that other extensions cannot read. Values that are sensitive or that must not be visible to other extensions are the natural fit, while shared business data is not. The data scope argument and the choice between plain and encrypted storage are the main levers a developer has.

M365.FM does not cover isolated storage in Business Central directly. The episode "Shared Data Reservoirs for Multi-Tenant Microsoft 365" (2026-05-11) discusses storage in a different sense: it contrasts isolated storage silos and fixed allocations with elastic shared data reservoirs, covering concepts such as Azure Elastic SAN, Azure SQL Hyperscale and elastic storage pools. That discussion concerns cloud storage architecture and capacity planning, not the Business Central AL feature, so the two uses of the word should not be confused.

isv-success-program.desc: ISV Success is a Microsoft program for software companies building B2B applications on the Microsoft Cloud and publishing them to Microsoft Marketplace.

faq.a: ISV Success is a twelve-month program inside the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program for software companies that build B2B applications on or integrated with the Microsoft Cloud and want to publish them in Microsoft Marketplace.
faq.q: What is ISV Success?

faq.a: The core package bundles Azure sponsorship credit, an Azure support plan, a Microsoft 365 developer subscription, Dynamics 365 sandboxes, Visual Studio Enterprise, GitHub Enterprise Cloud for new customers and one-to-one guidance on design, go-to-market and listing optimization.
faq.q: What does ISV Success include?

faq.a: Yes. According to the documentation, the program can be renewed for a further year once an offer has been published or made transactable and a renewal fee is paid.
faq.q: Can ISV Success be renewed?

isv-success-program.long:
ISV Success is a Microsoft program for software development companies that build business-to-business applications on or integrated with the Microsoft Cloud and want to publish them in Microsoft Marketplace. According to the official documentation, it is a twelve-month program inside the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program. It combines technical resources, guidance and cloud benefits so that an independent software vendor can move an application from development to a listed marketplace offer.

Eligibility depends on a few conditions. The company must not be headquartered in an embargoed country, and it needs an application project that is externally available, intended for recurring sales and has at least one assigned developer. Participants commit to start development within a few months, finish within the year and publish to the marketplace. Benefits are activated in Partner Center under Benefits.

The core package bundles several components: Azure sponsorship credit, an Azure support plan, a Microsoft 365 developer subscription, Dynamics 365 sandboxes, Visual Studio Enterprise, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud for new customers. It also includes one-to-one guidance on design, go-to-market and listing optimization. Larger packages exist for existing participants and for companies with a certified software designation, but these depend on Microsoft's discretion. The M365.FM description of the program also mentions Marketplace Rewards, with marketing support, technical resources and Azure sponsorship.

Sales and marketing benefits require a marketplace listing, which ties the program closely to the publishing process. The program can be renewed for a further year once an offer has been published or made transactable and a renewal fee is paid. For software companies, this means planning the release path early: the technical benefits support development, while the go-to-market benefits only become available after the offer is live on Microsoft Marketplace.

The M365.FM episode "The Hard Way to Get Listed on Microsoft Marketplace" places ISV Success within the preparation for a marketplace listing. The episode says developers should use the app certification checklist to identify packaging and deployment issues before submission, and should follow app design best practices to avoid common oversights during development. It also recommends engaging with the ISV Success team early in the process, since the team can offer insights into both the business and technical aspects of certification. The episode presents this early contact as a way to navigate the complexities of the marketplace more effectively.

In practice, ISV Success is relevant to teams deciding how to resource and sequence a first marketplace release. The questions it touches include whether the application meets the eligibility conditions, which benefits to activate in Partner Center, how to use the guidance on design and listing optimization, and when to plan the renewal. The documentation and the episode both point to the same pattern: preparation before submission, with the program serving as a source of credits, tooling and advice along the way.

it-manager.desc: IT manager (also IT-Leiter, Head of IT) is a job role that leads an organisation's IT team and operations, covering systems, budget, projects and service quality.

faq.a: An IT manager leads the IT team and IT operations of an organisation and is responsible for its systems, budget, projects and service quality. The role is also known as IT-Leiter or Head of IT.
faq.q: What does an IT manager do?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Cost Management - Simply Explained" names the IT manager among its target audience. Monitoring cloud spending and preventing budget surprises fit the budget responsibility of the role.
faq.q: How does an IT manager relate to Azure Cost Management?

faq.a: The episodes mention Microsoft Intune for device management and update scheduling, Microsoft Entra ID for automated user provisioning, and Azure Logic Apps and Power Automate in the context of policy and compliance workflows.
faq.q: Which tools do the M365.FM episodes mention in connection with IT managers?

it-manager.long:
An IT manager, also called IT-Leiter, IT-Manager or Head of IT, leads the IT team and the IT operations of an organisation. The role carries responsibility for the organisation's systems, for the IT budget, for projects and for the quality of the services that IT delivers to the business. In a Microsoft environment this typically means oversight of Microsoft 365, Azure, device management and identity, even though the day-to-day technical work is often carried out by administrators, engineers and architects who report into or work alongside the IT manager.

The IT manager sits between technical teams and the wider organisation. On one side are decisions about platforms, licences, cloud spending and security controls. On the other side are people and process questions such as who is responsible for a policy, how often it is reviewed and how changes are documented. Typical decisions include which tools to adopt, how to keep cloud costs predictable, how to reduce manual workload for IT staff and how to make sure policies reflect real-world needs.

Several M365.FM episodes name the IT manager as part of their intended audience or as a stakeholder. The episode "Azure Cost Management - Simply Explained" lists the IT manager alongside Azure administrators, cloud architects, DevOps engineers and people preparing for Microsoft certification exams. It presents Azure Cost Management as a way to monitor cloud spending, prevent budget surprises and support FinOps practices through dashboards, Power BI integration, exports, APIs and anomaly detection. This connects directly to the budget responsibility that belongs to the role.

In "Microsoft Intune - Simply Explained", an IT manager is quoted as having previously spent a week and a half on manual updates, which Microsoft Intune now allows to be scheduled during non-working hours to limit disruption. The same episode describes device setup time falling from 3 hours to 1 hour and savings of 280 hours per year for IT staff, and notes that remotely wiping lost devices improves data security. These examples show the kind of operational efficiency and risk reduction an IT manager weighs when evaluating device management.

The episode "SC-900 Exam Prep Part 2/8: Microsoft Entra ID" includes a case study of an organisation that moved to Entra ID and struggled with onboarding and offboarding employees. According to the episode, automating these processes streamlined operations and reduced the risk of human error, and an IT manager is quoted as saying that automating user provisioning felt like a dream come true because of the absence of manual errors. This illustrates how identity automation relates to the service-quality side of the role.

Governance and security reviews also involve the IT manager. In "Stop Microsoft Copilot Prompt Injection with Azure Logic Apps", a review table assigns workflow automation policy to the IT manager with an annual review frequency and workflow adjustment as the update method. The episode recommends involving security admins, compliance officers and IT managers in every policy review, and documenting every change when a policy is updated. In "Automate Compliance Workflows with Microsoft Power Automate", IT manager is named as a role that certifications such as the MCSE can lead to, alongside systems engineer and solutions architect, which places the position within a common career path in enterprise IT.

Taken together, the episodes describe the IT manager as a role that connects technology choices to budget, staffing effort, security and compliance. Related areas include cost management and FinOps in Azure, device management with Microsoft Intune, identity management with Microsoft Entra ID, and compliance and policy review processes.

it-service-management.desc: IT service management (ITSM) is the set of activities an organization performs to plan, build, deliver, run and manage IT services for its customers.

faq.a: ITSM covers the activities an organization performs to plan, build, deliver, run and manage IT services for its customers. It is typically organized through processes such as incident, request and change management.
faq.q: What does IT service management (ITSM) cover?

faq.a: According to the sources, ITIL distinguishes the service desk from a call center or help desk, which cover only part of the scope. The service desk is the single point of contact for incidents, service requests, change requests, third-party arrangements and software licensing.
faq.q: How does ITSM differ from a help desk?

faq.a: ITIL is the most prominent framework. Others named in the sources include COBIT, TOGAF, eTOM, FitSM, CMMI, ASL, USM, BiSL, the Microsoft Operations Framework and the certifiable standard ISO/IEC 20000.
faq.q: Which frameworks and standards are associated with ITSM?

it-service-management.long:
IT service management (ITSM) is the set of activities an organization performs to plan, build, deliver, run and manage IT services for its customers. It is typically organized through processes such as incident, request and change management. In contrast to technology-centred disciplines such as network or systems management, ITSM is process-oriented: it focuses on customer needs and on the services that are actually delivered, and it stresses continual improvement.

A central element of ITSM in practice is the service desk. Under ITIL, the service desk acts as the single point of contact between users and IT staff. It receives incident reports, handles service requests, and manages change requests, third-party arrangements and software licensing. ITIL distinguishes the service desk from a call center or help desk, since those cover only part of this scope. This distinction matters when an organization decides how broadly to define the function and which tasks should sit within it.

ITSM is usually guided by a framework or standard. ITIL is the most prominent one and is aimed at aligning IT with business needs. Other frameworks and standards named in the sources include COBIT, TOGAF, eTOM, FitSM, CMMI, ASL, USM, BiSL, the Microsoft Operations Framework and the certifiable standard ISO/IEC 20000. Professional bodies such as itSMF and HDI support the field, and common certifications include ITIL 4, TOGAF and COBIT. Choosing among these options is typically a question of how much structure, formal certification and process documentation an organization wants.

Routine ITSM tasks can be automated through IT process automation, which reduces manual handling of recurring requests and standard changes. ITSM tools are also often applied beyond the IT department, an approach known as enterprise service management, where the same request, workflow and service desk principles are used for other business functions.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, ITSM comes up when organizations connect service management platforms with Microsoft 365. The M365.FM episode "ServiceNow and Microsoft 365: From Intent to Business Action" (2026-01-26) addresses this in the context of integration planning. According to the episode, the starting point is an assessment of current systems and processes: identifying fragmentation and inefficiencies, evaluating current ITSM needs, and identifying pain points that an integration could address. The episode also recommends consulting the IT team to learn which features would be most beneficial, and considering how other Microsoft tools, such as Dynamics 365 or Azure DevOps, might fit into the broader strategy.

Taken together, the sources describe ITSM as both a discipline and a practical operating model. It defines how services are requested, delivered, changed and improved, which framework or standard gives the process its structure, and how tooling and automation support day-to-day work. Decisions around it typically concern the scope of the service desk, the choice of framework, the degree of automation, and whether service management practices should extend to non-IT areas of the organization.

it-services.desc: IT services is the industry of companies that plan, implement, run and support IT systems and software for other organisations, including Microsoft partners.

faq.a: It refers to companies that plan, implement, run and support IT systems and software for other organisations. Related German terms are IT-Dienstleister and Systemhaus.
faq.q: What does IT services mean as an industry?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) - Simply Explained" says CSP lets customers purchase IT services bundled with licenses from authorized partners, with monthly or annual billing and a single point of contact for support.
faq.q: How do IT services relate to the Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider program?

faq.a: The episode "Showback vs Chargeback for Cloud and Microsoft 365 Costs" describes showback as reporting IT costs to departments to improve visibility and cost accountability without actual billing.
faq.q: Why do IT services costs matter inside an organisation?

it-services.long:
IT services is the industry of companies that plan, implement, run and support IT systems and software for other organisations. In German-speaking markets the same type of company is often called an IT-Dienstleister or a Systemhaus. Instead of building products for a mass market, these providers work on behalf of customers: they select technology, put it into operation, keep it running and help users when problems occur.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, IT services providers act as an important link between the vendor and the customer organisation. One route described in the M365.FM episode "Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) - Simply Explained" is the Cloud Solution Provider program. According to the episode, the CSP program lets customers purchase IT services bundled with licenses from authorized partners. It lists several characteristics: tailored IT services, a choice between monthly or annual billing, a single point of contact for support, and the fact that CSP does not include Software Assurance. The episode also frames the model as a way to enhance customer engagement and build long-term relationships between provider and customer.

The term also appears from the customer's point of view. In the episode "Showback vs Chargeback for Cloud and Microsoft 365 Costs", the IT department is treated as a supplier of IT services to internal business units. Showback is described as a method of reporting IT costs to departments without enforcing actual billing. Its goal is to improve cost visibility and awareness, so that teams take ownership of what they spend on IT services. The episode lists reasons organisations adopt it: improved cost visibility, better decisions about resource allocation, a cost-conscious culture and alignment of spending with business needs. This shows that IT services can be delivered by an external company as well as by an internal team, and that both models need transparent cost reporting.

IT services also cover governance and operations of new technology. The episode "How Do You Successfully Deploy Microsoft 365 Copilot Across an Enterprise?" discusses transforming IT operations with agentic AI and aligning automation, intelligence and governance so that IT services are resilient, efficient and secure. It describes Microsoft's frameworks for managing AI agents and names Agent 365 as the control plane that gives one place to manage all AI agents. For IT services teams, this means that rolling out a product such as Microsoft 365 Copilot involves not only installation but also safety, rule compliance and ongoing management.

Support is another core part of the field. The episode "Multi-Agent AI with Copilot Studio and David Lorenzo Lopez [MVP]" points to resources for solving problems quickly, such as the Microsoft Community Hub for Copilot Studio, the official documentation and an IT support service at a university organisation named in the show notes. In the episode "Build Auditable AI Agents with Azure AI Foundry", IT services is listed as one of several sectors using AI, with AI app deployment and oversight as the stated use, and easier development processes and quicker rollouts as the stated benefits.

Typical decisions around IT services include whether to buy licenses and services through a partner or directly, whether to run operations in-house or externally, how to bill or report costs internally, and how to govern new AI capabilities. The M365.FM episodes touch on each of these from different angles: partner purchasing models, cost allocation, enterprise deployment and AI governance.

jamf-pro.desc: Jamf Pro is Jamf's enterprise device management platform for Apple devices such as Mac, iPhone and iPad, with integration options for Microsoft Intune.

faq.a: Jamf Pro is Jamf's enterprise device management platform for Apple devices such as Mac, iPhone and iPad.
faq.q: What is Jamf Pro?

faq.a: Jamf Pro can integrate with Microsoft Intune to share compliance signals.
faq.q: How does Jamf Pro relate to Microsoft Intune?

jamf-pro.long:
Jamf Pro is a device management platform from Jamf for enterprise environments that use Apple hardware. It is designed to manage Apple devices such as Mac, iPhone and iPad.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, Jamf Pro is relevant because it can integrate with Microsoft Intune to share compliance signals. This allows organizations that run Apple devices alongside Microsoft cloud services to connect device state information from Jamf Pro with Intune. The details of how this integration is configured are not covered here.

On M365.FM, Jamf Pro is tracked as a product entity. No specific episodes are linked to this page at present.

java.desc: Java is a general-purpose, object-oriented language compiled to bytecode for the JVM; M365.FM covers upgrading a Java 8 Spring app to Java 21 with AI agents.

faq.a: Java is a general-purpose, object-oriented programming language that is compiled to bytecode for the Java virtual machine.
faq.q: What is Java?

faq.a: It walks through modernizing a legacy Java 8-era Spring MVC app on AWS to Java 21, showing AI agents handling the upgrade work. The starting problems named are pinned dependencies, unpatched CVEs and idle compute waste.
faq.q: What does the episode "Upgrade Java 8 Apps to Java 21 with AI Agents" cover?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure DevOps - Simply Explained", Java is among the application types that its deployment strategies cover, alongside .NET, Node.js, Python, Ruby, Android and iOS.
faq.q: Does Azure DevOps support Java applications?

java.long:
Java is a general-purpose, object-oriented programming language. Source code is compiled to bytecode that runs on the Java virtual machine (JVM), which is the basis for running the same application on different platforms. In the Microsoft ecosystem it appears mostly as one of several languages that Azure and related developer tooling support, rather than as a Microsoft product itself.

The most direct treatment of Java on M365.FM is the episode "Upgrade Java 8 Apps to Java 21 with AI Agents" from 28 November 2025. It describes a real-world, end-to-end modernization of a legacy Java 8 Spring application to Java 21. The starting point is a Java 8-era Spring MVC app running on AWS that has drifted over time: dependencies are pinned, CVEs remain unpatched, compute sits idle, and the setup relies on "works on my laptop" folklore. The episode argues that this kind of upgrade is work teams keep postponing, and it shows AI agents doing that work, with the stated goal of ending up with an application that is faster and cheaper to run.

The scenario illustrates a common decision around Java: whether to keep an older runtime in place or move to a current version. In the episode's framing, the cost of staying on Java 8 shows up as security exposure from unpatched vulnerabilities, locked dependency versions that make further change harder, and wasted infrastructure. Doing the upgrade manually is described as burning cycles, which is why the episode presents automated, agent-driven modernization as an alternative to leaving the application untouched.

Java also comes up in other M365.FM episodes as one language among many. In "Fix Microsoft Copilot Agent Governance with a Control Plane", Java is listed alongside Go, C#, Python, JavaScript (Node.js), Ruby, PowerShell and Ansible as a language commonly used in enterprise environments for durable task programming. The episode says Java and C# are valued for their robustness and cross-platform capabilities and are often used in large-scale systems.

In "Azure DevOps - Simply Explained", Java is named among the application types that Azure DevOps deployment strategies can serve, together with .NET, Node.js, Python, Ruby, Android and iOS. The episode presents Azure DevOps as language- and platform-agnostic, with deployment targets such as VMs, Kubernetes, serverless Azure Functions and web apps across clouds, plus approval gates and rollout approaches like blue-green deployments, canary releases and rolling updates.

The episode "When to Use Python in Power Platform Automation" mentions Java in a popularity context, noting that in 2022 Python overtook Java and C in popularity for the first time in 20 years. In "Speed Power BI with OneLake and Direct Lake", the Java Virtual Machine appears as the processing basis of traditional execution engines, in contrast to the Native Execution Engine, which the episode says uses C++ and vectorized execution to process data in batches for faster analytical queries.

Taken together, the episodes position Java as an established enterprise language, relevant both to teams maintaining long-lived applications and to Azure-hosted or pipeline-driven delivery. The material does not go into language features or version-by-version differences; its focus is on modernization effort, deployment support and how Java compares with other languages and runtimes.

javascript.desc: JavaScript is the programming language of the web platform, used for front-end and back-end development, including Microsoft 365 apps, add-ins and Power Apps Code Apps.

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, JavaScript is used to build Microsoft 365 Copilot plugins and add-ins, Microsoft Teams apps, and Power Apps Code Apps. It is also listed among languages used for durable task programming in enterprise environments.
faq.q: What is JavaScript used for in the Microsoft ecosystem?
