faq.a: The episodes name Visual Studio Code, Node.js as the back-end runtime, the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit, the Yeoman Generator (yo office), and frameworks such as React and Vue. TypeScript is mentioned as an alternative to JavaScript.
faq.q: Which tools are commonly used with JavaScript for Microsoft 365 development?

faq.a: Yes. JavaScript is described as the language of the web platform for front-end and back-end development, with Node.js named as the back-end JavaScript runtime in the Teams app episode.
faq.q: Can JavaScript be used for both front-end and back-end development?

javascript.long:
JavaScript is the programming language of the web platform. It is used for front-end work in the browser as well as for back-end development, which makes it a common choice for building interactive applications. Within the Microsoft ecosystem, JavaScript appears in several development scenarios covered by M365.FM, from custom Copilot plugins to Microsoft Teams apps and Power Apps Code Apps.

In practice, JavaScript is rarely used in isolation. The episodes describe it together with related technologies: TypeScript as an alternative for teams that prefer typed code, React and Vue as frameworks for building user interfaces, and Node.js as the back-end JavaScript runtime. Visual Studio Code is named as the essential editor for JavaScript, TypeScript or SharePoint Framework (SPFx) development. Which language or framework a project uses typically depends on the skills of the team, as the episode "Build Custom Microsoft 365 Copilot Plugins" notes when it says developers can pick JavaScript or TypeScript based on their team's skills.

For Microsoft 365 extensibility, the episode "Build Custom Microsoft 365 Copilot Plugins" describes a starting workflow in which the command yo office is run in a terminal. After answering prompts about the project type, script language, add-in name and supported Office app, the generator creates a project folder with the essential files: the manifest, HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The episode presents this as a foundation for custom plugins that work in Microsoft 365. It also mentions the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit and the Yeoman Generator as ways to initialize the project structure, with HTML, CSS and JavaScript or TypeScript for the interface and React as a frequent choice for building user interfaces.

The episode "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions" places JavaScript in the toolchain for Teams app development. Its table lists Visual Studio Code for JavaScript, TypeScript or SPFx development, the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit for provisioning and deploying cloud resources, Node.js as the back-end JavaScript runtime necessary for app functionality, and Microsoft Teams for collaboration and testing. The choice of tools, according to the episode, affects how quickly a project can start and how easy it is to manage.

Power Apps Code Apps are another area where JavaScript is relevant. The episode "Power Apps Code Apps with Carike Botha [MVP]" states that Code Apps combine low-code speed with professional coding control, and that developers can use familiar tools such as Visual Studio Code, JavaScript, React and Vue to build rich, modern web applications. It also points to source control with GitHub for collaboration, versioning and deployment management, and to AI-assisted development for generating code and simplifying complex tasks. The episode "Power Apps Code Apps - Simply Explained" adds that using JavaScript, TypeScript and React allows responsive and interactive user interfaces and the implementation of complex business logic, which the episode links to rapid development cycles. It mentions access to over 1,500 connectors and built-in compliance features that support enterprise governance and security policies.

JavaScript is also named in the context of agent governance. In "Fix Microsoft Copilot Agent Governance with a Control Plane", JavaScript (Node.js) appears in a list of programming languages commonly used in enterprise environments for durable task programming, alongside Go, Java, C#, Python, Ruby, PowerShell and Ansible (YAML). The episode describes each language as having its own advantages, for example Go for its concurrency model and performance, Java and C# for robustness and cross-platform capabilities, and Python for simplicity.

Taken together, the episodes treat JavaScript as a shared foundation across several Microsoft products. Typical decisions around it include whether to use JavaScript or TypeScript, which UI framework to pair it with, and which tooling (Visual Studio Code, Node.js, the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit) to adopt for the target platform.

jira-service-management.desc: Jira Service Management is Atlassian's IT service management product built on Jira, used to receive, route and resolve service requests and incidents.

faq.a: Jira Service Management is Atlassian's IT service management product built on Jira. It is used to receive, route and resolve service requests and incidents.
faq.q: What is Jira Service Management?

faq.a: Yes, it can be integrated with Microsoft Teams. M365.FM covers this in the episode "Integrate Jira Service Management with Microsoft Teams".
faq.q: Can Jira Service Management be used with Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: Jira Service Management is made by Atlassian and is built on Jira.
faq.q: Which company makes Jira Service Management?

jira-service-management.long:
Jira Service Management is an IT service management product from Atlassian, built on Jira. It is used to receive, route and resolve service requests and incidents, giving teams a structured way to handle work that arrives from users or other systems.

The product can be integrated with Microsoft Teams. This connects the service management workflow with a collaboration platform that many organizations already use for day-to-day communication, so that request and incident handling can sit closer to the conversations where teams work.

On M365.FM, Jira Service Management appears in the episode "Integrate Jira Service Management with Microsoft Teams" (published 2025-11-03), which covers the connection between the Atlassian product and Microsoft Teams. This page is limited to what is stated in the available information; details such as specific features, editions or pricing are not covered here.

json.desc: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a plain-text format of label-value pairs, objects and lists used by almost every modern web API to exchange data.

faq.a: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a plain-text data format made of label-value pairs, objects and lists. Almost every modern web API uses it to exchange data.
faq.q: What is JSON?

faq.a: ARM Templates use declarative JSON files to define and deploy Azure resources through Azure Resource Manager. The M365.FM episode "ARM Templates - Simply Explained" describes them as the original Infrastructure as Code technology behind Azure.
faq.q: How is JSON used in Azure?

faq.a: The episode "ARM Templates vs Bicep: Why Azure Teams Are Switching" says the intricate JSON syntax can lead to a steep learning curve, maintainability challenges and error-prone deployments. Bicep is presented as a more readable alternative.
faq.q: Why do some teams move from JSON-based ARM Templates to Bicep?

json.long:
JSON, short for JavaScript Object Notation, is a plain-text data format built from label-value pairs, objects and lists. Almost every modern web API uses it to exchange data between systems. Because it is plain text, it can be read by people and processed by software in many programming languages, which is why it appears in so many corners of the Microsoft ecosystem.

The format is made up of a small number of building blocks. A label, usually called a key, is paired with a value. Several pairs can be grouped into an object, and values can be arranged in lists. Objects and lists can be nested inside one another, which allows a single JSON document to describe anything from a simple record to a deeply layered configuration. This nesting is both the strength of the format and, as several M365.FM episodes point out, a source of difficulty when documents grow large.

In the context of SharePoint and Microsoft Lists, JSON is one of the options discussed in the episode "CAML vs REST vs JSON for SharePoint Lists". The episode compares three approaches for working with list data and looks at how each behaves in real-world situations, including slow lists, complex filters and very large lists. The episode frames the choice between CAML, REST and JSON as a performance question, and it argues that the approach that seems most modern is not automatically the fastest. For anyone deciding how to query or shape list data, the practical takeaway is to test the options against the actual size and filter complexity of the list in question.

JSON also plays a central role in Azure infrastructure automation. ARM Templates are described in the episode "ARM Templates - Simply Explained" as the original Infrastructure as Code technology behind Azure Resource Manager. They let organizations define, deploy and manage Azure infrastructure using declarative JSON files, so that deployments become repeatable, predictable and version-controlled. In that model, JSON is the language in which the desired state of Azure resources is written down.

The same episodes also describe the drawbacks of using JSON for this purpose. The episode "Bicep - Simply Explained" notes that traditional methods can lead to debugging deeply nested JSON objects, and lists pain points such as growing complexity in larger environments, bloated files that are hard to maintain, and frequent merge conflicts. "ARM Templates vs Bicep: Why Azure Teams Are Switching" says that the intricate JSON syntax can produce a steep learning curve, maintainability challenges and error-prone deployments, and presents Bicep as a more user-friendly alternative with cleaner syntax and improved tooling.

A related comparison appears in "PowerShell vs Bicep for Azure Infrastructure Automation". It lists the available structured approaches for Azure automation side by side. ARM Templates use JSON to declaratively define and deploy Azure resources, deployed through the Azure portal or command line interface. Bicep is described as a simplified deployment language for Azure that is more readable than JSON, deployed via the Azure CLI or PowerShell. Other entries in the same list include Terraform, which uses HCL, and the Azure PowerShell module.

Taken together, the episodes show two sides of JSON in Microsoft environments. As an exchange format for APIs and list data, it is a common and widely supported way to move structured information. As an authoring format for large infrastructure definitions, the episodes treat it as workable but verbose, which is the reason many Azure teams look at Bicep. Decisions around JSON therefore usually come down to scale: for data exchange and moderate configuration it remains a natural fit, while very large, deeply nested deployment files are where readability and maintenance start to suffer.

json-rpc.desc: JSON-RPC is a lightweight remote procedure call protocol encoded in JSON; version 2.0 is the message format used by the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

faq.a: JSON-RPC is a lightweight remote procedure call protocol encoded in JSON. Version 2.0 is the message format used by the Model Context Protocol (MCP) between clients and servers.
faq.q: What is JSON-RPC?

faq.a: According to the episode "MCP (Model Context Protocol) - Simply Explained", MCP uses JSON-RPC 2.0 for bidirectional, message-driven communication, which supports efficient data exchange and streaming for long-running operations.
faq.q: How does MCP use JSON-RPC?

faq.a: No. The episodes also state that the agent2agent protocol (A2A) uses HTTP and JSON-RPC so that agents can identify each other, share capabilities and coordinate work.
faq.q: Is JSON-RPC only used by MCP?

json-rpc.long:
JSON-RPC is a lightweight remote procedure call protocol that encodes its messages in JSON. A remote procedure call lets one program ask another program, often running on a different machine or process, to perform an operation and return a result. In the Microsoft ecosystem and the wider AI tooling space, JSON-RPC appears mainly as the message format underneath agent and tool protocols rather than as a product that users configure directly. Version 2.0 is the version named in the M365.FM episode material, where it is the message format used by the Model Context Protocol (MCP) between clients and servers.

The M365.FM episodes describe JSON-RPC mostly through the protocols that rely on it. The episode "MCP (Model Context Protocol) - Simply Explained" says that MCP uses JSON-RPC 2.0 for bidirectional, message-driven communication between clients and servers. According to the episode, this supports efficient data exchange and streaming for long-running operations, which improves real-time data access. The episode also points to the transport layer, which allows machine-readable discovery so that capabilities can be queried dynamically at runtime. In that picture, JSON-RPC carries the structured messages, while the surrounding protocol defines what clients and servers say to each other.

The episode "Dynamics 365 ERP MCP Server - Simply Explained" places JSON-RPC in a table of protocols and technologies involved in the integration. There, JSON-RPC is described as the format used for message conversion between MCP protocol messages and client-server communication. It sits alongside the Model Context Protocol itself, which establishes secure, bi-directional communication between AI systems and data, standard input/output (stdio), which suits local resource integration with lightweight, synchronous messaging, and Server-Sent Events (SSE), which suits remote resource integration and multiple asynchronous server calls. This shows a useful separation: JSON-RPC defines how messages are shaped, while stdio and SSE describe how those messages travel between a client and a server.

JSON-RPC also shows up in agent-to-agent communication. The episode "Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Communication - Simply Explained" explains that the agent2agent protocol (A2A) provides a standardized way for AI agents to interact across platforms. By building on established web standards such as HTTP and JSON-RPC, A2A aims to stay compatible with existing systems. The episode lists standardized communication, interoperability, secure interactions and structured messaging as key features of A2A. The episode "Enterprise AI Agent Fabric: Architecture Beyond Chatbots" repeats the point that the A2A protocol uses HTTP and JSON-RPC to identify other agents, share capabilities and coordinate work. It treats agent-to-agent communication as the backbone of persistent agent fabrics, and it lists related requirements such as durable state management, resumable conversations and message persistence, which the episode says teams may have to address with custom solutions.

For anyone evaluating MCP servers or agent protocols, JSON-RPC is relevant mainly as a shared foundation. Because both MCP and A2A rely on it, tools built around either protocol exchange messages in a common, JSON-based request-and-response style. The material does not say that JSON-RPC itself provides state management, resumability or security; the A2A episode treats those as separate concerns that require extra design effort. When reading architecture discussions about agents, it helps to distinguish three layers: the message format (JSON-RPC), the transport (such as stdio, SSE or HTTP), and the higher-level protocol (MCP or A2A) that defines capabilities and behavior.

In short, JSON-RPC is a small, widely reusable building block. In the episodes covered by M365.FM it is never the main subject, but it recurs as the common message layer beneath MCP, the Dynamics 365 ERP MCP Server integration, and the A2A protocol used for agent networks.

jump-box.desc: A jump box, also called a jump server or jump host, is a hardened server that administrators connect to first before reaching other machines in a private network.

faq.a: A jump box is a hardened server, also called a jump server or jump host, that administrators connect to first and then use to reach other machines in a private network.
faq.q: What is a jump box?

faq.a: When it runs as a regular virtual machine, it needs patching and monitoring. It also needs an exposed management port, which has to be protected.
faq.q: What does a jump box require to operate safely?

faq.a: Yes. Jump server and jump host are alternative names for the same concept: a hardened server used as the first hop for administrative access.
faq.q: Are jump server and jump host the same as a jump box?

jump-box.long:
A jump box is a hardened server, also known as a jump server or jump host, that administrators connect to first and then hop from to other machines in a private network. It acts as a single, controlled entry point for administrative access instead of allowing direct connections to each machine.

The approach is used to manage systems that sit inside a private network. Administrators authenticate to the jump box and move on to the target machines from there. Concentrating access in one place gives teams a defined point at which administrative connections can be controlled.

A jump box also has costs. When it is deployed as a regular virtual machine, it needs patching and monitoring like any other server, and it requires an exposed management port so that administrators can reach it. Because it is the first point of contact for administrative traffic, its hardening and upkeep matter. The management port it exposes is part of what has to be protected and watched.

No related topics or episodes are linked to this entry on M365.FM at this time. The concept is summarized here as a general term for hardened administrative access points in private networks.

just-enough-administration.desc: Just Enough Administration (JEA) is a PowerShell security technology that delegates specific administrative tasks without granting full administrator rights.

faq.a: JEA is a Windows PowerShell security technology for delegated administration. It lets users perform specific administrative tasks, such as restarting certain services, without holding full administrator rights.
faq.q: What is Just Enough Administration (JEA)?

faq.a: A configurable management endpoint exposes only the permitted cmdlets, functions and external commands. Privileged actions run through virtual accounts or group-managed service accounts, and transcripts and logs record which commands were run.
faq.q: How does JEA limit what a user can do?

faq.a: "Secure PowerShell Remoting for Microsoft 365" lists JEA and least privilege per task as the authorization layer of a remoting security architecture. "PowerShell Automation for Azure and Microsoft 365 with Matthew Dowst [MVP]" lists it among security practices that limit user access to approved cmdlets.
faq.q: How do the M365.FM episodes treat JEA?

just-enough-administration.long:
Just Enough Administration (JEA) is a Windows PowerShell security technology for delegated administration. It allows an organization to give users the ability to carry out specific administrative tasks, such as restarting certain services, without making them full administrators of a machine. According to Microsoft Learn, JEA works for anything that can be managed with PowerShell and follows the principle of least privilege.

The core idea is that fewer people should need administrator rights on a system. Instead of adding a person to a highly privileged group, an administrator sets up a configurable management endpoint that exposes only the permitted cmdlets, functions and external commands. When a regular user connects to that endpoint, privileged actions run through virtual accounts or group-managed service accounts rather than through the user's own credentials. A temporary privileged virtual account lets someone with non-admin credentials execute commands that would normally require admin rights, and only within the limits the endpoint defines.

A typical example from the Microsoft Learn overview is a team of DNS administrators on a domain controller. Without JEA, those administrators would need membership in the Domain Admins group. With JEA, they receive only the commands they need, such as repairing the DNS cache or restarting the DNS server. They get no access to Active Directory, no ability to browse the file system and no way to run risky scripts. The privileges are therefore matched to the job instead of to a broad role.

Auditability is the second main benefit. JEA supports transcripts and logs that record which commands a user ran in a session, so activity performed through a delegated endpoint can be traced afterwards. This combination of restricted capability and a record of use is what makes delegation easier to defend in security reviews. Microsoft also provides samples and a DSC resource in a GitHub repository, and a separate article covers prerequisites.

JEA appears in M365.FM as one control within a wider PowerShell security approach. The episode "Secure PowerShell Remoting for Microsoft 365" places it in the authorization layer of a security architecture, next to modern authentication, credential hygiene and network restrictions. The notes describe authorization as JEA and least privilege per task, using custom constrained endpoints. In the same architecture the episode recommends preferring OAuth, app registrations or managed identities, disabling basic authentication, keeping secrets in Azure Key Vault and limiting which network segments can reach remoting endpoints.

The episode "PowerShell Automation for Azure and Microsoft 365 with Matthew Dowst [MVP]" mentions JEA in a list of security practices for PowerShell. There, JEA is described as limiting user access to approved cmdlets. It is listed together with enforcing constrained language mode to disable risky features, keeping PowerShell updated and reviewing logging settings. Taken together, the episodes treat JEA as one layer that narrows what an authenticated user may do, not as a replacement for strong authentication or secret handling.

In practice, the decision to use JEA usually comes down to who needs to perform which tasks. Where a help desk, an operations team or a service owner needs to run a small set of administrative commands, a constrained endpoint can expose just those commands. Where broad, unrestricted administration is genuinely required, JEA offers little. The sources provided do not state licensing requirements or explicit limitations, so details such as supported platforms and setup steps should be confirmed in the official prerequisites article before planning a rollout.

just-in-time-access.desc: Just-in-time access grants elevated permissions only when needed and for a limited time, so they expire automatically instead of staying permanently assigned.

faq.a: It is an access model in which elevated permissions are granted only when needed and for a limited time, then expire automatically instead of staying permanently assigned.
faq.q: What does just-in-time access mean?

faq.a: The episode "Privileged Identity Management (PIM) - Simply Explained" describes the Just-in-Time model as a standout feature of PIM, which grants permissions only when necessary and revokes them after a set time or when the task is complete.
faq.q: How is just-in-time access related to Privileged Identity Management?

faq.a: The episode "Govern Microsoft 365 Guest Access and Offboarding" describes it for external users, who receive temporary access for a specific project or time frame instead of permanent access.
faq.q: Where else is just-in-time access applied besides admin roles?

just-in-time-access.long:
Just-in-time access (often shortened to JIT access) is an access model in which elevated permissions are granted only when they are needed and only for a limited period. Once that period ends, or once the task is complete, the permissions expire automatically instead of remaining permanently assigned to an account. The model is used mainly for privileged accounts and sensitive resources, where standing high-level rights create more risk than short, deliberate elevation.

The core idea is to shorten the time during which a person or account holds powerful rights. M365.FM episodes describe this as a way to reduce the attack surface: an account that has no active elevated permissions offers less to an attacker or to someone misusing access. The episode "Privileged Identity Management (PIM) - Simply Explained" lists three characteristics of the model. It grants permissions only when necessary, it revokes access after a set time or upon task completion, and it aligns with the principle of least privilege, so that users hold only the rights required for the work at hand.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, just-in-time access is most closely tied to Privileged Identity Management (PIM). The same episode calls the JIT model one of the standout features of PIM, a set of technologies and practices that help secure, monitor and control access to sensitive resources by privileged users or accounts. The episode "Lock Down Microsoft Entra ID Before Phishing Hits" recommends adopting PIM to grant just-in-time access to sensitive accounts, noting that this limits the risk of privilege abuse. It presents this as one measure among others, alongside Conditional Access policies, single sign-on and user education about phishing.

The model also appears in guidance on administrator roles. The episode "Microsoft 365 Global Admin Power, Identity, and Governance" lists using privileged access management in Azure to allow just-in-time access for sensitive tasks as one of several steps for controlling powerful roles. The other steps named there include role-based access control to separate duties, multi-factor authentication for admin actions, approval by more than one admin for critical actions such as device wipes or role changes, conditional access policies, auditing of Azure AD roles with least privilege, and monitoring of sign-in activity. Just-in-time access is therefore treated as a complement to these controls, not a replacement for them.

Just-in-time access is also discussed for external collaborators. The episode "Govern Microsoft 365 Guest Access and Offboarding" explains that it gives external users the permissions they need only when they need them, which avoids granting permanent access to Microsoft 365 resources. Instead, temporary access is provided for a specific project or time frame. The episode says this limits the window of opportunity for misuse and supports a guest user management strategy, and it pairs the approach with expiration dates for guest accounts and approval workflows for different kinds of external collaboration, such as vendors, contractors or partners.

The episode "AD Tiering and Privileged Access with Viktor Hedberg [MVP-MCT]" covers the topic in the context of tiered administration. It describes just-in-time access as giving users temporary permissions only when needed, which reduces risk by limiting how long someone holds high-level rights, and says this supports privileged identity management. In the same discussion, a tiered access model creates clear boundaries between account types by blocking logins from lower tiers to higher ones, which keeps the most important systems separated from everyday accounts.

Typical decisions around just-in-time access include which roles or resources should require elevation instead of permanent assignment, how long an elevation should last, and whether approval from another administrator should be required. The episodes frame the benefit consistently: fewer standing privileges, a shorter window for misuse, and permissions that end by themselves rather than depending on someone remembering to remove them.

kaizen.desc: Kaizen is a lean practice of small, practical improvements made close to the work, often run as short kaizen events by the people who run the process.

faq.a: Kaizen is a Japanese word meaning improvement. In business it refers to the idea that large gains come from many small improvements, with participation from everyone in the organisation.
faq.q: What does Kaizen mean?

faq.a: A kaizen event, also called a kaizen blitz or workshop, focuses on one issue and often lasts about a week. It is typically carried out by the people who run the process.
faq.q: What is a kaizen event?

faq.a: The episode "Why Continuous Improvement Needs Better Data" says teams often cannot prove whether a countermeasure worked, where it worked, and under which conditions it stopped working. As a result, the same loss can reappear a few weeks after an event.
faq.q: Why do kaizen improvements sometimes not last?

kaizen.long:
Kaizen is a lean practice built on small, practical improvements made close to the work, usually by the people who run the process. The word is Japanese and means improvement. Outside Japan it became a business concept holding that large gains come from the cumulative effect of many small improvements, with participation from everyone, from the chief executive to assembly line workers. The aim is to eliminate waste and redundancy using the resources already available rather than large new investments.

The approach is usually traced through W. Edwards Deming's 1947 visit to Japan and statistical quality control, the wartime Training Within Industry program in the United States, and the Toyota Production System. Masaaki Imai popularized the term in 1986. Some sources describe the framing of kaizen as a Japanese philosophy as a later interpretation, so the history is not entirely uncontested.

A number of methods are associated with kaizen. These include the plan-do-check-act cycle, the five whys, 5S, and the seven wastes. The three Mu, which stand for waste, unevenness and overburden, are also part of the vocabulary, as is going to the source, meaning looking at the real process where the work happens. Several types are described: point kaizen for quick individual fixes, system kaizen, line kaizen, and cube kaizen, which spans suppliers and customers. Quick or blitz kaizen refers to a fast, focused format.

In practice, kaizen is often run as a kaizen event or workshop. These events focus on one issue and often last about a week. A small team that works in the process analyses a problem, tests a countermeasure and tries to make the result visible. This makes the method approachable, because it does not depend on a large project organisation.

The method also has recognised limits. Point improvements in one area can cancel benefits elsewhere, and events address a limited scope, which leaves unresolved issues for later events. These limits shape how organisations decide where to run events and how to connect them to the wider process.

The M365.FM episode "Why Continuous Improvement Needs Better Data" looks at this problem in a factory setting. The episode says that improvement work in many factories still depends on workshops, spreadsheets, isolated reports and what people remember from the previous shift. A kaizen event can create visible progress, but a few weeks later the same loss often appears again under slightly different production conditions. According to the episode, the issue is not always the quality of the improvement idea. The bigger problem is that teams often cannot prove whether a countermeasure actually worked, where it worked, and under which conditions it stopped working. The episode frames better data as the way to make continuous improvement compound into learning over time.

The term also appears in an AI context. The episode "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud" mentions a Kaizen funnel as a structured mechanism to crowdsource and prioritize ideas for AI initiatives. It lists this alongside an AI Center of Excellence, stronger governance for responsible scaling and mitigation of AI hallucinations, and continuous improvement practices such as 'Fix, Hack, Learn' weeks. In that discussion, the kaizen idea of gathering many small ideas from the people close to the work is applied to deciding which AI initiatives to pursue.

keda.desc: KEDA (Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling) is an open-source Kubernetes component that scales workloads based on events such as queue length or HTTP request rate.

faq.a: KEDA stands for Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling. It is an open-source Kubernetes component that scales workloads based on events such as queue length or HTTP request rate.
faq.q: What is KEDA?

faq.a: Yes. According to its description, KEDA supports scaling workloads down to zero when no events require processing.
faq.q: Can KEDA scale workloads to zero?

faq.a: Examples named in the description are queue length and HTTP request rate. The facts provided do not list further event sources.
faq.q: What kinds of events can trigger scaling with KEDA?

keda.long:
KEDA (Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling) is an open-source component for Kubernetes that scales workloads in response to events. Instead of relying only on resource metrics such as CPU or memory, it reacts to signals like the length of a message queue or the rate of incoming HTTP requests.

A defining capability of KEDA is that it can scale a workload down to zero when there is no work to process, and scale it back up when events arrive. This makes it relevant for event-driven and queue-based applications running on Kubernetes, where demand can be irregular and idle capacity is undesirable.

The available facts on this entry do not list related products, episodes, or official documentation links, so details such as supported event sources, configuration objects, or integration with specific Microsoft services are not covered here.

key-performance-indicator.desc: A key performance indicator (KPI) is a measure used to judge how well an organization, process or activity is meeting its objectives.
key-performance-indicator.long:
A key performance indicator (KPI) is a measure used to judge how well an organization, process or activity is meeting its objectives. It turns a goal into something that can be tracked, so that progress, drift or shortfall becomes visible rather than assumed.

One perspective discussed on M365.FM argues that a KPI should do more than report a number. In that view, a KPI works as a decision rule: it has a named owner, a defined trigger, and an action that was committed to in advance. The trigger describes the condition under which the measure calls for a response, and the pre-committed action describes what happens when that condition is met. Without these elements, a KPI risks becoming a figure on a dashboard that is observed but never acted on.

This framing is relevant to anyone who builds reports, scorecards or dashboards, because it shifts the question from "what can be measured" to "what decision does this measure support". Ownership makes responsibility explicit, the trigger removes ambiguity about when to act, and the agreed action reduces debate at the moment a threshold is crossed.

The concept appears on M365.FM as a perspective on how measurement should connect to decisions. No specific episodes, products or linked topics are listed for this entry at present.

key-person-dependency.desc: Key person dependency is an operational risk in which critical knowledge or capability sits with one or a few people, creating a single point of failure.

faq.a: It is an operational risk in which critical process knowledge or capability is concentrated in one or a few individuals. When they are absent or leave, it creates a single point of failure.
faq.q: What is key person dependency?

faq.a: The bus factor is the smallest number of team members who would have to leave suddenly before a project stalls because nobody else has the required knowledge. A bus factor of 1 means a single point of failure.
faq.q: How does key person dependency relate to the bus factor?

faq.a: The sources name reducing complexity, documenting and updating processes, cross-training and sharing information. The M365.FM episode on Excel shadow systems also points to governance, visibility and automation.
faq.q: How can key person dependency be reduced?

key-person-dependency.long:
Key person dependency is an operational risk in which critical process knowledge or capability is concentrated in one or a few individuals. When those people are absent or leave, the process, project or service can stall because nobody else knows how to run it. The concept describes a single point of failure that sits in people rather than in technology, and it is a common concern in operational resilience and continuity planning.

A closely related measure is the bus factor, also called the truck, lottery or circus factor. According to the Wikipedia article on the topic, it is the smallest number of team members who would have to leave suddenly before a project stalls because nobody else has the required knowledge. The article links the bus factor to key person risk but focuses on technical experts rather than on easily replaced managers or financial leaders. A person counts only if they are both key to the work and irreplaceable. A bus factor of 1 is a single point of failure, while higher values indicate more redundancy. The article gives the example of a 30-person bakery: if only five people can bake, the factor is five.

The cause is often undocumented or unshared work. In software, a component that only one person understands is a key dependency. The departure does not have to be dramatic: a new job or parental leave has the same effect as any other exit. The same source cites a 2015 to 2016 study of 133 popular GitHub projects that found 65 percent had a bus factor of two or less, which shows how common the pattern is even in widely used projects.

Typical mitigations named in the source are reducing complexity, documenting and updating processes, cross-training and sharing information. In practice, the decisions around this risk include which processes are critical, who currently holds the knowledge, and whether that knowledge lives in a form others can read, reuse and verify.

The M365.FM episode "Fix Excel Shadow Systems and Broken Business Processes" connects key person dependency to spreadsheet-based work. The episode says that relying on Excel and spreadsheets creates shadow data, key person dependency and static information. It describes these tools as a source of data integrity issues and information silos, and it argues that spreadsheets hide errors, slow the business and block real-time decisions. In that framing, a spreadsheet understood by only one person becomes exactly the kind of single point of failure described above.

The episode's recommended direction is to apply governance, visibility and automation to protect operations. It advises assessing the process architecture and choosing modern solutions that move beyond Excel and spreadsheets, with the stated goals of operational resilience, reduced risk and a team that is set up for growth. Taken together, the sources treat key person dependency as a risk to be identified and reduced through documentation, shared knowledge and more transparent, automated processes rather than as an unavoidable fact of how teams work.

keyword-search.desc: Keyword search is lexical retrieval that matches the exact words of a query to documents, often ranked with BM25, precise for exact terms but blind to meaning.

faq.a: Keyword search is traditional lexical search that matches the exact words of a query against documents, often ranked with the BM25 algorithm. It is precise for exact terms but does not understand meaning.
faq.q: What is keyword search?

faq.a: Keyword search misses results when a query and a document use different words for the same idea, for example time off versus vacation. The episodes describe combining it with vector search, semantic ranking and metadata filtering to cover both exact terms and meaning.
faq.q: Why is keyword search often combined with vector search?

faq.a: Examples in the episodes include Azure AI Search, which combines keyword search with vector search and semantic ranking, and Microsoft Purview audit search, which lets users enter keywords or phrases to search the audit log.
faq.q: Where does keyword search appear in Microsoft products?

keyword-search.long:
Keyword search is a traditional, lexical form of search that matches the exact words of a query against the words found in documents. Results are often ranked with the BM25 algorithm. Because it works on literal terms, it is precise when a user knows the exact word, code or phrase to look for, but it does not understand meaning: it cannot tell that two different words describe the same idea.

This behavior defines both the strength and the weakness of the approach. The episode "Azure AI Search Hybrid Retrieval - Simply Explained" describes keyword search as matching what the user types, which is ideal when a policy code is needed but useless when a user asks about time off and the document says vacation. In other words, keyword search rewards exact vocabulary overlap and offers no help when the query and the source use different wording for the same concept.

In practice, keyword search is used wherever exact terms matter: looking up identifiers, product names, codes, or specific phrases. A familiar example from the Microsoft ecosystem appears in the episode "Audit Microsoft 365 User Activity with Purview". There, Microsoft Purview audit search lets administrators enter keywords or phrases to search within the audit log. The same episode lists keyword search next to other filters, such as a date and time range in UTC with a maximum of 180 days, administrative units, friendly activity names, operation names and record types. Keyword search is therefore one narrowing tool among several, used together with structured filters to focus on specific user activities.

Keyword search also plays a role in modern AI retrieval design. The episode "Azure AI Search – Simply Explained" presents Azure AI Search as Microsoft's search and information retrieval service that combines traditional keyword search with vector search, semantic ranking and AI enrichment. It is described as a core component for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), AI agents and enterprise search solutions. In that setup, keyword search contributes the exact-match side of retrieval, while vector search and semantic ranking address meaning.

The episode "Improve Microsoft Copilot Accuracy Beyond Vector Search" makes a related design point. It argues that Copilot produces poor answers when it is given wrong or low-quality data, and recommends moving beyond pure vector search to a more structured retrieval strategy. That strategy combines techniques such as keyword search, metadata filtering and business rules so the AI reaches the most relevant and precise information. The episode's key takeaway is that vector search should be seen as one tool, not the foundation, and that retrieval strategy plays a central role in reliable Copilot systems.

Keyword search also appears in discussions of scale. The episode "Scaling Microsoft Copilot to 35 Million Pages: The Epstein Files" notes that large-scale investigations of massive document collections require more than keyword search, and that relationship discovery becomes the critical capability. Approaches mentioned there include semantic search, vector databases, knowledge graphs and RAG.

When deciding how to use keyword search, the main question is whether exact wording is reliable. Where users search for codes, names or fixed phrases, lexical matching is a precise fit. Where users phrase questions in natural language and source documents use different terms, keyword search alone tends to miss relevant content, which is why the episodes point toward hybrid retrieval that pairs it with vector search, semantic ranking and metadata filtering.

knowledge-article.desc: A knowledge article is a reviewed support answer in the Dynamics 365 knowledge base that agents search during cases and customers read through a self-service portal.

faq.a: It is a reviewed support answer stored in the Dynamics 365 knowledge base. Agents can search it while working on a case, and customers can read it through a self-service portal.
faq.q: What is a knowledge article in Dynamics 365?

faq.a: According to the episode "Dynamics 365 Knowledge Management - Simply Explained", it should start from a real customer or agent problem, use clear titles, keywords, categories and straightforward language, and give the main answer first before explaining the steps in order.
faq.q: How should a knowledge article be written?

faq.a: The episode "Extend Copilot in Dynamics 365 for CRM and ERP" says Copilot and AI agent capabilities provide knowledge article recommendations to agents, alongside suggested replies and case summarization.
faq.q: How do knowledge articles relate to Copilot?

knowledge-article.long:
A knowledge article is a reviewed support answer stored in the Dynamics 365 knowledge base. It serves two audiences at once: agents can search it while working on a customer case, and customers can read it through a self-service portal. Because the content has been approved before it is published, it acts as a shared source of guidance rather than an informal note kept in one person's files.

The main purpose of a knowledge article is to put approved information where the work happens. According to the M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Knowledge Management - Simply Explained", agents can reach approved guidance directly within their customer service workflow instead of switching between multiple applications and repositories. The same article can therefore answer a question for an agent in the middle of a case and for a customer who prefers to find the answer without contacting support.

The episode also describes what makes an article effective. A useful knowledge article starts with a real customer or agent problem, not with a topic chosen in the abstract. Clear titles, relevant keywords, categories and straightforward language make articles easier to discover. The article should provide the main answer quickly and then explain the necessary steps in the order that agents or customers need to follow them. The episode adds that organizations can connect related articles and organize knowledge around subjects, so that a reader who needs more detail can move to neighboring content.

Knowledge articles also appear inside the agent workspace. The episode "Dynamics 365 Customer Service Workspace - Simply Explained" describes the workspace as a browser designed around customer service, in which customers, cases, knowledge articles, product records and conversations are organized around the piece of customer work currently being handled. Opening a knowledge article there is meant to avoid a separate browser window for each item, so that agents can move between multiple customer issues without repeatedly losing and rebuilding context.

AI assistance is another place where knowledge articles come up. The episode "Extend Copilot in Dynamics 365 for CRM and ERP" states that Copilot and AI agent capabilities give agents suggested replies, knowledge article recommendations and case summarization. It says this works by analyzing historical tickets and customer segment data, with the aim of helping agents deliver faster and more consistent customer experiences. In that setting, the quality of the underlying articles matters, since recommendations can only point to answers that exist in the knowledge base.

In practice, decisions around knowledge articles concern authoring and structure rather than technology alone. Teams choose which real problems deserve an article, how to word titles and keywords so that agents and customers can find them, which categories and subjects to use, and which articles to link to one another. Keeping answers reviewed before publication is what allows both agents and self-service readers to rely on the same content. The sources provided here do not cover review workflows, versioning, licensing or portal configuration in detail, so those aspects are left to the product documentation and the full episodes.

knowledge-graph.desc: A knowledge graph is a data model that stores entities and typed relationships so software can follow connections, for example across production stages in a genealogy investigation.

faq.a: A knowledge graph is a data model that represents entities and typed relationships explicitly so software can traverse connections, for example across production stages in a genealogy investigation.
faq.q: What is a knowledge graph?

faq.a: The episodes say a knowledge graph supplies context that isolated records lack, which supports stronger AI grounding, better discovery of hidden patterns, and greater traceability.
faq.q: Why do the M365.FM episodes link knowledge graphs to AI?

faq.a: The episodes describe Microsoft Graph as connecting people, documents, and workflows into a single knowledge graph and as turning data silos into a trusted enterprise knowledge graph.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Graph relate to a knowledge graph?

knowledge-graph.long:
A knowledge graph is a data model that represents entities and the typed relationships between them explicitly, so that software can traverse those connections instead of treating each record as an isolated item. Rather than storing information only in separate tables or folders, the model records what things are (people, documents, products, processes, resources) and how they relate. One example given in the topic description is following links across production stages in a genealogy investigation, where each step can be traced back through the connections that joined it to the next.

The main purpose is to give software context. Isolated records can be read in large volumes, but they do not automatically explain how pieces fit together. In the M365.FM episode "What Is a PPR Knowledge Graph — and Why Manufacturing AI Needs One", this gap is described in a factory setting. Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems know the orders and Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES) hold their own data, yet the isolated records do not explain how a product, process, and resource (PPR) came together at any given moment. The episode presents a Product-Process-Resource knowledge graph as the connecting layer, and argues that this missing connection is where promising artificial intelligence initiatives lose their footing.

The same idea appears in the Microsoft 365 context. The episode "How Microsoft Graph Connects Microsoft 365 Data and Context" describes Microsoft Graph as transforming data silos into a trusted enterprise knowledge graph, and says this layer provides context for reliable AI applications. According to that episode, a proprietary knowledge graph lets organizations infuse AI with company-specific rules, while automated tagging adds rich metadata and reduces manual effort. It also mentions smart workflows that integrate with Logic Apps and Power Automate to create repeatable processes across Microsoft tools.

The episode "Graph-Powered AI Agents: An Enterprise Architecture Guide" describes Microsoft Graph as the digital nervous system of an organization, connecting people, documents, and workflows into a single knowledge graph. In that framing, the structure lets AI agents reach the right data at the right time, connect information, remember past actions, and reason through multi-step problems. The episode lists uses such as orchestrating AI agents with access to business data and content, streamlining workflows with Microsoft 365 Copilot, and extending agent capabilities by connecting to other data sources through APIs.

The episode "Microsoft Cowork IQ Knowledge Graph Architecture" looks at implementing knowledge graph architectures for hybrid work. It discusses how Microsoft Graph, Microsoft 365, AI-powered search, and Copilot-related capabilities help connect people, content, and conversations, with attention to compliance requirements. Practical scenarios named there include expertise discovery, employee onboarding, project collaboration, knowledge sharing, and organizational intelligence.

The episode "Microsoft Graph Architecture Beyond Folders and Hierarchies" contrasts graph-based thinking with folder-and-hierarchy structures. It presents a table of use cases and benefits that includes a Trend Micro AI security assistant with 20% better answers, fraud detection at NewDay with 10-15% fewer undetected cases, a BMW Group Cloud Data Hub with more than 1,000 use cases for 9,000 users, fraud investigations at Paysafe taking minutes instead of hours, and a Uber Config Knowledge Graph enabling early conflict detection. The episode says that future graph-based architecture brings better discovery of hidden patterns, stronger AI grounding, and greater traceability. These figures are attributed to the episode and are not independently verified here.

Taken together, the episodes treat a knowledge graph as a way to make relationships first-class. Typical decisions around it involve which entities and relationship types to model, which data sources to connect, how to keep the model adaptable as the environment changes, and how to supply the resulting context to AI applications and agents so their answers rest on connected, traceable information.

knowledge-management.desc: Knowledge management is the organized process of creating, sharing, using and maintaining an organization's knowledge, applied in M365.FM episodes to SharePoint and Dynamics 365.

faq.a: Knowledge management is the organized process by which an organization creates, shares, uses and maintains its knowledge and information. In M365.FM episodes it is applied to SharePoint as a company knowledge platform and to Dynamics 365 for customer service.
faq.q: What is knowledge management?

faq.a: The episode "Fix SharePoint Knowledge Management" says organizations fail when they treat SharePoint like a dumping ground, without a lifecycle, ownership or metadata. This leads to duplicate "final" files, broken search and shadow repositories in Teams, OneDrive and email.
faq.q: Why does SharePoint knowledge management often fail, according to M365.FM?

faq.a: According to the episode "Dynamics 365 Knowledge Management - Simply Explained", it gives teams a single, trusted source of approved knowledge articles that agents use while helping customers. This replaces searching old emails, shared folders or spreadsheets and supports consistent answers across channels.
faq.q: How does Dynamics 365 Knowledge Management support customer service?

knowledge-management.long:
Knowledge management is the organized process by which an organization creates, shares, uses and maintains its knowledge and information. The goal is that people can find reliable answers when they need them, instead of relying on scattered files, personal experience or outdated copies. In the Microsoft ecosystem the term appears in several product contexts, and the M365.FM episodes on this topic mainly apply it to SharePoint as a company knowledge platform and to Dynamics 365 for customer service.

The episode "Fix SharePoint Knowledge Management" starts from the premise that SharePoint does not fail on its own; organizations fail when they treat it like a dumping ground. According to the episode, the typical result is duplicate "final" files, broken search and shadow repositories in Teams, OneDrive and email. It names the causes as the absence of a lifecycle, ownership and metadata. The core ingredients of a functional knowledge platform, as described there, are navigation, lifecycle and metadata. The episode outlines a practical path toward a trusted "One Point of Truth" that is kept alive through governance and automation.

Governance is a recurring theme. The episode "Stop SharePoint Sprawl with Data and Automation Governance" treats the quality of knowledge management as dependent on clear rules and controls. It describes limiting who can create sites and teams to avoid unnecessary sprawl and outdated resources, and setting rules for private and shared channels in Teams. The same material discusses applying controls to how AI interacts with data and collaboration spaces, so that AI tools work safely and predictably within Microsoft 365 environments and the knowledge base does not fill up with stale content.

A second angle is AI-assisted organization of knowledge. The episode "Integrate Viva Topics with Search and SharePoint" describes Viva Topics as a knowledge assistant that finds and organizes knowledge from communication and content across Microsoft systems. It mentions topic cards that surface relevant information at the point of need, integration with SharePoint, and the role of subject matter experts who guide management and keep the knowledge base reliable. The stated benefits are less time spent searching and more confidence in the information used day to day.

A third angle is customer service. The episode "Dynamics 365 Knowledge Management - Simply Explained" describes how Dynamics 365 Knowledge Management helps customer service teams build a single, trusted source of knowledge that agents use while supporting customers. Instead of searching old emails, shared folders or spreadsheets, or depending on individual experience, teams create approved knowledge articles that give consistent answers across customer service channels. The episode "Optimize Dynamics 365 Business Processes for Faster Delivery" lists knowledge management alongside workflow automation and intelligent case routing as features of autonomous agents that support efficiency in customer service.

Taken together, the episodes show that knowledge management is less a single product than a set of practices: assigning ownership, defining a content lifecycle, using metadata and navigation, approving content before it is reused, and applying governance so the platform stays current. Which Microsoft tool fits depends on the audience, for example employees searching a company knowledge platform in SharePoint, or service agents needing approved articles in Dynamics 365. In each case, the episodes stress that tooling alone does not create trusted knowledge; consistent rules and maintenance do.

knowledge-source.desc: A knowledge source is content such as SharePoint sites, files, websites, Dataverse tables or connectors that a Copilot Studio agent grounds its answers on.

faq.a: It is content that an agent in Copilot Studio can ground its answers on, such as SharePoint sites, files, websites, Dataverse tables or connectors. The agent answers from this material instead of relying only on its language model's training.
faq.q: What is a knowledge source in Copilot Studio?

faq.a: According to the episode "Use SharePoint Lists as a Copilot Knowledge Base", not necessarily. It argues that Copilot Studio can work with data where it already lives, such as SharePoint lists, within the user's permissions.
faq.q: Does data have to be moved to Dataverse before an agent can use it?

faq.a: A knowledge source grounds answers in content, while the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is described as a discoverable bundle of capabilities that tells an agent which tools it can use. Choosing between them, or a connector, is a recurring design question.
faq.q: How does a knowledge source differ from MCP?

knowledge-source.long:
A knowledge source is content that an agent in Copilot Studio can ground its answers on. Typical examples are SharePoint sites, files, websites, Dataverse tables and connectors. In German-language material the concept appears as "Wissensquelle", and in some discussions it is called Copilot Studio knowledge. The term sits within Copilot Studio, the Microsoft tool in which such agents are built.

Grounding means that an agent answers from this material instead of relying only on what its language model learned in training. This ties answers to the organization's own information and is the practical form of Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in Copilot Studio. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Copilot Studio Knowledge Tuning - Simply Explained" starts from a common problem: an agent can sound completely sure of itself and still be wrong, because it answers from the wrong place, either its own general knowledge or a document that was never meant to be used. Deciding what knowledge actually means in Copilot Studio, and which content an agent should draw on, is therefore a central design step.

Several kinds of content can serve as a knowledge source. SharePoint and Dataverse are two of the most common places where such content lives, and a Connector can bring in data from other systems. The episode "Use SharePoint Lists as a Copilot Knowledge Base" describes adding SharePoint lists as a source so that people can interact conversationally with their data through an agent. According to that episode, every row and column in a list is available within the permissions of the person asking, which keeps access secure and relevant. It also argues against the habit of migrating data to Dataverse or Fabric first, noting that Copilot Studio can work with the data where it already exists, so no moving or copying is needed.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a related way for an agent to reach data and actions. The episode "From Demo to Production- Building Enterprise AI Agents That Actually Work with Microsoft Copilot Studio with Elliot Margot [MVP]" explains MCP as a structured, discoverable bundle of capabilities that tells an agent which tools are available and how to use them. Choosing between a knowledge source, a connector and an MCP server is a recurring design question when an agent has to connect to enterprise tools and APIs.

The quality of the underlying content strongly affects the quality of answers. The same episode with Elliot Margot warns that unstructured PDFs, duplicate files and outdated versions lead to slow, expensive and unreliable answers. It recommends a knowledge architecture in which the current, approved information is available to the agent while old versions are kept out of the production knowledge source. The episode "Beyond Copilot: Building Enterprise AI Agents That Actually Work with Copilot Studio with Manpreet Singh [MVP-MCT]" lists enterprise knowledge grounding, SharePoint as an AI knowledge source, and data quality, metadata and indexing among its topics, alongside Power Platform connectors, Microsoft Purview and DLP, and governance of agents.

Scope also matters when several agents are involved. In "Extending Microsoft 365 Copilot: Agents, MCP & Production-Grade AI with Yves Habersaat [MVP]", the recommendation is to avoid one enormous Copilot that holds every instruction, tool, knowledge source and responsibility. Instead, individual agents get clearly defined scopes. In an IT support example, a front-facing agent routes requests to specialized agents for Microsoft 365, Salesforce or other platforms, each of which can be tied to its own relevant content.

In practice, working with knowledge sources comes down to a few decisions: which content the agent should be allowed to use, where that content already lives, whether a connector or an MCP server is the better route for a given system, and how current and well structured the material is. Treating these as deliberate choices, rather than adding every available file, is the theme that runs through the related M365.FM episodes.

kql.desc: Kusto Query Language (KQL) is the Microsoft query language for analyzing log data in Microsoft Sentinel, Microsoft Defender and Azure Monitor.

faq.a: KQL is used to analyze log data in Microsoft Sentinel, Microsoft Defender and Azure Monitor. Analysts filter, aggregate and join events to investigate incidents, hunt for threats, troubleshoot failures and build alerts or dashboards.
faq.q: What is Kusto Query Language (KQL) used for?

faq.a: No. KQL is a language for reading and analyzing data, not for changing it.
faq.q: Can KQL change the data it queries?

faq.a: It is mentioned in "Microsoft Sentinel - Simply Explained", "Azure Monitor — Simply Explained", "Azure Functions - Simply Explained" and "Build Self-Healing Automation with Telemetry and Observability", mostly as the way to query logs and telemetry on those platforms.
faq.q: Where does KQL appear in the M365.FM episodes?

kql.long:
Kusto Query Language (KQL) is the query language used in Microsoft Sentinel, Microsoft Defender and Azure Monitor to analyze log data. It was developed by Microsoft and is classed under analytics and BI tooling. KQL is a language for reading and analyzing data, not for changing it. Analysts and administrators use it to filter, aggregate and join large volumes of events so that patterns, failures and suspicious behavior become visible.

In practice, KQL is the shared skill behind several Microsoft platforms. In security work, it supports investigating incidents, hunting for threats and building detection logic. KQL is related to Microsoft Defender, where it is used for advanced hunting across security data. In monitoring and operations, the same language is used to query logs collected by Azure Monitor, for example to troubleshoot failures or analyze performance trends. Because the language is the same across these services, a security analyst and a cloud administrator can work with log data from different sources in a similar way.

The M365.FM episodes that mention KQL are mainly about the platforms where it is used rather than about syntax. The episode "Microsoft Sentinel - Simply Explained" lists KQL among the core concepts of Sentinel, alongside data connectors, analytics rules, incidents, workbooks, threat hunting, automation rules, playbooks, watchlists and threat intelligence. According to the episode, Sentinel collects telemetry from Microsoft 365, Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Entra ID, Azure, AWS, Google Cloud and many third-party security products, and the discussion covers scenarios such as detecting ransomware attacks and identifying compromised accounts.

The episode "Azure Monitor — Simply Explained" presents KQL as the means of troubleshooting failures in Azure Monitor. It describes the creation of alerts, the analysis of performance trends and the use of Application Insights to understand application performance, user behavior, dependencies and exceptions. It also mentions integration with Microsoft Sentinel, Azure Automation and ITSM platforms for operational visibility.

The episode "Azure Functions - Simply Explained" touches on KQL in the context of monitoring. It notes that Azure Monitor integrates closely with Azure services and collects data automatically, but warns that there is a learning curve when moving to KQL for advanced queries. Its logging advice includes integrating Azure Functions with Application Insights for telemetry on function executions, dependencies and failures, and using correlation IDs in logs to trace requests across distributed components.

The episode "Build Self-Healing Automation with Telemetry and Observability" shows a further use. It describes creating an Application Insights resource in the Azure portal, sending telemetry from systems such as Supply Chain Management to it, and storing that data in Azure Monitor Logs, often in the customEvents table. Log queries written in KQL are then used to view and filter the collected data, which prepares clean and organized data for automation in Microsoft Power Automate.

Taken together, the episodes position KQL as the query layer that connects data collection to action. Telemetry is gathered by connectors, agents or Application Insights, stored in a log store, and then explored with KQL to drive alerts, investigations, workbooks and automated responses. Teams deciding where to invest learning time can see from these episodes that KQL spans security operations, application monitoring and automation scenarios, even though each episode treats it as one concept among many.

krbtgt-account.desc: The KRBTGT account is the Active Directory account whose key the Key Distribution Center uses to sign Kerberos tickets; rotating its password twice invalidates forged tickets.

faq.a: The KRBTGT account is the Active Directory account whose key the Key Distribution Center uses to sign Kerberos tickets.
faq.q: What is the KRBTGT account?

faq.a: Rotating the KRBTGT password twice invalidates forged Kerberos tickets that were signed with a previously compromised key.
faq.q: Why is the KRBTGT password rotated twice?

krbtgt-account.long:
The KRBTGT account is a built-in account in Active Directory. Its key is used by the Key Distribution Center (KDC) to sign Kerberos tickets, which makes the account a central part of how Kerberos authentication is trusted within a domain.

Because tickets are signed with the KRBTGT key, a compromise of that key can allow forged Kerberos tickets to be created. Rotating the KRBTGT password twice is the described way to invalidate such forged tickets. The account is therefore relevant to Active Directory security hygiene, incident response and recovery planning.

This page describes the concept only as far as it is known from the available facts. No related entities, official documentation links or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to the KRBTGT account, so no further details on procedures, scheduling or tooling are given here.

kv-cache.desc: The KV cache is the key-value memory that transformer language models hold during inference to store attention state for earlier tokens, growing with context and users.
kv-cache.long:
The KV cache (key-value cache) is a memory structure used by transformer-based language models during inference. It stores the attention state computed for previous tokens, so the model can refer back to earlier parts of a conversation or document without recomputing that state at every step.

Because the cache holds state for each token in the context, it grows as the context length increases. It also grows with the number of concurrent users, since each active session keeps its own cached state. For this reason, the KV cache can become a hardware bottleneck, particularly for self-hosted large language models (LLMs), where available accelerator memory limits how many users and how much context can be served at once.

Understanding the KV cache is relevant when planning capacity for self-hosted LLM deployments, since memory consumption depends not only on the model itself but also on context length and concurrency. The concept is useful for anyone weighing the trade-offs between longer context windows, the number of simultaneous users, and the hardware required.

No related topics, official documentation links or M365.FM episodes are currently associated with this entry.

langchain4j.desc: LangChain4j is an open-source Java library for building LLM-powered applications, with a unified model-provider API, tool calling, agents and RAG.

faq.a: LangChain4j is an open-source Java library for building LLM-powered applications. It provides a unified API over model providers plus tool calling, agents and RAG.
faq.q: What is LangChain4j?

faq.a: The episode "Stop Prompt Injection in LangChain4j and Copilot Studio" discusses how agents built with LangChain4j and Copilot Studio can become over-permissioned and unaudited. It covers prompt injection, over-scoped connectors and missing logs as the main risks.
faq.q: Why does LangChain4j come up in M365.FM security episodes?

faq.a: The episode recommends giving the agent its own identity, avoiding shared credentials and tenant-wide scopes, and treating it like a very dumb, very powerful user that is restrained by design.
faq.q: How does the episode suggest restraining an AI agent?

langchain4j.long:
LangChain4j is an open-source Java library for building applications powered by large language models (LLMs). It gives Java developers a unified API over different model providers, so application code does not have to be written against a single vendor's interface. On top of that common layer, the library offers tool calling, agents and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which are the building blocks most teams reach for when they move from a simple chat prompt to an application that can act on data and systems.

In practice, LangChain4j is used where an organization already runs Java services and wants to add LLM features without leaving that ecosystem. A unified provider API means the model behind the application can be changed without rewriting the surrounding logic. Tool calling lets a model invoke functions defined in the application, agents let the model plan and chain steps, and RAG lets it ground answers in documents or data retrieved at query time. Each of these capabilities extends what a model can reach, and that reach is exactly what makes governance and security a central concern.

The M365.FM episode "Stop Prompt Injection in LangChain4j and Copilot Studio" (2025-11-29) treats LangChain4j and Copilot Studio together as examples of AI agents that are shipping faster than change control. The episode describes how helpful copilots can quietly become data-leaking, over-permissioned shadow admins with no audit trail. It names three recurring problems: prompt injection, over-scoped connectors and missing logs, and it argues that these combine into reportable incidents. The recommended posture, as the episode frames it, is to give an agent its own identity, avoid shared credentials, avoid tenant-wide scopes, and to treat the agent like a very dumb, very powerful user that has to be restrained by design.

This framing is useful for anyone deciding how to deploy a LangChain4j-based agent. Because an agent can call tools and retrieve data, the permissions attached to those tools define the blast radius of a successful attack. A prompt that smuggles instructions into the model's context can only do as much damage as the identity and connectors behind the agent allow. Scoping access narrowly, separating identities per agent, and keeping an audit trail are therefore design decisions to make before an agent goes live, not clean-up tasks for afterwards.

LangChain4j appears in related M365.FM content on the same theme. "Stop Microsoft Copilot Prompt Injection with Azure Logic Apps" (2026-05-05) and "Indirect Prompt Injection Security for Enterprise AI" (2026-06-16) both list the LangChain4j episode among related listening, as does "Stop Outsourcing Human Judgment to Microsoft Copilot" (2026-02-03). Together these episodes place LangChain4j inside a broader discussion about prompt injection, indirect prompt injection and the governance of enterprise AI in the Microsoft ecosystem.

The topics most closely tied to LangChain4j are therefore prompt injection, agent identity and permissions, connector scope, and logging. LangChain4j supplies the Java-side mechanics for building agents and RAG pipelines, while the episodes focus on how to constrain and observe what those agents can do. Readers evaluating the library for an enterprise setting can use the episode's checklist-style guidance on identity, credentials, scopes and auditability as a starting point for review.

langgraph.desc: LangGraph is an open-source framework from LangChain for building stateful, multi-agent LLM applications as graphs of nodes and edges, with checkpointing and human approval.

faq.a: LangGraph is an open-source framework from LangChain for building stateful, multi-agent LLM applications as graphs of nodes and edges. It includes checkpointing and human approval steps.
faq.q: What is LangGraph?

faq.a: The episode "Persistent Context Architecture for Copilot and ChatGPT" describes LangGraph as extending LangChain with graph-based workflows and memory management, while LangChain provides memory modules and retrieval mechanisms.
faq.q: How does LangGraph relate to LangChain?

faq.a: Yes. The episodes say Hosted Agents in Microsoft Foundry can manage custom code and frameworks such as LangGraph, and that the Azure AI Foundry SDK supports LangGraph alongside Semantic Kernel, AutoGen, CrewAI and LlamaIndex.
faq.q: Can LangGraph be used with Microsoft Foundry?

langgraph.long:
LangGraph is an open-source framework from LangChain for building stateful, multi-agent applications based on large language models. Instead of describing an agent as a single linear chain of calls, LangGraph models an application as a graph made of nodes and edges. The framework adds checkpointing and human approval steps, which makes it relevant for workflows where state has to be kept across steps and where a person may need to confirm an action before the process continues.

The graph approach is the central idea. Nodes represent units of work, edges define how control moves between them, and the shared state travels along the graph. This structure lets developers split a complex task into smaller parts, assign those parts to specialized agents, and observe how a request moves through the system. The M365.FM episode "Graph-Powered AI Agents: An Enterprise Architecture Guide" places LangGraph, together with AutoGen, among the frameworks that support emergent cooperative behavior in multi-agent setups. The episode describes message passing and shared memory as the means of communication between agents, and it recommends modular graphs because they improve scalability and fault tolerance. It also advises assigning roles and tasks to agents according to their skills, a pattern that maps naturally onto a graph in which each node has a defined responsibility.

LangGraph is closely tied to LangChain. According to the episode "Persistent Context Architecture for Copilot and ChatGPT", LangChain provides memory modules and retrieval mechanisms for context management, and LangGraph extends LangChain with graph-based workflows and memory management. In that discussion LangGraph is one of several tools that help integrate persistent context, next to approaches such as reflection-based memory in Claude and embeddings and knowledge graphs in ChatGPT. The episode frames these tools as building blocks for a memory architecture that supports persistent context across interactions.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, LangGraph appears as a framework that can be used alongside Azure services. The episode "Microsoft Foundry AI Apps with Jannik Reinhard [MVP]" describes several agent types in Microsoft Foundry: Prompt Agents for testing ideas quickly, Workflow Agents that automate steps with visual or YAML-based tools, and Hosted Agents that let teams manage custom code and frameworks, such as LangGraph. This means a team that has already built its agent logic as a LangGraph graph can run it as a hosted agent rather than rewriting it in another tool. The episode "Production AI Agents with Microsoft Foundry and Edgar McOchieng [MVP]" adds that the Azure AI Foundry SDK supports popular frameworks including Semantic Kernel, AutoGen, CrewAI, LangGraph and LlamaIndex, so teams can choose the tools that fit their skills. The same episode mentions open protocols such as MCP and A2A, which allow agents to connect with external systems and cooperate across platforms.

Typical decisions around LangGraph concern how much structure an agent system needs. A simple prompt-and-response scenario may not call for a graph, while a process with several specialized agents, shared state, recovery after failures, or mandatory human sign-off benefits from explicit nodes, edges, checkpoints and approval points.
