Its summary frames Loop workspaces as a space where a team can collaborate effortlessly, gathering all project-related information in one place so that teamwork is smoother and more efficient. The episode is presented with a practical focus on what the feature is, how it works, and the decisions that matter for architecture, adoption, security, governance and day-to-day operations. Those areas are worth considering when planning a rollout, since a workspace holds shared content and its membership determines who can see it.

Loop workspaces are also mentioned in other M365.FM episodes as related listening. The episode "OneNote vs Loop vs Copilot with Karinne Diamond Bessette [MVP]" lists "Microsoft Loop Workspaces - Simply Explained" among related episodes, and "Microsoft Teams Hidden Features with Josh Blalock [MVP]" and "Microsoft Mesh - Simply Explained" both point to the Loop Workspaces episode as a relevant follow-up. Together these references place workspaces within wider conversations about collaboration tools in the Microsoft ecosystem, including how Loop compares with OneNote, Planner, Lists and Microsoft To Do.

lotus-1-2-3.desc: Lotus 1-2-3 was a spreadsheet program released by Lotus Development in 1983 that dominated the 1980s and was later overtaken by Microsoft Excel.

faq.a: Lotus 1-2-3 was a spreadsheet program released by Lotus Development in 1983. It was the dominant spreadsheet program of the 1980s.
faq.q: What was Lotus 1-2-3?

faq.a: Lotus 1-2-3 was later overtaken by Microsoft Excel, which took over as the leading spreadsheet application.
faq.q: What happened to Lotus 1-2-3's market position?

faq.a: Lotus 1-2-3 was released by Lotus Development in 1983.
faq.q: Who released Lotus 1-2-3?

lotus-1-2-3.long:
Lotus 1-2-3 is a spreadsheet program that was released by Lotus Development in 1983. It became the dominant spreadsheet application of the 1980s and is widely remembered as one of the defining business software products of that decade.

Spreadsheet programs are used to organize data in rows and columns, perform calculations and keep numerical models. Lotus 1-2-3 served this purpose for business users during the period when personal computers were becoming common in offices.

In later years, Lotus 1-2-3 was overtaken by Microsoft Excel. This shift is part of the history of Microsoft's productivity software and helps explain how Excel came to occupy the position it holds in the Microsoft ecosystem today. For readers following Microsoft 365, Lotus 1-2-3 serves as historical context for the evolution of spreadsheet software.

No linked topics or M365.FM episodes are currently associated with this entry, and no official product site or documentation is listed for it.

low-code-tool.desc: A low-code tool builds apps and automations with little or no programming; M365.FM episodes cover examples such as Copilot Studio, Power Pages and AI Builder.

faq.a: A low-code tool is a tool for building apps and automations with little or no programming. Makers assemble screens, data connections and workflow steps from ready-made building blocks instead of coding everything by hand.
faq.q: What is a low-code tool?

faq.a: The episodes describe Copilot Studio, Power Pages and AI Builder as low-code tools, and also mention Microsoft 365 Copilot as a low-code option for setting up declarative agents.
faq.q: Which Microsoft products are described as low-code tools on M365.FM?

faq.a: The episode on Copilot Connectors says pro-code tools such as Visual Studio Code with the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit or the Teams SDK are available when more advanced options are needed. Another episode points developers and data scientists building custom AI models toward Azure AI Foundry.
faq.q: When might a pro-code tool be used instead of a low-code tool?

low-code-tool.long:
A low-code tool is a tool for building apps and automations with little or no programming. Instead of writing every line by hand, makers assemble screens, data connections and workflow steps from ready-made building blocks. This allows people who work close to a business process to create solutions such as internal apps, automated approvals, chatbots or simple websites without a full development project. On M365.FM, "low-code tool" is a parent category, and several Microsoft products are described under it.

The category is defined mainly by who uses the tools and how much control they need. According to the episode "Copilot Studio vs Azure AI Foundry: Which Should You Use?", a business team that wants quick results and prefers a low-code tool is a good fit for Copilot Studio, while developers and data scientists who build custom AI models are pointed toward Azure AI Foundry, which offers more advanced options. The episode lists the primary users of Copilot Studio as low-code makers, IT admins and developers. This shows that low-code tools are not limited to non-technical staff, but are designed to lower the effort needed to get a working solution.

Low-code tools also sit next to pro-code tools rather than replacing them. The episode "Connect External Business Data with Microsoft 365 Copilot Connectors" contrasts the two approaches for agents. For a declarative agent, the low-code options are Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio, while the pro-code options are Visual Studio Code with the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit. For a custom engine agent, the low-code option is Copilot Studio, while the pro-code options are Visual Studio Code with the Teams SDK or Visual Studio 2022. The episode explains that low-code tools can be used to set up connections easily, and that pro-code tools are available when more advanced options are required. It also mentions plugins and Microsoft Graph Connectors as ways to give Copilot new abilities or connect it to unique data.

Other examples appear in the M365.FM catalog. The episode "Power Pages Licensing, Capacity Limits, and Alternatives" describes Power Pages as Microsoft's low-code tool for building secure, data-driven websites. It covers how Power Pages integrates with Dataverse and the Power Platform, and why organizations use it to create customer portals, partner sites and self-service web experiences without heavy custom development. The same episode addresses licensing, capacity limits and alternative solutions, which are typical decision points when choosing a low-code platform for a public-facing site.

The episode "Use AI Form Fill in Power Apps for Faster Data Entry" refers to AI Builder as a low-code tool that applies machine learning without advanced coding skills. According to the episode, it can automate tasks such as data entry and document processing, for example extracting data from invoices and entering it into a database to save time and reduce errors. The episode also mentions pre-built models for object detection, sentiment analysis and language understanding, which support tasks like image recognition and text analysis.

For related topics, Copilot Studio is classified as a low-code tool and is also part of the Power Platform. Building blocks such as connectors, Power Fx and knowledge sources are what makers combine inside these tools. Typical decisions around the category include whether a business team can reach its goal with a low-code tool or needs the control of a pro-code approach, how licensing and capacity limits affect a planned solution, and how external business data should be connected so that it becomes available in Microsoft Search and Copilot.

machine-learning.desc: Machine learning is an approach in which a program learns patterns from examples instead of hand-written rules and uses them to make predictions.

faq.a: Machine learning is an approach where a program finds patterns in examples instead of following rules a person wrote by hand, and then uses those patterns to make predictions. The episode "Azure Machine Learning - Simply Explained" describes this as the whole idea.
faq.q: What is machine learning in simple terms?

faq.a: The episodes mention Azure Machine Learning, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Open Datasets, Azure Databricks, Power BI, Azure Data Factory, Microsoft Defender, and Microsoft Sentinel. They cover model building, data sources, MLOps security, and machine learning used for threat detection.
faq.q: Which Microsoft services are connected to machine learning in the M365.FM episodes?

faq.a: The episode "Secure MLOps in Microsoft Cloud with Martin Dimovski [MVP-MCT]" lists data leakage, adversarial attacks, prompt injection, and model extraction attempts. It recommends secure-by-design AI, layered security, and continuous monitoring.
faq.q: What security risks are mentioned for machine learning pipelines?

machine-learning.long:
Machine learning is an approach in which a program learns patterns from examples instead of following rules written by hand, and then uses those patterns to make predictions. The M365.FM episode "Azure Machine Learning - Simply Explained" puts it plainly: machine learning is a program that finds patterns in examples instead of following rules a person wrote by hand, and that is the whole idea. The shift matters because the behavior of the system comes from the data it was shown rather than from logic a developer spelled out line by line.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, machine learning shows up in several places. The "Azure Machine Learning - Simply Explained" episode covers what machine learning really is and what the Azure Machine Learning service does. Its outline walks through the workspace, data and compute, building a model, turning it into predictions, and keeping it working over time. That sequence reflects a typical lifecycle: gather and prepare data, train a model on suitable compute, turn the trained model into something that produces predictions, and then maintain it so it continues to work.

Data is a central ingredient, since a model can only learn from the examples it receives. The episode "Azure Open Datasets - Simply Explained" describes curated public datasets hosted by Microsoft in Azure that can be used to build AI, analytics, and machine learning solutions. According to the episode, these datasets are meant to reduce the time spent searching for and cleaning data, and they work with Azure Machine Learning, Azure Databricks, Power BI, Azure Data Factory, and other Azure services. The episode compares the service to a public library where the books are already organized and sitting next to the workspace.

Machine learning can also be built on analytics platforms. The episode "Build Machine Learning Models in Microsoft Fabric" describes a path from Lakehouse data to production models. It names practical building blocks: curated data layers, reproducible notebooks, MLflow tracking, a governed model registry, and batch or real-time serving. The episode also mentions a 14-day rollout plan and reliability and ROI metrics as part of its blueprint. The emphasis is on moving from experiments to models that can be shipped and governed, rather than on isolated one-off analyses.

Once models are in use, operating them becomes its own discipline. The episode "Secure MLOps in Microsoft Cloud with Martin Dimovski [MVP-MCT]" frames MLOps as the management of machine learning operations that drive business decisions. It argues that resilient MLOps in the Microsoft Cloud calls for secure-by-design AI, layered security, and continuous monitoring. The episode lists risks that AI pipelines face, including data leakage, adversarial attacks, prompt injection, and attempts at model extraction that target data and APIs. It also says Microsoft Defender can provide real-time protection, data protection, and threat detection for such systems, and that security should be part of every step rather than an add-on.

Machine learning also appears as a supporting capability inside other products. In the episode "Microsoft Sentinel - Simply Explained", Sentinel's integration with Azure services is described as enabling real-time threat detection and response that draws on AI and machine learning to identify advanced threats. Here machine learning is not something an organization builds from scratch but a technique used within a security service.

For people deciding how to approach machine learning, the episodes point to a few recurring questions: where the training data comes from and how it is prepared, which platform hosts the notebooks, tracking, and model registry, how predictions are served in batch or real time, and how the running model is monitored and secured. The fundamental idea stays the same across these topics: instead of coding the rules, the system derives them from examples.

magma.desc: Magma is a multimodal foundation model from Microsoft Research for AI agents, combining vision and language input to generate grounded actions.

faq.a: Magma is a multimodal foundation model for AI agents from Microsoft Research. It is a vision-language-action model that takes text and visual input and generates grounded actions.
faq.q: What is Magma?

faq.a: According to its description, Magma generates grounded actions such as UI navigation and robotic manipulation.
faq.q: What kinds of actions can Magma generate?

faq.a: Magma comes from Microsoft Research.
faq.q: Who develops Magma?

magma.long:
Magma is a multimodal foundation model for AI agents developed by Microsoft Research. It is described as a vision-language-action model, meaning it processes both text and visual input and produces actions based on what it perceives.

The actions Magma generates are grounded in the input it receives. Two examples given in its description are UI navigation, where an agent acts within a software interface, and robotic manipulation, where an agent controls physical movements. This places the model in the area of agentic AI, in which a system perceives its environment and acts on it rather than only producing text.

The available information about Magma is limited to this short description. No related topics, documentation links, official site or version details are listed here, and no M365.FM episodes currently cover the model. This page will be extended if further verified information becomes available.

mai-1.desc: MAI-1 is Microsoft AI's in-house large language model family, a sparse mixture-of-experts design for multi-step reasoning, offered as a cloud-hosted model.

faq.a: MAI-1 is an in-house large language model family from Microsoft AI, built as a sparse mixture-of-experts model for deep, multi-step reasoning and offered as a cloud-hosted model.
faq.q: What is MAI-1?

faq.a: The episode "Phi-4 is the Runtime. MAI-1 is the Reason." describes them as playing different roles rather than competing: Phi-4 is the fast, efficient Runtime layer and MAI-1 is the deeper Reasoning layer.
faq.q: How does MAI-1 relate to Phi-4 according to M365.FM?

faq.a: According to eWeek, MAI-1-preview was Microsoft's first proprietary foundation model, a mixture-of-experts generalist trained on about 15,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. It was announced on 28 August 2025, aimed mainly at consumers, and tested publicly on LMArena.
faq.q: What was MAI-1-preview?

mai-1.long:
MAI-1 is a family of large language models developed in-house by Microsoft AI. It is built as a sparse mixture-of-experts model and is positioned for deep, multi-step reasoning. It is offered as a cloud-hosted model rather than as a small model intended to run locally. In the M365.FM material it is described as the reasoning layer in Microsoft's wider AI architecture.

Public documentation of the first release is limited to a preview. A technology news article from eWeek covers the announcement of MAI-1-preview, described there as Microsoft's first proprietary foundation model and one that competes directly with partner OpenAI. According to that article, it is a mixture-of-experts model designed as a generalist for everyday prompts, trained in-house on about 15,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. It handles general-purpose text tasks and is aimed mainly at consumers rather than enterprises. A separate Wikipedia entry on Microsoft AI confirms that MAI-1-preview and the voice model MAI-Voice-1 were announced on 28 August 2025 as among the first in-house models, after Microsoft's products had relied mainly on OpenAI's models. The article does not describe the deep multi-step reasoning focus or a later cloud-hosted offering, so only the preview model is documented in those sources.

At launch, MAI-1-preview was in public testing on the LMArena community evaluation forum, and testers could apply for early API access. Microsoft said it would begin collecting user feedback on certain text-generation uses of the model inside Copilot within weeks. These details show how the model was introduced: as a preview, evaluated by the public and feeding into Copilot, not as a finished enterprise standard.

The M365.FM episodes place MAI-1 in a broader strategic frame. The episode "Phi-4 is the Runtime. MAI-1 is the Reason." argues that Microsoft's AI strategy becomes easier to understand once the question shifts away from which model is better. According to the episode, asking whether MAI-1 can beat Phi-4, whether Phi-4 is more efficient, or which model should become the enterprise standard assumes that both models compete for the same job, and the episode says they do not. It describes Microsoft as building toward an architecture in which different forms of intelligence perform different roles: Phi-4 represents the fast, efficient Runtime layer, and MAI-1 represents the deeper Reasoning layer.

The same framing appears in the episode "The PCF Blueprint: Architecture Over UI", whose excerpt repeats the argument that organizations should stop selecting a winner and instead understand how the layers fit together. For decision-makers, the practical point drawn from these episodes is that model choice is treated as an architectural question about which layer handles which kind of work, with MAI-1 assigned to the reasoning-heavy part and Phi-4 to the fast runtime part.

When reading about MAI-1, it helps to separate two things: the documented preview model reported in the news, and the broader description of MAI-1 as a reasoning-oriented, cloud-hosted family. The first is a generalist text model announced in 2025 with consumer focus and Copilot testing. The second is the positioning described in the glossary entry and discussed in the episodes. Details such as pricing, versions, availability by region or specific enterprise features are not stated in the available material and are therefore not covered here.

mail-flow-rule.desc: A mail flow rule, also called a transport rule, is an Exchange Online rule that checks messages in transit against conditions and exceptions and applies actions.

faq.a: A mail flow rule, also called a transport rule, is an organization-wide Exchange Online rule that checks messages in transit against conditions and exceptions and applies actions before delivery.
faq.q: What is a mail flow rule?

faq.a: Rules are processed in priority order, with the top rule evaluated first. A setting can also stop the processing of further rules.
faq.q: In what order are mail flow rules processed?

faq.a: They can be managed in the Exchange admin center or with Exchange Online PowerShell, and rules created in the admin center start out disabled. The documentation describes test modes, with or without policy tips, and advises testing each rule and the combination of rules thoroughly.
faq.q: How are mail flow rules created and tested?

mail-flow-rule.long:
A mail flow rule, also known as a transport rule, is an organization-wide rule in Exchange Online. It inspects messages as they pass through the organization and, when certain conditions match, applies an action before the message is delivered. The M365.FM episode "Mail Flow Rules - Simply Explained" describes this as a layer of rules that every email in a company passes through, sitting between the send button and the inbox, usually without users ever seeing it.

According to the Microsoft Learn documentation, a rule consists of conditions, actions and optional exceptions. The conditions define which messages the rule applies to, and the exceptions carve out messages that should be left alone. The actions describe what happens to a matching message. Examples named in the documentation include prepending text to the subject, forwarding a message for approval, sending a policy tip to the sender and generating an incident report. The episode frames the logic of a rule around three questions that every rule asks, followed by what happens when a rule fires.

Beyond conditions, actions and exceptions, a rule has several settings. The rule mode can be set to enforce the rule or to test it, with or without policy tips. A severity value is available, but it only filters reports and does not change how the rule behaves. A time window can limit when the rule is active, and a setting can stop the processing of further rules. Another choice determines whether the sender address is matched in the message header, in the envelope or in both. Rules are processed in priority order, and the rule at the top of the list is evaluated first, so the order of rules matters when several of them could apply to the same message.

Administrators can manage mail flow rules in the Exchange admin center or with Exchange Online PowerShell. The documentation notes that rules created in the admin center start out disabled, so a new rule has to be enabled before it takes effect. The documentation includes an example that tags external mail sent to a distribution group, which shows a typical use: marking or handling messages based on where they come from and where they are going.

The episode covers the jobs people commonly give these rules, the limits that are rarely mentioned up front, and the mistakes beginners make. It also places mail flow rules within the wider context of Microsoft 365 and Azure. A recurring theme in both the episode and the documentation is testing. The documentation advises testing each rule and the combination of rules thoroughly, and points out that changes can take a while to apply and that report data can lag. The episode likewise includes a section on testing a rule before it affects real mail, which fits the availability of test modes in the rule settings.

In practice, decisions around mail flow rules include how specific the conditions should be, which exceptions are needed, where a rule belongs in the priority order, and whether it should first run in a test mode before being enforced. Because a rule acts on messages in transit across the whole organization, a poorly scoped or badly ordered rule can affect more mail than intended, which is why the sources stress testing the rule on its own and in combination with the other rules already in place.

main-account.desc: A main account in Dynamics 365 Finance is the ledger account that records what an amount relates to, such as cash, sales revenue or rent expense.

faq.a: A main account is a record in the chart of accounts that states what a ledger amount relates to, for example cash, sales revenue or rent expense. Every amount in the general ledger is assigned to a main account.
faq.q: What is a main account in Dynamics 365 Finance?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, the types include profit and loss, revenue and expense accounts as posting accounts, balance sheet, asset, liability and equity accounts as transaction accounts, total accounts that aggregate account intervals, and a reporting type used only for financial statement reporting in Brazil.
faq.q: What main account types exist?

faq.a: The episodes explain that financial statements do not create numbers but organize and summarize balances already recorded in the ledger. Main accounts are grouped into categories so that assets, liabilities and equity appear on the balance sheet and revenue and expenses feed the income statement.
faq.q: How do main accounts relate to financial statements?

main-account.long:
A main account in Dynamics 365 Finance is a record in the chart of accounts that states what a posted amount relates to financially. Cash, sales revenue, rent expense, wages, accounts receivable, accounts payable, loans and taxes can each have their own main accounts. Every amount in the general ledger is assigned to a main account that represents what happened financially, which makes the main account the basic building block of ledger data.

The main accounts together form the chart of accounts, which provides the structure used to organize financial transactions. The episode "Dynamics 365 General Ledger - Simply Explained" describes the chart of accounts as a financial filing cabinet in which each main account represents a specific category. Examples named there include cash, inventory, accounts payable, sales revenue and rent expense. The same episode says that these accounts are grouped into categories used for financial statements: assets, liabilities and equity appear on the balance sheet, while revenue and expenses contribute to the income statement. Correct account structures are therefore presented as the foundation for reliable reporting.

Each main account has a main account type, chosen when the account is created, and this type determines how the account is used. According to the Microsoft Learn page on main account types, the available types fall into several groups. Profit and loss, revenue and expense accounts are posting accounts that record revenue and expenses, and their sum determines the year-end result. Balance sheet, asset, liability and equity accounts are transaction accounts that record what a legal entity owns or owes. Total accounts aggregate account intervals and show the total of group balances. A reporting type exists that is used only for financial statement reporting in Brazil.

Some practical details come from the documentation. After the total type is selected, the Totals option on the General tab is opened to define the account intervals that the total account adds up. Total accounts cannot be suspended, so the documentation suggests using the Active from and Active to dates to simulate suspension. Main accounts can also be grouped into main account categories, which are used for reporting, and the documentation links to a separate article on setting them up.

The episode "Dynamics 365 Financial Reporting - Simply Explained" places main accounts at the start of the reporting process. It states that financial reporting starts with correctly structured accounting data. The general ledger contains the financial impact of customer invoices, supplier bills, payroll, bank payments, inventory adjustments and other business transactions, and each of these amounts is assigned to a main account. According to the episode, financial statements do not create these numbers; they organize and summarize balances that already exist in the ledger. The episode also introduces main account types and categories as the broad accounting classifications behind that summarizing.

In practice, decisions around main accounts concern which accounts a legal entity needs, which type each account should have, and how accounts are grouped into categories so that the balance sheet and income statement can be built from them. Because the type controls whether an account behaves as a posting account, a transaction account or a total, choosing it correctly when the account is created matters for how balances are accumulated and reported.

mainframe-computer.desc: A mainframe computer is a large, centralized computer shared by many users through terminals, with workloads queued and scheduled on a single host.

faq.a: A mainframe computer is a large, centralized computer shared by many users through terminals. Workloads are queued and scheduled on one host.
faq.q: What is a mainframe computer?

faq.a: Users connect through terminals that give access to the central host. The host handles the processing and schedules the submitted workloads.
faq.q: How do users access a mainframe?

mainframe-computer.long:
A mainframe computer is a large, centralized computer that many users share through terminals. Rather than each user running software on a personal machine, work is submitted to one host, where workloads are queued and scheduled.

The defining characteristic is centralization. Processing, storage and job scheduling sit on the central host, while terminals act as access points for the people who use it. This contrasts with distributed models, in which computing is spread across many separate devices or servers.

In discussions of the Microsoft ecosystem, the mainframe is often used as a reference point for how centralized, shared computing differs from later client-server and cloud approaches. Understanding the mainframe model helps explain concepts such as scheduled workloads, shared resources and terminal-based access.

No specific M365.FM episodes or related topics are linked to this entry at present.

managed-environments.desc: Managed Environments is a Power Platform governance suite that gives admins usage insights, sharing limits and solution checking to control environments at scale.

faq.a: Managed Environments is a suite of premium Power Platform capabilities that lets admins govern environments at scale, for example with usage insights, sharing limits and solution checking.
faq.q: What is Managed Environments in the Power Platform?

faq.a: According to the episode with Michael Roth, DLP policies operate in the context of environments and should be designed together with the environment strategy. Managed Environments and advanced connector policies can add granularity, but a single policy is not a complete governance program.
faq.q: How do Managed Environments relate to DLP policies?

faq.a: The episode "Power Platform Managed Environments Need Pro-Dev Practices" argues that organizations misunderstand what the feature solves, so governance can slow work without enabling delivery, with citizen and professional developers working separately.
faq.q: Why can Managed Environments fall short in practice?

managed-environments.long:
Managed Environments is a suite of premium Power Platform capabilities that lets administrators govern environments at scale. It is described as a governance layer meant to bring control, visibility and order to low-code environments. Typical capabilities named in the product description include usage insights, limits on how apps and resources can be shared, and solution checking. Official documentation for the feature is published on Microsoft Learn under the Power Platform admin section.

In practice, Managed Environments is applied to individual Power Platform environments. An environment is the container in which apps, flows, and Dataverse data live, and the episode "Power Platform Environments - Simply Explained" covers this in plain terms: what an environment actually is, the different environment types, the single Dataverse database per environment, who gets access and what they can touch, and environment groups described as folders for environments. In that episode Managed Environments is presented as "the premium switch", a setting turned on for an environment to add extra governance on top of the basic environment model. The same episode also touches on moving work safely with application lifecycle management and solutions, data policies as guardrails, and ways to tell which environment one is working in.

Managed Environments does not stand alone in a governance program. The episode "Power Platform Governance Without Killing Innovation: Security, DLP, Environments & Citizen Development with Michael Roth [MVP]" places it next to Data Loss Prevention policies. According to that episode, DLP policies operate in the context of environments, so they should be designed together with the environment strategy. Managed Environments and advanced connector policies can provide additional granularity, but the episode stresses that enabling a policy once does not constitute a complete governance program. The episode names four foundations that organizations should understand: tenant security settings, environment architecture, Data Loss Prevention policies, and clearly defined roles and responsibilities around citizen development.

The episode "Power Platform Managed Environments Need Pro-Dev Practices" takes a critical view. It argues that Managed Environments often fail to deliver on their promise because organizations misunderstand what they actually solve. As introduced there, they are meant to bring control and visibility to low-code environments, but in practice they can slow work down without enabling real delivery. The core problem described is that citizen developers are limited by governance while professional developers are not properly integrated into the platform, so the two groups work separately. The outcome the episode describes is neither agility nor quality. Its title points toward combining Managed Environments with professional development practices rather than relying on the feature alone.

The "Power Automate - Simply Explained" episode mentions Managed Environments in the context of data management, describing it as a feature that keeps data secure while providing visibility and control with less effort. In that episode it appears alongside automation across Excel, OneDrive and Teams and document processing built on Power Automate, Power Apps and Microsoft Dataverse.

Taken together, the episodes frame several decisions that surround Managed Environments: which environments warrant the premium governance switch, how environment groups are organized, how DLP and connector policies are aligned with the environment layout, and how both citizen developers and professional developers are supported so that governance enables delivery instead of blocking it. The sources describe the capability set only at a high level, so specific licensing terms, configuration steps and limits should be checked in the official Microsoft Learn documentation.

managed-identity.desc: A managed identity gives an Azure application or resource an identity whose credentials Azure creates and rotates, so no secret sits in code or configuration.

faq.a: It removes the need to store secrets such as passwords, API keys, certificates or connection strings in code or configuration files. Azure creates and rotates the credentials automatically.
faq.q: What problem does a managed identity solve?

faq.a: They appear in Azure Automation accounts and runbooks, in Azure File Sync, and as one of the authentication flows for PowerShell scripts that call Microsoft Graph.
faq.q: Where do the M365.FM episodes use managed identities?

faq.a: The episode on Azure automation recommends assigning only the roles and permissions each task needs, following the principle of least privilege.
faq.q: How should permissions be handled for a managed identity?

managed-identity.long:
A managed identity is an identity for an application or Azure resource whose credentials Azure creates and rotates automatically. The practical effect is that no secret, password, API key or connection string has to be stored in code or configuration files. Instead of asking a service "what do you have", an identity-based model asks "who are you", which is how the episode "Managed Identities - Simply Explained" frames the shift in thinking.

The concept addresses a familiar weakness of possession-based credentials. Certificates, SAS tokens, static API keys and passwords all work on the principle that whoever holds the secret is treated as the owner of the identity. Such secrets tend to spread into scripts, backups, repositories and logs, and they can expire without notice. The episode "Migrate Azure File Sync to Managed Identity" describes Azure File Sync's older authentication, built on local X.509 certificates and SAS tokens, in exactly these terms, and presents Managed Identity as the modern replacement in which each Storage Sync Service receives its own identity.

The comparison table in "Managed Identities - Simply Explained" shows the same pattern across scenarios. An application that previously reached a database with a static API key, a static password or a connection string for a message queue instead authenticates through a managed identity, a workload identity or a service account, so that no password, API key or connection string is needed. The access path stays the same, but the stored secret disappears from it.

Managed identities are widely used in automation. The episode "Secure Azure Automation with Ahmed Uzejnovic [MVP]" explains that an Azure Automation account can have a system-assigned managed identity enabled. This identity lets the automation reach resources protected by Azure Entra ID, such as Azure Key Vault. The episode stresses assigning only the roles and permissions each task requires, in line with the principle of least privilege, and names service principals as an alternative authentication method for the same account.

The episode "PowerShell Automation for Azure and Microsoft 365 with Matthew Dowst [MVP]" applies the idea to runbooks. A runbook in an Azure Automation account can start an Azure virtual machine with the Start-AzVM cmdlet, and the episode recommends using managed identity for secure authentication in the runbook rather than embedding credentials.

In script-based work against Microsoft 365, the episode "Use Managed Identity with PowerShell for Microsoft Graph" treats managed identity as one of three real-world authentication flows alongside device code and client credentials with certificates. It describes an API-first approach with REST calls to Microsoft Graph following a "token, headers, REST call" pattern, and ties access to the principle of least privilege. The choice between flows is a design decision: interactive scenarios, certificate-based app identities and Azure-hosted workloads each suit a different flow, and managed identity fits cases where the code runs on an Azure resource that can hold the identity.

Taken together, the episodes position managed identity as a way to remove stored secrets, reduce silent credential expiry and limit what a leaked credential could do, while keeping permissions narrow through role assignment. Typical decisions around it include whether to use a system-assigned identity tied to one resource, which roles to grant, and whether an existing certificate or SAS-based setup should be migrated.

managed-service-provider.desc: A managed service provider (MSP) is an outside company hired to run and manage a business's IT or cloud environment, including Microsoft 365, on its behalf.

faq.a: A managed service provider is an outside company that a business hires to run and manage its IT or cloud environment on its behalf.
faq.q: What is a managed service provider (MSP)?

faq.a: The episodes mention Intune, Microsoft Defender and Entra ID for securing MSP environments, as well as the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK for multi-tenant automation and license optimization.
faq.q: Which Microsoft tools are discussed in connection with MSPs on M365.FM?

faq.a: The episode "5 High-Margin Microsoft 365 Business Models" describes a healthcare IT MSP that focused on SharePoint consulting and, according to the episode, added $50,000 per month in revenue by optimizing clients' SharePoint environments.
faq.q: How can an MSP build a business around Microsoft 365?

managed-service-provider.long:
A managed service provider (MSP) is an outside company that a business hires to run and manage its IT or cloud environment on its behalf. Instead of staffing every technical function internally, an organization hands day-to-day operation of systems, users and security to a specialist provider. In the Microsoft ecosystem, this typically means managing Microsoft 365 tenants, identities, devices and security tooling for one or many client organizations.

Because an MSP serves several clients, its work is shaped by scale and repeatability. The M365.FM episode "Building a Secure Microsoft-First MSP: Intune, Defender & Entra ID at Scale with Albin Klinaku [MVP]" looks at this from a security angle. It describes Entra ID as playing a vital role in securing identities within MSP environments, offering protection against common attack vectors and treating identity as the new perimeter. The episode also notes that a single set of credentials lets employees reach their applications, which reduces password fatigue and supports secure remote work and collaboration. It further stresses that Microsoft Defender should remain a vital part of the security framework so that comprehensive protection is provided for clients. Intune is named in the episode title as part of the same Microsoft-first approach.

Automation is another recurring theme for MSPs. The episode "Run Your Full Stack Locally with .NET Aspire" includes show notes on PowerShell for Microsoft 365 administration. It says the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK is replacing many legacy modules (MSOnline, AzureAD, ExchangeOnline) and exposes unified Graph API capabilities, enabling richer automation and reporting. According to the episode, cross-tenant and delegated-administrator operations can be performed via PowerShell, which makes MSP automation and multi-tenant orchestration more powerful than the graphical admin interface allows. The same notes describe large-scale license optimization: detecting unused or underused seats, reassigning or revoking licenses automatically, and running scheduled scripts to save money. The episode also mentions that Microsoft 365 Cloud Shell and the Admin Center's in-browser PowerShell can be used to run management scripts.

MSPs are also discussed as a business model, not only a technical role. The episode "5 High-Margin Microsoft 365 Business Models" presents a case study of a healthcare IT MSP that transformed its business through Microsoft 365 consulting. According to the episode, this MSP focused on SharePoint consulting, optimized its clients' SharePoint environments, and increased revenue by an additional $50,000 per month. The episode attributes this to helping healthcare organizations streamline document management and improve collaboration. It also describes Teams and SharePoint as the backbone of many Microsoft 365 consulting solutions, supporting a connected and efficient enterprise environment.

Taken together, the episodes show typical decisions around the MSP concept: how to secure identities and devices across many client tenants, how to use scripting and the Graph-based tooling for multi-tenant administration and license management, and how to turn Microsoft 365 expertise into a repeatable service offering. For a client organization, hiring an MSP means shifting operational responsibility for the IT or cloud environment to an external company, while the provider's choices about identity protection, endpoint management and automation determine how that environment is secured and run.

managed-solution.desc: Managed and unmanaged solutions are the two Power Platform solution modes: an editable working copy for development and a locked copy for deployment.

faq.a: An unmanaged solution is the editable working copy used in development and is the source of the platform's assets. A managed solution is the locked copy exported for deployment to test, UAT, SIT and production, and its components cannot be edited directly.
faq.q: What is the difference between a managed and an unmanaged solution?

faq.a: No. According to the documentation notes, a managed solution cannot be imported into the same environment that holds the original unmanaged solution, so testing requires a separate environment. Managed solutions are meant for downstream environments, not the development environment.
faq.q: Can a managed solution be imported into the environment where it was developed?

faq.a: Deleting an unmanaged solution removes only the container, and the customizations stay active in the default solution. Deleting a managed solution removes its customizations and can cause data loss in the custom tables and columns it contains.
faq.q: What happens when a managed or unmanaged solution is deleted?

managed-solution.long:
Managed and unmanaged solutions are the two modes in which a Power Platform solution exists. An unmanaged solution is the editable working copy used in development environments, while a managed solution is the locked copy that is exported and deployed to test and production environments. The distinction shapes how customizations are built, moved between environments, maintained and removed, which makes it a basic concept for anyone working with application lifecycle management (ALM) on Power Platform and Dynamics 365.

An unmanaged solution is used in development and is regarded as the source of the platform's assets. It can be exported either as unmanaged or as managed. Exported unmanaged versions should be kept in source control. Unmanaged solutions are also described as the form used for development and testing, where changes can be made as needed. Deleting an unmanaged solution removes only the container: the customizations it held stay active as part of the default solution. In other words, removing the unmanaged wrapper does not remove the components themselves.

A managed solution is meant for deployment to test, UAT, SIT and production environments, but not to the development environment in which the solution was built. As an ALM practice, a managed solution is produced by exporting an unmanaged solution, and it is treated as a build artifact rather than something edited by hand. Components cannot be edited directly inside a managed solution. If a managed component is changed anyway, this creates a dependency that blocks uninstalling the managed solution. A managed solution also cannot be exported again, and it cannot be imported into the same environment that holds the original unmanaged solution, so testing a managed build requires a separate environment.

Removal behaves differently as well. Deleting a managed solution removes the customizations it contains, and this can cause data loss in the custom tables and columns that are part of the solution. For that reason, uninstalling a managed solution is a decision that needs care, particularly in production.

In practice the two modes map onto a simple flow. Customizations are created and changed in an unmanaged solution in a development environment. When they are ready to move, the solution is exported as managed and imported into the downstream environments. This keeps non-development environments stable, because the imported components cannot be modified there, and it keeps the editable source in one place where it can be versioned.

The M365.FM episode "Deploy Dynamics 365 Customizations with ALM Pipelines" covers this in the context of solution deployment strategy for Dynamics 365. The episode says managed solutions are designed for production environments and cannot be modified after import, which helps keep a system clean and stable. It describes unmanaged solutions as intended for development and testing, where changes can be made as needed. Its guidance is that customizations moving from non-production to production should be exported as managed solutions. The episode places this choice at the start of a deployment and ties it to hybrid ALM pipelines for full Dynamics 365 implementations.

When planning a deployment, the main decisions are therefore which environment holds the unmanaged source, where exported unmanaged versions are stored in source control, which separate environment is used to test the managed build, and how removal of a managed solution is handled given the possible loss of data in custom tables and columns.

managing-director.desc: Managing director is a senior executive role that runs a company, answers for strategy, results and compliance, and corresponds to the German Geschäftsführer.

faq.a: A managing director runs a company as its legal and executive head and is responsible for strategy, results and compliance. The role is treated as another name for the chief executive officer, who implements the board's targets and oversees day-to-day operations.
faq.q: What does a managing director do?

faq.a: The entity description states that managing director corresponds to the German Geschäftsführer, and both Geschäftsführer and Geschäftsführerin are listed as aliases. The reference material used for this page does not cover German law or the title Geschäftsführer in detail.
faq.q: Is a managing director the same as a Geschäftsführer?

faq.a: The reference material treats managing director as another name for the chief executive officer. In the United Kingdom it is often used in business and the charity sector instead of CEO, while in the United States CEO is the usual business term.
faq.q: How is managing director different from CEO?

managing-director.long:
Managing director is the title of the person who runs a company as its legal and executive head. The role carries responsibility for the company's strategy, its results and its compliance with applicable rules. In German-speaking contexts the title corresponds to Geschäftsführer or Geschäftsführerin, and the English form Managing Director is used as an alias for the same position. The term appears on M365.FM as a job entity, relevant wherever Microsoft-ecosystem topics reach the level of company leadership.

In general business language, the managing director is treated as another name for the chief executive officer, the top-ranking officer who manages a company or a nonprofit organization. According to the reference material used for this page, such an officer reports to the board of directors, leads strategy and key policy decisions, and implements the targets the board sets. The role also covers oversight of day-to-day operations such as marketing, finance and human resources, reporting on the company's status to the board, motivating staff, driving change, and communicating with the press, the public and employees. Ultimately, the person is accountable for business decisions.

Usage of the title differs by country. In the United Kingdom, managing director is often used in business and in the charity sector instead of CEO. Charities tend to avoid the word director for senior staff, in order to prevent confusion with unpaid trustees. In the United States, CEO is the usual business term, while executive director is used mainly in not-for-profit organizations, where the legal duties are distinct. In countries with a dual board structure, an executive board led by the CEO exists alongside a separate supervisory board with its own chair. The reference material does not discuss Germany or the specific title Geschäftsführer, so the mapping between the two terms rests on the short description of this entity rather than on a detailed legal comparison.

For readers working with Microsoft 365, Power BI, Fabric or related platforms, the managing director typically matters as the accountable decision-maker. Questions about strategy, compliance and results, which define the role, are the same questions that arise when an organization chooses how to govern data, security and identity. Because the role is ultimately accountable for business decisions, topics such as data governance and security posture often reach this level even when the technical work is done by specialists.

The M365.FM episode "Fix Duplicate Customer Identity in Power BI and Fabric" touches the term only indirectly. Its excerpt mentions Rajan Behal, described as an Advisory Managing Director at KPMG LLP, who points out that as organizations become more interconnected and software-driven, managing identities, especially non-human ones, becomes vital for security and smooth operations. The episode uses this to frame identity chaos, meaning situations in which data identities cannot be clearly identified or managed across systems, leading to multiple, changing or unclear identities that cause confusion and errors. In this context, managing director appears as a job title of an advisor quoted in the discussion, not as the subject of the episode. No further episode material on the role itself is available.

manufacturing.desc: Manufacturing is the industry that turns raw materials and components into physical goods in factories and workshops; M365.FM covers its data and AI topics.

faq.a: Manufacturing is the industry that turns raw materials and components into physical goods in factories and workshops. M365.FM covers it mainly through data, IT and AI topics such as unifying ERP, MES and shop floor data.
faq.q: What does manufacturing mean in the context of M365.FM?

faq.a: The episode "What Is a PPR Knowledge Graph — and Why Manufacturing AI Needs One" says factory AI can read large amounts of data but often lacks an understanding of the plant. A Product-Process-Resource graph is presented as a way to supply that missing connection between product, process and resource.
faq.q: Why do the episodes say manufacturing AI needs a knowledge graph?

faq.a: The episodes mention Microsoft Fabric, including OneLake, and Azure IoT Operations, in combination with protocols such as MQTT and OPC UA. They also cover FinOps principles for controlling cloud cost in industrial workloads.
faq.q: Which Microsoft technologies appear in the manufacturing episodes?

manufacturing.long:
Manufacturing is the industry that turns raw materials and components into physical goods, from single parts to series production, in factories and workshops. The term is also known under the aliases Fertigungsindustrie, Produktion and Fertigung. On M365.FM, the topic appears mainly from a data, IT and AI perspective: how information from plants, lines and machines can be brought together, understood and used in the Microsoft ecosystem.

A recurring theme in the episodes is that manufacturing data is spread across different systems. The episode "Microsoft Fabric for Manufacturing: One Source of Truth From ERP, MES and the Shop Floor" states that ERP, MES and shop floor data live in separate systems and that a single source of truth takes design. It discusses using Microsoft Fabric to unify those sources, covering OneLake, modeling and governance, and describes how to structure the platform around manufacturing use cases. The audience named for it includes data and analytics leads.

The episode "MQTT and OPC UA in Microsoft Manufacturing: Azure IoT Operations + Fabric Architecture" addresses why modern factories can still rely on manual exports and guesswork even when ERP, MES and Azure systems are in place. According to the episode, the core problem is a lack of trust in manufacturing data. It sets MQTT and OPC UA side by side and looks at the architecture that combines Azure IoT Operations with Fabric, with a focus on data that is disconnected from the plant floor.

Context for AI is the second major thread. The episode "What Is a PPR Knowledge Graph — and Why Manufacturing AI Needs One" says factory AI can read large amounts of data but often lacks an understanding of the actual plant environment. In its description, ERP systems know the orders and MES systems know the operations, but nothing automatically explains how a product, process and resource (PPR) came together at a given moment. The episode names this missing connection as the point where promising AI initiatives lose their footing, and presents a Product-Process-Resource knowledge graph as the way to supply it.

A related episode, "Knowledge Graphs for Manufacturing: Giving AI the Context of Your Factory", continues the idea. It states that AI answers improve when the AI understands the context of the factory, and discusses modeling equipment, processes and relationships in a graph and linking that graph to AI. It is aimed at data architects, AI teams and manufacturing engineers.

Cost is the third theme. In "FinOps for Manufacturing IT: Controlling Cloud Cost for Industrial Workloads", the episode argues that industrial workloads in the cloud need cost visibility that fits plants, lines and data volumes. It covers applying FinOps principles in manufacturing IT, including tagging, allocation, forecasting and ownership, with the aim of controlling cloud cost without slowing delivery. The stated audience includes IT managers and cloud architects.

Taken together, the episodes treat manufacturing as an industry where decisions often concern how to connect existing systems rather than replace them: unifying ERP, MES and shop floor data, choosing protocols such as MQTT and OPC UA for moving machine data, adding relationship-based context for AI, and keeping cloud spending traceable to plants and lines. The sources provided do not give further detail on specific products beyond the ones named in the episodes, so this page limits itself to what those episodes describe.

manufacturing-execution-system.desc: A manufacturing execution system (MES) is shop-floor software that records production activity against work orders and operations, such as material consumed at a station.

faq.a: An MES tracks and documents how raw materials become finished goods, recording production activity against work orders and operations, such as the actual material consumed at a station. It gives decision makers a view of current plant-floor conditions and produces an as-built record.
faq.q: What does a manufacturing execution system (MES) do?

faq.a: ANSI/ISA-95 places MES at Level 3, between ERP at Level 4 and process control at Levels 0 to 2. Part 3 of the standard divides Level 3 into production, quality, logistics and maintenance.
faq.q: Where does an MES fit in the ISA-95 model?

faq.a: It exchanges work instructions and set points with SCADA, PLC and DCS systems, often via OPC-UA, and exchanges data with ERP via B2MML. The M365.FM episode "Connect ERP, MES, and IoT — Without Replacing Anything" discusses aligning MES, ERP and IoT views of the same production situation.
faq.q: How does an MES connect to other systems?

manufacturing-execution-system.long:
A manufacturing execution system (MES) is shop-floor software that records production activity against work orders and operations, for example the actual material consumed at a station. More broadly, manufacturing execution systems are computerized systems that track and document how raw materials become finished goods. They give decision makers a view of current plant-floor conditions and produce an as-built record of the process, its data and its outcomes. That record is especially valuable in regulated industries such as food and pharmaceuticals.

In the ANSI/ISA-95 model, MES sits at Level 3, between enterprise resource planning (ERP) at Level 4 and process control at Levels 0 to 2. Part 3 of the standard splits Level 3 into production, quality, logistics and maintenance. This placement explains the role of an MES: it translates plans from the business layer into executable work on the plant floor and reports what actually happened back upward. The Manufacturing Execution System (MES) therefore describes operations as they are performed, while ERP describes them as they were planned and accounted for.

Typical MES functions include product definition management (master data, bills of material and recipes), resource management, scheduling of work orders received from ERP or planning systems, dispatching to work centers, execution reporting, data collection, performance analysis such as overall equipment effectiveness, and track and trace of lots and orders. The MESA association defined 11 functions in total. Cited benefits include less waste, rework and scrap, more accurate cost capture, less downtime, paperless workflows and lower inventory.

An MES does not work in isolation. It exchanges work instructions and set points with SCADA, PLC and DCS systems, often via OPC-UA, and it exchanges data with ERP via B2MML. Because of these interfaces, decisions around an MES usually concern integration as much as functionality: which system owns master data, how work orders flow down to the floor, how execution data flows back, and how equipment-level signals are captured.

The M365.FM episode "Connect ERP, MES, and IoT — Without Replacing Anything" (2026-10-22) approaches the topic from the point of view of a production line under pressure. The episode describes a familiar, reactive scramble in the middle of a shift: operators call maintenance, supervisors check the master production schedule, and team members cross-reference several digital systems. Someone opens the MES, someone else queries the ERP platform, and a new dashboard appears because each crisis seems to call for another screen. The episode calls this a multi-system disconnect: although several systems are running, they rarely describe the same operational situation. Each system holds its own view of the same event, and people on the floor are left to reconcile them manually.

Seen this way, the MES is one of several data sources that have to be aligned rather than a stand-alone answer. The episode's framing, connecting ERP, MES and IoT without replacing anything, points to integration of existing systems as the way to get a shared picture of production. For anyone evaluating or documenting an MES, the practical questions are therefore which work orders and operations it records, what consumption and quality data it captures at each station, how that data reaches ERP and equipment-level systems, and how the resulting as-built record is used for traceability, performance analysis and compliance.

mapi.desc: MAPI (Messaging Application Programming Interface) is a Microsoft messaging API and data model behind Exchange and Outlook, whose legacy structures still shape development.

faq.a: MAPI (Messaging Application Programming Interface) is a proprietary Microsoft messaging API and data model underlying Exchange and Outlook. Microsoft Learn describes it as providing the messaging architecture for Outlook 2013 and Outlook 2016.
faq.q: What is MAPI?

faq.a: Applications and transports use MAPI to work with email data, to create messages and the folders that hold them, and to receive notifications when MAPI-related data changes.
faq.q: What can applications do with MAPI?

faq.a: The episode "Migrate Exchange Web Services to Microsoft Graph with Glen Scales [MVP]" says that creating mail from raw MIME with MAPI extended properties can require rethinking workflows when moving to Graph.
faq.q: Why does MAPI come up in Exchange Web Services to Microsoft Graph migrations?

mapi.long:
MAPI, short for Messaging Application Programming Interface, is a proprietary Microsoft messaging API and data model that underlies Exchange and Outlook. Its legacy data structures still influence how developers work with Exchange data today, even when they use newer interfaces to reach it. The term is used both for the programming interface itself and for the way mailbox content is modeled beneath it.

According to the Microsoft Learn reference, MAPI is the Microsoft Outlook Messaging API and provides the messaging architecture for Outlook 2013 and Outlook 2016. It supplies interfaces, functions and data types that developers use to build Outlook messaging applications. Applications and transports use MAPI to work with email data, to create messages and the folders that hold them, and to receive notifications when MAPI-related data changes. The reference page applies only to Outlook 2013 and Outlook 2016 and does not list individual interfaces, functions or code examples.

The Microsoft Learn reference is organized into four parts: a getting-started overview, sample applications, concept guides for understanding and programming with MAPI, and the reference for its programming elements. For developers who are new to the area, the page points to a separate article on selecting the right API or technology for developing Outlook solutions. That guidance reflects a common decision: MAPI is one option among several, and the choice depends on the type of solution being built.

In practice, MAPI matters most when existing code has to be moved to newer technologies. The M365.FM episode "Migrate Exchange Web Services to Microsoft Graph with Glen Scales [MVP]" touches on this. The episode notes that some workflows need special attention when moving from Exchange Web Services to Microsoft Graph, especially those involving archive mailboxes or public folders. It also says that creating mail from raw MIME with MAPI extended properties can require rethinking a workflow, because that approach does not carry over unchanged. Advanced delta semantics are listed as another difference between EWS and Graph that may require rework of parts of the code.

The episode presents these points as a table of migration challenges: archive mailbox access and some mailbox import and export workflows require special attention, public folder scenarios need engagement with Microsoft for dependencies, and advanced delta semantics differ between the two APIs. MAPI extended properties appear in this list because they are one of the places where the older data model leaks into application code, so teams that depend on them have to review those parts of a migration separately.

For administrators and developers, the practical consequence is that knowledge of MAPI remains relevant for reading older Exchange and Outlook code, for understanding how messages, folders and notifications are structured, and for assessing the effort of a move to Microsoft Graph. Because the available sources describe MAPI mainly in the context of Outlook 2013 and Outlook 2016 and in the context of EWS-to-Graph migration, anyone planning work should confirm current support and requirements in the official documentation for the specific scenario.

mapping-data-flows.desc: Mapping data flows are visually designed, no-code data transformations in Azure Data Factory that run as pipeline activities on Spark clusters managed by the service.

faq.a: They are visually designed data transformations that require no code. The service translates the design and runs it on scaled-out Apache Spark clusters that it manages.
faq.q: What are mapping data flows in Azure Data Factory?

faq.a: It runs as an activity inside a pipeline, where the integration runtime and parameter values are selected. This lets it use the existing scheduling, control flow and monitoring features of pipelines.
faq.q: How does a mapping data flow run?

faq.a: The data preview works only when debug mode is switched on. The inspect tab shows no metadata when the source has no defined schema, which is typical for schema drift.
faq.q: Why is the data preview or metadata sometimes not shown?

mapping-data-flows.long:
Mapping data flows are visually designed data transformations in Azure Data Factory. According to Microsoft Learn, the page also applies to Azure Synapse Analytics. They let developers build transformation logic without writing code. The service takes care of code translation, path optimization and the execution of the data flow jobs, which run on scaled-out Apache Spark clusters that the service manages.

A mapping data flow does not run on its own. It is executed as an activity inside a pipeline. In that pipeline activity, the integration runtime and the parameter values are chosen. Because of this, a data flow can use the scheduling, control flow and monitoring features that already exist for Azure Data Factory pipelines, rather than needing a separate mechanism for orchestration.

The authoring experience is built around a canvas with three main areas. A top bar offers functions for saving, validating and viewing the JSON or script of the data flow. A graph shows the stream from source to sink, so the path of the data through the transformations is visible at a glance. A configuration panel appears for whichever transformation is selected. Each transformation provides tabs for its own settings, for partition optimization, for a read-only metadata inspection and for a data preview.

There are a few practical constraints noted in the documentation. The data preview works only when debug mode is switched on. The inspect tab shows no metadata when the source has no defined schema, which is typical for schema drift. Anyone designing flows against sources with changing structures should expect this behavior when inspecting metadata during development.

In typical situations, mapping data flows are chosen when transformation logic should be expressed visually instead of in code, while the surrounding pipeline handles triggers, scheduling and monitoring. The decision is mostly about where transformation work should live: in a graphical stream of transformations executed on managed Spark, or elsewhere in the data platform. The documentation also points to Dataflow Gen2 in Microsoft Fabric as a comparable technology, which is relevant for teams weighing Azure Data Factory against Fabric.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Data Factory - Simply Explained" covers mapping data flows under the heading "Transforming Without Code". It places them alongside the other building blocks of the service: pipelines and activities, linked services and datasets, integration runtimes, and triggers and scheduling. The same episode also compares Azure Data Factory with Fabric pipelines and discusses costs and best practices.

The episode "What Microsoft Fabric Means for Power BI Professionals" mentions mapping data flows in a learning outline for data ingestion and integration in Fabric. There, learning mapping data flows and data transformation is listed together with exploring connectors and practicing ingestion into OneLake, using Data Factory capabilities in Fabric. This shows how the concept appears in both the Azure Data Factory context and in discussions of the Fabric data platform.

markdown.desc: Markdown is a lightweight markup language with plain-text formatting syntax, used in Fabric notebooks, coding-agent context files, and Copilot skill definitions.

faq.a: Markdown is a lightweight markup language with plain-text formatting syntax. Files written in it usually use the .md extension and remain readable even without rendering.
faq.q: What is Markdown?

faq.a: Both store skills as Markdown (.md) files. The episode "Copilot Cowork - Simply Explained" says skills are defined in a simple Markdown file and that specific descriptions help Cowork decide when to use a skill.
faq.q: How do Copilot Studio and Copilot Cowork use Markdown?

faq.a: The episode with Andre Baltieri says that specifications and Markdown files can provide persistent project context for coding agents, which helps when long conversations lose important information.
faq.q: Why are Markdown files mentioned in connection with AI coding agents?

markdown.long:
Markdown is a lightweight markup language that uses plain-text formatting syntax. Content written in Markdown stays readable as ordinary text, and the same text can be rendered with headings, lists, emphasis, and other formatting by tools that understand the syntax. Files that contain Markdown typically carry the .md extension. In the Microsoft ecosystem, Markdown appears in several places: documentation inside notebooks, context files for AI coding agents, output returned by AI assistants, and the files in which Copilot Studio and Copilot Cowork store skills.

One common use is documentation inside data and machine learning work. The episode "Train AI Models with Microsoft Fabric Notebooks" describes structuring a notebook into separate cells, for example for feature engineering, exploratory analysis, and model training code. It also recommends adding Markdown cells to explain the logic and document experiments. According to the episode, this makes notebooks easier to read and share with others, while the separation into cells helps with debugging and rerunning parts of an experiment without repeating earlier steps.

Markdown also plays a role in AI-assisted software development. In "How AI Changed Software Development Forever — Building the Agentic Future with Andre Baltieri [MVP]", the discussion covers how context can degrade over a long AI conversation. One simple remedy mentioned is to finish a task, close the conversation, and start again with a clean context. The episode adds that specifications and Markdown files can provide persistent project context for coding agents, so that important information does not depend on a single long session. Because Markdown is plain text, such files can be written, versioned, and reviewed like any other project file.

Markdown is also relevant to what AI assistants return and what they can read. In "Stop Reinventing SPFx- Building Better SharePoint Solutions with PnP React Controls with Siddharth Vaghasia [MVP]", the point is made that an agent could surface richer, interactive interfaces through SharePoint Framework components instead of returning only text or Markdown. This positions Markdown as the baseline text format for agent output, with richer user interface components as a possible extension. On the input side, "SharePoint Isn't Boring Anymore: How Copilot Is Reinventing the Modern Workplace with Marcin Siewnicki [MVP]" notes that Copilot can work with different types of information, including text, HTML, Markdown, SharePoint lists, and content extracted from video transcripts. Markdown is therefore one of several content types that can become part of the knowledge available through AI in a Microsoft 365 environment.

A further use is the definition of skills. Copilot Studio and Copilot Cowork store skills as Markdown (.md) files. The episode "Copilot Cowork - Simply Explained" describes custom skills as playbooks that guide the AI in task execution. According to the episode, each user can create up to 20 custom skills, and defining a skill in a simple Markdown file keeps the setup straightforward. It also notes that specific descriptions in a skill help Cowork decide when to use it. In practice, this means the quality of a skill depends largely on how clearly the Markdown file states its purpose and steps.

Taken together, the episodes treat Markdown as a simple, human-readable format that works for people and for AI systems. Typical decisions around it include whether to document an experiment in Markdown cells inside a notebook, whether to keep persistent instructions for a coding agent in Markdown files instead of relying on long conversations, and how to write skill descriptions so that Copilot Cowork can select the right skill for a task. The sources do not describe specific Markdown syntax elements or dialects, so the format itself is covered here only at the level of a lightweight plain-text markup language.

market-development-funds.desc: Market development funds (MDF), also called co-op funds, are partner earnings Microsoft sets aside for approved marketing and enablement activities, to be spent within a set period.
market-development-funds.long:
Market development funds (MDF) are partner earnings that Microsoft sets aside for approved marketing and enablement activities. They are also known as co-op funds. The funds are not general-purpose income: they are earmarked for specific uses and must be spent within a set period.

In practice, MDF is a mechanism for directing part of a partner's earnings back into activities that promote and support the partner's business with Microsoft offerings. Because the funds are tied to approved activities and a time limit, partners who hold MDF need to plan how and when it is used.

The available facts do not specify how MDF is calculated, which activities qualify, how claims are submitted, or what the exact spending periods are. Those details depend on Microsoft's partner program terms and should be confirmed in the relevant program documentation.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this term, and no related topics have been connected to it yet.

marketing-manager.desc: Marketing manager is a job role that plans and runs campaigns, content, events and channels to reach and grow an audience or customer base.

faq.a: A marketing manager plans and runs marketing activities such as campaigns, content, events and channels. This includes analysing the market, choosing target segments, setting positioning and strategy through the marketing mix, managing vendors, and tracking progress with metrics and CRM tools.
faq.q: What does a marketing manager do?

faq.a: In small firms the role blends management with hands-on work. In large consumer firms it can resemble a general manager responsible for one product.
faq.q: How does the marketing manager role differ between small and large companies?

faq.a: The episode "Use Microsoft Graph API for Connected M365 Automation" describes a marketing manager who used Graph API data on reply times to priority clients. She found that faster responses correlated with higher sales win rates, a pattern not previously visible.
faq.q: How does the M365.FM episode connect a marketing manager to Microsoft Graph API?

marketing-manager.long:
A marketing manager is a professional role responsible for planning and running marketing activities such as campaigns, content, events and channels, with the aim of reaching and growing an audience or customer base. The role sits within the wider discipline of marketing management, which applies marketing orientation, techniques and methods inside an organisation and manages the resources and activities involved. Spellings such as Marketingmanager, Marketing-Manager and Marketing Manager refer to the same job.

According to the source material on marketing management, the work follows a recognisable cycle. Kotler's framing describes it as the analysis, planning, implementation and control of programmes designed to produce exchanges with target audiences. In practice, a marketing manager analyses the industry and competitors with tools such as Porter's five forces and SWOT, and runs market research that can be qualitative, quantitative, experimental or observational. Brand audits are another part of the analytical work. From this groundwork, the manager chooses attractive target segments and defines a brand's positioning around a differentiated key benefit.

Strategy is typically set through the marketing mix of product, price, place and promotion. A marketing plan commonly contains an executive summary, a situation analysis, objectives, the chosen strategy and segments, and an implementation section for each of the four Ps. Beyond planning a single campaign, marketing managers also work on improving core processes such as new product development, brand management and pricing. They manage vendors, for example agencies, and track progress using metrics, forecasts and CRM tools.

The scope of the role depends on company size. In small firms it tends to blend management with hands-on execution, so one person may both set direction and produce the work. In large consumer firms the role can resemble that of a general manager responsible for a single product. This variation is a common point of confusion when comparing job descriptions, since the same title can cover quite different levels of strategy and delivery.

The M365.FM episode "Use Microsoft Graph API for Connected M365 Automation" (2025-08-05) mentions a marketing manager in the context of operational data in Microsoft 365. The episode describes a marketing manager who used the Graph API to look at reply times to priority clients. She noticed that faster responses to certain clients correlated with higher sales win rates, a pattern that had not been visible before because nobody had the data.
