In practice, this means protecting endpoints before an attack succeeds, surfacing suspicious behavior when something gets through, and giving analysts the means to understand what happened and act on it. Automated investigation reduces manual triage effort, while advanced hunting lets analysts query collected data to look for activity that has not yet triggered an alert.

A recurring theme in the M365.FM episodes is that endpoint signals are valuable beyond the endpoint itself. The episode "Microsoft Defender for Endpoint - Simply Explained" describes how these signals support security operations and lists practical questions to answer before rolling the product out across a Microsoft 365 environment. That framing treats deployment as a planning exercise rather than a simple switch-on.

Defender for Endpoint also works as one building block of a larger detection picture. The episode "Microsoft Defender XDR - Simply Explained" explains that Microsoft Defender XDR connects Microsoft Defender for Endpoint with Defender for Office 365, Defender for Identity, Defender for Cloud Apps and Microsoft Entra ID so that attacks which individual tools might miss can be identified across the full attack chain. Concepts from that episode, such as incidents, alerts, automated investigation and remediation, threat intelligence, advanced hunting and AI-powered attack disruption, all draw on endpoint data among other sources.

Other episodes show the product in supporting roles. In "Detect Impossible Travel and Token Replay in Microsoft Entra ID", Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is listed among forensic tools in the Microsoft cloud, described there as monitoring behavior across virtual machines to detect suspicious activities, alongside Microsoft Sentinel and Azure VM snapshots. The episode "Harden Microsoft 365 Security Without User Friction" recommends pairing Defender for Office 365 with Defender for Endpoint and Conditional Access to build a layered security posture, and notes inconsistent Intune device governance as a recurring risk in many tenants.

The episode "Zero Trust Across Microsoft 365 and Dynamics 365" points to a further use: Conditional Access can enforce device state using signals from Intune, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint or partner signals. According to that episode, this makes it possible to require compliant devices even when full MDM enrollment is not feasible. Defender for Endpoint therefore contributes to access decisions as well as to detection and response.

Typical decisions around the product include choosing between Plan 1 and Plan 2 based on whether detection, investigation and hunting capabilities are needed, and deciding how endpoint telemetry should feed the wider security operations process. Related topics include Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Sentinel, Intune and Conditional Access.

microsoft-defender-threat-intelligence.desc: Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence (Defender TI) is a Microsoft threat intelligence platform built on RiskIQ, now being folded into Microsoft Defender.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft threat intelligence platform, built on the RiskIQ acquisition, that combines finished intelligence like threat actor profiles with raw internet data such as passive DNS and certificates. Its capabilities are being folded into Microsoft Defender.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence?

faq.a: The Intel explorer searches and filters across Microsoft and customer sources for campaigns, indicators, attack patterns, threat actors, tools, vulnerabilities and reports. Entity pages for IP addresses, domains, URLs and files add reputation data, sandbox results and infrastructure relationships.
faq.q: What can be searched in the threat intelligence experience of the Defender portal?

faq.a: It is part of Microsoft Defender. Microsoft Learn describes threat intelligence in the Defender portal as combining Microsoft's threat research, data from the organization's environment and Defender security context, applicable to Microsoft Defender XDR and Microsoft Sentinel in the Defender portal.
faq.q: How does Defender Threat Intelligence relate to Microsoft Defender?

microsoft-defender-threat-intelligence.long:
Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, often shortened to Defender TI, is a Microsoft threat intelligence platform built on the RiskIQ acquisition. It combines finished intelligence, such as threat actor profiles, with raw internet data such as passive DNS and certificates. The goal is to give security teams context about who may be behind an attack and what infrastructure they use, rather than leaving them with an alert that only shows that something broke. The product is part of Microsoft Defender, and its capabilities are being folded into the wider Defender experience.

In practice, threat intelligence of this kind is used to understand emerging threats, investigate threat actors and their infrastructure, judge how a threat affects an organization, and support hunting and incident response. Microsoft Learn describes this under the heading of threat intelligence in the Microsoft Defender portal, which combines Microsoft's threat research, intelligence from the organization's own environment and security context from Microsoft Defender. It applies to Microsoft Defender XDR and to Microsoft Sentinel in the Defender portal.

The documentation names several components. An Overview page presents an executive summary, the latest threats, high-impact threats and those with the greatest exposure, with optional email notifications. The Intel explorer searches and filters across Microsoft and customer sources for campaigns, indicators, attack patterns, threat actors, tools, vulnerabilities and reports. Entity pages for IP addresses, domains, URLs and files add reputation data, related reports, sandbox results and infrastructure relationships. Threat analytics reports can draw on data from the customer's own environment, and Microsoft Copilot in Defender can summarize and prioritize intelligence. Project Perception extracts indicators, maps techniques to MITRE ATT&CK and generates KQL hunting queries. The documentation notes that some parts are preview features and that ISOC customers need an ISOC workspace.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence - Simply Explained" approaches the topic from the analyst's viewpoint. According to its description, the alert on the screen never tells you who is attacking; it only tells you something broke and leaves you guessing. The episode covers what threat intelligence actually is, indicators of compromise described as breadcrumbs, threat actors as the parties behind an attack, infrastructure analysis as a way of following the trail, and how to use the intelligence in an investigation.

The topic also appears in the episode "Microsoft Security Exposure Management with Uros Babic [MVP-MCT]". There, the excerpt says that Microsoft's integrated security tools combine threat intelligence, contextual scoring and data sensitivity to bring the most urgent risks to the top. The episode states that Defender Threat Intelligence can be used to unmask adversaries and neutralize modern cyberthreats, and that this intelligence lets teams adjust security defenses before threats become incidents.

Typical decisions around the product involve how intelligence feeds into daily work: using indicators and actor profiles to enrich an investigation, pivoting across infrastructure such as domains, IP addresses and certificates, and turning findings into hunting queries. Because the capabilities are being folded into Microsoft Defender, teams evaluating the tooling should check current Microsoft Learn documentation to see where individual features now live in the Defender portal.

microsoft-defender-vulnerability-managem.desc: Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management is a Microsoft Defender capability that discovers devices and software, prioritizes weaknesses by risk, and tracks remediation.

faq.a: It continuously discovers devices and software, assesses weaknesses, prioritizes them by risk and context, and tracks remediation until devices no longer report the exposure.
faq.q: What does Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management do?

faq.a: It is organized into four areas: inventories, discovering and assessing threats, identifying and prioritizing risk, and taking action and tracking progress.
faq.q: How is the documentation for Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management organized?

faq.a: It is part of Microsoft Defender and, as described in the episode "Microsoft Defender XDR - Simply Explained", covers the assets component by providing visibility and remediation tools for vulnerabilities.
faq.q: How does it relate to Microsoft Defender XDR?

microsoft-defender-vulnerability-managem.long:
Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management is a capability within Microsoft Defender that continuously discovers devices and software, assesses their weaknesses, prioritizes those weaknesses by risk and context, and tracks remediation until devices no longer report the exposure. According to the Microsoft Learn documentation, its aim is to reduce cyber risk through continuous vulnerability discovery and assessment, risk-based prioritization and remediation.

The central problem it addresses is not finding vulnerabilities but deciding what to do about them. A vulnerability scan can return hundreds or thousands of CVEs, and the harder questions are which weaknesses create the most risk, what should be fixed first, who should fix it, and whether the remediation actually worked. The episode "Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management - Simply Explained" makes this point directly: the capability goes beyond running a scan and installing patches, and severity matters, but context matters more. A weakness on a laptop that handles sensitive information and is exposed to active threats is treated differently from the same weakness elsewhere.

The documentation organizes the capability into four areas that follow a flow of taking inventory, assessing, prioritizing, fixing and following progress. The first area, inventories, covers devices, software, browser extensions, certificates, and hardware and firmware assessment. This matches the episode's emphasis on discovery: before vulnerabilities can be prioritized, there has to be knowledge of what is actually present in the environment.

The second area, discovering and assessing threats, includes dashboard insights, the exposure score, Microsoft Secure Score for Devices, security baselines, searching for exposed devices and authenticated scanning for Windows. The third area, identifying and prioritizing risk, covers security recommendations, network share configuration assessment, exceptions for recommendations, planning for software that is no longer supported, handling zero-day vulnerabilities and an event timeline. The fourth area, taking action and tracking progress, covers remediating vulnerabilities, blocking vulnerable applications and a report on vulnerable devices.

Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management is part of Microsoft Defender. In the episode "Microsoft Defender XDR - Simply Explained", it appears among the core components of Microsoft Defender XDR, where it covers the assets layer and provides visibility and remediation tools for vulnerabilities. It sits alongside Defender for Endpoint for endpoints, Defender for Office 365 for email and collaboration, Defender for Identity and Microsoft Entra ID Protection for identities, and Defender for Cloud Apps for applications.

In practice, teams use it to move from a long list of findings to an ordered set of actions with an owner and a way to confirm the outcome. Typical decisions include which security recommendations to act on first, whether an exception is justified for a given recommendation, how to plan for software that is no longer supported, and whether a vulnerable application should be blocked while a fix is pending. Tracking continues until devices stop reporting the exposure, which closes the loop between assessment and verified remediation.

The Microsoft Learn landing page does not state licensing, platform requirements, limits or pricing, and it points to separate pages for an overview and for comparing offerings. Anyone planning a deployment would need to consult those pages for requirements and offering differences.

microsoft-delve.desc: Microsoft Delve was a Microsoft 365 service built on Microsoft Graph that surfaced documents colleagues were working on or had shared; it was retired in December 2024.

faq.a: Microsoft Delve was a Microsoft 365 service built on Microsoft Graph that surfaced documents colleagues were working on and had shared.
faq.q: What was Microsoft Delve?

faq.a: No. Microsoft retired Delve in December 2024, so references to it in older guidance should be treated as outdated.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Delve still available?

faq.a: The retrieved episodes do not discuss the product. The word "delve" appears in their text only as an ordinary English verb, for example in "delve into" or "delve deeper."
faq.q: Do the M365.FM episodes cover Microsoft Delve?

microsoft-delve.long:
Microsoft Delve was a Microsoft 365 service built on Microsoft Graph. Its purpose was to surface documents that colleagues were working on and had shared, so that people could find relevant content without searching folder by folder. Microsoft retired the service in December 2024, which makes it a product that now belongs mainly to the history of Microsoft 365 rather than to its current toolset.

The core idea behind Delve was discovery rather than storage. Documents themselves lived elsewhere in Microsoft 365, and Delve presented a view of them based on the relationships and activity that Microsoft Graph tracks across a tenant. Because the service depended on Microsoft Graph, what it showed for a given person was shaped by who that person worked with and which items had been shared with them. In this sense Delve acted as a window onto existing content and sharing, not as a separate repository.

This design is the reason Delve is often discussed in connection with permissions and information hygiene. A service that surfaces content based on sharing makes the quality of existing sharing visible. Where documents were shared too broadly, a discovery view could make that oversharing easier to notice. The facts available here describe the service only as one that showed documents colleagues were working on and had shared, so the exact mechanics of how items were ranked or displayed are not covered in this overview.

For organizations, the main practical decision around Delve today is about transition. Since the service was retired in December 2024, teams that relied on it for finding colleagues' recent documents need to use other parts of Microsoft 365 for discovery and search. Anyone reviewing older internal guidance, training material, or governance documents may still find references to Delve, and those references should be treated as outdated. Reviewing how content is shared and who can see it remains a sensible exercise regardless of which discovery surface is in use, since the underlying permissions are what determine what any such service can show.

The M365.FM episodes in the source material do not discuss Delve as a product. The name appears in the retrieved episode excerpts only through the ordinary English verb "delve," as in the phrases "delve into" or "delve deeper," found in episodes such as "SC-900 Cybersecurity Fundamentals: A Modern Security Guide," "DP-600 Training 4/4: Incremental Refresh, RLS, and OLS," "How to Build a Winning Microsoft Partner Strategy," "Enforce AI Agent Security Controls at Execution Time," and "Mainframe Architecture Lessons for Azure Cloud Design." These matches are word usage, not coverage of the service, and they should not be read as the episodes making any statement about Microsoft Delve itself.

In short, Microsoft Delve was a Microsoft 365 service built on Microsoft Graph that surfaced shared and in-progress documents from colleagues, and it was retired in December 2024. No official documentation links or related topic relations were provided for this entry, so the description here is limited to what is stated above. Readers who need current guidance on content discovery in Microsoft 365 should consult up-to-date official Microsoft documentation instead of relying on material written when Delve was still available.

microsoft-designer.desc: Microsoft Designer is an AI-powered graphic design app from Microsoft that turns text prompts into images, social media posts and other visuals.

faq.a: Microsoft Designer is an AI-powered graphic design app from Microsoft that creates images, social media posts and other visuals from text prompts. It is described as part of the Copilot family and as part of Microsoft 365.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Designer?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Create Business Content with Microsoft Designer", Designer auto-applies a brand kit with fonts, colors and logos so that on-brand assets can be created quickly. The episode adds that this works inside Microsoft 365 with collaboration across SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Designer support brand consistency?

faq.a: Microsoft Designer is listed as related to Microsoft 365 Copilot and is described as part of the Copilot family. Both are AI assistants within the Microsoft ecosystem.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Designer relate to Microsoft 365 Copilot?

microsoft-designer.long:
Microsoft Designer is an AI-powered graphic design app developed by Microsoft. It is used to create images, social media posts and other visuals from text prompts, and it is described as part of the Copilot family. The product is classed as a Microsoft tool and as an AI assistant, and it is listed as part of Microsoft 365. It is also related to Microsoft 365 Copilot. The product is also referred to simply as Designer, and an official site for it is maintained by Microsoft.

The core idea is that a user describes the desired result in text, and the app generates a visual starting point instead of requiring a design from scratch. Typical uses named in the available material are social media graphics and general visual content for business communication. This makes it relevant for roles that produce campaign assets regularly, such as marketing and communications teams, where speed and consistency of output matter more than custom illustration work.

One point stressed in the M365.FM material is brand consistency. The episode "Create Business Content with Microsoft Designer" says that Designer auto-applies a brand kit, meaning fonts, colors and logos, so that on-brand assets can be produced in seconds. According to the episode, this happens inside Microsoft 365 and supports real-time collaboration across SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams. In practice, that means design files and finished assets can sit in the same places where other business documents are already stored and shared, rather than moving through a separate tool chain.

The same episode places Microsoft Designer next to Fabric Dataflows Gen2, presenting both as ways to reduce busywork in marketing and analytics. Designer covers the content creation side, while Dataflows Gen2 is described as bringing AI-assisted Power Query to unify messy campaign data. The episode frames the combination as a way for marketing operations and reporting to become faster and cleaner. It also cites the statement that nearly nine out of ten companies now use AI for content creation, an adoption figure that the episode itself attributes to its own sources.

In terms of decisions around the product, the main considerations raised by the material are brand governance and collaboration. Teams that need consistent fonts, colors and logos across many assets can look at how a brand kit is applied automatically. Teams that already work in SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams can consider how shared editing fits their existing storage and review habits. Because Microsoft Designer is related to Microsoft 365 Copilot, organizations evaluating Copilot capabilities may also look at it as one of the AI-assisted creation options within the wider Microsoft 365 ecosystem.

Some other M365.FM episodes appear in connection with the term "designer", but they concern different tools. Episodes on Azure Logic Apps and Power Automate mention a visual designer for building workflows, which is a workflow-authoring interface and not the graphic design app. These should not be confused with Microsoft Designer, which is focused on image and visual creation from prompts.

For the most direct coverage of the product, the episode "Create Business Content with Microsoft Designer" from August 2025 is the relevant reference on the M365.FM feed. It describes the app in a business setting, covering brand kit application, collaboration across Microsoft 365 services and the pairing with analytics tooling. Detailed feature lists, pricing and licensing terms are not covered in the material summarized here and should be checked against official Microsoft documentation.

microsoft-dev-box.desc: Microsoft Dev Box is an Azure service offering developers self-service, preconfigured cloud workstations; new sign-ups have stopped as it moves to Windows 365.

faq.a: Microsoft Dev Box is an Azure service that gives developers self-service access to preconfigured, cloud-hosted Windows workstations. These are organised in dev centers, projects and pools.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Dev Box?

faq.a: According to the product description, Microsoft has stopped new sign-ups and is moving the service's capabilities to Windows 365. The documentation links a retirement guide for details.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Dev Box still available for new customers?

faq.a: The documentation lists hibernation, scheduled auto-stop, automatic deletion of unused dev boxes, quota increases and project policies as cost control options.
faq.q: How can costs be controlled in Microsoft Dev Box?

microsoft-dev-box.long:
Microsoft Dev Box is an Azure service that gives developers self-service access to preconfigured, cloud-hosted Windows workstations. A dev box is a full Windows workstation that runs in a Microsoft data center, and developers reach it from whatever screen they already own. The service is organised in dev centers, projects and pools, so that a team can define what a workstation looks like once and let developers create their own from that definition. According to the product description, Microsoft has stopped new sign-ups and is moving the capabilities of Dev Box to Windows 365.

The main purpose of Microsoft Dev Box is to remove the manual effort of setting up a development machine. Instead of waiting for hardware or installing tools by hand, a developer picks a project and a pool and receives a workstation that is ready to code. The documentation hub on Microsoft Learn describes it as powerful, preconfigured, ready-to-code cloud-based workstations with self-service access. The episode "Microsoft Dev Box - Simply Explained" frames the idea as a work computer that might never sit on a desk, and lists the four pieces that make Dev Box work as one of its topics.

The documentation groups the product's capabilities into several areas. Customizations cover team and user settings, dev center imaging, customization tasks and the imagedefinition and task YAML files; GitHub Copilot can help generate such files. The developer portal supports managing a dev box, self-service snapshots and restore, hibernation, multiple monitors, postponing or skipping a scheduled shutdown, and a troubleshoot-and-repair tool. Further topics address an MCP server, serverless GPU for AI workloads, and automation with the Azure CLI and REST API. Architecture and deployment guidance is included for larger rollouts.

Cost control and security are treated as separate concerns in the documentation. Cost control options include hibernation, scheduled auto-stop, automatic deletion of unused dev boxes, quota increases and project policies. On the security side, the documentation mentions conditional access through Intune, single sign-on, and access via dev tunnels from VS Code. These controls matter when workstations hold source code and credentials outside a physical office, and they are typical decision points when an organisation considers a cloud workstation approach.

The retirement of new sign-ups is the most important planning fact for anyone evaluating the service today. The documentation page links a retirement guide, but its content is not shown in the available material, and the page states no licensing requirements, prerequisites or concrete limits. Organisations that already use Microsoft Dev Box, or that are comparing cloud workstation options, should therefore consult the retirement guide and the Windows 365 documentation for the migration path rather than assume that the current feature set stays unchanged.

Dev Box appears in M365.FM mainly through the episode "Microsoft Dev Box - Simply Explained", which introduces what the service is and how its pieces fit together in plain terms. A second episode, "Test Microsoft 365 Apps with Visual Studio Dev Tunnels", mentions a dev box only in passing, as a general term for a development environment that can be exposed if a tunnel is left public or anonymous. That episode recommends locking tunnels down, logging them and shutting them off when testing is done. It concerns Visual Studio Dev Tunnels and is a separate topic from the Azure service, though the documentation also names dev tunnels as one way to reach a dev box from VS Code.

microsoft-edge.desc: Microsoft Edge is the browser from Microsoft; the M365.FM episode 'Microsoft Edge for Business' describes how it behaves differently once a work account is used.

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Microsoft Edge for Business - Simply Explained", it is not a second browser to install. It is the same Edge that is already in use, which behaves differently when someone signs in with a work account.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Edge for Business?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Edge for Business - Simply Explained" lists the work profile and the personal profile as a core topic, alongside the question of who controls the browser. The available excerpt does not give further detail on how the two profiles differ.
faq.q: What is the difference between the work profile and the personal profile in Microsoft Edge?

faq.a: No. Episodes such as "Edge vs. Cloud in Manufacturing- Why the Wrong Architecture Costs You More" and "Cloud Latency and Edge Computing Strategy" use "edge" to mean computing close to machines or users, which is a different topic from the browser.
faq.q: Do the edge computing episodes on M365.FM cover the Microsoft Edge browser?

microsoft-edge.long:
Microsoft Edge is a web browser from Microsoft. It is the entity covered here under the name Microsoft Edge, and the M365.FM material that mentions it centers on how the browser is used in work settings. The episodes also use the word "edge" in a different sense, as in edge computing, and that meaning is a separate topic from the browser product.

The most direct description comes from the episode "Microsoft Edge for Business - Simply Explained". According to its show notes, Microsoft Edge for Business is not a second browser that has to be installed. It is the same Edge that people already use, configured to behave differently as soon as someone signs in with a work account. The episode is part of the Simply Explained format and lists several themes: what Edge for Business actually is, the work profile and the personal profile, and who controls the browser. A section on Internet Explorer is also named in the excerpt, though the available text does not say what the episode states about it.

The work profile and personal profile distinction is the central idea in that episode's outline. Because Edge for Business is the same installation, the difference lies in how the browser acts once a work identity is present. This matters in practice for people who use one device for both private and professional browsing, and for administrators who need to understand where organizational control starts and where it ends. The question of who controls the browser is listed as its own topic in the episode, which signals that responsibility for settings and behavior is a point of attention when Edge is used in an organization.

Typical decisions around Microsoft Edge in a business context follow from this. Organizations have to decide how work and personal browsing are separated, who is responsible for configuring the browser, and how a work sign-in changes what users see and can do. The episode frames these as questions to understand before rolling out or standardizing on the browser, rather than as a separate product purchase, since no second installation is required.

The other M365.FM episodes that surface alongside Microsoft Edge use the word in the sense of edge versus cloud computing. "Edge vs. Cloud in Manufacturing- Why the Wrong Architecture Costs You More", "Edge or Cloud? Where Industrial Workloads Should Actually Run", "Cloud Latency and Edge Computing Strategy" and "How Machine Data Reaches Microsoft Fabric - From OPC UA to Real-Time Analytics" deal with where workloads and data processing should run. They discuss latency, bandwidth, resilience, security and cost, the role of Azure Arc and Azure IoT Operations, and how machine data moves from OPC UA through an edge layer and MQTT into Microsoft Fabric. These episodes concern edge computing as an architecture approach and are not about the Microsoft Edge browser, so the two meanings should not be mixed.

For readers searching for the browser, the relevant M365.FM source is the Simply Explained episode on Microsoft Edge for Business. For readers looking at industrial and cloud architecture, the edge computing episodes are the relevant ones. Keeping the two apart avoids confusion when the term appears in Microsoft ecosystem discussions, where the same word can refer to a product used by office workers or to a processing location close to machines on a factory floor.

microsoft-entra.desc: Microsoft Entra is Microsoft's family of identity and network access products, including Microsoft Entra ID, Cloud Sync, Domain Services and Private Access.

faq.a: Microsoft Entra is the family of identity and network access products from Microsoft, and it includes Microsoft Entra ID. It covers services that control who can sign in and what they can reach.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Entra?

faq.a: Both synchronize identities from on-premises Active Directory into Microsoft Entra ID. The episode on Cloud Sync describes it as a cloud-managed approach and compares it with Entra Connect, including the decision between the two.
faq.q: How do Microsoft Entra Connect and Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync differ?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode explains it for legacy applications that move to Azure but still expect a traditional Windows domain, for example with LDAP lookups, Kerberos authentication, Group Policy or domain-joined machines.
faq.q: When is Microsoft Entra Domain Services relevant?

microsoft-entra.long:
Microsoft Entra is the family of identity and network access products from Microsoft, and Microsoft Entra ID is one of its members. Microsoft develops the platform, and on M365.FM it is classified as a Microsoft tool and as an identity and security tool. The name is often shortened to Entra. It brings together the services that decide who can sign in, to which resources, and under which conditions, covering both people and non-human identities.

Because Entra is a family rather than a single product, a practical first step is to see which member addresses which problem. Microsoft Entra ID is the cloud identity service. Hybrid organizations that still run an on-premises Active Directory use synchronization products to connect it with the cloud. Two of these are covered in the M365.FM episodes: Microsoft Entra Connect and Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync. Microsoft Entra Domain Services serves a different case, in which older applications move to Azure but still expect a traditional Windows domain. Microsoft Entra Private Access, with its Quick Access feature, belongs to the network access side of the family. Related topics in the knowledge graph include Microsoft Entra Agent ID and identity lifecycle management.

The episode "Microsoft Entra Connect - Simply Explained" starts from the observation that Entra Connect is a technology almost everyone working with Microsoft 365 has heard about, while its actual job is often misunderstood. It asks why organizations need it, what exactly is synchronized between Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID, where passwords are checked, and what happens if synchronization stops working. "Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync - Simply Explained" presents Cloud Sync as a cloud-managed way to synchronize identities from on-premises Active Directory into Microsoft Entra ID. The episode explains how it differs from Entra Connect, why an organization might choose it, and what has changed in 2026. It walks through the identity problem, architecture, high availability, scoping, security, hybrid environments and the decision between the two tools.

"Microsoft Entra Domain Services - Simply Explained" addresses a specific migration situation. Microsoft Entra ID is built for modern cloud identity, but established Windows applications were designed around Active Directory and may require LDAP directory lookups, Kerberos authentication, Group Policy, service accounts or domain-joined machines. Moving such an application into Azure does not by itself provide those capabilities, and the episode explains how Entra Domain Services fits that gap.

Non-human access is the subject of "Entra Workload Identities - Simply Explained". The episode notes that modern cloud environments are no longer accessed only by people: applications, automation workflows, Azure services, DevOps pipelines, AI agents and background jobs all need secure access to business resources without human interaction. It contrasts user identities with workload identities and offers a practical foundation for administrators, cloud architects, developers, DevOps engineers and consultants who deal with secure application authentication.

On the network side, "Microsoft Entra Quick Access - Simply Explained" describes Quick Access as one feature inside Microsoft Entra Private Access. The episode frames it as a response to the company VPN feeling out of step with current ways of working, and mentions a Microsoft network spanning 70 regions as the scale behind it. It covers what Quick Access is, why a VPN feels wrong now, the three pieces that make it work, and what it does in practice.

Taken together, the episodes show typical decisions around Microsoft Entra: whether to synchronize on-premises identities with Entra Connect or Cloud Sync, whether a legacy application needs a managed domain through Entra Domain Services, how applications and automation should authenticate through workload identities, and whether private application access should replace a traditional VPN. Official product information is published by Microsoft on its Microsoft Entra security page.

microsoft-entra-id-p2.desc: Microsoft Entra ID P2 is the premium Microsoft Entra ID license tier that adds ID Protection, risk-based Conditional Access and Privileged Identity Management.

faq.a: P2 includes all listed P1 authentication features and adds risk-based Conditional Access, Identity Protection and Privileged Identity Management. It also lists access reviews, entitlement management with access packages and risk-based identity verification.
faq.q: What does Microsoft Entra ID P2 add compared with P1?

faq.a: Yes. Microsoft Entra ID P2 is included in Microsoft 365 E5. Per Microsoft Learn it is also part of Microsoft 365 E7, the Defender suites, Enterprise Mobility + Security E5 and the Defender and Purview suites for Business Premium.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Entra ID P2 included in Microsoft 365 E5?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, PIM features stop working and eligible role assignments are removed. Permanent role assignments stay in place.
faq.q: What happens when a Microsoft Entra ID P2 license expires?

microsoft-entra-id-p2.long:
Microsoft Entra ID P2 is a license tier of Microsoft Entra ID, the identity and access management service in the Microsoft ecosystem. It is the premium level above Microsoft Entra ID P1 and is sold on its own as well as part of several bundles. The tier is included in Microsoft 365 E5. According to Microsoft Learn, it also comes with Microsoft 365 E7, the Defender suites, Enterprise Mobility + Security E5 and the Defender and Purview suites for Business Premium.

P2 contains all of the listed authentication features of P1 and adds identity security capabilities on top. The episode "Microsoft Entra as a Complete IAM Platform" describes the split this way: P1 covers capabilities such as self-service password reset, dynamic group management and basic Conditional Access, while P2 adds advanced identity security in the form of risk-based Conditional Access policies, Identity Protection and Privileged Identity Management. Which tier an organization chooses depends on whether it needs these advanced, risk-based controls.

Risk-based Conditional Access is available only in P2. It works together with Identity Protection, which requires a P2 license. Identity Protection covers risk-based sign-in and user-risk policies that are enforced through Conditional Access. It also provides reports on risky users, risky sign-ins and risk detections, as well as notifications for users who are at risk. In practice, this lets access decisions respond to the detected risk of a sign-in or an account rather than relying only on static conditions.

Privileged Identity Management (PIM), including PIM for groups, is the other major part of the tier. Per Microsoft Learn, it needs P2 or Entra ID Governance for every user with eligible or time-bound assignments, for approvers and for access review participants. Further capabilities listed for P2 include risk-based identity verification, access reviews and entitlement management with access packages. Lifecycle Workflows and some access review features are not part of P2, and workload identities are licensed separately, so the scope of the tier should be checked against the actual requirements.

License lifecycle matters for administrators. Microsoft Learn notes that if a P2 license expires, PIM features stop working and eligible role assignments are removed, while permanent assignments stay in place. Planning renewals and license assignment for privileged-role users, approvers and reviewers therefore affects how privileged access is managed.

P2 also appears in the partner context. The episode "The FY26 Partner Designation Restructuring Is Coming — Most Partners Aren't Ready" mentions Entra ID P2 as an addition to the Identity and Access Management specialization that expands the pathways for partners to qualify. This shows the tier is relevant not only to tenant administrators but also to partners who build identity practices around it.

Within the product family, Microsoft Entra ID P2 is part of Microsoft Entra ID. Organizations running Microsoft 365 E3 or Microsoft 365 Business Premium can use Microsoft Entra IAM, as the episode "Microsoft Entra as a Complete IAM Platform" states, and move to P2 when they need risk-based controls and privileged access management beyond what P1 offers.

microsoft-entra-id-protection.desc: Microsoft Entra ID Protection scores sign-in risk and user risk so Conditional Access can require MFA, a password change or block access to Microsoft Entra ID.

faq.a: It detects, investigates and remediates identity-based risks by scoring sign-in risk and user risk. Conditional Access policies can use these scores to require MFA, require a password change or block access.
faq.q: What does Microsoft Entra ID Protection do?

faq.a: Sign-in risk concerns a single authentication attempt and whether it is likely made by the legitimate owner, while user risk concerns whether the account itself may be compromised. The episode "Microsoft Entra ID Protection - Simply Explained" covers both and what the risk levels mean.
faq.q: What is the difference between sign-in risk and user risk?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Defender for Identity - Simply Explained", Defender for Identity focuses on threats in Active Directory and post-authentication network activity, while Entra ID Protection focuses on access control and authentication risks.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Entra ID Protection differ from Microsoft Defender for Identity?

microsoft-entra-id-protection.long:
Microsoft Entra ID Protection is a security product that is part of Microsoft Entra ID. It detects, investigates and remediates identity-based risks. Instead of treating every sign-in the same way, it scores how risky a sign-in or an account appears to be, so that an organization can decide how to respond based on that score.

The product works with two kinds of risk: the user and the sign-in. Sign-in risk describes how likely it is that a particular authentication attempt is not made by the legitimate account owner. User risk describes how likely it is that an account itself has been compromised. Each of these is expressed through risk levels, and the levels are what policies act on. The episode "Microsoft Entra ID Protection - Simply Explained" walks through what Identity Protection watches, the difference between the two risk types, what the risk levels mean, and how risk turns into a decision.

The main purpose of Microsoft Entra ID Protection is to feed those risk signals into Conditional Access. A Conditional Access policy can use sign-in risk or user risk as a condition and then require multifactor authentication, require a password change, or block access. This links detection directly to enforcement: a low-risk sign-in can proceed normally, a more suspicious one can be challenged with MFA, and an account considered compromised can be forced through a password change or blocked until it is dealt with.

The focus on identity reflects how attacks commonly happen. According to the episode "Microsoft Entra ID Protection - Simply Explained", Microsoft says more than 97 percent of identity attacks are password attacks, and the usual way into a Microsoft 365 account is a password that leaked somewhere else rather than a clever hack. In that situation, a correct password alone is weak evidence that the person signing in is the real user, which is why a risk assessment of the sign-in and of the account adds useful context.

Microsoft Entra ID Protection also appears in wider security discussions in the M365.FM catalog. In "Microsoft Defender XDR - Simply Explained", it is listed together with Microsoft Defender for Identity as the part of Microsoft Defender XDR that detects threats and protects user identities. The episode "How Microsoft Graph Connects Microsoft 365 Data and Context" notes that Microsoft Graph can aggregate alerts and incidents from security providers such as Microsoft Entra ID Protection, Microsoft 365 Defender and Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, so identity risk can be seen alongside other security data.

The product is also relevant beyond human users. In "Entra Workload Identities - Simply Explained", Microsoft Entra ID Protection is named among the controls for governing workload identities, together with least privilege access, Conditional Access for workload identities, workload identity federation, certificate-based authentication, logging, monitoring, lifecycle management and ownership. The episode argues that application identities need the same governance as privileged user accounts, including a clearly assigned owner, minimal permissions and continuous monitoring.

Microsoft Entra ID Protection is often compared with Microsoft Defender for Identity. The episode "Microsoft Defender for Identity - Simply Explained" contrasts the two: Microsoft Defender for Identity focuses on detecting threats in Active Directory and monitors network activity for post-authentication attacks, while Entra ID Protection focuses on access control and authentication risks and performs authentication risk assessment. The two address different stages of an identity attack and can be used together.

microsoft-entra-kerberos.desc: Microsoft Entra Kerberos lets Microsoft Entra ID issue Kerberos tickets from the cloud so users can authenticate to services such as Azure Files.
microsoft-entra-kerberos.long:
Microsoft Entra Kerberos is a capability of Microsoft Entra in which Microsoft Entra ID issues Kerberos tickets from the cloud. Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication protocol traditionally associated with on-premises domain controllers. With Microsoft Entra Kerberos, users can authenticate to services that rely on Kerberos without those on-premises domain controllers being involved in issuing the tickets.

A stated use case is access to Azure Files, where users authenticate using Kerberos tickets obtained through Microsoft Entra ID. This allows Kerberos-based sign-in to cloud-hosted file shares from a cloud identity foundation rather than from an on-premises Active Directory environment.

Microsoft Entra Kerberos is part of Microsoft Entra, the identity and access product family it belongs to. The available facts do not describe specific configuration steps, supported client versions or licensing requirements, so those details should be checked in official Microsoft documentation.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity.

microsoft-entra-permissions-management.desc: Microsoft Entra Permissions Management is a CIEM solution that discovers, compares and right-sizes identity permissions across Azure, AWS and Google Cloud.

faq.a: It is a cloud infrastructure entitlement management (CIEM) solution that discovers the permissions of all identities across Azure, AWS and Google Cloud and compares granted permissions with those actually used. It helps right-size and monitor permissions.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Entra Permissions Management?

faq.a: It covers Azure, AWS and Google Cloud, which makes it relevant for multi-cloud environments where permissions would otherwise be reviewed separately in each platform.
faq.q: Which cloud platforms does Microsoft Entra Permissions Management cover?

faq.a: It helps answer who has access to what and whether that access is really needed. By surfacing unused or excessive permissions, it supports removing them and reducing the attack surface, as described in the M365.FM episodes on the topic.
faq.q: What problem does it help address?

microsoft-entra-permissions-management.long:
Microsoft Entra Permissions Management is a cloud infrastructure entitlement management (CIEM) solution that discovers the permissions of all identities across Azure, AWS and Google Cloud. It compares the permissions that have been granted with the permissions that are actually used, and it helps organizations right-size and monitor those permissions. The product is part of Microsoft Entra, the family of identity and access offerings from Microsoft.

The core question it addresses is one that grows harder as cloud estates expand: who has access to what, and do they really need it? The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Entra Permissions Management - Simply Explained" describes this as one of the biggest security questions in the cloud. As businesses adopt Azure, AWS and Google Cloud side by side, permissions become difficult to manage, and unnecessary risk can build up through excessive or unused access rights. A CIEM solution is meant to bring those entitlements into one view so they can be assessed rather than assumed.

The approach rests on comparing granted access with used access. Identities in a cloud environment often hold broad permissions that are never exercised, for example because roles were assigned generously at the start of a project or never revisited afterwards. By discovering the permissions of all identities and setting them against actual activity, Permissions Management makes the gap between what is allowed and what is needed visible. From there, permissions can be right-sized, meaning reduced toward what an identity actually uses, and then monitored over time so that new excess does not quietly accumulate.

The episode "Microsoft Entra as a Complete IAM Platform" places the product within the wider Microsoft Entra platform and presents it as a way to manage permissions across hybrid and multi-cloud environments. According to that episode, the tool gives complete visibility of permissions, makes it possible to spot unused or excessive permissions and remove them quickly, and in this way reduces the attack surface and helps keep data safe. In that framing, Permissions Management covers the entitlement side of identity, complementing other Entra capabilities that connect users, devices and apps.

Typical situations where the topic comes up include organizations that run workloads in more than one cloud and need a consistent way to review access, teams that want to find and remove permissions that are never used, and security or architecture discussions about limiting how much access any single identity holds. Decisions around the product usually involve which clouds and identities are in scope, how right-sizing is approached, and how ongoing monitoring fits into existing identity governance practices.

The product is closely related to other identity and governance topics covered by M365.FM. Several episodes list "Microsoft Entra Permissions Management - Simply Explained" as a related listen, including "Privileged Identity Management (PIM) - Simply Explained", "Azure Cost Management - Simply Explained" and "Microsoft Entra External ID - Simply Explained". These recommendations place it alongside privileged access management, cloud cost governance and external identity topics. According to the episode listings, the audience for this material includes Microsoft 365 administrators, architects, IT leaders and similar roles who want to understand how these services fit into the wider Microsoft ecosystem and where they can create practical value.

microsoft-entra-sign-in-logs.desc: Microsoft Entra sign-in logs record user and application sign-in attempts with status, error codes and Conditional Access results, and are the first stop for failed sign-ins.

faq.a: They record sign-in attempts to a tenant, capturing who signed in, with which client application and to which target resource, along with status, error codes and Conditional Access results. Entries are system-generated and cannot be changed or deleted.
faq.q: What do Microsoft Entra sign-in logs show?

faq.a: They are in the Microsoft Entra admin center under Monitoring and health. The minimum role named in Microsoft documentation is Reports Reader.
faq.q: Where are the sign-in logs found and who can view them?

faq.a: The preview experience separates interactive user sign-ins, non-interactive user sign-ins, service principal sign-ins and managed identity sign-ins. The legacy view shows only interactive user sign-ins.
faq.q: Which sign-in log types exist?

microsoft-entra-sign-in-logs.long:
Microsoft Entra sign-in logs are a set of activity logs in the Microsoft Entra admin center that record sign-in attempts to a tenant. They cover sign-ins to internal apps and resources, and each entry captures who signed in, with which client application and to which target resource. The logs include status information, error codes and Conditional Access results, which is why they are usually the starting point when a sign-in fails and an administrator needs to understand why. They belong to the broader Microsoft Entra topic area.

According to Microsoft documentation, the logs are used to analyze sign-in failures and patterns. Typical questions include how many users signed in to an application this week, how many sign-ins failed in the last 24 hours, which browsers or operating systems are in use, and which Azure resources were accessed by managed identities and service principals. Entries are generated by the system and cannot be changed or deleted, so they serve as a consistent record of sign-in activity. The logs also feed other Microsoft Entra features, including ID Protection and usage and insights reports.

The newer preview experience separates four log types: interactive user sign-ins, non-interactive user sign-ins, service principal sign-ins and managed identity sign-ins. The legacy view, by contrast, shows only interactive user sign-ins. This distinction matters in practice, because a failure may sit in a non-interactive or workload sign-in that the legacy view does not display. Filters can narrow the view to a user, application or time window, and agent logs cover agent activity. The logs are located in the Microsoft Entra admin center under Monitoring and health. The minimum role named in the documentation for viewing them is Reports Reader. The documentation page summarized here does not name license requirements, a retention period or export details, so those points should be checked separately before relying on the logs for long-term analysis.

Two M365.FM episodes mention the logs in the context of security work. In "Fix Microsoft Purview Information Protection Rollouts", the advice is to analyze Entra sign-in logs, use the 'What If' tool, and test new policies in report-only mode. The episode presents these steps as a way to find enforcement gaps and improve controls when a rollout does not behave as expected. The sign-in logs therefore support checking how Conditional Access policies actually applied to real sign-ins, rather than relying only on how the policies were intended to work.

In "When Microsoft Messaging Looks Secure but Isn't — Exchange Server, Hybrid and Microsoft 365 Security with Thomas Stensitzki [MVP]", the discussion covers Entra sign-in logs alongside suspicious sign-ins and impossible-travel alerts, as part of Microsoft Defender and security monitoring. The episode stresses that security tools and scores can guide decisions, but administrators still need to understand what each tool measures, what their licenses include and which protections their organization actually needs. Read together, the episodes position the sign-in logs as evidence for both troubleshooting and monitoring: they show what happened during a sign-in, and that record can be compared with the policies and alerts configured around it.

microsoft-entra-tenant-governance.desc: Microsoft Entra Tenant Governance is a Microsoft Entra capability for discovering related tenants, linking them through governance relationships and monitoring configuration drift.

faq.a: It provides visibility across an organization's tenants and helps keep them aligned with security and compliance requirements. It does this by discovering related tenants, establishing governance relationships, monitoring configuration and supporting secure tenant creation.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Entra Tenant Governance used for?

faq.a: According to the documentation, related tenants are detected through B2B access, multitenant applications and shared billing accounts.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Entra Tenant Governance find related tenants?

faq.a: No. The documentation describes the resource policy feature, still in preview, as acting only at request time: it evaluates Microsoft Graph requests and can block non-compliant changes, but it does not fix resources that already exist.
faq.q: Can the resource policy feature fix existing non-compliant resources?

microsoft-entra-tenant-governance.long:
Microsoft Entra Tenant Governance is a capability within Microsoft Entra that gives an organization visibility across all of its tenants and helps keep them aligned with security and compliance requirements. It addresses a common situation in larger organizations: several tenants exist side by side, for example after mergers, for sensitive workloads or for testing. Tenants created outside central oversight, often described as shadow IT tenants, are difficult to audit, and Tenant Governance is meant to bring them into view and under consistent control.

The capability has several parts. The first is discovery of related tenants. According to the documentation, related tenants are detected through B2B access, multitenant applications and shared billing accounts, so administrators can see which tenants are connected to their organization even if nobody registered them centrally.

The second part is governance relationships. These add invitation and approval workflows for cross-tenant administrator access, built on the least-privilege principle and supported by policy templates. Instead of granting administrator access between tenants informally, a relationship between the tenants is established through a defined process.

The third part is configuration management. Baselines are defined in a standard JSON format and describe the desired state. Monitors then run against these baselines and report drift, meaning deviations between the actual configuration and the desired one. Snapshots capture the current settings, and the documentation lists services such as Entra, Intune, Exchange Online, Teams, Purview and Defender as covered. This makes it possible to compare tenants against a common standard and to document the state of a configuration at a given point in time.

A fourth element is a resource policy feature, which is still in preview. It evaluates Microsoft Graph requests against policies and can block changes that do not comply. The documentation states a clear limit: it only acts at request time and does not fix existing resources. Non-compliant configurations that already exist therefore need to be found and corrected through other means, such as the drift monitoring described above.

Secure tenant creation completes the picture. When new tenants are created, a governance relationship can be attached automatically, so that new tenants do not start outside the governance structure. The service is offered in Basic and Premium tiers, and licensing details are documented separately by Microsoft, so planning a rollout includes checking which tier covers the required functions.

In practice, the capability is relevant for organizations that need to answer questions such as which tenants exist, who holds administrator access across them, and whether configurations match internal baselines. Typical decisions include which tenants to link first, which baselines to define, and whether to use the preview resource policy feature given its limits.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Entra Tenant Governance - Simply Explained" covers the topic as an introductory explanation. Its published show notes are brief and note that the episode includes AI-generated content, so they do not provide further detail beyond the topic itself. Tenant Governance is part of the broader Microsoft Entra family of identity and access capabilities.

microsoft-entra-verified-id.desc: Microsoft Entra Verified ID is a Microsoft service for issuing and verifying digital credentials that prove specific facts about a person, held in a wallet like Microsoft Authenticator.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft service for issuing and verifying digital credentials that prove specific facts about a person. The credentials are held in a wallet such as Microsoft Authenticator, and the product is part of Microsoft Entra.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Entra Verified ID?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Entra Verified ID - Simply Explained", passkeys and MFA help verify that someone controls a sign-in method but cannot prove real-world facts such as employment status or certifications. Verified ID credentials are meant to prove those facts.
faq.q: How does Verified ID differ from passkeys and MFA?

faq.a: The episode "Stop Deepfake Business Email Compromise with Verified ID" says the service enhances security by requiring proof of identity and authority for high-risk actions. It recommends combining this with verification steps in procedures, threat detection, monitoring and training.
faq.q: How is Verified ID relevant to deepfake business email compromise?

microsoft-entra-verified-id.long:
Microsoft Entra Verified ID is a Microsoft service for issuing and verifying digital credentials. A credential proves a specific fact about a person, and the holder keeps it in a wallet such as Microsoft Authenticator. The product is part of Microsoft Entra, the Microsoft identity and network access product family.

The service addresses a gap that sign-in methods leave open. According to the episode "Microsoft Entra Verified ID - Simply Explained", Microsoft Entra ID, passkeys and multi-factor authentication help confirm that someone controls a sign-in method, but they cannot prove real-world facts. The episode names examples such as employment status, completed security training, professional certifications, contractor relationships, and verified identity during account recovery. Verified ID is positioned as the layer that can carry this kind of proof, so that identity security extends beyond passwords and MFA.

The basic model has three roles: an issuer that creates a credential, a holder who stores it in a wallet, and a verifier who asks the holder to present it. Because the credential is held by the person in a wallet rather than looked up in a central directory at every request, the approach is described as decentralized. The episode "Microsoft Entra Private Access - Simply Explained" lists Entra Verified ID among the components of the Microsoft Entra family and describes it as providing decentralized, verifiable credentials to enhance security and privacy in identity verification.

One use highlighted in the episode "Microsoft Entra as a Complete IAM Platform" is verifying identities with confidence during onboarding and credential recovery. That episode says Microsoft Entra Verified ID offers advanced digital identity verification, including Face Check for real-time verification, and that it integrates with identity systems in over 190 countries. It also states that the service uses Azure AI services for facial identity verification, which is used when a user needs to prove who they are. These statements are attributed to the episode and describe how it presents the product within a wider IAM platform view.

Another scenario is defense against social engineering. The episode "Stop Deepfake Business Email Compromise with Verified ID" discusses deepfake business email compromise, where attackers imitate trusted people through realistic synthetic media. The episode says that Microsoft Entra Verified ID enhances security by requiring proof of identity and authority for high-risk actions. It pairs this with updated procedures that include verification steps for all types of communication, advanced threat detection tools that can identify unusual patterns, and continuous monitoring and training, since deepfake technology evolves quickly.

In practice, decisions around Verified ID tend to center on which facts are worth proving and who should issue and verify them. Candidates mentioned in the episodes include employment status, training completion, certifications, contractor relationships, onboarding identity checks, account recovery, and approval of high-risk requests. Verified ID is described as complementing, not replacing, Microsoft Entra ID, passkeys, MFA and Conditional Access, which continue to handle authentication and access decisions while credentials add verifiable claims about the person.

The M365.FM episodes treat Microsoft Entra Verified ID both as a standalone topic and as one component of the broader Microsoft Entra portfolio. Listeners who want a concise introduction can start with "Microsoft Entra Verified ID - Simply Explained", while the other episodes show how the product fits alongside identity governance, private access and IAM platform capabilities.

microsoft-fabric-apps.desc: Microsoft Fabric Apps are custom, AI-assisted web applications and dashboards built on Microsoft Fabric data, offered as an alternative or complement to Power BI reports.

faq.a: Microsoft Fabric Apps are custom, AI-assisted applications and dashboards built on Microsoft Fabric data. They are positioned as an alternative or complement to classic Power BI reports.
faq.q: What are Microsoft Fabric Apps?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Fabric Apps - Simply Explained", Fabric provides services such as servers, APIs, databases, authentication and hosting automatically. This lets developers focus on the business application instead of infrastructure.
faq.q: What does Fabric provide when building a Fabric App?

faq.a: The episode with Amit Chandak says semantic models can act as a reusable business layer between organizational data and multiple experiences. Fabric Apps, Data Agents and ontology-driven solutions can build on that layer.
faq.q: How do Fabric Apps relate to semantic models?

microsoft-fabric-apps.long:
Microsoft Fabric Apps are custom, AI-assisted applications and dashboards built on top of Microsoft Fabric data. Developed by Microsoft, they are part of Microsoft Fabric and belong to the analytics and BI tool category. They are positioned as an alternative or complement to classic Power BI reports, for situations where a purpose-built web application serves users better than a report page.

The core idea described in the M365.FM episode "Microsoft Fabric Apps - Simply Explained" is that data-driven web applications can be built directly inside Microsoft Fabric. Instead of managing servers, APIs, databases, authentication and hosting as separate concerns, Fabric provides these services automatically. Developers and data professionals can then concentrate on the business application itself rather than on infrastructure. According to the episode, a Fabric App can range from interactive dashboards to operational business applications, which lowers the barrier to building enterprise-grade solutions while keeping security, governance and scalability within the Microsoft ecosystem.

Because Fabric Apps sit on top of Fabric data, they connect naturally to what an organization already maintains there. A Semantic model is a typical foundation: it holds KPIs and business definitions in one place, and an app can present those definitions to users without redefining them. This is the same data layer that Power BI reports draw on, which is why Power BI is the closest related topic. A team that already has reports can treat Fabric Apps as a complementary way of delivering that data, for example when users need more interaction, workflow or a tailored interface than a standard report page offers.

The second episode, "Microsoft Fabric End-to-End: From Raw Data to Business Decisions with Amit Chandak [MVP]", places Fabric Apps in a wider architecture. The episode says that KPIs and business definitions encoded within a semantic model represent organizational knowledge, and that this knowledge can increasingly be consumed by experiences beyond traditional dashboards. Amit discusses how Data Agents, ontology-driven solutions and Fabric Apps can build on semantic models. In this view, the semantic model is not merely a Power BI component but a reusable business layer between organizational data and several human or AI-driven experiences.

The AI-assisted character of Fabric Apps links them to several related topics. Vibe coding describes building software by describing the desired result and letting AI generate the implementation, and Rayfin is listed as a related tool in this area. Microsoft 365 Copilot is related as part of the broader AI-assisted Microsoft environment. The sources do not detail how these pieces interact in practice, so decisions about which tool to use for a given task depend on the individual scenario.

Typical decisions around Fabric Apps concern when a classic Power BI report is sufficient and when a custom application is the better fit. Reports remain the established approach for analysis and sharing, while Fabric Apps address cases that call for an application experience built directly on Fabric data. Because hosting, authentication and related services are provided by the platform, the effort shifts from infrastructure to application design and to maintaining a well-governed semantic model underneath. Official documentation for Microsoft Fabric is available through Microsoft Learn.

microsoft-flow.desc: Microsoft Flow is the former name of Power Automate, the Microsoft workflow service renamed in November 2019 and still found in older documentation and searches.

faq.a: Microsoft Flow is the former name of Power Automate, a workflow service developed by Microsoft. It was renamed in November 2019 and continues as Power Automate.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Flow?

faq.a: Yes. Microsoft Flow, Flow and MS Flow are earlier names for the service now called Power Automate. Older documentation and community posts may still use the former names.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Flow the same as Power Automate?

faq.a: No. Episodes such as "Mail Flow Rules - Simply Explained" and "DP-600 Training 3/4: Data Flow, SQL, and Delta Optimization" only share the word flow. The workflow service itself is covered under Power Automate, for example in "Power Automate - Simply Explained".
faq.q: Do the M365.FM episodes about mail flow rules or data flows describe Microsoft Flow?

microsoft-flow.long:
Microsoft Flow is the former name of Power Automate, the workflow automation service developed by Microsoft. Microsoft renamed the service in November 2019, and the product continues today under the Power Automate name. The older names Flow, MS Flow and Microsoft Flow are still used in a large body of legacy material, including documentation, blog posts, connector names and community answers, which is why the term still turns up in searches.

The purpose of this entry is mainly to connect the old name with the current product. Microsoft Flow is an instance of a Microsoft tool and is directly related to Power Automate, which is the place where the service, its features and its further development are described. Anyone who reads a guide, forum thread or internal note that mentions Flow should treat it as a reference to Power Automate, while keeping in mind that the content may predate the rename and may therefore describe the service as it looked before November 2019.

In practice, the old name matters in a few situations. One is recognizing legacy flows and documentation: administrators and makers who inherit an environment may find assets, naming conventions or internal wikis that still talk about Microsoft Flow. Another is mapping older guidance to the current product during a migration or cleanup, so that advice written under the Flow name can be matched to the equivalent Power Automate capability. A third is simple search behavior: people who learned the product under its earlier name often continue to use it when looking for help.

How the service works is described under Power Automate. The episode "Power Automate - Simply Explained" describes it as a platform that helps automate repetitive tasks and streamline business processes, operating on a simple trigger-action model. Under that model, a trigger is defined that starts specific actions when a certain event occurs. The episode gives the example of a flow that sends a notification whenever an important email arrives. It also lists the main goals of Power Automate: automating routine processes to improve efficiency and improving employee productivity by streamlining time-consuming tasks. Because the product was formerly called Microsoft Flow, the word flow in this context refers to an automated workflow built in this service.

The word flow is also easy to confuse with unrelated Microsoft topics, and several episodes that surface for this term are not about the workflow service at all. "Mail Flow Rules - Simply Explained" covers Exchange mail transport rules that check every email between the send button and the inbox. "DP-600 Training 3/4: Data Flow, SQL, and Delta Optimization" discusses performance optimization for data flows and SQL queries, using tools such as the Monitoring Hub, DMVs and Query Insights. "Dynamics 365 Intelligent Order Management - Simply Explained" explains orchestration flows, which define how an order moves through an organization's process. These episodes share only the word flow with Microsoft Flow and should not be read as descriptions of the renamed product.

For current information on the service, its connectors and its capabilities, the Power Automate entry and the official Power Automate documentation from Microsoft are the appropriate references. This entry serves as a pointer: Microsoft Flow is the earlier name, Power Automate is the product as it exists today, and material that uses the old name should be interpreted with that history in mind.

microsoft-forms.desc: Microsoft Forms is a Microsoft 365 tool for building surveys, quizzes and polls whose responses flow into Excel, Power Automate and Teams.

faq.a: Microsoft Forms is used to create surveys, quizzes and polls. Typical uses named in the facts are feedback, registrations, knowledge checks and quick polls inside an organisation.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Forms used for?

faq.a: Responses flow into Excel, Power Automate and Teams. In Excel they can be analysed in a spreadsheet, and Power Automate can react to new responses to trigger follow-up actions.
faq.q: Where do Microsoft Forms responses go?

faq.a: No. Microsoft Forms is a survey and quiz tool included in Microsoft 365. Power Apps forms are a component of Power Apps that connect to data sources such as SharePoint lists, as covered in separate M365.FM episodes.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Forms the same as a Power Apps form?

microsoft-forms.long:
Microsoft Forms is a tool for creating surveys, quizzes and polls. It was developed by Microsoft, is part of Microsoft 365, and is included in the license. Microsoft classifies it as a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool. The product is also referred to simply as Forms. Its core purpose is to collect structured answers from people and make those answers easy to analyse or act on afterwards.

Typical uses are feedback collection, registrations, knowledge checks and quick polls inside an organisation. A form is built from questions, and the same building blocks can serve either as a survey or, when answers are scored, as a quiz. Because responses are stored in a structured way, they can be reviewed as they arrive rather than being gathered by hand from emails or chat messages.

The main value of Forms lies in where the responses go. Answers can flow into Microsoft Excel, where results can be evaluated in a spreadsheet. They can also be used with Power Automate, which can react to new responses and trigger automated follow-up actions. A form can also be shared with a team in Microsoft Teams, which keeps data collection close to the place where colleagues already work together. These three relationships are the ones the facts name explicitly: Microsoft Excel for analysis, Power Automate for automation, and Microsoft Teams for sharing.

The episode "Microsoft Forms - Simply Explained" presents Forms as the survey and quiz builder that many organisations already own. According to the episode description, it walks through the tool step by step: the tool you already own, building a first form, when a survey becomes a quiz, and branching, described as the form that rewrites itself depending on answers. It then covers collecting answers, answers that land in Excel by themselves, and letting Power Automate do the follow-up, and it also touches on the limits of the tool.

The decision around Forms is usually about fit. For short surveys, polls and quizzes where results should end up in Excel or start an automated process, a tool that is already included in Microsoft 365 can be a practical starting point. The episode's section on limits indicates that the tool is not meant for every scenario, so it is worth checking the requirements of a task against what Forms offers before building on it.

Other M365.FM episodes use the word form in a different sense. "Fix Power Apps Forms That Fail to Submit to SharePoint" deals with forms inside Power Apps, which depend on fields, data types and rules lining up with a SharePoint list. "Fix Power Apps After a Schema Change" and "Power Apps Galleries, Forms, and Screens - Simply Explained" also treat forms as a Power Apps component. These are separate from Microsoft Forms, which is a standalone survey and quiz tool, although both appear in the same ecosystem and can be combined with other Microsoft 365 services. Readers searching for Microsoft Forms should keep this distinction in mind to avoid mixing up the survey tool with Power Apps form controls.

microsoft-foundry.desc: Microsoft Foundry is Microsoft's paid platform for building, evaluating and operating AI applications and agents, formerly known as Azure AI Foundry.

faq.a: Microsoft Foundry is Microsoft's platform for building, evaluating and operating AI applications and agents. It combines a model catalog, an agent service, tools, evaluation and observability, and is part of Microsoft Azure.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Foundry?

faq.a: Yes. Microsoft Foundry was formerly known as Azure AI Foundry and, before that, as Azure AI Studio. The M365.FM episodes use these names interchangeably.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Foundry the same as Azure AI Foundry?

faq.a: Foundry Agent Service is part of the Foundry family and is the component for turning a model into an agent that performs tasks. The episode "Microsoft Foundry Agent Service - Simply Explained" covers its building blocks, including models, tools, knowledge and threads.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Foundry relate to Foundry Agent Service?

microsoft-foundry.long:
Microsoft Foundry is Microsoft's platform for building, evaluating and operating AI applications and agents. It brings a model catalog, an agent service, tools, evaluation and observability into one environment, so that teams do not have to assemble these pieces from separate services. The product was formerly called Azure AI Foundry and, before that, Azure AI Studio; all three names appear in the M365.FM episodes. It is a paid product, developed by Microsoft and part of Microsoft Azure.

The platform is aimed at developers, architects and IT professionals who want to move from experimenting with models to running AI solutions that do real work. The episode "Microsoft Foundry Agent Service - Simply Explained" makes this point directly: the Foundry catalog holds more than ten thousand AI models, but that number only matters if a model can be turned into something that actually performs tasks. The Foundry Agent Service is the part of the platform that addresses this. According to the episode, it is built around ideas such as models as a swappable brain, tools and knowledge that let an agent take action, and threads that keep track of a conversation.

Foundry is related to several other Microsoft products and technologies. Foundry Agent Service and Foundry Local belong to the Foundry family. Azure OpenAI Service is the related offering for access to models.
