Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are commonly used to give an AI agent access to tools, Azure Logic Apps can supply workflows, and GitHub Copilot supports the developer side of building. Microsoft Agent 365 comes into play when agents need to be managed after they are built. In this way Foundry sits between model access, agent construction and operational control.

The M365.FM episodes look at the platform from several perspectives. "Microsoft Foundry AI Apps with Jannik Reinhard [MVP]" discusses the vision behind Foundry, the developer experience it enables, and how Microsoft combines AI models, orchestration, security and related capabilities for building AI-powered apps and services. "From Data to Intelligent Agents: Building Trusted Enterprise AI with Microsoft AI Foundry with Shubhangi Goyal [MVP]" describes the shift from simple chatbots to intelligent agents that automate business processes and reason over enterprise data. The episode says that successful AI projects begin with a strong data foundation, meaning clean, governed and well-connected enterprise data.

A different angle comes from "Beyond Copilot: Building AI That Works in the Real World with Azure AI Foundry and Agentic AI for Frontline Workers with Fergus Kidd [MVP]". It argues that enterprise AI should reach beyond knowledge workers at desks and support frontline roles, with examples such as access to parts and pricing information for maintenance staff or safety procedures and inspection workflows for a wind-farm inspector. The same episode stresses that the worker does not need to understand the underlying architecture.

Governance is a recurring theme. "Prevent Shadow IT in Microsoft Foundry AI Agent Programs" warns that Foundry behaves like an agent factory and therefore needs governance before execution rather than after agents are already running. Related episodes listed alongside the introductory material include "Production AI Agents with Microsoft Foundry and Edgar McOchieng [MVP]", which covers building and deploying production-grade agents, and "Build Reliable Intune and Entra ID Agents with Azure AI Foundry".

Typical decisions around Foundry therefore include which models to use from the catalog, which tools and knowledge sources an agent may access, how agents are evaluated and observed in operation, and how the resulting agent program is governed. The official documentation for the product is published on Microsoft Learn under the Azure AI Foundry documentation area.

microsoft-graph-activity-logs.desc: Microsoft Graph activity logs record the HTTP requests Microsoft Graph processes for a tenant and can be exported through Azure Monitor diagnostic settings.

faq.a: They record the HTTP requests that the Microsoft Graph service receives and processes for a tenant, including app and user identity, request URI and method, response status, scopes and roles, and conditional access status.
faq.q: What do Microsoft Graph activity logs record?

faq.a: A tenant administrator enables them through diagnostic settings in Azure Monitor. Destinations are a Log Analytics workspace, an Azure storage account, or an Event Hubs namespace for streaming to external SIEM tools.
faq.q: How are Microsoft Graph activity logs enabled and where can they be sent?

faq.a: A Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 license, a supported admin role such as Security Administrator, and an Azure subscription with a destination. Diagnostic settings cannot filter the data, and only activity in the resource tenant is recorded.
faq.q: What is needed to use Microsoft Graph activity logs?

microsoft-graph-activity-logs.long:
Microsoft Graph activity logs are an audit trail of the HTTP requests that the Microsoft Graph service receives and processes for a tenant. They show which applications call which endpoints, by which identity, and with what outcome. The logs are part of Microsoft Graph and are used mainly for security monitoring, investigation and tenant-wide visibility into API usage.

The logs capture traffic from line-of-business apps, API clients, SDKs, AI clients and Microsoft apps such as Outlook and Teams. They are not enabled by default in a way that makes them queryable on their own: tenant administrators turn them on through diagnostic settings in Azure Monitor. From there, the data can be sent to a Log Analytics workspace, an Azure storage account, or an Event Hubs namespace for streaming to external SIEM tools. Records land in the MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs table, with fields for the app and user identity, request URI and method, response status, scopes and roles, client authentication method and conditional access status.

Typical uses include tracing what a specific app did, investigating the activity of a compromised account, reviewing unexpected privileged application permissions, and spotting unusual call volumes. Because every request is recorded with its identity and target, the logs help answer questions such as which service principal read which resources, from which IP address, and with which permissions.

Setup has a few prerequisites. A Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 license is required, along with a supported admin role such as Security Administrator, and an Azure subscription that hosts the chosen destination. Several limits matter when planning a deployment: only activity in the resource tenant is recorded, and diagnostic settings cannot filter the data, so the full stream is exported to whichever destination is selected. Request URIs are logged, so secrets must not be stored in directory attributes, since they could appear in the log data.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Graph Security Automation for Microsoft 365" covers the logs in the context of analyzing access patterns to identify potential security breaches. The episode describes using KQL (Kusto Query Language) against the MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs table, which it presents as an audit trail of HTTP requests processed by Microsoft Graph. It names the key columns for detection as AppId, IPAddress, RequestId, RequestMethod, RequestUri, Roles, Scopes, ServicePrincipalId, UserAgent and UserId. It also suggests using the parse_url() function to extract parameters from the RequestUri for more detailed analysis, and summarizing request statistics as part of the investigation.

In practice, the main decisions around Microsoft Graph activity logs concern the destination and the queries built on top of them. A Log Analytics workspace suits interactive KQL analysis and alerting, a storage account suits retention, and Event Hubs suits forwarding to an external SIEM. Because the export cannot be filtered at the diagnostic-settings level, any narrowing of the data happens later, at query or processing time.

microsoft-graph-data-connect.desc: Microsoft Graph Data Connect extracts Microsoft 365 datasets in bulk on a schedule into Azure storage for analytics, after admin approval of each request.

faq.a: It is a part of Microsoft Graph that extracts Microsoft 365 datasets in bulk on a schedule into Azure storage for analytics. Each data request must be approved by an administrator before extraction.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Graph Data Connect?

faq.a: The Graph API is queried one request at a time, while Data Connect exports large volumes of data as datasets into analytics platforms such as Microsoft Fabric, Azure Synapse Analytics or Azure Data Factory. The episodes also note that it has different throttling constraints for bulk operations.
faq.q: How does Data Connect differ from the Microsoft Graph API?

faq.a: It is used to feed reporting, business intelligence, AI and machine learning workloads with Microsoft 365 data. The episode "Enterprise Microsoft 365 Analytics with Graph Data Connect" describes it as a way to get complete, governed data instead of throttled or partial exports.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Graph Data Connect used for?

microsoft-graph-data-connect.long:
Microsoft Graph Data Connect is a part of Microsoft Graph that exports Microsoft 365 data in bulk into Azure storage so that organizations can analyze it at scale. It extracts datasets on a schedule, and each data request requires approval by an administrator before extraction can take place. It is positioned as an enterprise-scale data export solution for Microsoft 365 rather than a way to read individual items one at a time.

The central difference from the standard Microsoft Graph API is the access pattern. With the Graph API, an application queries data one request at a time. Data Connect instead delivers large volumes of data as datasets, which can then be loaded into analytics platforms. The sources name Microsoft Fabric, Azure Synapse Analytics and Azure Data Factory as typical destinations. From there the data can feed reporting, business intelligence, AI and machine learning workloads. The destination is Azure storage, so the data lands in an environment the organization controls and can process with its usual analytics tooling.

The administrator approval step is a core part of how the service works. Each request for data is reviewed and approved before extraction runs, which places governance at the point where data leaves Microsoft 365. This supports the idea, described in the episodes, of moving complete and governed data into analytics rather than relying on partial snapshots.

Typical situations for Data Connect arise when teams need more than the usual administrative tools can provide. The episode "Enterprise Microsoft 365 Analytics with Graph Data Connect" describes a common problem: big decisions made on small slices of Microsoft 365 data, caused by throttled exports, missing fields, short retention and brittle PowerShell scripts. The episode argues that traditional Office 365 APIs and admin exports were not built for enterprise analytics, and presents Data Connect as a way to move complete, governed data covering areas such as mail, Teams, SharePoint and audits into an analytics environment.

The design decision usually comes down to scale. In the episode "Microsoft Graph Automation Architecture: Beyond Scripts", Data Connect is recommended for large-scale operations because it handles bulk data extraction and has different throttling constraints from the regular API. The same episode lists practical measures for the request-based API, such as retry logic with exponential backoff, spreading calls to avoid bursts, delta queries for efficient scanning and service prioritization to reduce throttling risk. Data Connect is named as the option for bulk operations when those measures are not enough.

Data Connect sits within the wider Microsoft Graph platform. The episode "Microsoft Graph: The Enterprise Nervous System" lists it among Microsoft Graph capabilities, described as a way to build applications using Microsoft Graph Data Connect, alongside areas such as Outlook calendar and mail, Teams collaboration and Microsoft 365 Copilot connectors. The episode "How Microsoft Graph Connects Microsoft 365 Data and Context" points to related material, including "Microsoft Graph Data Connect - Simply Explained", "Find Missing Microsoft 365 Compliance Data with Graph" and "Microsoft Graph Connectors - Simply Explained".

The episode "Microsoft Graph Data Connect - Simply Explained" gives the overview in plain terms: a secure, bulk export path for Microsoft 365 data into analytics platforms, aimed at reporting, business intelligence, AI and machine learning. Official documentation for the product is available through Microsoft Learn under the Microsoft Graph Data Connect concept overview.

microsoft-graph-permissions.desc: Microsoft Graph permissions, or scopes, define what an app may access in Microsoft Graph, split into delegated and application (app-only) types.

faq.a: Delegated permissions let an app act on behalf of a signed-in user, while application (app-only) permissions let an app act with its own identity without a signed-in user. Application permissions often require administrator consent.
faq.q: What is the difference between delegated and application permissions in Microsoft Graph?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Graph Permissions and Consent Models Explained" says the cause is usually consent rather than code. Development tenants allow broad testing, while production tenants enforce policies that block risky scopes.
faq.q: Why do Microsoft Graph apps often fail at rollout?

faq.a: The episode recommends requesting the minimum viable scopes that match how the app actually runs, and documenting the granted permissions with their justification and approval records.
faq.q: How should an app choose which Microsoft Graph permissions to request?

microsoft-graph-permissions.long:
Microsoft Graph permissions, also called scopes, define what an app is allowed to access when it calls Microsoft Graph. They are the mechanism that decides which data and operations an application can reach, and they sit at the center of how apps are authorized against Microsoft 365 resources. The topic belongs to the broader subject of Microsoft Graph, and the official documentation describes it in its permissions overview.

Two permission models are in use. Delegated permissions let an app act on behalf of a signed-in user, so the app works in the context of that user. Application permissions, also called app-only permissions, let an app act with its own identity, without a signed-in user, and they apply across the organization rather than to one person's data. Application permissions often require administrator consent, which is why consent is a frequent point of friction when an app moves from development to production.

Choosing between the two models depends on how the app actually runs. An app that works with a user present, for example reading that user's own data after sign-in, fits the delegated model. A background service or automation job that runs without anyone signed in fits the application model. The episode "Microsoft Graph Permissions and Consent Models Explained" says that most Graph-powered apps fail at rollout not because of code but because of consent. It describes development tenants as allowing broad testing, while production tenants enforce tighter policies that block risky scopes. Its recommended approach is to understand the delegated and application models and to request the minimum viable scopes that match how the app really works.

The same episode lists several governance practices: document the granted Microsoft Graph API permissions together with their justification and approval records, watch for excessive permission usage, and train developers and administrators on the permission and consent model and on secure handling of credentials. These steps treat permissions as something that needs ongoing review rather than a one-time setup.

The topic appears in other M365.FM episodes as a practical prerequisite. In "Migrate Exchange Web Services to Microsoft Graph with Glen Scales [MVP]", the section on permissions and authentication states that moving to Microsoft Graph requires rethinking how apps handle permissions, and that Microsoft Graph uses a different permissions model than Exchange Web Services or Azure AD Graph. The episode notes that application permissions allow an app to access resources without a signed-in user.

In "Audit SharePoint Online Permissions at Scale", an Azure Automation account needs the right Microsoft Graph permissions to read and write data when runbooks collect information from SharePoint sites. In "Connect External Business Data with Microsoft 365 Copilot Connectors", building a custom connector involves registering an application and then granting admin consent for the required Microsoft Graph permissions in the Microsoft Entra admin center. The episode describes this as the step that ensures only authorized users and apps can access organizational data, and it advises reviewing permissions before connecting new data sources. Finally, "Fix Failed Microsoft 365 Copilot Rollouts" lists confirming that the required Microsoft Graph permissions and API access are provisioned and audited as part of the prerequisites for a Copilot rollout.

Taken together, these episodes treat Microsoft Graph permissions as a design and governance decision: pick the model that matches the app's runtime behavior, request only what is needed, obtain the appropriate consent, and keep a record of what was granted and why.

microsoft-graph-powershell.desc: Microsoft Graph PowerShell is a PowerShell SDK that wraps the Microsoft Graph APIs and replaces the retired Azure AD PowerShell and MSOnline modules.

faq.a: It is a PowerShell SDK that wraps the Microsoft Graph APIs and is used to manage Microsoft Entra ID and other Microsoft 365 services. It replaces the retired Azure AD PowerShell and MSOnline modules.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Graph PowerShell?

faq.a: It replaces the retired Azure AD PowerShell and MSOnline modules. The episode "Run Your Full Stack Locally with .NET Aspire" also lists ExchangeOnline among the legacy modules the SDK is replacing.
faq.q: Which older modules does Microsoft Graph PowerShell replace?

faq.a: The episodes stress understanding OAuth, delegated and application permissions, service principals and least-privilege access, and scoping permissions tightly instead of granting broad tenant-wide rights. They also recommend version control, testing, logging and approval workflows.
faq.q: What should be considered when automating with Microsoft Graph PowerShell?

microsoft-graph-powershell.long:
Microsoft Graph PowerShell is a PowerShell SDK that wraps the Microsoft Graph APIs. It is used to manage Microsoft Entra ID and other Microsoft 365 services from scripts and the command line, and it replaces the retired Azure AD PowerShell and MSOnline modules. It is part of Microsoft Graph, the unified API layer that sits behind many of the admin tools administrators already use in the portals.

The main purpose of the SDK is to give administrators a single, consistent way to automate work across the Microsoft ecosystem. Because Microsoft Graph exposes identities, users, groups, Teams, SharePoint, security, compliance and business data through one interface, the SDK lets a script touch several of these areas without switching between separate legacy modules. The episode "Microsoft Graph and PowerShell for Enterprise Automation" describes this as a way to automate repetitive tasks, manage large environments consistently, and build governance processes that cannot be achieved through manual portal administration.

The transition away from older modules is a recurring theme. The episode "Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK - Simply Explained" states that Microsoft retired two of the admin modules that PowerShell scripts relied on for years, and describes the replacement as friendlier than it sounds. The episode "Secure Azure Automation with Ahmed Uzejnovic [MVP]" also covers the move from the legacy AzureAD and MSOnline modules toward Microsoft Graph PowerShell and API-driven automation. A further episode, "Run Your Full Stack Locally with .NET Aspire", notes that the SDK is replacing many legacy modules, including MSOnline, AzureAD and ExchangeOnline, and exposes unified Graph API capabilities that allow richer automation and reporting.

Security and authentication are central to using the SDK. According to "Microsoft Graph and PowerShell for Enterprise Automation", understanding authentication, OAuth, delegated and application permissions, service principals and least-privilege access is essential for building secure enterprise automation. The episode "Secure Azure Automation with Ahmed Uzejnovic [MVP]" adds that, rather than giving automation tools broad tenant-wide permissions, organizations should isolate workloads, scope permissions tightly, and continuously monitor automated actions. It presents modern automation as an engineering discipline that requires version control, testing, logging, approval workflows and governance, and describes reusable automation frameworks as safer and more scalable than one-off administrative scripts.

For unattended scenarios, the episode "Use Managed Identity with PowerShell for Microsoft Graph" walks through preparing the system and environment so that scripts can access Microsoft Graph resources securely. It names the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK as the source of the cmdlets needed for this integration and lists requirements to check before installing: PowerShell version 7 or higher, .NET Framework 4.7.2 or later on macOS, an updated PowerShellGet, and a suitable execution policy. The aim of this preparation, the episode says, is smooth execution and secure access.

Typical decisions around the SDK include which permission model to use (delegated or application), how to scope permissions to the minimum needed, how to run scripts without stored secrets, and how to migrate existing scripts built on the retired modules. The episode "Run Your Full Stack Locally with .NET Aspire" also mentions that PowerShell can support cross-tenant and delegated-administrator operations, which it says makes multi-tenant orchestration for managed service providers more powerful than the graphical interface allows.

Official documentation for the SDK is published on Microsoft Learn under the Microsoft Graph PowerShell overview. Together, the episodes position Microsoft Graph PowerShell as the current scripting route to Microsoft Graph for Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Entra ID administration, with an emphasis on secure, governed and maintainable automation.

microsoft-graph-schema-extensions.desc: Microsoft Graph schema extensions add strongly typed, discoverable custom data to supported Microsoft Graph resources, defined once and usable by authorized apps in a tenant.

faq.a: They are a Microsoft Graph mechanism for adding strongly typed, discoverable custom data to supported Graph resources. The schema is defined once and can then be used by authorized apps in a tenant.
faq.q: What are Microsoft Graph schema extensions?

faq.a: Schema extensions are part of Microsoft Graph, where they extend supported resources with custom properties. Microsoft Graph is the broader topic under which this concept falls.
faq.q: How do schema extensions relate to Microsoft Graph?

faq.a: Microsoft documents the schemaExtension resource and its API operations on Microsoft Learn, in the Microsoft Graph API reference.
faq.q: Where is the official documentation for schema extensions?

microsoft-graph-schema-extensions.long:
Microsoft Graph schema extensions are a mechanism within Microsoft Graph for attaching custom data to supported Graph resources. Each extension is defined once as a schema, and the resulting custom properties are strongly typed and discoverable, rather than being stored as untyped or ad hoc values.

Once a schema extension has been defined, authorized apps in a tenant can use it to read and write the custom data on the resources it supports. This makes schema extensions a way to extend the shared Microsoft Graph data model with application-specific or organization-specific attributes while keeping the structure of that data explicit and consistent across the apps that rely on it.

Schema extensions sit under the broader topic of Microsoft Graph, the API surface used to work with data across the Microsoft ecosystem. They are one of several extensibility options for adding custom data to Graph resources, and they are described as a distinct resource type in the official Microsoft Graph documentation, which covers the schemaExtension resource and its API operations.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

microsoft-graph-security-api.desc: The Microsoft Graph security API is a single programmatic interface in Microsoft Graph that connects Microsoft security providers, for example to retrieve alerts or stream them to SIEM tools.

faq.a: It is a single programmatic interface within Microsoft Graph that connects multiple Microsoft security providers. It can be used, for example, to retrieve alerts or to stream them to SIEM tools.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft Graph security API?

faq.a: The episode "How Microsoft Graph Connects Microsoft 365 Data and Context" lists Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Identity, Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention and Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management, plus legacy alerts as the first generation of alerts in the API.
faq.q: Which alert sources does the Microsoft Graph security API aggregate?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Graph Security Automation for Microsoft 365", it enriches alerts with contextual information and automates security operations, for example automating access reviews and integrating compliance workflows. The episode "Graph API - Simply Explained" also names detecting unusual logins or suspicious behavior as a use case.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft Graph security API used for in automation?

microsoft-graph-security-api.long:
The Microsoft Graph security API is a programmatic interface that is part of Microsoft Graph and connects multiple Microsoft security providers behind one access point. According to the product description, it can be used to retrieve alerts or to stream them to SIEM tools. Instead of integrating each security product separately, a developer or security team works against a single, standardized interface that exposes security information from several sources.

The main purpose of the Microsoft Graph security API is to bring security alerts and threat intelligence from different sources into one consistent model. An episode titled "How Microsoft Graph Connects Microsoft 365 Data and Context" lists the kinds of services whose alerts are aggregated, including Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Microsoft Defender for Identity, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention and Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management. The same episode also mentions legacy alerts, described as the first generation of alerts in the Microsoft Graph security API. The episode says this aggregation gives a unified view of an organization's security posture.

A recurring theme in the episodes is consistency. The episode "How Microsoft Graph Connects Microsoft 365 Data and Context" states that Microsoft Graph ensures data from Teams, SharePoint and Exchange Online appears in a consistent format, and that this makes it easier to automate workflows and build reliable solutions. For the security API specifically, the episode "Microsoft Graph Security Automation for Microsoft 365" describes it as providing a standard interface to integrate security alerts and threat intelligence from multiple sources. It says this integration enriches alerts with contextual information and automates security operations.

Typical situations for using the Microsoft Graph security API center on automation and monitoring. The episode "Microsoft Graph Security Automation for Microsoft 365" gives examples such as automating access reviews and integrating compliance workflows, which it connects to meeting regulatory requirements like GDPR and HIPAA. The episode "Graph API - Simply Explained" names security monitoring as one of several Microsoft Graph use cases and says the Graph Security API can be used to detect unusual logins or flag suspicious behavior. In that episode, this sits alongside other scenarios such as onboarding automation, custom dashboards and meeting analytics.

Because the Microsoft Graph security API is part of Microsoft Graph, it follows the same overall approach as the wider platform: one API surface that gives access to data and context across Microsoft 365 services. Decisions around it usually concern which security providers to bring together, whether alerts should be pulled on demand or streamed to a SIEM tool, and how the aggregated alert data feeds into existing automation and compliance workflows. The official documentation provides an overview of the concepts behind the API for those who want to go deeper.

In summary, the Microsoft Graph security API acts as a unifying layer for security information in the Microsoft ecosystem. It is described in the episodes as a way to aggregate alerts from several Defender and Purview services, enrich them with context, and use them in automated security and compliance processes, all through the interface provided by Microsoft Graph.

microsoft-graph-toolkit.desc: Microsoft Graph Toolkit (MGT) is a set of reusable, framework-agnostic web components and authentication providers for building apps that work with Microsoft Graph.

faq.a: Microsoft Graph Toolkit (MGT) is a set of reusable, framework-agnostic web components and authentication providers for working with Microsoft Graph.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Graph Toolkit (MGT)?

faq.a: It can be used in web apps, Teams tabs and SharePoint web parts.
faq.q: Where can Microsoft Graph Toolkit (MGT) be used?

faq.a: Microsoft Graph Toolkit (MGT) is part of Microsoft Graph and provides components and authentication providers for building solutions that work with it.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Graph Toolkit (MGT) relate to Microsoft Graph?

microsoft-graph-toolkit.long:
Microsoft Graph Toolkit (MGT) is a collection of reusable, framework-agnostic web components together with authentication providers. It is designed for working with Microsoft Graph and is part of the wider Microsoft Graph ecosystem.

The components can be used in several kinds of solutions, including web apps, Teams tabs and SharePoint web parts. Because the components are framework-agnostic, they are not tied to a single front-end framework. The authentication providers handle sign-in and access to Microsoft Graph, so that the components can retrieve and display data on behalf of a user.

Microsoft Graph Toolkit (MGT) belongs to Microsoft Graph, the API layer for accessing data and services across Microsoft 365. Within that relationship, the toolkit serves as a UI and authentication layer on top of the underlying Graph APIs, giving developers prebuilt building blocks rather than requiring each interface element to be written from scratch.

No specific M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no official documentation or site links are listed in the available information.

microsoft-hololens.desc: Microsoft HoloLens is a mixed reality headset that overlays holograms on the physical world, used in enterprise settings such as training, guided work and remote assistance.

faq.a: Microsoft HoloLens is a mixed reality headset developed by Microsoft that overlays holograms on the physical world. It was used in enterprise scenarios such as training and field work.
faq.q: What is Microsoft HoloLens?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, HoloLens 2 includes Dynamics 365 Guides for learning new skills and Dynamics 365 Remote Assist for working with remote experts through Teams.
faq.q: Which software comes preinstalled on HoloLens 2?

faq.a: The episode with Fergus Kidd names cost, hardware fragility, difficult app integration and unclear business value as factors. It adds that in settings where devices can be dropped or used with PPE, a premium headset with a steep learning curve may be hard to justify.
faq.q: Why did HoloLens struggle in enterprise use according to the M365.FM episodes?

microsoft-hololens.long:
Microsoft HoloLens is a mixed reality headset developed by Microsoft that overlays holograms on the physical world. It was used mainly in enterprise scenarios such as training and field work, where people needed information or instructions placed directly in their line of sight while their hands stayed free for the task.

The hardware is described in Microsoft Learn documentation for HoloLens 2, the second-generation device. It is an untethered holographic computer that continues the first-generation HoloLens and runs the Windows Holographic operating system, a variant of Windows 10. The headset has a flip-up visor that holds the sensors and see-through holographic lenses, a headband with an adjustment wheel, buttons for brightness, volume and power, and a USB-C port. Its sensor set includes cameras for head tracking, infrared cameras for eye tracking, a time-of-flight depth sensor, an inertial measurement unit and an 8-megapixel camera. The device runs on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 850 chip with a second-generation holographic processing unit, and the documentation states an active battery life of two to three hours.

Interaction with HoloLens 2 relies on fully articulated two-handed tracking, real-time eye tracking and voice commands, while the headset builds a live mesh of the surrounding space. Natural-language voice input through Cortana needs an internet connection. A user account is required, the documentation says the device is not intended for children under 13, and the eye protection only meets basic impact ratings. These points matter when organizations consider using the headset on a shop floor or in similar environments.

HoloLens 2 ships with preinstalled business software. Dynamics 365 Guides is included for learning new skills, and Dynamics 365 Remote Assist is included for working with remote experts through Teams. These two applications reflect the typical use of the headset: step-by-step instructions anchored in the real workplace, and live help from a person who is somewhere else.

The M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Guides - Simply Explained" covers this use in plain English. It explains what the mixed reality application was designed to solve, how Microsoft HoloLens brought instructions into the physical workplace, how companies could capture expert knowledge, how Microsoft Teams enabled remote assistance, and how Dynamics 365, Dataverse, Power Platform, Power BI and AI could extend the experience. The episode also raises a strategic issue for organizations: according to its description, Microsoft has set December 31, 2026 as the end-of-availability date for Dynamics 365 Guides, which is relevant to anyone who built processes around the headset and the application.

The episode "Beyond Copilot: Building AI That Works in the Real World with Azure AI Foundry and Agentic AI for Frontline Workers with Fergus Kidd [MVP]" looks at why HoloLens, VR and consumer glasses struggled in enterprise settings. The discussion between Fergus Kidd and Mirko Peters names cost, hardware fragility, difficult app integration and unclear business value as factors. The episode points out that in industries where a device can be dropped, damaged or used while wearing PPE, a premium headset with a steep learning curve may be hard to justify. It contrasts this with approaches in which technology disappears into the workflow, for example by letting a worker talk to an AI assistant, call a manager through Teams, capture evidence, scan a code or document a repair without stopping the physical task.

Taken together, the sources describe Microsoft HoloLens as a capable but specialized device: a sensor-rich headset with hands, eye and voice input, paired with Dynamics 365 Guides and Remote Assist, whose enterprise adoption was shaped by cost, durability and the availability of the surrounding software.

microsoft-ignite.desc: Microsoft Ignite is Microsoft's annual conference for developers, IT professionals and partners, formerly known as TechEd and renamed Ignite from 2015.
microsoft-ignite.long:
Microsoft Ignite is Microsoft's annual conference for developers, IT professionals and partners. The event is the successor to TechEd, which held its first edition in 1993 in Orlando. After the 2014 TechEd in Barcelona, Microsoft adopted the Ignite name from 2015. From 2024 the former partner event Microsoft Inspire was merged into Ignite, so that a single event now serves both audiences.

In practice, Microsoft Ignite is a place to follow Microsoft's platform news, learn technical practices and meet other professionals. Editions typically run three to five days and combine several formats: presentations, whiteboard sessions, hands-on labs, access to experts and MVPs, and an exhibition area. A large session catalog is published in advance, which allows attendees to plan their schedule around the topics that matter to their role, whether that is development, IT administration or partner business.

The event has taken place in different cities and formats over time. The North American editions include Chicago in May 2015, Atlanta in September 2016, and Orlando from 2017 to 2019. Digital events followed in 2020 and 2021, a hybrid edition took place in Seattle in 2022, and Seattle hosted again in 2023. Chicago hosted the November 2024 edition, and a hybrid event at Moscone Center in San Francisco was held in November 2025. Before the Ignite name, regional TechEd editions ran in Africa, Australia, India, Israel, Latin America, the Middle East, New Zealand and Europe. Since 2020 the event has increasingly offered digital or hybrid participation, and the host city changes almost every year.

For professionals deciding how to use the event, the format determines the approach. The session catalog lets attendees prepare in advance, hands-on labs support practical learning, and expert and MVP access offers a way to ask questions directly. The exhibition area is a place to meet partners and vendors. Because digital and hybrid participation is available, attendance does not necessarily require travel.

Microsoft Ignite also appears as a learning resource in M365.FM content. The episode "D365FO Integration Architecture with Anitha Eswaran [MVP-MCT]" lists Microsoft Ignite in a table of resource types for staying current, under webinars and events, alongside user groups. The listed benefit is the latest trends and networking. The episode's accompanying tip is to bookmark favorite resources and visit them regularly to keep knowledge current. In that context the episode frames the D365FO integration strategy as a living process that needs continuous improvement, because technology and business needs change quickly and integrations must adapt to keep up.

Taken together, Microsoft Ignite serves as a recurring checkpoint for people working in the Microsoft ecosystem. It brings together learning content, direct contact with experts and community members, and a partner audience in one annual event, and it is one of several ways, alongside documentation and community forums, to keep skills and strategies up to date.

microsoft-information-protection.desc: Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) is Microsoft's framework for classifying, labeling and protecting sensitive data, now known as Microsoft Purview Information Protection.

faq.a: It is Microsoft's framework for classifying, labeling and protecting sensitive data, now known as Microsoft Purview Information Protection. It applies labels and protection such as encryption, access restrictions and visual marking across Microsoft 365 apps and services, on-premises systems and endpoints.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Information Protection (MIP)?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes describe MIP as integrating with DLP policies. Sensitivity labels aligned with MIP are set up as part of a DLP rollout, and the labels help DLP decide how labeled content is handled.
faq.q: How does MIP relate to data loss prevention (DLP)?

faq.a: According to the episode "Secure and Govern Microsoft 365 Copilot", MIP labels are enforced when Copilot processes or returns data, so Copilot may surface only appropriately labeled content. Another episode also names MIP for Dataverse as a control for discovering and classifying sensitive data.
faq.q: What role does MIP play with Microsoft Copilot?

microsoft-information-protection.long:
Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) is Microsoft's framework for classifying, labeling and protecting sensitive data. It is now known as Microsoft Purview Information Protection. The term covers a set of solutions and tools that help organizations find sensitive information, assign classifications to it, and apply protection so that the data remains controlled wherever it is stored or used.

According to the M365.FM episode "Fix Microsoft Purview Information Protection Rollouts", MIP helps classify, label and protect sensitive information across Microsoft 365 apps and services, on-premises systems and endpoints. Protection is applied through labels and can include encryption, access restrictions and visual marking. The same episode explains that MIP integrates with data loss prevention (DLP) policies, which is how it contributes to preventing data loss: labels and protection settings give DLP a consistent basis for deciding how content may be handled.

In practice, MIP is the classification and labeling layer on which other controls build. The episode "Configure Microsoft 365 DLP Policies in Purview" lists establishing data classification and sensitivity labels aligned with Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) as one of the early steps in a DLP rollout. Further steps named there include inventorying data locations such as Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, endpoints and third-party integrations, and mapping sensitive information types and custom detectors such as regex patterns, dictionaries and keywords. DLP policies are then created with scopes, conditions, actions and overrides. The episode recommends starting in test or audit mode to validate detections and limit user disruption before any blocking actions are enforced.

MIP also matters for generative AI scenarios. The episode "Secure and Govern Microsoft 365 Copilot" states that MIP classifies and labels content and that these labels are enforced when Copilot processes or returns data. As described there, this means Copilot may surface only appropriately labeled content, supports data loss prevention and integrates with compliance tools, so that data security and compliance are maintained when Copilot operates within the Microsoft 365 environment. The same episode discusses limiting access to data sources, applying DLP policies, and making sure AI agents and Copilot Studio configurations comply with the enterprise security posture and governance controls.

The episode "How to Govern Microsoft Copilot in the Enterprise" extends the topic to the Power Platform. It names the use of Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) for Dataverse to discover and classify sensitive data as one of several governance controls. Others mentioned alongside it include advanced connector policies to control data flows between Copilot and other services, sharing limits to reduce the risk of oversharing, and monitoring of agent protection status with remediation guidance. These controls are presented as ways to enforce governance policies and keep the environment secure.

The typical decisions around MIP concern scope and sequencing: which data locations to cover, which sensitivity labels to define, which sensitive information types are relevant to the organization, and how to introduce enforcement gradually. The episode "Fix Microsoft Purview Information Protection Rollouts" frames labeling as part of a broader rollout that also involves a continuous improvement process, which suggests that label taxonomies and policies are expected to be reviewed and adjusted over time rather than set once.

Because the product is now named Microsoft Purview Information Protection, documentation and episodes may use either name. Both refer to the same area: classifying, labeling and protecting sensitive data across Microsoft 365 and connected environments.

microsoft-learn.desc: Microsoft Learn is Microsoft's free learning platform with modules and learning paths on Microsoft products, usable as a content source in Viva Learning.

faq.a: Microsoft Learn is Microsoft's free learning platform with modules and learning paths on Microsoft products.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Learn?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn content can be turned on as a source in Viva Learning, which integrates within Microsoft Teams and brings learning resources into that environment.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Learn relate to Viva Learning?

faq.a: It offers self-paced modules and learning paths. The Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse episode, for example, lists modules such as an introduction to end-to-end analytics using Microsoft Fabric and getting started with lakehouses in Microsoft Fabric.
faq.q: What kind of content does Microsoft Learn offer?

microsoft-learn.long:
Microsoft Learn is Microsoft's free learning platform. It offers modules and learning paths on Microsoft products, so that people can build skills on a given technology step by step. Because the content is organized by topic and product, it is commonly used both for self-directed study and as a reference point when an organization plans training around the Microsoft ecosystem.

A modular structure is the core idea behind the platform. Individual modules cover a defined subject, and learning paths group several modules into a sequence that moves from fundamentals toward more specific tasks. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse - Simply Explained" illustrates this in practice. It lists a set of self-paced training modules for Microsoft Fabric, including an introduction to end-to-end analytics using Microsoft Fabric and a module on getting started with lakehouses in Microsoft Fabric. The episode describes these as hands-on training options that cover essential topics and help people learn the platform effectively.

Microsoft Learn also connects to Microsoft Viva Learning. According to the platform description, its content can be turned on as a source in Viva Learning. The episode "Microsoft Viva Learning - Simply Explained" explains that Viva Learning is a learning hub that integrates within Microsoft Teams, which allows employees to reach a range of learning resources without leaving the Teams environment. In that setting, Microsoft Learn content serves as one of the catalogs that can be surfaced next to other learning material, so that people can find modules and learning paths in the same place where they already collaborate. The same episode notes that Viva Learning offers a one-month free trial for organizations that want to explore its features before committing to a subscription, and that its design and mobile compatibility are intended to make learning convenient for busy professionals.

Typical decisions around Microsoft Learn concern how to use it alongside an organization's own training approach. Teams that introduce new technology, such as Microsoft 365 Copilot or Microsoft Fabric, often need a dependable set of free reference material. Microsoft Learn can fill that role for product-specific skills, while Viva Learning can bring the same content into the daily workflow in Teams. Administrators who manage Viva Learning decide whether the Microsoft Learn source is enabled, which determines whether its modules and learning paths appear for employees.

Several other M365.FM episodes touch on the surrounding topics where such training matters. "How Do You Successfully Deploy Microsoft 365 Copilot Across an Enterprise?" discusses enterprise rollout and the shift toward agentic systems, and "Beyond the Prompt: Mastering Microsoft Copilot for Real Productivity with Jess Stratton [MVP]" focuses on prompt engineering and integration across Microsoft 365 apps. "Agentic AI for IT Operations: Windows 365, Intune & Microsoft's AI Vision with Christiaan Brinkhoff [Nerdio]" covers endpoint management and governance with Windows 365, Microsoft Intune, Agent 365 and Microsoft Foundry. These episodes do not describe Microsoft Learn in detail, but they show the kinds of product areas where structured, product-focused learning material is relevant as adoption grows.

In summary, Microsoft Learn is a free, product-oriented source of modules and learning paths. It stands on its own as a learning platform and also acts as an enabled content source within Viva Learning, linking product training to the Teams environment where employees already work.

microsoft-lists.desc: Microsoft Lists is a Microsoft 365 tool for tracking information and work in customisable lists with views, rules and formatting, stored in SharePoint.

faq.a: Microsoft Lists is used to track information and work in customisable lists with views, rules and formatting. Typical examples are issue tracking, inventories and onboarding checklists.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Lists used for?

faq.a: The data is stored in SharePoint. Microsoft Lists is part of SharePoint and builds on its list technology, which is why it is also called SharePoint Lists.
faq.q: Where is the data in Microsoft Lists stored?

faq.a: The episode "Fix Power Apps Delegation Warnings in SharePoint Lists" says SharePoint was not engineered as a transactional database and that delegation and performance problems appear as scale grows. It positions Dataverse as the option built for data.
faq.q: Is SharePoint a good database for Power Apps?

microsoft-lists.long:
Microsoft Lists is a tool for tracking information and work in customisable lists. It offers views, rules and formatting, and the data is stored in SharePoint. It is included in Microsoft 365 and is also referred to as SharePoint Lists. Microsoft developed it, and it is classified as a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool. It is part of SharePoint, whose list technology it builds on.

The typical use of Microsoft Lists is structured record keeping that does not need a full database. Common examples are issue tracking, inventories and onboarding checklists. Users define the columns of a list, create views to filter and arrange the entries, and apply rules and formatting to make the content easier to read and act on. Because the data lives in SharePoint, a list inherits the collaboration setting of the platform it sits in.

Microsoft Lists is frequently combined with other products from the Microsoft ecosystem. Power Apps can build apps on top of a list, Power Automate can run workflows around list items, and Microsoft Teams can host lists in channels so that a team works on the same records where it already communicates. These combinations let a simple list grow into a small business process without moving the data elsewhere.

One recurring decision is where a list fits among the Microsoft 365 task and tracking tools. The episodes "Microsoft To Do vs Planner vs Lists vs Loop" and "Unify Microsoft 365 Tasks Across To Do, Planner, Lists, and Loop" describe the problem as unclear roles rather than too many apps. The operating model they present assigns To Do to personal focus, Planner to team visibility, Lists to structured and recurring workflows, and Loop to real-time capture that flows into the others. The episodes say that confusion appears when teams mix these roles, duplicate tasks across tools and have to update them by hand.

A second decision concerns how far a list should carry an application. "Fix Power Apps Delegation Warnings in SharePoint Lists" warns that SharePoint was never engineered to act like a real transactional database. According to the episode, an app built on a list can work well at first and then degrade as users, data size and queries grow, with delegation limits and filters causing performance problems. It contrasts this with Dataverse, which it describes as built for data, while SharePoint is described as built for collaboration metadata. "SharePoint Lists vs Model-Driven Apps: Avoid Overbuilding" looks at the opposite risk. It argues that Dataverse and model-driven apps bring licensing, security matrices, solution layers, environment sprawl and governance overhead, which can be excessive for problems that a shared list and a few notifications would solve.

The episode "Use SharePoint Lists as a Copilot Knowledge Base" covers a third use. It says that Copilot Studio can connect directly to SharePoint Lists, with permission-aware access and without copying the data. In the episode's argument, authentication replaces replication, governance is inherited from the existing access controls and audit setup, and answers reflect current list content. The episode presents this as an alternative to migrating data into other stores only so that Copilot can use it.

Taken together, the episodes treat Microsoft Lists as a practical tool for structured collaboration data. It suits tracking and workflow scenarios in Microsoft 365 and can feed apps, automations and Copilot, but it has limits when used as a foundation for large or transactional applications.

microsoft-loop.desc: Microsoft Loop is a collaborative workspace in Microsoft 365 built on portable components, pages and workspaces that stay in sync across Teams, Outlook and Word.

faq.a: A Loop component is a portable piece of content, such as a list or table, that stays in sync wherever it is placed, for example in Teams, Outlook and Word. A change in one location is updated in all the others.
faq.q: What is a Loop component in Microsoft Loop?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes on task tools, Loop covers freeform co-creation and real-time capture that flows into the other tools, while To Do handles personal focus, Planner team visibility and Lists structured or recurring workflows.
faq.q: What role does Loop play next to To Do, Planner and Lists?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Loop and Copilot Pages: Where Collaboration Content Should Live" says that Loop components and Copilot Pages add new places for content. It discusses how they fit with SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams in terms of storage, sharing and lifecycle.
faq.q: How is Microsoft Loop related to Copilot Pages?

microsoft-loop.long:
Microsoft Loop is a collaborative workspace developed by Microsoft and included in Microsoft 365. It is built around three building blocks: Loop components, Loop pages and Loop workspaces. The defining idea is portability. A component such as a list or a table can be placed in several locations, for example in Teams, Outlook and Word, and it stays in sync everywhere it appears. A change made in one place is therefore visible in all the others. Microsoft Loop is classified as a Microsoft tool and as a collaboration tool, and its public availability dates from November 2023.

In practice, Loop is used for working material that several people edit together: shared notes, action lists and other content that changes while a team works on it. Because components can be embedded in chats and messages, the content does not have to be copied between applications. The relationship to Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Outlook is central, since those are the places where components are typically shared. Loop workspaces add a place where project-related information can be gathered, so that a team can reach notes and documents without switching between several apps.

Loop also sits next to other Microsoft 365 tools, and a recurring question is which tool fits which job. The episode "OneNote vs Loop vs Copilot with Karinne Diamond Bessette [MVP]" discusses OneNote, Microsoft Loop and Copilot for notes and frames the topic as a challenge of information chaos in the modern workplace, with a focus on where each tool fits and which architecture, security, governance or operational choices matter. A related theme appears in task management. The episodes "Unify Microsoft 365 Tasks Across To Do, Planner, Lists, and Loop" and "Microsoft To Do vs Planner vs Lists vs Loop" argue that the problem is not too many task apps but unclear roles. In the operating model they describe, To Do covers personal focus, Planner covers team visibility, Lists covers structured or recurring workflows, and Loop covers freeform co-creation and real-time capture that flows into the other tools. According to the episodes, chaos appears when roles are mixed and tasks are duplicated across tools.

The episode "Microsoft Loop Workspaces - Simply Explained" describes Loop Workspaces as a space where a team collaborates and gathers all project-related information in one place. It points to the decisions that matter around Loop in architecture, adoption, security, governance and day-to-day operations, which is why a workspace is more than a convenience feature for an administrator or project lead.

Loop is also related to Microsoft 365 Copilot. The episode "Microsoft Loop and Copilot Pages: Where Collaboration Content Should Live" explains that Loop components and Copilot Pages add new places where content can live, and with them new questions about where it should live. It looks at how Loop, Copilot Pages, SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams fit together and how storage, sharing and lifecycle behave across them. The stated aim is to help organizations set practical guidance for where collaboration content belongs, so that users know whether a given piece of content belongs in a Loop component, a Copilot Page, a SharePoint library, OneDrive or a Teams conversation.

For organizations, the main decisions around Microsoft Loop concern roles and placement rather than features alone. Typical questions are which kinds of notes and working content go into Loop and which stay in OneNote, how Loop content is shared and stored relative to SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams, and how Loop relates to existing task tools. Official documentation for Microsoft Loop is available through Microsoft's support pages.

microsoft-lync.desc: Microsoft Lync was Microsoft's unified communications platform for messaging, presence, voice and meetings, later rebranded as Skype for Business and replaced by Teams.

faq.a: Microsoft Lync was Microsoft's unified communications platform for instant messaging, presence, voice and meetings. It was later rebranded as Skype for Business.
faq.q: What was Microsoft Lync?

faq.a: Lync was rebranded as Skype for Business, and Microsoft Teams later replaced that product. Teams is now the successor in this line of communication tools.
faq.q: What replaced Microsoft Lync?

faq.a: The episode "From Microsoft Lync to Teams with Carsten Lund Meilbak [MVP]" features Mirko Peters in conversation with Microsoft MVP Carsten Lund Meilbak about the evolution from Lync and Skype for Business to Microsoft Teams.
faq.q: Which M365.FM episode covers the history from Lync to Teams?

microsoft-lync.long:
Microsoft Lync was Microsoft's unified communications platform for instant messaging, presence, voice and meetings. It was later rebranded as Skype for Business, and Microsoft Teams eventually replaced that product. The name Lync therefore marks an early stage in the line of Microsoft communication and collaboration tools that leads to the Microsoft Teams ecosystem used today.

In practical terms, a unified communications platform brings several ways of reaching colleagues into one client. Lync combined instant messaging, presence (showing whether a person is available), voice and meetings. Organizations used it to let employees chat, call and join online meetings from a single application instead of relying on separate tools for each purpose. Searches for the term today usually come from people who encounter the name in older documentation, in migration projects or in the history of Skype for Business and Teams.

The lineage matters when planning or explaining a move to Teams. Lync became Skype for Business through a rebrand, and Teams later took over the role that both products had filled. This is why legacy Lync or Skype for Business environments appear as the starting point in many discussions about moving enterprise communication to Microsoft Teams, including its voice features. The comparison between the older platforms and Teams also shows how the focus shifted over time from messaging, presence and calls toward a broader collaboration environment.

The name has also survived in technical configuration. In the M365.FM episode "Customize Microsoft 365 Apps Deployment with ODT XML", Lync appears in a sample Office Deployment Tool configuration file. A comment in the XML notes that administrators can add or remove components as needed, listing Teams, OneDrive, Groove and Lync as examples. This reflects the way the Lync name remained visible in Microsoft 365 Apps deployment tooling for administrators who customize which components are installed.

The most direct treatment of the topic on M365.FM is the episode "From Microsoft Lync to Teams with Carsten Lund Meilbak [MVP]". In it, Mirko Peters speaks with Microsoft MVP Carsten Lund Meilbak about the evolution of enterprise communication and collaboration, from the early days of Microsoft Lync and Skype for Business to the modern Microsoft Teams ecosystem. The conversation explores how collaboration platforms have changed from simple messaging tools, and it looks at how collaboration technology continues to evolve, why user experience matters, and how organizations can build more effective and future-ready communication environments with Microsoft technologies.

That episode is referenced as a related listen in other M365.FM episodes on Microsoft Teams, including "Microsoft Teams Phone and Telephony | Simply Explained" and "Microsoft Teams Hidden Features with Josh Blalock [MVP]". Together these point listeners from the history of Lync toward current Teams topics such as telephony and lesser-known features. For readers new to the subject, the Lync story serves as background: it explains where the presence, voice and meeting capabilities in Teams come from and why the product names Lync, Skype for Business and Teams appear in the same conversations.

microsoft-marketplace.desc: Microsoft Marketplace is Microsoft's combined commercial marketplace that brings Azure Marketplace and AppSource together for buying and selling cloud solutions and AI apps.

faq.a: Microsoft Marketplace is Microsoft's combined commercial marketplace that brings Azure Marketplace and AppSource together. It is used for buying and selling cloud solutions and AI apps.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Marketplace?

faq.a: It combines the two. Azure Marketplace and Microsoft AppSource are the related offerings that Microsoft Marketplace brings together in one commercial marketplace.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Marketplace relate to Azure Marketplace and Microsoft AppSource?

faq.a: The episode "The Hard Way to Get Listed on Microsoft Marketplace" says that publishing involves technical requirements, certification and creating offers customers can find and buy, and that many partners underestimate this complexity. The episode "Your AppSource Listing Is Costing You Deals" adds that a listing is part of the buyer's evaluation journey.
faq.q: What do the M365.FM episodes say about getting listed?

microsoft-marketplace.long:
Microsoft Marketplace is the combined commercial marketplace of Microsoft. It brings Azure Marketplace and Microsoft AppSource together in one place, and it is used for buying and selling cloud solutions and AI apps. Microsoft develops the platform, and the official documentation for it is published on Microsoft Learn under the marketplace section. In the M365.FM knowledge base it is classified as a Microsoft tool, and it is closely related to the two marketplaces that were merged into it.

The platform serves two groups. Customers use it to find, evaluate and acquire solutions that fit into the Microsoft ecosystem. Publishers and partners use it to list their own offers so that customers can discover and buy them. Because both sides meet in a single commercial marketplace, decisions around Microsoft Marketplace tend to involve questions of discoverability, technical readiness, certification and how an offer is presented to a buyer.

The relationship to Azure Marketplace and Microsoft AppSource is central to understanding the term. Azure Marketplace and AppSource were separate storefronts, and Microsoft Marketplace is described as the combined commercial marketplace that unites them. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft AppSource - Simply Explained" describes AppSource as an online marketplace for business applications, offering solutions that integrate with Microsoft services and help organizations address specific business challenges. That episode frames the understanding of such a marketplace as important for getting the most out of it and for improving an organization's efficiency.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Marketplace - Simply Explained" is part of the Knowledge Nuggets series with Mirko Peters. It covers Microsoft Marketplace with a practical focus on what it is, how it works and the decisions that matter for architecture, adoption, security, governance or day-to-day operations. The episode describes the marketplace as one of the most important platforms in the Microsoft ecosystem and notes that it is often misunderstood, which makes a plain-language explanation a useful starting point for newcomers.

For publishers, the episode "The Hard Way to Get Listed on Microsoft Marketplace" looks at what it takes to publish solutions and services in Microsoft's commercial marketplace. It describes the path from meeting technical requirements and passing certification to creating offers that customers can actually find and buy. The episode says that many partners underestimate the complexity and then discover that getting approved is only one part of the work. A listing is therefore treated as something to plan for, not as a formality at the end of product development.

A related theme appears in "Your AppSource Listing Is Costing You Deals". The episode argues that an AppSource listing is part of a buyer's evaluation journey and not simply a publishing requirement. It names unclear positioning, weak proof, incomplete technical information and poor marketplace presentation as factors that can hurt results, and it aims to help listings become a real sales asset instead of a forgotten catalog entry within the Microsoft commercial marketplace.

The commercial side of the platform is also touched on in "The Partnership Mistakes That Cost Partners Millions". The episode explains that Microsoft partners often lose revenue through avoidable mistakes in positioning, co-sell execution, marketplace readiness and account alignment. It presents marketplace readiness as one element of a wider, repeatable partnership strategy in the Microsoft ecosystem, not as a stand-alone task.

In practice, organizations that look at Microsoft Marketplace typically weigh a few questions: whether a needed cloud solution or AI app is already available there, how it integrates with existing Microsoft services, and what governance or security review is needed before acquiring it. Partners weigh a different set: whether an offer is technically ready, how it will be positioned, and how it fits into co-sell and account plans. The official documentation on Microsoft Learn is the reference for the detailed requirements and processes.

microsoft-mesh.desc: Microsoft Mesh is a Microsoft 365 platform for immersive 3D experiences in Microsoft Teams, using avatars and custom virtual spaces for meetings and events.

faq.a: Microsoft Mesh is a platform from Microsoft for immersive 3D experiences in Microsoft Teams. It uses avatars and custom virtual spaces for meetings and events and is part of Microsoft 365.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Mesh?

faq.a: The immersive experiences of Microsoft Mesh are delivered in Microsoft Teams. The episode on hybrid events discusses running them using Microsoft Teams Immersive Spaces and Microsoft Mesh.
faq.q: How is Microsoft Mesh related to Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: The episode "High-Stakes Hybrid Events with Microsoft Teams and Mesh" mentions lagging avatars, broken spatial audio, synchronization issues, and low engagement as problems that can make even visually impressive virtual environments ineffective.
faq.q: What challenges does the M365.FM podcast mention for Mesh-based events?

microsoft-mesh.long:
Microsoft Mesh is a platform from Microsoft for immersive 3D experiences in Microsoft Teams. It combines avatars with custom virtual spaces so that meetings and events can take place in a shared three-dimensional environment rather than only in a conventional grid of video tiles. Microsoft Mesh is part of Microsoft 365 and is classed as both a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool. Its closest relationship is to Microsoft Teams, where the immersive experiences are delivered.

In practice, Microsoft Mesh is relevant wherever an organization wants more engagement from distributed participants than a standard call provides. Typical situations include hybrid events, larger gatherings, and meetings in which presence and a sense of shared space matter. Participants appear as avatars, and the virtual space itself can be customized, which is what distinguishes the platform from a regular Teams meeting. Technical documentation for the product is published by Microsoft in its Learn documentation area for Mesh.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Mesh - Simply Explained" introduces the product with a practical focus on what it is, how it works, and which decisions matter for architecture, adoption, security, governance, and day-to-day operations. The episode describes Microsoft Mesh as one of the most talked-about yet also one of the most misunderstood technologies in the Microsoft ecosystem. That framing is useful for anyone evaluating the product: understanding what Mesh actually does, and what it does not do, comes before any decision about rollout.

A second episode, "High-Stakes Hybrid Events with Microsoft Teams and Mesh", looks at the topic from an engineering angle. Rather than product marketing, it asks what it takes to run successful high-stakes hybrid events using Microsoft Teams Immersive Spaces and Microsoft Mesh. The episode notes that hybrid work has changed how organizations connect employees, but that creating engaging virtual events remains a challenge. It points to problems such as lagging avatars, broken spatial audio, synchronization issues, and low engagement, and says that even visually impressive virtual environments can become ineffective if the user experience falls short. The practical takeaway from that discussion is that planning for technical quality and participant experience matters as much as the design of the virtual space.

For decision makers, the questions around Microsoft Mesh are therefore less about whether a 3D space can be created and more about whether it works reliably for the intended audience and event type. Considerations that follow from the episodes include the stability of avatars and audio, the synchronization of participants, and the level of engagement the format actually produces compared with a standard Teams meeting. Governance, security, and operations are also named as areas where decisions matter, which is consistent with Mesh being embedded in Microsoft 365 rather than operating as a separate stand-alone service.

The name can cause confusion in search results. The term "mesh" also appears in unrelated Microsoft topics, such as data mesh governance with Microsoft Fabric domains or mesh configurations in Azure Virtual WAN. Those discussions concern data architecture and networking, not the immersive Teams platform. Microsoft Mesh, as covered here, refers specifically to the platform for immersive 3D experiences with avatars and virtual spaces in Microsoft Teams.

microsoft-mvp.desc: Microsoft MVP is the Most Valuable Professional award Microsoft gives to independent technology experts who share their knowledge with the community.

faq.a: Microsoft MVP stands for Most Valuable Professional. It is an award Microsoft gives to independent technology experts who share their knowledge with the community.
faq.q: What is a Microsoft MVP?

faq.a: Episode titles mark MVP guests with tags such as "[Microsoft MVP]", "[MVP]" or "[MVP-MCT]". The last tag combines the MVP award with the Microsoft Certified Trainer designation.
faq.q: How are MVPs shown in M365.FM episodes?

faq.a: The listed episodes cover Excel and dashboards, modern .NET with WPF, ASP.NET Core and gRPC, SharePoint Framework with PnP React Controls, GitHub Copilot and AI coding agents, and AI adoption with Microsoft Copilot, Copilot Studio and Power Platform.
faq.q: Which topics do the MVP guests on M365.FM cover?

microsoft-mvp.long:
Microsoft MVP stands for Most Valuable Professional. It is an award that Microsoft gives to independent technology experts who share their knowledge with the community. Holders of the award are people working with Microsoft technologies in many different roles, and the title is used as a public marker of community contribution rather than as an exam-based qualification.

In practice, the MVP designation shows up in the professional profiles of developers, architects, trainers and consultants who write, speak, teach and answer questions about Microsoft products. The M365.FM episodes that feature MVPs mark the guest's status in the episode title, for example with the tag "[Microsoft MVP]", "[MVP]" or "[MVP-MCT]". The last variant combines the MVP award with the Microsoft Certified Trainer designation, which indicates that a guest holds both.

The M365.FM episodes featuring MVPs cover a wide range of topics across the Microsoft ecosystem, which illustrates how varied the award's recipients are. In "From Excel Expert to Microsoft MVP: Empowering Millions with Data, Dashboards & AI with Karen Abecia [Microsoft MVP]", the focus is on Excel, dashboards and AI as tools for managing information and supporting decisions. The episode excerpt notes that nearly 90% of finance teams still rely on Excel for financial modeling, a figure attributed to that episode.

Other episodes show the developer side of the community. "Modern .NET: WPF, ASP.NET Core, and gRPC with Gábor Ruzsinszki [MVP]" discusses the evolution of modern .NET development, from legacy WPF desktop applications to ASP.NET Core, cloud-native architectures and gRPC services, including how .NET moved from a Windows-only framework to a cross-platform ecosystem. "Stop Reinventing SPFx- Building Better SharePoint Solutions with PnP React Controls with Siddharth Vaghasia [MVP]" looks at building production-ready SharePoint Framework (SPFx) solutions by combining Microsoft 365 technologies with reusable community components, so that every part does not have to be built from scratch.

AI and tooling are covered as well. In "GitHub Copilot, Clean Context, Automated Testing & AI Coding Agents with Lars Gyrup Brink Nielsen [MVP]", the conversation moves from AI code assistance to AI coding agents that can inspect repositories, modify files, run tests, analyze failures and create pull requests. Topics named in the episode include TypeScript, JavaScript, Nx, monorepos, GitHub Actions and Playwright. "From AI Hype to Business Value with Kayode Ajayi [MVP-MCT]" addresses how organizations can move from AI experimentation to measurable business value, with attention to Microsoft Copilot, Copilot Studio and Power Platform.

Taken together, the episodes show that the MVP title is not tied to one product area. The guests work with Excel, .NET, SharePoint, GitHub, Power Platform and Microsoft Copilot, and several of them describe long careers in the Microsoft technology stack, including teaching, software architecture and solution architecture. For readers evaluating a speaker, author or advisor, the MVP tag in an episode title signals that Microsoft has recognized the person's community involvement, while the details of their expertise are best judged from the content they share, as in the episodes above.

microsoft-partner-center.desc: Microsoft Partner Center is Microsoft's portal for partners to manage membership, benefits, incentives, customers, marketplace offers and support.

faq.a: It is Microsoft's portal where partners manage their relationship with Microsoft, including membership, benefits, incentives, customers and support.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Partner Center?

faq.a: According to the episode "The Hard Way to Get Listed on Microsoft Marketplace", a developer account is created through Partner Center, and the app submission form with details, screenshots and a logo is completed there before the certification process.
faq.q: How is Microsoft Partner Center used for Microsoft Marketplace listings?

faq.a: Yes. The episode "Microsoft Partner Center - Simply Explained" says the Partner Center dashboard shows metrics such as revenue, deal conversion rates and customer satisfaction.
faq.q: Can partners track their performance in Microsoft Partner Center?

microsoft-partner-center.long:
Microsoft Partner Center is Microsoft's portal where partners manage their relationship with Microsoft. According to the short description and the Microsoft documentation overview, it covers membership, benefits, incentives, customers and support. For organizations that build, sell or implement Microsoft solutions, it serves as the central place to sign up, track their standing in the partner program and handle administrative and commercial tasks tied to Microsoft.

The M365.FM episodes describe several typical uses. The episode "Microsoft Partner Center - Simply Explained" says that performance can be tracked through the Partner Center dashboard, with metrics such as revenue, deal conversion rates and customer satisfaction used to refine strategies and improve outcomes. The same episode notes that Partner Center provides technical support and troubleshooting assistance, and that partners can contact support when they run into problems while using the platform.

A second area is the partner program itself. The episode "How to Become a High-Performing Microsoft Partner" recommends starting by creating a free account in Partner Center to access resources. It points to the six core Solution Partner designations as a way to identify which fit matches a company's strengths. It also highlights the Partner Capability Score (PCS), which the episode links to certifying the team and tracking customer success metrics, and it names customer retention and revenue growth as measures of effectiveness. The episode "Microsoft Partner Journey: From Enrollment to Growth" adds that partners can reach a Solutions Partner designation by meeting specific customer outcome criteria, and that using Partner Center effectively helps manage partnerships and track performance. It also mentions advanced specializations as a way to build credibility and open new business opportunities, and warns against common mistakes such as skipping attribution setup and pursuing irrelevant certifications.

A third area is publishing applications. The episode "The Hard Way to Get Listed on Microsoft Marketplace" describes a sequence in which a developer account is created through Partner Center, an app package is prepared with a development platform such as Visual Studio or Xamarin, and an app submission form is completed in Partner Center with app details, screenshots and a logo. After that, the app goes through a certification process in which Microsoft checks compliance with policies and technical requirements. Once certified, the app is published and then monitored. In this flow, Partner Center acts as the submission and account entry point for Microsoft Marketplace listings.

Partner Center also appears from a developer perspective. The episode "How Microsoft Graph Connects Microsoft 365 Data and Context" lists Partner Center among the services whose data can be reached through Microsoft Graph, alongside core Microsoft 365 services, enterprise mobility and security tools, Windows features and Dynamics 365. This indicates that partner-related data is not only available through the portal interface but can also be integrated programmatically.
