It challenges the belief that deploying modern security controls such as MFA, EDR, Conditional Access and Zero Trust checklists makes an organization secure. Instead, the episode argues that security comes from engineering trust as a system and building resilience, particularly when AI accelerates both attacks and defensive response. In this framing, owning a tool is not the same as being protected by it.

Two further episodes show how tools are described and assessed. "Agent Feed - Simply Explained" presents Agent Feed as a tool for managing AI agents within Power Apps, with features such as real-time activity logs and assistance requests that support oversight of automated processes. "Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence - Simply Explained" includes a section on choosing tools for real-time data, listing evaluation criteria such as functionality fit, scalability, integration depth and usability, and advising that a tool should integrate well with existing systems to avoid data silos.

Taken together, the category and the episodes suggest a consistent approach: start from the problem, the architecture and the operating context, then evaluate candidate tools against criteria such as fit, scalability, integration and ease of adoption. The Microsoft tool category supplies the vocabulary for browsing the options, while the individual product and narrower category pages hold the detail needed to compare them.

microsoft-trust-center.desc: The Microsoft Trust Center is Microsoft's public site for security, privacy and compliance information on its cloud services, used for audits and assessments.

faq.a: It is Microsoft's public site for security, privacy and compliance information about its cloud services. It hosts documentation and resources that customers can use for audits and assessments.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft Trust Center?

faq.a: The overview page is organized into tabs for Microsoft Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Power Platform and additional products and services. Examples include Azure AI, Azure OpenAI Service, Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Power Apps and Power BI.
faq.q: Which products does the Microsoft Trust Center cover?

faq.a: The overview page itself lists no concrete certifications or audit results. Those details sit on the linked pages, which the overview reaches through its product tabs and its navigation to audit reports and related topics.
faq.q: Where do concrete certifications and audit results appear?

microsoft-trust-center.long:
The Microsoft Trust Center is Microsoft's public site for security, privacy and compliance information about its cloud services. It brings together documentation and resources that customers can use when they carry out audits and assessments, and it presents Microsoft products and services in terms of security, privacy, compliance and transparency. A short statement on the overview page says that data is handled securely and in line with privacy and legal requirements.

The Microsoft Trust Center Overview page is organized around product tabs. These cover Microsoft Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Power Platform and additional products and services. Example entries include Azure AI, Azure OpenAI Service, Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Power Apps and Power BI. For each product, the page links to topics such as security, privacy, GDPR, data location and compliance. For Azure AI, the links also include responsible AI, a transparency note and limited access.

Beyond the product tabs, the wider navigation covers data management, data access and data location. It also lists regulations such as DORA, the EU AI Act and NIS2, and it points to the Secure Future Initiative, Zero Trust, audit reports and Compliance Score. In practice the Trust Center works as a starting point: a reader chooses a product, then follows the links to the detailed security, privacy and compliance documents. The overview page itself names no licenses or prerequisites and contains no concrete certifications or audit results, because those details sit on the linked pages.

Typical situations in which people consult the Trust Center are compliance reviews, vendor assessments and preparations for audits. A security or compliance team can use it to find out where data is located, how data access is handled, which regulations Microsoft addresses for a given service, and which audit reports are available. Because the content is organized per product, the same site serves teams that work with Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 or the Power Platform.

The M365.FM episodes mention the Trust Center in two contexts. In "Enterprise AI Agents with Sailaja Mantripragada [MVP-MCT]", the discussion of protecting sensitive data as agents interact with different systems includes data loss prevention policies and monitoring through audit logs in the Power Platform admin center. The episode adds a tip to always follow Microsoft Trust Center guidelines to stay compliant with GDPR, HIPAA and other industry standards.

In "Prepare Microsoft 365 for German KRITIS Requirements", the Trust Center appears in connection with certifications. The episode says that certifications show Microsoft 365 following strict rules for data protection and backup, that Microsoft updates its certifications regularly to match new regulations, and that readers can check the Trust Center for the latest information. It lists ISO 27001, BSI C5 and GDPR in a table as supporting KRITIS, and says that certifications help show auditors that systems meet legal and industry standards.

Taken together, the Trust Center serves as a reference point rather than a configuration tool. It documents how Microsoft describes its services in terms of security, privacy and compliance, while decisions about policies, data residency and retention remain with the organization using the services. Anyone preparing evidence for an auditor would typically use the Trust Center to locate the relevant product page and the linked documents, then combine that information with the organization's own settings and processes.

microsoft-whiteboard.desc: Microsoft Whiteboard is a digital canvas for sketching, sticky notes and brainstorming, used in Teams meetings and on devices as part of Microsoft 365.

faq.a: Microsoft Whiteboard is a digital canvas for sketching, sticky notes and brainstorming. It is used for workshops, planning sessions and visual collaboration, including in hybrid meetings.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Whiteboard used for?

faq.a: Whiteboard is available in Teams meetings as a shared canvas, so participants can draw and add notes together during a meeting. It is also used on devices outside of Teams.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Whiteboard relate to Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: Yes. Microsoft Whiteboard is developed by Microsoft, is part of Microsoft 365, and is included in the license.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Whiteboard part of Microsoft 365?

microsoft-whiteboard.long:
Microsoft Whiteboard is a digital canvas for sketching, sticky notes and brainstorming. It is developed by Microsoft, is included in Microsoft 365, and is used in Teams meetings and on devices. In short, it gives participants a shared surface on which ideas can be drawn, noted and arranged together, instead of relying only on spoken discussion or slides.

The tool is classified as a Microsoft tool and as a collaboration tool. Its typical uses are workshops, planning sessions and visual collaboration, including hybrid meetings in which some participants are in a room and others join remotely. Because the canvas is shared, everyone taking part can contribute at the same time, which suits activities such as collecting ideas, grouping sticky notes or sketching a rough structure before it is formalised elsewhere.

The main connection of Microsoft Whiteboard is to Microsoft Teams, where it is available during meetings as a shared canvas. This makes it one of the collaboration options inside a meeting, next to chat, files and other apps. The same canvas can also be used on devices, so the experience is not limited to a single meeting window. Detailed feature descriptions are maintained in Microsoft's official support documentation for Whiteboard.

In practice, teams often have to decide whether a whiteboard is the right place for a given piece of work. A digital canvas is well suited to early, loosely structured thinking: brainstorming, mapping options, sketching a process or drafting a diagram together. Content that needs to be tracked, assigned or stored long term usually belongs in other tools. This question of where information should live is a recurring theme in discussions of the Microsoft 365 collaboration landscape.

Whiteboard appears in the M365.FM episodes mainly as one tool among several rather than as the central subject. The episode "Build Microsoft Teams Meeting Apps and Bots" describes Teams meetings as a live work hub and mentions that built-in and custom apps can enhance collaboration, giving examples such as running polls or brainstorming on a whiteboard. It also notes that bots can capture meeting notes, send reminders and act as virtual assistants, and it advises staying aware of security and compliance when using apps and bots.

The episode "OneNote vs Loop vs Copilot with Karinne Diamond Bessette [MVP]" places Whiteboard in a list of places where employees can store ideas, tasks, meeting notes, project updates and collaborative content, alongside OneNote, Loop, Teams, Copilot, Planner, Outlook and SharePoint. The episode frames the resulting spread of locations as information chaos and discusses how organisations can decide where information should actually live and keep it organised, searchable and actionable.

In the episode "Customize Dataverse for Complex Business Apps", a whiteboard is mentioned as the first step of an implementation plan: sketching an entity relationship diagram covering entities, keys, relationships and ownership before building tables. This illustrates a common use of a shared canvas, namely drafting a design collaboratively before it is turned into a working solution. The episodes do not go into feature-level detail about Whiteboard itself.

microsoft365dsc.desc: Microsoft365DSC is an open-source PowerShell module that applies Desired State Configuration to export, configure, compare and monitor Microsoft 365 tenant settings as code.

faq.a: Microsoft365DSC is an open-source PowerShell module that uses Desired State Configuration to manage Microsoft 365 tenant configuration as code. It can export, configure, compare and monitor tenant settings.
faq.q: What is Microsoft365DSC?

faq.a: Drift detection refers to identifying differences between a tenant's current configuration and its intended, defined state. Microsoft365DSC includes this as part of its monitoring capabilities.
faq.q: What does drift detection mean in Microsoft365DSC?

faq.a: It is a PowerShell module that relies on Desired State Configuration. This allows Microsoft 365 settings to be described and managed as code.
faq.q: What technology does Microsoft365DSC build on?

microsoft365dsc.long:
Microsoft365DSC is an open-source PowerShell module built on Desired State Configuration (DSC). It treats the configuration of a Microsoft 365 tenant as code, so that settings can be described in files, reviewed, reapplied and compared over time rather than managed only through administrative portals.

The module is used to export an existing tenant configuration, to configure a tenant from a defined configuration, and to compare a tenant's current state against a reference. It also supports monitoring, including drift detection: identifying where the live configuration has diverged from the intended, documented state.

Because the configuration is expressed as code, Microsoft365DSC fits into configuration-as-code and infrastructure-as-code practices for Microsoft 365 administration. Typical purposes include documenting a tenant, reproducing settings across environments, and keeping a tenant aligned with an approved baseline.

No linked topics or M365.FM episodes are currently associated with Microsoft365DSC in the knowledge base, so this page describes the product only on the basis of its general definition.

middleware.desc: Middleware is software between applications and systems that connects them; M365.FM episodes argue schedule-based, polling middleware adds hidden cost.

faq.a: Middleware is software that sits between applications and systems to connect them so they can exchange data. In M365.FM episodes it appears as custom connectors, central integration hubs and similar bridging layers.
faq.q: What is middleware?

faq.a: The episode "Replace Legacy Middleware with Policy-Driven Architecture" argues that legacy middleware adds complexity, cost and dependency between systems and can become a bottleneck that raises maintenance overhead.
faq.q: Why does an M365.FM episode call legacy middleware a silent tax?

faq.a: They point to event-driven platform services, direct control over data flows and protocol-level integration such as gRPC, which the Azure SQL episode links to smaller payloads and faster transmission.
faq.q: What alternatives to polling middleware do the episodes mention?

middleware.long:
Middleware is software that sits between applications and systems in order to connect them. It carries data and requests from one system to another so that platforms that were not designed to work together can still exchange information. In the M365.FM episodes that mention it, middleware appears both as a practical integration tool and as a source of cost and complexity.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, middleware shows up in several forms. The episode "D365FO Integration Architecture with Anitha Eswaran [MVP-MCT]" describes custom connectors and middleware as a way to bridge gaps when Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations (D365FO) has to talk to systems that have no out-of-the-box connector. Custom connectors let a team define how D365FO communicates with web services and REST APIs, and middleware fills the remaining gaps so the integration fits a specific business need. The episode "Dataverse MCP Integration with Nathan Rose [MVP]" describes custom integration as building unique solutions, such as middleware, code or special connectors, to link old and new platforms so data keeps flowing between systems that were not built to communicate. It also lists managing the complexity of connecting many systems through a central hub as one characteristic of this approach.

The central critique comes from "Replace Legacy Middleware with Policy-Driven Architecture". The episode argues that legacy middleware creates a silent tax on enterprises by adding unnecessary complexity, cost and dependency between systems. Instead of enabling integration, middleware often becomes a bottleneck that slows decision-making and increases maintenance overhead. The episode's core message is that modern platforms such as Microsoft 365 shift the focus away from best-of-breed stacks and toward unified ecosystems with strong control planes. It describes a transition from integration-heavy architectures to simplified, policy-driven systems in which automation and platform services take over work that middleware used to do. In this framing, schedule-based, polling middleware is the pattern that should dissolve into event-driven platform services.

The episode "Azure SQL Security Beyond Firewalls and IP Allowlists" raises related concerns. Its key takeaways say that managed connectors can create hidden dependencies that lead to system instability, and that relying on them alone for integration should be avoided. It describes middleware friction as something that slows data movement and recommends seeking direct control over data flows to improve performance. It also notes that REST polling wastes resources through unnecessary API requests, and it points to protocol-level integration such as gRPC, with smaller payloads and faster transmission, as important for AI workloads. A schema-first approach is mentioned as a way to make integration reliable and predictable.

A separate use of the word appears in "Fix OWASP Architectural Risks in .NET Applications". There, middleware refers to request-pipeline components in ASP.NET Core rather than integration software. The episode notes that ASP.NET Core provides antiforgery middleware, but that single-page apps, API endpoints or missing SameSite cookie settings can still leave CSRF exposures. This is a different meaning of the term, tied to application security instead of system integration.

Taken together, the episodes present a decision around middleware: where a gap between systems really needs a custom connector or middleware layer, and where platform-native, event-driven services and direct data flows can replace a polling hub. Teams weighing this choice are encouraged to question whether their workflows deliver time-to-value and agility, and to count the maintenance and dependency cost of each intermediary layer.

migration-coexistence.desc: Migration coexistence is a migration phase in which old and new environments, such as two Microsoft 365 tenants, run side by side while users move in batches.

faq.a: It is a migration phase in which the old and new environments, for example two Microsoft 365 tenants, run side by side and are linked. This keeps mail and collaboration working while users are moved in batches.
faq.q: What is migration coexistence?

faq.a: Users are moved in batches rather than all at once, so those who have moved and those who have not still need to work together. Coexistence links the two environments so that this remains possible during the transition.
faq.q: Why is coexistence used during a migration?

migration-coexistence.long:
Migration coexistence is a phase of a migration project in which the old and the new environment operate at the same time and are linked to each other. A typical example is a move between two Microsoft 365 tenants, where the source and target tenants run in parallel for a period instead of being switched over in a single step.

The purpose of coexistence is to keep mail and collaboration working while users are moved in batches. Because not all users change environments at the same moment, those who have already moved and those who have not yet moved still need to be able to communicate and work together. The link between the two environments is what makes this possible during the transition.

Coexistence is therefore usually discussed alongside batch-based migration approaches, where the migration is divided into groups of users rather than carried out as a single cutover. The phase ends when the last users have been moved and the old environment is no longer needed.

No related topics or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, so this page is limited to the general definition of the term.

migration-cutover.desc: Migration cutover is the point in a migration when users stop working in the old system or tenant and switch to the new one, usually in a planned quiet window.

faq.a: It is the moment when users stop working in the old system or tenant and switch to the new one, typically scheduled for a quiet window such as a weekend.
faq.q: What is a migration cutover?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, the network identity of the source computer moves to the destination. The destination takes over the source's name, IP addresses and Active Directory computer account, while the source keeps its files but is no longer available to users.
faq.q: What happens during a cutover in Storage Migration Service?

faq.a: The episode "Shared Data Reservoirs for Multi-Tenant Microsoft 365" recommends testing migration tooling before each cutover, scheduling windows during low-usage periods, validating data afterwards and documenting lessons learned after each phase.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode recommend for cutovers?

migration-cutover.long:
Migration cutover is the moment in a migration when users stop working in the old system or tenant and begin working in the new one. It is usually scheduled for a quiet window such as a weekend, so that the switch affects as few people as possible. Before the cutover, the source environment remains the working system; after it, the destination takes over. The term is used for many kinds of migrations in the Microsoft ecosystem, from moving file servers to consolidating data across several Microsoft 365 tenants.

The exact mechanics depend on the product involved. Microsoft Learn describes cutover in the Windows Server Storage Migration Service as the phase that moves the network identity of the source computer to the destination computer. In that case the source keeps its files but is no longer available to users and applications. The destination takes over the source's computer name, IP addresses and Active Directory computer account, so that clients reach it as if it were the original server. This is one product-specific example of the broader concept, and it covers file server migrations rather than the general planning of a cutover window.

In Storage Migration Service, some preparation is needed before the cutover starts. The network configuration for the destination has to be provided, and a new name can be chosen for the source. Firewall rules for SMB, Netlogon and WMI must be open on both machines. The cutover itself then runs a series of automated steps: connecting to both computers, setting Active Directory permissions, creating temporary accounts, removing the source from the domain, renaming and re-joining it with a new identity, then renaming the destination, replacing its IP addresses and joining it under the source's original account. The documentation also explains how to finish the process manually if the cutover fails at a known progress stage, and it notes that domain controller migration is not supported.

Typical decisions around a cutover include when to schedule it, how to test the tooling beforehand, and how to confirm afterwards that the data arrived intact. The episode "Shared Data Reservoirs for Multi-Tenant Microsoft 365" approaches the topic from a multi-tenant perspective. It recommends tracking cutover events and resolving issues quickly to keep the migration on schedule, testing migration tooling before each cutover, and scheduling cutover windows during low-usage periods. It also advises validating data after each migration cutover and documenting lessons learned after each migration phase.

The same episode presents a phased approach as a way to manage migration for multiple tenants. Because each phase ends with its own cutover, the plan can be adjusted as lessons emerge from the previous one. This lets a team refine its process, tooling and timing before the next group of users or the next tenant is switched. The episode also links migration to what follows it: lifecycle management keeps the shared data reservoirs healthy after migration, which includes automating policy enforcement across all workspaces.

In practice, cutover is the point of highest visibility in a migration, because it is when users notice the change. Planning around it therefore tends to cover the timing of the window, the preparation of the destination, a clear way to track progress during the switch, and a defined path for resolving problems if a step fails. Validation after the cutover closes the loop, confirming that the new system or tenant is ready for normal use before the migration phase is considered complete.

migration-factory.desc: A migration factory is a repeatable delivery model that moves workloads to the cloud in waves, using shared standards, runbooks, validation gates and rollback patterns.

faq.a: A migration factory is a repeatable delivery model for large cloud migrations. It moves workloads in waves and relies on shared standards, runbooks, validation gates and rollback patterns instead of one-off projects.
faq.q: What is a migration factory?

faq.a: In the AWS Cloud Migration Factory example, a wave is a group of applications and servers that share the same cutover date. The example schedule runs a three-week cycle of build, validation and cutover, with waves running in parallel.
faq.q: What is a wave in a migration factory?

faq.a: The episode "Move Legacy Systems to Azure Without Disrupting Work" recommends platform first, then a repeatable migration factory, then modernization. It warns that exceptions approved during migration become permanent debt.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode recommend about the order of work?

migration-factory.long:
A migration factory is a repeatable delivery model for large cloud migrations. Instead of treating each move as a one-off project, it moves workloads in waves and applies shared standards, runbooks, validation gates and rollback patterns to every wave. The idea is to turn migration into a production line: the same steps are executed in the same order, so effort, risk and duration become more predictable as the number of workloads grows.

The model is typically considered when an organization has many applications or servers to move and cannot afford to design the approach from scratch each time. Standardization is the central element. Runbooks describe the individual tasks, validation gates define what must be true before a workload advances to the next stage, and rollback patterns define how to return to a known state if a step fails. Because these artifacts are reused, lessons from earlier waves feed directly into later ones.

A concrete example of the concept is described in AWS Prescriptive Guidance for the Cloud Migration Factory solution, which automates large-scale server migrations to AWS. That page covers one vendor's implementation rather than the generic term, but it illustrates how a factory can be structured. The workflow has three phases. In pre-migration, the team prepares the implementation environment by deploying the factory, building a migration execution server and setting up the migration tooling. In migration implementation, predefined tasks automate the work: verifying prerequisites, pushing the replication agent to the source machines of a wave, checking replication status, launching servers for boot-up testing and scheduling a window for application cutover. Post-migration tasks depend on the scenario and may include removing servers from the source configuration database, decommissioning source machines and tuning performance on the target instances.

Waves are the unit of organization in this example. A wave is a group of applications and servers that share the same cutover date. The documented example schedule is a three-week cycle: a build stage in week one, validation and boot-up testing in week two, and cutover in week three. All waves run in parallel, so several groups can be in different stages at the same time. This overlap is what allows throughput to scale without restarting the process for each group.

The M365.FM episode "Move Legacy Systems to Azure Without Disrupting Work" places the migration factory inside a wider sequence. The episode argues for an order of platform first, then a repeatable migration factory, then modernization that compounds instead of fragments. It says that every exception approved during migration becomes permanent debt and that governance throughput can collapse quickly, which is why policy, networking, logging and subscription boundaries need to be settled before waves begin. According to the episode, cloud success is less about where workloads run and more about whether the enterprise can change safely, predictably and under control. It also notes that many organizations underestimate costs and overlook application dependencies when planning an enterprise migration strategy.

In practice, decisions around a migration factory include how to define waves, which validation gates are mandatory, who approves exceptions, and how rollback is rehearsed before cutover. The factory approach does not remove the need to assess individual applications, but it separates the repeatable mechanics of moving workloads from the case-by-case decisions about how each one should eventually be modernized.

migration-wave.desc: A migration wave is a group of applications and workloads migrated together, allowing a large estate to move in sequenced batches with lessons carried into each subsequent wave.

faq.a: A migration wave is a group of applications and workloads that are migrated together. A large estate is moved in sequenced batches, with each batch forming one wave.
faq.q: What is a migration wave?

faq.a: Waves let a large estate move in sequenced batches rather than all at once. The lessons from each wave carry into the next.
faq.q: Why are migrations organized into waves?

migration-wave.long:
A migration wave is a group of applications and workloads that are migrated together as one batch. Instead of moving an entire estate at once, the work is divided into sequenced waves, each with a defined scope.

The approach is used when a large estate has to be moved in stages. Grouping items into waves lets a team plan, execute and review each batch as a unit, rather than handling every application and workload separately. Because the waves run one after another, the lessons learned in one wave can carry into the next.

The term describes a way of structuring migration work rather than a specific product or tool. It applies to the sequencing of applications and workloads, with each wave forming a manageable portion of the overall effort.

No episodes on M365.FM are currently linked to this concept, and no related entities or official documentation links are recorded for it.

minimal-apis.desc: Minimal APIs in ASP.NET Core are a simplified approach for building HTTP APIs with minimal code and configuration, without using controllers.

faq.a: Minimal APIs are a simplified approach in ASP.NET Core for building HTTP APIs with minimal code and configuration, without using controllers.
faq.q: What are Minimal APIs in ASP.NET Core?

faq.a: Minimal APIs are a concept within the broader ASP.NET Core framework, offering an alternative to the controller-based way of defining HTTP APIs.
faq.q: How do Minimal APIs relate to ASP.NET Core?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn provides documentation on the route-to-code approach in the ASP.NET Core web API section.
faq.q: Where can official documentation on Minimal APIs be found?

minimal-apis.long:
Minimal APIs (ASP.NET Core) are a simplified approach for building HTTP APIs within ASP.NET Core. They are designed to require minimal code and configuration, and they do not rely on controllers, which are the traditional structure used for web APIs in the framework.

The approach is used when developers want to define HTTP endpoints directly and keep the surrounding setup small. Instead of organizing API logic into controller classes, endpoints are declared in a more compact, route-to-code style. This makes the concept relevant for small services and for scenarios where reducing ceremony is a priority.

Minimal APIs sit under the broader topic of ASP.NET Core, the Microsoft web framework for building web applications and services. Official documentation for the route-to-code approach is available from Microsoft Learn under the ASP.NET Core web API section.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity, so this page serves as a concise reference definition of the term within the Microsoft ecosystem.

mistral-ocr.desc: Mistral OCR is an optical character recognition API from Mistral AI that turns PDFs, scans and images into structured Markdown, including tables and layout details.

faq.a: Mistral OCR is an API from Mistral AI that extracts text and structured content from PDFs and images and returns it as Markdown, including tables, within a JSON response organized by page.
faq.q: What does Mistral OCR do?

faq.a: According to Mistral's documentation, inputs can be images such as PNG, JPEG and AVIF or documents such as PDF, PPTX and DOCX, supplied as a public URL, Base64 or an uploaded file. More than 40 languages are supported.
faq.q: Which file types and languages does Mistral OCR support?

faq.a: The episode "How to Build Private RAG with SharePoint and n8n" describes Mistral OCR, running in Azure AI Foundry, as a way to convert scanned documents into searchable data for the knowledge base behind a SharePoint and n8n based RAG solution.
faq.q: How is Mistral OCR used in the M365.FM episode on private RAG?

mistral-ocr.long:
Mistral OCR is an optical character recognition API from Mistral AI. It converts documents, including scans and tables, into structured Markdown so that their content can be searched, processed or passed on to other systems. In Mistral's documentation the capability appears under the name Document AI OCR processor, and the mistral-ocr-latest alias points to the newest OCR model. In the M365.FM episode on private retrieval augmented generation, it is used inside Azure AI Foundry.

The service extracts text and structured content from PDFs and images while preserving document structure and hierarchy. Supported inputs include images such as PNG, JPEG and AVIF, and documents such as PDF, PPTX and DOCX. A file can be passed as a public URL, as Base64 or as an uploaded file. The documentation lists support for more than 40 languages.

The result is returned as a JSON object that contains pages. Each page holds Markdown, images, tables, hyperlinks, header, footer, dimensions, confidence scores and blocks, and the response also includes model and usage information. Tables can be left inline in the Markdown or returned separately as Markdown or HTML tables through a table format parameter. Headers and footers can be extracted separately. Block extraction returns paragraph-level bounding boxes with structural labels such as title, list, table, equation, caption, code and signature, in reading order. Confidence scores can be requested at page, block or word level.

Some features depend on the model version. According to the documentation, table formatting and separate header or footer extraction require OCR version 2512 or newer, and block extraction requires OCR 4 or newer. For large volumes, Mistral recommends its Batch Inference service, and for structured output it points to Document Annotations. The documentation page itself does not mention Azure AI Foundry, so details of that hosting setup come only from the episode.

A typical situation is a knowledge base built from scanned or image-based documents. Text that exists only as a scan cannot be searched or retrieved by a language model until it has been recognized and converted. Mistral OCR addresses that step by producing Markdown that keeps headings, lists and tables, which is a more usable form for indexing than flat extracted text. Decisions around it usually concern the output format for tables, whether headers and footers should be kept or stripped, whether confidence scores are needed to flag uncertain passages, and whether batch processing is appropriate for the document volume.

The episode "How to Build Private RAG with SharePoint and n8n" (2026-06-06) places Mistral OCR in a private retrieval augmented generation setup. The episode states that tools like Mistral OCR help convert scanned documents into searchable data and thereby improve the knowledge base. It sits alongside correct SharePoint setup for document organization and retrieval, and workflow automation with n8n that connects SharePoint and manages data retrieval tasks. The episode also recommends regular testing and iteration so that the solution stays reliable and efficient, and notes that such a solution can be scaled by integrating multiple data sources and adapting workflows to an organization's needs.

mitre-attack.desc: MITRE ATT&CK is a free, public knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques from real-world observations, used as a shared language for describing attacks.

faq.a: MITRE ATT&CK is a free, public knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations, maintained by MITRE. It serves as a shared language for describing how attacks are carried out.
faq.q: What is MITRE ATT&CK?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, it is used inside Microsoft Defender to map alerts to attack stages, in Microsoft Sentinel for visualizing ATT&CK coverage, and in Microsoft Threat Analytics guidance that links techniques to hunting and incidents.
faq.q: Where does MITRE ATT&CK show up in Microsoft security tools?

faq.a: The episode "Turn Microsoft Threat Analytics into Real Security Action" describes pulling techniques into Advanced Hunting, linking findings to incidents in Microsoft Defender, and converting recommendations into actions in a read, test, act, verify rhythm.
faq.q: How can ATT&CK techniques be used in practice?

mitre-attack.long:
MITRE ATT&CK is a free, public knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques that is based on real-world observations of how attacks are carried out. It is maintained by MITRE and is widely used as a shared language: instead of describing an intrusion in ad hoc terms, security teams can refer to the same named tactics and techniques and understand each other across tools, teams and organizations.

The core idea is to break a cyberattack down into steps. Tactics describe the stage or goal of an attacker at a given point, and techniques describe how that goal is pursued. Because the entries come from observed adversary behavior rather than from theory, the framework works as a reference that defenders can map their own alerts, detections and findings onto. This makes it useful for threat analysis, for spotting gaps in defenses, and for communicating about incidents in a consistent way.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, MITRE ATT&CK appears in several security products and workflows. The episode "Microsoft Defender for Cloud Security and Compliance" describes relying on the MITRE ATT&CK framework inside Microsoft Defender to understand how attackers think. When an alert arrives, the mapping shows which stage of an attack is happening. According to the episode, this helps with analyzing threats using a common language and with finding gaps in defenses so they can be fixed quickly.

The episode "Microsoft Defender vs Sentinel: When You Need Both" lists MITRE ATT&CK coverage among the capabilities of Microsoft Sentinel. In that context, the framework is used to visualize security status, so that detection coverage can be viewed against known adversary techniques. The same capability list includes analytics that reduce alert noise and group alerts into incidents, threat intelligence from multiple sources, watchlists, workbooks and incident management, with ATT&CK coverage acting as one lens on the overall detection picture.

The episode "Microsoft Defender for Identity - Simply Explained" refers to MITRE ATT&CK when discussing proactive security assessments. It states that the PROID framework detected all thirty-one MITRE ATT&CK techniques in a simulated environment, and presents this as evidence that such assessments can address various tactics and layers of security. The episode places this within a wider argument for threat hunting and continuous monitoring as part of identity threat detection.

The episode "Turn Microsoft Threat Analytics into Real Security Action" shows a practical use of ATT&CK techniques in daily operations. It explains that Microsoft's security researchers map global telemetry, MITRE ATT&CK techniques and indicators of compromise into guidance written in the tenant's own language. The episode proposes a read, test, act, verify rhythm and a focused 60 minute workflow in which techniques are pulled into Advanced Hunting, findings are linked to incidents in Microsoft Defender, and recommendations are turned into concrete actions. In this workflow, ATT&CK techniques serve as the bridge between threat reports and hunting queries that can be run against a tenant.

Taken together, the episodes treat MITRE ATT&CK less as a product and more as a vocabulary and reference model. Typical decisions around it include which techniques to prioritize for detection, how to read coverage views in a SIEM, and how to translate a technique named in a threat report into a hunt or a configuration change. The framework itself does not detect anything; its value lies in structuring the conversation between analysts, tools and reports.

mixed-reality.desc: Mixed reality (MR) blends digital content such as instructions and 3D objects with the physical environment so both can be seen and used together.

faq.a: Mixed reality (MR) blends digital content such as instructions and 3D objects with the physical environment so both can be seen and used together. In the M365.FM episodes it appears mainly in frontline and field work scenarios.
faq.q: What is mixed reality?

faq.a: The episodes describe Dynamics 365 Guides as a mixed reality application that brings instructions into the user's field of view, and Dynamics 365 Remote Assist as a way to connect frontline workers with remote experts using live video, visual guidance, Microsoft Teams, and mixed reality scenarios.
faq.q: How does mixed reality relate to Dynamics 365 Guides and Remote Assist?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Mesh - Simply Explained", Microsoft Mesh is no longer a standalone metaverse platform and has become an integrated feature inside Microsoft's collaboration tools.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Mesh a metaverse platform?

mixed-reality.long:
Mixed reality (MR) is an approach in which digital content, such as instructions and 3D objects, is blended with the physical environment so that both can be seen and used together. Unlike a fully virtual setting, the real surroundings remain part of the experience, and the digital layer is placed on top of or alongside them. In the Microsoft ecosystem, the term appears mainly in workplace and frontline scenarios, where information is brought directly to the location where work is performed.

The M365.FM episodes describe several practical uses. In the episode "Dynamics 365 Guides - Simply Explained", the central idea is that information appears directly inside the user's field of view. The episode explains Dynamics 365 Guides as a mixed reality application, how Microsoft HoloLens brought instructions into the physical workplace, and how companies could capture expert knowledge. It also covers how Microsoft Teams enabled remote assistance and how Dynamics 365, Dataverse, Power Platform, Power BI, and AI could extend the experience. The episode additionally raises a strategic issue that organizations need to understand, noting that Microsoft has made changes affecting the product's direction.

A second use case is remote collaboration. The episode "Dynamics 365 Remote Assist - Simply Explained" looks at how frontline workers can connect with remote experts through live video, visual guidance, Microsoft Teams, mobile devices, and mixed reality. The scenarios covered include field service, manufacturing, maintenance, inspections, troubleshooting, and training. The core idea stated in the episode is that, instead of trying to describe a physical problem to someone who cannot see it, a worker can show the problem and receive guidance in context. The episode also ties this to Dynamics 365 Field Service and to Microsoft 365 identity and security.

Mixed reality also appears in connection with digital twins. The episode "Codify Business Logic into a Digital Twin for AI Agents" mentions that maintenance and operations teams use digital twins to create work instructions in mixed reality, which makes inspections and repairs more efficient. It also notes that simulation and training become more engaging with AR and VR, which helps transfer knowledge faster, and cites Boeing as an example of a company using digital twins to power AR aircraft inspection apps that generate synthetic images for training machine learning models.

In field service, the episode "Use Copilot in Dynamics 365 Field Service" describes the integration of mixed reality and guided workflows with Copilot. According to the episode, this allows Copilot to create context-aware checklists that align with AR overlays, which it says improves first-time fix rates. This sits alongside other capabilities discussed there, such as analyzing photos and short videos from customers or technicians to identify visible faults and attaching annotated evidence to work orders.

The term is also linked to Microsoft Mesh. The episode "Microsoft Mesh - Simply Explained" recalls that early announcements were accompanied by words like metaverse, mixed reality, and virtual worlds, and that many people assumed Microsoft was building a completely new digital universe for work. The episode states that the product has evolved considerably: Microsoft Mesh is no longer a standalone metaverse platform but has become an integrated feature inside Microsoft's collaboration tools. This illustrates a typical decision point around mixed reality, namely the difference between an ambitious vision and the concrete, integrated capabilities organizations actually use.

Taken together, the episodes present mixed reality less as a single product and more as a way of delivering guidance, expertise, and data in the physical context of a task. Typical situations include step-by-step instructions for technicians, live support from a remote expert, inspections and repairs supported by digital twin data, and training that benefits from immersive simulation. Organizations weighing such scenarios need to consider the devices involved, the connected Dynamics 365 and Microsoft 365 services, and the product direction changes that the episodes point out.

mixture-of-experts.desc: Mixture of experts (MoE) is a model architecture where a gating mechanism activates only some expert sub-networks per input, so large models use fewer parameters per inference.

faq.a: Mixture of experts is a model architecture in which a gating mechanism activates only a subset of expert sub-networks for each input. This lets a model have many parameters while using fewer of them per inference.
faq.q: What is mixture of experts (MoE)?

faq.a: A gating function takes the input and produces weights, the experts each produce outputs, and the final result is usually a weighted sum. In sparsely-gated MoE, only the top-k gate values are kept, with k typically 1 or 2, so only some experts run.
faq.q: How does the gating mechanism work in an MoE model?

faq.a: Known limits include load imbalance between experts, discrete routing that is harder to optimize, many interacting design choices and training stability. Techniques such as auxiliary losses, capacity factors and bias adjustments are used to address balancing.
faq.q: What challenges are associated with mixture of experts?

mixture-of-experts.long:
Mixture of experts (MoE) is a machine learning technique and model architecture in which several expert sub-networks divide a problem space into regions, while a gating mechanism decides which experts are used for each input. As a result, a model can hold a very large number of parameters while only a subset of them is active during any single inference. The idea comes from ensemble learning, where it was once described as committee machines, and it has become a common design pattern for large neural networks.

The core mechanism has two parts. A gating function takes the input and produces weights, and the experts each produce outputs. The final result is usually a weighted sum of the expert outputs, and the experts and the gate are trained jointly. In deep learning the main motivation is conditional computation: by keeping only the top-k gate values, with k typically 1 or 2, only some experts run for a given input. This approach, called sparsely-gated MoE, was introduced by Shazeer and colleagues at Google Brain in 2017. In Transformer models, MoE layers usually replace the feedforward layers within Transformer blocks.

Several well-known models use this design. The Switch Transformer uses top-1 routing, GLaM has 1.2 trillion parameters, Mixtral 8x7B has 46.7B parameters and 8 experts, and DBRX has 132B parameters and 16 experts. These examples show how the architecture is applied at very different scales, always with the same principle of activating only part of the network per input.

Training and operating MoE models involves a number of design decisions. Load balancing is one of them: without countermeasures, some experts can receive far more inputs than others, and approaches such as auxiliary losses or DeepSeek-style bias adjustments are used to even out the load. Other topics include capacity factors, token dropping, the distinction between shared and routed experts, and sparse upcycling, which converts a dense model into an MoE model. Known limitations include load imbalance, discrete routing that is harder to optimize, many interacting design choices and training stability.

The term also appears in discussions of enterprise AI. The M365.FM episode "Mixture of Experts for Enterprise Copilot and AI Agents" describes a Mixture of Experts approach in which specialized AI services collaborate and select specific models suited to the task at hand. According to the episode, this contrasts with traditional multi-model strategies that often rely on a single generalist model, and it presents MoE as a way to improve performance by drawing on the strengths of multiple experts. The episode also cites a figure from service providers reporting a 97% positive impact on customer satisfaction when specialized AI systems are adopted. That figure is attributed to the episode and is not a property of the architecture itself.

When evaluating MoE in practice, the central trade-off is between total parameter count and per-inference cost. A sparse model can offer large capacity while activating only a fraction of its parameters, but it brings routing, balancing and stability concerns that dense models do not have. Readers comparing the architectural meaning with the enterprise-oriented framing in the episode should note that the first describes routing inside a single neural network, while the second describes selecting among specialized AI services or models for a task.

mlops.desc: MLOps (machine learning operations) is a set of practices for managing the deployment and lifecycle of machine learning models, documented by Microsoft for Azure Machine Learning.
mlops.long:
MLOps (machine learning operations) is a concept that covers the management and deployment of machine learning models across their lifecycle. Microsoft describes it in its Azure Machine Learning documentation under the topic of model management and deployment.

The term is used for the practices that move a machine learning model from development into production use and keep it manageable afterward. In the Microsoft ecosystem, this subject is addressed in the context of Azure Machine Learning, where the official documentation explains how models are managed and deployed.

The facts available for this entry are limited. No related entities, aliases or detailed definitions are recorded here, so the entry points to the official Microsoft documentation as the authoritative source for specifics on workflows, tooling and terminology.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

mobile-application-management.desc: Mobile Application Management (MAM) in Microsoft Intune protects company data inside apps through app protection policies, with no device enrollment needed.

faq.a: No. According to the Microsoft documentation, MAM protects corporate data within an app and can be used without device enrollment. A full device wipe, however, is only possible on devices enrolled in MDM.
faq.q: Does Mobile Application Management (MAM) require device enrollment?

faq.a: Selective wipe removes only company data from the app and leaves personal data in place. The app checks for such a wipe request roughly every 30 minutes.
faq.q: What does selective wipe do in MAM?

faq.a: A user needs a Microsoft Entra account with an Intune license and membership in a targeted security group. The app must be integrated with the Intune App SDK or wrapped with the Intune App Wrapping Tool, and Android requires the Company Portal app.
faq.q: What is needed to apply app protection policies?

mobile-application-management.long:
Mobile Application Management (MAM) in Microsoft Intune is an approach that protects corporate data at the app level rather than managing the entire device. It is typically used on personal devices, where an organization wants to secure work or school data without taking control of the whole phone or tablet. Because protection applies to the app and the data inside it, the device itself does not have to be enrolled, and personal content outside the managed app stays out of scope.

MAM in Intune works through app protection policies. These policies are rules that are enforced when a user accesses or moves company data, and they can also block or monitor specific actions inside an app. The documentation describes support for multi-identity apps, in which only the work or school account is protected while any personal account in the same app is left alone. Policy options named in the sources include an app PIN with a configurable recheck interval and an optional data wipe after failed PIN attempts, encryption of company data only, and access conditions. Such conditions can include a minimum operating system version or app version, a Play Integrity verdict, and jailbreak or root checks.

A central capability is selective wipe. When this action is triggered, only company data is removed from the app, while personal data remains untouched. According to the Microsoft documentation, the app checks for such a wipe request roughly every 30 minutes. A full device wipe, by contrast, is only possible on devices that are enrolled in mobile device management (MDM), which is one of the practical differences between MAM and MDM.

Several requirements apply before MAM can take effect. A user needs a Microsoft Entra account with an Intune license and must be a member of a security group that is targeted by the policy. The app must be integrated with the Intune App SDK or wrapped with the Intune App Wrapping Tool. On Android, the Company Portal app is needed, and Office apps require matching Microsoft 365 licensing. The documentation also lists limits: behavior can be unreliable when apps depend on on-premises services, and PIN sharing rules differ by platform.

In practice, administrators choose between MAM and MDM depending on who owns the device and how much control is appropriate. MAM suits bring-your-own-device scenarios where only data inside apps needs protection, while MDM is used for managed corporate devices that are enrolled and configured through profiles and compliance policies. The two can also be combined as part of a broader endpoint strategy.

The episode "Microsoft Intune - Simply Explained" lists MAM among the key concepts of Intune, next to device enrollment, configuration profiles, compliance policies, application deployment, Windows Autopilot and MDM, and notes how Intune integrates with Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Defender and Conditional Access. The episode "Harden Intune Deployment for Zero Trust Compliance" recommends using Conditional Access policies so that only compliant devices reach company resources, and says to protect app data with Mobile Application Management (MAM). It also suggests using Endpoint Analytics for ongoing improvements and regularly reviewing logs and audits to keep an Intune environment secure.

model-driven-app.desc: A model-driven app is a Power Apps app type generated from the Dataverse data model, with forms, views and business process flows laid out automatically.

faq.a: A model-driven app is a Power Apps app type that is generated from the Dataverse data model. Forms, views and business process flows are laid out automatically instead of being designed screen by screen.
faq.q: What is a model-driven app?

faq.a: A canvas app follows a user interface first approach with full control over layout, while a model-driven app derives its structure from the data model and business rules in Dataverse. The choice depends on the business requirements.
faq.q: How does a model-driven app differ from a canvas app?

faq.a: The episode "SharePoint Lists vs Model-Driven Apps: Avoid Overbuilding" says Dataverse adds licensing, security matrices, solution layers and governance overhead. For problems that only need a shared list and a few notifications, SharePoint or Microsoft Teams may be simpler.
faq.q: When might a model-driven app be more than a solution needs?

model-driven-app.long:
A model-driven app is one of the two main app types in Power Apps. Instead of designing every screen by hand, the maker builds on the Dataverse data model, and the app is generated from it, with forms, views and business process flows laid out automatically. The app type is also referred to as model-driven apps or, in German, as a modellgesteuerte App. Microsoft documents the concept in its model-driven app overview for Power Apps makers.

The approach is data first. The structure of the application follows from the tables, relationships and business rules defined in Dataverse, rather than from a free screen layout. This makes model-driven apps a fit for data-heavy business applications with many related tables, where a consistent interface and a shared data model matter more than custom design. The counterpart is the canvas app, which follows a user interface first approach and gives the maker full control over layout and user experience. One episode summarizes the difference by saying that canvas apps let makers build custom layouts and screens, while model-driven apps use data models and business rules to build solutions.

Model-driven apps are related to two other topics. Power Apps is the broader platform in which the app type is built, alongside Power Automate, Power BI, Dataverse and Power Pages in the Microsoft Power Platform. Dataverse supplies the tables, relationships and security that the generated app depends on. Because the app is derived from the data model, decisions about the Dataverse schema directly shape what the app looks like and how it behaves.

Choosing between app types depends on business requirements. The episode "Canvas Apps vs Model-Driven Apps - Simply Explained" from Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets on M365 FM, presented by Mirko Peters, explains the differences in simple terms for IT professionals and citizen developers, and describes when each approach delivers the greatest value. The episode "Power Apps - Simply Explained" places both app types within the wider Power Apps platform and covers how they integrate with Microsoft 365 services such as SharePoint, Teams, Excel and Outlook, as well as Dynamics 365 and Azure. It also lists practical scenarios such as employee onboarding, asset management, inspections, help desk solutions, inventory tracking, approval processes and field service applications.

The episode "SharePoint Lists vs Model-Driven Apps: Avoid Overbuilding" takes a cautionary view. It argues that model-driven apps can look like a fix for every business problem, but that this belief can lead to complexity and low adoption. According to the episode, Dataverse brings licensing, security matrices, solution layers and governance overhead, and it warns of over-restrictive setups such as mis-scoped roles or business units that make records appear to disappear. Its advice is to build where people already work, automate what matters, and consider Microsoft Teams and SharePoint when a shared list and a few notifications are enough.

Model-driven apps also appear as a skill area in career guidance. The episode "Build a Power Platform Career with Nathalie Leenders [MVP-MCT]" lists power apps development for canvas and model-driven apps among the areas to learn, next to workflows in Power Automate, dashboards and reports in Power BI, connections with SharePoint and Dataverse, SQL, and JavaScript and JSON.

The episode "Power Apps Code Apps - Simply Explained" mentions the model-driven app as one of the traditional Power Apps app types, against which Code Apps are compared. Code Apps let developers build React-based web applications with familiar tools while still using Dataverse, Microsoft Entra authentication, connectors and managed deployments.

model-quantization.desc: Model quantization stores a model's weights in a lower-bit numerical format, such as four-bit NF4, to reduce memory requirements for running and fine-tuning large models.

faq.a: Model quantization is storing a model's weights in a lower-bit numerical format, for example four-bit NF4, to cut memory needs.
faq.q: What is model quantization?

faq.a: QLoRA combines model quantization with LoRA. It allows fine-tuning large models on a single GPU.
faq.q: What is QLoRA?

faq.a: It reduces the memory a model requires, which helps large models fit on limited hardware such as a single GPU.
faq.q: Why is quantization used?

model-quantization.long:
Model quantization is the practice of storing a model's weights in a lower-bit numerical format instead of higher-precision values. One example is the four-bit NF4 format. Because each weight occupies fewer bits, the overall memory needed to hold the model is reduced.

The main purpose is to make large models fit on limited hardware. Lower memory needs mean that models which would otherwise exceed the capacity of a single GPU can be loaded and used on more modest setups.

Quantization is often combined with LoRA, a technique for adapting a model by training a small set of additional parameters. This combination is known as QLoRA. With QLoRA, the base model weights are kept in a quantized form while the adaptation is trained, which allows fine-tuning of large models on a single GPU.

This page describes the concept in general terms. No related entities or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to it, so it serves as a reference definition for readers who encounter the term in discussions of AI model deployment and fine-tuning.

model-router.desc: Model router is a deployable chat model in Microsoft Foundry that selects an underlying large language model in real time to respond to each prompt.

faq.a: Model router is a deployable chat model in Microsoft Foundry that selects an underlying large language model in real time to respond to each prompt.
faq.q: What is Model router in Microsoft Foundry?

faq.a: No. Model router is part of Microsoft Foundry, formerly Azure AI Foundry, and is deployed within that platform.
faq.q: Is Model router a separate platform?

faq.a: Details such as supported models and deployment steps are in the Microsoft Learn how-to documentation for Model router in the Foundry OpenAI section.
faq.q: Where can the technical details of Model router be found?

model-router.long:
Model router is a deployable chat model in Microsoft Foundry, the platform formerly known as Azure AI Foundry. Rather than answering a prompt with a single fixed model, it chooses an underlying large language model in real time for each request and returns that model's response.

In practice, Model router is deployed like other chat models in Microsoft Foundry and called through a single endpoint. Because the selection of the underlying model happens per prompt, one deployment can serve requests that are handled by different models behind the scenes. This is the core idea behind the product: routing each prompt to a suitable model instead of requiring the application to pick one in advance.

Model router is part of Microsoft Foundry and is documented in the Microsoft Learn how-to guide for Model router in the Foundry OpenAI section. That documentation is the authoritative source for supported underlying models, deployment steps, configuration options and any limits, none of which are detailed here.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to Model router (Microsoft Foundry). Related topics on the site include Microsoft Foundry, the platform that hosts the deployment.

modern-work.desc: Modern Work is an umbrella term for the modern digital workplace, covering cloud identities, security and infrastructure as well as collaboration tools, generative AI and new ways of working.

faq.a: Modern Work is an umbrella term for the modern digital workplace. It covers the technical side, such as cloud identities, security and infrastructure, and the end-user side, such as collaboration tools, generative AI and new ways of working.
faq.q: What does Modern Work mean?

faq.a: The episode "Fix a Failing Microsoft 365 Rollout" says identity issues can block access to Copilot features and the Copilot app, and that outdated Office apps or operating systems can break integrations or hide features. Resolving these is described as essential to recovering a rollout.
faq.q: Why do identity and device requirements matter for Modern Work rollouts?

faq.a: Modern Work is a Solutions Partner designation covering Microsoft 365 productivity, collaboration and endpoint management. According to the episodes, it is also a prerequisite for the AI Business Solutions specialization, together with the Business Applications designation.
faq.q: How does Modern Work relate to the Microsoft partner program?

modern-work.long:
Modern Work is an umbrella term for the modern digital workplace. It describes two sides of the same subject: the technical foundation, which includes cloud identities, security and infrastructure, and the end-user experience, which includes collaboration tools, generative AI and new ways of working. The term is used both in everyday discussions about how organizations equip their staff and in the way Microsoft structures its partner programs.

The technical side concerns what IT teams build and operate so that people can work from different places and on different devices. Cloud identities determine who can sign in and what they can reach, security protects those identities and the data behind them, and infrastructure delivers the services and devices. The end-user side concerns what employees actually see and use: collaboration tools, generative AI features and the habits of working together that develop around them. Treating the two sides together matters because a rollout can fail on either one. A strong collaboration tool still disappoints if identities are misconfigured, and a well-secured environment still goes unused if people do not adopt it.

The M365.FM episode "Fix a Failing Microsoft 365 Rollout" illustrates how these sides interact. It notes that resolving identity issues is essential to recovering a stalled rollout, because identity problems can block access to Copilot features and to the office agent or Copilot app. The episode also says that some Copilot features and modern work scenarios expect updated clients and Windows 11 capabilities, and that outdated Office apps or operating system versions can break integrations, reduce performance or hide Copilot features in Microsoft Office. Ensuring devices meet requirements is described as a key implementation step. For AI adoption, the episode advises planning with clear governance and pilot projects to avoid rollout failures.

Modern Work also appears in the context of flexible and remote working. The episode "Azure Virtual Desktop - Simply Explained" describes Azure Virtual Desktop as a way to reach a Windows desktop from any device, running in the cloud, which reduces the need for expensive hardware and eases IT overhead. It presents this as a cost-effective option, especially for small and medium businesses, and links it to enhanced security and to adapting to modern work trends. This shows how the infrastructure part of Modern Work supports the way people work day to day.

A further meaning of the term is its use as a named area in the Microsoft partner ecosystem. The episode "How to Become a High-Performing Microsoft Partner" lists Modern Work as one of the Solutions Partner designations and describes it as covering Microsoft 365 productivity, collaboration and endpoint management. It sits next to designations for areas such as Infrastructure (Azure), Security and modern app development on Azure. According to the episode, advancing through partnership levels depends on criteria such as the Partner Capability Score, which includes metrics in skilling, customer success and performance.

The episode "Microsoft Partner Journey: From Enrollment to Growth" connects this designation to further specializations. It states that the AI Business Solutions specialization requires a Solutions Partner designation for Business Applications or Modern Work. This makes Modern Work a prerequisite for certain AI-related partner paths, which reflects how closely the workplace and generative AI are now linked in the term's meaning.

Collaboration culture is another thread. The episode "Use Minecraft for Workplace Team Building" frames Minecraft as a way to improve collaboration in modern work. It says that sandbox constraints, such as limited building blocks and physics, push teams to prioritize and solve problems iteratively, and that real-time spatial collaboration can expose communication gaps that are otherwise hidden. It also stresses regular feedback and making such exercises part of team building to strengthen trust and communication. Taken together, the episodes show that Modern Work spans technology decisions, rollout governance, partner qualifications and the human side of working together.

modular-monolith.desc: A modular monolith is a single deployable application divided into modules with clear internal boundaries, usually along business capabilities, allowing later extraction into services.

faq.a: It is an architecture with a single deployable unit that is divided into modules with clear internal boundaries, typically by business capability.
faq.q: What is a modular monolith?

faq.a: The module boundaries make it possible to extract parts into services later if needed, while the application remains one deployable unit in the meantime.
faq.q: Why divide a monolith into modules?

faq.a: It is associated with the episode ".NET Extensibility and Clean Architecture with Miguel Castro [MVP]", dated 2026-07-01.
faq.q: Where does the modular monolith appear on M365.FM?

modular-monolith.long:
A modular monolith is an architectural approach in which an application is built and deployed as a single unit, while its internals are organized into modules with clearly defined boundaries. These modules are typically drawn along business capabilities rather than technical layers, so each one groups the logic that belongs to a particular area of the domain.

The main purpose of this structure is to keep the operational simplicity of one deployable unit while retaining a separation of concerns inside the codebase. Because the boundaries between modules are explicit, individual parts can be extracted into separate services later if a need arises, without redesigning the whole application from scratch.

On M365.FM, the concept appears in the episode ".NET Extensibility and Clean Architecture with Miguel Castro [MVP]", published on 2026-07-01, which places it in the context of .NET extensibility and clean architecture. No further details about how the topic is treated in that episode are provided here.

monorepo.desc: A monorepo keeps multiple projects or systems in one shared repository while each can still be built and deployed independently.

faq.a: A monorepo is a version control strategy in which multiple projects or systems are kept in one shared repository while still being deployable independently.
faq.q: What is a monorepo?

faq.a: According to the episode with Lars Gyrup Brink Nielsen, they do not necessarily. Microservices and micro-frontends can live inside one monorepo and still be built and deployed independently.
faq.q: Do microservices need separate repositories?

faq.a: The episode "The Monorepo Myth: Why Your Architecture Is Fragmented" describes it as an organizational decision that shapes how teams communicate, coordinate changes, and deliver software, not only a question of Git performance or build times.
faq.q: Is choosing a monorepo only a technical decision?

monorepo.long:
A monorepo is a version control strategy in which multiple projects or systems are stored in one shared source-control repository. The defining point is that sharing a repository does not mean sharing a deployment. Individual projects inside a monorepo can still be built and released independently of one another, which separates the question of where code lives from the question of how it ships.

The concept is mainly used to manage the relationship between systems that depend on each other. According to the episode with Lars Gyrup Brink Nielsen, microservices and micro-frontends do not necessarily require separate repositories. They can exist within one monorepo while still being independently built and deployed. The episode names two advantages of this setup: dependencies between projects become easier to understand, and changes that span multiple systems can be tested together rather than coordinated across several repositories.

The choice between a monorepo and multiple repositories is often framed as a technical matter, with arguments about Git performance, build times, or repository size. The episode "The Monorepo Myth: Why Your Architecture Is Fragmented" argues that this framing is incomplete. It describes the decision as an organizational one that determines how teams communicate, coordinate changes, and deliver software. The episode challenges the belief that either monorepos or multirepos are automatically the better option, so the right structure depends on how an organization actually works rather than on a general rule.

In practice, teams weigh a monorepo when several projects change together or share dependencies and when visibility across those projects matters. A single repository makes cross-project changes visible in one place and allows them to be validated together. Teams that choose separate repositories instead accept more coordination between repositories in exchange for a different boundary between projects. Neither approach removes the need to define ownership, standards, and how changes are reviewed and released.

The topic also appears in the context of AI coding agents. In the episode "GitHub Copilot, Clean Context, Automated Testing & AI Coding Agents with Lars Gyrup Brink Nielsen [MVP]", the monorepo is explained alongside the idea that organizations can make architectural rules automatically enforceable instead of expecting an agent to remember every rule. Within a shared repository, such rules can be applied consistently across the projects it contains, which is why the episode treats repository structure and enforceable standards as connected concerns.

The monorepo is also referenced as related listening in several M365.FM episodes about architecture, including "Microsoft Cowork IQ Knowledge Graph Architecture", "Microsoft 365 Backup with Isolated Vault Architecture", and ".NET Extensibility and Clean Architecture with Miguel Castro [MVP]". In those listings it is grouped with other architecture-focused topics such as Microsoft Graph automation and enterprise AI agent design, which reflects its role as a structural decision about how a software estate is organized.

To summarize the points the episodes make: a monorepo is a repository strategy, not a deployment strategy; independent builds and deployments remain possible inside it; and the decision to adopt it is better understood as an organizational choice about communication and coordination than as a purely technical one.

monthly-active-users.desc: Monthly active users (MAU) is a usage metric counting unique users who actively use a product within a month, here applied to see whether Copilot adoption sticks.

faq.a: MAU counts the unique users who actively use a product within a month. What counts as activity, such as logging in or uploading content, is defined by each organization and is often not disclosed.
faq.q: What does monthly active users (MAU) measure?

faq.a: It is used to track whether adoption sticks, since it shows how many distinct people keep using the product over a month instead of only receiving a license.
faq.q: Why does MAU matter for Copilot adoption?

faq.a: According to the episode "The FY26 Partner Designation Restructuring Is Coming — Most Partners Aren't Ready", the Secure AI Productivity Specialization requires partners to demonstrate a growth of 2,500 MAU on specified workloads.
faq.q: How does MAU relate to Microsoft partner designations?

monthly-active-users.long:
Monthly active users (MAU) is a usage metric that counts the unique users who actively use a product within a calendar month. It belongs to the family of active-user measures, which also include daily active users and weekly active users. In the context of M365.FM, the metric is used to judge whether adoption of a product such as Copilot sticks, meaning whether people keep using it after an initial rollout rather than simply being assigned a license.

The general definition of an active user is a unique user who interacts with a product within a set period. How that interaction is defined is left to each organization. Companies compute the figure from their own data, using actions they treat as activity, such as logging in, visiting a home page, commenting or uploading content. Because the methods vary and are often not disclosed, two MAU figures from different products or companies are not automatically comparable. This is one of the main criticisms of the metric: there is no standard definition, simple actions can inflate counts, duplicate or fake accounts can distort the numbers, and the figure says little about loyalty or about user behavior before and after adoption.

MAU is typically used for social networks, games, mobile apps and online banking, in research on churn prediction, and as a figure presented to investors and advertisers. A related measure is the ratio of daily to monthly active users, which serves as a rough engagement indicator. The source material cites a ratio of 0.15 as a growth tipping point and sustained values of 0.2 and above as a sign of lasting success. Growth in active users also does not always translate into revenue, and collecting this kind of usage data raises consent and privacy questions.

In the Microsoft partner ecosystem, MAU appears as a concrete qualification threshold. The M365.FM episode "The FY26 Partner Designation Restructuring Is Coming — Most Partners Aren't Ready" describes updates to partner designations and specializations. According to the episode, the Secure AI Productivity Specialization has replaced the Teamwork Deployment specialization, and it now requires partners to demonstrate a growth of 2,500 Monthly Active Users (MAU) on specified workloads, along with a reduction in customer tenant requirements. In this setting, MAU is not only an internal product-analytics number but a measurable proof point that a partner's customers are actually using the workloads the partner deployed.

For practitioners, the decision points around MAU follow from its definition. Before relying on a MAU figure, it is useful to establish which actions count as activity, over which period, and for which workloads, since a login and a meaningful use of a feature are very different signals.
