Used alone, MAU shows breadth of use but not depth, so it is often read alongside engagement ratios and other usage indicators. In adoption work, a rising MAU after a rollout suggests that use is spreading, while a flat or falling count can indicate that licensed users are not returning.

The episode on the FY26 partner designation changes is the M365.FM reference that ties MAU to a specific program requirement. It places the metric among other changes listed there, including Entra ID P2 being added to the Identity and Access Management specialization and GitHub certifications becoming part of the Digital & App Innovation designation. Within that discussion, MAU serves as the yardstick for sustained workload usage rather than one-time deployment.

mqtt.desc: MQTT is a lightweight publish-and-subscribe messaging protocol where producers publish to topics on a broker that forwards messages to subscribers.

faq.a: MQTT is a lightweight publish-and-subscribe messaging protocol in which producers publish messages to topics on a broker, which forwards them to subscribed consumers. It includes quality of service levels for delivery.
faq.q: What is MQTT?

faq.a: The episodes describe them as complementary: OPC UA exposes the machine signal, an edge layer collects it, and MQTT can distribute it locally before Microsoft Fabric ingests and analyzes the stream.
faq.q: How do MQTT and OPC UA relate in the M365.FM episodes?

faq.a: According to the episode "Connectivity Is Not Integration", no. Fast signal delivery still leaves questions such as which shipment is at risk unanswered until MES, ERP, maintenance and quality data are combined.
faq.q: Does MQTT alone make a connected factory useful for decisions?

mqtt.long:
MQTT is a lightweight publish-and-subscribe messaging protocol. In this model, producers publish messages to named topics on a broker, and the broker forwards each message to the consumers that have subscribed to those topics. Producers and consumers do not need to know about each other directly; the broker and the topic structure sit between them. MQTT also defines quality of service levels, which govern how reliably a message is delivered. These characteristics make it a common choice for moving small, frequent messages such as sensor readings, alarms and status changes.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, MQTT appears mainly in industrial and manufacturing scenarios. The M365.FM episodes place it in a chain that starts at the factory floor: a programmable logic controller (PLC) holds raw tag values such as a temperature reading, a timestamp and a quality state; an industrial gateway or edge layer collects those signals; a message broker distributes them; and cloud services such as Azure IoT Hub or Microsoft Fabric ingest and analyze the resulting stream. The episode "From Sensor to Dashboard: The MQTT Pipeline Through Azure IoT Hub" follows this path and notes that older plants often run several generations of equipment, some using proprietary protocols or OPC UA, which makes a reliable architecture across sensors, gateways, brokers and cloud analytics necessary.

MQTT is frequently discussed together with OPC UA, and the episodes treat the two as complementary rather than competing. "MQTT and OPC UA in Microsoft Manufacturing: Azure IoT Operations + Fabric Architecture" argues that framing industrial connectivity as a winner-takes-all battle misses the real issue, which the episode describes as a lack of trust in manufacturing data. "How Machine Data Reaches Microsoft Fabric - From OPC UA to Real-Time Analytics" describes a division of roles: OPC UA exposes the machine signal, an edge layer collects it, MQTT can distribute it locally, and Microsoft Fabric can ingest and analyze the stream.

Another recurring topic is the Unified Namespace. The episode "Unified Namespace and MQTT on Azure: Architecture for Real-Time Plant Data" explains that a unified namespace makes plant data available in a consistent structure for many consumers. It covers MQTT basics and how to architect such a namespace on Azure, and it points to trade-offs, naming and governance questions that should be settled early. Because MQTT organizes messages by topic, the topic hierarchy and naming conventions become a design decision with lasting consequences for every consumer that subscribes.

The episodes also stress the limits of what MQTT solves. Moving a signal quickly is not the same as answering an operational question. "Connectivity Is Not Integration — Why Your Connected Factory Still Can't Answer the Right Questions" gives the example of a packaging machine that stops: the PLC reports the fault, OPC UA exposes the event, MQTT distributes it, and the dashboard updates immediately. Yet when a planner asks which customer shipment is now at risk, the answer still requires MES data, ERP records, maintenance history, quality status, production quantities and delivery commitments, often combined in a spreadsheet. The episode on machine data reaching Microsoft Fabric makes a similar point: the difficult part begins after the data arrives, when raw telemetry has to be turned into enough production context to support a decision.

In practice, decisions around MQTT therefore concern more than the protocol itself. They include where the broker runs, how topics are named and governed, how signals from different equipment generations are brought into one structure, and how the delivered messages are combined with business context downstream. The M365.FM episodes present MQTT as the transport and distribution layer within a larger architecture, with the value depending on the context and trust built around the data it carries.

mqtt-quality-of-service.desc: MQTT quality of service (QoS) defines delivery guarantees between client and broker: QoS 0 (at most once), QoS 1 (at least once) and QoS 2 (exactly once).

faq.a: MQTT defines three levels: QoS 0 (at most once), QoS 1 (at least once) and QoS 2 (exactly once). They differ in how acknowledgement and retry are handled between client and broker.
faq.q: What are the MQTT QoS levels?

faq.a: Azure IoT Hub supports QoS 0 and QoS 1. QoS 2, exactly once delivery, is not among the supported levels.
faq.q: Which MQTT QoS levels does Azure IoT Hub support?

faq.a: QoS 0 delivers a message at most once without a delivery guarantee. QoS 1 delivers at least once using acknowledgement and retry, which means a message can be received more than once.
faq.q: What is the difference between QoS 0 and QoS 1?

mqtt-quality-of-service.long:
MQTT quality of service (QoS) is a set of delivery levels in the MQTT messaging protocol. It governs how acknowledgement and retry work between a client and a broker, and therefore how reliably a message is expected to reach its destination.

Three levels are defined. QoS 0 means at most once: the message is sent without a guarantee of delivery. QoS 1 means at least once: delivery is acknowledged and retried as needed, so a message may arrive more than once. QoS 2 means exactly once: the message is delivered a single time through a more involved exchange between client and broker.

The choice of level is a trade-off between delivery assurance and protocol overhead, and it is typically set per message or per subscription depending on how important reliable delivery is for a given use case. In the Microsoft ecosystem, Azure IoT Hub supports MQTT with QoS 0 and QoS 1. QoS 2 is not among the levels supported by Azure IoT Hub, which is relevant when designing IoT devices and applications that connect to the service.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

ms-102.desc: Microsoft 365 Certified: Administrator Expert (MS-102) is a Microsoft expert certification for tenant, identity, security and compliance administration; the exam retires on 30 November 2026.

faq.a: It is an expert-level Microsoft certification for administering Microsoft 365 tenants, covering identity, security and compliance. The exam code is MS-102.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft 365 Certified: Administrator Expert (MS-102) certification?

faq.a: According to the available information, the MS-102 exam is scheduled to retire on 30 November 2026. The Microsoft Learn exam page is the place to confirm the current status.
faq.q: When is the MS-102 exam scheduled to retire?

faq.a: It covers Microsoft 365 as a whole, including Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive and the Microsoft 365 admin center.
faq.q: Which Microsoft 365 services does the certification cover?

ms-102.long:
Microsoft 365 Certified: Administrator Expert (MS-102) is an expert-level certification from Microsoft for administrators who manage Microsoft 365 tenants. It centers on the exam with the code MS-102 and addresses identity, security and compliance across a whole tenant. According to the available information, the exam is scheduled to retire on 30 November 2026, which matters for anyone planning to take it.

The certification is aimed at administrators who are responsible for a tenant as a whole rather than for a single workload. Instead of focusing on one service, it reflects the broader responsibility of keeping a Microsoft 365 environment organized, secure and compliant. That includes deciding how users and licenses are handled, how services are configured, and how protection and compliance requirements are met across the environment.

The topics linked to the certification show the areas it touches. It covers Microsoft 365 as the overall service, along with Exchange Online, SharePoint and OneDrive. Exchange Online represents mail, while SharePoint and OneDrive represent the file and content workloads that administrators have to configure and secure. The Microsoft 365 admin center is also part of the scope. It is the central place for managing users, licenses and services, and it is the day-to-day starting point for much tenant administration work.

In practice, someone preparing for MS-102 deals with tasks that cut across these services: setting up and maintaining the tenant, managing identities, applying security controls and meeting compliance needs. Because the exam is described as an expert-level credential, it assumes familiarity with these areas rather than introducing them from scratch. The official documentation page for the exam on Microsoft Learn is the reference point for the current skills outline and exam details, and it is the right place to check for the latest status of the retirement date.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Teams Governance with Entra ID as the Control Plane" mentions the certification in a list of training resources and credentials. There, Microsoft 365 Certified: Administrator Expert (MS-102) is described as the certification that evaluates, plans and manages Microsoft 365 services, listed alongside the MS-721 collaboration communications systems engineer path and the MS-700 course on Microsoft Teams. The episode presents these resources as a way to build skills and prepare for certification exams.

The same episode also offers a useful perspective for tenant administrators. It challenges the common belief that the Teams Admin Center is the central command for governance and describes it instead as a downstream service console. According to the episode, the real decisions about who gets in, what is blocked and which policy is enforced come from upstream identity controls. That view fits the tenant-wide scope of MS-102, where identity, security and compliance are treated as the foundation on which individual services such as Teams, Exchange Online, SharePoint and OneDrive depend.

ms-700.desc: Microsoft 365 Certified: Teams Administrator Associate (MS-700) is a Microsoft associate certification for planning, configuring and managing Teams, meetings and calling.

faq.a: The exam code is MS-700. It leads to the Microsoft 365 Certified: Teams Administrator Associate certification.
faq.q: What is the exam code for the Teams Administrator Associate certification?

faq.a: It covers Microsoft Teams, Teams Phone and Microsoft Teams Rooms, which together span collaboration, calling and meeting spaces.
faq.q: Which products does MS-700 cover?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Microsoft Teams Governance with Entra ID as the Control Plane", MS-700 focuses on managing Teams for collaboration and communication, while MS-721 covers managing Teams Phone, meetings and devices.
faq.q: How does MS-700 differ from MS-721?

ms-700.long:
Microsoft 365 Certified: Teams Administrator Associate, tested through the exam code MS-700, is an associate-level certification developed by Microsoft. It validates skills in planning, configuring and managing Microsoft Teams, including meetings and calling. The certification is directed at administrators who set up Teams in an organization, define policies and keep collaboration and voice services running.

The certification covers three product areas named in its description. Microsoft Teams is the core collaboration application. Teams Phone adds calling and telephony capabilities to it. Microsoft Teams Rooms brings the meeting experience into physical meeting spaces. Together these areas describe the main responsibilities of a Teams administrator: collaboration workloads, voice services and meeting room devices.

In practice, the role behind MS-700 involves deciding how Teams is rolled out and controlled. This includes defining policies, managing meetings and calling features, and operating the services day to day. Candidates typically prepare through Microsoft's own documentation and the official exam page on Microsoft Learn, which lists the exam details. Microsoft also offers hands-on instructor-led training for the exam under the course title MS-700: Managing Microsoft Teams.

The certification sits within a wider Microsoft certification family. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Teams Governance with Entra ID as the Control Plane" lists recommended training options in a table that places the Teams Administrator Associate (MS-700) next to related credentials. One of them is the Microsoft 365 Certified: Collaboration Communications Systems Engineer Associate (MS-721), which the episode describes as focused on managing Teams Phone, meetings and devices, and which also has a matching instructor-led course. The episode also mentions the Microsoft 365 Certified: Administrator Expert as a further certification in the list. This shows that MS-700 centers on managing Teams for collaboration and communication, while MS-721 leans toward the voice, meeting and device side.

The same episode also offers a governance perspective that is relevant for anyone studying this material. It challenges the idea that the Teams Admin Center is the central command for controlling Teams behavior and describes it as a downstream service console rather than the authority behind policy. According to the episode, decisions about access, blocking and enforcement originate in upstream identity controls, which is why it frames Entra ID as the control plane for Teams governance. For MS-700 candidates, this offers a useful frame for thinking about where governance is actually decided, even though the episode itself is not an exam guide.

The topic relates closely to Microsoft Teams, Teams Phone and Microsoft Teams Rooms, and indirectly to identity management through Entra ID. Choosing between MS-700 and a related certification such as MS-721 depends on whether the focus of the role is general Teams administration or specialized communications and device engineering, as the episode's comparison of the two credentials suggests.

mttr.desc: Mean time to resolution (MTTR) is an operational metric for the average time needed to restore a service after an incident, used in incident response and DevOps.

faq.a: MTTR stands for mean time to resolution, also read as mean time to recovery. It is the average time needed to restore a service after an incident.
faq.q: What does MTTR stand for?

faq.a: The episodes mention mean time to detection (MTTD) alongside MTTR. MTTD covers how quickly an issue is noticed, while MTTR covers how long restoring service takes, and agentic AI is described as reducing both.
faq.q: How is MTTR related to MTTD?

faq.a: The episodes point to Azure Service Health and Resource Health alerts, proactive monitoring, and AI agents that find information quickly and automate triage and repeatable fixes. One episode cites a 30-50% MTTR reduction for complex incidents with SharePoint AI agents.
faq.q: How can MTTR be reduced according to the M365.FM episodes?

mttr.long:
Mean time to resolution (MTTR) is an operational metric that describes the average time it takes to restore a service after an incident. The abbreviation is also read as mean time to recovery. It is regarded as a key measure for incident response and DevOps performance, because it condenses how quickly a team can move from a reported problem to a working service. A lower average generally indicates that disruptions are noticed, triaged and fixed faster, and that users and business processes are affected for a shorter period.

In practice, MTTR is used to track the health of operations over time, to compare the effect of process or tooling changes, and to support service-level discussions. Because it is an average, it is typically read alongside other indicators rather than on its own. One of the episodes pairs it with mean time to detection (MTTD), the time needed to notice that something is wrong, since resolution can only begin once an incident has been detected and triaged. Together, these measures describe the full path from the start of a disruption to restored service.

The M365.FM episodes mention MTTR in several contexts across the Microsoft ecosystem. In "Azure Monitor — Simply Explained" (2026-07-15), proactive monitoring is presented as essential for smooth operations in Azure. The episode says that enabling Service Health and Resource Health alerts gives timely notifications about Azure-wide or resource-specific issues, and that this helps reduce MTTR and lets teams act quickly to limit business impact. The same episode also stresses strict governance for dashboards so that the data shown in real-time monitoring remains trustworthy.

A second theme is the use of AI agents to shorten resolution times. In "Govern SharePoint Knowledge Agent with Human Oversight" (2025-11-03), the episode describes SharePoint AI agents as good at finding information and answering user queries quickly. It cites tool-calling accuracy of 90% or higher and responses in under 2.5 seconds, and says this fast response helps reduce MTTR by 30-50% for complex incidents that require coordination across teams. These figures are attributed to the episode and are not independently established here. The episode also describes concurrent orchestration, in which several AI tools analyze data in parallel, as part of how such agents work together.

In "How Do You Successfully Deploy Microsoft 365 Copilot Across an Enterprise?" (2026-07-29), MTTR appears as one of the benefits of agentic AI. The episode lists automated incident detection and remediation, in which agentic AI continuously monitors systems, triages alerts and executes repeatable fixes. According to the episode, this reduces both MTTD and MTTR while freeing engineers for higher-value work. It adds proactive problem prevention through predictive analytics and autonomous playbooks, and scalable self-service through intelligent assistants.

MTTR also shows up outside pure operations. In "Build Intelligent Power Apps with AI Builder" (2025-08-05), it is listed among the metrics that matter when automating business processes with AI. There it appears next to automation rate, accuracy, precision and recall, exception rate and human review throughput, model drift indicators, and business impact such as cost or time saved and SLA adherence. The episode also recommends running a pilot in shadow mode and comparing results against baseline KPIs, which is a way to judge whether a change actually improves resolution time.

When using MTTR, a few decisions recur: which events count as an incident, when the clock starts and stops, and whether the figure is reported as an average for all incidents or split by severity. Establishing a baseline before introducing monitoring alerts, dashboards or AI agents makes it possible to attribute any change in the metric to the new approach. The sources provided here do not prescribe a single calculation method, so teams define these boundaries themselves and apply them consistently.

multi-access-edge-computing.desc: Multi-access edge computing (MEC) places compute, storage and application hosting close to where data is generated, typically alongside a 5G network, to cut latency.

faq.a: MEC is a network architecture concept defined by ETSI that places compute, storage and application hosting close to where data is generated, typically alongside a 5G network. It was formerly called mobile edge computing and lets applications run at base stations or other edge nodes.
faq.q: What is multi-access edge computing (MEC)?

faq.a: The sources list lower latency, reduced core signaling load and lower hosting cost. Processing closer to users also reduces network congestion and improves application performance.
faq.q: What are the benefits of MEC?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode "Cloud Latency and Edge Computing Strategy" describes combining private 5G with MEC to bring processing close to devices, often within the same building or campus. Private 5G provides a dedicated wireless network, while MEC handles the local processing.
faq.q: How does MEC relate to private 5G?

multi-access-edge-computing.long:
Multi-access edge computing (MEC) is a network architecture concept that places compute, storage and application hosting physically close to where data is generated, typically alongside a 5G network. It enables real-time processing without round trips to a distant cloud region. The term was formerly known as mobile edge computing. According to the source material, the concept is defined by ETSI and brings cloud computing and an IT service environment to the edge of cellular networks and, more generally, of any network. ETSI created an Industry Specification Group for it in 2014.

The core idea is to run applications and processing closer to users. Doing so reduces network congestion and improves application performance. MEC is designed to run at cellular base stations or other edge nodes. This lets operators deploy new services quickly and open their radio access network (RAN) to authorized third parties such as developers and content providers. Listed benefits include lower latency, reduced core signaling load and lower hosting cost.

The central component is a MEC application server that is integrated with the RAN. It offers compute, storage, connectivity and real-time RAN information in a multitenant hosting environment. Applications are delivered to this environment as virtual machine images or containers. Because the server sits at or near the network edge, applications can use local radio information and avoid sending every request across the wider network to a central data center.

Typical use cases named in the sources include computational offloading, content delivery and caching, mobile big data analytics, connected cars, smart venues, healthcare, smart grids and indoor positioning. A common thread across these scenarios is that responsiveness matters and that moving all data to a distant cloud region would add delay or cost. The same material notes that few applications had adopted MEC at the time of writing, and it names AWS Wavelength as the first larger-scale commercial MEC product.

In practice, deciding where to run a workload comes down to what needs to happen locally and what can wait for the cloud. The M365.FM episode "Cloud Latency and Edge Computing Strategy" frames this as a strategy of processing workloads at the edge, filtering out noise and sending only what matters to the cloud, which it says keeps systems responsive and cost-effective. The episode describes breaking through the latency wall by combining private 5G networks with MEC. In that picture, data processing moves even closer to where devices operate, often within the same building or campus, so that not every piece of data has to travel to a distant cloud.

The episode also explains the role of the private 5G network in this combination. A private 5G network gives a dedicated wireless network in which the operator controls who connects and how data flows. Together with MEC, this arrangement keeps both connectivity and processing local, while the cloud remains the destination for the data that is worth forwarding.

MEC therefore sits between devices and the central cloud as an intermediate tier. It does not replace cloud regions; it complements them by handling latency-sensitive or high-volume processing nearby and passing on filtered results. Teams evaluating the concept typically weigh the latency requirements of the application, the volume of data generated at the site, and the cost of transporting that data, which are the same considerations the episode raises when discussing responsiveness and cost-effectiveness.

multi-agent-architecture.desc: Multi-agent architecture is an AI solution design in which several agents with their own scope, instructions and tools work together, often behind a routing front agent.

faq.a: It is an AI solution design in which several agents each have their own scope, instructions and tools. Typically a front agent routes requests to specialized agents.
faq.q: What is a multi-agent architecture?

faq.a: The Azure Architecture Center guidance advises starting with the lowest complexity that works and moving to several agents when prompt complexity, tool overload or security boundaries make a single agent unreliable.
faq.q: When should a multi-agent architecture be used instead of a single agent?

faq.a: The guidance names coordination overhead, added latency, multiplied model calls, growing context windows, error propagation and endless loops in group chat or handoff patterns. The M365.FM episode on private RAG security also mentions more complex protocol design and error handling.
faq.q: What are the drawbacks of multi-agent designs?

multi-agent-architecture.long:
Multi-agent architecture is an AI solution design in which several agents each have their own scope, instructions and tools. A common form uses a front agent that receives a request and routes it to specialized agents. Instead of one agent handling every task, responsibility is divided so that each agent focuses on a defined area. The term is used in the Microsoft ecosystem when building agents for Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio and custom development.

According to the M365.FM episode "Extending Microsoft 365 Copilot: Agents, MCP & Production-Grade AI with Yves Habersaat [MVP]", an agent needs instructions that define its responsibilities and boundaries, knowledge sources with relevant organizational information, tools that allow it to perform actions, and an orchestration layer that decides how requests are processed. In a multi-agent architecture, a front agent can delegate tasks to specialized agents. Depending on the task, those agents can then access internal knowledge sources, external systems, APIs and MCP servers.

The Azure Architecture Center guidance on AI agent orchestration patterns describes the idea as coordinating several specialized agents so they can work together on complex tasks. An orchestrator or a peer-based protocol handles task distribution, context passing and result aggregation. The guidance credits this design with specialization, easier scaling and simpler testing, and it allows each agent to have its own model, knowledge sources and tools. It names five orchestration patterns: sequential, concurrent, group chat, handoff and magentic. They differ in how work is routed and in whether a manager adapts a task list on the fly. Microsoft Agent Framework and Semantic Kernel are named as code-level options for implementing such designs.

The same guidance advises choosing the lowest complexity that works. The suggested progression is a direct model call first, then a single agent with tools, and only then several agents. Typical reasons to move to multiple agents are prompt complexity, tool overload or security boundaries that make a single agent unreliable. The costs and risks it lists include coordination overhead, added latency, multiplied model calls, growing context windows, error propagation and endless loops in group chat or handoff designs. Because agent output is nondeterministic, the guidance recommends testing with rubrics or an LLM judge rather than exact comparison, and it expects observability, authentication and guardrails.

Security is one of the motivations discussed in the M365.FM episode "Private RAG Security: Authorization-Aware Data Retrieval". The episode compares single-agent and multi-agent retrieval-augmented generation. In its comparison table, multi-agent RAG shows higher accuracy and higher transparency, but slower processing time. The episode's figures show surgical states captured at 50% versus 90%, drug costs at 50% versus 80%, and administration costs at 0% versus 80% for single-agent versus multi-agent setups. The episode also notes that moving to a multi-agent architecture can bring challenges such as more complex protocol design and stricter error-handling requirements. It argues that the benefits for security and efficiency often outweigh these challenges and connects the approach to Zero Trust principles in data security.

In practice, the decision around multi-agent architecture is a trade-off. Splitting scope across agents can make each agent easier to instruct, test and secure, and it lets different agents use different tools or knowledge sources. In return, routing logic, hand-offs and error handling add design effort, latency and cost. The sources therefore treat it as a step to take when a simpler design proves unreliable, not as a default starting point.

multi-agent-system.desc: A multi-agent system is an architecture in which several AI agents collaborate, typically with an orchestrating agent delegating tasks to specialized child agents.

faq.a: It is an architecture in which several AI agents work together, typically with one orchestrating agent delegating tasks to specialized child agents. Each agent can have its own role, knowledge and decision-making capabilities.
faq.q: What is a multi-agent system?

faq.a: The episodes say single agents can stall on complex workflows, such as Intune, Entra ID and Microsoft Graph tasks. Multiple agents can split roles like planning, operating and reviewing, and cross-verify information to improve reliability.
faq.q: Why use several agents instead of one?

faq.a: The Azure AI Foundry episode describes planner, operator, reviewer and concierge agents. The Copilot Studio episode mentions agents that create content, review quality, check user experience, validate requirements or orchestrate a workflow.
faq.q: Which roles appear in the example multi-agent systems?

multi-agent-system.long:
A multi-agent system is an architecture in which several AI agents work together instead of a single agent handling every task. In a common pattern, one orchestrating agent receives a goal and delegates parts of the work to specialized child agents, each with a defined role. The approach is used when a single agent struggles with complex, multi-step workflows or when work benefits from separation of duties, checks and review.

The episode excerpts describe the idea in several ways. According to the show notes for "Multi-Agent AI with Microsoft Copilot and SharePoint – Reshmee Auckloo [MVP]", multi-agent systems are suited to complex problem-solving because they use the collective intelligence of specialized AI agents. Each agent operates independently, has its own knowledge base and decision-making capabilities, and still collaborates with the others toward shared objectives. The same notes mention proactivity, where agents anticipate future needs and challenges by observing their environment and acting accordingly, and structured communication channels that let agents exchange information so the system runs smoothly.

A practical example appears in "Build Reliable Intune and Entra ID Agents with Azure AI Foundry". The episode builds a small, self-healing, governed multi-agent system for enterprise IT using Azure AI Foundry and Semantic Kernel. It explains why single agents stall on real Intune, Entra ID and Microsoft Graph workflows, and shows how planner, operator, reviewer and concierge agents collaborate to deliver faster and safer automation. The patterns covered include tool-driven remediation, identity-scoped actions, content safety and observability, which the episode then applies to several real-world scenarios.

The division of roles is also a theme in "From Demo to Production- Building Enterprise AI Agents That Actually Work with Microsoft Copilot Studio with Elliot Margot [MVP]". There, different agents take on distinct roles such as creating content, reviewing quality, checking user experience, validating requirements or orchestrating a workflow. Instead of expecting one model to get everything right on the first attempt, a multi-agent system can improve, audit and refine its work. The episode describes this as AI starting to resemble a coordinated digital team rather than a simple prompt-and-response experience.

Auditability and decision quality are the focus of "Build an Auditable Multi-Agent Copilot in Microsoft 365". Its excerpt states that multi-agent collaboration fosters richer interactions and cites an empirical study of a multi-agent conversational system called MultiColleagues compared with single-agent baselines. According to the episode, participants rated the multi-agent system significantly higher for complementary strengths and diverse perspectives, and the results showed improved decision-making. The notes also say that diversity among agents contributes to more reliable outcomes, because agents can cross-verify information and enhance accuracy.

The broader operating context is covered in "Agentic Operating Model for Enterprise AI and Copilot". The excerpt lists a 1,445% increase in multi-agent system inquiries by 2025 as one trend, alongside task-specific AI agent integration reaching 40% by 2026 and 72% of executives expecting small language models to surpass large language models in relevance by 2030. The episode advises building agentic systems on open standards for flexibility and prioritizing operational readiness, data infrastructure and change management, with pilot programs aimed at measurable results.

Taken together, the episodes treat a multi-agent system as a design decision about how to split work: a planner or orchestrator coordinates, specialized agents act, and reviewer-style agents check results. Related considerations raised in the notes include governance, identity-scoped actions, observability and the quality of retrieved knowledge, such as the role of metadata in retrieval-augmented generation.

multi-cloud.desc: Multi-cloud is a strategy of running workloads across several public cloud providers such as Azure, AWS and Google Cloud, trading portability for added complexity.

faq.a: Multi-cloud is a strategy of running workloads across more than one public cloud provider, such as Azure, AWS and Google Cloud. It aims for portability and less vendor lock-in but adds operational complexity.
faq.q: What is multi-cloud?

faq.a: The episode "Reduce the Multi-Cloud Network Tax Across Azure, AWS, and GCP" uses the term for the combined cost of egress fees, port and cross-connect fees in a colocation meet-me, latency, and the overhead of running IAM, gateways, monitors and DNS in each cloud.
faq.q: What is the multi-cloud network tax?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Arc - Simply Explained", Azure Arc projects on-premises or multi-cloud servers into Azure and manages them similarly to native Azure virtual machines, applying consistent policies and governance. It also extends to Kubernetes clusters.
faq.q: How can Azure manage resources in a multi-cloud setup?

multi-cloud.long:
Multi-cloud is a strategy in which an organization runs workloads across more than one public cloud provider, for example Azure, AWS and Google Cloud. The usual motivation is portability and reduced vendor lock-in: if no single provider holds every workload, the dependence on any one platform is lower. The cost of this approach is added operational complexity, because each provider brings its own identity model, networking, monitoring and tooling that must be run side by side.

In the M365.FM episode "Public vs Hybrid vs Multi-Cloud Azure Architecture", the central argument is that organizations rarely choose public cloud, hybrid or multi-cloud on purpose. According to the episode, these architectures emerge over time: one exception, one acquisition, one regulatory constraint, one latency issue at a time. The episode says those accumulated decisions later determine who can ship, who can comply and who gets blamed when something breaks. It frames the result as configuration rather than intent, and says that when intent is not enforced through a coherent control plane, entropy fills the gap. In that reading, multi-cloud is less a strategy someone drafted and more the visible outcome of many separate decisions that were never governed together.

The cost side is covered in the episode "Reduce the Multi-Cloud Network Tax Across Azure, AWS, and GCP". It describes multi-cloud as sounding like freedom until physics and billing collide. Connecting Azure, AWS and GCP, according to the episode, creates a toll road: egress fees to leave one cloud, port and cross-connect fees at a colocation meet-me point, and the operational overhead of running three of everything, including IAM, gateways, monitors and DNS. Latency adds a further hidden cost, even when private interconnects are used. The episode calls this combination the multi-cloud network tax.

The design advice in that episode is disciplined rather than product-driven. It recommends picking a primary cloud, meaning the place where the data lives, and treating the other clouds as satellites. It also recommends preferring shared services and APIs over bulk data copies, and placing compute near storage instead of moving large datasets between providers. The point is to avoid designs that move data back and forth in circles and generate repeated charges.

Multi-cloud also shows up in Azure management tooling. The episode "Azure Arc - Simply Explained" describes Azure Arc as a way to project on-premises or multi-cloud servers into Azure and manage them similarly to native Azure virtual machines. Once a server is connected as an Arc-enabled server, it is integrated into the Azure control plane, so consistent policies and governance can be applied across environments. The episode says this central approach improves operational consistency and reduces configuration drift, and that Azure Arc extends the same idea to Kubernetes clusters, which can be managed alongside other resources.

The episode "Azure Resource Manager - Simply Explained" touches on the same theme from the governance side. It describes Azure Resource Manager (ARM) as the central control plane for managing Azure resources and suggests exploring multi-cloud strategies with ARM to keep a unified governance model across different cloud environments. By contrast, "PowerShell vs Bicep for Azure Infrastructure Automation" notes that Bicep is specifically designed for Azure, which makes it unsuitable for multi-cloud environments. Tooling choices therefore matter: a language or service built for one provider limits how far automation can be reused across several.

Taken together, the episodes present multi-cloud as a decision with trade-offs rather than a default. Portability and reduced lock-in are the stated benefits, while network charges, duplicated operational work, latency and fragmented governance are the stated costs. The recurring recommendation is to make the architecture intentional: define a primary platform, limit cross-cloud data movement, and use a unifying control plane where multiple environments must be managed together.

multi-repo.desc: Multi-repo (polyrepo) is a repository strategy where services, libraries or products live in separate, independently versioned repositories coordinated through APIs and contracts.
multi-repo.long:
Multi-repo, also called polyrepo, is a repository strategy in which services, libraries or products are stored in separate repositories rather than in one shared codebase. Each repository is versioned independently, so a component can be changed, released and tracked on its own timeline.

Because the code is split across repositories, teams coordinate their work through explicit interfaces. APIs, contracts and versioning define how one component depends on another, and changes that cross repository boundaries are managed through those agreed interfaces instead of through a single combined change.

The approach is commonly discussed as a counterpart to keeping many projects in one repository. Choosing between the two is a question of how code is organized, owned and released, and it affects how teams share libraries, manage dependencies and handle changes that span several components.

On M365.FM, Multi-repo (polyrepo) is listed as a concept in the knowledge base. No specific episodes or related topics are linked to it at this time.

multi-user-authorization.desc: Multi-user authorization (MUA) for Azure Backup requires a second approval from a separate Resource Guard owner before critical vault operations, such as disabling soft delete.
multi-user-authorization.long:
Multi-user authorization (MUA) for Azure Backup is a feature that adds a second layer of approval to sensitive operations on a backup vault. Instead of allowing a single administrator to carry out a critical change alone, MUA requires authorization through a Resource Guard that is owned by a different person.

The feature is aimed at protecting backup data from unauthorized or accidental changes. Examples of critical operations that fall under this control include disabling soft delete or reducing the level of protection on a vault. Because the Resource Guard sits with a separate owner, a compromised or mistaken account with access to the vault cannot complete these actions by itself.

In practice, MUA is relevant to organizations that want separation of duties around their Azure Backup configuration and a safeguard against destructive changes to recovery points. The concept is described in Microsoft's Azure Backup documentation on multi-user authorization.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic, and no further related entities are recorded for it.

multimodal-ai.desc: Multimodal AI covers models and applications that process more than one input type, such as text, images, voice and video, in one system or workflow.

faq.a: Multimodal AI refers to models and applications that process more than one input type, such as text, images, voice and video. The underlying research field is called multimodal learning, which combines several kinds of data, called modalities, to give a fuller picture than a single type.
faq.q: What is multimodal AI?

faq.a: Common approaches include early fusion, where embeddings are merged before prediction, intermediate fusion of separately processed representations, and cross-attention. Many multimodal LLMs convert an encoder's output into tokens interleaved with text tokens.
faq.q: How do multimodal models combine different data types?

faq.a: According to an M365.FM episode, computer vision supports tasks such as OCR for serial numbers, barcode and QR scanning to retrieve records, and photo-based checks like verifying a window installation, although advanced visual checks require significant effort.
faq.q: How does multimodal AI apply to frontline work?

multimodal-ai.long:
Multimodal AI refers to models and applications that process more than one type of input, such as text, images, voice and video. In the research literature the underlying field is called multimodal learning, a branch of deep learning that combines several kinds of data, known as modalities. These can include text, images, audio, video and, in robotics, proprioception. The central idea is that combining modalities gives a fuller picture than any single data type can provide.

Multimodal approaches are used for tasks such as visual question answering, cross-modal retrieval, text-to-image generation and image captioning. Beyond these, applications named in the sources range from search and recommendation to healthcare diagnostics, robotics, emotion recognition and code search. In enterprise settings, the same principle shows up when a system accepts a photo, a spoken request or a document alongside written text and uses all of it to complete a task.

Technically, a multimodal model has to represent the information from each modality jointly. Several approaches exist. In early fusion, the embeddings of the different modalities are merged before a prediction is made. In intermediate fusion, each modality is first processed separately and the resulting representations are then combined. Cross-attention is another mechanism for relating one modality to another. A common recipe for multimodal large language models converts the output of an encoder into tokens that are interleaved with text tokens, often using a frozen image encoder. Examples named in the sources include CLIP for joint image-text representations, LLaVA, Whisper for audio and DALL-E for generation. The field was proposed in 2011, and large multimodal models such as Google Gemini and GPT-4o have become popular since 2023.

The M365.FM episode "Beyond Copilot: Building AI That Works in the Real World with Azure AI Foundry and Agentic AI for Frontline Workers with Fergus Kidd [MVP]" places multimodal AI in the context of frontline work. The episode describes computer vision as having immediate practical value in the field. OCR can capture long serial numbers without a technician having to read them aloud, and barcode and QR scanning can quickly identify equipment and retrieve the right records. More advanced visual quality checks, such as verifying a window installation from a photo, are described as possible but requiring significant additional effort. The episode frames this as the point where enterprise AI becomes operational: it does not merely generate text, it connects people with the right data and helps them complete real tasks, moving between knowledge retrieval, notes and reporting within the same session.

The episode "How Microsoft Built an Enterprise AI Architecture Advantage" lists multimodal AI among the areas of AI innovation it discusses. It describes advances in AI generation that combine text, audio and images for richer user experiences, alongside other areas such as AI copilots integrated into business applications and machine learning for energy management.

Several open challenges are associated with multimodal systems according to the source material. Aligning the modalities with each other is one. Deciding how and when to fuse them is another, as is handling situations in which one modality is missing. Choosing data sources that complement each other also matters. Privacy is a further concern, because combining several data sources can make it possible to re-identify people. These points are relevant when evaluating whether a multimodal capability fits a given scenario, particularly where images, audio or video of people or equipment are captured as part of everyday workflows.

multitenancy.desc: Multitenancy is a software architecture in which a single application instance serves multiple customers, called tenants, while keeping each tenant's data isolated.

faq.a: Multitenancy is a software architecture in which one instance of an application serves multiple customers, called tenants. Each tenant's data is kept isolated from the others.
faq.q: What is multitenancy?

faq.a: A tenant is a customer served by the shared application instance. The architecture ensures that a tenant's data remains separate from the data of other tenants.
faq.q: What is a tenant in a multitenant architecture?

multitenancy.long:
Multitenancy is a software architecture in which a single instance of an application serves multiple customers, known as tenants. Each tenant's data is kept isolated from the data of the others, even though the underlying application and infrastructure are shared.

In this model, tenants use the same running software rather than each receiving a separate copy. The central design concern is isolation: one tenant should not be able to see or affect another tenant's data. This distinguishes multitenancy from single-tenant approaches, where each customer is served by its own dedicated instance.

Multitenancy is a general concept in software design and is commonly discussed in the context of cloud and software-as-a-service offerings. On M365.FM, it is part of the knowledge base as a concept relevant to understanding how shared services are structured. No specific episodes, product relations or official documentation links are currently associated with this entry.

n8n.desc: n8n is a fair-code workflow automation platform that connects apps, APIs and AI models through nodes on a visual canvas, available as a cloud service or self-hosted.
n8n.long:
n8n is a workflow automation platform distributed under a fair-code model. It lets users build automated processes by connecting apps, APIs and AI models. Each step in a workflow is represented by a node placed on a visual canvas, and nodes are linked together to define how data moves between services.

The platform can be used as a cloud service or run self-hosted. This gives teams a choice between a managed environment and operating the software on their own infrastructure. Typical uses include linking separate applications, calling external APIs, and incorporating AI models into automated sequences.

On M365.FM, n8n is listed as a product entity in the knowledge base covering the Microsoft ecosystem. No related topics, documentation links or episodes are currently associated with this entry, so the page will be extended as connections to Microsoft services and episode coverage are added.

named-entity-recognition.desc: Named entity recognition (NER) is a natural language processing technique that identifies and classifies entities such as people, organizations, locations and dates in text.
named-entity-recognition.long:
Named entity recognition (NER) is a natural language processing technique that identifies and classifies entities in text. Typical entity categories include people, organizations, locations and dates. The technique reads unstructured text and marks the spans that refer to these entities, assigning each one a category.

NER is often used to enrich documents with metadata. Once the entities in a document have been extracted and labeled, that metadata can support retrieval, since content can be searched, filtered or grouped by the people, organizations, places or dates it mentions rather than by raw text alone.

No specific products, services or related topics are linked to this entry, and no M365.FM episodes are currently associated with it. The entry therefore covers the concept in general terms only: what NER does, which kinds of entities it targets, and why it is applied to documents as a way to add structured information that makes text easier to find and organize.

nearshoring.desc: Nearshoring is the outsourcing of business processes, especially IT work, to companies in a nearby country, typically one or two time zones away.

faq.a: Nearshoring is the outsourcing of business processes, especially IT work, to companies in a nearby country. The provider is typically one or two time zones away.
faq.q: What is nearshoring?

faq.a: The partner is typically located in a country that is one or two time zones away from the client. This proximity is what characterizes nearshoring.
faq.q: How far away is the partner in nearshoring?

faq.a: Nearshoring covers business processes in general, with a particular emphasis on IT work.
faq.q: What kind of work is usually nearshored?

nearshoring.long:
Nearshoring is the practice of outsourcing business processes, especially IT work, to companies located in a nearby country. The partner is typically one or two time zones away from the client, which is the defining feature that separates nearshoring from other sourcing models.

Because of the small time-zone gap, teams on both sides can share most of their working hours. This is the reason the approach is commonly considered for IT activities where regular communication between the client and the external provider matters.

Nearshoring is one way of organizing outsourced work alongside other models. In general terms, it describes the geographic proximity of the provider rather than a specific technology or product. It is therefore a sourcing and delivery concept that can apply to many kinds of business processes, with IT services being the most frequently cited example.

This page does not currently link nearshoring to specific Microsoft products, services or M365.FM episodes. It serves as a concept reference for the term as it is used when discussing outsourcing and the organization of IT work.

nested-groups.desc: Nested groups are groups that are members of other groups, so a user's effective access can arrive indirectly through several layers of group membership.

faq.a: Nested groups are groups that are members of other groups. A user's effective access can therefore come indirectly, through several layers of group membership, rather than through a single direct assignment.
faq.q: What are nested groups?

faq.a: They can create access paths that are hard to see. The episode "Audit SharePoint Online Permissions at Scale" describes a tool that finds users who have access through groups inside other groups, alongside direct and inherited permissions, so hidden access paths are not missed.
faq.q: Why do nested groups matter for permission audits?

faq.a: The episodes give two angles. "Design Around Microsoft 365 Service Limits" recommends preferring direct members over deep nested groups for Teams at scale, while "Fix Automated Microsoft 365 Licensing Failures" suggests composing separate dynamic group rules via nested groups to keep licensing automation easier to change.
faq.q: Should nested groups be used in Teams and licensing setups?

nested-groups.long:
Nested groups are groups that are members of other groups. Instead of adding every person directly to every group that grants access, an administrator can place one group inside another, so that the members of the inner group inherit whatever the outer group has been granted. As a result, a user's effective access can come indirectly, through several layers of group membership, rather than from a single, visible assignment.

The concept matters mainly because of what it does to visibility. When permissions are assigned to a group, and that group itself contains other groups, the list of people who actually have access is no longer obvious from looking at the top-level group alone. Someone can reach a site, list or item through a chain of memberships that is easy to overlook. This is why auditing work in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem treats nested groups as a category of their own, next to direct permissions and inherited permissions.

The M365.FM episode "Audit SharePoint Online Permissions at Scale" addresses this directly. It describes a permissions audit that needs to show all types of access, including the ones that are hard to find. According to the episode, the tool it discusses checks nested groups, direct permissions and inherited permissions, with the aim of giving a complete picture of the access structure. For nested groups specifically, the system finds users who have access through groups inside other groups, so that hidden access paths are not missed. The episode contrasts this with direct permissions, where users and groups have access to sites, lists or items explicitly, and with inherited permissions, which come from a parent object.

Nested groups also appear as a design choice in the episode "Design Around Microsoft 365 Service Limits". In its guidance on running Teams at scale and avoiding silent failures, the episode recommends tracking member and channel counts with alerts at 70, 85 and 95 percent thresholds. It also advises preferring direct members over deep nested groups, and auditing guests regularly. The reasoning implied in that advice is that deep nesting makes membership harder to reason about and to monitor, while the episode places it alongside other practices such as splitting mega-teams into functional teams and archiving unused channels.

A third perspective comes from the episode "Fix Automated Microsoft 365 Licensing Failures". There, nested groups are used constructively as a way to make automation easier to change. The episode suggests splitting dynamic group rules by concern, for example role (title or job code) versus region versus business unit, and then composing the results via nested groups. It pairs this with other practices for change-ready automation, such as adopting name prefixes so that a startsWith rule survives renames, reviewing rules quarterly, treating the HR system as the source of truth for synchronization into Entra, and keeping a living catalog of groups, rules, attributes and license intent.

Taken together, the episodes show nested groups as a trade-off. They can organize access and licensing logic into smaller, reusable building blocks, but each additional layer makes the effective membership of a user less transparent. Typical decisions therefore include how many layers to allow, when to use direct members instead, and how to document group structures so that reviewers can follow them. For audits, the practical takeaway from the episodes is that a permissions review which ignores nested groups risks missing real access paths, and that tooling able to resolve membership through multiple levels gives a more accurate view than inspecting only the groups named in a permission assignment.

network-density.desc: Network density describes the depth of trusted relationships with operators and experts, as distinct from audience size, and is linked to faster learning and easier collaboration.

faq.a: Network density is the depth of trusted relationships with operators and experts, as opposed to the size of a passive audience. It emphasizes the quality of connections over the number of followers.
faq.q: What is network density?

faq.a: The episode describes it as speeding up learning and opening lower-friction paths to collaboration. Trusted relationships make it easier to gain knowledge and to start working with others.
faq.q: Why does network density matter according to the episode?

faq.a: It appears in the episode "Lessons from Publishing 500 Microsoft 365 Podcast Episodes," dated 2026-03-19.
faq.q: Where is network density discussed on M365.FM?

network-density.long:
Network density is a concept that refers to how deep and trusted a person's relationships are with operators and experts. It is contrasted with the size of a passive audience, which measures reach rather than the strength of connections. In this framing, a smaller group of people who know and trust one another can matter more than a large following that does not interact.

The concept is associated with two practical effects described in the source episode. First, dense networks speed up learning, since people with direct access to practitioners can get information and context more quickly. Second, they open lower-friction paths to collaboration, because existing trust reduces the effort needed to start working together.

On M365.FM, network density appears in the episode "Lessons from Publishing 500 Microsoft 365 Podcast Episodes" (2026-03-19), where it is discussed in connection with publishing a long-running Microsoft 365 podcast. The episode uses it to distinguish between building a large audience and building meaningful relationships with the operators and experts in the field.

network-file-system.desc: Network File System (NFS) is the standard network file system protocol for Linux and Unix systems, and Azure Files supports it alongside SMB.

faq.a: NFS is the standard network file system protocol for Linux and Unix systems. It is used to access files on a remote server over a network.
faq.q: What is Network File System (NFS)?

faq.a: Yes. Azure Files supports NFS alongside SMB, so both protocols can be used depending on the clients and workloads involved.
faq.q: Does Azure Files support NFS?

network-file-system.long:
Network File System (NFS) is a network file system protocol that serves as the standard for Linux and Unix systems. It allows files stored on a remote server to be accessed over a network in a way that is comparable to working with local storage.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, NFS is relevant because Azure Files supports it alongside SMB. This means that Azure Files can be used with Linux and Unix workloads that rely on NFS, while SMB remains available for other client types. The protocol choice depends on the operating systems and applications that need to reach the shared file storage.

The available information on M365.FM does not currently link NFS to specific episodes or related topics, so this page covers only the core definition and its connection to Azure Files.

network-security-group.desc: A network security group (NSG) is an Azure control that filters inbound and outbound traffic between resources in a virtual network using prioritized security rules.

faq.a: A network security group filters inbound and outbound traffic between Azure resources in an Azure virtual network by applying security rules that allow or deny traffic. Rules are evaluated by priority, and the first matching rule is applied.
faq.q: What does a network security group do in Azure?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Network Security Groups - Simply Explained", an NSG is a logical firewall service that filters at the network layer (Layer 4) and operates on individual resources. Azure Firewall is described as a managed service with stateful packet inspection, application-level protection and centralized management.
faq.q: How is an NSG different from Azure Firewall?

faq.a: An NSG is associated with a subnet or with a network interface. Default rules allow traffic within the virtual network and deny other inbound traffic, and they can be overridden with higher-priority rules.
faq.q: Where is a network security group applied?

network-security-group.long:
A network security group (NSG) is an Azure networking control that filters network traffic between Azure resources in an Azure virtual network. It does this with security rules that allow or deny inbound or outbound traffic. The NSG is a basic building block for segmenting and protecting workloads that run in a virtual network, such as virtual machines, and it is often the first layer of traffic control that administrators configure.

Each security rule in an NSG has a name, a priority, a source and destination, a protocol, a direction, a port range and an action. The priority is a number between 100 and 4096. Rules are processed in priority order, with lower numbers evaluated first, and processing stops at the first matching rule. Evaluation is based on the five-tuple of source, source port, destination, destination port and protocol. Flows are tracked statefully, so reply traffic for an allowed connection does not need a separate rule in the opposite direction.

Every NSG also contains default rules. These allow traffic within the virtual network and from the Azure load balancer, and they deny other inbound traffic. The default rules cannot be deleted, but they can be overridden by creating rules with a higher priority, meaning a lower number. This makes it possible to open specific ports or sources while keeping the restrictive baseline in place.

To keep rule sets manageable, NSGs support several grouping constructs. Service tags group the IP address prefixes of an Azure service, so a rule can refer to a service by name instead of by a list of addresses. Application security groups group virtual machines, so that policy follows the workload and does not depend on manually maintained IP lists. Augmented rules allow multiple IP addresses and ports to be placed in a single rule, which reduces the number of rules needed. An NSG takes effect once it is associated with a subnet or with a network interface.

NSGs are not the only place where traffic rules can be applied. Security admin rules from Azure Virtual Network Manager are evaluated before NSG rules, which gives central network teams a way to set guardrails that individual NSGs do not override. A further platform behavior documented by Microsoft is that outbound SMTP traffic on port 25 is blocked for several subscription types, which is relevant when mail-related workloads are planned.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Network Security Groups - Simply Explained" places NSGs next to Azure Firewall. According to the episode, the two serve different purposes. It describes Azure Firewall as a managed, cloud-based network security service with stateful packet inspection, application-level protection and centralized management for resources in a virtual network. It describes an NSG as a logical firewall service that filters at the network layer (Layer 4) and operates on individual resources. The episode frames this comparison as a way to choose the right tool for a given security need.

NSGs also appear as a prerequisite in other Azure scenarios. The episode "Azure Chaos Studio - Simply Explained" lists setting up a Network Security Group to allow inbound and outbound traffic for Chaos Studio among the setup requirements, together with a managed identity and a virtual network with subnets for the target resources. In that context the NSG is part of the network preparation needed before the service can be deployed.

network-slicing.desc: Network slicing runs multiple logical networks, each with its own performance and security boundaries, on shared physical 5G infrastructure.

faq.a: Network slicing is a method of running multiple logical networks on the same physical 5G infrastructure. Each logical network can have its own performance characteristics and security boundaries.
faq.q: What is network slicing?

faq.a: It is used to isolate different kinds of traffic from each other. One example is separating safety-critical traffic from video or guest traffic.
faq.q: What is network slicing used for?

network-slicing.long:
Network slicing is a concept in 5G networking that allows multiple logical networks to operate on the same physical infrastructure. Each logical network, often called a slice, can have its own performance characteristics and security boundaries, so that different types of traffic do not interfere with one another.

A typical use is the isolation of safety-critical traffic from other traffic types, such as video streams or guest access. By separating these workloads into distinct slices, an operator or organization can apply different performance and security expectations to each one while still relying on a single underlying network.

No specific products, services or related topics are linked to this entry, and no M365.FM episodes currently reference network slicing. The entry therefore covers only the general definition and purpose of the concept.

neural-processing-unit.desc: A neural processing unit (NPU) is a specialized processor that accelerates AI and machine learning workloads while drawing much less power than a CPU or GPU.
neural-processing-unit.long:
A neural processing unit (NPU) is a specialized processor built to accelerate artificial intelligence and machine learning workloads. It is designed to run the repetitive mathematical operations that AI models depend on, and it does so with much lower power draw than a general-purpose CPU or a GPU.

Because an NPU handles this kind of AI math efficiently, it is typically used to take on AI tasks that would otherwise consume more energy on other processors. The practical benefit is lower power consumption for sustained AI work, which matters most on devices where energy use is a constraint.

On M365.FM, the NPU is covered as a concept within the broader Microsoft ecosystem discussion of AI hardware and how AI workloads are processed. No specific episodes or linked topics are currently listed for this entry, so this page limits itself to the general definition of the term.

new-commerce-experience.desc: The new commerce experience (NCE) is Microsoft's commerce model for CSP subscriptions, built on term commitments and a short cancellation window for seat reductions.

faq.a: NCE is Microsoft's commerce model for CSP subscriptions. It uses term commitments of one month, one year or three years and limits how seats can be reduced after a short cancellation window.
faq.q: What is the new commerce experience (NCE)?

faq.a: Subscriptions under NCE can have a monthly, annual or three-year term commitment.
faq.q: What term lengths are available under NCE?

faq.a: Options to reduce seats are limited. After the short cancellation window has passed, reducing seat counts is not freely possible.
faq.q: Can seats be reduced after purchase under NCE?

new-commerce-experience.long:
The new commerce experience (NCE) is Microsoft's commerce model for subscriptions sold through the Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) program. It governs how licenses are purchased, renewed and changed, and it replaces a more flexible approach to subscription management with fixed term commitments.

Under NCE, a subscription is bought with a defined term: monthly, annual or three-year. Once a subscription is created, there is only a short cancellation window in which it can be cancelled. After that window closes, options to reduce the number of seats are limited, which means license quantities are effectively tied to the chosen term. This makes the term length and the planned seat count important decisions when a subscription is ordered.

NCE is relevant mainly for organizations that buy Microsoft cloud services through CSP partners, as well as for the partners who manage those subscriptions on behalf of customers. Planning license counts, renewal dates and the choice between monthly and longer terms are common topics connected to the model.

No episodes of M365.FM are currently linked to this entry, and no further related topics have been recorded here.

nis2.desc: NIS2 Directive is the EU cybersecurity directive for essential and important entities, requiring risk management measures and timely incident reporting.

faq.a: NIS2 is the EU directive on cybersecurity for essential and important entities. It covers sectors such as energy, transport, health and digital infrastructure.
faq.q: What is the NIS2 Directive?

faq.a: It requires risk management measures and timely incident reporting from the entities within its scope.
faq.q: What does NIS2 require from organizations?

faq.a: Sectors named in the directive's scope include energy, transport, health and digital infrastructure.
faq.q: Which sectors does NIS2 cover?

nis2.long:
The NIS2 Directive is a European Union directive on cybersecurity. It applies to essential and important entities in sectors such as energy, transport, health and digital infrastructure.

The directive sets two main obligations for the organizations it covers: they must put risk management measures in place, and they must report incidents in a timely manner. These requirements make cybersecurity a compliance matter as well as a technical one, which is why NIS2 is often discussed alongside governance, security operations and incident response in organizations that run Microsoft environments.

On M365.FM, NIS2 is treated as a concept within the wider Microsoft ecosystem, where regulatory requirements influence how organizations plan security, monitoring and reporting. No specific episodes, related topics or official documentation links are currently listed for this entry, so the page stays limited to the definition and scope given above.

nist-ai-risk-management-framework.desc: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary US framework for managing AI risks, organized around governing, mapping, measuring and managing risk.

faq.a: It is a voluntary framework from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology for managing AI risks. It is organized around governing, mapping, measuring and managing risk.
faq.q: What is the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?

faq.a: No. The episodes describe it as voluntary and note that, although it includes provisions such as decommissioning, it lacks regulatory enforcement.
faq.q: Is the NIST AI Risk Management Framework mandatory?

faq.a: The episode with Peter Rising says Microsoft Purview supports responsible AI enablement by aligning with global standards like the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, which guides the AI lifecycle from governance to risk mapping, measurement and management.
faq.q: How does the NIST AI Risk Management Framework relate to Microsoft Purview?

nist-ai-risk-management-framework.long:
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary framework published by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. It helps organizations manage risks that come with building, deploying and operating artificial intelligence. It is organized around four activities: governing, mapping, measuring and managing risk. Because it is voluntary, it works as guidance that organizations can adopt to structure their own policies and practices, not as a law that carries enforcement.

In practice, the framework serves as a reference point for AI governance. Organizations use it to define policies, assess risks and support transparency. The M365.FM episodes describe it as one of several frameworks that organizations commonly draw on, alongside the OECD Principles on AI and the EU AI Act. One episode lists it under the United States as a voluntary framework for managing AI risks, with an emphasis on trustworthiness, safety and fairness. That description places it among other responsible-AI guidance, some of it non-binding but influential in shaping policy.

The four activities give the framework its structure. Governing covers the policies, roles and accountability that surround AI use. Mapping establishes the context in which an AI system operates and identifies where risk can arise. Measuring assesses and tracks those risks. Managing addresses them through action. The episode with Peter Rising describes this as guidance that runs through the AI lifecycle, from governance to risk mapping, measurement and management. The same episode says Microsoft Purview supports responsible AI enablement by aligning with global standards such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and it mentions the Microsoft Responsible AI Council as a body that puts responsible AI policies into action.

Typical decisions around the framework concern how to anchor an organization's AI governance. The episode "Grounding Microsoft Copilot for Trusted Enterprise AI" recommends a cross-functional AI governance board with clear roles and responsibilities to oversee AI strategy and accountability. It suggests using the NIST AI Risk Management Framework together with the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications to address core risks and to validate controls throughout the AI lifecycle. The same episode advises testing and updating policies regularly and notes that ongoing validation and oversight keep an AI platform aligned with business goals.

The framework also appears in discussions of AI agents. The episode "Enterprise AI Agents with Sailaja Mantripragada [MVP-MCT]" says organizations building agents with Microsoft Copilot Studio and the Power Platform often follow governance frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the OECD Principles on AI and the EU AI Act. It adds that AI governance is not a one-time task and that agents need to be monitored, audited and improved on an ongoing basis.

The episode "Microsoft Entra Agent ID: Secure Identity for AI Agents" looks at the framework's limits. It says the framework includes provisions for decommissioning AI agents but lacks regulatory enforcement. It contrasts this with the EU AI Act, which the episode says has no mandatory sunset clauses or specific decommissioning procedures for orphaned agents, and with ISO/IEC 42001:2023, which defines a retirement phase for AI agents but relies on voluntary compliance. According to the episode, none of these require automatic termination of orphaned agents after a set period, emergency shutdown mechanisms, or standardized handover when an agent's creator ceases operations.

Taken together, the episodes treat the NIST AI Risk Management Framework as a structured, voluntary reference for organizations that want to align AI governance with an established model. They also make clear that using it is a choice made by the organization, and that its provisions, for example on decommissioning, are not backed by enforcement.

node-js.desc: Node.js is a cross-platform, open-source JavaScript runtime built on Google's V8 engine, used to run JavaScript outside the browser, often for web back ends.

faq.a: Node.js is a cross-platform, open-source JavaScript runtime that runs JavaScript outside the browser on Google's V8 engine. It is commonly used for web back ends.
faq.q: What is Node.js?

faq.a: The episode "Fix Broken SPFx Live Data Updates" says that using the wrong Node.js version or installing packages globally instead of locally can cause upgrade issues. It recommends checking the Node.js version before any upgrade, since SPFx works best with specific versions.
faq.q: Why does Node.js version matter for SharePoint Framework projects?

faq.a: The episodes mention Node.js APIs hosted on Azure App Service and a Node.js Microservices Workshop that uses Azure Container Apps to teach microservices fundamentals.
faq.q: Where can Node.js applications run on Azure according to the episodes?

node-js.long:
Node.js is a cross-platform, open-source JavaScript runtime that executes JavaScript outside the browser. It runs on Google's V8 engine and is commonly used for web back ends. Because it is a runtime and not a framework or a hosted service, it appears in the Microsoft ecosystem as a prerequisite, a build dependency or a hosting option for applications written in JavaScript or TypeScript.

In the M365.FM episodes, Node.js shows up in several different roles. In the episode "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions", Node.js is listed among the tools needed to build custom Teams apps and is described as the back-end JavaScript runtime environment necessary for app functionality. It sits in a toolset alongside Visual Studio Code, the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit, Microsoft Teams itself, and the developer tools in Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome. For developers working in JavaScript, TypeScript or the SharePoint Framework (SPFx), having Node.js installed is therefore part of preparing the development machine.

The episode "Fix Broken SPFx Live Data Updates" treats Node.js from the perspective of environment setup.
