The episode "Microsoft Loop Workspaces - Simply Explained" notes that Microsoft 365 and SharePoint infrastructure must be reachable, and that firewall or proxy settings should follow the Office 365 URLs and IP address ranges. It also says that WebSocket traffic to the office.com domain, along with another Microsoft domain, needs to be allowed for real-time collaboration features. The same requirement appears in "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Settings and Configuration", which lists full WebSocket (WSS) connectivity from user devices to the office.com domain and a cloud.microsoft domain. That episode names blocked WSS, TLS inspection and aggressive proxy timeouts as common network configuration issues that can affect Copilot, and it says Microsoft consolidates Copilot experiences under the cloud.microsoft domain.

The office.com address also serves as an entry point to other Microsoft 365 experiences. In "Integrate Viva Topics with Search and SharePoint", the episode says that when a search query matches a topic, Microsoft Search returns topic cards as primary answers. These cards can be found on the SharePoint start page, on Office.com or within SharePoint pages. The episode describes SharePoint as the backend for organizing and accessing project files, while Viva Topics uses AI to organize knowledge.

Office on the web is also one of the environments in which Office Add-ins can run. According to "Build Office Add-Ins for Excel and Word Without VBA", Office Add-ins are web apps that run inside Office, with a small XML manifest controlling where they appear and the Office JavaScript API letting code read and write documents. The episode says an add-in can be built once and run on Windows, Mac and Office on the web, and that updates can be shipped like any modern web app.

In summary, Office on the web is the browser-delivered layer of the Office apps within Microsoft 365. It connects closely to OneDrive and SharePoint for storage, depends on correct network and endpoint settings for real-time features, and shares its surrounding ecosystem with tools such as Microsoft Loop, Copilot and Viva Topics.

office-scripts.desc: Office Scripts is an Excel automation feature that records steps or lets users write script code, and scripts can be run from Power Automate flows.

faq.a: Office Scripts automates everyday tasks in Excel by recording manual steps or writing script code, then replaying them as reusable scripts. An example from Microsoft Learn is a daily CSV clean-up that removes columns, formats a table, adds formulas and builds a PivotTable.
faq.q: What is Office Scripts used for?

faq.a: Scripts can be called from Power Automate flows, for example in response to emails or on a schedule. The documentation notes that scheduling from within Excel is temporarily disabled and names Power Automate as the alternative.
faq.q: How can Office Scripts run outside of Excel?

faq.a: The episode "When to Use Python in Power Platform Automation" says Python suits analytics, machine learning and Fabric notebooks but not everyday orchestration in Microsoft 365. It presents Office Scripts, Copilot and agent-style orchestration as better fits for that glue work.
faq.q: How does the M365.FM episode relate Office Scripts to Python?

office-scripts.long:
Office Scripts is a Microsoft product for automating everyday tasks in Excel. Users record manual steps in a workbook and replay them as reusable scripts, or write and refine script code directly. Scripts are described in the M365.FM material as TypeScript-flavoured, and they are stored in OneDrive. The feature sits between manual spreadsheet work and heavier automation approaches, and it connects Excel to the wider Power Platform through Power Automate.

The feature has two main parts according to Microsoft Learn. The Action Recorder captures actions such as editing cells, formatting and creating tables, and saves them as a script. A Copy as code option turns recorded actions into script code without saving the whole script. The Code Editor is then used to refine recorded or newly written scripts, adding logic such as conditions and loops, or functions that the Excel interface does not offer directly. This makes it possible to start from a recording and extend it into something more flexible.

A typical use is a repeatable data preparation task. The example on the Microsoft Learn page is a daily CSV clean-up: the script removes unneeded columns, formats a table, adds formulas and builds a PivotTable in a new worksheet. Once such a routine is captured as a script, it no longer has to be repeated by hand each day. A script can also be attached to a workbook, so teammates who have access to that workbook can see and run it.

Office Scripts can run outside the workbook when called from Power Automate flows, for example in response to emails or on a schedule. This is the route for unattended automation. The documentation notes that scheduling from within Excel is temporarily disabled and names Power Automate as the alternative. Licensing details are left to other articles, so they are not covered here.

The M365.FM episode "When to Use Python in Power Platform Automation" places Office Scripts in a decision about tooling. The episode argues that Python is well suited to analytics, machine learning and Fabric notebooks, but a poor choice for everyday orchestration inside Power Automate, Power BI Dataflows Gen2, Dataverse and Microsoft 365. In that framing, Office Scripts, together with Copilot and agent-style orchestration such as type-agent, can write and run the glue code. The episode describes this approach as relying on typed contracts, native connectors and AI-generated scripts that respect schemas and governance, in contrast to brittle Python running in Azure Functions.

The decision the episode raises is where each language belongs. Python stays in places where it is strong, such as Fabric notebooks and advanced analytics, while workbook-level and flow-level automation in Microsoft 365 is handled with Office Scripts and Power Automate. For teams, this means choosing Office Scripts when the work is centred on Excel files and flows, and reserving Python for analytical workloads rather than routine orchestration.

Related topics include Power Automate as the runner for scripts outside Excel, Copilot as an aid for generating scripts, and the Power Platform tools mentioned in the episode, such as Dataverse and Power BI Dataflows Gen2, which form the surrounding environment where such automation is evaluated.

okta.desc: Okta is a San Francisco identity and access management company whose cloud platform provides single sign-on, and M365.FM cites it as a separate identity system.

faq.a: Okta is an identity and access management company based in San Francisco. Its cloud platform provides single sign-on to many applications.
faq.q: What is Okta?

faq.a: The episodes cite Okta as a separate identity system that can be consolidated into Microsoft Entra ID. It also appears in a list of identity governance solutions alongside SailPoint and Saviynt, compared with Microsoft Entra ID P1 and P2.
faq.q: How does Okta relate to Microsoft Entra ID in the M365.FM episodes?

faq.a: The episodes use the 2020 Okta breach, in which attackers stole credentials and exposed sensitive support case information, as an example of credential compromise and weak access-point security.
faq.q: Why is Okta mentioned in security-related episodes?

okta.long:
Okta is an identity and access management company based in San Francisco. Its cloud platform provides single sign-on to many applications, which means that users can sign in once and reach multiple business systems through a central identity service. On M365.FM, Okta appears as a reference point in discussions about identity, access governance and security in the Microsoft ecosystem, mostly as an example of a separate identity system next to Microsoft Entra ID.

In the episode material, Okta is described in two roles. First, it is named as a separate identity system that can be consolidated into Microsoft Entra ID. Organizations that run several identity platforms side by side often face duplicated identities, unclear permissions and gaps in visibility about who has access to what. Bringing these systems together under one identity foundation is one way to reduce that complexity, and Okta is cited as one of the systems an organization might fold into Microsoft Entra ID.

Second, Okta appears as one of several identity governance solutions. The episode "Close the Microsoft Teams Channel Governance Gap" lists Okta together with SailPoint and Saviynt under identity governance solutions. According to that episode, such tools help organizations shift from reactive to proactive governance, with stronger security, continuous compliance and operational efficiency. In the same comparison, Microsoft Entra ID P1 and P2 are presented as options that provide advanced identity and access management features, such as rules for who can see or edit information and alerts when someone tries to access restricted data.

Okta is also used in the episodes as a case study for security incidents. In "Fix Microsoft 365 Compliance Drift Beyond Green Dashboards", the episode describes a 2020 data breach in which attackers stole credentials and exposed sensitive support case information. The episode uses this incident to illustrate how inadequate security measures around access points can lead to severe consequences, including damage to reputation. A similar reference appears in "Microsoft Entra External ID for Digital Trust and Growth", where the Okta breach is named as an example of credential compromise dominating high-profile incidents. That episode argues for a flexible, claim-centric approach built on zero trust principles, where every user and device is verified and trust is earned continuously.

A further mention comes from "Fix Duplicate Customer Identity in Power BI and Fabric". There, the episode says that companies like Okta have faced challenges aligning identity systems after acquisitions. The point of the example is that confusing or duplicated identities create security risks and visibility gaps, and that unclear permissions can follow when identity systems do not align. The episode names Zluri as a platform that helps by automating access reviews and onboarding and offboarding, reducing risks from orphaned access and compliance failures.

Taken together, the M365.FM episodes treat Okta less as a product to configure and more as a recurring reference in three recurring decisions: whether to consolidate separate identity systems into Microsoft Entra ID, whether to add a dedicated identity governance layer, and how to learn from credential-based breaches. For anyone researching Okta in a Microsoft context, these episodes offer examples of how identity sprawl, governance tooling and breach lessons connect to Microsoft Entra ID and zero trust thinking.

ollama.desc: Ollama is an open-source tool for downloading and running large language models on a local machine or server, exposing them through a local REST API.

faq.a: Ollama is an open-source tool for downloading and running large language models on a local machine or server. It exposes the models through a local REST API.
faq.q: What is Ollama?

faq.a: Applications communicate with the model through the local REST API that Ollama provides. This allows other software on the same machine or server to send requests to the locally running model.
faq.q: How do applications use models run with Ollama?

ollama.long:
Ollama is an open-source tool for downloading and running large language models on a local machine or server. Instead of sending prompts to a hosted cloud service, models are executed on hardware the user controls, and they are made available to other software through a local REST API.

The REST API is the main way applications interact with a model run through Ollama. Because the interface is exposed locally, scripts, internal tools and other programs can send requests to the model running on the same machine or on a server within the same environment. This makes the tool relevant for scenarios where keeping model execution local is preferred.

On M365.FM, Ollama is listed as a product entity. No related topics, linked entities or episodes are currently associated with this page, so no further connections to the Microsoft ecosystem are described here. Additional details will be added as related content is published.

on-behalf-of-flow.desc: The OAuth 2.0 On-Behalf-Of flow (OBO) lets a middle-tier service exchange a signed-in user's token for a token to a downstream API, keeping the user's identity.
on-behalf-of-flow.long:
The OAuth 2.0 On-Behalf-Of flow (OBO) is an OAuth 2.0 flow in which a middle-tier service exchanges the token of the signed-in user for a token to a downstream API. The downstream call is then made with the user's identity and permissions rather than with the identity of the service itself.

The flow is relevant when a client application calls a web API, and that API in turn needs to call another API while acting for the same user. Instead of using its own credentials, the middle-tier service presents the access token it received from the user and requests a new token scoped to the downstream API. This allows the downstream API to apply authorization decisions based on the actual signed-in user.

Microsoft documents the flow as part of the Microsoft identity platform in Microsoft Entra, and the official documentation is available on Microsoft Learn under the title of the OAuth 2.0 On-Behalf-Of flow.

No related topics or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

on-premises-data-gateway.desc: The on-premises data gateway is a Windows application that carries data between on-premises sources and Microsoft cloud services such as Power BI, Power Apps and Fabric.

faq.a: It carries data between on-premises sources, such as local SQL servers and file shares, and cloud services like Power BI, Power Apps, Power Automate and Microsoft Fabric. It uses outbound connections only, so the data stays behind the firewall until it is requested.
faq.q: What is the on-premises data gateway used for?

faq.a: It runs in standard mode or personal mode. The facts available only state that these two modes exist.
faq.q: What modes does the on-premises data gateway run in?

faq.a: The episode "Troubleshoot the Power BI On-Premises Data Gateway" says that issues between the gateway and the Power BI service can cause subtle failures. It also notes that auto-updates may be disabled by default in some environments, which can lead to "gateway not working" errors.
faq.q: Why might a gateway stop working?

on-premises-data-gateway.long:
The on-premises data gateway, often called the Power BI gateway, is a Windows application installed inside a private network. It carries data between on-premises data sources and Microsoft cloud services such as Power BI, Power Apps, Power Automate and Microsoft Fabric. It does this using outbound connections only, so the cloud service does not need to open an inbound path into the corporate network. The gateway runs in one of two modes, standard or personal.

The main purpose of the gateway is to let cloud services use data that stays behind a firewall. In the Power BI context, the M365.FM episode "Troubleshoot the Power BI On-Premises Data Gateway" describes it as the component that brings secure, on-premises data into the cloud capabilities of Power BI without moving that data outside the firewall. Typical sources named there are local SQL servers and file shares, which the gateway connects to the Power BI service.

The same gateway concept appears across several Microsoft products, not only Power BI. The episode "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" explains that secure ingestion of on-premises data into Microsoft Fabric typically uses an on-premises data gateway or a virtual network data gateway to bridge on-premises sources and cloud services. The episode recommends combining gateways with firewall-enabled Azure Data Lake Storage, VNet integration and role-based secure access, so that data is encrypted in transit and at rest and leakage is limited during ETL and ingestion workflows.

In automation scenarios the gateway provides hybrid connectivity. The episode "Power Automate vs Azure Logic Apps for Enterprise Integration" states that Azure Logic Apps can reach legacy systems behind corporate firewalls through the on-premises data gateway, which supports automating processes and exchanging data securely. The episode "Build Enterprise Automation with Azure Logic Apps" adds that, together with Hybrid Connections, the gateway lets Logic Apps securely access legacy databases, file shares and APIs, so that business processes can span cloud and on-premises environments.

The gateway also matters for Power Apps and custom connectors. In "Build Secure Custom Connectors for Power Apps", the on-premises data gateway is listed as the option for reaching internal APIs from a custom connector. That episode places this advice alongside other practices, such as storing secrets in Azure Key Vault or environment variables, limiting who can create connections and applying data loss prevention policies to the connector.

Operationally, the gateway is a component that needs attention, because it is installed and maintained on a machine inside the network. The troubleshooting episode points out that problems between the gateway and the Power BI service can cause subtle failures. It also notes that auto-updates are available but disabled by default in some environments, which can lead to unexpected "gateway not working" errors. Keeping the gateway current and checking its connection to the cloud service are therefore part of a stable setup.

When choosing between the modes and related gateway types, the decision depends on who uses the connection and where the data lives. The standard mode is the shared gateway for multiple users and services, while the personal mode is intended for individual use. For sources inside an Azure virtual network, the Fabric episode mentions the virtual network data gateway as an alternative to the on-premises variant. Official Microsoft documentation describes the gateway in more detail.

one-stop-shop-vat.desc: The EU VAT One Stop Shop (OSS) lets a business declare and pay VAT due in several EU member states through its home tax authority in one return.
one-stop-shop-vat.long:
The VAT One Stop Shop (OSS) is an EU mechanism that allows a business to declare and pay the VAT it owes in several member states through a single channel, namely its home tax authority. Instead of registering for VAT separately in each country where VAT is due, the business reports those amounts in one return.

One point stressed in the source material is that local input VAT cannot be deducted in the OSS return. VAT a business has paid on purchases in another member state therefore has to be handled outside the OSS return and cannot be offset there.

The topic is relevant to organisations that sell or invoice across EU borders and need to understand how VAT obligations in different member states are reported. This page is limited to the facts available about the concept and does not cover eligibility rules, thresholds, filing deadlines or specific invoicing requirements.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no related topics or official documentation links are listed.

onecopy.desc: The OneCopy principle in Microsoft Fabric means data is stored once in OneLake and read directly by Spark, SQL and Power BI instead of being duplicated.

faq.a: It means data is stored once in OneLake and read directly by multiple engines such as Spark, SQL and Power BI, rather than being copied between tools.
faq.q: What does the OneCopy principle mean in Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: No. The principle describes a logical copy, and physical redundancy still exists. Database mirroring creates a copy, and shortcuts depend on the availability of their source.
faq.q: Does OneCopy mean there is never any duplicated data?

faq.a: Shortcuts act as references to data stored elsewhere, such as other workspaces, Azure storage, Amazon S3 or Dataverse, so teams can share data without duplicating it.
faq.q: How do shortcuts relate to the OneCopy principle?

onecopy.long:
The OneCopy principle is a design idea in Microsoft Fabric. Data is stored once in OneLake, and the different analytics engines work directly on that single copy instead of each tool keeping its own duplicate. Engines such as Spark, SQL and Power BI read the same stored data, so there is no need to move it between tools before it can be used somewhere else.

The principle rests on OneLake, the unified data lake that comes automatically with every Microsoft Fabric tenant. One OneLake exists per tenant. It builds on Azure Data Lake Storage and stores tables in open formats such as Delta Parquet or Iceberg. Because the format is open and shared, all Fabric analytics engines can operate on the same files. According to Microsoft Learn, a table created with T-SQL can be read by Spark without special connectors or exports, and Power BI reports can read the data directly through Direct Lake.

In practice, the principle is meant to remove a common source of friction in analytics projects: copying data from one system to another so that a different team or engine can use it. Each copy adds storage cost, needs a pipeline to keep it current, and can drift out of sync with the original. With OneCopy, a data engineer working in Spark, an analyst writing T-SQL and a report author in Power BI all point at the same data. The episode "Microsoft Fabric OneLake - Simply Explained" lists this among its key takeaways: use the OneCopy principle to access data without unnecessary duplication, which the episode links to saving storage costs. It also presents OneLake as a way to centralize analytics data and reduce duplication, which it says improves collaboration among teams.

Shortcuts are the mechanism for data that does not live in the same place. A shortcut acts as a reference to data stored elsewhere, for example in another workspace, in Azure storage, in Amazon S3 or in Dataverse. Teams can then share and use that data without creating a duplicate inside their own workspace. Security is meant to follow the data as well: according to the documentation notes, security roles apply consistently at folder, table, row and column level across SQL, Spark and Power BI, so access rules do not have to be rebuilt for each engine. The episode similarly points to OneLake's governance features for data security and compliance.

There are limits to how literally the principle should be read. A shortcut depends on the availability of its source, so if the referenced system is unavailable, the data behind the shortcut is as well. Database mirroring does create a copy, which means it is an exception to the one-copy idea in the strict sense. The documentation also describes OneCopy as a logical copy: physical redundancy still exists underneath, so the principle is about having one logical version of the data to work with, not about the absence of any replication in the storage layer.

Typical decisions around the principle involve choosing between reading data in place through a shortcut, mirroring it into OneLake, or ingesting it as a new table. Teams weigh the benefit of avoiding duplicate pipelines and storage against the dependency on the source system and the fact that mirroring produces a copy. Integration with other Microsoft tools, such as Power BI and Teams, is described in the episode as a way to streamline workflows and improve decision-making, and it also mentions performance benefits such as faster data queries and reduced operational overhead.

onedrive.desc: OneDrive is Microsoft's cloud storage for personal work files, syncing folders across devices and integrating with SharePoint, sharing controls and Microsoft 365 apps.

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft OneDrive - Simply Explained", they are two separate accounts that only look alike, even though they share the OneDrive name.
faq.q: Is the OneDrive on a home computer the same as OneDrive at work?

faq.a: Files shared in Teams chats are stored in OneDrive, while team files live in SharePoint.
faq.q: Where are files stored when they are shared in a Teams chat?

faq.a: The episodes say full library sync causes storage use, performance slowdowns, sync conflicts and governance risks, and recommend shortcuts to the source instead.
faq.q: Why do the episodes advise against syncing entire SharePoint libraries?

onedrive.long:
OneDrive, also referred to as Microsoft OneDrive, is Microsoft's cloud storage service for personal work files. It keeps folders available across devices, connects to File Explorer through sync, and works together with sharing controls and the Microsoft 365 apps. It is developed by Microsoft, is included with Microsoft 365, and is classified on M365.FM as a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool. The service dates back to 2007-08.

OneDrive is used to store and access a person's own working files from different devices, to share those files with colleagues or external recipients, and to protect work through version history and folder backup. It relates closely to Microsoft Word, Microsoft Excel, Microsoft PowerPoint and Microsoft OneNote, since documents created in these applications can be saved to and opened from OneDrive. It also relates to Microsoft Teams and SharePoint: files that people share in Teams chats are stored in OneDrive, while team files live in SharePoint. This split between personal storage and team storage is a recurring theme when organizations decide where a given file should be kept.

The episode "Microsoft OneDrive - Simply Explained" points out that the name OneDrive covers two different products. The OneDrive on a home laptop and the OneDrive provided by an employer are separate accounts that only look alike. The episode also walks through how files get onto a computer, how sharing and permissions work, the folder backup that users did not explicitly ask for, and the undo options provided by version history.

Sync is the area where most practical questions arise. The episode "OneDrive Sync: Setup and Troubleshooting | Simply Explained" describes OneDrive Sync as the mechanism that connects SharePoint and OneDrive files to File Explorer, so people can work with familiar folders while Microsoft 365 keeps collaboration and cloud storage connected. The episode covers how sync works, why common problems occur, and how teams can use it safely at scale.

Several episodes discuss the limits of syncing everything. "SharePoint Sync vs Add Shortcut to OneDrive" says that syncing entire SharePoint libraries to local devices creates unnecessary storage usage, performance slowdowns, sync conflicts and governance risks. According to the episode, large synced libraries increase metadata overhead and network traffic and raise the likelihood of duplicate or outdated files across devices. It also argues that locally copied files can bypass SharePoint retention policies, version history and sensitivity labels, weakening compliance. The proposed alternative is to use shortcuts rather than full library sync. "Stop OneDrive Sync Conflicts with SharePoint Shortcuts" makes a similar case, describing OneDrive shortcuts as a way to turn a slow, overloaded laptop into a curated workspace by pointing to the source instead of copying it.

A related decision is covered in "SharePoint Network Drive vs OneDrive Sync". That episode examines mapping SharePoint or SharePoint Online as a network drive, explains how SharePoint document libraries work behind the scenes and how mapped drives behave in Windows, and notes that treating SharePoint like a traditional file share can lead to slow performance, sync problems and missing features. Taken together, the episodes frame OneDrive as one part of a wider Microsoft 365 file architecture in which SharePoint, Teams and local sync each have a distinct role.

onedrive-files-on-demand.desc: OneDrive Files On-Demand is a OneDrive sync feature that lists all cloud files in File Explorer as online-only placeholders and downloads them only when opened.

faq.a: According to Microsoft Support, a blue cloud marks an online-only file. It is downloaded when opened and cannot be opened while the device is offline.
faq.q: What does the blue cloud icon mean in OneDrive Files On-Demand?

faq.a: The documentation says it works with OneDrive, SharePoint in Microsoft 365, and SharePoint Server 2019 team sites. It needs a supported Windows 10 or Windows Server version and a signed-in OneDrive account.
faq.q: Which services does OneDrive Files On-Demand work with?

faq.a: The episode "Fix OneDrive Files On-Demand Sync Issues" explains four core components (filter driver, sync engine, cache database, cloud module), where each can break, and a step-by-step playbook for diagnosing red Xs, "file not available" messages, and ghosted folders.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode on Files On-Demand sync issues cover?

onedrive-files-on-demand.long:
OneDrive Files On-Demand is a feature of the OneDrive sync client that gives access to every file in OneDrive cloud storage without downloading all of them and without using local disk space for each one. Files appear in File Explorer as placeholders. The actual content is fetched only when a user opens a file, which keeps the local disk free of data that is rarely needed.

File Explorer shows the state of each item with a status icon. According to Microsoft Support documentation, a blue cloud marks an online-only file that is downloaded when opened and cannot be opened while offline. A green check marks a file that was opened and is now locally available. A green circle with a white check marks a file that has been set to always stay on the device. Right-click commands let users keep items on the device or free up space again, and Storage Sense can return unused files to online-only status after a period the user chooses. New files appear as online-only by default, unless they are created inside a folder that is marked to always keep files on the device.

The feature works with OneDrive, with SharePoint in Microsoft 365, and with SharePoint Server 2019 team sites. It requires a supported Windows 10 or Windows Server version and a signed-in OneDrive account. The documentation lists several limits. Desktop search finds online-only files by name only, not by their content. The feature is not supported when Windows Information Protection is enabled, and some third-party antivirus products are incompatible with it. Deleting an online-only file removes it from OneDrive on all devices, although the recycle bin can restore it. These points matter when planning a rollout, because users who expect a placeholder to behave like a local file may be surprised by offline access or search behavior.

The M365.FM episode "Fix OneDrive Files On-Demand Sync Issues" (2025-08-05) looks at the feature from a troubleshooting angle. It describes common symptoms such as files that spin forever, red Xs, "file not available" messages, and ghosted folders. The episode explains the problems through four core components: a filter driver, a sync engine, a cache database, and a cloud module. It discusses where each component can fail and says that small factors, such as path length or a bloated cache, can stall sync. The episode also presents a step-by-step playbook for diagnosing these problems before a team loses working time.

Files On-Demand also appears in discussions about how to organize shared content. The episode "SharePoint Sync vs Add Shortcut to OneDrive" (2026-05-26) is aimed at administrators, architects, developers, security professionals, and business leaders who need a practical foundation before making implementation decisions. It lists the Files On-Demand troubleshooting episode among related listening, alongside episodes on stopping OneDrive sync conflicts with SharePoint shortcuts and on comparing a SharePoint network drive with OneDrive sync. Together these episodes place Files On-Demand in the wider question of how SharePoint libraries and OneDrive content reach the desktop and how reliably that works.

In practice, decisions around the feature usually concern which folders should always stay available offline, how aggressively Storage Sense should free up space, and how to handle sync problems when they appear. The documentation and the episodes together suggest that understanding the online-only, locally available, and always-keep states, and the components behind them, makes it easier to explain unexpected behavior and to troubleshoot it in a structured way.

onedrive-selective-sync.desc: OneDrive selective sync is a sync app setting that lets users choose which OneDrive folders are synced to a device, leaving unchecked folders in the cloud.

faq.a: It is a OneDrive sync app setting, called Choose folders, that controls which OneDrive folders are synced to a device. Folders that are not selected stay only in the cloud.
faq.q: What is OneDrive selective sync?

faq.a: Unchecked folders are not synced to the device and remain only in the cloud.
faq.q: What happens to folders that are unchecked?

faq.a: It is available in the OneDrive sync app under the Choose folders option.
faq.q: Where is the selective sync setting found?

onedrive-selective-sync.long:
OneDrive selective sync is a setting in the OneDrive sync app, labeled Choose folders, that controls which OneDrive folders are synced to a particular device. Folders that are left unchecked are not synced to that device and remain only in the cloud.

The setting is used to decide what is stored locally on a given computer. Because the choice is made per device, the folder selection on one device does not have to match another. The selection can be changed through the Choose folders option in the sync app.

This page is based on a short description of the concept only. No related topics, official documentation links or M365.FM episodes are currently associated with OneDrive selective sync, so further details are not covered here.

onedrive-shortcuts.desc: Add shortcut to OneDrive places a cloud-managed link to a shared SharePoint library or folder in a user's OneDrive instead of syncing a separate copy.

faq.a: It adds a link to a shared SharePoint library or folder in the user's OneDrive, so the content appears in My files without a separate replica being synced. The content stays with its owner.
faq.q: What does Add shortcut to OneDrive do?

faq.a: No. According to Microsoft Support, a shortcut uses no storage of its own, because the content counts against the owner of the shared folder.
faq.q: Does a shortcut use the user's OneDrive storage?

faq.a: The episode warns that deleting or renaming a shortcut can affect the shared source. Microsoft Support states that removing a shortcut deletes only the link, and that a rename is visible only to the person who set it.
faq.q: What happens if a shortcut is deleted or renamed?

onedrive-shortcuts.long:
Add shortcut to OneDrive is a OneDrive feature that places a link to a shared SharePoint library or folder in a user's OneDrive, instead of syncing a replica of that content to the device. The shortcut is managed in the cloud and points to the shared source. The user reaches the shared content from their own My files area while the data stays in its original location. Microsoft Support describes the same idea for shared folders: a shortcut is a link that puts a shared folder in My files, using the Add shortcut to My files command.

The feature exists to make shared folders easier to reach and edit. It is available from the Shared view: the user selects a folder and uses the circle on its tile or the right-click menu. On a PC or Mac where the OneDrive app syncs the shortcut, the content can also be opened locally. A shortcut can be renamed, and the new name is visible only to the person who set it. Because a shortcut is only a link, it uses no storage of its own. The content counts against the owner of the shared folder.

The feature comes up mostly in comparison with traditional library syncing. The episode "SharePoint Sync vs Add Shortcut to OneDrive" describes syncing entire SharePoint libraries to local devices as a growing problem for modern enterprises. According to the episode, it creates unnecessary storage usage, performance slowdowns, sync conflicts and governance risks. Large synced libraries increase metadata overhead and network traffic, and they raise the likelihood of duplicate or outdated files across devices. The episode also says that files copied locally can bypass SharePoint retention policies, version history and sensitivity labels, which weakens compliance. A shortcut avoids a full local replica of the library and keeps the content under the source's controls.

The episode "Stop OneDrive Sync Conflicts with SharePoint Shortcuts" covers the move away from syncing. Its guidance includes stopping the sync before deleting any synced folders, and disabling the sync button in the SharePoint admin settings to prevent new syncs. It also advises promoting the "Add shortcut to OneDrive" feature to users and monitoring usage while providing support during the transition. One tip from that episode is not to disable offline client availability, because shortcuts need it to function properly.

Handling the shortcut needs some care. The short description of the feature, based on the episode, warns that deleting or renaming a shortcut can affect the shared source. The Microsoft Support page describes a narrower behavior: removing a shortcut deletes only the link, so the folder stays with its owner, and a rename is visible only to the person who made it. Removing a shortcut also removes it from synced computers. Anyone planning a rollout should weigh the episode's caution against this documented behavior and check how the shortcut behaves in their own tenant.

The documentation lists several requirements and limits. Users need to be signed in with a Microsoft account and need edit rights on the shared folder. Only folders are supported, not single shared files. The page states limits of 100 folder shortcuts per person and 1,000 shortcuts overall for files and folders. If the owner stops sharing the folder, it disappears from OneDrive. These points matter when deciding whether shortcuts can replace library syncing for a team, since access follows the sharing permissions of the source.

In practice, the choice is between syncing a library to each device and linking to it from OneDrive. Shortcuts suit shared content that people want in their own OneDrive without copying it. The two episodes frame this as a way to reduce sync conflicts, storage use and governance gaps, while keeping files under the policies applied in SharePoint.

onedrive-sync-engine.desc: The OneDrive sync engine is the OneDrive software on a computer that detects local and cloud changes and keeps files in both places identical.
onedrive-sync-engine.long:
The OneDrive sync engine is the OneDrive sync software that runs on a computer. It detects changes made to files locally and changes made in the cloud, and it keeps the files in both locations identical.

Among the mechanisms associated with it are chunked, resumable and differential uploads. Chunked uploads divide a file into parts, and resumable uploads allow a transfer to continue after an interruption rather than starting over. Differential uploads transfer only the changed portions of a file instead of the entire file.

The OneDrive sync engine is relevant to anyone working with files that exist both on a local device and in cloud storage, since its role is to reconcile the two copies. Its behavior determines how quickly and reliably edits appear on each side.

No related topics, official documentation links or M365.FM episodes are currently listed for this entry, so this page limits itself to the basic definition and the upload methods described above.

onelake.desc: OneLake is the single, organization-wide logical data lake in Microsoft Fabric, which lets workloads share data and use shortcuts instead of duplicate copies.

faq.a: OneLake is the single, organization-wide logical data lake that comes with Microsoft Fabric. It gives all Fabric workloads one shared place for analytics data.
faq.q: What is OneLake?

faq.a: Shortcuts let workloads reference data stored in other locations without importing a duplicate copy of it. This helps avoid the multiplying copies and refresh jobs described in the episodes.
faq.q: What are shortcuts in OneLake?

faq.a: The episode "Speed Power BI with OneLake and Direct Lake" says Power BI can query lakehouse tables directly through Direct Lake with performance similar to Import mode, without duplicate copies or complex refresh cycles.
faq.q: How does OneLake relate to Power BI and Direct Lake?

onelake.long:
OneLake is the single, organization-wide logical data lake that comes with Microsoft Fabric. It serves as the central location for an organization's analytics data, so that the different Fabric workloads can work against the same storage rather than each keeping its own separate copy. Shortcuts are a key mechanism in this design: they let a workload reference data that lives in another location without importing a duplicate of it.

The problem OneLake addresses is data duplication. The episode "OneLake - Simply Explained" describes a familiar scenario in which one sales table exists in a warehouse, a lakehouse, a Power BI import model and several team folders. Each copy begins as a convenience, but over time the numbers diverge, reports become stale, and someone inherits yet another refresh job. The episode presents OneLake as the answer to this mess, aimed at stopping the cost of copying data across systems.

According to the episode "Microsoft Fabric OneLake - Simply Explained", OneLake is the unified data lake at the heart of Microsoft Fabric and provides one centralized place for all of an organization's analytics data. Every Fabric workload, from Power BI and Data Engineering to Data Science and Data Warehouse, can access the same data. The stated effects are less duplication and fewer data silos. The episode "Microsoft Fabric End-to-End: From Raw Data to Business Decisions with Amit Chandak [MVP]" places OneLake alongside common Fabric capacity and the Delta format as shared foundations, so that lakehouses, warehouses, Power BI and other Fabric experiences operate as parts of one platform rather than isolated services. In that episode, Amit Chandak compares OneLake conceptually to OneDrive: instead of every analytics workload creating independent storage, workloads share a common foundation.

OneLake also plays a role in the way Power BI handles data. The episode "Speed Power BI with OneLake and Direct Lake" explains that, with OneLake and Direct Lake, Power BI can query lakehouse tables directly with performance similar to Import mode, without creating duplicate copies or maintaining complex refresh cycles. The pattern described there runs from Dataflows Gen2 into a Lakehouse, through Pipelines and a Semantic Model, to a Direct Lake report, with OneLake as the storage layer underneath.

In the episode "Eliminate Data Silos with Microsoft Fabric and OneLake", OneLake is described as one storage plane within Fabric's wider approach to fragmentation, alongside one identity through Entra. The episode argues that a stack made of Power BI, ad hoc pipelines, shadow CSVs and several conflicting dashboards amounts to entropy rather than a coherent platform, and it frames Fabric as a response to that fragmentation. Related themes raised there include data silos, lack of governance, scalability, and security and compliance.

For decisions about adopting OneLake, the episodes point to a few recurring considerations. Teams weighing whether to copy data into each workload can instead consider referencing it through shortcuts. Teams building Power BI models can consider Direct Lake over lakehouse tables as an alternative to import refresh cycles. Teams planning a broader platform can look at how shared foundations such as OneLake, Fabric capacity and the Delta format reduce the number of separate services and storage technologies to manage. Further technical detail is available in the official Microsoft Learn overview of OneLake.

onelake-security.desc: OneLake security is a role-based access control model for data in OneLake, with row-level and object-level rules defined once and applied across Fabric engines.

faq.a: OneLake security is a role-based access control model for data stored in OneLake. Administrators define roles that grant access to folders or tables in a Fabric item and assign them to users or groups, and the permissions apply across Fabric engines.
faq.q: What is OneLake security?

faq.a: New SQL analytics endpoints start in delegated identity mode and are not protected by OneLake security. The access mode must be switched to the user's identity mode for the roles to take effect.
faq.q: Why do SQL analytics endpoints need a configuration change?

faq.a: DefaultReader is a role that new items come with, and its membership is virtualized, so anyone with a permission such as ReadAll is automatically a member. Since it grants full access, users should be removed from it once they are placed in a more restrictive role.
faq.q: What is the DefaultReader role?

onelake-security.long:
OneLake security is a role-based access control model for data stored in OneLake, the unified storage layer of Microsoft Fabric. It lets administrators define access rules once, directly on the data, so the same rules apply across Fabric engines and endpoints instead of being rebuilt separately in each tool. Row-level and object-level restrictions are part of the model, which allows access to be narrowed to specific folders, tables, rows or columns.

In practice, an administrator creates security roles that grant access to specific folders or tables inside a Fabric item and then assigns those roles to users or groups. Row-level and column-level security can narrow table access further. A ReadWrite permission, available only for lakehouses, allows writing through Spark notebooks, the OneLake file explorer or OneLake APIs without granting rights to manage Fabric items. Creating roles requires write and reshare permission, which workspace admins and members usually hold. According to the Microsoft Learn documentation, lakehouses and mirrored items are listed as supported.

New items come with a DefaultReader role. Its membership is virtualized, so anyone who holds the needed permission, such as ReadAll, is automatically a member. Because this role grants full access, the documentation notes that users should be removed from it once they are placed in a more restrictive role; otherwise the broader access remains in effect. Users who have no data access role at all see no data in the item.

SQL analytics endpoints need specific attention. New endpoints start in delegated identity mode and are not protected by OneLake security until the access mode is switched to the user's identity mode. This is a typical decision point when rolling out OneLake security, since the protection only reaches that endpoint once the mode is changed.

OneLake security is one layer in a wider security picture. The episode "Microsoft Fabric End-to-End: From Raw Data to Business Decisions with Amit Chandak [MVP]" describes security across multiple layers, starting with Fabric workspace roles and continuing through item-level access, OneLake security and semantic-model security. In that discussion, Amit Chandak recommends using security groups rather than managing individual users wherever possible. Microsoft Entra provides the identity and group foundation, while Fabric applies those identities and groups to workspaces, items and data access. Assigning OneLake security roles to groups fits this approach.

The episode "Microsoft Fabric 2025 Updates Explained" mentions OneLake Security improvements alongside new governance tools, describing them together as part of an enterprise-grade foundation for secure data operations. The episode frames these changes in the context of real-time intelligence and the wider set of Fabric updates it covers.

Taken together, the sources present OneLake security as a way to centralize data-level access control in Fabric: roles are defined on the data in OneLake, assigned to Entra identities and groups, and enforced consistently by the engines that read the data, provided the endpoint is configured to use the user's identity.

onelake-shortcuts.desc: OneLake shortcuts are pointers in Microsoft Fabric's OneLake that reference data stored elsewhere, so the data is reachable in a lakehouse without being copied.

faq.a: A OneLake shortcut is a pointer in Microsoft Fabric's OneLake that references data stored elsewhere, inside Fabric or in external storage. The data stays at its target path while the shortcut appears in a lakehouse or other item.
faq.q: What is a OneLake shortcut?

faq.a: Shortcuts avoid physical data movement. The episode "Build ETL with Microsoft Fabric Dataflows Gen2" says this reduces both storage and compute costs, since redundant ingestion pipelines and repeated copies are not needed.
faq.q: Why are OneLake shortcuts used instead of copying data?

faq.a: The episode "Use Microsoft Fabric Domains for Data Mesh Governance" names OneLake Shortcuts as the way to share high-quality data as a product between domain teams. The episode "Build a Trusted Semantic Layer in Microsoft Fabric" lists shortcuts as an engineering output, separate from governance policies such as sensitivity labels.
faq.q: How do OneLake shortcuts relate to data mesh and governance?

onelake-shortcuts.long:
OneLake shortcuts are pointers in Microsoft Fabric's OneLake that reference data stored in another location, either inside Fabric or in external storage, without copying that data. The data stays at its target path, while the shortcut appears as an entry in a lakehouse or another Fabric item. Because only a reference is created, users and workloads can read the data as if it were part of the item they are working in, while the original location remains the single place where the data actually lives.

The main purpose of OneLake shortcuts is to avoid physical data movement. Without shortcuts, making the same data available in several places typically means building ingestion pipelines and storing duplicate copies. With a shortcut, one team can expose data to another team or workspace by reference. This is why shortcuts come up in discussions of data architecture in Fabric: they change the question from how to move data to where the data should live and who should be able to reach it.

The M365.FM episode "Build ETL with Microsoft Fabric Dataflows Gen2" covers shortcuts from a cost and capacity angle. It lists factors that raise compute usage, such as cross-region access with higher latency, repeated transformations and redundant ingestion pipelines, and contrasts them with OneLake shortcuts, which the episode says reduce physical data movement and therefore lower storage and compute costs. In that context, shortcuts are presented as one way to keep ETL operations efficient and predictable, alongside managing compute resources carefully and using managed staging.

Shortcuts also appear in the governance and data mesh discussion. The episode "Use Microsoft Fabric Domains for Data Mesh Governance" maps data mesh principles to Fabric features. Under the principle of data as a product, it names shared access to high-quality data through OneLake Shortcuts. In that model, domain teams own and manage their own data and workspaces, and shortcuts are one mechanism for letting other teams consume that data without taking over ownership or duplicating it. The episode pairs this with semantic models, metadata-rich catalogs, role-based access and cataloging for compliance.

A third episode, "Build a Trusted Semantic Layer in Microsoft Fabric", places OneLake shortcuts on the technical side of a split between governance and engineering. According to the episode, the governance side produces policies, sensitivity labels and data ownership definitions, while the engineering side, owned by data engineers, Fabric administrators and developers, produces validated datasets, automated workflows and OneLake shortcuts. The episode argues that separating these concerns lets an organization address governance and security effectively, with shortcuts belonging to integration and data availability rather than to policy setting.

In practice, decisions around OneLake shortcuts concern where data should be stored, which team owns the target location, and how access is controlled when the same data is surfaced in several lakehouses or items. Since a shortcut is only a reference, the target path remains the authoritative copy, and ownership, quality and access rules defined there continue to matter for every place the shortcut appears. Shortcuts therefore connect naturally to topics such as lakehouses, domains, data products and ETL design in Microsoft Fabric.

onenote.desc: Microsoft OneNote is a digital notebook for typed notes, ink, images and web clippings, organised in notebooks, sections and pages and synced through OneDrive.

faq.a: Microsoft OneNote is a digital notebook for typed notes, ink, images and web clippings. It is typically used for meeting notes, research collections, project documentation and personal knowledge management.
faq.q: What is Microsoft OneNote used for?

faq.a: Notebooks are organised into sections and pages and are synced through OneDrive, so the same notes are available across devices. OneNote is included in the Microsoft 365 licence as part of Microsoft 365 Apps.
faq.q: How does OneNote store and sync notes?

faq.a: "Build a OneNote System for Notes and Follow-Ups" describes a workflow built on tags, linked pages and templates. "OneNote vs Loop vs Copilot with Karinne Diamond Bessette [MVP]" compares OneNote with Loop and Copilot, and "Copilot in Office Apps: The Governance Checklist" covers governance when Copilot works with notes through Microsoft Graph.
faq.q: What do the M365.FM episodes say about OneNote?

onenote.long:
Microsoft OneNote is a digital notebook for typed notes, ink, images and web clippings. Content is organised in a hierarchy of notebooks, sections and pages, and notebooks are synced through OneDrive, so the same notes are available across devices. It was developed by Microsoft, first released in 2003, and is included in the Microsoft 365 licence as part of Microsoft 365 Apps. In the M365.FM knowledge base it is classified both as a Microsoft tool and as a collaboration tool.

OneNote is typically used for meeting notes, research collections, project documentation and personal knowledge management. Because a page can hold typed text, handwritten ink, images and clipped web content side by side, it suits situations where information arrives in mixed formats and needs to be kept in one place. The notebook, section and page structure gives a familiar way to group related material, for example one notebook per project or topic, with sections for areas of work and pages for individual notes.

Storage and sync work through OneDrive. Notebooks live there, which is how notes stay consistent when opened on different devices. This link to OneDrive also shapes decisions about where notebooks are kept and who can reach them. OneNote is also closely related to Microsoft Teams, where notebooks are commonly shared with a team and used alongside meetings and channels. An episode on organising projects in Teams lists native access to Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OneNote, SharePoint and Outlook among the benefits of the Microsoft 365 integration, since it supports document collaboration and version control in one workspace.

The M365.FM episode "Build a OneNote System for Notes and Follow-Ups" argues that most people use only about ten percent of OneNote and end up with a digital junk drawer that hides decisions and weakens follow-ups. It describes turning OneNote into a working system built on action-ready tags, linked pages, smart templates and a workflow-first notebook structure, so that less time goes into searching and more into acting on notes. The emphasis is on how the notebook is organised rather than on adding more features.

A second line of discussion concerns where OneNote fits among other Microsoft tools for notes. The episode "OneNote vs Loop vs Copilot with Karinne Diamond Bessette [MVP]" compares OneNote, Microsoft Loop and Copilot for notes. It approaches the topic from the problem of information chaos in the modern workplace and focuses on how each option works, where it fits, and the architecture, security, governance and operational choices that matter in real Microsoft environments.

Copilot is the third theme. The episode "Copilot in Office Apps: The Governance Checklist" notes that Copilot is presented as available across Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and OneNote. It explains that Copilot draws on emails, files, meetings and notes through Microsoft Graph, and that privacy, data loss prevention and audit workloads increase once it is switched on. For OneNote this means notes can become part of the data Copilot works with, which makes governance of where notes are stored and who can access them a practical concern. The episode "Microsoft 365 Copilot Prompts That Deliver Better Results" also mentions organising notes in OneNote as one of the daily routines in which clear, contextual prompts help Copilot deliver useful results.

Taken together, the sources describe OneNote as a flexible notebook whose value depends on how it is structured, how it is shared through OneDrive and Microsoft Teams, and how it is governed once AI features such as Copilot are involved.

ontological-design.desc: Ontological design is a design philosophy holding that the things people create in turn shape the people who use them, from software to workplace tools.

faq.a: It is a design philosophy holding that the things people design and create in turn shape the people who use them. It was first formulated in the 1986 book Understanding Computers and Cognition by Terry Winograd and Fernando Flores.
faq.q: What is ontological design?

faq.a: In the M365.FM episode with Tracy van der Schyff, the concept is applied to software, Microsoft Teams, intranets, and Copilot: the things people create eventually change them. The episode also says Copilot may expose existing permission and information-management problems rather than create them.
faq.q: How does ontological design relate to Microsoft 365 and Copilot?

ontological-design.long:
Ontological design is a design philosophy holding that the things people design and create in turn shape the people who use them. Rather than treating design as the neutral production of useful objects, the concept asks what design fundamentally is and does. Its core idea, as summarized by Anne-Marie Willis in an Eye on Design article, is that people design their world while the world acts back on them and designs them. Design therefore shapes the conditions under which people exist and understand themselves.

The concept was first formulated in the 1986 book Understanding Computers and Cognition by Terry Winograd and Fernando Flores. That work drew on Humberto Maturana and Martin Heidegger and made the claim that in designing tools, people are designing ways of being. Later contributors to the idea include Anne-Marie Willis, Tony Fry, who frames it as design that sustains or diminishes futures, and Arturo Escobar. The perspective is popular in design academia, although the same source admits it is abstract and hard to apply in practice.

Several key claims run through the literature. Design structures what is possible, often unnoticed. Unintended consequences are treated as central rather than incidental. People are inside the loop before they become aware of it, which can make alternatives seem unrealistic. For this reason, the perspective suggests that narrow problem-solving should give way to asking what worlds design creates. It also questions the celebration of individual iconic designers and examines topics such as branding.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the concept is useful as a way of thinking about digital workplaces. The M365.FM episode "How Microsoft 365 & Copilot Are Redesigning the Way We Work with Tracy van der Schyff [MVP]" includes a section titled "Ontological design: the things we create change us." The episode notes describe the concept as sounding complicated, while Tracy van der Schyff explains it in a very practical way: people create things, and the things they create eventually change them. According to the episode, this applies to software, applications, intranets, processes, social media, Microsoft Teams, Copilot, and almost every digital environment people interact with.

The same episode connects this way of thinking to how organizations experience Copilot. The show notes say that organizations can come to believe Copilot created a problem when the underlying permissions, sharing practices, or information-management issues may have existed for years. In the episode's words, the AI did not necessarily create the mess; it exposed it. Read through the lens of ontological design, a tool introduced into a workplace does not simply perform a task. It also changes how people work, what becomes visible, and which practices are treated as normal.

For teams that build or roll out Microsoft 365 solutions, the concept points to a practical decision: tools, intranets, and workflows are designed for how people are expected to work, and they in turn influence how people actually work. Asking what kind of working environment a design produces, and not only whether it solves the immediate problem, is the shift in perspective the concept encourages. Because the effects are often unnoticed and unintended consequences are treated as central, the sources suggest paying attention to them early rather than treating them as side issues.

ontology.desc: An ontology is a formal set of shared definitions that names the types of things in a domain and the relationships between them, so people and systems read data alike.

faq.a: An ontology is a formal set of shared definitions for a domain that specifies the types of things and the relationships that may connect them. Its aim is that people and systems interpret data the same way.
faq.q: What is an ontology?

faq.a: According to the episode "Connectivity Is Not Integration — Why Your Connected Factory Still Can't Answer the Right Questions", a schema defines the shape of a record, an ontology defines the shared meaning of concepts and relationships, and a graph stores and queries the connected entities.
faq.q: How does an ontology differ from a schema and a graph?

faq.a: The episodes describe an ontology as a layer that can describe relationships across several semantic models and give AI systems a structure for navigating enterprise information. It also gives a chatbot or agent a formal model of the business domain to reason with.
faq.q: How does an ontology relate to semantic models and AI agents?

ontology.long:
An ontology is a formal set of shared definitions for a domain. It specifies the types of things that exist in that domain and the relationships that may connect them, so that people and systems interpret data in the same way. In practice it acts as a common vocabulary with rules: instead of each team or system describing a customer, a machine, or an order in its own terms, the ontology states what those concepts mean and how they relate to one another.

The main purpose is to keep meaning consistent across teams, tools, and AI systems. The episode "Fabric IQ - Simply Explained" illustrates the problem with a familiar situation: two teams call the same customer two different things. The episode describes this as data that is fine, while the meaning behind it has quietly drifted apart. An ontology addresses that drift by fixing shared definitions rather than only storing records. That episode covers the ontology as one part of Fabric IQ, alongside how it connects to semantic models and how it grounds AI agents.

An ontology is often discussed next to two related ideas, a schema and a graph, and the episode "Connectivity Is Not Integration — Why Your Connected Factory Still Can't Answer the Right Questions" separates them clearly. A schema defines the shape of a record, for example by requiring fields such as asset ID, event timestamp, fault code, work-order ID, or engineering unit. An ontology defines the shared meaning of the concepts and relationships used across the factory. A graph provides a practical way to store and query those connected entities. According to the episode, once those relationships exist, the same machine event becomes more useful for planning and decision-making, because it can be read with context such as whether output is released, restricted, or held, and which relationships were valid when the event happened.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the concept appears in the context of digital twins. The episode "Microsoft Fabric Digital Twin Builder Explained" describes the ontology in the digital twin builder as a semantic model that defines entities, relationships, and properties. According to the episode, this lets teams structure data into an ontology and create comprehensive digital replicas, and it allows disparate data, including OT data, to be mapped into a consistent schema, which simplifies digital twin creation.

The concept also relates to AI. The episode "Codify Business Logic into a Digital Twin for AI Agents" states that ontology and semantics shape how a chatbot reasons and interacts. In that framing, the ontology gives a formal model of the business domain, defining relationships and business logic, and creates a structured framework for the AI system. The episode describes this as a shift from unstructured data to structured, semantic reasoning, and says it improves consistency and reliability. It also mentions combining tools such as Databricks for storage and Stardog for knowledge graphs to model relationships within data.

The episode "Everyone Wants Copilot—but Is Your Data Ready: Microsoft Fabric Architecture with Walter Calcagno [MVP-MCT]" adds an architectural view. Large organizations often have many semantic models across departments and domains, and the episode notes that solving this by building one enormous semantic model is not necessarily the answer. Walter Calcagno highlights the ontology as another layer: rather than forcing everything into a single semantic model, an ontology can describe relationships across models and provide a structure through which AI systems can navigate enterprise information. In his view, semantic models combined with ontology models are an increasingly important foundation for connecting enterprise data with large language models.

Taken together, the episodes treat an ontology as a layer of meaning that sits above raw data and records. Typical decisions around it include whether a schema alone is sufficient, whether relationships need to be modeled explicitly, how an ontology relates to existing semantic models, and how its definitions can be used to ground AI agents in business terms.

opc-ua.desc: OPC UA (OPC Unified Architecture) is an industrial communication standard that exchanges machine data in a structured information model with typed values and status codes.

faq.a: OPC UA (OPC Unified Architecture) is an industrial communication standard that exchanges data in a structured information model. It uses typed values, status codes, client-server subscriptions and certificate-based application security.
faq.q: What is OPC UA?

faq.a: The episodes describe them as complementary: OPC UA exposes the machine signal, an edge layer collects it, MQTT can distribute it locally, and Microsoft Fabric can ingest and analyze the stream. One episode rejects the idea of a winner-takes-all battle between the two.
faq.q: How does OPC UA relate to MQTT in a Microsoft manufacturing setup?

faq.a: According to the episode "Connectivity Is Not Integration", it does not. A fault event can reach a dashboard immediately, but questions such as which shipment is at risk still require MES, ERP, maintenance and quality data.
faq.q: Does OPC UA connectivity alone answer operational questions?

opc-ua.long:
OPC UA, short for OPC Unified Architecture, is an industrial communication standard for exchanging data between machines, controllers and higher-level systems. Instead of passing around loose, unlabeled values, it exposes data in a structured information model. Values are typed, they carry status codes, and clients can subscribe to changes. Application security is based on certificates, so that the applications taking part in an exchange can be identified and trusted.

In practice, OPC UA is the layer that makes a machine signal available in the first place. The episode "How Machine Data Reaches Microsoft Fabric - From OPC UA to Real-Time Analytics" describes the typical chain: OPC UA exposes the machine signal, an edge layer collects it, MQTT can distribute it locally, and Microsoft Fabric can ingest and analyze the resulting stream. Machine alarms, sensor values, production counters and fault events are examples of the kind of data that travels along this path. The same episode stresses that the hard part begins after the data arrives, because raw telemetry still has to be turned into enough production context to support an actual decision.

The client-server pattern with subscriptions is one of the defining traits of the standard. A client connects to a server that represents a device or a control system and subscribes to the nodes it cares about, receiving updates when values change. The typed values and status codes matter because a reading such as a temperature is only useful together with its data type and an indication of whether the value can be trusted. The episode "From Sensor to Dashboard: The MQTT Pipeline Through Azure IoT Hub" points to the same idea from the PLC side: a raw tag value comes with a timestamp and a quality state, and older plants often run several generations of equipment that use proprietary protocols or OPC UA.

OPC UA is often discussed together with MQTT, but the episodes treat them as complementary rather than competing. The episode "MQTT and OPC UA in Microsoft Manufacturing: Azure IoT Operations + Fabric Architecture" rejects the framing of industrial connectivity as a winner-takes-all battle and instead places the discussion in the context of a broader problem, a lack of trust in manufacturing data. According to the episode, factories can have ERP, MES and Azure systems in place and still rely on manual exports and guesswork. Because PLCs rarely speak cloud MQTT directly, the pipeline episode describes an industrial gateway on the operational technology (OT) network that bridges the gap by normalizing data into a common message shape, managing collection frequency and forwarding state changes immediately.

An information model also raises the question of how machine-level structures relate to the rest of the business. The episode "What Is an Industrial Data Model" gives an example: a single machine may appear as a work center in ERP, an asset number in maintenance, a resource in MES, a group of OPC UA nodes in the control system, and a different friendly name on the shop floor. According to the episode, an industrial model does not force all of these systems to share one identifier. It records how the different references relate to the same physical or logical object, which gives the factory a stable identity layer without destroying the local structures each source system needs. In this view, OPC UA nodes are one of several representations of an asset, not the complete picture.

The episode "Connectivity Is Not Integration — Why Your Connected Factory Still Can't Answer the Right Questions" makes the limits of connectivity explicit. A packaging machine stops, the PLC reports the fault, OPC UA exposes the event, MQTT distributes it and a dashboard updates immediately, yet a planner asking which customer shipment is now at risk still needs MES data, ERP records, maintenance history, quality status, production quantities and delivery commitments, often combined in a spreadsheet. The takeaway from the episodes is that OPC UA solves the problem of getting a well-described machine signal out of the plant, while contextualization, shared identity and integration with business data remain separate design decisions.

Typical decisions around OPC UA therefore concern where the signal is collected (an edge or gateway layer), how it is distributed (for example via MQTT), how it reaches analytics (for example Microsoft Fabric) and how it is tied to production context so that the data can answer operational questions.

openai.desc: OpenAI is an AI research and product company behind ChatGPT and the GPT models, and a Microsoft partner whose models are offered through Azure OpenAI Service.

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure OpenAI Service - Simply Explained", Azure OpenAI Service runs the same models but Microsoft hosts them inside the customer's own Azure space, with the customer's own keys, limits and privacy rules.
faq.q: What is the difference between Azure OpenAI Service and ChatGPT?

faq.a: The episodes describe a partnership that includes OpenAI's commitment to run workloads on Azure, and Microsoft offers the models through Azure OpenAI Service. One episode also lists OpenAI among Microsoft's strategic AI partnerships.
faq.q: How does OpenAI relate to Microsoft?

faq.a: The episode "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud" says smaller models can handle simple tasks well and cost less, while larger models such as GPT-4o offer advanced reasoning but increase expenses.
faq.q: How can the cost of using OpenAI models in Azure be kept down?

openai.long:
OpenAI is an AI research and product company known for ChatGPT and the GPT models. In the Microsoft ecosystem the name comes up mainly through its partnership with Microsoft, which includes a commitment to run workloads on Azure, and through Azure OpenAI Service, the way many organizations consume its models inside their own Microsoft cloud environment.

The M365.FM episode "Azure OpenAI Service - Simply Explained" clarifies a frequent point of confusion: Azure OpenAI Service is not ChatGPT with a Microsoft logo on it. According to the episode, it runs the same models, but Microsoft hosts them inside the customer's own Azure space, with the customer's own keys, limits and privacy rules. The episode walks through the building blocks of the service: the models behind it, deployments as a customer's own copy of a model, endpoints and keys that let apps connect, tokens as the unit everything is measured in, quotas and rate limits, built-in content filtering, and data privacy as the aspect that matters most to IT teams.

A second use of OpenAI models appears in "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform". The episode argues that adding a connector is not an AI strategy and describes a pattern in which Power Apps or Dynamics 365 are paired with Power Automate for orchestration, Azure OpenAI for the intelligence, and Azure API Management for security, throttling and observability. It covers cleaning and enriching payloads in flows, choosing the right model and prompts per use case, such as classification versus summarization, plus a step-by-step build plan, KPIs to track and guardrails intended to keep performance predictable and compliant.

Cost is the focus of "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud", which combines Azure OpenAI with Copilot Studio, Power Platform and practical cost controls. The episode notes that smaller models can handle simple tasks well and cost less, while larger models such as GPT-4o offer more advanced reasoning but raise expenses, so the model choice should be reviewed against the task. This ties directly to the token-based measurement described in the service overview.

OpenAI models also appear as a building block in retrieval-augmented generation. In "How to Build Private RAG with SharePoint and n8n", an Azure OpenAI account is listed among the prerequisites for generating embeddings and using language models. The other components named in the episode are a SharePoint account for storing and organizing documents, an n8n account for automating workflows, Microsoft Graph access to connect SharePoint with other Microsoft services, a PostgreSQL or Supabase account for storing vectors and enabling semantic search, Mistral OCR access for scanned documents and images, and an Open WebUI account for the user interface. The episode also advises having admin rights or the correct permissions on each platform.

Finally, "How Microsoft Built an Enterprise AI Architecture Advantage" places OpenAI within Microsoft's broader AI strategy. The episode lists strategic partnerships with companies such as OpenAI and NVIDIA as one factor strengthening Microsoft's AI capabilities, alongside heavy research and development investment and tools like Microsoft Copilot that bring AI into everyday applications. The episode attributes to Microsoft a commitment of at least $40 billion over five years to AI technologies and a 20% share of the global cloud market for Azure.

Typical decisions around OpenAI in a Microsoft context therefore concern how the models are accessed (through Azure OpenAI Service rather than directly), which model fits a task, how tokens, quotas and rate limits affect cost and reliability, and how security, throttling and observability are handled when apps and agents call the models.

openapi.desc: OpenAPI is an open specification for machine-readable descriptions of web APIs, used by Semantic Kernel and Microsoft 365 Copilot to describe plugin and extension capabilities.

faq.a: OpenAPI is an open specification for machine-readable descriptions of web APIs. In the Microsoft ecosystem it is used by Semantic Kernel and Microsoft 365 Copilot to describe what plugins and extensions can do.
faq.q: What is OpenAPI?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, an OpenAPI or Swagger file is used to build custom connectors in Power Apps, and importing an openapi.json file is part of creating an MCP custom connector for Copilot Studio.
faq.q: Where is OpenAPI used with Power Apps and Copilot Studio?

faq.a: The episode "Build Custom Microsoft 365 Copilot Plugins" lists API plugins based on OpenAPI as a way to connect external systems so Copilot can retrieve data and invoke business processes.
faq.q: How does OpenAPI relate to Microsoft 365 Copilot plugins?

openapi.long:
OpenAPI is an open specification for describing web APIs in a machine-readable form. An OpenAPI document states what an API offers and how it can be called, so that other tools and services can understand it without custom documentation or guesswork. In the Microsoft ecosystem it is used by Semantic Kernel and by Microsoft 365 Copilot to describe what plugins and extensions can do.

The core purpose is a standard, shared way of describing an API. When an API is described in this format, tools that consume it can learn how to call it, which makes integration easier and more reliable.
