The M365.FM episode "Build Microsoft Copilot Plugins with Azure Functions" makes this point directly: OpenAPI describes an API in a standard way so that other tools and services can understand how to call the underlying functions. That episode presents OpenAPI as one of the integration patterns for connecting Azure Functions to external systems, and it includes a table to help decide when to use certain integration patterns and when not to.

OpenAPI appears in several places across Copilot and Power Platform work. For Microsoft 365 Copilot, the episode "Build Custom Microsoft 365 Copilot Plugins" lists API plugins based on OpenAPI as one way to connect external systems, alongside Microsoft Graph connectors and custom connectors built in Azure. According to the episode, these approaches let Copilot retrieve data, invoke business processes and integrate with systems such as ERP, CRM or proprietary databases, so that Copilot chat and actions become more conversational and context-aware. In this role the OpenAPI description tells Copilot what an API plugin can do.

In Power Apps, OpenAPI files, also referred to as Swagger files, are used to define custom connectors. The episode "Build Fusion Apps with Power Apps and Azure Functions" describes a pattern in which an Azure Function is protected with API Management, a new API is created for the function, and a custom connector is then built in Power Apps from an OpenAPI or Swagger file that shows what the function does and adds security. Once the connector exists, the app calls the API through it as a data source. The episode "Build Secure Custom Connectors for Power Apps" covers a related path, walking through creating a secure custom connector for an API, including authentication, OpenAPI, error handling and throttling, so that apps can work with live business data rather than CSV exports or copy-paste.

OpenAPI also features in connecting Model Context Protocol servers to Copilot Studio. The episode "MCP Custom Connector in Copilot Studio: The Complete Integration Guide" outlines a procedure that starts in the Copilot Studio Tools area, adds a new tool of the custom connector type, and then, in Power Apps, creates a new custom connector by importing an OpenAPI file. The steps include naming the connector, uploading an openapi.json file, reviewing the configuration settings, creating the connector and then refreshing the Tools tab in Copilot Studio to see the new connector.

In practice, the decisions around OpenAPI usually concern which surface consumes the description. For a Copilot plugin, the OpenAPI document describes the plugin's capabilities. For a Power Apps custom connector, it defines the operations the connector exposes, with security added separately. For an MCP connector in Copilot Studio, an openapi.json file serves as the import for the connector definition. Across these scenarios the shared benefit named in the episodes is that a single, standard description lets different Microsoft tools understand and call an API consistently.

openfga.desc: OpenFGA is an open source fine-grained authorization engine inspired by Google Zanzibar and hosted by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.

faq.a: OpenFGA is an open source fine-grained authorization engine inspired by Google Zanzibar. It is hosted as a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project.
faq.q: What is OpenFGA?

faq.a: It answers authorization checks, such as whether a user can access a given object.
faq.q: What kind of question does OpenFGA answer?

faq.a: OpenFGA is inspired by Google Zanzibar, the authorization approach that underlies its fine-grained access checks.
faq.q: Which project inspired OpenFGA?

openfga.long:
OpenFGA is an open source fine-grained authorization engine. It is inspired by Google Zanzibar and is hosted as a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project.

The engine is used to answer authorization checks, for example whether a given user can access a given object. This relationship-based approach to access control is the core of its purpose: instead of embedding permission logic in individual applications, access decisions are evaluated by a dedicated authorization service.

The available facts do not list specific Microsoft products, linked topics, documentation pages or M365.FM episodes related to OpenFGA, so no further integration details are stated here. As a neutral reference, the entry describes OpenFGA as an authorization engine within the open source and cloud native ecosystem, relevant to readers who encounter the term while researching fine-grained access control and Zanzibar-style authorization models.

openid-connect.desc: OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an authentication layer on OAuth 2.0 that signs users in with signed ID tokens and, via federation, removes stored secrets from pipelines.

faq.a: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization protocol, and OpenID Connect extends it with authentication. OIDC adds the ID token, a signed JWT that lets a client verify the user and read claims about them.
faq.q: What is the difference between OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect?

faq.a: It needs an app registration in Microsoft Entra ID, a matching registered redirect URI and ID token issuance enabled. The sign-in request must include the client ID, the id_token response type, the openid scope and a nonce.
faq.q: What does an app need to sign users in with OIDC on the Microsoft identity platform?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode "Service Principal Security: Stop Using Personal Accounts" describes OIDC and Federated Credentials replacing long-lived secrets in GitHub Actions and other pipelines. The pipeline exchanges tokens with Entra ID instead of storing credentials.
faq.q: How is OIDC used in CI/CD pipelines?

openid-connect.long:
OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an authentication protocol built on top of OAuth 2.0. OAuth 2.0 describes how an application obtains authorization, while OpenID Connect adds a standard way to establish who the user is. This extension makes single sign-on possible between OAuth-enabled applications. According to the material behind this page, Microsoft recommends OIDC as the default for new cloud apps, and it relies on compact JSON-based tokens to handle sign-in.

The central element is the ID token. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) signed with public-key cryptography, and a client can use it to verify the user and read claims about that user. On the Microsoft identity platform, OIDC is supported by several endpoints: a discovery document published on a well-known path, a key endpoint used to verify token signatures, an authorize endpoint and a token endpoint, a logout endpoint, and a UserInfo endpoint. The UserInfo endpoint returns claims according to the openid, profile and email scopes.

To use OIDC with Microsoft Entra ID, an application needs an app registration, a matching registered redirect URI, and ID token issuance enabled. A sign-in request must include the client ID, the id_token response type, the openid scope and a nonce. Apps that rely on ID tokens are expected to validate both the signature and the claims, ideally with a token validation library rather than custom code. The documentation notes that native apps and single-page apps gain little from such validation. It also states that tokens issued for other Microsoft APIs should not be read or validated by the client.

Some practical details affect implementation. Sign-out needs two parts: the redirect to the end-session endpoint and clearing the application's own session. Because responses delivered in the URL fragment are limited in length, the form_post response mode is recommended.

Beyond interactive user sign-in, OIDC also appears in automation and DevOps scenarios. The M365.FM episode "Service Principal Security: Stop Using Personal Accounts" describes Federated Credentials and OpenID Connect as replacements for long-lived secrets in GitHub Actions, CI/CD pipelines and multi-cloud integrations. The episode presents static secrets as one of the largest liabilities in enterprise automation. It covers how OIDC token exchange works with Entra ID, why workload federation removes the need for stored credentials, and why temporary trust is described as stronger than permanent passwords.

The episode "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD" mentions OIDC in a similar deployment context. It says GitHub supports OpenID Connect for secure deployments to cloud platforms, alongside features such as reusable workflows, artifact attestations, deployment rules that control who can deploy and when, and a deployment history useful for audits and compliance checks.

In practice, the choice to use OIDC usually comes up in two situations: adding sign-in to a new app registered in Microsoft Entra ID, and replacing client secrets in pipelines with federated trust. In both, the protocol exchanges short-lived signed tokens instead of relying on passwords or static secrets kept by the application or the pipeline.

openrewrite.desc: OpenRewrite is an open-source ecosystem for automated source-code refactoring that applies recipes to migrate frameworks, fix security issues and reduce technical debt.

faq.a: OpenRewrite is an open-source ecosystem for automated source-code refactoring. It runs recipes that perform framework migrations, security fixes and stylistic consistency changes, with the goal of eliminating technical debt.
faq.q: What is OpenRewrite?

faq.a: It modifies Lossless Semantic Trees that represent the source code and then prints the changed trees back as source. This keeps changes minimally invasive and preserves the original formatting, so the result can be reviewed as a diff.
faq.q: How does OpenRewrite change code without disrupting formatting?

faq.a: In the episode "Upgrade Java 8 Apps to Java 21 with AI Agents", a modernization agent auto-applies OpenRewrite recipes, which drive the migration of Java APIs during the upgrade. Changes stay traceable in Git.
faq.q: What role does OpenRewrite play in the Java 8 to Java 21 episode?

openrewrite.long:
OpenRewrite is an open-source ecosystem for automated source-code refactoring. Its stated goal is to help developers eliminate technical debt in their repositories by running prepackaged, open-source recipes for framework migrations, security fixes and stylistic consistency. The aim is to reduce work that would otherwise take hours or days to a matter of minutes. OpenRewrite was originally focused on Java, and the community is widening its language and framework coverage.

The central concept is the recipe. Recipes are the units that users run, and they are built from visitors, which make the actual modifications to the code. The OpenRewrite documentation gives one example: a visitor that turns assertTrue calls into static imports consistently across all test files. Because recipes are composed from such visitors, a larger migration can be expressed as a set of smaller, repeatable code changes that run in the same way every time.

Technically, OpenRewrite does not edit source files as plain text. It modifies Lossless Semantic Trees, which represent the source code, and then prints the changed trees back out as source. Because of this design, changes are minimally invasive and preserve the original formatting of the code. The practical result is a clean diff that a developer can review and commit like any other change. Recipes are run on one repository at a time through Gradle and Maven plugins. For running the recipe catalogue across many repositories, with mass commits and impact analysis, the documentation describes Moderne as a commercial platform. Moderne offers a free public service for open-source projects, and a multi-repo command-line interface is also available. The documentation further notes that recipes are moving from Maven Central to the Code Genome Project.

Typical situations for using OpenRewrite include upgrading the Java version of an application, moving from one framework version to another, and applying security fixes in bulk. In each case, the value lies in applying a known, reviewable transformation instead of hand-editing many files, with each modification visible in version control.

OpenRewrite appears in the M365.FM episode "Upgrade Java 8 Apps to Java 21 with AI Agents" (2025-11-28). In that episode, a co-pilot-style modernization agent takes over much of the repetitive work of moving a Java 8 application to Java 21 on Azure. According to the episode description, the agent inventories the entire stack, ranks CVEs by real reachability, auto-applies OpenRewrite recipes, aligns BOMs, fixes illegal reflective access and keeps every change traceable in Git. In this workflow, OpenRewrite recipes drive the migration of Java APIs during the upgrade, while the agent coordinates the surrounding steps. The same episode extends the scenario beyond the code upgrade to platform decisions such as Azure App Service versus Azure Spring Apps, migration to Azure SQL Database, Dockerfile generation, GitHub Actions CI/CD and secrets handling with Key Vault and managed identities.

The combination described in the episode reflects a common pattern: deterministic, recipe-based refactoring handles well-understood API migrations, while an AI agent handles inventory, prioritization and orchestration. Keeping the changes as reviewable diffs in Git is what makes the result auditable.

opentelemetry.desc: OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral, open-source observability standard and framework for instrumenting applications to emit traces, metrics and logs.

faq.a: OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral, open-source observability standard and framework for instrumenting applications so they emit traces, metrics and logs.
faq.q: What is OpenTelemetry?

faq.a: According to the episode "Why Microservice Architecture Slows Software Delivery", it supports distributed tracing, which follows a request across services and helps reveal where delays and bottlenecks occur.
faq.q: How does OpenTelemetry help with microservices?

faq.a: The episodes describe using it, for example with Azure AI Foundry, to visualize how agents run, which tools they call and how they make decisions, and to monitor pilot agent deployments.
faq.q: How is OpenTelemetry used with AI agents in the Microsoft ecosystem?

opentelemetry.long:
OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral, open-source observability standard and framework for instrumenting applications so that they emit traces, metrics and logs. It gives teams a common way to describe what a running system is doing, independent of the monitoring product that eventually stores or visualizes the data. Because the approach is not tied to a single vendor, the same instrumentation can in principle feed different backends, which is why it appears in discussions of cloud, microservice and AI workloads alike.

The three signal types named in its definition each answer a different question. Traces follow a single request as it moves through the components of a system. Metrics capture aggregated measurements over time, such as latency or request counts. Logs record individual events and decisions. OpenTelemetry is used to produce all three in a consistent form, so that data coming from different services, languages and frameworks can be correlated rather than analyzed in isolation.

One of the clearest use cases in the M365.FM material is distributed tracing in microservice architectures. The episode "Why Microservice Architecture Slows Software Delivery" explains that distributed tracing lets teams follow a request across many services, with each service adding its own processing time and network delay. It lists OpenTelemetry alongside Jaeger and Zipkin as tracing tools that connect the dots and show the full path of a request. According to the episode, this makes it easier to spot where delays happen, exposes bottlenecks and accelerates debugging, so teams can identify latency sources and improve reliability.

OpenTelemetry also comes up in the context of AI agents. The episode "Secure AI Agents and Shadow IT in Microsoft 365" describes framework fragmentation as a governance problem: different AI frameworks use different metrics and logging styles, which complicates observability and integration. The episode suggests that tools such as Datadog and OpenTelemetry can give better visibility into AI workflows, helping teams track decision paths and identify issues before they escalate, and it stresses continuous monitoring to detect misuse, policy violations and changes in AI behavior early.

The same theme appears in two further episodes about building agents on Microsoft's cloud. "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud" addresses debugging opacity, where agents make decisions that are hard to trace. It recommends structured reasoning logs and using Azure AI Foundry with OpenTelemetry to visualize how agents run, which tools they call and how they make decisions. "Production AI Agents with Microsoft Foundry and Edgar McOchieng [MVP]" advises starting with a low- or medium-risk pilot project and monitoring everything with tools like OpenTelemetry, alongside least-privilege access for agent actions and a human in the loop for important decisions.

Cost is another angle. In "Azure Monitor — Simply Explained", OpenTelemetry appears in a list of ways to tune the amount of telemetry collected and keep Azure monitoring costs under control. The episode mentions using OpenTelemetry metric instruments and aggregating metrics to reduce data volume, next to limiting reported data and disabling unneeded instrumentation. The underlying idea is to collect only the signals that are necessary while keeping visibility into the environment.

Taken together, the episodes treat OpenTelemetry as an instrumentation layer rather than a monitoring product in itself. It produces traces, metrics and logs; tools such as Jaeger, Zipkin, Datadog or Azure Monitor are the places where such data is examined. Typical decisions around it include which signals to collect, how much data to send in order to manage cost, and how to apply it to both classic microservices and AI agent workflows where decision paths need to be traceable.

opentofu.desc: OpenTofu is an open source infrastructure-as-code tool forked from Terraform, governed by the Linux Foundation under the MPL 2.0 license.

faq.a: OpenTofu is an open source infrastructure-as-code tool forked from Terraform. It is governed by the Linux Foundation and released under the MPL 2.0 license.
faq.q: What is OpenTofu?

faq.a: It was started by Gruntwork, Spacelift, Harness, env0, Scalr and others after HashiCorp moved Terraform from an open source license to the Business Source License, which the project calls ambiguous for companies and developers.
faq.q: Why was OpenTofu created?

faq.a: Its website describes OpenTofu as a drop-in replacement for Terraform that preserves existing workflows and configurations, and the project aims for feature parity with Terraform.
faq.q: How does OpenTofu relate to Terraform?

opentofu.long:
OpenTofu is an open source infrastructure-as-code (IaC) tool that began as a fork of Terraform. The fork was started by Gruntwork, Spacelift, Harness, env0, Scalr and others after HashiCorp moved Terraform from an open source license to the Business Source License, which the project describes as ambiguous for companies and developers. OpenTofu is governed by the Linux Foundation and is released under the MPL 2.0 license. Its website describes it as a drop-in replacement for Terraform that preserves existing workflows and configurations.

Infrastructure as code means describing cloud resources in configuration files instead of creating them by hand, so that environments can be deployed repeatedly and consistently. OpenTofu is used for this purpose. According to its website, it manages resources across clouds through providers, and the site gives examples such as AWS S3 buckets, Cloudflare DNS records and GitHub repositories. The project cites an ecosystem of more than 3,900 providers and 23,600 modules, and a registry search site lets users look up providers and modules.

The project describes itself as community driven and aims for feature parity with Terraform. Contributions come through GitHub discussions, issues, RFC reviews and code, and the website credits more than 180 community contributors along with sponsors who support hosting and monitoring. Because it sits under the Linux Foundation's stewardship, the direction of the tool is not tied to a single vendor.

The website highlights several features by release. Version 1.7 introduced client-side state encryption, with key providers such as PBKDF2, AWS KMS, GCP KMS and OpenBao. Version 1.8 added early evaluation of variables and locals in module sources. Version 1.9 added the -exclude flag and provider for_each. These items show the project's focus on state protection, module flexibility and provider handling, although the sources do not describe them in more detail.

Typical decisions around OpenTofu concern licensing and compatibility. Teams that already have Terraform configurations may weigh a tool that keeps existing workflows against the license terms of the original product. Teams starting new IaC work on a cloud platform will also compare it with other options, since several tools exist for the same job.

In the M365.FM episode "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained", OpenTofu appears in a list of widely used IaC tools for Azure. The listed tools are Terraform, OpenTofu, ARM Templates, Bicep Templates, Ansible, Pulumi, Chef and SaltStack. The episode excerpt goes on to explain ARM templates, which use JSON files to define and deploy Azure resources, so OpenTofu is mentioned there as one option among several rather than examined in depth.

openusd.desc: OpenUSD (Universal Scene Description) is an open-source framework and file format, originally developed by Pixar, for describing, composing and exchanging 3D scenes.
openusd.long:
OpenUSD (Universal Scene Description) is an open-source framework and file format for describing, composing and exchanging 3D scenes between tools and engines. It was originally developed by Pixar.

The framework is used to represent 3D scene content in a form that different applications can read and work with. Because it covers both the description of a scene and the way scene elements are composed together, it serves as a shared basis for workflows in which several tools and engines need to exchange the same 3D data.

The available facts about OpenUSD (Universal Scene Description) do not list specific related products, topics or documentation links, so this page keeps to the general definition. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity. Further details on features, versions or integrations should be taken from the official OpenUSD project materials rather than from this summary.

operational-technology.desc: Operational technology (OT) is the hardware, software and work used to monitor and control physical production processes and equipment, distinct from IT.

faq.a: OT monitors and controls physical production processes and equipment, while IT covers business, computing and data services. OT stresses availability and real-time control, whereas IT security centers on confidentiality, integrity and availability.
faq.q: What is the difference between OT and IT?

faq.a: OT includes industrial control systems such as SCADA, distributed control systems, remote terminal units and programmable logic controllers, as well as IoT and industrial IoT devices and building automation.
faq.q: Which systems count as operational technology?

faq.a: According to the episode "From Sensor to Dashboard: The MQTT Pipeline Through Azure IoT Hub", an industrial gateway on the OT network translates data into a common message shape, manages collection frequency and buffers data locally during network outages.
faq.q: How does OT data reach cloud services like Azure IoT Hub?

operational-technology.long:
Operational technology (OT) refers to the hardware and software that detects or causes change by directly monitoring and controlling industrial equipment, assets, processes and events. It is usually defined in contrast to information technology (IT), which covers business computing and data services. A common shorthand describes OT as IT in the non-carpeted areas of a facility, meaning the plant floor, the field and the physical infrastructure rather than the office.

OT environments include industrial control systems such as SCADA, distributed control systems, remote terminal units and programmable logic controllers (PLCs). They also cover IoT and industrial IoT devices and building automation. These systems regulate physical values such as temperature, pressure and flow, which means they need real-time or near-real-time processing and high reliability. They typically communicate through specialized protocols such as Modbus, DNP3, Profibus, BACnet and OPC-UA rather than the general-purpose protocols common in office networks. The term was introduced by Gartner in 2006, first in connection with power utility control systems.

The priorities of OT and IT differ. OT stresses availability and real-time control of a physical process, while IT security is usually framed around confidentiality, integrity and availability. Security in OT was long based on isolation and obscurity. Since at least 2005, OT has been connected to IT systems, which created new risks. Stuxnet is cited as an illustration. Typical weaknesses include weak segmentation, plaintext protocols and legacy devices without authentication. Recommended responses include layered defenses, continuous anomaly monitoring and the ISA/IEC 62443 series of standards.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, OT mostly appears where plant data meets cloud services. The episode "From Sensor to Dashboard: The MQTT Pipeline Through Azure IoT Hub" describes the situation in older plants, which often run several generations of equipment with proprietary protocols or OPC UA. PLCs therefore rarely speak cloud MQTT directly. According to the episode, an industrial gateway deployed on the OT network bridges this gap. It normalizes data by translating disparate formats, scales and engineering tags into a common message shape. It manages collection frequency by aggregating high-frequency scans into meaningful intervals while forwarding state changes immediately. It also buffers data locally during network outages and replays it once connectivity returns.

The second angle is data governance. In "Microsoft Purview for Copilot Security with Peter Rising [Microsoft]", the guidance includes segmenting OT and IT data and sharing only aggregated insights with the cloud. The episode pairs this with multi-factor authentication for supervisors, contractors and suppliers, keeping Copilot from indexing outdated or risky shared files, and Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies that monitor and block sensitive files from leaving secure channels. The stated aim is to protect intellectual property and control who can access it. The episode's tip is to review the data segmentation strategy and make sure only necessary information moves to the cloud.

Taken together, the sources show OT as a distinct domain with its own protocols, reliability needs and risk profile. Decisions around it usually concern where the boundary between OT and IT lies, which data crosses that boundary, in what form, and how that crossing is secured and governed.

operator-connect.desc: Operator Connect is a Teams Phone option in which a Microsoft-certified carrier supplies PSTN connectivity, numbers and session border controllers, managed in the Teams admin center.

faq.a: Operator Connect is a Teams Phone connectivity option where a Microsoft-certified operator provides PSTN connectivity, phone numbers and session border controllers. Administrators manage users and numbers in the Teams admin center.
faq.q: What is Operator Connect?

faq.a: Microsoft covers Teams services and administration. The operator handles PSTN connectivity, number provisioning and porting, calling services and PSTN-related support.
faq.q: Who is responsible for what with Operator Connect?

faq.a: The documentation lists the required Teams Phone licenses, users in Teams Only mode, suitable admin permissions, a certified operator in the target countries or regions and a network that meets Teams requirements.
faq.q: What is needed to use Operator Connect?

operator-connect.long:
Operator Connect is a Teams Phone connectivity option that links Microsoft Teams to the public switched telephone network (PSTN) through a Microsoft-certified operator. The operator runs the PSTN infrastructure, including the numbers and the session border controllers, while administrators manage users and numbers in the Teams admin center. The stated aim is a simpler Teams Phone deployment, because an organization does not have to run and maintain its own session border controllers.

The model suits organizations that already work with a carrier taking part in the Operator Connect program and want to keep that relationship while using Teams for voice. Administrators enable the chosen operator in the Teams admin center and then assign phone numbers. Depending on the situation, they can buy new numbers, port existing ones or migrate users from another Teams Phone PSTN option. Because numbers are handled in the same admin interface used for other Teams administration, voice management stays in one place.

Several prerequisites apply. The documentation lists the required Teams Phone licenses, users in Teams Only mode, suitable admin permissions, a certified operator that is available in the target countries or regions, and a network that meets Teams requirements. Country and region coverage therefore matters early in planning, since the choice of operator depends on which operators serve the locations where users work.

Onboarding follows four steps: check the prerequisites, choose an operator, plan a number strategy and configure Operator Connect. The number strategy step is worth attention, because it determines whether numbers are newly acquired, ported from an existing provider or carried over when users are migrated from another Teams Phone PSTN option.

Responsibilities are split between Microsoft and the operator. Microsoft covers Teams services and administration. The operator handles PSTN connectivity, number provisioning and porting, calling services and PSTN-related support. In practice, this means that questions about the Teams client or admin center belong with Microsoft, while questions about call routing to the PSTN, number porting or carrier-side services belong with the operator.

Operator Connect is only one of several PSTN connectivity options for Teams Phone. The episode "Microsoft Teams Phone and Telephony | Simply Explained" describes it alongside Microsoft Calling Plans and Direct Routing and presents the comparison as a way to understand which approach best fits a given set of business requirements. The same episode covers Teams Telephony features such as voicemail, call forwarding, Auto Attendants, Call Queues, presence integration, call transfers and hybrid work support, and it notes that Teams Phone works with mobile devices, Teams-certified desk phones and meeting room systems. Choosing between the connectivity options is therefore a decision about who supplies and operates the PSTN link, not about which Teams voice features are available.

optical-character-recognition.desc: Optical character recognition (OCR) reads characters in images or documents and converts them to machine-readable text without understanding what the text means.

faq.a: OCR reads the characters visible in an image or document and turns them into machine-readable text. It does not by itself know what that text means.
faq.q: What does OCR do?

faq.a: The episode "Communication Compliance - Simply Explained" lists OCR as a way to handle text inside images when strengthening policies. It generates signals rather than conclusions, so reviewers still evaluate the full conversational context.
faq.q: How is OCR used in Communication Compliance?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure AI Search – Simply Explained", OCR is part of document enrichment, used together with entity recognition to improve the data being searched and make results more accurate and complete.
faq.q: What role does OCR play in Azure AI Search?

optical-character-recognition.long:
Optical character recognition (OCR) is a technology that reads the characters visible in an image or document and turns them into machine-readable text. It does this without by itself knowing what that text means. The output is text that other systems can store, search, filter or analyze, but any interpretation of that text has to come from a separate step or tool.

The core purpose of OCR is to make text that is locked inside pixels accessible to software. A scanned page, a photograph of a form or a screenshot contains letters and numbers that a person can read, but a computer treats the file as a picture. OCR bridges that gap by extracting the visible characters. Once the content exists as text, it can be used in processes that normally work only on typed or digital text, such as keyword matching, indexing and downstream data processing.

The M365.FM episodes mention OCR in three different settings. In "Communication Compliance - Simply Explained", OCR is listed among the techniques that organizations can use to strengthen communication policies, alongside custom keywords, phrase dictionaries, contextual conversation analysis and configurable review sampling percentages. There it is used for text inside images, so that content shared as a picture can still be evaluated by a policy. The episode stresses that these technologies generate signals rather than conclusions. Reviewers are meant to evaluate communications within their complete conversational context before deciding whether a policy has actually been violated. This fits the nature of OCR: it supplies the text, while judging its meaning and relevance remains a separate, human-guided task.

In "Azure AI Search – Simply Explained", OCR appears as part of document enrichment. The episode describes Azure AI Search as using AI tools such as Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and entity recognition to improve the data being searched. In this context OCR extracts text from content that would otherwise not be searchable, and entity recognition then works on that text. The episode says this leads to more accurate and complete search results. The relationship illustrates a common division of labor: OCR produces the raw text, and other AI capabilities add structure or meaning on top of it.

In "Automate Power Platform Data Entry with AI Tools", OCR is one of the techniques used by an AI Form Filler, together with text cleaning and tokenization. According to the episode, text cleaning removes irrelevant data such as punctuation and duplicates, tokenization breaks text into manageable units, and OCR extracts text from images or PDFs. The episode presents this as a way to manage data more effectively than manual methods and lists benefits such as faster data cleaning and analysis, fewer human errors in processing, and the ability to handle large datasets.

Typical decisions around OCR follow from these examples. When content arrives as images or scanned PDFs, a team has to decide whether the text inside needs to be extracted so that it can be searched, checked against policies or entered into forms and other systems. Because OCR only recognizes characters, it is usually combined with further steps, such as entity recognition, tokenization, keyword or phrase matching, or human review, depending on whether the goal is search, compliance monitoring or data entry automation.

Taken together, the episodes treat OCR as an enabling building block rather than a standalone solution. It converts visible characters into text, and the value comes from what is done with that text afterwards: enriching a search index, feeding a compliance policy that produces review signals, or populating fields in an automated workflow.

organism-as-a-service.desc: Organism as a Service is a concept from Sonny Gillissen: AI-driven agent loops in Azure Logic Apps let integrations interpret context and react instead of only running fixed workflows.

faq.a: Organism as a Service is a concept described by Sonny Gillissen. It describes integrations that use AI to interpret context, react to unexpected situations and respond, instead of only executing predefined workflows.
faq.q: What is Organism as a Service?

faq.a: Azure Logic Apps is used as the example platform. Agent loops in Azure Logic Apps illustrate how an integration can act on context rather than follow a fixed sequence of steps.
faq.q: How does Azure Logic Apps relate to Organism as a Service?

faq.a: It is covered in the episode "AI Turns Integration into an Organism as a Service — How Azure Logic Apps Are Changing Enterprise Integration with Sonny Gillissen [MVP]", dated 2026-08-18.
faq.q: Where is Organism as a Service discussed on M365.FM?

organism-as-a-service.long:
Organism as a Service is a concept described by Sonny Gillissen that frames enterprise integration as something closer to a living system than a fixed pipeline. In this view, AI allows an integration to interpret context, react to unexpected situations and respond, rather than only executing a predefined workflow step by step.

The concept is illustrated through agent loops in Azure Logic Apps. Traditional integration workflows follow a set sequence of triggers and actions defined in advance. Under the Organism as a Service idea, an AI component inside the workflow can assess what is happening, adapt to conditions that were not anticipated at design time and decide how to proceed. The term is a conceptual description of this shift, not a product or a licensed Microsoft service.

Organism as a Service appears on M365.FM in the episode "AI Turns Integration into an Organism as a Service — How Azure Logic Apps Are Changing Enterprise Integration with Sonny Gillissen [MVP]", published on 2026-08-18. The episode discusses how AI is changing enterprise integration with Azure Logic Apps and introduces the concept as a way to describe that change.

organizational-brain.desc: Organizational brain is a context layer described by Rishi Sapra, built from five layers that ground AI agents in an organization's certified knowledge.

faq.a: It is a context layer described by Rishi Sapra that grounds AI agents in an organization's certified knowledge. It is organized into five layers: data, logic, tools, skills and governance.
faq.q: What is the Organizational brain?

faq.a: The five layers are data, logic, tools, skills and governance. Together they form the context that AI agents are grounded in.
faq.q: What are the five layers of the Organizational brain?

faq.a: It is discussed in the episode "From Financial Data to AI-Ready Decisions: Power BI, Microsoft Fabric, Semantic Models & AI Agents with Rishi Sapra [MVP]", dated 2026-09-16.
faq.q: Where does the Organizational brain appear on M365.FM?

organizational-brain.long:
Organizational brain is a concept described by Rishi Sapra. It refers to a context layer that grounds AI agents in an organization's certified knowledge, so that agents work from approved, trusted information rather than unverified sources.

The concept is structured around five layers: data, logic, tools, skills and governance. Together, these layers describe the kinds of context an AI agent draws on when it supports decisions inside an organization. The facts available for this entry do not detail how each layer works or how the layers are implemented in practice, so this page limits itself to the layer names and the grounding purpose.

Organizational brain appears on M365.FM in the episode "From Financial Data to AI-Ready Decisions: Power BI, Microsoft Fabric, Semantic Models & AI Agents with Rishi Sapra [MVP]", published on 2026-09-16. The episode title places the concept alongside Power BI, Microsoft Fabric, semantic models and AI agents, which are the topics discussed in that conversation.

organizational-debt.desc: Organizational debt is the accumulated cost of unresolved decisions, unclear ownership and inconsistent processes, paid as ongoing coordination overhead rather than in code.
organizational-debt.long:
Organizational debt is the accumulated cost of unresolved decisions, unclear ownership and inconsistent processes within an organization. The cost is paid over time as ongoing coordination overhead: effort spent aligning people, clarifying who is responsible and reconciling different ways of working.

The term is distinct from technical debt. Technical debt lives in the code, while organizational debt lives in how teams are structured, how decisions are made and how responsibilities are assigned. The two can interact, since unclear ownership and inconsistent processes often show up in the way systems are built and maintained, but they describe different kinds of accumulated cost.

The concept is used to explain why coordination effort keeps growing even when no single technical problem can be pointed to. Each decision left open, each area without a clear owner and each process that differs from team to team adds to the overhead that has to be paid on later work.

On M365.FM, organizational debt is discussed in the episode "The Monorepo Myth: Why Your Architecture Is Fragmented" (2026-07-19), which connects the topic to questions of architecture and fragmentation.

organizational-unit.desc: An organizational unit (OU) is a container in Active Directory, similar to a labeled folder, used to group accounts and to scope tasks such as synchronization.
organizational-unit.long:
An organizational unit (OU) is a container inside Active Directory. It works like a labeled folder: accounts and other directory objects can be placed in it so that they are grouped in a way that matches how an organization wants to manage them.

OUs are used to organize accounts and to scope administrative tasks. One example is synchronization, where an OU can define which part of the directory a particular task applies to. By placing accounts in a specific OU, administrators can limit an operation to that group instead of the entire directory.

The concept is relevant to anyone working with Active Directory in a Microsoft environment, particularly when deciding how to structure accounts and which accounts should be included in a given process.

No related topics or episodes are currently linked to this entry on M365.FM.

orphaned-flows.desc: Orphaned flows are Power Automate flows whose owner has left, is disabled or was never a real person, leaving no one accountable while they may keep running or fail silently.
orphaned-flows.long:
Orphaned flows are Power Automate flows that no longer have an accountable owner. The owner may have left the organization, the account may be disabled, or the flow may have been created under an identity that was never a real person in the first place. In each case, nobody is clearly responsible for the flow's behavior.

The core issue is that an ownerless flow can continue to run without anyone watching it. It may keep executing on its trigger, or it may fail silently when a connection, credential or dependency changes, and no one is positioned to notice or fix the problem. Because accountability is missing, questions about what the flow does, what data it touches and whether it is still needed often go unanswered.

The concept is used in governance and administration discussions around Power Automate to describe a category of risk and cleanup work: identifying flows without a valid owner, deciding whether they are still required, and assigning responsibility or retiring them. Treating orphaned flows as a defined concept helps teams talk about ownership as a basic requirement for any automation that stays in production.

No specific episodes, tools or related topics are linked to this entry on M365.FM at this time.

orphaned-sites.desc: Orphaned sites are SharePoint or Teams sites with no active owner, often after the owner leaves, while content and permissions stay in the tenant.

faq.a: An orphaned site is a SharePoint or Teams site without an active owner, typically because the original owner left the organization. Its content and permissions remain in the tenant.
faq.q: What is an orphaned site in Microsoft 365?

faq.a: The episode "Secure Microsoft Copilot with Entra ID and Zero Trust" recommends aggressive discovery of orphaned sites and external shares, followed by quick remediation, to prevent exposure before a broad rollout.
faq.q: Why are orphaned sites a risk for Microsoft Copilot rollouts?

faq.a: The episode "Teams Private Channels vs Shared Channels" advises keeping at least two channel owners and using scripted checks for private channels so that no site is left without an owner.
faq.q: How can orphaned sites be prevented?

orphaned-sites.long:
Orphaned sites are SharePoint or Teams sites that no longer have an active owner. The usual cause is that the original owner left the organization or changed roles and nobody took over responsibility. The site itself does not disappear in that case: its content and its permissions remain in the Microsoft 365 tenant, even though no one is accountable for reviewing who has access or what is stored there.

The concept matters mainly for governance and security. A site without an owner has no person who can approve access requests, remove outdated members, correct oversharing or decide when the content is no longer needed. Over time, permissions drift away from current business reality, and old content stays reachable by people who may no longer need it. For this reason, orphaned sites are usually discussed together with external sharing, permission audits and data classification, since each of these areas depends on someone being responsible for the site.

The M365.FM episode "Secure Microsoft Copilot with Entra ID and Zero Trust" places orphaned sites in the context of collaboration risk. According to the episode, organizations should keep a catalog of external integrations, assign each a risk score, and use aggressive discovery to find orphaned sites and external shares, then remediate issues quickly to prevent exposure. The same episode recommends enforcing Purview sensitivity labels and DLP for Microsoft Copilot interactions before a broad rollout. The connection is that content in sites nobody manages can still be reachable by Microsoft Copilot through the permissions that remain in place.

The episode "Microsoft Copilot Governance Without Waiting for Perfect Data" treats orphaned sites as a normal feature of real environments rather than a reason to postpone a rollout. It describes environments as inherently messy, with orphaned sites, inconsistent data classification and fragmented ownership. The episode argues that waiting for perfect governance before deploying creates governance debt and delays value. Instead, governance should run as a continuous track alongside deployment, using automation, prioritization and real-time controls to manage risk.

In "Automate Microsoft 365 Governance Beyond Static Checklists", the reduction of orphaned sites and teams is named as one of the metrics for measuring the success of governance automation. The other metrics listed alongside it are fewer external sharing incidents, fewer access-related security alerts, better compliance audit results and higher policy adoption by business users. The episode mentions that dashboards and reports from tools such as SysKit Point or native Microsoft 365 reports can provide these indicators.

The episode "Audit SharePoint Online Permissions at Scale" covers the detection side. It says that centralized dashboards help spot outdated access and orphaned sites, that automation saves time and reduces errors, and that regular reviews of sensitive libraries keep the environment secure. It recommends combining built-in and third-party tools to move from manual checks to proactive governance.

Prevention is addressed in "Teams Private Channels vs Shared Channels". Its guidance on owner turnover is to always keep at least two channel owners and, for private channels, to use scripted checks so that orphaned sites do not arise. The point is that ownership should never depend on a single person, because a single departure is enough to leave a site without an owner.

Taken together, the episodes describe a practical cycle: discover sites without active owners, review their permissions and content, remediate by assigning ownership or restricting access, and prevent recurrence through multiple owners and automated checks. Orphaned sites are therefore treated both as a risk indicator and as a measurable governance outcome.

orphaned-workspace.desc: An orphaned workspace is a Microsoft 365 team, group or SharePoint site that remains active but has no current owner managing its membership, sharing and lifecycle.

faq.a: It is a collaboration space such as a team, group or SharePoint site that is still active but no longer has a current owner. As a result, no one is responsible for its membership, sharing and lifecycle decisions.
faq.q: What is an orphaned workspace in Microsoft 365?

faq.a: The description names teams, groups and SharePoint sites as examples of Microsoft 365 collaboration spaces that can lose their owner.
faq.q: Which types of spaces can become orphaned?

faq.a: Owners are responsible for membership, sharing and lifecycle decisions. Without one, those decisions may not be made, even though the workspace remains active.
faq.q: Why does a missing owner matter?

orphaned-workspace.long:
An orphaned workspace is a Microsoft 365 collaboration space, such as a team, group or SharePoint site, that is still active but no longer has a current owner. Without an owner, nobody is clearly responsible for decisions about who belongs to the space, how its content is shared and when it should be archived or removed.

The term is used in Microsoft 365 governance discussions to describe a gap in accountability rather than a specific product feature. A workspace can become orphaned when its owner leaves the organization, changes roles or is otherwise removed, while the space itself continues to hold content and members. Because the space keeps running, the missing ownership can go unnoticed.

The main concerns are the three areas that owners normally handle: membership, sharing and lifecycle. Membership may drift as people join or leave without review. Sharing settings may stay open longer than intended. Lifecycle decisions, such as retention, archiving or deletion, may never be made. Addressing orphaned workspaces generally means identifying spaces without an owner and assigning a new responsible person or retiring the space.

No specific episodes or related topics are currently linked to this term on M365.FM.

outcome-based-pricing.desc: Outcome-based pricing is a model in which clients pay for measurable business results rather than billable hours, often via build fees plus retainers or licences.

faq.a: It is a pricing model for consulting and IT services in which clients pay for measurable business results rather than billable hours. It is often delivered as build fees plus recurring retainers or licences.
faq.q: What is outcome-based pricing?

faq.a: Time-and-materials contracts pay for inputs such as man-hours, while outcome-based contracts pay for results the business wants. The CIO article reports that time-and-materials is still the most common model and that outcome-based contracts are at most about 15 percent of new deals.
faq.q: How does outcome-based pricing differ from time-and-materials contracts?

faq.a: The CIO article names difficulty agreeing on outcomes between executives, limited vendor control over external factors, the risk of gaming metrics and uneven results. The M365.FM episode on computer-using agents adds that agent and outcome must be clearly defined.
faq.q: What challenges come with outcome-based pricing?

outcome-based-pricing.long:
Outcome-based pricing is a pricing model for consulting and IT services in which the client pays for measurable business results instead of billable hours. In practice it is often structured as a build fee combined with recurring retainers or licences, so that the price is tied to the value delivered rather than to the time a provider spends on the work. The term is used both in outsourcing contracts and in discussions about how Microsoft ecosystem partners package their services.

The idea is easiest to understand by contrast with input-based contracts. A CIO article on outsourcing describes task-based, or input, contracts as agreements that pay for resources such as servers, hardware or man-hours, while outcome-based contracts pay for results the business actually wants. A consultant quoted in that article notes that clients generally want business results rather than infrastructure. The article also reports that time-and-materials contracts remain the most common model, followed by fixed price, and that outcome-based contracts make up at most about 15 percent of new deals and may cover only part of the work.

The same source lists several challenges. Agreeing on the outcome can be difficult when the CEO, CFO and CIO want different things. The vendor has limited control over factors such as marketing and economic conditions that influence results. Metrics such as customer satisfaction can be gamed, and results may be uneven. Forrester's listed advantages include more cohesive delivery, less monitoring of individual staff, stronger incentives to innovate and potential long-term savings. The drawbacks it names are less transparency into how work is done, limited cost visibility and extra effort for root-cause analysis. Both sides can resist the model: clients give up day-to-day control and need trust, while vendors absorb more risk the higher the outcome sits on the value chain.

In the M365.FM episode "5 High-Margin Microsoft 365 Business Models", the shift from hourly billing to outcome-based pricing is presented as part of a broader change in how Microsoft 365 services are sold. The episode says that as complexity in the Microsoft ecosystem increases, organizations struggle with governance, which creates demand for specialists who design and operate control systems rather than deliver one-time projects. In that framing, value is tied to measurable business impact such as risk reduction, automation and efficiency gains, and the episode links this to recurring revenue streams rather than traditional consulting engagements.

The episode "Computer-Using Agents: How CUA Could Transform SaaS" approaches the topic from the software side. It says organizations redefine value in contracts and shift to outcome-based pricing as agent-driven systems become more common. According to the episode, pricing models evolve and require clear definitions of what counts as an agent and what counts as an outcome. It also states that advanced instrumentation and real-time data observability become essential for compliance, and that SaaS companies need to adapt to avoid obsolescence.

Taken together, the sources point to the same practical decisions. A provider and client need a shared, measurable definition of the outcome before any price is set. Both need a way to observe results, which is why instrumentation and observability come up in the episode on computer-using agents. They also need to decide how risk is split, how the build work is charged, and whether ongoing value is billed as a retainer or a licence. The CIO article adds that the model may cover only part of a contract and is not yet the dominant form of engagement, so it is often used alongside other pricing methods rather than as a full replacement.

outlook.desc: Microsoft Outlook is the email, calendar, contacts and tasks client of Microsoft 365, connecting to Exchange Online and other mail accounts.

faq.a: Microsoft Outlook is the Microsoft 365 client for email, calendar, contacts and tasks. It connects to Exchange Online and other mail accounts and is used to organize communication and schedules.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Outlook used for?

faq.a: Exchange Online hosts the mailboxes that Outlook connects to, while Outlook on the web is the browser version of the same environment. Together they give access to the same mail and calendar data from different clients.
faq.q: How does Outlook relate to Exchange Online and Outlook on the web?

faq.a: "Build Internal Outlook Newsletters with Dynamic Groups" describes an internal newsletter pipeline using Dynamic Distribution Groups, a shared mailbox and a reusable template. "Use Microsoft Loop Components Across Teams and Outlook" covers Loop components that update in several places at once, and "Beyond the Prompt: Mastering Microsoft Copilot for Real Productivity with Jess Stratton [MVP]" covers Copilot across Microsoft 365 apps including Outlook.
faq.q: What do the M365.FM episodes say about Outlook?

outlook.long:
Microsoft Outlook is the email, calendar, contacts and tasks client of Microsoft 365. It connects to Exchange Online as well as to other mail accounts and is used to organize communication and schedules in one place. The catalog lists its release as 1997-01-16 and describes it as included with Microsoft 365 licensing. The product is also referred to as Outlook, as the new Outlook, or as Outlook for Windows.

Outlook is developed by Microsoft and is classed as a Microsoft tool and as a collaboration tool. It is part of Microsoft 365 Apps. Its closest technical relationship is with Exchange Online, which hosts the mailboxes that the client reads and writes. Outlook on the web is the browser-based counterpart, so the same mailbox and calendar can be reached either through the desktop client or through a web browser.

In day-to-day use, Outlook covers four connected areas: email for sending and receiving messages, a calendar for appointments and meetings, contacts for people and addresses, and tasks for to-do items. Because it can connect to accounts beyond Exchange Online, it can serve as a single client for several mailboxes. Its calendar is tightly connected to Microsoft Teams, which matters for scheduling and joining meetings. Microsoft 365 Copilot is also related to Outlook, since it can assist with drafting and summarizing within the mail environment.

The M365.FM episodes show how Outlook fits into wider Microsoft 365 workflows. The episode "Build Internal Outlook Newsletters with Dynamic Groups" argues that many internal updates get lost in Teams noise and that the fix is wiring together tools an organization already owns rather than adopting a new platform. It describes a repeatable newsletter pipeline: targeting audiences with Dynamic Distribution Groups that rely on Entra ID attributes, sending from a shared mailbox for branding and continuity, composing with a reusable Outlook template, and then scaling the same pattern to other departments. According to the episode, the aim is that updates are no longer buried, audiences only see what matters to them, and leaders can measure engagement without extra licenses.

The episode "Use Microsoft Loop Components Across Teams and Outlook" looks at Loop components as living, embeddable data that updates everywhere at once. It contrasts this with copy-paste and scheduled syncs between systems such as CRM, Power BI and Teams, and describes how a single canonical object can appear in several places, including Outlook, without the numbers drifting apart. The episode also points to gotchas to watch when adopting this approach.

Copilot in Outlook is addressed in "Beyond the Prompt: Mastering Microsoft Copilot for Real Productivity with Jess Stratton [MVP]". The episode notes describe Microsoft Copilot as working inside Microsoft 365 apps and connecting Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams into one system. Guest Jess Stratton recommends multi-part prompts that divide larger projects into small steps, and follow-up prompts to adjust writing style, correct errors and add missing context to AI drafts.

Outlook also appears as an integration point in other episodes. "Microsoft Places - Simply Explained" notes that Microsoft Places features are embedded in Teams and Outlook so they can be used in the flow of work, such as for desk booking in hybrid work. "Dynamics 365 Customer Service - Simply Explained" lists Outlook among the products the service platform integrates with, alongside Teams, Microsoft 365, Power Platform, Copilot and Azure, so that support agents have the information they need to resolve issues.

For decisions around Outlook, the relevant questions are usually which mailbox platform it connects to, whether the new Outlook or another variant is deployed, how groups and shared mailboxes are structured for communication, and how adjacent services such as Teams and Copilot are combined with it.

outlook-actionable-messages.desc: Outlook actionable messages let recipients take quick actions or fill in fields in an Adaptive Card inside an email, without leaving Outlook.
outlook-actionable-messages.long:
Outlook actionable messages are a feature that extends email in Outlook so that recipients can act on a message directly. Instead of opening a separate web page or application, a recipient can take a quick action or complete fields that appear in an Adaptive Card embedded in the message.

The approach is used when an email needs a response or a small piece of input, such as confirming a choice or entering a few values. Because the interaction happens within Outlook, the recipient stays in the mail client while completing the task. The card format is Adaptive Card, which defines the layout and input elements shown in the message.

The feature is documented by Microsoft in its Outlook developer documentation, which is the reference for how actionable messages are built and used. No related topics or specific implementation details are listed here beyond that official documentation.

No episodes on M365.FM are currently linked to Outlook actionable messages. This page will be updated if related content is added.

outlook-web.desc: Outlook on the web (OWA) is the browser version of Outlook for mail, calendar and contacts, hosted by Exchange Online and developed by Microsoft.

faq.a: Outlook on the web is the browser version of Outlook for mail, calendar and contacts. It is hosted by Exchange Online and is also known as Outlook Web App or OWA.
faq.q: What is Outlook on the web?

faq.a: No. It is used through a browser from any computer with an internet connection, so no desktop application has to be installed.
faq.q: Does Outlook on the web require installing software?

faq.a: Exchange Online provides the mailbox service behind both. Mailbox data stays there, so the same mail and calendar appear in the browser and in the installed Microsoft Outlook client.
faq.q: How does Outlook on the web relate to Microsoft Outlook and Exchange Online?

outlook-web.long:
Outlook on the web is the browser version of Outlook. It provides mail, calendar and contacts without installing a desktop application and is hosted by Exchange Online. It is also known as Outlook Web App or OWA, and it is reached through a browser from any computer with an internet connection. According to the catalog data, it is included with the relevant Microsoft 365 licensing, so no separate purchase is described for it.

The product is developed by Microsoft and is part of Office on the web, the set of browser versions of Office applications. It is classed as a Microsoft tool and as a collaboration tool. It is closely related to Microsoft Outlook, the full client, and to Exchange Online, which provides the mailbox service behind both. Because mailbox data stays in Exchange Online, the same mail and calendar content appears in the browser and in the installed client.

According to Microsoft Support, Outlook on the web is a browser-based way to keep email, calendar and contacts close at hand and to work together with other people. Messages can be sent and files shared, and the page mentions suggested replies and a like button as ways to save time. A focused inbox prioritizes important messages. A search function covers mail, appointments and contacts, which helps when looking for a specific message or person.

The calendar is another central part. A meeting can be started by clicking a time slot, with further settings available under more options. Smart time suggestions point to slots when all attendees are free. An appointment can be turned into a Teams meeting, and suggested locations are offered. A Microsoft 365 account can also be connected to LinkedIn to exchange messages and files with contacts. Typical uses named in the documentation are collaboration through email and file sharing, scheduling, and organizing meetings. The Microsoft page is an overview without step-by-step instructions and names no licenses, system requirements, plans or limitations.

In practice, typical scenarios include accessing mail from a shared or unmanaged device, using email on a computer where Office is not installed, and administering shared mailboxes or calendar settings from a browser. For administrators, it can also be a quick way to check how a user's mailbox looks without the influence of a local client profile, since the view comes directly from the service rather than from a locally configured application.

The decision between the browser version and the installed Microsoft Outlook usually depends on the device and the working situation. The browser version needs no installation and works wherever a browser is available, while the full client is the related desktop option for the same Exchange Online mailbox. No M365.FM episode is currently linked to Outlook on the web in the catalog, so there are no episode statements to summarize here. Related topics for further reading are Microsoft Outlook, Exchange Online and Office on the web.

owasp.desc: OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, is a public community project whose shared web-attack resources underpin the managed rules of web application firewalls.

faq.a: OWASP is the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a public community project that maintains shared resources on common web attacks. Its Core Rule Set is the basis of managed WAF rules.
faq.q: What is OWASP?

faq.a: According to the episode "Run Azure Application Gateway Without Public IP Exposure", Azure WAF applies managed rules maintained by Microsoft that are based on OWASP vulnerabilities. These help protect against threats like SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
faq.q: How does OWASP relate to Azure WAF?

faq.a: The episodes say OWASP recognizes prompt injection as a critical AI security risk, and one episode recommends using the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications together with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework when governing Microsoft Copilot.
faq.q: Does OWASP cover AI and Copilot security?

owasp.long:
OWASP stands for the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. It is a public community project that maintains shared resources on common web attacks. Its work is referenced widely in application security, and its Core Rule Set is the basis of managed WAF rules. In practice, the name OWASP appears whenever teams discuss typical web vulnerabilities, how to rank application risks, or how to configure a web application firewall.

One of the most concrete uses of OWASP material in the Microsoft ecosystem is the web application firewall. The episode "Run Azure Application Gateway Without Public IP Exposure" describes Azure WAF as a protection layer against threats such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS). According to that episode, Azure WAF applies managed rules maintained by Microsoft that are based on OWASP vulnerabilities, and it also supports custom rules tailored to a specific application. The WAF can run in two modes: Detection mode logs suspicious requests, while Prevention mode blocks malicious requests. It is deployed with Azure Application Gateway by associating a WAF policy with the gateway, which allows centralized protection, and integration with Azure Monitor supports real-time monitoring. In this setup, OWASP provides the knowledge base about common attacks, while the managed rule set turns that knowledge into enforceable rules.

OWASP is also discussed in the context of application architecture. The episode "Fix OWASP Architectural Risks in .NET Applications" addresses the belief that upgrading to the latest .NET framework makes an application safe. The episode argues that this belief does not hold. With the OWASP update reshaping how risks are ranked and understood, it says that modern attacks no longer focus on individual controller functions but on the seams and the glue between components, such as dependencies a build relied on or a base container layer that reached production unnoticed. The episode frames this as a shift from a checklist mindset to an ecosystem problem. For teams building .NET applications, this means that reviewing risk categories at the architecture and supply-chain level matters alongside code-level fixes.

OWASP guidance has also been extended to AI systems. The episode "Indirect Prompt Injection Security for Enterprise AI" notes OWASP's recognition of prompt injection as one of the most critical AI security risks. The episode explains why organizations should stop viewing documents as passive data and start treating them as potential instructions. It covers sources that AI systems consume, including poisoned knowledge bases, hidden text, document metadata, SharePoint repositories, Teams chats, Outlook emails and vector databases, as well as attack patterns such as delayed activation, retrieval abuse and context manipulation.

The episode "Grounding Microsoft Copilot for Trusted Enterprise AI" connects OWASP to governance. It recommends a cross-functional AI governance board with clear roles and responsibilities, and suggests using frameworks like the NIST AI Risk Management Framework together with the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. According to the episode, these resources help address core risks and validate controls throughout the AI lifecycle, and it adds that policies should be tested and updated regularly so the platform stays aligned with business goals and regulatory requirements.

Taken together, the episodes show three typical places where OWASP appears: as the basis of managed WAF rules protecting web applications, as a reference for architectural risk in .NET applications, and as a source of risk frameworks for large language model and Copilot deployments. In each case OWASP serves as shared, community-maintained reference material that teams use to name risks, prioritize them and check their controls.

pac-validation.desc: PAC validation is a Kerberos check that verifies the Privilege Attribute Certificate in a ticket against the KDC signature to reject forged or tampered group claims.

faq.a: It checks the Kerberos Privilege Attribute Certificate in a ticket against the KDC signature. This confirms that the PAC and its group claims have not been forged or tampered with.
faq.q: What does PAC validation check?

faq.a: It helps reject tickets with forged or modified group claims, such as silver tickets, because their PAC will not match the signature produced by the KDC.
faq.q: Which attacks does PAC validation help reject?

faq.a: The Privilege Attribute Certificate is the part of a Kerberos ticket that carries authorization data, including group membership claims.
faq.q: What is a PAC in Kerberos?

pac-validation.long:
PAC validation is a security check in Kerberos authentication. It examines the Privilege Attribute Certificate (PAC) carried inside a Kerberos ticket and compares it against the signature created by the Key Distribution Center (KDC). The PAC holds authorization data, including group membership claims, so confirming its integrity is central to trusting what a ticket asserts about a user.

The purpose of the check is to reject tickets whose PAC has been forged or altered. Silver tickets are one example: because such a ticket is crafted without the KDC's involvement, its group claims can be fabricated. When validation against the KDC signature is performed, a PAC that does not match is rejected instead of being accepted at face value.

PAC validation is therefore relevant to defending Kerberos-based environments against privilege escalation through manipulated ticket contents. It is a verification step rather than a separate authentication protocol, and it works by tying the authorization data in a ticket back to a signature the KDC produced.

No related topics or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no official documentation link is available in the source facts.

packml.desc: PackML is a packaging machine standard from the Organization for Machine Automation and Control (OMAC) that defines a common set of machine states and modes.

faq.a: PackML is a packaging machine standard from the Organization for Machine Automation and Control (OMAC). It defines a common set of machine states and modes.
faq.q: What is PackML?

faq.a: The standard defines machine states such as stopped, execute, held and complete, along with modes for operating a machine.
faq.q: Which states does PackML define?

faq.a: PackML comes from the Organization for Machine Automation and Control (OMAC).
faq.q: Who publishes PackML?

packml.long:
PackML is a standard for packaging machines published by the Organization for Machine Automation and Control (OMAC). It defines a common set of machine states and modes so that equipment can be described and controlled in a consistent way. Examples of states named in the standard include stopped, execute, held and complete.

A shared state model of this kind is used to describe what a machine is doing at any given moment and how it moves from one condition to another. Because the vocabulary of states and modes is the same across machines, packaging lines built from equipment of different origins can be discussed, programmed and monitored using the same terms.

On M365.FM, PackML is listed as a concept entry within the knowledge base. No related topics or episodes are currently linked to it, and no further details beyond its definition as an OMAC machine state and mode standard are recorded here.

paginated-reports.desc: Paginated reports are fixed-layout, print-oriented reports in Power BI and SQL Server Reporting Services, defined in RDL with precise control over pages.

faq.a: Paginated reports are fixed-layout, print-oriented reports in Power BI and SQL Server Reporting Services, defined in RDL. They allow precise control over page size, margins, headers, footers and page breaks.
faq.q: What are paginated reports?

faq.a: The episode "Power BI Paginated Reports: Service vs Report Builder vs SSRS" describes exporting a dashboard to PDF as closer to a screenshot. Paginated reports are presented as the way to produce print-perfect, audit-ready PDFs.
faq.q: How do paginated reports differ from exporting a Power BI dashboard to PDF?

faq.a: The episode "Power Platform - Simply Explained" states that Premium Per User includes paginated reports and that Fabric capacity supports all Premium features. "Deploy Power BI with Development, Test, and Production Pipelines" also names Premium and Premium Per User for paginated reports.
faq.q: Which Power BI licenses include paginated reports?

paginated-reports.long:
Paginated reports are fixed-layout, print-oriented reports available in Power BI and in SQL Server Reporting Services (SSRS). They are defined in RDL (Report Definition Language) and give the author precise control over page size, margins, headers, footers and page breaks. Because the layout is fixed rather than responsive, a paginated report is meant to look the same on screen, in a PDF and on paper, which is why it is associated with formal documents such as invoices, statements and audit-ready output.

The main contrast is with interactive Power BI dashboards and reports, which are built for exploration on screen. The M365.FM episode "Power BI Paginated Reports: Service vs Report Builder vs SSRS" frames this as a question of using a tool for the right job. It argues that exporting an interactive dashboard to PDF produces something closer to a screenshot than a controlled document, and that paginated reports are the way to deliver print-perfect PDFs that executives and auditors ask for. In that framing, dashboards are for interactive analysis and paginated reports are for precisely laid-out, repeatable output.

There are several ways to author a paginated report. The episode compares three routes: the Power BI Service, Report Builder, and Visual Studio, alongside SSRS as the on-premises reporting platform. In the Power BI Service, the episode describes a quick and straightforward approach in which a report is generated from a dataset by choosing the option to create a formatted table. This suits users who want a fast result without detailed design work. Report Builder and Visual Studio offer more design control for layouts that need fine-grained structure, and the episode's stated goal is to help listeners decide which tool fits a given requirement.

Licensing and capacity are a recurring decision around paginated reports. The episode "Power Platform - Simply Explained" lists Power BI license tiers and notes that Premium Per User (PPU), at $24 per user per month in that episode, includes paginated reports, while the Free and Pro tiers are described differently, and Microsoft Fabric capacity supports all Premium features. The episode "Deploy Power BI with Development, Test, and Production Pipelines" makes a related point: Power BI Premium or Premium Per User is the choice when advanced capacities, paginated reports, larger model sizes or deployment pipelines are needed at scale. It contrasts this with Power BI Embedded, which it describes as targeting ISVs and applications that embed interactive reports for customers.

Paginated reports also appear in the context of Microsoft Fabric. In "What Microsoft Fabric Means for Power BI Professionals", implementing paginated reports, together with conversational analytics through Copilot, is listed under analytics and report development skills that apply where relevant within Fabric. This places paginated reports alongside building reports and dashboards, mastering DAX and optimizing datasets as part of the skill set for Power BI professionals working in Fabric.

In practice, the decision usually comes down to the output requirement. When users need to explore data interactively, standard Power BI reports fit. When the requirement is a controlled, paginated document with defined page layout that can be printed or archived, a paginated report fits. The remaining choices are the authoring tool, the platform (Power BI or SSRS) and the license or capacity that includes paginated report support.

parameter-sniffing.desc: Parameter sniffing is SQL Server-style query-plan behavior: a plan is compiled for the parameter values seen at compile time, then reused for later executions.

faq.a: It is the behavior of SQL Server-style engines that compile a query plan for the parameter values seen at compile time and reuse the cached plan. This can perform poorly when later parameter values differ greatly. It is also called parameter sensitivity.
faq.q: What is parameter sniffing?
