faq.a: According to Microsoft's query processing guide, the hint makes the optimizer treat parameters and local variables as compile-time constants that can be folded into literals, which can help with highly variable or skewed data. The query is recompiled on every execution, which can be expensive, so the effect on the whole workload should be measured first.
faq.q: How can OPTION (RECOMPILE) affect parameter sniffing problems?

faq.a: No. The documentation states that values of local variables are not sniffed at compile time. The optimizer instead estimates from density information or, without statistics, uses fixed percentage guesses for equality and range comparisons.
faq.q: Are local variables sniffed in the same way as parameters?

parameter-sniffing.long:
Parameter sniffing is a behavior of SQL Server-style database engines in which a query plan is compiled for the parameter values seen at compile time and the cached plan is then reused. It is also called parameter sensitivity. The behavior is not a defect in itself: the engine inspects the current parameter values while compiling or recompiling a query and passes them to the query optimizer, which can then produce a more efficient execution plan for those values. The difficulty appears when the cached plan is later used for parameter values that look very different from the original ones, because a plan that suits one value can perform poorly for another.

Microsoft's query processing architecture guide for SQL Server describes parameter sniffing in a section on parameter sensitivity. According to that guide, the process applies to stored procedures, queries run through sp_executesql, and prepared queries. It interacts directly with plan reuse, because compiled plans are stored in the plan cache and can be picked up again by later executions. The first set of values that triggers a compilation therefore shapes the plan that subsequent calls receive, which is why results can vary depending on which call happened to compile the plan.

The guide names one remedy: the OPTION (RECOMPILE) query hint. With this hint, the optimizer treats parameters and local variables as compile-time constants, which can be folded into literals. The values used are those in effect right before the statement runs, which are not necessarily the values originally passed in. This can help when input data is highly variable or skewed. The guide also warns that the hint recompiles the query on every execution, which can be expensive, and advises measuring the effect on the whole workload before adopting it. The guide also points to a separate article on the Parameter Sensitive Plan optimization for further reading.

A related detail from the same documentation concerns local variables. Their values are not sniffed at compile time. Instead, the optimizer estimates from density information, or, when no statistics are available, uses fixed percentage guesses for equality and range comparisons. This distinction matters when diagnosing a slow query, since a parameter and a local variable can lead to different estimates and therefore different plans.

In practice, parameter sniffing shows up as queries that run fast for some inputs and slowly for others, or as performance that changes after a plan is evicted and recompiled. The M365.FM episode "Fix Bad Data Upstream with T-SQL Contracts" lists parameter sniffing among common enterprise failures, describing it as something that can masquerade as randomness. The episode also frames plan shapes as a governance matter, saying that if plan shapes change, spend and reliability change with them, so that plan behavior translates into cost stability and operational risk.

The episode "Design Reliable and Resilient Azure Architectures" places parameter sniffing in a troubleshooting workflow for Azure SQL Database. It suggests enabling Intelligent Insights and Query Performance Insight, capturing long-running queries, reviewing execution plans, and identifying missing indexes or parameter sniffing. It further mentions Azure SQL's automatic tuning recommendations and index suggestions via Azure Advisor, along with query optimization, appropriate indexing, and considering scaling DTUs or vCores or moving to Hyperscale.

Taken together, the sources treat parameter sniffing as a plan-caching trade-off: reusing a compiled plan saves compilation work, while a plan tuned to one parameter value may not suit others. Typical decisions around it involve examining execution plans, checking whether data distribution is skewed, and weighing the compile cost of options such as OPTION (RECOMPILE) against the benefit of more suitable plans.

partner-admin-link.desc: Partner Admin Link (PAL) is an Azure capability that ties a partner's Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program ID to the credentials used to manage a customer's Azure resources.

faq.a: Partner Admin Link (PAL) is an Azure capability that links a partner's Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program ID to the credentials used to manage a customer's Azure resources. It lets Microsoft recognize the partner's influence on Azure consumption.
faq.q: What is Partner Admin Link (PAL)?

faq.a: It connects the partner's Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program ID to the credentials the partner uses to manage a customer's Azure resources.
faq.q: What does PAL connect to a partner's ID?

faq.a: Microsoft documents the process for linking a partner ID for Azure performance on Microsoft Learn, under the Partner Center membership documentation.
faq.q: Where can the official steps for PAL be found?

partner-admin-link.long:
Partner Admin Link (PAL) is an Azure capability that associates a partner's Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program ID with the credentials used to manage a customer's Azure resources. Through this link, Microsoft can recognize the partner's influence on the customer's Azure consumption.

PAL is used by partners who administer or deploy Azure environments on behalf of customers. Instead of relying on a separate record, the partner ID is attached to the account or credentials the partner already uses to access the customer's resources. This allows the work performed under those credentials to be attributed to the partner within the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program.

The concept sits within the wider area of Azure administration and the Microsoft partner ecosystem, where partner contribution to cloud usage is tracked and acknowledged. Microsoft documents the process of linking a partner ID for Azure performance on Microsoft Learn, which is the reference for the exact steps and requirements.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no related entities have been specified. For detailed procedures, eligibility conditions and any program benefits, the official Microsoft documentation is the authoritative source.

partner-capability-score.desc: The Partner Capability Score (PCS) is a composite score of up to 100 points per solution area in the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program, used to qualify for Solutions Partner designations.

faq.a: It is a composite score of up to 100 points per solution area in the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program. It measures Performance, Skilling and Customer Success using data in Partner Center and determines eligibility for the Solutions Partner designation.
faq.q: What is the Partner Capability Score (PCS)?

faq.a: A partner needs at least 70 points in a solution area, and more than zero points on every metric of that area on at least one day in the qualification period.
faq.q: How many points are needed to qualify?

faq.a: Performance and customer success data usually refresh by the 20th of each month, and skilling data within about ten days of a certification. The score history shows the current and previous five months.
faq.q: How often is the Partner Capability Score updated?

partner-capability-score.long:
The Partner Capability Score (PCS) is a composite point value in the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program. It measures how a partner performs in three categories, Performance, Skilling and Customer Success, and it uses data that is already available in Partner Center. A score of up to 100 points is calculated for each of six solution areas, and that score determines whether the partner qualifies for the Solutions Partner designation in the area concerned.

Each of the three categories draws on a different kind of data. Performance counts net customer additions. Skilling counts certified people who are linked to the partner organization, at intermediate and advanced level. Customer Success looks at usage growth and deployments. Because the score is calculated per solution area, a partner can hold different scores in different areas and qualify in some but not in others.

Qualification follows two conditions. A partner needs at least 70 points in a solution area, and it needs more than zero points on every metric of that area on at least one day in the qualification period. The qualification status is shown as in progress, qualified or enrolled. Qualifying alone does not always complete the process: partners without legacy gold or silver status must purchase the designation to become enrolled, while legacy partners are enrolled automatically once they qualify. Enrollment lasts 13 months from purchase.

In day-to-day use, the score is something partners track over time rather than check once. The score history in Partner Center shows the current month and the previous five months. According to the documentation notes, performance and customer success data usually refresh by the 20th of each month, while skilling data updates within about ten days of a certification. Expired certifications can reduce skilling points, so keeping certifications current is part of maintaining a score.

The M365.FM episode "How to Become a High-Performing Microsoft Partner" lists the Partner Capability Score among its key takeaways. It advises partners to focus on the score by certifying their team and tracking customer success metrics, and it connects this to the six core Solution Partner designations, which help a partner identify the area that best fits its business strengths. The episode also points to customer retention and revenue growth as performance metrics for measuring effectiveness.

The episode "Microsoft Partner Journey: From Enrollment to Growth" places the score within the enrollment process. After a company profile is set up in Partner Center, company details are verified, and the partner is expected to maintain compliance with program rules and track its Partner Capability Score. The same episode stresses that the company name must match official documents and that the primary and legal contacts are specified accurately, since this verification precedes any work on the score.

In practice, the score connects several decisions: which solution area to focus on, how many team members to certify and keep certified, and how to grow customers and usage in that area. Because the three categories draw on certifications, net customer additions and usage data, improving the score typically involves both skilling and customer engagement rather than one alone.

partner-development-manager.desc: Partner development manager (PDM) is a Microsoft role that manages a partner relationship, helping the partner navigate Microsoft programs and connect with field sellers.

faq.a: A partner development manager (PDM) is a Microsoft role that manages a partner relationship. The role helps the partner navigate Microsoft programs and connect with Microsoft field sellers.
faq.q: What is a partner development manager (PDM)?

faq.a: A PDM supports the partner in finding its way through Microsoft programs and helps establish connections with Microsoft field sellers.
faq.q: What does a PDM do for a partner?

partner-development-manager.long:
A partner development manager (PDM) is the Microsoft role responsible for managing a relationship with a partner. The role centers on helping the partner understand and move through Microsoft programs and on connecting the partner with Microsoft field sellers.

In practice, the term describes a point of contact on the Microsoft side for organizations that work within the Microsoft partner ecosystem. A PDM acts as a link between the partner and the wider Microsoft organization, including the sales teams that engage directly with customers.

The available information on this concept is limited. No linked products, programs or related topics are recorded for it at this time, and no specific M365.FM episodes are currently associated with the term. The entry therefore covers only the role definition: a Microsoft-side relationship manager for partners, focused on program navigation and introductions to field sellers.

pass-the-hash.desc: Pass-the-hash is a lateral movement technique that reuses a captured NTLM password hash to authenticate to other systems without the clear-text password.

faq.a: Pass-the-hash is a lateral movement technique in which a captured NTLM password hash is reused to authenticate to other systems without knowing the clear-text password.
faq.q: What is pass-the-hash?

faq.a: The episodes mention blocking credential theft from LSASS, using privileged access workstations for privileged tasks, tiering and least privilege, and detecting the technique with Defender for Identity alerts combined with blocking, password reset and device isolation.
faq.q: How do the M365.FM episodes suggest defending against pass-the-hash?

faq.a: According to the episode "Harden Azure AD Connect Against Hybrid Identity Breaches", it follows an initial phished user as lateral movement, before privilege escalation such as DCSync or a Golden Ticket leads to domain-wide control.
faq.q: Where does pass-the-hash fit in an attack chain?

pass-the-hash.long:
Pass-the-hash is a lateral movement technique in which an attacker takes a captured NTLM password hash and reuses it to authenticate to other systems, without ever learning the clear-text password. Because the hash itself acts as the credential, an attacker who obtains it from one machine can try it against further machines and services. This makes the technique a common step once an initial foothold has been gained inside a Windows or hybrid environment.

In the M365.FM episodes, pass-the-hash appears as one stage in a larger attack chain rather than as an isolated event. The episode "Harden Azure AD Connect Against Hybrid Identity Breaches" describes how breaches rarely depend on zero-day vulnerabilities and instead accelerate through identity abuse. Its example path starts with one phished user, moves to lateral movement through pass-the-hash or ticket reuse, continues with privilege escalation such as DCSync or a Golden Ticket, and ends with domain-wide control. The episode names three weak areas that do most of the damage: an oversized admin blast radius without tiering or least privilege, lax PKI and certificate templates, and sloppy hybrid identity synchronization that can turn an on-premises compromise into a cloud compromise.

Several defensive measures discussed in the episodes target the conditions that make pass-the-hash possible. The episode "Detect Microsoft 365 Attack Chains with Entra and Sentinel" lists blocking credential theft from LSASS as a defense technique, noting that preventing unauthorized access to LSASS memory breaks common attack paths such as Pass-the-Hash and Pass-the-Ticket. The same episode mentions other protections in the same list, including blocking Office child processes and advanced ransomware protection, as part of reducing the room an attacker has to operate undetected.

The episode "AD Tiering and Privileged Access with Viktor Hedberg [MVP-MCT]" approaches the problem through isolation of privileged work. It describes privileged access workstations (PAWs) that handle only privileged tasks and are not used for email, web browsing or other daily work. According to the episode, this isolation keeps credentials safe and prevents lateral movement, and it also protects against attacks like pass-the-hash that use stolen credentials to move through a network. The episode adds that PAWs support compliance through strong access controls and detailed logs of privileged actions, and that they help operational resilience if other parts of the network are compromised.

Detection and response are covered in the episode "Conditional Access with Defender for Identity Signals". In its mapping of signals to responses, credential theft techniques such as Pass-the-Hash and Pass-the-Ticket correspond to a Defender for Identity security identity alert. The suggested response is to block the account and require a password reset, isolate the device through Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and disable legacy protocols on the offending endpoints. The episode recommends starting in audit or monitor mode for one to two weeks and then switching responses to enforcement per alert class.

Taken together, the episodes treat pass-the-hash as a technique to address on several layers: reducing credential exposure on endpoints, limiting how far a single stolen credential can travel through tiering and dedicated admin workstations, hardening the hybrid identity path between on-premises Active Directory and the cloud, and detecting the behavior with identity-focused alerts tied to automated responses. Typical decisions around the topic include which accounts may sign in to which tiers of systems, whether privileged tasks run on separate devices, and how aggressively alerts should trigger blocking or device isolation once monitoring has been validated.

pass-through-authentication.desc: Microsoft Entra pass-through authentication (PTA) is a hybrid sign-in method where Microsoft Entra ID validates passwords against on-premises Active Directory via local agents.

faq.a: It is a hybrid identity sign-in method in which Microsoft Entra ID validates a user's password against on-premises Active Directory at sign-in time. The validation is performed through local authentication agents.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Entra pass-through authentication?

faq.a: The password is validated against on-premises Active Directory at the moment of sign-in. Local authentication agents connect Microsoft Entra ID to the on-premises directory for this check.
faq.q: Where is the password validated with pass-through authentication?

faq.a: It is a concept within the broader Microsoft Entra family, serving as one of the sign-in methods used in hybrid identity scenarios.
faq.q: How does pass-through authentication relate to Microsoft Entra?

pass-through-authentication.long:
Microsoft Entra pass-through authentication (PTA) is a hybrid identity sign-in method. When a user signs in, Microsoft Entra ID validates the user's password against on-premises Active Directory at sign-in time, using authentication agents installed in the local environment.

PTA is used in hybrid identity setups where organizations want users to sign in to cloud resources with their on-premises Active Directory credentials, while the password check itself happens against the on-premises directory rather than being evaluated only in the cloud. The local authentication agents act as the link between Microsoft Entra ID and Active Directory for this validation step.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, PTA sits under the broader Microsoft Entra family of identity and access capabilities. It is one of the sign-in options available in hybrid identity configurations, alongside other approaches described in Microsoft's hybrid identity documentation. Microsoft Learn includes a dedicated article on how pass-through authentication works, which covers its operation in more detail.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

passive-dns.desc: Passive DNS is a historical record of the IP addresses that domain names resolved to over time, used in threat intelligence to link attacker infrastructure.

faq.a: Passive DNS is a historical record of which IP addresses domain names resolved to over time. It is used in threat intelligence to connect attacker infrastructure.
faq.q: What is Passive DNS?

faq.a: Analysts use the historical resolution records to link domains and IP addresses to one another. This helps connect separate indicators that belong to the same attacker infrastructure.
faq.q: How is Passive DNS used in threat intelligence?

faq.a: Because the record covers past resolutions, it shows how domains and IP addresses were associated over time, not only their current relationship.
faq.q: What does the historical aspect add?

passive-dns.long:
Passive DNS is a historical record of which IP addresses domain names resolved to over time. Instead of showing only where a domain points today, it preserves earlier resolutions, so an analyst can see how a name and an address were associated at different points in the past.

In threat intelligence, this history is used to connect attacker infrastructure. When a suspicious domain or IP address is identified, passive DNS data can show which other domains resolved to the same address, or which addresses a given domain used before. These overlaps help analysts relate separate indicators to one another and map the infrastructure behind an activity.

The concept belongs to the broader practice of investigating network indicators such as domains and IP addresses. It is a data source that supports pivoting from one known indicator to related ones, rather than a detection product or service by itself.

passkey.desc: A passkey is a phishing-resistant sign-in credential built on a FIDO2 public/private key pair, with the private key kept on the user's device.

faq.a: A passkey is a phishing-resistant sign-in credential based on a public/private key pair defined by the FIDO2 standards. The private key stays on the user's device and is unlocked with a biometric or PIN.
faq.q: What is a passkey?

faq.a: No shared secret is sent to the service, and the service holds only the public key. The episode "Passkeys vs Passwords in Microsoft Entra ID" notes that stealing public keys is useless for authentication.
faq.q: Why are passkeys considered resistant to phishing?

faq.a: The episode "Passkeys and FIDO2 - Simply Explained" says passkeys have been made the default way to sign in to Microsoft 365 and already appear in Microsoft 365 and Azure. Microsoft Entra ID documentation covers enabling passkeys (FIDO2).
faq.q: Where are passkeys relevant in Microsoft environments?

passkey.long:
A passkey is a phishing-resistant sign-in credential based on a public/private key pair, as defined by the FIDO2 standards. The private key stays on the user's device and is unlocked locally with a biometric or a PIN. Passkeys are described as digital credentials that replace traditional passwords, and they rely on public key cryptography to protect an identity while making sign-in simpler.

The central idea is that no shared secret travels between the user and the service. In a password model, the same secret is typed by the user and stored or verified by the service, so it can be phished, guessed or reused. With a passkey, the service holds only the public key, and the private key never leaves the device. The episode "Passkeys vs Passwords in Microsoft Entra ID" makes this point by noting that stealing passkey-related data, meaning public keys, is useless for authentication. According to that episode, this forces attackers to target endpoints or social-engineering vectors instead, which are described as higher-effort and often easier to detect.

Passkeys are used wherever an organization wants to move away from passwords toward phishing-resistant sign-in. In the Microsoft ecosystem, the official documentation for enabling passkeys (FIDO2) in Microsoft Entra ID is the reference for configuring them. The episode "Passkeys and FIDO2 - Simply Explained" states that Microsoft has made passkeys the default way to sign in to Microsoft 365. That episode walks through what a passkey is, how the keys do their work without ever sharing a secret, and why phishing stops working once the secret is gone.

The same episode also covers practical decisions. It distinguishes two kinds of passkey and discusses which one suits which person, and it addresses what happens when a phone or security key goes missing. It also looks at where passkeys already appear in Microsoft 365 and Azure, and it includes a section on the "honest catches" that are rarely mentioned. Anyone planning a rollout will want to consider these points, particularly device loss and recovery, before passwords are retired.

Passkeys also appear in the context of identity modernization. The episode "Move Active Directory Groups to Microsoft Entra ID" lists passwordless methods such as Windows Hello for Business alongside synced passkeys and passkey profiles. It describes these as providing phishing-resistant sign-in experiences that make it easier for users to access their accounts securely, and it connects them to higher user satisfaction and less frustration. In that framing, passkeys are one part of a broader move to Microsoft Entra ID in which each sign-in is evaluated while security and productivity are kept in balance.

In summary, a passkey replaces a typed password with a cryptographic key pair governed by FIDO2. The private key remains on the device and is released only after a biometric or PIN check, and the service stores only the public key. This design removes the secret that phishing relies on. The decisions that remain for administrators and users concern which type of passkey to adopt, how to handle lost devices, and where in Microsoft 365 and Azure the credential will be used.

password-hash-synchronization.desc: Password hash synchronization (PHS) is a hybrid identity sign-in method that syncs protected hashes of on-premises Active Directory passwords to Microsoft Entra ID.

faq.a: Password hash synchronization is a hybrid identity sign-in method that syncs protected hashes of on-premises Active Directory passwords to Microsoft Entra ID. Users can then sign in to cloud services with the same password.
faq.q: What is password hash synchronization (PHS)?

faq.a: No. With password hash synchronization, the readable password is not sent to the cloud. Only a protected hash of the on-premises Active Directory password is synchronized to Microsoft Entra ID.
faq.q: Is the actual password sent to the cloud with PHS?

faq.a: PHS is used in hybrid identity environments that combine an on-premises Active Directory with Microsoft Entra ID, allowing the same password to work for cloud service sign-in.
faq.q: Where is PHS used?

password-hash-synchronization.long:
Password hash synchronization (PHS) is a hybrid identity sign-in method. It synchronizes protected hashes of on-premises Active Directory passwords to Microsoft Entra ID, so users can sign in to cloud services with the same password they use on-premises.

The readable password is not sent to the cloud. Only a protected hash derived from the on-premises password is synchronized. This allows Microsoft Entra ID to validate sign-ins in the cloud using the synchronized hash, while the user keeps a single set of credentials across the on-premises and cloud environments.

PHS is used in hybrid identity scenarios where an organization maintains an on-premises Active Directory and also uses Microsoft cloud services that rely on Microsoft Entra ID. It is one of the sign-in options available in this kind of hybrid setup, and its main characteristic is that cloud authentication does not require the on-premises directory to be reachable at the moment of sign-in.

The official Microsoft Learn documentation for Microsoft Entra Connect describes the feature in more detail. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

password-writeback.desc: Password writeback is an optional feature that sends a password changed or reset in the cloud back to on-premises Active Directory so both accounts keep the same password.
password-writeback.long:
Password writeback is an optional feature that must be deliberately configured. When a password is changed or reset in the cloud, the feature sends that new password back to on-premises Active Directory. As a result, the cloud account and the on-premises account keep the same password.

The feature is typically relevant in hybrid environments, where user identities exist both in the cloud and in an on-premises Active Directory. Without a mechanism that returns cloud-side password changes to the directory, the two passwords could drift apart. Password writeback addresses this by keeping the credentials aligned after a change or reset made in the cloud.

Because it is not enabled by default, organizations decide whether to turn it on as part of their identity configuration. The available facts do not describe specific prerequisites, licensing, supported scenarios, or configuration steps, so those details are not covered here.

pay-as-you-go-pricing.desc: Pay-as-you-go pricing is the default cloud billing model in which charges are applied after the fact for the resources actually consumed.

faq.a: It is the default cloud billing model in which a customer is billed after the fact for the resources actually consumed. Cost therefore follows usage rather than a fixed upfront commitment.
faq.q: What is pay-as-you-go pricing?

faq.a: The episodes mention Azure Key Vault, certain cloud features of Microsoft Purview, and Windows 365 for Agents. For Purview, the episodes say that availability varies by feature and recommend checking the pricing page and the Microsoft 365 agreement.
faq.q: Which Microsoft services are mentioned with pay-as-you-go pricing in the episodes?

faq.a: The episodes say that it lowers running costs because payment applies only for active use. This is described as a good fit for changing agent work.
faq.q: Why is pay-as-you-go pricing described as useful for agent workloads?

pay-as-you-go-pricing.long:
Pay-as-you-go pricing is the default cloud billing model in which a customer is billed after the fact for the resources actually consumed. Instead of purchasing a fixed quantity of capacity or a licence in advance, usage is measured and charged afterwards. In the Microsoft ecosystem the term appears in connection with several services, and the M365.FM episodes mention it mainly as a cost-related property of those services rather than as a topic on its own.

The core idea is the link between cost and consumption. When usage is low, the bill is correspondingly low, and when usage grows, the bill grows with it. This is why the model is often described as a way to manage costs according to usage and needs. It suits situations where demand is hard to predict, where a service is only needed for limited periods, or where an organisation wants to start small and scale gradually without committing to a fixed amount up front. The trade-off is that the final cost is only known once the consumption has taken place, so monitoring usage matters.

The episode "Azure Key Vault - Simply Explained" mentions the model in the context of Azure Key Vault. The episode says that the pay-as-you-go pricing model allows organizations to manage costs effectively based on their usage and needs. It lists this alongside other characteristics of the service, such as role-based access control, compliance with industry standards, and protection features like soft-delete and purge protection. In that framing, pay-as-you-go is one of the factors an organisation weighs when deciding to adopt a managed service for secrets and keys.

The episodes "Microsoft Purview vs Azure Information Protection" and "What Is Microsoft Intune Used For?" contain the same passage on Microsoft Purview. They explain that licensing for Purview combines Microsoft 365 SKUs and add-on options, and that some Purview services are available with pay-as-you-go pricing for certain cloud features. The practical advice given is to check the Purview pricing page and the organisation's Microsoft 365 agreement. This shows that pay-as-you-go can coexist with other licensing approaches within the same product family, and that availability can differ by feature.

The episodes "Agentic AI for IT Operations: Windows 365, Intune & Microsoft's AI Vision with Christiaan Brinkhoff [Nerdio]" and "How Do You Successfully Deploy Microsoft 365 Copilot Across an Enterprise?" discuss it in relation to Windows 365 for Agents. The episodes list pay-as-you-go pricing among the features of that offering and say that it lowers running costs because payment applies only for active use. They describe this as well suited to changing agent workloads, where the amount of automation work varies over time. The same feature list names observability and real-time monitoring, cross-platform support for Windows, Linux and browsers, and controls over sessions, networking, capacity and data location.

Taken together, the episodes treat pay-as-you-go pricing as a cost model that fits variable or usage-driven workloads such as key management, selected data protection features and agent execution environments. A typical decision is whether usage-based billing or a fixed licensing arrangement better matches the expected pattern of use, and the episodes point to the official pricing pages and existing agreements as the place to confirm the details for a given service.

payables-agent.desc: Payables Agent is a Microsoft AI agent in Dynamics 365 Business Central that reads vendor invoice PDFs from email and prepares purchase invoices for human review.

faq.a: It retrieves vendor invoice PDFs attached to Microsoft 365 emails, imports them as inbound e-documents, uses Azure Document Intelligence for OCR and creates purchase invoices that a user can review, release and post.
faq.q: What does the Payables Agent do in Business Central?

faq.a: The documentation focuses on overhead costs such as rent, utilities, leasing, catering, phone bills and software subscriptions, not on supply chain spending.
faq.q: Which types of invoices is the Payables Agent meant for?

faq.a: Only PDF attachments from Microsoft 365 email are supported. Complex scenarios, matching against open purchase orders and e-invoices through channels such as PEPPOL are named as future topics.
faq.q: What are the limits of the first version of the Payables Agent?

payables-agent.long:
Payables Agent is an AI agent built by Microsoft for Dynamics 365 Business Central. It automates parts of accounts payable and accounting work by reading vendor invoices that arrive as attachments to Microsoft 365 emails and turning them into purchase invoices in Business Central. The stated goal is to save time and reduce errors in a routine, repetitive process. The agent prepares the documents; people review them before anything is posted.

According to the Business Central release plan documentation, the agent follows three stages. In the first stage, it collects PDF attachments from a Microsoft 365 mailbox and imports them as inbound e-documents. In the second stage, Azure Document Intelligence performs optical character recognition (OCR) on the documents. The results are stored in the e-document, and an enlarged PDF viewer supports validation of the extracted data. In the third stage, the agent creates a purchase invoice document that the user can release and post. It categorizes the expense and posts it to the general ledger, drawing on purchase history or on the company's accounting rules.

The documentation describes a specific focus for the agent: overhead costs rather than supply chain spending. Typical examples named are rent, utilities, leasing, catering, phone bills and software subscriptions. These are invoices that recur and often have predictable coding, which makes them a practical fit for pattern-based categorization. Spending tied to the supply chain is outside the described scope.

Setup and scope are also covered in the source. Administrators, makers or analysts can enable the agent. In its first version, only PDF attachments from Microsoft 365 email are supported. The documentation names several topics as future areas rather than current capabilities: complex scenarios, matching against open purchase orders, and e-invoices through channels such as PEPPOL. The page does not describe licensing or costs, so those questions are not answered by the source material available here.

The M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Copilot - Simply Explained" places the Payables Agent among the AI agents in Business Central and supply chain scenarios. The episode says that agents extend AI assistance into more defined operational workflows, and that a Payables Agent can work with vendor invoices and prepare invoice drafts for review. It groups this with a Sales Order Agent that analyzes customer requests arriving through email and with supplier-focused agents that support repetitive communication in supply chain operations. The episode stresses that such agents can automate parts of routine work, while people remain responsible for reviewing exceptions and approving actions that affect customers, inventory, payments and other important business processes.

The episode "AI and Copilot in D365FO Finance with Billur Samdancioglu [MVP-MCT]" describes a related invoice processing scenario in Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations. In that discussion, a user opens an invoice in the invoice capture workbench and asks the agent for suggestions. The agent retrieves historical postings and supplier patterns from the ERP and returns a summary with recommended general ledger accounts and dimension values for each line item. The episode presents this as a way to transform the accounts payable process with Copilot in Dynamics 365.

In practice, the decision points around the Payables Agent concern which invoices suit the agent, how accounting rules or purchase history guide categorization, and how review is organized before posting. Because the agent creates purchase invoices that a user releases and posts, the review step remains part of the workflow, consistent with the episode's point that people stay responsible for exceptions and approvals.

pbix.desc: PBIX is the Power BI Desktop file format that bundles report pages, data model, queries and visuals in one file; emailing it around is not version control.

faq.a: A PBIX file is the Power BI Desktop file format. It bundles report pages, the data model, queries and visuals in a single file.
faq.q: What does a PBIX file contain?

faq.a: No. The episode "Power BI Version Control with GitHub and Azure DevOps" argues that passing PBIX files around by email is not version control; it suggests Git commits for a real version history.
faq.q: Is emailing PBIX files a form of version control?

faq.a: No. According to Microsoft Learn, reports built on uploaded local Excel or CSV files, reports published before late 2016 and content deployed through deployment pipelines cannot be downloaded, and an administrator can disable the download feature.
faq.q: Can every report be downloaded from the Power BI service as a PBIX file?

pbix.long:
A PBIX file is the file format used by Power BI Desktop. It bundles the report pages, the data model, the queries and the visuals of a Power BI report into a single file with the .pbix extension. Report authors open it in Power BI Desktop to build and edit content, and they publish it from there to the Power BI service. Because everything lives in one file, a PBIX file is convenient to hand over, but it is also a single binary artifact, which matters as soon as several people work on the same report.

The PBIX format also plays a role in the other direction. Microsoft Learn describes how a report or a semantic model can be downloaded from the Power BI service into Power BI Desktop as a .pbix file. Depending on the case, the download can contain the report together with its data, a report with a live connection to the semantic model in the service (so the file holds no data), or an empty report that carries only the semantic model. At least the Contributor role in the workspace is required, and Power BI Desktop must be installed to open the file; using the current Desktop version is advised.

The documentation also lists cases in which a download is not possible. Examples include reports built on uploaded local Excel or CSV files, reports published before late 2016, and content deployed through deployment pipelines. Direct Lake models and models with incremental refresh can only be reached through a live connection, and semantic models with automatic aggregations cannot be exported as .pbix. Models above 50 GB are not supported for a data download. An administrator can also switch the download feature off, in which case it does not appear in the service. These limits are relevant when a team plans to treat the service as a source for recovering PBIX files.

The central point in the M365.FM episode "Power BI Version Control with GitHub and Azure DevOps" is that sending PBIX files around by email is not version control. The episode describes how Power BI developers and BI teams can adopt version control for Power BI reports. As a starting point it suggests saving work as a PBIX file in Power BI Desktop and optionally extracting a Power BI project file for Git integration. Regular commits to a Git repository capture the version history and allow the team to revert unwanted changes.

The episode also mentions combining this with a workspace connected to Git, or storing PBIP text files in a Git repository, so that the BI team can collaborate, manage changes and keep previous versions. In this approach the PBIX file remains the everyday working format in Power BI Desktop, while the text-based project format is the one suited for tracking changes in a repository. The episode frames this as a choice between built-in version control approaches and external tooling, with the shared goal of a traceable history instead of copies of files passed between colleagues.

Typical decisions around PBIX files therefore concern where the authoritative copy lives, how changes are tracked, and who may download or publish content. Teams that rely on PBIX files alone usually end up with several copies of the same report. Teams that add a Git repository, with or without the project format, gain a version history and a way to roll back. Knowing which reports can still be downloaded from the service as .pbix, and which cannot, is part of that planning.

pdca-cycle.desc: The PDCA cycle (Plan-Do-Check-Act) is an iterative four-step method used in lean and continuous improvement to test a change before making it standard.

faq.a: PDCA stands for Plan-Do-Check-Act, the four steps of an iterative improvement method used in lean and continuous improvement.
faq.q: What does PDCA stand for?

faq.a: The cycle is used to test a change against expected results before making it standard, so that improvements are verified rather than assumed.
faq.q: What is the purpose of the PDCA cycle?

faq.a: No. It is iterative, meaning the steps are repeated so that each round of results informs the next round of planning.
faq.q: Is the PDCA cycle a one-time process?

pdca-cycle.long:
The PDCA cycle (Plan-Do-Check-Act) is an iterative four-step improvement method used in lean and continuous improvement. Each pass through the cycle tests a change against expected results before that change is adopted as the standard way of working.

The four steps are plan, do, check and act. In the plan step, a change and its expected outcome are defined. In the do step, the change is carried out, typically on a limited scale. In the check step, the actual results are compared with the expected results. In the act step, the change is either made standard or revised, and the cycle can begin again with new learning.

Because the cycle is repeated, improvement is treated as an ongoing process rather than a one-time project. This makes PDCA a common reference point in discussions of lean practices, process improvement and structured experimentation.

No related topics or episodes are currently linked to this entry on M365.FM, and no official documentation or website is associated with the concept in the available facts.

pegging.desc: Pegging is the automatic link created during master planning between a demand transaction and the supply expected to cover it.

faq.a: Pegging is the automatic link that the planning calculation creates between a demand transaction and the supply expected to cover it.
faq.q: What is pegging in master planning?

faq.a: No. The link is generated automatically as part of the master planning calculation.
faq.q: Is pegging created manually?

pegging.long:
Pegging is a concept in master planning. It refers to the automatic link that the planning calculation creates between a demand transaction and the supply that is expected to cover that demand.

In practice, a pegging relationship connects the two sides of a planning result: the requirement on one side and the planned or existing supply on the other. Because the link is generated by the planning calculation itself, it does not need to be maintained by hand. It records which supply is intended to satisfy which demand.

The concept is used to understand and trace planning outcomes. Following a pegging link allows a planner to see which demand a given supply transaction is meant to serve, or which supply is expected to cover a given demand.

No related topics, official documentation or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, so details on specific products, configuration options or usage scenarios are not covered here.

per-tenant-extension.desc: A per-tenant extension (PTE) is a Business Central extension built for a single customer's environment instead of being published for all Business Central customers.
per-tenant-extension.long:
A per-tenant extension (PTE) is a Business Central extension created for one customer's own environment. Unlike an extension published for all Business Central customers, a PTE is specific to a single tenant.

PTEs are typically used to support a process that is unique to a particular company. When a business has requirements that standard Business Central functionality does not cover and that would not be relevant to other customers, a per-tenant extension is the approach used to add that functionality to the customer's environment.

The key distinction is audience. A per-tenant extension targets one customer, while a broadly published extension is made available to all Business Central customers. This makes the PTE the concept associated with company-specific customization within Business Central.

No episodes of M365.FM are currently linked to this topic, and no further related topics or official documentation links are recorded for it here.

permission-creep-index.desc: The Permission Creep Index (PCI) is a risk metric in Microsoft Entra Permissions Management that compares granted permissions with the permissions an identity actually uses.

faq.a: It compares the permissions an identity has been granted with the permissions it actually uses. A higher score means more unused, excessive permissions.
faq.q: What does the Permission Creep Index measure?

faq.a: It applies to the authorization systems monitored by Microsoft Entra Permissions Management: AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud Platform. Default service accounts and GCP-managed service accounts are excluded from the calculation.
faq.q: Which environments does the PCI cover?

faq.a: Identities are grouped into Low, Medium and High PCI categories and shown in a bubble chart and heatmap. A trend view and a downloadable PCI history report show how the index changes over time.
faq.q: How is the PCI displayed on the dashboard?

permission-creep-index.long:
The Permission Creep Index (PCI) is a risk metric in Microsoft Entra Permissions Management. It compares the permissions an identity has been granted with the permissions that identity actually uses. A higher score indicates more unused, excessive permissions, which widens the potential impact of a compromised or misused account. The index is intended to make this gap between granted and used access visible so that it can be reviewed and reduced.

The PCI appears on the Microsoft Entra Permissions Management dashboard and covers the authorization systems monitored by the product: AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud Platform. The documentation does not publish a formula or value ranges for the score. It does describe high risk in terms of the number of users whose permissions go beyond what they normally or necessarily use. Default service accounts and GCP-managed service accounts are not counted in the calculation.

The dashboard presents the index in several ways. Identities are grouped into Low, Medium and High PCI categories. A bubble chart highlights high-risk identities, and a list shows which authorization systems have seen the largest recent change. A heatmap shows how many users contribute to a given score, while a trend view and a downloadable PCI history report show how the index develops over time. Alongside the index, findings are split into identity findings, such as inactive or over-provisioned roles, and resource findings, such as unencrypted storage buckets or open security groups.

In practice, the PCI supports the principle of least privilege. Permissions tend to accumulate as roles change, projects end and access is granted for one-off tasks, and the index puts a measurable number on that accumulation. Typical decisions around it include which high-scoring identities to review first, whether to remove permissions that are never used, and whether a rising trend in one authorization system calls for a closer look at how access is granted there.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Entra Permissions Management - Simply Explained" presents the PCI as a vital feature that measures the risk of excessive permissions for administrative accounts. The episode says that tracking the index helps ensure administrators have only the permissions they need, in line with least privilege, and that this proactive approach reduces the risk of unauthorized access and potential security incidents.

One point to note is the status of the underlying documentation. The documentation page describing the dashboard data is archived because Microsoft Entra Permissions Management was announced for retirement. Anyone relying on the PCI should therefore treat the source material as historical and check the current product status before building processes around it.

permission-debt.desc: Permission debt is the accumulated backlog of overly broad, inherited or outdated access rights that stays hidden until AI tools such as Copilot surface the data.
permission-debt.long:
Permission debt describes the accumulated backlog of overly broad, inherited or outdated access rights within an organization's systems. A typical example is content that has been shared with everyone. These rights often remain unnoticed for long periods because nobody actively searches for the data they expose.

The concept is mainly used to explain why access problems become visible after AI tools are introduced. According to the definition, the debt stays latent until tools like Copilot surface the data at machine speed. Information that was technically reachable but practically hard to find can then be returned in responses to users who were never meant to see it.

For administrators, the term frames permission cleanup as a form of maintenance work that builds up over time, much like other types of technical debt. Reviewing, tightening and removing outdated access rights reduces the amount of data that AI-assisted search can expose.

On M365.FM, the topic appears in the episode "Microsoft Graph and PowerShell for Enterprise Automation" (2026-07-02), which relates to automating administrative tasks in the Microsoft ecosystem.

permission-drift.desc: Permission drift is the gradual divergence of an access model from business reality through local decisions, role changes, leftover groups and unremoved exceptions.

faq.a: Permission drift is the gradual divergence of an access model from current business reality, caused by local decisions, role changes, leftover groups and exceptions that are never removed.
faq.q: What is permission drift?

faq.a: According to the episode "The Architecture of Intelligence- Why the Chatbox is the Wrong Model for Enterprise AI", Copilot does not create the permission problem but makes existing drift more visible by increasing the discoverability of information users could already access.
faq.q: How does permission drift relate to Microsoft Copilot?

faq.a: The episodes recommend regular permission audits, breaking inheritance on sensitive libraries, applying DLP policies, monitoring user activity, and setting up governance and information architecture before migrations.
faq.q: How can permission drift be reduced?

permission-drift.long:
Permission drift is the gradual divergence of an access model from current business reality. It occurs because access keeps evolving through local decisions, role changes, leftover groups and exceptions that are never removed. A permission structure that matched the organization at one point in time slowly stops matching it, without any single change that looks like the cause. In the Microsoft 365 context, the term is mostly used in discussions about SharePoint, Teams and Copilot governance.

The concept matters because access rarely stays where it was designed. Typical sources of drift named in the M365.FM episodes include orphaned Teams, broadly shared sites, inherited permissions, old sharing links and shadow sites. Each of these can be individually small, but together they leave content technically accessible to people who no longer have a business reason to see it. The episode "Block Copilot Access to Sensitive SharePoint Documents with Purview DLP" describes the problem as user permissions changing unintentionally over time, and it suggests regularly auditing permissions and breaking inheritance on sensitive libraries to stop governance gaps and keep data access tightly controlled.

The topic has gained attention because of AI assistants. The episode "The Architecture of Intelligence- Why the Chatbox is the Wrong Model for Enterprise AI" challenges the assumption that Copilot itself creates an entirely new permission problem. Instead, it argues that AI dramatically increases the discoverability of information users could already access. A poorly governed SharePoint environment may contain years of permission drift, and information that once required knowing the correct site, library, folder, filename or search terminology can become much easier to find with natural-language AI. In that reading, drift is an existing condition that AI makes visible rather than a new risk the tool introduces.

A related argument appears in "Fix Wrong Microsoft 365 Copilot Answers with SharePoint Governance". The episode says that Copilot, search and AI agents give confident but wrong answers inside Microsoft 365 largely because of governance rather than prompts, models or tools. It lists permission drift together with orphaned Teams, ROT data and shadow sites as factors that poison AI grounding. According to the episode, AI reads structure, permissions, labels and residue, not intent, so cleaning up the environment changes the quality of the answers.

Drift is also a migration concern. The episode "Microsoft 365 Structural Debt from Default Governance" recommends setting up control models and a clear information architecture before modernizing legacy environments. The stated reasoning is that this prevents permission drift and audit gaps by avoiding the transfer of old problems into a new system. Its tip is to review the governance framework before and after any migration.

Permission drift is not limited to document libraries. In "Build Custom Microsoft Teams Bots, Tabs, and Extensions", it is named as the biggest risk for custom Teams apps, because policy or scope changes can silently break bots. The mitigation suggested there is simple logging and regular audits.

Across the episodes, the recommended responses are consistent in kind: audit permissions on a regular schedule, break inheritance on sensitive libraries where needed, apply data loss prevention policies, monitor user activity for unusual behavior, and establish governance before modernization or AI rollout rather than after. The common decision point is whether access reviews happen routinely or only after an incident, since drift by definition accumulates unnoticed.

permission-inheritance.desc: Permission inheritance in SharePoint is the concept by which child items take their access rights from the parent site, library or list rather than defining their own.

faq.a: It is the concept by which items lower in a SharePoint hierarchy receive their access rights from the parent object above them instead of having their own separate permissions.
faq.q: What is permission inheritance in SharePoint?

faq.a: Permission inheritance is a concept within SharePoint, which is listed as its broader topic. It describes how access control is applied across SharePoint's structure.
faq.q: How does permission inheritance relate to SharePoint?

permission-inheritance.long:
Permission inheritance (SharePoint) is a concept within SharePoint that describes how access rights are passed down through a hierarchy. In this model, objects placed lower in the structure receive the permissions of the object above them, instead of having a separate set of permissions assigned to each one.

The concept is used to keep access control consistent and manageable across a SharePoint environment. When permissions are set once at a higher level, the objects beneath it follow the same rules, which reduces the need to configure access item by item.

Permission inheritance (SharePoint) is a subtopic of SharePoint, which is its broader topic on M365.FM. It is relevant wherever questions about who can see or change content in SharePoint are discussed.

No specific episodes, official documentation links or further details are currently listed for this entry, so this page is limited to the basic definition and its relationship to SharePoint.

permissions-on-demand.desc: Permissions on demand is a Microsoft Entra Permissions Management feature for requesting narrowly scoped cloud permissions for a limited time, with automatic expiry.

faq.a: Permissions on demand is a Microsoft Entra Permissions Management feature. It lets identities request narrowly scoped cloud permissions for a limited time.
faq.q: What is Permissions on demand?

faq.a: Approval is optional. A request can include an approval step, after which the permissions are granted for the requested period.
faq.q: Does Permissions on demand require approval?

faq.a: The permissions expire automatically once the limited time period is over, so they do not need to be removed by hand.
faq.q: What happens when the requested time ends?

permissions-on-demand.long:
Permissions on demand is a feature of Microsoft Entra Permissions Management. It lets identities request cloud permissions that are narrowly scoped and available only for a limited time, instead of holding those permissions continuously.

The feature supports an optional approval step, so a request can be reviewed before access is granted. Once the requested period ends, the permissions expire automatically, which means access does not have to be removed manually afterward.

The approach is used to limit standing access in cloud environments. By granting access only when it is requested and only for a defined duration, organizations can reduce the amount of permission that remains in place when it is not needed.

The available facts do not describe specific configuration steps, supported cloud platforms, licensing or related Microsoft Entra topics, so this page does not cover them. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this term.

persistent-context.desc: Persistent context is a design approach for Microsoft 365 Copilot in which reusable intent and a governed set of sources carry across conversations instead of being re-entered.

faq.a: It is a design approach in which reusable intent (instructions, constraints, definitions) and a curated, governed set of sources persist beyond a single conversation, rather than being re-entered in every prompt.
faq.q: What is persistent context in Microsoft 365 Copilot?

faq.a: In episodic use, each interaction starts from an immediate prompt. The episode "Persistent Context Architecture for Copilot and ChatGPT" argues this prevents Copilots and agents from becoming effective because identity, goals, constraints, history and provenance are not carried forward in a structured, auditable way.
faq.q: How does persistent context differ from episodic AI use?

faq.a: The episodes link persistent context to auditable provenance, authoritative data and lifecycle governance. Without these, carried-forward information can become unreliable, and automation can drift into sprawl and permission creep.
faq.q: Why does governance matter for persistent context?

persistent-context.long:
Persistent context is a design approach for Microsoft 365 Copilot in which reusable intent and a curated, governed set of sources persist beyond a single conversation. Instead of re-entering instructions, constraints and definitions in every prompt, these elements are defined once and carried forward. The idea contrasts with episodic AI use, where each interaction starts from an immediate prompt and little else.

The approach rests on two kinds of material. The first is reusable intent: instructions, constraints and definitions that describe how an assistant should behave and what terms mean in a given organization. The second is a curated, governed set of sources the assistant can draw on. Keeping both stable across conversations is meant to make results more consistent and to reduce the effort of repeating the same background information.

The M365.FM episode "Persistent Context Architecture for Copilot and ChatGPT" (February 2026) treats persistent context as a foundational architectural layer rather than a convenience feature. The episode argues that most organizations treat AI as a series of immediate prompts, and that this episodic design prevents agents and Copilots from becoming truly effective. In its framing, context consists of identity, goals, constraints, history and provenance, and it needs to be carried forward in a structured and auditable way for AI systems to scale reliably in the enterprise. The episode subtitle, "Why Episodic AI Is Slowing You Down", summarizes that position.

Persistent context also appears in discussions of automation and agents. The episode "Architect Scalable SharePoint Automation for Enterprise Workflows" (February 2026) lists persistent context alongside identity boundaries, execution contracts and lifecycle governance as elements that keep automation from turning into unmanaged sprawl, permission creep and fragile outcomes. It describes treating automation as products with owners, enforcing execution constraints and grounding actions in authoritative data.

The episode "Enterprise AI Agent Fabric: Architecture Beyond Chatbots" (June 2026) states that traditional conversational chatbots often fail to deliver persistent context or true automation. It describes architecture over chat as a way for agentic systems to maintain natural language interactions and remember past decisions, and it points to Microsoft Agent 365 as a practical example of agentic AI operating securely and at scale across the enterprise.

Memory is a related theme. In "The Future of AI Software Factories- OpenCLAW, Agent Orchestration & The Intelligence Age with Mark Smith [MVP]" (August 2026), the discussion distinguishes short-term, medium-term and long-term memory for autonomous agents. The episode says agents need enough persistent context to understand what was created months earlier and why particular decisions were made, and that documentation such as a wiki can serve as institutional memory for an AI development organization, which agents can consult when making later decisions.

The episode "Microsoft Work IQ: The Intelligence Layer for Microsoft 365" (June 2026) describes a Memory Layer that creates lasting organizational knowledge. According to the episode, this layer lets the AI remember preferences and historical decisions, supports mapping relationships between dispersed data, and moves Copilot from a stateless assistant toward a learning partner that builds an understanding of a user's working style.

Taken together, the episodes present persistent context as a design decision with governance implications. What persists, who curates the sources, and how provenance is tracked determine whether the carried-forward information is reliable and auditable. Typical decisions include which instructions belong in reusable form, which sources count as authoritative, and how long accumulated context should be retained. Persistent context is therefore discussed as an architectural concern for Copilot and agents, not only as a prompting technique.

persona.desc: A persona in user experience design represents the goals, responsibilities and working environment of a specific user group, and is used to guide product and agent design.

faq.a: A persona represents the goals, responsibilities and working environment of a specific user group. It gives designers a concrete reference for the people a product or agent is meant to serve.
faq.q: What is a persona in user experience?

faq.a: In the M365.FM discussion, personas such as a field engineer or finance analyst define what a Copilot Studio agent must know and do. The persona sets the scope of the agent's knowledge and tasks.
faq.q: How do personas relate to Copilot Studio agents?

faq.a: A field engineer and a finance analyst are given as examples. Each has different responsibilities and a different working environment, which leads to different agent requirements.
faq.q: Which example personas are mentioned?

persona.long:
A persona (user experience) is a representation of a specific user group. It describes the goals, responsibilities and working environment of the people in that group, so that design decisions can be made with a concrete user in mind rather than an abstract audience.

Personas are used to define what a solution needs to support. In the context discussed on M365.FM, they help determine what a Copilot Studio agent must know and do. A persona such as a field engineer or a finance analyst sets out the tasks that user performs and the setting in which the work takes place, which in turn shapes the knowledge and actions an agent should cover.

The examples used to illustrate the concept are a field engineer and a finance analyst. These two roles differ in responsibilities and working environment, which shows why separate personas lead to different agent requirements. Defining the persona first gives a reference point for scoping an agent's capabilities and content.

The concept appears in an episode of the M365.FM podcast that covers building agents with Copilot Studio. No further related topics or official documentation links are listed for this entry.

persona-driven-insights.desc: Persona-driven insights is an approach that starts analytics and AI work from defined personas, their decisions and business questions, before models, reports or agents are built.

faq.a: It is an approach that starts analytics and AI work from defined personas, including their decisions, pain points and business questions, before semantic models, reports and agents are built.
faq.q: What is persona-driven insights?

faq.a: It starts from personas and the decisions and business questions they need to address, and builds semantic models, reports and agents from that basis.
faq.q: What does the approach start from instead of data or tools?

faq.a: It is discussed in the episode "From Financial Data to AI-Ready Decisions: Power BI, Microsoft Fabric, Semantic Models & AI Agents with Rishi Sapra [MVP]".
faq.q: Where does persona-driven insights appear on M365.FM?

persona-driven-insights.long:
Persona-driven insights is an approach to analytics and AI work that begins with defined personas rather than with data sources or tooling. Each persona is described by the decisions it has to make, the pain points it faces and the business questions it needs answered.

The approach is used to guide what gets built. Once the personas and their questions are clear, semantic models, reports and agents are designed to serve those specific needs, instead of being assembled first and matched to users afterward. This keeps the focus on the decisions that people actually need to support.

In the context of the Microsoft ecosystem, the concept connects to semantic models, reports and AI agents, which are the artifacts that this method aims to shape. The framing applies to both traditional reporting and newer agent-based scenarios, since both depend on a clear understanding of who is asking which questions.

On M365.FM, the concept appears in the episode "From Financial Data to AI-Ready Decisions: Power BI, Microsoft Fabric, Semantic Models & AI Agents with Rishi Sapra [MVP]", published on 2026-09-16, which covers financial data, semantic models and AI agents in relation to decision-making.

personal-branding.desc: Personal branding is the practice of shaping how a professional is perceived so that they are known for specific expertise, using content, speaking and social media.

faq.a: Personal branding is the practice of deliberately shaping how a professional is perceived, for example through content, speaking and social media, so that they are known for specific expertise.
faq.q: What is personal branding?

faq.a: No. The episode "How to Futureproof Your Career in the AI Era with Sarah Jones" says a strong reputation does not require becoming an influencer, but rather consistently providing value and building meaningful professional relationships.
faq.q: Does personal branding mean becoming an influencer?

faq.a: According to the sources, employers increasingly screen applicants' online histories and platforms such as LinkedIn act as professional profiles, so a visible and consistent public presence can influence how candidates are evaluated.
faq.q: Why does personal branding matter in hiring?

personal-branding.long:
Personal branding is the practice of deliberately shaping how a professional is perceived, so that they become known for specific expertise. It is typically pursued through content creation, public speaking and social media, and it aims to build credibility and visibility among a defined audience. In its broader description, personal branding is a strategic effort to create, position and maintain a favorable public perception of oneself, built on individual traits and a differentiated narrative aimed at a target audience.

The idea draws on marketing theory and on self-presentation theory, which deals with identity, reputation and image. According to the source material, McNally and Speak defined a personal brand in 2003 as a perception or emotion maintained by somebody other than you, which underlines that a brand lives in the minds of others rather than in what a person claims about themselves. Tom Peters is credited with coining the term through his 1997 article The Brand Called You, followed by The Brand You 50 in 1999. The internet and social media later made the practice accessible to a much wider group of professionals, since publishing and networking no longer depended on traditional gatekeepers.

Recommended practices described for building a personal brand include defining an audience and a specialization, creating original content, and publishing across several channels. Keeping a consistent image, staying authentic and responsive, building a complete professional profile and using a visual identity are also listed. Platforms such as LinkedIn serve as professional profiles, and employers increasingly screen applicants' online histories, which is one reason the topic is relevant for job seekers and for people who want to advance within their field.

Personal branding is also debated. Critics argue that it commodifies the self, that it can turn artificial because platform logic shapes how people present themselves, and that it puts pressure on people to conform. Supporters say it helps people stand out. These points matter in practice because they frame a decision many professionals face: how much visibility to pursue and in what form.

The M365.FM episode "How to Futureproof Your Career in the AI Era with Sarah Jones" treats personal branding as a major focus within a wider discussion of career resilience, what recruiters look for when evaluating candidates, and a job market increasingly supported by AI-powered hiring tools. In the episode, Sarah Jones discusses how professionals can build credibility and visibility through networking, community engagement, content creation, public speaking and authentic participation in industry conversations. The episode emphasizes that building a strong reputation does not require becoming an influencer. Instead, it stresses consistently providing value and developing meaningful professional relationships. Listeners are offered actionable advice on how to stand out in a highly competitive job market.

Taken together, the sources present personal branding as a set of repeatable habits rather than a single campaign: choose a specialization, share useful work, take part in the community, keep the public profile complete and consistent, and stay authentic. The approach is relevant for anyone in the Microsoft ecosystem who wants to be associated with a particular skill area, whether to attract opportunities, support a career change or strengthen standing with peers and recruiters.

personally-identifiable-information.desc: Personally identifiable information (PII) is data that can identify a specific person, such as names, contact details or ID numbers, and must be protected.

faq.a: PII is information that can be used to identify a specific person, such as names, contact details or identification numbers. In customer service it must be protected, for example through redaction and access controls.
faq.q: What is personally identifiable information (PII)?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, Microsoft Purview automatically scans and classifies data, identifies sensitive PII and tags it according to compliance requirements. It also offers data lineage, role-based access control and a compliance dashboard.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Purview deal with PII?

faq.a: The Dataverse episode describes data masking rules that replace sensitive values with masked strings for unauthorized users. The Copilot episode says users only see responses based on data they can access and that anonymization techniques remove PII.
faq.q: How can PII be protected in Dataverse and Copilot scenarios?

personally-identifiable-information.long:
Personally identifiable information (PII) is information that can be used to identify a specific person. Typical examples are names, contact details and identification numbers. Because such data points to real individuals, organizations treat it as sensitive and protect it through technical and organizational measures. In customer service, for instance, PII is expected to be shielded by redaction and access controls so that only the people who need the data can see it.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, PII appears in several contexts: compliance tooling, data loss prevention, application platforms and AI assistants. The M365.FM episodes on these topics describe the same underlying goal in different products: find the personal data, label it, limit who can reach it, and keep a record of how it is handled.

The episode "Microsoft Purview Information Protection - Simply Explained" describes automatic data classification as one building block. According to the episode, Microsoft Purview scans and classifies data, identifies sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) and tags it according to compliance requirements. The same episode points to a compliance dashboard that gives real-time insight into an organization's compliance status, so that adherence to guidelines can be tracked and data protection measures stay effective.

The episode "Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management - Simply Explained" connects PII handling to regulations such as GDPR and HIPAA. It lists data classification, data lineage, access control and a compliance dashboard as features that support compliance. Data classification tags identified PII according to GDPR requirements. Data lineage tracks the flow of personal data, which supports accountability and auditability. Role-based access control ensures that only authorized personnel can access sensitive data.

In "Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) - Simply Explained", PII is named among the sensitive data types that DLP can protect, alongside financial records, health information and intellectual property. The episode explains that DLP policies in Microsoft Purview can be adapted to an organization's needs, including the definition of sensitive data types and the enforcement actions that apply. It recommends reviewing DLP policies at least quarterly so that they stay aligned with evolving data security needs, and it notes that Microsoft Purview can take action when a policy is violated.

For application data, the episode "Dataverse Security - Simply Explained" looks at data masking. It describes creating masking rules to protect PII by replacing sensitive data with masked strings, so that only authorized users can access the original values. The episode also describes upcoming technology intended to help identify and classify sensitive data across environments, improving the understanding of the data estate and the compliance posture.

The episode "Grounding Microsoft Copilot for Trusted Enterprise AI" covers PII in the context of AI assistance. It states that users only see responses based on data they personally have access to, which is meant to prevent data leakage, and that data anonymization techniques are used to remove PII. It also mentions EU Data Boundary compliance, which keeps EU customer data within EU boundaries, and specialized data boundaries for HIPAA compliance to protect patient information.

Taken together, the episodes show a common pattern for working with PII: discover and classify it, restrict access through roles and permissions, mask or redact it where full values are not needed, monitor and audit its use, and review policies regularly. Which of these measures applies depends on the regulation involved, the type of data and the system in which it is stored or processed.

pester.desc: Pester is an open-source test and mock framework for PowerShell used to run unit and integration tests on scripts and modules, commonly within CI/CD pipelines.

faq.a: Pester is the open-source test and mock framework for PowerShell. It is used to run unit and integration tests for scripts and modules.
faq.q: What is Pester?

faq.a: It is used to test PowerShell code, including scripts and modules, and to mock dependencies during tests. It is commonly run in CI/CD pipelines.
faq.q: What is Pester used for?

faq.a: Yes. Pester is described as an open-source framework for testing and mocking in PowerShell.
faq.q: Is Pester open source?

pester.long:
