Teams choosing a delivery service for a globally used web application look at how close edge locations are to their users and how requests are routed to origins. Because PoPs are operated by the provider, the practical choices are about which Front Door tier to use and how to configure routing, caching and security rules, rather than about the placement of the edge locations themselves.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Front Door - Simply Explained" discusses these benefits from the viewpoint of using Azure Front Door as a CDN. The episode says that Front Door reduces latency by routing requests to the nearest point of presence, which leads to faster TCP handshake times and quicker SSL setup. It also says that median round-trip times have been halved, resulting in better availability and faster page load times, and that this improvement is particularly noticeable after new PoP locations were added, especially in regions like Africa. The excerpt also points to high availability as an advantage of the service.

In short, a point of presence is the first contact point between a user and a provider's network. For Azure Front Door, the density and placement of these edge locations, combined with the private backbone to the origin, are central to how the service reduces latency and applies caching and security close to users.

policy-as-code.desc: Policy as code expresses governance, security and compliance rules as versioned code that is evaluated automatically to allow or block changes during deployment.

faq.a: Policy as code is the practice of expressing governance, security and compliance rules as versioned code that is evaluated automatically, for example during deployment, to allow or block changes.
faq.q: What is policy as code?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes name Azure Policy, which the episode "Compliance as Code: The Architect's Blueprint for Automated Trust" recommends for enforcing compliance across cloud resources at the right scope. Third-party tools are also mentioned as options.
faq.q: Which Microsoft tool is mentioned for policy as code?

faq.a: The episodes list Policy as Code alongside Infrastructure as Code, Golden Paths and platform engineering as ways to enforce governance consistently, so that standards are applied by the pipeline or platform rather than by manual review.
faq.q: How does policy as code relate to Infrastructure as Code and platform engineering?

policy-as-code.long:
Policy as code is the practice of writing governance, security and compliance rules as versioned code instead of keeping them in documents or relying on manual review. Because the rules are code, they can be stored in source control, reviewed, tested and evaluated automatically, for example during deployment, where the result decides whether a change is allowed or blocked.

The main purpose is consistency. When policies are embedded directly into the software delivery process, every deployment is held to the same standard regardless of who triggers it or which environment it targets. The episode "Scaling CI-CD: The Governance Blueprint" describes this approach: policies, security controls and quality gates belong inside the delivery pipeline rather than being added as an afterthought, so that every deployment follows the same trusted standards automatically. The episode lists Policy as Code alongside Infrastructure as Code, automated testing, security scanning, compliance validation, approval workflows and continuous monitoring, and contrasts this with manual reviews, noting that successful organizations build pipelines that enforce governance consistently across every environment.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, Azure Policy is the tool most often named in connection with the practice. The episode "Compliance as Code: The Architect's Blueprint for Automated Trust" recommends using Azure Policy to enforce compliance across cloud resources and applying governance policies at the right scope through an inheritance system. It also mentions policy enforcement points that apply governance rules automatically, and presents policy as code as a way to enhance automation and consistency. The same episode pairs this with continuous monitoring, which gives ongoing visibility into compliance status and helps identify gaps quickly.

Policy as code also appears in infrastructure and security discussions. In "Azure Infrastructure as Code and DevOps with Maik van der Gaag [MVP]", it is mentioned as part of secure coding and access control practices. The episode suggests scanning code for vulnerabilities with Static Application Security Testing (SAST) to find problems early, and using Policy as Code to enforce rules and compliance, with Azure Policy and third-party tools named as options. It also recommends least-privilege access, giving users and services only the permissions they need, which reduces the risk of accidental changes or security breaches.

The concept extends beyond infrastructure to data and AI governance. In "How Probabilistic AI Changes Power Platform Design", policy as code is listed among practices for reliable AI outcomes that depend on data quality and governance. The episode suggests adopting it to manage access and retention, alongside active metadata and lineage, machine-learning-based classification of sensitive data, risk-based controls, human approvals and automated evidence collection for audits and compliance.

At the organizational level, "The DevOps Tax: Why Your Platform is Failing" places Policy as Code among the building blocks of Platform Engineering, together with Golden Paths, Infrastructure as Code and AI-ready governance. The episode frames the DevOps Tax as the hidden productivity cost created when developers spend most of their time solving infrastructure problems instead of building products. In that framing, encoding policy into the platform is one way to reduce the burden on individual teams, because standards are enforced by the platform rather than rediscovered by each developer.

Typical decisions around policy as code include where to evaluate rules (for example at deployment time in a pipeline), at which scope to apply them, which tools to use, and how to combine automated enforcement with human approval where judgment is needed. Standardized deployment templates, mentioned in the "Scaling CI-CD: The Governance Blueprint" episode together with platform engineering, are one way to help development teams move quickly while staying inside the same guardrails.

policy-decision-point.desc: A policy decision point (PDP) is the access control component that evaluates an authorization request against defined policies and returns a deterministic permit or deny decision.

faq.a: A PDP evaluates an authorization request against defined policies and returns a deterministic permit or deny decision.
faq.q: What does a policy decision point (PDP) do?

faq.a: Its outcome follows from the defined policies and the request being evaluated, so it results in a clear permit or deny decision rather than an ambiguous one.
faq.q: Why is a PDP described as deterministic?

policy-decision-point.long:
A policy decision point (PDP) is a component of an access control architecture. It evaluates an authorization request against defined policies and returns a deterministic permit or deny decision.

In a typical access control design, the PDP is the part that makes the decision, while other components send requests to it and act on the result. Separating decision-making from enforcement allows policies to be defined and evaluated in one place instead of being embedded in each application or resource. The PDP takes the request details, applies the relevant policies, and produces an outcome that can be consistently reproduced for the same inputs.

The term is relevant for people studying authorization models, zero trust approaches and policy-based access control, where decisions are expected to follow explicit rules rather than ad hoc checks.

No related topics or episodes are currently linked to this entry on M365.FM, and no official documentation links have been provided. The description here is therefore limited to the general definition of the concept.

policy-enforcement-point.desc: A policy enforcement point (PEP) is an architectural component that checks a request against policy synchronously and allows or denies it before the state change commits.

faq.a: A PEP is an architectural component that evaluates a request against policy synchronously and allows or denies the action before the state change commits.
faq.q: What is a policy enforcement point (PEP)?

faq.a: The policy decision point is the counterpart to the PEP. The PEP applies the allow or deny outcome to the request in the request path, while the decision point is the component associated with deciding that outcome.
faq.q: How does a policy enforcement point differ from a policy decision point?

faq.a: A PEP acts synchronously, before the state change commits. A denied action therefore does not take effect, unlike controls that only detect or report an action afterwards.
faq.q: When does a PEP act on a request?

policy-enforcement-point.long:
A policy enforcement point (PEP) is an architectural component that evaluates a request against policy at the moment the request is made. It works synchronously: the check happens in the request path, and the action is either allowed or denied before the resulting state change is committed. Because the decision is made before commit, a denied action never takes effect.

In access-control and governance architectures, the PEP is the counterpart to a policy decision point (PDP). The two roles are commonly described as separate responsibilities: the decision point determines what the outcome of a policy evaluation should be, while the enforcement point is where that outcome is applied to the actual request. Keeping the roles distinct allows policy logic to be defined and evaluated in one place while enforcement happens wherever requests flow.

The concept is used when designing systems in which rules must be applied consistently and in real time, rather than detected or reported after the fact. A PEP sits in the path of the operation it governs, which distinguishes it from after-the-fact auditing or monitoring approaches.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no further product-specific details are recorded here. The description above covers the general architectural meaning of the term only.

policy-tip.desc: A policy tip is a short notice in Outlook, Teams or other apps telling users that a data loss prevention rule applies to the content they are working with.

faq.a: A policy tip is a notice shown by a data loss prevention policy to tell users that the content they work with conflicts with a DLP rule. In Outlook it is shown to the sender while composing a message.
faq.q: What is a policy tip in Microsoft Purview DLP?

faq.a: According to the Microsoft Purview reference, they are not available in SharePoint and OneDrive desktop clients, mobile Office apps, third-party cloud apps or on-premises content. Teams files get no tips either.
faq.q: Where do policy tips not work?

faq.a: In Teams, a flagged message shows a prompt where users can review the detected sensitive information types and, if the admin allows it, override or report a mistake. Whether this is possible depends on how the administrator configured the policy.
faq.q: Can users override a policy tip?

policy-tip.long:
A policy tip is a short notice that a data loss prevention (DLP) policy shows to a user when the content they are working with conflicts with a DLP rule. In Outlook, for example, the sender sees the notice while composing a message and learns that a rule or policy applies to it. Policy tips are part of Microsoft Purview data loss prevention and are documented in the Microsoft Purview policy tips reference.

The main purpose of a policy tip is to make a compliance rule visible at the moment it matters. Instead of silently blocking an action or reporting it afterwards, the policy tip tells the user what has been detected, so that they can change what they are doing. The reference describes supported conditions that can trigger such a notice, including content shared from Microsoft 365, sensitive information types, sensitivity labels, keywords in the subject or body, and sender or recipient conditions.

How a policy tip looks depends on the application. According to the reference, Outlook offers default and customized oversharing dialogs, a wait-on-send dialog and a custom compliance link that can point users to further education, with availability depending on the client. In Teams, a flagged message triggers a prompt where users can review the detected sensitive information types and, if the administrator allows it, override the block or report a mistake. This means the tip can work both as information and as a point where the user may respond.

Support for policy tips varies widely between locations, and this affects how a DLP rollout is planned. The reference lists policy tips as working in SharePoint and OneDrive on the web, in Office apps on the web for documents already stamped by a policy, in Teams messages, on endpoint devices, and in Fabric and Power BI. They are not available in SharePoint and OneDrive desktop clients, in mobile Office apps, in third-party cloud apps or for on-premises content. Teams files get no tips, and Windows Office apps show them only for a limited set of conditions and actions. Administrators who rely on policy tips for user guidance should therefore check which client and workload their users actually work in.

The M365.FM episode "Configure Microsoft 365 DLP Policies in Purview" treats policy tips as an educational element of DLP. The episode advises adding helpful advice to the alert, reminding users about compliance rules and safe data handling, and using policy tips often. It describes DLP as a teaching tool and not just a way to block actions: when users see a policy tip, they understand the risk and can change their behavior, which the episode says builds a culture of security and responsibility.

The same episode places policy tips next to admin notifications. While the policy tip informs the person who triggers the rule, email notifications keep administrators informed about DLP incidents so that they can respond quickly to possible data leaks. Used together, the two give the user immediate guidance and give administrators visibility into what happened.

post-quantum-cryptography.desc: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) covers algorithms built to resist quantum-computer attacks, including NIST-standardized ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA.

faq.a: PQC is a set of cryptographic algorithms designed to resist attacks by quantum computers. Examples standardized by NIST include the lattice-based ML-KEM and ML-DSA and the hash-based SLH-DSA.
faq.q: What is post-quantum cryptography (PQC)?

faq.a: It is the risk that long-lived sensitive data is captured today and decrypted later, once quantum computers capable of breaking current public-key algorithms exist. It is a named driver for starting PQC planning early.
faq.q: What is the "harvest now, decrypt later" risk?

faq.a: Cryptographic agility is the ability to change algorithms quickly and safely. Microsoft Learn recommends it as the foundation, together with a cryptographic inventory, governance and review of vendor timelines, because migration is a multi-year program.
faq.q: Why is cryptographic agility important for PQC readiness?

post-quantum-cryptography.long:
Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) refers to cryptographic algorithms designed to resist attacks by quantum computers. Among the algorithms standardized by NIST are the lattice-based ML-KEM and ML-DSA and the hash-based SLH-DSA. The concept is framed as preparation for the possibility that future quantum computers could break some of the public-key algorithms that security controls rely on today.

A central reason for acting early is the "harvest now, decrypt later" risk. In this scenario, long-lived sensitive data is captured now and decrypted once a sufficiently capable quantum computer exists. Data that must stay confidential for many years is therefore exposed earlier than the date on which quantum attacks become practical. Cryptography underpins authentication, digital signatures, software integrity and secure communication such as TLS, so the affected scope is broad. It spans applications, identity systems, VPN and network equipment, storage, IoT and operational technology, and partner integrations.

The guidance in Microsoft Learn, "Plan cryptographic agility and post-quantum readiness", treats cryptographic agility as the foundation. Cryptographic agility means being able to change algorithms quickly and safely, without rebuilding every system that depends on them. Alongside agility, the page recommends an inventory of cryptographic use and trust chains, clear governance, and a review of vendor timelines. These steps make it possible to know where vulnerable algorithms are in use and which suppliers can support new ones.

The suggested approach runs in several stages: discovering where vulnerable algorithms are used, evaluating vendor support, planning phased migration waves with rollback options, and implementing changes with testing and evidence tracking. High-value assets, identity systems and long-lived data are prioritized. Migration is described as a multi-year program rather than a single project, and some systems will need new libraries, certificates or firmware, or even replacement hardware.

The M365.FM episode "Cryptographic Agility for Post-Quantum Security" (2026-06-12) looks at how cryptographic agility can be used to defend against quantum risks. According to the episode, the platform follows a phased approach to upgrading its security. The first phase integrates PQC algorithms into foundational components such as SymCrypt, so that cryptographic security stays consistent across platforms. The second phase updates core infrastructure services, such as authentication and key management, to provide quantum safety, with the most sensitive components prioritized. The third phase extends PQC to all Microsoft services and endpoints.

In practice, decisions around PQC concern sequencing and readiness rather than a single switch. Organizations weigh which assets hold long-lived data, which identity systems anchor trust, and which vendors have published support timelines. Because some algorithms may need replacing in systems that were not designed for change, the emphasis on agility, inventory and governance is meant to reduce the effort and risk of each later migration wave.

power-apps-barcode-scanner.desc: The Power Apps barcode scanner control is a canvas app control that reads barcodes and QR codes through the device's native scanner; Microsoft has retired it.

faq.a: It is a canvas app control that opens the device's native scanner to read barcodes and QR codes, making the scanned result available to the app.
faq.q: What does the Power Apps barcode scanner control do?

faq.a: Microsoft has retired the control in favor of the barcode reader control. Makers should consult the Microsoft documentation for the current status.
faq.q: Is the Power Apps barcode scanner control still supported?

faq.a: It is part of Power Apps and is used in canvas apps.
faq.q: Which product does the barcode scanner control belong to?

power-apps-barcode-scanner.long:
The Power Apps barcode scanner control is a control for canvas apps in Power Apps. It opens the native scanner on a device so that an app can read barcodes and QR codes, and the scanned value can then be used inside the app.

The control is part of Power Apps and was used by makers who needed to capture codes, for example to look up or record items by scanning. Microsoft has since retired this control in favor of the barcode reader control, so new work is directed toward the replacement rather than the older scanner control.

Microsoft documents the control in its Power Apps documentation on canvas app controls. That reference page is the authoritative place to check the current status of the control and details of its properties.

No episodes on M365.FM are currently linked to this topic.

power-apps-containers.desc: Containers in Power Apps are canvas app layout controls that position child controls automatically, using manual or horizontal and vertical auto-layout instead of X and Y formulas.

faq.a: Containers are layout controls in Power Apps canvas apps. They contain child controls and position them either manually or through horizontal or vertical auto-layout.
faq.q: What are containers in Power Apps?

faq.a: They allow screens to respond to different sizes without requiring X and Y formulas on each control, because the container handles the positioning of its children.
faq.q: Why are containers used in canvas apps?

faq.a: Child controls can be positioned manually, or the container can arrange them automatically in a horizontal or vertical auto-layout.
faq.q: What layout options do containers offer?

power-apps-containers.long:
Containers (Power Apps) are layout controls in Power Apps canvas apps. They hold other controls as children and arrange those children according to the container's layout settings. Containers can position child controls manually, or they can use horizontal or vertical auto-layout to place them automatically.

The main purpose of containers is to help screens respond to different sizes. Because the container manages the placement of its child controls, an app maker does not need to write X and Y position formulas for each control to achieve a layout that adapts. This makes containers a core building block for responsive design in canvas apps, as described in the Microsoft documentation on building responsive canvas apps.

Containers fall under the broader topic of Power Apps, the Microsoft platform for building apps. Within that scope, they belong to the layout and design side of canvas app development, where structure and sizing decisions determine how an app behaves across different screens and devices.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic. The official Microsoft Learn documentation on building responsive canvas apps is the referenced source for the behavior described here.

power-apps-for-figma.desc: Power Apps for Figma is a Figma plugin by Microsoft MVP Lukas Pavelka that moves designs, components and design systems to and from Power Apps canvas apps.

faq.a: It is a Figma plugin created by Microsoft MVP Lukas Pavelka and published by Power Plugins. It moves designs, components and design systems between Figma and Power Apps canvas apps.
faq.q: What is Power Apps for Figma?

faq.a: Layers carry supported name prefixes, and the plugin turns them into YAML code shown in a Code view. The YAML is copied to the clipboard and pasted into the Power Apps builder, as described in the M365.FM episode with Lukas Pavelka.
faq.q: How does a design get from Figma into Power Apps?

faq.a: It comes in a free version and a pro version. The help article mentions extra settings and a Get PRO button for free users, but its own tab counts are inconsistent, so feature details should be confirmed in the plugin.
faq.q: Is Power Apps for Figma free?

power-apps-for-figma.long:
Power Apps for Figma is a Figma plugin that connects design work in Figma with app building in Power Apps. It was created by Microsoft MVP Lukas Pavelka and is published by Power Plugins. The plugin moves designs, components and design systems between Figma and Power Apps canvas apps, and it is available in a free version and a pro version. It is treated as part of the wider Power Apps ecosystem.

The core purpose, according to the plugin's help article, is to prepare Figma designs so they can be exported to Power Apps. Controls and screens in a Figma file carry name prefixes that the plugin recognizes as supported Power Apps control types. The plugin reads these prefixed layers and turns them into YAML code that can be pasted into the Power Apps builder. It also works in the other direction: an import function brings YAML and Base64 images into Figma, so existing app visuals can be brought back into a design file.

The interface is organized into tabs. The Editor tab manages designs before export. It offers a Layout view that lists the selected screens and controls with supported prefixes, and a Code view that shows the generated YAML. A theme and style tool works from design tokens or saved styles. A bottom action bar provides several functions: Compile, which adds prefixes automatically; a dependency model showing screen navigation; PDF export; YAML export, delivered as a ZIP when several screens are selected; resizing for mobile or tablet; translation; and a bulk manager for renaming layers. A Generate tab, described in the documentation as alpha, is an AI chat that creates modern Power Apps controls from prompts, with custom controls planned. Further tabs cover settings, help with the supported prefixes, and a history that compares versions.

The documentation separates a free version from a PRO version. Free users see extra settings and a Get PRO button, although the article's own count of tabs is inconsistent, so the exact split of features between the two versions should be checked in the plugin itself.

Typical situations involve a designer or maker who wants an app's look to be defined in Figma first and then carried into a canvas app, instead of rebuilding each screen by hand in the Power Apps builder. Decisions around the plugin include whether to start from a UI kit in Figma, how to name layers so the prefixes are recognized, whether to rely on the Compile function to add prefixes automatically, and whether the pro features are needed.

The M365.FM episode "Figma to Power Apps Development with Lukas Pavelka [MVP]" covers the workflow in practice. According to its show notes, the plugin has to be installed before starting. To edit a control, the user selects it in Figma with the right prefix, opens the AI chat in Figma, describes the edit as a prompt, opens Power Apps for Figma in the YAML Code Viewer, presses the copy-to-clipboard button and pastes the code into the Power Apps builder. The episode adds a tip that repeating these steps refreshes a design, so app visuals can be updated quickly. It also describes importing a Figma design into Power Apps after installing the plugin, starting with choosing a UI kit in Figma that fits the project.

power-apps-maker-portal.desc: The Power Apps maker portal is the browser-based, point-and-click environment in Power Apps where makers build apps, flows and solutions, and prototype quickly.

faq.a: It is the browser-based, point-and-click environment where makers build apps, flows and solutions. The episodes also describe it as the place to manage solution components, create and edit Dataverse tables, and add connections.
faq.q: What is the Power Apps maker portal used for?

faq.a: It is well suited to prototyping but offers limited control over moving work between environments. For deployments, the episodes point to solutions, environment variables, solution layering and ALM pipelines.
faq.q: Is the Power Apps maker portal suitable for moving work between environments?

faq.a: According to the episode "Design Scalable Dataverse Data Models", the maker portal is used to create and edit tables, columns, relationships, views and forms. Advanced tasks can be handled with tools such as the Dataverse Web API and Power Query.
faq.q: How is the maker portal used with Dataverse?

power-apps-maker-portal.long:
The Power Apps maker portal is the browser-based part of Power Apps in which makers build apps, flows and solutions through a point-and-click experience. It is part of Power Apps and acts as the main workspace where low-code work is created, edited and organized. Because it runs in the browser and relies on visual tools rather than code, it is well suited to prototyping, where an idea needs to be turned into a working app or flow quickly. At the same time, it offers only limited control over moving work between environments, which is why teams that go beyond prototypes usually look at additional deployment approaches.

In practice, the maker portal is used to view and manage the components that make up a solution. The episode "Deploy Dynamics 365 Customizations with ALM Pipelines" describes solutions that contain items such as Power Automate cloud flows, connection references, APIs, plug-ins and workflows, as well as user interface components like web resources (HTML, JavaScript and images) and metadata for custom ribbon buttons. According to that episode, the Power Apps maker portal can be used to view and manage these components, and proper organization of them supports solution deployment and reduces errors during automation. The same episode stresses consistent naming and versioning across development, testing and production, which helps avoid problems such as case-sensitivity issues.

The maker portal also plays a central role in data modeling. In "Design Scalable Dataverse Data Models", the portal is named as the place to create and edit tables, columns, relationships, views and forms in Dataverse. The episode contrasts it with more advanced tools such as the Dataverse Web API for programmatic tasks and Power Query for data import and transformation, and it points to solutions as the way to package model changes. For validating a model, the episode suggests testing with model-driven apps and canvas apps, reporting with Power BI, and using test data to confirm that related data and business rules behave as expected. It also recommends solution layering and environment variables to manage deployments across environments so that data stays consistent across multiple applications.

Connections are another area where the maker portal appears. In "Replace Legacy RPA with Copilot Studio Computer Use", the portal is the place to create a new connection if the expected Copilot Studio connection is missing. The episode explains that a connection list should contain an entry with the API ID /providers/Microsoft.PowerApps/apis/shared_microsoftcopilotstudio, and that its presence means the connection exists. If it is absent, the connection can be added manually through the Power Apps maker portal. After that, the agent is published in Copilot Studio, the connection string and agent name are checked under the web app channel to confirm they match the Power Apps environment, and Power Automate flows triggered by the agent are tested.

Taken together, these episodes show the maker portal as the hands-on authoring surface of Power Apps: it is where tables, apps, flows, connections and solution components are created and inspected. A typical decision is when to stay in the portal and when to rely on more structured practices. For quick prototypes and everyday maintenance, the point-and-click experience is sufficient. When work has to move reliably between development, testing and production, the episodes point toward solutions, environment variables, solution layering, consistent naming and versioning, and ALM pipelines, since the portal alone gives limited control over that movement.

The maker portal therefore relates closely to several neighboring topics: Dataverse for tables and relationships, Power Automate for cloud flows and connection references, Copilot Studio for agents and their connections, and Dynamics 365 for solution-based customizations. Understanding what the portal covers well, and where other tools take over, helps makers choose an appropriate approach for each stage of an app's life.

power-apps-premium.desc: Power Apps Premium is a per-user Power Apps license for running apps that use Dataverse, model-driven apps and premium connectors beyond Microsoft 365 rights.

faq.a: It covers apps that use premium capabilities such as Dataverse, model-driven apps and premium connectors. These are not covered by the Power Apps rights included in Microsoft 365.
faq.q: What does Power Apps Premium cover that Microsoft 365 does not?

faq.a: According to the episode "Avoid the Dataverse Licensing Trap in Power Apps", the per-app plan covers one custom app or one Power Pages website per user, while Power Apps Premium is a per-user license for unlimited apps.
faq.q: How does Power Apps Premium differ from the per-app plan?

faq.a: Yes. The episodes on Power Apps Code Apps state that end users need a Power Apps Premium license to access Code Apps.
faq.q: Is a Power Apps Premium license needed for Code Apps?

power-apps-premium.long:
Power Apps Premium is a per-user license for Power Apps. It allows a user to run apps that rely on premium capabilities, such as Microsoft Dataverse, model-driven apps and premium connectors. These capabilities are not covered by the Power Apps rights that are included in Microsoft 365. The license is part of the Power Apps product family and is one of several licensing options for the platform.

The main purpose of the license is to give end users access to apps that go beyond the standard use cases covered by Microsoft 365. When an app uses a premium connector or stores its data in Dataverse, each user who runs it needs an appropriate license. The per-user model is aimed at people who work with several apps. A per-app plan, in contrast, covers a single application for each user.

The episode "Avoid the Dataverse Licensing Trap in Power Apps" compares the main plan choices. According to the episode, the free plan includes 2 GB of Dataverse space and up to 750 automation flows per month. The Power Apps Per App plan costs $5 per app per user and covers one custom app or one Power Pages website, with a 50 MB database and 400 MB file storage. Power Apps Premium is listed at $20 per user, or $12 per user for 2,000 or more users, with unlimited apps, 2 GB of files, 250 MB of Dataverse space and premium connectors. A pay-as-you-go option billed through an Azure subscription is also described. The episode summarizes the trade-off this way: the per-app plan suits a single app, while the per-user plan suits people who need many apps. These figures are attributed to the episode and may differ from current official pricing.

Licensing questions also arise with newer app types. The episode "Avoid the Generative Pages Power Apps Licensing Trap" says that using generative pages with Microsoft Dataverse brings licensing issues, because each viewer needs a Power Apps Premium license once a page has been created. According to the episode, this turns the app from a standard app into a premium one. To limit unexpected costs, it suggests keeping Dataverse components in separate environments so that other apps are not pulled into premium licensing.

Code Apps are another area where the license matters. The episodes "Power Apps Code Apps with Carike Botha [MVP]" and "Power Apps Code Apps - Simply Explained" both state that a Power Apps Premium license is required for end users to access Code Apps. In the first episode, the license appears in a list of prerequisites alongside Visual Studio Code, Node.js (LTS version), Git, the Power Apps CLI and the Power Platform Tools extension for VS Code. The second episode says that a standard Power Apps Premium license is needed and describes it as ensuring access to advanced features within the Power Platform. It also notes that Code Apps can be deployed to a Power Apps environment with the command pac code push.

The license also comes up in discussions of scale. The episode "Power Platform Scalability Limits and Fixes" explains that licensed user types contribute different entitlements to tenant-level capacity and request limits. It says that for many users or many apps, appropriate licensing tiers such as Power Apps Premium and a suitable architecture should be considered, so that load is distributed across environments. Platform constraints named there include concurrent sessions, Dataverse capacity and environment-level limits.

In practice, the decision around Power Apps Premium usually involves three questions: whether an app uses Dataverse or premium connectors, how many apps each user needs to run, and how many users are involved. The answers determine whether a per-app plan, a per-user plan or pay-as-you-go billing fits better. The episodes consistently recommend checking licensing before building, since the cost model can change once premium features are added to an app.

power-apps-sdk.desc: Power Apps SDK (code apps) is an open-source Node.js package that generates typed model and service files for data sources and links custom code to Power Platform services.
power-apps-sdk.long:
Power Apps SDK (code apps) is an open-source Node.js package used by Power Apps code apps. It generates typed model and service files for data sources, giving custom code a structured way to work with the data and services an app depends on.

The SDK also connects custom code to Power Platform services such as connectors and authentication. In this role it acts as the bridge between code written by a developer and the platform capabilities that Power Apps provides, so that an app built in code can reach the same connected services as other Power Apps.

The package is part of Power Apps code apps, the approach in which an app is built with custom code rather than assembled only in a low-code designer. Within that approach, the SDK supplies the typed models and services and the connection to the platform.

No further details, such as versions, installation steps, or supported data sources, are included in the information available for this entry, and no M365.FM episodes are currently linked to it.

power-apps-vibe.desc: Power Apps vibe experience is an AI-native, prompt-driven preview feature in Power Apps where makers describe an app and AI generates the plan, data model and app.

faq.a: It is an AI-native, prompt-driven experience in Power Apps, currently in preview, where makers describe what they want and AI generates the plan, data model and app.
faq.q: What is the Power Apps vibe experience?

faq.a: The Power Apps vibe experience is part of Power Apps, the Microsoft platform for building business applications.
faq.q: How does it relate to Power Apps?

faq.a: It is described as being in preview, so its features and behavior may change. Microsoft Learn documentation provides the current details.
faq.q: Is the Power Apps vibe experience generally available?

power-apps-vibe.long:
Power Apps vibe experience is an AI-native, prompt-driven experience in Power Apps, currently in preview. Makers describe in natural language what they want to build, and AI generates the plan, the data model and the app itself, rather than the maker assembling each part by hand.

The experience is part of Power Apps, Microsoft's low-code platform for building business applications. Within that platform, the vibe experience focuses on starting from a description of intent. The generated output covers the planning step, the underlying data model and the resulting app, which the maker can then work with.

Because the experience is in preview, its capabilities and behavior may change before general availability. Microsoft documents the feature in its Power Apps documentation on Microsoft Learn, which is the reference point for current details on scope and usage.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity. As more coverage is added, related episodes will appear alongside the Power Apps topic.

power-architect.desc: Power architect is a role or cross-functional responsibility for designing how decision rights, data ownership, access and escalation paths flow through an organization.

faq.a: In the M365.FM episode "The Power Architect Role in Microsoft 365 Transformation", the power architect is a role or cross-functional responsibility for designing how decision rights, data ownership, access and escalation paths flow through an organization.
faq.q: What is a power architect?

faq.a: The episode argues that tools do not solve a broken operating model. It describes a gap between how organizations are designed on paper and how they operate in reality, which behavioral patterns and decision flows shape.
faq.q: Why does the episode say Microsoft 365 and AI do not fix transformation on their own?

faq.a: The main episode is "The Power Architect Role in Microsoft 365 Transformation". It is also listed as a related episode in "Leading AI Transformation and Community with Areti Iles [MVP]".
faq.q: Which M365.FM episodes cover the power architect concept?

power-architect.long:
Power architect is a concept framed in the M365.FM episode "The Power Architect Role in Microsoft 365 Transformation" as a role, or a cross-functional responsibility, focused on how power and decisions move through an organization. The role is concerned with designing how decision rights, data ownership, access and escalation paths flow, so that a transformation actually changes how work moves rather than only changing the tools people use.

The starting point of the concept is a gap that the episode describes between how organizations are designed on paper and how they truly operate in reality. According to the episode, digital transformation efforts can fail even when the right technology is in place. Tools such as Microsoft 365 and AI do not by themselves solve a broken operating model. The power architect is presented as the figure who addresses this hidden gap, which the episode treats as a question of who actually fixes these failures.

The four elements named in the description give the concept its structure. Decision rights concern who is allowed to decide what, and where a decision is made in practice. Data ownership concerns who is accountable for information and who controls it. Access concerns who can reach which resources and under what conditions. Escalation paths concern how issues and exceptions travel upward or sideways when the normal flow does not resolve them. The power architect designs how these four flow across the organization, and the cross-functional framing indicates that the work is not tied to a single department or a single technical product.

The episode also points to behavioral patterns and decision flows as the factors that shape real outcomes. In this view, what an organization achieves with Microsoft 365 depends less on feature availability and more on how people behave around decisions, ownership and access. Because of that, the role looks at the operating model itself instead of treating a rollout as a purely technical project. A transformation can be considered successful, in this framing, when the way work moves has changed, not only when new software has been deployed.

Typical situations where the concept becomes relevant are Microsoft 365 and AI initiatives that stall or deliver little change despite sound technology choices. In such cases the decisions for the organization include who holds decision rights, who owns data, how access is granted and how escalation works. Naming the power architect as a role or responsibility gives these questions an explicit owner, instead of leaving them spread across IT, security, compliance and business teams without coordination.

The concept is also referenced in a later M365.FM episode, "Leading AI Transformation and Community with Areti Iles [MVP]", which lists "The Power Architect Role in Microsoft 365 Transformation" among related episodes on transformation topics, alongside "Microsoft 365 Copilot Enterprise Transformation Strategy" and "Use Fabric Notebooks for Data Transformation and ML". Listeners who want the full explanation of the concept should start with the episode of the same name as the term.

power-automate-desktop.desc: Power Automate Desktop (PAD) is a Microsoft RPA tool for Windows that records and runs desktop flows to automate repetitive tasks in desktop and web applications.

faq.a: It is used to automate repetitive tasks in desktop and web applications on Windows by recording and running desktop flows. It is especially relevant for applications that offer no interface for other systems to connect to.
faq.q: What is Power Automate Desktop used for?

faq.a: Desktop flows run on a Windows PC, while cloud flows in Power Automate can trigger them. This lets a process combine cloud services with steps in a legacy application.
faq.q: How do desktop flows relate to cloud flows?

faq.a: According to the episode "Power Automate Desktop Attended vs Unattended - Simply Explained", an attended robot works at the desk while the user watches, and an unattended robot works while the user is away. The episode notes that the two do not cost the same.
faq.q: What is the difference between attended and unattended robots?

power-automate-desktop.long:
Power Automate Desktop, also called Power Automate for desktop or PAD, is a robotic process automation (RPA) tool for Windows developed by Microsoft. It records and runs desktop flows that automate repetitive tasks in desktop and web applications, including applications that offer no interface through which other systems could connect to them. It is part of Power Automate and is classed as a low-code tool.

The core idea is to let software repeat work that a person would otherwise perform step by step on a PC. Many business processes still run through applications that were never built to exchange data with other services. A desktop flow can operate such an application the way a user would, which makes it useful where no standard connection is available. The catalog data lists it as an included offering. The episode "Power Automate Desktop - Simply Explained" describes it as a free robot already sitting on a Windows PC that most people never switch on, and presents it as Microsoft's answer to work done the same way, over and over, in apps that cannot talk to anything else.

Desktop flows are one of two flow types discussed in that episode, the other being cloud flows. The episode covers the difference between desktop flows and cloud flows and also looks at how the recorder turns actions into a flow. The two types can work together: cloud flows in Power Automate can trigger desktop flows, so a process can combine services in the cloud with steps in a legacy application on a PC.

A second decision around the tool concerns how the robot runs. The episode "Power Automate Desktop Attended vs Unattended - Simply Explained" distinguishes two kinds of robot. One sits with the user at the desk and works while the user watches. The other works while the user is away. The episode notes that the two do not cost the same, so the choice between attended and unattended operation is both a practical and a licensing question for anyone planning an RPA project. The episode walks through when each robot fits and what the real difference between them is.

Power Automate Desktop also appears in discussions of skills and careers. The episode "Build a Power Platform Career with Nathalie Leenders [MVP-MCT]" mentions the PL-500 certification as validating skills in designing and deploying RPA solutions using Power Automate Desktop, alongside other Power Platform certifications such as PL-400 for developers. The catalog notes that PL-500 is now retired, and it covered Power Automate Desktop together with Power Automate. The episode frames certifications and practical experience as steps toward roles such as Power Platform consultant, solution architect or team leader.

In other episodes the tool is mentioned as one option within wider integration landscapes. The episode "Scale HR Operations with Copilot Studio AI Agents" lists Power Automate Desktop (PAD) in a comparison of integration approaches, noting that it integrates with various systems and suits organizations looking for desktop automation. The episode "Service Accounts vs App Registrations for Power Automate Email" touches on running Power Automate desktop flows in the context of community forums and testing new features.

Related topics are Power Automate as the parent product, automation in general, and the low-code approach, in which flows are assembled from actions rather than written as conventional code. Taken together, the episodes position Power Automate Desktop as the part of Power Automate that reaches into Windows applications and web interfaces, complementing cloud-based flows rather than replacing them.

power-automate-process-license.desc: Power Automate Process license (per flow) is a licensing option that licenses an individual automated flow rather than each user, formerly known as the per flow plan.

faq.a: It is a Power Automate licensing option that licenses a single automated process (flow) instead of each user. One licensed flow can serve many users.
faq.q: What is the Power Automate Process license (per flow)?

faq.a: It was formerly known as the per flow plan.
faq.q: What was the Process license (per flow) previously called?

faq.a: It is aimed at high-volume scenarios, where one automated process serves many users and licensing each user individually would not fit.
faq.q: When is a per-flow license used?

power-automate-process-license.long:
The Power Automate Process license (per flow) is a licensing option within Power Automate. Instead of assigning a license to each user, it licenses an individual automated process, known as a flow. It was formerly known as the per flow plan.

The model is intended for high-volume scenarios. Because the license is tied to the flow and not to individual people, a single licensed flow can serve many users. This makes it relevant where one automated process is used broadly across an organization and per-user licensing would be impractical to assign and track.

The Process license (per flow) is part of Power Automate, Microsoft's service for building automated workflows. It sits alongside other ways of licensing the service, with the main distinction being that the licensed unit is the process itself rather than the person who triggers or benefits from it.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no further details about pricing, limits or capabilities are recorded here.

power-automate-run-history.desc: Power Automate run history is the list of past runs of a cloud flow, kept for a limited retention period and used mainly as a debugging aid, not an audit record.

faq.a: It is the list of past runs of a Power Automate cloud flow. Entries are kept only for a limited retention period.
faq.q: What is Power Automate run history?

faq.a: No. It is meant as a debugging aid, and because it is retained only for a limited time it should not be treated as a long-term audit trail.
faq.q: Is Power Automate run history a permanent audit record?

faq.a: The information available here does not state a specific duration, only that retention is limited. The exact period should be confirmed in Microsoft's official documentation.
faq.q: How long is Power Automate run history kept?

power-automate-run-history.long:
Power Automate run history is the list of past runs of a Power Automate cloud flow. Each entry represents an earlier execution of the flow, and the list is retained only for a limited retention period rather than indefinitely.

Because of that time limit, run history is best understood as a debugging aid. It lets flow authors look back at recent runs to see what happened and to investigate problems. It is not a permanent audit record, so it should not be relied on as the long-term source of evidence for what a flow did or when it did it.

The concept sits under the broader topic of Power Automate, where it forms part of how cloud flows are monitored and troubleshot. The practical consequence of the retention limit is that anything that must be kept beyond that window, such as records needed for compliance or accountability, has to be captured by other means instead of depending on the run list.

The point that run history is a debugging aid rather than a permanent audit record is emphasized in an M365.FM episode that discusses the topic. No specific retention duration is stated in the information available here, so the exact period should be checked in Microsoft's official documentation for Power Automate.

power-automate-trigger.desc: A trigger in Power Automate is the event that starts a flow, such as a new email, a submitted form, a button click or a schedule.

faq.a: A trigger is the event that starts a Power Automate flow. Examples include a new email, a submitted form, a button click or a schedule.
faq.q: What is a trigger in Power Automate?

faq.a: Every flow has one trigger, followed by one or more actions.
faq.q: How many triggers can a Power Automate flow have?

faq.a: The trigger starts the flow, and the actions that follow it run in response. The trigger comes first, and the actions define what the flow does.
faq.q: How does a trigger relate to actions?

power-automate-trigger.long:
A trigger in Power Automate is the event that starts a flow. Examples include a new email arriving, a form being submitted, a button being clicked or a defined schedule being reached. Every flow has exactly one trigger, followed by one or more actions that run once the trigger fires.

The trigger determines when and why a flow runs, so it is usually the first element chosen when a flow is designed. The actions that follow define what the flow does in response, such as processing data or sending a message. Because a trigger always comes first, it sets the starting point and the input context for everything else in the flow.

Trigger (Power Automate) is a concept within the broader topic Power Automate. Microsoft documents triggers in its Power Automate documentation under an introduction to triggers, which is the official reference for how they work.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

power-bi-data-alerts.desc: Power BI data alerts are notifications in the Power BI service that fire when a value on a dashboard tile crosses a set threshold, such as on cards, gauges and KPIs.

faq.a: They are notifications in the Power BI service that fire when a value on a dashboard tile crosses a threshold.
faq.q: What are Power BI data alerts?

faq.a: Alerts are limited to tiles pinned to dashboards, such as cards, gauges and KPIs.
faq.q: Which tiles support Power BI data alerts?

faq.a: They are part of Power BI, specifically the Power BI service.
faq.q: What product are Power BI data alerts part of?

power-bi-data-alerts.long:
Power BI data alerts are a feature of Power BI, the Microsoft analytics platform. They are notifications in the Power BI service that trigger when a value shown on a dashboard tile crosses a defined threshold.

Data alerts are limited to tiles pinned to dashboards. The tile types named in the available facts are cards, gauges and KPIs. Alerts therefore apply to single-value visuals on a dashboard rather than to every visual type in a report.

The typical use of a data alert is to monitor a number on a dashboard without checking it manually. When the monitored value passes the configured threshold, the alert fires and a notification is delivered through the Power BI service.

Power BI data alerts are part of Power BI. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic, and no official documentation link is recorded in the source facts.

power-bi-desktop.desc: Power BI Desktop is a free Windows application from Microsoft for connecting to data, modelling it and authoring reports before publishing to the Power BI service.

faq.a: It is used to connect to data, model it with relationships and measures, and design report pages and visuals. The finished reports are then published to the Power BI service for sharing.
faq.q: What is Power BI Desktop used for?

faq.a: Power Query is used in Power BI Desktop for loading and transforming data, and DAX is used for calculations in the data model. Both are part of everyday report authoring in the application.
faq.q: How do Power Query and DAX relate to Power BI Desktop?

faq.a: Yes, it is a free Windows application from Microsoft. Reports built in it are typically published to the Power BI service for sharing and refresh.
faq.q: Is Power BI Desktop free?

power-bi-desktop.long:
Power BI Desktop is a free Windows application from Microsoft for connecting to data sources, modelling the data and authoring Power BI reports. Report authors use it to shape data, define relationships and measures, and design visuals and pages. The finished report is then published to the Power BI service, where it can be shared with others and refreshed. It is part of Power BI, is classed as an analytics and BI tool, and is sometimes abbreviated as PBI Desktop.

The typical workflow in Power BI Desktop starts with getting data. Data is connected through the Get Data function, and loading and transforming it is done with Power Query. Calculations in the data model are written in DAX, so both Power Query and DAX are closely related to everyday work in the application. Once the model and the visuals are in place, the report is published to the Power BI service. This split between authoring on the desktop and sharing in the service is the central design of the product.

The M365.FM episodes describe several concrete data scenarios. "Connect Power BI Desktop to SharePoint Folders" deals with using SharePoint as a data source. SharePoint is described there as a place that can grow into a maze of lists, libraries, document versions, old folders and columns added by people who have since left. The episode frames the task as turning that jumble into something that can be reshaped, filtered, modelled and presented clearly, starting from the site URL. "Embed Power BI and Fabric Analytics in Dynamics 365" covers a Dataverse connection: open Power BI Desktop, choose Get Data, select Dataverse as the source, enter the Dynamics 365 organization URL, pick the entities needed and load them. From there, relationships, calculations and visuals can be added.

Power BI Desktop also appears in the episodes in the context of larger, team-based development. "Power BI DAX and Semantic Models with Bernat Agulló Roselló [MVP]" covers filter context, relationships and the difference between measures and calculated columns. The episode says advanced semantic models quickly become difficult to manage in Power BI Desktop alone, which makes automation and scripting with Tabular Editor important for scalable BI solutions. This points to a common decision: when a model outgrows manual work in the desktop application, enterprise tooling becomes relevant.

The lifecycle topics follow the same pattern. "Deploy Power BI with Development, Test, and Production Pipelines" describes the development workspace as the place where authors open Power BI Desktop, change tables, rebuild DAX calculations, try new visuals and adjust Power Query steps. Changes are promoted to a test stage and then to production, so that experiments do not affect other users. "Power BI Version Control with GitHub and Azure DevOps" notes that Power BI Desktop files use the binary PBIX format. According to the episode, teams therefore often rely on source control strategies, such as saving report parts as separate JSON files or using the ALM Toolkit. It also mentions workspaces, deployment pipelines and the XMLA endpoint as ways to mimic development, test and production branches.

Taken together, the episodes position Power BI Desktop as the authoring environment where data connection, Power Query transformation, DAX modelling and report design come together. It is the starting point for the Power BI service, deployment pipelines and version control practices, while the sources describe it as free to use on Windows.

power-bi-org-apps.desc: Org apps are a Microsoft Fabric item type that packages Power BI reports and other items for consumers, with multiple apps allowed per workspace.

faq.a: Org apps are a Microsoft Fabric item type that content creators use to package Power BI reports and other items for consumers.
faq.q: What are org apps in Microsoft Fabric and Power BI?

faq.a: Yes. Org apps allow multiple apps per workspace, so creators can package content separately from the same workspace.
faq.q: Can a workspace contain more than one org app?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode presents them as the single governed doorway for report distribution, i.e. one controlled entry point through which consumers access packaged content.
faq.q: Why are org apps described as a governed doorway?

power-bi-org-apps.long:
Org apps (Microsoft Fabric and Power BI) are an item type in Microsoft Fabric that content creators use to package Power BI reports and other items for consumers. Instead of sharing individual reports one by one, a creator bundles the relevant content into an app that consumers open as a single unit.

A workspace can contain multiple org apps. This allows content creators to assemble separate packages from the same workspace, for example for different audiences or purposes. On M365.FM, org apps are described as the single governed doorway for report distribution, meaning the app serves as the controlled entry point through which consumers reach reports and related items.

Org apps sit at the intersection of Microsoft Fabric and Power BI, since they are a Fabric item type built around distributing Power BI content. Detailed behavior, configuration options and current capabilities are documented in the official Microsoft Learn article on org app items in the Power BI consumer documentation.

power-bi-premium.desc: Power BI Premium is a capacity-based Power BI offering with dedicated resources that lets content reach viewers without per-user Pro licenses; Fabric capacity now replaces it.

faq.a: Power BI Premium is a capacity-based Power BI offering that provides dedicated resources and allows content to be distributed to viewers without per-user Pro licenses. It was sold in sizes called P1 through P5.
faq.q: What is Power BI Premium?

faq.a: Yes. Microsoft now steers new customers to Fabric capacity, and the episode "Fabric vs Power BI Premium - Simply Explained" states that one of the two names in its title is being retired.
faq.q: Is Power BI Premium being replaced by Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: The episode "Reduce Power BI Premium Costs with Better Data Models" recommends moving to a star schema with lean fact tables and avoiding bloated columns, lazy imports and tangled relationships, since these consume capacity.
faq.q: How can Power BI Premium capacity costs be reduced?

power-bi-premium.long:
Power BI Premium is a capacity-based offering within Power BI. Instead of licensing every individual who consumes content, an organization buys dedicated resources and distributes reports to viewers without requiring a per-user Pro license for each of them. Microsoft now steers new customers toward Fabric capacity, so the name is in the process of being retired in favor of Microsoft Fabric.

The episode "Fabric vs Power BI Premium - Simply Explained" describes Power BI Premium as the shared engine an organization bought so that hundreds of people could open the same report. It came in sizes called P1 through P5. The same episode covers the two names that people often mix up, what Power BI Premium was built to do, and what Fabric is and why Power BI Premium is being replaced by it. For anyone planning purchases or reading older documentation, this distinction matters, because much existing material still refers to Premium and its P-series sizes.

In practice, Power BI Premium is used when a report audience is large and a per-user licensing model becomes impractical. Dedicated capacity also gives an organization predictable resources for refreshes, queries and heavy models rather than relying on shared infrastructure. The episode "Deploy Power BI with Development, Test, and Production Pipelines" describes the governance side: Power BI Premium's governance framework adapts as data volumes and complexity grow, and the platform connects to enterprise data sources such as SAP, Oracle, SQL Server, Azure Synapse, Snowflake and BigQuery. It handles large datasets with in-memory compression and optimized storage, incremental data refresh reduces load and improves performance, and composite models allow multiple data sources to be combined. That episode also recommends a sustainable operating model and strict security and governance as usage grows.

Capacity is a shared, finite resource, which makes data model quality a cost factor. The episode "Reduce Power BI Premium Costs with Better Data Models" argues that bloated columns, careless imports and tangled relationships put a load on Power BI Premium capacity and can add up to real money over a year. Its proposed remedy is architectural: moving from loosely organized models to a star schema with lean fact tables, rather than relying on a plug-in. Better modeling is presented as a way to lower capacity consumption and improve report speed at the same time.

Copilot is another area where capacity plays a role. The episode "Connect Microsoft Copilot to Predictive Power BI" tells listeners to check tenant settings and make sure the organization has the right capacity before enabling Copilot in Power BI. It mentions Power BI Premium or eligible Pro licenses as the route to advanced AI features, and it recommends high-quality data sources such as Excel and SQL Server, role-based access to protect sensitive data, and training for the users who get access to Copilot features.

The transition to Fabric is the most relevant current decision around the product. The episode "What Microsoft Fabric Means for Power BI Professionals" includes migration guidance for moving from Power BI Premium to Microsoft Fabric. It suggests starting with a health check: take an inventory of all content, including reports, datasets and dashboards, and identify anything stale or underused so that unnecessary data is not carried over into the new environment. The aim is a smooth migration that keeps existing business intelligence projects running.

Power BI Premium is part of Power BI, and the official documentation on Microsoft Learn covers it under the enterprise Power BI section of Fabric. Taken together, the episodes treat Power BI Premium as an established capacity model whose concepts, such as dedicated resources, governance and model efficiency, carry over into Fabric capacity, while the product name and purchasing path are being phased out.

power-bi-premium-per-user.desc: Power BI Premium Per User (PPU) is a per-user license for most Power BI Premium features that does not provision a Fabric capacity.
power-bi-premium-per-user.long:
Power BI Premium Per User (PPU) is a per-user license that gives individual users access to most Power BI Premium features. It is part of Power BI Premium and is licensed per person rather than through a shared capacity.

A PPU license does not provision a Fabric capacity. Content hosted in a PPU workspace is also subject to a licensing rule: users who consume that content need a PPU license as well. As a result, the license model applies to both the people who create content and the people who view it in those workspaces.

PPU is relevant when evaluating how Power BI Premium features can be obtained per user instead of through capacity-based licensing. The official Microsoft documentation for Power BI Premium Per User is provided as an FAQ in the Microsoft Fabric enterprise documentation, which covers licensing questions in more detail.

No episodes on M365.FM are currently linked to this topic.

power-bi-pro.desc: Power BI Pro is a per-user Power BI license for creating, publishing, sharing and collaborating on Power BI content, and part of the wider Power BI product.

faq.a: Power BI Pro is a per-user license that is part of Power BI. It lets users create, publish, share and collaborate on Power BI content.
faq.q: What is Power BI Pro?

faq.a: According to the episode "Secure External Data Sharing with Power Pages and Nicholas Hayduk [MVP]", you and your external users may need Power BI Pro or Premium licenses, so the organization's plan should be checked before sharing.
faq.q: Do external users need a Power BI Pro license to view shared reports?

faq.a: The episode "What Microsoft Fabric Means for Power BI Professionals" says Fabric can be adopted alongside Power BI licensing and that organizations using Power BI Pro may evaluate upgrades depending on scale and governance needs.
faq.q: How does Power BI Pro relate to Microsoft Fabric?

power-bi-pro.long:
Power BI Pro is a per-user license within Power BI. It allows a licensed user to create, publish, share and collaborate on Power BI content such as reports and dashboards. Microsoft documents the differences between license types in its Power BI fundamentals material, which is the reference point for deciding what a Pro license covers compared with other options.

In practice, Power BI Pro is the license that turns Power BI from a personal analysis tool into a collaborative one. A user who builds a report in Power BI Desktop can publish it to the Power BI service and share it with colleagues. One of the M365.FM episodes summarizes the requirement list for embedded analytics in this way: a Power BI Pro license is essential for creating, sharing and collaborating on reports, report sharing allows distribution of reports to other Pro users within the organization, collaborative workspaces enable shared team spaces, and data refresh keeps reports current through scheduled refreshes. These are the capabilities most closely tied to the license in the episode material.

The license shows up in several typical scenarios. In the episode "Monitor Business Central Telemetry with Power BI", the Power BI app for Business Central is combined with a connection from Power BI Desktop to Application Insights. Custom dashboards then highlight KPIs such as performance bottlenecks, page load times, extension failures and user activity patterns. The episode states that with a Power BI Pro license, teams can publish and share these dashboards across the organization, supporting governance, capacity planning and decisions about performance tuning.

A second scenario appears in "Embed Power BI and Fabric Analytics in Dynamics 365". There, the episode lists licensing and permissions that need to be checked before starting an embedded analytics setup, and puts Power BI Pro first on that list. A third appears in "Power Platform - Simply Explained", where a Power BI Pro license is named among the prerequisites for sharing the Power BI report that is part of the CoE Starter Kit, alongside items such as access to an Office 365 mailbox for the Office 365 Outlook connector and an Azure app registration for collecting usage information.

Licensing also matters when content leaves the organization. In "Secure External Data Sharing with Power Pages and Nicholas Hayduk [MVP]", the answer to whether special licenses are needed to share Power BI reports externally is yes: both the sharer and the external users may need Power BI Pro or Premium licenses. The episode advises checking the organization's plan before sharing and notes, attributed to Nicholas Hayduk, that licensing affects both access and collaboration options. It also recommends reviewing shared data and permissions at least every quarter, with continuous monitoring for sensitive data.

Power BI Pro is also discussed in the context of larger-scale decisions. In "What Microsoft Fabric Means for Power BI Professionals", the episode explains that Microsoft Fabric can be adopted alongside Power BI licensing, that some Fabric capabilities overlap with Power BI Premium features, and that organizations using Power BI Pro may evaluate upgrades depending on scale and governance needs. Power BI Premium capacity combined with Fabric is described there as delivering enterprise-grade performance and management for BI at scale.

Taken together, the sources present Power BI Pro as the per-user entry point for authoring and sharing in Power BI. Questions about who needs the license, whether external recipients need one, and when capacity-based options become relevant are the main decisions that arise around it.

power-bi-project-pbip.desc: Power BI Desktop project (PBIP) stores report and semantic model definitions as plain-text files in a folder structure, enabling source control with tools like Git.

faq.a: A PBIP is a way of saving Power BI Desktop work in which the report and semantic model definitions are stored as plain-text files in a folder structure instead of a single binary PBIX file.
faq.q: What is a Power BI Desktop project (PBIP)?

faq.a: Plain-text files in folders can be managed with source control tools such as Git, which allows changes to be tracked and compared more easily than with a single binary file.
faq.q: Why use PBIP instead of PBIX?

faq.a: It is part of Power BI Desktop, where a report and its semantic model can be saved as a project.
faq.q: Which product does the PBIP format belong to?

power-bi-project-pbip.long:
A Power BI Desktop project (PBIP) is a save format in Power BI Desktop that stores the definitions of a report and its semantic model as plain-text files inside a folder structure. This differs from the single binary PBIX file, which packages everything into one opaque container.

Because the contents are saved as individual text files, a PBIP can be tracked with source control tools such as Git. Changes to the report or the semantic model can be compared, reviewed and versioned at file level, which is difficult with a binary file. The folder-based layout also makes it easier for several people to work on the same Power BI content and to integrate it into development workflows.

The Power BI Desktop project is a capability of Power BI Desktop, the authoring application for Power BI reports and models. It is documented by Microsoft as part of the Power BI developer documentation on projects.

No episodes on M365.FM are currently linked to this topic. For details on the folder structure, supported items and current limitations, the official Microsoft Learn documentation on Power BI Desktop projects is the reference.

power-bi-report-builder.desc: Power BI Report Builder is Microsoft's free desktop authoring tool for paginated (RDL) reports, which are previewed locally and published to the Power BI service.

faq.a: It is used to author paginated (RDL) reports that are print-friendly, multi-page and pixel-perfect. Reports are previewed locally and then published to the Power BI service.
faq.q: What is Power BI Report Builder used for?

faq.a: The download is free. With a free license, publishing is limited to My Workspace, while Pro or Premium Per User allows publishing to other workspaces with at least the Contributor role and build permission on the dataset.
faq.q: Is Power BI Report Builder free?

faq.a: Sources include SQL Server, Oracle, Power BI semantic models, Analysis Services, Azure SQL and OData. Reports can be exported to formats such as PDF, Excel, Word, CSV and XML.
faq.q: Which data sources and export formats does it support?

power-bi-report-builder.long:
Power BI Report Builder is a desktop authoring tool from Microsoft for creating paginated reports in the RDL format. It is part of the Power BI family and is used to design reports that are published to the Power BI service. Paginated reports are print-friendly, multi-page and pixel-perfect, and they can show every row of a table, which distinguishes them from interactive dashboards that summarize data on a single canvas.

A report built in Power BI Report Builder consists of a report definition. This definition specifies which data is used, where the data comes from and how the layout looks. Authors can preview the report locally before publishing it. Wizards help create common elements such as tables, matrices, charts and maps, while free-form layouts suit document-style output such as invoices. Reports support grouping, sorting, expressions, conditional formatting, parameters, drillthrough and document maps. The tool can open existing reports created in SQL Server Data Tools.

Data for a report can come from several sources, including SQL Server, Oracle, Power BI semantic models, Analysis Services, Azure SQL and OData. Output can be exported to formats such as PDF, Excel, Word, CSV and XML, and subscriptions can deliver published reports by e-mail. This makes the tool relevant where documents need a fixed layout, repeatable printing or distribution to people who do not work inside Power BI itself.

The download of Power BI Report Builder is free, but publishing depends on licensing. With a free license, publishing is limited to My Workspace. A Pro or Premium Per User license allows publishing to other workspaces, provided the author has at least the Contributor role and build permission on the dataset. Documented limits include that a parameter cannot be both multivalue and allow-null, and that running the tool as a virtualized application, such as a Citrix published app, is not supported.

A typical decision is where to create a paginated report. The M365.FM episode "Power BI Paginated Reports: Service vs Report Builder vs SSRS" compares the options. According to the episode, the Power BI service suits quick and straightforward report creation, while Power BI Report Builder is the choice for advanced design features and professional layouts. The episode also recommends using styles and templates to keep formatting consistent, making manual adjustments for precise element placement, and using Lookup functions to enrich data with additional context. It advises building shared datasets to keep data consistent and to streamline report creation, and engaging with users to improve reports continuously based on their needs.

In practice, the tool fits situations in which layout control matters more than interactivity: operational documents, statements, invoices and long tabular listings. Because the finished reports are published to the Power BI service, they live alongside other Power BI content, and the authoring work stays on the desktop where detailed design, expressions and parameters can be configured and previewed before publication.

power-bi-report-themes.desc: Power BI report themes are JSON-based files that apply colors, fonts and visual formatting consistently across a Power BI report and can be shared as organizational themes.

faq.a: Power BI report themes are JSON-based theme files that apply colors, fonts and visual formatting consistently across a Power BI report.
faq.q: What are Power BI report themes?

faq.a: Yes. Report themes can be distributed centrally as organizational themes, so a common visual standard can be applied to reports.
faq.q: Can report themes be shared across an organization?

faq.a: They are defined in JSON-based theme files.
faq.q: In what format are Power BI report themes defined?

power-bi-report-themes.long:
Power BI report themes are JSON-based theme files used to define the look of a Power BI report. A theme specifies settings such as colors, fonts and visual formatting, and applies them across the report so that individual visuals share a consistent appearance instead of being formatted one by one.

The main purpose of a report theme is consistency. Because the formatting is stored in a single file, the same design settings can be reused across multiple reports. Report themes can also be distributed centrally as organizational themes, which allows a common visual standard to be maintained for reports created within an organization.
