Power BI report themes belong to the broader topic of Power BI, Microsoft's business analytics and reporting product. Within that area, they address report design and formatting rather than data modeling or data access. Because themes are defined in JSON, they are stored as a structured text file that can be created, edited and shared.

Official Microsoft documentation on report themes in Power BI Desktop is available on Microsoft Learn. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

power-bi-shape-map.desc: The shape map visual in Power BI Desktop is a preview visual that colors predefined regions such as countries, states or custom TopoJSON boundaries by a measure.

faq.a: It colors predefined regions, such as countries, states or custom TopoJSON boundaries, according to a measure. It does not plot points on a map.
faq.q: What does the shape map visual in Power BI do?

faq.a: It is described as a Power BI Desktop preview visual, so it is not a fully released visual.
faq.q: Is the shape map visual a released or preview feature?

faq.a: Yes. Besides predefined regions such as countries and states, it can use custom TopoJSON boundaries.
faq.q: Can the shape map visual use custom regions?

power-bi-shape-map.long:
The shape map visual (Power BI) is a preview visual in Power BI Desktop that displays data by coloring predefined regions rather than plotting points on a map. Regions can be countries, states or boundaries supplied as custom TopoJSON, and each region is shaded according to the value of a measure.

This approach differs from point-based map visuals. Instead of placing markers at coordinates, the shape map fills whole areas, which makes it suited to comparing a measure across geographic or administrative regions. The use of custom TopoJSON boundaries allows regions beyond the built-in options to be defined and used in a report.

The shape map visual is part of Power BI and is available in Power BI Desktop. Because it is described as a preview feature, its availability and behavior may differ from fully released visuals. Further details are provided in Microsoft's official documentation for the visual.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity.

power-bi-workspace-app.desc: A Power BI workspace app is a curated bundle of reports and dashboards published from a workspace, with audiences controlling which content each group sees.

faq.a: A Power BI workspace app is a curated bundle of reports and dashboards published from a workspace. It is part of Power BI and groups related content for consumers.
faq.q: What is a Power BI workspace app?

faq.a: Audiences control which content each group of users sees within the app. This lets one app show different reports and dashboards to different groups.
faq.q: What do audiences do in a Power BI workspace app?

power-bi-workspace-app.long:
A Power BI workspace app is a curated collection of reports and dashboards that is published from a workspace in Power BI. It packages selected content into a single, organized unit so that consumers can open related items together instead of browsing the workspace directly.

A defining feature of a workspace app is its audiences. Audiences control which content each group of users can see, so the same app can present different reports and dashboards to different groups. This makes it possible to share a common set of analytics while limiting each group to the content that applies to it.

A Power BI workspace app is part of Power BI. It is used to distribute finished content to end users, with the workspace serving as the place where that content is prepared before publication. Microsoft documents how end users work with these apps in its Power BI documentation on end-user apps.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity, and no further details beyond the description above are recorded here.

power-fx-user-defined-functions.desc: User-defined functions in Power Fx are named, reusable functions defined at app level in Power Apps canvas apps to centralize repeated logic.

faq.a: They are named, reusable Power Fx functions defined at app level in Power Apps canvas apps. They let a maker write a piece of logic once and call it by name in multiple places.
faq.q: What are user-defined functions in Power Fx?

faq.a: They are used to centralize repeated logic, such as model normalization, type coercion and payload assembly.
faq.q: What are user-defined functions used for?

faq.a: They are defined at the app level in Power Apps canvas apps.
faq.q: Where are user-defined functions defined?

power-fx-user-defined-functions.long:
User-defined functions (Power Fx) are named, reusable Power Fx functions that are defined at the app level in Power Apps canvas apps. Rather than repeating the same formula in many controls or properties, a maker defines the logic once under a name and calls it wherever it is needed.

They are used to centralize repeated logic. Typical examples include model normalization, type coercion and payload assembly. Keeping this logic in a single named function means a change is made in one place instead of in every formula that depends on it, which supports consistency and easier maintenance across an app.

The concept belongs to the Power Fx formula language used in canvas apps within the Power Apps part of the Microsoft ecosystem. No related topics, episodes or official documentation links are currently listed for this entry on M365.FM, so the description here is limited to the definition and common use cases above.

power-pages.desc: Power Pages is Microsoft's low-code service in the Power Platform for building secure, data-driven business websites such as customer and partner portals.

faq.a: Power Pages is used to build secure, data-driven business websites such as customer portals, partner portals and self-service sites. These let external visitors work with business data without direct access to internal systems.
faq.q: What is Power Pages used for?

faq.a: Dataverse usually stores the data that a Power Pages site displays and edits, while Power Fx is the formula language used across the Power Platform. Power Pages itself is part of the Power Platform.
faq.q: How does Power Pages relate to Dataverse and Power Fx?

faq.a: No. Power Pages is a paid Power Platform service, and the episode "Power Pages Licensing, Capacity Limits, and Alternatives" covers how its licensing and capacity limits compare with alternative solutions.
faq.q: Is Power Pages free to use?

power-pages.long:
Power Pages, also referred to as Microsoft Power Pages, is a low-code service for building secure, data-driven business websites. It is developed by Microsoft, belongs to the Power Platform and is classed as a low-code tool. It first appeared in February 2022 and is a paid service. Its focus is on external-facing scenarios: customer portals, partner portals, self-service sites and public-facing business applications in which visitors work with business data without having direct access to internal systems.

In practice, Power Pages is used when an organization wants to give people outside the company a controlled view of its data and processes. Typical examples named in the M365.FM material are customer portals, partner sites and self-service web experiences that can be created without heavy custom development. Data usually sits in Dataverse, the data platform that Power Pages is related to, so that a site can display and edit records that are already part of the organization's business data. Power Fx, the formula language used across the Power Platform, is a related topic for logic and configuration.

Because Power Pages sites are exposed to people outside the organization, security and architecture are recurring themes. The episode "Secure External Data Sharing with Power Pages and Nicholas Hayduk [MVP]" describes the risks of sharing data externally, such as data leaks and unauthorized access, and recommends double-checking permissions, classifying data into sensitive and non-sensitive categories and sharing only what is necessary. It presents Power Pages as a way to manage access while keeping compliance and user experience in focus, and argues that external users should not be treated like internal employees.

The episode "Building Multi-Tenant SaaS with Power Pages and Dataverse" looks beyond simple portals and discusses what changes when a platform must support multiple customers, strict security boundaries, enterprise governance and large-scale growth. According to the episode, many Power Platform projects struggle when they move beyond a single environment, and it covers topics such as Microsoft Entra External ID, governance and ALM practices, and performance as architectural decisions that become critical at that stage.

Licensing and capacity are another decision area. The episode "Power Pages Licensing, Capacity Limits, and Alternatives" explains what Power Pages is, how it integrates with Dataverse and the Power Platform, why organizations use it for quick portal creation, and how its licensing, capacity limits and alternative solutions compare. Since it is a paid service, these points matter when planning a site that may grow in users or data volume.

Existing portals are also a topic. "Modernize Legacy Power Apps Portals and Power Pages" addresses the move from older portal implementations to Microsoft Power Pages and warns about shadow logic: business rules, automations or workflows that operate outside official oversight and can create a hidden security risk. The episode lists unofficial workflows, hidden automations and untracked logic as common forms and recommends recognizing them early in a migration.

For a general introduction, "Power Pages - Simply Explained" from the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets series, presented by Mirko Peters, explains the platform in simple terms and shows how organizations can rapidly create customer portals, partner portals, self-service websites and public-facing business applications. It also frames the practical questions of architecture, adoption, security and governance that accompany such projects.

Taken together, the sources place Power Pages as the web-facing part of the Power Platform: a low-code way to publish business data externally, with Dataverse as the usual data layer and security, governance and licensing as the main points to settle before a site goes live.

power-pages-server-logic.desc: Power Pages server logic lets makers run JavaScript on the server, close to Dataverse, for operations that should not run in the browser, with access controlled by web roles and table permissions.

faq.a: It is a Power Pages feature that lets makers run JavaScript on the server, close to Dataverse, for operations that should not run in the browser.
faq.q: What is Power Pages server logic?

faq.a: Access is controlled by web roles and table permissions, the same security mechanisms used elsewhere in Power Pages.
faq.q: How is access to server logic controlled?

faq.a: Server logic is part of Power Pages.
faq.q: Which product is server logic part of?

power-pages-server-logic.long:
Power Pages server logic is a capability of Power Pages that lets makers run JavaScript on the server rather than in the visitor's browser. The code executes close to Dataverse, which suits operations that should not be exposed to or performed on the client side.

In practice, server logic is used for operations that need to stay off the browser, such as working with Dataverse data in a controlled environment. Because the code runs on the server, the logic itself is not delivered to the page visitor in the way client-side scripts are.

Access to server logic is not open by default. It is controlled by web roles and table permissions, the same security building blocks Power Pages uses to govern what authenticated and anonymous users can see and do with Dataverse data. This ties server logic directly to the site's existing security model rather than introducing a separate one.

Server logic is part of Power Pages, the Microsoft low-code platform for building external-facing business websites on top of Dataverse. Makers who already configure web roles and table permissions for their sites apply the same concepts when deciding who may call server logic.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic. The official Microsoft Learn documentation provides an overview of server logic in Power Pages.

power-pages-table-permissions.desc: Power Pages table permissions control which Dataverse records site users can access and what actions they can perform, scoped globally, by contact or by account.

faq.a: They are settings in Power Pages that control which Dataverse records site users can access and what they can do with those records.
faq.q: What are Power Pages table permissions?

faq.a: Table permissions are assigned through web roles. Users who hold a web role receive the access defined by the table permissions associated with that role.
faq.q: How are table permissions assigned to users?

faq.a: Examples of scope include global access, access by contact, and access by account, which determine the set of records the permission applies to.
faq.q: What scopes can a table permission have?

power-pages-table-permissions.long:
Power Pages table permissions are a security concept in Power Pages that defines which Dataverse records a site user can access and what that user can do with them. They apply to the Dataverse tables that a Power Pages site reads from or writes to, and they form part of how access to business data is limited on a site.

Each table permission has a scope that determines which records it covers. Documented examples of scope include global access, access limited to records related to the signed-in contact, and access limited to records related to the contact's account. A permission is not applied to users directly; it is assigned through web roles, so that the users holding a given web role receive the rights granted by the table permissions linked to it.

Table permissions are a sub-topic of Power Pages, the Microsoft platform for building websites that work with Dataverse data. They matter whenever a site shows lists or forms based on Dataverse tables, because the permissions determine which records appear and which operations are allowed on them.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic. Further detail on configuration is available in the official Microsoft Learn documentation on table permissions.

power-pages-web-api.desc: The Power Pages Web API lets site pages create, read, update and delete Dataverse table records from client-side JavaScript, governed by enabled tables, fields and permissions.

faq.a: It lets site pages create, read, update and delete Dataverse table records from client-side JavaScript.
faq.q: What can the Power Pages Web API do?

faq.a: Access is controlled by the tables that are enabled for the API, the fields that are allowed, and the table permissions applied to users.
faq.q: How is access to data controlled in the Power Pages Web API?

faq.a: It is part of Power Pages, where it is used to work with Dataverse data from site pages.
faq.q: Which product does the Power Pages Web API belong to?

power-pages-web-api.long:
The Power Pages Web API is a feature of Power Pages that allows pages on a site to create, read, update and delete records in Dataverse tables. Calls are made from client-side JavaScript running in the browser, so a page can work with Dataverse data without a separate custom backend for those operations.

Access through the Power Pages Web API is not open by default. It is controlled by three layers: the tables that have been enabled for the API, the fields on those tables that are allowed, and the table permissions that determine what a given user may do with the records. Together these settings define which data can be reached from a site and which operations are permitted.

The Power Pages Web API is part of Power Pages, Microsoft's platform for building websites that surface Dataverse data. It is typically relevant where a page needs to display records, submit forms, or update data dynamically from script, while keeping access limited to what the site's configuration allows.

No M365.FM episodes are linked to this entry yet. Further technical detail is available in the official Microsoft Learn documentation for the Web API overview in Power Pages.

power-pivot.desc: Power Pivot adds advanced data modeling to Microsoft Excel, relating multiple tables and using DAX calculations; introduced in 2010, it later became a Power BI building block.

faq.a: Power Pivot provides advanced data modeling in Microsoft Excel. It lets users relate multiple tables in a data model and write calculations in DAX, and it was introduced in 2010.
faq.q: What is Power Pivot?

faq.a: Power Pivot uses DAX for its calculations. The episode "Data Analysis Expressions (DAX) - Simply Explained" describes DAX as the calculation language behind Power BI, Excel Power Pivot, and SQL Server Analysis Services, and Power Pivot later became one of the building blocks of Power BI.
faq.q: How does Power Pivot relate to DAX and Power BI?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes mention Power Query for transforming data, Power Pivot for data modeling with DAX, Power View for visualizations, and Power Q&A for natural language queries.
faq.q: Which tools are commonly mentioned alongside Power Pivot?

power-pivot.long:
Power Pivot is a data modeling feature in Microsoft Excel. It lets users bring several tables into a single data model, define relationships between them, and write calculations in DAX (Data Analysis Expressions). It was introduced in 2010 and later became one of the building blocks of Power BI.

The core idea behind Power Pivot is to move analysis beyond a single flat worksheet. Instead of combining everything into one large table, users keep related data in separate tables and connect them in a data model. Reports and PivotTables can then draw on that model. One of the M365.FM episodes describes this as relational data modeling, one of the capabilities that distinguishes Excel when work involves heavy data analysis.

Calculations in Power Pivot are written in DAX. The episode "Data Analysis Expressions (DAX) - Simply Explained" describes DAX as the calculation language that powers Microsoft Power BI, Excel Power Pivot, and SQL Server Analysis Services. According to the episode, DAX is more than simply using Excel formulas inside Power BI, because it works across complete tables and data models rather than individual spreadsheet cells. The episode also covers the difference between calculated columns and measures, a distinction that matters when building calculations on top of a Power Pivot data model.

Power Pivot is often mentioned together with Power Query. In "Excel vs Google Sheets with David Benaim [MVP]", the two are presented as tools that let users manipulate and model data in complex ways: Power Query is associated with cleaning and transforming data from various sources, while Power Pivot is associated with relational data modeling. The episode frames these features as a reason Excel may be essential for users whose work involves heavy data analysis, in contrast to alternatives such as Google Sheets.

The pairing also appears in the context of data volumes. The episode "Fix Power Apps Excel Data Limits with Dataverse" says that Excel's data limitations are often overstated and that, with Power Query and Power Pivot, Excel can handle large datasets beyond the traditional one million row limit. The episode attributes these misconceptions to a lack of training on modern Excel capabilities. The same episode is nonetheless about the limits of Excel as a data source for Power Apps and the move to Dataverse, so Power Pivot is one part of a broader discussion about choosing the right data platform.

Power Pivot is also listed among the Microsoft tools relevant to reporting. In "Power BI Paginated Reports: Service vs Report Builder vs SSRS", the takeaways include using Power Query for data transformation, using Power Pivot for data modeling with DAX, creating visualizations with Power View, and using Power Q&A for natural language queries. The episode presents these as strategies for producing visually accurate, high-quality reports.

Typical decisions around Power Pivot involve where the data model should live and which tool should own the calculations. Because the same DAX language is used in Excel Power Pivot, Power BI, and SQL Server Analysis Services, skills in writing measures and understanding relationships carry across these products, as the DAX episode explains. Users who start with a data model in Excel can therefore recognize the same concepts when working in Power BI, which is consistent with Power Pivot's role as one of the building blocks of that product.

power-platform-admin-center.desc: The Power Platform admin center (PPAC) is Microsoft's central portal for managing Power Platform environments, data policies, capacity, tenant settings and analytics.

faq.a: It is the central portal for administering the Power Platform, covering environments, data policies, capacity, tenant settings and analytics. It is also used to monitor and manage governance responsibilities.
faq.q: What is the Power Platform admin center used for?

faq.a: DLP policies, which govern how connectors may be combined, are managed in this portal. They are one of the main governance controls applied through it.
faq.q: How does the Power Platform admin center relate to data loss prevention?

faq.a: No. The Microsoft 365 admin center serves the wider Microsoft 365 tenant, while the Power Platform admin center is the portal for the Power Platform. Some tasks, such as enabling Microsoft 365 Copilot, involve several admin centers.
faq.q: Is the Power Platform admin center the same as the Microsoft 365 admin center?

power-platform-admin-center.long:
The Power Platform admin center, often shortened to PPAC, is the central portal for administering the Power Platform. It is developed by Microsoft and is part of the Power Platform. Administrators use it to manage environments, data policies, capacity, tenant settings and analytics. According to the catalog data, it is included with the platform and does not require a separate purchase.

The core concept behind the portal is the environment. The episode "Power Platform Admin Center - Simply Explained" presents environments as the one idea that makes the rest of the portal make sense. It also points to a situation many tenants share: Microsoft creates a default environment automatically for every tenant, and apps and flows can accumulate there without anyone having planned it. The admin center is where administrators see and manage these environments and decide how they are separated and used.

Governance is the main reason administrators work in the portal. Many governance decisions, such as how environments are separated and which connectors may be combined, are applied here. Data loss prevention (DLP) policies, which control how connectors can be used together, are managed in this portal. The related Microsoft 365 admin center serves the wider Microsoft 365 tenant, while the Power Platform admin center covers the Power Platform side. The product documentation is published on Microsoft Learn under the Power Platform admin documentation.

The episode "Power Platform Governance Best Practices with Craig White [MVP]" discusses how to adopt low-code tools in a secure and scalable way with a structured governance strategy that balances innovation, security and operational control. According to the episode, consistency across an organization can be supported with Managed Environments and the Center of Excellence starter kit. It also recommends regularly checking database activity, system jobs and API calls to maintain platform health and compliance, and says the admin center should be used to monitor and manage these responsibilities. On environment strategy, the episode advises creating dedicated environments that support application lifecycle management (ALM) and governance, each with a clearly defined purpose.

"Power Platform Tenant Governance and Security Risks" describes the admin center as a central hub for managing environments, offering tools to enforce governance and improve security, along with governance features and reporting capabilities. The episode asks whether the platform is dangerous for the enterprise and argues that its security is enterprise-grade while the real risk lies elsewhere. The episode "Govern Power Platform Environments Instead of Disabling Them" argues that low-code solutions still introduce risk, since inadequate governance can expose organizations to data leakage, shadow IT and regulatory noncompliance. It says analytics from the admin center and the Center of Excellence toolkit reveal adoption, maker activity and risky apps, which allows governance actions to be targeted. It further states that patterns such as environment strategy, ALM pipelines and managed metadata scale across hundreds of makers and thousands of apps, and that governance tasks such as environment provisioning and policy enforcement can be automated.

The portal also appears in the Microsoft 365 Copilot context. "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Settings and Configuration" lists the Power Platform admin center among the admin centers where Copilot can be enabled, alongside the Microsoft 365 admin center, the SharePoint admin center and the Copilot dashboard. The episode also points to the Microsoft Purview portal for reviewing security updates and policies. Taken together, the episodes show the admin center as the place where environment structure, policy, capacity and monitoring come together for the Power Platform.

power-platform-alm.desc: Application lifecycle management (Power Platform) is the practice of managing apps through development, testing and production, typically by moving solutions between environments.

faq.a: It is the practice of managing Power Platform apps through development, testing and production. This is typically done by moving solutions between environments.
faq.q: What is application lifecycle management in Power Platform?

faq.a: It is a concept that falls under Power Platform as a broader topic. It describes how apps built on the platform are managed across their lifecycle.
faq.q: How does application lifecycle management relate to Power Platform?

faq.a: Microsoft provides an overview of application lifecycle management in its Power Platform documentation on Microsoft Learn.
faq.q: Where can the official description be found?

power-platform-alm.long:
Application lifecycle management (Power Platform) is the practice of managing Power Platform apps through development, testing and production. In this context, it typically involves moving solutions between environments so that changes can be built, checked and released in a controlled way.

The concept sits under Power Platform as a broader topic. It is relevant wherever apps and related components are created by more than one person or need to run reliably in a production environment. Working with separate environments for development, testing and production is the usual way to separate in-progress work from what users rely on.

Microsoft documents the approach in its Power Platform documentation, which includes an overview of application lifecycle management. That overview is the reference point for how the practice is described for the platform.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry. The topic is covered here as a concept within the Power Platform area of the Microsoft ecosystem.

power-platform-center-of-excellence.desc: A Power Platform Center of Excellence (CoE) is a team and set of practices that supports makers and governs and nurtures Power Platform adoption in an organization.

faq.a: It is a team and a set of practices that supports makers and administers, governs and nurtures Power Platform adoption across an organization, beyond tooling and dashboards.
faq.q: What is a Power Platform Center of Excellence (CoE)?

faq.a: No. The CoE is the team and its practices, while the CoE Starter Kit provides tooling, templates and governance practices, such as dashboards and app inventories, that a CoE can use for monitoring and governance.
faq.q: Is the CoE the same as the CoE Starter Kit?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft 365 Admins: From Gatekeepers to Cloud Architects" lists CoE leadership, a governance architect, a security specialist and a training coordinator as example roles.
faq.q: Which roles can a CoE team include?

power-platform-center-of-excellence.long:
A Power Platform Center of Excellence (CoE) is a team and a set of practices that supports makers and administers, governs and nurtures Power Platform adoption across an organization. In the official guidance, the CoE is described as going beyond tooling and dashboards: it covers the people, responsibilities and routines that surround the platform, not only the technical assets used to monitor it. It sits within the broader Power Platform topic, which includes low-code apps and automation built by makers inside the business.

The purpose of a CoE is to bridge IT and business units. The episode "Microsoft 365 Admins: From Gatekeepers to Cloud Architects" describes the CoE as a team that guides governance efforts and helps organizations deliver value quickly while protecting their assets. The same episode lists example roles that such a team can include: CoE leadership, which oversees the CoE and its initiatives; a governance architect, who designs governance frameworks and policies; a security specialist, who ensures compliance and security measures are in place; and a training coordinator. These roles show that a CoE is organized around decisions about who does what, how data is protected and how apps keep running smoothly.

A CoE is often associated with the Power Platform CoE Starter Kit, although the two are not the same thing. The Starter Kit is tooling and templates, while the CoE itself is the team and the practices. The episode "Govern Power Platform Environments Instead of Disabling Them" says the Starter Kit provides tooling, templates and governance practices to govern Power Platform at scale. According to that episode, it helps implement governance controls, environment strategy, monitoring, app lifecycle management and adoption strategy, and it supports scaling low-code solutions while letting citizen developers deliver value without creating shadow IT or data governance issues. The episode's framing is to govern environments rather than disable them.

Monitoring and compliance are a recurring theme in the episodes. "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform" says the Starter Kit gives dashboards, app inventories and automation tools, and that these can be used to monitor usage, check compliance and document business reasons for settings. The episode adds that the kit can scan for new environments so that governance stays up to date, and it recommends reviewing policies regularly to support sustainable growth. It also lists related practices such as tagging resources, setting up a team structure for environments, and using activity logs and analytics to monitor usage.

The episode "Automate Microsoft 365 Compliance Tasks with Power Automate" places the CoE Starter Kit inside a wider governance checklist. In its monitoring, logging and auditing section, the episode lists enabling and centralizing audit logging for Power Platform activities, configuring the CoE Starter Kit for governance and monitoring, watching for flow run failures, performance anomalies and unusual usage patterns, and retaining logs according to regulatory and organizational retention policies. Other items in the same checklist include reviewing connector permissions and consent scopes regularly and mapping Power Platform components to applicable regulatory requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA and SOC.

Taken together, the sources present a CoE as a combination of organizational structure and governance practice. Typical decisions around it include how to structure the team, which governance framework and policies to apply to environments, how to monitor usage and compliance, and how to support makers through training and adoption work. The official documentation is the reference for the full definition of the CoE and its role in Power Platform adoption.

power-platform-cli.desc: Power Platform CLI (PAC CLI, pac) is a Microsoft command-line tool for developing, packaging and deploying Power Platform components in a repeatable way.

faq.a: It is used to develop, package and deploy Power Platform components from the command line. The episodes describe tasks such as packing and unpacking solutions, versioning, dependency checks and plug-in registration.
faq.q: What is Power Platform CLI used for?

faq.a: Yes. PAC CLI and pac are alternative names for the Power Platform CLI, a free developer tool from Microsoft that is part of Power Platform.
faq.q: Is PAC CLI the same as Power Platform CLI?

faq.a: According to the episodes, it runs inside Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions to unpack and pack solutions, support Solution Checker runs and dependency reports, and automate deployments and test triggers.
faq.q: How does PAC CLI fit into CI/CD pipelines?

power-platform-cli.long:
Power Platform CLI, also called PAC CLI or simply pac, is a command-line tool for developing, packaging and deploying Power Platform components. It was developed by Microsoft, is classed as a developer tool and is part of Power Platform. The knowledge base lists it as free of charge. Instead of working through the portal, developers and administrators issue commands, so that tasks such as packing solutions or managing environments can be scripted and repeated.

The main purpose of the tool is to replace manual, click-heavy steps with scripted ones. This matters most when solutions move between development, test and production environments. The episode "Build Reusable Components with Power Platform CLI" says that Power Platform chaos across dev, test and prod is not inevitable and that PAC CLI turns fragile manual moves into repeatable DevOps. It names scripted solution packaging, versioning, dependency checks and plug-in registration as areas where the tool helps. It also recommends isolating authentication per tenant, packing managed solutions with all their references, and automating plug-in deployments. According to the episode, the intended results are predictable migrations, fewer "works in dev" surprises and cleaner rollbacks.

Because pac runs on the command line, it fits naturally into build and release pipelines. The episode "Set Up Power Platform ALM with GitHub Actions" describes a source, build, test and deploy flow in which solutions are kept in Git in unpacked form using PAC CLI, so that pull requests produce readable differences. It suggests committing both managed (release) and unmanaged (dev) exports, tagging them with the solution version, and storing a configuration folder per environment for environment variables and connection reference mappings. In the build stage, GitHub Actions use PAC CLI to unpack and pack solutions, run Solution Checker, generate a dependency report and publish artifacts such as a managed solution file. The same episode advises using service principals for deployments rather than individual people, for consistency and traceability.

PAC CLI also appears in testing and deployment guidance. "Automated Testing for Power Apps and Dataverse" mentions it as a native tool for automating deployments and triggering tests within CI/CD pipelines, alongside third-party tools such as EasyRepro for end-to-end tests that mimic real user actions. The episode explains that automated tests in a pipeline give fast feedback and support quality gates, meaning checkpoints that an app must pass before moving to the next stage. "Build Fusion Apps with Power Apps and Azure Functions" lists packaging apps with the Power Platform CLI among its practices for deploying fusion development solutions, next to source control with GitHub, CI/CD pipelines in Azure DevOps and securing APIs with Azure API Management.

The episode "Dataverse Business Skills for Scalable Power Platform Solutions" compares PAC CLI with two other tools, MCP Server and the Python SDK, as options for working with Dataverse. It presents each tool as having its own strengths and suggests choosing according to need. MCP Server is described there as a natural language interface for inserting, updating and searching data without writing code, which contrasts with the command-driven, scriptable approach of pac.

Typical decisions around PAC CLI involve how to structure solutions in source control, which authentication method to use in pipelines, and how to separate managed and unmanaged artifacts across environments. The tool does not replace a pipeline platform; the episodes position it as the component that performs Power Platform-specific steps inside systems such as Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions. Official documentation for the tool is published on Microsoft Learn in the developer section of the Power Platform documentation.

power-platform-dataflows.desc: Power Platform dataflows use Power Query to ingest, transform and load data into Dataverse or other destinations, on demand or on a schedule.

faq.a: They are a self-service, cloud-based data preparation technology built on Power Query. They ingest, transform and load data into Dataverse, a Power BI workspace or Azure Data Lake Storage, and can run on demand or on a schedule.
faq.q: What are Power Platform dataflows?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, no dataflow-specific license is required. The feature is covered by the licensing of Power Apps, Power BI or Dynamics 365 Customer Insights.
faq.q: Do Power Platform dataflows need a separate license?

faq.a: The episode "Migrate Dataverse Data Between Environments Safely" lists Power Platform Dataflows as one of several migration paths, together with the Dataverse Migration Utility, Azure Data Factory and third-party ETL solutions.
faq.q: How do dataflows relate to Dataverse migration?

power-platform-dataflows.long:
Power Platform dataflows are a self-service, cloud-based data preparation technology in Microsoft Power Platform. They are built on Power Query and are used to ingest data from a source, transform it and load the result into a destination such as Microsoft Dataverse, a Power BI workspace or an organization's Azure Data Lake Storage account. Dataflows are part of Power Platform and can run on demand or on a schedule.

The main purpose of a dataflow is to keep transformation logic in one central place, separate from the modeling and visualization layer in Power BI. Because the prepared tables are stored centrally, several solutions can reuse them instead of each report or app repeating the same Power Query code. Other services read the results through Dataverse, the dataflow connector or the data lake. According to Microsoft Learn, these consumers include Power BI, Power Apps, Power Automate and Dynamics 365 applications.

In terms of sources, the documentation lists more than 80 supported data sources. Sources that sit on premises require an on-premises data gateway. The transformation step uses the Power Query experience, which means that data shaping tasks such as cleaning, combining and reshaping tables are defined in the same query language used elsewhere in the Microsoft data stack.

Typical scenarios named in the documentation include migrating legacy data into Dataverse, replacing ETL tooling when building a data warehouse or star schema, and avoiding duplicated Power Query code across reports. Dataflows are therefore relevant both for application builders who need data in Dataverse and for analytics teams who want a shared, reusable preparation layer.

On licensing, no dataflow-specific license is required. The feature is covered by the licensing of Power Apps, Power BI or Dynamics 365 Customer Insights. Microsoft Learn also notes a generation distinction on the Power BI side: Power BI dataflow Gen1 is described as legacy and receives no new features, while Gen2 is recommended for Premium customers with Fabric access.

The M365.FM episode "Migrate Dataverse Data Between Environments Safely" lists Power Platform Dataflows among several migration paths for Dataverse data, alongside the Dataverse Migration Utility, Azure Data Factory and third-party ETL solutions. The episode says the right path depends on scale and complexity, and that complex data types and relationships such as option sets, lookups, polymorphic lookups and hierarchies require careful mapping to preserve integrity and behavior.

The episode "Power Apps Code Apps - Simply Explained" mentions dataflows in the context of connecting Power Apps Code Apps with other services. It names Power Automate cloud flows for synchronizing data and Power Platform dataflows for data management across environments as examples of such integrations. Taken together, the episodes position dataflows as one data movement and preparation option within the wider Power Platform, used next to Dataverse, Power Automate and other tools rather than as a replacement for them.

power-platform-developer.desc: A Power Platform developer builds apps, automations and reports with Power Apps, Power Automate, Power BI and Copilot Studio, often using connectors and Dataverse.

faq.a: A Power Platform developer builds apps, automations and reports using Power Apps, Power Automate, Power BI and Copilot Studio, often with connectors and Dataverse.
faq.q: What does a Power Platform developer do?

faq.a: The episode "From SharePoint Developer to Power Platform Architect with Michel Mendes [MVP]" lists PL-400: Power Platform Developer Associate, which focuses on advanced development skills. It suggests starting with fundamentals such as PL-900 first.
faq.q: Which certification is aimed at Power Platform developers?

faq.a: According to the episode "Build a Power Platform Career with Nathalie Leenders [MVP-MCT]", the platform lets people make apps, automate jobs and look at data without needing to know a lot of code.
faq.q: Do Power Platform developers need to write a lot of code?

power-platform-developer.long:
A Power Platform developer is a professional who builds apps, automations and reports on the Microsoft Power Platform. The role draws on Power Apps, Power Automate, Power BI and Copilot Studio, and it often involves connectors and Dataverse. The job title also appears under related names such as Power Platform Entwickler and Power Apps developer. The common thread is the use of low-code tools to deliver business solutions without relying on extensive traditional coding.

The work covers several kinds of deliverables. Apps are created for business users, repetitive tasks are turned into automated workflows, and data is analysed and presented in reports. Connectors link these solutions to other services, while Dataverse typically serves as the data layer. With Copilot Studio, the scope extends to AI agents. The episode "Copilot Studio AI Agents and RAG with Nilüfer Doğan [MVP]" addresses this area: it explains how agents can retrieve relevant company information instead of relying solely on the underlying language model, and it stresses governance, security, and why high-quality business data is essential for reliable AI outcomes. The episode names Power Platform developers among its intended listeners.

The episode "Build a Power Platform Career with Nathalie Leenders [MVP-MCT]" looks at the role from a career angle. It says a person can begin as a Power Platform developer by learning low-code tools, and that the platform lets people make apps, automate jobs and look at data without needing to know a lot of code. According to the episode, people choose this path because the platform works well with other Microsoft tools and because companies look for people who know automation. It also recommends meeting new people, gaining real-world experience through projects and internships, and building a portfolio to demonstrate skills to future employers.

Certification is another recurring topic. The episode "From SharePoint Developer to Power Platform Architect with Michel Mendes [MVP]" lists a path of Microsoft certifications: PL-900 (Power Platform Fundamentals), PL-100 (Power Platform App Maker Associate), PL-200 (Power Platform Functional Consultant Associate), PL-400 (Power Platform Developer Associate) and PL-600 (Power Platform Solution Architect Expert). The PL-400 certification is the one aimed at advanced development skills. The episode's tip is to start with the fundamentals and move to advanced certifications with experience, and to explore related certifications in Microsoft 365, Azure or Dynamics 365 to understand the wider Microsoft ecosystem. The episode title itself reflects a progression from SharePoint developer toward Power Platform architect.

The role is also changing as AI becomes part of development. The episode "AI, Power Platform & Developer Experience: The Next Frontier with Reza Niroomand [MVP]" discusses how AI is reshaping developer productivity and how the boundaries between low-code and pro-code continue to disappear. It highlights the need to balance AI-generated code with solid engineering principles, security, maintainability and scalable solution design as organizations adopt AI-first development strategies. The episode frames these themes as relevant for Power Platform developers, solution architects, IT professionals and Microsoft consultants, and says it covers which skills will matter most as the platform evolves.

In practice, decisions around the role tend to involve choosing the right Power Platform component for a task, deciding how data is stored and connected, and judging when a solution needs more engineering discipline. The sources describe the position as sitting between business needs and technical delivery, with a path that can lead toward functional consulting or solution architecture over time.

power-platform-environment.desc: A Power Platform environment is a container in Microsoft Power Platform that holds and manages business data, apps, chatbots and flows within a tenant and region.

faq.a: It is a container in Microsoft Power Platform where business data, apps, chatbots and flows are stored and managed together. Each environment belongs to a Microsoft Entra tenant, is bound to a region and can hold at most one Dataverse database.
faq.q: What is a Power Platform environment?

faq.a: According to the episode "Power Platform Admin Center - Simply Explained", Microsoft creates a default environment automatically for every tenant. The episode notes it can fill up with apps and flows that nobody planned.
faq.q: What is the default environment?

faq.a: The episode "Power Platform Governance Best Practices with Craig White [MVP]" says sandbox environments give a safe space to test new ideas and features. They isolate data and users, so experiments do not affect production systems.
faq.q: Why are sandbox environments used?

power-platform-environment.long:
A Power Platform environment is a container in Microsoft Power Platform where business data, apps, chatbots and flows are stored and managed together. Each environment belongs to a Microsoft Entra tenant, is bound to a region and can hold at most one Dataverse database. The environment is the basic unit around which the rest of the platform is organized, which is why the M365.FM episode "Power Platform Admin Center - Simply Explained" describes environments as the one idea that makes the rest of the admin center make sense.

In practice, environments are used to separate resources by purpose, audience or risk. The episode "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform" lists the choice or creation of an appropriate Power Platform environment, with separate development, test and production stages, as one step in a deployment checklist. The same checklist places environment-level data loss prevention (DLP) policies, license checks for Power Apps, Power Automate and Power Virtual Agents, and the registration of a custom connector for Azure OpenAI alongside that environment choice. Because policies and data sit at environment level, the way environments are planned directly shapes how an organization can control what makers build.

Every tenant also has a default environment. According to the episode "Power Platform Admin Center - Simply Explained", Microsoft creates it automatically for every tenant, and it can quietly fill up with apps and flows that nobody planned. This is one of the typical situations that makes environment strategy a governance topic: without deliberate decisions, work accumulates in a shared space where ownership and oversight are unclear. The episode introduces the Power Platform admin center as the place where environments are managed and covers who gets access to them.

Governance is the recurring theme in other episodes. "Power Platform Governance Best Practices with Craig White [MVP]" discusses sandbox environments as a safe place to test new ideas and features. The episode says sandboxes isolate data and users, which protects sensitive information and allows experimentation without affecting production systems. It also describes using Power Automate to automate governance tasks, including enforcing DLP policies and running audit workflows, and says this supports a secure, well-managed environment and consistent, accountable practices across the tenant.

The risk side appears in "Modernize Legacy Power Apps Portals and Power Pages", which describes shadow logic as business rules, automations or workflows that operate in a Power Platform environment outside official oversight. The episode presents this as a hidden security risk that can expose data and processes, and says it should be addressed early when moving from legacy systems to Microsoft Power Pages. Similarly, "Microsoft 365 Admins: From Gatekeepers to Cloud Architects" notes that broken workflows in a Power Platform environment can disrupt operations and expose an organization to risk, and frames the admin role as shifting toward architecting policies, automation and guardrails rather than manual oversight.

Taken together, the episodes treat the Power Platform environment as both a technical boundary and a governance boundary. It determines where data lives, which region and tenant it belongs to, whether a Dataverse database exists, and where policies such as DLP apply. Decisions around it typically cover how many environments to create, how to separate development, test and production, how to use sandboxes, and how to handle the default environment. The environment concept sits under the broader Power Platform topic and underlies the apps, flows and chatbots built there.

power-platform-pipelines.desc: Pipelines in Power Platform is a built-in feature that moves solutions between development, test and production environments to simplify ALM for smaller teams.

faq.a: They are the native deployment pipelines built into Power Platform that move solutions between environments such as development, test and production. They are aimed at simplifying ALM for smaller teams.
faq.q: What are Pipelines in Power Platform?

faq.a: Per Microsoft Learn, they do not deploy Dataverse table data, handle one solution per deployment, do not support cross-tenant deployment, allow one development environment per solution and one host per environment.
faq.q: What limits apply to Pipelines in Power Platform?

faq.a: The sources do not say they replace them. The M365.FM episodes describe Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions as popular tools for CI/CD in Power Platform projects, including automated testing, while the built-in pipelines simplify ALM with less setup.
faq.q: Do Pipelines in Power Platform replace Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions?

power-platform-pipelines.long:
Pipelines in Power Platform are the native deployment pipelines built into Power Platform. They move solutions between environments such as development, test and production and are aimed at simplifying application lifecycle management (ALM) for smaller teams. According to Microsoft Learn, the feature serves as a built-in way to handle ALM and CI/CD automation across Power Platform and Dynamics 365, without requiring a team to assemble its own tooling first.

The setup is organised around a central pipelines host environment. Administrators configure the deployment pipelines in that host, and the environments taking part are linked to it and typed as either development or target environments. Makers can then deploy solutions straight from their development environment, while developers can run pipelines with the Power Platform CLI. This split lets administrators keep control of the stages while makers carry out the day-to-day deployments.

Several checks and controls are part of how a deployment runs. Before deploying, the pipeline checks for missing dependencies and validates connections and variables. The same solution artifact moves through the stages in a fixed order without being exported again, so the package that was tested is the package that reaches the next stage. Approvals can be handled through delegated deployments. At each deployment, managed and unmanaged solutions are backed up in the host. An audit log and Power BI reports are included, and earlier solution versions can be redeployed when rollback is enabled.

Licensing and environment requirements affect planning. Developer-type development and test environments need no standalone license, while other environments must be managed environments, and a production target needs licenses with premium rights. Documented limits include that Dataverse table data is not deployed, that each deployment covers one solution, that cross-tenant deployment is not supported, that each solution has one development environment, and that each environment can be linked to one host. Teams that need to move reference data, span tenants or build more elaborate release flows will have to consider these boundaries.

Pipelines in Power Platform sit alongside other approaches to ALM rather than replacing all of them. The M365.FM episode "Automated Testing for Power Apps and Dataverse" discusses integrating automated testing with CI/CD pipelines and names Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions as popular tools for building such pipelines in Power Platform projects. The episode describes adding approvals, deploying with service principals for secure automation, and running tests as part of a workflow. That is a code-first, tool-driven route, in contrast to the built-in feature described above.

The episode "Deploy Dynamics 365 Customizations with ALM Pipelines" covers the same subject for Microsoft Dynamics 365. It states that pipelines in Power Platform simplify ALM for Microsoft Dynamics 365, bringing automation, continuous integration and continuous delivery, and it lists elements of a strong pipeline architecture: version control with Azure Repos, automated build and release steps, code review requests and minimum branching options for simplicity. It also stresses structuring environments and a branching strategy to support multiple development and deployment stages.

In practice, the choice comes down to team size, governance needs and how much customisation of the release process is required. Smaller teams that mainly need to promote a solution from development through test to production can use the built-in pipelines with limited setup. Teams that need automated testing gates, source control integration or more complex flows may combine them with, or choose, Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions, as the episodes outline.

power-platform-solution.desc: A Power Platform solution is a container that carries an app and its customizable components, such as flows, tables and connectors, between environments.

faq.a: It is a container in Power Platform that carries an app and its customizable components, such as flows, tables and connectors, between environments. It holds metadata and configuration, not business data.
faq.q: What is a Power Platform solution?

faq.a: No. A solution carries metadata and configuration only. Moving records stored in Dataverse is a separate task from deploying the solution package.
faq.q: Does a Power Platform solution contain business data?

faq.a: According to the episode "Migrate Dataverse Data Between Environments Safely", customizations can be transferred and deployed across dev, test and prod environments using solution packages, which supports repeatable and automated migration pipelines.
faq.q: How are solutions used across development, test and production?

power-platform-solution.long:
A Power Platform solution is a container in Power Platform that carries an app together with all of its customizable components from one environment to another. Typical components include apps, flows, tables and connectors. A solution holds metadata and configuration, not business data, which makes it the unit that packages how an application is built rather than the information the application stores.

The main purpose of a solution is to move work between environments in a controlled way. Teams commonly separate development, test and production environments, and a solution is what travels along that path. Because everything that belongs to the application is grouped in a single package, the same set of components can be deployed repeatedly instead of being rebuilt by hand in each environment. Official documentation on solution concepts in application lifecycle management (ALM) describes this role in more detail, and solutions sit within the broader Power Platform family of low-code tools.

In practice, a solution is used whenever an app, a flow or a data model has to leave the place where it was created. A maker builds the components in a development environment, adds them to a solution, and then exports the solution as a package. That package can be imported into a test environment and later into production. The episode "Migrate Dataverse Data Between Environments Safely" connects this to migration work: it says that customizations can be transferred and deployed across environments (dev, test, prod) using solution packages, which enables repeatable and automated migration pipelines. The same episode treats Dataverse migration as a foundation for a Power Platform solution, noting benefits such as unified administration, an integrated platform that combines ERP, CRM and Power Apps, and fewer silos.

The distinction between configuration and data matters for planning. Since a solution carries metadata and configuration only, moving the records stored in tables is a separate task. This is why discussions of migration treat the transport of customizations through solution packages and the transfer of Dataverse data as related but different activities. Anyone planning a deployment needs to decide how components will be packaged and how any existing business data will be handled.

The term also appears in conversations about architecture and careers. In "Architecting Power Platform for Complex Enterprise Solutions with Ian Tweedie [MVP]", the host and a Power Platform Solution Architect discuss what happens when Power Platform applications become business-critical, highly integrated and more complex than a simple maker-first approach. The episode states that low-code does not mean low architecture, and that enterprise solutions almost always include requirements beyond standard low-code capabilities. Structuring components into well-defined packages is part of that kind of disciplined design, although the episode excerpt focuses on the broader architectural questions.

The phrase "Power Platform solution" is also used more loosely in other contexts. In "Microsoft Marketplace - Simply Explained", it appears as an example of something a business leader might look for when searching a global commerce platform that connects customers, software vendors, consultants, AI solutions and cloud services. In career-oriented episodes such as "From SharePoint Developer to Power Platform Architect with Michel Mendes [MVP]" and "Build a Power Platform Career with Nathalie Leenders [MVP-MCT]", the Power Platform Solution Architect Expert certification (PL-600) is described as testing the ability to design, secure and deliver Power Platform solutions. In these cases the wording refers to a delivered business solution in general, while the technical concept described above is the packaging container used for application lifecycle management.

For readers deciding how to approach the topic, the useful starting points are the environment strategy (which environments exist and how work moves between them), the components that belong together in one package, and the separation of configuration from business data. The linked official documentation on solution concepts in ALM covers the underlying model, and the M365.FM episodes above show how the idea appears in migration, enterprise architecture and certification contexts.

power-platform-tenant-isolation.desc: Power Platform tenant isolation is an admin setting that blocks Microsoft Entra ID-based connector connections to other tenants unless they are explicitly allowed.

faq.a: When switched on, it blocks cross-tenant connections made through Microsoft Entra ID-based connectors in both directions, except for tenants on an allow list. It affects only canvas apps and flows.
faq.q: What does Power Platform tenant isolation block?

faq.a: Exceptions are allow-list entries given as a domain or tenant ID, applied to inbound, outbound or both directions. A wildcard entry allows every tenant in a direction.
faq.q: How are exceptions to tenant isolation defined?

faq.a: At runtime, apps and flows that violate the policy fail. At design time, canvas apps cannot add the connection and flows are saved but suspended.
faq.q: What happens to existing apps and flows that use cross-tenant connections?

power-platform-tenant-isolation.long:
Power Platform tenant isolation is a Power Platform administration setting that controls cross-tenant connections made through connectors. It lets administrators decide which Microsoft Entra tenants may be reached from the tenant (outbound) and which external tenants may connect into it (inbound). The stated aim is to keep connector use secure within the tenant and to reduce the risk of data exfiltration. It is a feature of Power Platform and is configured as part of that platform's tenant-level security settings.

The setting applies only to connectors that authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID, such as Office 365 Outlook or SharePoint. It is separate from the Entra-wide tenant restrictions feature, so access outside Power Platform is not affected by it. According to the documentation notes, only canvas apps and flows are affected, and the Azure DevOps connector is not covered because it uses its own OAuth flow. These boundaries matter when judging what tenant isolation does and does not protect.

The behavior depends on whether the setting is switched on. According to the Microsoft Learn documentation, by default the setting is off, and cross-tenant connections work as long as valid Entra credentials are supplied. When isolation is switched on, all tenants are blocked in both directions except those on an allow list. Each allow-list entry can apply to inbound traffic, outbound traffic or both, and can be specified as a domain or as a tenant ID. A wildcard entry allows every tenant in a given direction. The short description of this topic states that the episode context describes the isolation as enforced by default, which can break cross-tenant flows that were never documented. That wording differs from the documentation notes, so the effective default in a given tenant is worth verifying in the admin center.

Administrators configure tenant isolation in the Power Platform admin center under the security and identity settings. The documentation mentions that a Power Platform administrator role is relevant for viewing and setting it. Because the effect is tenant-wide, a typical preparation step is to inventory which apps and flows rely on connections to partner or other tenants, then add those tenants to the allow list in the correct direction before enabling the restriction.

The consequences of a block differ between design time and runtime. At design time, canvas apps cannot add a connection that violates the policy, and flows can still be saved but are suspended. At runtime, apps and flows that violate the policy fail. This is why undocumented cross-tenant dependencies are a common source of surprises: a flow built years earlier that quietly reads a SharePoint site or sends mail through a connection in another tenant can stop working once isolation is enforced, even though nothing in the flow itself changed.

In practice, decisions around tenant isolation come down to balancing collaboration with data-exfiltration risk. Organizations that work with partners or subsidiaries in separate tenants need deliberate allow-list entries, while organizations without such needs can leave the allow list empty and block every external tenant. Using specific domains or tenant IDs is narrower than the wildcard, which opens a whole direction. Since the topic sits under the broader Power Platform area, it is usually reviewed together with other governance and data-protection settings for environments, connectors and flows.

power-platform-tools-vs-code-extension.desc: Power Platform Tools is a Visual Studio Code extension that integrates the Power Platform CLI and supports downloading, editing and uploading Power Pages site content.

faq.a: It is a Visual Studio Code extension that brings the Power Platform CLI into VS Code. It is part of the Power Platform and is used for working with Power Pages site content from the editor.
faq.q: What is the Power Platform Tools extension for Visual Studio Code?

faq.a: It supports downloading, editing and uploading Power Pages site content. This lets site content be worked on locally in Visual Studio Code and then uploaded again.
faq.q: What can the extension do with Power Pages site content?

faq.a: Installation guidance is provided in Microsoft Learn documentation on installing the Visual Studio Code extension for Power Platform development.
faq.q: Where can installation instructions be found?

power-platform-tools-vs-code-extension.long:
Power Platform Tools extension for Visual Studio Code is a Visual Studio Code extension that brings the Power Platform CLI into the VS Code editor. It is part of the Power Platform ecosystem and is aimed at developers who prefer to work with Power Platform assets from a code editor rather than only through browser-based designers.

According to the available description, the extension supports downloading, editing and uploading Power Pages site content. This allows site files to be retrieved to a local workspace, modified with the editing features of Visual Studio Code, and then uploaded back to the Power Platform environment. Because the extension exposes the Power Platform CLI inside VS Code, command-line operations can be run from within the same development environment.

Installation and usage details are described in Microsoft's official developer documentation for installing the Visual Studio Code extension. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity, so this page is limited to the product description and its relationship to Power Platform.

power-query-m.desc: Power Query M is the functional, case-sensitive formula language used to express data mashups in Power Query across Power BI, Excel and other Microsoft services.
power-query-m.long:
The Power Query M formula language, often shortened to Power Query M, is the formula language behind Power Query. It is described as functional and case-sensitive, and it is used to express data mashups: the steps that connect to data sources, shape the data and combine it into a result.

Power Query M sits within the broader Power Query topic. Power Query appears in several Microsoft products, including Power BI and Excel, as well as other Microsoft services, and the M language is the common formula language used to express queries across them. Because the language is case-sensitive, names of functions and identifiers need to be written exactly as defined.

Official reference material for the language is published in the Microsoft Learn documentation for Power Query M. That documentation is the primary source for language syntax, function references and specification details.

On M365.FM, Power Query M is tracked as a concept entity that links to the broader Power Query topic. No specific episodes are associated with this entry at this time.

power-usage-effectiveness.desc: Power usage effectiveness (PUE) is the ratio of a data center's total facility energy to the energy consumed by its IT equipment, with values above 1.0 showing overhead.
power-usage-effectiveness.long:
Power usage effectiveness (PUE) is a metric that compares the total energy used by a data center facility with the energy used by the IT equipment inside it. It is expressed as a ratio, so a facility whose entire energy draw went to IT equipment would score 1.0.

In practice, values are above 1.0 because a facility also consumes energy for overhead such as cooling and power conversion. The further a value sits above 1.0, the larger the share of total facility energy that goes to something other than the IT equipment itself.

PUE is used to describe and compare the energy overhead of data center operations, for example when tracking changes in a facility over time or discussing infrastructure efficiency. Because it is a ratio of facility energy to IT energy, it describes overhead rather than the amount of useful computing work performed.

No related topics or M365.FM episodes are linked to this entry at present.

power-virtual-agents.desc: Power Virtual Agents (PVA) was Microsoft's no-code chatbot builder in the Power Platform and has since been merged into Microsoft Copilot Studio.

faq.a: Power Virtual Agents (PVA) was the no-code chatbot builder of the Power Platform, developed by Microsoft. It allowed people without programming skills to create chatbots through a graphical interface.
faq.q: What was Power Virtual Agents?

faq.a: According to the catalog data, it was merged into Microsoft Copilot Studio. The name now mostly appears in older documentation and existing environments, so current capabilities should be checked under Copilot Studio.
faq.q: What happened to Power Virtual Agents?

faq.a: It was one component of the Power Platform alongside Power Apps, Power Automate and Power BI. The M365.FM episodes mention it as the part used to build chatbots for customer support and routine tasks.
faq.q: How does Power Virtual Agents relate to the rest of the Power Platform?

power-virtual-agents.long:
Power Virtual Agents, abbreviated PVA, was the no-code chatbot builder of the Power Platform. It let people without programming skills create conversational bots through a graphical interface. The product was developed by Microsoft and is classed as both a Microsoft tool and a low-code tool. According to the catalog data, it was first released in November 2019 and has since been merged into Microsoft Copilot Studio, so the name now appears mainly in older documentation, existing environments and legacy material.

The purpose of Power Virtual Agents was to make chatbot creation available to people outside traditional development teams. The M365.FM episodes describe it as a way to create intelligent chatbots that improve customer service and automate common tasks without coding skills. Typical uses mentioned in the episodes include customer support and engagement, as well as handling routine requests that would otherwise need staff time. Because the building work happened in a visual interface rather than in code, the product fit the low-code approach that defines much of the Power Platform.

Power Virtual Agents was part of the Power Platform, where it sat next to Power Apps, Power Automate and Power BI. In that family, Power Apps covers custom applications, Power Automate covers workflow automation, Power BI turns raw data into reports, and Power Virtual Agents covered conversational bots. The episode "Power Platform Scalability Limits and Fixes" notes that license types affect access to premium connectors such as Microsoft Dataverse and Power Virtual Agents, which shows that licensing and capacity were part of planning any solution that included bots. The episode "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform" describes rendering Azure OpenAI responses as Adaptive Cards and integrating them into Power Virtual Agents or Teams bots, aiming for rich conversational interfaces without heavy front-end code.

The M365.FM episodes place the product within the wider platform story. "Power Platform - Simply Explained" introduces the Power Platform as an integrated low-code platform and lists Power Virtual Agents among its components, alongside the point that the platform integrates with Microsoft 365 applications to support collaboration and operational efficiency. "Reduce Developer Backlogs with Citizen Automation" mentions Power Virtual Agents as a way to build chatbots that improve customer support, and stresses that strong governance should accompany citizen development so that data security and compliance are maintained while users innovate. "AI, Power Platform & Developer Experience: The Next Frontier with Reza Niroomand [MVP]" discusses AI capabilities in Power Virtual Agents as a way to create tailored interactions for users.

For readers who meet the name PVA today, the practical point is terminology. Since the product has been merged into Microsoft Copilot Studio, current capabilities should be looked up under that name, and older guides may describe screens, terms or licensing that no longer match the present product. Existing bots and environments created under the old name may still be encountered, which is why the term remains relevant when maintaining or migrating older solutions. Checking the current Microsoft documentation is the reliable way to confirm present terminology and capabilities.

In short, Power Virtual Agents represents the earlier stage of Microsoft's no-code approach to conversational bots within the Power Platform. Its role, building chatbots visually without coding, continues under the Copilot Studio name, while the older name persists in legacy material and in the episodes that describe the platform's components.

powerpages-chat-participant.desc: The @powerpages chat participant is a GitHub Copilot Chat feature in Visual Studio Code, part of the Power Platform Tools extension, offering Power Pages-aware code help in preview.

faq.a: It is a participant in GitHub Copilot Chat for Visual Studio Code, included in the Power Platform Tools extension. It provides Power Pages-aware code generation and explanations.
faq.q: What is the @powerpages chat participant?

faq.a: According to the documentation, it supports code generation and explanations for Power Pages, with Liquid and form validation given as examples.
faq.q: What kinds of tasks does the @powerpages chat participant support?

faq.a: No. The feature is described as being in preview, so its behavior and availability may change.
faq.q: Is the @powerpages chat participant generally available?

powerpages-chat-participant.long:
The @powerpages chat participant is a participant in GitHub Copilot Chat for Visual Studio Code. It is delivered as part of the Power Platform Tools extension and is documented as a preview capability.

Its purpose is to provide Power Pages-aware code generation and explanations inside the editor. Examples named in the documentation include help with Liquid templates and form validation. By addressing the participant by name within Copilot Chat, a developer can direct a question or request to Power Pages-specific context rather than to general-purpose assistance.

As a preview feature, its behavior and availability may change. Details on configuration and usage are described in Microsoft Learn under the Power Pages documentation for GitHub Copilot Chat.

No episodes on M365.FM are currently linked to this topic, and no related entities have been specified in the available facts.

powerpoint.desc: Microsoft PowerPoint is the Microsoft 365 presentation application for slides, templates, animations and live presenting, with co-authoring and Copilot support.

faq.a: Microsoft PowerPoint is used to create slides, apply templates and animations, present live, and co-author decks with others. It is commonly applied to meetings, training material and reports.
faq.q: What is Microsoft PowerPoint used for?

faq.a: Microsoft 365 Copilot can draft and edit slides, and PowerPoint supports Copilot-generated decks that provide a first draft of a presentation. The M365.FM episodes also discuss where Copilot helps and where it still has limits.
faq.q: How does Copilot relate to PowerPoint?

faq.a: Yes, PowerPoint for the web is the browser version and is listed as a related product. PowerPoint itself is part of Microsoft 365 Apps and is included with the Microsoft 365 license.
faq.q: Is there a browser version of PowerPoint?

powerpoint.long:
Microsoft PowerPoint is the presentation software of Microsoft 365. It is used to build slides, apply templates and animations, present live, and work on a deck together with other people through co-authoring. It also supports Copilot-generated decks, in which a first draft of a presentation is created with AI assistance. The product is developed by Microsoft and has been available since 1990, according to the product data.

PowerPoint belongs to Microsoft 365 Apps, the group of installable Office applications, and is classed as both a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool. Typical uses include meetings, training material and reports. A browser version, PowerPoint for the web, is available as a related product, and Microsoft Teams is the place where presentations are commonly shared and shown during meetings. Licensing is included with Microsoft 365, so organizations that already use the Microsoft 365 Apps have the application available without a separate product.

A central decision around PowerPoint is how much of the work to standardize and how much to leave to individual authors. Corporate templates are one lever: they define layout and design once so that decks look consistent across a company. Another is the choice between the installed application and PowerPoint for the web, depending on whether a user needs the full desktop feature set or quick access and shared editing in a browser. Co-authoring adds a third consideration, since several people can edit the same deck instead of passing files back and forth.

Copilot is the other main topic linked to PowerPoint. Microsoft 365 Copilot is related to PowerPoint because it can draft and edit slides, and the M365.FM material describes it working across Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams. The episode "Use GPT-5 in Microsoft 365 Copilot" says the move to GPT-5 is meant to give first-try outputs that match a user's voice and goal, including smarter charts and slides, and to reduce time spent on formatting.
