The episode "Replace Traditional M365 Training with In-Flow Learning" describes Copilot giving contextual tips inside apps such as Word, Excel and PowerPoint while users work.

The episode "PowerPoint Like a Pro- Hidden Features, Corporate Templates & Copilot with Fiona Walsh [MVP]" features a Microsoft PowerPoint MVP who has more than 20 years of experience helping organizations improve presentations and presentation skills. The episode says PowerPoint is one of the most widely used business applications in the world, yet many professionals only use a small part of it. It covers features that experienced users tend to overlook, corporate templates, and where Copilot genuinely helps and where it still has work to do.

The episode "Beyond the Prompt: Mastering Microsoft Copilot for Real Productivity with Jess Stratton [MVP]" looks at Copilot across the Microsoft 365 apps. It recommends multi-part prompts, in which a large project is divided into small steps, and follow-up prompts that refine a draft by adjusting style, correcting errors and adding missing context. These approaches apply to drafting slide content as well as text documents.

Governance is the final theme. The episode "Copilot in Office Apps: The Governance Checklist" explains that Copilot draws on emails, files, meetings and notes through Microsoft Graph, and says that privacy, data loss prevention and audit workloads increase once Copilot is switched on. For PowerPoint, that means the content of decks and the sources Copilot can reach should be considered before wide rollout. Official documentation for the application is published on Microsoft's support site.

powerpoint-online.desc: PowerPoint for the web is the browser version of Microsoft PowerPoint for creating, presenting and co-authoring slide decks without installing the desktop app.

faq.a: PowerPoint for the web, also called PowerPoint Online, is the browser version of Microsoft PowerPoint. It is used to create, present and co-author slide decks without installing the desktop app, and it is included in Microsoft 365.
faq.q: What is PowerPoint for the web?

faq.a: It is a related product developed by Microsoft that opens and edits presentations from the desktop application, Microsoft PowerPoint. It belongs to Office on the web, together with the browser versions of Word, Excel, OneNote and Outlook.
faq.q: How does PowerPoint for the web relate to Microsoft PowerPoint?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Settings and Configuration" states that Copilot needs third-party cookies enabled to work with Office web applications such as PowerPoint Online. Blocking them can cause failures when retrieving files to reference.
faq.q: Why do third-party cookies matter for Copilot in PowerPoint Online?

powerpoint-online.long:
PowerPoint for the web, also known as PowerPoint Online or PowerPoint im Web, is the browser version of PowerPoint for creating, presenting and co-authoring slide decks. It was developed by Microsoft and runs in a web browser, so no installation of the desktop application is needed. It is included in Microsoft 365 and is classified both as a Microsoft tool and as a collaboration tool.

PowerPoint for the web is part of Office on the web, the set of browser-based Office applications that also includes the web versions of Word, Excel, OneNote and Outlook. It is related to Microsoft PowerPoint, the desktop application, and it opens and edits presentations that originate there. In practice this means a deck started in the desktop app can be continued in a browser, and the reverse also applies.

The product is typically used in situations where flexibility matters more than the full desktop feature set. Teams use it to prepare presentations together with colleagues, to co-author the same deck at the same time, to make last-minute changes shortly before a meeting, and to present directly from a browser on any device. Because the work happens in the browser, it suits environments where installing software is restricted or where a person switches between devices.

A typical decision around the product is whether to work in the browser version or in the desktop app. The web version covers creating, presenting and co-authoring, which fits collaborative and ad hoc work. Anyone who depends on the desktop application for a particular task can continue to use Microsoft PowerPoint alongside it, since both work on the same presentations. Official documentation for the product is published by Microsoft in its PowerPoint support pages.

One M365.FM episode touches on this topic: "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Settings and Configuration" (2025-11-03). The episode explains why Microsoft Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot sometimes work well and sometimes do not respond, and attributes much of that to configuration, licensing and the tight dependencies Copilot has on the rest of the environment. In its troubleshooting steps, the episode states that for Copilot to work with Office web applications such as Word Online, PowerPoint Online and Excel Online, third-party cookies must be enabled. According to the episode, blocking third-party cookies can cause failures when Copilot tries to retrieve files to reference, and it recommends checking the browser settings and enabling third-party cookies to avoid connectivity problems. The episode is about Copilot in general and does not cover PowerPoint for the web in any other detail.

For anyone using PowerPoint for the web together with Copilot, the practical takeaway from that episode is that browser configuration is part of the setup. Cookie settings in the browser can influence whether features that rely on file access behave as expected, so they are one of the first items to check when something does not work in the web apps.

powershell.desc: PowerShell is Microsoft's command-line shell and scripting language for Windows and other platforms, used to automate tasks across Windows, Azure and Microsoft 365.

faq.a: PowerShell is Microsoft's command-line shell and scripting language for Windows and other platforms. It is used to automate repetitive tasks and manage systems, including Windows, Azure and Microsoft 365.
faq.q: What is PowerShell?

faq.a: No. The episode "PowerShell - Simply Explained" says it is about saving time by replacing repetitive clicks with repeatable automation, and it is aimed at IT professionals, administrators and developers alike.
faq.q: Is PowerShell only for programmers?

faq.a: The episode "PowerShell vs Bicep for Azure Infrastructure Automation" says PowerShell reaches its limits for modern cloud infrastructure at scale and presents Azure Bicep as the preferred Infrastructure as Code language for deploying and maintaining Azure resources.
faq.q: When is Bicep discussed as an alternative to PowerShell?

powershell.long:
PowerShell is Microsoft's command-line shell and scripting language for Windows and other platforms. It is used by IT professionals, administrators and developers to automate repetitive tasks, manage systems at scale and control many aspects of Windows, Azure and Microsoft 365. The M365.FM episode "PowerShell - Simply Explained" stresses that PowerShell is not only a tool for programmers: its core value is saving time by replacing repetitive clicks with repeatable, reliable automation.

In practice, PowerShell serves as both an interactive shell and a scripting environment. Administrators can run single commands to query or change settings, or combine commands into scripts that run the same way every time. The episode "PowerShell Automation with Harm Veenstra [MVP]" describes it as far more than a scripting language for administrators and instead as an automation platform. According to that episode, it can simplify repetitive tasks, connect services and save many hours in different environments, from Microsoft 365 and Azure automation to local system management, reporting, APIs and DevOps workflows. The session covers practical automation examples from several of these areas.

PowerShell is closely tied to Microsoft 365 administration. For years, PowerShell scripts formed the foundation of Microsoft 365 automation. The episode "Modern Microsoft 365 Automation Beyond PowerShell Scripts" explains that IT admins built large script libraries to onboard users, assign licenses, provision devices, configure Exchange, manage permissions and automate other operational work across cloud and hybrid environments. The same episode also discusses why enterprise IT is changing and why traditional PowerShell-driven approaches are being questioned. It points to challenges around legacy automation, including excessive permissions, credential handling, deprecated modules and maintenance overhead, and it notes that Microsoft continues to standardize its tooling.

A related topic is Microsoft Graph. The episode "Microsoft Graph and PowerShell for Enterprise Automation" describes Microsoft Graph as far more than another API and as the operational backbone of Microsoft 365. It argues that relying only on admin portals limits scalability, visibility and automation, while Microsoft Graph offers a unified interface for managing identities, users, groups, Teams, SharePoint, security, compliance and business data across the Microsoft ecosystem. In this context, PowerShell is the scripting layer from which such interfaces can be used for enterprise automation.

For Azure, the episode "PowerShell vs Bicep for Azure Infrastructure Automation" draws a distinction. It states that PowerShell has become the automation standard for Microsoft environments but reaches its limits when managing modern cloud infrastructure at scale. The episode presents Azure Bicep as the preferred Infrastructure as Code language for deploying and maintaining Azure resources and warns that relying solely on PowerShell can create long-term operational challenges. The discussion centers on the difference between imperative and declarative automation: PowerShell scripts describe the steps to perform, while Bicep describes the desired state of resources.

Typical decisions around PowerShell therefore involve choosing the right tool for the task. Short administrative jobs, reporting, connecting services and day-to-day Microsoft 365 operations are natural uses for scripts, while large-scale Azure infrastructure deployment is discussed in the episodes as better suited to a declarative language. Teams that maintain older script libraries also face questions about permissions, credential handling and module lifecycles. Across the episodes, the common theme is that PowerShell remains a central automation skill in the Microsoft ecosystem, while its role is being weighed against newer approaches for specific scenarios.

powershell-module.desc: A PowerShell module is a package of commands for a specific job or service, installed once and loaded when needed, as in the Az and Microsoft Graph modules.

faq.a: A PowerShell module is a package of PowerShell commands for a specific job or service. It is installed once and loaded when needed, for example the Az module for Azure resources.
faq.q: What is a PowerShell module?

faq.a: The episodes show the Install-Module command, for example installing the Az module from the PSGallery repository with the CurrentUser scope. They advise keeping modules updated for security patches and new features.
faq.q: How is a PowerShell module installed?

faq.a: The episodes name the Azure Active Directory, MicrosoftTeams, ExchangeOnlineManagement, Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell and MSOnline modules, plus the Microsoft Graph PowerShell module and the Az module for Azure.
faq.q: Which PowerShell modules are mentioned for Microsoft 365?

powershell-module.long:
A PowerShell module is a package of PowerShell commands built for a specific job or service. It is installed once and then loaded into a session when the commands are needed. Instead of writing every task from scratch, administrators and developers rely on modules that bundle the cmdlets for a given product, such as Azure, Exchange Online, SharePoint or Microsoft Teams.

The M365.FM episodes show that modules are the usual way to reach Microsoft cloud services from a script. The episode "Azure CLI vs PowerShell: Which Should You Use?" explains that Azure PowerShell consists of cmdlets packaged as a PowerShell module named Az, while Azure CLI offers executable commands that run in several shells. In the comparison given there, Azure PowerShell works on Windows, macOS and Linux and requires Windows PowerShell or PowerShell. The same episode notes that these tools can be combined with Azure Functions and GitHub Actions to build event-driven workflows, an approach it says many DevOps teams use to keep cloud resources in sync.

For Microsoft 365, the episode "Run Your Full Stack Locally with .NET Aspire" lists several modules by task. The Azure Active Directory module is named for user and group management. The MicrosoftTeams module helps control teams and meetings. The ExchangeOnlineManagement module manages mailboxes and email settings. The Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell module gives access to SharePoint sites and permissions. The MSOnline module is described as a way to manage users, groups and licenses in a Microsoft 365 tenant and to automate user creation and license assignment. The episode advises always installing the latest version of each module, because new versions include security updates and new features for Microsoft 365.

Installing a module is typically done with the Install-Module command. The episode "PowerShell Automation for Azure and Microsoft 365 with Matthew Dowst [MVP]" shows installing the Az module with the CurrentUser scope from the PSGallery repository, and stresses keeping modules updated to receive current features and security patches. It also mentions that the account used for such work should have a suitable administrator role, such as Exchange Administrator or SharePoint Administrator, and that multi-factor authentication should be enabled for extra security.

Modules also appear in unattended automation. The episode "Use Managed Identity with PowerShell for Microsoft Graph" describes setting up the Microsoft Graph PowerShell module. Its listed requirements are PowerShell 7.2 or later, .NET Framework 4.7.2 or newer and the latest PowerShellGet module. After installing the module, a session connects to the tenant with the Connect-MgGraph command and the scopes the task needs, for example User.ReadWrite.All and Directory.ReadWrite.All. The episode notes that scopes can be adjusted to the needs of the automation.

Modules matter for governance and cost work as well. In "Build an Automated Azure Cleanup Engine to Reduce Cloud Waste", the latest Azure PowerShell module is called essential for scripting and automation. According to the episode, it can loop through subscriptions and resource groups and find role assignments with an object type of 'Unknown' so they can be removed. The episode pairs it with Azure CLI and Resource Graph for advanced queries and reporting, and recommends granting permissions at the smallest effective scope using built-in Azure RBAC roles.

In practice, choosing a PowerShell module means matching the module to the service being managed, keeping it current, and granting only the permissions the task requires. Whether to use a module-based approach such as Azure PowerShell or a shell-independent tool such as Azure CLI is a decision the episodes frame around the platform, shell and workflow in use.

powershell-pipeline.desc: The PowerShell pipeline is the mechanism, written as a vertical bar, that passes the output of one command as input to the next so small commands can be chained.
powershell-pipeline.long:
The PowerShell pipeline is a core concept in PowerShell. It is written as a vertical bar placed between two commands, and it sends the output of the command on the left to the command on the right as its input.

The pipeline is used to combine small, single-purpose commands into longer sequences. Instead of writing one large command that does everything, a user can chain several commands so that each one handles a single step and hands its result to the next. This approach is a common way of building scripts and one-line administrative tasks in PowerShell.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, PowerShell is widely used for administration and automation, and the pipeline is the feature that lets commands from different areas be linked together in one expression.

No specific M365.FM episodes, linked topics or official documentation are recorded for this entry at present, so this page limits itself to the definition and general purpose of the concept.

ppr-knowledge-graph.desc: A PPR knowledge graph links product, process and resource data from ERP, MES, historian and maintenance records so people and AI can trace how production came together.

faq.a: PPR stands for product-process-resource. The model describes a production system through the products being made, the processes that make them and the resources that carry those processes out.
faq.q: What does PPR stand for in a PPR knowledge graph?

faq.a: The episode says ERP, MES and other systems each hold isolated records that do not automatically explain how a product, process and resource came together. A PPR knowledge graph links those records so AI can work with that context.
faq.q: Why does manufacturing AI need a PPR knowledge graph?

faq.a: According to the research paper, the graph is paired with large language model chatbots so operators, production planners and engineers can query it in natural language.
faq.q: How can people query a PPR knowledge graph?

ppr-knowledge-graph.long:
A PPR knowledge graph is a knowledge graph built on the product-process-resource (PPR) model. It connects records that normally sit in separate manufacturing systems, so that people and AI can trace how a given product, the process that made it and the resources used came together at a particular moment in production. The term is explained in the M365.FM episode "What Is a PPR Knowledge Graph — and Why Manufacturing AI Needs One".

The underlying PPR model describes a production system through three things: the products being made, the processes that make them and the resources that carry those processes out. According to a research paper on Product-Process-Resource Asset Knowledge Graphs, the model can be traced to ISA-95 and VDI 3682. The paper builds on it to propose a PPR Asset Knowledge Graph, an industry-oriented semantic model implemented as an OWL ontology. The point of such a graph is that product, process and resource are not treated as separate lists but as explicitly related things.

The problem it addresses is described in the episode. Factory AI can often read large volumes of data but lacks an understanding of the actual plant environment. ERP systems know the orders, MES know what happened on the line, and other systems hold sensor histories and maintenance records. These isolated records do not automatically explain how a product, process and resource came together at any given time. The episode says this missing connection is where promising AI initiatives lose their footing. A PPR knowledge graph is presented as the layer that supplies that connection by linking ERP, MES, historian and maintenance records.

The research paper gives a concrete picture of how such a graph can be used. It aims to close gaps in conventional model-driven engineering of cyber-physical production systems, especially in representing undesired conditions and errors in flexible production such as robotic workcells, where Industry 4.0 flexibility can undermine classic quality assurance. The graph is paired with large language model chatbots so that operators, production planners and engineers can query it in natural language. The authors evaluated the approach on electric vehicle battery remanufacturing and report that it supports resource allocation based on explicitly modelled capabilities and helps identify and reduce undesired conditions.

Typical situations where this matters include tracing why a product was made under certain conditions, deciding which resource is suitable for a process based on its modelled capabilities, and finding the context behind an error or undesired condition. For AI use in a plant, the decision is less about the model itself and more about whether the underlying data carries the relationships between products, processes and resources. A graph makes those relationships explicit, which is what lets a chatbot or analysis tool answer questions with context rather than from isolated records.

One caveat applies to the sources. The research paper is an abstract and does not itself mention linking ERP, MES, historian or maintenance records; that framing comes from the M365.FM episode. The paper supports the PPR model, the ontology-based graph, the natural-language querying and the battery remanufacturing evaluation, while the episode supplies the plant-data integration perspective.

predictive-analytics.desc: Predictive analytics applies statistical or AI models to historical and current data to forecast outcomes such as churn, delays or pipeline conversion.

faq.a: Predictive analytics uses historical and current data with statistical or AI models to forecast likely future outcomes, such as supply delays, pipeline conversion or customer churn.
faq.q: What is predictive analytics?

faq.a: The episodes mention it in Excel with AI, in Copilot, in Dynamics 365 Project Operations, in Power BI combined with Copilot, and in CRM-style apps built with Power Apps.
faq.q: Where does predictive analytics appear in the Microsoft ecosystem according to M365.FM?

faq.a: The episode "Connect Microsoft Copilot to Predictive Power BI" describes surfacing forecasts, trends and risk indicators in conversational workflows, moving from "What happened?" to "What is likely to happen next?", and it emphasizes governance and data quality.
faq.q: What does the Power BI and Copilot episode say about predictive analytics?

predictive-analytics.long:
Predictive analytics is the use of historical and current data together with statistical or AI models to forecast likely future outcomes. Typical examples include supply delays, pipeline conversion and customer churn. Instead of describing only what has already happened, the approach estimates what is likely to happen next, which gives teams a basis for acting earlier.

In practice, predictive analytics is used to anticipate trends, risks and customer needs so that decisions can be made proactively. The M365.FM episodes place it in several Microsoft-related settings. In Excel, AI-assisted features are described as a way to forecast trends from historical data and to make more informed decisions about future outcomes. In customer-facing scenarios, predictive analytics is described as a way to anticipate customer needs so that issues can be addressed before they escalate. In project delivery and sales scenarios, it is presented as a way to look ahead at outcomes rather than only report on the past.

The episode "From Excel Expert to Microsoft MVP: Empowering Millions with Data, Dashboards & AI with Karen Abecia [Microsoft MVP]" describes predictive analytics as one capability of AI in Excel. According to the episode, it allows users to forecast trends based on historical data. The same discussion contrasts isolated calculations with automating entire workflows, and names automated data entry and importing data from various sources as related uses of AI.

The episode "Microsoft 365 Copilot Agents: Real Business Value with Steve Corey [MVP]" lists predictive analytics in Copilot among the business benefits it discusses, alongside collaboration tools, personalized customer interactions and reduced administrative overhead. In this framing, the forecasting element helps businesses anticipate customer needs and improve service by addressing problems proactively.

The episode "Dynamics 365 Project Operations with Joe Griffin [MVP]" covers predictive analytics in Dynamics 365 Project Operations. It describes the use of AI and machine learning to forecast project outcomes with greater accuracy, with real-time insights into performance, risks, costs and resource needs. The episode connects this to proactive project management, and it mentions skills matching and workload balancing as neighboring capabilities that support optimization.

The episode "Connect Microsoft Copilot to Predictive Power BI" treats predictive analytics as a key theme. It describes Power BI as a semantic and analytical layer that feeds AI-powered experiences, so that users can ask questions in natural language through Copilot and receive contextual answers backed by governed Power BI models. By combining Copilot with Power BI datasets, organizations can surface forecasts, trends, risk indicators and business predictions inside conversational workflows. The episode describes this as a move from asking "What happened?" to "What is likely to happen next?" and "What actions should we take?" It also stresses governance and data quality as important conditions for this kind of use.

The episode "Power Apps Code Apps with Carike Botha [MVP]" mentions predictive analytics in the context of a sales pipeline and CRM management application, where centralizing lead data and automating reminders go together with gaining predictive analytics.

Across these episodes, a common point is that the quality of a forecast depends on the data behind it. Governed models, reliable historical data and clear business questions are the recurring prerequisites mentioned, while the specific forecasting method, whether a statistical model or machine learning, depends on the product and scenario in use.

predictive-lead-scoring.desc: Predictive lead and opportunity scoring in Dynamics 365 Sales uses a model trained on historical sales outcomes to rank leads and opportunities.

faq.a: It uses a model trained on historical sales outcomes to score leads and opportunities by their likelihood to convert or close, helping sellers prioritize their work.
faq.q: What does predictive lead and opportunity scoring do in Dynamics 365 Sales?

faq.a: According to the episode "Predictive Lead Scoring with Dynamics 365", it requires Dynamics 365 Sales with Sales Insights or predictive scoring enabled in the license, and enough historical leads with a closed status, both won and lost, with consistent close reasons.
faq.q: What is needed before predictive lead scoring can be enabled?

faq.a: The episode "Dynamics 365 Sales Accelerator - Simply Explained" lists predictive scoring among the capabilities that help teams prioritize leads and opportunities within the guided selling experience.
faq.q: How does predictive scoring relate to Sales Accelerator?

predictive-lead-scoring.long:
Predictive lead and opportunity scoring is a capability of Dynamics 365 Sales that applies a model trained on historical sales outcomes to score leads and opportunities by their likelihood to convert or close. It is also referred to as predictive lead scoring, predictive opportunity scoring or simply predictive scoring. The purpose is to help sellers decide where to spend their attention, so that records with a higher likelihood of a successful outcome can be worked first.

The approach rests on past results. The episode "Predictive Lead Scoring with Dynamics 365" describes the model as blending several kinds of signal: who a lead is, what the lead did, how fast and in what order those actions happened, and how similar leads ended. That includes patterns such as the number of actions and desktop versus mobile behavior. In the episode's words, the score combines these elements into a single indication that a seller can act on, instead of relying on gut feeling alone.

Setup is described in the same episode as a task of roughly 15 to 45 minutes once the prerequisites are in place. The prerequisites it names are Dynamics 365 Sales with Sales Insights or predictive scoring enabled in the license, and a sufficient volume of historical leads with a closed status, both won and lost, along with consistent close reasons. Scoring is then turned on in the Sales Insights settings under predictive models, where lead scoring is selected. The administrator chooses the target entity, confirms the outcome fields and picks a training data window, for example the last 6 to 18 months. Fields and filters are chosen next, and the episode advises including meaningful columns rather than overloading the model. The official documentation for configuring predictive lead scoring covers the same configuration path in more detail.

The data quality point is practical. Because the model learns from closed leads, inconsistent close reasons or too little history limit what it can learn. Teams considering the feature therefore need to decide how far back training data should reach and which fields describe the business meaningfully, and they need to keep outcome recording consistent in daily use.

Predictive scoring is one part of the wider Sales Insights offering. The episode "Dynamics 365 Sales Insights - Simply Explained" places predictive lead and opportunity scoring alongside the Sales Insights assistant, Auto Capture, Email Engagement, relationship intelligence, conversation intelligence and forecasting. The shared idea in that episode is using AI and activity signals to help sales teams focus their attention and know what to do next.

Scores also feed guided selling. The episode "Dynamics 365 Sales Accelerator - Simply Explained" describes Sales Accelerator as a guided selling experience inside Dynamics 365 Sales, with an Up Next work list and sequences, and lists predictive scoring among the capabilities that help teams prioritize leads and opportunities and organize daily activities. The episode adds that automation helps in some areas while human judgment remains essential, which is a sensible way to read any score: as input to a seller's decision, not a replacement for it.

A further episode, "LinkedIn Sales Navigator and Dynamics 365 Sales Integration", summarizes predictive scoring as machine learning that predicts the success of leads and opportunities based on historical data, and sets it next to relationship analytics and the LinkedIn integration. Together these describe how scoring complements other sources of customer insight. The episode "Connect Microsoft Copilot to Predictive Power BI" mentions predictive scoring in a different context, as part of predictive models in a business intelligence pipeline, which is a separate topic from the Dynamics 365 Sales feature.

predictive-maintenance.desc: Predictive maintenance uses condition evidence such as sensor data to flag developing equipment faults early enough for maintenance to plan action before failure.

faq.a: Predictive maintenance uses condition evidence such as sensor measurements to warn about developing equipment faults early enough for maintenance to plan an intervention before functional failure.
faq.q: What is predictive maintenance?

faq.a: The episode "Predictive Maintenance on Azure for Manufacturers: What You Actually Need Before the Model" says to start with the maintenance decision and work back to the evidence, data and process needed before choosing a model.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode on predictive maintenance on Azure recommend as a starting point?

faq.a: No. The episode "Upgrade Java 8 Apps to Java 21 with AI Agents" describes predictive maintenance applied to legacy Java runtime environments, using system logs, performance metrics and usage patterns to detect potential failures before they happen.
faq.q: Is predictive maintenance only used for physical machinery?

predictive-maintenance.long:
Predictive maintenance is an approach to equipment upkeep that uses condition evidence, such as sensor measurements, to warn about developing faults early enough for maintenance teams to plan an intervention before a functional failure occurs. The central idea is timing: a warning only has value if it arrives with enough lead time for people to act on it. A prediction that comes too late, or that nobody is set up to respond to, does not change the outcome for the asset.

In practice, predictive maintenance links three things: evidence from the equipment, an analytical method that interprets that evidence, and a maintenance process that turns a warning into a planned job. The evidence is typically sensor readings taken from an asset while it runs. The analytical step can involve data platforms and machine learning, but the show notes stress that the model is not the starting point. The starting point is the maintenance decision that the warning is meant to support, and the evidence and data needed to support that decision follow from it.

The M365.FM episode "Predictive Maintenance on Azure for Manufacturers: What You Actually Need Before the Model" takes this decision-first view. The episode is part of the iFAKT series and says that predictive maintenance on Azure only pays off when a warning arrives early enough for a team to act on it. It proposes working backward from the maintenance decision to the evidence, data and process required before choosing a model. According to the description, the episode follows one hypothetical asset from sensor reading onward and covers how to connect Azure data and machine learning to the maintenance process that technicians already follow. It is aimed at maintenance managers, reliability engineers, plant and production leaders, and OT and IT architects. A second listing of the same episode repeats this framing: define the decision first, then connect Azure data to the maintenance process.

Predictive maintenance also appears in other M365.FM episodes, mostly as one item in a broader list of benefits. The episode "From Pilot to Production: Building Enterprise AI That Actually Delivers with Leon Gordon [MVP]" mentions manufacturing AI that improves production efficiency, minimizes downtime with predictive maintenance and improves sustainability. In the same discussion, tools for building enterprise AI are described as needing to integrate with existing systems while offering governance and compliance features, and Microsoft Fabric is presented there as a unified data platform. That context shows how predictive maintenance is typically positioned: as an industrial use case that depends on a solid data foundation.

The episode "Upgrade Java 8 Apps to Java 21 with AI Agents" uses the term in a software setting. There, predictive maintenance is described as AI that monitors legacy Java runtime environments continuously and detects potential failures before they happen by analyzing system logs, performance metrics and usage patterns. The stated benefit is avoiding costly downtime and reducing maintenance effort by scheduling updates and fixes at suitable times. This shows the concept applied to IT systems rather than physical machinery, using logs and metrics as the condition evidence instead of sensor measurements.

The episode "Scale Azure Logic Apps Beyond Custom Connectors" touches the topic more loosely. It argues that automating repetitive tasks reduces maintenance costs and frees a team to focus on higher-value work, naming predictive maintenance and testing strategies as examples of that work.

Typical decisions around predictive maintenance follow from these sources. Teams need to define which maintenance decision a warning should support, determine what evidence is available from the asset, check that the data can reach the place where it is analyzed, and confirm that the maintenance workflow can use the warning in time. Only after those questions are answered does the choice of model become meaningful. The M365.FM material consistently treats the model as the last piece rather than the first.

premium-connectors.desc: Premium connectors in Power Platform are connectors classified as premium, requiring additional licensing beyond the standard connectors included with Microsoft 365.
premium-connectors.long:
Premium connectors (Power Platform) are connectors within Power Platform that are classified as premium rather than standard. They typically cover specialized or external systems, and custom connectors fall into this category as well. Using them requires additional licensing beyond what is included with Microsoft 365.

The distinction matters when planning apps, flows and other solutions built on Power Platform. Standard connectors are available under the licensing already included with Microsoft 365, while a solution that relies on a premium connector needs extra licensing for the people or workloads that use it. Checking the connector classification early helps avoid licensing gaps when a solution moves from design to production.

Premium connectors sit under the broader topic of Power Platform, which is the family of low-code tools in which connectors are used to link apps and automations to data and services. This page covers the concept only at a general level; no specific connector lists, license names or prices are given here.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

prep-data-for-ai.desc: Prep data for AI is a Power BI feature that lets model authors simplify the schema and add instructions so Copilot can return more accurate answers.

faq.a: Prep data for AI is a Power BI feature that lets model authors simplify the schema and add instructions so that Copilot gives more accurate answers.
faq.q: What is Prep data for AI?

faq.a: It is intended for model authors, who adjust the model so that Copilot can interpret it more accurately.
faq.q: Who uses Prep data for AI?

faq.a: By simplifying the schema and adding instructions, the feature aims to make the answers Copilot gives more accurate.
faq.q: What does Prep data for AI change about Copilot answers?

prep-data-for-ai.long:
Prep data for AI is a feature in Power BI aimed at model authors. It is used to prepare a semantic model so that Copilot can interpret the data more reliably and respond with more accurate answers.

According to its description, the feature works in two main ways: simplifying the schema and adding instructions. Simplifying the schema reduces what Copilot has to interpret, while the added instructions give it guidance on how the model should be understood. Both steps are carried out by the person who builds and maintains the model, rather than by the end user asking questions.

The concept is relevant wherever Copilot is used with Power BI data, since the quality of its answers depends on how clearly the underlying model is described and structured. Preparing the data in this way is a model-authoring task that sits upstream of everyday report consumption.

No further details, such as specific settings, supported scenarios, or related products, are listed in the available information for this entry, and no M365.FM episodes are currently linked to it.

preservation-hold-library.desc: The Preservation Hold library is a hidden SharePoint and OneDrive library that keeps preserved copies of content edited or deleted while a retention policy, label or hold applies.

faq.a: It is a hidden library in SharePoint and OneDrive that stores preserved copies of content that is edited or deleted while a retention policy, retention label or hold applies.
faq.q: What is the Preservation Hold library?

faq.a: Content is preserved there when it is edited or deleted while a retention policy, retention label or hold applies to it.
faq.q: When does content end up in the Preservation Hold library?

faq.a: No. It is a hidden library and is not part of the normal browsing experience in SharePoint or OneDrive.
faq.q: Is the Preservation Hold library visible to users?

preservation-hold-library.long:
The Preservation Hold library is a hidden library in SharePoint and OneDrive. It stores preserved copies of content that is edited or deleted while a retention policy, retention label or hold applies to that content.

In practice, the library works as a background store for retention and hold scenarios. When an item subject to retention or a hold is changed or removed by a user, a preserved copy is kept in the Preservation Hold library instead of being lost. Because the library is hidden, it is not part of the normal browsing experience for users of a site or OneDrive.

The concept is relevant to administrators and compliance teams who work with retention policies, retention labels and holds in the Microsoft ecosystem, and who need to understand where preserved content ends up when files are modified or deleted. It also matters when reasoning about storage, since preserved copies are kept in addition to the live content.

No related entities, official documentation links or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic, so this page is limited to the definition and role of the library.

principal-agent-problem.desc: The principal-agent problem is a conflict of interest that arises when an agent acts for a principal while their goals and information differ, including when AI agents act on instructions.

faq.a: It is a conflict of interest that arises when one party (the agent) acts on behalf of another (the principal) while their goals and information diverge.
faq.q: What is the principal-agent problem?

faq.a: M365.FM applies it to AI agents that follow literal instructions rather than business intent, so the outcome can differ from what the principal actually wanted.
faq.q: How does the principal-agent problem apply to AI agents?

principal-agent-problem.long:
The principal-agent problem is a conflict of interest that arises when one party, the agent, acts on behalf of another party, the principal, while the goals and information of the two parties diverge. Because the agent may hold knowledge or incentives the principal lacks, the agent's actions can drift from what the principal actually wants.

On M365.FM the concept is applied to AI agents. In that framing, an AI agent follows the literal instructions it is given rather than the underlying business intent behind them. The gap between the stated instruction and the intended outcome mirrors the gap between principal and agent: the organization or user that delegates a task is the principal, and the AI agent carrying it out is the agent.

This perspective is used to explain why delegating work to AI agents can produce results that are technically compliant with the instruction but misaligned with what the business wanted. It highlights the difference between specifying a task and communicating the purpose behind it.

No specific episodes, product links or related entities are listed for this topic in the available information, so it is presented here as a general concept used within the M365.FM discussion of AI agents.

private-5g.desc: Private 5G is a dedicated cellular network for a single enterprise site, using SIM-based identity and network slicing to give operational technology predictable latency.

faq.a: Private 5G is a dedicated cellular network operated for a single enterprise site, such as a factory, port or hospital. It uses scheduled access, SIM-based device identity and network slicing to provide predictable latency for operational technology workloads.
faq.q: What is Private 5G?

faq.a: The episode "Cloud Latency and Edge Computing Strategy" says combining private 5G with Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) brings data processing closer to the devices, often within the same building or campus, instead of sending all data to a distant cloud.
faq.q: How does Private 5G relate to edge computing?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, it was an Azure service for deploying and managing 5G core network functions on an Azure Stack Edge device as part of an on-premises private mobile network. The documentation page is archived because the service was announced for retirement, with migration to partner solutions recommended.
faq.q: What was Azure Private 5G Core?

private-5g.long:
Private 5G is a dedicated cellular network that is operated for a single enterprise site, such as a factory, port or hospital. Instead of sharing capacity with public mobile users, the site runs its own 5G environment and controls who and what can connect to it. The approach relies on scheduled access to the radio resources, SIM-based device identity and network slicing, with the goal of delivering predictable latency for operational technology workloads.

The main purpose of a private 5G network is to give machines, sensors and other devices on a defined location a connection that behaves consistently. Operational technology workloads often depend on timing: a response that arrives too late can matter as much as one that does not arrive at all. Scheduled access helps keep latency predictable, SIM-based identity ties each device to a credential that the site operator manages, and network slicing allows different traffic types to be separated within the same network.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, one documented building block was Azure Private 5G Core. According to Microsoft Learn, it is an Azure cloud service for deploying and managing 5G core network functions on an Azure Stack Edge device, forming part of an on-premises private mobile network for an enterprise. A packet core instance at each site includes functions such as AMF, SMF, UPF, PCF, AUSF, UDM and UDR, with an optional 4G mode for private LTE. The service connects to standards-compliant 4G and 5G standalone radio access networks and aims at low-latency, secure connectivity for IoT devices and local data processing that does not depend on cloud connectivity.

Management of such a setup happens centrally through the Azure portal and ARM APIs. SIMs and eSIMs are provisioned through SIM partners, and the documentation lists integration with Azure Monitor, Resource Health, Event Hubs and Azure RBAC. A high-availability configuration uses two devices. Several parts are explicitly outside the service and come from the customer or partners: radio equipment, SIMs, Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes and gateway routers. The named use cases include manufacturing analytics, warehouse automation, public safety, utilities and smart farming. The Microsoft Learn page is archived, because the service was announced for retirement, and migration to partner solutions is recommended. Anyone planning a private 5G project should check the current status of any product they consider.

Private 5G is closely tied to edge computing. The M365.FM episode "Cloud Latency and Edge Computing Strategy" discusses how latency limits cloud-centric designs and how data volume sent to the cloud can be reduced. The episode says Azure Stack Edge helps handle AI workloads at the edge, filter out noise and send only what matters to the cloud, which keeps systems responsive and cost-effective. It also says the latency wall can be broken by combining private 5G networks with Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC). In this integration, data processing moves closer to where devices operate, often within the same building or campus, so that not every piece of data has to travel to a distant cloud.

Typical decisions around private 5G therefore concern where processing should run, which workloads need local handling because of latency or connectivity requirements, and which components the organization sources itself versus from partners. Because the radio network, SIM provisioning and local compute are separate pieces, a deployment is usually an assembly of several parts rather than a single product. The concept itself, a site-specific cellular network with controlled access and predictable latency, remains the same regardless of which vendor supplies the individual components.

private-branch-exchange.desc: A private branch exchange (PBX) is a private telephone system that connects internal extensions within an organization and links them to the public telephone network.

faq.a: A private branch exchange (PBX) is a private telephone system that connects internal extensions within an organization and links them to the public telephone network.
faq.q: What is a private branch exchange (PBX)?

faq.a: A PBX connects the internal extensions of an organization to each other and to the public telephone network.
faq.q: What does a PBX connect?

private-branch-exchange.long:
A private branch exchange (PBX) is a private telephone system used within an organization. It connects internal extensions to one another and links them to the public telephone network, so that employees can call colleagues directly and place or receive calls outside the organization.

The term describes the role the system plays in an organization's telephony setup rather than a single product. Organizations use a PBX to manage internal extensions and to route calls between those extensions and external telephone lines.

On M365.FM, the PBX is covered as a concept within the Microsoft ecosystem knowledge base. No specific relations to other topics, products or episodes are recorded for this entry at this time.

private-channels.desc: Private channels in Microsoft Teams are visible only to invited team members and each use a separate SharePoint site, which affects files, apps and governance.

faq.a: A private channel is a Teams channel visible only to invited members of the team. It is backed by its own separate SharePoint site, so its files are kept apart from the team's main site.
faq.q: What is a private channel in Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: The episode "Design a Microsoft Teams Structure That Actually Works" says each private channel gets its own SharePoint site collection and separate file library accessible only to channel members. Standard channels use folders in the team's primary SharePoint site.
faq.q: How do private channels store files?

faq.a: The episode "Teams Private Channels vs Shared Channels" suggests a separate team for long-running, regulated programs needing labels, holds and audits, and for heavy app or tab use such as Power BI, Planner, bots and flows.
faq.q: When should a separate team be used instead of a private channel?

private-channels.long:
Private channels are a channel type in Microsoft Teams that is visible only to the members who have been invited to it. They sit inside a team but restrict access to a selected subset of that team's members, which makes them a common choice for sensitive or confidential discussions. Each private channel is backed by its own separate SharePoint site, so its files are stored apart from the rest of the team.

The separate storage is the feature that most shapes how private channels behave. According to the M365.FM episode "Design a Microsoft Teams Structure That Actually Works", private channels get their own SharePoint site collection. Standard channels, by contrast, map to folders inside the team's primary SharePoint site, while a private channel creates a separate site collection and a separate file library that only channel members can access. This is what keeps the content limited to invited members, but it also means that site and its permissions have to be accounted for in governance planning.

In practice, teams choose between three channel types: standard, private and shared. The episode "Microsoft Teams Channels vs Chat: When to Use Each" describes standard channels as open to all team members for general communication and file access, private channels as limited to selected members and suited to confidential topics, and shared channels as a way to collaborate with external users without creating extra accounts. The same episode recommends choosing the channel type according to project needs, balancing collaboration against security, and notes that SharePoint is used for document storage in all channel types.

The episode "Teams Private Channels vs Shared Channels" focuses on the decision between a private channel, a shared channel and a brand-new team. It points to places where private channels can quietly break workflows, including shadow SharePoint sites, missing apps and blocked guests. It offers a decision framework with role-specific do's and don'ts, plus compliance guidance. In its summary of when to pick each option, a separate team is suggested for long-running, regulated programs that need labels, holds and audits, and for work that depends heavily on apps and tabs such as Power BI, Planner, bots and flows. A separate team is also described as giving a cleaner lifecycle and dedicated compliance and ownership. Shared channels are presented as the option for native cross-tenant collaboration without guest oversharing.

The episode "Microsoft Teams Hidden Features with Josh Blalock [MVP]" mentions private channels among features for keeping sensitive discussions organized and focused, noting that only invited members can access these spaces. It contrasts them with shared channels, which allow collaboration with external partners without switching apps.

Taken together, the episodes treat private channels as a middle option. They are more restricted than a standard channel and lighter than a separate team, but they bring their own SharePoint site, possible gaps in app availability and different guest behavior. Typical decisions therefore revolve around who needs access, whether external participants are involved, how long the work will run, and whether compliance requirements such as retention or audit call for the clean ownership of a dedicated team. The episode on Teams structure also recommends assigning team owners to maintain structure and accountability and gathering user feedback to refine how channels are organized.

privileged-access-management.desc: Privileged access management (PAM) covers solutions and practices for controlling, brokering and monitoring privileged accounts and administrative permissions in Microsoft environments.

faq.a: PAM refers to solutions and practices for controlling, brokering and monitoring access to privileged accounts and administrative permissions. It is described as a subset of identity and access management that combines people, processes and technology.
faq.q: What is privileged access management (PAM)?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Security, Privileged Identity Management centers on time- and approval-based role activation. PAM is broader and also covers aspects such as password management, session recording and monitoring of privileged activity.
faq.q: How does PAM differ from Privileged Identity Management?

faq.a: Typical capabilities include just-in-time and just-enough access, automated password management, multifactor authentication, secure remote access through gateways, recording of privileged sessions, analysis of unusual activity and account lifecycle automation.
faq.q: Which capabilities does a PAM solution typically include?

privileged-access-management.long:
Privileged access management (PAM) refers to solutions and practices for controlling, brokering and monitoring access to privileged accounts and administrative permissions. Microsoft Security describes it as an identity security approach that watches for, detects and prevents unauthorized privileged access to critical resources. It combines people, processes and technology, and it is treated as a subset of identity and access management. Its particular focus is on what privileged users are allowed to do and what they actually do after they have signed in.

The purpose of privileged access management is to reduce the risk that comes with powerful accounts. The stated aims are to limit how many users hold administrative capabilities, to narrow the blast radius of an incident, to reduce attack paths, and to support audits through activity logs. Privileged accounts are not limited to human administrators. The documentation names domain administrators, service accounts, local and application administrator accounts, and emergency accounts as typical privileged account types, and all of them fall within the scope of a PAM approach.

A PAM solution typically brings together several capabilities. These include just-in-time and just-enough access, so that elevated rights exist only for the time and scope needed; automated password management; multifactor authentication; secure remote access through gateways; recording of privileged sessions; analysis of unusual activity; and automation of the account lifecycle. Together these controls make elevated access an exception that is requested, granted, observed and withdrawn, rather than a standing permission attached to an account.

Implementation generally begins with visibility. The first step is to identify all privileged accounts and to apply least privilege, meaning that each account receives only the permissions its tasks require. The next steps are controlling how elevation happens, monitoring and auditing privileged activity, and automating the discovery and management of privileged accounts so that the inventory stays current. The same source stresses that technology alone is not considered enough, which reflects the people and process elements of the approach, such as defined roles, approval rules and regular reviews.

PAM is often mentioned alongside Privileged Identity Management, but the two are contrasted in the documentation. Privileged Identity Management centers on time- and approval-based role activation, whereas PAM is the broader discipline of governing privileged access as a whole. In practice, role activation with approval is one building block within a wider privileged access program.

In the M365.FM episode "Prepare Microsoft 365 for German KRITIS Requirements" (3 November 2025), PAM appears in a checklist for the Identity & Access Management area. The checklist lists multifactor authentication for all administrative and privileged accounts, Privileged Access Management and Just-In-Time access for elevated roles, Conditional Access policies enforcing risk-based access controls, location restrictions and device compliance, Azure AD Privileged Identity Management configured for role activation and access review, and least privilege applied to user, service and admin roles and groups. In that context PAM is one of several identity controls that are expected to work together when an organization prepares Microsoft 365 for the requirements of German critical infrastructure.

Typical decisions around PAM include which accounts count as privileged, which roles should be activated only on request instead of being permanently assigned, how elevation is approved, and how privileged sessions and password changes are logged for later audit. Because audit evidence is one of the stated benefits, activity logs and access reviews are usually planned together with the access controls themselves.

privileged-access-workstation.desc: A privileged access workstation (PAW) is a dedicated, hardened device reserved for administrative tasks, limiting where sensitive administrator credentials are exposed.

faq.a: A privileged access workstation (PAW) is a dedicated, hardened device used only for administrative tasks. It exists so that sensitive administrator credentials are exposed on as few systems as possible.
faq.q: What is a privileged access workstation (PAW)?

faq.a: Restricting the device to administrative use reduces the number of systems on which privileged credentials are exposed. This keeps those credentials away from devices used for general activities.
faq.q: Why is a PAW used only for administrative tasks?

privileged-access-workstation.long:
A privileged access workstation (PAW) is a dedicated, hardened device used only for administrative tasks. Its purpose is to keep sensitive administrator credentials exposed on as few systems as possible.

The core idea behind a PAW is separation. Administrative work is performed on a device that is set aside for that purpose, rather than on a general-purpose workstation also used for everyday activities. Reducing the number of systems on which privileged credentials appear narrows the places where those credentials could be exposed.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the term is used in discussions of securing administrative access and protecting high-privilege accounts. A PAW is typically described as one element of a broader approach to privileged access, rather than a complete solution on its own.

No specific M365.FM episodes, linked topics, or official documentation links are currently associated with this entry, so this page limits itself to the definition and the underlying principle of dedicated, hardened administrative devices.

privileged-identity-management.desc: Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) replaces standing admin rights with eligible assignments activated just in time, with MFA, justification and optional approval.

faq.a: An eligible assignment requires the user to activate the role before using it, while an active assignment gives the rights immediately. Both can be time-bound or permanent.
faq.q: What is the difference between eligible and active assignments in PIM?

faq.a: Activation can require multifactor authentication, a justification and an approval workflow, and assignments can have start and end dates. Notifications, access reviews and audit history support oversight.
faq.q: What controls can be applied when a role is activated?

faq.a: PIM manages access to resources in Entra ID, Azure, Microsoft 365 and Intune, covering Entra roles, Azure resource roles and PIM for Groups. Microsoft Graph APIs allow programmatic access.
faq.q: Which resources and role types does PIM cover?

privileged-identity-management.long:
Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) is a service in Microsoft Entra ID for managing, controlling and monitoring access to important resources in Entra ID, Azure, Microsoft 365 and Intune. It belongs to Microsoft Entra. Its stated goal is to reduce the number of people who hold sensitive access and to provide just-in-time elevation to privileged roles, so that administrator rights are not available around the clock to every account that might need them.

The central idea is the difference between eligible and active assignments. An eligible assignment means the user holds a role in principle but must activate it before it can be used. An active assignment means the rights are available immediately. Both kinds can be time-bound or permanent. In practice, PIM replaces standing admin rights with eligible assignments, and activation can be tied to several conditions: a start and end date, a required justification, multifactor authentication on each activation, and an optional approval workflow in which a designated approver must confirm the request.

Beyond activation, PIM provides notifications, access reviews and downloadable audit history. These support oversight of who holds privileged roles, who activated them, when and why. The service also protects against removing the last active Global Administrator and Privileged Role Administrator, which helps prevent an organization from locking itself out of its own administration.

Management in PIM covers Entra roles, Azure resource roles and PIM for Groups. Microsoft Graph APIs are available for programmatic access, which is relevant for organizations that want to automate assignment or reporting. Using the service requires licenses; the official overview leaves the details to the Entra ID Governance licensing documentation, so licensing should be checked there before planning a rollout.

Typical decisions around PIM include which roles should be eligible rather than permanently active, how long an activation should last, which roles need an approval step, and how often access reviews should run. These choices balance security against the effort administrators face when they need to perform work quickly.

The M365.FM episode "Harden Intune Deployment for Zero Trust Compliance" lists PIM among best practices for making an Intune setup safer. It describes the tool as a way to give limited access to important features so that only allowed users can perform critical tasks, alongside role-based access control, phishing-resistant authentication such as FIDO2 security keys, Multi-Admin Approval and emergency procedures.

The episode "Copilot in Microsoft Entra ID - Simply Explained" connects PIM to Copilot's Access Governance functionality. According to the episode, this feature integrates with PIM to manage and monitor privileged access, and natural language queries can be used to determine least privileged roles based on tasks, enabling role activation without leaving the Copilot chat.

pro-code-development.desc: Pro-code development is traditional software development in which professional developers write custom code, usually contrasted with no-code and low-code platforms such as Power Platform.

faq.a: Pro-code development is traditional software development by professional developers who write custom code. It is usually contrasted with low-code and no-code approaches such as Power Platform.
faq.q: What is pro-code development?

faq.a: The episode "No-Code vs Low-Code vs Pro-Code: Which Should You Choose?" says pro-code usually gives stronger security because the developer controls every detail, while no-code may rely on what the platform provides.
faq.q: How does pro-code compare with no-code on security according to M365.FM?

faq.a: The episodes say yes. They recommend governance that covers both low-code and pro-code needs, and they advise treating Logic Apps as code and deploying them through CI/CD.
faq.q: Do low-code solutions still need pro-code practices?

pro-code-development.long:
Pro-code development is traditional software development in which professional developers write custom code. In the Microsoft ecosystem the term is usually used as a contrast to low-code and no-code approaches, such as building apps and automations on Power Platform. Where low-code tools offer visual designers and prebuilt components, pro-code means writing and maintaining the solution directly in a programming language, with full responsibility for how it is built, tested and deployed.

The M365.FM episode "No-Code vs Low-Code vs Pro-Code: Which Should You Choose?" frames the topic as a choice of development strategy. It describes the goal as helping teams decide how to speed up delivery or build complex enterprise systems. On security, the episode says pro-code development usually gives stronger security because the developer controls every detail. No-code, by comparison, makes app building easy for many people but may depend on what the platform itself offers. The episode presents each approach as having strengths and weaknesses rather than one being universally correct.

Pro-code also appears in discussions of cost and economics. The episode "Power Platform Automation Arbitrage for Cost Savings" describes Power Platform as an arbitrage layer that sits between expensive pro-code development and the hidden cost of manual work. In that framing, pro-code is the costly end of the spectrum, which is why low-code automation can create savings when a process does not need custom engineering.

Governance is a further theme. The episode "Power Platform Managed Environments Need Pro-Dev Practices" recommends a dual approach to governance that accommodates both low-code and pro-code development needs. Managed Environments are presented as a way to improve control and visibility over Power Platform solutions, with governance meaning the rules, roles and processes that keep data, apps and reports secure and compliant and that control who can create, share and change solutions. The title itself suggests that professional development practices belong in low-code environments as well.

In practice, pro-code work in Microsoft 365 often means building with developer frameworks. The episode "Stop Reinventing SPFx- Building Better SharePoint Solutions with PnP React Controls with Siddharth Vaghasia [MVP]" describes a modern SharePoint Framework (SPFx) project as a combination of several technologies: TypeScript, React, Fluent UI, PnPjs and PnP React Controls. TypeScript provides stronger typing and compile-time checks, and Fluent UI helps custom solutions fit the surrounding experience. According to the episode, pro-code suits cases that need control over the user interface, complex data handling, reusable components, APIs or sophisticated application experiences directly inside SharePoint. The guest also argues that generative AI coding tools are challenging the traditional assumption that pro-code takes longer than low-code.

The boundary between the two approaches is not always sharp. In "AI Turns Integration into an Organism as a Service — How Azure Logic Apps Are Changing Enterprise Integration with Sonny Gillissen [MVP]", codeful workflows are discussed as an attempt to bridge visual Logic Apps development and traditional pro-code approaches. The same episode says low code does not mean abandoning software engineering practices: Logic Apps should be treated as code and deployed through CI/CD, because manual deployment between environments creates risk.

Taken together, the episodes treat pro-code development as one option within a spectrum rather than a replacement for low-code. The decision typically turns on the need for control, security detail, complexity, delivery speed and cost, and on whether the organization can apply engineering and governance practices consistently across both styles.

process-criticality.desc: Process criticality describes how much damage a business process causes when it fails, slows down or produces wrong outcomes, typically assessed by frequency, dependency and consequence.
process-criticality.long:
Process criticality is a concept that describes how much damage a business process causes when it fails, slows down or produces wrong outcomes. It is used to judge how important a given process is to an organization and how much attention, protection or oversight it warrants.

Criticality is typically assessed along three dimensions: frequency, dependency and consequence. Frequency refers to how often the process runs or is affected. Dependency refers to how many other processes, systems or people rely on its outcome. Consequence refers to the severity of the impact when the process fails, is delayed or delivers an incorrect result. Considering these factors together allows processes to be compared and ranked rather than treated as equally important.

Assessing process criticality is generally used to prioritize work such as risk management, continuity planning, monitoring, automation and quality control. Processes with a higher criticality can be given stronger safeguards, closer observation or more rigorous testing, while lower-criticality processes can be handled with lighter controls.

No related products, topics or episodes are currently linked to this entry on M365.FM, so this page limits itself to the general definition of the concept.

process-debt.desc: Process debt is the accumulated cost of unresolved process shortcuts, such as unclear decision rights and temporary fixes that became permanent, which automation can hide and scale.

faq.a: Process debt is the accumulated cost of unresolved process shortcuts, such as unclear decision rights, unretired exceptions and temporary fixes that became permanent.
faq.q: What is process debt?

faq.a: Automation can hide process debt and scale it. A flawed process that is automated may run faster and more smoothly while still repeating the same underlying problems.
faq.q: Why does process debt matter for automation?

faq.a: It appears in the episode "Frictionless Automation Can Digitize Business Chaos", published on 2026-04-21.
faq.q: Where is process debt covered on M365.FM?

process-debt.long:
Process debt is the accumulated cost of unresolved process shortcuts in how work is done. Typical examples include unclear decision rights, exceptions that were never retired, and temporary fixes that became permanent. As with other forms of debt, the cost builds up over time and is paid later, often by the people who inherit the process.

The concept is mainly used to explain why automation does not automatically improve a process. When a workflow that carries process debt is automated, the underlying shortcuts can be hidden behind a smooth interface and then repeated at greater scale. The unresolved problems remain, but they become harder to see and harder to question.

In practice, the term is applied when reviewing a process before automating it. It prompts questions about who actually decides, which exceptions are still needed, and which workarounds were only meant to be temporary.

On M365.FM, process debt is discussed in the episode "Frictionless Automation Can Digitize Business Chaos" (2026-04-21), which addresses how automation can digitize existing disorder instead of removing it.

process-historian.desc: A process historian is an operational historian: a plant system that stores time-stamped process records from production equipment, often serving as a source of machine data.
process-historian.long:
A process historian, also called an operational historian, is a plant system that stores time-stamped process records collected from production equipment. Each record ties a measured or recorded value to the moment it occurred, which makes the stored data suitable for looking back at how a process behaved over time.

In many plants a process historian already exists alongside the production equipment. Because of this, it is often treated as an existing source of machine data. Rather than connecting to every machine individually, teams can draw on the records the historian has already gathered, using it as a point of access to equipment-level information.

The concept is relevant wherever machine and process data needs to be made available to other systems or analyses. The available information describes the process historian in general terms and does not tie it to a specific product, vendor, protocol or Microsoft service, so details of any particular implementation are outside what is stated here.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no related topics are listed.

product-dimensions.desc: Product dimensions in Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management are color, size, style, configuration and version, which identify the specific variant of a product master.

faq.a: There are five product dimensions: color, configuration, size, style and version. They identify the specific variant of a product master.
faq.q: Which product dimensions exist in Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management?

faq.a: No. Physical measurements are set on the product master and apply to all variants, whereas product dimensions are the characteristics that distinguish one variant from another.
faq.q: Are physical measurements product dimensions?

faq.a: A product master needs at least one product dimension to generate variants. The dimensions are combined into dimension groups that are assigned to the product master.
faq.q: How many product dimensions does a product master need?

product-dimensions.long:
Product dimensions are the characteristics in Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management that identify the specific variant of a product master. There are five of them: color, configuration, size, style and version. Because they distinguish one variant from another, they allow items that belong to the same product family but are not interchangeable to be managed separately in inventory, on orders and in other supply chain processes.

The product master acts as the parent definition, and the variants are the individual members of that family. Each variant can have its own inventory availability, labels, barcodes and operational requirements. The episode "Dynamics 365 Product Information Management - Simply Explained" describes it this way and walks through the five dimensions. Color and size are the straightforward examples from clothing. Style can separate variations such as a regular fit from a slim fit. Configuration can identify a particular build or setup, for instance different equipment specifications. Version is used to distinguish versions of a product.

In practice, the product dimensions are combined into dimension groups, and those groups are assigned to product masters. A product master needs at least one product dimension in order to generate variants. Values for size, color and style are created in the dimension and variant group setup, while configuration values usually come from the product configurator or the dimension-based configurator. When orders are entered, the dimensions on the order line select the wanted variant.

Not every theoretical combination has to exist. The official documentation gives the example of jeans offered in three colors and six sizes: of the eighteen possible combinations, only nine are actually created as variants. This is a typical decision when setting up a product master, since only the variants that are really offered need to be generated.

Physical measurements are not product dimensions. They are set on the product master and apply to all variants of that master, so they should not be confused with size, which is a variant-defining dimension.

The version dimension helps manufacturers track several product versions across the supply chain. Its values are created as needed over the life cycle of the product. There are limits to be aware of: the version dimension is not supported in several areas, such as vendor catalogs, and it is not supported in Commerce channels. Enabling it in a production environment requires checking customizations that reference inventory dimensions, and it is turned on by default only for new systems from a certain release.

For planning a product information model, product dimensions are a central decision. They determine how variants are defined, which attributes are variant-specific and which are shared by the whole product master, and how items are selected on order lines. The M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Product Information Management - Simply Explained" places them within the wider discussion of product masters and variants in Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management.

product-genealogy.desc: Product genealogy is the record of how input materials become manufactured outputs through assembly, transformation, rework and component replacement.

faq.a: Product genealogy is the record of how input materials contribute to manufactured outputs through assembly, transformation, rework and component replacement. One source describes it as the complete digital record of how a product was made.
faq.q: What is product genealogy?

faq.a: According to a manufacturing software vendor's blog post, traceability follows materials and products forward and backward through production. Genealogy covers the full set of relationships, including materials, batches, equipment, operators, inspections and process data, that produced the finished product.
faq.q: How does product genealogy differ from traceability?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode "Connect ERP, MES, and IoT — Without Replacing Anything" lists product genealogy among the functions of the MES, alongside dispatching, operator tracking and electronic batch records.
faq.q: Where does product genealogy sit in an ERP, MES and IoT landscape?

product-genealogy.long:
Product genealogy is a manufacturing concept that describes how input materials contribute to manufactured outputs. It covers the records created as materials are assembled, transformed, reworked or replaced, so that a finished product can be traced to the components and steps behind it.
