In plain terms, it is the history of what went into a product and what happened to it along the way.

A vendor blog post on manufacturing execution systems from GE Vernova Software defines genealogy as the complete digital record of how a product was made. Such a record links materials, batches, equipment, operators, inspections and process data. The same source separates genealogy from traceability. Traceability follows materials and products forward and backward through production, while genealogy covers the full set of relationships that produced the finished product. The source is a vendor page and not a neutral standards document, so its definition is best read as one industry description rather than a formal specification.

The source names several components of genealogy. Forward traceability runs from a received lot to a customer shipment. Backward traceability runs from a finished product to its suppliers and ingredient lots. Lot genealogy covers consumption, splits, merges, intermediate inventory and rework. Batch genealogy links recipes, equipment and parameters to each batch. As-built records capture what actually happened during production and underpin electronic batch records. According to the source, these records are captured automatically as work happens, so the history does not have to be rebuilt later from spreadsheets, paper or machine logs.

The purpose of genealogy is mostly practical. The source argues that complete genealogy lets manufacturers limit a recall to the affected products rather than a wider population. It also supports root cause analysis and corrective action, because the path a product took can be examined step by step. It is further linked to compliance topics such as 21 CFR Part 11 and GMP, where documented production history matters.

In the M365.FM episode "Connect ERP, MES, and IoT — Without Replacing Anything", product genealogy appears as one of the functions of the Manufacturing Execution System. The episode describes MES as execution control: it takes planned work from the ERP and turns it into controlled shop floor execution, managing dispatching, operator tracking, electronic batch records and product genealogy. This places genealogy on the execution layer, between planning in the ERP and the physical evidence captured by industrial IoT close to the equipment.

The same episode points to a related design decision: production states should not be forced into generic words such as "complete". A part can be physically manufactured but still awaiting inspection, pending material posting, or redirected into rework loops. This matters for genealogy because rework and inspection outcomes are part of the record of how an output came to exist. Recording granular states, rather than a single completion flag, keeps those events visible in the product history.

Typical situations where genealogy is relevant include investigating a quality defect, scoping a recall, documenting a batch for regulatory review, and tracking which component replacements or rework steps a unit went through. The sources do not describe specific Microsoft tooling for genealogy; the episode frames it as a capability of the MES layer within a landscape that also includes ERP and IoT systems.

product-information-management.desc: Product information management (PIM) keeps one central, shared product definition, covering numbers, names, units, categories, attributes, images and translations.

faq.a: PIM is the practice of keeping one central, shared product definition, including numbers, names, units, categories, attributes, images and translations, that other business processes use. It acts as a hub that gathers scattered product data and distributes it to sales channels.
faq.q: What is product information management (PIM)?

faq.a: According to the sources, a PIM distributes product data to e-commerce sites, print catalogues, marketplaces such as Amazon and Google Shopping, social media and trading-partner data feeds.
faq.q: Which channels does a PIM typically supply with product data?

faq.a: The episode "Dynamics 365 Product Information Management - Simply Explained" explains how the product creates a shared product definition across the business. It covers products, product masters, variants, dimensions, configurations, categories, attributes, legal entities and integrations.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode on Dynamics 365 Product Information Management cover?

product-information-management.long:
Product information management (PIM) is the practice of keeping one central, shared definition of each product so that other business processes can rely on the same data. That definition includes product numbers, names, units, categories, attributes, images and translations. Wikipedia describes PIM as the process of managing all the information needed to market and sell products through distribution channels, using data created internally to support a multichannel strategy.

The core idea is to replace scattered product data with a single hub. In many organisations, product details sit in different departments and formats, such as spreadsheets, supplier files and separate systems. A PIM gathers this data in one place and then distributes it to the channels that need it, for example e-commerce sites, print catalogues, marketplaces such as Amazon and Google Shopping, social media and trading-partner data feeds. The goal is that customers and employees see consistent, current information regardless of where they encounter a product.

Typical PIM functions listed in the sources include centralisation of product data, multi-language and multi-market support, maintenance within a central catalogue, automation of product creation, data governance and output, catalogue grouping for target markets, access control through a web administration interface, and links to ordering and inventory systems. Exchange standards such as Open ICEcat are supported. Technically, a PIM runs over or alongside a database and application server and may use XML-based exchange. It is most relevant to B2C and B2B firms that sell through several channels.

PIM is related to, but distinct from, several neighbouring disciplines. Wikipedia relates it to product data management, product lifecycle management, digital asset management and master data management. It notes that generic master data management often lacks product-specific enrichment, validation and workflow rules, which is one reason product information is handled with dedicated PIM capabilities.

The problem a PIM addresses is easy to recognise in practice. A supplier changes a specification, one spreadsheet gets updated, another system does not, and customers receive outdated information or employees order the wrong item. A shared product definition reduces this kind of inconsistency because changes are made once and reused by the processes that depend on them.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Product Information Management - Simply Explained" (2026-08-21) covers this topic. In it, Mirko Peters explains how Dynamics 365 Product Information Management creates a shared product definition across the business. The episode says it manages products, product masters, variants, dimensions, configurations, categories, attributes, legal entities and integrations, and describes Dynamics 365 Product Information Management as a central place for defining and maintaining product information.

When considering a PIM, the main decisions revolve around which product attributes belong in the shared definition, how variants and categories are structured, which channels and markets need output, and how governance and access are controlled. The sources frame PIM as a way to support these choices with one consistent data foundation rather than as a replacement for ordering or inventory systems, to which it links.

product-lifecycle-management.desc: Product lifecycle management (PLM) is engineering software and practice for managing product design intent, including CAD models, drawings, tolerances and approved revisions.

faq.a: PLM is engineering software and practice that manages product design intent. It covers items such as drawings, CAD models, material requirements, tolerances and approved revisions.
faq.q: What is product lifecycle management (PLM)?

faq.a: PLM manages design-related information, including CAD models, drawings, material requirements, tolerances and approved revisions of a product.
faq.q: What kind of information does PLM manage?

faq.a: Based on the available facts, PLM is described as both software and a practice, not as one specific product. No particular vendor or Microsoft service is linked to it here.
faq.q: Is PLM a single product?

product-lifecycle-management.long:
Product lifecycle management (PLM) is a combination of engineering software and practice used to manage product design intent. The information it governs includes drawings, CAD models, material requirements, tolerances and approved revisions.

In practice, PLM serves as the controlled source for what a product is meant to be. By holding approved revisions alongside the design data they apply to, it helps ensure that teams work from the current, sanctioned definition of a product rather than from outdated or unapproved versions.

The available information for this entry is limited. No linked topics, product documentation or official sites have been recorded for PLM on M365.FM, and no episodes are currently associated with this term. The entry therefore describes the concept in general terms only and does not tie it to a specific vendor product or Microsoft service.

product-master.desc: In Dynamics 365, a product master is the parent record for a product family, holding shared details and the rules used to create individual product variants.

faq.a: A product master is the parent record for a product family. It holds the shared details and the rules from which individual product variants are created.
faq.q: What is a product master in Dynamics 365?

faq.a: A simple product represents one fixed item with no choices that create separate variants. A product master represents a whole family of related products, such as jeans that come in different colors and sizes.
faq.q: What is the difference between a simple product and a product master?

faq.a: According to the Dual-write episode, Finance and Operations often owns product creation because operations controls product master information and stock units. Dual-write can then send the product information into Dataverse for sales users.
faq.q: Which application usually owns product master information when Dual-write is used?

product-master.long:
A product master in Dynamics 365 is the parent record that represents an entire family of related products. It stores the information shared by every member of the family and the rules from which individual product variants are created. It is one of the two product types in Dynamics 365 product information management, the other being the simple product.

The distinction between the two types is easiest to see through the choices a product offers. A simple product represents one fixed item without choices that would create separate variants. A product master is used when one product comes in several forms that the business has to tell apart. The M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Product Information Management - Simply Explained" uses a pair of jeans as its example. Customers may think of the jeans as one product, but a warehouse must distinguish blue medium jeans from black large jeans. The product master holds the information common to all the jeans, while the variants carry the differences, such as color and size.

In practice, this structure separates what is true of the whole family from what is true of one specific item. Shared details are maintained once on the product master instead of being repeated on every variant. The rules on the master determine which variants can exist, so each distinguishable item that operations needs to stock, sell, or ship is created from the same definition. This is why the product master matters for planning, inventory, and fulfilment, where the exact variant is what gets counted and moved, even though customers often browse and buy at the level of the family.

The same episode also points out that translations allow the same underlying product to have appropriate names and descriptions for different languages and markets. Product naming and descriptions are therefore part of the wider product information that surrounds a product master, helping customers recognize products in their own context.

Product masters also come up where Dynamics 365 applications exchange data. The episode "Dynamics 365 Dual-write - Simply Explained" describes products as an example where ownership becomes important. According to the episode, Finance and Operations often owns product creation because operations controls product master information, stock units, and other details needed to sell and deliver products. Once a product is prepared for customer-facing work, Dual-write can send the related product information into Dataverse, so sales users can work with those products without someone manually recreating the product catalog in another application.

The term also appears more generally in discussions of data consistency. The episode "Microsoft Fabric Digital Twin Builder Explained" mentions asset and product master data in the context of building a single source of truth, stating that unified master data supports consistency and reliability across an organization. That usage refers to master data as a data management discipline rather than to the Dynamics 365 record type, but it reflects the same underlying idea: keep the authoritative description of a product in one governed place.

Typical decisions around a product master include whether an item needs variants at all, in which case a simple product is enough, and which attributes distinguish the variants. Teams also decide which application owns product creation and how the finished product reaches customer-facing applications. The sources do not go into further technical detail, such as specific dimension names, configuration steps, or field definitions, so those points are left to Microsoft's own documentation for the relevant Dynamics 365 application.

product-owner.desc: Product owner: the single accountable role in Scrum and agile product development that ranks the backlog, decides what is built next and accepts delivered changes.

faq.a: A product owner is the single accountable role that ranks the backlog, decides what gets built next and accepts delivered changes. The role is known from Scrum and agile product development.
faq.q: What does a product owner do?

faq.a: The episodes cite it in three contexts: as part of the developer experience of an Azure platform, as a key role that needs proper training to help Copilot and AI efforts scale, and as a dedicated role that maintains momentum in Dynamics 365 business process delivery.
faq.q: Why do the M365.FM episodes mention the product owner role?

faq.a: The episode "Why Enterprise AI and Copilot Pilots Fail to Scale" says that assigning roles such as scrum master and product owner without proper training causes confusion and weakens the team.
faq.q: What problem does the episode on Copilot pilots associate with the role?

product-owner.long:
A product owner is the single accountable role that ranks the backlog, decides what gets built next and accepts delivered changes. The role is known from Scrum and agile product development, where it gives a team one clear point of accountability for priorities. Instead of work being driven by competing requests, one person is responsible for ordering the backlog and for deciding whether a delivered change counts as done.

In practice, the role covers three connected responsibilities. The first is ranking the backlog, which means putting the work items in an order that reflects what matters most to the business and to users. The second is deciding what is built next, which turns that ranking into concrete commitments for the team. The third is accepting delivered changes, which closes the loop by confirming that what was built meets the intent behind the request. Together these responsibilities keep delivery connected to business needs rather than to technical preference alone.

The role appears in several M365.FM episodes, each time as part of a wider operating model rather than as a topic on its own. In "Platform Engineering: The New Operating Model for Azure", the developer experience enhancements of an internal platform include a product owner, alongside measurement of key metrics such as developer satisfaction and time-to-first-deploy. The episode describes this as part of how a platform is treated as a product with its own accountable owner, in a setting where teams report a 40-50% reduction in cognitive load for developers. The product owner role here supports the idea that a platform needs someone who decides what the platform offers and in what order.

The episode "Why Enterprise AI and Copilot Pilots Fail to Scale" approaches the role from the angle of skills and staffing. It states that teams need the right people in key roles, such as scrum master and product owner, and warns that organizations sometimes assign these roles without proper training, which causes confusion and weakens the team. The episode also stresses that non-technical roles are just as important as technical talent, because they represent customer needs and keep the business aligned. According to the episode, when teams lack these skills they cannot deliver value or scale their efforts, and skill gaps stall innovation.

In "Optimize Dynamics 365 Business Processes for Faster Delivery", the product owner appears in a discussion of how to improve operational efficiency and responsiveness. The hosts advocate a structured approach that breaks work into stages named qualify, commit and deliver, with actionable criteria at each stage. They highlight data-driven decision-making and the role of a dedicated product owner in maintaining momentum. The episode presents these methods as a way to reduce cycle times, raise productivity and support a culture of continuous improvement.

Taken together, the episodes point to a consistent pattern. A product owner is most often discussed where a team needs a single decision point: choosing what to build next, keeping delivery moving, and keeping work aligned with what the business and its users need. The decisions around the role are mainly organizational. They include who holds it, whether that person has been trained for it, and whether the role is dedicated rather than added on top of other duties. The sources in these episodes frame a dedicated, trained owner as a factor that supports delivery, and an untrained or unclear assignment as a source of confusion.

product-process-resource.desc: Product, process, resource (PPR) is a manufacturing modeling structure that links the product to be built, the process needed to build it, and the resources that perform the work.

faq.a: PPR stands for product, process, resource. It names the three elements that the structure links together.
faq.q: What does PPR stand for?

faq.a: The product is what is to be built. The process is what is required to build it. The resources are the machines, tools and people that can perform the work.
faq.q: What are the three parts of a PPR structure?

faq.a: It is used to model manufacturing by connecting the product, the build process and the resources capable of doing the work, instead of keeping these separate.
faq.q: What is PPR used for?

product-process-resource.long:
Product, process, resource (PPR) is a manufacturing modeling structure that connects three elements: the product to be built, the process required to build it, and the resources that can carry out the work. Resources in this context include machines, tools and people.

The purpose of a PPR structure is to describe manufacturing in a connected way rather than treating product data, process steps and shop-floor resources as separate sets of information. By linking the three, a model can show what is being made, how it is made, and which machines, tools or people are able to perform each part of the work.

The concept is relevant to anyone working with manufacturing data, production planning or digital representations of production. Because it describes relationships between product, process and resource, it can serve as a common frame of reference when these areas need to be discussed or modeled together.

No related topics, official documentation or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, so this page limits itself to the general definition of the concept.

productized-services.desc: Productized services are consulting offerings standardized into named programs with a fixed scope, defined deliverables, a fixed timeline and a set price.

faq.a: Productized services are consulting offerings standardized into named programs. Each one has a fixed scope, defined deliverables, a fixed timeline and a set price.
faq.q: What are productized services?

faq.a: Custom consulting is typically scoped individually, while a productized service is packaged in advance with predefined deliverables, timeline and price. This makes the offer repeatable and easier to compare.
faq.q: How do productized services differ from custom consulting?

faq.a: It includes a fixed scope, defined deliverables, a fixed timeline and a set price, usually bundled under a program name.
faq.q: What does a productized service include?

productized-services.long:
Productized services are consulting offerings that have been standardized into named programs. Instead of selling open-ended hours or custom proposals, a provider packages its expertise into a repeatable offer with a fixed scope, defined deliverables, a fixed timeline and a set price.

The approach is used to make consulting easier to describe, buy and deliver. A client can see in advance what is included, how long the engagement runs and what it costs, while the provider can repeat the same structure across engagements. Each program typically has its own name, which distinguishes it from general-purpose or time-and-materials consulting work.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, the concept is relevant to consultants and partners who want to turn recurring advisory or implementation work into clearly bounded programs. No specific Microsoft products, tools or documentation are linked to the term in the available information.

No M365.FM episodes are currently associated with this topic, and no related entities are listed. This page will be extended as related content is added.

programmable-logic-controller.desc: A programmable logic controller (PLC) is a ruggedized industrial computer that runs the local machine sequence of production equipment based on inputs.

faq.a: A PLC is a ruggedized industrial computer that controls manufacturing processes, machines and assembly lines. It runs the local machine sequence and responds to inputs within a limited time as a hard real-time system.
faq.q: What is a programmable logic controller (PLC)?

faq.a: It repeats a scan cycle of reading inputs, executing the program and writing outputs, which typically takes tens of milliseconds. Programming is commonly done under IEC 61131-3, for example in ladder logic.
faq.q: How does a PLC execute its program?

faq.a: According to the episode "From Sensor to Dashboard: The MQTT Pipeline Through Azure IoT Hub", PLCs rarely speak cloud MQTT directly because plants often use proprietary protocols or OPC UA. An industrial gateway on the OT network bridges that gap and normalizes the data.
faq.q: Why does a PLC usually need a gateway to reach Azure IoT Hub?

programmable-logic-controller.long:
A programmable logic controller (PLC) is a ruggedized industrial computer used to control manufacturing processes, machines and assembly lines. In the M365.FM knowledge base it is described as the industrial controller that runs the local machine sequence of production equipment, handling its steps and conditions in response to inputs. It is designed for reliability, ease of programming and fault diagnosis, and it sits at the boundary between physical equipment and the data systems that sit above it.

According to the reference notes, a PLC is a hard real-time system: it must produce outputs within a limited time after its inputs change. Its main parts are a CPU, a power supply, memory, an I/O interface and a communications interface. It works in a repeating scan cycle: it reads the inputs, executes the program and writes the outputs, a cycle that typically takes tens of milliseconds. Inputs and outputs are either discrete, such as on/off signals from limit switches, or analog, such as pressure or temperature; a 4-20 mA loop, for example, maps to a range of 0 to 32,767.

PLCs began in the late 1960s in the US car industry as a replacement for hard-wired relays and sequencers. The first, the Modicon 084, followed a 1968 General Motors request. The main programming standard is IEC 61131-3, which defines Structured Text, Instruction List, ladder logic, function block diagram and sequential function chart. Ladder logic remains popular because its scan-based execution is predictable. PLCs connect over Ethernet, serial ports and protocols such as Modbus, and they are usually paired with HMIs and SCADA systems. Safety PLCs meet SIL requirements. Programs are not fully portable between vendors, which is a practical consideration when equipment from several generations or suppliers is mixed in one plant.

In the context of Azure and Microsoft-based manufacturing data platforms, the PLC is the source of raw signals. The episode "From Sensor to Dashboard: The MQTT Pipeline Through Azure IoT Hub" gives the example of a packaging line where a conveyor motor temperature rises beyond normal operating limits. At that moment the PLC holds a raw tag value, such as a temperature reading, together with a timestamp and a quality state. The episode points out that older plants often run multiple generations of equipment using proprietary protocols or OPC UA, so PLCs rarely speak cloud MQTT directly. An industrial gateway deployed on the operational technology (OT) network bridges this gap, including by normalizing data before it moves toward cloud ingestion layers.

The PLC also appears as a boundary for control, not only for data. The episode "IoT Hub vs Event Hubs — Why Most Manufacturers Pick the Wrong Service" describes commands as requests telling a device or gateway to perform an action with specific intent, such as collecting diagnostics or testing a connection. According to the episode, commands carry execution responsibility and must respect local PLC and safety boundaries. This means that cloud-side messaging services request actions, while the local machine sequence and safety behavior stay with the controller on the plant floor.

Typical decisions around a PLC therefore concern where the line between local control and cloud integration is drawn: which tag values are exposed, which gateway translates between OT protocols and cloud messaging, and which commands may reach a device at all. The same distinction helps when separating telemetry, commands, state and business messages in a cloud design, since only the controller itself is responsible for the real-time machine sequence.

progressive-disclosure.desc: Progressive disclosure is a design pattern for AI agent skills in which only each skill's name and description stay in context, while full instructions load on demand.

faq.a: It is a design pattern in which only each skill's name and description stay in context, and the full instructions, scripts and resources load only when a request matches the skill.
faq.q: What is progressive disclosure in AI agent skills?

faq.a: Three. Level 1 is the name and description (about 100 tokens per skill, always loaded), level 2 is the SKILL.md body (expected under about 5,000 tokens, loaded on a match), and level 3 is bundled files and scripts opened only when needed.
faq.q: How many levels of loading does a Claude skill have?

faq.a: The description is what Claude matches against the request, so it must say what the skill does and when to use it. According to the documentation, vague descriptions make triggering unreliable.
faq.q: Why does the description of a skill matter?

progressive-disclosure.long:
Progressive disclosure is a design pattern for AI agent skills in which only each skill's name and description remain in the model's context, and the full instructions, scripts and resources are loaded only when a request matches the skill. The aim is to keep the context window free of material that the current task does not need, while still giving the agent access to a large body of specialised know-how.

The pattern addresses a problem that the M365.FM episode "The End of AI Bloat: Why Modern Agents Need Skills" calls the Context Tax. According to the episode, an enterprise agent often starts with a relatively small system prompt describing its role, tone, business rules and guardrails, and then grows as more requirements are added. The episode argues that the underlying issue is not the model but the architecture, and that monolithic prompts create this tax. It presents modular Skills, combined with progressive disclosure, as the solution, and describes Skills as becoming an architectural foundation for modern AI agents across Microsoft Copilot Studio, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code and the broader enterprise AI ecosystem.

The Claude documentation on Agent Skills uses progressive disclosure to explain how skills avoid filling the context window. A skill is a directory containing instructions, metadata and optional resources such as scripts and templates, and it is loaded in three levels. Level 1 is the name and description taken from the YAML frontmatter. This level is always present at startup and costs roughly 100 tokens per skill. Level 2 is the body of the SKILL.md file, which is read only when a request matches the description, and which is expected to stay under about 5,000 tokens. Level 3 consists of bundled files, references and scripts that are opened only when needed. Files that are never accessed cost no tokens, and for scripts only their output enters the context, not the code itself.

Because only names and descriptions occupy context until a skill triggers, many skills can be installed without a meaningful penalty. This is the practical benefit of the pattern: capability can grow by adding skills, whereas a single monolithic prompt would grow in size and cost with every added rule. The agent effectively reads an index first and consults the detailed material only for the task at hand.

The description is the part that carries the most weight in day-to-day use. It is what Claude matches against the incoming request, so it needs to state both what the skill does and when it should be used. The documentation notes that vague descriptions make triggering unreliable. It also lists limits: a name of at most 64 characters and a description of 1 to 1,024 characters. Authors therefore face a design decision about how much to put in the always-loaded description, how much in the SKILL.md body, and how much in separate reference files or scripts that are loaded or run only on demand.

In summary, progressive disclosure is a loading strategy rather than a product feature of a single vendor: keep a minimal, always-visible summary of each capability, load detailed instructions when a request calls for them, and open supporting resources only at the last step. The episode places this strategy at the centre of the argument for replacing bloated prompts with modular Skills.

project.desc: Microsoft Project is paid project management software for schedules, resources and Gantt charts, with cloud scheduling continuing in Planner premium.

faq.a: Microsoft Project is paid project management software used for schedules, resources and Gantt charts. It helps plan tasks, assign people and track progress against a timeline.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Project used for?

faq.a: According to the facts on record, cloud scheduling continues in Planner premium. The episode with Joe Griffin adds that Microsoft Project Online is approaching retirement, which gives organisations a reason to review how they deliver projects.
faq.q: What happens to cloud scheduling for Microsoft Project?

faq.a: Microsoft Planner is where cloud scheduling continues, and Microsoft Teams is a common place for project communication and collaboration. Both are listed as related topics to Microsoft Project.
faq.q: How is Microsoft Project related to Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Planner?

project.long:
Microsoft Project is project management software from Microsoft for building schedules, managing resources and visualising work in Gantt charts. It is a paid product, first released in 1984, and is also referred to as MS Project or simply Project. It is classified as a Microsoft tool and is documented through Microsoft's support pages and an official product site.

The core purpose of Microsoft Project is to plan work against a timeline. Project managers use it to define tasks, assign people to those tasks and follow progress over time. The Gantt chart is the central view for this kind of planning, because it shows how tasks, durations and resources fit together across a schedule. Resource planning is a second pillar: knowing who is available, and for which work, is one of the recurring questions in any project environment.

The facts on record also note that cloud scheduling continues in Planner premium. This matters for organisations that have relied on older Project services, because the direction of cloud-based scheduling points toward Microsoft Planner. Microsoft Planner is therefore the most closely linked product to Microsoft Project in the relationship data. Microsoft Teams is the other related topic: Teams is commonly the place where project teams communicate and collaborate, so project planning tools and Teams are often considered together when organisations decide how to organise delivery work.

The M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Project Operations with Joe Griffin [MVP]" addresses the situation most directly. The episode says that Microsoft Project Online is approaching retirement and that organisations face a critical decision: simply replace an aging project management tool, or use the opportunity to modernise how projects are delivered across the business. The guest, Joe Griffin, is introduced as a Microsoft MVP, CEO of proMX UK and an expert in Dynamics 365 Project Operations, and the conversation explores the future of project management within the Microsoft ecosystem.

A related perspective comes from "Dynamics 365 Project Operations - Simply Explained". The episode describes how customer projects can become complicated quickly because different roles need different information: sales holds the customer relationship and quote, project managers hold schedules and tasks, resource managers need to know who is available, consultants record hours and expenses, and finance needs to understand costs, revenue and what can actually be invoiced. This framing helps explain why planning software alone is sometimes only one part of a larger decision about how projects are run and billed.

The episode "Microsoft Teams Project Management: A Practical Guide" looks at project management from the Teams side. It discusses common problems such as disorganisation and communication breakdowns even when the right tools are available, and describes turning Teams into a structured project command center through task tracking, file management, clear file structures, automated status updates and strategic channel planning.

One caution on naming: the episode "Fix Common Azure AI Foundry Project Failures" concerns AI projects in Azure AI Foundry and only shares the word "project" with Microsoft Project. It is not about the scheduling product. Typical decisions around Microsoft Project therefore centre on whether to keep using existing scheduling tools, how to move toward Planner premium for cloud scheduling, and whether broader solutions such as Dynamics 365 Project Operations fit the organisation's needs.

project-management-office.desc: A project management office (PMO) is an organizational unit that sets project standards, oversees projects and reports across them, as covered on M365.FM.

faq.a: A PMO is a group or department inside an organization that sets and maintains project management standards, provides documentation, guidance and metrics, and reports on project progress. Its aim is to standardize execution and improve efficiency.
faq.q: What is a project management office (PMO)?

faq.a: An enterprise PMO is the type with the broadest remit. It gives a portfolio-wide view of all projects, aligns them with strategy and usually reports to the CEO or an equivalent role.
faq.q: What is an enterprise PMO?

faq.a: A PMO can be supportive (consultative), controlling (requires compliance with its standards) or directive (takes over project management). Which level fits depends on how much authority the organization wants the PMO to hold.
faq.q: What levels of control can a PMO have?

project-management-office.long:
A project management office (PMO) is a group or department inside a business, agency or enterprise that sets and maintains project management standards. Its purpose is to standardize how projects are executed and to gain efficiency from repeated practice. An enterprise PMO is the form with the widest remit: it provides a portfolio-wide view of all projects in an organization and aligns them with strategy.

A PMO typically acts as the source of documentation, guidance and metrics for project work. Many PMOs build their frameworks on established methods such as PRINCE2 or the PMBOK guide. Common functions include defining the methodology, facilitating or owning portfolio management, monitoring active projects and portfolios, and reporting progress to top management. That reporting helps leadership decide which projects to continue and which to cancel.

PMOs are often described by their level of control over projects. A supportive PMO takes a consultative role. A controlling PMO requires compliance with its standards. A directive PMO takes over project management itself. Several organizational types are also described. The enterprise PMO usually reports to the CEO or an equivalent role. The divisional PMO serves a single business unit. The project PMO exists for one large project or program. A project management center of excellence is another variant. Some researchers argue that PMOs cannot be sorted into fixed types and that many PMO practices lack supporting evidence, even though a PricewaterhouseCoopers survey of 1,524 organizations cited in the source material names an established PMO among the top three drivers of successful delivery.

In practice, organizations weigh how much authority a PMO should hold. A lightweight, advisory setup suits teams that mainly need templates and guidance, while a controlling or directive model fits organizations that need strict adherence to a common framework. The decision also depends on whether the PMO is meant to serve one project, one division or the whole enterprise.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Planner for Enterprise PPM with Erik van Hurck [MVP]" places the PMO within the building blocks of enterprise project and portfolio management. In that discussion, the Project Management Office is described as a centralized function that defines and maintains the enterprise project management framework, providing guidance and monitoring adherence to methodologies. The episode lists it alongside related areas such as enterprise project governance, which outlines authority, roles, responsibilities and decision-making processes, as well as resource management and risk management. Read together, these areas show the PMO as the function that keeps the framework consistent while governance, resource allocation and risk handling operate around it.

For people searching for the term, the key points are that a PMO standardizes methods, monitors delivery and reports across projects, and that its scope and level of control vary by organization. The enterprise PMO is the variant most closely tied to portfolio-level visibility and strategic alignment.

faq.a: Microsoft's lifecycle information states that Project Online is being retired on September 30, 2026. Microsoft points customers to Planner, Project Server or Dynamics 365 Project Operations.
faq.q: When is Microsoft Project Online being retired?

faq.a: Project Online is a SharePoint-based cloud service for project portfolio management. Its web interface is Project Web App, and it works with the Project desktop application.
faq.q: What is Project Online built on?

faq.a: The episode "Dynamics 365 Project Operations with Joe Griffin [MVP]" presents the retirement as a decision between replacing an aging tool and modernizing project delivery. It describes Project Operations as combining resource management, budgeting, financial tracking, time and expense management, invoicing and AI-powered insights on Microsoft Dataverse.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode on Dynamics 365 Project Operations say about the retirement?

project-online.long:
Microsoft Project Online is Microsoft's cloud service for project portfolio management. It is built on SharePoint, delivers its web interface through Project Web App, and works together with the Project desktop application. It is part of the wider Microsoft Project family. Project Online is scheduled to be retired on September 30, 2026, and Microsoft's lifecycle documentation points customers toward Planner, Project Server or Dynamics 365 Project Operations as alternatives.

The service is aimed at organizations that need more than basic task tracking. According to the M365.FM episodes, Project Online and Microsoft Project remain relevant for complex project management and enterprise scheduling with advanced resource management. Features such as task dependencies, timeline views, Gantt charts and detailed schedule-driven planning are the typical reasons teams look at Project Online rather than lighter tools. The episode "Microsoft To Do vs Planner vs Lists vs Loop" notes that Planner does not natively support task dependencies or traditional Gantt charts and is intended as a lightweight, kanban-style project management tool. For dependency management and advanced scheduling, that episode points to Microsoft Project or Project Online.

Project Online also appears in the Microsoft 365 licensing landscape. The episode "Set Up Microsoft Copilot in Teams Step by Step" lists Project Online Essentials among the eligible plans for Copilot access, alongside other plans such as Visio Plan 1 and Plan 2, SharePoint Plan 1 and Plan 2, and OneDrive for Business Plan 1 and Plan 2. The episode states that one of these plans is required for each user who will access Copilot, and it advises asking the IT administrator if the organization's plan is unclear.

In day-to-day collaboration, Project Online is often discussed next to Microsoft Teams. The episode "Organize Projects Properly in Microsoft Teams" describes Teams as project management software for many teams, combining chat, meetings, file sharing and task management through Planner and Project for the web. For complex project management or enterprise scheduling with advanced resource management, the episode says Microsoft Project or Project Online may still be needed, and that Teams integrates with both to give a unified project management experience.

The approaching retirement shapes most current decisions about the product. The episode "Dynamics 365 Project Operations with Joe Griffin [MVP]" frames the retirement as a choice for organizations: replace an aging project management tool, or use the occasion to modernize how projects are delivered across the business. Joe Griffin, described as a Microsoft MVP, CEO of proMX UK and an expert in Dynamics 365 Project Operations, discusses the future of project management within the Microsoft ecosystem. The episode describes Dynamics 365 Project Operations as covering resource management, budgeting, financial tracking, time and expense management, invoicing and AI-powered insights within a single platform built on Microsoft Dataverse.

For organizations still running Project Online, the practical question is which successor fits their needs. Based on the sources, the options named by Microsoft are Planner for lightweight task and kanban-style work, Project Server for organizations that want a server-based portfolio solution, and Dynamics 365 Project Operations for a broader platform that combines project delivery with financial and resource management. The official lifecycle page for Project Online is the reference for the retirement timeline and supported dates.

project-portfolio-management.desc: Project portfolio management (PPM) is the discipline of managing projects, programs and portfolios together, covering resources, finances, risks and strategic alignment.
project-portfolio-management.long:
Project portfolio management (PPM) is the discipline of managing projects, programs and portfolios together. It covers resources, finances, risks and strategic alignment, and it provides an enterprise view that sits above individual project schedules.

Where project management focuses on planning and delivering a single piece of work, PPM looks across many initiatives at once. Typical concerns include how limited resources are shared between projects, how spending is tracked across the portfolio, which risks affect several projects at the same time, and whether the work being done supports the organization's strategic goals.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, PPM is a recurring theme when organizations move from tracking single projects to governing a whole set of initiatives. This page treats it as a general concept rather than a specific product feature.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no related topics have been recorded for it yet.

project-server.desc: Microsoft Project Server is Microsoft's on-premises enterprise project management server and the predecessor platform to Project Online, part of Microsoft Project.
project-server.long:
Microsoft Project Server is an on-premises enterprise project management server from Microsoft. It forms part of the Microsoft Project product family and is regarded as the predecessor platform to Project Online.

As a server-based offering, Project Server was designed to support project management at the organizational level rather than for individual users alone. Among the enterprise features it provided were enterprise custom fields, which allow organizations to define their own data fields and apply them consistently across projects.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, Project Server relates to Microsoft Project as one of its components. Its role as an earlier, self-hosted platform is relevant for readers comparing on-premises project management infrastructure with the cloud-based Project Online that followed it.

No episodes of M365.FM are currently linked to this entry, and no official documentation links are listed in the available facts.

projectum-xpm.desc: Projectum xPM is a project, portfolio and resource management solution from Context& built on the Microsoft Power Platform and Dataverse, formerly known as Power PPM.

faq.a: Projectum xPM is a project, portfolio and resource management solution from Context& that is built on the Microsoft Power Platform and Dataverse.
faq.q: What is Projectum xPM?

faq.a: Projectum xPM was formerly known as Power PPM.
faq.q: What was Projectum xPM called before?

faq.a: It is positioned as a Project Online replacement, offering project, portfolio and resource management on Power Platform and Dataverse.
faq.q: How is Projectum xPM positioned relative to Project Online?

projectum-xpm.long:
Projectum xPM is a project, portfolio and resource management solution developed by Context&. It is built on the Microsoft Power Platform and uses Dataverse as its data layer. The product was formerly known as Power PPM.

The solution is positioned as a replacement for Project Online. Organizations that manage projects, portfolios and resources in Project Online can therefore consider Projectum xPM as an alternative that runs on Power Platform and Dataverse rather than on the older Project Online service.

Because it is based on Power Platform and Dataverse, Projectum xPM sits within the broader Microsoft ecosystem for business applications and data. No further details about specific features, editions, pricing or versions are provided here, and no related topics or episodes are currently linked to this entry on M365.FM.

prompt.desc: A prompt is the instruction or question given to an AI model; clear prompts state goal, context, format and constraints, and they also matter for AI security.

faq.a: A clear prompt states the goal, the context, the desired output format and any constraints. Describing the task precisely narrows the answers the model can give, which is why good prompting is described as the fastest way to better Copilot results.
faq.q: What makes a prompt clear?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Indirect Prompt Injection Security for Enterprise AI", it is a threat in which hidden commands in trusted content such as documents, emails, SharePoint pages or Teams conversations influence AI behavior. It works because retrieved content becomes part of the model's context and models do not reliably separate data from instructions.
faq.q: What is indirect prompt injection?

faq.a: The episode "The End of AI Bloat: Why Modern Agents Need Skills" says system prompts tend to grow as rules, procedures and examples are added, until they reach thousands of tokens. Every request then forces the model to process all instructions, even irrelevant ones, which the episode calls the context tax.
faq.q: Why can long system prompts be a problem for agents?

prompt.long:
A prompt is the instruction or question given to an AI model. It tells the model what to do, and the quality of that instruction strongly shapes the quality of the answer. In the Microsoft ecosystem, prompts are the main way users interact with Microsoft 365 Copilot, and they are a core concept within the broader field of Generative AI.

A clear prompt usually states four things: the goal (what the user wants to achieve), the context (the background the model needs), the desired format (for example a summary, a table or an email draft) and any constraints (length, tone, scope or sources to avoid). The same model can return very different results depending on how precisely the task is described, which is why good prompting is regarded as the fastest way to get better Copilot results. A vague request leaves the model to guess, while a specific one narrows the range of plausible answers.

Prompts are used wherever a person or a system hands work to an AI model. In Microsoft 365 Copilot, a user types a prompt in an app such as Word, Outlook or Teams, and the answer is grounded in that user's own work data. Prompts are not limited to short questions typed by end users. Agents, for example in Copilot Studio, also rely on a system prompt that describes the agent's role, tone, business rules and guardrails. The episode "The End of AI Bloat: Why Modern Agents Need Skills" describes how such a system prompt can grow over time as policies, compliance rules, procedures, examples, edge cases and department-specific workflows are added, until it becomes thousands of tokens long. Because every user request forces the model to process every instruction, even those that are irrelevant to the task, the episode frames this as a "context tax" and discusses skills as an alternative approach.

Prompts also have a security dimension, because instructions can reach a model through the content it reads and not only through what a user types. The episode "Indirect Prompt Injection Security for Enterprise AI" explains that retrieved content such as documents, emails, SharePoint pages, Teams conversations and knowledge bases becomes part of the model's context. Because models do not reliably separate data from instructions, hidden commands, poisoned documents, metadata or embedded instructions can influence AI behavior. The episode presents indirect prompt injection as a risk that is easy to overlook, in contrast to hallucinations, which many organizations treat as the main concern.

The episode "Stop Microsoft Copilot Prompt Injection with Azure Logic Apps" takes a related position. It argues that the real security problem is not weak prompts or missing filters but the architecture behind how AI models process retrieved information. According to the episode, systems like Microsoft Copilot retrieve data and treat it as context, which opens the door to prompt injection, and it discusses intercepting threats before they reach Copilot using Azure Logic Apps alongside Microsoft security tooling. The episode "Stop Prompt Injection in LangChain4j and Copilot Studio" adds that over-scoped connectors, missing logs and over-permissioned agents can turn helpful copilots into data-leaking tools, and it recommends strict access controls and regular monitoring of AI systems.

On the productivity side, the episode "Beyond the Prompt: Mastering Microsoft Copilot for Real Productivity with Jess Stratton [MVP]" looks at how Copilot integrates into Microsoft 365 and how users can move beyond basic interactions. It covers advanced prompt engineering and deeper integration of Copilot into daily work, with insights from Jess Stratton.

Taken together, the episodes show two sides of the same concept. Writing a precise prompt improves the usefulness of Copilot output, while treating everything a model reads as potential instructions explains why prompt-related risks cannot be solved by wording alone. Typical decisions around prompts therefore include how to phrase requests, how much instruction an agent should carry in its system prompt, and which controls limit the damage if untrusted content contains hidden instructions.

prompt-chaining.desc: Prompt chaining is a prompting technique in which one AI prompt's output feeds the next, linking several steps into a single workflow such as one spanning Microsoft 365 apps.

faq.a: Prompt chaining is a prompting technique in which the output of one AI prompt feeds the next, linking several steps into one workflow. The Claude documentation describes it as breaking a task into sequential API calls where each call's output feeds the next.
faq.q: What is prompt chaining?

faq.a: The Claude documentation names two situations: when intermediate outputs need to be inspected, and when a specific pipeline structure has to be enforced. Otherwise, it says, the model now handles most multistep reasoning internally.
faq.q: When is explicit prompt chaining still useful?

faq.a: The episode "Enterprise AI Agents with Sailaja Mantripragada [MVP-MCT]" lists it among capabilities of AI management platforms, alongside instruction pipelines and agent orchestration. The episode "Enterprise AI Agent Engineering with Karthikeyan VK [MVP]" describes orchestrating LLMs through prompt chaining and structured reasoning as a common approach in agent development.
faq.q: How do the M365.FM episodes mention prompt chaining?

prompt-chaining.long:
Prompt chaining is a prompting technique in which the output of one AI prompt becomes the input of the next, so that several steps are linked into one workflow. Instead of asking a model to complete a large task in a single request, the task is broken into a sequence of smaller prompts, each building on the result of the previous one. In the Microsoft ecosystem, the technique is described, for example, as a way to connect work across Excel, Word, Outlook and Teams with Microsoft 365 Copilot.

The core idea is sequential hand-off. A first prompt produces a result, such as an analysis, a draft or a summary. That result is passed into a second prompt, which transforms or extends it, and so on until the workflow is complete. According to the Claude Platform documentation, prompt chaining means breaking a task into sequential API calls in which each call's output feeds the next. Because every step is a separate call, each one can be logged, evaluated or branched on. The documentation describes this as the main practical benefit compared with using one large prompt.

A common pattern named in that documentation is self-correction in three steps: generate a draft, have the model review the draft against stated criteria, then refine the draft using that review. This shows how chaining adds structure to a task. Each stage has a narrow purpose, and the output of the review stage directly shapes the final refinement stage.

The documentation also qualifies when explicit chaining is needed. It says that with adaptive thinking and subagent orchestration, Claude now handles most multistep reasoning internally, so explicit chaining is no longer the default way to get multistep reasoning. It remains worthwhile in two situations: when intermediate outputs need to be inspected, and when a specific pipeline structure has to be enforced. Where chaining is not required, the documentation suggests asking the model to check its own work within a single prompt instead. The source offers only this short description and no dedicated example, and it does not cover Microsoft 365 Copilot scenarios.

Prompt chaining also appears in M365.FM discussions of enterprise AI agents. The episode "Enterprise AI Agents with Sailaja Mantripragada [MVP-MCT]" covers monitoring and management of agents after deployment. It says that AI management platforms can be used to define workflows and orchestrate interactions, and that these tools support prompt chaining, instruction pipelines and agent orchestration. The same episode mentions real-time dashboards and analytics for tracking agent performance, lifecycle management tools such as Azure ML or Databricks for versions and deployments, and policy engines and context-aware authorization for enforcing rules and adding security.

The episode "Enterprise AI Agent Engineering with Karthikeyan VK [MVP]" places prompt chaining in the context of LLM-centric agent development. It says developers and organizations often focus on orchestrating LLMs through prompt chaining and structured reasoning, and that this trend boosts productivity and flexibility. The episode also describes multi-agent systems in which specialized agents collaborate, workflow-oriented frameworks that blend deterministic pipelines with agent-based decision-making, and enterprise-grade platforms that add governance and compliance controls. It then raises a hidden problem that arises when teams rely too heavily on LLM-centric approaches.

In practice, decisions around prompt chaining often come down to how much visibility and control a workflow needs. A chain gives explicit checkpoints, which suits cases where intermediate results must be reviewed or where a fixed order of steps matters. A single, well-formed prompt may be sufficient when those needs are absent. The technique relates closely to instruction pipelines and agent orchestration, which the episodes mention alongside it as part of managing AI workflows.

prompt-engineering.desc: Prompt engineering is the practice of crafting and refining instructions to get better outputs from a generative AI model, and it recurs in M365.FM Copilot episodes.

faq.a: Prompt engineering is the practice of crafting and refining instructions to get better outputs from a generative AI model. M365.FM describes it as the skill of asking the right questions to get useful answers.
faq.q: What is prompt engineering?

faq.a: The episodes discuss it as a skill users need for good Copilot results, and note that missing prompt engineering training can lead to poor results and lost confidence during a rollout.
faq.q: How does prompt engineering relate to Microsoft 365 Copilot?

faq.a: Several M365.FM episodes say it is not. They argue for context engineering, agent-based designs, and workflow architecture to address inconsistent results and limited scalability.
faq.q: Is prompt engineering enough for enterprise AI?

prompt-engineering.long:
Prompt engineering is the practice of crafting and refining instructions to get better outputs from a generative AI model. The term covers the skill of asking the right questions in the right way so that an AI system returns useful answers. In the Microsoft ecosystem it is most often discussed in connection with Microsoft 365 Copilot, where users type requests into assistants that work inside everyday applications.

The core idea is iterative. A user writes an instruction, reviews the result, and adjusts the wording until the output matches the intent. How well this works depends on the person writing the prompt, which is one reason organizations talk about training. One M365.FM episode, "Fix Failed Microsoft 365 Copilot Rollouts", describes prompt engineering as the skill of asking the right questions to get useful answers. It lists a lack of prompt engineering training as a rollout problem: users get poor results and lose confidence, and employees may not realize they have access to Copilot at all. The episode frames structured onboarding as a way to avoid wasting the tool's potential.

Prompt engineering also appears as a skill to build in its own right. The episode "Beyond the Prompt: Mastering Microsoft Copilot for Real Productivity with Jess Stratton [MVP]" presents advanced prompt engineering alongside deep integration strategies across Microsoft 365 apps. According to the episode, Copilot works inside applications such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams, and the guidance is aimed at gaining productivity and overcoming AI overwhelm. In this framing, prompt skills are one part of using Copilot well rather than the whole picture.

Several M365.FM episodes argue that prompt engineering alone does not scale. "Build a Copilot That Respects DLP with Context Engineering" says that many Microsoft 365 Copilot projects fail even when the prompts look fine, and that the real issue is context engineering rather than prompt engineering. The episode describes context engineering as the systematic design, management, and governance of all information a Copilot can access, and says that when Copilot lacks structured, governed, and relevant information, results become inconsistent, low-quality, or misleading. In that view, many AI failures are context failures rather than model failures.

A related argument appears in "How to Build a Microsoft Copilot Agent Fabric". The episode states that the era of prompt engineering is ending, and says that teaching employees to write better prompts creates inconsistent results, limits scalability, and keeps humans involved in every workflow step. It contrasts this with specialized agents that collaborate, reason, and execute tasks autonomously instead of relying on a single chatbot. The episode describes this as the direction for enterprise AI and approaches it with a focus on architecture, security, governance, and operations.

The same shift is described for creative work in "AI Movie Production with Copilot, Seedance, and Higgsfield". The episode says creators increasingly use specialized systems for ideation, scripting, storyboarding, shot planning, character consistency, motion generation, editing, and post-production instead of relying on one model to generate an entire movie. It names a key theme as the move from prompt engineering to architecture design: the challenge is no longer writing better prompts but designing workflows that coordinate multiple AI models and creative stages. The episode compares this to how software evolved from standalone applications into distributed architectures.

Taken together, these episodes position prompt engineering as a foundational skill for individual users, and as a starting point rather than an endpoint. Typical decisions around it include whether to invest in user training during a Copilot rollout, how much to rely on individual prompt quality versus governed context, and when to move toward agent-based or multi-model workflows. The episodes present these as complementary layers: prompts shape a single interaction, context engineering governs the information behind it, and architecture design coordinates multiple systems.

prompt-injection.desc: Prompt injection is an attack where hidden instructions in documents, web pages or emails push an AI system to ignore its rules or leak data.

faq.a: In the indirect form, the malicious instruction is hidden in content the AI system retrieves, such as documents, emails, SharePoint content or Teams conversations, rather than typed in by a user. The episode "Indirect Prompt Injection Security for Enterprise AI" focuses on this indirect route.
faq.q: What is the difference between direct and indirect prompt injection?

faq.a: According to the episode "Stop Microsoft Copilot Prompt Injection with Azure Logic Apps", the problem lies in the architecture: models cannot reliably separate data from instructions, so retrieved content becomes part of the model's context.
faq.q: Why is prompt injection hard to prevent with filters alone?

faq.a: The sources point to limiting permissions, filtering inputs and requiring human approval for sensitive actions. The episodes also recommend least-privilege access, permission audits, logging and treating AI agents as privileged accounts.
faq.q: Which defences are commonly recommended?

prompt-injection.long:
Prompt injection is an attack in which hidden or malicious instructions placed in a document, web page or email trick an AI system into ignoring its rules or leaking data. It belongs to the broader field of generative AI security, because the attack targets how language models treat text. An injected instruction is, in the end, just text that the model processes like any other prompt, which is why the technique is difficult to separate cleanly from legitimate content.

The attack is most discussed in its indirect form. Instead of a user typing a harmful request directly, the malicious instruction is embedded in content the AI system later retrieves, such as trusted documents, emails, SharePoint content, Teams conversations or knowledge bases. The episode "Indirect Prompt Injection Security for Enterprise AI" describes how every piece of retrieved content becomes part of the model's context, so hidden commands, poisoned documents, metadata and embedded instructions can influence AI behavior without the attacker ever interacting with the system directly. The episode argues that many organizations see hallucinations as the biggest enterprise AI risk, while this less visible threat is among the most dangerous.

The underlying problem is architectural. The episode "Stop Microsoft Copilot Prompt Injection with Azure Logic Apps" says the core issue is not weak prompts or missing filters but the way AI models process information. Systems such as Microsoft Copilot retrieve data from multiple sources, and the model cannot reliably separate data from instructions. For that reason the episode treats prompt injection as a design and workflow question rather than something a single filter can fully solve, and it discusses using Azure Logic Apps for security workflows, including advice to use prewarmed instances and monitor performance so these workflows stay responsive when data volumes are high.

The risk grows when the AI system can act, not only answer. This links prompt injection closely to the AI agent: an agent that reads content and takes actions can turn a manipulated instruction into a real consequence. The episode "Stop Prompt Injection in LangChain4j and Copilot Studio" warns that over-scoped connectors, over-permissioned agents and missing logs can create reportable incidents, and it recommends strict access controls to prevent data leaks and unauthorized actions, along with regular monitoring of AI systems and a governance framework aligned with organizational goals and legal requirements.

The episode "Secure Microsoft Copilot with Entra ID and Zero Trust" frames the exposure through what it calls the "Lethal Trifecta": Microsoft Copilot can access sensitive data, read untrusted content and communicate externally. It names EchoLeak as an example of a prompt injection attack that can exploit such conditions. Microsoft's recommendation, as presented there, is explicit verification and least-privilege access, together with auditing permissions and treating AI agents as privileged accounts.

Across the sources, the typical defences are consistent: limit the permissions of the AI system, filter inputs, and require human approval for sensitive actions. The episode "Secure MLOps in Microsoft Cloud with Martin Dimovski [MVP-MCT]" places prompt injection within a wider AI security picture that also covers infrastructure, models, training data, inference pipelines and generated outputs, and it describes prompt injection as becoming one of the biggest AI security concerns today, alongside risks such as open-source model supply chains, compromised dependencies, API key leakage and poisoned public models.

In practice, decisions around prompt injection concern which data an assistant or agent may read, which external channels it may use, which actions require a person to confirm, and how activity is logged for later review. Combining narrow permissions, input handling and approval steps reflects the point made across the episodes that no single control removes the risk.

protected-health-information.desc: Protected health information (PHI) is health, care or payment data linked to an individual and governed in the US by HIPAA; relevant to Microsoft 365, Azure and AI compliance.

faq.a: PHI is information about an individual's health, medical care or payment for care that can be linked to that individual. In the US its use and disclosure are governed by HIPAA.
faq.q: What is protected health information (PHI)?

faq.a: The episode "What Is SharePoint Premium - Simply Explained" names sensitivity labels for PHI, access logging and encryption as SharePoint Premium compliance features for regulated industries.
faq.q: Which Microsoft 365 features do the episodes connect to PHI?

faq.a: According to "How to Stop AI Agents from Deleting Important Emails", using AI systems that are not HIPAA-compliant to process PHI leads to regulatory violations, and most AI email tools lack Business Associate Agreements with healthcare organizations.
faq.q: Why does PHI matter when using AI tools?

protected-health-information.long:
Protected health information (PHI) is information about an individual's health, medical care or payment for care that can be linked to that individual. In the United States, the use and disclosure of PHI are governed by HIPAA. The term is central to compliance planning in the Microsoft ecosystem because many organizations that store documents, run email, or build AI solutions on Microsoft platforms also handle data of this kind.

The M365.FM episodes treat PHI mainly as a compliance trigger. When a system processes PHI, the organization has to show that technical, physical and administrative controls are in place. The episode "Public vs Hybrid vs Multi-Cloud Azure Architecture" lists HIPAA among the compliance standards that shape architecture choices and says it applies to organizations holding PHI in the USA. It places HIPAA next to PCI, GDPR and CCPA as requirements that influence whether a public, hybrid or multi-cloud design meets legal obligations, especially in highly regulated industries.

In document management, PHI shows up as a labeling and protection question. The episode "What Is SharePoint Premium - Simply Explained" says SharePoint Premium addresses compliance requirements for regulated industries and names sensitivity labels for protected health information (PHI), access logging and encryption as features. The episode describes this as an integrated approach so that governance policies are applied consistently across a Microsoft 365 environment, which reduces the complexity of compliance management. In practice, labeling content that contains PHI is one way to make the sensitivity of that content visible to people and to policy enforcement.

The episode "Viva Connections - Simply Explained" lists compliance measures in which Personal Identifiable Information (PII) and PHI are stored securely. Its table names technical, physical and administrative controls, access controls and information security policies to prevent unauthorized access, regular backups, audit controls and encryption protocols, SSL technology for secure transmission, and continuous monitoring of systems for security threats. These items illustrate the kinds of safeguards the episode associates with handling PHI alongside other personal data.

PHI also matters for AI projects. In "From Data to Intelligent Agents: Building Trusted Enterprise AI with Microsoft AI Foundry with Shubhangi Goyal [MVP]", HIPAA appears in a list of laws and regulations relevant to AI, described as compliance for AI systems processing PHI, alongside the EU AI Act, CCPA and financial regulations such as GLBA. To ensure compliance, the episode recommends defining data governance policies, implementing technical controls for data access, and monitoring agent behavior against the applicable regulations.

The episode "How to Stop AI Agents from Deleting Important Emails" gives a concrete warning. It says that using AI systems that are not HIPAA-compliant to process PHI leads to regulatory violations. It also points to a Business Associate Agreement gap: according to the episode, most AI email tools do not have BAAs with healthcare organizations, which can cause unauthorized disclosures of PHI. The episode frames these legal points as a reminder that AI cleanup and automation tools must comply with privacy laws and regulations, and that failure to do so can bring serious penalties and loss of trust.

Taken together, the episodes suggest a typical decision sequence: identify whether data qualifies as PHI, check which regulations such as HIPAA apply, choose platform features such as sensitivity labels, access logging and encryption, and confirm that any third-party or AI tool that touches the data is covered by the required agreements and governance policies before it is deployed.

protected-users.desc: The Protected Users security group is a global Active Directory group that shields privileged accounts from credential theft by restricting NTLM, delegation and ticket lifetimes.

faq.a: It is a global Active Directory security group intended to protect privileged accounts against credential theft. Members are subject to stricter authentication restrictions than regular accounts.
faq.q: What is the Protected Users security group?

faq.a: Members cannot use NTLM authentication, face limits on Kerberos delegation, and receive shorter Kerberos ticket lifetimes.
faq.q: What restrictions apply to members of the Protected Users group?

faq.a: It is designed for privileged accounts, where protecting credentials from theft is especially important.
faq.q: Which accounts is the Protected Users group meant for?

protected-users.long:
The Protected Users security group is a global security group in Active Directory. It is designed to protect privileged accounts against credential theft by applying a set of non-configurable restrictions to the accounts that belong to it.

According to the available description, members of the group cannot authenticate using NTLM, are limited in how Kerberos delegation can be applied to them, and receive shorter Kerberos ticket lifetimes. Together these restrictions reduce the ways in which a member's credentials could be captured and reused by an attacker.

The group is typically relevant for administrators and other high-privilege accounts in Windows Server environments that rely on Active Directory, where reducing exposure of reusable credentials is a common hardening goal. Because membership changes how an account can authenticate, the behavior of applications and services that depend on NTLM or delegation should be reviewed before accounts are added.

The group's behavior and requirements are described in Microsoft's documentation on credentials protection and management for Windows Server. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

protocol-buffers.desc: Protocol Buffers (protobuf) is a language-neutral mechanism from Google for defining and serializing structured data, used as the interface definition language of gRPC.

faq.a: Protocol Buffers is used to define and serialize structured data in a language- and platform-neutral way. It is the interface definition language of gRPC, where service contracts are written in a .proto file and client and server code is generated from it.
faq.q: What is Protocol Buffers used for?

faq.a: According to the episode with Gábor Ruzsinszki, gRPC uses Protocol Buffers to serialize data, and the services and messages are described in a .proto file. Code for both client and server is generated from that file.
faq.q: How does Protocol Buffers relate to gRPC?

faq.a: The episode "Fix OWASP Architectural Risks in .NET Applications" recommends Protocol Buffers, or JSON with strict schema validation, as safer alternatives to unsafe serialization formats. It also advises validating data before deserialization.
faq.q: Why do the M365.FM episodes mention Protocol Buffers in a security context?

protocol-buffers.long:
Protocol Buffers, often shortened to protobuf, is a language-neutral and platform-neutral mechanism from Google for defining and serializing structured data. Developers describe the shape of their data and the operations of a service in a schema, and that schema is then used to produce a compact binary representation of the data. Protocol Buffers also serves as the interface definition language of gRPC, which is the context in which it appears most often in the M365.FM episodes.

The working model is schema-first. Service contracts are defined in a .proto file, which describes the messages and services an application wants to use. From that file, code is generated for both the client and the server. Because both sides are generated from the same definition, they know exactly what to expect from each other. The episode "Azure SQL Security Beyond Firewalls and IP Allowlists" describes this as defining the data structure up front, which prevents errors and interface drift.

The episode "Modern .NET: WPF, ASP.NET Core, and gRPC with Gábor Ruzsinszki [MVP]" introduces gRPC as a way to call methods on a server from a client as if they were local, aimed at high-performance remote procedure call scenarios where data must be sent and received quickly even when applications run on different machines. It states that gRPC uses Protocol Buffers to serialize data, and that this can be applied in several kinds of applications, including WPF desktop apps, ASP.NET web apps, and cloud services. In that setting, the .proto file is the shared contract from which the generated client and server code originates.

A recurring theme is the compactness of the binary encoding.
