The episode "Azure SQL Security Beyond Firewalls and IP Allowlists" says that gRPC payloads are smaller because of binary encoding, that Protocol Buffers reduce serialization size and speed up integration, and that this saves bandwidth and lowers infrastructure costs. The same episode says gRPC outperforms REST by up to nine times as load increases, with benefits showing up for large data transmissions or many simultaneous clients. These are figures attributed to the episode, not independently verified measurements.

The episode "Custom Connectors vs Model Context Protocol for Enterprise AI" frames Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) within an architectural shift away from verbose text-based communication toward machine-optimized binary transport. It contrasts oversized JSON payloads and repetitive REST requests with the compact binary messages that Protobuf transmits. The topics it lists include how binary serialization reduces payload size, why Protobuf reduces CPU overhead, the performance gains of schema-first communication, and how strongly typed contracts eliminate interface drift.

Protocol Buffers also comes up in a security context. In "Fix OWASP Architectural Risks in .NET Applications", the discussion of insecure deserialization notes that parsers may mishandle malformed data, leading to crashes or data corruption. The recommended practice is to avoid unsafe serialization formats and use safer alternatives such as JSON with strict schema validation or Protocol Buffers. The episode also advises validating incoming data before deserialization and restricting the types an application accepts, and it suggests replacing insecure serializers with secure, validated formats during modernization.

Typical decisions around Protocol Buffers therefore involve choosing between text-based formats such as JSON over REST and a schema-first binary approach, weighing payload size and throughput against the need to maintain .proto contracts and generated code. The episodes treat Protocol Buffers less as a standalone product and more as the contract and encoding layer that gives gRPC its typed, compact, predictable behavior.

provisioned-throughput-units.desc: Provisioned throughput units (PTU) reserve dedicated model processing capacity for Azure OpenAI and Microsoft Foundry deployments, as an alternative to pay-as-you-go token billing.

faq.a: A PTU is the unit of measure for provisioned deployments in Microsoft Foundry and Azure OpenAI, where each unit represents a fixed amount of model processing capacity reserved exclusively for the deployment.
faq.q: What is a provisioned throughput unit (PTU)?

faq.a: PTUs are billed hourly per unit regardless of tokens consumed, with Azure Reservations available as a discounted commitment option. Standard deployments use pay-as-you-go token billing on shared capacity.
faq.q: How are PTUs billed compared with standard deployments?

faq.a: No. The documentation states that quota does not guarantee capacity and that reservations do not guarantee it either, so creating the deployment first is advised.
faq.q: Does having PTU quota guarantee capacity?

provisioned-throughput-units.long:
Provisioned throughput units (PTU) are the normalized unit used to reserve dedicated model processing capacity for Azure OpenAI deployments. Microsoft's documentation describes a provisioned throughput unit as the unit of measure for provisioned deployments in Microsoft Foundry, where each unit represents a fixed amount of model processing capacity. PTUs serve as an alternative to pay-as-you-go token billing, in which capacity is shared and cost follows the number of tokens consumed.

The central idea is reservation. The chosen number of units is reserved exclusively for the deployment whether or not requests arrive. Because the capacity is not shared the way it is in standard deployments, latency is more predictable. The documentation positions provisioned throughput for steady traffic, latency-sensitive applications, high production volumes and real-time scenarios such as chats, copilots or agents.

Several parameters shape how PTUs are obtained and used. Quota is model-independent but is granted per subscription, region and deployment type. Each model has a minimum unit count and its own tokens-per-minute yield per unit, so the same number of PTUs delivers different throughput depending on the model. Deployment types include global provisioned, data zone provisioned and regional provisioned. An optional spillover feature can send overflow requests to a standard deployment when the provisioned capacity is exceeded, although it is not available for every model family.

Billing for PTUs is hourly per unit, regardless of how many tokens are consumed. Azure Reservations are offered as a discounted commitment option. Sizing a deployment relies on request rates, prompt and response sizes and cache rates, and the Azure portal includes a capacity calculator to support that estimate. The documentation also cautions that quota does not guarantee capacity, which can fluctuate, and that reservations do not guarantee it either. For that reason, creating the deployment first is the advised order of steps before committing to a reservation.

A typical decision around PTUs is whether workload patterns justify reserved capacity or whether pay-as-you-go billing is sufficient. Steady, high-volume or latency-sensitive production traffic matches the scenarios the documentation names for provisioned throughput, while variable or low-volume usage is the situation standard token billing is built for. The hourly billing model means the cost is tied to the reserved units rather than to usage, which is why sizing matters.

The M365.FM episode "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud" places PTUs within the wider cost structure of building agents. In its overview of billing layers, the episode lists Provisioned Throughput Units as the cost of throughput in Foundry and gives a figure of $1 per PTU. It sets this beside other cost items such as agent logging and observability costs, which vary with logging volume, and the Microsoft Agent Pre-Purchase Plan, described as a unified plan with discounts on AI services at $19,000 for 20,000 ACUs. The episode says the pre-purchase plan covers over 30 services and offers a single governance path for AI projects, and it frames an understanding of these billing layers as a way to make better decisions and keep AI costs under control.

psdataverse.desc: PSDataverse is an open-source PowerShell module by Reza Niroomand that brings the Dataverse Web API to PowerShell 7+ for moving data in and out of Power Platform.
psdataverse.long:
PSDataverse is an open-source PowerShell module created by Reza Niroomand. It exposes the Dataverse Web API to PowerShell 7 and later, so that data operations against Dataverse can be scripted from the command line instead of being built by hand against the API.

The module is aimed at moving large amounts of data into and out of Power Platform. To support this, it offers piping, batching and parallelism. Piping lets results from one command flow into the next in the usual PowerShell style, batching groups multiple operations into fewer requests, and parallelism allows work to run concurrently rather than one record at a time.

Typical uses follow from that design: bulk data loads, exports, and other scripted data tasks against Dataverse environments, particularly where volume makes manual or one-by-one approaches impractical. Because it is a PowerShell module, it fits into existing automation and administration scripts that already run on PowerShell 7+.

No official site, documentation link or related topics are listed in the information available for this entry, and PSDataverse is not yet linked to any specific M365.FM episode.

pseudonymization.desc: Pseudonymization replaces personal identifiers with artificial ones while a key to re-identify exists, so under GDPR the data remains personal data.

faq.a: Pseudonymization is a de-identification technique that replaces personal identifiers with artificial ones while a key to re-identify the person still exists. Under GDPR, pseudonymized data remains personal data.
faq.q: What is pseudonymization?

faq.a: With pseudonymization, re-identification is still possible through a key, so the data stays personal data under GDPR. Anonymization removes the link to a person so that identification is no longer possible.
faq.q: How does pseudonymization differ from anonymization?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, Purview applies pseudonymization of usernames in audit log collection and in Communication Compliance investigations, together with role-based access control and other privacy protections.
faq.q: Where does pseudonymization appear in Microsoft Purview?

pseudonymization.long:
Pseudonymization is a de-identification technique in which personal identifiers, such as a name or username, are replaced with artificial identifiers. The defining feature is that a key or other additional information still exists that allows the original identity to be restored. Because re-identification remains possible, pseudonymized data is still treated as personal data under GDPR. This distinguishes pseudonymization from anonymization, where the link to a person is removed so that identification is no longer possible.

The technique is used to reduce exposure of identities while keeping data useful for analysis, review or processing. A pseudonym lets someone work with records, events or content without immediately seeing who is behind them, while an authorized party holding the key can still reverse the mapping when it is legitimately necessary. Typical situations include investigations, audits, analytics and AI workloads where the data has value but the identity of the individual should not be visible to every person who handles it. Pseudonymization lowers privacy risk but does not remove the need for governance, since the key itself and the resulting data still require protection.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, pseudonymization appears mainly in compliance and governance tooling. The M365.FM episode "Communication Compliance - Simply Explained" describes Microsoft Purview Communication Compliance as a process in which potential issues may be dismissed, resolved through coaching, escalated to Human Resources, referred to compliance teams, or transferred into Microsoft Purview eDiscovery for formal legal investigations. According to the episode, role-based access control, pseudonymization, reviewer accountability, privacy protections and documented governance procedures help keep such investigations fair, proportionate and aligned with applicable legal and organizational requirements. Here pseudonymization is one safeguard among several, intended to limit how much reviewers see about the people involved.

The episode "Audit Microsoft 365 User Activity with Purview" covers the same idea in the context of audit logs. It says that Microsoft Purview captures audit logs across Microsoft 365 services while protecting user identities through pseudonymization and role-based access controls. The episode adds that granular collection policies let administrators specify which sensitive information types and AI interaction details to collect, and that retention policies help manage how long audit data is kept, preventing unnecessary storage. Similarly, "Protect Microsoft Copilot with Purview, DLP, and Insider Risk with Alan Cox [MVP]" notes that Purview supports pseudonymization of usernames for privacy, alongside capabilities for monitoring compliance, finding electronic information for legal cases, and retaining or deleting content as required.

Pseudonymization also features in architecture and AI governance discussions. In "How to Design Sovereign Cloud Architecture for Microsoft Azure", the episode lists encryption and pseudonymization as a best practice for meeting sovereignty rules, recommending strong encryption for data at rest and in transit and noting that cryptographic keys should be kept secret with good controls and classification. This is relevant because the key that enables re-identification is itself a sensitive asset. The episode "Stop Prompt Injection in LangChain4j and Copilot Studio" lists anonymization and pseudonymization as techniques for transforming personal data so that compliance can be maintained while AI remains effective, as part of a broader governance framework that also includes security measures and regular staff training.

When deciding whether to use pseudonymization, the main questions concern who may hold the re-identification key, under what conditions it can be used, and how the pseudonymized data is protected. Because the data stays personal data under GDPR, the usual obligations around lawful processing, access control, retention and documentation continue to apply. The episodes treat pseudonymization as a complement to, not a replacement for, role-based access control, encryption, key management and retention policies.

psreadline.desc: PSReadLine is a PowerShell module that customizes command-line editing, with a searchable command history and suggestions drawn from previously run commands.
psreadline.long:
PSReadLine is a PowerShell module that customizes the command-line editing experience. It is used in the PowerShell console to change how text is entered and edited at the prompt.

Among the capabilities described for the module are a searchable command history and suggestions based on commands that were run earlier. These features are intended to make it easier to recall and reuse previous input without retyping it.

Official reference documentation for the module and its commands is published on Microsoft Learn under the PowerShell module reference for PSReadLine.

No related topics or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

pstn.desc: The public switched telephone network (PSTN) is the worldwide telephone infrastructure that Microsoft Teams voice reaches through Calling Plans, Operator Connect, Teams Phone Mobile or Direct Routing.

faq.a: It is the worldwide telephone network of phone lines, mobile networks and switching infrastructure. Teams needs a PSTN connection so users and voice apps can place and receive calls outside the organization.
faq.q: What is the PSTN in the context of Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: No. Calls between Teams users stay inside Teams and never touch the PSTN. A PSTN connection is only needed for calls to and from outside phone numbers.
faq.q: Do calls between Teams users use the PSTN?

faq.a: No. Users need a Teams Phone license plus a separate PSTN solution. The license grants calling features, while the PSTN solution provides numbers and network access, including emergency calling.
faq.q: Is a Teams Phone license enough to make external calls?

pstn.long:
The public switched telephone network (PSTN) is the worldwide system of telephone lines, mobile networks and switching infrastructure that allows a call to reach a phone number anywhere. It is the shared layer that connects separate carriers and countries, so that a person on one network can ring a number on another. In the Microsoft ecosystem the term matters because Microsoft Teams voice is a software-based calling service that needs a path into this network whenever a call leaves the organization.

In Teams, PSTN connectivity lets users place and receive calls outside the company, for example to customers, suppliers or mobile phones. It is also needed for voice apps such as auto attendants and call queues, which require phone numbers to be reachable from outside. Calls between Teams users are different: they stay inside Teams and never touch the PSTN. This distinction is useful when planning, because only external calling and externally reachable voice apps depend on a PSTN connection.

Microsoft's planning documentation describes four ways to connect Teams to the PSTN. With a Microsoft Calling Plan, Microsoft acts as the carrier and supplies the numbers. With Operator Connect, a certified third-party carrier provides the service. With Teams Phone Mobile, a mobile operator number becomes the user's Teams number; this option supports user numbers only. With Direct Routing, an organization links any carrier to Teams through a certified session border controller. These options can be combined within a single tenant, so different users or sites can use different approaches.

A frequent point of confusion is the difference between a license and a PSTN solution. According to the documentation, users need a Teams Phone license plus a PSTN solution, and the two are separate. The license grants the calling features in Teams, while the PSTN solution supplies the phone numbers and the access to the public network, including emergency calling. Choosing a connection option therefore does not replace the license, and holding the license does not by itself provide numbers or outside connectivity.

The episode "Microsoft Teams Phone and Telephony | Simply Explained" covers the PSTN options for Teams Telephony. It states that each option has its own benefits and suits different organizational needs, and it starts its breakdown with Microsoft Calling Plans. According to the episode, Microsoft acts as the PSTN carrier in that model, managing the phone numbers and calls, and it lists a simple setup process among the advantages. This fits the broader decision that organizations face: a Calling Plan keeps carrier relationships with Microsoft, whereas Operator Connect, Teams Phone Mobile and Direct Routing bring in an outside carrier or an existing telephony setup.

When evaluating the choice, typical considerations include country availability, whether existing carrier contracts or equipment should be kept, whether mobile numbers should serve as Teams numbers, and how emergency calling is handled. The documentation points to external directories for availability by country and mentions emergency support only for the United States, so details for other regions need to be checked separately. The documentation does not give prices, so costs must be taken from the respective provider or licensing sources.

psychological-safety.desc: Psychological safety is a shared team belief that people can speak up, ask questions, admit mistakes or challenge decisions without social penalty.

faq.a: Psychological safety is a shared belief in a team that people can speak up, ask questions, admit mistakes or challenge decisions without social penalty. One M365.FM episode describes it as feeling comfortable sharing ideas and concerns without fear of embarrassment or punishment.
faq.q: What is psychological safety?

faq.a: The episodes mention sharing experiences openly, including challenges with AI, using peer reviews, setting clear guidelines, rewarding learning and making it safe to experiment. Peer advisory groups and trust-building in diverse or global teams are also named.
faq.q: How do the M365.FM episodes suggest building psychological safety?

faq.a: According to an M365.FM episode, research shows that psychological safety enhances team learning and effectiveness. The same episode cites a positive correlation between work quality and team learning behavior, supporting continuous learning and knowledge sharing.
faq.q: Why does psychological safety matter for teams?

psychological-safety.long:
Psychological safety is a shared belief within a team that people can speak up, ask questions, admit mistakes or challenge decisions without being penalized socially. It describes a feature of the working climate rather than a tool or a product. In the M365.FM episodes that mention it, the term appears in connection with leadership, communication across cultures, workplace isolation, collaboration platforms and the introduction of new technology.

In practice, psychological safety is used as a goal for teams and for the people who lead them. One episode describes it as a situation in which everyone feels comfortable sharing ideas, asking questions and expressing concerns without fear of embarrassment or punishment. The idea is that when this environment exists, a team can close communication gaps and make better use of what its members know. Leaders are described as playing a vital role in creating that environment, since they set the tone for how mistakes, questions and disagreement are received.

The episode "Leadership, AI, and Imposter Syndrome with Daniel "Dan" Barber [MVP]" connects psychological safety to the use of AI. Its recommendations for leaders include setting clear guidelines for how AI is used in the organization, using peer reviews to highlight the value of human judgment, and sharing personal experiences with AI, including the challenges, as a way to build psychological safety. The episode also lists normalizing imposter syndrome and holding open conversations among its strategies. In this framing, AI can increase demands and complexity, but it also creates opportunities for growth when approached with the right mindset, and responsible, contextual use is said to help leaders and teams build confidence and resilience.

The episode "Cultural Nuance in Global Meetings Beyond Translation" places psychological safety within global and multilingual teams. It describes the leader's role in creating a safe environment so that people can share ideas and concerns despite differences in language and culture. It also points to collaboration platforms with live translation and intelligent recaps as helpful for frontline workers who face language and digital barriers. Clear and inclusive communication is the shared concern, and psychological safety is presented as part of the same effort.

In "Why High Performers Burn Out from Workplace Isolation", psychological safety appears as a counterweight to loneliness and isolation. The episode describes peer advisory groups as safe spaces where people can share experiences without fear of judgment, and it states that research shows psychological safety enhances team learning and effectiveness. It also cites a study reporting a positive correlation between work quality and team learning behavior, which the episode reads as evidence that psychological safety supports continuous learning and knowledge sharing.

The episode "Fix Microsoft Teams Governance Sprawl with Enforced Decisions" lists psychological safety among strategies for challenging an organizational illusion, next to continuous improvement and rewarding learning. There it is summarized as making it safe to share ideas and experiment. The episode names stronger trust, a supportive environment, clearer views of contributions and less friction as benefits of facing the illusion head-on.

Finally, "From Microsoft Lync to Teams with Carsten Lund Meilbak [MVP]" mentions psychological safety in the context of inclusive communication after the pandemic. The advice is to build trust and psychological safety so that open dialogue and better collaboration can happen, alongside practices such as active listening, open questions, cross-functional projects and shared goals. The episode adds that organizations focused on inclusivity see higher employee engagement and job satisfaction.

Across these episodes, psychological safety is treated as a practical condition for learning, communication and collaboration rather than as a standalone program. Typical decisions around it include how leaders model openness, which guidelines to set when introducing new technology, and where to create protected spaces such as peer groups for honest exchange.

public-key-infrastructure.desc: Public key infrastructure (PKI) is the system of roles, services and processes that creates, distributes, renews and revokes digital certificates based on key pairs.

faq.a: Public key infrastructure (PKI) is the system of roles, services and processes that creates, distributes, renews and revokes digital certificates. These certificates are based on public and private key pairs.
faq.q: What is public key infrastructure (PKI)?

faq.a: A PKI handles the lifecycle of digital certificates: creating them, distributing them, renewing them and revoking them when needed.
faq.q: What does a PKI do with digital certificates?

faq.a: Based on the available description, PKI is a system of roles, services and processes rather than one individual product or feature.
faq.q: Is PKI a single product?

public-key-infrastructure.long:
Public key infrastructure (PKI) is the system of roles, services and processes that creates, distributes, renews and revokes digital certificates. These certificates are built on public and private key pairs, which allow identities and keys to be bound together and verified.

A PKI covers the full lifecycle of a digital certificate. This includes issuing certificates, distributing them to the users, devices or services that need them, renewing them before they expire, and revoking them when they should no longer be trusted. Because it combines technology, defined roles and operational processes, a PKI is generally treated as an infrastructure rather than a single product or feature.

On M365.FM, public key infrastructure (PKI) is recorded as a concept within the Microsoft ecosystem knowledge base. No related topics or episodes are linked to this entry at present, and no official documentation links have been associated with it. Further detail on how PKI relates to specific Microsoft products or services is not included in the information available for this page.

public-sector.desc: Public sector refers to government bodies, authorities and publicly owned organisations that provide public services, often with strict compliance needs on Microsoft platforms.

faq.a: The public sector is the part of the economy made up of government bodies, authorities and publicly owned organisations that provide public services. It is also referred to as government or public administration.
faq.q: What does public sector mean?

faq.a: The episodes group government with banking, finance and healthcare because these industries must follow strict regulatory frameworks to protect sensitive data and maintain trust, which affects how workflows, AI agents and networks are set up.
faq.q: Why do M365.FM episodes mention the public sector alongside banking and healthcare?

faq.a: The episodes link it to Microsoft Copilot Studio with Microsoft Purview, Power Automate approval workflows, Azure AI Foundry for citizen support and system security, and Azure Virtual WAN for secure connections between agencies and departments.
faq.q: Which Microsoft topics connect to the public sector in the episodes?

public-sector.long:
The public sector is the part of the economy made up of government bodies, authorities and publicly owned organisations that provide public services. The term is also expressed as government, public administration or, in German, Öffentliche Verwaltung. On M365.FM it is treated as an industry, and it appears in episodes mainly when the topic is compliance, data protection, auditability and secure connectivity in Microsoft cloud and AI scenarios.

Organisations in this area typically work under specific regulatory frameworks and handle sensitive data on behalf of citizens. For that reason, technology decisions in the public sector are often shaped less by feature lists and more by questions of oversight, data residency, traceability and trust. The M365.FM episodes that mention the sector do so in this context, usually listing government alongside other heavily regulated industries such as banking, finance and healthcare.

The episode "Scaling Copilot Studio with Isha Kapoor [MVP]" names banking, government and healthcare as industries with unique compliance challenges. According to the episode, each of these sectors must follow specific regulatory frameworks to protect sensitive data and maintain trust, and Microsoft Copilot Studio supports these needs by aligning with global and industry-specific standards. The episode describes tools for regulatory alignment, data protection and responsible AI, integrated with Microsoft Purview for end-to-end oversight. It also covers data residency: Microsoft Copilot Studio uses Azure's global infrastructure to give organisations secure options for controlling where their data lives.

The episode "Build Audit-Ready Power Automate Approval Workflows" points to the same risk profile. It says that finance, healthcare and government organisations must follow strict laws, and that a SharePoint approval process which does not meet these standards can lead to extra scrutiny. The episode recommends reviewing a Power Automate approval workflow regularly and making sure every approval and piece of evidence meets compliance rules. Missing approval logs or weak controls are described as a source of regulatory risk in regulated settings.

In "Build Auditable AI Agents with Azure AI Foundry", the public sector appears in a list of application areas. The episode lists "Government & Public Sector" as using the platform for citizen support and internal system security, with the stated outcomes of safe AI utilization and improved public administration. This places the sector among industries where AI agents must be auditable as well as useful.

The episode "Azure Virtual WAN - Simply Explained" addresses connectivity. It states that government and public sector organisations prioritise security and compliance, and that Azure Virtual WAN allows them to connect securely with various agencies and departments. Here the sector is presented as a typical user of managed wide-area networking where multiple bodies must exchange data safely.

"Build a Microsoft AI Agent Control Plane" touches on the sector more indirectly. In a discussion of honesty and trust, the episode says that government agents must be honest and that their lies can harm democracy and public trust. It also notes that AI agents can spread misinformation and that ethical guidelines are needed for their responsible use, with transparency and ethical practices as the basis for rebuilding trust.

Taken together, the episodes describe a consistent picture: in the public sector, compliance, data protection, auditability, secure networking and public trust are recurring decision criteria when adopting Microsoft services such as Copilot Studio, Power Automate, Azure AI Foundry and Azure Virtual WAN.

publisher.desc: Microsoft Publisher is a desktop publishing application for flyers, newsletters and brochures, part of Microsoft 365 Apps, with support ending in October 2026.

faq.a: Microsoft Publisher is a desktop publishing application for creating flyers, newsletters and brochures. It allows text and graphics to be placed freely on a page for print or digital distribution.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Publisher used for?

faq.a: According to the facts on record, Microsoft ended support for Publisher in October 2026. Organizations with existing Publisher files typically plan a move to other tools.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Publisher still supported?

faq.a: Microsoft Publisher is related to Microsoft Word and Microsoft PowerPoint, which can cover many layout and document tasks. It is also part of Microsoft 365 Apps and can be excluded from a deployment via an Office Deployment Tool XML configuration, as discussed in "Customize Microsoft 365 Apps Deployment with ODT XML".
faq.q: Which tools relate to Microsoft Publisher?

publisher.long:
Microsoft Publisher is a desktop publishing application from Microsoft for creating flyers, newsletters and brochures. It is classified as a Microsoft tool and is part of Microsoft 365 Apps. According to the facts on record, it was first released in May 1991, and Microsoft ended support for the product in October 2026. For that reason, the topic matters today mainly for people who still hold existing Publisher files or who are planning a move to other tools.

The application is used for page layout work in which text and graphics are placed freely on a page and prepared for print or digital distribution. Typical results are single-page flyers, multi-page newsletters and folded brochures. Unlike a word processor, a desktop publishing application focuses on the arrangement of elements on the page rather than on continuous text, which is why Publisher has been associated with small-scale marketing and communication material.

Publisher is related to two other Microsoft applications, Microsoft Word and Microsoft PowerPoint. Many layout tasks, such as newsletters or simple printed documents, can also be handled in Microsoft Word, while visually driven documents and presentations are the domain of Microsoft PowerPoint. When an organization has to replace Publisher after the end of support, these two applications are the related tools named in the facts. Which one fits depends on how the existing Publisher files are used: for print-oriented documents, for on-screen material, or for a mix of both.

Because Publisher ships as part of Microsoft 365 Apps, administrators also meet it in deployment planning. The M365.FM episode "Customize Microsoft 365 Apps Deployment with ODT XML" touches on this. It describes how a default Click-to-Run installation can lead to the wrong apps being installed, for example HR receiving Publisher it never wanted, while finance lacks Power Query. The episode says the remedy is a tailored Office Deployment Tool XML configuration that removes unneeded apps, locks the update channel, pre-installs languages, enables shared device activation and reduces update prompts. It also recommends segmenting configurations by persona, since finance, marketing and other groups need different app sets. In that context, Publisher is an example of an application that can be excluded from a deployment when a group has no use for it.

The word "publisher" also appears in other M365.FM episodes, but with different meanings that should not be confused with the application. "Deploy Dynamics 365 Customizations with ALM Pipelines" discusses solution publishers in Dynamics 365, which act as the identity and prefix for customizations. "Event Grid - Simply Explained" describes an event publisher as the source that sends events to Azure Event Grid. "The Hard Way to Get Listed on Microsoft Marketplace" lists Publisher and Offer ID issues as common submission errors, and "Migrate Exchange Web Services to Microsoft Graph with Glen Scales [MVP]" mentions publisher info as part of an app registration. None of these refer to the desktop publishing product.

For current guidance on the product, Microsoft maintains a support page for Publisher. In practice, decisions around Publisher come down to three points: inventorying existing Publisher files, choosing a replacement tool such as Microsoft Word or Microsoft PowerPoint for future documents, and deciding whether Publisher should still be included in Microsoft 365 Apps deployments.

publisher-verification.desc: Publisher verification is a Microsoft Entra program that marks an app's publisher as verified, so consent policies can limit user consent to verified publishers.

faq.a: It shows that Microsoft has confirmed the publisher of the app through a verified Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program account linked to the app registration. It says nothing about the quality of the app and is not a certification.
faq.q: What does the blue verified badge in publisher verification mean?

faq.a: Administrators can use the verification status as a criterion in user consent policies, for example to allow user consent only for apps from verified publishers.
faq.q: How can administrators use publisher verification?

faq.a: No. The documentation notes state that there is no fee and no license. The process does require a verified partner account and specific admin roles in Entra and Partner Center.
faq.q: Does publisher verification cost anything or require a license?

publisher-verification.long:
Publisher verification is a program in the Microsoft identity platform that gives users and administrators information about the authenticity of the organization behind an application. When an app integrated with Microsoft Entra is verified, a blue verified badge appears on the consent prompt and on the enterprise applications page. The badge shows that Microsoft has confirmed the publisher's identity. It does not describe the quality of the app and is not a certification.

The confirmation works through a verified Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program account. The partner ID of that account is linked to the app registration, and Microsoft uses this link to establish who publishes the app. Administrators can then use the verification status as a criterion in user consent policies. This allows an organization to restrict user consent so that people can only approve apps from verified publishers, while other apps require administrator review.

Several requirements apply. The partner account has to be the verified global account of the organization. The app must be registered in a Microsoft Entra tenant with a work or school account, not in Azure AD B2C, and that tenant has to be associated with the partner account. The publisher domain must match the e-mail domain used during verification and cannot be an onmicrosoft.com domain. The user who starts the process needs an application administrator role in Entra and an admin role in Partner Center, and must sign in with multifactor authentication. There is no fee and no license for the program.

The feature mainly applies to multitenant apps that use OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect. National clouds are currently not supported, according to the documentation notes. Organizations that run apps in those environments therefore cannot rely on this mechanism today.

In practice, publisher verification is one building block of governing third-party apps and integrations in Microsoft 365. Without any guardrail, users may grant permissions to unknown applications, which creates exposure for organizational data. Combining a consent policy that requires verified publishers with a review process for everything else gives administrators a more manageable approval path. Because the badge only confirms who publishes an app, it works best alongside other checks, such as reviewing the permissions an app requests.

The M365.FM episode "Leadership and Microsoft 365 Governance Beyond Central Control" mentions publisher verification in its governance checklist. The episode lists reviewing and governing third-party apps and integrations with Microsoft 365, naming app consent and publisher verification, as one of the recurring governance tasks. It places this next to regular risk assessments, compliance gap analysis, budgeting for governance tools and administration, and periodic governance reviews with executive sponsorship. In that framing, controlling app consent is part of a continuous governance cycle rather than a one-time setting.

pull-request.desc: A pull request is a request to merge one branch into another, giving reviewers a place to comment on and approve changes before the merge happens.

faq.a: A pull request asks for one branch to be merged into another and lets reviewers comment on, request corrections to, or approve the change first. The episode "Git - Simply Explained" describes reviewers examining commits, files and individual lines.
faq.q: What is a pull request used for?

faq.a: The episode "Manage Git Integration for Microsoft Fabric Notebooks" describes opening a pull request when feature-branch work is finished, so teammates can review it. After approval, the branch is merged back into development or testing.
faq.q: How are pull requests used with Microsoft Fabric notebooks?

faq.a: Yes. The episode "Git - Simply Explained" says automated checks can build the project and run tests, and "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD" mentions required status checks as part of branch protection rules.
faq.q: Can automated checks run on a pull request?

pull-request.long:
A pull request is a request to merge one branch into another. It gives reviewers a place to comment on, discuss and approve a change before it is merged. In Git-based workflows, it is the usual step between finishing work on a branch and bringing that work into a shared branch such as main, development or testing.

The M365.FM episode "Git - Simply Explained" places pull requests within the wider set of Git concepts. Clone creates a connected copy, push sends committed work outward, and pull brings shared work back to a local copy. When a branch is ready, teams commonly open a pull request before merging it into main. The pull request asks teammates to inspect the proposed changes. Reviewers can examine commits, files and individual lines, leave comments, request corrections, or approve the work. According to the episode, this keeps the discussion attached directly to the changes instead of spreading decisions across emails and chat messages. The episode also notes that automated checks can build the project and run tests as part of the process.

Pull requests also appear in team practices around Microsoft Fabric. The episode "Manage Git Integration for Microsoft Fabric Notebooks" describes a feature-branch workflow: when work in a feature branch is finished, a pull request is opened so teammates can review the changes. The episode says this helps catch mistakes, share knowledge and improve notebooks. After approval, the feature branch is merged back into a development or testing branch, and the cycle repeats until the changes are ready for production. Its tip is to always use pull requests for merging, since code reviews help maintain high standards.

Repository setup is another place where pull requests come up. The episode "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD" lists a pull request template among the items to configure in a new GitHub repository, alongside issue templates, a default branch (main) with branch protection rules, CODEOWNERS and contribution guidelines. It also mentions configuring branch protection rules such as required reviews and status checks. In practice these settings determine what must happen on a pull request before a merge is allowed.

In discussions of AI-assisted development, pull requests are described as both an output and a measurement point. The episode "GitHub Copilot, Clean Context, Automated Testing & AI Coding Agents with Lars Gyrup Brink Nielsen [MVP]" describes AI coding agents that can potentially inspect a repository, understand an issue, modify multiple files, run automated tests, analyze failures, make corrections and prepare a pull request. The question shifts, in the episode's framing, from whether AI can generate code to whether it can safely perform engineering work inside a real software architecture. The pull request is where a human can still review that work.

The episode "The Productivity Illusion: Why AI is Breaking Your Engineering KPIs" looks at pull requests as a metric. According to the presentation it summarizes, pull request throughput has nearly doubled as AI generates a significant portion of production code, yet production incidents, code churn, review times and cognitive load have also increased. The episode argues that AI has moved engineering constraints downstream into review, testing, operations and governance, so a dashboard showing more merged pull requests does not by itself show more value.

Taken together, the episodes describe a pull request as a review gate and a record of discussion tied to specific changes. Typical decisions around it include which branches require pull requests, how many approvals and which automated checks are needed before merging, and how review capacity keeps pace with the volume of changes being proposed.

purchase-order.desc: A purchase order is a formal document from a buyer to a vendor stating the items or services, quantities, agreed prices, delivery dates and payment terms of a purchase.

faq.a: A purchase order states the items or services being bought, the quantities, the agreed prices, the delivery dates and the payment terms. The episode on Dynamics 365 Finance also mentions delivery details and other information associated with the purchase.
faq.q: What does a purchase order contain?

faq.a: According to the episode "Dynamics 365 Procurement and Sourcing - Simply Explained", procurement covers the request, approval, purchase order, receipt, invoice and payment. The purchase order follows approval and comes before goods receipt and invoice processing.
faq.q: Where does the purchase order fit in the source-to-pay process?

faq.a: The episode on Dynamics 365 Warehouse Management says the purchase order tells the organization which products, quantities and arrival time to expect. Employees can compare the physical delivery with it, so a shortfall such as 98 of 100 expected cases becomes visible immediately.
faq.q: Why is a purchase order useful in the warehouse?

purchase-order.long:
A purchase order is a formal document that a buyer sends to a vendor. It states the items or services being bought, the quantities, the agreed prices, the delivery dates and the payment terms. In practice it is the organization's formal request to the supplier, and it gives both sides a defined record of what was ordered. That shared record becomes important later in the process, when goods arrive and an invoice has to be checked against what was originally agreed.

In the M365.FM episodes, the purchase order appears as one step in a longer chain of business activity rather than as an isolated document. The episode "Dynamics 365 Procurement and Sourcing - Simply Explained" describes procurement as managing what happens when an organization actually buys something: the request, approval, purchase order, receipt, invoice, and eventually payment. Together, these activities form the source-to-pay process, which the episode describes as the complete journey from identifying a business requirement to paying the supplier. The purchase order sits in the middle of that journey, after a need has been identified and a vendor selected, and before goods are received and the invoice is processed.

The episode "Dynamics 365 Finance - Simply Explained" places the purchase order directly after approval. In its example, a request for laptops is reviewed by a manager, who can question or reject it before the organization places an order. This moves financial control earlier in the process instead of discovering unnecessary spending only after the invoice arrives. Once the request is approved, Purchasing can create the purchase order. The episode says it can describe the laptops, quantities, agreed prices, delivery details, payment terms and other information associated with the purchase.

The purchase order also matters for warehouse work. According to the episode "Dynamics 365 Warehouse Management - Simply Explained", warehouse activity frequently begins with a purchase order. The order tells the organization which products it expects from a supplier, the expected quantities, and usually the expected arrival time. When a truck reaches the warehouse, employees can scan the products or pallets and compare the physical delivery with the expected purchase order. The episode gives the example of 100 cases being expected while only 98 arrive, in which case the discrepancy can become visible immediately.

Planning is a further area where purchase orders play a role. The episode "Dynamics 365 Master Planning - Simply Explained" explains that a customer delivery date creates a chain of dependent dates stretching backward through production and purchasing. If a supplier requires ten days to deliver wheels, the purchase order must be placed considerably earlier than the production start. Lead times therefore determine when a purchase order needs to be created so that components are available when the production schedule requires them.

Finally, the purchase order connects to invoice handling. The episode "Dynamics 365 Accounts Payable - Simply Explained" notes that an invoice record can contain the vendor, invoice number, invoice date, currency, amounts, lines, tax information, purchase order references and supporting documents. A purchase order reference on the invoice links the supplier's bill back to the original order, which supports the comparison between what was ordered, what was received and what is being charged.

Taken together, the episodes treat the purchase order as the document that turns an approved need into a defined commitment with a supplier. It supports approval and financial control before spending occurs, gives the warehouse an expectation to check deliveries against, informs planning decisions about order timing, and provides a reference point for accounts payable when the invoice arrives.

purchase-requisition.desc: A purchase requisition is an internal request to buy goods or services that states what is needed, how much and where, before any vendor commitment is made.

faq.a: A purchase requisition is an internal request to buy goods or services that states what is needed, how much and where it should be delivered. It does not yet create a commitment with a vendor.
faq.q: What is a purchase requisition?

faq.a: According to the episode "Dynamics 365 Procurement and Sourcing - Simply Explained", this gives the organization a chance to review the requirement, check budgets, apply purchasing policies and obtain approvals before purchasing.
faq.q: Why does a purchase requisition come before any vendor commitment?

faq.a: The episodes describe automated approval workflows for purchase requisitions and agents that read an equipment request and create a requisition. One episode also describes supply chain monitoring that auto-creates a requisition, with actions logged and auditable.
faq.q: Can purchase requisitions be created or approved automatically?

purchase-requisition.long:
A purchase requisition is an internal request to buy goods or services. It records what an organization needs, in what quantity and, where relevant, where the purchase should be delivered. Its defining feature is timing: a requisition comes before any commitment to a vendor. It is a request inside the organization, not an order placed with a supplier.

Because no commitment exists yet, the requisition gives the organization room to act before money is spent. The episode "Dynamics 365 Procurement and Sourcing - Simply Explained" describes this as an opportunity to review the requirement, check budgets, apply purchasing policies and obtain the appropriate approvals before the purchase proceeds. In practice, the requisition separates the person who has a need from the process that decides whether and how that need is met.

The same episode explains that requisitions apply to many kinds of purchases. It lists examples such as laptops, office furniture, training, repairs, cleaning, software and legal services, and notes that Dynamics 365 can support both goods and services while maintaining controlled purchasing processes. An employee typically specifies the item or service, the quantity and the delivery location, and the request then moves through the organization's review steps.

In Microsoft's business applications, the purchase requisition is an early step in procurement. Dynamics 365 Procurement and Sourcing treats it as the internal request stage, ahead of the commitments made with vendors. Typical decisions around it include who may raise a requisition, which budgets it is checked against, which purchasing policies apply and who must approve it. Those rules are what turn a simple request into a controlled purchasing process.

The term also appears in discussions of automation. The episode "Orchestration-First Architecture for Business Logic" lists the automation of purchase requisition or expense report approvals as an example of an approval workflow, stating that this reduces approval times and ensures accountability. Here the requisition is the item moving through a workflow, with approvals handled by automated steps rather than manual hand-offs.

Autonomous agents are a further context. In "Autonomous AI Agents: Use Cases, Risks, and Governance", a procurement scenario has an employee request new equipment, after which the agent reads the request and creates a purchase requisition. This shows the requisition as the structured record that turns an informal request into a trackable procurement item, which is also why governance matters when software creates such records on behalf of people.

The supply chain perspective adds another use. In "Supply Chain Visibility with Fabric and Dynamics 365 SCM", closed-loop actions include automatically creating a purchase requisition, advancing an alternate supplier or splitting a shipment, with each action logged and auditable. In that scenario, a requisition can be triggered by monitoring conditions such as predictive exceptions, and the audit trail keeps the resulting actions traceable.

Across these episodes, the purchase requisition acts as a control point. It captures need, quantity and delivery details early, keeps the organization free of vendor commitments while checks happen, and provides a record that approvals, workflows and automation can attach to. Whether a person or an automated process creates it, the requisition marks the step where a need is formally stated and reviewed before any purchase order or vendor agreement follows.

purview.desc: Microsoft Purview is Microsoft's family of data governance, protection and compliance tools, covering labels, DLP, retention, eDiscovery, audit and insider risk.

faq.a: Microsoft Purview is Microsoft's family of data governance, protection and compliance tools. It covers sensitivity labels, data loss prevention, retention, eDiscovery, audit and insider-risk management across Microsoft 365 and other data sources.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Purview is a Trap: The Hard Truth About Data Governance" argues that treating it as one is a common mistake. It says relying on Purview without a clear strategy can lead to chaotic data environments and confusion over permissions.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Purview a complete data governance solution on its own?

faq.a: According to the facts and episodes, Purview works with content in Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive, and the episodes also mention Exchange Online and Microsoft Fabric as places where data lives and moves.
faq.q: Which Microsoft 365 services does Microsoft Purview work with?

purview.long:
Microsoft Purview is Microsoft's family of data governance, protection and compliance tools. It covers sensitivity labels, data loss prevention, retention, eDiscovery, audit and insider-risk management across Microsoft 365 and other data sources. Microsoft develops the product, and it is a paid offering. On M365.FM it is classified as a Microsoft tool and as an identity and security tool, and it is related to the topics of data governance and Microsoft Agent 365.

The purpose of Purview follows from how data behaves in a Microsoft 365 environment. According to the episode "Microsoft Purview Data Map - Simply Explained", an employee might answer email in Outlook, collaborate in Teams, save documents in SharePoint and OneDrive, analyze information in Microsoft Fabric, export a report, change numbers in Excel and send the spreadsheet to several colleagues. Each individual application may be secure, but the information keeps moving, being copied, renamed, shared and sometimes forgotten. Purview addresses this by providing tools to classify, protect, retain, search and monitor that information wherever it lives.

The capabilities named in the product description map to distinct tasks. Sensitivity labels and data loss prevention are used to classify content and to control how it is shared. Retention and records management define which documents are kept and for how long. eDiscovery supports searches and evidence preservation. Audit records user and administrator activity. Insider-risk management looks at risky behavior inside the organization. Because Purview works with content in Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive, it is often rolled out together with identity and device controls.

Several M365.FM episodes in the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets series walk through individual parts of Purview. "Microsoft Purview Records Management - Simply Explained" covers contracts, financial reports, employee records, policies and other business documents that must be retained for legal, regulatory and operational reasons. The episode describes how organizations still need clear rules defining which documents become official records, how long they must be preserved and when they can safely be deleted, even though work happens across SharePoint Online, OneDrive, Microsoft Teams and Exchange Online.

"Microsoft Purview Audit - Simply Explained" focuses on a different need. Employees open files, share documents, send email, modify Teams settings and update compliance policies every day. When a security incident, compliance investigation or legal request occurs, organizations need clear answers about what happened, who performed the action and when it took place. Audit records are the basis for those answers.

"Microsoft Purview eDiscovery — Simply Explained" addresses situations such as a regulator requesting company records, an HR investigation or legal teams needing to preserve critical evidence. The episode points out that searching through Outlook mailboxes, Teams chats, SharePoint sites and OneDrive folders manually is slow, error-prone and often impossible at enterprise scale, which is the problem eDiscovery is meant to solve.

The episode "Microsoft Purview is a Trap: The Hard Truth About Data Governance" adds a cautionary view. It says many organizations mistakenly treat Purview as a complete solution for data governance, and that relying on it without a clear strategy may result in chaotic data environments and confusion over permissions. The episode's point is that recognizing the limitations of the tool is essential for organizations that want to build a successful data governance framework. In practice this means that deciding what to classify, retain, audit and investigate, and who owns those decisions, comes before configuring the tooling. Official documentation for Purview is published by Microsoft on Microsoft Learn.

purview-data-map.desc: Microsoft Purview Data Map is the technical layer of Microsoft Purview that scans connected data sources and stores metadata about data assets.

faq.a: It is the technical layer of Microsoft Purview that scans connected data sources and stores metadata about data assets. The Unified Catalog builds on this metadata.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft Purview Data Map?

faq.a: According to the episode summaries, it holds the metadata for discovering and describing data assets, sources, classifications and relationships.
faq.q: What kind of information does the Data Map hold?

faq.a: The episodes describe it as the means to discover sensitive data, after which policies such as sensitivity labels and DLP rules can be enforced across Microsoft 365 data and cloud services.
faq.q: How does the Data Map relate to data protection in Microsoft Purview?

purview-data-map.long:
Microsoft Purview Data Map is the technical layer of Microsoft Purview that scans connected data sources and stores metadata about the data assets it finds. It is part of Microsoft Purview, the portfolio Microsoft uses for data security, compliance and governance. The Unified Catalog builds on the metadata that the Data Map holds, which makes the Data Map the foundation underneath the more visible catalog and governance experiences.

The purpose of the Data Map follows from the problem it addresses. Microsoft 365 data rarely stays in one place. An employee might answer email in Outlook, collaborate in Teams, save documents in SharePoint and OneDrive, analyze information in Microsoft Fabric, export a report, change numbers in Excel and send the spreadsheet to several colleagues. Each application may be secure on its own, but the information keeps moving, being copied, renamed, shared and sometimes forgotten. A metadata layer that records where data sits and what it looks like gives organizations a way to find and understand that data before they try to protect or govern it.

According to the episode summaries, the Data Map provides the metadata foundation for discovering and describing data assets, sources, classifications and relationships. In practical terms, it works by connecting to data sources, scanning them, and storing the resulting metadata rather than acting as a place where the business data itself lives. The classifications recorded during discovery are one of the elements the Data Map keeps, alongside descriptions of the assets, the sources they come from and the relationships between them.

Typical situations in which the Data Map comes up involve information architects and governance teams who need an inventory of data across several systems. The episode "Microsoft Purview Data Governance for Information Architects" frames the Data Map within a broader approach to managing data across its lifecycle using Purview capabilities and accountable roles. In that discussion the Data Map answers the question of what exists and where, while the governance features and roles decide who is responsible for it and how it is handled.

The Data Map also appears in discussions about data protection. The episodes "Microsoft Purview vs Azure Information Protection" and "What Is Microsoft Intune Used For?" carry a shared passage stating that Microsoft Purview works with Data Loss Prevention (DLP) and Microsoft Defender, using sensitivity labels, policy-based DLP rules and activity monitoring. In that passage the Data Map is named as the way to discover sensitive data, after which policies can be enforced across Microsoft 365 data and cloud services, and data security investigations can be accelerated when incidents occur.

The most direct treatment is the episode "Microsoft Purview Data Map - Simply Explained", part of the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets series on M365 FM. It starts from the scenario of data moving between Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, Microsoft Fabric and Excel, and explains how Microsoft Purview helps organizations find, understand, protect and govern that information. The episode places the Data Map as the discovery and understanding step in that chain.

A recurring decision around the Data Map is how it fits into a wider tooling landscape. The episode on data governance for information architects notes that Purview is deeply integrated with Microsoft security and compliance services, while Collibra is often positioned as a broader independent governance platform, and that the right choice depends on architecture and scope. The same episode confirms that Microsoft continues to use Purview as its unified data security, compliance and governance portfolio, so the Data Map remains a component of an actively used product family.

purview-data-security-investigations.desc: Microsoft Purview Data Security Investigations is a Microsoft Purview solution for investigating data security incidents such as data leaks and identifying exposed sensitive data.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft Purview solution for investigating data security incidents such as data leaks. It helps teams find where sensitive data is and what was exposed.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Purview Data Security Investigations?

faq.a: Microsoft Purview Data Security Investigations is part of Microsoft Purview, where it addresses the investigation of data security incidents.
faq.q: How does it relate to Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: It is used for data security incidents such as data leaks, where the goal is to identify the location of sensitive data and the extent of exposure.
faq.q: What kinds of incidents is it used for?

purview-data-security-investigations.long:
Microsoft Purview Data Security Investigations is a solution within Microsoft Purview designed for investigating data security incidents, such as data leaks. It helps teams find where sensitive data is located and determine what was exposed during an incident.

The product is used when a security or compliance team needs to understand the scope of a data incident. Instead of only noting that a leak occurred, investigators can work to locate the sensitive data involved and assess what information was affected.

Microsoft Purview Data Security Investigations is part of Microsoft Purview, the broader Microsoft family of data security, governance and compliance capabilities. Its role within that portfolio is focused on the investigation stage, complementing the other areas that Microsoft Purview covers.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic, and no further product details are provided here beyond its purpose and its place within Microsoft Purview.

purview-unified-catalog.desc: Microsoft Purview Unified Catalog is the business-facing data catalog in Microsoft Purview, organized by governance domains, data products and glossary terms.

faq.a: It is used to discover, understand and request access to data. It organizes data into governance domains, data products and glossary terms, and adds data quality scores and governance health controls.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Purview Unified Catalog used for?

faq.a: Governance domains, data products, glossary terms, critical data elements, and objectives and key results. Data products can bundle tables, files or Power BI reports for a use case.
faq.q: What are the main building blocks of the Unified Catalog?

faq.a: Not yet. Microsoft Learn states that the new experience requires upgrading to the enterprise version of the new Purview experience, which is being rolled out gradually by environment and region.
faq.q: Is the Unified Catalog available in every environment?

purview-unified-catalog.long:
Microsoft Purview Unified Catalog is the business-facing data catalog within Microsoft Purview. It is the place where people discover, understand and request access to data. Microsoft Learn describes it as the data governance platform within Microsoft Purview, an integrated software-as-a-service framework built on an inventory of data assets together with their metadata and lineage. It is part of Microsoft Purview and is aimed at making organizational data findable rather than leaving employees to ask colleagues which numbers to use.

The Unified Catalog supports several governance tasks: data discovery, secure access, curation by data owners and stewards, measuring governance health, and linking data to business goals. Its approach is federated governance. Central standards are defined once, while responsibilities for data sit in the business units that know the data best. This ownership model is also discussed in the episode "Map Real User Behavior in Microsoft 365 Governance". The episode says that Purview assigns specific accountabilities and so bridges gaps between business needs and technical implementation, with technical ownership covering how governance requirements are implemented within Purview. It also says that since adopting the Unified Catalog, organizations have seen improved data governance practices, because individual groups take ownership of their data and embed governance into daily operations. The same episode notes that communication breakdowns and poor workflow visibility across teams can still cause misunderstandings and inefficiencies.

The catalog is organized around a small set of building blocks. Governance domains group data by business concept. Data products bundle tables, files or Power BI reports for a specific use case. Glossary terms give shared business definitions. Critical data elements and objectives and key results (OKRs) connect data to business priorities. The episode "Microsoft Purview Unified Catalog - Simply Explained" walks through the same structure, covering the underlying data problem, what the catalog is, domains, data products, glossary terms, data quality and who uses it. Its starting point is that company data is often not missing but spread across different systems and therefore hard to find.

Governance health and data quality are part of the product. Health controls score the governance state, and health actions suggest improvements. Data quality rules and scores exist for governance domains, data products and individual assets, so that consumers can judge whether data is suitable for their purpose. Access is handled through access policies, which let users request access to data products instead of negotiating it informally.

Users can search or browse the catalog to find data, and an AI-based copilot is available as an additional way to interact with it. Typical situations include a business analyst looking for the authoritative dataset for a report, a data owner publishing a data product for others to consume, and a governance team tracking whether domains meet their quality and policy goals.

Availability is an important planning point. According to Microsoft Learn, using the new experience requires upgrading to the enterprise version of the new Purview experience. This is being rolled out gradually by environment and region, so it is not yet available everywhere. Numeric limits and pricing are covered in separate linked documentation and are not described here.

python.desc: Python is a general-purpose programming language that M365.FM episodes place around Power Platform automation, Azure Quantum, Azure Automation and the Microsoft Agent Framework.

faq.a: The episode "Use Python with Power Platform for Scalable Automation" presents a three-tier hybrid architecture with Power Platform as the orchestrator. "When to Use Python in Power Platform Automation" cautions against using Python as default glue code and says native connectors, Copilot and agent-style orchestration can be better in many cases.
faq.q: How does Python relate to Power Platform according to M365.FM?

faq.a: It is named as a runbook option in Azure Automation alongside PowerShell and graphical runbooks, as part of hybrid quantum jobs with QAOA in Azure, and as a language to verify when setting up the Microsoft Agent Framework.
faq.q: Where does Python appear in Azure scenarios covered by the episodes?

faq.a: According to the quantum episode excerpt, Q# is the primary language and is designed specifically for quantum programming. The episode also covers running hybrid quantum jobs in Azure with Python and QAOA.
faq.q: Is Python the primary language for quantum programming in Azure?

python.long:
Python is a programming language that appears in the Microsoft ecosystem as a scripting and integration option rather than as a product with its own admin surface. On M365.FM it comes up in several contexts: automation around Microsoft Power Platform, hybrid quantum jobs in Azure, runbooks in Azure Automation, and setup steps for the Microsoft Agent Framework. This page summarizes what the episodes say about it and does not describe the language beyond that.

The most direct treatment is in the episodes about Power Platform. "Use Python with Power Platform for Scalable Automation" reframes Microsoft Power Platform as a control plane for enterprise workflows instead of a low-code productivity toy. It introduces a three-tier hybrid architecture in which Power Platform acts as the orchestrator, with code-based components handling the heavier work. The point of the episode is that automation should be engineered for scale and hybrid scenarios, with Python as one part of that design.

"When to Use Python in Power Platform Automation" takes a more critical angle. The episode argues that Python is not the language of AI inside the Microsoft stack and that treating it as one quietly harms Power Platform projects. It describes the pattern of cramming Python into Power Automate, Power BI, Fabric or custom connectors as glue code, and says this can inflate defects and cost. It contrasts that pattern with options such as Copilot and agent-style orchestration, which the episode says can write and run the glue with typed contracts, native connectors and generated scripts that respect schemas and governance. The practical decision here is when Python adds value and when a native or agent-based approach fits better.

Python also appears on the Azure side. In "Run Hybrid Quantum Jobs in Azure with Python and QAOA", the episode explains why classical optimization struggles with NP-hard problems and how hybrid quantum methods such as QAOA on Azure can help. It covers qubits, superposition, entanglement and interference, and describes a classical optimizer steering parameters while Azure Quantum workspaces, simulators and quantum processing units run the quantum part. The excerpt also notes that several quantum programming languages are supported, with Q# named as the primary one designed for quantum programming, and that Python is used to drive these jobs.

In "Azure Automation - Simply Explained", Python is listed alongside PowerShell and graphical runbooks as a way to execute administrative tasks within an Automation Account. The episode describes schedules and webhooks for automated or event-driven workflows, Hybrid Runbook Workers for running automations on on-premises servers or machines outside Azure, and common scenarios such as starting and stopping virtual machines to reduce costs, patch management and user provisioning. In this setting Python is one of the runbook types an administrator can choose.

Finally, "Microsoft Agent Framework - Simply Explained" mentions Python in its implementation steps. The first step is to clone the laboratory repository and verify the Python version. The remaining steps cover creating an Azure AI Foundry resource and project, deploying required models and services, configuring an Azure Search Service and connecting it for grounding with Bing Search. The episode adds that the framework supports multiple programming languages, including .NET and Python.

Taken together, the episodes treat Python as a flexible option across automation, cloud administration, quantum experiments and agent development. The recurring decision is where it belongs: as a deliberate tier in a hybrid architecture, as a runbook language in Azure Automation, or as a prerequisite for a framework, rather than as default glue code added without a clear reason.

python-in-excel.desc: Python in Excel runs Python code directly in worksheet cells for analysis and visualization, executed in the Microsoft cloud and returned to the grid.

faq.a: The code is executed in the Microsoft cloud, not on the local computer. The results are returned into the worksheet grid.
faq.q: Where does Python in Excel run the code?

faq.a: A paid Microsoft 365 license for the desktop apps is required, and the Microsoft 365 connected experiences must be switched on. Free or perpetual home licenses do not support it.
faq.q: What is needed to use Python in Excel?

faq.a: No. Excel for iPad, iPhone and Android cannot recalculate Python cells and shows an error instead.
faq.q: Can Python cells be recalculated on mobile devices?

python-in-excel.long:
Python in Excel is a feature of Microsoft Excel that lets users write and run Python code directly in worksheet cells. It was developed by Microsoft and is classified as a Microsoft tool and as an analytics and BI tool. The code does not run on the local computer. It is executed in the Microsoft cloud, and the results are returned into the grid, so analysts can use Python for statistics, data cleaning and charts without leaving Excel. The feature is also referred to as Excel Python, and its license is listed as included.

The main purpose is to bring more demanding data analysis and advanced visualizations into the spreadsheet. Users write Python formulas in the Excel grid and gain access to open-source Python libraries under enterprise-level security. Typical scenarios include exploratory analysis of a table with Python libraries instead of long formula chains, building visualizations that standard Excel charts do not offer, and handing colleagues a single workbook that holds both the data and the analysis logic. Workbooks that use Python can be shared and refreshed with colleagues, which fits team-based work with shared files.

Python in Excel relates to other tools in the Microsoft ecosystem. It is often used together with Power Query: Power Query shapes and loads the data into the workbook, and Python then analyzes or visualizes it. It also relates to Microsoft 365 Copilot, which can assist users in working with data in Excel. Because Python in Excel is part of Microsoft Excel itself, the data, the transformation steps and the Python-based analysis can live in one file.

Availability depends on licensing and configuration. According to the Microsoft support documentation, a paid Microsoft 365 license for the desktop apps is required, and free or perpetual home licenses do not support the feature. The Microsoft 365 connected experiences must also be switched on. On Windows, the feature depends on specific update channels and build versions, and Excel for the web is available to enterprise and business users. Device-based subscriptions and shared computer activation are not supported. Excel for iPad, iPhone and Android cannot recalculate Python cells and shows an error instead.

Compute options are another point to consider. Without the add-on license, only standard compute and automatic recalculation are offered. The add-on adds premium compute as well as manual and partial recalculation modes. Premium compute is capped per month and falls back to standard compute once the cap is reached. Teams planning heavier analysis should check which compute tier and recalculation mode fit their workbooks.

Because execution happens in the Microsoft cloud, the feature suits shared workbooks, but organizations should consider where sensitive data is processed before using it. This is a governance decision as much as a technical one, since the data leaves the local machine for calculation. The M365.FM data for this entry contains no episodes, so no episode content is summarized here; the description above is based on the product overview and the Microsoft support documentation.

q-sharp.desc: Q# is Microsoft's open-source, high-level programming language for writing quantum programs, included in the Quantum Development Kit and usable with Azure Quantum.

faq.a: Q# is Microsoft's open-source, high-level programming language for writing quantum programs. It is included in the Quantum Development Kit.
faq.q: What is Q#?

faq.a: Q# programs can be used with Azure Quantum, Microsoft's cloud service for quantum computing.
faq.q: How does Q# relate to Azure Quantum?

faq.a: Yes. Q# is described as an open-source language and is part of the Quantum Development Kit.
faq.q: Is Q# open source?

q-sharp.long:
Q# is a high-level programming language from Microsoft designed for writing quantum programs. It is open source and is part of the Quantum Development Kit, the set of tools Microsoft provides for quantum development.

Q# programs can be used with Azure Quantum, Microsoft's cloud service for quantum computing. In practice, the language serves as the way developers express quantum algorithms and operations, with the Quantum Development Kit supplying the surrounding tooling.

Microsoft documents the language through its official Azure Quantum overview of Q#, which is the primary reference for its design and usage.

Q# is listed as a product entity in the M365.FM knowledge base.
