The comparison table in the episode places regression testing on the automated side: automation is described as best for repetitive tests and regression testing, and as ideal for frequent tests and large-scale test automation. Manual testing, by contrast, is described as better suited to complex, unique scenarios that need human judgment, to rare or short-term tests, and to usability and complex user flows. The episode notes that automation frees up testers for more complex tasks and gives faster feedback. The practical decision is therefore which checks are repeated often enough to justify automating them.

The episode "Unit vs Integration vs Frontend Testing" looks at how different test levels contribute to regression testing. It says unit tests catch regressions at the function or component level by failing quickly when internal logic changes break expected behavior. Integration tests can detect regressions in interactions, configuration or integration points that unit tests might miss. The episode summarizes the split as unit tests for narrow, fast feedback and integration tests for cross-component regressions. It also covers techniques such as mocks, stubs, fakes and dependency injection, which replace external dependencies so a unit test focuses on the code under test and reduces flakiness.

Regression testing also shows up as a risk-reduction step around change events. In "Migrate Bing Maps to Azure Maps in Power BI", the episode lists risks such as increased operational or customer impact when issues arise after migration, and decisions driven by deadlines rather than strategic planning. To mitigate them, it recommends a structured testing approach with thorough regression testing in a controlled environment before moving to production, so issues are identified and resolved early. It also mentions the Power BI conversion function, including the 'Upgrade maps' button, for converting existing Map and Filled map visuals to Azure Maps visuals.

In "Deploy Dynamics 365 Customizations with ALM Pipelines", regression testing is one of several recommended testing methods alongside user acceptance testing, data validation testing and API testing. The episode describes it as checking that updates do not break existing features, with the example of testing workflows after a Dynamics 365 update. It also advises defining critical business scenarios and automating repetitive tests, with role-based testing used to check permissions and access controls.

The episode "Debug Quantum Programs with VS Code and Azure Quantum" applies the idea to quantum development. Its best practices include using simulators in CI for regression testing and running limited hardware tests selectively. It also recommends logging telemetry and metrics for experiments so runs can be compared and regressions spotted, and versioning code, dependencies and experiment configurations for reproducibility.

Taken together, the episodes treat regression testing as a recurring safeguard rather than a one-off activity. It is usually automated, placed in pipelines or CI, layered across unit and integration levels, and run in a controlled environment before changes reach production. The description of this topic also notes that AI agents can expand a regression suite by generating tests from observed failures, so that each discovered problem becomes a permanent check.

regular-expressions.desc: Regular expressions (regex) are character sequences that define text match patterns, used in data classification to detect structured sensitive data such as ID numbers.

faq.a: Regular expressions (regex) are character sequences that specify text match patterns. They are used to find text that fits a defined structure.
faq.q: What are regular expressions (regex)?

faq.a: In data classification, regex enables fast, pattern-based detection of structured sensitive data such as ID numbers. A pattern describes the expected format, and matching text can be flagged.
faq.q: How are regular expressions used in data classification?

faq.a: Structured data with a consistent, predictable format, such as ID numbers, suits regex-based detection because its structure can be expressed as a pattern.
faq.q: What kind of data suits regex-based detection?

regular-expressions.long:
Regular expressions (regex) are character sequences that specify patterns for matching text. A pattern describes the form a piece of text must take, such as a fixed number of digits or a defined arrangement of letters and separators, so that matching strings can be located automatically.

In data classification, regex is used for fast, pattern-based detection of structured sensitive data. Identifiers that follow a consistent format, such as ID numbers, are well suited to this approach because their structure can be expressed as a pattern. A regex-based rule can then scan content and flag text that fits that structure, supporting the identification of sensitive information.

The approach is pattern-driven, so it relies on the data having a recognizable and predictable format. It is most relevant where sensitive values appear in a regular structure rather than as free-form text.

No related topics or M365.FM episodes are linked to this entry at present, so there is no further ecosystem-specific detail to report here.

regulatory-templates.desc: Regulatory templates are ready-made blueprints in Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager with the controls and improvement actions used to create assessments.

faq.a: They are ready-made blueprints containing the controls and improvement actions for a regulation, standard or certification. They are used to create assessments in Compliance Manager.
faq.q: What are regulatory templates in Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager?

faq.a: An M365.FM episode says they map to standards such as GDPR, HIPAA, ISO and industry-specific requirements.
faq.q: Which standards do regulatory templates map to?

faq.a: The episodes describe regulatory templates and improvement actions as centralizing compliance activities and making it easier to track evidence and update status, while the compliance score measures progress and highlights areas for improvement.
faq.q: How do regulatory templates relate to improvement actions and the compliance score?

regulatory-templates.long:
Regulatory templates are ready-made blueprints in Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager. Each template contains the controls and improvement actions that belong to a particular regulation, standard or certification, and it serves as the starting point for creating an assessment. Instead of building a compliance checklist from scratch, an organization selects a template that matches an obligation and works from the structure the template provides.

In practice, regulatory templates are used to translate legal, regulatory and internal governance obligations into concrete, trackable work. An episode of M365.FM describes them as templates that map to standards such as GDPR, HIPAA, ISO and industry-specific requirements. Once a template is applied, the resulting assessment lists the controls that need to be addressed and the improvement actions linked to them, so teams can see what is expected and where they currently stand.

The templates work together with other parts of Compliance Manager. The compliance score measures progress and highlights areas for improvement, while improvement actions break the requirements of a template into specific steps with guidance for teams. According to the episode "Microsoft 365 as an Enterprise Operating System", regulatory templates and improvement actions centralize compliance activities, which makes it easier to track evidence and update status. The same episode places them alongside pre-built assessments for common industry and regional standards, custom assessments for unique needs, workflow capabilities that streamline risk assessment, and step-by-step guidance that helps teams align with regulations.

Typical decisions around regulatory templates concern which obligations apply to the organization and whether a ready-made template fits them. Where a standard is covered by a template, it can be used to create an assessment directly. Where the needs are unusual, the episode points to custom assessments as an additional option. Because the templates tie requirements to improvement actions, they also help organizations decide which compliance work to prioritize and how to document the evidence that supports each control.

In the episode "Microsoft 365 Audit Readiness and Governance Debt", regulatory templates are named as one element of the broader Microsoft 365 compliance ecosystem. That ecosystem also includes data protection through information protection and governance, privacy controls, eDiscovery and audit capabilities, and the compliance score. The episode describes these capabilities as central to classifying and protecting sensitive data, retaining and disposing of content according to policy, detecting and responding to insider risks, and producing evidence for investigations. Within that picture, regulatory templates provide the regulatory mapping that connects the technical controls to named standards.

The episode "Control Rogue AI Data Risks with Microsoft Purview" connects regulatory templates to the governance of AI use. It lists them together with compliance scoring, automated sensitivity labeling, and retention and disposition policies as Purview capabilities that map to industry requirements. According to that episode, these capabilities help organizations manage AI in regulated contexts, so that AI interacting with customer data or health records stays governed, auditable and compliant when using Microsoft 365, Copilot or third-party AI tools.

Taken together, the episodes treat regulatory templates as a structuring tool rather than a standalone control. They define what a given regulation, standard or certification expects, and they feed the assessments, improvement actions and compliance score that Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager uses to show progress and support audit readiness.

rehost.desc: Rehost (lift and shift) is a cloud migration path that moves an existing server or application to Azure with few changes, usually onto a virtual machine.

faq.a: It is a cloud migration path in which an existing server or application is moved to Azure with few changes. The workload typically runs on a virtual machine instead of on-premises hardware.
faq.q: What is Rehost (lift and shift)?

faq.a: A rehosted workload typically runs on a virtual machine in Azure, replacing the on-premises hardware it previously used.
faq.q: Where does a rehosted workload usually run in Azure?

rehost.long:
Rehost (lift and shift) is a cloud migration path in which an existing server or application is moved to Azure with few changes. Instead of running on on-premises hardware, the workload typically runs on a virtual machine in the cloud.

The approach is generally used when an organization wants to move a workload to Azure without redesigning or rewriting it. Because the application itself is left largely as it is, the main change is where it runs: the underlying infrastructure shifts from physical or locally hosted servers to cloud-hosted virtual machines.

Rehost is one of several possible migration paths. Other paths typically involve modifying or rebuilding applications to make greater use of cloud services, whereas a rehost keeps changes to a minimum.

No related products, episodes or official documentation links are currently listed for this term on M365.FM.

released-product.desc: A released product in Dynamics 365 is a shared product definition approved for use in a specific legal entity, where it receives its own local settings.

faq.a: It is a shared product definition that has been approved for use in a specific legal entity. The legal entity then adds its own local settings.
faq.q: What is a released product in Dynamics 365?

faq.a: Local settings let each legal entity configure the product for its own use, while the underlying product definition remains shared.
faq.q: Why does a released product have local settings?

released-product.long:
A released product in Dynamics 365 is a shared product definition that has been approved for use in a specific legal entity. The legal entity then adds its own local settings to that definition. The term describes the step at which a product that exists as a common definition becomes usable within an individual company.

The concept separates two layers of product information. The shared product definition holds the details that apply across the organization, while the released product holds the settings that apply only to the legal entity in which the product has been released. This allows each legal entity to configure the product according to its own requirements without changing the shared definition.

The facts available for this entry are limited to this definition. No related topics, episodes or documentation links are currently associated with it on M365.FM.

remaining-useful-life.desc: Remaining useful life (RUL) is an estimate of how long a component can keep meeting its required function under assumed future operating conditions, with uncertainty.
remaining-useful-life.long:
Remaining useful life (RUL) is an estimate of how long a component can continue to meet its required function under assumed future operating conditions. Ideally, the estimate is stated together with its uncertainty rather than as a single fixed value.

The concept is used to describe how much service time is expected to remain before a component no longer performs as required. Because the estimate depends on assumed future operating conditions, a change in those assumptions changes the result. Stating uncertainty alongside the estimate makes clear how much confidence can be placed in it.

On M365.FM, no linked topics or episodes are currently associated with this entry, and no official documentation or site is listed for it. The entry therefore covers the general definition only, without product-specific detail from the Microsoft ecosystem.

remote-desktop-protocol.desc: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is Microsoft's proprietary protocol for connecting to a remote computer's graphical desktop, using port 3389 by default.

faq.a: RDP is Microsoft's proprietary protocol for connecting to the graphical desktop of a remote computer. It allows a user to view and operate the remote system's desktop over a network.
faq.q: What is Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP)?

faq.a: RDP listens on port 3389 by default.
faq.q: Which port does RDP use by default?

faq.a: RDP ports that are open on the internet are a frequent attack target. For this reason, exposing the default port directly to the public internet is generally regarded as risky.
faq.q: Why are open RDP ports considered a security concern?

remote-desktop-protocol.long:
Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is a proprietary protocol from Microsoft that allows a user to connect to and control the graphical desktop of a remote computer. By default, RDP listens on port 3389.

RDP is used to reach a desktop session on another machine over a network, so that the remote system's screen and interface can be operated from a different device. Because the protocol exposes a full graphical session, how it is made reachable matters for security.

RDP ports that are open to the internet are a frequent attack target. Exposing the default port 3389 directly to the public internet is therefore commonly treated as a risk, and this is a recurring consideration when remote access is planned for Windows-based systems.

In the context of the Microsoft ecosystem, RDP is a foundational concept for remote administration and remote desktop access. No related topics or episodes are currently linked to this entry on M365.FM, so this page serves as a concise definition of the term and its main security consideration.

report-definition-language.desc: Report Definition Language (RDL) is the XML-based file format that defines paginated reports in SQL Server Reporting Services and Power BI.

faq.a: Report Definition Language (RDL) is an XML-based file format that defines paginated reports. It is used in SQL Server Reporting Services and Power BI.
faq.q: What is Report Definition Language (RDL)?

faq.a: RDL is used to define paginated reports in SQL Server Reporting Services and in Power BI.
faq.q: Which Microsoft products use RDL?

report-definition-language.long:
Report Definition Language (RDL) is an XML-based file format used to define paginated reports. An RDL file describes a report as structured XML, and it is the report definition format used by SQL Server Reporting Services and Power BI.

Because RDL is expressed in XML, a report's definition is stored as text that tools can read, create and modify. This makes the format a common point of reference when working with paginated reports across the Microsoft reporting products named above.

The M365.FM knowledge base lists Report Definition Language (RDL) as a concept entity. No related entities or episodes are currently linked to this page, so it serves as a short definition of the term within the Microsoft ecosystem.

reprompt-attack.desc: Reprompt attack is a single-click data exfiltration technique against Microsoft Copilot, disclosed by Varonis, that injects prompts through a URL parameter.

faq.a: It is a single-click data exfiltration attack on Microsoft Copilot, disclosed by Varonis. It injects prompts through a URL parameter and chains follow-up instructions to leak data over multiple turns.
faq.q: What is the Reprompt attack?

faq.a: Varonis disclosed the Reprompt attack.
faq.q: Who disclosed the Reprompt attack?

faq.a: The initial prompt is injected via a URL parameter, so the attack needs only a single click. Follow-up instructions are then chained across multiple turns to leak data.
faq.q: How does the Reprompt attack deliver its prompts?

reprompt-attack.long:
Reprompt attack is a single-click data exfiltration attack targeting Microsoft Copilot. It was disclosed by Varonis. The attack relies on injecting a prompt into Copilot through a URL parameter, so that a user only needs to open a crafted link for the injected instructions to be processed.

According to the available description, the technique does not stop at the first injected prompt. It chains follow-up instructions so that Copilot continues to receive further prompts over multiple turns, which allows data to be leaked gradually rather than in a single request. The name reflects this repeated prompting behavior.

The concept is relevant to anyone assessing prompt injection and data exfiltration risks in AI assistants that are integrated with Microsoft services. It illustrates how input that arrives through a link, rather than typed by the user, can influence an assistant's behavior and how multi-turn chaining can extend the reach of an initial injection.

No further technical details, affected versions, mitigations or timelines are included in the facts available for this entry. Readers who need specifics should consult the original Varonis disclosure and Microsoft's own security guidance. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

request-for-quotation.desc: A request for quotation (RFQ) is a request sent to several vendors to bid on the same requirement, letting the buyer compare prices, delivery dates and terms.
request-for-quotation.long:
A request for quotation (RFQ) is a procurement request that a buyer sends to several vendors, asking each to bid on the same requirement. Because every supplier responds to an identical specification, the resulting quotes can be compared directly.

The main purpose of an RFQ is to support a supplier decision. By collecting offers on a common basis, the buyer can weigh prices, delivery dates and terms side by side before choosing a supplier. The comparison covers more than price alone, since delivery timing and contractual terms are part of what each vendor puts forward.

In practice, an RFQ is a structured way to gather and evaluate competing offers for a defined need. The quality of the comparison depends on how clearly the requirement is described, because vendors must be quoting against the same scope for their answers to be comparable.

On M365.FM, the term is catalogued as a concept entry. No related topics or episodes are linked to it at this time.

requirements-management.desc: Requirements management is the discipline of capturing, structuring, validating and tracing system requirements, increasingly supported by AI tools.

faq.a: It is the discipline of capturing, structuring, validating and tracing the requirements of a system. It helps answer what a system must do, why a requirement exists, who agreed to it and which parts of the solution implement it.
faq.q: What is requirements management?

faq.a: Traceability records the life of each requirement, including its origin, changes and links to parent and child requirements, tests and requesters. Change control receives change requests, analyzes their impact, implements approved ones, checks them through quality assurance and closes them.
faq.q: What do traceability and change control mean in this context?

faq.a: Microsoft 365 Copilot can help draft, summarize and structure requirement documents from existing material. In an Agentic SDLC, agents take part in turning requirements into code, tests and reviews.
faq.q: How does AI relate to requirements management?

requirements-management.long:
Requirements management is the discipline of capturing, structuring, validating and tracing the requirements of a system. It answers practical questions: what the system must do, why a requirement exists, who agreed to it and which parts of the solution implement it. The topic is also known as Anforderungsmanagement or requirements engineering. Its purpose is to keep a project aligned with its goals as scope and understanding change, and it is increasingly supported by AI.

According to the Wikipedia description of the field, requirements management is an ongoing process of documenting, analyzing, tracing and prioritizing requirements, getting stakeholders to agree on them, controlling changes and keeping stakeholders informed. A requirement is a capability that the product or service must meet. The overall aim is to confirm that the needs of customers and other stakeholders are understood, verified and satisfied, starting with the first analysis of objectives and continuing until after release.

Two mechanisms stand out. Traceability documents the life of each requirement: its origin can be followed, every change is recorded, and links connect parent and child requirements, tests and the people who requested them. This supports reports on compliance, completeness, coverage and consistency. Change control is the second mechanism. It receives and records change requests, analyzes their impact, implements the approved ones, checks them through quality assurance and then closes them. The same source describes work across phases such as investigation, feasibility, design, construction and test, and release, and names four verification methods: analysis, inspection, testing and demonstration.

In practice, organizations handle this in different ways. Some work only with documents, while others use tools that provide a database, traceability links, baselines and version control. The source advises adopting such tools incrementally, as part of wider process improvement rather than as a one-time switch. Whatever the storage format, the value comes from a shared, traceable description that business and technical people can both rely on.

The topic connects to several areas of the Microsoft ecosystem. Microsoft 365 Copilot can help draft, summarize and structure requirement documents from existing material, which can shorten the effort of turning notes and meeting results into a coherent specification. Agentic SDLC is related because agents take part in turning requirements into code, tests and reviews, which makes clear, verifiable requirements an input that automated steps depend on. Governance is also related, since traceability and approval of requirements are part of how an organization controls what gets built and how it changes over time.

Typical scenarios include collecting requirements for a new business application, keeping a record of decisions during a Microsoft 365 rollout, and checking that tests cover what was agreed. In each case, decisions revolve around how formal the process needs to be, which tooling to use and who approves changes.

No M365.FM episode in the knowledge base is linked to this topic directly, so there are no episode-specific statements to report here. Listeners interested in the surrounding areas can look at episodes covering Microsoft 365 Copilot, Agentic SDLC and Governance, which touch the contexts in which requirements are written, automated and controlled.

reranking.desc: Reranking is a retrieval step in which a second model rescores the top search candidates so the most relevant results go on to a language model, for example in RAG.

faq.a: Reranking is a second retrieval step in which a model rescores the top candidates from an initial search so the most relevant ones are passed on to a language model. It reorders existing results rather than finding new ones.
faq.q: What is reranking in a RAG pipeline?

faq.a: No. According to the Azure AI Search documentation, the semantic ranker reorders only the existing result set and generates no new text. Documents missed by the first-stage retrieval are not added.
faq.q: Does reranking generate new content or find new documents?

faq.a: Hybrid retrieval combines vector and keyword search to produce candidates, and reranking can then prioritize the most relevant of them. The episode "Improve Microsoft Copilot Accuracy Beyond Vector Search" describes modern tools using semantic reranking alongside hybrid retrieval.
faq.q: How does reranking relate to hybrid retrieval?

reranking.long:
Reranking is a retrieval step in which a second model rescores the top candidates returned by an initial search, so that the most relevant results are passed on, for example to a language model in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. The first search stage is built to find many plausible candidates quickly. The reranking stage then looks more closely at a limited set of those candidates and reorders them by how well they answer the query.

The approach can be seen in the semantic ranker of Azure AI Search, described in Microsoft Learn documentation. This ranker is a set of query-side capabilities that re-scores an initial result list produced by keyword ranking or reciprocal-rank-fusion ranking. It works on text queries, on the text part of vector queries, and on hybrid queries, and it relies on multilingual deep-learning models adapted from Bing. Only a limited set of top results is passed to the second stage. For each document, selected fields from a semantic configuration, such as title, keywords, and content, are combined into one summary string, which is truncated if it is too long. The ranker then assigns a new relevance score on a fixed scale, where a higher score means a better answer to the query.

Besides reordering, the semantic ranker can return captions with highlights and, optionally, a direct answer, both taken verbatim from the indexed content. Query rewriting is available in preview. The documentation describes the feature as suited to prose-heavy content such as knowledge bases and documentation. It is a billed premium feature offered in selected regions, with a free monthly allowance. Its limits are stated plainly: it reorders only the existing result set and generates no new text. If the first-stage retrieval misses a relevant document, reranking cannot recover it.

In practice, reranking is one decision among several in designing a retrieval pipeline. Teams choose how candidates are first retrieved, such as pure vector search, keyword search, or a hybrid of both, and then decide whether a second scoring stage is worth its added cost and processing step. Because reranking only reorders what the first stage returns, its value depends on the quality of that candidate list and on which fields are supplied to the ranking model.

The M365.FM episode "Improve Microsoft Copilot Accuracy Beyond Vector Search" places reranking within a discussion of retrieval accuracy. It states that pure vector search often lacks accuracy and context, and that hybrid retrieval, which combines vectors and keywords, improves precision and trust in AI responses. According to the episode, modern tools use semantic reranking to prioritize relevant answers, and it presents hybrid RAG as essential for business success. The episode also cites approximate figures for BIRD execution accuracy, putting pure vector search on quantitative queries at roughly 0% to 10%.

The episode "Build a Copilot That Respects DLP with Context Engineering" treats reranking from the angle of context engineering. It lists reranking strategies, described as sorting content by relevance so that important information is prioritized, alongside other practices such as defining contextual boundaries to avoid overload and structuring and standardizing context data. In that framing, reranking is one tool for deciding which material reaches the model's limited context, rather than a stand-alone feature.

resource-drift.desc: Resource drift is any change to Terraform-managed infrastructure made outside Terraform, leaving the real environment out of line with configuration and state.
resource-drift.long:
Resource drift is any change to infrastructure managed by Terraform that Terraform did not make. When such a change occurs, the real environment no longer matches the Terraform configuration and the recorded state.

Drift is detected by running a plan or a refresh-only plan. These operations compare the actual infrastructure with what Terraform expects, which makes differences visible before any changes are applied. The refresh-only variant is used to inspect and record what has changed in the environment without proposing modifications to the configuration.

The concept matters for anyone who relies on Terraform as the source of truth for infrastructure. Because configuration and state describe the intended and last-known condition of resources, any change made outside Terraform creates a gap between that description and reality. Identifying the gap is the first step in deciding whether to bring the environment back in line with the configuration or to update the configuration to reflect the change.

No specific M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic, and no additional related entities have been recorded.

responsible-ai.desc: Responsible AI means using AI in safe, accountable and useful ways, with governance, human judgment and monitoring across Microsoft technology initiatives.

faq.a: The episode "Responsible AI Is Good Business — Featuring Wiebke Apitzsch" describes it as helping organizations use AI in ways that are safe, accountable and useful, with governance, adoption and human judgment turning it into practical business value.
faq.q: What does Responsible AI mean according to M365.FM?

faq.a: In "Microsoft Purview for Copilot Security with Peter Rising [Microsoft]", Purview is described as supporting responsible AI adoption through data governance, sensitivity labels and Data Loss Prevention, so that Copilot respects existing security controls.
faq.q: How does Responsible AI relate to Microsoft Purview and Copilot?

faq.a: The episodes frame it as ongoing. One recommends post-deployment monitoring and making continuous improvement part of the AI strategy, while another says governance should be built in from the beginning rather than added later.
faq.q: Is Responsible AI a one-time task?

responsible-ai.long:
Responsible AI is an approach to designing, deploying and operating artificial intelligence so that it is safe, accountable and useful. In the Microsoft ecosystem the term appears in several contexts: governance frameworks for enterprise AI, security and compliance work around Microsoft 365 Copilot, platform capabilities in Azure AI Foundry, and agent building in Copilot Studio. Across the M365.FM episodes that touch on the topic, it is presented less as a stand-alone policy document and more as a set of practices that sit alongside technical delivery.

The episode "Responsible AI Is Good Business — Featuring Wiebke Apitzsch" frames the idea in practical terms. Its quick answer describes responsible AI as a way for organizations to use AI safely and accountably while still gaining value, and it explores how governance, adoption and human judgment can turn responsible AI from a policy discussion into business value across Microsoft technology initiatives. The excerpt also points to post-deployment monitoring as a recommendation of governance frameworks, and names Azure Machine Learning as offering real-time monitoring and explainability features that support this process. The episode's tip is to make continuous improvement part of the AI strategy by regularly reviewing AI governance policies and involving stakeholders.

Governance is the most recurring theme. In "Enterprise AI Agents with Sailaja Mantripragada [MVP-MCT]", the discussion highlights balancing innovation with governance so that AI solutions stay aligned with security, compliance and responsible AI principles. The episode argues that governance has to be built into AI initiatives from the beginning rather than added later. Topics it lists include data access, permissions, agent lifecycle management, citizen development, risk management, and frameworks that let organizations scale AI safely and confidently. In this reading, responsible AI is closely tied to who can build agents, what data those agents can reach, and how their lifecycle is managed.

Data protection forms a second angle. "Microsoft Purview for Copilot Security with Peter Rising [Microsoft]" connects responsible AI adoption to data governance, security and compliance. The excerpt states that Microsoft Purview helps address AI risks and supports AI enablement, and that a Copilot deployment should respect existing security controls. Its key takeaways mention sensitivity labels, used to classify and protect sensitive information so that Copilot honors those controls, and Data Loss Prevention as a further measure. Here responsible AI is expressed through concrete data-handling controls applied before and during Copilot rollout.

A third angle concerns regulated environments and development platforms. "Scaling Copilot Studio with Isha Kapoor [MVP]" says that organizations in regulated industries need to address identity governance, data leakage and compliance with laws such as HIPAA and GDPR, and that operational control while protecting sensitive data supports responsible AI. "Azure AI Foundry - Simply Explained" lists responsible AI among the core concepts of the platform, next to the model catalog, AI agents, prompt flows, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), fine-tuning, evaluations and observability. Evaluations and observability are the kinds of capabilities that make it possible to check AI behavior over time rather than only at launch.

Taken together, the episodes describe responsible AI as a lifecycle concern. Decisions arise before deployment (classifying data, setting permissions, defining who may build agents), at deployment (choosing platform features and compliance settings), and afterwards (monitoring, explainability and regular policy review with stakeholders). Human judgment remains part of the picture in the Wiebke Apitzsch episode, which places it alongside governance and adoption. For anyone searching the term, the practical takeaway from these sources is that responsible AI is carried out through governance structures, data protection tooling and ongoing review, rather than through a single product or one-time checklist.

responsible-ai-dashboard.desc: The Responsible AI dashboard is an Azure Machine Learning interface that combines tools such as error analysis, explanations and fairness assessment to debug models.

faq.a: It is a single interface in Azure Machine Learning that combines responsible AI tools, such as error analysis, model interpretability and fairness assessment, to evaluate and debug models.
faq.q: What is the Responsible AI dashboard?

faq.a: It supports regression and classification on tabular data, registered MLflow scikit-learn style models and parquet pandas datasets. AutoML models are not supported, and the number of visualized points is capped.
faq.q: Which model and data types does the Responsible AI dashboard support?

faq.a: No. According to the documentation, it is used for assessment and debugging, while mitigation is handled by separate tools.
faq.q: Does the Responsible AI dashboard fix the problems it finds?

responsible-ai-dashboard.long:
The Responsible AI dashboard is a single interface in Azure Machine Learning that brings several responsible AI tools together. It is used to evaluate and debug machine learning models and to support data-driven decisions about them. Instead of working with separate tools for fairness, error patterns, explanations and causal questions, a team can open one dashboard and move between these views for the same model and dataset.

According to the Azure Machine Learning documentation, the dashboard is made up of several components. Data analysis helps examine the dataset. The model overview includes a fairness assessment based on Fairlearn. Error analysis is used to locate cohorts, meaning subsets of data, where a model fails. Model interpretability provides global and local feature importance. Counterfactual what-if analysis lets users explore how changes to inputs would affect predictions, and causal analysis looks at the effect of treatment features. The dashboard can be customized so that only the tools relevant to a specific use case are included, and it is accompanied by a PDF scorecard that exports responsible AI metadata and findings.

The dashboard can be created through the Azure Machine Learning CLI v2, the Python SDK v2 or the studio. The components are designed to be combined in typical flows. One example is moving from the model overview to error analysis and then to data analysis, which helps trace where a model performs poorly and why. Another is moving from data analysis to causal inference, which helps separate correlation from causation. The documentation names data scientists and risk officers among the intended audiences, which reflects its use both for technical debugging and for review and oversight.

The documentation also lists limits. The dashboard supports regression and classification on tabular data. It works only with registered MLflow scikit-learn style models and with parquet pandas datasets. The number of points that can be visualized is capped, and AutoML models are not supported. Mitigation of the issues it surfaces is handled by separate tools, so the dashboard is oriented toward assessment and debugging rather than fixing problems itself.

The M365.FM episode "Secure and Govern Microsoft 365 Copilot" mentions the Microsoft Responsible AI Dashboard in a governance context. The episode describes an organization that may develop a Responsible AI Standard covering fairness, reliability, privacy and inclusiveness, with an Office of Responsible AI overseeing these efforts and checking that rules are followed. In that picture, the Responsible AI Dashboard is named as a tool that might be used to monitor AI systems and manage governance. The episode also stresses training on ethical principles for AI use and the importance of having easy ways to report concerns about Copilot or AI use.

Taken together, the product documentation and the episode show two sides of the topic. The documentation describes a concrete, model-level toolset inside Azure Machine Learning with defined components and defined limits. The episode places such tooling within a wider organizational framework of standards, oversight, training and reporting channels. Teams considering the dashboard would need to check whether their models fit the supported model and data types before planning around it.

rest-api.desc: A REST API is a web interface where one program requests data or actions from another using a URL, an HTTP verb, headers and a status-coded response.

faq.a: A REST API is a web interface through which one program requests data or actions from another. A request uses a URL, an HTTP verb and headers, and the response includes a status code. The term REST comes from Roy Fielding's 2000 dissertation.
faq.q: What is a REST API?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes mention the Power BI REST API for programmatic deployment, the SharePoint REST API for working with lists and documents, Microsoft Graph for tasks, and the Fabric REST API for Warehouse Snapshots. Custom connectors in Power Platform can also call any REST API.
faq.q: Where do REST APIs appear in Microsoft 365 and related services?

faq.a: The Microsoft Graph example in "Build Custom Microsoft 365 Copilot Plugins" sends a bearer token in the Authorization header and advises always using secure authentication. The Fabric example mentions generating API authorization tokens, and Azure API Management is described as a place to apply security policies, rate limits and logging.
faq.q: How is access to a REST API usually secured in these examples?

rest-api.long:
A REST API is a web interface through which one program requests data or actions from another. A request is built from an address (URL), an HTTP verb and headers, and the server answers with a response that carries a status code. The term REST comes from Roy Fielding's 2000 dissertation. In the Microsoft ecosystem, REST APIs are the common way to read, write and automate things in services such as Power BI, SharePoint, Microsoft Graph and Microsoft Fabric without using their graphical interfaces.

The basic mechanics are visible in the examples that appear in M365.FM episodes. A call to Microsoft Graph for Planner tasks is sent to a versioned address and includes an Authorization header with a bearer token, and the JSON result is then read from the response. The episode "Build Custom Microsoft 365 Copilot Plugins" stresses that secure authentication should always be used when connecting to Microsoft Graph, so that data stays protected. The same episode describes the SharePoint REST API, which lets a solution interact with SharePoint lists and documents. REST calls are used there to read, write and update items, automate updates, pull project statuses and manage files, which supports real-time project management and reporting and helps unify data from different sources.

REST APIs also play a role in release and deployment work. In "Deploy Power BI with Development, Test, and Production Pipelines", the Power BI REST API is listed as a way to deploy programmatically: reports can be uploaded and deployments managed by script rather than by hand. The episode places this next to automated publishing with CI/CD tools such as Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions, and next to parameterized data sources, so that content can move through development, test and production while dependencies between datasets, reports and data sources are handled.

In "Use Microsoft Fabric Warehouse Snapshots Correctly", the Fabric REST API is one of several interfaces for creating and managing Warehouse Snapshots, alongside the Fabric portal and T-SQL. The episode presents this choice as flexibility, so teams can pick the method that fits their workflow. It also mentions practical steps such as giving each snapshot a unique name, optionally specifying the creation time in UTC, and generating API authorization tokens before calling the Fabric API.

REST APIs are also the bridge for custom integrations. According to "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform", custom connectors in Power Platform can connect to any REST API, including advanced Azure OpenAI endpoints. The episode describes registering the API in Azure API Management, which supports managing access, monitoring usage and applying security policies, and which provides a unique endpoint along with rate limits and logging rules. The connector definition in Power Platform then defines triggers, actions and security settings.

The episode "When Azure SQL Becomes an Application Platform- APIs, Automation and AI with Dirceu Resende" lists REST API integration among the topics in a conversation about Azure SQL Database moving beyond traditional data storage. The discussion covers APIs, automation, external services, security, performance, Microsoft Fabric, Power BI, AI, vector search, RAG and observability, and the changing architectural role of databases inside modern applications.

Taken together, the episodes treat the REST API as a common integration pattern. Typical decisions concern which API surface to call, how to authenticate, whether to automate through CI/CD or scripts, and how to manage access, limits and logging when an API is exposed to other tools.

restricted-access-control.desc: Restricted access control is a SharePoint Advanced Management site-level control that limits a site and its content to members of specified groups, regardless of sharing links.

faq.a: It limits access to a SharePoint site and its content to members of specified groups, regardless of existing sharing links. It is a site-level control in SharePoint Advanced Management.
faq.q: What does restricted access control do?

faq.a: The episodes explain that Copilot only accesses content the user is authorized to view, so restricting site access narrows what can be surfaced. They recommend enforcing restricted access control on critical sites as part of Copilot security setup.
faq.q: How does restricted access control relate to Microsoft Copilot?

faq.a: They mention sensitivity labels, Microsoft Purview DLP and auto-labeling, Insider Risk Management policies, and restricting company-wide sharing groups and Anyone links at the tenant level.
faq.q: Which other controls do the episodes pair with restricted access control?

restricted-access-control.long:
Restricted access control is a site-level control in SharePoint Advanced Management. It limits access to a SharePoint site and its content to members of specified groups, regardless of any sharing links that already exist on that site. In some episode excerpts it is abbreviated as RAC. Its purpose is to keep business-critical or sensitive sites reachable only by the people who are meant to work with them, even when files or folders have previously been shared more widely.

The central idea is that the group list on the site takes precedence over sharing. A site can contain content that was shared through links over time, and those links can quietly widen who is able to open the material. With restricted access control in place, access to the site and its content is tied to membership in the groups that were named for it. That makes it a useful guardrail for sites holding contracts, financial material, or other information where oversharing would be a concern. In the episode "What Is SharePoint Premium - Simply Explained", the feature is described as allowing site access to be limited to specific security groups.

That same episode places restricted access control within the security and compliance pillar of SharePoint Premium, next to other governance features. It lists Data Access Governance reports, which provide sitewide reports on overshared content and exposure levels; a block download policy for view-only access; an inactive site policy that detects inactive sites for review and possible deletion; site lifecycle governance for creation approval and ownership audits; and conditional access for SharePoint. Restricted access control is one tool in that set, aimed specifically at narrowing who can reach a given site.

Several episodes connect the control to Microsoft Copilot readiness. The episode "Connect Microsoft Copilot to Salesforce, ServiceNow, and APIs" explains that Copilot works on the principle of least privilege and can only access content the signed-in user is authorized to view, so permission and security settings determine what data Copilot can reach. It states that restricted access control enforces default access restrictions for critical sites during provisioning, and it lists it alongside sensitivity labels, which require site sensitivity labels to enforce privacy and sharing controls. The practical implication given in these episodes is that tightening site access reduces what an AI assistant can surface for users who should not see it.

The episode "Set Up Microsoft Copilot in Teams Step by Step" lists enforcing restricted access control for business-critical sites as part of configuring security and compliance. In the same list it recommends disabling or restricting company-wide sharing groups and Anyone links at the tenant level, using Microsoft Purview Information Protection to require site sensitivity labels during provisioning, configuring auto-label and default sensitivity labels, and enabling Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management policies. The episode "Protect Microsoft Copilot with Purview, DLP, and Insider Risk with Alan Cox [MVP]" follows a similar pattern: it describes establishing secure defaults by enforcing restricted access control for critical sites and turning off company-wide sharing groups, then adding guardrails such as auto-labeling and DLP policies, and continuing to review and improve them using Purview reporting and risk assessments.

The episode "AI Contract Management with SharePoint Premium and Copilot" frames restricted access control policies as a way to define who can access specific content based on security groups, so that only authorized personnel can view or edit sensitive documents. It pairs this with sensitivity labels, which classify content by sensitivity level so that compliance with legal standards can be enforced.

Taken together, the episodes treat restricted access control as one layer in a broader approach rather than a standalone fix. It addresses who may enter a site, while sensitivity labels, data loss prevention, insider risk policies, and tenant-level sharing settings address how content is classified, shared, and monitored. Further technical details are maintained in the official Microsoft documentation page for restricted access control.

restricted-content-discovery.desc: Restricted content discovery is a SharePoint Advanced Management site-level control that keeps a site's content out of organization-wide search and Microsoft 365 Copilot results.

faq.a: It keeps the content of a SharePoint site out of organization-wide search and Microsoft 365 Copilot results. It is applied at the site level as part of SharePoint Advanced Management.
faq.q: What does Restricted content discovery do?

faq.a: No. It does not change who can access the site. It only limits whether the site's content is surfaced in organization-wide search and Microsoft 365 Copilot results.
faq.q: Does Restricted content discovery change site permissions?

restricted-content-discovery.long:
Restricted content discovery is a site-level control in SharePoint Advanced Management. It prevents the content of a selected SharePoint site from appearing in organization-wide search and in Microsoft 365 Copilot results.

The control changes discoverability only. It does not change who can access the site, so existing permissions stay as they are. Users who already have access to the site's files can still reach them directly, while the content is no longer surfaced through organization-wide search or Copilot responses.

Typical use is to reduce unintended exposure of content, for example when a site's permissions are broader than intended and a tenant wants to limit what search and Copilot can surface while access settings are reviewed. The feature works per site, so administrators can apply it to individual sites rather than to the whole tenant.

Restricted content discovery belongs to the SharePoint Advanced Management capabilities that support governance of SharePoint sites in Microsoft 365. Official documentation for the feature is published on Microsoft Learn. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

restricted-sharepoint-search.desc: Restricted SharePoint Search is a Microsoft 365 setting that limits organisation-wide search and Copilot to an admin-curated allow list of SharePoint sites.

faq.a: It lets administrators keep an allow list of SharePoint sites that organisation-wide search and, temporarily, Copilot Chat and agent experiences may draw from. It is off by default and the list starts empty.
faq.q: What does Restricted SharePoint Search do?

faq.a: No. Microsoft Learn states it is not a security boundary and does not change site permissions. It is a temporary measure that gives admins time to review permissions before content is overshared.
faq.q: Is Restricted SharePoint Search a security feature?

faq.a: No. There is no deny list, only an allow list with a size cap. A hub site counts as a single entry, and the feature is being phased out in favour of Restricted Content Discovery.
faq.q: Can Restricted SharePoint Search block individual sites?

restricted-sharepoint-search.long:
Restricted SharePoint Search is a feature in SharePoint in Microsoft 365 that lets administrators maintain an allow list of SharePoint sites. Only the sites on that list are used by organisation-wide search and, for the time the feature is active, by Copilot Chat and agent experiences. It is off by default, and the allow list starts out empty. The feature is aimed at organisations that want to limit which content Copilot and search can surface while they review how widely their data is shared.

Microsoft Learn describes Restricted SharePoint Search as a temporary measure. Its purpose is to give administrators time to review and correct permissions before content is overshared through search or Copilot. It is explicitly not a security boundary, and it does not change site permissions. A site left off the allow list is not locked down; users who have access to it can still open it directly. What changes is where search and Copilot look when they assemble results and answers.

Administrators manage the feature with PowerShell cmdlets. These are used to enable or disable it and to add or remove sites on the allow list. Changes take effect within about an hour. The allow list is capped in size, and a hub site counts as a single entry, which can help when many related sites should be included together. There is no deny list, so the feature cannot be used to block individual sites while leaving everything else searchable. Admins have to build the list from the sites they want to include.

Several content sources remain reachable even when the feature is switched on. Answers can still draw on content the user can already reach, such as their own OneDrive files, chats, mail and calendar, and files they have recently used or that were shared with them directly. Because the searchable set of SharePoint sites is narrower, Copilot may give less complete answers while Restricted SharePoint Search is enabled. This trade-off is part of the decision whether to turn it on, and for how long.

The documentation recommends pairing the feature with permission cleanup rather than relying on it alone. SharePoint Advanced Management and Microsoft Purview are named as tools for that work. The idea is that the allow list buys time while oversharing is addressed at the source, after which the restriction is no longer needed. The page also notes that Restricted SharePoint Search is being phased out in favour of Restricted Content Discovery, so organisations planning long-term governance should account for that direction.

The M365.FM episode "How I Built a JARVIS-Like Microsoft Copilot Assistant" lists Restricted SharePoint Search among upcoming data governance features. The episode says it will let admins control which sites show up in search results and Copilot, which helps manage data sharing and stay compliant with company rules. The episode "Move Canvas Apps from SharePoint to Dataverse" places restricted SharePoint search in a wider governance layer meant to stop Copilot from leaking secrets, alongside DLP enforcement, label-based blocking, permission hygiene and connector approvals. It argues that Copilot amplifies whatever governance already exists, good or bad, and that sensitivity labels do a lot to protect a tenant.

Taken together, the sources treat Restricted SharePoint Search as a stopgap within a broader Copilot readiness effort: restrict the searchable surface, fix permissions and labelling, then move toward the successor capability.

retail.desc: Retail, also called Einzelhandel or retail trade, is the industry that sells goods to consumers or businesses through stores, online channels or both.

faq.a: Retail is the industry that sells goods to consumers or businesses, in stores, online or both. It is also known as Einzelhandel, Handel or retail trade.
faq.q: What does the term Retail cover?

faq.a: According to the episode "Dynamics 365 Commerce - Simply Explained", it is Microsoft's platform for connecting the processes behind selling across physical stores, websites and other channels, including point of sale, inventory, pricing, orders and loyalty.
faq.q: How does Dynamics 365 Commerce relate to retail?

faq.a: The episodes mention inventory management and employee scheduling with Power Apps, fast checkouts and loyalty rewards in the context of cloud latency, personalized shopping experiences with AI agents, and retail data analysis with Copilot Studio.
faq.q: Which retail use cases do the M365.FM episodes mention?

retail.long:
Retail is the industry that sells goods to consumers or businesses, in physical stores, online or in a combination of both. The same field is also referred to as Einzelhandel, Handel or retail trade. In the context of the Microsoft ecosystem, retail appears as a use-case area where business applications, data tools and automation are applied to everyday trading processes such as products, inventory, pricing, customers, orders, loyalty and fulfillment.

The M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Commerce - Simply Explained" (August 2026) describes the most direct link between retail and Microsoft products. It explains Dynamics 365 Commerce as Microsoft's platform for connecting the processes behind selling products across physical stores, websites and other commerce channels. According to the episode, the idea is not to treat stores, websites and back-office systems as separate environments, but to provide a connected foundation for omnichannel retail. The topics it covers include point of sale, products, inventory, pricing, customers, orders, loyalty, fulfillment and retail operations. This reflects a common situation in retail: the same product, price and customer record must be consistent whether a purchase happens at a checkout counter or in an online shop.

Other episodes touch on retail as one example among several industries. In "Power Platform - Simply Explained" (July 2026), retail and e-commerce are listed alongside healthcare and life sciences, financial services and industrial scenarios. For retail, the episode names inventory management and employee scheduling, enhanced with real-time updates through canvas apps in Power Apps. This points to a typical decision in retail environments: whether to build tailored, lightweight apps for store staff and operations on top of existing data, rather than relying only on large standard systems.

The episode "Cloud Latency and Edge Computing Strategy" (June 2026) looks at retail and smart spaces from a performance perspective. It says that when a store or smart building is operated, speed matters, because customers expect fast checkouts, instant loyalty rewards and real-time inventory updates. The episode states that systems relying on distant cloud servers risk delays that frustrate shoppers and slow down operations, and that latency affects the speed of transactions. In this framing, retail is a scenario where the placement of computing close to the point of sale becomes an architectural question.

In "5 High-Margin Microsoft 365 Business Models" (March 2026), retail appears in a case study about the Agentic Workflow Factory model. The episode describes a retail company that used AI to create personalized shopping experiences and reports, as stated in the episode, a 20% revenue increase and a 25% rise in customer satisfaction through automated customer interactions and offers tailored in real time. The episode's advice is to start small by automating a few key workflows with AI agents, measure the impact and expand gradually. These figures are attributed to the episode and are presented there as a success story.

Finally, "Query Microsoft Fabric in Plain English with Copilot Studio" (November 2025) lists retail data analysis as a practical use case for Microsoft Copilot Studio. The episode says that real-time insights can support decision-making in retail operations and names inventory management as one of the impacted areas, presented in a table of use cases and benefits.

Taken together, the episodes treat retail as a domain where several Microsoft building blocks meet: a commerce platform for omnichannel selling, low-code apps for operational tasks, edge and cloud design for responsiveness, AI agents for personalization, and analytics for inventory and sales data. The recurring themes are connected channels, current inventory and customer information, and speed at the point of transaction.

retention-labels.desc: Retention labels are Microsoft Purview labels applied to individual items such as documents or emails to control when retention starts, how long it lasts and what happens afterwards.

faq.a: A retention label defines when retention begins, how long the item must be kept and what happens once the retention period ends. It is applied to individual items such as documents or emails.
faq.q: What do retention labels define?

faq.a: Retention policies apply organization-wide rules to entire Microsoft 365 locations such as mailboxes, SharePoint sites, OneDrive accounts or Teams chats. Retention labels apply directly to individual emails or documents, allowing item-level lifecycle rules.
faq.q: How do retention labels differ from retention policies?

faq.a: Yes. According to the episodes, retention labels can be auto-applied, for example using trainable classifiers and policies based on content patterns, and Microsoft Syntex can also auto-apply retention labels.
faq.q: Can retention labels be applied automatically?

retention-labels.long:
Retention labels are Microsoft Purview labels that attach lifecycle rules directly to individual items such as documents, emails and other business records. Each label defines three things: when the retention period begins, how long the content must remain protected, and what should happen once that period expires. Because the rule travels with the individual item, retention labels are used where different pieces of content in the same location need different treatment.

The concept is usually explained in contrast to retention policies. According to the episode "Data Lifecycle Management - Simply Explained", retention policies provide organization-wide rules that apply to entire Microsoft 365 locations such as Exchange Online mailboxes, SharePoint sites, OneDrive accounts or Microsoft Teams chats. They suit situations where large amounts of similar content need identical retention behavior. Retention labels, by comparison, apply to individual emails or documents. The episode also describes combining approaches, for example retaining information first and deleting it automatically later, and stresses that a lifecycle strategy begins with understanding why information exists before deciding how long it should be kept.

The episode "Microsoft Purview Records Management - Simply Explained" places retention labels within records management. It describes defining retention triggers, required retention periods and approved disposition actions. The episode says that this distinction prevents unnecessary retention while ensuring that important business records stay protected throughout their required lifecycle. In that framing, a retention label is the mechanism that expresses a specific lifecycle rule for a specific item, whereas broad retention policies apply baseline rules across locations.

Labels do not have to be chosen manually by users. The episode "Microsoft 365 Governance as Code Beyond Written Policies" notes that retention labels can be auto-applied, including through trainable classifiers and retention policies that label and retain or delete content based on content patterns rather than only on manual user choice. Similarly, the episode "Automate Document Processing with Microsoft Syntex" lists auto-applying retention labels, sensitivity labels and classification tags among the ways Syntex supports compliance and governance at scale, alongside metadata extraction that can trigger Power Automate flows and Power Apps.

Retention labels also appear in broader governance discussions. The episode "Why Microsoft 365 Governance Strategies Fail" argues that implementing retention labels, retention policies and automated disposition as part of a Microsoft 365 governance strategy reduces storage, discovery complexity and compliance risk over time. It presents automated lifecycle management as a cost saver and, in the same context, recommends content types, metadata and the Microsoft Purview catalog over rigid folder hierarchies for discoverability and governance.

A typical decision around retention labels is whether a requirement is better met by a location-wide retention policy or by a label on individual items. Where all content in a mailbox, site or chat location should behave the same way, a policy fits. Where individual documents or emails carry different retention triggers, periods or disposition actions, a label is the more precise tool. Retention labels are commonly considered together with sensitivity labels, which the governance episode describes as persisting protection such as encryption, watermarking and access restrictions across Word, Excel and PDF files, though the two label types serve different purposes: one governs how long content is kept, the other how it is protected.

retention-policies.desc: Retention policies in Microsoft Purview keep or delete Teams messages, chats and site files for a defined period, regardless of what users delete.

faq.a: They keep or delete content such as Teams channel messages, chats and site files for a defined period. They apply independently of what users delete.
faq.q: What do retention policies do in Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft 365 Retention Policies vs Records Management" says that mixing the two up can lose evidence, break audits and confuse eDiscovery. It covers precedence rules and how auto-apply labels can collide with site policies.
faq.q: How do retention policies differ from records management?

faq.a: No. The episode "Microsoft 365 Backup with Isolated Vault Architecture" says standard backup and retention policies do not fully protect against today's threats, and it points to short windows and complexity as limits of retention policies.
faq.q: Are retention policies the same as backup?

retention-policies.long:
Retention policies are Microsoft Purview policies that keep or delete content for a defined period. They apply to content such as Teams channel messages, chats and site files, and they work independently of what users delete. A user who removes a message or a file does not change the retention outcome, because the policy governs the content at the service level rather than leaving the decision to individuals. This makes retention policies a core building block of data lifecycle management in Microsoft 365.

The main purpose of a retention policy is to support compliance and governance. Organizations use them to make sure that content is available for as long as it must be kept, and removed when it no longer needs to be held. The episode "Microsoft Purview for Copilot Security with Peter Rising [Microsoft]" places retention policies within data lifecycle management and says they help keep data protected from creation to deletion. The same episode describes them alongside sensitivity labels, which classify documents, emails and Teams chats, as part of the controls that Copilot respects.

Retention policies are often discussed together with records management, and the two are easy to confuse. The episode "Microsoft 365 Retention Policies vs Records Management" argues that mixing up retention policies and records management can lose evidence, break audits and confuse eDiscovery. According to the episode, the topics worth understanding include the precedence rules across Exchange, SharePoint and Teams, how auto-apply labels can collide with site policies, and a step-by-step approach for mapping business requirements to retention settings. It is aimed at M365 administrators and records managers who run Purview policies and labels, at governance leaders preparing for audits and data subject access requests, and at project owners migrating legacy file shares to Microsoft 365.

The episode "Microsoft 365 Governance as Code Beyond Written Policies" covers a related point: retention labels can be applied automatically. It says that trainable classifiers and sensitivity or retention policies can label and retain or delete content based on content patterns, not only on manual user choice. The same episode notes that governance policy effects such as retention, DLP and sharing restrictions can differ for guest identities compared with internal users, so policies need to account for guests explicitly.

Gaps in retention are treated as a governance risk. In "Microsoft 365 Audit Readiness and Governance Debt", missing retention policies appear in a list of governance debt examples, where the stated consequence is compliance failures. Alongside items such as unaudited SharePoint permissions and a lack of naming conventions for Teams, the episode presents unmanaged retention as something that accumulates over time and surfaces during audits.

Retention policies are also distinguished from backup. The episode "Microsoft 365 Backup with Isolated Vault Architecture" states that standard backup and retention policies do not fully protect against today's threats, and that high availability keeps services online without guaranteeing data protection or disaster recovery. It describes retention policy limits, including short windows and complexity, as a reason traditional Microsoft 365 backup falls short. In that view, retention keeps or deletes content on a schedule, while recoverability after an incident is a separate requirement.

In practice, decisions around retention policies include which locations to cover, how long to keep content, whether to keep it, delete it or both, and how policies interact with labels and records management settings. The episodes recommend mapping business requirements first and understanding precedence before layering policies, so that the resulting retention behavior can be explained and defended during an audit or an eDiscovery request.

retry-pattern.desc: The Retry pattern is a resilience pattern in which a failed call to a remote dependency is automatically attempted again to recover from brief transient faults.
retry-pattern.long:
The Retry pattern is a resilience pattern in which a failed call to a remote dependency is automatically attempted again. It is intended to recover from brief transient faults, where the dependency is unavailable or erroring only for a short moment and a later attempt is likely to succeed.

In practice, the pattern is applied with limits. Retries are ideally bounded, meaning the number of attempts is capped so that a persistent failure does not cause calls to repeat indefinitely. They are also ideally combined with jitter, which adds a small random variation to the timing between attempts so that many clients do not retry at the same instant.

The Retry pattern is used in software that depends on remote services, such as cloud applications that call other services over a network. It addresses a specific class of problem, the short-lived fault, and is not a substitute for handling longer outages.

No related topics or M365.FM episodes are linked to this entry at present, so this page covers only the general definition of the concept.

return-on-security-investment.desc: Return on security investment (ROSI) is a ratio that compares the reduction in expected loss from security controls with the cost of those controls.
return-on-security-investment.long:
Return on security investment (ROSI) is a concept used to express the financial value of security controls. It compares the reduction in expected loss achieved by those controls with what they cost to implement and operate.

The calculation is given as: exposure before the control, minus exposure after the control, minus the security cost, divided by the security cost. In this form, the first two terms describe how much expected loss the control removes, and the cost term is subtracted so the result reflects net benefit relative to spending. A positive result indicates that the reduction in expected loss exceeds the cost of the control, while a result at or below zero indicates it does not.

ROSI is typically applied when security spending needs to be justified or compared across options, since it translates risk reduction into a single comparable figure. The quality of the result depends on how exposure is estimated before and after a control is in place, because both values are expected-loss figures rather than observed outcomes.

There are no specific M365.FM episodes or related entities linked to this concept at present.

revoscaler.desc: RevoScaleR is a Microsoft R package with rx-prefixed functions for importing, transforming and analyzing large data sets, used in SQL Server Machine Learning Services.

faq.a: RevoScaleR is a Microsoft R package with rx-prefixed functions for importing, transforming, summarizing, visualizing and analyzing data at scale. It ships with SQL Server Machine Learning Services and SQL Server 2016 R Services.
faq.q: What is RevoScaleR?

faq.a: Its functions work on large data sets in parallel and on distributed file systems. Data that does not fit in memory is processed in chunks and the results are merged afterwards.
faq.q: How does RevoScaleR differ from base R?

faq.a: It is used to set compute contexts and define SQL Server data sources. A common approach is to develop with a SQL Server compute context and then wrap the finished R code in sp_execute_external_script.
faq.q: How is RevoScaleR used with SQL Server?

revoscaler.long:
RevoScaleR is a Microsoft R package that supports distributed computing, remote compute contexts and high-performance data science algorithms. Its functions carry an rx or Rx prefix, and the package covers data import, transformation, summary, visualization and analysis. It ships with SQL Server Machine Learning Services and with SQL Server 2016 R Services, where it is used to set compute contexts and to define SQL Server data sources.

The main difference from base R is how data is handled. Base R generally needs a data set to fit in memory, whereas RevoScaleR functions work on large data sets in parallel and on distributed file systems. Data that does not fit in memory is processed in chunks, and the partial results are merged afterwards. This is the reason the package is relevant when R work slows down or stalls on very large tables.

The package reference groups its functions into several areas. Data sources and compute contexts define where data lives and where computation runs. DDL helpers support working with database objects. ETL functions such as rxImport and rxDataStep import and transform data. Further groups include plotting functions, descriptive statistics, and modeling functions such as linear models, logistic regression, decision trees, forests and k-means. Prediction and summary tasks are handled by functions such as rxPredict and rxSummary.

A typical workflow described in the documentation is to develop locally while using a SQL Server compute context. In that setup a model can be trained on the server, which avoids moving the data out of the database. Once the R code works, it is wrapped in sp_execute_external_script, ideally as a single function with clearly defined inputs and outputs. This keeps the code that runs inside SQL Server easy to reason about and to maintain.

The documentation also names limits that affect design decisions. Stored procedure calls are not supported as a data source. Some statistics functions do not chunk data, so they do not gain the same scale benefit. There are also output restrictions on rxPredict and rxSummary. These points matter when planning which parts of an analysis should rely on RevoScaleR functions and which should be handled differently.

The M365.FM episode "Stop R Freezing on Millions of SQL Server Rows" places RevoScaleR in the context of integrating R with SQL Server. According to the episode, the integration improves security, boosts performance and supports advanced analytics, and it lists RevoScaleR's handling of large data sets as a performance benefit. The episode also points to ease of use through familiar tools, support for statistics and machine learning, and collaboration between DBAs, analysts and developers.

In practice, RevoScaleR is relevant for teams that already work in R and need to run analyses against SQL Server data without pulling millions of rows into a local session. Choosing a compute context, defining the data source and deciding which steps run in the database are the central choices when using the package.

rework-rate.desc: Rework rate is a software delivery metric showing the share of recently written code that is rewritten, deleted or rolled back soon after, used as a signal of code durability.

faq.a: In software delivery, rework rate measures what share of recently written code is rewritten, deleted or rolled back shortly afterwards, and it is used as a signal of code durability. Related episodes apply the same idea to unplanned deployments, repeated automation steps and edits after approval.
faq.q: What does rework rate measure?

faq.a: The episode "The Productivity Illusion: Why AI is Breaking Your Engineering KPIs" recommends expanding the traditional DORA metrics with rework rate. Another episode, "Platform Engineering: The New Operating Model for Azure", lists deployment rework rate next to failed deployment recovery time and change failure rate.
faq.q: How is rework rate related to the DORA metrics?

faq.a: No. The M365.FM episodes also describe it as the percentage of repeated steps in Power Automate processes and as edits after approval in Microsoft 365 usage analysis.
faq.q: Is rework rate only used for code?

rework-rate.long:
Rework rate is a software delivery metric that measures what share of recently written code is rewritten, deleted or rolled back shortly after it was produced. It is used as a signal of code durability: the higher the share of fresh work that has to be redone, the less stable the output of a team or pipeline appears to be.
