Because it looks at what happens to work after it has been delivered, it complements metrics that only count how much was shipped.

In the M365.FM episode "The Productivity Illusion: Why AI is Breaking Your Engineering KPIs", rework rate appears in a list of flow metrics alongside flow efficiency, queue age, review cycle time, work in progress (WIP) and bottleneck identification. The episode frames these as measures that reveal where work actually becomes blocked, instead of simply counting completed deployments. Its argument is that AI has shifted engineering constraints from development toward review and verification, which makes flow measurement more valuable than raw throughput metrics. Rather than asking how much was shipped, the episode suggests asking how efficiently work moves through the system. The same episode also lists "DORA 5 and rework rate" as one of its practical recommendations, pointing to an expansion of the traditional DORA delivery metrics.

The term is used in a closely related way in the episode "Platform Engineering: The New Operating Model for Azure". There, a deployment rework rate is described as the ratio of unplanned deployments occurring due to incidents in production. It is listed next to failed deployment recovery time, which is the time taken to recover from a failed deployment requiring immediate intervention, and change failure rate (CFR), the ratio of deployments needing immediate intervention after release, often resulting in rollbacks. The episode states that these metrics confirm platform engineering enables developers to ship code quickly and reliably, and it recommends reviewing them monthly or quarterly to gauge the platform's value and its effect on team performance.

Rework rate is not limited to code. In "High-Performance Automation Control Plane for Power Automate", it is defined as the percentage of steps repeated due to errors, and it is described as highlighting areas where automation may need refinement. It sits in a set of metrics that also includes cycle time, the total duration of a process, and SLA compliance, the frequency of meeting deadlines. Here the idea is the same as in software delivery: repeated work is a sign that something upstream did not hold up the first time.

A further variant appears in "Link Microsoft 365 Usage to Real Business Results", where rework rate is defined as edits after approval and is classed as a bridge metric. In that episode it sits between usage signals and outcome metrics such as cycle time, win rate, CSAT, SLA hit percentage and revenue per rep, together with other bridge metrics like handoffs avoided and the async ratio of comments versus meetings. Edits after approval serve as an indicator of how often supposedly finished work has to be reopened.

Across these sources, the common thread is that rework rate measures work that has to be done again. In software delivery this means rewritten, deleted or rolled-back code or unplanned deployments after incidents; in automation it means repeated process steps; in collaboration scenarios it means edits after approval. Typical decisions around it include which definition to adopt, over what time window to look, and which other metrics to read alongside it. The episodes position it as one signal among several, to be interpreted together with flow and delivery metrics rather than used in isolation.

ring-based-deployment.desc: Ring-based deployment is a safe release practice that rolls a change out to successive rings of users or environments, with validation before each expansion.

faq.a: It is a safe deployment practice that releases a change to successive cohorts (rings) of users or environments, moving from an internal team to pilot users to broad production.
faq.q: What is ring-based deployment?

faq.a: Exit criteria are the validation conditions a ring must satisfy before the change is expanded to the next ring. They act as a checkpoint between stages of the rollout.
faq.q: What are exit criteria in a ring-based deployment?

faq.a: Releasing in stages allows problems to be found in a smaller group first, so a rollout can be stopped or adjusted before it reaches broad production.
faq.q: Why are changes released in rings instead of all at once?

ring-based-deployment.long:
Ring-based deployment is a safe deployment practice in which a change is released to successive cohorts, called rings, of users or environments rather than to everyone at once. A typical progression moves from an internal team, to a group of pilot users, and then to broad production.

The defining feature of the approach is that each ring acts as a checkpoint. Validation and exit criteria are defined for a ring, and the change is only expanded to the next, larger ring once those criteria are met. If problems appear in an early ring, the rollout can be paused or corrected before it reaches the wider user base, which limits the number of users or systems affected by a faulty change.

The concept is used to manage risk when introducing updates, configuration changes, or new capabilities in controlled stages. How many rings exist, who belongs to each one, and what counts as a passing result are decisions made for each deployment.

risk-register.desc: A risk register is a risk-management record of identified risks with likelihood, impact and status, and a core input for governance, risk and compliance (GRC) reporting.

faq.a: A risk register is a record used in risk management to track identified risks along with their likelihood, impact and status. It is a core input for governance, risk and compliance (GRC) reporting.
faq.q: What is a risk register?

faq.a: The guidance lists a unique ID, an open or closed status, a category, a one-sentence description, probability, impact and a priority with a documented calculation method. It also lists a level, a management strategy of mitigate, accept, avoid or transfer, the controls, an owner with escalation path, and a closure date.
faq.q: What fields does a risk register entry contain according to the Cloud Adoption Framework?

faq.a: The Cloud Adoption Framework recommends reviewing it on a regular schedule and after events such as new technology or audits, and presenting it to the executive sponsor.
faq.q: How often should a risk register be reviewed?

risk-register.long:
A risk register is a record used in risk management to track identified risks together with their likelihood, impact and status. It serves as a core input for governance, risk and compliance (GRC) reporting, because it gives an organization a single, structured list of what could go wrong, how serious each item is and who is dealing with it.

In the Cloud Adoption Framework on Microsoft Learn, a risk register is described as a list of cloud risks that holds all the information needed to identify, categorize, prioritize and manage them. It is built in the step of documenting cloud risks and then serves as the basis for deriving governance policies. The guidance recommends consistent wording so that everyone reads the risks in the same way, and it presents the register as something to maintain rather than a one-off document.

The sources name the typical fields of an entry. Each risk carries a unique ID for traceability and a management status of open or closed. A category places the risk in an area such as security, cost or regulatory compliance, and a one-sentence description states the threat. Probability and impact are recorded separately, and a priority combines the two using a documented calculation method. Each entry also records a level and a management strategy, which can be mitigate, accept, avoid or transfer. The concrete controls that enforce the strategy are listed, along with an owner, an escalation path and a closure date. The sample table in the guidance shows risks such as unauthorized access to cloud services, mitigated with multifactor authentication and periodic access reviews.

How the register is used matters as much as its structure. The guidance recommends reviewing it on a regular schedule and also after events such as the introduction of new technology or an audit. The results are presented to the executive sponsor, which links the register to decision-making and to the governance policies derived from it. Typical decisions around it include which strategy fits a given risk, which controls to put in place, who owns the risk and when it can be closed.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft 365 Maturity Model Based on 500 Tenant Audits" mentions the risk register in the context of governance and risk management. In its list of characteristics, a governance framework covering Teams, SharePoint and Power Platform, policy lifecycle management with regular reviews, third-party app and API access controls, and a risk register with mitigation plans for Microsoft 365 services appear together under the heading Governance & Risk Management. In that framing, the risk register is one element of a mature approach to running Microsoft 365, alongside access controls and policy reviews, and it sits next to assessment and roadmap items such as maturity assessments, target levels with owners and a quarterly review cadence.

Taken together, the sources show the risk register as a practical working tool. It captures risks in consistent language, ties each one to a strategy, controls and an owner, and feeds governance policies and reporting. Keeping it current through scheduled and event-driven reviews is what allows it to support GRC reporting and Microsoft 365 governance over time.

riskiq.desc: RiskIQ is a security company known for internet-scale threat intelligence and attack surface data, acquired by Microsoft in 2021.

faq.a: RiskIQ is a security company known for internet-scale threat intelligence and attack surface data. It was acquired by Microsoft in 2021.
faq.q: What is RiskIQ?

faq.a: Microsoft acquired RiskIQ in 2021, and RiskIQ's technology underpins Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence.
faq.q: How is RiskIQ related to Microsoft?

faq.a: It is known for threat intelligence and attack surface data at internet scale, used to understand threats and externally visible assets.
faq.q: What is RiskIQ known for?

riskiq.long:
RiskIQ is a security company known for internet-scale threat intelligence and attack surface data. Its work centered on collecting and organizing information about internet-facing assets and the threats associated with them, giving security teams a view of an organization's external footprint.

Microsoft acquired RiskIQ in 2021. Its technology underpins Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, which places RiskIQ's data and approach within the Microsoft security portfolio. In the Microsoft ecosystem, the name is therefore mostly encountered in discussions of threat intelligence, external attack surface visibility, and the Defender family of security products.

This entity page currently lists no linked topics or episodes. As M365.FM adds coverage of Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence and related security subjects, this page can be expanded to reflect how RiskIQ's technology appears in those discussions.

role-based-access-control.desc: Role-based access control (RBAC) assigns permissions by role instead of individual, so a person can open only the specific resources their work requires.

faq.a: RBAC grants permissions through roles instead of to individual users. The M365.FM episode "Azure Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) - Simply Explained" compares it to a keycard that opens specific doors for a specific person, rather than a light switch that turns access on or off for a whole room.
faq.q: What is role-based access control (RBAC) in simple terms?

faq.a: RBAC is one way to apply least privilege, since permissions are tied to roles and limited to what a task requires. The zero trust episode lists RBAC together with just-in-time access and regular audits and revocation as best practices for this.
faq.q: How does RBAC relate to least privilege?

faq.a: The episodes mention RBAC in the context of Azure Resource Manager governance, Azure Key Vault access to secrets, Microsoft Fabric data pipelines and zero trust security for AI with Microsoft Copilot and Azure.
faq.q: Where does RBAC appear in other Microsoft topics covered by M365.FM?

role-based-access-control.long:
Role-based access control (RBAC) is an authorization approach in which permissions are granted through roles rather than handed out one by one to individual users. In the Microsoft ecosystem, the term is most closely tied to Azure, where Azure role-based access control governs who can do what with which resources. The M365.FM episode "Azure Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) - Simply Explained" uses an analogy to describe it: RBAC is a keycard, not a light switch. A light switch is either on or off for a whole room, while a keycard opens specific doors for a specific person.

The purpose of RBAC is to limit access to what is needed. Instead of giving someone broad rights to an entire environment, an administrator assigns a role that covers only the required actions, and only for the required part of the environment. This fits the principle of least privilege, which the same episode lists among its topics. The episode outline also covers what RBAC actually does, the three pieces of every role assignment, the four sizes of scope, and the roles that administrators meet most often in practice.

The structure the episode points to is that every role assignment is made of a small number of parts and applies at a certain scope. Scope matters because it determines how far a permission reaches. A role granted at a wide scope applies to many resources, while a role granted at a narrow scope applies to few. Choosing the right scope is therefore one of the main decisions when assigning access, and it is closely linked to the least privilege idea of giving no more reach than the task requires.

RBAC also appears as a building block in the wider Azure governance picture. The episode "Azure Resource Manager - Simply Explained" lists role-based access control alongside subscriptions, resource groups, resource providers, management groups, tags and locks. In that discussion, Azure Resource Manager is presented as a centralized control plane that supports consistent deployments, governance and security across Azure services, and RBAC is one of the mechanisms that makes that governance enforceable. Organizing resources into logical groups and applying access rules to them is a typical scenario the episode describes.

Several other episodes treat RBAC as a standard security measure. In "Azure Key Vault - Simply Explained", the episode states that RBAC ensures only authorized users can access sensitive information, which strengthens the security of stored secrets. In "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines", RBAC is recommended to limit who can reach sensitive data, with permissions assigned based on user roles. That episode also advises regularly reviewing access permissions so that only trusted users keep access, and it pairs RBAC with managed identities, encryption of data at rest and in transit, and Azure Key Vault.

The episode "Zero Trust AI Security with Microsoft Copilot and Azure – Mourtaza Fazlehoussen [MVP]" places RBAC in a zero trust context. It lists RBAC among best practices for enforcing least privilege access, described as assigning permissions based on user roles to limit access. Alongside it, the episode names just-in-time access, which provides temporary access only when needed, and regular audits and revocation, which keep access rights current and necessary. Continuous monitoring is described as a further layer for spotting anomalies and responding to threats.

Taken together, the episodes treat RBAC less as a standalone feature and more as a recurring control that appears wherever access must be limited: in Azure resource management, in secret storage, in data pipelines and in AI security scenarios. Typical decisions around it include which role fits a task, at which scope to assign it, and how often to review and revoke assignments so that permissions do not outlive their purpose.

routing-diagnostics.desc: Routing diagnostics in Dynamics 365 Customer Service records the intake, classification and assignment stages of each work item to show why it was routed as it was.

faq.a: It records the intake, classification and assignment stages of each work item. This lets administrators see why a work item was routed where it went.
faq.q: What does routing diagnostics record in Dynamics 365 Customer Service?

faq.a: It is aimed at administrators who manage unified routing in Dynamics 365 Customer Service and need to understand or troubleshoot how work items are routed.
faq.q: Who uses routing diagnostics?

faq.a: Microsoft publishes it on Microsoft Learn under the Dynamics 365 Customer Service administration section, on the page for unified routing diagnostics.
faq.q: Where can the official documentation for routing diagnostics be found?

routing-diagnostics.long:
Routing diagnostics (Dynamics 365) is a unified routing feature in Dynamics 365 Customer Service. It records the stages a work item passes through, namely intake, classification and assignment, so that administrators can review how and why the item reached its destination.

In practice, the feature is used to troubleshoot routing behavior. When a work item is assigned to an unexpected queue or agent, or is not assigned at all, the recorded stages give administrators a trail to inspect instead of having to infer the outcome from the configuration alone. This supports checking that unified routing rules and settings behave as intended.

Routing diagnostics sits within the broader Dynamics 365 family of business applications and is part of the administration tooling for unified routing in Customer Service. Further details on its behavior and configuration are described in the official Microsoft Learn documentation for unified routing diagnostics.

row-level-security.desc: Row-level security (RLS) filters which rows of a semantic model or warehouse table each user can see, using roles and filter rules in Power BI and Fabric.

faq.a: RLS filters which rows of a semantic model or warehouse table each user can see, based on roles and filter rules. Users who open the same report can therefore see different subsets of the data.
faq.q: What does row-level security (RLS) do?

faq.a: RLS restricts which rows a user can see, while OLS concerns restricting access to objects in the model. The episode "DP-600 Training 4/4: Incremental Refresh, RLS, and OLS" covers both as part of Power BI data security.
faq.q: How does RLS differ from object-level security (OLS)?

faq.a: The episode "Deploy Power BI with Development, Test, and Production Pipelines" recommends validating RLS rules in isolated pipeline stages instead of assuming they are static and checking them only in production.
faq.q: Should RLS be tested before production?

row-level-security.long:
Row-level security (RLS) is a data access control that filters which rows of a semantic model or warehouse table each user can see. Access is based on roles and filter rules, so two people can open the same report or query the same table and still see different subsets of the data. The goal is to expose to each user only the rows relevant to their role, rather than building separate reports or copies of the data for each audience.

In practice, RLS is used to protect sensitive information and to support compliance with privacy rules. The M365.FM episode "DP-600 Training 4/4: Incremental Refresh, RLS, and OLS" discusses RLS together with Object-Level Security (OLS) as part of data security and analytics in Power BI. According to the episode, these features matter for data trust and for decision-making, because RLS lets organizations restrict data visibility at a granular level so that users see only the data relevant to their roles. The episode presents this as especially important for confidentiality and compliance in sensitive industries, and it refers to a conversation with a financial services client as an illustration.

RLS and OLS address different parts of a model. RLS decides which rows a user may see, while OLS, covered in the same DP-600 episode, concerns restricting access to objects in the model. Treating them as complementary controls helps when planning how a semantic model should expose data to different groups.

The episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" describes RLS as a way to control who can see which data in reports and dashboards. It says that in Microsoft Fabric, RLS can be set up in semantic models so that each user only views the data they are allowed to access, and that it can enforce data access policies across an organization. In that episode, RLS appears alongside other semantic model features such as calculation groups and field parameters, which are presented as ways to make a model scalable and easier to build on and maintain. Placing the security rules in the shared semantic model, instead of in individual reports, fits the idea of a reusable model that many reports draw from.

RLS also affects how models are deployed and tested. The episode "Deploy Power BI with Development, Test, and Production Pipelines" recommends validating RLS rules in isolated pipeline stages. It calls this surprising because RLS is often assumed to be static and only checked in production. The same episode recommends automated dataset refresh validations in a test stage and keeping gateway configuration separate from pipeline artifacts, since gateways are environment resources. Together these points describe RLS as something to be tested like any other part of a release, not configured once and left alone.

RLS has side effects on report design and performance. In "Build Accessible Power BI Themes with WCAG Contrast", the episode lists RLS among the factors that can cause different users to see different color assignments, because the data each person sees differs. This is relevant when a report relies on automatic colors for categories. In "Power Query Folding and Execution Order in Power BI", RLS is described as enforcing user-level data filtering within Power BI models. The episode notes this is especially important with DirectQuery, because backend databases often cannot tell users apart without Kerberos delegation. It also advises that RLS filters should support query folding, that the underlying tables should be indexed on the columns used by RLS to improve performance, and that security settings should be monitored continuously.

When deciding how to apply RLS, the episodes point to several recurring considerations: define roles and filter rules that match how users should see the data, place them in the semantic model so they apply consistently across reports, test them in pre-production stages, and design the filters so they do not undermine query performance.

runbook.desc: A runbook in Azure Automation is a script, typically PowerShell or Python or a graphical workflow, that the service runs on demand, on a schedule, from an alert or via a webhook.

faq.a: A runbook is a script, usually PowerShell or Python, or a graphical workflow that Azure Automation runs. It encapsulates an operational task so the service can execute it without manual steps.
faq.q: What is a runbook in Azure Automation?

faq.a: A runbook can be run on demand, on a schedule, from an alert, or via a webhook.
faq.q: How can a runbook be started?

faq.a: Runbooks are usually written in PowerShell or Python, and graphical workflows are also supported as a runbook type.
faq.q: Which scripting languages do runbooks use?

runbook.long:
A runbook (Azure Automation) is a unit of automation within the Azure Automation service. It is a script, usually written in PowerShell or Python, or a graphical workflow, that Azure Automation executes on behalf of the user. Runbooks are used to codify operational tasks so that they can be run repeatedly and without manual steps.

According to the available facts, a runbook can be started in several ways: on demand, on a schedule, from an alert, or through a webhook. This allows the same script to serve manual administration tasks as well as event-driven or time-based automation scenarios.

In terms of topic structure, Runbook (Azure Automation) sits beneath the broader concept Azure Automation, which is the service that hosts and runs these scripts. Microsoft documents the different runbook types, such as script-based and graphical variants, in its Azure Automation documentation on runbook types.

saas-fulfillment-apis.desc: SaaS fulfillment APIs are Microsoft commercial marketplace APIs that publishers use to manage the subscription lifecycle of transactable SaaS offers.

faq.a: They are Microsoft commercial marketplace APIs that publishers integrate to manage the subscription lifecycle of transactable SaaS offers, including activation, plan changes and cancellation.
faq.q: What are SaaS fulfillment APIs?

faq.a: Publishers of transactable SaaS offers in the Microsoft commercial marketplace integrate these APIs so their service can handle subscription lifecycle events.
faq.q: Who uses SaaS fulfillment APIs?

faq.a: Microsoft documents the APIs in its Partner Center marketplace offers documentation on the SaaS fulfillment APIs, available on Microsoft Learn.
faq.q: Where is the official documentation for SaaS fulfillment APIs?

saas-fulfillment-apis.long:
SaaS fulfillment APIs are Microsoft commercial marketplace APIs that publishers integrate to manage the subscription lifecycle of transactable SaaS offers. They cover lifecycle events such as activation, plan changes and cancellation.

The APIs are used by software publishers who sell SaaS offers through the Microsoft commercial marketplace. By integrating them, a publisher's own service can respond to what happens to a customer's subscription in the marketplace, for example when a subscription is activated, when the customer switches to a different plan, or when the subscription is cancelled.

The APIs apply specifically to transactable SaaS offers, meaning offers that are sold through the marketplace and therefore have a subscription whose state needs to be kept in sync between Microsoft and the publisher. Detailed technical requirements, supported operations and integration guidance are described in Microsoft's Partner Center documentation on the SaaS fulfillment APIs.

safe-attachments.desc: Safe Attachments is a Microsoft Defender for Office 365 feature that opens email attachments in an isolated sandbox and judges them by behaviour.

faq.a: Safe Attachments is a feature that opens email attachments in an isolated sandbox and judges them by behaviour before or while they are delivered. It is part of Microsoft Defender for Office 365.
faq.q: What is Safe Attachments in Microsoft Defender for Office 365?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes present both as scanning layers of Defender for Office 365: Safe Links checks URLs and Safe Attachments checks files, so users reach neither until they are judged safe.
faq.q: How is Safe Attachments related to Safe Links?

faq.a: The episode "Tune Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Against Phishing" says the cause is often misaligned layers, where Safe Links, Safe Attachments, anti-phishing machine learning and mail flow rules overlap, conflict or leave gaps. It describes Defender for Office 365 as something to tune continuously.
faq.q: Why can phishing still get through when Safe Attachments is enabled?

safe-attachments.long:
Safe Attachments is a feature of Microsoft Defender for Office 365. It opens email attachments in an isolated sandbox and judges them by what they do rather than by what they look like, and it does this before or while the message is delivered. The aim is to catch malicious files, including ones that signature-based scanning might miss, before a user opens them.

In the M365.FM episodes, Safe Attachments appears together with Safe Links as one of the two scanning layers that make up the advanced protection in Defender for Office 365. The episode "Microsoft Defender for Office 365 - Simply Explained" lists both under its key takeaways: Safe Links and Safe Attachments scan URLs and files to ensure they are safe before a user accesses them. The same episode places them next to real-time threat prevention, AI-based advanced threat detection, customizable security settings, reporting and user education. In this description, Safe Attachments is the file-focused part of a broader email protection service.

Safe Attachments also relates to Exchange Online Protection (EOP). The episode "Exchange Online Protection (EOP) - Simply Explained" describes advanced protection as an addition on top of the EOP baseline: Microsoft Defender for Office 365, with features like Safe Links and Safe Attachments. EOP provides the underlying mail filtering for Exchange Online, while Safe Attachments belongs to the extra layer that adds behaviour-based inspection of files.

A recurring theme in the episodes is that having the feature available does not mean it is configured well. "Hidden Microsoft 365 Tenant Security Risks" states that email security is often misconfigured. Advanced protections such as Safe Links, Safe Attachments and anti-spoofing policies are commonly left incomplete or disabled, which reduces protection against phishing and business email compromise (BEC). The episode treats this as one of several hidden tenant risks, alongside inactive accounts, permissions sprawl and underused audit logs.

The episode "Tune Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Against Phishing" goes further into why phishing can still reach users even when Defender for Office 365 is described as fully enabled. According to the episode, the cause is often misaligned layers: Safe Links, Safe Attachments, anti-phishing machine learning and mail flow rules that overlap, conflict or leave gaps. It stresses that Defender for Office 365 is not set-and-forget. The episode recommends tuning it as a living system so that security stops breaking business and business stops breaking security, and it mentions enabling dynamic delivery as one of the tuning steps.

In "Harden Microsoft 365 Security Without User Friction", the hosts name Safe Attachments among the Defender for Office 365 capabilities that help stop modern threats, together with anti-phishing policies, safe links, real-time alerts and analytics. They recommend pairing Defender for Office 365 with Defender for Endpoint and Conditional Access to build a layered security posture. They also note that technical controls alone are not enough, which is why the episodes repeatedly connect Safe Attachments to reporting and user education.

Typical decisions around Safe Attachments therefore concern configuration rather than activation alone. Administrators decide how the feature interacts with mail flow rules, how it is aligned with Safe Links and the anti-phishing policies, and how reporting is used to check that it works as intended. The episodes point to the Microsoft 365 admin center and the reporting features of Defender for Office 365 as the places to monitor effectiveness and find areas for improvement.

safe-links.desc: Safe Links is a Microsoft Defender for Office 365 feature that rewrites URLs and checks them at the moment of click in email, Microsoft Teams and Office apps.

faq.a: Safe Links rewrites URLs and checks them at the moment of click in email, Microsoft Teams and Office apps. It is a feature of Microsoft Defender for Office 365.
faq.q: What does Safe Links do?

faq.a: The episode "Defender for Office 365: Tuning Anti-Phishing and Safe Links Policies" says these policies only help if they are tuned to the organization rather than left at defaults. Tuning aims to reduce both missed threats and false positives.
faq.q: Is Safe Links effective with default settings?

faq.a: The episodes describe both as Defender for Office 365 features that check content before users access it: Safe Links covers URLs, and Safe Attachments covers files. They are meant to work together with anti-phishing policies and mail flow rules.
faq.q: How does Safe Links relate to Safe Attachments?

safe-links.long:
Safe Links is a feature of Microsoft Defender for Office 365 that rewrites URLs and checks them at the moment a user clicks. It applies to links in email, in Microsoft Teams and in Office apps. Because the check happens at click time rather than only when a message arrives, a link that was harmless on delivery but later points to a malicious destination can still be evaluated when someone tries to open it.

Within Defender for Office 365, Safe Links sits alongside several other protections. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Defender for Office 365 - Simply Explained" describes Safe Links and Safe Attachments as features that scan URLs and files to ensure they are safe before a user accesses them. It places them in the context of real-time threat prevention, AI-based advanced threat detection, customizable security settings and regular reporting. In this framing, Safe Links is the part that deals with the link-based path of phishing and malware, while Safe Attachments deals with files.

A recurring point in the episodes is that Safe Links does not deliver full value when left unmanaged. The episode "Defender for Office 365: Tuning Anti-Phishing and Safe Links Policies" states that anti-phishing and Safe Links policies only help if they are tuned to the organization rather than left at defaults. It covers tuning impersonation protection, preset policies, Safe Links, Safe Attachments and reporting, with the aim of reducing both missed threats and false positives. That wording frames policy tuning as a balance: settings that are too loose let threats through, and settings that are too aggressive create false positives that disrupt users.

The episode "Tune Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Against Phishing" makes a related argument. It says users can still click phishing links even when Defender for Microsoft 365 is described as fully enabled, and attributes this to misaligned layers rather than to the attackers alone. According to the episode, Safe Links, Safe Attachments, anti-phishing machine learning and mail flow rules can overlap, conflict or leave gaps. It treats Defender as a living system that needs ongoing tuning instead of a set-and-forget product, and it traces how a phishing email can slip through when these layers are not aligned. The excerpt also mentions steps such as working by risk group and enabling dynamic delivery.

The episode "Hidden Microsoft 365 Tenant Security Risks" lists email security misconfiguration as a common tenant risk. It says advanced protections such as Safe Links, Safe Attachments and anti-spoofing policies are often left incomplete or disabled, which reduces protection against phishing and business email compromise. In practice, this makes a review of whether Safe Links is actually configured and applied a routine part of a tenant security assessment, rather than an assumption that the feature is working because a license is present.

The episode "Harden Microsoft 365 Security Without User Friction" positions Defender for Office 365 as a key control against modern threats, naming anti-phishing policies, Safe Links, Safe Attachments, real-time alerts and analytics. It recommends pairing Defender for Office 365 with Defender for Endpoint and Conditional Access to build a layered security posture. It also notes that technical controls alone are not enough, so Safe Links is presented as one layer among identity, endpoint and user-awareness measures rather than a standalone safeguard.

Typical decisions around Safe Links therefore concern scope and tuning: which users or risk groups a policy covers, how it fits with preset policies and anti-phishing settings, and how reporting is used to spot missed threats and false positives. The episodes treat these as ongoing administrative tasks rather than one-time setup.

saga-pattern.desc: The Saga pattern splits a distributed transaction into local steps across systems, each paired with a compensating action that undoes earlier steps if a later one fails.

faq.a: The Saga pattern is a way to handle distributed transactions by splitting a process into local steps across systems. Each step has a compensating action that undoes earlier steps if a later step fails.
faq.q: What is the Saga pattern?

faq.a: A compensating action is an operation paired with a saga step that reverses the effect of that step. It is run when a later step fails, so earlier completed steps are undone.
faq.q: What is a compensating action in a saga?

faq.a: The pattern is described in the Azure Architecture Center on Microsoft Learn as a cloud design pattern for distributed transactions.
faq.q: Where is the Saga pattern documented by Microsoft?

saga-pattern.long:
The Saga pattern is a design approach for managing distributed transactions. Instead of running one transaction across several systems, it divides a business process into a sequence of local steps. Each step is executed within a single system and commits on its own.

Every step in a saga has a compensating action. If a later step fails, the compensating actions for the steps that already completed are run to undo their effects. This keeps data consistent across the participating systems without relying on a single transaction that spans all of them.

The pattern is used when a process touches multiple services or data stores and a failure partway through must not leave the overall outcome in an inconsistent state. It is documented in the Azure Architecture Center as a cloud design pattern, where Microsoft describes it as a way to coordinate steps and handle failures through compensation.

No related topics or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, so the description here is limited to the definition of the pattern itself. Further detail on implementation choices is available in the official Microsoft Learn documentation for the Saga pattern.

salami-slicing-attack.desc: A salami-slicing attack is a fraud technique that achieves a large overall effect through many small, individually inconspicuous steps, such as tiny account transfers.

faq.a: It is an attack or fraud technique that reaches a large overall result through many small, individually inconspicuous steps, such as transfers that drain accounts one tiny piece at a time.
faq.q: What is a salami-slicing attack?

faq.a: Each individual step is small enough to appear unremarkable, so the effect only becomes clear when the many small actions are viewed together.
faq.q: Why is a salami-slicing attack hard to notice?

salami-slicing-attack.long:
A salami-slicing attack is an attack or fraud technique in which a large effect is achieved through many small steps, each of which is too minor to attract attention on its own. The name refers to cutting a salami into thin slices: no single slice appears significant, yet together they add up to the whole sausage.

A typical example is a series of transfers that drain accounts one tiny piece at a time. Because every individual transaction is small, it is easy to overlook, and the cumulative loss may only become visible when the totals are examined across many transactions or over a long period.

The central idea behind the concept is that detection depends on looking at the pattern rather than at single events. Controls that only flag large or unusual individual actions may miss an approach that stays below such thresholds by design. For this reason, the term is often used when discussing why aggregated review and monitoring of many small actions can matter alongside checks on single large ones.

No related topics, official documentation links or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, so it serves as a general definition of the concept.

sales-order-agent.desc: Sales Order Agent is a Microsoft AI agent in Dynamics 365 Business Central that reads customer order emails and prepares draft sales quotes or orders for review.

faq.a: It reads customer order requests received by email in Dynamics 365 Business Central, identifies the customer, extracts the requested products and quantities, checks stock and prepares draft sales quotes or orders for review.
faq.q: What does the Sales Order Agent do?

faq.a: No. The drafts go to a person for review and approval. The episodes say people remain responsible for exceptions such as unusual pricing, missing products, incorrect customer information or orders that do not match established patterns.
faq.q: Does the Sales Order Agent approve orders by itself?

faq.a: It focuses on incoming customer order requests. The episodes name a Payables Agent for vendor invoice drafts and supplier-focused agents for repetitive supply chain communication as separate agents.
faq.q: How does the Sales Order Agent differ from other Business Central agents?

sales-order-agent.long:
Sales Order Agent is an AI agent built by Microsoft for Dynamics 365 Business Central. It supports the order intake process by reading customer order requests that arrive by email, checking stock and preparing draft sales quotes or sales orders. A person reviews and approves the result, so the agent prepares the work and does not close it on its own.

The purpose of the agent is to take over repetitive order-entry work. Customer orders can arrive through email and other channels, and employees normally have to interpret the request, enter the information, verify details and prepare a confirmation. According to the episodes, the Sales Order Agent can support this process from initial entry through confirmation, so staff spend less time on routine typing and more on the cases that need judgment.

The episode "Dynamics 365 Agents - Simply Explained" describes the typical sequence. The agent reads an order request received through email, identifies the customer, extracts the requested products and quantities, and prepares order information for review. The episode "Dynamics 365 Copilot - Simply Explained" describes it in similar terms: the agent analyzes customer requests arriving through email and helps prepare the corresponding sales order information. The facts for this product also mention a stock check before a draft quote or order is created.

Human oversight is a central theme in how the episodes present the agent. The episode "Dynamics 365 Agents - Simply Explained" says that people remain responsible for exceptions such as unusual pricing, missing products, incorrect customer information, or orders that do not match established patterns. The episode "Dynamics 365 Copilot - Simply Explained" makes the same point for agents in general: they can automate parts of routine work, but people remain responsible for the outcome. In practice, the agent handles the standard, repeatable order and passes anything unusual back to an employee.

The Sales Order Agent belongs to a wider group of agents in Dynamics 365. The episodes place it next to a Payables Agent, which works with vendor invoices and prepares invoice drafts for review, and next to supplier-focused agents that support repetitive communication in supply chain operations. They also set it beside Copilot features in Business Central, such as matching electronic vendor invoice lines to purchase orders or suggesting matches during bank reconciliation. The agents extend AI assistance into more clearly defined operational workflows, while Copilot features assist within a task the user is already doing.

The episode "Use Copilot in Dynamics 365 Business Central" (published 2025-11-03) frames the topic more broadly. It says Microsoft Copilot in Business Central can act as a sales order agent by suggesting line items, validating pricing and inventory, generating sales order drafts and automating routine entry tasks. It adds that this can speed up order fulfillment and reduce errors by using ERP data and business systems across the sales order lifecycle, and that the work happens inside the Business Central environment with Azure AI and Microsoft 365 Copilot integration.

The episode "Dynamics 365 Autonomous Agents - Simply Explained" (2026-08-19) lists the Sales Order Agent among its examples of repetitive business work and places it alongside agents for sales, where salespeople still decide which opportunities deserve attention and review communications. Official documentation on the order-processing flow is available on Microsoft Learn under the Business Central section for the Sales Order Agent.

For organizations considering the agent, the main decisions concern which orders suit automated drafting and who reviews the drafts. Standard orders with clear customers, products and quantities fit the described workflow. Orders with special pricing, items not in the catalog or unclear customer data fall under the exceptions the episodes assign to people.

salesforce.desc: Salesforce is a cloud software company known for its CRM platform; M365.FM episodes cover its role as an integration target for Microsoft 365 Copilot.

faq.a: Salesforce is a cloud software company known for its customer relationship management (CRM) platform. On M365.FM it appears mainly as an external business system that can be connected to Microsoft 365 tools.
faq.q: What is Salesforce?

faq.a: According to the episode "Connect Microsoft Copilot to Salesforce, ServiceNow, and APIs", Copilot out of the box sees only surface-level data like emails, chats and documents, not a Salesforce pipeline. Connecting it requires an integration approach with governed identity, least-privilege access and audit trails.
faq.q: Can Microsoft 365 Copilot see Salesforce data by default?

faq.a: The episodes mention Microsoft 365 Copilot connectors, Copilot extensibility with custom agents, and Azure Logic Apps as ways to connect Salesforce with Microsoft 365 and the Power Platform.
faq.q: Which Microsoft tools are mentioned for integrating Salesforce?

salesforce.long:
Salesforce is a cloud software company known for its customer relationship management (CRM) platform. In the Microsoft ecosystem, the name mostly comes up in connection with integration: the question of how data held in a CRM system can be reached from Microsoft 365 tools such as Copilot, Logic Apps and Power Automate. The M365.FM episodes that mention Salesforce treat it as one of several business systems that sit outside the core Microsoft 365 data layer.

The episode "Connect Microsoft Copilot to Salesforce, ServiceNow, and APIs" frames the central problem. According to the episode, Microsoft 365 Copilot out of the box sees only surface-level data such as emails, chats and documents, and not the systems that actually run a business. A Salesforce pipeline is given as an example of data that Copilot does not see by default, alongside ServiceNow incidents. The episode describes this blind spot as something that affects real decisions and discusses how to close it with governed identity, least-privilege access and full audit trails. It also separates what it calls AI theater from production-ready setups.

A related episode, "Connect External Business Data with Microsoft 365 Copilot Connectors", looks at the connector approach in more detail. The episode explains that connectors allow Copilot to reach beyond Outlook, SharePoint and Teams and pull in insights from Salesforce, Dynamics 365, custom databases, line-of-business apps and other external systems. In this view, connectors turn Copilot into a unified search layer that bridges scattered data silos and the employees who need the information. The episode also discusses the difference between Microsoft's prebuilt connectors and other options.

Salesforce also appears in the context of workflow automation. The episode "Build Enterprise Automation with Azure Logic Apps" lists Salesforce among the third-party systems, together with SAP, ServiceNow and custom APIs, across which Azure Logic Apps can act as an automation layer spanning Microsoft 365 and the Power Platform. The episode covers when to use Logic Apps versus Power Automate and how to build a production-ready flow with triggers, actions, connectors and error handling, and how to scale with governance and monitoring.

In "Microsoft 365 Copilot Extensibility with Gautam Sheth [MVP]", Salesforce is named together with Jira as an example of third-party apps that can be integrated to streamline processes. The key takeaways listed there also mention customizing Copilot to fit a workflow, creating custom agents with low-code tools, and regularly assessing security and maintaining custom tools. Here Salesforce is one of the applications that extensibility features can connect to.

Salesforce is also mentioned in "The Future of Work with Fabio Bonolo [MVP]", but in a different sense. In that episode it appears as a company example in a discussion of hybrid work and employee engagement: the episode says that Salesforce builds communities for connection, in contrast with other companies named in the same passage. This is a workplace-culture reference and not a technical one.

Taken together, the episodes position Salesforce as an external business system rather than a Microsoft product. Typical decisions around it include whether Copilot should gain access to CRM data, which connector or integration route to use, how identity and permissions are governed, and how access is audited. The episodes emphasize least-privilege access and audit trails as part of that design, and they recommend assessing security and maintaining integrations over time.

saml.desc: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an older XML-based federation standard for corporate single sign-on, using signed assertions from an identity provider.

faq.a: SAML is an older XML-based federation standard widely used for corporate single sign-on. An identity provider sends signed assertions about a user to an app.
faq.q: What is Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)?

faq.a: In SAML-based single sign-on, the identity provider issues a signed assertion about the user, and the application accepts it instead of collecting credentials directly.
faq.q: What does SAML do in single sign-on?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn provides a SAML vs. OIDC decision guide in its Microsoft Entra enterprise apps documentation.
faq.q: Where can guidance on choosing between SAML and other protocols be found?

saml.long:
Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an XML-based federation standard that is widely used for corporate single sign-on. In a SAML exchange, an identity provider sends signed assertions about a user to an application, so the application can trust the sign-in without handling the user's credentials itself.

SAML is generally described as an older standard compared with newer identity protocols. It is commonly used to connect enterprise applications to a central identity provider, allowing users to sign in once and access multiple apps. The signed assertion carries information about the user that the receiving application relies on to grant access.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the choice between SAML and other protocols such as OpenID Connect is covered in Microsoft Learn guidance on enterprise apps in Microsoft Entra, including a SAML vs. OIDC decision guide. That documentation helps administrators weigh protocol options when integrating applications with Microsoft Entra.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no related topics have been recorded for it yet.

sandboxing.desc: Sandboxing runs programs in an isolated, restricted environment so failures or compromised code cannot spread, and is applied to AI agents in M365.FM episodes.

faq.a: Sandboxing is a security mechanism that runs programs in an isolated environment with restricted access, so failures or compromised code cannot spread. The M365.FM episodes apply it to OS-level isolation of AI agents.
faq.q: What is sandboxing?

faq.a: The episode "Indirect Prompt Injection Security for Enterprise AI" recommends using sandboxing to isolate core instructions from outside data. It is listed together with input validation, output filtering and human review for high-risk actions.
faq.q: How does sandboxing help against indirect prompt injection?

faq.a: According to the episodes, no. Sandboxing is described as one layer alongside authentication, authorization, monitoring, policy enforcement, audit logs and human oversight.
faq.q: Is sandboxing used on its own in AI security?

sandboxing.long:
Sandboxing is a security mechanism that runs programs in an isolated environment with restricted access, so that failures or compromised code cannot spread to the rest of a system. In the M365.FM episodes that mention it, the concept is applied to the OS-level isolation of AI agents and to the handling of untrusted instructions and code in enterprise AI setups.

The basic idea is containment. Code or an agent that runs inside a sandbox can only reach the resources it has been explicitly given. If the code behaves unexpectedly, is buggy, or has been manipulated by an attacker, the damage stays inside the boundary instead of reaching data, systems or other agents outside it. This makes sandboxing a common building block in layered security designs, where no single control is expected to stop every threat.

The episode "Indirect Prompt Injection Security for Enterprise AI" lists sandboxing among the controls against indirect prompt injection. The recommendation there is to isolate core instructions from outside data using sandboxing, alongside other measures: treating all documents as if they could contain executable code, never trusting external data until it has been checked, cleaning and validating inputs before they reach the AI, filtering outputs, requiring human review for high-risk actions, and using model-side defenses such as adversarial fine-tuning and security layers. The episode refers to the OpenClaw incident of March 2026, in which malicious instructions hidden in a normal file were processed by an AI and led to a leak of sensitive data without any user action. That kind of scenario illustrates why separating trusted instructions from untrusted content matters.

In "MCP (Model Context Protocol) - Simply Explained", isolation and sandboxing appear as one layer of control within MCP security. The episode's overview table describes the objective of this layer as preventing unvetted code from executing outside a controlled environment. It sits next to authentication and authorization, provenance tracking, inline policy enforcement and centralized governance, each addressing a different security objective.

"Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Communication - Simply Explained" mentions sandboxing as part of a layered defense for agent communication channels. The episode names authentication, sandboxing and human oversight as combined measures, together with continuous monitoring to detect anomalies and potential security threats. The point is that agents exchanging information and tasks should not be able to act without limits.

In "Agentic Operating Model for Enterprise AI and Copilot", sandboxing is listed as an operating pattern in which high-risk actions run in safe environments before going live. It appears next to policy constraints, audit logs, escalation triggers, a centralized orchestrator, hierarchical orchestration, decentralized swarms and a governed context layer. In this framing, sandboxing works as a safe testing and containment step for risky agent actions rather than as a standalone safeguard.

The episode "Secure MLOps in Microsoft Cloud with Martin Dimovski [MVP-MCT]" places sandboxing in the context of integration risks in machine learning operations. Integrating diverse tools and data sources creates complex attack surfaces, and the episode says that patching policies, sandboxing and network segmentation should be enforced to reduce those risks. It also points to supply chain attacks on third-party components and to the need for strict separation between environments and monitoring for anomalous activity.

Across these episodes, sandboxing is presented as one control among several rather than a complete answer. Typical decisions around it include which actions count as high-risk and should run in isolation first, how strictly external data should be separated from core instructions, and how isolation is combined with authentication, monitoring, policy enforcement and human review.

sap.desc: SAP is a German enterprise software company known for its ERP systems, cited on M365.FM as a typical ERP source whose data is unified with CRM data via Fabric connectors.

faq.a: SAP is a German enterprise software company best known for its ERP systems.
faq.q: What is SAP?

faq.a: SAP is cited as a typical ERP source whose data is unified with CRM data through Fabric connectors.
faq.q: How does SAP relate to Fabric on M365.FM?

sap.long:
SAP is a German enterprise software company best known for its ERP (enterprise resource planning) systems. Organizations use ERP software of this kind to manage core business processes and the data that comes with them.

On M365.FM, SAP appears as an example of a typical ERP source. In the discussion, data from an ERP system such as SAP is brought together with CRM data through Fabric connectors, so that information from different business systems can be unified in one place.

The available facts about SAP on this site are limited to that role: an ERP data source in a scenario involving Fabric connectors and CRM data. No further product details, versions or integration specifics are covered here.

sap-ecc.desc: SAP ECC (ERP Central Component) is SAP's legacy ERP system, the predecessor of SAP S/4HANA, with mainstream maintenance ending in 2027.

faq.a: SAP ECC (ERP Central Component) is the core of SAP ERP, introduced in 2004 as the successor to SAP R/3 Enterprise. It is now considered legacy technology and has been superseded by SAP S/4HANA.
faq.q: What is SAP ECC?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode description states that mainstream maintenance for SAP ECC ends in 2027. The reference material mentions 2031 to 2033 only for a private-edition transition option, so contract-specific terms should be checked with SAP.
faq.q: When does mainstream maintenance for SAP ECC end?

faq.a: The sources name Financial Accounting, Controlling, Sales and Distribution, Materials Management, Production Planning, Quality Management, Plant Maintenance and Human Resources, among others.
faq.q: Which modules does SAP ECC include?

sap-ecc.long:
SAP ECC, short for SAP ERP Central Component, is the core of SAP ERP, the enterprise resource planning software from SAP SE that covers a company's central business functions. It is regarded as legacy technology and the predecessor of SAP S/4HANA. According to the episode summary on M365.FM, mainstream maintenance for SAP ECC ends in 2027, which is why many organisations running it have to decide where their ERP landscape will live and how they will migrate.

The product has a long lineage. SAP ERP as a product family dates back to 1972 according to the reference material, and it grew from SAP R/3, which launched on 6 July 1992. In 2004 SAP ERP was introduced and replaced R/3 Enterprise with the ERP Central Component, SAP ECC. This release merged SAP Business Warehouse, Strategic Enterprise Management and the Internet Transaction Server into a single instance. SAP ERP 6.0 followed in 2006, and from then on new functions were delivered through optional enhancement packages. The last of these, EhP8 in 2016, is described as concluding the evolution of ECC 6.0 and as the foundation for the move to S/4HANA.

SAP ECC is used to run core processes through a set of modules. The modules named in the sources include Financial Accounting, Controlling, Sales and Distribution, Materials Management, Production Planning, Quality Management, Plant Maintenance and Human Resources. Together they cover finance, logistics, manufacturing and personnel topics in one integrated system, which is why replacing or migrating it touches nearly every part of a business.

Traditional SAP ERP implementations are described as running through five phases, from preparation to go-live support. The reference material also cites unattributed cost estimates of more than 100 million dollars for projects at Fortune 500 companies, which illustrates why ERP changes are treated as major programmes rather than routine upgrades. These figures are estimates reported by the source and are not a statement about any specific migration.

The typical decision around SAP ECC concerns the move to SAP S/4HANA. The M365.FM episode "SAP S-4HANA - Simply Explained" is aimed at IT and business people who need to understand what S/4HANA is, how it connects to Microsoft tools, and where such projects usually go wrong. Its chapters cover what SAP S/4HANA actually is and the role of the in-memory approach, and its framing is that most companies still running SAP ECC must settle on a hosting location and a migration path before the 2027 deadline.

A note on dates: the reference material does not give a standard maintenance end date for SAP ECC itself. The only dates it mentions, 2031 to 2033, relate to a private-edition transition option. The 2027 date for mainstream maintenance comes from the description used by M365.FM, so organisations should confirm the current maintenance terms for their own contracts and editions directly with SAP.

Within the M365.FM knowledge base, SAP ECC is relevant mainly as the starting point of an SAP migration, where the connection between the ERP system and Microsoft tools becomes part of the planning. The episode treats the topic in plain language and is the main source on M365.FM for how the ECC-to-S/4HANA transition relates to the Microsoft ecosystem.

sap-fiori.desc: SAP Fiori is SAP's role-based, tile-oriented user experience and design language for SAP applications, used for many tasks in place of the transaction-driven SAP GUI.

faq.a: SAP Fiori is the user experience and design language for SAP applications. It offers role-based, task-focused, tile-oriented apps and replaces the transaction-code-driven SAP GUI for many tasks.
faq.q: What is SAP Fiori?

faq.a: The SAP Fiori Launchpad is the role-based, personalised entry point for users. It shows app tiles according to roles defined in the SAP system and includes a search and explore bar.
faq.q: What is the SAP Fiori Launchpad?

faq.a: According to SAP Learning, the stack includes SAPUI5, the Fiori front-end server for the ABAP platform, SAP Gateway with the OData protocol, SAP Business Application Studio and SAP Analytics. Clients include HTML5 browsers, SAP Business Client and SAP Mobile Start.
faq.q: Which technologies does SAP Fiori rely on?

sap-fiori.long:
SAP Fiori is the user experience for SAP software and the design language for enterprise applications. It is role-based and tile-oriented, and it was first used with SAP S/4HANA. For many tasks it replaces the transaction-code-driven SAP GUI with apps that are built around what a given user actually needs to do. SAP Learning describes it as replacing dense, transaction-centric screens with role-based, task-focused apps for frequent tasks such as approvals, lookups and self-service.

The typical use case is a business user who works with a limited set of recurring tasks. An example from SAP Learning is an Approve Purchase Orders app, which shows approvers the key information quickly instead of requiring navigation through several transaction screens. SAP introduced Fiori 3 in 2019 to give all SAP products one consistent design, so that applications from different areas of the SAP portfolio look and behave in a coherent way.

The design guidelines are built on several principles. Apps are meant to be role-based, adaptive across desktop, tablet and phone, coherent, simple and delightful. The guidelines also include a 5-1-2 principle: five interactions to reach important tasks, one primary action per screen and feedback within two seconds. These rules give developers and designers concrete targets when deciding how much to put on a screen and how many steps a task should take.

The SAP Fiori Launchpad is the entry point for users. It is role-based and personalised, and it shows app tiles according to the roles defined in the SAP system, together with a search and explore bar. In this way the tile-oriented approach controls which applications a user sees and how they reach them.

The technology stack behind SAP Fiori includes SAPUI5, a framework built on JavaScript, CSS and HTML5. Further components named by SAP Learning are the Fiori front-end server for the ABAP platform, SAP Gateway with the OData protocol, SAP Business Application Studio for development and SAP Analytics. Clients can be any HTML5 browser, SAP Business Client or SAP Mobile Start.

For teams that build or adapt Fiori apps, a recurring decision is how much custom development is justified. The M365.FM episode "Fix Poor Microsoft 365 Tenant Design with Practical Governance" touches on this in a discussion of overengineering in enterprise environments. Among its examples is implementing intricate logic in SAP Fiori or freestyle UI5 apps instead of using simpler Fiori Elements standard list reports. Another is building overly complex custom ABAP modules when standard functionality in SAP S/4HANA suffices. The episode says such choices can create systems that are difficult to maintain and understand, and that complexity is often mistaken for sophistication while it tends to produce confusion and inefficiency.

Taken together, the sources present SAP Fiori both as a user experience standard and as a development model. The standard defines how apps should look and behave, while the choice between freestyle UI5 development and Fiori Elements standard floorplans determines how much custom code has to be maintained over time. The episode's point is that the simpler standard option is often sufficient and easier to keep running than bespoke logic.

sap-hana.desc: SAP HANA is SAP's in-memory database that holds its data in RAM but still depends on very fast storage for logs, backups and snapshots.

faq.a: SAP HANA is SAP's in-memory database. It keeps its data in RAM but still needs very fast storage for logs, backups and snapshots.
faq.q: What is SAP HANA?

faq.a: The episodes name Ultra Disk as a fit for SAP HANA, citing up to 400,000 IOPS and 10,000 MB/s, and list SAP HANA among the workloads supported by Azure NetApp Files.
faq.q: Which Azure storage options do the M365.FM episodes link to SAP HANA?

faq.a: Yes. The episode "Azure Backup - Simply Explained" lists SAP HANA among the workloads that Azure Backup protects, together with Azure Virtual Machines, Azure Files, SQL Server and hybrid environments.
faq.q: Can Azure Backup protect SAP HANA?

sap-hana.long:
SAP HANA is SAP's in-memory database. It keeps its working data in RAM, which is the core of its design, but it does not run on memory alone: it still needs very fast storage for logs, backups and snapshots. That combination of memory-resident data and demanding persistent storage is what shapes most infrastructure decisions around the product, especially when it runs on cloud platforms.

In the M365.FM episodes, SAP HANA appears mainly as a workload that other Azure services are built to support or protect. It is not covered as a standalone product in these episodes. Instead, it shows up in the context of storage, backup and automation, and the way it is mentioned reflects the two sides of its profile: data in memory, and performance-sensitive storage underneath.

On the storage side, the episodes "Azure Managed Disks - Simply Explained" and "Azure Disk Storage - Simply Explained" both name SAP HANA as a typical use case for Ultra Disk. Ultra Disks are described there as the highest-performance option among Azure Managed Disks, suited to data-intensive applications such as SAP HANA and Oracle Database. The episodes list a maximum disk size of 65,536 GiB, a maximum throughput of 10,000 MB/s and up to 400,000 IOPS, and note that an Ultra Disk cannot be used as an OS disk. They position it for transaction-heavy workloads that need consistent, low-latency performance. "Azure Disk Storage - Simply Explained" also mentions Premium SSD v2 as a more flexible alternative, where throughput and IOPS can be adjusted separately, although its examples for that tier refer to SQL Server rather than SAP HANA.

The episode "Azure NetApp Files - Simply Explained" places SAP HANA among the enterprise workloads that Azure NetApp Files supports, alongside Oracle databases, Azure VMware Solution, Azure Virtual Desktop, AI, analytics and high-performance computing. The episode describes the service as providing sub-millisecond latency and dynamic performance scaling, and explains its building blocks: NetApp accounts, capacity pools, volumes, performance tiers, snapshots, replication, backups, security and high availability. For SAP HANA, this offers a file-based storage route as an alternative to disk-based options.

Backup is the other recurring theme. "Azure Backup - Simply Explained" states that Azure Backup protects Azure Virtual Machines, Azure Files, SQL Server, SAP HANA and hybrid environments. The episode covers backup policies, recovery points, retention, snapshots, incremental backups, encryption and restore options, and explains how soft delete, immutable backups and geo-redundant storage help protect against ransomware and accidental data loss. It also separates Azure Backup from Azure Site Recovery, which helps clarify when a team needs backup and when it needs disaster recovery for a system such as SAP HANA.

Finally, "Autonomous AI Agents: Use Cases, Risks, and Governance" uses SAP HANA as an example of a business system that an AI agent can write to. In its example, an AI agent analyzes invoices and updates SAP HANA automatically, so that people do not have to enter the data by hand. The episode presents this as part of automating repetitive tasks, and the governance and risk discussion in that episode applies equally to agents that touch a core database such as this one.

Taken together, the episodes show SAP HANA as a memory-based database whose operation depends on three decisions: which storage tier backs its logs and persistence, how its data is backed up and restored, and which automated systems are allowed to read from or write to it.

sap-s4hana.desc: SAP S/4HANA is SAP's ERP suite, released in 2015 as the successor to SAP ECC, running only on the in-memory SAP HANA database.

faq.a: SAP S/4HANA is SAP's ERP suite, released in 2015 as the successor to SAP ECC. It runs only on the in-memory SAP HANA database.
faq.q: What is SAP S/4HANA?

faq.a: The episode "SAP S-4HANA - Simply Explained" states that most companies running SAP ECC have to decide where S/4HANA lives and how to migrate before the 2027 deadline.
faq.q: Why is the 2027 deadline relevant for SAP S/4HANA?

faq.a: The Azure Architecture Center guide describes Fiori front-end servers, SAP Web Dispatcher, application servers and a Central Services cluster, with SAP HANA on clustered Linux VMs using HANA System Replication and automatic failover. HANA must run on SAP-certified VM types with premium-class disks for production.
faq.q: How is SAP S/4HANA typically deployed on Azure?

sap-s4hana.long:
SAP S/4HANA is SAP's ERP suite. It was released in 2015 as the successor to SAP ECC and runs only on the in-memory SAP HANA database. This tie to a single database platform is one of the defining traits of the product and shapes many of the architecture and migration decisions that organizations face when they move from older SAP landscapes.

The main reason the product comes up in enterprise planning is the migration path from SAP ECC. The M365.FM episode "SAP S-4HANA - Simply Explained" describes the situation in plain language: most companies running SAP ECC have to decide where S/4HANA will live and how to migrate before the 2027 deadline. The episode is aimed at IT and business people who need to understand what S/4HANA is, how it connects to Microsoft tools, and where projects usually go wrong. Its outline starts with what SAP S/4HANA actually is and then moves to why the in-memory approach matters.

A typical production layout for S/4HANA is described in the Azure Architecture Center guide on running SAP S/4HANA on Linux in Azure. The guide does not define S/4HANA itself, but it shows how the system is commonly built with high availability and disaster recovery. The application layer consists of Fiori front-end servers, SAP Web Dispatcher, application servers and a Central Services cluster. The database layer uses SAP HANA on clustered Linux virtual machines, with HANA System Replication and automatic failover. Fiori can also be embedded directly in the S/4 system, which removes the need for separate front-end virtual machines.

Several design points from that guide are relevant for planning. Central Services contain single points of failure, so they require highly available NFS storage and fencing. Networking follows a hub-and-spoke design with separate subnets per tier, load balancers and network security groups. SAP HANA must run on VM types certified by SAP, and production storage must use premium-class disks rather than standard disks. Spot VMs are not suitable for production, and cross-region disaster recovery is needed to survive a regional outage. Required SAP licences remain the customer's responsibility.

S/4HANA also appears in discussions about keeping custom development proportionate. The episode "Fix Poor Microsoft 365 Tenant Design with Practical Governance" lists overengineering examples from enterprise environments, including building overly complex custom ABAP modules when standard functionality in SAP S/4HANA suffices, and implementing intricate logic in SAP Fiori or freestyle UI5 apps instead of using simpler Fiori Elements standard list reports. The episode argues that such choices create systems that are difficult to maintain and understand, and that complexity should not be mistaken for sophistication.

Taken together, the available material points to three recurring decision areas: when and how to migrate from SAP ECC given the 2027 deadline, where to host the system and how to design its availability, and how closely to stay with standard functionality rather than extending it. The episodes also touch on the connection between S/4HANA and Microsoft tools, which is why the product is covered on a knowledge base focused on the Microsoft ecosystem.
