The episode "Data Loss Prevention in Microsoft 365: Policies That Actually Work" states that DLP policies fail when they either block everything or catch nothing, and that the workable middle ground takes iteration. It covers scoping, sensitive information types, policy tips, simulation mode and tuning, and recommends rolling out DLP in stages while measuring whether it actually reduces risk. Choosing the right type, adjusting confidence and testing in simulation before enforcement are therefore part of normal policy design.

In summary, sensitive information types are the detection building blocks that connect content to protection decisions in Microsoft Purview. They differ from trainable classifiers, which recognize documents that fit categories based on examples of business content, and from Exact Data Match, which the episodes mention as a separate capability. Pattern-based types are suited to structured data with recognizable formats, and they feed into DLP conditions, automatic labeling and AI interaction scanning.

sensitivity-labels.desc: Sensitivity labels (Vertraulichkeitsbezeichnungen) are Microsoft Purview labels that classify and protect documents, emails and meetings with encryption and markings.

faq.a: Sensitivity labels are Microsoft Purview labels that classify and protect documents, emails and meetings. A label can add encryption, visual markings and access restrictions that stay with the file.
faq.q: What are sensitivity labels?

faq.a: "Sensitivity Labels Rollout Playbook: From Pilot to Production" says rollout design decides success, not licensing. It covers label taxonomy, default behavior, user communication, auto-labeling and measuring adoption, and advises keeping the label set small.
faq.q: What does the episode say about rolling out sensitivity labels?

faq.a: According to "Fix Sensitivity Labels and Data Silos for Microsoft Copilot", labels that are static, incomplete and poorly maintained appear to enforce governance but are ineffective in dynamic, AI-driven environments.
faq.q: Why can sensitivity labels give a false sense of security?

sensitivity-labels.long:
Sensitivity labels, also known by the German term Vertraulichkeitsbezeichnungen, are labels from Microsoft Purview that classify and protect documents, emails and meetings. A label is applied to a piece of content and can add encryption, visual markings and access restrictions. These protections travel with the file wherever it goes, so the handling rules do not depend only on the location where the file happens to be stored.

Sensitivity labels are part of Microsoft Purview, the platform that brings together data security, compliance and governance capabilities. In the Purview portfolio they belong to the information protection area, where organizations discover, classify, label and protect sensitive data across Microsoft 365. The episode "Microsoft Purview Information Protection - Simply Explained" describes this as a combination of sensitivity labels, encryption and policy controls that supports safer sharing and clearer handling rules, so users can keep working productively without losing control of important business information.

In practice, labels are used to express how sensitive a piece of content is and what should happen because of that. Typical decisions include which labels to offer, what each label should enforce, which label is applied by default, and whether labeling is left to users or automated. Labels are typically used together with data loss prevention, which acts on sensitive content, and the wider Purview toolset covered in "Microsoft Purview - Simply Explained", which lists sensitivity labels alongside Data Loss Prevention, Information Protection, Data Lifecycle Management, eDiscovery, Audit, Insider Risk Management, Communication Compliance, Compliance Manager and Data Governance.

Rollout design is a central topic. The episode "Sensitivity Labels Rollout Playbook: From Pilot to Production" states that sensitivity labels succeed or fail on rollout design, not on the licensing line item. It outlines a path from pilot to production covering label taxonomy, default behavior, user communication, auto-labeling and how to measure adoption. It also advises keeping the label set small and avoiding common user frustration, which are points that affect whether people actually use the labels in daily work.

Labels also matter for AI. Microsoft 365 Copilot works with the content users can reach, so the quality of classification influences what an AI assistant can surface. The episode "Fix Sensitivity Labels and Data Silos for Microsoft Copilot" argues that sensitivity labels are widely misunderstood and often give organizations a false sense of security. According to the episode, labels can appear to enforce governance while in reality being static, incomplete and poorly maintained, which makes them ineffective in dynamic, AI-driven environments. The episode places the core issue not in the labeling technology itself but in how organizations use it, and points to measures such as reducing permission sprawl, automating classification and redesigning how data flows across the organization. Its key takeaway is that successful AI adoption depends on fixing the underlying data and access foundations.

The same principle appears in the context of governance for AI outputs. The episode "Microsoft Work IQ: The Intelligence Layer for Microsoft 365" says that the platform integrates existing permissions, sensitivity labels and data-loss prevention policies, so AI outputs follow the organization's rules and information stays protected. In that description, sensitivity labels are one of the existing controls that governance builds on rather than a separate mechanism.

Taken together, the episodes treat sensitivity labels as a foundation for data protection in Microsoft 365 that depends on careful design, maintenance and automation. A small, well-defined label set, clear defaults, user communication and measurement of adoption are presented as the practical ingredients, while static or incomplete labeling is presented as a risk, especially once Copilot and other AI features act on organizational content.

sentiment-analysis.desc: Sentiment analysis estimates whether text or a conversation reads as positive, neutral or negative, giving agents and leaders a signal rather than a verdict.

faq.a: It estimates whether text or a conversation appears positive, neutral or negative. In customer service it is described as a signal for agents to listen more carefully, not a verdict.
faq.q: What does sentiment analysis do?

faq.a: The episode "Reduce Escalations with Sentiment Routing in Dynamics 365" describes sentiment analysis as a key component of natural language processing, which lets AI systems interpret human language and detect emotions such as frustration.
faq.q: How is sentiment analysis related to NLP?

faq.a: M365.FM episodes mention it in Dynamics 365 Customer Service, in Microsoft Fabric notebooks, in .NET 10 applications, and in executive leadership reporting.
faq.q: Where does sentiment analysis appear in the Microsoft ecosystem?

sentiment-analysis.long:
Sentiment analysis is a technique that estimates whether a piece of text or a conversation appears positive, neutral or negative. In customer service it works as a signal that tells an agent to listen more carefully, not as a verdict about what a customer feels or intends. M365.FM treats the concept across several episodes, covering customer support, executive reporting, data science notebooks and application development.

The approach rests on natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning. According to the episode "Reduce Escalations with Sentiment Routing in Dynamics 365", NLP lets AI systems understand and interpret human language, which is what makes it possible to detect customer emotions such as frustration. Sentiment analysis is described there as a key component of NLP that classifies customer sentiment as positive, negative or neutral. The episode adds that recent advances use deep learning models, including deep neural networks and transformer architectures such as BERT, which capture complex textual relationships and emotional subtleties better than traditional methods.

In customer service, the typical use is routing and prioritisation. The same episode connects sentiment detection to reducing escalations in Dynamics 365: when a conversation reads as negative or frustrated, it can be handled differently from one that reads as neutral. The episode "Dynamics 365 Customer Service - Simply Explained" lists sentiment analysis among the AI-powered customer insights in that product, alongside intelligent case routing, as part of how agent productivity and customer experiences are supported. The short description of the concept keeps the intended role modest: the output prompts attention from a human and does not replace judgement.

Sentiment analysis also appears in data and development work. In "Train AI Models with Microsoft Fabric Notebooks", the Sentiment Analysis function is presented as a way to understand the tone of text such as customer reviews or social media posts, for example to flag negative comments and respond quickly. The episode says this works out of the box in notebooks without complex code, and that built-in functions can be combined with custom pytorch models. The episode "Build AI Applications with .NET 10" mentions adding text generation and sentiment analysis to applications, for instance through the OpenAI API, and points to tutorials for adding sentiment analysis to ASP.NET Core apps.

A further use is leadership reporting. The episode "Sentiment Analysis for Executive Leadership Reporting" argues that traditional dashboards show data but not meaning, and that advanced sentiment analysis addresses this by capturing how people feel, what drives behaviour, and where risks or opportunities are emerging. In that framing, reporting shifts from static KPIs toward context, including why something is happening. The episode also advises reviewing dashboard metrics on a regular schedule so the data stays relevant and aligned with goals, and focusing on meaningful metrics instead of vanity metrics that look good but do not drive real business results.

Several decisions follow from these sources. Teams choose where the signal is used: as an alert for agents, as an input to routing rules, as a flag in a notebook workflow, or as a contextual layer in executive reporting. They also decide how much weight the result carries. Since the concept is described as an estimate, it fits best as one input among others, reviewed by people, and checked against the business questions that leadership actually needs answered.

separation-of-duties.desc: Separation of duties (segregation of duties, SoD) is an internal control principle requiring more than one person or identity to complete a sensitive task.

faq.a: Separation of duties, also called segregation of duties (SoD), is an internal control principle that requires more than one person or identity to complete a sensitive task, so no single actor can both perform and approve it.
faq.q: What is separation of duties?

faq.a: The episode "Agent Governance Explained- How IT Can Enable the AI Agent Revolution with Thomas Zou [Microsoft]" links it to lifecycle management, where every change to an AI agent goes through review, testing and approval to minimize risks from unauthorized changes.
faq.q: How does separation of duties apply to AI agents according to M365.FM?

faq.a: It appears in episodes on Microsoft Fabric data pipeline security, managed identities with access certification, and Microsoft Graph and PowerShell automation, where enforcing it is listed as a way to lower security risks.
faq.q: Where else do the M365.FM episodes mention separation of duties?

separation-of-duties.long:
Separation of duties, also called segregation of duties (SoD), is an internal control principle. It requires that more than one person or identity take part in completing a sensitive task, so that no single actor can both perform and approve the same action. The idea is to reduce the risk of error, misuse and unauthorized change by splitting responsibilities across different roles.

In practice, the principle is applied wherever a change or an access right could cause harm if one party controlled it end to end. A typical pattern is a workflow in which one party prepares or implements a change and another party reviews and approves it. The same logic applies to identities as well as people: a task that touches sensitive data or configuration is divided so that the identity doing the work is not the one granting or approving the permission to do it.

The M365.FM episodes that mention the concept treat it as one control among several in identity, automation and data platform governance. In "Agent Governance Explained- How IT Can Enable the AI Agent Revolution with Thomas Zou [Microsoft]", separation of duties is tied to the lifecycle management component of a governance framework for AI agents. The episode says that this component ensures every change to an AI agent goes through a review, testing and approval process, and that this controlled approach minimizes risks associated with unauthorized changes. The same framework lists risk management, described as a defense-in-depth strategy, as a separate component.

In the context of data platforms, "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" connects separation of duties to workload isolation. The episode describes a graded approach: for moderate isolation, use one workspace per data product, and for high isolation, use multiple workspaces and enforce strict separation of duties. It also recommends consolidating data products only when necessary and isolating sensitive workloads to reduce risk. The same episode covers managed identities for authentication, which removes the need for hard-coded credentials.

The episode "Managed Identities - Simply Explained" places separation of duties inside identity governance. It suggests adopting Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) solutions to gain visibility into user access and help prevent unauthorized access, and says that regular access rights certification together with Separation of Duties (SoD) policies can further enhance security in an Azure environment.

Two episodes on automation, "Microsoft Graph Automation Architecture: Beyond Scripts" and "Microsoft Graph and PowerShell for Enterprise Automation", give a similar set of practices for automated identity workflows. They recommend documenting every automated identity workflow, including ownership, approval paths and rollback procedures, and testing changes in a limited scope before rolling them out across a tenant. Enforcing separation of duties is listed alongside these practices, and the episodes say it lowers security risks. They also recommend configuration-driven, parameterized scripts to keep automation flexible.

Across these sources the common thread is that separation of duties works as a design decision rather than a single feature: roles for building, approving and operating are kept distinct, approval paths are documented, and sensitive workloads are isolated. Decisions around the principle usually concern how finely to split responsibilities, how much isolation a workload needs, and how access is reviewed over time. The episodes treat it as a way to limit the impact of mistakes and unauthorized changes in AI agent, identity, automation and data pipeline scenarios.

server-message-block.desc: Server Message Block (SMB) is the standard Windows network file sharing protocol, supported by Azure Files, with data-in-transit encryption from SMB 3.0 onward.

faq.a: Server Message Block (SMB) is the standard Windows network file sharing protocol. It lets clients access files and shares on remote systems over a network.
faq.q: What is Server Message Block (SMB)?

faq.a: Yes. Azure Files supports SMB, so Azure-hosted file shares can be accessed using the same protocol commonly used for Windows network shares.
faq.q: Does Azure Files support SMB?

faq.a: SMB 3.0 and higher encrypt data in transit. Earlier versions of the protocol do not offer this encryption.
faq.q: Does SMB encrypt data in transit?

server-message-block.long:
Server Message Block (SMB) is a network protocol used for file sharing between computers. It is the standard file sharing protocol in Windows environments, allowing clients to access files and shares hosted on remote systems over a network.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, SMB is relevant for cloud-based file storage as well as traditional on-premises file servers. Azure Files supports SMB, so file shares hosted in Azure can be accessed using the same protocol that Windows clients already use for network shares.

Security is a key consideration when working with SMB. Versions 3.0 and higher of the protocol encrypt data in transit, which protects file traffic as it moves across the network. The protocol version in use therefore affects whether data transfer is encrypted.

SMB is tracked as a concept in the M365.FM knowledge base. No specific episodes or additional relations are linked to this entry at present.

serverless-computing.desc: Serverless computing is a cloud model where the provider runs and scales the servers while customers supply code that runs on events and pay per use.

faq.a: No. The episode "Serverless Computing - Simply Explained" notes that computing without servers does not exist. The term means the provider runs and scales the servers, so the customer does not rent or manage machines that sit mostly unused.
faq.q: Does serverless computing mean there are no servers?

faq.a: Billing is based on the executions and resources actually used rather than on idle machines. The episode "Azure Functions - Simply Explained" says Azure Functions consumes resources only while the code is running.
faq.q: How is serverless computing billed?

faq.a: Code runs in response to events. The "Azure Functions - Simply Explained" episode names examples such as a file uploaded to Azure Storage, an HTTP request, a timer, or a message arriving in Azure Service Bus.
faq.q: What triggers serverless code to run?

serverless-computing.long:
Serverless computing is a cloud execution model in which the cloud provider runs and scales the servers, while the customer supplies only code or workflows that run in response to events. Billing follows the executions and resources actually used rather than the time a machine sits idle. The name is widely seen as misleading: servers still exist, but they are no longer something the customer rents, patches or sizes. The M365.FM episode "Serverless Computing - Simply Explained" opens on exactly this point, describing the word "serverless" as one that trips up almost everyone, while the idea behind it is more useful than the label suggests.

The central purpose is to stop paying for machines that are barely used. In a traditional setup, a virtual machine or server is provisioned for a workload and costs money whether it is busy or not. In a serverless model, code runs only when something triggers it, and resources are consumed only while that code executes. The episode covers how serverless decides when to run and what it costs, which are the two questions that usually matter most when comparing it with always-on infrastructure.

Event-driven design is the core mechanism. According to the episode "Azure Functions - Simply Explained", typical triggers include a file being uploaded to Azure Storage, an HTTP request being received, a timer firing, or a message arriving in Azure Service Bus. In each case Azure Functions responds immediately and consumes resources only while the code is running. The episode explains how Azure Functions fit into modern cloud architectures and why they are a key building block for event-driven applications. It also covers triggers and bindings, the different hosting plans, and automatic scaling, which lets an application handle anything from a few requests per day to millions of executions without manual intervention.

Serverless does not remove architectural decisions, and networking is one example. The episode "Secure Azure Networking with Rex de Koning [MVP-MCT]" discusses how Virtual Network integration, private endpoints and network isolation allow serverless workloads to reach private resources without exposing services to the public internet. It also looks at the networking options available for Azure Functions across different hosting plans and the architectural reasoning behind them. This shows that the flexibility of serverless computing can be combined with the protection of sensitive workloads, a combination the episode describes as increasingly essential for secure cloud-native applications.

Choosing between execution options is another recurring theme. The episode "Copilot Studio Code Interpreter vs Azure Functions" contrasts the Code Interpreter in Copilot Studio with Azure Functions, which it presents as the more mature runtime: scalable, governed and auditable. It frames the discussion around functionality, use cases, performance and cost, and around how to move from a prototype to production without causing problems in a tenant. For anyone evaluating where code should run, the episode treats serverless computing as one of the factors to weigh against the needs of the project.

Serverless also sits within a longer history of platform shifts. In the episode "How AI Changed Software Development Forever — Building the Agentic Future with Andre Baltieri [MVP]", the progression from desktop to web, mobile, cloud, containers, microservices and serverless computing is described as the path software development has taken, before the guest argues that the move to AI feels fundamentally different because it changes how humans interact with software rather than simply introducing another platform or framework.

In practice, serverless computing suits workloads that are triggered by discrete events, vary widely in volume, or do not need a server running continuously. The decisions around it typically concern which trigger starts the code, which hosting plan to use, how the workload scales, how it connects securely to private resources, and how its costs compare with idle capacity. The M365.FM episodes listed here approach these questions from a plain-language introduction, a specific Azure service, a networking perspective and a comparison with another execution option.

service-account.desc: A service account is a shared non-human account that runs automation under one set of credentials; for AI agents it lacks attribution, ownership and lifecycle control.

faq.a: A service account is a shared non-human account used to run automation under one set of credentials. It lets scripts, connectors or services sign in without a person present, but it is still a user-style identity.
faq.q: What is a service account?

faq.a: According to the episode "AI Agent Identity Security: Beyond Service Accounts", a shared service account lacks per-agent attribution, ownership, lifecycle and policy enforcement. Dedicated agent identities are recommended instead.
faq.q: Why are service accounts a problem for AI agents?

faq.a: The episode "Replace Service Accounts with Entra Workload Identities" compares service accounts with managed identities and workload identities. Workload identities use secretless or short-lived credentials, have an owner and reviews, and provide a centralized sign-in and entitlement trail.
faq.q: What can replace a service account?

service-account.long:
A service account is a shared, non-human account used to run automation under a single set of credentials. Scripts, integrations, connectors and background services sign in with it so that they can reach data or systems without a person present. It is a long-standing pattern in many environments, and it appears in several M365.FM episodes as both a practical building block and a source of governance risk.

In day-to-day Microsoft work, service accounts show up in many places. The episode "Troubleshoot the Power BI On-Premises Data Gateway" refers to the gateway service account (PBIEgwService), which needs read permission on a folder so that data refreshes succeed, and recommends updating the stored credentials in the gateway settings after a password change to avoid refresh failures. The episode "How to Run Local Llama on SharePoint Files Securely" lists a permission-denied error as a typical problem and advises reviewing SharePoint permissions to confirm that the service account has the right access. In these cases the service account is a pragmatic way to give a technical component a stable identity.

The episodes also describe why the pattern is fragile. "Service Accounts vs App Registrations for Power Automate Email" points out that a service account is still a user. Delegated authentication, MFA prompts, password expiry and Conditional Access changes are all designed for humans, and they sit in front of a flow that has no human to respond. The episode describes such setups as brittle, over-privileged and hard to audit cleanly, and says that a change to Conditional Access or a password policy can make a flow fail loudly or, worse, half-silently.

The governance side is covered in "AI Agent Identity Security: Beyond Service Accounts". According to the episode, service account security risks often go unnoticed because traditional systems lack proper oversight. Service accounts may be created automatically by developers without a centralized tracking system, each cloud platform handles identity management differently, and visibility suffers when no manager is assigned to each account. The episode connects this to what it calls Shadow Agents, and argues that AI agents bring challenges that legacy identity and authorization models cannot handle. For AI agents, the core gaps are the lack of per-agent attribution, ownership, lifecycle and policy enforcement, which is why dedicated agent identities are recommended instead of a shared service account.

The alternative is laid out in "Replace Service Accounts with Entra Workload Identities". Its comparison matrix contrasts the three approaches. A service account relies on static passwords, has broad or user-like scope, rarely has Conditional Access or risk policies applied, follows an ad hoc lifecycle and leaves sparse audit data. A managed identity is secretless within Azure, has an Azure-centric scope and offers limited policy control and basic lifecycle handling, with audit coverage coming from Azure logs. A workload identity uses secretless or short-lived credentials with rotation, can cover any workload such as apps, scripts and connectors, is policy-driven where supported, has an owner with reviews and decommissioning, and provides a centralized sign-in and entitlement trail that supports audits. The episode also lists credential hygiene practices such as short-lived secrets, certificates and a key rotation policy, together with unified visibility into sign-ins, tokens, resource access and change history.

In practice, the decision around a service account comes down to what the account runs and who is accountable for it. Where a component such as a gateway or a local indexing process needs a technical identity, the episodes stress correct permissions and careful credential handling, for example using environment variables rather than plain text. Where the account supports automation that touches Microsoft 365 data or acts on behalf of AI agents, the episodes recommend moving to app registrations, managed identities, Entra workload identities or dedicated agent identities, so that each workload has its own attributable identity, a named owner, reviews and a decommissioning path.

service-catalog.desc: A service catalog is a central record of the software services an organization runs, listing each service's owner, documentation, dependencies, status and support links.

faq.a: A service catalog is a central record of the services an organization runs. For software services it shows each service's owner, documentation, dependencies, status and support links, so teams can quickly see what exists and who is responsible.
faq.q: What is a service catalog?

faq.a: Entries typically include a named accountable owner, a name or identifier, a description, a category and related services, access information, costs where relevant, how the service is requested and fulfilled, and escalation points and key contacts. In developer settings, source code, dashboards and operational status are also listed.
faq.q: What does a service catalog entry usually contain?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode "Internal Developer Platforms (IDPs) - Simply Explained" describes the service catalog as the central map of running software within an internal developer platform, alongside golden paths that let developers provide only key details while the platform handles the setup.
faq.q: How does a service catalog relate to an internal developer platform?

service-catalog.long:
A service catalog is a central record of the services an organization runs. In the software context described on M365.FM, it acts as a map of running software and shows, for each service, who owns it, where its documentation and source code live, what it depends on, what its operational status is, and where to find dashboards and support information. The term is also used more broadly in IT and business settings, where a service catalog is a curated collection of services kept in a digital registry that doubles as a knowledge management tool.

The main purpose is visibility. As organizations accumulate hundreds or thousands of applications and services, understanding what exists becomes increasingly difficult. A service catalog helps developers and operations teams answer basic questions quickly, such as which team owns a given service, how it connects to other services, and whom to contact when something goes wrong. In the broader IT service management sense, a catalog also centralizes services so that distributed parts of an organization use the same ones instead of duplicate local versions, and it can reveal gaps and redundancies.

A typical catalog entry carries a defined set of attributes. According to general descriptions of the concept, an entry usually has a named accountable owner, a name or identifier, a description, a category, related request types and supporting services, information on who may request or view it, any costs, how it is requested and fulfilled, and escalation points and key contacts. Services in such a catalog are typically repeatable, with controlled inputs, outputs and procedures. Some implementations also track demand metrics such as the most and least used services, approval and delivery times, and spending.

Users usually search or browse the catalog by category, review the details of a service, submit a request and follow its status. Under ITIL, an IT service catalogue is the published part of the service portfolio, and cloud service catalogues often work as self-service portals with standardized definitions. These descriptions focus on business and IT services and requests; a developer-oriented catalog of software components is a related but distinct framing, and the two should not be assumed to be identical.

The M365.FM episode "Internal Developer Platforms (IDPs) - Simply Explained" presents the service catalog as one building block of an internal developer platform. It appears alongside golden paths, where developers supply only the information that matters, such as the service name, owner, environment, runtime and approved options, while the platform handles the underlying setup. In that context the catalog provides the central map of what is running, including ownership, documentation, dependencies, source code, operational status, dashboards and support information.

The episode "High-Performance Azure Cloud Governance to Reduce Waste" uses the term in a governance sense. It lists a cloud service catalog as one governance strategy, described as a list of approved services that standardizes consumption and mitigates risks. It appears next to a cloud governance framework, cloud service management, cloud security, cloud cost management and cloud compliance. Here the catalog functions less as a map of existing software and more as a controlled set of approved offerings that guides how cloud services are consumed.

When deciding how to use a service catalog, the main considerations are which meaning applies and what the entries must contain. A catalog meant to document running software needs reliable ownership, dependency and status information, while a catalog meant to govern consumption needs a clear definition of approved services and who may request them. In both cases the value depends on entries having a named owner and staying current, since a record that is incomplete or outdated cannot answer the ownership and support questions it exists to address.

service-mesh.desc: A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that manages service-to-service traffic, mTLS and policy enforcement in distributed applications, often using sidecar proxies.

faq.a: A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that manages service-to-service traffic, mTLS and policy enforcement in distributed applications. It is often based on sidecar proxies.
faq.q: What is a service mesh?

faq.a: Istio and Linkerd are named as examples of technologies on which a service mesh is often based, using sidecar proxies.
faq.q: Which technologies are associated with a service mesh?

faq.a: It manages traffic between services, mutual TLS (mTLS) and policy enforcement within distributed applications.
faq.q: What does a service mesh manage?

service-mesh.long:
A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that manages communication between services in a distributed application. It is often built on sidecar proxies, with Istio and Linkerd being commonly cited examples of such implementations.

The layer is used to handle service-to-service traffic, mutual TLS (mTLS) between services, and the enforcement of policies. By placing these responsibilities in the infrastructure rather than in each application, the approach separates networking and security concerns from application code.

The concept applies to distributed architectures in which many services communicate with one another, such as microservice-based systems. In these environments, traffic management, encryption between services and consistent policy enforcement are recurring requirements, and a service mesh is one way to address them.

No related topics or episodes are currently linked to this entry on M365.FM.

service-principal.desc: A service principal is the identity an application uses to sign in within a Microsoft Entra tenant, and agent identities are built as a special kind of it.

faq.a: A service principal is the identity an application uses to sign in within a Microsoft Entra tenant. Agent identities are built as a special kind of service principal.
faq.q: What is a service principal in Microsoft Entra?

faq.a: The episode "Service Principal Security: Stop Using Personal Accounts" describes enterprise workflows tethered to personal user accounts as a hidden risk. "Build App-Only Microsoft Graph Integrations" adds that delegated, user-tied automations can break through session timeouts, MFA prompts and role changes.
faq.q: Why do the episodes advise against using personal accounts for automation?

faq.a: According to "Microsoft Graph Permissions and Consent Models Explained", scopes and roles are represented in the app registration and in the service principal in each tenant. Roles are used for application permissions when an app runs without a user context.
faq.q: How does a service principal relate to an app registration and Graph permissions?

service-principal.long:
A service principal is the identity that an application uses to sign in within a Microsoft Entra tenant. Instead of a person signing in with a username and password, the application authenticates as its own identity and receives access according to the permissions assigned to it. In the Microsoft Entra model described in the M365.FM material, agent identities are built as a special kind of service principal, which places the concept at the center of how automation and AI agents are represented in a tenant.

The service principal is closely tied to the app registration. The episode "Microsoft Graph Permissions and Consent Models Explained" says that scopes and roles are part of the Microsoft identity platform model and are represented in the app registration and in the service principal in each tenant. Scopes apply to delegated access, where an app acts on behalf of a signed-in user, while roles are used for application permissions and map to what an app can do when running without a user context. The same episode describes registering an application under App registrations in Microsoft Entra ID and then adding required Microsoft Graph permissions, choosing between delegated and application permissions.

A common use of a service principal is unattended, app-only automation. The episode "Build App-Only Microsoft Graph Integrations" argues that automations built on delegated permissions tied to human users tend to break at scale because of session timeouts, MFA prompts and role changes. It recommends shifting to app-only permissions with Microsoft Graph, so that jobs run headless through a service principal with least-privilege access and an audit trail, without an interactive login or an expiring session. The setup it outlines covers app registration, Application permissions, admin consent and storing secrets in Key Vault, and it extends the pattern with Graph webhooks for real-time workflows across SharePoint, Teams and Outlook.

The security side of this topic is the focus of the episode "Service Principal Security: Stop Using Personal Accounts". It describes a hidden risk in Microsoft 365 automation: enterprise workflows that run on borrowed identity, tied to personal user accounts. The typical scenario it gives is an engineer who builds a Power Automate flow or connects a Logic App using their own account, so the workflow depends on that person's identity. Moving such workloads to a service principal separates the automation from any individual's account and from changes to that person's access.

Service principals also appear as managed identities in other Microsoft services. The episode "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" explains that a Fabric workspace identity acts as a managed service principal, so credentials do not need to be stored in pipelines. According to the episode, this reduces the risk of leaking sensitive information, and it sits alongside Microsoft Entra ID authentication with access tokens and Conditional Access policies.

The identifier of a service principal is also needed in integration work. In "Microsoft Graph Connectors - Simply Explained", the first implementation step is to get the service principal object ID, using PowerShell or the Microsoft Graph API, because that ID is required for authentication when configuring an OIDC provider for a connector such as one for ServiceNow.

Taken together, the episodes treat the service principal as the preferred identity for non-interactive workloads: it is registered per application, receives explicit permissions or roles, can be granted least-privilege access, and does not depend on a person's account, password or MFA state.

servicenow.desc: ServiceNow is a software company whose cloud platform is widely used for IT service management and ticketing, and it appears often in Microsoft 365 integration scenarios.

faq.a: ServiceNow is a software company whose cloud platform is widely used for IT service management and ticketing. The M365.FM episode "ServiceNow and Microsoft 365: From Intent to Business Action" argues that ticketing was only the entry point and that the platform serves a broader role in turning requests into tracked business action.
faq.q: What is ServiceNow?

faq.a: The episodes describe several routes: Microsoft Graph Connectors that index external sources and apply security trimming, and custom connectors that bring data from systems such as ServiceNow into Microsoft Graph. The episode "Connect Microsoft Copilot to Salesforce, ServiceNow, and APIs" stresses identity, least-privilege access and audit trails.
faq.q: How can ServiceNow data be made available to Microsoft 365 Copilot?

faq.a: Yes. The episode "Build Enterprise Automation with Azure Logic Apps" lists ServiceNow among third-party systems that Logic Apps can connect to Microsoft 365 and the Power Platform, and it discusses when to choose Logic Apps versus Power Automate.
faq.q: Can ServiceNow be automated together with Microsoft 365 services?

servicenow.long:
ServiceNow is a software company whose cloud platform is widely used for IT service management and ticketing. In the M365.FM knowledge base it appears mainly as a business system that organizations connect to the Microsoft ecosystem, rather than as a Microsoft product. The episodes that mention it treat ServiceNow as one of several third-party platforms, alongside Salesforce, SAP, Jira and Confluence, whose data and processes sit outside Microsoft 365 but matter to everyday work.

The episode "ServiceNow and Microsoft 365: From Intent to Business Action" (January 2026) challenges the common view of ServiceNow as only a ticketing system. According to the episode, ticketing was the entry point, not the destination. It argues that the real enterprise problem is not tool sprawl but that work has no single authoritative state, no durable ownership, and no enforceable path from "someone asked" to "it's done". The episode describes enterprises as digitally rich, with many platforms, apps and automations, yet operationally fragmented because they lack a true operating layer. It then lays out an architectural model that explains where Microsoft is the place where intent is expressed and how that intent can be turned into tracked business action.

A second recurring theme is making external systems visible to Microsoft Copilot. The episode "Connect Microsoft Copilot to Salesforce, ServiceNow, and APIs" (December 2025) states that out of the box, Microsoft 365 Copilot only sees surface-level data such as emails, chats and documents. It does not see systems such as a Salesforce pipeline, ServiceNow incidents or proprietary APIs unless they are connected. The episode covers how Copilot sees data, why this is often misunderstood, and the difference between demonstration-style AI and production-ready setups, with attention to identity, least-privilege access and full audit trails.

The episode "Microsoft Graph Connectors - Simply Explained" (July 2026), presented by Mirko Peters, names ServiceNow among the third-party sources that organizations can index through Microsoft Graph Connectors. As described there, Graph Connectors crawl external data sources, create searchable indexes and apply security trimming, so that the content can surface in Microsoft Search, Microsoft Copilot and other Microsoft 365 experiences. This means ServiceNow records can become part of the same search and Copilot experience as Microsoft 365 content, rather than staying inside a separate portal.

Automation is the third angle. In "Build Enterprise Automation with Azure Logic Apps" (November 2025), ServiceNow is listed with SAP, Salesforce and custom APIs as a third-party system that Azure Logic Apps can link to Microsoft 365 and the Power Platform. The episode frames Logic Apps as an enterprise-grade automation layer and discusses when to use it instead of Power Automate, including triggers, actions, connectors, error handling, governance and monitoring.

The episode "Use Power Automate to Increase Microsoft Copilot ROI" (November 2025) mentions ServiceNow in the context of custom connectors. It describes integrating data from external systems such as Salesforce, ServiceNow and Jira into Microsoft Graph to broaden the data Copilot can draw on. The steps it outlines include defining a schema for the custom connector, registering the connection in Microsoft Entra ID, and writing code to pull and push data.

Taken together, the episodes position ServiceNow as a system of record for service and workflow data that organizations typically want to reach from Microsoft 365. The decisions they discuss are which integration path to use (Graph Connectors for search and Copilot grounding, Logic Apps or Power Automate for workflow automation, custom connectors for bespoke data), and how to keep identity, access control and auditing intact when external data is exposed to Copilot.

session-border-controller.desc: A session border controller (SBC) sits at the edge of a SIP voice network to translate signaling, handle media and protect calls; Teams Direct Routing requires a certified one.

faq.a: It is a customer-provided, Microsoft-certified device that connects an organization's own telephony infrastructure to Microsoft Teams Phone over SIP with TLS. It lets organizations use existing PSTN carriers and third-party telephony systems.
faq.q: What is a session border controller in Teams Direct Routing?

faq.a: A Microsoft-certified controller, at least one PSTN trunk, a publicly reachable IP address, an FQDN in a verified tenant domain with a public DNS record, and a public trusted certificate. Firewall rules must also allow the Teams IP ranges.
faq.q: What is needed to deploy an SBC for Direct Routing?

faq.a: Direct Routing connects Teams to the PSTN through the organization's own SBC, offering high flexibility. Operator Connect lets certified providers connect directly to Teams, which simplifies the setup.
faq.q: How does an SBC differ between Direct Routing and Operator Connect?

session-border-controller.long:
A session border controller (SBC) is a network element at the edge of a SIP-based voice network. It translates signaling, handles media and protects the voice path between an organization's own telephony environment and an external network. In the Microsoft ecosystem the term is most often met in connection with Microsoft Teams Phone, where a certified SBC is a requirement for Direct Routing.

In Teams Direct Routing, the session border controller is a customer-provided, supported device. It links the organization's own telephony infrastructure to Microsoft Teams Phone. Because of this, organizations can keep using existing PSTN carriers, integrate third-party telephony systems and retain more control over their voice infrastructure. Typical scenarios named in Microsoft's planning guidance are PSTN carriers, third-party PBXs, analog devices and contact centers.

The connection works over SIP with TLS between the SBC and the Microsoft SIP proxy. Microsoft provides primary, secondary and tertiary connection points, with automatic failover between them. Media normally flows through Microsoft media processors; media bypass is treated as a separate planning option. The device may also prioritize or restrict codecs such as SILK, G.711, G.722 and G.729, which is part of how an SBC shapes the voice path.

Several prerequisites apply before an SBC can be used with Direct Routing. The controller must be certified by Microsoft, and at least one PSTN trunk is needed. The SBC requires a publicly reachable IP address and a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) in a verified domain of the Microsoft 365 tenant, with a public DNS record. A public trusted certificate is also required, and firewall rules must allow the Teams IP ranges. These items are the usual checklist when planning a deployment.

Support boundaries matter in practice. Microsoft may decline support for devices that are not certified, and support requests go first through the device vendor. Another stated limit is that media cannot be re-targeted during an active call. These points influence both the choice of device and how operational responsibilities are divided between the organization, the SBC vendor and Microsoft.

The SBC is also the main point of difference between the PSTN connectivity options for Teams. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Teams Phone and Telephony | Simply Explained" describes Direct Routing as connecting Microsoft Teams to the PSTN through the organization's own Session Border Controller, which gives high flexibility and allows the telephony setup to be customized. It contrasts this with Operator Connect, where certified providers connect directly to Microsoft Teams and the process is simplified, so no customer-managed SBC is involved. The choice therefore depends on whether an organization wants to use its existing telephony infrastructure or preferred providers with maximum flexibility, or prefers a simpler provider-led connection.

shadow-ai.desc: Shadow AI refers to AI tools and agents that employees install or sign up for on their own, running outside the view and control of the IT team.

faq.a: Shadow AI means AI tools and agents that employees install or sign up for on their own, running outside the view and control of the IT team. Because they bypass normal oversight, they can create data leaks and compliance issues.
faq.q: What is Shadow AI?

faq.a: The episode on shadow data discovery with Microsoft Purview lists unsanctioned SaaS and shadow AI tools as a common source of shadow data, because these tools can store information in unauthorized cloud services.
faq.q: How does Shadow AI relate to shadow data?

faq.a: The episodes recommend updating governance policies, educating employees on safe AI usage, enhancing visibility with monitoring tools that track AI agent activity, and offering a sanctioned option such as Private LoRA on a secure platform.
faq.q: What do the M365.FM episodes recommend against Shadow AI?

shadow-ai.long:
Shadow AI is the use of AI tools and agents that employees install or sign up for on their own, without the knowledge or approval of the IT team. Because these tools run outside the view and control of IT, they are not covered by the security, compliance and governance measures an organization applies to sanctioned software. The term is closely related to shadow IT, and the M365.FM episode "Secure AI Agents and Shadow IT in Microsoft 365" treats the two together, noting that employees may turn to unauthorized tools such as ChatGPT and that this raises concerns about shadow IT and data security.

The main concern around shadow AI is data. When people paste documents, customer information or internal knowledge into an unsanctioned AI service, that data can leave the controlled environment and end up in cloud services that the organization has not reviewed. The episode "Shadow Data Discovery and Governance with Microsoft Purview" lists unsanctioned SaaS and shadow AI tools as one of the common sources of shadow data, alongside test or development databases and personal devices with mobile or cloud sync leaks. In that framing, shadow AI is one route by which information escapes formal oversight and grows unnoticed until a problem occurs.

The episodes also attach figures to the risk. The episode "AI Upskilling Strategy for Measurable Business ROI" states that unsanctioned AI tools often bypass security and governance controls and cites a data breach cost of $4.63 million per incident for shadow AI, compared with $3.96 million for standard breaches. It further says that shadow AI accounts for 20% of all data breaches, with detection taking up to 247 days and remediation lasting 94 days. These numbers are attributed to that episode and are presented there as a reason shadow AI can undermine the return on AI investments.

In regulated sectors the issue is framed as one of accountability. The episode "Automated Red Teaming for Multi-Model AI in Finance" says shadow AI poses significant risks and that organizations must identify and manage unauthorized AI tools. It also recommends establishing clear ownership and traceability for AI decisions to improve accountability and compliance, and adopting a proactive, multi-layered defense strategy for financial systems. The same episode points to automated red teaming and continuous monitoring as ways to detect threats in real time across multi-model AI environments.

The episodes describe several practical responses. "Secure AI Agents and Shadow IT in Microsoft 365" lists three takeaways: understand that unsanctioned AI tools can lead to data leaks and compliance issues, update governance policies regularly to address emerging risks, and educate employees on safe AI usage. It also recommends enhancing visibility with monitoring tools that track AI agent activities and identify potential problems. These measures combine policy, training and technical oversight rather than relying on a single control.

Another approach discussed is giving employees a sanctioned alternative. The episode "Private LoRA for Secure AI on Proprietary Enterprise Data" argues that using Private LoRA reduces the risk of shadow AI and helps safeguard data. It describes the Azure AI platform as providing enterprise-grade security that adheres to privacy, security and compliance standards, and integration with OpenAI models that keeps sensitive data protected and not used for training foundational AI models. The same episode notes that regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act and ISO/IEC 42001 now call for organizations to demonstrate accountability and risk control in their AI systems, which makes unmanaged AI usage harder to justify.

Taken together, the M365.FM material presents shadow AI as a governance and visibility problem more than a purely technical one. The typical decisions concern which AI tools are approved, how data is classified and protected, how agent activity is monitored, and how staff are trained to use sanctioned options. Related topics that appear in the episodes include shadow IT, shadow data discovery with Microsoft Purview, AI agent security in Microsoft 365, red teaming and AI regulation.

shadow-automation.desc: Shadow automation is automation that runs without explicit ownership or oversight, such as flows on personal connections that outlive their purpose.

faq.a: Shadow automation is automation that runs without explicit ownership or oversight. An example is a flow on a personal connection that keeps running after its original purpose has passed.
faq.q: What is shadow automation?

faq.a: Shadow IT typically refers to unsanctioned tools or services. Shadow automation executes actions, such as moving data or changing records, which gives it a more direct effect on business information.
faq.q: How does shadow automation differ from shadow IT?

shadow-automation.long:
Shadow automation refers to automated processes that operate without clear ownership or oversight. A typical example is a flow built on a personal connection that continues to run after the purpose it was created for has ended. Because no one is accountable for it, such automation can persist unnoticed.

The term is often compared with shadow IT. The difference lies in what the technology does. Shadow IT usually describes tools or services used outside official channels, while shadow automation actively executes actions, for example moving data or changing records. This makes the lack of ownership more consequential, since the automation continues to act on live information rather than simply existing as an unsanctioned tool.

The concept is used to describe governance gaps around automated workflows: who owns a flow, whose credentials it relies on, and whether it is still needed. Identifying and assigning ownership to such automation is a common theme when discussing oversight of automated processes in the Microsoft ecosystem.

No related topics or M365.FM episodes are linked to this entry at present, and no official documentation links are provided.

shadow-data.desc: Shadow data is unknown or overlooked copies of sensitive information that sit outside an organization's IT security and governance frameworks.

faq.a: Shadow data is any unknown, hidden or overlooked copy of sensitive information that exists outside an organization's IT security and governance frameworks, such as forgotten storage accounts, personal drives or AI training data sets.
faq.q: What is shadow data?

faq.a: The episode "Shadow Data Discovery and Governance with Microsoft Purview" says that assuming Purview cannot see what does not exist creates a dangerous blind spot. Data outside governed sources often has no label, retention policy or audit trace.
faq.q: Why is shadow data a governance risk?

faq.a: According to the episode "Fix Copilot Notebooks GDPR and Governance Risks", AI-generated summaries and similar outputs contain fragments of sensitive sources but inherit none of the original label, retention policy or audit trace, forming a "Shadow Data Lake".
faq.q: How can AI tools create shadow data?

shadow-data.long:
Shadow data is any unknown, hidden or overlooked copy of sensitive information that exists outside an organization's IT security and governance frameworks. Typical examples are forgotten storage accounts, personal drives and AI training data sets. Because these copies are not tracked, they usually carry no sensitivity label, retention policy or audit trail, and security and compliance teams may not know they exist.

The concept matters because governance tooling can only protect what it can see. The M365.FM episode "Shadow Data Discovery and Governance with Microsoft Purview" addresses this directly. It explains that Microsoft Purview provides strong visibility into governed data sources, but that many organizations assume that what Purview cannot see does not exist. According to the episode, that assumption creates a dangerous blind spot and makes shadow data one of the biggest hidden risks in modern data governance. The practical decision for governance teams is therefore not only how to classify and protect known data, but how to discover data that sits outside the governed estate in the first place.

Shadow data can arise in several ways. One path is spreadsheets and ad hoc files. The episode "Fix Excel Shadow Systems and Broken Business Processes" describes reliance on Excel and spreadsheets as creating shadow data, key person dependency and static information, alongside data integrity issues and information silos. It argues that governance, visibility and automation are needed to protect operations, and it recommends assessing process architecture and moving to modern solutions rather than leaving critical business logic in uncontrolled files.

Another path is AI-generated content. The episode "Fix Copilot Notebooks GDPR and Governance Risks" describes how outputs such as summaries, paragraphs and bullet lists are derived content that contains fragments of sensitive sources but inherits none of the original sensitivity label, retention policy, audit trace or Purview detection scope. The episode calls the result a "Shadow Data Lake": a large body of unlabeled, untraceable derivative insight. Its stated core problem is not the Microsoft security model itself but the fact that governance frameworks assume lineage, while AI output does not generate lineage.

The remedies discussed in that episode follow from this diagnosis. They include treating AI output as first-class content, labeling it by default, applying derived data policies, time-boxing notebook containers, limiting sharing and making AI summaries review-gated. The underlying idea is that productivity gains from AI should not come at the cost of unmanaged copies of sensitive information.

Shadow data is closely tied to Microsoft Purview, which the episodes treat as the main tool for visibility, classification and governance in the Microsoft ecosystem. The overview episode "Microsoft Purview - Simply Explained" lists the shadow data episode among related listening, alongside episodes on Purview for Copilot security, AI security, DLP, Insider Risk and real-time AI sensitivity labeling. The episode "Scaling CI-CD: The Governance Blueprint" also lists the shadow data episode among related governance topics, next to compliance as code and AI-powered metadata classification.

In summary, shadow data describes a visibility gap rather than a specific product. Addressing it combines discovery of unknown copies, consistent labeling and retention for derived content, and governance processes that cover spreadsheets, personal storage and AI-generated material, as discussed across the M365.FM episodes listed above.

shadow-it.desc: Shadow IT describes IT systems, services or tenants created by departments or employees without the knowledge or administration of central IT.

faq.a: Shadow IT refers to IT systems, services or tenants created by departments or employees without the knowledge or administration of central IT. Central IT therefore lacks visibility into these assets and their data.
faq.q: What is Shadow IT?

faq.a: According to the episode "Power Platform Governance Without Creating More Shadow IT", the platform itself is not the real risk; poor governance is. The episode notes that Shadow IT predates Power Platform through tools like Excel, Access and macros.
faq.q: Does Power Platform cause Shadow IT?

faq.a: The episode "Secure AI Agents and Shadow IT in Microsoft 365" describes AI agents, Copilot Studio bots and Power Automate flows as a new form of Shadow IT. It warns that agents running with human identities can move data faster than existing controls can see.
faq.q: How does Shadow IT relate to AI agents?

shadow-it.long:
Shadow IT is the term for IT systems, services or tenants that departments or individual employees create and use without the knowledge or administration of central IT. Because these assets sit outside normal oversight, central IT cannot see what data they hold, who has access to them, or how they are secured. In the Microsoft ecosystem, the topic appears in several forms: unsanctioned apps registered in a Microsoft 365 tenant, bots and connectors added by users or guests, flows and apps built with low-code tools, and, more recently, AI agents.

The M365.FM episode "Power Platform Governance Without Creating More Shadow IT" points out that Shadow IT existed long before Power Platform, through tools such as Excel, Access and macros. The episode argues that Power Platform itself is not the real risk; poor governance is. In its view, low-code tools make this type of development faster and more visible, which means they reveal whether an organization is capable of governing what people build. The main takeaway of that episode is that governance has to be established before capabilities are scaled, including AI capabilities.

The episode "Power Platform Governance: From Shadow IT to Secure Scale" challenges the assumption that anything from Microsoft is automatically secure. It states that Power Platform is enterprise-grade secure by design but becomes risky once governance is missing, and that organizations tend to fail because of missing governance rather than because of vulnerabilities or attackers. This frames Shadow IT less as a technical flaw of a product and more as a gap in ownership, process and oversight.

A practical, detection-oriented view is offered in "Detect Shadow IT in Microsoft 365". The episode describes tenants that may contain unknown apps, risky OAuth scopes and connectors installed by guests, and it recommends exposing what is hiding in the logs using Microsoft-native tools. It also covers taming app consent through Conditional Access and approval workflows, with the stated aim of moving a tenant from unmanaged to well-governed without breaking productivity. The approach combines visibility first with controlled consent and approval, rather than blanket blocking.

Newer episodes extend the concept to AI. "Secure AI Agents and Shadow IT in Microsoft 365" describes Shadow IT as having evolved into AI agents that move data faster than controls can see. It names Copilot Studio bots and Power Automate flows as new sources of Shadow IT inside Microsoft 365, and warns that agents running with human identities create governance and security problems. The episode also cites figures, saying that 60% of organizations have AI agents in production, 94% view them as a strategic priority, and 75% of knowledge workers use AI at work, often through unauthorized tools such as ChatGPT.

The episode "Prevent Shadow IT in Microsoft Foundry AI Agent Programs" applies the same reasoning to Microsoft Foundry, which it describes as an agent factory rather than just another AI feature to approve and forget. It argues that if execution comes before governance, the next generation of Shadow IT is almost guaranteed, and that many future AI incidents will stem from autonomous agents rather than from models hallucinating answers. The common thread across the episodes is that accessibility and speed, which make these platforms attractive, are the same traits that allow unmanaged assets to spread when governance, visibility and approval processes are not in place first.

shared-access-signature.desc: A shared access signature (SAS) token is a time-limited cryptographic token derived from a secret tied to an identity, used for example by devices to authenticate to Azure IoT Hub.

faq.a: A SAS token is a cryptographic, time-limited token derived from a secret tied to an identity. It allows a holder to authenticate without directly sharing the secret.
faq.q: What is a shared access signature (SAS) token?

faq.a: Devices can use a SAS token to authenticate to Azure IoT Hub. The token is derived from a secret associated with the device's identity and is valid for a limited time.
faq.q: How are SAS tokens used with Azure IoT Hub?

shared-access-signature.long:
A shared access signature (SAS) token is a cryptographic, time-limited token that is derived from a secret associated with an identity. Because the token is generated from that secret rather than exposing it directly, a holder can present the token to prove authorization without handing over the underlying key.

One documented use is device authentication to Azure IoT Hub. In this scenario, a device uses a SAS token to authenticate itself to the service. The time-limited nature of the token means that access is granted only for a defined period, after which a new token must be produced from the secret.

The available facts for this entry are limited. No related topics, official documentation links or M365.FM episodes are currently associated with the term, so this page describes only the general concept and its use with Azure IoT Hub.

shared-channels.desc: Shared channels are Microsoft Teams channels that can include people from outside the team or tenant, with their own SharePoint site and separate membership.

faq.a: Shared channels are Teams channels that can include people from outside the team or tenant, for example through B2B direct connect. They have their own SharePoint site and their own membership.
faq.q: What are shared channels in Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: The episode "Teams Private Channels vs Shared Channels" says private channels can break workflows through a separate SharePoint site, limited apps and blocked guests, while shared channels suit cross-organization work.
faq.q: How do shared channels differ from private channels?

faq.a: According to "Organize Projects Properly in Microsoft Teams", admins enable cross-tenant settings, define allowed domains and apps, configure shared channels policies in the Teams Admin Center, and decide who can create channels and invite external users.
faq.q: What do admins need to configure for shared channels?

shared-channels.long:
Shared channels are a channel type in Microsoft Teams that allows collaboration with people who are not members of the parent team and, in some cases, not part of the same tenant. They are described as channels that can include external participants, for example through B2B direct connect, and they come with their own SharePoint site and their own membership list. This sets them apart from standard channels, which follow the membership of the team, and from private channels, which restrict visibility to invited team members.

The main purpose of shared channels is cross-team and cross-organization work. The episode "Design a Microsoft Teams Structure That Actually Works" says shared channels break down barriers between teams: colleagues from different teams can work together without leaving their own workspace, sharing information, documents and conversations. The episode "Microsoft Teams Hidden Features with Josh Blalock [MVP]" makes a similar point for external partners, noting that the feature allows communication without switching apps.

A key design decision is choosing between a private channel, a shared channel and a separate team. The episode "Teams Private Channels vs Shared Channels" offers a decision framework for this. It describes where private channels can quietly break workflows. Examples it lists include a separate SharePoint site that leads to different retention, eDiscovery, labels and automation endpoints, limited apps and tabs where some bots, flows and Power BI scenarios fail, and guest restrictions, since private channel users must be in the tenant and guests are often blocked. According to the episode, shared channels are the better fit for cross-organization work, while certain edge cases still call for a separate team.

The episode "Microsoft Teams Channels vs Chat: When to Use Each" places shared channels alongside standard and private channels. It covers how naming and descriptions affect collaboration, why files should be organized inside each channel, and what administrators should know about permissions, access issues and deletion. This framing treats the shared channel as one of three channel types, each with its own membership and access behavior.

Administration is covered in "Organize Projects Properly in Microsoft Teams". For secure external collaboration it recommends enabling cross-tenant settings for inbound and outbound access, defining which domains and applications can be used, and configuring shared channels policies in the Teams Admin Center. Admins also decide who can create shared channels and who can invite external users. The episode adds role-based access control to assign permissions by job function, domain lists, multi-factor authentication and sensitivity labels to protect project data, plus monitoring of activity logs and alerts for unusual actions.

Because a shared channel has its own SharePoint site and membership, governance questions follow from that structure. Retention, labeling and eDiscovery are tied to the channel's own site rather than to the parent team's site, and membership has to be reviewed separately. The episodes consistently pair the feature with policy configuration and periodic review of who has access, especially when external users are involved.

In practice, shared channels fit situations such as joint projects with partner organizations or work spanning several internal teams. A team or tenant boundary no longer forces a separate chat tool or a new team for every collaboration, though the episodes stress that the choice should follow requirements for access, compliance and app support.

shared-mailbox.desc: A shared mailbox in Exchange Online is a mailbox that multiple users can access and send from, giving a team one consistent sender identity.

faq.a: A shared mailbox is a mailbox in Exchange Online that multiple users can access and send from. It works as a common address for a team rather than belonging to one person.
faq.q: What is a shared mailbox in Exchange Online?

faq.a: The episode "Build Internal Outlook Newsletters with Dynamic Groups" says a shared sender supports branding and continuity and builds trust, since readers see the same sender identity on every issue regardless of who prepares it.
faq.q: Why use a shared mailbox as the sender of an internal newsletter?

faq.a: The episode "Shared Data Reservoirs for Multi-Tenant Microsoft 365" suggests connecting to Exchange Online with PowerShell, generating audit reports for inactive or unused mailboxes, and checking the last logon timestamp for each shared mailbox to spot dormant accounts.
faq.q: How can inactive shared mailboxes be found?

shared-mailbox.long:
A shared mailbox is a mailbox in Exchange Online that multiple users can access and send from. Instead of belonging to a single person, it acts as a common address that a group of people can work in together. The Microsoft documentation for shared mailboxes covers how this type of mailbox is set up and used within Exchange Online collaboration scenarios. In the M365.FM episodes, the shared mailbox appears in several different roles, from a sender identity to an intake point for automated processing.

One of the clearest uses is as the consistent sender identity for an internal newsletter. The episode "Build Internal Outlook Newsletters with Dynamic Groups" describes a repeatable newsletter pipeline built from tools already present in Microsoft 365. In that pipeline, recipients are targeted with Dynamic Distribution Groups based on Entra ID attributes, and the newsletter is sent from a shared mailbox for branding and continuity. The episode says that a shared sender builds trust, because readers see the same familiar origin on every issue rather than the name of whichever employee happened to send it. This also supports continuity: the sender identity does not change when the person preparing the newsletter changes.

The same episode places the shared mailbox inside a larger workflow. Segmentation keeps messages relevant, a reusable Outlook template gives a predictable layout, and an intake, approval and send workflow built with Forms, Planner or Loop, and Power Automate removes the need for individual heroics. Measurement follows with Exchange traces and Delivery Reports feeding Power BI. In this arrangement the shared mailbox is the fixed point at the sending end of the chain, while the other components handle audience selection, composition, process and analytics.

Shared mailboxes also appear as a monitoring and security concern. In "Stop Microsoft Copilot Prompt Injection with Azure Logic Apps", a dedicated Office 365 shared mailbox is listed among the prerequisites, alongside an Azure subscription and Microsoft Security Copilot being enabled. The workflow monitors new emails arriving in the shared mailbox for potential threats, determines whether an email originated from Defender or Sentinel, exports the raw email content, handles attachments, and parses the message with an Azure Function. Here the mailbox serves as the ingestion point for an automated review process.

From a governance perspective, "Shared Data Reservoirs for Multi-Tenant Microsoft 365" treats shared mailboxes as something to audit. The episode suggests using PowerShell to connect to Exchange Online and manage mailboxes across client tenants, and to generate audit reports that identify inactive or unused mailboxes. It also recommends checking the last logon timestamp for each shared mailbox to spot dormant accounts, and says that regularly reviewing shared mailboxes and their activity helps reduce dark data and improve security. Because a shared mailbox is easy to create and may outlive the purpose it was created for, periodic review is part of keeping a tenant tidy.

The Dynamics 365 episodes mention shared mailboxes in a different light. "Dynamics 365 Omnichannel - Simply Explained" and "Dynamics 365 Contact Center - Simply Explained" both describe a traditional customer service setup in which email arrives in a shared mailbox while chat and phone are handled in separate applications. The episodes use this as an example of fragmentation: employees switch between systems, the customer's story is split across channels, and the customer may have to repeat information. The episodes present Dynamics 365 Omnichannel and Dynamics 365 Contact Center as ways to treat these interactions as one connected customer conversation.

Taken together, the episodes show the shared mailbox as a simple building block with several uses: a stable sender for communications, an intake address for automation, an item to audit for dormant accounts, and, in customer service, a channel that can become isolated when it is not connected to other systems. Decisions around it usually concern who needs access, what the mailbox is meant to do, and how its activity is reviewed over time.

shared-responsibility-model.desc: The shared responsibility model splits cloud security duties between provider and customer; in SaaS, the customer still owns its data, identities, devices and access.

faq.a: In SaaS, the provider runs and secures the platform, while the customer keeps responsibility for its data, identities, devices and access. In Microsoft 365, the episodes describe this as the customer managing users and data while Microsoft secures the infrastructure.
faq.q: What does the shared responsibility model mean in SaaS?

faq.a: The episodes mention multi-factor authentication, role-based access control, regular audits of permissions and sharing settings, diagnostic logging, backups, and a Zero Trust approach that verifies every access and action.
faq.q: Which customer-side controls do the M365.FM episodes associate with the model?

faq.a: The episodes say that understanding it clarifies security roles and prevents gaps, since a customer may otherwise assume the provider covers tasks that actually fall to the customer, such as protecting its own data and settings.
faq.q: Why do the episodes stress understanding the model?

shared-responsibility-model.long:
The shared responsibility model describes how security duties are divided between a cloud provider and its customer. The provider secures the underlying platform, while the customer remains accountable for the parts it controls. In a software-as-a-service (SaaS) setting such as Microsoft 365, the provider runs the platform, and the customer keeps responsibility for its data, identities, devices and access. The model exists to clarify who owns which control, so that neither side assumes the other is covering a task that nobody is actually performing.

The model is used in practice as a way to define security roles and to find gaps. Several M365.FM episodes return to it as a starting point for planning and review. The episode "SC-900 Exam Prep Part 1/8: Security Fundamentals" presents it as a foundational concept, saying that it defines who is responsible for what when it comes to security and compliance. It notes that cloud providers such as Microsoft Azure or AWS handle the security of the infrastructure, and that the customer's side of the arrangement is where things can become unclear.

In the context of Microsoft 365, the episode "Harden Microsoft 365 Security Without User Friction" states that Microsoft 365 security relies on a shared responsibility model, in which the customer manages users and data while Microsoft secures the infrastructure. The same episode ties this split to concrete customer-side measures: multi-factor authentication (MFA) to add a protective layer, role-based access control to give users only the permissions they need, and regular audits of permissions and sharing settings. It describes a combined approach of technical controls and user awareness so that the environment stays safe while users remain productive.
