For Azure, the episode "Hidden Microsoft 365 and Azure Cloud Security Risks" lists understanding the shared responsibility model among its recommendations, alongside regularly reviewing cloud configurations to avoid misconfigurations, enabling diagnostic logging for critical resources, running audits to remove orphaned resources, applying a Zero Trust approach that verifies every access and action, and using Microsoft Defender for Cloud. The point made there is that clarifying security roles prevents gaps, and that many of the listed tasks fall on the customer side of the line.

The model also appears in posture and migration work. In "Hidden Microsoft 365 Tenant Security Risks", security leaders are described as identifying blind spots by running a posture assessment that correlates logs from the security stack, audits critical accounts and permissions, and reviews the shared responsibility model for cloud services. The episode links weak identity security, such as reused passwords or missing MFA, to openings for initial access and lateral movement, which are the kinds of risk that sit with the customer rather than the platform provider. In "Plan a Secure and Cost-Controlled Azure Migration", the model is cited with the reminder that the customer must protect its own data and settings. That episode also connects it to backups against accidental deletion or ransomware, to continuous visibility into resources, to compliance obligations such as GDPR or HIPAA, and to the risks of shadow IT and unapproved tools.

Taken together, the episodes treat the shared responsibility model less as a product feature and more as a planning lens. It helps teams decide where a provider's assurances end and where their own configuration, identity management, device management, data protection and access governance have to begin. Because the exact division depends on the service type, the model is typically revisited whenever a workload moves to a new cloud service or a tenant's configuration changes.

sharegate.desc: ShareGate is a software vendor offering Microsoft 365 migration, consolidation and governance tools, covered in M365.FM episodes on SharePoint and Copilot.

faq.a: ShareGate is a software vendor of Microsoft 365 migration, consolidation and governance tools. M365.FM episodes mention it in connection with SharePoint migration, sprawl management, permissions auditing and compliance monitoring.
faq.q: What is ShareGate?

faq.a: The episode "Classic vs Modern SharePoint: Which Should You Use?" lists ShareGate as a migration tool that promotes subsites, optimizes site structure and manages permissions. It appears next to the Modernization Scanner and the Microsoft Page Transformation Tool.
faq.q: How does ShareGate relate to SharePoint modernization?

faq.a: "Copilot Inherits Your Mess: Modernizing Microsoft 365 for AI with Richard Harbridge [MVP]" features Richard Harbridge, a Microsoft MVP and industry advisor at ShareGate. It discusses why AI readiness depends on Microsoft 365 modernization and governance.
faq.q: Which M365.FM episode features someone from ShareGate?

sharegate.long:
ShareGate is a software vendor that provides tools for Microsoft 365 migration, consolidation and governance. Its products are used by administrators and IT teams who need to move content, restructure environments and keep an overview of how Microsoft 365 is used. In the M365.FM material, ShareGate appears mainly in discussions of SharePoint administration, permissions auditing, compliance monitoring and AI readiness.

In the episode "Classic vs Modern SharePoint: Which Should You Use?", ShareGate is listed among the tools and resources that make migration from classic to modern SharePoint easier. The episode describes it as a tool that promotes subsites, optimizes site structure and manages permissions during migration. It appears alongside the Modernization Scanner, which identifies sites ready for group connection and restructuring, and the Microsoft Page Transformation Tool, which converts classic pages to modern site pages. This places ShareGate in the migration and restructuring phase of a SharePoint modernization project, where content, site hierarchy and permissions all have to be handled together.

Governance and cleanup are the second area in which ShareGate is mentioned. The episode "Find and Remove Orphaned SharePoint Sites" discusses SharePoint sprawl, also called content sprawl, and recommends using Microsoft 365 tools to administer the environment better. According to the episode, tools like ShareGate and analytics can help monitor usage and manage sprawl. The same episode advises promoting user training, encouraging site ownership among users and balancing governance with team empowerment, so that collaboration continues while compliance and security are maintained.

Permissions auditing is a third context. In "Audit SharePoint Online Permissions at Scale", ShareGate is named with SysKit, AvePoint, Orchestry and DeliverPoint as third-party options that organizations use to strengthen SharePoint permissions auditing and compliance. The episode says these solutions help manage audits at scale and give deeper insight than native tools, and it states that ShareGate simplifies permissions management and provides clear audit trails. For organizations with many sites and complex sharing, this kind of reporting is the main reason to look beyond built-in features.

The episode "Fix Microsoft 365 Compliance Drift Beyond Green Dashboards" mentions ShareGate Protect in a list of tools for compliance monitoring. The episode describes it as automating data discovery, classification and compliance monitoring, which it says enhances governance. It is listed next to Purview Compliance Manager, ConfigCobra and Rubrik, each described with a different focus such as control tracking, configuration drift detection or continuous data classification. The surrounding discussion stresses continuous monitoring as protection against compliance gaps rather than relying on a dashboard that only appears healthy.

ShareGate also connects to the AI readiness theme. In the episode "Copilot Inherits Your Mess: Modernizing Microsoft 365 for AI with Richard Harbridge [MVP]", host Mirko Peters speaks with Richard Harbridge, identified as a Microsoft MVP and industry advisor at ShareGate. The conversation addresses why AI readiness is tied to Microsoft 365 modernization and governance, and asks what kind of Microsoft 365 environment is being exposed to AI. A central idea in the episode is that Copilot does not create the mess but amplifies it, and that technical debt which could stay hidden in traditional Microsoft 365 management becomes visible once AI is involved.

Taken together, the episodes position ShareGate within the practical work around Microsoft 365 environments: migrating and restructuring SharePoint, reducing sprawl, auditing permissions, monitoring compliance and preparing content and governance for Copilot. The episodes treat it as one option among several in each category, and they pair tool use with organizational measures such as training and clear site ownership.

sharepoint-2013-workflows.desc: SharePoint 2013 workflows are the legacy workflow engine for SharePoint lists and libraries, being retired in SharePoint Online in favor of Power Automate.

faq.a: Until the shutdown, existing workflows keep running and stay editable. After it, they can only be viewed as raw XML files and no longer run. Microsoft's notice gives the date for existing tenants.
faq.q: What happens to SharePoint 2013 workflows after the retirement date?

faq.a: Microsoft recommends Power Automate, the built-in approvals feature, and partner solutions. The Microsoft 365 Assessment tool can help find where existing workflows are in use.
faq.q: What replaces SharePoint 2013 workflows?

faq.a: On-premises SharePoint Server versions keep supporting 2013 workflows until their own end of support. The staged retirement described by Microsoft concerns SharePoint Online.
faq.q: Does the retirement affect on-premises SharePoint Server?

sharepoint-2013-workflows.long:
SharePoint 2013 workflows are the legacy workflow engine for SharePoint. A workflow in SharePoint automates the movement of documents or list items through the steps of a business process, and organisations have used this engine to attach business logic to lists and libraries. Typical examples include routing a document for review or moving a list item through approval stages. These workflows were usually built and published with SharePoint Designer 2013, while developers could also create them with Visual Studio.

Microsoft is retiring SharePoint 2013 workflows in SharePoint Online in stages. The older SharePoint 2010 workflows were switched off first. The 2013 workflows were then switched off for new tenants, and removal from existing tenants, including government clouds, follows on the date given in Microsoft's retirement notice. Until that shutdown, existing workflows keep running and remain editable. After the shutdown, they can only be viewed as raw XML files, which means the logic is no longer executed but can still be read as a reference when planning a rebuild. Administrators can block the creation of new 2013 workflows with a PowerShell tenant setting, which helps stop further technical debt from accumulating while migration work is under way.

The retirement applies to SharePoint Online. On-premises SharePoint Server versions keep supporting these workflows until their own end of support, so the decision about timing differs depending on whether an organisation runs Microsoft 365, an on-premises farm, or both. Microsoft recommends Power Automate as the replacement, alongside the built-in approvals feature and partner solutions. To find where workflows are in use before planning any migration, the Microsoft 365 Assessment tool can be used to inventory them across a tenant.

In practice, the main decisions around SharePoint 2013 workflows are which workflows are still needed, which can be retired without replacement, and which should be rebuilt. Because the workflow logic and the data are separate concerns, the lists and libraries themselves generally stay in place; what needs replacing is the automation attached to them. An inventory of active workflows, their owners and the processes they support is a sensible first step, followed by prioritising by business impact and rebuilding in the recommended platform.

The M365.FM episode "Replace SharePoint 2013 Workflows Before Retirement" frames the issue as one of legacy workflows rather than an outdated SharePoint. The episode argues for modernising without rebuilding everything: keep the existing lists and libraries, then layer Power Apps for usable front-ends, Power Automate for reliable approvals, AI Builder to auto-classify and extract data from PDFs, and Copilot Studio for conversational retrieval and actions. It also stresses urgency, noting that SharePoint 2010 workflows are already affected by the retirement sequence.

The episode "Service Principal Security: Stop Using Personal Accounts" places the retirement in a wider platform context. It lists the retirement of SharePoint 2013 workflows alongside the deprecation of Azure AD Graph and the disappearance of service-principal-less authentication, and says app-only modern authentication is becoming mandatory. According to the episode, Microsoft's direction is that automation must have its own identity, so rebuilt workflows should not depend on personal user accounts. For anyone replacing SharePoint 2013 workflows, this suggests treating the migration as an opportunity to review how automations authenticate as well as how they are built.

sharepoint-admin-agent.desc: SharePoint admin agent is a Microsoft AI agent in SharePoint Advanced Management that helps administrators find and fix tenant issues in natural language.

faq.a: It is an AI agent from Microsoft, part of SharePoint Advanced Management, that helps SharePoint administrators find and fix tenant problems such as inactive sites, oversharing and permission sprawl using natural language.
faq.q: What is the SharePoint admin agent?

faq.a: Copilot works with the data and permissions already present in a tenant, so oversharing and permission sprawl become more visible once it is used. The agent helps find and clean up such issues, which supports Copilot governance.
faq.q: How does the SharePoint admin agent relate to Copilot governance?

faq.a: The episode "Secure Microsoft Copilot with Entra ID and Zero Trust" recommends using the Microsoft Purview portal and the SharePoint Admin Agent to run scheduled reports as part of ongoing permission cleanup and monitoring.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode say about the SharePoint Admin Agent?

sharepoint-admin-agent.long:
The SharePoint admin agent, also referred to as Admin Agent for SharePoint or SharePoint Admin Agent, is an AI agent developed by Microsoft that helps SharePoint administrators find and fix problems in their tenant using natural language. It is classified as a Microsoft tool and an AI assistant, and it belongs to SharePoint Advanced Management. The problems it targets are typical governance issues: inactive sites, oversharing and permission sprawl.

The core idea is to replace manual report building and hand-written scripts with a conversational approach. Instead of assembling queries or reports step by step, an administrator describes what they want to know or change, and the agent supports the analysis. This makes the agent relevant for the everyday work of keeping a SharePoint tenant tidy, where questions such as which sites are no longer used or where access is broader than intended come up repeatedly.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem the agent sits at the intersection of several topics. It is related to the general concept of an AI agent, meaning software that acts on a task described by a user rather than only returning search results. It is also related to Copilot governance, which deals with controlling what Microsoft Copilot can reach in a tenant. Because Copilot works with the data, identities and permissions that already exist, weaknesses in SharePoint permissions become more visible once Copilot is in use. Finding and cleaning up oversharing and permission sprawl is therefore a common preparation step for a Copilot rollout.

The agent is also related to PnP PowerShell, the community module that administrators often use for scripted SharePoint management. Scripts remain an option for repeatable or highly customized tasks, while the agent offers a natural-language route for investigating and addressing tenant problems. How the two are combined depends on the administrator's preferences and the task at hand.

Typical scenarios include preparing a tenant for a Copilot rollout, reviewing sites that nobody uses any more, and tracking down sites with overly broad access. Each of these involves surveying the tenant, deciding which findings matter, and then acting on them, which is the workflow the agent is meant to support.

The M365.FM episode "Secure Microsoft Copilot with Entra ID and Zero Trust" is not specifically about this agent, but it covers the surrounding context. The episode argues that the biggest security risk in Copilot is not the model itself but the data, identities and permissions it can access. Among its recommendations are starting with a readiness assessment to address open links and misconfigurations, and using the Microsoft Purview portal and the SharePoint Admin Agent to run scheduled reports. It also advises educating site owners and users on labeling, sharing and responsible Copilot use, automating label inheritance, enforcing policies before scaling, and setting up ongoing KPI dashboards to monitor DLP hits and guardrail efficiency. The episode stresses that continuous monitoring and permission cleanup remain essential, and it recommends involving stakeholders early and focusing on quick wins to build foundational governance.

sharepoint-advanced-management.desc: SharePoint Advanced Management (SAM) is a Microsoft set of SharePoint governance and lifecycle tools, included with Microsoft 365 Copilot and part of SharePoint Premium.

faq.a: SAM is a set of governance and lifecycle tools for SharePoint from Microsoft. It includes site access reviews, inactive site policies, restricted access control and oversharing reports, and it is part of SharePoint Premium.
faq.q: What is SharePoint Advanced Management (SAM)?

faq.a: SAM is included with Microsoft 365 Copilot and is used for Copilot governance. The M365.FM episode "Reduce SharePoint Premium SAM and PAYG AI Costs" describes it as the backbone that keeps Copilot from turning oversharing into a data leak.
faq.q: How is SAM related to Microsoft 365 Copilot?

faq.a: Yes, SAM can be automated with PnP PowerShell. The SharePoint admin agent also builds on SAM as an AI helper for administrators.
faq.q: Can SAM be automated?

sharepoint-advanced-management.long:
SharePoint Advanced Management, abbreviated SAM, is a set of governance and lifecycle tools for SharePoint developed by Microsoft. It includes site access reviews, inactive site policies, restricted access control and oversharing reports, and it is included with Microsoft 365 Copilot. SAM is part of SharePoint Premium and is classed as both a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool. Its documentation is published on Microsoft Learn.

The purpose of SAM is to help administrators keep a growing SharePoint estate under control. Sites accumulate over time, permissions drift, and content is shared more widely than intended. When Microsoft 365 Copilot is introduced, existing permissions become more visible, because Copilot can surface whatever a user already has access to. SAM addresses this by giving administrators ways to find overshared content, limit who can see a site, review who holds access, and deal with sites that are no longer in use.

The components named in the sources cover several tasks. Site access reviews let site owners confirm who should keep access, which makes owners accountable for their own sites. Inactive site policies support the lifecycle side, so that unused sites can be identified and handled. Restricted access control limits visibility of a site to a defined group. Oversharing reports, together with Data Access Governance, help administrators spot risky sites so they can prioritize remediation. One M365.FM episode also mentions AI Insights as a way to prioritize fixes.

SAM sits next to several related technologies. It is related to SharePoint itself, to Copilot governance, and to Microsoft Purview, which handles information protection and compliance, including sensitivity labels and data loss prevention. SAM can be automated with PnP PowerShell, and the SharePoint admin agent builds on it as an AI helper for administrators. Through its licensing, SAM is tied to Microsoft 365 Copilot. One episode describes SAM as offering tenant-wide guardrails in SharePoint, while Purview supplies labeling and data loss prevention.

The M365.FM episode "Reduce SharePoint Premium SAM and PAYG AI Costs" presents SAM as the governance backbone that keeps Copilot from turning oversharing into a data leak. It uses an analogy in which role-based access control is the moat, SAM builds the walls, and Data Access Governance and AI Insights act as watchtowers. The episode walks through spotting risky sites with Data Access Governance, locking down visibility with Restricted Access Control, and making owners accountable with Site Access Reviews. It also points to related features such as Microsoft 365 Archive for managing storage costs and Microsoft 365 Backup for business continuity.

Other episodes place SAM within wider governance practice. "Govern Microsoft Fabric Data Agents in Copilot Studio" lists SAM among the measures for monitoring and controlling external sharing and access to sensitive files, alongside Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels and Conditional Access in Microsoft Entra. "Why Microsoft 365 Native Controls Are Not Real Governance" describes SAM as helping to govern content lifecycle and security in SharePoint and OneDrive, and argues that governance is an ongoing discipline with clear ownership rather than a one-time project. "AI Contract Management with SharePoint Premium and Copilot" names SAM as the source of tenant-wide guardrails, and "Save Time with Microsoft Copilot in Fabric" lists it among the tools that still need a human to apply them thoughtfully.

In practice, the decisions around SAM concern which sites to review first, who owns each site, which sites should have restricted visibility, and how inactive sites are handled. The episodes consistently frame SAM as one layer in a wider approach rather than a complete answer on its own.

sharepoint-agents.desc: SharePoint agents are Copilot agents grounded on a chosen SharePoint site or document library that answer questions about that selected content.

faq.a: A SharePoint agent is a Copilot agent grounded on a specific SharePoint site or document library. It answers questions about that selected content.
faq.q: What is a SharePoint agent?

faq.a: The episode "Block Copilot Access to Sensitive SharePoint Documents with Purview DLP" describes using data policies to prevent shadow agents and Microsoft Purview DLP to block agents from processing confidential data, even when users can see it.
faq.q: How can SharePoint agents be kept away from confidential content?

faq.a: The episode with Marcin Siewnicki says the concept has become less prominent as Copilot itself gains broader capabilities for interacting directly with SharePoint information.
faq.q: Are SharePoint agents still prominent in Copilot?

sharepoint-agents.long:
SharePoint agents are Copilot agents grounded on a specific SharePoint site or document library. Instead of drawing on everything a user can reach across Microsoft 365, such an agent answers questions about the content that has been selected for it. This makes the answers tied to a defined body of material, such as a team site, a policy library or a collection of project documents.

The basic idea is straightforward: SharePoint already holds much of an organization's documents, pages and lists, and an agent scoped to part of that content gives people a conversational way to ask about it. The episode "SharePoint Agents - Simply Explained" describes an AI assistant that is already switched on in every SharePoint site. It covers what SharePoint agents actually are, the two kinds of agents a user will meet, and how an agent finds the right answer, and it also looks at where agents earn their keep in daily work.

A second episode, "SharePoint Isn't Boring Anymore: How Copilot Is Reinventing the Modern Workplace with Marcin Siewnicki [MVP]", places SharePoint agents in the wider Copilot landscape. It describes them as dedicated AI experiences grounded in selected SharePoint sites, document libraries or information sources. The discussion also touches on how the concept has become less prominent as Copilot itself gains broader capabilities for interacting directly with SharePoint information, including content such as lists and text extracted from video transcripts. For anyone deciding whether to build a dedicated agent or simply use Copilot against SharePoint content, this positioning is a useful reference point.

Governance is a recurring theme in the episodes that mention SharePoint agents. "Block Copilot Access to Sensitive SharePoint Documents with Purview DLP" focuses on keeping agents from processing confidential data. It describes setting data policies so that makers cannot create shadow agents wired to the wrong content, and wiring Microsoft Purview DLP so that agents are blocked from processing confidential material even when users can see it. The stated aim is for Copilot and SharePoint agents to be powerful, safe and predictable. The practical consequence is that the scope of an agent, the sensitivity of the underlying site and the policies around it need to be considered together, not left to default behavior.

The episode "Govern SharePoint Knowledge Agent with Human Oversight" approaches the topic from the administration side. It frames the question of SharePoint agent versus human admin and argues that AI helps streamline routine tasks while human administrators contribute skills that remain essential. The episode cites statistics on SharePoint use in enterprises and reported cost savings; these figures are the episode's own claims. The takeaway is that agents support administration and content work but still call for human oversight.

SharePoint agents also appear as an extensibility option in "Connect External Business Data with Microsoft 365 Copilot Connectors". There, the recommendation is to use Copilot Studio and SharePoint agents for extensibility alongside integrating data from systems such as ERP and CRM, working with teams to find use cases, building proof-of-concepts, offering training and tracking adoption. In that context SharePoint agents are one building block among several for extending Copilot with business content.

In practice, typical decisions around SharePoint agents include which site or library an agent should be grounded on, who is allowed to create agents, and how data loss prevention and data policies apply to the content the agent can read. Because an agent answers from selected content, the quality and permissions of that content shape the quality and safety of its answers.

sharepoint-architect.desc: A SharePoint architect designs the structure, governance and integration of SharePoint and related Microsoft 365 content and collaboration solutions.
sharepoint-architect.long:
A SharePoint architect is a job role responsible for designing the structure, governance and integration of SharePoint and related Microsoft 365 content and collaboration solutions. The role is also referred to in German-language contexts as SharePoint-Architekt or SharePoint Architekt.

In practice, the role covers planning how content and collaboration solutions are organized, how they are governed, and how they connect with other parts of the Microsoft 365 ecosystem. The architect's work sits at the design level, translating organizational needs into a coherent SharePoint-based solution landscape rather than focusing on day-to-day administration alone.

This entity page is a short reference for the job title. No linked topics, official documentation or specific M365.FM episodes are currently associated with it, so the description is limited to the role definition above. Further detail on responsibilities, skills or tooling is not stated in the available facts.

sharepoint-autofill-columns.desc: SharePoint autofill columns use natural-language prompts to extract or generate metadata from files and fill library columns automatically, as a pay-as-you-go feature.

faq.a: They are a SharePoint feature that uses natural-language prompts to extract or generate metadata from files and automatically populate columns in a library.
faq.q: What are SharePoint autofill columns?

faq.a: Yes. The feature is part of the document processing capabilities of Microsoft Syntex, also known as SharePoint Premium.
faq.q: Is autofill columns part of Microsoft Syntex?

faq.a: Autofill columns is a pay-as-you-go feature. Further pricing details are not given here and can be found in the official Microsoft documentation.
faq.q: How is the feature billed?

sharepoint-autofill-columns.long:
SharePoint autofill columns are a pay-as-you-go SharePoint feature that uses natural-language prompts to extract or generate metadata from files and populate library columns automatically. The feature is part of the document processing capabilities of Microsoft Syntex, also referred to as SharePoint Premium.

In practice, autofill columns are used to reduce manual metadata entry in document libraries. Instead of typing values into columns for each file, a prompt describes the information to be found or produced, and the system fills the column based on the content of the file. This supports the organization and retrieval of documents by keeping column values consistent and complete.

Because autofill columns are billed on a pay-as-you-go basis, they belong to the group of Microsoft 365 capabilities where usage is metered rather than included in a standard license. The available facts do not describe specific pricing, supported file types, or configuration steps; those details are covered in the official Microsoft Learn documentation on the autofill overview.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity.

sharepoint-content-types.desc: SharePoint content types are reusable definitions that bundle site columns and settings for a category of items, such as a policy or contract, to keep metadata consistent.

faq.a: A SharePoint content type is a reusable definition that bundles site columns and settings for a category of documents or items, such as a policy or contract.
faq.q: What is a SharePoint content type?

faq.a: They keep metadata consistent across libraries and sites by letting the same set of columns and settings be applied wherever a given kind of item is stored.
faq.q: Why are content types used in SharePoint?

sharepoint-content-types.long:
SharePoint content types are reusable definitions in SharePoint that describe a category of documents or items, for example a policy or a contract. Each content type bundles together a set of site columns and related settings, so that every item of that kind carries the same structure.

The main purpose of content types is consistency. Because the definition is created once and then applied wherever it is needed, the same metadata fields appear across different libraries and sites rather than being rebuilt separately each time. This helps keep how information is described and organized uniform across a SharePoint environment.

In practice, content types are used when an organization wants documents or list items of one kind to share common properties, regardless of where they are stored. A policy, for instance, can be defined with its required columns and settings in a single place and then reused in multiple locations.

No specific M365.FM episodes are linked to this topic at present, and no related entities are listed in the available information.

sharepoint-designer.desc: SharePoint Designer is a legacy Microsoft desktop application used to customize SharePoint sites and build workflows, now being replaced by Power Automate.

faq.a: SharePoint Designer is a locally installed desktop application for customizing SharePoint sites and building applications and workflows without writing code. It supports data-driven pages, views, forms, web parts, navigation, branding files and workflow design.
faq.q: What is SharePoint Designer used for?

faq.a: The Microsoft Support page states that support for SharePoint Designer 2013 is scheduled to end in July 2026.
faq.q: When does support for SharePoint Designer 2013 end?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes describe Power Automate as the newer workflow solution integrated with modern SharePoint. They say it supports integrations across multiple Microsoft 365 applications and third-party services, unlike classic workflows in SharePoint Designer.
faq.q: What replaces SharePoint Designer workflows?

sharepoint-designer.long:
SharePoint Designer is a legacy Microsoft desktop application for customizing SharePoint sites and building SharePoint workflows. According to Microsoft Support, SharePoint Designer 2013 is a locally installed web and application design program that allows users to create and customise SharePoint sites and applications, and the documentation states that this can be done without writing code. It targets SharePoint 2013 and later sites.

The tool covers several areas of site design. Users can build data-driven pages, workflow-based solutions and site designs, and can package a finished solution as a template. SharePoint Designer connects to lists and libraries as well as to external data such as SQL Server, OLE DB, SOAP and REST services, XML files, and external content types through Business Connectivity Services. Views, forms, web parts and navigation can be designed within the application. For branding, it supports work with master pages, page layouts and CSS files, although by default only site collection administrators may edit them. Administrators can restrict features through a settings page, and some data options are not available in every SharePoint deployment.

Workflows are one of the main reasons organizations used SharePoint Designer. Workflows are assembled from events, conditions, actions and steps, and there is an import path from Visio. In classic SharePoint, together with InfoPath, these tools supported complex business process automation. The episode "Classic vs Modern SharePoint: Which Should You Use?" notes that such legacy workflows helped organizations manage approvals, document routing and notifications. It adds that Microsoft has since shifted its focus to newer workflow solutions, and that modern SharePoint integrates with Power Automate, which it describes as a more flexible and user-friendly way to build workflows.

That shift has practical consequences for organizations that still rely on SharePoint Designer. The Microsoft Support page states that support for SharePoint Designer 2013 is scheduled to end in July 2026. The same episode advises that teams depending on classic workflows may need to plan for migration. Typical decisions therefore involve inventorying existing workflows built in SharePoint Designer, deciding which are still needed, and rebuilding them on a supported platform.

The episode "Replace SharePoint 2013 Workflows Before Retirement" addresses this migration in more detail. It contrasts classic workflows in SharePoint Designer, which it describes as limited to the SharePoint environment, with Power Automate, which supports integrations across multiple Microsoft 365 applications and third-party services. According to the episode, this flexibility allows a wider range of users to develop workflows independently and improves the reliability of business processes. It suggests replacing outdated approval workflows with Power Automate to streamline processes and reduce long-term maintenance for IT teams.

In summary, SharePoint Designer remains relevant mainly for understanding and maintaining older SharePoint customizations. It is a no-code design tool for pages, data connections, branding and workflows in SharePoint 2013 and later sites, but its announced support end date and the move toward modern SharePoint and Power Automate mean that current projects are generally directed toward newer tools, while existing solutions call for migration planning.

sharepoint-document-libraries.desc: SharePoint document libraries are containers in SharePoint for storing, organizing and co-editing files, with metadata columns, custom views and flexible permissions.

faq.a: A SharePoint document library is a container for storing, organizing and co-editing files. It supports metadata columns, custom views and permissions that can be set at library, folder or file level.
faq.q: What is a SharePoint document library?

faq.a: Yes. The episode "SharePoint Sync vs Add Shortcut to OneDrive" says SharePoint document libraries can be added directly into Teams channels, giving access to folders, files and shortcuts without switching between apps.
faq.q: Can SharePoint document libraries be used in Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: According to the episode "Automate Document Processing with Microsoft Syntex", Syntex uses machine learning to extract information and classify documents stored in SharePoint document libraries, for example invoices, contracts and forms.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Syntex relate to document libraries?

sharepoint-document-libraries.long:
SharePoint document libraries are the containers in SharePoint where files are stored, organized and edited together. Beyond simply holding documents, a library adds structure through columns that describe each file with metadata, custom views that present the same content in different ways, and permissions that can be set at library, folder or file level. Libraries are the main place where document-based work in a SharePoint site takes place, and they also serve as the source for several other Microsoft 365 experiences.

In practice, a document library is used to keep team or project files in one governed location, to let several people co-edit the same document, and to find content through metadata rather than relying only on folder names. Columns make it possible to tag documents with information such as type or status, while views filter, sort and group that information so that different audiences can see the files in the way that suits them. Permissions can be inherited from the site or narrowed down to a single folder or file when specific content needs tighter control.

Document libraries sit inside the wider SharePoint site structure. According to the episode "Classic vs Modern SharePoint: Which Should You Use?", hub sites organize multiple modern team sites and communication sites under shared navigation, theme and search scope, while site-level permissions and content such as lists and SharePoint document libraries remain independent for each site. The same episode notes that modern team sites are typically created together with Microsoft 365 Groups, which provision shared resources such as an Exchange mailbox and Planner alongside the SharePoint team site.

Libraries also connect to other Microsoft 365 tools. The episode "SharePoint Sync vs Add Shortcut to OneDrive" describes adding SharePoint document libraries directly into Microsoft Teams channels, so that folders, files and shortcuts can be reached without switching apps. According to that episode, this avoids sync conflicts and reduces the need to add one shortcut after another to OneDrive, and it supports real-time co-authoring in a single workspace. The episode "Microsoft Viva Learning - Simply Explained" mentions that Viva Learning can surface learning content, such as onboarding guides or compliance training, that is stored in SharePoint document libraries.

Libraries are also where content processing happens. The episode "Automate Document Processing with Microsoft Syntex" explains that Syntex is an AI-powered content management service that applies machine learning to extract information from documents, classify them automatically and turn unstructured content into structured data. It says Syntex works on content stored in SharePoint document libraries, so that documents such as invoices, contracts and forms can be evaluated and processed where they are uploaded.

The episode "Improve SharePoint Document Libraries with New UX and Copilot" covers newer capabilities for libraries. It describes a new document library experience that includes enhanced breadcrumbs, Forms, Autofill and Copilot, and frames them as a way to move away from disorganized file collections, illustrated by the example of a file named "final_v3_REALLY_final.docx", toward a workflow that guides work instead of hiding it. The episode encourages experimenting with AI-driven insights and improved navigation to streamline document management tasks.

Typical decisions around document libraries include how to model metadata with columns, which views to offer, where to break permission inheritance, and whether to connect a library to Teams, OneDrive or other services. The sources attached to this topic describe these building blocks at a high level; detailed configuration steps are outside what the episode excerpts cover.

sharepoint-embedded.desc: SharePoint Embedded (SPE) is an API-first Microsoft 365 content platform for storing and managing documents in custom apps with built-in security and compliance.

faq.a: SharePoint Embedded is an API-first content platform from Microsoft that lets developers store and manage documents for their own apps in Microsoft 365. The files use Microsoft 365 security and compliance without appearing as a SharePoint site.
faq.q: What is SharePoint Embedded?

faq.a: No. The episode "SharePoint Embedded - Simply Explained" covers why it is not a SharePoint site: it is a headless backend that stores files for apps, while the app provides its own user interface.
faq.q: Is SharePoint Embedded the same as a SharePoint site?

faq.a: Applications work with the stored content through Microsoft Graph, and Microsoft Purview provides compliance and information governance capabilities for that content.
faq.q: How does SharePoint Embedded relate to Microsoft Graph and Microsoft Purview?

sharepoint-embedded.long:
SharePoint Embedded, also referred to as SPE, is an API-first content platform from Microsoft that lets developers store and manage documents for their own applications inside Microsoft 365. The files kept in it benefit from the security and compliance features of Microsoft 365, yet they do not appear as a SharePoint site. It is a paid offering, classified as a Microsoft tool and a developer tool, and it is part of SharePoint.

The central idea is that the platform stores files for apps instead of for people. The episode "SharePoint Embedded - Simply Explained" describes it as a part of Microsoft 365 that has no screen at all. A related episode, "What Is SharePoint Premium - Simply Explained", describes SharePoint Embedded as a headless version of SharePoint. In that description, developers and software vendors create customized user interfaces of their own while relying on SharePoint's secure backend for data storage, which supports compliance and data governance. In other words, the application supplies the interface, and Microsoft 365 supplies the storage layer behind it.

The typical audience is software vendors and internal development teams who need document storage inside their own products or line-of-business apps. Instead of building a separate file store and then re-implementing security, retention and auditing, they use Microsoft 365 as the backend. The "SharePoint Embedded - Simply Explained" episode walks through the main building blocks of the topic: the container idea, where the files live, the security story, what is built in, why it is not a SharePoint site, how billing works and where people tend to meet it in practice.

SharePoint Embedded is related to two other Microsoft topics. Microsoft Graph is the interface through which applications work with the stored content, which fits the API-first nature of the product. Microsoft Purview supplies compliance and information governance capabilities for that content, so organizations can apply their existing governance approach to documents that live in a custom application. Because the content sits in Microsoft 365 rather than in a vendor-specific silo, it can be governed alongside other Microsoft 365 data.

The topic also appears in neighbouring episodes. In "What Is SharePoint Premium - Simply Explained", SharePoint Embedded is listed under the Content Experiences pillar, which focuses on enriching how users interact with documents through a more intuitive and engaging interface. In "Microsoft Loop Workspaces - Simply Explained", SharePoint Embedded comes up in the context of storage management. The episode recommends regular audits of storage usage and a review of growth trends in SharePoint Embedded, alongside automated notifications for users nearing storage limits, user training on cleaning up outdated Loop Components, clear governance policies and periodic cleanups.

For anyone deciding whether the platform fits a project, the main points from the sources are these: it is intended for apps rather than end users, it is not a SharePoint site, it is billed as a paid service, and it works through APIs and Microsoft Graph. Official documentation is available from Microsoft Learn under the SharePoint developer section for SharePoint Embedded.

sharepoint-framework.desc: SharePoint Framework (SPFx) is Microsoft's client-side development model for extending SharePoint and Microsoft 365 with web parts, extensions and form customizers.

faq.a: SPFx is Microsoft's client-side development model for extending SharePoint and Microsoft 365 with web parts, extensions and form customizers. It is typically built with React and TypeScript.
faq.q: What is SharePoint Framework (SPFx)?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, SPFx is also used to build Adaptive Card Extensions for Viva Connections dashboards and appears in Microsoft Teams development toolchains alongside Visual Studio Code and Node.js.
faq.q: Can SPFx be used outside SharePoint pages?

faq.a: The episodes with Julie Turner and Siddharth Vaghasia discuss using SPFx together with Microsoft Graph, PnPjs and PnP React Controls, so that data access and reusable components do not have to be built from scratch.
faq.q: How do PnPjs and Microsoft Graph relate to SPFx?

sharepoint-framework.long:
SharePoint Framework (SPFx) is Microsoft's client-side development model for extending SharePoint and Microsoft 365. Solutions built with it include web parts, extensions and form customizers, and they are typically written with React and TypeScript. Because SPFx runs on the client side, it fits teams that already work with JavaScript and TypeScript tooling rather than server-side code.

In practice, SPFx is used to add custom experiences to SharePoint pages and sites and to surface Microsoft 365 data in places where users already work. The M365.FM episode "Customize Microsoft Viva Connections Dashboards" points to one such use: Adaptive Card Extensions (ACE) built with SPFx can give Viva Connections dashboards interactive card experiences that go beyond simple links. The same episode notes that such cards can show data from Microsoft Graph and can trigger Power Automate flows, for example to start approvals or notifications from the dashboard.

SPFx also appears in the Microsoft Teams development toolchain. The episode "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions" lists Visual Studio Code as an essential tool for JavaScript, TypeScript or SharePoint Framework (SPFx) development, alongside Node.js as the back-end JavaScript runtime and the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit, which simplifies provisioning and deploying cloud resources. This shows that SPFx work usually sits inside a broader Node.js-based toolset rather than a standalone environment.

A recurring theme in the episodes is not building everything from scratch. In "Stop Reinventing SPFx- Building Better SharePoint Solutions with PnP React Controls with Siddharth Vaghasia [MVP]", host Mirko Peters talks with Microsoft MVP Siddharth Vaghasia about building production-ready SPFx solutions by combining the right Microsoft 365 technologies with reusable community components such as PnP React Controls. The episode description also raises the question of when SPFx should actually be used, since not every SharePoint requirement calls for it. That decision is part of solution design: SPFx is one option among several Microsoft 365 extensibility approaches, and the episode frames the choice around the requirement at hand.

The episode "Building Modern Microsoft 365 Solutions with SharePoint Framework, Microsoft Graph, PnPjs & Great User Experiences with Julie Turner [MVP]" covers SPFx together with Microsoft Graph, PnPjs, open-source development, UX design and AI-assisted coding. Microsoft MVP Julie Turner discusses designing enterprise-grade Microsoft 365 solutions that remain scalable, secure and maintainable. The pairing of SPFx with Microsoft Graph and PnPjs reflects a common pattern: the framework provides the client-side hosting model, while Graph and helper libraries supply the data access.

Troubleshooting is another topic where SPFx comes up. The episode "Fix Broken SPFx Live Data Updates" offers a checklist for cases where live data is not updating in an SPFx web part. Its steps include confirming the scope of the issue (reproduction steps, affected users, the specific page or web part), checking recent changes such as deployments, configuration, code merges, tenant-level settings or package updates, and validating the network by using the browser DevTools Network tab to verify requests and response payloads. The approach is systematic: narrow down where the problem occurs, review what changed, and inspect the traffic.

For anyone evaluating SPFx, the sources suggest looking at it in context. It is a client-side model for SharePoint and Microsoft 365 extensions, it is commonly built with React and TypeScript, it works with Microsoft Graph and community libraries such as PnPjs and PnP React Controls, and it extends into areas like Viva Connections dashboards and Microsoft Teams development. Official documentation provides an overview of the framework on Microsoft Learn.

sharepoint-global-navigation.desc: Global navigation in the SharePoint app bar is a tenant-wide navigation layer that shows consistent top-level links across sites once a home site is set.

faq.a: Global navigation is the tenant-wide navigation layer in SharePoint. It is shown in the SharePoint app bar and provides consistent top-level links across all sites.
faq.q: What is global navigation in SharePoint?

faq.a: It appears once a home site has been set. The home site is the prerequisite for showing this tenant-wide navigation in the app bar.
faq.q: When does global navigation appear in the SharePoint app bar?

faq.a: Microsoft describes it in its documentation on the SharePoint app bar in the Viva Connections section of Microsoft Learn.
faq.q: Where is global navigation documented?

sharepoint-global-navigation.long:
Global navigation (SharePoint app bar) is the tenant-wide navigation layer in SharePoint. It appears in the SharePoint app bar once a home site has been set, and it gives users a consistent set of top-level links across all sites in the tenant.

The purpose of global navigation is to give users the same entry points regardless of which SharePoint site they are visiting. Because the links are defined at tenant level rather than per site, navigation stays uniform across the organization instead of varying from site to site. The dependency on a home site is central to the concept: the app bar's global navigation is tied to the site designated as the home site.

The feature is described in Microsoft's documentation on the SharePoint app bar within the Viva Connections area. That documentation is the official reference for how the app bar and its navigation behave.

No related entities or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic, so this page is limited to the definition above.

sharepoint-home-site.desc: A SharePoint home site is a communication site set as an organization's intranet landing point and the base for Viva Connections news, dashboard and resources.

faq.a: It is a communication site with special capabilities that serves as the branded landing point of an organization's intranet and as an entry to other portals. It also forms the base for the SharePoint app in Teams, formerly Viva Connections.
faq.q: What is a SharePoint home site?

faq.a: The home site is the foundation from which Viva Connections pulls its news, dashboard and resources. The M365.FM episode "Customize Microsoft Viva Connections Dashboards" describes Viva Connections as turning the home site into a dynamic dashboard inside Microsoft Teams.
faq.q: How does the home site relate to Viva Connections?

faq.a: The documentation advises swapping the root site before designating the home site, since doing it the other way round can lose settings. Setup also involves audience targeting, page approval and checking performance with page diagnostics.
faq.q: What should be considered when setting up a home site?

sharepoint-home-site.long:
A SharePoint home site is a communication site with special capabilities that serves as the branded landing point of an organization's intranet and as an entry to other portals. It is the site an organization designates as its home site, and it forms the base for the SharePoint app in Teams, formerly known as Viva Connections. The Microsoft Learn page on the topic frames the home site as an addition to the intranet design rather than a replacement for it, and recommends using the organization's root site for this role.

The home site matters because several intranet-wide capabilities attach to it. Search across sites, news and files is available at the intranet level through the home site. It also acts as the default official source of organization news, and news published there gets priority on the SharePoint start page. A further capability is global navigation in the SharePoint app bar. This navigation can only be edited from the home site's own start page, so the home site becomes the place where navigation for the whole organization is maintained.

In terms of how it works, the home site is the foundation from which Viva Connections pulls its news, dashboard and resources. The episode "Customize Microsoft Viva Connections Dashboards" describes Viva Connections as a platform that turns a SharePoint home site into a dynamic dashboard. According to the episode, this gives employees a single entry point for company updates, tasks and important links, and it works inside Microsoft Teams so people do not have to switch between different apps. The episode also says the experience can be personalized for each employee, so that everyone sees what matters most to them.

Building a home site involves a sequence of steps described in the documentation. The starting point is creating the communication site. Audience targeting is then enabled, and page approval is set up. Page diagnostics are used to check performance. One ordering point is called out explicitly: if the root site is swapped, that swap should happen before the home site is designated, because designating the home site before the root swap can lose settings. This is a typical planning decision for organizations that already have an established intranet on a different site.

There are also licensing and scope considerations. A Connections experience requires enterprise, frontline or academic licenses, and additional experiences need Viva licensing. Among the documented limits, integration with the SharePoint start page is not available, and a featured link is suggested as a workaround. Because the home site underlies both the intranet landing experience and the Teams-based dashboard, decisions about which site to use, how to structure global navigation and how to target audiences tend to be made together.

In practice, the home site is relevant for intranet owners, SharePoint administrators and communications teams who want a consistent, branded entry point to company news and resources. It connects the SharePoint intranet with Microsoft Teams through Viva Connections, so that the same news, links and navigation can be reached from either place. The M365.FM episode on Viva Connections dashboards approaches the topic from the dashboard side and shows how the home site serves as the underlying platform that the Teams experience is built on.

sharepoint-html-pages.desc: HTML pages in SharePoint are Site Pages built from HTML content that can be created with Copilot or uploaded, and run in a sandboxed iframe inside the tenant.

faq.a: They are SharePoint pages built from HTML content and stored in the Site Pages library like modern pages. They can be generated with Copilot or created by uploading a .html file or folder.
faq.q: What are HTML pages in SharePoint?

faq.a: A Microsoft 365 Copilot license is needed to create or edit these pages with Copilot. Contributors can upload and publish HTML pages without one.
faq.q: Is a Microsoft 365 Copilot license required?

faq.a: The HTML renders in a sandboxed iframe isolated from the SharePoint header and navigation, with Content Security Policy rules. Outbound API calls and cross-tenant communication are blocked, and external links require the domain on the site's HTML Field Security allow list.
faq.q: How is custom HTML kept secure in SharePoint?

sharepoint-html-pages.long:
HTML pages in SharePoint are a page type that lets a team publish custom HTML content as a page in SharePoint, for example content generated with the help of AI. The pages are stored in the Site Pages library, like modern pages, and stay inside the tenant's security boundary. The appeal is that a team can present something designed freely, such as an interactive overview or a styled report, without hosting it on an external site.

According to Microsoft Support documentation, there are two main ways to create such a page. The first is to create it with Copilot from a prompt; the generated page uses the site theme and aims for accessibility. The second is to upload a single .html file or a folder containing its files, where the HTML file may be up to 10 MB. Existing pages can be edited directly on text and images, or through a Copilot chat pane. Publishing makes the page visible only to people who already have permission, so existing SharePoint permissions continue to apply.

Security is a central part of the design. The HTML renders in a sandboxed iframe that is isolated from the SharePoint header and navigation, with Content Security Policy rules applied on top. Arbitrary fetch or outbound API calls and cross-tenant communication are blocked. JavaScript may run only if it is inline in the same file or loaded from Microsoft-managed libraries, such as Chart.js, Mermaid, React, Fluent UI and Babylon. localStorage is unavailable. Links to external domains require that the domain is on the site's HTML Field Security allow list.

Licensing and administration follow a split. Creating or editing with Copilot needs a Microsoft 365 Copilot license, while contributors can upload and publish without one. Site owners can disable HTML files per site, but tenant admins cannot disable them tenant-wide. The documentation also lists unsupported items: co-authoring, comments, mobile editing, templates and promoting a page to news.

The topic is related to SharePoint, which is the broader product where the pages live and where existing permissions and governance apply. It is also related to Microsoft 365 Copilot, which can help produce HTML content from a description, and to Vibe coding, since describing a page in plain language and letting an AI generate the markup is a typical way to create this kind of content.

Typical scenarios include an internal knowledge page, a project dashboard or an onboarding guide that needs more layout freedom than standard SharePoint page parts offer. Content created this way should still be reviewed before publishing, because generated markup can contain mistakes. No M365.FM episode in the knowledge base is linked to this topic directly, and the exact capabilities and limits are best checked in the official Microsoft documentation.

sharepoint-hub-sites.desc: SharePoint hub sites group related team and communication sites into a flat cluster with shared navigation, branding and search scope, without changing permissions.

faq.a: No. Associating a site with a hub does not change its permissions, and content rolled up in the hub is security-trimmed so people only see what they can already access.
faq.q: Do SharePoint hub sites change the permissions of associated sites?

faq.a: No. A site belongs to only one hub, although a site can move between hubs without its URL changing, and hubs can be associated with each other to widen the search scope.
faq.q: Can a SharePoint site belong to more than one hub?

faq.a: Associated sites inherit the hub's theme and shared navigation. The hub also provides a search scope and web parts such as News, Highlighted content, Sites and Events that roll up content from its sites.
faq.q: What do associated sites inherit from a hub site?

sharepoint-hub-sites.long:
SharePoint hub sites are a SharePoint feature for organizing an intranet by connecting families of related team sites and communication sites. Instead of building a strict hierarchy, a hub expresses relationships as associations. A site is associated with a hub, and it can later move to another hub without its URL changing. Because the structure is flat, the hub does not own the sites that join it, and association does not alter who can access them.

A hub is usually created from a communication site. Creating one requires SharePoint administrator rights, while hub site owners manage it afterwards, and administrators can also control who is allowed to associate sites with a hub. Once a site is associated, it inherits the hub's theme and shared navigation, so visitors see a consistent look and a common set of links across the cluster. A site can belong to only one hub, although hubs can be associated with each other to widen the shared search scope.

One purpose of a hub is to bring content from its member sites into a single place. Hub web parts such as News, Highlighted content, Sites and Events can roll up content from all associated sites or from a chosen subset. News flows from the associated sites up to the hub, not in the opposite direction. The hub also provides a search scope that covers its associated sites, which lets users search across the whole group at once.

Permissions are an important point when planning hubs. Associating a site with a hub does not change its permissions, and rolled-up content is security-trimmed, meaning people only see items they can already access. A hub therefore organizes and surfaces content without opening it up to additional audiences. Access still has to be managed on each individual site.

Typical designs follow how an organization is structured. Functional hubs group sites by business area, for example HR, finance or IT, while regional or location hubs group sites by geography. The Microsoft Learn planning guidance also lists recommended and technical limits for hubs, navigation links and search scope, which are worth checking before a hub design is finalized. Subsites remain a classic SharePoint feature, and hubs are the association-based alternative for relating sites to one another.

Hub sites also appear in discussions of Microsoft 365 architecture. The M365.FM episode "7 Microsoft 365 Architecture Mistakes That Cost Millions" lists hub site design among the frameworks for defining a strategic vision. In that episode, using SharePoint hub sites to create a logical structure sits alongside consistent metadata and taxonomy, simplified permission management, lifecycle governance and user-centric navigation based on user journeys. The episode frames these as ways to support adoption, noting that a platform employees do not use generates no return.

In practice, decisions around hub sites concern which sites belong together, which site serves as the hub, who may associate sites, and how navigation and branding should be shared. Because hubs do not change permissions, they are often paired with separate permission and governance planning. The official documentation does not state specific license requirements for hub sites.

sharepoint-knowledge-agent.desc: SharePoint Knowledge Agent is the preview name for the agent now documented as Copilot in SharePoint, which answers questions, suggests metadata and runs workflows on SharePoint content.
sharepoint-knowledge-agent.long:
SharePoint Knowledge Agent is an agent for SharePoint that works on the content stored in sites and libraries. It was previewed under this name and is now documented by Microsoft as Copilot in SharePoint; the older name survives mainly in PowerShell parameter names. According to the Microsoft Learn page on getting started, the agent brings agentic abilities into SharePoint, so teams can ask questions in natural language, run workflows, and generate sites, pages, interactive reports and Office files from SharePoint content.

In practice, the agent is used for three kinds of work that the sources describe. It can suggest metadata for documents, which makes content easier to find and use. It can apply simple rules written in natural language to automate parts of document handling. And it can answer questions directly from SharePoint content across libraries, so users do not have to browse folder structures to find an answer. The episode "Multi-Agent AI with Microsoft Copilot and SharePoint – Reshmee Auckloo [MVP]" places the agent in the context of multi-agent AI solutions, describing it as a way to manage content, automate workflows and enrich documents with metadata inside a shared SharePoint environment.

Licensing and billing are part of the decision. Microsoft Learn states that everyday tasks are covered by a Microsoft 365 Copilot license, while heavier work such as processing large content sets, building whole sites or running multi-step AI workflows needs usage-based billing and Copilot credits. Without credits, advanced tasks stop and the agent explains what it could not finish. A Microsoft-managed OpenAI reasoning model is used and needs no configuration by the tenant.

Governance is the main theme of the episode "Govern SharePoint Knowledge Agent with Human Oversight" (2025-11-03). The episode describes the agent as marketed as an autonomous librarian but behaving, in practice, like an overconfident intern that needs supervision. It says the agent amplifies whatever disorder already exists: auto-tagging mirrors inconsistencies in the library, such as duplicate or variant columns, and rules do not always fire reliably. The recommendation that follows from the episode is to keep a human reviewing the agent's suggestions and to clean up metadata structures before relying on automated tagging. This theme is repeated in the related-episode list of "The Human Side of CRM with Thomas Sandsør [MVP]", which groups the governance episode with others on human judgment and oversight of autonomous AI agents.

Administrators have several controls according to Microsoft Learn. Availability can be managed through site AI settings, through Restricted Content Discovery, or through a tenant-level PowerShell scope setting that is limited to a fixed period. These options let an organization restrict where the agent operates while content structure and permissions are reviewed.

There are also stated limits. The agent is not available in GCC, GCC High, DoD, air-gapped clouds or the cloud operated by 21Vianet. Language support is limited to languages that appear in both the SharePoint and Copilot language lists. Organizations evaluating the agent therefore need to check their cloud environment and languages first, then decide on licensing, credit consumption and the level of human review applied to tagging and rule results.

sharepoint-managed-metadata.desc: SharePoint managed metadata uses centrally managed term sets in the term store and managed metadata columns to give sites consistent vocabularies for tagging, navigation and search.

faq.a: It is a SharePoint feature that lets organizations define centrally managed term sets in the term store and use them in managed metadata columns across sites. This gives consistent vocabularies for tagging, navigation and search.
faq.q: What is SharePoint managed metadata?

faq.a: The term store is the central location where term sets are defined and managed. Managed metadata columns on sites draw their values from these term sets.
faq.q: What is the term store in SharePoint?

faq.a: It is used to keep tagging consistent across sites and to support navigation and search by reusing the same centrally managed terms.
faq.q: What is SharePoint managed metadata used for?

sharepoint-managed-metadata.long:
SharePoint managed metadata is a feature of SharePoint that allows organizations to define centrally managed term sets in the term store and apply them through managed metadata columns across sites. It provides a shared, controlled vocabulary instead of free-text tagging that varies from site to site.

The term store is the central location where term sets are created and maintained. A managed metadata column in a list or library draws its allowed values from a term set, so contributors select from an agreed list of terms rather than typing their own. Because the same terms are reused across sites, content is labeled consistently.

This consistency supports three main uses named in the Microsoft documentation: tagging content, building navigation, and improving search. Consistent terms can be used to organize and filter items, to drive navigation structures, and to make search results more predictable, since items sharing a term are described in the same way.

Managed metadata is a concept within the broader Microsoft ecosystem of SharePoint information architecture. Further technical detail is available in the official Microsoft Learn documentation for SharePoint managed metadata. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic.

sharepoint-premium.desc: SharePoint Premium is an add-on for SharePoint covering document processing, content AI, eSignature and advanced management, formerly marketed as Microsoft Syntex.

faq.a: SharePoint Premium is the current name for the capabilities formerly marketed as Microsoft Syntex. The episode "Automate Document Processing with Microsoft Syntex" describes Syntex being folded into SharePoint Premium.
faq.q: Is SharePoint Premium the same as Microsoft Syntex?

faq.a: It provides document processing, content AI, eSignature and advanced management for SharePoint. Examples from the episodes include extracting fields such as vendor, totals and dates, and supporting governance with SharePoint Advanced Management.
faq.q: What can SharePoint Premium do?

faq.a: The episodes say that structured, governed content gives Copilot better material to answer from. SharePoint Premium is presented as a way to prepare content so Copilot answers are grounded rather than guessed.
faq.q: How does SharePoint Premium relate to Copilot?

sharepoint-premium.long:
SharePoint Premium is a set of add-on capabilities for SharePoint, developed by Microsoft, that covers document processing, content AI, eSignature and advanced management. It was formerly marketed as Microsoft Syntex, and the older name still appears in some episodes and documentation. It is classified as a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool, and it is part of SharePoint rather than a separate platform.

The product is aimed at organisations that want to extract information from documents, automate content-heavy processes and govern content at scale. In practice this means turning files in SharePoint and OneDrive into structured, searchable content. The episode "End Content Silos with Microsoft Syntex" describes classifiers and extractors that tag details such as vendor, totals and dates, so that files can be organised automatically, drive Power Automate workflows and surface information across Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Purview.

One framing in the episodes is that SharePoint Premium brings three areas together: content experiences, content processing and governance. "Automate Document Processing with Microsoft Syntex" describes this as a brain (content experiences), muscle (content processing) and bouncer (governance). The episode argues that folding Syntex into SharePoint Premium is Microsoft consolidating these areas into one platform, so that content becomes structured, governed and queryable, which in turn gives Copilot better material to answer from. For getting started, the episode recommends using prebuilt models first, measuring the time saved and then scaling.

Governance is a second major theme. "Reduce SharePoint Premium SAM and PAYG AI Costs" discusses SharePoint Premium together with SharePoint Advanced Management (SAM) as the governance backbone that keeps Copilot from turning oversharing into a data leak. The episode walks through Data Access Governance (DAG) to spot risky sites, Restricted Access Control (RAC) to limit visibility, Site Access Reviews to make site owners accountable, and AI Insights to prioritise fixes. Its title also points to cost considerations around SAM and pay-as-you-go (PAYG) AI usage.

"AI Contract Management with SharePoint Premium and Copilot" applies the same ideas to a concrete scenario. It describes how data drifts into disorder over time and how structure, governance and AI models give content purpose. The episode presents practical steps for deploying AI on content so that Copilot answers are grounded in governed, cleaner data rather than guesswork. Contracts are a typical example because they combine repeating fields, approval steps and compliance requirements.

SharePoint Premium is related to several other Microsoft offerings. AI Builder also offers document-oriented AI models, so teams choosing a document-processing approach often compare the two. Microsoft Purview supplies compliance and information protection that complement the governance side. SharePoint Advanced Management administers content and sites and is the part most closely tied to oversharing control.

"What Is SharePoint Premium - Simply Explained" gives an overview for readers new to the topic. It explains what the product is, where it fits in a SharePoint environment, and which practical questions to ask before using it for business processes and content at scale. It also lists features such as e-signatures and document processing as part of the add-on. Because it is an add-on, a typical decision is whether the volume and value of document-driven processes justify enabling it, and where to start.

sharepoint-quick-steps.desc: SharePoint quick steps are custom command bar buttons for SharePoint and Microsoft Lists that run an action, such as moving a file or setting a status, in one click.
sharepoint-quick-steps.long:
SharePoint quick steps are custom commands for a SharePoint or Microsoft Lists list or library. They appear in the command bar and run an action on the selected item with a single click.

Typical actions described for quick steps include moving a file or setting a status on an item. Instead of opening an item, editing a field or copying a file by hand, a user selects the item and chooses the quick step from the command bar. This makes repeated tasks in a list or library faster and more consistent.

Quick steps belong to the list or library where they are defined, so the commands shown in the command bar depend on the location in which they were set up. They apply to the item or items the user has selected at that moment.

No further details, such as setup steps, licensing requirements or availability by plan, are provided in the source facts for this entry, and no M365.FM episodes are linked to it yet.

sharepoint-sharing-links.desc: SharePoint sharing links grant access to a file or folder through the Share option in SharePoint and OneDrive, using scopes such as anyone, organization or specific people.

faq.a: They are links created with the Share option in SharePoint and OneDrive that grant access to a file or folder.
faq.q: What are SharePoint sharing links?

faq.a: The scopes listed are anyone, people in the organization, people with existing access, and specific people.
faq.q: What scopes can a SharePoint sharing link have?

faq.a: They are created with the Share option in both SharePoint and OneDrive.
faq.q: Where can sharing links be created?

sharepoint-sharing-links.long:
SharePoint sharing links are links created with the Share option in SharePoint and OneDrive. Each link grants access to a specific file or folder, so a person can open the item without needing to locate it in a library themselves.

A sharing link is defined by its scope, which determines who can use it. The scopes described for these links are anyone, people in the organization, people with existing access, and specific people. The choice of scope controls how broadly a link can be used and whether recipients must be identified individually.

Because the same Share option appears in both SharePoint and OneDrive, sharing links are a common way of giving access to content stored in either service. The link scope is the main setting that distinguishes one type of sharing link from another.

No related topics or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no further details beyond the scopes above are available here.

sharepoint-site-provisioning.desc: SharePoint site provisioning is the governed creation of SharePoint sites and Teams workspaces through request, approval and templates that apply ownership and lifecycle rules.

faq.a: It is the governed process of creating SharePoint sites and Teams workspaces through a request and approval step and standard templates, so that ownership, naming, sensitivity and lifecycle settings are applied from the start.
faq.q: What is SharePoint site provisioning?

faq.a: The episode "Automate SharePoint Sites with Site Scripts and PnP Templates" says automation saves time, reduces errors, gives every site the same structure, applies permissions correctly from the start and scales as an organization grows.
faq.q: Why automate SharePoint site provisioning?

faq.a: The episode "PnP PowerShell vs PnP Framework" describes PnP PowerShell as imperative, fast and surgical, and PnP Framework provisioning as declarative, consistent and scalable for repeatable, audited site builds.
faq.q: What is the difference between PnP PowerShell and PnP Framework for provisioning?

sharepoint-site-provisioning.long:
SharePoint site provisioning is the governed process of creating SharePoint sites and Teams workspaces. Instead of letting sites appear ad hoc, creation runs through a request and approval step and uses standard templates, so that ownership, naming, sensitivity and lifecycle settings are applied from the start. The goal is a consistent starting point for every site, rather than cleaning up settings after a workspace already exists.

In practice, provisioning covers the decisions made at the moment a site is created: who owns it, what it is called, how it is classified, which structure it starts with, and how long it is expected to live. The episode "Automate SharePoint Sites with Site Scripts and PnP Templates" describes the manual route as selecting "Create", picking a site collection, adding details such as title and URL, setting permissions and finishing the creation. It then explains why automation is attractive: it saves time, reduces errors, makes every site follow the same structure, applies permissions correctly from the start and scales as an organization grows. Automation also lets users trigger site creation and configuration themselves, so administrators spend less time on repetitive tasks.

Templates are the core mechanism. The same episode covers site scripts and PnP templates as ways to automate the configuration of new sites. The episode "PnP PowerShell vs PnP Framework" compares two approaches to repeatable, audited, at-scale site builds. It describes PnP PowerShell as imperative, fast and surgical, and PnP Framework provisioning as declarative, consistent and scalable. It also discusses a decision playbook, modular template patterns, versioning strategies and a migration path, and it addresses the common problem of templates that work in a development environment but fail in production.

Provisioning also sits within wider governance. The episode "Why Microsoft 365 Governance Strategies Fail" lists lifecycle and provisioning as a governance area.
