The same episode names other trade-offs, such as product availability restrictions compared with agreements like the Enterprise Agreement, and contrasts them with advantages such as flexible monthly or annual billing and a single point of contact for support. For an organization deciding between CSP and a traditional agreement, the presence or absence of Software Assurance is therefore one of the factors to weigh.

The second context is cost estimation for Azure Files and Azure File Sync. The episode "Azure Files - Simply Explained" says that when estimating the total cost of ownership for Azure Files, the licensing costs for servers registered with Azure File Sync should be considered, along with discounts for Software Assurance. The episode "Migrate Azure File Sync to Managed Identity" repeats this point. It describes per-server licensing fees as monthly fees for each Windows File Server registered with Azure File Sync, and notes that discounts are available with Software Assurance and Azure Arc. These fees are described as not part of Azure billing but as adding to the total cost of ownership. In these cases Software Assurance appears as a possible way to reduce ongoing licensing expenses for on-premises servers that are connected to a cloud service.

Taken together, the episodes show Software Assurance as a factor that influences both which licensing agreement fits an organization and how the cost of hybrid setups is calculated. It matters most for organizations that keep on-premises Microsoft software in use alongside cloud services. When evaluating options, the sources suggest checking whether the chosen agreement includes Software Assurance, whether it affects discounts for specific services such as Azure File Sync, and how that compares with agreements that lack it. For exact terms, benefits and eligibility, the official Software Assurance FAQ in Microsoft's licensing documentation is the authoritative source, since the episode excerpts only touch on the topic in passing.

software-bill-of-materials.desc: A software bill of materials (SBOM) is a machine-readable inventory of the components and dependencies that make up a piece of software, used for security management.

faq.a: A software bill of materials (SBOM) is a machine-readable inventory of the components and dependencies that make up a piece of software. It documents what a software artifact contains so that its composition can be reviewed.
faq.q: What is a software bill of materials (SBOM)?

faq.a: According to the repository documentation, the tool outputs SPDX 2.2 by default and can be set to SPDX 3.0. Both versions can be validated with the tool, while redaction only works for SPDX 2.2 SBOMs.
faq.q: Which formats does Microsoft's SBOM tool produce?

faq.a: It hashes the files of a drop directory and lists them in the SBOM, and it scans a build components path for project files such as csproj or package.json using the Component Detection library. License information is filled in through the ClearlyDefined API.
faq.q: How does the SBOM tool detect components?

software-bill-of-materials.long:
A software bill of materials (SBOM) is a machine-readable inventory of the components and dependencies that make up a piece of software. It records what a software artifact contains, including packages and files, so that the composition of a product can be inspected, tracked and checked. In practice, an SBOM serves as the list that a team or a customer can consult when they need to know which parts a given piece of software is built from.

The purpose of an SBOM is closely tied to security and supply chain management. When the contents of a software package are documented in a structured form, it becomes easier to manage components, identify what is installed and handle questions about dependencies. An episode of M365.FM touches on this in a PowerShell security context: in "Run Your Full Stack Locally with .NET Aspire", the episode lists the Software Bill of Materials as one of several security features and describes it as listing all components in install packages for better security management. It appears alongside other measures such as antimalware scanning of script blocks, Constrained Language Mode, Application Control and encrypted SecureString transfer in remoting sessions.

How an SBOM is produced can be seen in Microsoft's open-source SBOM tool, which generates software bills of materials for software artifacts of any variety. According to its repository documentation, the output is compatible with SPDX 2.2 by default, and SPDX 3.0 can be selected as well. Both versions can be validated with the tool. To build the inventory, the tool hashes the files in a drop directory and lists them in the files section of the SBOM. It also scans a build components path for project files such as csproj or package.json in order to detect packages and dependencies, using the Component Detection library. License information is filled in through the ClearlyDefined API. Each generated SBOM receives a unique namespace that is based on an organization-wide base URI.

The tool offers commands for generating an SBOM for a given package name, version and supplier, for validating an existing SBOM, and for redacting file references. Typical use is inside automated build processes: integration into CI/CD is described for GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps pipelines. For installation, the repository lists several routes, namely WinGet, Homebrew, a .NET tool, a Docker image and a NuGet package. This range of options lets teams on different platforms add SBOM generation to their existing build and release workflow.

There are limits to keep in mind when working with generated SBOMs. Redaction of file references only works for SPDX 2.2 SBOMs. The components that are detected also depend on the package formats that Component Detection supports, so an SBOM reflects what the scanner can recognize rather than guaranteeing a complete picture of every possible dependency. Teams therefore need to check that their package formats are covered and validate the output instead of assuming completeness.

A further decision concerns the format version. Because SPDX 2.2 is the default and SPDX 3.0 is optional, a team has to choose which version fits its consumers and tooling, and if redaction is required, the documentation indicates that SPDX 2.2 is the version that supports it. The episode on PowerShell security also places the SBOM next to change tracking and logging advice for a Microsoft 365 tenant, which frames it as one part of a broader set of practices for keeping software and environments manageable and secure.

software-entropy.desc: Software entropy is the gradual rise of disorder, complexity and unpredictability in software systems as undocumented changes, exceptions and dependencies accumulate.
software-entropy.long:
Software entropy is a concept describing the gradual increase of disorder, complexity and unpredictability in a software system over time. It arises when undocumented changes, one-off exceptions and growing dependencies accumulate without active maintenance, so that the system becomes harder to understand and to predict.

The term is used to explain why software that was once well structured tends to degrade if it is left unattended. Each individual change may seem small, but the combined effect of exceptions, hidden dependencies and missing documentation makes later changes riskier and less predictable. Active maintenance is the counterweight, since without it the accumulated disorder continues to grow.

In practice the concept serves as a way to discuss the long-term health of systems, including how changes are recorded, how dependencies are tracked and how exceptions are handled. It is a general idea rather than a feature of a specific product.

No specific episodes or related topics are currently linked to this entry on M365.FM, so this page limits itself to the general definition of the concept.

software-extensibility.desc: Software extensibility is a design principle for building systems so new functionality can be added or parts swapped later without rewriting the core.

faq.a: Software extensibility is a design principle of building systems so that new functionality can be added or parts swapped later without rewriting the core.
faq.q: What is software extensibility?

faq.a: It is commonly achieved through plug-ins, hooks and abstractions, which provide defined ways to add or replace behavior in a system.
faq.q: How is software extensibility typically achieved?

software-extensibility.long:
Software extensibility is a software design principle in which a system is built so that new functionality can be added, or existing parts replaced, at a later point without rewriting the core of the system. It is treated as a property planned into the architecture rather than something added afterward.

In practice, extensibility is typically achieved through mechanisms such as plug-ins, hooks and abstractions. Plug-ins allow separate components to be attached to a host application. Hooks define points where custom behavior can be inserted into existing processes. Abstractions separate what a component does from how it is implemented, so that one implementation can be exchanged for another while the surrounding system stays unchanged.

The concept is relevant wherever a platform is expected to serve needs that its original developers cannot fully anticipate, since it lets those needs be addressed by adding to the system instead of modifying its foundation.

No specific episodes, product relations or official documentation are linked to this entry on M365.FM at this time.

software-supply-chain-security.desc: Software supply chain security protects applications against risks from third-party packages, transitive dependencies, build pipelines and deployment artifacts.

faq.a: It is the protection of applications against risks introduced through third-party packages, transitive dependencies, build pipelines and deployment artifacts.
faq.q: What is software supply chain security?

faq.a: It covers the components and processes used to build and deliver software, including dependencies, build pipelines and deployment artifacts.
faq.q: Which parts of the software lifecycle does it cover?

faq.a: They are dependencies an application pulls in indirectly through the packages it uses directly. They are one of the risk sources that software supply chain security addresses.
faq.q: What are transitive dependencies in this context?

software-supply-chain-security.long:
Software supply chain security is the practice of protecting applications against risks that enter through the components and processes used to build and deliver them. These include third-party packages, transitive dependencies, build pipelines and deployment artifacts.

The concept covers the full path from source code to a running application. A weakness or compromise at any point along that path, such as a dependency pulled in indirectly or a step in a build pipeline, can affect the final software even when the application's own code is sound. For that reason, the topic is usually treated as a distinct area of security rather than only a matter of reviewing first-party code.

On M365.FM, Software supply chain security is listed as a concept in the knowledge base. No related entities or episodes are currently linked to it, and no official documentation links are associated with this entry. Further detail will be added if more information becomes available.

solution-architect.desc: A solution architect designs end-to-end technical solutions that meet business requirements and fit an organisation's existing systems and standards.

faq.a: A solution architect designs end-to-end technical solutions that meet business requirements and fit an organisation's existing systems and standards.
faq.q: What does a solution architect do?

faq.a: The episodes mention Azure Solutions Architect Expert and AZ-305 on the Azure side, and Power Platform Solution Architect Expert (PL-600) on the Power Platform side.
faq.q: Which Microsoft certifications relate to the solution architect role?

faq.a: The episode "7 Levels of Azure Administration: Beginner to Cloud Architect" describes starting with AZ-900 and Azure administration skills, from which professionals can move into roles such as Solutions Architect.
faq.q: How do people move into a solution architect role according to the episodes?

solution-architect.long:
A solution architect (also written solutions architect, or Lösungsarchitekt in German) is a role that designs end-to-end technical solutions. The work centres on two questions: does the design meet the stated business requirements, and does it fit the systems and standards an organisation already has in place? The role therefore sits between business needs and technical implementation, translating the first into a structure that engineering and operations teams can build and run.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the title appears in several career paths and in certification names. The episode "7 Levels of Azure Administration: Beginner to Cloud Architect" describes a staged route through Azure administration, starting with the AZ-900 certification and the basic terms of subscriptions, resource groups and workloads. According to the episode, professionals who excel in Azure administration can move into roles such as Solutions Architect or DevOps Engineer, which it links to job stability and earning potential. In this view the solution architect role builds on hands-on administration experience rather than replacing it.

Certifications are a recurring theme around the role. The episode "Automate Compliance Workflows with Microsoft Power Automate" lists Azure Solutions Architect Expert and DevOps Engineer Expert as examples of the Expert certification level, aimed at advanced professionals, alongside Foundational, Associate and Specialty levels. The same episode cites figures on pay and productivity for certified Microsoft professionals; these are the episode's claims and should be read as such. The episode "5 Microsoft Certifications That Boost Salary—and 3 to Skip" names AZ-305 among the high-value certifications for job prospects, together with SC-100, CISSP, AWS Certified Solutions Architect and PMP. It advises weighing the cost of a certification against the potential salary increase, aligning choices with long-term career goals, and combining certifications with real-world experience.

The role also exists on the Power Platform side. The episode "From SharePoint Developer to Power Platform Architect with Michel Mendes [MVP]" presents the Microsoft Certified: Power Platform Solution Architect Expert certification (PL-600) as the most important certification for a Power Platform Architect. The episode says this exam tests the ability to design, secure and deliver Power Platform solutions. It sets this against related certifications that cover fundamentals (PL-900), app making (PL-100) and functional consulting (PL-200). The episode "Build a Power Platform Career with Nathalie Leenders [MVP-MCT]" lists the Power Platform Solution Architect (PL-600) exam among the Power Platform certifications, next to PL-100, PL-200, PL-300, PL-400 and PL-500, and recommends choosing a certification that matches the kind of work a person wants to do.

Taken together, the episodes treat the solution architect as a senior step on a path that usually starts with fundamentals and practical experience. Typical decisions around the role include which platform to specialise in (Azure or Power Platform in the sources), which certification to pursue and in what order, and how to demonstrate design ability beyond an exam. The sources agree that a certification alone is not the whole picture; the episodes pair it with practical experience and with a deliberate career plan that is reviewed over time.

The material in the sources describes the role mainly through career and certification paths. It does not define a fixed list of deliverables or a single official job description, so the common thread is the one in the short definition: designing end-to-end solutions that satisfy business requirements and remain consistent with existing systems and standards.

solution-dependencies.desc: Solution component dependencies are relationships where one Power Platform or Dynamics 365 solution component relies on another, such as a flow depending on a table.

faq.a: It is a relationship in which one Power Platform or Dynamics 365 solution component, such as a flow, form or business rule, relies on another component like a table or field.
faq.q: What is a solution component dependency?

faq.a: Missing dependencies are a common cause of failed solution imports into another environment, because a component may refer to something that is not available in the target.
faq.q: Why do missing dependencies matter?

faq.a: Microsoft describes how to check solution dependencies in its Power Platform ALM documentation on Microsoft Learn.
faq.q: Where is this documented?

solution-dependencies.long:
Solution component dependencies describe relationships in Power Platform and Dynamics 365 in which one solution component relies on another. For example, a flow, form or business rule may depend on a table or field. These relationships determine which components must be present for others to work as intended.

The concept matters most when solutions are moved between environments. Missing dependencies are a common cause of failed solution imports into another environment. If a component refers to a table or field that does not exist in the target environment and is not included in the imported solution, the import can fail. Reviewing dependencies before export and import helps identify which components need to be included or already installed.

Microsoft documents how to check solution dependencies in its application lifecycle management (ALM) guidance for Power Platform. This guidance is the main reference for understanding how dependencies are surfaced and examined.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic, and no related entities are listed in the available information.

solution-layers.desc: Solution layers in Dataverse stack component definitions from a system layer through managed layers to one unmanaged layer, and the top layer usually sets runtime behavior.

faq.a: They are the component-level stacking of definitions in Dataverse: a system layer at the bottom, managed solution layers above it and a single unmanaged layer on top. The top layer usually determines runtime behavior.
faq.q: What are solution layers in Dataverse?

faq.a: The episode "Deploy Dynamics 365 Customizations with ALM Pipelines" recommends checking it before every release. It helps reveal which solution defines a component and whether an unmanaged change is overriding it.
faq.q: Why should the Solution Layers view be checked before a release?

faq.a: Managed solutions form the layers above the system layer, while changes made directly in an environment go into the single unmanaged layer on top. The episode advises using managed solutions for production environments.
faq.q: How do solution layers relate to managed and unmanaged solutions?

solution-layers.long:
Solution layers are the component-level stacking of definitions in Dataverse. Each component, such as a table, form or app element, can be defined in more than one place, and Dataverse keeps those definitions in an ordered stack instead of replacing one with another. At the bottom sits the system layer. Above it come managed solution layers, and on top there is a single unmanaged layer. In general, the top layer determines how a component behaves at runtime, which is why the concept matters whenever a change seems to have no effect in an environment.

The stack is built per component, not per solution. Two managed solutions that touch the same component each contribute a layer, and the order in which they were applied affects what the environment ends up using. Edits made directly in an environment, outside a managed package, land in the unmanaged layer and sit above everything beneath them. Because that unmanaged layer is one layer rather than a history of changes, a direct edit can override what a managed solution delivers without any visible deployment step.

This behavior ties solution layers closely to managed and unmanaged solutions. The episode "Power Platform Solutions - Simply Explained" lists managed and unmanaged as the two modes of a solution and covers solution layers as a topic of their own next to publishers, prefixes, dependencies and moving an app between environments. Together these explain why a component can look different in development than in a downstream environment, and why removing something can be blocked by what depends on it.

The practical decisions around solution layers concern what is deployed into which environment. The episode "Deploy Dynamics 365 Customizations with ALM Pipelines" names deploying unmanaged solutions into UAT or Production for quick fixes as a common mistake that can lead to long-term chaos and painful troubleshooting. Its advice is to use managed solutions for production environments and to check the Solution Layers view before every release. Reviewing the layers of a component shows which solution currently defines it and whether an unmanaged customization is sitting on top of it.

Solution layers also appear as a design device and as a cost of complexity. The episode "Microsoft Dataverse as a Business Data Backbone" describes standing up solution layers named Core, Extensions and App as part of application lifecycle management, structuring customizations so that foundation, additions and the application itself are kept apart. The episode "SharePoint Lists vs Model-Driven Apps: Avoid Overbuilding" lists solution layers among the things that Dataverse brings along, together with licensing, security matrices, environment sprawl and governance latency. It argues that for simple needs these overheads can outweigh the benefit, so the layering model is worth taking on only when the scenario actually calls for Dataverse.

In short, solution layers describe where a component's definition comes from and which definition wins. Knowing the order of system, managed and unmanaged layers helps with troubleshooting unexpected behavior after a deployment, with keeping production environments clean, and with planning how customizations are packaged across environments.

solution-publisher.desc: A solution publisher is the owner label of a Power Platform solution that sets a naming prefix and controls which components other publishers may change.

faq.a: It acts as the owner of components created in its solutions, decides which changes other publishers may make to them, and defines the prefix added to the names of custom metadata such as tables and columns.
faq.q: What does a solution publisher control in Power Platform?

faq.a: No. Metadata names cannot be renamed after creation, so the prefix should be set before any apps or metadata are built. A publisher set on a component in a managed solution also cannot be changed.
faq.q: Can the publisher prefix be changed after components are created?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn advises creating a dedicated publisher with a meaningful name instead of using the default, and using a single publisher so the layering model can be changed later.
faq.q: Should a project use the default publisher?

solution-publisher.long:
A solution publisher is the owner label attached to a Power Platform solution. Every solution has a publisher, which is chosen when the solution is created. The publisher indicates who developed the app and acts as the owner of the components created in its solutions. It also defines the prefix that is added to the names of custom tables and columns. In Dynamics 365 and Power Platform projects, the publisher is one of the first things to settle before any customization work begins.

The publisher serves two main purposes. First, it identifies ownership. The owner decides which changes other publishers may make to the components it owns, and ownership can move within one publisher but not across publishers. Second, it supplies a prefix, such as a short company name, which is added to the names of the metadata the publisher creates. This prefix helps avoid naming collisions when solutions from different publishers are installed in the same environment. The episode "Deploy Dynamics 365 Customizations with ALM Pipelines" describes the publisher as the identity for customizations: it tells the system who created each component, which matters when solutions move between environments or when several teams work in the same system. It gives the example of a publisher prefix "abc", which the system then adds to every new component, such as a new table.

Timing matters because metadata names cannot be renamed after creation. The prefix should therefore be set before any apps or metadata are built. The same applies to the publisher itself: once a publisher is set on a component in a managed solution, it cannot be changed. A prefix chosen casually, or left at a default value, stays attached to the components that carry it.

Without a custom solution, work lands in the default system solutions, which are tied to default publisher settings. Microsoft Learn advises creating a dedicated publisher with a meaningful name instead of relying on the default. It also advises using a single publisher across solutions, so that the layering model can be changed later. Using one consistent publisher keeps ownership clear and avoids situations where components of one solution cannot be modified from another because they belong to a different publisher.

In practice, the publisher comes up in several typical situations. A team starting a new project creates the publisher first, sets a short and recognizable prefix, and then creates the solution. A team that automates deployments uses clear naming and versioning together with the publisher, so that the same identity travels from development to test and production environments. A company with several teams or partners has to decide whether to share one publisher or separate them, keeping in mind that ownership cannot be transferred across publishers and that components from different publishers can only be changed as far as their owner allows.

The publisher should not be confused with a marketplace publisher. The episode "The Hard Way to Get Listed on Microsoft Marketplace" covers a different concept: Publisher and Offer IDs that must be correct and active when an app is submitted for review, with incorrect or inactive IDs listed as a common error. That publisher account concerns marketplace listing, while the solution publisher discussed here concerns component ownership and naming inside Power Platform environments.

In short, the solution publisher is a small setting with long-lasting effects. It determines the naming prefix of custom tables and columns, records who owns each component, and governs how other publishers can change those components. Because neither the prefix nor the publisher on a managed component can be changed afterward, the recommended approach in the sources is to define one dedicated, meaningfully named publisher up front and use it consistently.

solutions-partner-designation.desc: Solutions Partner designation: Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program status per solution area, earned via the Partner Capability Score, replacing Silver and Gold competencies.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program designation awarded per solution area, such as Modern Work, Security or Data & AI. A partner earns it by reaching the required Partner Capability Score.
faq.q: What is the Solutions Partner designation?

faq.a: It replaced the former Silver and Gold competencies. According to the M365.FM episode on partner designation restructuring, legacy designations no longer qualify for incentives.
faq.q: What did the Solutions Partner designation replace?

faq.a: By reaching the required Partner Capability Score in a given solution area. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Partner Journey: From Enrollment to Growth" describes this as meeting specific customer outcome criteria.
faq.q: How does a partner earn a designation?

solutions-partner-designation.long:
The Solutions Partner designation is a status within the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program that is awarded per solution area, for example Modern Work, Security or Data & AI. A partner earns it by reaching the required Partner Capability Score for that area. The designation replaced the former Silver and Gold competencies, which means that the older competency model no longer serves as the basis for partner benefits.

The purpose of the designation is to show that a partner meets defined, measurable requirements in a specific solution area. Instead of a single general competency level, the model works area by area. A partner that is active in several areas can pursue a designation for each of them, and each designation is tied to its own thresholds. The M365.FM episode "How to Become a High-Performing Microsoft Partner" notes that each solution area has specific thresholds that must be met, and that understanding these levels and criteria helps a partner position itself within the program.

The score behind the designation is the Partner Capability Score, which is introduced in Microsoft's partner documentation. Reaching the required score in a solution area is the condition for the designation. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Partner Journey: From Enrollment to Growth" describes this in terms of customer outcome criteria: partners can achieve a Solutions Partner designation by meeting specific criteria tied to customer outcomes. The same episode lists related building blocks of the partner journey, including access to training and marketing resources through the Microsoft Partner Program, the use of the Microsoft Partner Center to manage partnerships and track performance, and advanced specializations that can add credibility and open further business opportunities.

The transition away from Silver and Gold is a recurring theme in the episodes. According to "The FY26 Partner Designation Restructuring Is Coming — Most Partners Aren't Ready", legacy designations such as the Silver and Gold competencies no longer qualify for incentives, and from October 1, 2023 only partners who achieve the new Microsoft Solutions Partner designation are eligible for those benefits. The episode frames this as a reason to adapt partner strategy to the new requirements and lists anticipated benefits of the restructuring, such as enhanced market recognition. The episode "How to Become a High-Performing Microsoft Partner" states that the new model replaces the Silver and Gold standards by January 22, 2025 and that transitioning to the Solutions Partner designation is essential for continued benefits. The two episodes give different dates for the replacement, so partners should check the current dates in the official partner documentation before planning.

In practice, a partner deciding how to approach the designation typically has to identify which solution areas match its business, understand the Partner Capability Score thresholds for those areas, and track progress through Partner Center. The episodes also describe the program benefits as being organized into three packages, and they point to performance metrics as the way a partner demonstrates its standing. Because the designation depends on measurable results rather than on a one-time qualification, ongoing attention to customer success and to the underlying metrics is part of keeping the status.

In summary, the Solutions Partner designation is the current per-area recognition in the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program. It is earned by reaching the required Partner Capability Score, it superseded the Silver and Gold competencies, and it is the status that governs eligibility for program incentives and benefits. The related M365.FM episodes treat it as a central step in the partner journey, from enrollment through growth, and as the main point to address for partners still operating under the legacy competency model.

source-of-authority.desc: Source of authority (SOA) names the directory with final say over an object's identity attributes in hybrid identity; Entra ID can take over synced groups and users.

faq.a: It is the directory that has final say over an object's identity attributes. Microsoft Entra ID can take over the source of authority for synced groups and users from on-premises Active Directory.
faq.q: What does source of authority mean in hybrid identity?

faq.a: No. According to the documentation, the change applies only to the named group and is not recursive, so nested groups stay on-premises unless each is converted individually.
faq.q: Is a source of authority change applied to nested groups automatically?

faq.a: Yes. Cloud-managed groups can be provisioned back to AD DS with Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync, which requires steps such as universal group scope and a directory extension mapping for the distinguished name.
faq.q: Can a cloud-managed group still be used by on-premises applications?

source-of-authority.long:
Source of authority (SOA) is a concept in hybrid identity. It describes which directory holds final say over an object's identity attributes. In a hybrid setup, an object such as a user or a group may appear in both on-premises Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID, but only one of the two is the place where it is authoritatively created, changed and deleted. Microsoft Entra ID can take over the source of authority for synced groups and users from on-premises Active Directory, which moves day-to-day management of those objects to the cloud.

The topic matters because objects that are synced to Entra ID but still ruled by on-premises Active Directory can be limited in what the cloud can do with them. The episode "Use Entra ID Group Writeback for Legacy File Servers" describes such objects as "zombies": visible in Entra but governed on-premises, which it says blocks modern governance such as dynamic membership, access reviews and APIs, and slows HR-driven provisioning. The episode's recommendation is to decide the source of authority per object rather than treating the whole directory the same way. Groups that matter to cloud workloads should be cloud-managed, while Group Writeback is used only where legacy systems still need on-premises visibility.

The Microsoft Entra documentation on group source of authority describes the mechanism for groups. Converting the source of authority of a group allows its management to move from Active Directory Domain Services to the cloud. The stated aims are more flexibility, modern governance and simpler administration. After conversion, security groups are managed in the Microsoft Entra admin center and through Microsoft Graph. The episode refers to this state as cloud-managed, using the isCloudManaged property.

Cloud-managed groups do not have to disappear from on-premises Active Directory. According to the documentation, they can be provisioned back to AD DS using Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync. This requires steps such as setting the group scope to universal and mapping the distinguished name through a directory extension. This pattern fits legacy file servers and other on-premises applications that still read group membership from Active Directory while administrators manage the group in the cloud. Typical uses listed in the documentation include cleaning up groups in AD that are no longer needed, moving distribution lists and mail-enabled security groups to Microsoft 365 groups, and writing Microsoft 365 groups back to AD for on-premises apps.

The documentation also names several limits that affect planning. The change applies only to the named group and is not recursive, so nested groups stay on-premises unless each one is converted individually. Local edits made to a cloud-managed group in Active Directory are overwritten at the next provisioning run. Dynamic membership rules are not carried over, and a custom LDAP connector is not supported. Security-enabled Microsoft 365 groups cannot be used to grant Exchange shared mailbox permissions. Rollback is only possible when the object's original authority was Active Directory.

The path outlined in the episode begins with an inventory: identify which groups exist, purge the "zombie" groups that are no longer needed, and classify what should stay on-premises and what should move. Together with the documentation, this gives a practical sequence for decisions around SOA: choose the authoritative directory per object, convert where cloud governance is needed, write back only for legacy dependencies, and account for the non-recursive scope and overwrite behavior before changing nested or heavily used groups.

sovereign-landing-zone.desc: Sovereign landing zone (SLZ) is an Azure landing zone variant with sovereignty controls for data residency, encryption and policy, built for regulated and public-sector customers.

faq.a: A Sovereign landing zone (SLZ) is a variant of the Azure landing zone that adds sovereignty controls for data residency, encryption and policy. It is built for regulated and public-sector customers.
faq.q: What is a Sovereign landing zone?

faq.a: It builds on the Azure landing zone and keeps its governed, pre-configured foundation, but adds stricter guardrails aimed at proving where data lives and who can control it.
faq.q: How does it differ from an Azure landing zone?

faq.a: Typical scenarios are government agencies, regulated industries and companies in the European Union that need clear evidence for data residency and control, often linked to Compliance and GDPR obligations.
faq.q: Which organizations typically need a Sovereign landing zone?

sovereign-landing-zone.long:
The Sovereign landing zone, abbreviated SLZ and also referred to as Sovereign Landing Zones, is a variant of the Azure landing zone that adds sovereignty controls. These controls cover data residency, encryption and policy. The variant is built for regulated and public-sector customers who have to show where their data lives and who can control it. It sits within the broader topic of Microsoft Azure and is documented in Microsoft's industry sovereignty guidance.

The concept builds directly on the Azure landing zone. An Azure landing zone is a pre-configured, governed foundation for running workloads in Azure, and the Sovereign landing zone keeps that idea while placing stricter guardrails on top. The practical purpose is to give organizations a structured starting point in which sovereignty requirements are expressed as part of the environment itself, rather than handled as separate checks after workloads have been deployed.

Three areas define the added controls. Data residency addresses the question of where data is stored and processed. Encryption addresses how data is protected and who holds control over it. Policy addresses how rules are enforced across the environment so that deployments stay within the boundaries an organization has set. Together these support customers who must provide evidence of residency and control, which is a common expectation in government agencies, regulated industries and companies operating in the European Union.

The Sovereign landing zone is closely related to Compliance and to GDPR. Data protection and regulatory obligations are the main reasons organizations look for sovereignty features in the first place, and a landing zone with built-in controls is one way to align a cloud environment with local and international regulations. Typical decisions around it include whether a standard Azure landing zone is sufficient or whether the stricter sovereign variant is needed, and which residency, encryption and policy requirements apply to the workloads that will run in it.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Infrastructure as Code and DevOps with Maik van der Gaag [MVP]" touches on this area. According to its description, many organizations now embed compliance and governance into their cloud strategies to align with local and international regulations, and the demand for regulatory compliance and data sovereignty drives the adoption of hybrid and sovereign cloud models. The episode says that Sovereign Landing Zones in Azure give a structured way to meet regional requirements and simplify policy management. It also states that with Azure infrastructure as code, both public and private environments can be managed from a single platform, which supports effective infrastructure management and helps keep deployments secure and compliant.

The episode does not describe the sovereign variant in technical detail, but its themes explain how the concept is typically applied. Landing zones of this kind are generally deployed as code, so the same practices discussed in the episode, such as Infrastructure as Code and DevOps, shape how a Sovereign landing zone is built, repeated and kept consistent. Treating the sovereignty controls as part of a code-managed foundation is what allows policy management to be simplified across environments.

In summary, the Sovereign landing zone is best understood as the Azure landing zone with sovereignty added: the same governed foundation, extended with controls for data residency, encryption and policy, aimed at customers who must demonstrate compliance and control over their data in Microsoft Azure.

sp-invoke-external-rest-endpoint.desc: sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint is a system stored procedure that lets Azure SQL Database and SQL Server 2025 call external HTTPS REST endpoints directly from T-SQL.

faq.a: It is a system stored procedure that calls an HTTPS REST endpoint passed in as an argument, so T-SQL code can reach external services such as Azure Functions, Event Hubs or Azure OpenAI.
faq.q: What does sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint do?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn lists SQL Server 2025, Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance and SQL database in Microsoft Fabric. On SQL Server 2025 and Managed Instance it must first be enabled through sp_configure.
faq.q: Where is sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint available?

faq.a: Only HTTPS is supported, redirects are not followed automatically, and payload size and concurrent calls are capped. In Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, only allowed Azure endpoints can be called directly; other targets must go through Azure API Management.
faq.q: What limits apply to sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint?

sp-invoke-external-rest-endpoint.long:
sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint is a system stored procedure that calls an HTTPS REST endpoint passed to it as an input argument. It makes it possible for T-SQL code to communicate with services outside the database engine. According to Microsoft Learn, it is available in SQL Server 2025, Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance and SQL database in Microsoft Fabric.

The procedure is typically used to connect the database with other cloud services. Documented examples include calling Azure Functions, reading or writing blob files, sending messages to Event Hubs and calling Azure OpenAI. For authentication it can use a managed identity or a database scoped credential. This turns a call to an external service into a single statement that can sit inside a stored procedure, a script or other T-SQL logic.

The procedure is controlled through a set of parameters. These cover the URL, the payload, headers, the HTTP method, a timeout, the credential, the response output and a retry count. The HTTP method is POST by default. The return value indicates the outcome: zero means the call ended with an HTTP 2xx status, while any other status code received is returned as the result. Retries happen only for certain status codes, and redirects are not followed automatically.

Several prerequisites and limits apply. A caller needs the EXECUTE ANY EXTERNAL ENDPOINT permission. On SQL Server 2025 and on Managed Instance, the feature is off until it is enabled through sp_configure. Only HTTPS endpoints can be called, there is a ceiling on payload size and a cap on concurrent calls. In Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, only a list of allowed Azure endpoints can be called directly; other targets have to be reached through Azure API Management. These restrictions matter when deciding whether a given integration can be built directly in the database or needs an intermediate layer.

Security is an explicit consideration. The Microsoft Learn page warns that the procedure can send data to an external location. Granting the permission, choosing the credential and limiting which endpoints are reachable are therefore decisions that belong to database and security administrators as much as to developers.

The M365.FM episode "When Azure SQL Becomes an Application Platform- APIs, Automation and AI with Dirceu Resende" names sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint as an important example of cloud capabilities in Azure SQL Database. The episode says it allows Azure SQL Database to communicate directly with REST endpoints, and describes this seemingly simple capability as something that fundamentally changes what developers can consider doing inside or close to the database. It frames this under the idea of the database becoming an active application component, in contrast to traditional architectures where the database sits passively behind an application layer. The same episode notes that Azure SQL Database receives cloud capabilities that may arrive later in traditional SQL Server releases, and that Microsoft Fabric and Power BI can consume Azure SQL information through increasingly integrated architectures.

In practice, the topic touches API integration, automation and AI scenarios. Teams weighing it typically compare calling an endpoint from T-SQL against placing that logic in an application tier, taking into account the supported endpoints, authentication method, error handling through the return value, and the data-exfiltration risk noted in the documentation.

sparkplug-b.desc: Sparkplug B adds industrial conventions to MQTT: a defined topic namespace, typed binary protobuf payloads, and birth and death messages for lifecycle state.

faq.a: It adds a standard topic namespace, a compact typed binary payload based on Google Protocol Buffers, and birth and death messages that describe the lifecycle state of edge nodes and devices.
faq.q: What does Sparkplug B add to MQTT?

faq.a: A death certificate uses the MQTT Last Will and Testament mechanism to tell applications that a device has gone offline, while a birth certificate describes the device and the data it can send.
faq.q: How does Sparkplug B show that a device is offline?

faq.a: No. According to the M365.FM episode on MQTT and OPC UA in Microsoft manufacturing, it adds industrial rules to MQTT but teams still need to define the meaning of their production events, including types, units and lineage.
faq.q: Does Sparkplug B define what production events mean?

sparkplug-b.long:
Sparkplug B is a specification that adds industrial conventions on top of MQTT publish/subscribe messaging. MQTT itself leaves topic naming and payload format open, so two systems that both speak MQTT can still be unable to understand each other. Sparkplug B closes part of that gap by fixing a topic structure, a typed binary payload format, and a set of messages that describe the lifecycle state of edge nodes and devices.

The topic namespace is built from a group ID, an edge node ID, an optional device ID and a message type. The message types named in the documentation are NBIRTH and NDEATH for edge nodes, DBIRTH and DDEATH for devices, NDATA and DDATA for data, NCMD and DCMD for commands, and STATE for the host application. Because every participant follows the same pattern, applications can predict where messages will appear and subscribe accordingly instead of relying on ad hoc naming agreements.

Payloads use a compact binary format based on Google Protocol Buffers. This keeps message size and bandwidth low, which is useful on WLAN or cellular links, and it supports richer data types than free-form text. Typed values are the main difference from loosely structured JSON, where meaning depends on convention and documentation outside the message.

The birth and death messages carry the lifecycle state. A birth certificate describes the device and the data it can send, which allows applications to discover sources automatically. A death certificate relies on the MQTT Last Will and Testament mechanism to tell applications that a device has gone offline. Data is sent by exception, meaning only changes are published, and connections are persistent with session awareness. The specification builds on MQTT 3.1.1 and 5.0 and is managed by the Eclipse Foundation within the Eclipse Tahu project.

In practice, Sparkplug B is considered when an edge or plant-floor environment needs interoperable MQTT communication between devices, gateways and host applications, and when knowing whether a source is online or offline matters as much as the values it sends. Decisions around it usually concern how far a team wants to standardize topics and payloads versus designing its own conventions on plain MQTT.

The M365.FM episode "MQTT and OPC UA in Microsoft Manufacturing: Azure IoT Operations + Fabric Architecture" places Sparkplug B in the context of Microsoft manufacturing architectures. The episode describes it as adding industrial rules to MQTT, such as defined topics and birth/death lifecycle state, but says it still does not replace the need to define what production events actually mean. In the same discussion the episode stresses semantic contracts covering types, units and lineage, warns against the cost of casual JSON, and notes that topic names are case-sensitive and call for strict lowercase conventions. It also connects the topic to Azure IoT Operations and Microsoft Fabric, which it describes as an edge data plane pattern running modular services on Arc-enabled Kubernetes and requiring hybrid IT/OT skills for a production-ready deployment.

spatial-audio.desc: Spatial audio renders voices by where speakers sit in a virtual space, so nearby people sound louder and distant ones quieter, as in Microsoft Teams and Mesh meetings.

faq.a: It is an audio option in which each participant's voice seems to come from their relative position on the meeting screen, helping listeners link a voice to a person in the gallery view. In 3D settings such as Microsoft Mesh, voices are rendered by position in the virtual space.
faq.q: What is spatial audio in Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Support, it needs wired USB stereo headphones or speakers, or a device's built-in stereo speakers; Bluetooth audio devices are not supported at present. The gallery must also show more than two participants.
faq.q: What is needed to use spatial audio in a Teams meeting?

faq.a: The documentation lists one-to-one calls and very large meetings as not yet supported. Teams also turns the feature off automatically when network bandwidth or memory runs short.
faq.q: Where is spatial audio not supported?

spatial-audio.long:
Spatial audio is a way of rendering voices according to where each speaker is positioned in a virtual space. People who are close sound louder and people who are farther away sound quieter. This makes it possible to hold natural side conversations in a 3D meeting, much as people do in a physical room, instead of mixing every voice into one flat stream.

In the Microsoft ecosystem the term appears in two related settings. The first is Microsoft Mesh, which, according to the episode "Microsoft Mesh - Simply Explained", is no longer a standalone metaverse platform. It has become an integrated feature inside Microsoft Teams that allows colleagues to meet in immersive 3D environments using avatars, spatial audio, and shared virtual meeting spaces. In that context spatial audio is one of the building blocks that makes a shared three-dimensional space feel like a place where people can move, gather in groups, and talk to those nearby.

The second setting is the standard Teams voice and video meeting. Microsoft Support describes spatial audio there as an immersive audio option in which each participant's voice seems to come from their relative position on the meeting screen. This lets listeners associate a voice with a person in the gallery view. It is switched on with a toggle in the audio settings, either before a meeting through the device settings or during a meeting through the more-actions menu, and the choice applies to future meetings.

The documentation lists several requirements and limits. The feature needs wired USB stereo headphones or speakers, or a device's built-in stereo speakers, and Bluetooth audio devices are not supported at present. The gallery must show more than two participants, so one-to-one calls are not supported, and very large meetings are also listed as not yet supported. Teams turns the feature off automatically when network bandwidth or memory runs short. With live interpretation, the original and translated audio play at the same volume unless the feature is turned off and the meeting rejoined, and music mode does not deliver high-fidelity audio while spatial audio is on. The support page names no licence requirement.

These details matter for anyone deciding whether to rely on the feature. Because it depends on the audio device and on available bandwidth and memory, results can differ between participants in the same meeting. Choosing wired stereo output, checking the gallery size, and knowing that automatic fallback can occur are practical points that follow from the documentation.

The episode "High-Stakes Hybrid Events with Microsoft Teams and Mesh" places spatial audio in the context of event quality. It introduces the "Ghost Town Effect", where participants abandon virtual experiences because of poor performance, lagging avatars, broken spatial audio, synchronization issues, and low engagement. The episode's point is that a visually impressive virtual environment can quickly become ineffective if the user experience suffers, and spatial audio that does not work properly is named among the causes. Both episodes treat spatial audio as part of the immersive experience in Mesh and Teams Immersive Spaces, and as something that has to perform reliably to add value over a traditional video call.

spec-driven-development.desc: Spec-driven development is an approach in which work begins from a written specification of a feature, which is turned into a code scaffold and then refined.
spec-driven-development.long:
Spec-driven development is an approach to building software in which work starts from a written specification of the intended feature. Rather than beginning with code, the specification describes what the feature should do, and that description serves as the starting point for implementation.

In this approach, the specification is turned into a code scaffold, which is then refined. AI coding agents can generate that scaffold from a plain-language spec, so the written description can be expressed in ordinary language rather than in a programming language. The generated scaffold is not treated as a finished result but as a base for further refinement.

The concept is relevant to anyone looking at how AI coding agents fit into software development workflows, since it frames the specification as the primary input and the generated code as a derived and adjustable output.

No related topics or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no official documentation or site is listed for the concept.

spec-kit.desc: Spec Kit is GitHub's open-source toolkit for spec-driven development with AI coding agents, using a constitution, specifications, plans and tasks.

faq.a: Spec Kit is GitHub's open-source, MIT-licensed toolkit that gives AI coding agents structured processes, templates and documented outcomes. Its core process is Spec-Driven Development, built around a constitution, specifications, plans and tasks.
faq.q: What is Spec Kit?

faq.a: It requires Python 3.11 or newer, uv and a supported AI coding agent, on Linux, macOS or Windows. Offline and air-gapped use and private catalogs are supported.
faq.q: What does Spec Kit require to run?

faq.a: The episode "How AI-Generated Identity Configuration Breaks Entra Security" describes it as the enforcement layer that binds architectural intent to executable rules. It says Spec Kit integrates with Microsoft Entra to lock identity policies and to support compliance reporting.
faq.q: How does the M365.FM episode describe Spec Kit?

spec-kit.long:
Spec Kit is an open-source, MIT-licensed toolkit from GitHub that gives AI coding agents structured processes, reusable templates and documented outcomes. Its core process is Spec-Driven Development, in which a written specification, rather than an ad hoc prompt, drives what the agent builds. The toolkit is organized around four artifacts: a constitution, specifications, plans and tasks.

In the standard workflow, a constitution is set up once per project. It states guiding principles such as code quality, testing and maintainability. For each feature, commands are then run in the agent chat. The specify command describes what to build, plan sets the technical approach, and tasks breaks the plan into work items. The implement and converge steps build the code and check it until convergence is reported. Optional steps cover clarification, checklists and consistency analysis. This sequence moves from intent to executable work in a defined order.

Bundled extensions add further processes. A bug-fixing extension ends in a verified, partial or failed verdict, and an idea-assessment extension ends in go, needs-clarification or kill. Custom processes can be assembled from integrations, extensions, presets, workflows and bundles. Community catalogs can be searched, though the documentation warns that listings are not audits or endorsements. Spec Kit requires Python 3.11 or newer, uv and a supported AI coding agent on Linux, macOS or Windows. Offline and air-gapped use and private catalogs are supported.

The M365.FM episode "How AI-Generated Identity Configuration Breaks Entra Security" (2025-12-31) places Spec Kit in a Microsoft identity context. There it is described as the enforcement layer that binds architectural intent to executable rules. According to the episode, architectural intent serves as a blueprint for system design, guiding technology choices and keeping them aligned with business goals. Enforcing that intent is said to improve reliability and security by validating that security controls function as intended.

The episode also says that Spec Kit integrates with Microsoft Entra to lock identity policies, supporting compliance with governance frameworks. It further says that automating compliance reporting with Spec Kit simplifies documentation and speeds up auditing, that strict permissions management minimizes unauthorized access to sensitive data and resources, and that real-time monitoring and alerts help identify compliance problems. These points are the episode's account of how the toolkit is used in that scenario, whereas the repository documentation describes the general spec-driven workflow.

Typical decisions around Spec Kit concern how much of a project's intent to capture in the constitution and specifications, which extensions or presets to adopt, and whether to use community catalogs or a private one. Teams working in restricted environments can rely on the offline and air-gapped support. Because the toolkit shapes how an AI coding agent produces code, it is relevant wherever AI-generated output, such as identity configuration for Microsoft Entra, needs to be checked against stated rules before it is accepted.

spf.desc: Sender Policy Framework (SPF) is an email authentication record published in DNS that lists the servers permitted to send mail on behalf of a domain.

faq.a: SPF is an email authentication record in DNS. It lists the servers that are allowed to send mail for a domain.
faq.q: What is Sender Policy Framework (SPF)?

faq.a: An SPF record is published in DNS as part of a domain's DNS configuration.
faq.q: Where is an SPF record stored?

faq.a: SPF is used to help receiving mail systems verify whether a message came from a server authorized to send email for the domain it claims to represent.
faq.q: What is SPF used for?

spf.long:
Sender Policy Framework (SPF) is an email authentication mechanism implemented as a record in DNS. The record lists the servers that are allowed to send email for a particular domain.

The purpose of SPF is to help receiving mail systems check whether a message claiming to come from a domain was sent by a server the domain owner has authorized. A receiving system can compare the sending server against the list in the domain's SPF record and use the result when deciding how to treat the message.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, SPF is one of the email authentication concepts that domain owners configure through DNS when setting up mail for their domains.

No related topics or episodes are linked to this entry on M365.FM at this time, so this page covers the definition and basic purpose of SPF only.

splunk.desc: Splunk is software for searching, monitoring and analyzing machine-generated data, used for log aggregation and SIEM, and discussed in M365.FM security episodes.

faq.a: Splunk is software for searching, monitoring and analyzing machine-generated data, used for log aggregation and SIEM. The M365.FM episodes mention it for centralized security monitoring and as a destination for telemetry and Azure data.
faq.q: What is Splunk used for?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Sentinel - Simply Explained" describes Splunk Enterprise Security as pay-per-ingested data plus a license, with a higher upfront cost but more control. Microsoft Sentinel is described as pay-per-data ingestion, with costs that rise with log volume.
faq.q: How does Splunk Enterprise Security pricing compare with Microsoft Sentinel in the episodes?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Event Hubs - Simply Explained" lists configuring integrations such as the Splunk Add-on as one step when working with Azure Event Hubs. Data is first sent to an Event Hub, for example using Azure Monitor.
faq.q: How can Azure data be sent to Splunk?

splunk.long:
Splunk is software for searching, monitoring and analyzing machine-generated data. It is typically used for log aggregation and as a SIEM (security information and event management) platform, where events from many systems are collected in one place so that security teams can search them, monitor them and look for anomalies. In the M365.FM episodes, Splunk appears mainly in a security operations context and as one of several tools that can sit alongside Microsoft services.

The episode "Microsoft Sentinel - Simply Explained" places Splunk Enterprise Security next to other SIEM and security options. In its pricing comparison, Microsoft Sentinel is described as pay-per-data ingestion, where costs rise with log volume. CrowdStrike Falcon is described as priced per endpoint, with a higher base price but lower add-on costs. Splunk Enterprise Security is described as pay-per-ingested data plus a license, with a higher upfront cost but more control. The episode lists data ingestion volume and retention settings as cost factors to consider when evaluating Microsoft Sentinel, noting that retention settings after the first 90 days may incur costs. The episode summary for this topic also frames a security operations stack being consolidated from Splunk into Microsoft Sentinel, which is a common decision point when organizations weigh a separate SIEM against a Microsoft-native one.

In "Azure Event Hubs - Simply Explained", Splunk shows up as an integration target. The episode's setup steps include creating an Event Hub namespace in the Azure portal, sending data to the Event Hub using Azure Monitor, setting up authentication with Azure AD, assigning roles for data access and configuring integrations such as the Splunk Add-on. This describes a pattern in which streaming data from Azure is forwarded to Splunk for analysis, so Splunk can remain part of the pipeline even when the data originates in Azure services.

Two episodes connect Splunk to Microsoft Copilot security. In "Protect Microsoft Copilot with Purview, DLP, and Insider Risk with Alan Cox [MVP]", Splunk Enterprise Security is named among the solutions to explore, together with Opsin, Wiz and CrowdStrike Falcon, to strengthen security posture alongside Microsoft Purview controls such as sensitivity labels, DLP and activity-log monitoring. In "Secure a Microsoft Copilot Rollout with Microsoft Purview", a table of tools describes Splunk Enterprise Security as providing centralized monitoring and analytics for Copilot activity and detecting anomalies and violations. In that table, Opsin helps security teams understand what Copilot can access and detect oversharing risks, while Microsoft Purview classifies and labels information. The episode pairs these with permission hygiene audits to enforce least-privilege access.

Splunk also appears in an automation context. In "Build Self-Healing Automation with Telemetry and Observability", it is listed among the connector options for telemetry integration, described as a source for logs and telemetry data. The same list includes Telegraf, NLog, Open Telemetry, Serilog, Fluent Bit and Logstash, and the episode notes that Microsoft Power Automate can link such sources to workflows so that responses can be automated based on real-time insights.

Across these episodes, Splunk is treated as one option in a wider tooling landscape rather than a Microsoft product. The recurring decisions are whether to keep Splunk as a separate SIEM, how its ingestion-based licensing compares with Microsoft Sentinel's pay-per-ingestion model, and how Azure Event Hubs or other connectors feed data into it.

spreadmart.desc: Spreadmart is a pejorative BI term for spreadsheet-based reporting built outside a governed data mart or warehouse, marked by duplicated datasets and inconsistent metric logic.

faq.a: Spreadmart is short for spreadsheet data mart. It refers to a setup built on spreadsheets or desktop databases that individuals or groups maintain to do work a data mart or data warehouse could do in a more structured way.
faq.q: What does the term spreadmart mean?

faq.a: Different people build them at different times with different data sources and metric definitions, which creates a fragmented view of the enterprise. Because the data is disconnected from its source, it cannot be verified or refreshed automatically, and undefined data can support false conclusions.
faq.q: Why do spreadmarts cause problems?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" describes spreadmart-style dashboards as a result of copy-paste sprawl in Power BI. It recommends a model-first approach in which the semantic model is a shared enterprise asset reused across reports and teams.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Fabric relate to the spreadmart problem?

spreadmart.long:
Spreadmart, short for "spreadsheet data mart", is a pejorative term from business intelligence. It describes a reporting and analysis setup built on spreadsheets or other desktop databases that individuals or small groups maintain themselves, doing work that a governed data mart or data warehouse could do in a more structured way. Wayne Eckerson of TDWI coined the term in 2002 as a criticism of this pattern.

A spreadmart usually appears when standard BI reporting feels too slow or too inflexible. A typical sequence is that an analyst exports a table into Excel and builds a private report. Copies of that file are then emailed around, edited, and re-saved. Once exported, the data is disconnected from its source, so it cannot be verified against the original system and cannot be refreshed automatically. Because different people build their own versions at different times, with different data sources and different definitions of the same metric, the organization ends up with a fragmented, decentralized view of the business. The core risk named in the sources is that undefined, disconnected data can support false conclusions and costly wrong decisions.

The term is a label for a symptom rather than a product or feature. In practice, discussions around spreadmarts focus on duplicated datasets, conflicting calculations and a lack of trust: two reports can show different numbers for what appears to be the same measure, and nobody can easily say which one is correct. The main alternatives are the structured approaches the term is defined against, namely data marts and data warehouses, where data is modeled once, sourced from governed pipelines, and shared.

The concept is not without counterarguments. Stephen Samild argues that spreadmarts fill roles that warehouses cover poorly. He names handling unstructured data, read-write analysis, avoiding long lead times when a new data source is needed, and free-form presentation. This view frames spreadmarts as a response to real gaps in formal BI rather than only as a governance failure, which is why the decision is often about balancing agility against consistency rather than eliminating spreadsheets outright.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the term comes up in discussions about Power BI sprawl. The M365.FM episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" (2025-08-12) describes environments that start fast and then stall under copy-paste sprawl: duplicated PBIX files, conflicting measures and "spreadmart" dashboards that nobody fully trusts. The episode says the fix is not another naming convention but a model-first architecture. In that approach, Microsoft Fabric treats the semantic model as an enterprise asset, one definitional layer reused across reports, workspaces and teams. The episode also points to calculation groups as a way to avoid endless YTD, QTD and TTM variants, keeping time intelligence, KPIs and business rules centralized and auditable.

Taken together, the sources present the spreadmart as both a historical BI criticism and a recurring modern pattern. The practical question for teams is where metric definitions live and who owns them. When definitions are scattered across individual files, the spreadmart pattern emerges; when they are centralized in a shared, governed model, reports can be built on a single consistent layer while still allowing self-service analysis on top of it.

sql.desc: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard domain-specific language for querying and managing data in relational database systems.

faq.a: SQL stands for Structured Query Language. It is the standard domain-specific language for querying and managing data in relational database systems.
faq.q: What does SQL stand for?

faq.a: SQL is used to query and manage data stored in relational database systems. This includes retrieving data and making changes to the data and its structure.
faq.q: What is SQL used for?

sql.long:
SQL, short for Structured Query Language, is the standard domain-specific language used to query and manage data in relational database systems. It is designed for working with structured data organized in tables, and it provides a common way to retrieve, insert, update and delete records as well as to define and manage database structures.

As a domain-specific language, SQL is focused on data operations rather than general-purpose programming. Its statements describe what data is wanted or what change should be made, and the database system determines how to carry that out. This makes it a foundational skill for anyone who works with relational databases, data analysis or reporting.

In the context of the Microsoft ecosystem, SQL is relevant wherever relational data is stored and queried. On M365.FM, SQL is documented as a concept entity. No specific related topics or episodes are linked to this entry at present.

sql-analytics-endpoint.desc: The SQL analytics endpoint is a read-only T-SQL surface over Delta tables that Microsoft Fabric provisions for items such as lakehouses.

faq.a: It is a read-only T-SQL surface over Delta tables that Microsoft Fabric provisions for items such as lakehouses. It lets users query lakehouse data with SQL.
faq.q: What is the SQL analytics endpoint in Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: No. It is described as read-only, so it is used for querying and analytics rather than for changing tables.
faq.q: Can the SQL analytics endpoint be used to write data?

faq.a: The episode says that using it as the default path for every workload is a major driver of capacity unit consumption, so routing all workloads through it can raise capacity use.
faq.q: Why does the SQL analytics endpoint matter for capacity?

sql-analytics-endpoint.long:
The SQL analytics endpoint is a read-only T-SQL surface over Delta tables that Microsoft Fabric provisions for items such as lakehouses. It gives people and tools a familiar SQL way to query data that is stored in OneLake, without requiring them to work through Spark. Microsoft documents the feature in its lakehouse SQL endpoint article under the Fabric data engineering section.

In practice, the endpoint is used for interactive analytics and for SQL-based reporting on lakehouse data. One episode describes the Lakehouse SQL Analytics Endpoint as a dedicated endpoint for running lakehouse SQL queries and interactive analytics. According to that episode, performance is helped by separating compute from storage, which allows compute resources to be scaled for query-heavy workloads, and by using optimized formats such as Delta tables to reduce IO and speed up query planning and execution. Because the surface is read-only, it is a way to read and analyze data, not a place where tables are written or transformed.

The endpoint also acts as a connection point for external tools. An episode on the Fabric data warehouse notes that the SQL analytics endpoint connects with third-party tools such as SQL Server Management Studio, so that users can run queries in an environment they already know. This is one reason the endpoint is often the first access path that SQL-oriented teams reach for.

The SQL analytics endpoint also has a cost dimension. The short description of the topic notes that, in the episode, using it as the default path for every workload is a major driver of capacity unit consumption. The takeaway is that the endpoint is convenient, but routing every workload through it is not neutral from a capacity standpoint. Choosing deliberately between SQL access and other ways of working with lakehouse data is part of managing capacity in Microsoft Fabric.

Governance and lineage are another area where the endpoint appears. The episode "Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Governance and Data Lineage" explains that lineage is shown at the artifact level, with the lakehouse and the warehouse appearing as separate nodes even when they share data in OneLake. It adds that a SQL analytics endpoint in a lakehouse can sometimes create extra nodes in the lineage view, and that different connection methods can create multiple nodes for the same source or destination. The episode also states that the lakehouse and warehouse cannot currently be merged into a single lineage node.

The topic is covered in several M365.FM episodes. "Optimize Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Performance" discusses how the endpoint affects performance. "Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse - Simply Explained" places it within the wider lakehouse picture, alongside OneLake, Delta tables and the medallion flow from raw files to trusted tables. "Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse - Simply Explained" mentions it as the way third-party SQL tools connect. Together, these episodes frame the SQL analytics endpoint as a read-only SQL access layer over Delta data whose use should be weighed against capacity consumption, performance needs and lineage clarity.

sql-database-in-fabric.desc: SQL database in Microsoft Fabric is a transactional database on the Azure SQL Database engine whose data is automatically replicated into OneLake for analytics.

faq.a: It is a transactional SQL database inside Microsoft Fabric, built on the same SQL Database Engine as Azure SQL Database. It is part of the Fabric Database workload and serves as an operational OLTP store.
faq.q: What is SQL database in Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: Data is automatically replicated into OneLake as Delta Lake parquet files, so it is available for analytics almost in real time. An SQL analytics endpoint is also created automatically in the workspace.
faq.q: How does its data become available for analytics?

faq.a: Billing runs through Fabric capacity. Access is authenticated with Microsoft Entra and requires read permission on the database item.
faq.q: How is SQL database in Microsoft Fabric billed and accessed?

sql-database-in-fabric.long:
SQL database in Microsoft Fabric is a developer-friendly transactional database that runs inside Microsoft Fabric. It is built on the same SQL Database Engine as Azure SQL Database and belongs to the Fabric Database workload. Its main role is that of an operational OLTP store: applications write and read transactional data in it, while the same data becomes available for analytics inside the Fabric platform.

The central mechanism is automatic replication. Data stored in the database is replicated into OneLake as Delta Lake parquet files, so it is available for analytical use almost in real time. An SQL analytics endpoint is created automatically in the workspace, which gives analytical workloads a way to query the replicated data without building a separate pipeline. This links transactional and analytical workloads in one environment, a combination that the documentation names as typical scenarios such as translytical applications, operational data stores and reverse ETL, alongside intelligent applications.

Developers can work with the database through several tools. The Fabric portal offers a web query editor, and SQL Server Management Studio, the MSSQL extension for Visual Studio Code and GitHub Copilot are also supported. Further features described in the documentation include automatic tuning with automatic index creation, vector data types for semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, a GraphQL API, and Git integration. On the security side, the documentation lists row-level and object-level security, customer-managed keys at workspace level, SQL auditing, and sharing without granting workspace access. Authentication uses Microsoft Entra, and access requires read permission on the database item.

Billing for the database runs through Fabric capacity rather than through separate Azure SQL pricing constructs. This matters when deciding between this item and a standalone Azure SQL Database, because consumption is tied to the capacity that the workspace already uses. The documentation also lists limits that influence that decision: only the default connection policy is supported, elastic pools in the Azure SQL sense do not exist, and some monitoring features are still in preview.

In the context of M365.FM, the product appears in the episode "Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse - Simply Explained".
