The choice between them is one of the central decisions in a telephony project, and the migration episode lists "calling plans or direct routing" as part of the planning work, alongside inventory and number planning, devices, emergency calling and user adoption.

Typical situations in which Teams Phone comes up are PBX replacement and the cloud migration of an existing telephone setup. The episode "Teams Phone Migration: Moving From a PBX to Cloud Calling Without Surprises" describes such a move as rarely a pure technology project, because numbers, devices, sites and people each run on their own timelines. It covers how to plan a migration, including taking inventory of what exists today, planning numbers, deciding on a connection model, selecting devices, handling emergency calling and supporting user adoption.

Other M365.FM episodes treat the topic from different angles. "Microsoft Teams Phone and Telephony | Simply Explained" is presented by Mirko Peters and explains how organizations can replace traditional PBX systems with a telephony platform integrated with Microsoft 365, supporting both internal collaboration and external voice calling. "Microsoft Teams Phone - Simply Explained" is a further explainer, but only a short description is on record for it. The episode "Set Up Microsoft Copilot in Teams Step by Step" touches on Teams Phone in its FAQ, stating that Copilot can assist in scenarios involving Teams Phone and hybrid meetings, for example by transcribing audio and generating recaps for attendees who joined by phone. It adds that availability may depend on the organization's configuration and on whether Teams Phone audio is captured for transcription.

Teams Phone also appears in a recommended-listening list in the episode "Shadow Data Discovery and Governance with Microsoft Purview", where the Teams Telephony explainer is suggested for understanding Teams calling and communication foundations. This reflects how the topic connects to governance and compliance subjects in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem. Official documentation for the feature is published by Microsoft on Microsoft Learn under the Teams Phone System overview.

teams-premium.desc: Teams Premium is an add-on licence for Microsoft Teams that adds meeting protection, branded meetings, AI-generated recaps and webinar features.

faq.a: Teams Premium is an add-on licence for Microsoft Teams that adds advanced meeting protection, branded meetings, AI-generated recaps and webinar features. It is a separate licence, not simply Teams at a higher price.
faq.q: What is Teams Premium?

faq.a: Both bring AI help into meetings, so organisations often have to decide which to buy first. The episode "Microsoft 365 Copilot vs Teams Premium: What to Buy First" compares the two for that decision.
faq.q: How does Teams Premium relate to Microsoft 365 Copilot?

faq.a: According to the episode "Cultural Nuance in Global Meetings Beyond Translation", features like live translation and Intelligent Recap improve accessibility and post-meeting analysis but do not interpret intent. The episode warns against overtrusting AI output.
faq.q: Does Teams Premium interpret meaning in global meetings?

teams-premium.long:
Teams Premium, also called Microsoft Teams Premium, is an add-on licence for Microsoft Teams. It was developed by Microsoft, is part of Microsoft Teams and is classified as a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool. It is not a separate meeting application. It is a licence layer that switches on capabilities which the normal Teams licence leaves off. According to the available facts, it was released in February 2023 as an add-on rather than a replacement for existing Teams licensing.

The product addresses several areas of meeting and event work: advanced meeting protection, branded meetings that carry a consistent company look, AI-generated recaps, and webinar features for larger events. It is aimed at organisations that hold sensitive meetings, want meetings to reflect their corporate identity, or run bigger events. The episode "Microsoft Teams Premium - Simply Explained" structures the topic in this way, walking through what the add-on is, meetings that think, keeping the meeting in the room, looking like your company, big events, appointments and bookings, features for the IT team, and who actually needs it. The same episode stresses that Teams Premium is not simply Teams with a higher price tag but a distinct add-on licence.

Because it is licensed as an add-on, a typical decision for administrators is whether the extra features justify licensing them for some or all users. Official Microsoft documentation on Teams add-on licensing is the reference for which features are included and how the licence is assigned. The episode "Set Up Microsoft Copilot in Teams Step by Step" notes that certain advanced capabilities, such as enhanced meeting recaps, deeper integrations or tenant-level controls, may be tied to Teams Premium or to specific Microsoft 365 plans, and recommends checking the organisation's licensing to see which features are enabled for a given account.

Teams Premium is related to Microsoft 365 Copilot, since both bring AI help into meetings. The episode "Microsoft 365 Copilot vs Teams Premium: What to Buy First" frames the choice between them as a purchasing-order question. It describes Copilot in Teams as an orchestration layer across meetings, chats and a central intelligence hub, running on Microsoft Graph so that it only surfaces what a user already has permission to see. In meetings, the episode says, Copilot turns live transcription into decisions, actions and mid-call catch-ups that can be exported when allowed. The comparison helps organisations judge whether meeting protection and branding, or broader AI assistance, comes first.

The episode "Cultural Nuance in Global Meetings Beyond Translation" discusses Teams Premium as an enabler rather than a solution. It says features such as live translation and Intelligent Recap improve accessibility and post-meeting analysis but do not interpret intent. Their value, according to the episode, lies in helping teams revisit conversations, identify ambiguity and analyse signals such as weak commitments or unclear ownership after the meeting. The episode also warns against overtrusting AI output in cross-cultural settings, where participants may never explicitly disagree yet still resist decisions later.

Governance is a further angle. In "Microsoft 365 Structural Debt from Default Governance", the discussion of Microsoft Teams Premium and advanced collaboration recommends including advanced access controls, meeting and recording retention, sensitivity labelling for meetings and files, usage policies and review workflows. The point made there is that these governance features should be configured so that data is protected and compliance requirements are met, rather than left at defaults.

In summary, Teams Premium extends Microsoft Teams for organisations with specific needs around protected meetings, branded experiences, AI recaps and webinars. Its value depends on licensing fit, on how it is configured alongside governance controls, and on how it is positioned next to Microsoft 365 Copilot.

teams-templates.desc: Teams templates are predefined or custom Microsoft Teams structures with channels, tabs, apps and settings, managed in the Teams admin center for creating new teams.

faq.a: A template can hold the type, name, description, visibility, team settings, channels, tabs and apps. It cannot hold members, the team picture, files, connectors, or private and shared channels.
faq.q: What can a Teams template contain?

faq.a: They are managed in the Teams admin center or with PowerShell. Developers can also create teams from templates through Microsoft Graph.
faq.q: Where are Teams templates managed?

faq.a: Microsoft's prebuilt industry templates can be duplicated but not edited. A duplicate can serve as the basis for a custom template, and custom templates can also be created from scratch or from an existing team.
faq.q: Can the prebuilt industry templates be changed?

teams-templates.long:
Teams templates are predefined or custom Microsoft Teams structures that include channels, tabs, apps and settings. They are managed in the Teams admin center, and new teams can be created from them. According to Microsoft Learn, a team template defines the structure of a team for a particular business need or project, so administrators can roll out consistent teams and users can start collaboration spaces with predefined settings, channels and apps.

A template can hold the team type, name, description, visibility, team settings, channels, tabs and apps. Several items are not part of a template: members, the team picture, files, connectors, and private and shared channels. Each template also has size limits on channels, tabs per channel and apps, although more of these can be added after a team has been created. Sensitivity labels are not supported in GCC environments.

Templates can be created and managed in the Teams admin center or with PowerShell. Custom templates can be built from scratch, from an existing team, or from another template. Microsoft also supplies prebuilt industry templates. These can be duplicated but not edited, and some of them are connected templates that add SharePoint pages and lists as tabs. Developers can create teams from templates through Microsoft Graph as well.

Which templates users see is controlled by template policies. These policies determine which templates appear for which users and groups, so different parts of an organization can be offered different starting points. Typical decisions around Teams templates include whether to duplicate a prebuilt industry template or create a custom one, which channels, tabs and apps belong in a standard structure, and which groups of users should be able to see a given template.

In the M365.FM episode "Automate Microsoft 365 Governance Beyond Static Checklists", Teams templates appear in a list of governance automation practices. The episode recommends using Teams templates and provisioning solutions to enforce standards, alongside automating user and group provisioning and deprovisioning, implementing group expiration and renewal, and standardizing on automation platforms such as Power Automate, Microsoft Graph and Azure Automation. In that framing, templates are one building block for making team creation consistent rather than relying on manual checklists.

The episode "Microsoft Teams Governance with Entra ID as the Control Plane" lists Microsoft Teams templates among its key strategies for managing the Teams admin center. The episode says to use Microsoft Teams templates to streamline team setups. The same list covers relying on groups for tailored policies, controlling private channel creation for sensitive discussions, customizing meeting policies, establishing messaging policies for different user groups, managing app access, using analytics, and controlling external and guest access. Templates are presented as one part of a broader approach to consistent, governed team setup.

teams-toolkit.desc: Teams Toolkit, also called Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit, is free Microsoft developer tooling for building apps and agents for Microsoft Teams and Copilot.

faq.a: Teams Toolkit is free developer tooling from Microsoft for building apps and agents for Microsoft Teams. It is now also called the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit and covers agents and Copilot extensibility in Microsoft 365.
faq.q: What is Teams Toolkit?

faq.a: According to the episode "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions", it simplifies development by providing tools for provisioning and deploying cloud resources. It is used together with Visual Studio Code, Node.js and Microsoft Teams.
faq.q: What does the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit do in a Teams app project?

faq.a: Both are ways to extend Microsoft 365 Copilot. The episode "Copilot Studio vs Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit" compares them and highlights production concerns such as grounding, governance, monitoring and cost control.
faq.q: How does the toolkit relate to Copilot Studio?

teams-toolkit.long:
Teams Toolkit is developer tooling from Microsoft for building apps and agents for Microsoft Teams. It is now also known as the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit, a name that reflects its wider scope: besides Teams apps, it supports agents and Copilot extensibility across Microsoft 365. In the knowledge base it is classified as a Microsoft tool and a developer tool, and it is listed as free.

The toolkit is used to create, run and publish extensions. Developers reach for it when a project needs custom code and control rather than a purely low-code approach. Microsoft's documentation describes the fundamentals of the toolkit on its Microsoft Learn platform pages. In the M365.FM episodes, the toolkit appears mainly as part of a developer's starting kit, rather than as a standalone subject.

One episode, "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions", lists the toolkit in a table of main tools and their purposes. According to the episode, the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit simplifies the development process by providing tools for provisioning and deploying cloud resources. It appears alongside Visual Studio Code, which the episode describes as essential for JavaScript, TypeScript or SharePoint Framework (SPFx) development, and Node.js, described as the back-end JavaScript runtime needed for app functionality. Microsoft Teams itself is named as required for collaboration and testing, and Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome are recommended for their developer tools when debugging.

The same toolkit shows up in the episodes about extending Microsoft 365 Copilot. "Extend Microsoft 365 Copilot with Agents, Plugins, and Connectors" names the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit and Copilot Studio as the first essential tools and resources for starting copilot development. It also mentions a Microsoft 365 subscription (with or without a copilot license), a development environment setup, and admin permissions for sideloading custom apps. The Microsoft 365 Developer Program is described there as giving access to a dedicated sandbox environment suited to testing and prototyping copilot extensions. "Build Custom Microsoft 365 Copilot Plugins" lists the toolkit, together with the Yeoman Generator for Office Add-ins, as a way to scaffold and manage projects, and advises installing the latest version of Visual Studio with the Office/SharePoint development workload. It further notes that a Microsoft 365 developer account is needed for plugin development.

"Microsoft 365 Copilot Extensibility with Gautam Sheth [MVP]" describes custom tools that automate tasks, integrate apps and personalize workflows. The episode says that the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit, connectors and APIs can be used to create agents that streamline daily work, and it gives examples of repetitive tasks that custom agents can handle.

A typical decision around the toolkit is whether to build with code or with a low-code tool. "Copilot Studio vs Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit" compares the two paths. The episode argues that rolling out Microsoft 365 Copilot is only the starting point and that production exposes harder challenges: grounding answers in authoritative sources, governance to prevent agent sprawl, monitoring for reliability, and licensing and cost controls. It suggests thinking in layers, from the foundation model and orchestrator to grounding, and mentions that agents can use the conversational reasoning of Microsoft 365 Copilot through the Search MCP server.

Because the toolkit targets Microsoft Teams as a host, it is closely related to Microsoft Teams, where many of the apps it produces run, including bots, tabs and extensions. Its alias, the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit, is the name used in most of the more recent episode material.

teamsfx.desc: TeamsFx SDK is a deprecated Microsoft SDK for building custom Microsoft Teams apps; existing TeamsFx solutions need to be migrated to alternatives such as SPFx or Power Apps.

faq.a: TeamsFx SDK is a Microsoft SDK for building custom Microsoft Teams apps. It has been deprecated.
faq.q: What is TeamsFx SDK?

faq.a: Existing TeamsFx solutions need to be migrated. Options discussed include moving them to SPFx or Power Apps.
faq.q: What happens to existing TeamsFx solutions?

teamsfx.long:
TeamsFx SDK is a Microsoft software development kit that was used to build custom apps for Microsoft Teams. It has been deprecated, which means it is no longer the recommended foundation for new Teams app development.

Because of the deprecation, solutions that were already built with TeamsFx SDK need to be migrated. Possible migration targets mentioned in the context of M365.FM include SPFx (SharePoint Framework) and Power Apps. Which path fits depends on the existing solution and its requirements, and the available facts do not describe specific migration steps.

The topic is discussed in an M365.FM episode that covers the migration of TeamsFx solutions to SPFx or Power Apps. Further technical documentation on the SDK is published by Microsoft on Microsoft Learn, in the Teams platform section on the Teams Toolkit and the TeamsFx SDK.

technical-debt.desc: Technical debt is the future rework cost of choosing quick or ungoverned solutions over sound, maintainable ones, a recurring theme in M365.FM episodes.

faq.a: Technical debt is the future cost of rework caused by choosing quick or ungoverned solutions instead of sound, maintainable ones. The cost shows up later as maintenance effort and slower change.
faq.q: What is technical debt?

faq.a: The episodes mention regular refactoring, interfaces and design patterns such as Dependency Injection in .NET, well-designed Dataverse structures, standardizing connectivity with MCP, and avoiding overengineering or premature microservice decomposition.
faq.q: How do the M365.FM episodes suggest reducing technical debt?

faq.a: According to the episode "Scale Azure Logic Apps Beyond Custom Connectors", each custom connector adds complexity, and teams must track versions, manage security and ensure compliance, which raises hidden maintenance costs over time.
faq.q: Why can custom connectors in Azure Logic Apps create technical debt?

technical-debt.long:
Technical debt is the future cost of rework that results from choosing quick or ungoverned solutions instead of sound, maintainable ones. The term works as a financial metaphor: a shortcut taken today may deliver something faster, but the cost does not disappear. It returns later as extra maintenance effort, slower changes and growing complexity. Technical debt is not tied to a single product; it appears in custom code, architecture decisions, integrations and low-code solutions alike.

The concept matters because the cost of technical debt is often hidden. An episode on Azure Logic Apps points out that such costs rarely show up on a balance sheet, yet they affect results month after month. Teams that accumulate shortcuts tend to spend more time maintaining what already exists than improving the business. For decision-makers, the practical question is therefore not only how fast a solution can be delivered, but how expensive it will be to keep, change and secure over time.

M365.FM episodes connect technical debt to several different areas of the Microsoft ecosystem. In ".NET Extensibility and Clean Architecture with Miguel Castro [MVP]", the advice centers on keeping code clean and flexible. The episode recommends using interfaces to define clear contracts between components, which reduces tight coupling and improves testability, and refactoring regularly so that technical debt does not accumulate. It also names proven design patterns such as Dependency Injection and the Strategy Pattern, and it cautions against overengineering by focusing on current needs and keeping the design simple.

In "Scale Azure Logic Apps Beyond Custom Connectors", technical debt is linked to custom connectors. The episode explains that every new connector adds complexity to an automation environment, because versions must be tracked, security managed and compliance ensured. Over time, according to the episode, these hidden costs can become overwhelming and slow a team down, turning automation that should drive efficiency into a recurring expense.

The episode "Dataverse Business Skills for Scalable Power Platform Solutions" approaches the topic from data modeling. It argues that successful solutions depend on strong Dataverse foundations rather than simply creating forms, workflows or user interfaces. Well-designed Dataverse structures, the episode says, help organizations maintain consistency, improve governance and reduce technical debt as applications scale across departments and business units. It also describes turning business processes into reusable, governed capabilities that Copilot and AI agents can use.

Technical debt also appears in the context of AI integration. "MCP Architecture for Microsoft Copilot and AI Agents" recommends using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to standardize connectivity and integration across agents, with the stated aim of scaling AI solutions and reducing technical debt. Finally, "Why Microservice Architecture Slows Software Delivery" describes how poorly governed microservice environments can create organizational bottlenecks and technical debt. The episode stresses that architectural decisions should follow business boundaries and operational realities rather than trends, and that decomposing systems too early, without clear domain ownership, team maturity, observability and deployment understanding, can lead to a fragmented landscape.

Taken together, the episodes describe recurring causes and countermeasures: tight coupling, ungoverned custom components, weak data foundations and premature architectural splits on one side, and clear contracts, regular refactoring, governed reusable capabilities, standardized protocols and simple designs on the other.

technical-debt-ratio.desc: Technical debt ratio (TDR) is a metric that expresses the cost to fix existing technical debt as a percentage of total investment, applied here to automation portfolios.

faq.a: It expresses the cost to fix existing technical debt as a percentage of the total investment. It is a proportion that shows how much remediation effort has accumulated relative to overall spend.
faq.q: What does the technical debt ratio (TDR) measure?

faq.a: In the M365.FM episode, the metric is applied to automation portfolios such as Power Automate flows. It is used to frame the cost of fixing accumulated debt across a set of workflows against the total investment in them.
faq.q: How is TDR applied to Power Automate?

faq.a: It appears in the episode "Power Automate vs Azure Logic Apps for Scalable Workflows," dated 2026-04-26.
faq.q: Where is the technical debt ratio discussed on M365.FM?

technical-debt-ratio.long:
Technical debt ratio (TDR) is a metric that expresses the cost of fixing existing technical debt as a percentage of the total investment in a system or portfolio. It gives teams a single proportion for comparing how much remediation work has built up against the overall effort spent on building and maintaining a solution.

On M365.FM, the term is applied to automation portfolios, such as collections of Power Automate flows. In that setting, the ratio is a way to describe how much rework a set of workflows might require relative to what was invested in creating and running them. A higher percentage points to a larger share of investment tied up in fixing earlier shortcuts, while a lower one points to a smaller remediation burden.

The concept appears in the episode "Power Automate vs Azure Logic Apps for Scalable Workflows" (2026-04-26). There it is used as a lens for thinking about how automation choices affect long-term maintainability as workflows scale. No further formulas, thresholds or tooling are specified in the available material, so the explanation here is limited to the definition and its application to automation portfolios.

telemetry.desc: Telemetry is a time-ordered record of repeated device measurements, such as machine sensor readings, whose meaning comes from the sequence of values.

faq.a: Telemetry is a time-ordered record of repeated measurements sent by devices, such as machine sensor readings. Its meaning comes from the sequence of values rather than from any single value.
faq.q: What is telemetry?

faq.a: According to the IoT Hub and Event Grid episode, continuous telemetry such as temperature or vibration readings builds an operational history for later analysis, while a discrete event such as a device disconnect signals a change that may require a response. Treating them as the same can create noisy workflows and unnecessary processing.
faq.q: How does telemetry differ from an event?

faq.a: The episodes mention telemetry in Azure IoT scenarios, in Dynamics 365 Business Central (performance data, user behavior, errors and system activity), and in Microsoft 365, where Entra sign-ins, Teams activity and SharePoint file operations can be correlated.
faq.q: Where does telemetry appear in Microsoft products according to the episodes?

telemetry.long:
Telemetry is a time-ordered record of repeated measurements sent by devices, for example the sensor readings of a machine. Its meaning comes from the sequence rather than from any single value: one temperature reading says little, while a series of readings over time shows how a machine behaves, drifts or fails. In the M365.FM episodes, the term appears in two main settings: industrial IoT and manufacturing on Azure, and the operational data of Microsoft cloud products such as Dynamics 365 Business Central and Microsoft 365.

The episode "IoT Hub Message Routing vs Event Grid — Why Telemetry and Events Are Not the Same Problem" (released in two versions, dated 2026-09-18 and 2026-10-02) frames the core distinction. A temperature reading, a vibration sample, a machine cycle and a device disconnect may all be described as events, but the episode argues they do not represent the same architectural problem. Continuous telemetry such as temperature readings, vibration data, cycle counts, power consumption and operating states creates an operational history that engineers, data teams, maintenance teams and production systems may need to analyze later. A device disconnect is different because it represents a change that may require a response.

From this the episode contrasts Azure IoT Hub Message Routing with Azure Event Grid. According to the episode, one is designed around operational data, the other around notifying systems that something changed and may require a response. It warns that confusing continuous telemetry with discrete events can create noisy workflows, incomplete production histories and unnecessary processing, and that treating the two as interchangeable can leave an architecture with expensive workflows processing data that was never meant to trigger them. In practice, the decision is whether a message belongs to a stream that should be kept and analyzed as history or to a notification that should start an action.

Telemetry also plays a role in automation and observability. The episode "Build Self-Healing Automation with Telemetry and Observability" describes how automation is evolving from simple scripts into systems that monitor themselves and fix problems automatically. It says modern automation uses telemetry data, such as logs, metrics and traces, to understand what is happening inside systems in real time. The idea of self-healing automation is presented as a response to the slow and poorly scalable practice of waiting for alerts and troubleshooting manually, with systems reacting instantly instead.

Product-level telemetry is covered in "Monitor Business Central Telemetry with Power BI". The episode describes telemetry in Dynamics 365 Business Central as one of the most valuable and often underused capabilities. It captures performance data, user behavior, errors and system activity, giving administrators a view of how their environment is running. The episode explores turning this data into insights with Microsoft Power BI.

The episode "Correlate Microsoft 365 Telemetry for Better Insights" argues that dashboards often isolate metrics and that the real signal appears when several sources are triangulated: Azure AD/Entra sign-ins, Office/M365 audit data for SharePoint and Teams, and usage and licensing information. The episode offers a pragmatic model, KQL queries, a Power BI schema and automations aimed at catching risky access, among other goals.

Across these episodes a common thread emerges. Telemetry is valuable because of its continuity and context: it is kept as a sequence, analyzed over time, and correlated with other sources. Whether the source is a factory machine, a Business Central environment or Microsoft 365 sign-ins and file operations, the practical questions are the same: what is being measured, how it is routed and stored, and whether a given signal should be treated as history to analyze or as a trigger for action.

temporary-access-pass.desc: Temporary Access Pass is a short-lived, time-limited passcode in Microsoft Entra for first sign-in and for registering passwordless authentication methods.
temporary-access-pass.long:
Temporary Access Pass is a time-limited passcode in Microsoft Entra. It lets a user sign in without an existing password or other registered credential, so that the user can set up stronger authentication methods.

The passcode is short-lived by design. Its main purpose is to bootstrap a user's sign-in: after using it for the first sign-in, the user registers passwordless methods such as the Authenticator app or a security key. This makes it relevant for onboarding new accounts and for situations in which a user needs to register or re-register authentication methods.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, Temporary Access Pass belongs to the area of identity and access management with Microsoft Entra, particularly passwordless authentication. It is not meant as a permanent credential. It serves as a temporary step toward a lasting passwordless setup.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no further related topics have been recorded for it.

tenant-to-tenant-migration.desc: Tenant-to-tenant migration is the planned move of users, mailboxes, files, Teams and settings from one Microsoft 365 tenant to another, e.g. after a merger.

faq.a: It is the process of moving users, mailboxes, files, Teams and settings from one Microsoft 365 tenant to another. It is typically triggered by events such as a merger or divestiture.
faq.q: What is a tenant-to-tenant migration?

faq.a: Two tenants are separate environments, and according to the M365.FM episode nothing carries over on its own. The work involves planning, mapping and cutover, and it covers mailboxes, sites, Teams and settings, not only documents.
faq.q: Why is a tenant-to-tenant migration more than copying files?

faq.a: It relates to Exchange Online for mailboxes, SharePoint for sites and documents, and Microsoft Teams for collaboration. Governance decisions on policies, permissions and ownership also have to be made for the target tenant.
faq.q: Which Microsoft 365 areas are involved in a tenant-to-tenant migration?

tenant-to-tenant-migration.long:
Tenant-to-tenant migration, also called T2T migration, tenant migration or Mandantenmigration, is the process of moving users, mailboxes, files, Teams and settings from one Microsoft 365 tenant to another. A tenant is the separate organizational container in which a company's Microsoft 365 accounts and data live. Because two tenants are independent of each other, content does not move between them by itself; it has to be transferred deliberately as part of a structured effort.

The usual trigger is a business event. In a merger, two separate Microsoft accounts have to become one. In a divestiture, a part of the organization is split off and needs its own environment, or is absorbed into the tenant of the acquiring company. In both cases the IT work follows a decision made at the business level, which is why the topic often arrives with tight timelines and many stakeholders.

A tenant-to-tenant migration is a project rather than a simple file copy. It involves planning, mapping and cutover phases. Planning clarifies what exists in the source tenant and what the target tenant should look like. Mapping decides how users, mailboxes, sites, Teams and settings in the source correspond to objects in the target. Cutover is the point at which users switch from the old environment to the new one. The sources do not prescribe specific tools or a fixed sequence, so the details depend on the individual situation.

The topic touches several workloads within Microsoft 365, which is its broader parent topic. Mailboxes and calendars belong to Exchange Online. Sites and documents belong to SharePoint. Chats, channels and collaboration spaces belong to Microsoft Teams. Each of these areas has its own structure, and the migration has to account for how they depend on one another, for example when a Team is backed by a SharePoint site and a group mailbox.

Governance is the other closely related subject. Policies, permissions and ownership have to be decided deliberately for the target tenant instead of being copied blindly from the source. A merger or divestiture is also an opportunity to review who has access to what and which rules should apply going forward, rather than carrying over unexamined settings.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft 365 Tenant-to-Tenant Migration - Simply Explained", part of the Simply Explained series, addresses a common misconception. According to the episode, most companies think a Microsoft 365 migration is just copying files from one account to another, and that assumption is exactly what sinks the project. The episode explains what a tenant really is and why nothing carries over on its own when two accounts have to become one after a merger or a sale of a division. It is the episode to start with for an overview of what has to be planned and why.

tensorrt.desc: NVIDIA TensorRT is an NVIDIA product in the Microsoft-ecosystem knowledge base M365.FM; this page covers the name and its place in the catalog.

faq.a: NVIDIA TensorRT is a product by NVIDIA that is listed as an entity on M365.FM. No further description has been recorded in the available facts, so this page does not detail its functionality.

faq.a: No episodes are currently linked to NVIDIA TensorRT in the available data. Related episodes can be added to this page as they become available.
faq.q: Does M365.FM have episodes about NVIDIA TensorRT?

tensorrt.long:
NVIDIA TensorRT is a product by NVIDIA, listed as a product entity in the M365.FM knowledge base, which covers the Microsoft ecosystem.

The information currently available for this entry is limited. No description, linked topics, official documentation or related episodes have been recorded for NVIDIA TensorRT, so this page does not make claims about its features, versions, supported platforms or typical use cases. terraform.desc: Terraform from HashiCorp is a multi-cloud infrastructure-as-code tool that describes infrastructure in readable files and manages Azure through a provider.

faq.a: Terraform is a multi-cloud infrastructure-as-code tool from HashiCorp. It describes infrastructure in readable files that can be reviewed and run again, and it manages platforms such as Azure through providers.
faq.q: What is Terraform?

faq.a: Bicep is Azure-only and made by Microsoft, while Terraform works across several clouds, including Azure, AWS and Google Cloud. The episodes also note that Terraform relies on a state file that must be managed carefully, whereas Bicep does not.
faq.q: How does Terraform differ from Bicep?

faq.a: The episode "Terraform - Simply Explained" describes plan and apply as a safety net. Terraform first shows what it intends to change, and the change is carried out only in the apply step.
faq.q: What do the plan and apply steps do in Terraform?

terraform.long:
Terraform, also called HashiCorp Terraform, is a multi-cloud infrastructure-as-code tool from HashiCorp. It describes infrastructure in files that can be read, reviewed and run again, and it connects to cloud platforms through providers, including a provider for Azure. It is classified as a developer tool and is closely tied to the practice of infrastructure as code.

The core idea is that infrastructure should not depend on manual steps. The episode "Terraform - Simply Explained" puts it this way: Terraform exists because Azure portal clicks cannot be rebuilt twice. Writing the infrastructure down as a file makes it repeatable, reviewable and easy to run again. That episode walks through the main building blocks in order: what Infrastructure as Code really means, what Terraform actually is, how providers let Terraform talk to a cloud, the plan and apply steps described as a safety net, the state file as Terraform's memory, modules for avoiding rebuilding the same thing, remote state for working with other people, and drift, where reality quietly diverges from what was written.

Several of these parts are what set Terraform's day-to-day use apart. Providers are the layer through which Terraform reaches a platform such as Azure, AWS or Google Cloud. The plan and apply workflow separates previewing a change from carrying it out. The state file records what Terraform manages, which is why the episodes stress handling it carefully. One of them warns that state files must be managed carefully to avoid issues, and another says Bicep's lack of native state management is a limitation, so state is a recurring point in the comparisons. Modules support reuse, and remote state matters once more than one person works on the same infrastructure.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, Terraform is most often compared with Bicep. Bicep is Azure-only and made by Microsoft, while Terraform spans several clouds. The episode "Terraform vs Azure Bicep: Which IaC Tool Should You Choose?" says Terraform stands out when multi-cloud infrastructure as code is needed, since the Terraform CLI and configuration files offer the same workflow across Azure, AWS, Google Cloud and many other platforms. The same episode describes Bicep files as simple to read and write, and notes that Bicep avoids the state-file handling that Terraform requires. It does not name a universal winner; the right choice depends on the organization's architecture and cloud strategy.

The episode "Bicep vs ARM Templates vs Terraform for Azure" places Terraform in a wider comparison with ARM templates and Bicep. It refreshes the role of ARM templates as a long-standing standard, introduces Bicep as a cleaner and more maintainable alternative, and compares readability, modular design and parameter handling. The episode "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained" covers the same tools, including Azure Bicep, ARM Templates, Terraform and PowerShell, and explains where each fits within the Microsoft ecosystem. It also links infrastructure as code to Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions, CI/CD pipelines, governance and security policies.

Another episode, "Azure Bicep at Scale: Modular Infrastructure as Code", lists limitations of Bicep such as no native state management and a smaller ecosystem than Terraform or Pulumi. Taken together, the episodes suggest that Terraform is a candidate when work spans more than Azure or when a mature provider ecosystem and a state-based workflow are wanted, while Bicep is the Azure-focused option.

terraform-provider.desc: A Terraform provider is a plugin that lets Terraform communicate with a single platform, such as Azure, AWS or GitHub, through that platform's API.
terraform-provider.long:
A Terraform provider is a plugin that teaches Terraform how to talk to a single platform through its API. Examples of such platforms include Azure, AWS and GitHub. Without a provider for a given platform, Terraform has no way to interact with that platform's resources.

Providers are distributed separately from Terraform itself. They are listed in the Terraform Registry, which serves as the place where available providers can be found. This separation means that support for a platform is delivered by its own plugin rather than being built into the core Terraform tool.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the relevant case is a provider for Azure, which allows Terraform to work with Azure through its API. The same concept applies to other platforms, so a single Terraform workflow can involve more than one provider when several platforms are in use.

M365.FM has no linked episodes or related topics for the Terraform provider concept at this time, and no official documentation links are recorded here.

terraform-state.desc: Terraform state is the record Terraform keeps of managed infrastructure, mapping configuration to real objects; it can hold secrets and belongs in a locked remote backend.

faq.a: Terraform uses its state to match the resources in a configuration with the real objects that were deployed. This tells Terraform which resources to add, update or delete when changes are planned and applied.
faq.q: What is Terraform state used for?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, local state is poor for teams, can expose sensitive information because the file may contain secrets in plain text, and carries a higher risk of accidental deletion. A remote backend is the recommended alternative.
faq.q: Why should Terraform state not be kept locally?

faq.a: The state can be kept in an Azure Storage blob container using the azurerm backend, configured with a storage account name, a container name and a key for the state file. Blob storage locks the state before write operations and encrypts data at rest.
faq.q: How can Terraform state be stored in Azure?

terraform-state.long:
Terraform state is the record that Terraform keeps of the infrastructure it manages. It maps the resources described in a configuration to the real remote objects that exist in a cloud environment. Terraform reads this record to decide which changes to make: which resources to add, which to update and which to delete. Because the state acts as the source of truth for everything Terraform manages, how it is stored and protected has a direct effect on how safely deployments run.

In practice the state is held in a state file. One M365.FM episode, "Terraform vs Azure Bicep: Which IaC Tool Should You Choose?", describes Terraform as relying on a state file to track the current status of infrastructure and stresses that state management must be handled carefully to avoid issues that can disrupt deployments. The same episode notes that the state file can be stored locally or remotely, with remote options including cloud buckets and similar storage. The choice between local and remote storage is one of the central decisions around Terraform state.

Microsoft Learn documentation on storing Terraform state in Azure Storage explains why that choice matters. By default, Terraform stores state locally. The documentation describes this as a poor fit for teams, because the file may expose sensitive information, since it can contain secrets in plain text, and because there is a greater risk of accidental deletion. The recommended pattern is to keep the state remotely in an Azure Storage blob container through the azurerm backend. That backend is configured with the storage account name, the container name and a key that names the state file.

The documentation also covers how access to that storage is handled. The access key is best supplied through an environment variable rather than being written to disk, and it can also be stored in Key Vault. Azure Blob storage locks the state automatically before write operations, which prevents concurrent changes that could corrupt it, and the data is encrypted at rest. The example in the documentation uses an access key and open network access, which the page marks as unsuitable for production. For production use, it points to firewalls, service endpoints or private endpoints, together with the most secure supported authentication method.

Typical situations where state comes up include team collaboration, pipeline-based deployments and reviewing planned changes. The episode "Azure Infrastructure as Code and DevOps with Maik van der Gaag [MVP]" mentions using Terraform state files to track the current state of resources, which helps in planning and applying changes safely. It places this alongside other practices such as sharing code through Terraform modules, requiring code reviews before changes are merged, and using continuous deployment to deliver updates to an Azure environment reliably and with less risk of human error. The episode also mentions combining Terraform with tools such as Ansible or PowerShell for end-to-end automation.

Taken together, the sources point to a consistent set of practices. Terraform state should be treated as sensitive data, kept in a remote backend rather than on a local machine, protected by locking so that two operations cannot change it at the same time, and placed behind access controls. Understanding what the state contains, and who or what can read or modify it, is part of operating Terraform responsibly, particularly when several people or automated pipelines work against the same infrastructure. The same concern for state handling is one of the points the first episode raises when comparing Terraform with Azure Bicep for infrastructure as code.

thin-client.desc: A thin client is a simple computer optimized for connecting to a desktop or computing environment that runs remotely on a server or in the cloud.

faq.a: A thin client is a simple computer optimized for connecting to a desktop or computing environment that runs remotely on a server or in the cloud.
faq.q: What is a thin client?

faq.a: The environment a thin client connects to runs remotely, either on a server or in the cloud, rather than on the thin client device itself.
faq.q: Where does the computing environment of a thin client run?

thin-client.long:
A thin client is a simple computer designed primarily to connect to a desktop or computing environment that runs remotely, either on a server or in the cloud. Instead of performing most processing locally, the device acts as an access point to a workspace hosted elsewhere.

The concept is relevant wherever organizations deliver desktops and applications from central infrastructure rather than from each individual device. Because the computing environment runs on a server or in the cloud, the endpoint itself can remain comparatively simple.

On M365.FM, the term is part of the knowledge base covering the Microsoft ecosystem. No specific episodes, related products or official documentation links are currently associated with this entry, so it serves as a general definition of the concept.

threat-actor.desc: A threat actor is a person or group that carries out cyberattacks; Microsoft tracks them in profiles and names them using a weather-themed taxonomy.

faq.a: A threat actor is a person or group that carries out cyberattacks. Microsoft tracks such actors in profiles and assigns them names so they can be referred to consistently.
faq.q: What is a threat actor?

faq.a: Microsoft uses a weather-based taxonomy in which the family name signals the category, such as Typhoon for China-linked nation-state activity, Blizzard for Russia, Sandstorm for Iran, Sleet for North Korea and Tempest for financially motivated actors. An adjective distinguishes actors within a family.
faq.q: How does Microsoft name threat actors?

faq.a: A Storm label with a number is a temporary designation for clusters of activity that are still unclear or in development. It is used until the activity can be assigned to a defined actor.
faq.q: What does a Storm label mean?

threat-actor.long:
A threat actor is a person or group that carries out cyberattacks. In security work the term covers a wide range of adversaries, from government-directed teams to criminal groups, and it gives defenders a common way to talk about who or what is behind a set of malicious activity. Microsoft tracks threat actors in profiles and names them using a weather-themed scheme, so that analysts and customers can refer to the same actor consistently.

Microsoft's documentation on how it names threat actors sorts the actors it tracks into five categories. Nation-state actors work for or are directed by a government program. Financially motivated actors are behind activity such as ransomware, business email compromise and phishing. Private sector offensive actors are commercial companies that build and sell cyber weapons. Influence operations run manipulative information campaigns. The fifth category is groups in development, a provisional label used for unknown or emerging activity that has not yet been resolved into a defined actor.

The naming scheme is based on weather. The family name signals the category of the actor. For example, Typhoon is used for China-linked nation-state activity, Blizzard for Russia, Sandstorm for Iran and Sleet for North Korea, while Tempest is used for financially motivated actors. An adjective distinguishes individual actors within a family. For clusters whose origin or nature is still unclear, Microsoft uses a temporary Storm label with a number. Microsoft states that the goal of this approach is to help organizations prioritize risk and to help researchers track threats. It also notes that attribution of origin is an assessment rather than a certainty, and that the mapping between Microsoft's names and the names used by other vendors is updated over time.

In practice, knowing the category and name of a threat actor helps security teams decide how seriously to treat a given alert and which techniques to expect. A financially motivated group points toward concerns such as ransomware or phishing, while a nation-state actor may imply longer-term, more persistent intrusion. Actor profiles also support intelligence reading: they collect the techniques, tools and behavior associated with a named group so defenders can compare them with what they see in their own environment.

This context is central to threat hunting, which the M365.FM episode "Turn Microsoft Threat Analytics into Real Security Action" discusses. The episode says that understanding the context of threat actor techniques is crucial for identifying evidence of their activities. It describes centralizing data from networks, applications and security systems in a SIEM platform to improve the ability to detect long-term trends and to detect advanced persistent threats more effectively. It also outlines a threat hunting process made up of preparing baselines, developing hypotheses, executing hunts, validating results and receiving feedback to improve future hunts, and it recommends identifying critical assets and sensitive data to focus hunting efforts.

Taken together, the term threat actor links the human or organizational side of an attack to the technical evidence defenders collect. Naming conventions such as Microsoft's make that link easier to use, but the labels remain working assessments: Storm designations are temporary, and attribution can change as more is learned about an actor.

threat-explorer.desc: Threat Explorer is a Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 tool for searching email detections, delivery actions and campaigns across a tenant.

faq.a: Threat Explorer is a near real-time reporting tool in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 2. It lets security teams search email detections, delivery actions and campaigns, and take actions such as remediating messages.
faq.q: What is Threat Explorer?

faq.a: Real-time detections, available in Plan 1, show only the state of a message at delivery. Threat Explorer offers more views, filtering with saved queries and actions, and also shows post-delivery activity.
faq.q: How does Threat Explorer differ from real-time detections?

faq.a: A Defender for Office 365 licence and suitable permissions are required. Permissions can come through Defender XDR roles, email and collaboration roles, or Entra roles, with least privilege advised.
faq.q: What is needed to access Threat Explorer?

threat-explorer.long:
Threat Explorer is a near real-time reporting tool in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 that helps security operations teams investigate and respond to threats. It is included in Plan 2 of Defender for Office 365. A lighter report, real-time detections, is available in Plan 1. Threat Explorer offers more views, more filtering including saved queries, and more actions than that real-time report. The tool is used to search email detections, delivery actions and campaigns across a tenant.

The tool is organized into views that cover all email, malware, phish, campaigns, content malware, and URL clicks. Analysts can filter by date range, message properties, file properties and threat properties. Charts can be pivoted by values such as delivery action, sender domain, and detection technology, which makes it possible to look at the same set of messages from several angles. Data can be exported as CSV for further analysis or reporting outside the portal.

Beyond reading data, Threat Explorer supports action. Admins can remediate selected messages, preview or download an email, or move into hunting. Preview and download work only while the message still exists in a cloud mailbox or quarantine. This is one practical difference from the real-time detections report, which shows only the state of a message at the time of delivery. Threat Explorer also shows post-delivery activity, so an investigation can follow what happened to a message after it reached the mailbox.

Access requires a Defender for Office 365 licence and suitable permissions. These can be granted through Defender XDR roles, email and collaboration roles, or Entra roles, and least privilege is advised. Teams that only hold Plan 1 work with the real-time detections report rather than the full Threat Explorer experience, which is a typical licensing decision to check before planning investigation workflows.

The M365.FM episode "Tune Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Against Phishing" places Threat Explorer in the context of ongoing tuning. According to the episode, Safe Links, Safe Attachments, anti-phishing and mail flow rules are often not tuned together. It recommends layered policies per risk group, dynamic delivery, tighter impersonation protection, removal of conflicting transport rules, and weekly reviews that use Threat Explorer together with Message Trace. The episode frames Defender as a living system rather than a checklist, with Threat Explorer serving as one of the review tools.

The episode "Build Better Phishing Reports with Defender and Power BI" uses Threat Explorer from a reporting angle. It says that surface statistics do not equal risk, and that Threat Explorer, automated investigation and response (AIR), and user submissions reveal the narrative behind "blocked" totals. The episode points to near-miss telemetry, such as who clicked, who reported and how fast an incident was contained, as more informative than raw block counts. It also covers feeding this data into Power BI dashboards and normalizing data before visualizing it.

In practice, Threat Explorer is the place where analysts check what was detected, how a message was delivered, which campaign it belongs to and whether further remediation is needed. Its filtering, pivoting and export functions make it suited to both ad hoc investigations and recurring review routines.

threat-hunting.desc: Threat hunting is the proactive search through security data for threats that automated detections have not flagged, for example using queries in Microsoft Defender XDR.

faq.a: Threat hunting is the proactive search through security data for threats and suspicious activity that automated detections have not flagged, for example with queries in Microsoft Defender XDR.
faq.q: What is threat hunting?

faq.a: According to the episode on Microsoft Defender for Office 365, proactive threat hunting lets security admins actively search for threats instead of waiting for alerts, which improves visibility into things like phishing campaigns.
faq.q: How does threat hunting differ from waiting for alerts?

faq.a: The episodes mention Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint with KQL-based advanced hunting, and Microsoft Sentinel for complex hunting across large volumes of logs. They also stress baselining normal activity and continuous monitoring.
faq.q: Which tools and skills are mentioned for threat hunting in the M365.FM episodes?

threat-hunting.long:
Threat hunting is the proactive search through security data for threats and suspicious activity that automated detections have not flagged. Instead of waiting for an alert to fire, security staff actively look for signs of compromise, for example by running queries in Microsoft Defender XDR. The goal is to find risks before they escalate into incidents, and to improve visibility into activity such as phishing campaigns that might otherwise go unnoticed.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, threat hunting is closely tied to the security tools that collect and correlate telemetry. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Defender for Endpoint - Simply Explained" lists advanced threat hunting as a capability that uses data-driven insights and KQL (Kusto Query Language) for precise threat detection, which it describes as strengthening proactive security measures. The episode "Microsoft Defender for Office 365 - Simply Explained" names proactive threat hunting as a benefit type: it enables security administrators to search for threats actively rather than waiting for alerts, which improves visibility and response to phishing campaigns. Both episodes place hunting alongside automation, such as Automated Investigation and Response, which handles routine and lower-severity items so that analysts can concentrate on more complex issues.

The split between automated detection and manual hunting also shapes the choice of tools. The episode "Microsoft Defender vs Sentinel: When You Need Both" describes Defender as strongest where immediate protection and automated response are needed, and Sentinel as strongest where the challenge involves large volumes of logs, complex threat hunting, or correlating events across disconnected systems. According to the episode, Sentinel gathers material ranging from firewall logs to identity events to build a full forensic timeline, while Defender feeds Sentinel high-fidelity alerts. In that picture, hunting benefits from broad, correlated data rather than from a single product's view.

Threat hunting also applies to identity infrastructure. The episode "Harden Azure AD Connect Against Hybrid Identity Breaches" includes a section on threat hunting in Active Directory and stresses continuous monitoring as essential for detecting identity-based attacks before they escalate. It recommends establishing a baseline of normal activity so that anomalies pointing to a possible breach become easier to recognize. A baseline is what turns a hunt from an open-ended search into a comparison of observed behavior against what is expected.

The episode "Turn Microsoft Threat Analytics into Real Security Action" frames hunting as one element of a wider threat intelligence practice. Its key points include integrating real-time threat intelligence to improve detection and response times, using threat hunting to identify risks proactively, breaking down data silos to support collaboration and comprehensive analysis, and applying user behavior analytics to detect insider threats early. It also advises acting on threat data promptly, adopting continuous monitoring to follow the evolving threat landscape, and measuring and communicating the effectiveness of threat intelligence efforts so that analytics lead to actionable results.

Typical decisions around threat hunting therefore include which data sources to bring together, who owns the hunting work, how findings feed back into detections and automated response, and how outcomes are reported to management. Because hunting depends on query skills such as KQL and on reliable, well-connected data, the episodes consistently connect it to data integration, baselining and continuous monitoring rather than treating it as a standalone activity.

threat-intelligence.desc: Threat intelligence is continuously updated information about malicious IP addresses, domains and attack patterns that security tools use to alert on or block threats.

faq.a: Threat intelligence is continuously updated information about known malicious IP addresses, domains and attack patterns. Security tools use it to alert on or block threats.
faq.q: What is threat intelligence?

faq.a: Azure Firewall can filter traffic based on Microsoft threat intelligence. The episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" lists threat intelligence next to network rules, application rules and NAT rules.
faq.q: How does Azure Firewall use threat intelligence?

faq.a: "Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence - Simply Explained" covers what threat intelligence is, Indicators of Compromise, threat actors, infrastructure analysis, and how to use this information in an investigation.
faq.q: What topics does the Defender Threat Intelligence episode cover?

threat-intelligence.long:
Threat intelligence is continuously updated information about known malicious IP addresses, domains and attack patterns. Security tools use this information to raise alerts on suspicious activity or to block traffic and behavior that matches known threats. Instead of waiting for something to break and then guessing at the cause, a security team can compare what it observes in its own environment with what is already known about attackers and their infrastructure.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence - Simply Explained" starts from a common frustration: an alert on the screen says that something broke, but it does not say who is attacking. The episode walks through what threat intelligence actually is and breaks it into several building blocks. Indicators of Compromise are described as breadcrumbs, the observable traces an attack leaves behind. Threat actors are the parties behind an attack, and knowing who they are helps put an incident in context. Infrastructure analysis follows the trail of the servers, domains and addresses an attacker uses. The episode also covers how this material is used in an investigation and mentions community-related aspects of the topic.

One direct application of threat intelligence is network filtering. The episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" describes Azure Firewall as a cloud-native, fully managed network security service that protects Azure workloads from internal and external threats. Besides network rules, application rules and NAT rules, threat intelligence is one of the concepts the episode explains. Azure Firewall can filter traffic based on Microsoft threat intelligence, which means traffic to or from known malicious IP addresses and domains can be flagged or blocked without administrators maintaining those lists by hand. The episode also compares the Basic, Standard and further Azure Firewall tiers, which is relevant when deciding which capabilities a given environment needs.

Threat intelligence also plays a role in exposure and risk prioritization. In the episode "Microsoft Security Exposure Management with Uros Babic [MVP-MCT]", the discussion states that Microsoft integrates threat intelligence into exposure management so that emerging risks can be spotted and defenses adjusted. According to the episode, the platform combines threat intelligence, contextual scoring and data sensitivity to highlight urgent risks, and Defender Threat Intelligence is named as a way to unmask adversaries and neutralize modern cyberthreats. The practical point is prioritization: a gap that matches active attacker behavior deserves attention before a gap that is only theoretical.

The episode "AI Security and Microsoft Purview with Danilo Nogueira [Microsoft]" connects threat intelligence with predictive analysis. It says that AI in cybersecurity analyzes global threat data and can help forecast attack patterns, with cryptocurrency mining malware campaigns given as an example of a trend that can be predicted. The episode lists threat intelligence alongside user behavior analytics, network security and vulnerability management as areas where predictive models contribute, and it states that organizations rely on threat intelligence to stay ahead of attackers.

A recurring caution appears in "Turn Microsoft Threat Analytics into Real Security Action". The episode argues that threat analytics is useless if it does not lead to action, and that this leaves an organization vulnerable. Its takeaways include assessing threat analytics regularly so that it produces actionable insight, acting on threat data promptly to avoid financial losses and security breaches, and integrating real-time threat intelligence to improve detection and response times. It also recommends threat hunting to identify risks before they escalate, breaking down data silos for collaboration and comprehensive analysis, using user behavior analytics to detect insider threats early, and adopting continuous monitoring.

Taken together, the episodes treat threat intelligence as an input that only has value when it is connected to tools and processes. It feeds automated controls such as Azure Firewall filtering, informs investigations in Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, shapes risk prioritization in exposure management, and supports proactive hunting. The decisions around it are mostly about integration and follow-through: which tools consume the intelligence, how quickly findings are acted on, and how the results are measured and communicated.

threat-modeling.desc: Threat modeling is a structured security exercise in which developers and security experts review an application's design to find what can go wrong and where gaps exist.

faq.a: Threat modeling is a structured security exercise in which developers and security experts review an application's design to identify what can go wrong and where security gaps are. It is ideally done early in development.
faq.q: What is threat modeling?

faq.a: The episodes recommend doing it during planning and design rather than after deployment. The episode on secure MLOps states that security should start in the planning and design phase.
faq.q: When should threat modeling be done?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microservice Dependency Poisoning and Cascading Cloud Latency", traditional threat modeling identifies threats, assets and mitigations through system decomposition and risk enumeration, while toxic flow analysis tracks how sensitive or high-risk data moves through systems using graph-based data flow mapping.
faq.q: How does threat modeling differ from toxic flow analysis?

threat-modeling.long:
Threat modeling is a structured security exercise in which developers and security experts review the design of an application to identify what can go wrong and where security gaps are. It is meant to happen early in development, while the design can still be changed at low cost, rather than after a system is already deployed. The result is a shared understanding of likely threats, the assets worth protecting and the mitigations that should be built in.

The practice is used in several contexts described in M365.FM episodes. In the episode "Secure MLOps in Microsoft Cloud with Martin Dimovski [MVP-MCT]", threat modeling appears as part of a secure-by-design approach to machine learning operations. The episode says that security should start in the planning and design phase, not after deployment, and lists threat modeling alongside identity protection, secure pipelines, infrastructure hardening, API security and governance. It also stresses that security teams should work with developers and DevOps teams as partners rather than blockers, which is the collaborative setup that threat modeling depends on. The same discussion explains that AI systems need protection across infrastructure, models and further layers, and that they introduce new attack surfaces while amplifying existing weaknesses.

In the episode "Fix OWASP Architectural Risks in .NET Applications", threat modeling is linked to the OWASP Top 10 and to the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS). The episode states that using ASVS and threat modeling early in .NET projects yields targeted controls such as input validation, access control and logging, and that this consistently lowers exposure to Top 10 categories. It contrasts newer .NET Core defaults, which include HSTS, stricter cookie policies and safer serialization choices, with many legacy .NET Framework applications that remain vulnerable unless they are modernized. In that framing, threat modeling is a way to decide which controls a given application needs instead of applying generic checklists.

The episode "Multi-Agent AI with Copilot Studio and David Lorenzo Lopez [MVP]" mentions threat modeling as one element of secure development under the Software Development Lifecycle (SDL). Alongside encrypting data at rest and in transit, keeping production and test environments separate and documenting secure coding practices, the episode says that threat modeling must be completed and that audit logs of all agent interactions must be kept. Here it appears as a required item within a wider set of security and compliance assessments.

The episode "Microservice Dependency Poisoning and Cascading Cloud Latency" compares traditional threat modeling with toxic flow analysis. According to the episode, traditional threat modeling focuses on identifying potential threats, assets and mitigations, using system decomposition and risk enumeration. Toxic flow analysis, by contrast, tracks the movement of sensitive or high-risk data through systems, using graph-based data flow mapping and risk propagation tracing. The comparison is offered to help readers understand exposure and remediation in distributed microservice environments.

The episode "Microsoft 365 Security Through Clear Accountability" approaches the topic from the people side. It mentions training such as a threat modeling practitioner course as a way to build skills and to understand how attackers think, which it presents as helping people become stronger defenders in their organization and catch threats early. In that context it sits next to a culture in which everyone feels responsible for security.

Taken together, the episodes treat threat modeling as an early, collaborative design activity. Typical decisions around it include when to run it in the project lifecycle, who takes part (developers, DevOps and security experts), how its findings map to concrete controls such as those in ASVS, and whether additional techniques like data flow analysis are needed for complex, distributed or AI-based systems.

three-way-matching.desc: Three-way matching is an accounts payable control that compares the purchase order, the product receipt and the vendor invoice before an invoice is paid.

faq.a: Three-way matching is an accounts payable control that compares the purchase order, the product receipt and the vendor invoice before the invoice is paid.
faq.q: What is three-way matching?

faq.a: The three documents are the purchase order, the product receipt and the vendor invoice.
faq.q: Which documents are compared in three-way matching?

faq.a: It checks that the ordered, received and invoiced items are consistent before payment, so that discrepancies can be reviewed before an invoice is paid.
faq.q: Why is three-way matching used?

three-way-matching.long:
Three-way matching is an accounts payable control. Before a vendor invoice is paid, it compares three documents: the purchase order, the product receipt and the vendor invoice itself.

The purpose of the control is to confirm that what was ordered, what was received and what was billed are consistent with one another. An invoice that does not line up with the purchase order or the product receipt can be held back for review instead of being paid automatically. This reduces the risk of paying for goods that were never ordered, were not delivered, or were billed at a different quantity or price than agreed.

In practice, the three documents represent three stages of a procurement process. The purchase order records the commitment made to the vendor, the product receipt records the delivery of the goods, and the vendor invoice records the amount the vendor is claiming. Matching them against each other links purchasing, receiving and payment into one verification step.

No related products, topics or episodes are currently linked to this entry on M365.FM, so this page covers the concept in general terms only.

throttling.desc: Throttling limits how many requests or how much compute a service accepts, shown as HTTP 429 in Microsoft Graph and as delays or rejected jobs in Fabric capacities.

faq.a: According to the episodes, 429 is the response code for throttling. The recommended handling is to use the Retry-After delay to recover from throttling quickly.
faq.q: What does HTTP 429 mean in Microsoft Graph?

faq.a: The episode on how Microsoft Graph connects Microsoft 365 data says efficient querying and data management help avoid throttling and improve application performance.
faq.q: How can applications reduce the risk of throttling?

faq.a: The Fabric cost episode says that if usage exceeds the available capacity for too long, queuing or throttling can occur, leading to delays or rejected jobs.
faq.q: How does throttling relate to Microsoft Fabric?

throttling.long:
Throttling is a mechanism in which a service slows down, delays or rejects requests when a client or workload exceeds what the service is willing or able to handle. In the Microsoft ecosystem it appears in several places: as an HTTP status code in Microsoft Graph, as a side effect of connector-based integrations, and as a capacity-related behavior in Microsoft Fabric. The M365.FM episodes treat it mainly as something developers and architects need to plan for, rather than as an unusual fault.

In Microsoft Graph, throttling is reported with the HTTP status code 429. The episode "Microsoft Graph Automation Architecture: Beyond Scripts" lists it next to other common responses: 403 for access denied and 404 for not found. It recommends preparing an application to handle these errors, using the @odata.nextLink property to work through paged results, and handling authentication and authorization errors early. According to the episode, robust error handling keeps an automation reliable.

The episode "Migrate Exchange Web Services to Microsoft Graph with Glen Scales [MVP]" gives a concrete best practice in a table of HTTP error codes. For a 429 response, it advises using the Retry-After delay to recover from throttling quickly. The same table suggests showing a simple "Access denied" message for a 403 and notes that some deleted resources can be restored within 30 days when a 404 occurs. In that episode, throttling handling is part of the groundwork for replacing EWS calls with Microsoft Graph API calls.

The episode "How Microsoft Graph Connects Microsoft 365 Data and Context" links throttling to query design. It says that efficient querying and data management help avoid throttling and improve application performance. It also pairs this advice with the principle of least privilege for permissions and with general automation best practices such as consistency and compliance.

In integration scenarios, throttling can also be a performance factor. The episode "Azure SQL Security Beyond Firewalls and IP Allowlists" describes latency and throttling as a cost of connector-based approaches. It names serialization overhead, where data is serialized and deserialized several times, and retry storms, which can occur when connectors hit throttling. The episode says this overhead grows with enterprise scale and may show up as delays in integration pipelines that handle large data volumes for AI or analytics.

In Microsoft Fabric, throttling is tied to capacity. The episode "Reduce Microsoft Fabric Costs by Optimizing Compute Workloads" explains that when several jobs run at once, total CU usage cannot exceed the available capacity. If demand spikes, queuing or throttling may occur, and some capacities can autoscale by borrowing extra resources, which adds to the bill. According to the episode, short bursts may not cause issues, while long periods of overuse can lead to delays or rejected jobs. Throttling therefore connects performance behavior directly to cost decisions.

Across these episodes, practical responses are consistent: expect throttling responses, honor the Retry-After delay, keep queries efficient, avoid unnecessary repeated calls, and size or smooth workloads so that sustained demand does not exceed allocated capacity.

time-to-decision.desc: Time to decision is a metric measuring how long it takes to move from an identified issue to a committed action, showing whether decision authority flows or pools in a workflow.

faq.a: It measures how long it takes from an identified issue to a committed action. The result indicates whether decision authority is flowing or pooling in a particular workflow.
faq.q: What does time to decision measure?

faq.a: The metric is used to show where decision authority moves or accumulates, which can only be observed within a defined workflow. Looking at one workflow makes the handoffs between issue and action visible.
faq.q: Why is time to decision tied to a specific workflow?

faq.a: It appears in the episodes "AI Upskilling Strategy for Measurable Business ROI" and "Why Microsoft 365 Copilot Strategy Fails".
faq.q: Where is time to decision discussed on M365.FM?

time-to-decision.long:
Time to decision is a metric that measures the elapsed time between an identified issue and a committed action. It is used to show whether decision authority is flowing or pooling within a specific workflow. A short interval suggests that decisions move to the people and systems able to act on them, while a long interval points to places where authority accumulates and work waits.

The metric is tied to a defined workflow rather than to an organization as a whole. Because it tracks the span from recognizing a problem to committing to an action, it focuses attention on the handoffs, approvals, and escalations in between, not on the speed of individual tasks.

On M365.FM, the concept appears in discussions of how organizations evaluate technology and skills investments. It is referenced in the episode "AI Upskilling Strategy for Measurable Business ROI", where measurable outcomes are the theme, and in "Why Microsoft 365 Copilot Strategy Fails", which examines why Microsoft 365 Copilot strategies fall short. In both contexts, time to decision serves as a way to describe whether changes in tooling or training affect how quickly decisions are made.

time-to-first-token.desc: Time to first token (TTFT) is a latency metric for generative AI that measures the delay between a submitted request and the first token of the answer.
