faq.a: It measures the time between a user submitting a request to a generative AI system and the first token of the answer appearing. It is typically expressed in milliseconds.
faq.q: What does time to first token (TTFT) measure?

faq.a: According to Microsoft's Azure OpenAI performance and latency documentation, total response time equals time to first token plus the average gap between tokens multiplied by the number of tokens generated.
faq.q: How does TTFT relate to total response time?

faq.a: Streaming shortens the wait for the first output and improves perceived responsiveness in chat interfaces. It does not change how long the full answer takes and matters less for batch jobs.
faq.q: Does streaming reduce time to first token?

time-to-first-token.long:
Time to first token (TTFT) is a latency metric for generative AI systems. It measures the time between a user submitting a request and the first token of the answer appearing. It is usually expressed in milliseconds and describes how quickly a model starts responding, not how long the complete answer takes.

TTFT is used to judge responsiveness. In chat interfaces and other interactive scenarios, the wait before any output appears shapes how fast a system feels to the person using it. Microsoft's Azure OpenAI performance and latency documentation treats the metric as the interval between submitting a prompt and receiving the first token. It also places it in a simple relationship: total response time equals time to first token plus the average gap between tokens multiplied by the number of tokens generated. TTFT is therefore one component of overall latency, and the generation phase that follows contributes the rest.

Several factors influence the value. According to the documentation, larger prompts raise the first-token delay, although prompt size usually matters less than how much text is generated. Heavy load on a deployment and many simultaneous requests can also slow responses. For this reason, a single TTFT reading is hard to interpret without context. The documentation recommends reading latency metrics together with a token metric such as processed prompt tokens, so that a slow response can be related to the amount of input that was processed.

In Azure Monitor, the Time to Response metric corresponds to time to first token and suits streaming workloads. A normalized variant divides first-byte latency by prompt token count. That variant is meant for comparing across different prompt sizes, not for diagnosing absolute latency. The documentation gives no concrete target values for TTFT, so acceptable thresholds depend on the application and its users.

Streaming is closely tied to the metric. Streaming shortens the wait for the first output and improves perceived responsiveness in chat interfaces, but it does not change how long the full answer takes. It matters less for batch jobs, where nobody watches the output arrive and total completion time is the more relevant figure. Choosing which latency number to optimize therefore depends on whether the workload is interactive or batch-oriented.

The M365.FM episode "Real-Time AI Sensitivity Labeling in Microsoft Purview" (2026-05-12) uses the term in a data-protection setting. The episode says that Time to First Token measures how quickly AI starts analyzing data, and that Microsoft Purview delivers results in milliseconds, so protection appears applied almost as soon as a file is saved or shared. It presents this rapid response as a way to reduce the risk of leaks and mistakes, and it cites figures for tuned models of over 95% precision for Tier 0 data and recall above 90%. These figures are attributed to the episode.

In practice, TTFT is one of several measures used when evaluating or monitoring generative AI workloads. It describes the start of a response, while the gap between tokens and the number of tokens generated describe the rest. Considering all of these together, along with prompt size and deployment load, gives a fuller picture of how a model deployment performs.

tls-inspection.desc: TLS inspection decrypts selected encrypted web traffic under organizational policy so content checks such as file filtering can be applied, and it affects Microsoft 365 setups.

faq.a: TLS inspection lets an organization decrypt and inspect selected encrypted web traffic under its policy, so that content-based checks such as file filtering can be applied.
faq.q: What is TLS inspection?

faq.a: The episode "Maintain Hybrid Exchange Beyond the Configuration Wizard" recommends exempting EXO traffic from TLS inspection where possible, along with disabling SSL offload that breaks client certificate chains.
faq.q: Should TLS inspection be applied to Exchange Online traffic in a hybrid setup?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Entra Private Access - Simply Explained", TLS inspection is not supported on Private Network connector traffic and can stop the connector from reaching the Global Secure Access service.
faq.q: Is TLS inspection supported for Microsoft Entra Private Access connector traffic?

tls-inspection.long:
TLS inspection is a security technique in which an organization decrypts and inspects selected encrypted web traffic under its own policy, so that content-based checks such as file filtering can be applied. Because most web traffic is encrypted, network controls that only see addresses and ports cannot evaluate what is actually inside a connection. Inspection at the TLS layer makes the content visible to the inspecting control, which can then apply policy before the traffic reaches its destination. The word "selected" matters: inspection is normally applied to defined categories or destinations rather than to every flow.

In the M365.FM episodes, TLS inspection appears in two roles. First, it is a capability that security services offer. The episode "Global Secure Access - Simply Explained" describes a Secure Web Gateway (SWG) that applies organizational security policies before users reach websites, SaaS applications, AI services, and cloud platforms. The discussion there covers URL filtering, SaaS visibility, AI governance, Microsoft Purview integration, TLS inspection, file protection, and cloud application discovery. In that context, inspection supports protection against unauthorized uploads, malicious websites, shadow IT, and emerging AI services that may carry compliance or data protection risks. The episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" places TLS inspection in the Premium tier of Azure Firewall, alongside an Intrusion Detection and Prevention System (IDPS), and describes that tier as intended for enterprises with high network security demands.

Second, TLS inspection appears as a common source of problems for Microsoft 365 connectivity, because breaking and re-establishing an encrypted session can interfere with services that depend on intact certificate chains or long-lived connections. The episode "Maintain Hybrid Exchange Beyond the Configuration Wizard" gives the hint to exempt Exchange Online (EXO) traffic from TLS inspection where possible. It lists this alongside other hybrid hygiene points: disable SSL offload that breaks client certificate chains, and make sure a reverse proxy preserves headers and supports large POST requests for mailbox moves. The episode frames these as items to check when validating a hybrid deployment after the Hybrid Configuration Wizard has run.

The episode "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Settings and Configuration" lists TLS inspection among common network configuration issues that can affect Microsoft 365 Copilot, together with a blocked WebSockets (WSS) protocol and aggressive proxy timeouts. It advises ensuring full WSS connectivity from user devices to the *.cloud.microsoft and *.office.com domains, and suggests checking network settings when Copilot shows errors or does not respond.

The episode "Microsoft Entra Private Access - Simply Explained" covers a related case in its troubleshooting notes. It states that TLS inspection is not supported on Private Network connector traffic and can interfere with the connector's ability to connect to the Global Secure Access service. The same notes mention that a proxy server between the connector and the resource can cause failures, since the connector needs direct connectivity, and that a certificate chain validation error can arise from proxy misconfiguration even when the connector status shows as Active.

For administrators, the recurring decision is where inspection adds value and where it should be bypassed. Inspection is useful where content-level controls such as file filtering are wanted for general web and SaaS traffic. It is a candidate for exemption on paths the episodes name as sensitive to interception: Exchange Online traffic in hybrid setups, Microsoft 365 Copilot connectivity, and Private Network connector traffic for Entra Private Access. When a service shows certificate errors, dropped WebSocket connections, or connectors that cannot reach their cloud service, checking whether an inspecting proxy or firewall sits in the path is a reasonable early step according to these episodes.

tls-termination.desc: TLS termination ends the encrypted TLS connection at a proxy or load balancer so back-end servers get plain requests and certificates are managed centrally.

faq.a: TLS termination means ending the encrypted TLS connection at a proxy or load balancer, such as a gateway. The back-end servers then receive plain requests, and certificates are managed in one place. It is also called TLS or SSL offloading.
faq.q: What is TLS termination?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Front Door - Simply Explained" lists SSL/TLS termination as a core concept of Azure Front Door. The episode "Azure Container Apps - Simply Explained" describes Envoy as an edge HTTP proxy that handles TLS termination.
faq.q: Which Azure services use TLS termination according to the M365.FM episodes?

faq.a: No. The episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" notes that application FQDN filtering rules filter outbound traffic to a defined list of domain names without needing TLS termination.
faq.q: Does every kind of traffic filtering require TLS termination?

tls-termination.long:
TLS termination is the practice of ending an encrypted TLS connection at an intermediary, such as a proxy, a load balancer or a gateway, instead of at the back-end server that finally handles the request. The client opens an encrypted session to the intermediary, which decrypts the traffic and forwards a plain request to the servers behind it. The technique is also known as TLS offloading or SSL offloading, and the two names are used interchangeably in this context.

The main reason to terminate TLS at a single point is operational. Because the encrypted connection ends in one place, certificates are managed in one place as well, rather than being installed and renewed on every back-end server. The back-end servers also receive plain requests, which removes the work of encrypting and decrypting from them. A typical decision around the topic is whether the traffic between the intermediary and the back end stays unencrypted or is protected again by a new connection. The facts available here describe the basic pattern of plain requests towards the back end and do not go further into that choice.

TLS termination appears as a building block in several Azure services that M365.FM has covered. In the episode "Azure Front Door - Simply Explained", SSL/TLS termination is listed among the core concepts of the service, alongside global load balancing, health probes, URL routing, caching and Web Application Firewall (WAF). The episode presents Azure Front Door as an entry point for internet-facing applications and compares it with Azure Load Balancer, Azure Traffic Manager and Azure Application Gateway. In that setting, terminating TLS at the front door of an application fits together with the other functions of such an edge service, for example inspecting and routing requests before they reach the back end.

The episode "Azure Container Apps - Simply Explained" shows the same idea inside a hosting platform. It describes Envoy acting as an edge HTTP proxy that manages traffic routing and secures connections through TLS termination. Applications in the environment can then communicate smoothly and securely, with the proxy handling the encrypted side of the connection. Here the termination is part of the platform and does not have to be built into each container app.

The episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" mentions TLS termination in a contrasting way. It describes application FQDN filtering rules that filter outbound traffic to a defined list of fully qualified domain names without needing TLS termination. This shows that some filtering tasks can be done without decrypting the traffic, while other inspection functions depend on terminating the encrypted connection. Whether termination is needed therefore depends on what the intermediary is expected to do with the traffic.

In practice, TLS termination is considered when an application sits behind a gateway or load balancer and the team wants central certificate handling and simpler back-end servers. It is closely related to load balancing, reverse proxying, web application firewalls and edge routing, since these functions often run on the same component. The three M365.FM episodes mentioned above give a view of the concept from different angles: as part of a global edge service, as part of a container platform's proxy, and as an option that some firewall rules deliberately avoid.

tmdl.desc: Tabular Model Definition Language (TMDL) is a human-readable, text-based syntax for defining tabular semantic models, such as tables, measures and relationships.

faq.a: TMDL is a human-readable, text-based syntax for defining tabular semantic models, including tables, measures and relationships.
faq.q: What is Tabular Model Definition Language (TMDL)?

faq.a: TMDL can be used to store Power BI semantic models as a folder of text files.
faq.q: How can TMDL be used with Power BI?

tmdl.long:
Tabular Model Definition Language (TMDL) is a text-based syntax for defining tabular semantic models. It is designed to be human-readable and describes model objects such as tables, measures and relationships in plain text rather than in a binary or opaque format.

TMDL can be used to store Power BI semantic models as a folder of text files. Because the model definition is held in readable text, individual objects can be inspected and edited directly, and the files can be handled with standard text-based tooling.

Microsoft documents TMDL in its Analysis Services documentation, where an overview of the language is available. At present no related topics or episodes are linked to this entry on M365.FM, so no further context from the show is available here.

toil.desc: Toil in operations is repetitive, manual work such as alert triage or log analysis that adds no lasting value and that SRE and DevOps teams aim to automate away.

faq.a: Toil is repetitive, manual operational work, such as recurring alert triage or log analysis, that creates no lasting value.
faq.q: What is toil in operations?

faq.a: Site reliability and DevOps teams aim to reduce toil mainly through automation of the repetitive tasks.
faq.q: How do teams reduce toil?

faq.a: The term is used by site reliability engineering (SRE) and DevOps teams to describe operational work that should be minimized.
faq.q: Which teams use the term toil?

toil.long:
Toil (operations) is repetitive, manual operational work that creates no lasting value. Typical examples are recurring alert triage and log analysis, where the same steps are carried out again and again without improving the underlying system.

The concept is used by site reliability engineering (SRE) and DevOps teams to identify work that consumes time without moving a service forward. Once a task is recognized as toil, the usual goal is to reduce it, most often through automation, so that engineers can spend more time on work with lasting impact.

In practice, naming something as toil helps teams distinguish it from engineering work such as building tooling, improving reliability or removing the root cause of recurring problems. Reducing toil is therefore treated as an ongoing part of operating services rather than a one-time cleanup.

No specific M365.FM episodes, product links or related topics are listed for this entry yet.

token-theft.desc: Token theft is an attack in which an adversary steals and replays a session or access token to act as a user without the password or another MFA prompt.

faq.a: Token theft is an attack in which an adversary steals a user's session or access token and replays it to act as that user. Because the token already reflects a completed sign-in, the attacker does not need the password or a new MFA prompt.
faq.q: What is token theft?

faq.a: Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing is a common way to obtain a token: the attacker intercepts a legitimate sign-in and captures the resulting token. The episode "Stop OAuth Consent Attacks in Microsoft Entra ID" names AiTM phishing and token theft as techniques that can bypass MFA.
faq.q: How does token theft relate to adversary-in-the-middle phishing?

faq.a: The episodes point to Conditional Access, MFA, token hygiene with continuous access evaluation (CAE), clear device tiers, time-bound privileged roles, regular permission reviews, monitoring and a token theft response plan.
faq.q: What do the M365.FM episodes suggest for reducing token theft risk?

token-theft.long:
Token theft is an attack in which an adversary steals a user's session or access token and replays it to act as that user. Because the token already represents a completed sign-in, the attacker does not need the password and does not have to pass multi-factor authentication (MFA) again. A common route to a stolen token is adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing, in which the attacker sits between the user and the real sign-in service and captures the token that results from a legitimate authentication. Microsoft documents this scenario in a dedicated token theft playbook within its security operations guidance.

The concept matters because it undermines a common assumption: that enabling MFA is enough to protect an account. The episode "Stop OAuth Consent Attacks in Microsoft Entra ID" describes phishing that can bypass MFA using techniques such as AiTM phishing and token theft. According to the episode, these methods exploit weaknesses in the authentication process and allow unauthorized access without the victim completing an MFA challenge, and the episode notes that such attacks are becoming more frequent.

Token theft also appears as a step inside broader attack chains. The episode "Detect Microsoft 365 Attack Chains with Entra and Sentinel" lists token theft and forgery among the common privilege escalation methods. In that phase, attackers steal or forge authentication tokens to gain unauthorized access and move toward higher-level access to sensitive data and resources. The episode presents this alongside API abuse and the exploitation of configuration flaws, and recommends stricter access controls and regular reviews of user permissions as a way to reduce the risk.

Configuration is a recurring theme in how the episodes treat prevention. "Hidden Microsoft 365 Tenant Security Risks" warns that without Conditional Access and multi-factor authentication, the risk of token theft increases, because attackers can steal access tokens and use them to bypass security controls. It also advises monitoring the Microsoft 365 environment for signs of suspicious activity and reviewing permissions regularly. This frames token theft as one of several consequences of tenant misconfiguration rather than an isolated threat.

"Fix Conditional Access Loopholes in Microsoft 365" treats token theft as one of three trust problems in a messy Conditional Access setup, alongside overbroad exclusions and unclear device compliance. The episode proposes replacing permanent exceptions with time-bound authentication contexts, stronger MFA and clear device tiers (compliant, hybrid joined, Azure AD joined, registered). Its suggested baseline of five inclusive policies includes one for token hygiene and continuous access evaluation (CAE), together with all-users MFA, step-up for unmanaged devices, strong authentication for admins and an emergency bypass through authentication context, followed by a safe rollout approach.

Administrative access is another area where token theft planning is mentioned. In "Microsoft Intune - Simply Explained", the episode says Microsoft recommends a defense-in-depth strategy for securing Intune administration. That includes Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management for time-bound role assignments, strong authentication methods and a token theft response plan, so that unusual administrator activity can be monitored and answered.

Taken together, the sources describe token theft as a threat that is addressed through layered controls rather than a single setting: Conditional Access policies, device state requirements, token hygiene with CAE, time-bound privileges, permission reviews and monitoring, plus a prepared response plan for the case where a token is compromised. Microsoft's token theft playbook is the official reference for how to approach investigation and response.

tool-contract.desc: A tool contract is a standardized, versioned definition of an action an AI agent may call, covering inputs, outputs, executing identity, logging and approval gates.

faq.a: A tool contract is a standardized, versioned definition of an action an AI agent may call. It specifies allowed inputs, structured outputs, the executing identity, provenance logging and approval gates for irreversible steps.
faq.q: What is a tool contract?

faq.a: Like an API contract, it defines precisely what an action accepts and returns, so behavior is predictable. It adds agent-specific controls such as executing identity, provenance logging and approval gates.
faq.q: How is a tool contract similar to an API contract?

faq.a: Approval gates apply to irreversible steps, so that actions which cannot be undone require explicit approval before they run.
faq.q: Why do tool contracts include approval gates?

tool-contract.long:
A tool contract is a standardized, versioned definition of an action that an AI agent is permitted to call. It works in a similar way to an API contract: instead of leaving an agent free to improvise, the contract states exactly what the action does and under which conditions it may run.

According to the available description, a tool contract specifies the allowed inputs for the action, the structured outputs it returns, the identity under which it executes, and the provenance logging that records what happened. It also defines approval gates for irreversible steps, so that actions which cannot be undone require explicit sign-off before they proceed. Because the definition is versioned, changes to an action can be tracked over time rather than altering behavior silently.

The concept is used to make agent behavior predictable and auditable. By constraining inputs, fixing the shape of outputs, tying execution to a defined identity and recording provenance, a tool contract gives organizations a clearer basis for governing what an agent can do.

On M365.FM, the topic appears in the episode "MCP Custom Connector in Copilot Studio: The Complete Integration Guide" (published 2025-11-12), which covers integration in the context of an MCP custom connector in Copilot Studio.

total-cost-of-ownership.desc: Total cost of ownership (TCO) is the full lifetime cost of a system, covering operations, maintenance, staffing and infrastructure, not just the purchase or migration price.

faq.a: TCO covers the full cost of a system over its lifetime, including operations, maintenance, staffing and infrastructure, not only the initial purchase or migration cost. Episodes also name scalability, support and resource requirements as part of the evaluation.
faq.q: What does total cost of ownership (TCO) include?

faq.a: The episode on Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows 365 says tools like the Azure Pricing Calculator can help estimate costs and understand TCO. It also stresses choosing suitable resources such as VM sizes and storage configurations.
faq.q: How is TCO used when planning an Azure Virtual Desktop deployment?

faq.a: The episode "Platform Engineering - Simply Explained" cites up to 9% potential TCO reduction from auto-scaling and up to 7% from right-sizing instances. "Microsoft Sentinel - Simply Explained" attributes a lower TCO versus traditional SIEM solutions to flexible pricing and efficient data handling.
faq.q: Which factors can reduce TCO according to the episodes?

total-cost-of-ownership.long:
Total cost of ownership (TCO) is the full cost of a system over its lifetime. It includes operations, maintenance, staffing and infrastructure, and not only the initial purchase or migration cost. The concept is used to compare technology options on a longer horizon, so that a low entry price does not hide high running costs, and a higher upfront investment is weighed against what it saves later.

In practice, TCO is a way of structuring a budget discussion. An evaluation typically separates initial costs from operational expenses, and adds factors such as scalability, support and resource requirements. The M365.FM episode "Vector Databases - Simply Explained" describes TCO as an evaluation of long-term costs, including initial and operational expenses, scalability, support and resource requirements, in order to align a deployment with budget and growth needs. The same episode points out that ongoing costs such as cloud service charges, maintenance fees and scaling costs can rise as data and query volumes increase, so a cloud service may become more expensive as usage grows.

TCO also appears when comparing delivery models. The episode "Azure Virtual Desktop vs Windows 365 with Dieter Kempeneers [MVP] & Dominiek Verham [MVP]" mentions using the Azure Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and understand TCO when planning a migration to Azure Virtual Desktop. It also notes that choosing resources such as VM sizes and storage configurations is important, which are decisions that feed directly into the cost picture. For Windows 365, the episode describes Microsoft handling much of the underlying infrastructure, which shifts where administration effort sits.

Several episodes link TCO to specific levers. "Platform Engineering - Simply Explained" lists a potential TCO reduction of up to 9% through auto-scaling and up to 7% from right-sizing instances, presented as figures in that episode's cost-benefit table. These numbers are attributed to the episode and are not general benchmarks. The episode "Microsoft Sentinel - Simply Explained" says that organizations can experience a lower TCO with Microsoft Sentinel compared with traditional SIEM solutions, and attributes this to a flexible pricing model and efficient data handling.

The architecture-focused episode "Public vs Hybrid vs Multi-Cloud Azure Architecture" treats TCO alongside return on investment (ROI). It recommends continuously evaluating and iterating an architecture so that both ROI and TCO stay optimized over time, rather than treating cost as a one-time calculation at design stage. It also frames cost as one of several trade-offs that business stakeholders should consider together with other architectural pillars as a workload becomes production-ready.

Taken together, the episodes treat TCO as a recurring question rather than a single figure. Typical decisions where it matters include choosing between virtual desktop options, selecting a data platform such as a vector database, picking a security monitoring approach, and setting up scaling and sizing practices. In each case the useful comparison covers the whole lifetime of the system: the cost of getting started, the cost of running and staffing it, and how those costs change as usage grows.

traceability.desc: Traceability is the ability to follow the recorded history of material and products through receipt, production and delivery, supporting recall and containment decisions.

faq.a: It is the ability to follow the recorded history of material and products through receipt, production and delivery. It is used to support recall and containment decisions.
faq.q: What is traceability in manufacturing?

faq.a: According to the episode "Traceability and Genealogy: Tracking Every Part From Supplier to Customer", it needs consistent identifiers and connected systems, including lot and serial concepts and well-managed system handoffs.
faq.q: What does traceability need in order to work?

faq.a: No. M365.FM episodes also use the term for audit trails in approval workflows, for governance of emissions data, and for accountability of AI decisions.
faq.q: Is traceability only relevant to physical parts?

traceability.long:
Traceability is the ability to follow the recorded history of material and products through receipt, production and delivery. In manufacturing, it is used to support recall and containment decisions: when a problem is found in a part, a lot or a finished product, a traceable record shows where that item came from, where it went and which other items may be affected. The same idea also appears in compliance and governance contexts, where it refers to being able to follow decisions and actions back through a documented trail.

In a production setting, traceability depends on data foundations rather than on any single tool. The M365.FM episode "Traceability and Genealogy: Tracking Every Part From Supplier to Customer", part of the iFAKT series, states that tracing every part from supplier to customer needs consistent identifiers and connected systems. The episode covers lot and serial concepts, system handoffs and typical gaps, and explains how to design traceability that supports quality, recalls and audits. Lot and serial identifiers give each batch or unit a reference that can be carried from one step to the next, while handoffs between systems are the points where records can be lost or broken. Genealogy, the companion term used in that episode title, describes the connected history of what went into a product and where it ended up.

Typical decisions around traceability concern how identifiers are assigned, how they are kept consistent across receiving, production and shipping, and how the systems involved pass that information to one another. Gaps tend to appear where identifiers change format, where records are entered manually, or where one system does not pass its data on to the next. The episode frames these gaps as a central design topic, because a recall or containment decision is only as reliable as the connected record behind it.

Beyond manufacturing, the term appears in several other M365.FM episodes, always in the sense of a followable record. The episode "Build Audit-Ready Power Automate Approval Workflows" says that auditors may demand clear evidence or traceability, that missing audit trails and weak access controls create compliance gaps, and that approval logs should capture details such as who approved and when. The episode "Microsoft Carbon Control Plane for Enterprise Sustainability" lists centralized governance, traceability and audit readiness among the key characteristics of an approach in which emissions data is integrated with systems of record such as ERP, procurement, energy platforms and cloud services.

Two episodes link traceability to AI. In "Automated Red Teaming for Multi-Model AI in Finance", the episode says that establishing clear ownership and traceability for AI decisions enhances accountability and compliance. In "Graph-Powered AI Agents: An Enterprise Architecture Guide", the episode says Microsoft Graph addresses compliance and traceability requirements by integrating Microsoft Purview APIs, so that prompts and responses from AI applications can be sent programmatically into Microsoft Purview for compliance tracking.

Across these sources, the common thread is a recorded, connected history that can be followed after the fact. Whether the subject is a manufactured part, an approval, an emissions figure or an AI decision, traceability depends on consistent identifiers or logging, on systems that hand information on without loss, and on governance that defines who is responsible for the record. The sources summarized here describe the concept and its data requirements, not a specific product feature, so the practical design depends on the systems and processes already in place.

trainable-classifiers.desc: Trainable classifiers are machine-learning classifiers in Microsoft Purview that learn to recognize document types from examples and serve as conditions in DLP and labeling policies.

faq.a: They are machine-learning classifiers that learn to recognize a kind of document, such as contracts or source code, from example documents. They can be used as conditions in DLP and labeling policies.
faq.q: What are trainable classifiers in Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: Sensitive information types use pattern-based detection for structured data like credit card numbers. Trainable classifiers recognize documents that fit a category based on examples, even when the content follows no fixed pattern.
faq.q: How do trainable classifiers differ from sensitive information types?

faq.a: According to the episodes, they can serve as conditions in DLP policies and in automatic or recommended sensitivity labeling. They also scan user prompts and responses during AI interactions.
faq.q: Where can trainable classifiers be used?

trainable-classifiers.long:
Trainable classifiers are machine-learning classifiers in Microsoft Purview that learn to recognize a kind of document, such as contracts or source code, from example documents. Instead of matching a fixed pattern, a classifier is taught what a category of content looks like, and it can then be used as a condition in Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies and in sensitivity labeling policies. They are one of several detection methods in Purview for finding and protecting sensitive information.

The purpose of trainable classifiers is to cover content that cannot be described with a simple rule. Pattern-based detection, such as sensitive information types, works well for structured data like credit card numbers and health identifiers. Many business documents, however, do not follow a fixed pattern. A resume, a patent, a contract or a piece of source code is recognizable by its overall content and structure rather than by a single string. The episodes describe trainable classifiers as a way to recognize documents that fit specific categories using examples of business content, which improves the accuracy of data classification and reduces the need to write manual rules.

Within Purview, trainable classifiers sit alongside other classification capabilities. The episode "Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) - Simply Explained" lists them together with sensitive information types, Exact Data Match and Document Fingerprinting. Exact Data Match compares content against an approved dataset to reach higher accuracy and fewer false positives, while Document Fingerprinting identifies copies or near-copies of known documents. Trainable classifiers differ from these in that they generalize from example content to a whole category of documents, even when individual files do not match any known pattern or reference file.

A typical use is in DLP. The episode "Configure Microsoft 365 DLP Policies in Purview" states that built-in and trainable classifiers help detect complex content such as resumes, source code or patents, which reduces manual rule creation when planning a Microsoft 365 DLP setup. A classifier can be set as a condition so that a policy acts when matching content is shared, moved or accessed. The same episode places this next to DLP logs and Activity Explorer entries that support investigations, and next to Endpoint DLP, which can enforce controls on managed devices.

Trainable classifiers also support labeling. According to the episode "Fix Microsoft Purview Information Protection Rollouts", Purview can automatically apply or recommend sensitivity labels using sensitive information types, patterns and trainable classifiers, so that labeling scales without constant user intervention. The episode "Protect Microsoft Copilot with Purview, DLP, and Insider Risk with Alan Cox [MVP]" adds that sensitive information types and trainable classifiers scan user prompts and responses during AI interactions, and that applied sensitivity labels give a visible layer of protection in apps such as Word and Outlook. Automating label application means the process does not depend on users labeling every file or email.

The episode "Shadow Data Discovery and Governance with Microsoft Purview" frames classification as a prerequisite for protection: sensitive data must be classified before it can be protected. It presents trainable classifiers as the tool for recognizing documents that fit a category even when they follow no fixed pattern, and pairs them with pattern-based detectors, Exact Data Match and document fingerprinting. In practice, the choice between these methods depends on the data. Structured identifiers suit pattern-based types, approved reference datasets suit Exact Data Match, known documents suit fingerprinting, and categories of free-form business content suit trainable classifiers. Further detail on how classifiers are created and trained is available in the official Microsoft documentation for trainable classifiers in Microsoft Purview.

transact-sql.desc: Transact-SQL (T-SQL) is Microsoft's extension of SQL, used by SQL Server, Azure SQL Database and related SQL products and services to query and manage data.

faq.a: Transact-SQL (T-SQL) is Microsoft's extension of SQL used by Microsoft SQL Server and related SQL products and services. According to Microsoft Learn, all tools and applications that talk to a SQL Server database do so by sending T-SQL commands.
faq.q: What is Transact-SQL (T-SQL)?

faq.a: The Microsoft Learn reference lists SQL Server, Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, Azure Synapse Analytics and several Microsoft Fabric items such as the warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint. Individual articles may apply only to certain products, as shown in their applies-to notes.
faq.q: Which Microsoft products does T-SQL apply to?

faq.a: The episode "SQL vs T-SQL: Key Differences for Microsoft Data Teams" suggests T-SQL when using Microsoft SQL Server or Azure SQL Database, when portability across vendors is not required, and when procedural logic is needed. Standard SQL is preferred for cloud-agnostic or multi-vendor systems.
faq.q: When should a team choose T-SQL over standard SQL?

transact-sql.long:
Transact-SQL (T-SQL) is Microsoft's extension of SQL, the structured query language for relational databases. It is the dialect used by Microsoft SQL Server and by related SQL products and services. The Microsoft Learn reference for the Database Engine states that all tools and applications that talk to a SQL Server database do so by sending T-SQL commands, which makes the language central to the Microsoft data platform.

In practice, T-SQL covers the statements that most people associate with working in a relational database. The reference names SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE as common statements for reading and changing data. Beyond these, the documentation links to system objects that administrators and developers query or call, including catalog views, dynamic management views, system functions and system stored procedures. Related languages such as XQuery and MDX are also referenced from the same documentation area.

The scope of T-SQL extends across several Microsoft products. According to the reference, it applies to SQL Server, Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, Azure Synapse Analytics and several Microsoft Fabric items, such as the warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint. Individual articles may be valid only for certain products, which is indicated by the applies-to notes shown on each page. Checking those notes is therefore part of using the documentation correctly, especially when moving workloads between an on-premises SQL Server instance and a cloud service.

Several tools are built around T-SQL. The reference lists SQL Server Management Studio, the MSSQL extension for Visual Studio Code, SQL Server Data Tools and sqlcmd as tools that use the language. In SQL Server Management Studio, pressing F1 on a keyword opens the matching reference article, which gives a quick path from a statement in an editor to its documented syntax and behavior. Details on how T-SQL relates to SQL standards are covered in a separate document rather than on the reference entry page.

A recurring decision for data teams is whether to write standard SQL or to use T-SQL features. The M365.FM episode "SQL vs T-SQL: Key Differences for Microsoft Data Teams" addresses this with a checklist under the keyword t-sql vs sql. According to the episode, a team using Microsoft SQL Server or Azure SQL Database should prefer T-SQL, while multi-vendor or cloud-agnostic systems point toward standard SQL. On portability, the episode says standard SQL fits queries that must run across different relational database systems such as Oracle, MySQL and PostgreSQL, whereas T-SQL is the choice when portability is not required. The excerpt also lists procedural logic as a reason to use T-SQL, and the episode advises consulting Microsoft's documentation and testing T-SQL features in the target environment to get reliable and well-performing database operations.

For teams working with Microsoft data services, T-SQL is therefore both the everyday query language and a platform-specific layer on top of SQL. Understanding which statements and system objects are available in a given product, and which are portable, helps when planning migrations, choosing tooling and deciding how tightly to tie code to the Microsoft platform.

transactional-outbox-pattern.desc: The transactional outbox pattern writes a record change and a matching outbox table entry in one transaction so downstream services can reliably process every event.

faq.a: It is an integration pattern in which a record change and a matching entry in a dedicated outbox table are written in the same transaction. This lets a downstream service reliably pick up and process every event.
faq.q: What is the transactional outbox pattern?

faq.a: Writing both in one transaction means they succeed or fail together. The outbox therefore holds an entry for each committed change, so downstream processing does not miss events.
faq.q: Why is the outbox entry written in the same transaction as the data change?

transactional-outbox-pattern.long:
The transactional outbox pattern is an integration pattern in which a change to a record and a matching entry in a dedicated outbox table are written in the same transaction. Because both writes succeed or fail together, the outbox contains an entry for every committed change, and none for changes that were rolled back.

The pattern is used so that a downstream service can reliably pick up and process every event. Instead of publishing a message directly while updating data, which can leave the two out of step if one step fails, the application records the event in the outbox table alongside the data change. A separate process or service then reads the outbox entries and handles them.

The available facts describe the pattern in general terms and do not tie it to a specific Microsoft product, service or implementation. No related entities, documentation links or M365.FM episodes are currently listed for this topic.

triple-peak-workday.desc: The triple peak workday is a pattern described in Microsoft research in which knowledge work activity peaks in the morning, the afternoon and the late evening.

faq.a: It is a pattern described in Microsoft research in which knowledge work activity peaks in the morning and afternoon and then peaks again in the late evening.
faq.q: What is the triple peak workday?

faq.a: A traditional pattern is described by two peaks, morning and afternoon. The triple peak workday adds a third peak of activity in the late evening.
faq.q: How does it differ from a traditional workday pattern?

triple-peak-workday.long:
The triple peak workday is a concept from Microsoft research that describes how knowledge work activity is distributed across a day. Instead of the traditional two peaks, one in the morning and one in the afternoon, activity rises a third time in the late evening.

The term is used to describe changing daily rhythms of knowledge workers. It is relevant to discussions of work patterns, scheduling and how people balance working time with personal time, since an evening peak means that some work takes place outside the conventional workday.

The available information on this page is limited to the definition above. No related topics, official documentation links or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, so further detail on the underlying data, methodology or recommendations is not covered here.

truesec.desc: Truesec is a cybersecurity company offering services such as penetration testing, incident response and proactive security.

faq.a: Truesec is a cybersecurity company that provides services such as penetration testing, incident response and proactive security.
faq.q: What is Truesec?

faq.a: The listed services are penetration testing, incident response and proactive security.
faq.q: What services does Truesec provide?

truesec.long:
Truesec is a cybersecurity company. According to the information available, its services include penetration testing, incident response and proactive security work.

Penetration testing involves simulating attacks against systems to identify weaknesses, while incident response covers the handling of security incidents once they occur. Proactive security refers to measures taken in advance to reduce risk. These service areas are typical of organizations that help others assess and improve their security posture.

trunk-based-development.desc: Trunk-based development is a source-control practice where developers commit small changes to one shared trunk branch at least daily, with branches lasting hours.

faq.a: It is a source-control branching model in which developers collaborate on one branch, the trunk (usually main in Git), committing small changes at least once every 24 hours and avoiding long-lived development branches.
faq.q: What is trunk-based development?

faq.a: Yes. Larger teams use pull requests, but the feature branches must be short-lived and come from one developer workstation, existing for code review and CI checks rather than for building or publishing artifacts.
faq.q: Can teams use pull requests with trunk-based development?

faq.a: Larger changes are handled with branch by abstraction and feature flags so they can be merged without disrupting the trunk. Releases are made from the trunk, with fix-forward corrections, or from release branches cut just in time, hardened and deleted.
faq.q: How are larger changes and releases handled in trunk-based development?

trunk-based-development.long:
Trunk-based development is a source-control branching model in which developers collaborate on a single shared branch, the trunk, which in Git is usually main. Instead of keeping long-lived development branches apart for weeks, developers commit small changes to the trunk at least once every 24 hours, and any branches that exist live for hours rather than weeks. The aim is to avoid the merge problems and broken builds that tend to appear when separate lines of work drift away from each other.

The practice is used to support continuous integration and continuous delivery. Because everyone integrates into the same branch frequently, the codebase stays close to a state that can be released on demand. Teams that adopt the model replace long-lived branches with a set of documented techniques. These include running a full pre-integration build on the developer workstation before committing, using a build server that confirms each commit does not break the build, and practising eager code review so changes do not wait long before they are merged.

How the model works in practice depends on team size. Small teams may commit straight to the trunk. Larger teams commonly use pull requests, but the feature branches behind them must be short-lived and created from a single developer workstation. Such short-lived branches exist for code review and CI checks, not for building or publishing artifacts. This keeps the trunk as the single source of truth and avoids the situation in which people cannot tell which version is the real one.

Two techniques are central when a change is too large to finish in a day. Branch by abstraction allows a larger change to be made gradually inside the trunk, and feature flags let unfinished functionality be merged without being visible or active for users. Together they make it possible to integrate continuously while still delivering larger pieces of work over time.

Releases are handled differently from models built around permanent release lines. If release branches are used at all, they are cut from the trunk just in time, hardened, and then deleted. Alternatively, a team can release directly from the trunk and fix forward, meaning problems are corrected with a new commit on the trunk rather than patched on a separate branch. According to the source material, Google practises trunk-based development with a monorepo and reportedly about 35,000 developers. The same source compares GitHub Flow as a similar approach that differs mainly in where releases come from.

The M365.FM episode "Git Branching Strategies - Simply Explained" places trunk-based development among several common strategies and describes it as the fast one, next to Git Flow, described as the structured one, and GitHub Flow, described as the simple one. The episode also covers what a branch is, why branching strategies exist, the three building blocks of branching, pull requests, merge versus rebase, how to choose a strategy for small and large teams, and common mistakes beginners make. Within that framing, trunk-based development is one option to weigh according to team size, release needs and how much discipline around testing and review a team can sustain.

Choosing the model is therefore a decision about trade-offs. Frequent integration into one branch reduces merge conflicts and keeps the build healthy, but it relies on small changes, automated checks on the build server, and tools such as feature flags to keep unfinished work safe. Teams weighing it against other strategies typically look at how often they need to release, how large their team is, and whether they can keep the trunk releasable at all times.

trusted-platform-module.desc: The Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is a hardware security chip that stores cryptographic keys and helps prove a device's identity and boot integrity.

faq.a: It is a hardware chip that works as a secure cryptographic processor with physical tamper-resistance. It generates, stores and limits the use of cryptographic keys and records measurements of boot components.
faq.q: What is the Trusted Platform Module (TPM)?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn names Windows Hello, BitLocker and System Guard. Windows Autopilot pre-provisioning and self-deploying modes also require TPM attestation to prove the device's identity.
faq.q: Which Windows features depend on TPM?

faq.a: New and upgraded Windows 11 devices need TPM 2.0. Device health attestation with TPM 2.0 additionally requires UEFI firmware.
faq.q: Which TPM version does Windows 11 need?

trusted-platform-module.long:
The Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is a hardware-based security feature: a chip on a device's motherboard that acts as a secure cryptographic processor. Its specifications are defined by the Trusted Computing Group. The chip includes several physical tamper-resistance mechanisms, so malware cannot interfere with the protections it provides. In the Microsoft ecosystem, TPM serves as a hardware anchor for device identity and for features that need to trust that a key or a system state has not been altered.

The module generates, stores and limits the use of cryptographic keys. Keys can be configured so that they never leave the module, which keeps them out of reach of software running on the operating system. Authorization values can be attached to keys, and dictionary-attack protection is triggered after too many failed attempts. A device can also be authenticated through a unique RSA key held in the chip. In addition, the TPM records measurements of boot components such as firmware and the operating system. Because of these measurements, a key can be made usable only when the system started with the expected software. Windows initializes and takes ownership of the TPM automatically.

Several Windows security features rely on the TPM. According to Microsoft Learn, Windows Hello, BitLocker and System Guard all use it. Typical uses include certificates bound to the device, replacing smart cards, BitLocker Network Unlock and device health attestation. In device health attestation, an MDM server asks a health service about the device's settings, such as whether Secure Boot is enabled, and the TPM provides the measured evidence behind that answer. Device health attestation with TPM 2.0 requires UEFI firmware.

TPM also matters for provisioning. Windows Autopilot pre-provisioning and self-deploying modes require TPM attestation to prove the device's identity. In practice this means a device without a usable TPM cannot take part in those deployment modes, which makes the chip a hardware prerequisite to check when planning device purchases or Autopilot rollouts. New and upgraded Windows 11 devices need TPM 2.0, so the version of the module is a relevant decision point when assessing existing hardware.

The M365.FM episode "Windows 365 Link - Simply Explained" places TPM in the context of a thin-client access device. The episode describes a design with a minimal local footprint that avoids the traditional risks of locally stored files, installed applications, administrator accounts and unmanaged software. It explores how Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Intune, Trusted Platform Module (TPM), Secure Boot, BitLocker encryption, Microsoft Defender and strict application controls work together to protect both the access device and the cloud-hosted desktop environment. Combined with Zero Trust identity verification and centralized device management, the episode says, organizations gain a highly secure endpoint while significantly reducing operational complexity.

In summary, the TPM is the hardware component that ties together several layers: key protection, disk encryption, sign-in, boot integrity measurement and remote attestation. Administrators typically encounter it when verifying Windows 11 hardware requirements, enabling BitLocker, configuring device health attestation or preparing devices for Autopilot pre-provisioning and self-deploying deployments.

typescript.desc: TypeScript is a Microsoft programming language that adds static types to JavaScript to catch mistakes early, and it is used for Power Apps code components.

faq.a: TypeScript is a programming language from Microsoft that builds on JavaScript with static types to catch mistakes early. It is used, among other things, to write Power Apps code components.
faq.q: What is TypeScript?

faq.a: According to the episodes, Code Apps let teams build custom web applications with technologies such as React and TypeScript, developing locally and running within the Power Platform. App logic can be written in TypeScript or JavaScript using Visual Studio Code and the Power Apps SDK.
faq.q: How is TypeScript used in Power Apps Code Apps?

faq.a: The episode on PnP React Controls describes TypeScript as providing stronger typing and compile-time checks within a modern SPFx stack that also includes React, Fluent UI, PnPjs and PnP React Controls.
faq.q: What role does TypeScript play in SharePoint Framework development?

typescript.long:
TypeScript is a programming language from Microsoft that builds on JavaScript by adding static types. The aim of those types is to catch mistakes early, before code runs, rather than leaving them to surface at runtime. In the Microsoft ecosystem it is used to write Power Apps code components, and it appears across other developer scenarios covered by M365.FM, including SharePoint Framework (SPFx) development, Power Apps Code Apps, infrastructure as code and AI-assisted software engineering.

Because TypeScript is built on JavaScript, teams that already know JavaScript can work with it without learning an entirely separate language. The core idea is stronger typing combined with compile-time checks. The episode "Stop Reinventing SPFx- Building Better SharePoint Solutions with PnP React Controls with Siddharth Vaghasia [MVP]" describes TypeScript as providing stronger typing and compile-time checks, and places it alongside React, Fluent UI, PnPjs and PnP React Controls as part of a modern SPFx technology stack. In that breakdown, no single framework carries a project; several technologies each play a defined role. TypeScript contributes the typing layer, Fluent UI helps custom solutions keep the familiar Microsoft user experience, and PnPjs simplifies interaction with SharePoint, Microsoft Graph and other Microsoft 365 services by replacing repetitive REST request code with reusable abstractions.

TypeScript is also central to Power Apps Code Apps. The episode "Power Apps Code Apps - Simply Explained" explains that Code Apps let teams create custom web applications using familiar coding tools within the Power Platform, drawing on modern web technologies such as React and TypeScript. These apps can be developed locally and run within the Power Platform. According to the episode, the significance lies in better control over architecture, user interface and complex business logic, which makes them suitable for advanced applications and sets them apart from Canvas and Model-Driven Apps. Teams are advised to understand these characteristics before adopting Code Apps in a Microsoft environment.

The episode "Power Apps Code Apps with Carike Botha [MVP]" adds the tooling side. It describes writing app logic in languages such as TypeScript and JavaScript, using frameworks such as React and Vue for the user interface, and working in Visual Studio Code, which integrates with the Power Apps SDK so that code apps can be developed, tested and packaged within the editor. The episode also mentions access to more than 1,500 connectors for data integration, including Dataverse and SQL data sources.

TypeScript is not limited to application front ends. In "Bicep vs ARM Templates vs Terraform for Azure", Pulumi is presented as an option for teams that prefer languages they already know: it allows infrastructure as code to be written in Python, TypeScript, Go, C# or Java. The episode lists benefits such as using familiar languages, fitting into current development workflows and not needing to learn a new syntax, and notes that this applies to Azure resources and other cloud platforms.

TypeScript also comes up in discussions of AI-assisted development. In "GitHub Copilot, Clean Context, Automated Testing & AI Coding Agents with Lars Gyrup Brink Nielsen [MVP]", Mirko Peters and the guest cover GitHub Copilot, AI coding agents, developer experience, automated testing, TypeScript, JavaScript, Nx, monorepos, Polygraph, GitHub Actions and Playwright, along with the architectural foundations needed for agentic software engineering at enterprise scale. In that context TypeScript is one of the languages and ecosystems around which such workflows are discussed.

Typical decisions around TypeScript concern where it fits in a given solution: as the language for Power Apps code components, as the typed layer of an SPFx project, as the language for a Power Apps Code App built with React, or as an alternative to a domain-specific language for infrastructure code. In each case the shared reasoning in the episodes is the same: familiar web tooling combined with typing that surfaces errors early.

unattended-desktop-flow.desc: An unattended desktop flow is a Power Automate desktop flow run mode where a bot signs in to a free machine without a user present, using a paid unattended license.

faq.a: It is a desktop flow run mode in which the bot signs in to a free machine and runs the flow without a user present.
faq.q: What is an unattended desktop flow?

faq.a: Yes. Running a desktop flow unattended requires a paid unattended license.
faq.q: Does an unattended desktop flow need a license?

faq.a: No. It cannot run while any user session is open, and it also cannot run with elevated rights.
faq.q: Can an unattended desktop flow run while someone is signed in to the machine?

unattended-desktop-flow.long:
An unattended desktop flow is a run mode for desktop flows in which the bot signs in to a free machine and runs the automation without a user being present. Unlike an attended run, no person needs to watch or interact with the session while the flow executes.

This mode is used for automations that should run on their own, such as scheduled or triggered tasks that do not depend on someone being logged in. The bot starts its own session on the target machine, which must be available for the run.

Several conditions apply. Running a desktop flow unattended requires a paid unattended license. The run cannot take place while any user session is open on the machine, so the machine has to be free of active sessions. In addition, an unattended run cannot be performed with elevated rights.

These constraints shape how machines are prepared and scheduled for unattended automation: the target machine needs to be idle and without a signed-in user at the time the flow starts, and the flow has to work without administrator-level privileges.

More details on running desktop flows unattended are available in Microsoft's Power Automate documentation. No episodes on M365.FM are currently linked to this topic.

unconstrained-delegation.desc: Unconstrained delegation is an Active Directory Kerberos setting that lets a service act as users toward any other service, which attackers can abuse if the host is compromised.

faq.a: It is a Kerberos delegation setting that lets a service cache users' TGTs and request tickets to any service on their behalf. Because it is not limited to specific services, a compromised host can be abused to impersonate users.
faq.q: What is unconstrained delegation in Active Directory?

faq.a: Its account security posture assessments cover unsecure Kerberos delegation, including unconstrained delegation, for entities that are not domain controllers. The recommendation is to disable delegation or use a constrained type with a defined list of allowed services.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Defender for Identity treat unconstrained delegation?

faq.a: In "Move Active Directory Groups to Microsoft Entra ID", the episode states that domain controllers cannot use unconstrained delegation during ADMT use. It suggests installing and running the ADMT apps on the target domain controller to remove the need for delegation.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode on moving Active Directory groups say about it?

unconstrained-delegation.long:
Unconstrained delegation is a Kerberos delegation setting in Active Directory. Kerberos delegation in general lets an application request end-user credentials so that it can reach resources on behalf of the originating user. Unconstrained delegation is the broadest of the available types. A service or computer configured this way can cache the TGTs of users who authenticate to it and can then request tickets to any other service in the user's name. Microsoft Defender for Identity lists it alongside constrained delegation and resource-based constrained delegation as one of the kinds of Kerberos delegation it evaluates.

The main concern is trust. With unconstrained delegation the environment has to trust the application to behave correctly, because the entity holding the setting can impersonate a user toward any other service. If that host is compromised, an attacker can reuse the cached tickets. Microsoft Defender for Identity illustrates this with a web site running under an application pool account that has unconstrained delegation. After a domain admin signs in to the site, the site could request a service ticket for a SQL server in that admin's name. It could also be used to change the Enterprise Admins group or to obtain the KRBTGT hash. Any service can be abused in this way if one of its delegation entries is sensitive.

In Microsoft Defender for Identity, unsecure Kerberos delegation is covered by the account security posture assessments. The assessment applies to entities that are not domain controllers and flags those with unsecure delegation configured. Its stated recommendation is to disable delegation or to switch to a constrained type. In practice that means trusting the computer for delegation to specified services only and listing the services it is allowed to delegate to, instead of allowing delegation to any service.

Typical situations in which the term comes up are security reviews of Active Directory, posture assessments of service accounts and servers, and migration projects. Reviewers look for accounts and computers with unconstrained delegation because each one widens the impact of a single host compromise. Administrators weighing whether delegation is needed at all can decide between removing it, using constrained delegation with an explicit list of target services, or using resource-based constrained delegation, which the Defender for Identity page names as a third option.

Unconstrained delegation also appears in the M365.FM episode "Move Active Directory Groups to Microsoft Entra ID". In its table of common ADMT problems, the episode notes that domain controllers cannot use unconstrained delegation. The suggested solution is to install and run the ADMT apps on the target domain controller, which removes the need for delegation. This shows that the setting can matter during directory migrations as well as in security hardening, and that some tooling requirements can be met without enabling it.

In summary, unconstrained delegation trades convenience for exposure. It allows a service to act for users toward any other service, but it concentrates risk on every host that holds the setting. The guidance in the sources is to disable it where possible, move to constrained delegation with a defined service list where delegation is needed, and treat any entity still configured this way as sensitive.

unified-namespace.desc: Unified namespace (UNS) is an architecture pattern: a governed, shared event space, typically on an MQTT broker, where factory data is published once and consumed by any approved system.

faq.a: A unified namespace is an architecture pattern that provides a governed, shared event space, typically on an MQTT broker, where machine data and other current factory events are published once and consumed by any approved system.
faq.q: What is a unified namespace (UNS)?

faq.a: No. The M365.FM episode on MQTT and OPC UA describes it as a common event space where IT and OT publish facts, not a new master database or a magic bullet that creates a shared operating model without effort.
faq.q: Is a UNS a new master database?

faq.a: The topic hierarchy lets data be found by navigation, and the episode advises mirroring an enterprise-to-cell structure such as ISA-95, keeping transient context like product codes and order numbers out of static topic paths, and using strict lowercase because topic names are case-sensitive.
faq.q: Why does topic design matter in a UNS?

unified-namespace.long:
A unified namespace (UNS) is an architecture pattern that provides a governed, shared event space, typically built on an MQTT broker. Machine data and other current factory events are published into this space once and can then be consumed by any approved system. The approach is used in manufacturing to bring operational technology (OT), IT and business systems onto a common footing without wiring every system to every other system.

The core mechanism is publish-subscribe messaging. Publishers send events to topics, and subscribers choose which topics they want to receive. Because data publishers do not need to know who is consuming their events, producers and consumers are decoupled. Subscribers can use wildcards and filtering to limit the traffic they receive. This decoupling is the main reason the pattern is discussed as an alternative to point-to-point integrations, whose maintenance burden grows as more systems are connected.

The topic hierarchy is central to how a UNS stays usable. Documentation from HiveMQ, which is vendor content, recommends that the hierarchy mirror the organisation, for example sites, lines, processes and assets, so data can be found by navigation and sprawl is avoided. The M365.FM episode on MQTT and OPC UA describes ISA-95, the enterprise-to-cell hierarchy, as a naming contract: a stable map for locating assets consistently before changing business context such as work orders and products is applied. The same episode warns against stuffing transient context, such as product codes and order numbers, into static topic paths, and notes that topic names are case-sensitive and call for strict lowercase conventions.

A broker alone does not make a UNS. The HiveMQ material argues that it must also support high-throughput messaging, fine-grained access control, interoperability between edge and cloud, and integration of historical data. Further requirements named there include scaling, schema registries that enforce data contracts and add context such as units, topic-level access control with TLS, and persistence through time-series databases and retained messages. The UNS is built for real-time exchange, so history needs separate persistence. Without data modelling it can become a chaotic message hub.

The M365.FM episodes place the concept within Microsoft manufacturing scenarios. In "Connect ERP, MES, and IoT — Without Replacing Anything", the UNS is presented as one of the architectural patterns, alongside edge computing, that lets factories escape point-to-point connections by decoupling data publishers from system consumers. The episode also stresses protecting system boundaries: data platforms and low-code applications must not become shadow systems where users can freely alter live production orders or inventory balances outside approved workflows.

The episode "MQTT and OPC UA in Microsoft Manufacturing: Azure IoT Operations + Fabric Architecture" addresses what it calls the UNS hype. It describes the UNS as a common event space in which IT and OT publish facts. It is explicitly not a new master database, and it is not a magic bullet that creates a shared operating model without effort. Mapping data once in the shared space, rather than five times in different downstream systems, is the benefit the episode points to, but the organisational work of agreeing on naming, context and ownership remains.

In practice, the decisions around a UNS concern topic and payload design, the choice of naming hierarchy, who may publish and who may subscribe, how data contracts are enforced, and where history is stored. Treating the UNS as a governed event space for current facts, rather than as a system of record, keeps its role clear relative to ERP, MES and data platforms.

unified-tenant-configuration-management.desc: Unified Tenant Configuration Management (UTCM) is a set of Microsoft Graph APIs, in preview since 2026, for baseline snapshots and drift monitoring of Microsoft 365 tenant configuration.
unified-tenant-configuration-management.long:
Unified Tenant Configuration Management (UTCM) is a set of Microsoft Graph APIs introduced in preview in 2026. It is designed for working with the configuration of a Microsoft 365 tenant: capturing a baseline snapshot of how a tenant is configured and then monitoring the live tenant for configuration drift.

In practice, this means an administrator or an automation process can record a reference state of tenant settings and later compare the current tenant against that reference. Differences between the baseline and the live configuration are what is described as configuration drift. Because UTCM is exposed through Microsoft Graph APIs rather than a single console, it is aimed at scenarios where tenant configuration is handled programmatically.

UTCM is still in preview, so its scope and behavior may change before general availability. No further details about supported workloads, permissions or licensing are included in the information available for this page.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

unit-economics.desc: Unit economics measures cost and value per unit of work instead of in aggregate, applied to AI as cost per decision, per insight or per automated workflow.

faq.a: Unit economics means measuring costs and value per unit of work rather than in aggregate. The unit can be chosen to match the outcome being evaluated.
faq.q: What is unit economics?

faq.a: On M365.FM it is framed as cost per decision, cost per insight or cost per automated workflow. This ties AI spending to specific results instead of a total figure.
faq.q: How is unit economics applied to AI?

faq.a: It is discussed in the episode "Microsoft 365 Copilot Prompts That Deliver Better Results", published on 2025-11-03.
faq.q: Where does unit economics appear on M365.FM?

unit-economics.long:
Unit economics is a concept that measures costs, and the value they produce, per unit of work rather than as a single aggregate figure. Instead of asking what a service costs in total, it asks what each individual output costs and what that output is worth.

In the context of AI, the unit can be defined in several ways. The framing discussed on M365.FM includes cost per decision, cost per insight and cost per automated workflow. Each of these ties spending to a concrete result, which makes it possible to compare approaches and to judge whether a particular use of AI is worth its cost.

The concept appears on M365.FM in the episode "Microsoft 365 Copilot Prompts That Deliver Better Results" (published 2025-11-03). There it is applied to AI usage, linking the way work is requested and structured to the cost and value of what comes back. No further details on specific figures or tools are given in the available material.

As a general reference point, unit economics is a way of reasoning about efficiency: define the unit that matters, measure what it costs to produce, and compare that with the value it delivers.

unit-testing.desc: Unit testing is a software testing practice that checks small, isolated pieces of code, such as a single method or function, against expected behavior.

faq.a: A unit test checks a small, isolated piece of code, such as a single method, function or formula, against expected behavior. In "Unit vs Integration vs Frontend Testing", a login function in a .NET app is given as an example.
faq.q: What does a unit test check?

faq.a: According to the episode "Unit vs Integration vs Frontend Testing", unit testing checks one part of the code by itself, integration testing checks that different parts work together, and frontend testing looks at everything from the user's point of view.
faq.q: How does unit testing differ from integration and frontend testing?

faq.a: The episode ".NET Extensibility and Clean Architecture with Miguel Castro [MVP]" says that standardized interfaces allow mock versions to be created. This makes unit testing easier and faster, because tests do not depend on real dependencies.
faq.q: Why do interfaces and mocks matter for unit testing?

unit-testing.long:
Unit testing is a software testing practice that checks small, isolated pieces of code, such as a single method or function, against expected behavior. Each test looks at one part of the code on its own, without depending on the rest of the application. The approach is fast and cheap to run, but it cannot see failures that only appear when components interact or when a user works with the interface.

The M365.FM episode "Unit vs Integration vs Frontend Testing" places unit testing next to two other levels of automated testing. In the episode's description, unit testing checks whether one part of the code works by itself, integration testing makes sure different parts of an app work together, and frontend testing looks at everything from the user's point of view. The episode gives the example of testing a login function in a .NET app as a unit test. This comparison explains the scope limit of unit tests: because they isolate a single piece of code, they cannot show whether the pieces cooperate correctly or whether the interface behaves as users expect.

Unit testing also appears in low-code and data-platform work. The episode "Automated Testing for Power Apps and Dataverse" describes unit testing as checking small pieces of logic, such as formulas or functions. According to the episode, unit tests are used to confirm that each part works on its own, which helps find errors early and keeps business rules reliable. The same episode treats integration testing as a separate type of testing, used to validate how Dataverse, connectors and external systems work together. Choosing among these types is presented as a decision about which kinds of issues a team wants to catch.

A further connection is design for testability. In the episode ".NET Extensibility and Clean Architecture with Miguel Castro [MVP]", the discussion of interfaces and loose coupling includes the point that interfaces allow mock versions to be created. The episode says this makes unit testing easier and faster, because tests do not need to rely on real dependencies. In other words, the way code is structured affects how simply individual units can be isolated and tested.

Unit testing is also discussed in terms of what is missing from infrastructure-as-code tooling. The episodes "Azure Bicep at Scale: Modular Infrastructure as Code" and "Terraform vs Azure Bicep: Which IaC Tool Should You Choose?" both list testing and validation among the limitations of Azure Bicep. They describe a lack of robust unit testing or simulation capabilities for deployments, and the second episode calls testing awkward because there is no first-class unit testing, which makes it difficult to simulate changes or mock deployments. This shows that unit testing is treated as a capability teams expect from their tooling, and that its absence is weighed when choosing between tools.

Taken together, the episodes position unit testing as the lowest and most granular level of automated testing. It is used to verify business logic, formulas and functions early and cheaply, to support code that is built around interfaces and mocks, and to give quick feedback on individual changes. It is typically combined with integration testing and frontend testing, since each level catches a different class of problem and none of them covers the others' blind spots.
