unity-catalog.desc: Unity Catalog is the unified governance layer for data and AI in Azure Databricks, providing access control, auditing, lineage and discovery across workspaces.

faq.a: Unity Catalog is the unified governance layer for data and AI in Azure Databricks. It controls access, tracks lineage automatically and records activity for auditing across workspaces.
faq.q: What is Unity Catalog in Azure Databricks?

faq.a: Tables, views, volumes, functions and models use a three-level namespace of catalog, schema and object. Privileges on these securable objects are granted to users, service principals or groups.
faq.q: How are objects organized in Unity Catalog?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, it is on automatically for workspaces created after November 2023. Workspaces created before that must be upgraded to use it.
faq.q: Is Unity Catalog enabled by default?

unity-catalog.long:
Unity Catalog is the governance layer of Databricks. In Azure Databricks it is described as the unified governance layer for data and AI. Once it is enabled for a workspace, it works underneath all data and AI interactions there. It provides centralized access control, auditing, lineage and discovery across workspaces, so that rules about who may see or change data are defined in one place instead of being repeated in each workspace.

The documentation describes how this works in practice. Unity Catalog controls access whenever a table is queried or a model is called. It tracks lineage automatically and records activity for auditing. Access to the catalog is available through Catalog Explorer, SQL, the Databricks CLI and REST APIs. Everything that is governed is a securable object, and privileges on these objects are granted to users, service principals or groups. Tables, views, volumes, functions and models are organized in a three-level namespace made up of a catalog, a schema and the object itself.

A distinction that matters for storage decisions is the one between managed and external objects. Tables and volumes can be managed, in which case Unity Catalog handles the storage lifecycle as well as governance. They can also be external, in which case Unity Catalog handles governance only and the storage stays outside its lifecycle management. Choosing between the two is a typical design decision when data already lives in existing storage locations.

The functional areas named in the Microsoft Learn documentation go beyond basic permissions. They include access control with attribute-based policies and row and column filters, discovery, lineage, audit logs exposed as a system table, data classification, data quality monitoring, data sharing across organizations and clouds, and AI governance. This means one layer covers both analytical data and AI assets such as models, rather than treating them as separate governance problems.

On availability, Unity Catalog is turned on automatically for workspaces created after November 2023. Workspaces created earlier must be upgraded to use it. The documentation also notes that an open-source implementation of Unity Catalog exists, and it points to a separate page for requirements and limitations that should be checked before planning a rollout.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Databricks - Simply Explained" places Unity Catalog within its overview of the platform. Its outline covers what Azure Databricks is, why the lakehouse idea exists, Apache Spark, notebooks, clusters and Delta Lake, and then groups "Workspaces, Accounts, and Unity Catalog" together as one topic. The episode also closes with guidance on when to use Databricks, Fabric or Synapse. In that framing, Unity Catalog is the part that explains how several workspaces under one account can share a consistent governance model, which is relevant when comparing Databricks with other Microsoft data platforms.

For people searching for the term, the short version is that Unity Catalog answers the questions of who can access which data or model, where that data came from, who used it, and how it can be found or shared. Because it is enforced at the point where tables are queried or models are called, and because lineage and audit records are generated automatically, it forms the basis for governance in Azure Databricks rather than an optional add-on.

unstructured-data.desc: Unstructured data is information without a predefined data model, such as chat messages, meeting transcripts and documents, and it is stored, governed and analyzed in Microsoft services.

faq.a: Unstructured data is information that does not follow a predefined data model. Examples named in the sources include chat messages, meeting transcripts, documents, images, videos, backups and logs.
faq.q: What is unstructured data?

faq.a: The episodes describe Azure Blob Storage as an object storage service for unstructured data, organized as blobs in containers. It sits within Azure Storage Accounts, which provide a unique namespace for stored objects.
faq.q: Where can unstructured data be stored in Azure?

faq.a: According to the episodes, Microsoft Purview can discover and map data across structured and unstructured sources and apply sensitivity labels in real time. This is presented as a response to fast growth and the limits of manual tagging.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Purview relate to unstructured data?

unstructured-data.long:
Unstructured data is information that does not follow a predefined data model. Typical examples are chat messages, meeting transcripts and documents, and the M365.FM episodes also name images, videos, backups, logs and application files. Unlike rows in a relational table with fixed columns, this kind of content has no schema that tells a system what each part means. Large language models can now analyze unstructured data for patterns, which is one reason the topic receives attention in Microsoft-focused architecture and governance discussions.

In practice, unstructured data raises three recurring questions: where to store it, how to analyze it, and how to protect it. For storage, the episode "Azure Blob Storage - Simply Explained" describes Azure Blob Storage as Microsoft's scalable object storage service for large amounts of unstructured data such as images, videos, documents, backups, logs and application files. Instead of a traditional file system, data is kept as objects called blobs inside containers, and it can be reached through REST APIs or Azure SDKs. The episode presents this model as durable, cost-effective and accessible from anywhere.

The episode "Azure Storage Accounts - Simply Explained" covers the layer above that. It describes Azure Storage Accounts as the foundation for managing different data types in the cloud, including unstructured data, files, messages and NoSQL data. Each storage account creates a unique namespace, so every stored object has a distinct URL, which the episode says simplifies data management and accessibility across the Azure platform. Choosing a storage account and a service within it is therefore one of the first decisions when unstructured data has to be kept at scale.

For analytics, the episode "Optimize Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Performance" notes that Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse environments support unified analytics across structured and unstructured data. It stresses that performance work remains necessary for scalability, cost control and reliable reporting, and it lists data modeling strategies, partitioning best practices, query tuning, workload management and storage optimization as the main levers. The point for unstructured data is that combining it with structured data in one lakehouse still requires deliberate design.

Governance is the third area. In "Real-Time AI Sensitivity Labeling in Microsoft Purview", the episode says unstructured data is growing by 55-65% each year and that manual tagging covers only about 30% of intellectual property, leaving security gaps. It describes real-time AI in Microsoft Purview as intercepting files, analyzing content and applying sensitivity labels instantly when a file is created or uploaded, so that governance works as invisible infrastructure instead of a productivity interruption. These figures are attributed to the episode.

The episode "Shadow Data Discovery and Governance with Microsoft Purview" addresses the risk of data that sits outside known controls. It says shadow data causes exposure, lack of accountability and higher breach costs, and that only 32% of organizations have policies to manage AI use. According to the episode, Microsoft Purview uses continuous discovery and real-time data mapping to give visibility across structured and unstructured data in hybrid and multi-cloud environments, and it integrates with Azure and Office 365.

Taken together, the episodes treat unstructured data as a lifecycle topic. It must be stored in a suitable service such as Azure Blob Storage within an Azure Storage Account, analyzed alongside structured data, for example in a Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse, and discovered and labeled so that sensitive content is protected as volumes grow. The common thread is that the lack of a predefined model makes automation, whether for classification, discovery or analysis, more practical than manual handling.

user-defined-routes.desc: User-defined routes (UDR) are custom routes in an Azure route table, associated with a subnet, that override Azure's default system routes to control traffic paths.

faq.a: User-defined routes are custom routes placed in an Azure route table and associated with a subnet. They override Azure's default system routes so that traffic follows a path chosen by the administrator.
faq.q: What are user-defined routes (UDR) in Azure?

faq.a: A typical use is sending outbound traffic from a subnet through a firewall or virtual appliance by setting that appliance as the next hop.
faq.q: What is a typical use of a UDR?

faq.a: A UDR overrides Azure's default system routes. When a custom route applies to a destination, it replaces the default routing behavior for the associated subnet.
faq.q: How does a UDR relate to Azure's default routes?

user-defined-routes.long:
User-defined routes (UDR) are custom routes defined in an Azure route table and associated with a subnet. They override Azure's default system routes, which allows network administrators to decide where traffic leaving a subnet is sent instead of relying on the routing Azure applies automatically.

A common use is directing outbound traffic through a firewall or other virtual appliance by specifying that appliance as the next hop. In this pattern, traffic from workloads in the subnet is forced through a central inspection or filtering point rather than following the default path. Because the route table is associated with a subnet, the custom routes apply to the resources deployed in that subnet.

User-defined routes are a building block of Azure network design, particularly where traffic must be inspected, filtered or steered through specific network appliances. They work together with system routes: where a user-defined route matches a destination, it takes precedence over the default behavior described for system routes.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic, and no related entities have been recorded for it yet.

user-experience-design.desc: User experience (UX) design is a user-centered approach to designing products around usability, accessibility and how people perceive and use them.
user-experience-design.long:
User experience (UX) design is a user-centered approach to designing products. It focuses on usability, accessibility and on how people perceive and use what they are given, rather than on technical features alone.

On M365.FM, the concept is discussed in the context of Power Apps business applications. In that setting, UX design refers to shaping these applications so that the people who work with them can use them effectively and can understand and access them without unnecessary barriers.

The available information describes UX design at this general level. No specific methods, frameworks, tools or guidelines are named in the source material, so this page does not attribute any to the concept. No related entities or episode titles are linked to this topic at present.

value-stream-mapping.desc: Value stream mapping is a lean method that visualizes how material, information and decisions flow through a product family, including steps, queues and handoffs.

faq.a: It shows how material, information and decisions flow through a product family, including the process steps, the queues where work waits and the handoffs between them.
faq.q: What does a value stream map show?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes describe it as a way to see where problems occur in a workflow and how long each step takes, helping to identify bottlenecks before automation or notifications are added.
faq.q: How is value stream mapping used in workflow and automation work?

faq.a: According to the episode "Can Value Stream Mapping Become a Live Data Model?", the map is static while the factory keeps changing, so it can end up describing yesterday's operation.
faq.q: What is the main limitation of a traditional value stream map?

value-stream-mapping.long:
Value stream mapping is a lean method for visualizing how material, information and decisions move through a product family or process. It records the process steps involved, the queues where work waits, and the handoffs between people, teams or systems. The result is a map that makes the full flow visible in one place, so that delays and inefficiencies can be seen as part of a system rather than as isolated problems.

The method originates in Lean Manufacturing, where it is used to understand how a production system actually operates. Because it covers material flow, information flow and decision points together, it helps different functions look at the same picture. In a factory context this can bring together production, planning, quality, maintenance, supply chain and operations, each of which sees a different part of the flow in daily work. Mapping the steps and the waiting time between them shows where time is spent and where improvements are possible.

Value stream mapping is also applied outside the factory floor. The M365.FM episode "Replace Reactive Dashboards with Proactive Notifications" mentions it alongside workflow process maps, Lean concepts and Six Sigma methods as a way to see where problems occur in a team's workflow and where notifications are needed. The episode describes mapping each step of a workflow to decide which steps need alerts, and presents value stream mapping as a way to spot where information gets stuck or events are missed.

In automation work, the method is treated as a way to find bottlenecks before technology is applied. The episode "Frictionless Automation Can Digitize Business Chaos" lists value stream mapping among several approaches for identifying bottlenecks, noting that it shows how long each step takes. The same list includes process mining, which shows real workflows and variations, a complexity/value matrix analysis for deciding which steps to improve first, and data readiness checks. The episode's broader point is to optimize workflows before implementing automation rather than digitizing broken processes, and it also recommends reviewing performance metrics and logs to find slow actions, inefficient loops or outside services that slow down Power Automate flows.

A recurring limitation of the traditional approach is that a map is a snapshot. The episode "Can Value Stream Mapping Become a Live Data Model?" points out that the factory keeps changing while the map does not. A setup takes longer than expected, or material waits in the wrong location, and the map hanging on the wall still describes yesterday's factory. The episode explores whether a value stream map could become something more than a static drawing, namely a live data model that stays connected to what is actually happening.

Typical decisions around value stream mapping include which product family or process to map, which steps and queues to record, and how to use the result. Teams commonly use the map to decide where to improve first, where waiting time can be reduced, and where handoffs create friction. Because the method describes the current flow rather than prescribing a fix, it works as a starting point for discussion and prioritization, and it can be combined with other analysis techniques such as process mining or performance data when a more detailed or current view is needed.

vat-in-the-digital-age.desc: VAT in the Digital Age (ViDA) is an EU legislative package that modernises VAT through e-invoicing and digital reporting, platform rules and single VAT registration.

faq.a: ViDA covers real-time digital reporting based on e-invoicing (Directive 2025/516), platform economy rules (Regulation 2025/517) and single VAT registration (Implementing Regulation 2025/518). Each act was adopted on 11 March 2025 and published on 25 March 2025.
faq.q: What are the three pillars of ViDA?

faq.a: Since April 2025, member states may mandate domestic e-invoicing without a derogation. From 1 July 2030, structured e-invoices are required for cross-border B2B and B2G supplies by VAT-registered businesses, with a harmonised real-time system planned for 1 January 2035.
faq.q: When do the ViDA e-invoicing requirements apply?

faq.a: The episodes describe ViDA as a fundamental shift from delayed, periodic VAT reporting to continuous, transaction-level control. They say it removes the time buffer that previously absorbed errors and corrections.
faq.q: How do the M365.FM episodes describe the impact of ViDA?

vat-in-the-digital-age.long:
VAT in the Digital Age (ViDA) is a European Commission package, proposed on 8 December 2022, to modernise the EU VAT system and reduce the VAT gap. The cited figure for that gap is 99 billion euros of lost revenue in 2020. The Commission projected up to 18 billion euros of additional annual VAT revenue and about 5 billion euros in yearly compliance savings. Adoption required unanimity among member states, and Estonia's resistance delayed agreement for about two years.

ViDA rests on three pillars, each a legal act adopted on 11 March 2025 and published on 25 March 2025. The first is real-time digital reporting based on e-invoicing (Directive 2025/516). The second covers platform economy rules (Regulation 2025/517). The third is single VAT registration (Implementing Regulation 2025/518). Together they change how businesses issue invoices, report transactions and register for VAT across the EU.

The dates matter for planning. Since April 2025, member states may mandate domestic e-invoicing without needing a derogation. From 1 July 2030, VAT-registered businesses must issue structured e-invoices for cross-border B2B and B2G supplies, with a harmonised real-time system planned for 1 January 2035. From 1 July 2028, platforms for short-term accommodation and passenger road transport are treated as the deemed supplier, although member states may postpone this to 2030. The One Stop Shop extends to more B2C supplies starting 1 January 2027, with the extension finishing on 1 July 2028.

The M365.FM episode "7 Common ViDA Mistakes in Dynamics 365—and How to Avoid Them" treats ViDA less as a compliance upgrade and more as a fundamental shift in how VAT operates. According to the episode, traditional VAT models relied on time gaps between a transaction and its reporting, and those gaps absorbed errors, corrections and ambiguity. ViDA removes that buffer by requiring structured e-invoices and near real-time digital reporting. The episode describes the result as a move from delayed, periodic reporting to continuous, transaction-level control, in which VAT corrections can no longer wait until a later period.

In the same episode, the three pillars are described as converging into a single transaction pipeline that must be provable end to end. This includes platform-based deemed supplier rules alongside e-invoicing and reporting. For organisations running Dynamics 365, the episode's framing is that VAT logic, invoicing and reporting have to be consistent within one traceable flow, rather than treated as separate periodic tasks. The episode title points to common mistakes that arise when ViDA is approached as a routine compliance update.

The topic also appears in the M365.FM episode "Design an End-to-End Auditable ESG Compliance Stack", whose excerpt repeats the same explanation of ViDA as a shift to continuous, transaction-level control. This suggests the episodes connect ViDA to the broader theme of auditable, end-to-end compliance architecture, where evidence must be traceable from the original transaction through to what is reported.

Typical decisions around ViDA concern timing and scope: whether a business is affected by domestic e-invoicing mandates that member states may now introduce, how cross-border B2B and B2G supplies will be handled before the 2030 requirement, and whether the business operates through or as a platform that may be treated as a deemed supplier. Because the national and EU timelines differ, the sources suggest tracking both the EU-wide dates and any member state choices, including possible postponements.

vba.desc: Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) is Microsoft's event-driven programming language built into most desktop Office applications, used to automate tasks in Excel.

faq.a: Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) is an event-driven programming language from Microsoft. It is built into most desktop Microsoft Office applications.
faq.q: What is Visual Basic for Applications (VBA)?

faq.a: VBA is used to automate tasks inside Office applications. Excel is a common example of an application where VBA is used for this purpose.
faq.q: What is VBA used for?

vba.long:
Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) is an event-driven programming language from Microsoft. It is built into most desktop Microsoft Office applications, which allows users and developers to write code that runs inside those programs rather than as separate software.

VBA is commonly used to automate tasks. A typical example is Excel, where VBA code can take over work that would otherwise be done by hand in the application. Because the language is event-driven, code can be set up to run in response to actions or events within the host application.

On M365.FM, VBA is listed as a product entity within the Microsoft ecosystem. No related topics, linked entities or specific episodes are currently associated with this page, so no further details are given here beyond the definition and the Excel automation use case described above.

vector-store.desc: A vector store is a database that finds content by meaning using embeddings rather than exact words, and serves as the memory layer for retrieval-augmented generation.

faq.a: A vector store is a database optimized for searching embeddings by meaning rather than exact words. It is commonly used as the memory for retrieval-augmented generation.
faq.q: What is a vector store?

faq.a: Content and queries are converted into vectors by embedding models, and the store returns the nearest neighbors to the query vector. This allows matches based on meaning, such as dog and canine, instead of shared keywords.
faq.q: How does a vector store find matches?

faq.a: Yes. The Azure AI Search documentation describes hybrid search that combines vector and keyword queries in one request. Filtering uses a separate text or numeric field because vector fields themselves are not filterable.
faq.q: Can a vector store be combined with keyword search?

vector-store.long:
A vector store is a database optimized for searching embeddings by meaning rather than by exact words. Instead of matching keywords, it holds content as numeric vectors and returns the items whose vectors are most similar to the vector of a query. In practice it is used as the memory for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where an AI system looks up relevant passages in stored material before producing an answer.

The approach rests on embeddings. An embedding model converts text into a vector, and queries are encoded with the same kind of model so that both sides can be compared. According to the Azure AI Search documentation on Microsoft Learn, each vector field gets an internal vector index built on a nearest-neighbors approach, and a query returns the closest k neighbors. Because matching depends on similarity rather than shared terms, the search can connect related ideas such as dog and canine, work across languages, and span different content types such as text and images.

Getting vectors into a store can happen in two ways. In Azure AI Search, embeddings can be created through integrated vectorization in an indexer pipeline, which uses an indexer, a supported data source and a skillset. Alternatively, embeddings can be generated externally and written into vector fields. The same documentation lists typical scenarios: similarity search, hybrid search that combines vector and keyword queries in one request, multimodal and multilingual search, and filtered vector search. The service can also be used as a pure vector store that acts as long-term memory, a knowledge base, or the retrieval layer for RAG.

Some practical constraints are mentioned in the documentation. Vector fields themselves are not filterable, so filtering relies on a separate text or numeric field stored alongside the vector. Services created before 2019 do not support vector workloads. These points matter when planning an index, since filters and metadata need to be designed in addition to the vectors.

The M365.FM episode "How to Build Private RAG with SharePoint and n8n" shows how a vector store fits into a workflow. The episode describes building semantic search for an AI agent in n8n by connecting storage to a retrieval pipeline. Its steps include adding nodes to fetch source data from storage, inserting a Vector Store node, and selecting an embedding model that matches the storage setup. It also covers adding a Default Data Loader node, choosing a chunking strategy, and configuring chunk size and overlap parameters. The episode further recommends adding metadata to the stored content for better search results, creating a separate workflow for querying the store, and configuring the agent to use that retrieval workflow.

Taken together, the decisions around a vector store follow a consistent pattern: choosing an embedding model, deciding how content is split into chunks and how much they overlap, attaching metadata that supports filtering and relevance, and separating the ingestion workflow from the query workflow. The vector store itself provides the similarity search, while the surrounding pipeline determines what goes in and how an agent or application uses what comes back.

veeam.desc: Veeam is a vendor of backup and recovery software for hybrid and multi-cloud environments, including a data protection offering for Microsoft 365.

faq.a: Veeam is a vendor of third-party backup and recovery software for hybrid and multi-cloud environments. Its software covers virtual, cloud-native, SaaS, Kubernetes and physical workloads, including Microsoft 365.
faq.q: What does Veeam do?

faq.a: Veeam launched Veeam Backup for Microsoft Office 365 in 2016 and now lists Microsoft 365 among the platforms it protects. M365.FM episodes also mention Veeam Data Cloud as an option for independence and operational separation.
faq.q: How is Veeam connected to Microsoft 365?

faq.a: "Microsoft 365 Backup with Isolated Vault Architecture" cites the Veeam Data Protection Report for 2024, which puts average recovery time without a dedicated backup above three weeks. "Microsoft 365 Data Sovereignty Beyond Technical Custody" names Veeam Data Cloud as a solution for independence and operational separation.
faq.q: What do the M365.FM episodes say about Veeam?

veeam.long:
Veeam is a vendor of third-party backup and recovery software for hybrid and multi-cloud environments. Veeam Software Group is a privately held, US-based company, owned by Insight Partners, that develops backup, disaster recovery and data protection software for virtual, cloud-native, SaaS, Kubernetes and physical workloads. In the Microsoft ecosystem, Veeam is relevant mainly because it offers dedicated backup for Microsoft 365 data as an alternative or complement to what the platform provides natively.

According to its Wikipedia entry, Veeam was founded in 2006 by Ratmir Timashev and Andrei Baronov, who had earlier sold Aelita Software to Quest. Its first products handled monitoring and reporting for virtual infrastructure. Veeam Backup & Replication launched in 2008 for VMware vSphere, with Hyper-V support following in 2012. Later products include Veeam Backup for Microsoft Office 365, introduced in 2016, and agents for Windows and Linux in 2017. The company has since expanded to protect data on AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Microsoft 365 and Kubernetes.

The company's corporate history includes several transactions. Insight Partners announced a deal of about 5 billion dollars to buy it in January 2020. Acquisitions listed on the same page include Kasten for Kubernetes in 2020 and Coveware, a ransomware response firm, in April 2024, plus an announced plan in October 2025 to buy Securiti AI for 1.725 billion dollars. The page reports revenue above 1 billion dollars in 2019 and about 6,100 employees in 2025, and it gives conflicting information about the headquarters.

In M365.FM coverage, Veeam appears in two contexts. The episode "Microsoft 365 Backup with Isolated Vault Architecture" cites the Veeam Data Protection Report for 2024 in a discussion of human error. The episode says that employees delete emails, Teams messages or entire folders by mistake, and that without a dedicated backup the average recovery time exceeds three weeks, according to that report. It lists common Microsoft 365 risks such as unmonitored application consent and OAuth permissions, inactive mailboxes, shared accounts, excessive admin privileges and human error, and argues for a backup solution that protects against mistakes and restores data quickly.

The second appearance is in "Microsoft 365 Data Sovereignty Beyond Technical Custody". The episode lists strategies for more control over sensitive workloads and for following data residency rules: end-to-end encryption, zero-trust access controls, and choosing solutions such as Veeam Data Cloud for independence and operational separation. It also stresses the difference between data residency and data sovereignty and the lessons organizations learn when balancing technical custody with business sovereignty in Microsoft 365.

Typical decisions around Veeam therefore concern whether Microsoft 365 data needs a backup that sits outside the production tenant, how quickly lost mailboxes, Teams messages or files must be restorable, and how operational separation supports sovereignty and compliance goals. Because the available episode material is limited to these two references, details such as specific product editions, licensing or deployment steps are not covered here and should be checked against the vendor's own documentation.

vendor-posting-profile.desc: A vendor posting profile in Dynamics 365 sets which general ledger accounts vendor transactions post to, using rules defined for a vendor or vendor group.
vendor-posting-profile.long:
A vendor posting profile is a configuration concept in Dynamics 365 that determines which general ledger accounts are used when vendor transactions are posted. The profile applies rules that can be set for an individual vendor or for a vendor group.

In practice, a vendor posting profile links the vendor side of the accounting process to the general ledger. Instead of selecting accounts manually for each transaction, the system uses the profile that matches the vendor or the vendor group to decide where the related postings go. This helps keep the posting of vendor-related transactions consistent with the account structure that has been defined.

Because the rules can be defined at the level of a single vendor or a vendor group, the same mechanism can cover both broad defaults and more specific cases. The available facts describe the concept at this level only; details such as individual fields, transaction types or setup steps are not covered here.

There are currently no M365.FM episodes linked to this entry and no related topics assigned. The entry will be expanded if further information becomes available.

verifiable-credentials.desc: Verifiable credentials are W3C-based digital credentials in which an issuer makes a claim about a holder that a verifier can check, optionally with selective disclosure.

faq.a: They are digital credentials based on W3C open standards in which an issuer makes a claim about a holder. The holder can present the claim, and a verifier can check it, optionally with only the needed information disclosed.
faq.q: What are verifiable credentials?

faq.a: Microsoft Entra Verified ID provides verifiable credentials. The episode "Microsoft Entra External ID for Digital Trust and Growth" describes it as enabling portable trust, while Entra External ID acts as the orchestration and governance layer for external identities.
faq.q: Which Microsoft product uses verifiable credentials?

faq.a: Account-centric identity focuses on storing and managing accounts. Claim-centric identity, as described in the episode "Microsoft Entra External ID for Digital Trust and Growth", focuses on verifying trusted claims when they are needed.
faq.q: How do verifiable credentials differ from account-centric identity?

verifiable-credentials.long:
Verifiable credentials are digital credentials built on W3C open standards. They allow an issuer to make a claim about a holder, for example that a person is an employee or holds a certification. The holder can then present that claim to a verifier, and the verifier can check it. Depending on the setup, the holder can disclose only the information that is needed for a given purpose instead of handing over a full record. The concept sits at the center of decentralized identity models, where trust is carried by the credential itself rather than by repeated lookups in a central account store.

The model involves three roles. The issuer creates and signs the credential. The holder keeps it and decides when and to whom to present it. The verifier receives the presentation and validates it. Because the claims are cryptographically verifiable, the verifier does not need to contact the issuer's directory every time a credential is shown. In the episode "Microsoft Entra as a Complete IAM Platform", this is described as organizations issuing cryptographically verifiable claims, such as employee badges or certifications, that work without constant contact with central directories.

In practice, verifiable credentials are used where an organization needs to confirm something about a person or entity without storing a full account for them. Typical situations include proving employment, proving a qualification, or verifying a trusted attribute during onboarding or access decisions. The approach shifts attention from managing accounts to verifying claims when they are needed. The episode "Microsoft Entra External ID for Digital Trust and Growth" describes this as a move from account-centric identity to claim-centric identity, where organizations focus less on storing accounts and more on verifying trusted claims at the point of need.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, verifiable credentials appear in Microsoft Entra Verified ID. The episode "Microsoft Entra External ID for Digital Trust and Growth" explains that Entra External ID acts as the orchestration and governance layer for external identities, while Verified ID enables portable trust through verifiable credentials. In the same episode, passkeys, verifiable credentials and decentralized identity models are presented together as changes to the future of authentication, aimed at making trust portable, secure and policy-driven.

Verified ID is also listed as one component of a wider security framework in "Microsoft Entra Private Access - Simply Explained". There it is described as providing decentralized, verifiable credentials to enhance security and privacy in identity verification, alongside other Microsoft Entra capabilities such as Identity Governance and Conditional Access. The episode presents these components as working together to form a framework that adapts to an organization's changing needs.

The main decisions around verifiable credentials concern which claims are worth issuing, who acts as issuer, and which verifiers need to trust them. Because the standards are open, the credential is not tied to a single directory, which is the basis for the portability the episodes emphasize. Selective disclosure matters for privacy, since a verifier can receive only the attribute it requires. Verifiable credentials complement rather than replace other identity controls: the episodes place them next to passkeys, access governance and policy-based access decisions as part of a broader identity and access management approach.

vertipaq.desc: VertiPaq is the in-memory columnar storage engine behind Power BI import models, compressing data column by column to support fast queries.

faq.a: VertiPaq is the in-memory columnar storage engine used by Power BI import models. It compresses data column by column so queries run fast.
faq.q: What is the VertiPaq engine?

faq.a: The episodes say VertiPaq processes star schema models faster because they need fewer joins and simpler queries, and that it compresses data better with star schemas, reducing memory use.
faq.q: Why do star schemas matter for VertiPaq?

faq.a: According to the episodes, Direct Lake queries are processed by the VertiPaq engine, giving performance comparable to Import mode without scheduled refresh cycles.
faq.q: How is VertiPaq related to Direct Lake?

vertipaq.long:
The VertiPaq engine is the in-memory columnar storage engine used by Power BI import models. Instead of storing data row by row, it compresses data column by column, which allows queries to run quickly against data held in memory. It sits beneath the semantic model layer, so report authors rarely interact with it directly, but its behavior shapes how fast reports respond and how much memory a model consumes.

One point made in the M365.FM episode "Data Analysis Expressions (DAX) - Simply Explained" concerns how VertiPaq treats data. The episode states that the engine operates independently of data types: strings, floating-point numbers and dates use similar memory and perform at comparable speeds because of dictionary encoding. It also notes that mixing data types in expressions can force conversions. Some of these conversions are efficient, while others place more demand on the formula engine, which can affect performance. In practical terms, this means data type choices matter mostly where DAX expressions combine or convert values.

Model design has a direct effect on how well VertiPaq performs. The episode "Build a Power BI Star Schema for Faster Reports" says the engine processes star schema models faster because they require fewer joins and less complex queries. Its recommendations include aggregating data before loading to reduce size, avoiding many-to-many relationships that can produce incorrect results and slow performance, and flattening snowflake structures into a star schema to minimize joins. The episode "Reduce Power BI Premium Costs with Better Data Models" makes a related argument: VertiPaq compresses data better with star schemas, which speeds up queries and reduces memory use, and a clear model is also easier to maintain.

The same episode warns against overly complex models. Cramming too much data into wide tables or adding unnecessary calculated columns is described as a common mistake that can hurt report performance. Keeping relationships simple and clear, and avoiding circular or ambiguous links, is presented as part of the same approach. Because memory use is tied to Premium capacity costs in that discussion, efficient modeling for VertiPaq is framed as a way to reduce those costs.

VertiPaq also appears in the Microsoft Fabric context. The episodes "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" and "Speed Power BI with OneLake and Direct Lake" explain that Direct Lake queries are processed by the VertiPaq engine. According to these episodes, this gives performance comparable to Import mode without scheduled refresh cycles, since data is queried directly from OneLake without being moved or duplicated. The episodes add that only the necessary data is loaded into memory, which makes it possible to analyze data volumes that exceed memory limits, and that Direct Lake fits into existing Fabric investments, such as the gold analytics layer in a medallion lakehouse architecture.

Taken together, the episodes treat VertiPaq as the common query engine across Import mode and Direct Lake. Decisions about schema shape, relationship types, calculated columns and data types are all discussed in terms of how they help or hinder this engine, which makes it a central concept for anyone tuning Power BI or Fabric semantic models.

vibe-coding.desc: Vibe coding is building software by describing it in natural language and letting an AI generate and refine the code or app, as discussed in Power Apps episodes.

faq.a: Vibe coding is building software by describing what you want in natural language and letting an AI generate and refine the code or app. The builder guides the result through prompts and feedback rather than writing every line manually.
faq.q: What is vibe coding?

faq.a: It appears in Generative pages, which create Dataverse-aware React pages from plain-English prompts, and in Power Apps code apps, where developers work in code with AI assistance. GitHub Copilot is a related coding assistant.
faq.q: Where does vibe coding appear in Power Apps?

faq.a: The episode "Canvas App UI vs Generative Pages: Which Should You Use?" cites read-only generated output, prompt ambiguity and hidden licensing, and notes that speed can mask fragility. Another episode describes hitting a wall where prompting alone no longer resolves a problem.
faq.q: What risks do the M365.FM episodes mention?

vibe-coding.long:
Vibe coding is the practice of building software by describing what is wanted in natural language and letting an AI generate and refine the code or app. Instead of writing every line by hand, the person steers the result through prompts and feedback. The concept is also described as prompt-driven development or AI-assisted app building, and it is closely tied to how much the quality of a prompt shapes the output.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, vibe coding appears mainly in Power Apps. Generative pages turn plain-English prompts into responsive, Dataverse-aware React pages, which replaces much of the manual layout work familiar from canvas apps. Power Apps code apps take a different route: developers work in code, keep their source outside the platform, collaborate with others and retain a history of every change, while AI helps generate components, optimize code and define a data model. GitHub Copilot is a related coding assistant, and one of the episodes uses its agent mode in the context of multi-file changes.

The typical benefit named in the episodes is speed. In "Power Apps AI and Vibe Coding with Keith Atherton [MVP-MCT]", the guest describes coming from traditional .NET and SQL development and valuing how Power Apps reduces the time spent rebuilding the same forms, logic and app structures, so that more effort goes into solving business problems. The episode presents a vision in which AI makes app creation accessible to more people, while experienced builders still need frameworks to deploy enterprise-grade solutions safely.

The episodes also stress the trade-offs. "Canvas App UI vs Generative Pages: Which Should You Use?" says the speed of generated pages can mask fragility. It names read-only generated output, prompt ambiguity and hidden licensing as risks, and notes that technical debt can shift rather than disappear. It suggests manual UI where unique micro-interactions matter and Generative pages for repeatable, data-driven enterprise apps, with a blend of both possible. Governance is described as coming partly from Dataverse metadata and roles.

A second theme is what happens when a vibe-coded project meets complexity. "Use GitHub Copilot Agent Mode for Multi-File Changes" quotes a developer describing the moment when something breaks, an edge case appears and it is no longer possible to simply prompt a way out. Fixes in one place can create problems elsewhere, and patchwork changes can leave a codebase without cohesion. This is the situation where structured, multi-file assistance and conventional engineering practice are presented as helpful.

"Power Apps Vibe Code vs Low-Code: Which Fits Your Team?" frames the decision as a comparison of approaches for developers and citizen builders, and "Power Apps Code Apps with Carike Botha [MVP]" covers the developer-oriented side with source control and AI-assisted generation of React components. Together, the episodes treat vibe coding less as a replacement for low-code or traditional development and more as an additional way of working. The practical questions they raise are who owns the generated code, how it is governed, how it is maintained over time and which team skills fit the chosen approach.

vibe-engineering.desc: Vibe engineering is a term for disciplined, AI-assisted software and agent development in which experienced engineers own setup, security and governance.

faq.a: Vibe engineering is a term for disciplined, AI-assisted software and agent development in which experienced engineers own setup, security and governance.
faq.q: What is vibe engineering?

faq.a: Vibe coding is presented as the casual counterpart. Vibe engineering is contrasted with it by emphasizing that experienced engineers take responsibility for setup, security and governance.
faq.q: How does vibe engineering differ from vibe coding?

vibe-engineering.long:
Vibe engineering is a term for disciplined, AI-assisted software and agent development. In this approach, experienced engineers take responsibility for the setup, security and governance of the work, rather than leaving those decisions to the AI tooling.

The term is used in contrast to casual vibe coding. Where vibe coding describes a loose, informal way of building software with AI assistance, vibe engineering stresses structure and accountability. The defining feature is that human engineers with relevant experience remain in charge of how the environment is configured, how security is handled and how governance is applied to what gets built.

The concept is discussed on M365.FM as a way of separating careful, professionally owned AI-assisted development from more improvised practices. No specific tools, products, frameworks or methods are tied to the term in the information available here, so it is best understood as a description of an approach and a set of responsibilities rather than a fixed methodology.

virtual-desktop-infrastructure.desc: Virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) hosts desktops on central servers or in the cloud, which users reach remotely, so profiles and app data must load fast.

faq.a: VDI hosts desktops on central servers or in the cloud, and users connect to them remotely. In the common form, multiple desktop operating system instances run as virtual machines on a server under a hypervisor, giving each user an individual desktop.
faq.q: What is virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI)?

faq.a: VDI gives each user an individual desktop operating system, while remote desktop sessions share one server operating system and use far fewer resources. VDI licensing costs more and is less flexible.
faq.q: How does VDI differ from remote desktop sessions?

faq.a: According to an M365.FM episode, Azure Virtual Desktop is VDI on Azure with multi-session, shared desktops and full IT control, while Windows 365 is desktop-as-a-service with single-user, dedicated cloud PCs and simplified management.
faq.q: How do Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows 365 relate to VDI?

virtual-desktop-infrastructure.long:
Virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) is an approach in which desktops are hosted on central servers or in the cloud and users connect to them remotely. The desktop environment and its applications are separated from the physical device used to access them. Only display, keyboard and mouse data travel over the network through a remote display protocol, while the data itself stays on the remote system. Clients can be PCs, thin clients, tablets or phones.

In its most common form, VDI runs several desktop operating system instances as virtual machines on a server under a hypervisor. Each user receives an individual desktop operating system, and personal workspaces can be preserved between sessions. Reference material on desktop virtualization notes that the term VDI is often misused to mean any kind of desktop virtualization, although it describes this specific virtual-machine-based model. It is distinct from remote desktop sessions, where users share a single server operating system. Shared sessions use far fewer resources, while VDI licensing costs more and is less flexible.

Because desktops are central, the way user profiles and application data are delivered matters a great deal. User profiles and app data must load quickly from central storage, since a slow sign-in or slow data access is directly visible to users. Supporting technologies named in the sources include application virtualization, user virtualization that separates personal settings from the operating system, and desktop layering. These help keep the base image manageable while preserving each user's individual settings.

Typical reasons for choosing VDI include centralised management, easier disaster recovery and improved security, because no data is stored on user devices. VDI also makes it possible to run Windows applications on non-Windows devices. Organizations can operate such an environment themselves or use cloud options, which the sources describe as managed VDI and desktop as a service.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the M365.FM episode "Windows 365 – Simply Explained" compares Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows 365. According to its comparison table, Azure Virtual Desktop is a virtual desktop infrastructure on Azure with multi-session, shared desktops, requires full control and maintenance by IT, is highly scalable with custom scaling options, and uses usage-based pricing tied to Azure resources. Windows 365 is described as desktop-as-a-service, a cloud PC with single-user, dedicated desktops, simplified management through a Microsoft portal, linear scaling with per-user provisioning. The choice between them therefore depends on how much control and operational effort an organization wants to take on.

The episode "Azure Virtual Desktop vs Windows 365 with Dieter Kempeneers [MVP] & Dominiek Verham [MVP]" places VDI in a market context. It cites a projection of growth at a CAGR of 12.5% from 2025 to 2035, reaching approximately USD 59.02 billion by 2035, and attributes this to the increasing need for flexible and secure work environments. The episode also says that AI technologies are changing the VDI landscape: AI-driven automation is described as reducing downtime and improving user satisfaction, and as enhancing security by detecting unusual user activity. It frames choosing the right virtual desktop strategy as an important decision for businesses navigating the AI era, and notes that Azure Virtual Desktop offers a full Windows experience with flexibility for various scenarios.

virtual-machine.desc: A virtual machine is a complete computer simulated inside another computer, with its own operating system, memory and storage, isolated more strongly than a container.

faq.a: A virtual machine is a complete computer simulated inside another computer, with its own operating system, memory and storage. It provides stronger isolation than a container but is larger and slower to start.
faq.q: What is a virtual machine?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets - Simply Explained" describes a single VM as having a fixed limit. If traffic grows tenfold and one VM handles every request, pages slow down and visitors may leave, which is the case for scaling out across multiple machines.
faq.q: Why is one virtual machine often not enough for a growing workload?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Managed Disks - Simply Explained" lists Standard HDD, Standard SSD, Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disks, and describes choosing among them based on performance, latency and cost.
faq.q: Which disk types can be used with Azure virtual machines?

virtual-machine.long:
A virtual machine is a complete computer simulated inside another computer. It has its own operating system, its own memory and its own storage, and it behaves like a separate physical machine even though it runs on shared hardware. Because each virtual machine carries a full operating system, it offers stronger isolation than a container. The trade-off is size and speed: a virtual machine is larger than a container and takes longer to start.

Virtual machines are used when a workload needs a full operating system environment, a clear boundary between workloads, or control over the system that a lighter packaging format does not provide. In Azure, the virtual machine is a basic unit of compute, and several Azure services are built around creating, sizing, storing and scaling virtual machines. The M365.FM episodes touch on these related areas rather than the virtual machine in isolation, so the concept appears in them as a building block of larger Azure designs.

One recurring theme is scaling. The episode "Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets - Simply Explained" starts from a simple problem: a website suddenly receives ten times more visitors, but only one virtual machine handles every request. Pages slow down, people wait, and some may leave before the application responds. The episode frames this as a fixed limit of a single virtual machine, which is why the topic of virtual machine scale sets is introduced as a way to move beyond one machine. The episode "Azure AI Infrastructure Architecture for C-Level Leaders" returns to the same idea from a planning angle. It recommends configuring autoscaling through Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets so that resources adjust to workload demand and avoid over-provisioning, and it advises reviewing VM sizes and configurations against actual usage, with Azure Advisor mentioned for tailored recommendations. It also mentions distributed training with frameworks such as Horovod and PyTorch across multiple VMs.

Capacity and cost are another part of the picture. The episode "Azure Compute Fleet – Simply Explained" notes that creating one virtual machine is straightforward, but when a workload suddenly needs hundreds or thousands of workers, choosing one exact VM size can become a major limitation. The selected size might not have enough capacity in the preferred region, another size could work at a different price, and Spot VMs can reduce costs but can be reclaimed by Azure. Managing all of those options by hand quickly becomes difficult, and the episode describes shifting the question from how to get a set number of identical VMs to how to get the compute capacity a workload needs.

Storage for virtual machines is covered in "Azure Managed Disks - Simply Explained". That episode explains the difference between OS disks and data disks, and walks through the available disk types: Standard HDD, Standard SSD, Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disks. It describes choosing among them based on performance, latency and cost, and it also covers snapshots, backups, encryption, availability zones and redundancy options. Managed disks are presented as a way to simplify virtual machine storage so administrators can concentrate on workloads rather than storage operations.

Virtual machines also appear in automation and permissions work. In "PowerShell Automation for Azure and Microsoft 365 with Matthew Dowst [MVP]", a table of permissions lists the virtual machine write permission for the Microsoft.Compute provider as part of the steps needed to create an extension on a virtual machine, alongside permissions on workspaces and automation accounts. This shows that virtual machines are managed through the same role and permission model as other Azure resources.

When deciding between a virtual machine and a container, the main factors drawn from the concept are isolation and overhead. A virtual machine gives a stronger boundary because it includes its own operating system, while a container is lighter and starts faster. Choices around size, disk type, scaling and capacity then follow from the workload's needs for performance, availability and cost.

virtual-network-data-gateway.desc: The virtual network (VNet) data gateway is a Microsoft-managed gateway that links Power BI and Microsoft Fabric to data sources in an Azure virtual network.
virtual-network-data-gateway.long:
The virtual network (VNet) data gateway is a Microsoft-managed data gateway that connects Power BI and Microsoft Fabric to data sources located inside an Azure virtual network. Unlike a traditional gateway, it does not require gateway software to be installed on a machine.

It is used when data sources sit within a private Azure network and cloud services such as Power BI or Microsoft Fabric need to reach them securely. Because Microsoft manages the gateway, the usual work of hosting, installing and maintaining gateway software on a server or virtual machine is not part of the setup.

The VNet data gateway belongs to the data integration capabilities documented by Microsoft, and its official overview is available in Microsoft Learn. No related topics or episodes are currently linked to it on M365.FM.

virtual-network-peering.desc: Azure virtual network peering connects two virtual networks so traffic flows privately over the Microsoft backbone, including across regions via global peering.

faq.a: It connects two virtual networks so that traffic between them flows privately over the Microsoft backbone. Resources in the peered networks can communicate with each other without leaving that private path.
faq.q: What does Azure virtual network peering do?

faq.a: Yes. Global peering connects virtual networks across Azure regions, in addition to peering between networks in the same region.
faq.q: Can peered virtual networks be in different regions?

faq.a: If network A is peered with B and B is peered with C, A and C are not automatically connected. A separate peering between A and C is required for those two networks to communicate directly.
faq.q: Why is peering described as not transitive?

virtual-network-peering.long:
Azure virtual network peering is an Azure feature that connects two virtual networks so that traffic between them flows privately over the Microsoft backbone. It is a capability of Azure Virtual Network, the broader service for building private networks in Azure.

Peering is used to let resources in separate virtual networks communicate with each other as though they were part of one network. Global peering extends this to virtual networks located in different Azure regions, so the connected networks do not need to share a region.

Two constraints are central to planning a peering design. The address spaces of the peered virtual networks must not overlap, which makes IP address planning an early step when networks are expected to be connected. In addition, peering is not transitive: if one virtual network is peered with a second, and the second is peered with a third, the first and third do not gain connectivity to each other through that chain. A direct peering is needed between any two networks that must communicate.

The topic belongs to the networking area of the Microsoft ecosystem and relates directly to Azure Virtual Network. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entity. Further details on behavior and configuration are described in the official Microsoft Learn documentation on virtual network peering.

virtual-network-service-endpoints.desc: Virtual network service endpoints are an Azure Virtual Network feature that limits access to selected Azure services to traffic from chosen subnets over the Azure backbone.

faq.a: They let a chosen subnet reach selected Azure services over the Azure backbone, and a virtual network rule on the service restricts access to that network. The service keeps its public endpoint.
faq.q: What do virtual network service endpoints do?

faq.a: No. According to the Microsoft Learn overview, endpoints do not cover traffic from on-premises, and DNS records for the service still resolve to public addresses.
faq.q: Do service endpoints cover traffic from on-premises networks?

faq.a: Microsoft recommends Private Link and private endpoints as the preferred option. Service endpoints are enabled per subnet and per service and carry no extra charge.
faq.q: Are service endpoints or private endpoints preferred?

virtual-network-service-endpoints.long:
Virtual network service endpoints are an Azure Virtual Network feature that restricts access to certain Azure services so that only traffic from a chosen virtual network subnet is allowed. The service keeps its public endpoint, but a rule on the service limits who may use it. In practice, resources in the subnet reach the service over the Azure backbone network, and the service can be locked down so that the public internet no longer has access to it.

The feature is used when workloads in a virtual network need to talk to platform services such as storage or databases while the service itself should not be reachable from everywhere. According to the Microsoft Learn overview, the supported services include Storage, SQL Database, Cosmos DB, Key Vault, Service Bus, Event Hubs, App Service and Container Registry. Resources in the subnet can use these services without public IP addresses of their own.

The setup has two parts. First, the endpoint is enabled on a subnet for a given service. Endpoints are switched on per subnet and per service, and several services can be combined on one subnet. Second, a virtual network rule is configured on the target service so that access is limited to that network. Enabling the endpoint requires a special permission on the subnet, and no extra charge applies for the feature itself.

Several related building blocks interact with service endpoints. Service tags can be used in network security groups to allow or deny traffic to the relevant services. Service endpoint policies filter access to specific resources of a service rather than the whole service. Routing is also affected: routes with the next hop type VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint take precedence over BGP routes and user-defined routes. One visible side effect is that the source address of traffic changes from a public IP address to the private IPv4 address of the virtual network, which matters for firewall rules that were written against the old public address.

There are limits to keep in mind when deciding on this approach. Service endpoints do not cover traffic coming from on-premises networks. DNS records for the service still resolve to public addresses, because the service keeps its public endpoint. For these reasons, Microsoft recommends Private Link and private endpoints as the preferred option, with service endpoints remaining a simpler alternative for subnet-level access control.

The topic appears in two M365.FM episodes. In "Azure Virtual Network - Simply Explained", the episode lists virtual network service endpoints among the features that support secure internal communication, describing them as extending the private address space of a virtual network to Azure services and securing them within the VNet. It places them alongside virtual network peering, which connects multiple VNets, and network security groups, which apply stateful rules to filter traffic. In "Microsoft Foundry AI Apps with Jannik Reinhard [MVP]", the episode names virtual network service endpoints together with Azure Firewall as network security features that help shield AI applications from external threats, as part of a broader layered security picture that also covers identity, encryption and threat detection.

virtual-private-network.desc: A virtual private network (VPN) creates an encrypted tunnel from a remote device into a private network over an untrusted network such as the internet.

faq.a: A virtual private network (VPN) creates an encrypted tunnel from a remote device into a private network over an untrusted network such as the internet.
faq.q: What is a virtual private network (VPN)?

faq.a: A VPN is traditionally used for remote access to company resources, allowing a remote device to connect into a private network through the encrypted tunnel.
faq.q: What is a VPN traditionally used for?

virtual-private-network.long:
A virtual private network (VPN) is a networking concept in which an encrypted tunnel is established between a remote device and a private network. The tunnel runs over an untrusted network, such as the internet, so that traffic between the device and the private network is protected while in transit.

Traditionally, a VPN has been used for remote access to company resources. A user or device outside the corporate network connects through the tunnel and can then reach internal systems as though it were attached to the private network itself. This model has long been a standard way to extend access to employees working away from the office.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, the VPN is relevant as a reference point for how remote access to organizational resources is understood and discussed. The concept describes the encrypted-tunnel approach to connecting remote devices to a private network, which is often contrasted with other ways of providing access to company applications and data.

No specific episodes, product relations or official documentation links are currently associated with this entry on M365.FM, so the description here is limited to the general definition and traditional use of a VPN.

virtual-table-data-provider.desc: A virtual table data provider translates Dataverse requests for a virtual table into calls to an external system and returns the results as Dataverse rows.

faq.a: It translates Dataverse requests for a virtual table into calls to an external system and returns the results to Dataverse as rows.
faq.q: What does a virtual table data provider do?

faq.a: Dataverse includes an OData v4 data provider and also supports custom data providers.
faq.q: Which data providers are available for virtual tables in Dataverse?

virtual-table-data-provider.long:
A virtual table data provider is a component that handles the connection between Dataverse and an external system for a virtual table. When Dataverse receives a request for data in a virtual table, the data provider translates that request into one or more calls to the external system. It then returns the results to Dataverse as rows, so the external data can be treated like other Dataverse table data.

Dataverse includes an OData v4 data provider, which can be used when the external system exposes an OData v4 interface. Dataverse also supports custom data providers, which allow developers to implement the translation logic themselves when the external system does not fit the built-in provider.

The data provider is the piece that defines how data from the external source is read and surfaced in Dataverse, which makes it a central part of any virtual table setup. No related topics or M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

visio.desc: Microsoft Visio is a paid Microsoft diagramming application for flowcharts, org charts, network and process diagrams, offered as a desktop app and as Visio for the web.

faq.a: Microsoft Visio is a diagramming application used for flowcharts, org charts, network diagrams and process diagrams. Typical uses are documenting business processes, mapping IT infrastructure and presenting organisational structures.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Visio used for?

faq.a: No. Visio is a paid product and not part of the standard Microsoft 365 licence. It is licensed through the Microsoft 365 platform and has to be assigned to the users who need it.
faq.q: Is Visio included in the standard Microsoft 365 licence?

faq.a: Yes. Visio is related to SharePoint and Microsoft Teams, where diagrams can be stored, shared and discussed with colleagues.
faq.q: Does Visio work with Teams and SharePoint?

visio.long:
Microsoft Visio is a diagramming application developed by Microsoft. It is used to create flowcharts, organisational charts, network diagrams and process diagrams. The product is available in two forms: as a desktop app and as Visio for the web, which runs in the browser. Visio is classified as a Microsoft tool and is a paid product rather than a part of the standard Microsoft 365 licence.

The typical purpose of Visio is to turn information that is hard to explain in text into a visual representation. Common situations include documenting a business process step by step, mapping IT or network infrastructure, and presenting how a team or company is structured. Because diagrams of this kind are often shared and maintained over time, they are usually created with the audience and the review process in mind, not only the person drawing them.

Visio is related to several parts of the Microsoft ecosystem. It is connected to Microsoft 365, the platform through which Visio is licensed and used alongside other apps. It is also related to SharePoint and Microsoft Teams, where diagrams can be stored, shared and discussed with colleagues. In practice, this means a diagram does not have to stay in a single file on one computer; it can be placed where a team already works and collaborates.

The licensing side matters for administrators. Since Visio is a paid product that sits outside the standard Microsoft 365 licence, it has to be assigned deliberately to the users who need it. Visio plans are mentioned in M365.FM episodes in exactly this licensing context, as one of several add-on products that organisations have to track.

The M365.FM episodes assigned to Visio touch it only indirectly. The episode "Set Up Microsoft Copilot in Teams Step by Step" lists Visio Plan 1 and Plan 2 among the other eligible plans that can qualify a user for Copilot, and states that one of these plans is needed for each user who will access Copilot. The episode stresses that activating Copilot is not enough and that setup, licensing, permissions and governance decide its value. Anyone unsure which plan their organisation uses is advised to check with their IT administrator.

The episode "Fix Automated Microsoft 365 Licensing Failures" approaches Visio from the licence-management side. It describes why automatically assigned licences can seem to disappear, pointing to brittle dynamic group rules, drifting attributes and slow recalculation. As part of right-sizing, it recommends reviewing add-ons such as Audio Conferencing, Project and Visio, and Power BI Pro, removing unused SKUs, adding missing base SKUs, and tracking reclaimed licences and monthly savings so the results can be shared with Finance. This is relevant wherever Visio licences are handed out through groups rather than assigned manually.

In summary, Microsoft Visio is the diagramming option within the Microsoft ecosystem for process, organisational and infrastructure diagrams. Decisions around it usually concern which form to use (desktop app or Visio for the web), where to store and share the diagrams (SharePoint and Microsoft Teams), and how to license and review its use alongside the rest of Microsoft 365.

visual-studio.desc: Visual Studio is a Microsoft development product; M365.FM episodes cover its Dev Tunnels feature for testing Microsoft 365 apps, alongside related tooling.

faq.a: According to the episode "Test Microsoft 365 Apps with Visual Studio Dev Tunnels", Dev Tunnels in Visual Studio expose local Teams, SharePoint, or Power Platform services to the internet without an Azure deployment, so changes can be tested quickly.
faq.q: What does Visual Studio do in the context of Microsoft 365 testing?

faq.a: The episode recommends a named, persistent tunnel with Private, authenticated access tied to Microsoft Entra ID, and warns that leaving a tunnel Public or anonymous can expose the whole development machine. It also advises logging and shutting the tunnel off when done.
faq.q: How should a Dev Tunnel be secured?

faq.a: The episodes treat them separately. Dev Tunnels are described in Visual Studio, while the Bicep, ARM template, and Power Apps Code Apps episodes refer to Visual Studio Code as an editor with extensions and IntelliSense.
faq.q: Is Visual Studio the same as Visual Studio Code in these episodes?

visual-studio.long:
Visual Studio is a development product from Microsoft. In the M365.FM episodes that mention it, it appears in two roles: as the environment that hosts the Dev Tunnels feature for testing Microsoft 365 apps, and as a point of reference in discussions of related developer tools such as Visual Studio Code. This page summarizes only what those episodes state and does not describe the full product.

The clearest use case in the source material is Dev Tunnels. The episode "Test Microsoft 365 Apps with Visual Studio Dev Tunnels" explains that Dev Tunnels in Visual Studio let developers expose local Teams, SharePoint, or Power Platform services to the internet within minutes, without an Azure deployment. The episode recommends configuring a named, persistent tunnel and using Private, authenticated access tied to Microsoft Entra ID. According to the episode, this keeps tests secure and keeps OAuth redirect URIs stable. It also describes real-time feedback in Microsoft 365 as a way to shorten iteration loops, and it mentions that tunnels can be managed with the Dev Tunnels CLI.

The same episode raises a security warning. It names leaving a tunnel Public or anonymous as the biggest risk, because one missed setting can expose an entire development machine. Its guidance is to lock the tunnel down, log activity, and shut the tunnel off when testing is finished. For anyone deciding how to test a locally running Microsoft 365 app, the practical choice described is between an authenticated, Entra ID-bound private tunnel and an anonymous public one, with the episode favoring the former.

Other episodes in the source set mention Visual Studio Code rather than Visual Studio itself. The episode "Bicep - Simply Explained" notes that IntelliSense in Visual Studio Code helps catch errors and improves coding speed when working with Bicep, a language that compiles to ARM templates for Azure infrastructure. The episode "ARM Templates - Simply Explained" lists Visual Studio Code as a lightweight editor with Azure extensions that offer code completion and error highlighting, next to the Azure CLI and the ARM template test toolkit. These references show how editors in the Visual Studio family fit into infrastructure-as-code workflows, although they concern Visual Studio Code specifically.

Power Platform development is a further area where the family appears. The episodes "Power Apps Code Apps - Simply Explained" and "Power Apps Code Apps with Carike Botha [MVP]" describe Code Apps as a way for developers to build modern web applications, for example with React, using familiar tools like Visual Studio Code. These apps still draw on Power Platform capabilities such as Dataverse, Microsoft Entra authentication, connectors, security policies, and managed deployments. The episodes also mention source control with GitHub for collaboration, versioning, and deployment management, and AI-assisted development for generating code. They present Code Apps as an extension of the platform for scenarios that need full control over user experience and architecture, not as a replacement for low-code development.

Taken together, the episodes position Visual Studio and its related editor as everyday tools for developers working across Microsoft 365, Azure, and the Power Platform. Choices that recur in the material include whether to test locally through a tunnel or deploy first, how to secure that tunnel with Microsoft Entra ID, and which editor to use for infrastructure code and custom apps. Details beyond these points, such as editions, versions, or pricing, are not covered in the available sources.

viva.desc: Microsoft Viva is a set of employee-experience apps in Teams and Microsoft 365, covering communities, work patterns, learning and a branded employee start point.

faq.a: Microsoft Viva is a set of employee-experience apps inside Teams and Microsoft 365, including Viva Engage, Viva Insights, Viva Learning and Viva Connections. It is developed by Microsoft.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Viva?

faq.a: Most Viva experiences are surfaced in Microsoft Teams, for example as apps or as the employee portal provided by Viva Connections.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Viva relate to Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Microsoft Viva Insights - Simply Explained", the first view it opens is meant for the individual user, covering topics such as focus time and quiet time, before manager and leader views are explained.
faq.q: Is Viva Insights only a tool for managers?

viva.long:
Microsoft Viva is a set of employee-experience apps inside Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365. It is developed by Microsoft and classed as both a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool. Rather than being one single application, Viva bundles several services under one name, including Viva Engage for communities, Viva Insights for personal and team work patterns, Viva Learning for training content and Viva Connections for a branded start point in Teams. It was released in February 2021, and organizations use it to support communication, learning and well-being at work. Product documentation is published by Microsoft on its Learn site.

The modules address different parts of daily work. Viva Engage focuses on communities, leadership communication and knowledge sharing. Viva Insights shows work patterns and gives individuals, managers and leaders different views of the same underlying data. Viva Learning brings learning content and discovery into the flow of work across Microsoft 365 and Teams. Viva Connections acts as a central hub within the Viva suite. In the description quoted in the M365.FM episode on it, Microsoft calls Viva Connections "a gateway to other Viva apps and services" that can curate specific content and tools and give easy access to resources, news, announcements and popular destinations. Viva Topics is another part of the family; it uses AI to build topic pages from content across Microsoft 365, including SharePoint, and can show topic cards inside apps such as Outlook and Teams.

Viva is closely tied to Microsoft Teams, because most Viva experiences are surfaced there, for example as apps or as the employee portal that Viva Connections provides.
