Administrators also need to make sure users have an organizational account, since personal accounts cannot be used for the cloud-hosted services. Related topics are the services the app connects to: Windows 365 Cloud PCs, Azure Virtual Desktop, Microsoft Dev Box and Remote Desktop Services.

Note that the name "Windows app" also appears in unrelated contexts. In the episode "SCCM vs Intune: Key Differences | Simply Explained", the phrase refers to the ConfigMgr console being a Windows application, which is not the remote-access client described here.

windows-autopatch.desc: Windows Autopatch is a Microsoft managed service on Intune and Windows Update for Business that builds update rings, watches rollouts and pauses them on bad health signals.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft managed service on top of Intune and Windows Update for Business that creates update rings, monitors rollouts and pauses them when health signals turn bad. It covers updates for Windows, Microsoft 365 Apps for enterprise, Microsoft Edge and Microsoft Teams.
faq.q: What does Windows Autopatch do?

faq.a: Policy decisions, exclusions and accountability stay with the organization. The service handles ring creation, monitoring and pausing, but it only delivers updates to devices that have been registered.
faq.q: Who remains responsible for patching decisions when using Windows Autopatch?

faq.a: Microsoft documentation lists Business Premium, A3+, E3+ and F3 as intended licensing. Support requests to the service engineering team require E3+ or F3.
faq.q: Which licenses are intended for Windows Autopatch?

windows-autopatch.long:
Windows Autopatch is a cloud service from Microsoft that automates updates for Windows, Microsoft 365 Apps for enterprise, Microsoft Edge and Microsoft Teams. It sits on top of Microsoft Intune and Windows Update for Business. It creates update rings, monitors rollouts and can pause them when health signals turn bad. Policy decisions, exclusions and accountability stay with the organization using it.

The service addresses a chore that nearly every Windows environment shares: patching hundreds of machines every month, indefinitely. The M365.FM episode "Windows Autopatch - Simply Explained" frames this as an unpaid job that never ends, and says IT teams usually fall behind because the work has no finish line, not because they are careless. According to Microsoft documentation, the stated goals of Windows Autopatch are keeping devices current for security, adopting new features quickly, reducing routine IT effort and limiting disruption to users.

Updates move through successive deployment rings instead of reaching every device at once. Reliability and compatibility signals feed into the rollout, so a problem seen in an early ring can slow or stop the release before it reaches later rings. After a device is registered with the service, the Intune admin center exposes role-based access control, update rings and Autopatch groups. Autopatch groups bundle Microsoft Entra groups with update policies. The service only delivers updates to registered devices, so registration is the starting point for any rollout.

The documented scope covers several update types: quality updates, hotpatch (monthly security updates without a restart), feature updates, and driver and firmware updates. Reporting and device alerts are part of the offering as well. Microsoft states two aims: at least 95 percent of up-to-date devices on the latest quality update, and at least 90 percent of eligible devices on a supported Monthly Enterprise Channel build. These are objectives, not guarantees.

Licensing is another point that matters when planning. Intended licensing covers Business Premium, A3+, E3+ and F3. Support requests to the service engineering team require E3+ or F3. Teams evaluating the service therefore need to check which licenses they hold before relying on it.

The second episode, "Windows Update Management: Autopatch, Update Rings and Feature Updates Explained", places Autopatch within a broader operating model. It describes patching as a continuous activity instead of a monthly event, since updates now run continuously and exploits can arrive within days. The episode covers Windows Update for Business, Intune update rings, feature update policies, Windows Autopatch, expedited updates, drivers, reporting and troubleshooting. Its stated aim is an operating model that turns patching into a governed process. In this view, Autopatch is one building block next to manually configured rings and policies, not a replacement for understanding them.

Windows Autopatch also appears in the episode "Windows 365 – Simply Explained", where it is listed among the components around Windows 365. There it is described as automating the patching of Cloud PCs to keep them updated, alongside Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Intune and Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager. That makes it relevant both for physical Windows devices and for Cloud PC deployments that already depend on Intune.

The main decision around Windows Autopatch is how much of the update process to hand to the managed service. Rings, monitoring and pausing are handled by the service, while exclusions, policy choices and accountability for outcomes remain with the organization.

windows-autopilot.desc: Windows Autopilot is a set of Microsoft technologies that set up and pre-configure new Windows devices and enroll them into Microsoft Intune.

faq.a: Windows Autopilot is used to set up and pre-configure new Windows devices and enroll them into Microsoft Intune, so that a device can configure itself for an organization without IT staff building it manually.
faq.q: What is Windows Autopilot used for?

faq.a: The documented deployment modes include user-driven, self-deploying, and pre-provisioning. Each suits a different way of handing a device to its user.
faq.q: Which deployment modes does Windows Autopilot offer?

faq.a: Windows Autopilot enrolls the device into Microsoft Intune, which then applies configuration profiles, compliance policies, and application deployments. The episodes on Intune and on SCCM versus Intune both list Autopilot as part of device provisioning.
faq.q: How does Windows Autopilot relate to Microsoft Intune?

windows-autopilot.long:
Windows Autopilot is a collection of Microsoft technologies used to set up and pre-configure new Windows devices and enroll them into Microsoft Intune. Its purpose is to replace the traditional approach in which an IT department builds and images every laptop by hand before it reaches an employee. With Windows Autopilot, a device can be shipped directly from a supplier to the user, who unpacks it, connects it to the internet, signs in, and lets the organization's policies configure the machine.

The technology supports several deployment modes. The user-driven mode is the scenario in which an employee unboxes a device and signs in with a work identity. The self-deploying mode is intended for devices that are set up without a user performing the sign-in steps. The pre-provisioning mode allows part of the preparation to take place before the device is handed to its end user. Which mode fits depends on how the device will be used and who will receive it, and the official documentation describes each of these scenarios.

Windows Autopilot works together with Microsoft Intune, which is the management service that receives the enrolled device and applies configuration profiles, compliance policies, and application deployments. For this reason it appears in discussions of endpoint management more broadly, including device enrollment, mobile device management, security baselines, and software updates. A device that arrives pre-configured and enrolled can be productive on its first day instead of waiting for manual preparation.

The M365.FM episode "Windows Autopilot - Simply Explained" describes the idea as unboxing a brand-new work laptop and watching it set itself up for the company without an IT person in the room. According to the episode, this is why a new hire can be productive on day one instead of day five. The episode outlines what Autopilot actually is, why IT teams made the switch, and how a device gets claimed.

Other episodes place Windows Autopilot in the wider context of device management. "SCCM vs Intune: Key Differences | Simply Explained" covers device provisioning, co-management, and cloud versus on-premises administration, and lists Windows Autopilot among the topics when comparing Configuration Manager with Intune. "Microsoft Intune - Simply Explained" names Windows Autopilot alongside device enrollment, configuration profiles, compliance policies, application deployment, and endpoint security as key Intune concepts.

The episode "Licensing, Security & Management: Making Microsoft 365 Defender and Intune Work Together with Videsh Chavan" has a section on Windows Autopilot and zero-touch provisioning. It states that Autopilot fundamentally changes traditional corporate device provisioning, because IT departments no longer need to manually build and image each laptop, and devices can be sent straight from suppliers to users. The same episode recommends structured security baselines and manageable policy architectures instead of large numbers of disconnected policies, so that endpoint management stays understandable and maintainable.

Finally, "Building a Secure Microsoft-First MSP: Intune, Defender & Entra ID at Scale with Albin Klinaku [MVP]" discusses Windows Autopilot as part of cloud-native device management, together with compliance policies and security baselines. The conversation covers how managed service providers can standardize deployments, automate repetitive tasks, and scale securely across multiple tenants. Official documentation for the technology is published by Microsoft Learn.

windows-autopilot-device-preparation.desc: Windows Autopilot Device Preparation is a simpler Windows Autopilot flavor that groups and configures a device at enrollment, without pre-registering a hardware hash.
windows-autopilot-device-preparation.long:
Windows Autopilot Device Preparation is a newer, simpler flavor of Windows Autopilot. It groups and configures a device at the moment the device enrolls, so the hardware hash does not need to be registered beforehand. It supports Microsoft Entra join only and runs on Windows 11.

The feature is part of Windows Autopilot, the broader Microsoft approach to setting up and configuring new Windows devices. Within that family, Windows Autopilot Device Preparation covers the scenario in which a device is joined to Microsoft Entra and prepared during enrollment instead of being identified in advance through a pre-registered hardware hash.

The main differences from the earlier Autopilot flavor follow from the facts above: enrollment-time grouping and configuration, no hardware hash pre-registration, Microsoft Entra join as the only supported join type, and Windows 11 as the supported operating system. Organizations that need other join types or earlier Windows versions should check the official Microsoft documentation, since these details are outside the scope of this page.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this topic. Further technical details are available in the official Microsoft Learn documentation for Windows Autopilot Device Preparation.

windows-enterprise-multi-session.desc: Windows Enterprise multi-session is a Windows 10/11 Enterprise edition for Azure Virtual Desktop that allows several users to share one virtual machine at once.

faq.a: It is a Windows 10/11 Enterprise edition for Azure Virtual Desktop that lets multiple users hold interactive sessions on one virtual machine at the same time.
faq.q: What is Windows Enterprise multi-session?

faq.a: Its use depends on eligible Windows Enterprise or Microsoft 365 licenses.
faq.q: What does Windows Enterprise multi-session require in terms of licensing?

faq.a: It is used with Azure Virtual Desktop, where several users share a single virtual machine in separate interactive sessions.
faq.q: Where is Windows Enterprise multi-session used?

windows-enterprise-multi-session.long:
Windows Enterprise multi-session is an edition of Windows 10 and Windows 11 Enterprise designed for use with Azure Virtual Desktop. Its defining capability is that multiple users can hold interactive sessions on a single virtual machine at the same time, rather than each user requiring a dedicated machine.

The edition is used to host shared desktop environments in Azure Virtual Desktop, where several people sign in to the same virtual machine and work in separate sessions. Use of the edition depends on eligible Windows Enterprise or Microsoft 365 licenses, so licensing is a prerequisite for deployment.

Within the Microsoft ecosystem, Windows Enterprise multi-session sits at the intersection of Windows client operating systems, Azure Virtual Desktop and Microsoft 365 licensing. No specific episodes of M365.FM are linked to this entry at present, and no further technical details are recorded here beyond the description above.

windows-hello-for-business.desc: Windows Hello for Business is the managed form of Windows Hello that replaces passwords with a device-bound key pair unlocked by a PIN or biometrics for work accounts.

faq.a: It is the managed business version of Windows Hello. It replaces passwords with a device-bound key pair that a PIN or biometrics unlock, and it signs users into Microsoft Entra ID or Active Directory work accounts.
faq.q: What is Windows Hello for Business?

faq.a: The episode "Windows Hello for Business - Simply Explained" addresses this directly with the point that a PIN is not a password. The PIN unlocks a device-bound key rather than acting as a shared secret for the account.
faq.q: Is the Windows Hello for Business PIN the same as a password?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes name FIDO2 security keys such as YubiKeys, passkeys, Microsoft Authenticator passwordless sign-in and Azure AD certificate-based authentication.
faq.q: Which other passwordless methods are mentioned alongside it?

windows-hello-for-business.long:
Windows Hello for Business is the managed business version of Windows Hello. It replaces passwords with a device-bound key pair that the user unlocks with a PIN or with biometrics such as a fingerprint or facial recognition. It is used to sign users into work accounts in Microsoft Entra ID or Active Directory. Because the credential is tied to the device rather than typed in and sent as a shared secret, it removes the password from the sign-in process instead of trying to make the password stronger.

The reasoning behind this approach is described in the M365.FM episode "Windows Hello for Business - Simply Explained". The episode states that Microsoft's cloud sees over three hundred million fraudulent sign-in attempts every day, and that almost all of them are aimed at passwords. Its argument is that a longer password is not the real fix; the real fix is to take the password out of the picture. The episode walks through why passwords fail, what Windows Hello for Business is, why a PIN is not a password, where a face and fingerprint data go, and the chip that holds the key. It also covers how the sign-in works and mentions key trust and certificate trust, which are deployment models for the feature.

In practice, Windows Hello for Business is one of several passwordless options an organization can choose. Other M365.FM episodes list it alongside FIDO2 security keys, Microsoft Authenticator passwordless sign-in, passkeys and Azure AD certificate-based authentication. The episode "Build Custom Microsoft 365 Copilot Plugins" describes Windows Hello for Business as using biometric data, such as fingerprints or facial recognition, for secure, passwordless access, and presents it as one of the methods that remove the risks that come with passwords. Choosing among these methods is described there as a decision about how users and services prove their identity.

The episode "Lock Down Microsoft Entra ID Before Phishing Hits" mentions Windows Hello for Business and FIDO2 security keys as options to implement, especially for users in privileged roles. It frames passwordless authentication as both more secure and more convenient, since users no longer need to remember complex passwords. It also cites an expectation that organizations with advanced identity-first security programs will experience 50% fewer identity-related breaches by 2026 than those without, and says that moving to passwordless authentication can support that direction.

Privileged access is another context in which the feature comes up. In "ENTRA PIM EXPLAINED: Securing Privileged Access with Mark Orr [MVP]", the guest recommends moving organizations toward Windows Hello for Business, passkeys, Microsoft Authenticator passwordless sign-in and hardware security keys such as YubiKeys. The episode says that passwordless authentication should be an organization's first goal. According to the episode, besides improving security it improves the user experience by eliminating forgotten passwords, while protecting users from phishing attacks and credential theft.

Windows Hello for Business also appears in connection with remote work scenarios. The episode "Azure Virtual Desktop - Simply Explained" lists passwordless authentication, including FIDO keys and Windows Hello for Business, among the supported authentication methods for connecting to Azure Virtual Desktop with a Microsoft Entra ID account. The other methods listed there are smart cards, passwords, multifactor authentication and federation with third-party identity providers. The episode recommends single sign-on for a seamless experience, so that users reach their virtual desktop without repeatedly entering credentials.

Taken together, the episodes treat Windows Hello for Business as a building block of a passwordless strategy built around Microsoft Entra ID rather than as a standalone feature. Typical decisions around it include which passwordless methods to offer to which users, whether privileged roles should be moved first, and which trust model fits an environment that uses Microsoft Entra ID, Active Directory or both.

windows-laps.desc: Windows LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) assigns each device a unique, regularly rotated local administrator password stored in the directory with restricted read access.

faq.a: Windows LAPS gives each device a unique local administrator password and rotates it regularly. The passwords are stored in the directory with restricted read access.
faq.q: What does Windows LAPS do?

faq.a: Using a different password per device means a single compromised credential does not by itself expose other machines. Regular rotation also limits how long any one password stays valid.
faq.q: Why use unique, rotated local administrator passwords?

faq.a: Microsoft publishes the Windows LAPS overview on Microsoft Learn, in the Windows Server identity documentation section.
faq.q: Where can the official Windows LAPS documentation be found?

windows-laps.long:
Windows LAPS, short for Windows Local Administrator Password Solution, is a Microsoft product that manages the password of the local administrator account on each device. Instead of reusing one shared password across many machines, it gives every device its own unique password and changes it on a regular basis.

The generated passwords are stored in the directory, and read access to them is restricted. This lets authorized administrators retrieve a device's local administrator password when needed, such as for troubleshooting or recovery, while limiting who can see it. Because each password is unique and rotated, exposure of one device's credential does not by itself reveal the passwords of other devices.

Typical uses include reducing the risk that a single compromised local administrator password can be reused to move between machines, and providing a controlled way to access local administrator accounts when other sign-in methods are unavailable.

Official documentation for Windows LAPS is available through Microsoft Learn in the Windows Server identity section. No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry.

windows-recall.desc: Recall (Windows) is an opt-in feature on Copilot+ PCs that stores encrypted snapshots of the screen locally and lets users search past activity in natural language.

faq.a: Recall is an opt-in Windows feature on Copilot+ PCs that saves encrypted snapshots of the screen locally. Users can then search their past activity using natural language.
faq.q: What is Recall in Windows?

faq.a: The snapshots are saved locally on the device and are encrypted, rather than being stored elsewhere.
faq.q: Where are Recall snapshots stored?

faq.a: No. Recall is described as an opt-in feature, meaning it only runs when a user chooses to enable it.
faq.q: Is Recall enabled by default?

windows-recall.long:
Recall (Windows) is an opt-in Windows feature available on Copilot+ PCs. It periodically saves snapshots of what appears on the screen and keeps them in encrypted form on the device itself. Because the feature is opt-in, it only operates when a user chooses to turn it on.

The purpose of Recall is to help users find things they have previously seen or done on their PC. Instead of browsing through folders, browser history or open windows, a user can describe what they are looking for in natural language and search across their saved past activity.

The snapshots are stored locally rather than being kept elsewhere, which is a central design point of the feature. Microsoft documents Recall for developers and administrators in its Windows AI documentation on Microsoft Learn, which is the primary official reference for how the feature is described and exposed.

On M365.FM, Recall (Windows) is tracked as a product entity within the Microsoft ecosystem. No episodes or related entities are currently linked to this page, so the description here is limited to what Microsoft states about the feature itself.

windows-server.desc: Windows Server is Microsoft's server operating system, licensed at the physical host level and usable in Azure via Azure Hybrid Benefit where eligible.

faq.a: Windows Server is Microsoft's server operating system. Its licensing can be applied at the physical host level and, where eligible, it can be used in Azure via Azure Hybrid Benefit.
faq.q: What is Windows Server?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Site Recovery - Simply Explained", Windows Server 2025 and 2022 are supported, 2019 and 2016 are supported for Server Core and Server with Desktop Experience, and 2012 R2 and 2012 are also listed as supported.
faq.q: Which Windows Server versions does Azure Site Recovery support?

faq.a: The episode "Manage Microsoft 365 Update Overload" lists Windows Server 2022 as supported while in Mainstream Support with an end date of October 2026, while Windows Server 2019 and 2016 ended on October 14, 2025.
faq.q: What do the episodes say about Windows Server support dates?

windows-server.long:
Windows Server is Microsoft's server operating system. Its licensing can be applied at the physical host level, and where a customer is eligible, Windows Server can also be used in Azure through Azure Hybrid Benefit. Beyond the licensing model, the product appears across the Microsoft ecosystem as a base operating system for virtual machines, as a selectable image in cloud services, and as a platform that other Microsoft tools must support.

In practice, Windows Server shows up in several places in the M365.FM episodes. In "Azure Image Builder - Simply Explained" (August 2026), Windows Server is named as one of the Azure Marketplace images that Azure Image Builder can use as a starting point. The same episode lists Windows 11, Ubuntu and other supported operating systems alongside it, and notes that organizations can also begin with images they have already created, including images stored in Azure Compute Gallery. The idea is that a known source image becomes the starting point for future virtual machines, so administrators do not have to configure each new VM manually. The episode also points out that Image Builder itself does not create production VMs.

Business continuity is another area where the operating system version matters. "Azure Site Recovery - Simply Explained" (July 2026) includes a support overview for protecting VMs by copying them from one area to another. According to the episode, Windows Server 2025 and Windows Server 2022 are supported, Windows Server 2019 and Windows Server 2016 are supported for both Server Core and Server with Desktop Experience, and Windows Server 2012 R2 and Windows Server 2012 are also listed as supported. For anyone planning disaster recovery, this kind of table is a practical checkpoint before relying on replication for a given server.

Support lifecycle is a recurring theme as well. In "Manage Microsoft 365 Update Overload" (November 2025), the episode states that Microsoft 365 updates only work on supported devices and operating systems, and it lists Windows Server versions with their support status. According to the episode, Windows Server 2022 is supported while in Mainstream Support, with an end-of-support date given as October 2026. Windows Server 2019 and Windows Server 2016 are listed as ended on October 14, 2025, and Windows Server 2012 R2 is listed as no longer supported since January 14, 2020. The episode's advice is to check that computers and servers meet the requirements before relying on updates.

Windows Server is also one of the operating system choices for virtual desktops. In "Azure Virtual Desktop vs Windows 365 with Dieter Kempeneers [MVP] & Dominiek Verham [MVP]" (July 2026), Azure Virtual Desktop is described as a virtual desktop solution that delivers a full Windows experience, with a choice between Windows 11, Windows 10 or Windows Server, in both single-session and multi-session configurations. This positions Windows Server as an option when the desktop environment is hosted in Azure rather than on local hardware.

Security baselines refer to Windows Server too. In "Microsoft Defender for Endpoint - Simply Explained" (July 2026), the episode notes that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint supports industry standards for configuration comparison. These include Center for Internet Security (CIS) benchmarks for Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server 2008 R2 and above, as well as Security Technical Implementation Guides (STIG) benchmarks for Windows 10 and Windows Server 2019. This lets administrators measure server configuration against a known benchmark.

Taken together, the episodes show the typical decisions around Windows Server: which version to run given the published support dates, whether it is covered by recovery and update tooling, which image to use as a base for new virtual machines, and how licensing, including Azure Hybrid Benefit where eligible, applies when workloads move between on-premises hosts and Azure.

windows-server-update-services.desc: Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) is a Windows Server role that downloads, approves and distributes Microsoft updates from an internal server to networked computers.

faq.a: WSUS is a Windows Server role that lets IT administrators deploy Microsoft product updates. It manages the distribution of updates published through Microsoft Update to computers on the network.
faq.q: What is Windows Server Update Services (WSUS)?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, WSUS is deprecated and gets no new features, but it remains supported for production with security and quality updates according to its lifecycle.
faq.q: Is WSUS still supported?

faq.a: Configuration Manager uses WSUS for patch management. The episode "SCCM vs Intune: Key Differences | Simply Explained" also says that using SCCM and WSUS can streamline the patch management process.
faq.q: How does WSUS relate to Configuration Manager?

windows-server-update-services.long:
Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) is a server role in Windows Server that lets IT administrators deploy Microsoft product updates. It manages the distribution of updates published through Microsoft Update to computers on the network. Instead of every device reaching out to Microsoft on its own, the updates are downloaded once to an internal server, reviewed and approved by administrators, and then handed out to the managed machines.

According to Microsoft Learn, the stated aims of update management with WSUS are operational efficiency, protection against vulnerabilities and a stable production environment. Administrators decide which updates reach which computers and when, which is the core of the approval model. Administration is done through a management console, and PowerShell cmdlets cover the main tasks and allow routine administration to be automated. This makes it possible to script recurring work rather than repeating it by hand in the console.

Several technical characteristics are described in the documentation. SHA-256 is supported for added security. The Windows Update Agent can be deployed independently of the server. A single WSUS server can act as the update source for other WSUS servers, so update distribution can be arranged in tiers. At least one WSUS server in the network must be able to connect to Microsoft Update in order to learn which updates exist, and how many servers connect directly is left to the administrator's design. The documentation lists Windows Server 2016 through 2025 as well as Windows 10 and Windows 11 as applicable. For Windows 11 clients, WSUS supports Unified Update Platform updates only after an update has been installed or MIME types have been added in IIS.

WSUS is part of Windows Server and is also the update mechanism that Configuration Manager uses for patch management. This ties it to the wider discussion of how organizations manage devices, whether with on-premises tools or with cloud services. The product is deprecated and receives no new features, but it remains supported for production use, with security and quality updates, according to its lifecycle. Anyone planning an update infrastructure therefore has to weigh a still-supported role against the fact that its feature set is no longer evolving.

The M365.FM episode "SCCM vs Intune: Key Differences | Simply Explained" touches on WSUS in the context of patch management. The episode says that organizations facing the challenges of manual update methods should implement aggressive automation and centralization, and that using tools like SCCM and Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) can significantly streamline the patch management process. According to the episode, this approach reduces the manual workload and minimizes errors. The same episode contrasts this with Intune, which it presents as a strong choice for organizations adopting cloud-first strategies, so WSUS appears there as part of the traditional, server-based side of the comparison.

Typical decisions around WSUS therefore concern how many servers should connect directly to Microsoft Update, whether downstream servers should take their updates from an upstream WSUS server, how approvals are organized, and whether routine administration is automated with PowerShell. Because the role is deprecated but supported, teams also have to consider how long it fits their lifecycle plans, especially when Configuration Manager relies on it for patching.

windows-subsystem-for-linux.desc: Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) runs a Linux environment directly on Windows, without a traditional virtual machine or dual-boot setup; WSL 2 uses a real Linux kernel.

faq.a: WSL is a Windows feature that runs a GNU/Linux environment, including most command-line tools and applications, directly on Windows. Microsoft states that Linux runs unmodified and without the overhead of a traditional virtual machine or a dual-boot setup.
faq.q: What is Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL)?

faq.a: Both versions exist and Microsoft provides a dedicated comparison page. WSL 2 uses a real Linux kernel in a lightweight virtual machine, and the M365.FM episode "Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) - Simply Explained" covers the difference between the two.
faq.q: What is the difference between WSL 1 and WSL 2?

faq.a: Distributions can be obtained from the Microsoft Store, and the documentation notes that other distributions can be used as well. Installation guides exist for Windows, Windows Server and manual setups.
faq.q: How are Linux distributions installed for WSL?

windows-subsystem-for-linux.long:
Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) is a Windows feature that lets developers run a GNU/Linux environment, including most command-line tools, utilities and applications, directly on Windows. According to Microsoft's documentation, Linux runs unmodified and without the overhead of a traditional virtual machine or a dual-boot setup. WSL is available on Windows 10 and Windows 11, and installation guides exist for Windows, for Windows Server and for manual setups.

The main reason people look at WSL is that a large share of development tutorials, scripts and tools assume a Linux shell. The M365.FM episode "Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) - Simply Explained" opens with exactly this point: half the tutorials online assume the reader is not on Windows, which used to suggest having the wrong machine. The episode describes WSL as a free feature that runs real Linux right beside Windows. The Microsoft documentation names typical uses such as Node.js and web development, scripting, and remote development with Visual Studio Code. Its linked videos also cover GPU-accelerated machine learning with WSL 2 and running Linux GUI apps.

Two versions exist, WSL 1 and WSL 2, and Microsoft maintains a dedicated page that compares them. The short description of the product states that WSL 2 uses a real Linux kernel in a lightweight virtual machine. The episode lists the real difference between WSL 1 and WSL 2 as one of its topics, which makes the version choice one of the first decisions when setting up WSL. The documentation itself does not state system requirements, licensing terms or concrete limitations on its landing page and refers readers to the install, comparison and FAQ pages for those details.

Linux distributions are obtained from the Microsoft Store, and the documentation notes that other distributions can be used as well. Once a distribution is installed, the documentation covers how files are shared in both directions: accessing Linux files from Windows and Windows files from within WSL. Further documented topics include connecting USB devices to WSL 2 and a memory reclaim feature. These pieces describe the practical day-to-day side of working in a Linux environment while staying on a Windows machine.

WSL is also developed in the open. A Microsoft blog post announces that WSL is open source, and issues are tracked on GitHub. For people who want early access to new builds, preview versions are available through the Windows Insiders channels Dev, Beta and Release Preview, which differ in stability. Choosing a channel is therefore a trade-off between access to newer builds and the expected stability of the build.

In practice, the decisions around WSL tend to follow a simple order: confirm that the Windows edition in use is covered by the relevant installation guide, decide between WSL 1 and WSL 2 using the comparison page, pick a distribution from the Microsoft Store or another source, and then decide how Windows and Linux files and tools should work together. For readers who want a plain-language introduction before reading the technical documentation, the M365.FM episode "Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) - Simply Explained" is aimed at explaining why Linux tools keep appearing in Windows tutorials, what WSL actually is, and how the two WSL versions differ.

windows-update-for-business.desc: Windows Update for Business is a free set of policy controls built into Windows for deferring updates, setting deadlines and managing restarts on company devices.

faq.a: No. It is a free set of controls built into Windows, and Microsoft Learn describes it as a free service for Windows 10 and Windows 11 Pro, Education and Enterprise editions. Devices download updates directly from Windows Update.
faq.q: Is Windows Update for Business a product that has to be purchased?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, feature updates can be deferred for up to 365 days and quality updates for up to 30 days. Updates can also be paused for 35 days.
faq.q: How long can updates be deferred with Windows Update for Business?

faq.a: Settings are applied through Group Policy or through an MDM solution such as Microsoft Intune. Windows Update for Business reports and Windows Autopatch build on these same policies.
faq.q: How are Windows Update for Business settings applied?

windows-update-for-business.long:
Windows Update for Business is a set of policy controls built into Windows that lets organizations decide which updates their devices receive and when. It is not a product that is purchased and not a server that has to be operated. Devices connect directly to the Windows Update service, and administrators shape the behavior through policy. According to Microsoft Learn, the feature used to be called Windows Update for Business and is now documented as Windows Update client policies, so both names appear in documentation and in discussions of the topic.

The service is free and applies to Windows 10 and Windows 11 in the Pro, Education and Enterprise editions. Its purpose is to keep devices current with security and feature updates while giving administrators influence over timing. A central idea is staged deployment: updates can be tested on a subset of devices before a wider rollout, so that problems are found early and do not reach the whole organization at once. Settings are applied through Group Policy or through an MDM solution such as Microsoft Intune.

The controls cover several areas. Administrators can defer feature updates for up to 365 days and quality updates for up to 30 days, and they can pause updates for 35 days. They can set installation deadlines and control restarts, so that updates do not interrupt users at inconvenient moments. A branch readiness level can be chosen, and driver updates as well as Microsoft product updates can be managed. The two main update categories are feature updates, which bring larger changes, and quality updates, which are the regular fixes and security patches.

The documentation also names limits. Feature updates are not offered to LTSC devices, Click-to-Run Office is not supported, and the Update Baseline applies only to Group Policy. These points matter when deciding whether the policies cover every device and application in an environment.

Windows Update for Business is also the foundation for other tooling. Intune update rings, feature update policies, expedited updates, Windows Update for Business reports and Windows Autopatch all build on these policies. In practice, the decision is often between configuring rings and deadlines directly and handing more of the orchestration to a managed service such as Windows Autopatch.

The M365.FM episode "Windows Update for Business - Simply Explained" describes it as a free set of controls already built into Windows that sits unused on most company laptops, and it explains why updates often seem to land at the worst time. The episode "Windows Update Management: Autopatch, Update Rings and Feature Updates Explained" argues that updates now run continuously and that exploits arrive within days, so patching should be a governed, ongoing process rather than a monthly event. It covers update rings, feature update policies, Windows Autopatch, expedited updates, drivers, reporting and troubleshooting. The episode "Manage Microsoft 365 Update Overload" uses Windows Update for Business as a point of comparison, describing cloud update options for Microsoft 365 that offer control similar to it, including deployment rings, configurable rollout timing, deadlines and exclusion dates around important business events.

winui.desc: WinUI is Microsoft's native XAML-based UI framework for Windows desktop apps, supporting C# and C++ and delivered as part of the Windows App SDK.

faq.a: WinUI is used to build native Windows desktop applications with a XAML-based programming model in C# or C++. It is part of the Windows App SDK and targets modern, responsive apps that follow the Fluent Design System.
faq.q: What is WinUI used for?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, WinUI runs on Windows 10 version 1809 and later, including Windows 11. Apps can run on x86, x64 and ARM devices.
faq.q: Which Windows versions and architectures does WinUI support?

faq.a: Both use XAML. The episode "Modern .NET: WPF, ASP.NET Core, and gRPC with Gábor Ruzsinszki [MVP]" says that the XAML-based architecture of WPF influenced newer technologies such as .NET MAUI and WinUI, and it discusses migration challenges for large legacy WPF systems.
faq.q: How does WinUI relate to WPF?

winui.long:
WinUI is Microsoft's native user interface framework for building Windows desktop applications. It uses a XAML-based programming model, supports C# and C++, and is part of the Windows App SDK. In Microsoft's documentation, WinUI 3 is described as the recommended native UI framework for new Windows desktop applications.

The framework is intended for modern, responsive desktop apps that follow the Fluent Design System. According to the documentation, it provides a broad set of modern controls and styles, high-performance rendering, advanced pixel processing, high-DPI rendering and smooth animations. Apps can accept input from touch, pen, keyboard and mouse, and they can run on x86, x64 and ARM devices. Through the Windows App SDK, WinUI apps also reach modern Windows APIs, and the SDK supplies tooling for development and deployment. WinUI runs on Windows 10 version 1809 and later, including Windows 11.

WinUI is used inside Microsoft as well. The documentation notes that parts of the Windows shell and several built-in apps are built with WinUI, and it cites PowerToys as an open-source example of an application using the framework. The project itself is developed in public on GitHub in the microsoft-ui-xaml repository, where contributions are accepted.

For developers who want to get started, the Microsoft Learn material includes a project walkthrough, tools and samples, and the WinUI 3 Gallery, an app with interactive samples of the available controls. The documentation page targets Windows desktop apps and does not state licensing terms or explicit technical limitations, so decisions that depend on those points need to be checked against further sources.

Typical decisions around WinUI concern which UI framework fits a given project. The M365.FM episode "Modern .NET: WPF, ASP.NET Core, and gRPC with Gábor Ruzsinszki [MVP]" touches on this question from the perspective of existing enterprise software. In that conversation, Gábor Ruzsinszki discusses why many enterprise companies still rely on WPF today and explains its strengths and its XAML-based architecture. The episode says that this XAML heritage influenced newer technologies such as .NET MAUI and WinUI, which places WinUI in a line of XAML-based UI technologies on the Microsoft platform.

The same episode compares alternatives such as Avalonia and Uno Platform and discusses the migration challenges that large legacy systems face. This is relevant context for WinUI, because teams with long-lived WPF applications have to weigh the effort of moving to a newer framework against the benefits described in the documentation, such as modern controls, Fluent Design and access to current Windows APIs.

In summary, WinUI is the XAML-based, native option within the Windows App SDK for new Windows desktop apps. It connects to the broader XAML family of WPF, .NET MAUI and related frameworks, and the available material points to Microsoft Learn for technical details and to the "Modern .NET" episode for a practitioner's view on how it relates to WPF and other alternatives.

word-online.desc: Word for the web, also called Word Online, is the browser version of Microsoft Word for writing and co-authoring documents without a desktop installation.

faq.a: Word for the web, also called Word Online, is the browser version of Word. It lets users write and co-author documents without installing the desktop app, and it is part of Office on the web.
faq.q: What is Word for the web?

faq.a: No. Microsoft Word is the desktop application, while Word for the web is its browser-based counterpart. The two are related and work with the same documents.
faq.q: Is Word for the web the same as Microsoft Word?

faq.a: The episode "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Settings and Configuration" says Copilot needs third-party cookies enabled to work with Office web apps such as Word Online. Blocking them causes failures when retrieving files to reference.
faq.q: Why do third-party cookies matter for Copilot in Word for the web?

word-online.long:
Word for the web is the browser-based version of Word, also known as Word Online or, in German-language environments, Word im Web. It allows documents to be written, edited and co-authored directly in a web browser, without installing the Word desktop app. It is developed by Microsoft, is included in Microsoft 365, and is part of Office on the web, the family of browser versions of Office apps.

In practice, Word for the web is used for quick edits, for reviewing and commenting on shared documents, and for working on devices where the desktop application is not available. Because the document is opened in the browser, several people can work on the same file at the same time, which is why the product is classified both as a Microsoft tool and as a collaboration tool. It is closely related to Microsoft Word, the desktop application, and it opens and edits the documents that Word creates.

A typical decision around Word for the web is whether a task can be handled in the browser or whether the full desktop app is needed. For short editing sessions, shared drafts and review rounds, the browser version avoids any installation step. For other work, organizations and users often keep the desktop application alongside it. The two are meant to work with the same documents rather than replace one another, and the choice usually depends on the device, the situation and the task at hand.

Because Word for the web runs in a browser, browser settings can influence how it behaves, particularly when other services connect to it. The M365.FM episode "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Settings and Configuration" (2025-11-03) touches on this. According to the episode excerpt, Copilot relies on third-party cookies to access files and provide intelligent support in Microsoft 365 web apps. For Copilot to work with Office web applications such as Word Online, PowerPoint Online and Excel Online, third-party cookies must be enabled. The episode says that blocking third-party cookies results in a failure when retrieving files to reference, and it recommends checking browser settings and enabling third-party cookies to avoid connectivity problems.

The same episode places this point in a broader context. It looks at the frustrations users face when Microsoft Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot do not behave as expected. It explains that the difference between a helpful and an unresponsive Copilot often comes down to configuration, licensing and the dependencies Copilot has on the surrounding Microsoft 365 environment. Word for the web is one of the web apps mentioned in this discussion, but the episode does not focus on Word for the web alone.

For readers searching for the term, the main points are straightforward: Word for the web is the browser edition of Word, included in Microsoft 365, built for writing and co-authoring without installing the desktop app, and part of Office on the web. Official product help for Word is available through Microsoft support documentation.

work-in-progress.desc: Work in progress (WIP) is material or product that has entered production but is not finished; excess WIP ties up material and space and hides flow problems.

faq.a: Work in progress is material or product that has started its production route but is not yet finished. It is also called work in process or in-process inventory, and the term can refer either to the partially finished items or to their value.
faq.q: What does work in progress (WIP) mean?

faq.a: Excess WIP ties up material and space and can hide problems in the flow. In lean thinking, excessive processing of goods or WIP is counted as one of the seven wastes because it adds no value.
faq.q: Why is too much WIP considered a problem?

faq.a: The episode "The Productivity Illusion: Why AI is Breaking Your Engineering KPIs" lists Work in Progress (WIP) among the flow metrics that reveal where work becomes blocked, next to flow efficiency, queue age, review cycle time, bottleneck identification and rework rate.
faq.q: How does WIP relate to engineering metrics in the M365.FM episode?

work-in-progress.long:
Work in progress (WIP) is material or product that has started its production route but is not yet finished. The term is also written work in process or in-process inventory. In its original manufacturing sense it covers a company's partially finished goods that await completion and sale, and it can also refer to the value of those items. Because the idea describes work that has been started but not completed, it has since been applied beyond factories, including to the way engineering teams measure how work moves through a delivery system.

In supply chain management and accounting, WIP is an input for inventory on the balance sheet, where it is grouped with raw materials and finished goods under current assets. A commonly cited end-of-period calculation is beginning WIP inventory plus production costs minus finished goods. Production costs in this calculation include raw materials, labour and overhead. The tax authority HMRC has no specific definition of the term and distinguishes between manufactured products, service contracts and construction contracts, so the way WIP is treated can depend on the kind of work involved.

In lean thinking, excessive processing of goods or WIP counts as one of the seven wastes, because it adds no value. Too much WIP ties up material and space and can hide problems in the flow, since unfinished items sit in queues where delays and defects are harder to notice. For that reason, low WIP levels are generally regarded as ideal, and efficient inventory management is described as a way to lower costs.

Managing WIP involves a trade-off. Higher WIP levels can absorb surges in demand and shorten cycle time, but they also raise storage costs and the risk of obsolescence, and they create waste if demand falls short of expectations. Holding the right amount therefore requires coordination across internal functions as well as with suppliers and customers. Demand forecasting software is mentioned as one tool that can help keep enough WIP in place without building up excess stock.

The M365.FM episode "The Productivity Illusion: Why AI is Breaking Your Engineering KPIs" (2026-07-25) brings the concept into software engineering. The episode argues that organizations should replace activity-based thinking with flow-based measurement. Instead of asking how much was shipped, the question becomes how efficiently work moves through the system. Work in Progress (WIP) appears in the episode's list of important flow metrics, alongside flow efficiency, queue age, review cycle time, bottleneck identification and rework rate. According to the episode, these metrics show where work actually becomes blocked, rather than simply counting completed deployments.

The same episode presents the view that AI has shifted engineering constraints away from development and toward review and verification. In that framing, flow measurement, including how much work is in progress at any point, is described as far more valuable than raw throughput metrics. Tracking WIP alongside queue age and review cycle time is presented as a way to see where work accumulates, which parallels the manufacturing view that unfinished items pile up where the flow is constrained.

In practice, teams and operations managers use WIP as a signal rather than a target on its own. A rising WIP count can indicate a bottleneck or a queue that is growing faster than it is being cleared, while a low and stable count suggests work is moving through without long waits. The decisions around it usually concern whether to limit how much work is started at once, where to add capacity, and how to balance the buffer that protects against demand swings against the costs and risks of holding unfinished work.

work-iq.desc: Work IQ is Microsoft's intelligence layer that grounds Microsoft 365 Copilot and agents in an organization's work context, people, projects and data.

faq.a: Work IQ is Microsoft's intelligence layer that grounds Microsoft 365 Copilot and agents in an organization's work context and data. It aims to give Copilot an understanding of people, teams, projects and organizational knowledge.
faq.q: What is Work IQ?

faq.a: No. The episode "Work IQ: Simply Explained" states that it only sees what a user is allowed to see, so the context it uses follows existing access permissions.
faq.q: Does Work IQ show users data they are not allowed to see?

faq.a: The episode "MCP Architecture for Microsoft Copilot and AI Agents" lists Work IQ tools within scoped, governed agent tooling and mentions a Work IQ CLI that connects AI coding assistants with Microsoft 365 data for better context in coding tasks.
faq.q: How does Work IQ relate to MCP and AI agents?

work-iq.long:
Work IQ is Microsoft's intelligence layer that grounds Microsoft 365 Copilot and agents in the work context and data of an organization. Rather than treating Copilot as an assistant that only reads a single document or prompt, Work IQ builds a contextual understanding of how work happens across Microsoft 365. The aim is for answers, recommendations and agent behavior to reflect the people, teams, projects and organizational knowledge involved, instead of relying on files alone.

The episode "Microsoft Work IQ: The Intelligence Layer for Microsoft 365" describes Work IQ as the next major evolution for Microsoft 365 Copilot, one that moves it from a simple AI assistant toward a layer that understands people, teams, projects and organizational knowledge. According to that episode, this contextual understanding enables more accurate answers, better recommendations and smarter AI agents. The core idea is that useful AI output depends on knowing the surrounding context of the work, not only the content of one item.

The episode "Work IQ: Simply Explained" frames the problem in plain terms: an AI tool that reads one pasted file and then forgets the team and the projects lacks the most important information about the work. Its outline covers what Work IQ actually is, why Copilot needed a memory, the three layers in plain words, how it understands people and relationships, and the point that it only sees what a user is allowed to see. That last point links Work IQ to permissions: the context it draws on respects what a given person has access to.

Work IQ also appears in the discussion of the Model Context Protocol. The episode "MCP Architecture for Microsoft Copilot and AI Agents" lists Work IQ tools among the pieces that support enterprise security and governance, with admin control, scoped permissions and continuous evaluation for accuracy and reliability. It also mentions multi-platform integration, so that Work IQ tools can be used across different development environments, and a Work IQ CLI that bridges AI coding assistants with Microsoft 365 data to improve context awareness in coding tasks. The episode presents Microsoft's commitment to MCP as a way for agents to operate across platforms, maintain compliance and adapt to changing enterprise requirements.

Two further episodes place Work IQ alongside related architecture. In "Microsoft Copilot Cowork Engine for Context-Driven Work", Work IQ is described as helping the co-work engine understand a user's needs, which in turn supports smarter suggestions and faster results. In "Microsoft Cowork IQ Knowledge Graph Architecture", Work IQ is said to help Copilot understand skill profiles and collaboration frequency. That episode connects this to Microsoft Graph and the Semantic Index, which it describes as mapping organizational boundaries and permission structures so that AI can interpret intent and organizational language rather than match keywords alone, while respecting enterprise security and data governance.

In practice, Work IQ matters to people deciding how to roll out Microsoft 365 Copilot and agents. The material points to a few recurring considerations: whether the context an agent uses reflects real working relationships, whether permissions are scoped so users only see what they are entitled to see, and how agent tooling is governed by administrators. The episodes also suggest starting small, for example by focusing on one workflow and measuring results, when introducing context-driven Copilot capabilities.

Taken together, the episodes describe Work IQ as the layer that supplies context to Copilot and agents, built on organizational data and relationships and bounded by existing access rules. The sources do not give version details, pricing or availability, so those aspects are not covered here.

work-order.desc: A work order is a job record that follows a maintenance or repair task from first report to completion, holding tasks, workers, parts, status and costs.

faq.a: According to the episodes, a work order can hold the problem description, required activities or tasks, responsible workers, schedule, parts or products, safety instructions, labor, costs and the final outcome. In Field Service it can also include customer details, service address, equipment and appointment window.
faq.q: What does a work order contain?

faq.a: The episode "Dynamics 365 Asset Management - Simply Explained" says work orders can originate from scheduled maintenance, inspections, equipment breakdowns, or follow-up work identified by technicians.
faq.q: Where do work orders come from in Dynamics 365 Asset Management?

faq.a: The episode "Use Copilot in Dynamics 365 Field Service" says Copilot lets users update work order fields with natural language (text or speech), ask questions about stored data and get on-demand work order summaries.
faq.q: How does Copilot relate to work orders in Dynamics 365 Field Service?

work-order.long:
A work order is a job record that follows a maintenance or repair task from the first report to completion. It holds the tasks to be done, the workers assigned, the parts required, the current status and the costs. In the M365.FM episodes it appears as the central record in several Microsoft Dynamics 365 scenarios, and as one of the key relationships in connected-factory architectures.

The episode "Dynamics 365 Field Service - Simply Explained" describes the work order as the central record in Dynamics 365 Field Service, a kind of digital job folder for a customer visit. The episode says it can contain the customer's information, the service address, the equipment requiring attention, a description of the problem, the priority, the agreed appointment window, tasks, required products and other information needed to complete the job. In that setting, Field Service becomes relevant when solving a problem requires somebody to physically visit the customer. The work order then manages the visit, the scheduling, the technician, the work performed, the parts consumed, the equipment history and the outcome. The episode's heading for this section is "One job, one source of facts."

The episode "Dynamics 365 Asset Management - Simply Explained" places the work order in a maintenance context. When a maintenance need becomes actual work, Dynamics 365 uses a work order. According to the episode, the work order acts as the job ticket connecting the problem, the required activities, the responsible workers, the schedule, parts, safety instructions, labor, costs and the final outcome. Work orders can originate from scheduled maintenance, inspections, equipment breakdowns, or follow-up work identified by technicians. The same episode discusses early warning for equipment: the aim is not to predict every breakdown perfectly, but to give maintenance teams more time to respond before equipment necessarily fails.

The episode "Use Copilot in Dynamics 365 Field Service" covers how work orders are handled day to day. It describes Dynamics 365 Copilot for Field Service as using artificial intelligence and voice recognition to reduce manual data entry, inefficiencies and the risk of data loss and human error. According to the episode, users can ask questions in natural language about data stored in the system, update work order fields with text or speech, and request on-demand work order summaries to quickly assess status and next actions.

Work orders also appear in manufacturing discussions, where the term refers to production jobs as well as maintenance jobs. In "Connectivity Is Not Integration — Why Your Connected Factory Still Can't Answer the Right Questions", the episode argues that answering operational questions requires relationships between the machine, the active operation, the work order, the product, material status, quality state, maintenance information and customer demand. It follows a single packaging-machine alarm through several systems: the PLC knows what happened at the machine, MES understands which operation and work order are active, and ERP knows demand. No single system holds the complete answer on its own.

The episode "What Happens When Sales Promises an Urgent Order" makes a similar point. A machine record, a work order, a material quantity, an operator roster and a customer due date are useful facts, but they support urgent-order decisions only when the relationships between them are explicit. The episode gives examples of such relationships: an operation belongs to a particular work order, that work order supports a particular customer commitment, the operation can run on certain approved resources, and material is allocated to it.

Taken together, the episodes treat the work order as a unit that ties a problem or task to people, schedule, materials, cost and outcome. Decisions around it typically concern where the record originates (a scheduled task, an inspection, a breakdown or a customer request), who is assigned, which parts are needed, and how its status connects to other systems such as ERP or MES.

workday.desc: Workday is a cloud-based enterprise suite from Workday, Inc. for human capital management and finance, built around configurable business processes, routing and approvals.

faq.a: Workday is a cloud-based enterprise application suite from Workday, Inc. for human capital management and finance. It is built around configurable business processes, routing and approvals.
faq.q: What is Workday?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Cowork IQ Knowledge Graph Architecture" says business data can be ingested through Copilot Connectors so that agents can reason over data from WorkDay, Adobe and many other sources. It lists WorkDay as a structured data source with a high security level.
faq.q: How does Workday relate to Microsoft 365 according to M365.FM?

faq.a: No. In episodes about notifications, Teams features and Copilot Cowork, "workday" means the working day and the interruptions within it, not the Workday suite.
faq.q: Do the other M365.FM episodes that mention workday cover the Workday product?

workday.long:
Workday is a cloud-based enterprise application suite from Workday, Inc. that covers human capital management and finance. It is organized around configurable business processes, routing and approvals, which means that actions such as requests or changes in HR and finance data move through defined steps and are passed to the people responsible for them. Organizations use it as a system of record for people and financial information, and as the place where those approval-driven workflows are run.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, Workday matters mainly as a data source that sits next to Microsoft 365 rather than inside it. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Cowork IQ Knowledge Graph Architecture" describes the layer of data underneath Microsoft 365, which holds information about people, relationships, projects and communications. According to that episode, business data from other systems can be ingested through Copilot Connectors, so that agents can reason over data from WorkDay, Adobe and hundreds of other sources. The episode lists WorkDay among the sources with structured data and states a high security level for it, alongside Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 and Power Apps.

The episode presents this ingestion as a way to improve productivity and decision-making while keeping security standards in place. It frames the point as context-aware insights that respect privacy and security. For teams deciding how to use Workday data with Copilot-style agents, the practical question raised there is which external sources are connected, what kind of data they hold (structured or unstructured), and what security level applies to each. Workday is presented in that context as a structured business source, comparable in role to other line-of-business systems that feed information into the Microsoft 365 data layer.

Workday also appears indirectly in other M365.FM episodes, but only through the phrase "workday" in its everyday sense of a working day, not as the product. Episodes such as "Reduce Microsoft 365 Notification Overload and Protect Focus", "Microsoft Teams Hidden Features with Josh Blalock [MVP]", "Replace Reactive Dashboards with Proactive Notifications" and "Microsoft Copilot Cowork Engine for Context-Driven Work" talk about notifications, focus, Teams features and time lost to email during the workday. These discussions concern Microsoft 365 behavior and user productivity, not the Workday suite, and should not be read as statements about the product.

For readers searching for the term, the distinction is useful. Workday, written as a product name, refers to the HR and finance suite from Workday, Inc. The lowercase word "workday" in several episodes refers to the working day and the interruptions that notifications and email cause within it. The connection between the product and the Microsoft ecosystem documented in the available episode material is the Copilot Connectors scenario, where Workday data is brought into the context that Microsoft 365 agents can use.

The sources do not describe Workday's modules, pricing, versions or configuration in detail, so this page limits itself to the definition above and to the integration scenario named in the episode. Anyone planning an actual connection between Workday and Microsoft 365 would need to consult the official documentation of both vendors for current capabilities and requirements.

workflows-agent.desc: Workflows agent is an agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot that turns natural-language descriptions into working automations across Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Planner.

faq.a: It is an agent in Microsoft Copilot that creates workflows from natural-language descriptions, using supported Microsoft 365 services such as Outlook, SharePoint, Teams and Planner, without code.
faq.q: What is the Workflows agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot?

faq.a: According to the documentation, workflows cannot be shared, only a limited set of Microsoft connectors is supported, errors in existing workflows are not fixed automatically, and ambiguous site or channel names may be mismatched. A Power Platform DLP policy must also allow the needed connectors.
faq.q: What are the main limitations of the Workflows agent?

faq.a: Power Automate is the pointer for advanced needs. The episode "Copilot Workflows Agent vs Power Automate: What to Migrate" compares the two and describes hybrid patterns where the agent is the front end and Power Automate is the backbone.
faq.q: How does the Workflows agent relate to Power Automate?

workflows-agent.long:
Workflows agent is an agent in Microsoft Copilot that automates tasks across Microsoft 365. Instead of building a flow step by step in a designer, a user describes in natural language what should happen, and the agent generates a working workflow from supported Microsoft 365 services without code. It is positioned as a conversational, intent-driven way to automate everyday work.

According to Microsoft's getting-started documentation, the agent can automate actions in Outlook, SharePoint, Teams and Planner. Workflows can run on a schedule or in response to events, and they can use data such as a calendar, tasks or lists. Teams can also be used to collect user input through adaptive cards. The agent identifies the services it needs from the names mentioned in the prompt and connects with the user's Microsoft 365 account. After a workflow is generated, it can be tested, and an Activity page shows run history and errors. Workflows can be turned on or off or deleted from there.

Availability and requirements matter for planning. At the time of the documentation page, Workflows agent was part of the experimental Frontier early access program, rolling out first in the United States in English to select Microsoft 365 personal and premium plans. Administrators control availability under the Copilot settings for agents. A Power Platform data loss prevention (DLP) policy must allow the connectors that a workflow needs, which ties the agent directly into existing governance rules.

The documentation also lists limitations. Workflows cannot be shared, only a limited set of Microsoft connectors is supported, and errors in existing workflows are not fixed automatically. Ambiguous site or channel names in a prompt may be matched to the wrong target, so precise naming in prompts is relevant. For more advanced needs, the documentation points to Power Automate.

The relationship to Power Automate is the central decision around this product. The M365.FM episode "Copilot Workflows Agent vs Power Automate: What to Migrate" (2025-11-26) compares the two head-to-head and asks whether hand-built cloud flows have become the slower or more expensive option. The episode describes where conversational, intent-driven automation can outperform traditional designer-driven flows for everyday work across Outlook, Teams and SharePoint, and it weighs the two approaches on points such as governance and licensing cost. It covers DLP, environments, auditability and SLAs, and it describes hybrid patterns in which the agent acts as the front end while Power Automate remains the backbone. The episode frames its conclusion as knowing what to keep in Power Automate and what to migrate.

The related episode "Automate Compliance Workflows with Microsoft Power Automate" (2026-03-07) places Power Automate in a wider Microsoft ecosystem context and links back to the Workflows agent comparison in its list of related M365.FM episodes. Together, the sources suggest a practical split: lightweight, personal or team-level automations described in plain language on one side, and governed, auditable, more complex processes on the other. Because the agent depends on DLP policies, supported connectors and admin settings, teams considering it typically need to check those controls first, and then decide per scenario whether a prompt-generated workflow is sufficient or whether a Power Automate flow is the better fit.

workload-identity-federation.desc: Workload identity federation (WIF) lets external workloads such as GitHub Actions pipelines swap a trusted token for a short-lived Microsoft Entra access token without stored secrets.

faq.a: It removes the need to store secrets or certificates in a workload. An external token from a trusted provider, such as a GitHub Actions pipeline, is exchanged for a short-lived Microsoft Entra access token.
faq.q: What problem does workload identity federation solve?

faq.a: The terms are used as aliases. Workload identity federation, abbreviated WIF, is the concept, and federated identity credentials (FIC) is the name used for the credential configuration that establishes the trust.
faq.q: Is workload identity federation the same as federated identity credentials?

faq.a: No. The episode "Entra Workload Identities - Simply Explained" lists federation alongside least privilege, Conditional Access, monitoring, lifecycle management and clear ownership, and says workload identities need governance like privileged user accounts.
faq.q: Does federation replace governance of workload identities?

workload-identity-federation.long:
Workload identity federation, also called WIF or federated identity credentials, is a concept within Microsoft Entra Workload ID. It allows a workload that runs outside Azure, for example a GitHub Actions pipeline, to exchange a token issued by a trusted external identity provider for a short-lived Microsoft Entra access token. The central point is that no secret has to be stored: the workload does not hold a password, client secret or certificate that could leak, expire unnoticed or be copied.

The approach addresses a common problem with application identities. Pipelines, services and bots need to authenticate to resources protected by Microsoft Entra, and traditionally this meant creating a credential and keeping it somewhere, such as in a pipeline variable or a configuration file. Every stored credential has to be rotated, protected and eventually retired. With federation, trust is established once between the Microsoft Entra application and the external token issuer. After that, the external token serves as proof of identity, and Microsoft Entra returns a short-lived access token that the workload then uses to reach the target resource.

The M365.FM episodes mention federated identity credentials in several settings. In "Entra Workload Identities - Simply Explained", workload identity federation appears in a list of measures for securing workload identities in Microsoft Azure. The episode treats workload identities as needing governance in the same way as privileged user accounts, and it names least privilege access, Conditional Access for workload identities, certificate-based authentication, Microsoft Entra ID Protection, logging, monitoring, lifecycle management and ownership alongside federation. The host argues that every workload identity should have a clearly assigned owner, minimal permissions, continuous monitoring and regular security reviews, and that neglected application identities often leave unused service principals behind.

In "Copilot in Microsoft Entra ID - Simply Explained", Federated Identity Credentials (FIC) are listed among the key benefits discussed. The episode says they improve security by eliminating the need for persisted secrets and certificates for bot registration. The same list also mentions IT control, which lets administrators block risky agents from operating, and customer managed encryption keys.

The episode "MCP Custom Connector in Copilot Studio: The Complete Integration Guide" gives a practical recommendation. Among the lessons from organizations that integrated MCP with Copilot Studio, it advises using federated identity credentials for passwordless Power Platform authentication. This sits next to other points from the episode, such as bridging MCP to Copilot Studio through Power Platform custom connectors and letting user identity flow through the entire stack from the OAuth token to the business logic.

Typical decisions around workload identity federation concern where a secret can be removed altogether and how the trust relationship is scoped. Because federation replaces a stored credential with a trust relationship, the surrounding controls matter more: the federated application still needs an owner, narrowly scoped permissions and monitoring, as the governance discussion in the first episode emphasizes. Federation is therefore one part of a wider approach to workload identity hygiene rather than a replacement for it.

Workload identity federation sits under the broader topic Microsoft Entra Workload ID, which covers identities for applications, services and automated processes rather than for people. Within that area, federation is the option for workloads that already have a trusted identity elsewhere and need to obtain access to Microsoft Entra-protected resources without introducing a new secret to manage. Microsoft's documentation page on workload identity federation describes the mechanism in more detail.

workplace-loneliness.desc: Workplace loneliness is low connection, thin trust and weak relational redundancy among people at work, which can persist even in connected, productive teams.

faq.a: Workplace loneliness describes low connection, thin trust and weak relational redundancy among people at work. It can persist even in highly connected and productive teams.
faq.q: What is workplace loneliness?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode "Why High Performers Burn Out from Workplace Isolation" says isolation can harm communication, cause misunderstandings and conflicts, and erode trust. It also cites research linking it to increased stress and emotional exhaustion.
faq.q: How does workplace loneliness affect teams?

faq.a: Yes. The description of the concept states that it can persist in highly connected, productive teams, and general sources on loneliness note that people with successful careers can still be lonely.
faq.q: Can productive or successful people experience loneliness at work?

workplace-loneliness.long:
Workplace loneliness describes a state of low connection, thin trust and weak relational redundancy among people at work. It can persist even in highly connected and productive teams, which is why it is easy to overlook: calendars may be full, meetings frequent and output strong, while the relationships underneath remain shallow. The term applies the general idea of loneliness to the professional setting.

The general concept of loneliness, as described in the Wikipedia article on the topic, is an unpleasant emotional response to perceived or actual social isolation. It is subjective: a person can feel lonely in a crowd and content when alone, and loneliness is distinct from solitude. The same article separates social loneliness, meaning the lack of a wider network or community, from emotional loneliness, meaning the lack of close, nurturing relationships. It also separates short-term from chronic loneliness, with the chronic form linked to poorer health. The article notes that people with successful careers can still be lonely, which matches the description of workplace loneliness persisting in productive teams. The article has no dedicated section on the workplace, so the application to work is drawn from the episode material rather than from that source.

The M365.FM episode "Why High Performers Burn Out from Workplace Isolation" (2026-03-25) addresses the topic with a focus on high performers. According to the excerpt, loneliness can make it harder to innovate and solve problems effectively, and it can disrupt team dynamics. The episode says that when team members feel isolated, communication often suffers.
